_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that makes me wish I could give it a neutral rating rather than forcing me to say yes or no to it. I like what it was going for, it did a lot of really neat things but ultimately it fell flat in both presentation and execution of those unique ideas.The biggest problem with this game is its attempt to emulate what Portal did. The trope of being a test subject in a strange facility where a robotic female voice narrates is extremely tired and played out at this point and unless your writing is stellar it's going to fall flat because everyone is just going to compare it to Portal. Unfortunately this game's writing did fall flat. It wasn't funny when it was trying to be funny and it wasn't profound when it was trying to be profound. It felt like the kind of thing a high school kid would write after playing Portal for the first time. They even copy the idea of breaking out of the test environment just like in Portal and since we've all done that 15 years ago it has zero impact. At no point do you actually feel like you're breaking the rules, you always know that's exactly what was intended for you to do.That being said none of that really matters if the puzzles themselves are great and unfortunately despite having some really great ideas the game continually falls short of the target. One of the biggest problems is that the only items you can interact with are the ones used to solve the puzzle so you quickly get into a routine of searching for the item that causes your cursor to change and then scaling it up or down to move to the next part. And while the style of puzzle changes over time the premise largely remains the same. I'd say about 10% of the puzzles actually had interesting solutions, the rest were either extremely obvious or obtuse, expecting you to meander around until you found out how to break the scene and move to the next area.I feel like there is a lot of filler where you're just wandering that didn't add much to the game, I would have preferred a tighter delivery so that it felt like you were figuring things out rather than just walking through trippy spaces. And don't get me wrong, many of the spaces are interesting it just wasn't enough to make me really feel engaged.The interface is also quite annoying. When playing with a controller there is an acceleration on the movement that can't be turned off and the actual interacting with items and scaling them up or down often feels like trial and error more than a mechanic you have full control over.The game is quite short, it can be beat in under 3 hours even if you get stuck for a few minutes on the puzzles. Even worse is that the last 1/3rd or so of the game is essentially a walking simulator with obnoxious loops and attempts at being profound that fell mostly flat. If they tightened the game up and focused only on the puzzles it would be a very short experience.I don't hate this game but I am really surprised it has an overwhelmingly positive rating. I'd say it's a solid 6.5/10 and you should only buy it on a deep discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since I saw that pawn scale when I watched a youtuber play it, I needed to check this out. As Expected, the game had me invested from beginning to end with all through the power of Perception and dreams. It made me realize that im grateful for my perceptive skills and how the game approaches the player with these challenges in not just visual aspects, but also mechanically. The game allows you to manipulate perception in such ways that you may not be thinking about real life by the time your journey with it is over. It was phenomenal, from well, thought out puzzles, to deception of mindbreaking gameplay, Its a test to how perceptive you are with the problems you face in life. A testament to how looking through the lens of another can be possible if you look hard enough. In fact, the game has taught me a very valuable lesson in terms of how to approach my problems: to think about them from another perspective. It reminded me of Portal, but within a Dreamscape inside Stanley's Parable. a bold comparison, sure, but thats what I thought of it, thats how real it was to me. The music was top tier piano Jazz.In the game, you play as an Unknown subject who is testing somno-technology. after your brief introduction to the mechanics and the initial dream phase, your goal is to wake up through the layers of the mind using an elevator at the end of each level. However after many multiple failed attempts, you find yourself lost within your own mind, struggling to find the connection between the dreamworld and reality. But not everything is what it seems..Honestly, this has been one of the best medias I had ever experienced and I thank my mother for giving me such a brain to make way for the challenges that await me in life. And I hope that Pillow Castle can continue to make gems like these.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Despite an absolute gem of a trailer, Superliminal might be more full of regrets than full of dreams. The puzzle themselves are incredibly simple, considering the gameplay mechanics at work. And unless you want to invest some serious time to finish the achievements, I'd say you'd get as short of a game as you might expect for the price. On the other hand, if you really want to fight with the perspective controls to the next level... There is actually a level design tool given with the product, using the same gameplay mechanic. (Why can't you easily place walls and objects, in a manner that would make more sense and take less of your precious time? Bites me. “Somnasculpt works exactly like it wants to”.)Don't get me wrong though, the game is good looking and mostly runs smoothly. Which is an achievement in and on itself, considering what it is. Be it that you suddenly asks for the game to add polygons as crazy; or that you shrink yourself until you get impossibly close and personal, with textures that have to stay the correct resolution. As for the terrible lag experienced near the ending (with less texture and polygons!), I mostly have myself to blame for playing it on a minimal requirement machine. But what really hurts the game the most... is its unbearably pretentious tone about therapy and dreams. Now one might try to give points to the game for exposing the complete and utter sham that psychiatry is, and will ever be; with bonus points for shaming the player into considering his life might be more crap than it really is. Or literally exposing the fact, that this kind of "treatment", is considered so fool-proof as to be repetitively and forcefully administered when it exacerbates the problem. But then it goes the whole mile in the other direction, by delivering as an ending, the most pathetic discourse about control and change I have ever heard. And maybe it would have worked better if the game HAD been frustratingly tough... But without a correlation in reality, it just felt insulting. (Which I guess it should, since you are supposed to be an unwilling participant?)Where it succeed the most is in playing with your visual expectations. Or with its Soda Machine humour. Most particularly during the more "horror" segments of the game. (Which are downright chilling! Though will probably not have an immense replay value.) But while it tries as much as it dares, Superliminal isn't as abstractly immense as NaissanceE, nor as mind bending and twisted as Manifold Garden. Two games that hadn't the need to point fingers and pretend it was all a joke. Or plant tidbits of information as if it was meant to mean so much more... In fact both these games have the puzzles and ambiences themselves actually make a point, with a bit of flair and poetry.From the little of the theme in the trailer; I've should have known better. I guess my standard got twisted before I got here.Isn't "Portal" anyone that would. And now you know. You'll end this wishing harder, than ever before, that "Memory of a Broken Dimension" was done and available.Well maybe I'm too harsh with it. Maybe the point was to be this linear shape association grid. And not a maze of any kind... Maybe the player isn’t supposed to feel lost. Or trapped in something grander than he or she is. Maybe the real message is that anyone trying to tell you what you are, and how to think, is in actuality selling you a ride through oversimplifications. Often unable to fill and content their own whitescape with the relevance they are searching for. Maybe I am supposed to be angry with it. And if it was its goal, it temporarily succeeded. Maybe I shouldn't have had any expectations about this being mindbogglingly relevant or anything. Maybe it was just meant to look the part; for realism's sake.But I am willing to give it the benefit of the doubt here... and not just uninstall it. After all, I did buy it willingly. So it is my burden now.If this convince you to buy the game, then you’ll be responsible to play with your own perceptions.

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. It's a puzzle game with a gimmick, the gimmick being that you can change the size of objects you pick up based on their perspective with the environment, and I find that the game makes use of that gimmick in fun and original ways. The levels are beautifully designed, and combined with the excellent soundtrack, were really fun to just walk around in and soak up the vibes. There are also an enormous amount of secrets in each level that uncovering become a game unto themselves. I wish they could've done a little more at fleshing out the few characters that you encounter, though (especially the GLaDOS-esque AI that guides you through the levels).When I was approaching the end of the game, I actually started to feel sad that my journey was coming to an end, because I didn't want it to stop. It's been a while since a game made me feel that way. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is a fairly short & simple game, but its mechanic is very cool & clever, making it totally worth my time (I played through it in one session across much of a day).Superliminal feels reminiscent of both "The Stanley Parable" and "Portal", for some fairly obvious reasons, but that does not make it derivative of either. Having loved both of those games, I felt this game was immediately familiar.The main gameplay is nearly devoid of overly-frustrating elements, though players looking for bonus stuff/secrets will frustrate themselves for sure (I did), as the game mechanic doesn't lend itself to precise placement of objects. But again: this is not relevant to the main gameplay, which is rarely actively frustrating. If you have basic puzzle/problem-solving skills and patience, you'll be fine. You'll probably have a good time with your initial confusion or confounding feelings giving way to an "ah hah" moment, and happily running along to the next puzzle.I am not a hard-core gamer or puzzle person. I only enjoy a mild amount of challenge at this point in an irritatingly challenging life, so games that make things unnecessarily difficult for no reason other than "IT'S HARD" tend to irritate me. That is not the case here at all. With Superliminal, I only struggled with one main puzzle area because I assumed a set of six (?) windows were all equally non-interactive (one WAS) and therefore lost a lot of time and some patience running around trying to figure out what I missed until accidentally noticing that single of multiple identical items was indeed interactive. That's mostly on me, but I felt that there could've been a hint in the game itself to make sure that five out of six items being non-interactive does not imply what it implied to me (ie "don't bother, these are all static objects"). That's the sum total of my annoyance with the main game.(side note: I worked very hard to get on top of a couple of objects looking for secrets, only to feel like I was mislead and not rewarded for those efforts... I'm still not sure what's going on there, such as a greybox town that is entirely facade, except for one top floor that's got a real room but seems non-interactive... which slightly dampened the game's end narration, but that's me starting to try to find hidden things and fringe achievements, which isn't the point of the main gaming experience)The plot/story is minimal, but that's fine, since it's just the framing for a puzzle game with an original mechanic. I did find the end-monologue to be fairly touching, though. This was enhanced by the way the voice actor very subtly shifted from "possibly incompetent mad scientist with good intentions" to "sincere healthcare professional with pathos", with such a subtle touch reminiscent of David Tennant... And silly me, I thought the Dr. Pierce voice actor WAS David Tennant until the end credits! (The voice actor is Max Howarth, by the way; props to him for his skill here)I recommend this game to anyone. It played very well on Mac OS. I don't recall, a day later, any memorable bugs or performance issues aside from a painfully time-consuming initial load that seemed to have failed, but did eventually run without further issues.

_childDocuments_.review: "I'm a real doctor who went to doctor school." is a puzzle-based adventure game from Pillow Castle.  The main story will take players between two and four hours to complete without a guide and moderate exploration.  There is some replayability in collectibles, challenge modes, and level design.The player controls a nameless patient of Somnascult for treatment of an disclosed anxiety-based disorder.  The patient is placed in a dream state during treatment.  As the player progresses, it becomes clear that the treatment is highly experimental, the facility is too low-budget, and the treatment is going wrong.  The player must help the patient escape their dream. centers around a forced-perspective mechanic.  Beginning in a test-chamber structure, the player develops a basic understanding of the mechanic's rules.  The player must then expand on their understanding as they work to escape.  The mechanic expands beyond the resize-the-thing-to-use-it-as-a-ramp concept.  Objects can become "real" if certain two-dimensional plains are aligned.  In some areas, all objects are duplicated when selected.  Doorways can be used to alter the player's size.  While fairly short, the two-to-four hour initial playthrough ensures that the games mechanics do not overstay their welcome.  Puzzles are fresh, well-designed, and sufficiently varied.Humor is a fundamental component of .  Humor can come from the computerized program manager, the disembodied voice of Dr. Glenn Pierce, and a few points of unexpected nuggets found while exploring.  The humor is fairly subdued.  Unfortunately, toward the end of the game, the humor dissipates as it tries to take itself seriously.There is simply no way not to compare  with .  It's a puzzle-based game with a novel mechanic in which the player learns to control the environment through testing chambers while being monitored by a computer and then needs to escape while humor dialog narrates.   does what it does better because it wasn't trying to be anything.  However,  deserves to be rated on its own merits.  It is a fun experience that stretches on what a puzzle can be in a virtual world.  Fans of  or  will certainly enjoy .

_childDocuments_.review: I really really wanted to enjoy this game. I got it through humble recently and thought this would be a great time to pick up this game as I was always hesitant to grab it at full price in the past.When the game starts it sets up an expectation that you're playing a puzzle game, and there are puzzles but personally I found them very lacking. Mostly amounting to "walk forward and interact with the only thing you can in the room", and usually through the simple act of blind interaction the puzzle would be solved. Very quickly I realized this isn't a puzzle game, it's a walking simulator (which can be good and I have enjoyed in the past), but it's a walking simulator with almost nothing worth walking through.This game has such good ideas but in the end I can't justify the price tag on what amounts to being a subpar puzzler stapled onto a subpar walking simulator. If the game had ditched some of the puzzle aspects and focused solely on making an optical illusion based walking sim then it would have been a better time. But because the game needed so many restrictions for the puzzle aspect it made the rest of the, rather large, environments seem barren and not worth walking around (which I did alot of).The gimmick is cool but the execution feels like it's ripping off both Portal and Stanley's Parable but ignoring the core of what made either so much fun to interact with. The game shines most when it's just an optical illusion showcase/ TED talk (if you see the ending you'll get what I mean about it being a TED talk lol)Decent buy on sale but I can not recommend at full price

(suggestion: placeable props to assemble others, ability to throw/recall camera (to fixed spots?))TL;DR: If you like perspective-based puzzles and moderate exploration, 8/10 (9/10 if on sale); else, avoid.

_childDocuments_.review: hey guys I played superliminal following a recommendation from a disappointed player of maquette, and I've got to say I was very disappointed. It doesn't live up to the hype that's being circulated around it.The puzzles are well designed, but the story is appallingly written - bland and repetitive, aping other well-made popular culture games like Portal 2 or The Stanley Parable that had a clearer vision, but ultimately offering little more than the sound of those games - the impression of a menacing machine voice/narrator.  I enjoyed the puzzles but always found myself dreading the next line of dialogue. Like these games, you are trapped in a lab and eventually find holes in the walls to escape through, but Subliminal doesn't seem to know what do with this feature - bringing it back time and time again until it's ultimately meaningless. I've played some very good puzzle games that never used dialogue - antichamber, the witness - or ones that did - the talos principle, stanley parable - and I think I would recommend these games to players who like myself were disappointed with subliminal (and perhaps by extension maquette). Subliminal unfortunately is the kind of game that makes me worry about the state of the games industry today - especially since I was roped in like everyone else by that highly giffable unique mechanic. It's a shame it has very little else to offer; they could have delivered a narrative that is a natural extension of that mechanic describing its meaning, rather than just the spectacular appearance of a narrative (the sound and inferences of it) for the benefits of promotion.  Games can be so much more than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit:I feel cheated. I feel dirty too. Pretty much cruised through 99% of the game almost no problems, then have to look up a guide for the last two puzzles. Why? Because they changed the rules into abstract instead of logical thinking, and I have no patience for that. And after I had to look up a guide, the spell broke, and for all the good the 99% of the game did, the ending ruined just like that. The various different room turned to blank black and white scenes, the white which honestly kind of hurt to look at and compelled me to want to turn my brightness down. the pretentiousness of it all, the removal of logical puzzles for think outside of the box "puzzles" which really just translated to figure out what rule we changed, two of which I just accidentally stumbled on while having no idea what the hell I was supposed to do because there's no reasoning to it, and the rules fly in the face of what you were to do before, and it all just felt irritating, irritating enough to completely sour my mood on the whole thing and spoil my whole opinion on the game.in retrospect, it revealed to me some annoying parts in the previous sections too, like the many areas that relied on pitch darkness to add challenge to navigation, which is about as fun as stumbling in the dark usually is. and the fact that a lot of the game is the same puzzle over and over again, with only a few deviations or alterations to the mechanic to make it interesting. and the entire setting lacks the surreal qualities it needed throughout a lot of it, boiling down to dull rooms with slight reality twists. Stanley Parable did the boring hum drum office well because it was connected to the story and had a funny and interesting narrative to back it up. this....doesn't. Spoilers spoilersIt's all made up. Yeah, it's all a dream, but there's no stakes. The early story hints at things going horribly wrong Portal-style, and a Glados impersonator seems to be the root cause, which, while derivative, still packs a sort of punch as i haven't played Portal in a while, but then.......they reveal it was all part of the plan. The errors, the danger, the threat of possibly being trapped in your mind forever, all of it was a lie, and boy, that, right there, was when I felt truly and utterly cheated.My original positive review just said, "spoilers, it was all a dream", jokingly, but it turned out I was actually right. It was all a dream, because the entire story was all just a lie to push some pretentious message about changing perspective, a theme which other games can do simply though gameplay, or through better story telling. Congratulations devs, writer's specifically, you managed to make a game about dreaming, and still created a story with the exact same disappointing ending that people expect from a plot with a "it was all a dream" trope.Now, there are still a lot of good, trippy set pieces here and there, especially at the end just before the rug is pulled out from under you, but all that excitement and interest was just totally sucked out of me as soon as I realized  that the stakes, the danger, the chaos, the weirdness was all by design, and the illusion broke.

_childDocuments_.review: SubparliminalWhen I first played this game shortly after it released on Epic, I came away unimpressed. I felt the extent of the mechanic was explored in the first 20 minutes and that nothing that would follow would expand on it or use it in a new, clever way. So I stopped playing it and refunded. But people kept praising the game, especially after its Steam release. Maybe I was wrong?I wasn't wrong. To be clear, it's well-made and extremely unique. Very polished outside of weird pixelated lighting and massive seams (especially in the secret ending they added). Feels good and the forced perspective mechanic works flawlessly. The minimal story is fine - nothing amazing, a bit predictable, but handled well and ties into the gameplay in some nice ways. But the fun just simply does not last as long as the game does.It does have cool puzzles. It does have some neat twists. But it's far longer than it needs to be and did nothing to keep it interesting as time goes on. The game is a supplementary mechanic for a bigger game that has yet to happen. It's worth the price, but not worth the time.I liked the business card from SDD2016 tho.

_childDocuments_.review: Forget everything you know about reality, depth perception and perspective.In Superliminal, you play as a patient undergoing a sketchy medical treatment to 'cure feelings of self-doubt'. During your dreams, you explore beautiful but eerie dreamscapes where things aren't always what they seem to be. The soothing voice of your therapist will be by your side as you solve mind-bending puzzles that will get you stuck and frustrated. Most of these puzzles can be solved by changing your perspective on them, often having solutions that are completely logical but don't make sense at the same time. Around halfway through the game, your brain will have been rewired to think outside the box and you will approach every room with a new mindset.Gameplay and story are closely intertwined, as you get deeper into the dreamscapes you get this feeling of being completely lost when in reality you're going exactly where you're meant to go. Puzzles you solve can be compared to real-life problems, and their out of the box solutions show that any problem can be solved by changing your outlook on it. Superliminal carries a strong message of succeeding in the face of adversity which comes together during the final chapter of the game, as you reflect on everything you have accomplished.While the game is short (around 3.5 hours for a blind playthrough), it does offer extra challenge rooms that can be compared to Portal's challenge mode as interactions with the level are limited. It also has two speedrunning achievements that are pretty satisfying to get as you breeze through the entire game in under half an hour after just a bit of practice.

_childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is a game unlike any others I've played. Within the first 30 seconds of gameplay, logic is thrown out the window by showcasing the game's main gimmick, which is changing the size of an object based on the player's "perception" of where the object is placed. This ability is present through most of the game, with some exceptions. However, it does not overstay its welcome, as the game itself is only around 5-6 hours in length, with a total of 8 different levels to play (not including the small Epilogue at the conclusion of the game). While short, the game introduces a new theme or zone to explore in each level, allowing the player to consistently interact with new elements. Without getting into spoilers, there are other gimmicks that are popularized in specific levels, so keep a sharp eye. I highly recommend this product to anyone who enjoys games that stand out and are unique in what they do. Because in this game, Perception is Reality.

_childDocuments_.review: More mixed than positive, but more positive than negative: Fun game with engaging mechanics. I enjoyed my time with it in two playthroughs, including once with the developers' commentary. However, the game is quite short and doesn't make the most of its mechanics. Comparisons to Portal are unavoidable due to the style of humour and certain puzzles, but the game is more visually stimulating than the Valve titles. However, whereas Portal (and particularly its sequel) introduced mechanics and built them up to give you more complicated scenarios that tested your skill at incorporating those different mechanics to solve its puzzles, Superliminal really just runs out of steam in the last quarter, and the challenge level is always minimal. Put another way, the game doesn't live up to the potential of its concept and seems to lose interest in its mechanics as the game winds down. In their place, the story attempts to pick up the slack, and it really is more story-driven than puzzle-driven. I think, however, that it misses the mark and fumbles the conclusion. It's not bad, but the message doesn't resonate as well as the game thinks it does. Had the game's difficulty steadily increased, until the end resulted in a multifaceted, complex puzzle that required every previous skill to solve, then the ending narration would have more weight, but the "meta-narrative" falls flat.I wish the game was longer and had more puzzles. There is a challenge mode, but limiting how many times one can jump or pick up objects is not the same as designing more complicated and engaging puzzle sequences. I bought it on the Summer sale, so I don't think I wasted my money, but I wouldn't pay full price for it. I hope that the developer will take the mechanics of this game and design a sequel that expands on the concept and takes the gameplay to new levels of challenge and innovation.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't go into it expecting something like Portal, where new mechanics are introduced and feed into puzzles with increasing complexity. Each puzzle section hinges on one particular mechanic, and with the exception of the primary "make thing bigger or smaller" trick, you don't make use of them again. There were a few neat puzzles, but nothing that left me in awe after finding the solution. I would have liked to have seen several of these ideas put into play at the same time to create more complex puzzles.Towards the end of the game (and it's short) there's less puzzles and more walking until the environment changes unexpectedly or you fall through the floor. It's not as shocking as intended as many games have done this already, or at least included similar sequences, and arguably in a better way.I was also disappointed with the setting and story. In this regard it's like a less interesting mash up of the Stanley Parable and Portal. You're in some "dream simulation" that has clearly gone wrong, complete with a misanthropic AI with a computerized female voice and a bumbling doctor guiding you along. But nothing really happens and it wraps everything up, in frankly a trite way, with a message about how you're a better person because now you can think outside of the box. Not happy about spending 20 bucks on it. If you're into walky-talky kind of games you'd probably like it more than I did. As a puzzle game, give it a go at a cheaper price but don't expect to be blown away.

_childDocuments_.review: Now because I've played this game first on the Nintendo Switch where the game was already optimized for the system hardware, there the game played very smoothly though maybe not at the same level as the Playstation systems. The con with playing this game on the PC is that if you didn't check the graphics settings, the game will not look as good as it should be. At least 3 times throughout a single playthrough I had to change the Graphics settings but could never find the proper settings to make it look as good as on the Nintendo Switch. Plus the cursor moved sluggishly on the menus, compared to other games like the Stanley Parable. I think this is the reason I prefer Consoles like Nintendo over the PC. The game was already optimized for the console while in the PC you have to change Graphic Settings for best results. Feels like a Hassle.Oddly, once I unlocked the Developer's Commentary, the game looked and ran much more smoothly like on the Nintendo Switch. To be honest, I only brought this PC version because it had new unlockables modes, like the Developer's Commentary. Although, the new ability to see how long you've been playing one playthrough with a Timer option made it more reassuring when I attempted to go for the Speedrun acheivement of an hour.Gameplay wise: The Puzzles were virtually unchanged from the Console version I played. Although, in one "looping" puzzle, they added a little chime to indicate you're going the right path. Which is nice as it was the one puzzle where I had to look at a video walkthrough to get by. The Console version I played on Switch didn't have that correct chime.Final verdict The Game plays fine, but it's best to know which graphical settings for your PC will work to make the game look and run smoothly. Personally I prefer my Nintendo Switch for normal smooth gameplay and likely will over play the PC version for Commentary, Challenge mode and maybe the speedrun timer.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically just a tech demo, walking simulator pretending to be a puzzle game and have gameplay.This garbage is essentially the offspring of  but then what happened is a deformed useless garbage with no substance or depthAnd I mean that seriously, all the controls are WASD + mouse left click, the game wasn't joking as it is playing with your perspective and desperately trying make you see depth where there is noneAfter the first time it introduced a mechanic IT NEVER WENT BACK TO IT, nope, everything was a one time thing, instead of building on the rules it established it constantly did the "subvert your expectations, HA! you didn't expected that right? wink wink nudge nudge" But no matter how good it tried to present the idea of "perspective" the game was still shallow and ended up shallow, by the halfway point I was dying of boredom, and even the people on my stream started pointing it out, disappointed.I truly hated how even after realizing this walking simulator kept trying to appear deep and appear having substance by narrating nonsense over and over trying to copy what Stanley Parable did right, and trying to seem esoteric with non-euclidian geometry like Antichamber, while having effectively zero puzzle elements other than to just walk forward and positioning looking towards a direction, every, single, time, had infuriated me, it sounded like those pseudo philosophical artsy scammers that sugarcoat stuff to seem more valuable when it was actually stretching time on purpose to avoid the Steam 2 hour refund threshold. I did not look into any external solutions at any point and avoided watching anything about the game to not be spoiled. My complete playtime from beginning to end was 1.5 hours (an hour and a half) entirely in a single session, the "puzzles" were games-journalist level of shallowness and impressionability.Times like these I wish I just watched other people play and avoided disappointing myself with these bait and switch games that pad out time on purpose to avoid being refunded. _childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game with a caveat: That what you actually want is a surreal walking simulator/hidden object game with a few front-loaded traditional puzzle elements and some mild feel-good philosophy. However, if you were expecting Portal or the Talos Principle or the Turing Test with a perspective based puzzle focus, this isn't that, at least not for very long.After what feels like the intro section, the more overt puzzle elements start to disappear and it becomes a game of 'find the thing you're actually allowed to interact with, and interact with it' and 'walk through the doorway that may or may not actually look like a doorway'.Throughout most, but not all, of the game I didn't actually feel like I was solving anything, and that feeling just ended up being frustrating more than anything else, to the point that I quit at what turned out to be 10 minutes before the credits because I'd had enough.If the narrative felt less bare-bones, or the puzzle elements didn't fade into frustrating hidden object gameplay, I'd have enjoyed more of my time with this and been able to recommend it. But as it happens it's stuck in a limbo between being a good walking sim and being a good puzzle game and not really succeeding at either. On a meta level, it's fitting given the setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Nominated for most innovative gameplay.This is contemporary art that's worth your money, lads.Using videogame as a vessel to impart higher meanings.Just as my mom used to tell me: "Study, child, for the pen is lighter then the shovel", I would dare reply to her that there are thoughts that weigh a thousand pounds. It's impossible not to remember (and point out) a couple of preliminary things: 1. CodeParade's (and others) videos on non-euclidean geometry, how it would be applied to videogames and the development of non-euclidean videogame engines, that is to say, the shortest path from point A to point B is no longer a straight line. Just how warped can reality get?2. Portal. Superliminal is as influenced by Portal as my children would be, if I had any, influenced by me. This is not to say it's unoriginal. The puzzle landscape is evolving, and one could only imagine how trippy it would be to play this on VR. Portal kindled a beautiful fire for videogames that will burn for ages. Reality-bending puzzlery, like God itself beckoned to you . But this is about Superliminal, which stands on its own as a Titan that not only breaks the 4th wall, but freaking demolishes it, crumbles it down to dust and sucks you in for that deep philosophical (and visual!!!) experience. Man, this needs to be on VR stat.3. Miegakure , "A Puzzle Platformer in Four Dimensions", a game which is trying to visualize the fourth dimension, something hard (but not impossible) even to conceive firstly, that is to say, create it out of nothingness in the blank space of thought, imagine developing a  entirely based on it. It'll be by far the most efficacious way of visualizing 4D yet invented, in my feeble understanding.4. Lucid dreaming. From dream journaling, wake up calls to symbolic representation inside dreams, this game did its research on the topic. Everything is included, and it feels like one is lucid dreaming while playing this game. They warn you that the game could trigger dissociation, and I'm not surprised. My last question would be: How does I-LIDS work, really, and can it be compared to Elon Musk's ? (And this is where reality meets Sci-fi). (Treating spine diseases my ass! You can see the smirk of excitement on Elon's face as he showcases what will be )5. Optical illusions. Namely, the perspective kind. Google "T-Rex Optical Illusion" for a classic!I write this review just after finishing the game. It took me  to do so, but I paused to piss and didn't finish it in one sitting. So I guess the game is short, but I'm off to achievement hunting, trying to speedrun some parts, checking out extras, anyway, doing my thing. If you're like me, doing these should extend playtime a little bit. No button-mashing extravaganza here. It matters little (as one TF2 boi would say), because difficulty for its own right isn't the focus here at all: mechanics mean nothing to Superliminal. Instead, what you'll find is that it forces you to use your brain in different and totally new fun ways despite looking like a walking simulator at first glance (which is not the case at all! I say this in regards to mechanics ). are not cutting edge, but very sufficient to convey the message and well optimized (Tip: Turn off V-Sync in-game and enable fast V-Sync on Nvidia Control Panel. Way less input lag).As I move on to talk about the  I end this part here: Story and puzzles. This is what this game's about. Just like life reveals its meaning steadily, you will embark on a journey that progresses to a satisfying resolution, that is to say, the game has a thoughtful and well-defined story to tell, about Dr. Glenn Pierce, his  new Somnasculpt Dream Therapy, and how it can be applied to lessen suffering... and you'll find some interesting stuff along the way. With that out of the way, I can only imagine the amount of work poured into this. I cannot distill the essence of this game, I'll still play more so I'll just point out some stuff that caught my eye right off the bat (first experience + possible mini-spoiler, if you want to jump in blind, read this not, yes?):1. I feel like the Standard Orientation Protocol (the woman that tells you everything is going wrong) could be compared to the anxious voice inside our own heads, the inner judge that tells us we're inadequate, insufficient, ugly and that everything's trash all the time. Because she is as robotic, cold and judgmental as we are, when anxious, talking to ourselves stuck in some sort of feedback loop. She tells you that it is all your fault, and if you would just be like everyone else and , all this suffering would not be happening. Talk about reminding of weird embarassing things you said out loud in the past!!! She also reminds me of GLaDOS (This is the last time Portal will be mentioned on this abhorrent review, I apologize).2. Close to finishing the game, one finds oneself in a room with music playing. This teleported me instantly to Aperture Science, listening to the unforgettable "Still Alive" radio tune while waking up as a lab rat. But there's also loud ass music playing in the OTHER room (???), and a lot of other details and little easter eggs I will try to see by replaying the game...3. It really feels like being in therapy in this game, and the sheer manipulation of childlike objects, task completion and problem solving (as one does, in therapy when child) all immerses you deeper into this feeling of being a lab rat and having no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clue of what's going on. I feel like the concept has been explored to the brim, but weirdly enough I think there still should exist more to be said about this (sequel? anyone?). Your vision only appears 3D because you have two eyes, which causes an effect known as stereo-something, binocular vision or something. If you close one eye, the image that appears looks a hell of a lot 2D, like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ snapshot of the scene you're watching. Just thinking about this simple fact can make one trip to endless depths. So is my eye a camera now? Just what design came first? Is a camera more sophisticated than my eye, a complex evolutionary machine developed during the course of millions of years? How many frames per second can my freaking eye render? Is 4K quality analogous to the human eye, is it better, or is it worse? Is that lamppost out there some real object located far away or just a small little stick that I could grab with the tips of my fingers if I wanted to? Are my eyes reliable or could there possibly be some other, better way to see?For instance, imagine if you will a machine that's labeled "EYES". You would be able to look through it, and by doing so, you would actually SEE ALL of the electromagnetic spectrum (including X rays, gamma rays, infrared and ultraviolet, not just the visible spectrum, a.k.a. light. How would ultraviolet look like? Like violet, but more saturated? Maybe that's why they used "ULTRA"?)Yes. The senses are trippy, and work in tandem to form some weird amalgam (or illusion) we call "reality". Shadows, sounds, smells, proprioception etc. all render reality for us, but it is easily bendable, as you will see "clearly" (paradox much? get used to it) with Superliminal.What is reality? And where does actuality ends and subjectivity begins? Is there not a clear line? Or are they all tangled up together, inside this thing called conscious awareness, the superliminal, human experience?Yes. Very confusing and pleasant stuff.A well-deserved 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I without a doubt enjoyed my time with Superliminal. The puzzles are a nice mix of logic, and perception. It's definitely along the same lines as Viewfinder, but I feel like its more fleshed out than Viewfinder. Pros:-The puzzles are challenging enough to make you think about them, but not so hard that you rage out at the game. And the 'Ah-Ha' moment when you solve them feels very satisfying. -The background music is very well chosen for the type of game this is and the setting your character is in. -The walking speed of the character is perfect. I've played some games like this where the walking speed is miserably slow and I don't feel like this game suffers from that, which helps the levels feel like they're going by quickly.-The way the story is told through recordings at specific points feels very nice and helps with immersion.-Level design is well thought out and if you enjoy speedrunning you can find lots of intentional, and unintentional, ways to move quickly though some levels. Cons:-MANTLING. Man, The mantling mechanics can be really frustrating in certain situations(looking at you floaty bouncy house)-Due to the nature of the game, sometimes your perception and the games perception of placement don't line up always, which can lead to some frustrating situations. Especially in challenge mode.-The amount of certain collectibles seems SLIGHTLY excessive. So, if you're the type of person that wants ALL collectibles it can feel a little grindy. In conclusion, I give this game a solid 8.0/10. 23/27 achievements. 10.1 hours played. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: obvious influences of Portal and The Stanley Parable, but forges its own path to something different. I would have preferred some more of the standard puzzles before the game went mental, but overall highly recommended.As mentioned in the TLDR, immediately two games sprung to mind for me: Portal and The Stanley Parable. Then by extension games like The Spectrum Retreat. But this isn't too derivative, and the developers really have introduced some fresh new concepts to the genre. The puzzles are ingenious. And there are a few times where you really want to slap yourself as your expectations lead you one way, but your expectations are the issue. i.e. "There's a wall there. Why is there a wall? Well because I see a window. But is there really a wall, you're assuming there's a wall" etc. It works wonderfully.For the most part it wasn't too challenging. I consulted guides a couple of times, one where I was just not getting it and another time where I kind of broke the game. I had got myself into quite a pickle and as I was breaking the game issues with the level itself started to lead me into thinking I was doing the right thing. But that aside, I never ran into any issues.My only slight grumble/wish was that it had stayed a more literal puzzle game, playing more with the mechanics I had learned before going down the 'weird' rabbit hole that these games are often wont to do. I still enjoyed it and there's some really nice mind-bending stuff, but it was the 'end' that felt like it outstayed its welcome as just dragging on a bit too much.But really, go get this game if you like any of the ones I've mentioned above. It's a great and fresh addition to the genre. What that genre is... puzzle-walkingsimulator-madness genre perhaps.. I don't know. But I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, as I'm sure other people have said, half puzzle game and half walking simulator and it kind of fails at both.The puzzles are Portal-like, as in push a button to get through a door, where the operative mechanic is the ability to change the size of objects.  Most of the time the idea of forced perspective isn't very important, effectively all you're doing is scaling objects.  There are a few set pieces where they play around with paintings becoming real, and sometimes you scale yourself instead of the object, but these are usually one-off situations, they never mix the ideas and so the puzzles end up being very easy.With the walking simulator part they want to be the Stanley Parable.  Occasionally the atmosphere is comparable: some parts are genuinely creepy and there's a fair amount of non-Euclidean architecture.  But I think it fails in two aspects. Firstly, it never feels like the game's responding to what you're doing.  With the Stanley Parable you'd try something and the narrator would comment on it which would change what you did which the narrator would comment on and so on.  Superliminal feels more like a guided tour.  Secondly, Superliminal is very linear.  With the Stanley Parable the whole point was the ability to choose between paths, until the narrator made it clear it didn't matter what path you chose you had no control over the world.  With Superliminal, you're told you're not doing what you're supposed to but there's only ever one option to continue.  So the walking simulator feels very forced.I suppose you could argue the walking simulator is more similar to the behind-the-scenes parts of Portal 2, which is also linear, but the loading screen and the environment seem heavily Stanley Parable inspired.The technology in the game is impressive and I think they could make a really good game with the ideas they have, but Superliminal isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short but sweet puzzle game. Really interesting core mechanic that's genuinely never been done before, utilized satisfyingly, occasionally makes you go 'wow' and doesn't outstay its welcome. Sound familiar? _childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is one of those puzzle games that really wants to be Portal. Unfortunately, this is one of those games where it feels like it actually tried REALLY hard to be clever, and ended up falling on its face. Superliminal has a really cool premise, but it fails to actually do something interesting with it. You play as a patient of Dr. Pierce’s Somnasculpt dream therapy program. The premise of the game is that you are asleep, and you are going through your dreams, solving puzzles to deal with your personal problems.Naturally, as you might expect from such a game, the experience doesn’t exactly go smoothly, and soon you find yourself lost in a strange dreamscape while you have to keep solving puzzles to try and get back out. The game has what seems to be a cool central premise: you can manipulate your environment using the power of perspective. You can pick up an object and make it huge by dropping it against a distant backdrop, or tiny by dropping it up close. This is the central mechanic of the game, and most of the game consists of manipulating objects by grabbing them and growing/shrinking them.Unfortunately, the game does very little with this. There are a few other mechanics that are introduced that involve perspective – such as aligning an object to make it pop out of the scenery from a 2D image, or doing the reverse – but unfortunately, this is never really expanded on in a particularly interesting or creative way. It is all just about lining up the perspective, and that’s it.Indeed, the game ends up frequently devolving into a game of “find the interactive object or location in this space”. Towards the end of the game, you end up walking around an area for a bit trying to look at everything, and then you see the one thing you can interact with, or a hole in the wall, or whatever. This happens a LOT. While there are some slightly clever puzzles, like dropping an item into an area to make it into a 3D space instead of a flat 2D space, or making “holes” into solid spaces by putting objects on them, but it ends up never really evolving much.And that’s the problem. The game is not actually very clever, and the puzzles don’t tend to have very clever solutions; as a result, YOU, the player, don’t feels super smart for solving them. While it reinforces the whole “perception is reality” thing, as you have to think about how to perceive things the way that it is intended to progress, in the end, it ends up falling short.I wanted to like this game, and it kept introducing and toying with cute concepts, like picking up and moving doors to make the world inside bigger or smaller when you went through them, but in the end, it fails to actually go anywhere clever with them. A lot of the ideas are basically “Here is an idea!”, then the most basic executions of it, before moving on without doing further clever things.But in the end, it just ended up kind of mediocre. I liked the ideas it had a lot, but the execution was often wanting. It had clever ideas, and then didn’t really explore them in an interesting way. The bit that really sold Portal, where you took these basic ideas and then expanded on them in clever ways, was a big part of what made that game work so well, and that last extra step is lacking here.The story, too, doesn’t actually deliver; while it ends up poking at some of the same ideas as an AI that refuses to admit that it is wrong and the vain creator whose ideas aren’t as good as they think, in the end, neither end up really connecting with the player.Overall, I can’t really recommend it. If you get it for free, it’s not a terrible thing to experience, but it won’t knock your socks off; as a paid experience, I can’t really see buying this over other, better things.

And now with the multiplayer update I'm super exciting to play probably my favorite game of all time with my friends. If you like puzzle games like Portal, this game is absolutely for you. _childDocuments_.review: Graphics are beautiful and pleasing to the eye.Runs well with zero performance issues from my own play-through.Overall extremely polished and well made.So what is my issue? - Why can't I recommend it?Well I managed to beat the game in 21 minutes and I am by no stretch of the imagination a "speed runner" Personally I believe the developers should look to extend the gameplay - Maybe with a more concrete narrative, the game mechanic is so incredibly fun and new that it is outright criminal they did not wrap a bow around it with an intriguing narrative, all we get are little bits and pieces of an otherwise non-invasive story.I think the final message would've been so powerful, but it lacked the punch to make an impact and I was left seriously shocked asking myself "is this really the end?" Simply put, despite being a truly refreshing and VERY fun idea Superliminal is just too short an experience to be worth the $20 or even $15 dollars I paid for on discount, I've played free Demos that last longer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most thought provoking and relaxing games I have ever played.After playing this game the way I view the world around me has changed.The most obvious amazing aspect of the game is how unexpected everything is! You pick up a cube expecting it to be what it appears and then it just shatters into pieces. You try to put a chess piece on a button but it suddenly becomes a part of the interior design. While roaming the seamlessly endless dreams an announcer constantly comments on how you broke the things that cannot be broken. These passive-aggressive announcements are hilarious and made me want to play the game even further just to hear the opinion of the invisible commentator.The end of the game ,  once again , flips everything you've learnt about it while playing and allows you to see the truth.Thank you, Superliminal, for letting me dream.

_childDocuments_.review: A good aside to portal. TLDR: I'd recommend the experience.Think of this as a good once through journey, that like portal & limbo will be fun to watch your friends try to play through. Portal challenges your thinking but also requires some reflex/skill that could be a barrier to non-gamers (eg my mom).This game is very casual paced/does not require reflex timing style skill, so that entry barrier is gone.But it will challenge your thinking more & your ability to comprehend how to properly shrink/grow objects could be the same frustration for a non-gamer.(and hey, one of my friends spent 3min trying to catch himself in portal, before he realized the person disappearing right as he entered was his own character! People will vary in comprehension. My dad who struggles with phones and computers surprisingly picked Gran Turismo up right away) Most of the puzzles are kind of the same in principle, but the world changes and messes with you, and the variety of messing with you really expands near the end. Think of it as more an experience in messing with your brain, rather than an absolute difficult puzzle solving challenge.I enjoyed the whole ride and never found myself bored.I did look up 1 puzzle that got stuck on.Like portal and limbo, this short but good. I finished the main game in 3hrs, including searching for and finding some secrets. I feel like I got my money's worth. Plus, there are other modes and community levels to try as well.

_childDocuments_.review: ~ DIFFICULTY ~🔲 My 90 year old grandma could play it✅ Easy🔲 Normal🔲 Hard🔲 Dark Souls~ GRAPHICS ~🔲 MS Paint🔲 Bad🔲 Meh🔲 Graphics dont matter in this game✅ Good🔲 Beautiful~ MUSIC ~🔲 Bad🔲 Not special✅ Good🔲 Eargasm~ STORY ~🔲 This game has no story🔲 Like playing Temple Runners for the story🔲 It's there for the people who want it✅ Well written🔲 Epic story~ PRICE ~🔲 Free🔲 Underpriced🔲 Perfect Price✅ Could be cheaper🔲 Overpriced🔲 Complete waste of money~ REQUIREMENTS ~🔲 You can run it on a microwave✅ Average🔲 High end🔲 NASA computer~ LENGTH ~🔲 Very Short (0 - 3 hours)✅ Short (3 - 15 hours)🔲 Average (15-50 hours)🔲 Long (50-90 hours)🔲 Extremely long (90-110 hours)🔲 No ending~ FUN ~🔲 I'd rather watch paint dry🔲 Hard to enjoy🔲 Repetitive🔲 Actually pretty amusing✅ Ride of your life~ REPLAYABILITY~🔲 It's a one-time experience🔲 Only for achievements✅ If you wait a few months/years🔲 Definitely🔲 Infinitely replayable~ WORTH BUYING ~🔲 No🔲 Wait for sale✅ Yes----------------Superliminal is a puzzle game that plays with your perception of reality. You can manipulate objects by changing their size and shape depending on how you look at them. The game challenges you to think outside the box and explore the surreal environments that you find yourself in.The gameplay is simple and still unlike anything you will have seen before. The way you perceive objects and items in this game, especially when interacted with, will change the way each level is played. Extremely unique experiences lead to the gameplay being extremely versatile and a lot of fun!The story is about a lucid dreaming experiment gone wrong. You are a participant who gets trapped in a series of dreams that become increasingly bizarre and unstable. You have to follow the voice of Dr. Glenn Pierce, the creator of the experiment, who tries to guide you to wake up. Along the way, you encounter various messages and signs that hint at a deeper meaning behind your experience.The music is atmospheric and relaxing, creating a contrast with the sometimes unsettling and confusing nature of the puzzles. The soundtrack features ambient sounds and soft piano melodies that enhance the mood of each level. The music also adapts to your actions and changes depending on what you do.Overall, Superliminal is a unique and innovative game that offers a fresh perspective on puzzle-solving. It is a short but memorable experience that will make you question your own perception and reality. If you enjoy games that are creative and mind-bending, you should definitely give Superliminal a try.Superliminal gets a 7/10.For more reviews check my Steam profileHope you enjoyed my review, god bless you

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of the game certainly has some legs, and as a puzzle game it is genuinely interesting and does hold your attention. It definitely isn't anywhere near as enjoyable as some of my favourite other puzzle games, but it's still a good time. The game encourages different ways of thinking about puzzles, but gives you a very slim toolkit to work with, making it a bit repetitive (even for the short runtime). I'd say pick it up for sub £10 and it's definitely worth it, but measure your expectations. 6/10. Innovative core premise, fairly repetitive Gameplay loop, middling story, incredibly short runtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is the best puzzle game I've ever played.Superliminal has simplistic but brilliantly executed mechanics that feel incredibly fun and rewarding to figure out. Alongside these mechanics are a narrative told by recordings from the patient care team as well as the dream environment you are currently in. The atmosphere and narrative are wonderfully entwined. Each level feels unique in design and especially in the art direction. The music is also pretty great. All around, there is few things I can criticize with the game.Superliminal is a strong and fast burn that could jerk a few tears. There are few games I'd recommend for everyone but Superliminal is undoubtedly among them.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a terrible game. It was a clever idea, and mechanically it works fine.  This game takes place in a dream world. The basic premise revolves around perception. You can pick up an item, position it so that it looks bigger, and it will  bigger. Early on, this was fun enough. The occasional dialogue was amusing, and I was curious about more details about what was happening. As the game went on, I felt as though there was very little development. There were a handful of good puzzles sprinkled throughout the game, but a lot of them did just feel like the same thing over again. "Find the box. Make it bigger so you can use it as a stool." As time went on, there was more space between the puzzles as well, so it was less about the puzzles and more about walking from place to place, waiting for the next thing to happen. (You cannot sprint. This was fine during puzzles, but frustrating during the many "walking" bits.) The more the game went on, the more it felt like it was relying on the story side of the game, rather than puzzles or actual gameplay. This would have been fine except that, like the puzzles, there was a lot of time spent walking from short dialogue to short dialogue, and they never went as deep as I'd have liked. I had been looking forward to this game. I was a bit disappointed with some aspects listed above, but I wasn't planning to leave a negative review. The concept was still clever, it seems to have been programmed quite skillfully, the music was nice- it had its upsides. My issue was with the ending. Bear in mind- this is not a "multiple choice" type of game. There is one path you can take, with one solution to each puzzle. Sometimes it makes it  like you have multiple choices, but it's kind of like with portal. The way you're "supposed" to go (in-universe) is blocked, but the devs have a different route planned out. By itself, this is totally fine. But that really felt like it undercut the story here. There's a line at the end where . But the fact is,   There are two parts to this. The gameplay, and the story. The gameplay was a nice idea, but wasn't fleshed out enough to really be . The story could have been cool, and had nice intentions, but once again, wasn't fleshed out enough to be . But combined, it felt as though they were intended to compliment each other, and ended up contradicting instead. Either alone would have been passable, but combined, they sadly ended up tripping over each other and dragging the whole thing down.

_childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is a mind-bending puzzle game where the player enters a dream world full of obscure places and objects and everything revolves around the word "perspective".The story is pretty simple. You signed up for sleep therapy. Who knows why? Something about failure, trial and error, fear... It's a dream game. There isn't a lot that makes sense. But it's definitely a captivating ride!The visuals in this game are fantastic. Not too over the top, just plain and simple, yet still kinda charming. Nothing looks really real, it rather all fits into a liminal-space-style aesthetic, very dream-like. The music is really good, too. The game mostly consists of classic music and it really fits whatever tone the game is going for. Even without the game, the music is pretty relaxing and nice, a bit like elevator music. I recommend you listen to it closely.The game is performing very well on technical points. No lag, no weird collision, no bugs and extremely rare out-of-bounds clips. You'd really have to provoke that. Otherwise it doesn't happen. Except for multiplayer. That part of the game is still a bit difficult to grasp... You can get stuck in the lobby while trying to load a level  when everybody else already loaded in and half the props are missing for each player when you begin the first level without signing the paper in the first room.The achievements are kind of whack. You have 5 different collectibles in the game: Blueprints, Fire Alarms, Fire Extinguishers, Zodiac Signs and Chess Pieces. The fire alarms need to be all triggered and the fire extinguishers need to be all emptied in the whole level. The other collectibles are pretty well hidden. Other than that there's also an achievement for standing around AFK for 5 minutes and then there are achievements like uploading a dream or a workshop item.I did it all, but apart from the sharing stuff on Steam part, everything else was actually pretty fun. I suggest you go to bed and think about whether or not this game would be for you. I woke up the next morning willing to play.

_childDocuments_.review: The Portal of the mind.Story:You play as an unnamed person who has decided to attend the Pierce institute to test their new dream therapy, where a person is placed into a dream world where they can shift reality at will. You wind up being stuck and you're trying to find a way out, while traversing your dreams.Similarly to Portal, Superliminal delivers it's story through characters chiming in once in a while and updating you on what's going on. This ranges to pre recorded messages of an announcer speaking to you or tapes left by Dr. Pierce about the dream therapy. Overall it's decent stuff, it has a nice message by the end of it, but I feel like the game is so impressive that the story is sort of throw to the side because of it.Graphics:Superliminal is a simplistic looking game. It has a minimalistic approach to both the environments and the items you can interact with. It uses it to it's advantage so you naturally know where to go and what to do. However when the game does decide to make the environments more complex it makes sure to really make your jaw drop.Audio:The voice acting while very little of it, is very good. Dr. Pierce has a very naturally soothing voice and it helps match the dreamlike state of the game. You're exploring these crazy twisty worlds and hearing his voice just sort of really matches the tone. The music is also very relaxing, you never feel pressure or anything of the sort, it helps you build a very atmosphere (apart from one chapter if you know the one I'm talking about).Gameplay:I believe everyone at this point has at least seen a gif or a video of what Superliminal is about, but if you're not aware here's a brief rundown. Superliminal is a puzzle game where you use shifting perspectives to solve puzzles. You pick up and item and depending from your perspective it can be a giant item or a tiny thing. There's also other things like creating doorways from perspectives and others I don't want to spoil in this section.First of all I loved this mechanic and it's used to absolutely great potential, however I always felt that these puzzles mostly boiled down to finding the right size for the item to be and then using it advance. However each chapter introduces a new mechanic to the mix to help keep things fresh and that helps a lot, even though the game is pretty short.The only negative I really have with the game is that sometimes to get a right perspective for the item to change is pretty janky and requires a bit of tinkering. I could usually get an item large no problem, but have tons of trouble shrinking it down without messing up constantly.Verdict:Superliminal is a brilliant little game. I know it's been compared to Portal to death, but it's honestly a great twist on the puzzle genre and I absolutely loved my time with it. The campaign is short, however there's also a dream creator which allows a lot of creative people to create some great maps. So if you like this type of game, definitely check out Superliminal.Final Rating:9/10Pros:+ The shifting mechanic is awesome+ Great art design+ Each new level brings new puzzle mechanics Cons:- Short- Sometimes shifting is kind of jankyIf you liked this review please consider joining  and

_childDocuments_.review: I'd almost forgotten what a genuinely clever game feels like. Superliminal is such a game.The puzzles are excellent. A few are finicky, but the central mechanic is explored very effectively. As is the central theme of perception. Each level is confidently themed in a way that doesn't feel forced or overbearing; each level has an Idea, explores it thoroughly, and ends when it is satisfied with this exploration. It respects the player's time, and rewards creative thinking. Every puzzle felt right when it "clicked".The tone, however, is what makes it truly exemplary. Superliminal is as warm as it is clever. It delights in surprising the player, but it's a contagious delight. It invites a smile and a chuckle when it surprises the player, rather than basking in its wittiness. It is overall a comedic game that does not take itself too seriously, but at the same time, it is suffused with a wonderfully unfashionable sincerity.As you can see from my five hours clocked in, this is not a long game, but every minute I spent with it was time well spent. And I played through it twice, the second time with (genuinely interesting!) developer commentary, appreciating the foreshadowing and nudges built into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Superliminal is a game that takes puzzle-solving to new heights, offering a unique and mind-bending experience that is both challenging and engaging.  This first-person puzzle game has captured the attention of gamers worldwide, thanks to its innovative mechanics and surreal atmosphere.One of the standout features of Superliminal is its use of forced perspective, which allows players to manipulate the size and position of objects in the environment by adjusting their perspective. This creates a range of fascinating and challenging puzzles that require players to think critically and use their spatial reasoning skills to solve.As players progress through Superliminal, they are taken on a surreal journey through a world that defies the laws of physics and perception. The environments are filled with strange and abstract imagery that often shifts and changes as the player moves through them, creating a constant sense of wonder and surprise.Despite its challenging puzzles, Superliminal is an accessible game that is easy to pick up and play. The controls are intuitive, and the game offers a range of difficulty levels to suit players of all skill levels. This makes it an ideal game for anyone looking for a fun and engaging puzzle-solving experience.The game's soundtrack is another standout feature, with jazz standards that perfectly complements the game's surreal and dreamlike atmosphere. The sound effects are also well-done, adding to the immersion and overall sense of relaxation.The story involves you, the dreamer, being subjected to a new kind of sleep therapy, in which you have to complete challenging puzzles while you are dreaming. Time goes from 12:00 AM to 8:00 AM as the game continues, as seen through alarm clocks scattered throughout the game. Unfortunately, things go wrong, and the sleep therapy company Somnasculpt is forced to intervene to help you get back on track. the writing is clever and often humorous, and adds a good deal of character to this game, even though there are almost no characters in this game.  The ending left me both shocked and calmed, as if I had arrived at a new world. Finishing this game left me with an overwhelming  sense of joy,  the ultimate lesson of this story is that to accomplish a seemingly impossible task, one must look at it from a different point of view. In addition to its single-player campaign, Superliminal also offers a range of additional modes, including a speedrun mode and a sandbox mode that allows players to experiment with the game's mechanics and create their puzzles. This adds to the game's replay value, giving players plenty of reasons to come back and explore the game's world again and again.The game's graphics are stunning, with a clean and minimalist aesthetic that perfectly captures the game's surreal and dreamlike atmosphere. The environments are well-designed, with plenty of detail and visual interest, and the game's use of lighting and shadows is particularly impressive.Superliminal's story is also engaging, with a mysterious and intriguing narrative that keeps players engaged throughout the game. The game's ending is particularly well-done, offering a satisfying conclusion that ties together the various threads of the story in a satisfying way.The game's pacing is also excellent, with a steady progression of difficulty that keeps players engaged without overwhelming them. The game's difficulty ramps up gradually, introducing new mechanics and puzzles at a pace that is manageable and never frustrating.Finally, Superliminal is a game that is full of surprises and unexpected moments, creating a sense of excitement and wonder that is hard to find in other puzzle games. Whether it's the game's use of forced perspective, its surreal environments, or its engaging story, Superliminal is a game that constantly surprises and delights, offering a truly unique and unforgettable gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, after playing Superliminal, I'm pulling every fire alarms and empty every fire extinguisher I can find just for the sake of my sanity. They say I'm crazy but they don't understand, that they're all still dreaming!! Jokes aside. This game is short but it surprises you every now and then. Most of the puzzles aren't very difficult (except for one or two), but the creativity behind the concepts and buildings of the puzzles are pretty nice. Playing with the perspective of objects within a room is really refreshing. As a person who is reading and practicing concepts of buddhism, the whole idea of "you are still dreaming" is really familiar. So instead of the Inception idea of "we need to go deeper", the buddhism idea is: "you need to wake up". And the phrases "perception is (not) reality" brings the concept of the game to your daily life. As from a psychological point of view, this is an essential part of constructivism. So yea, you can see this game as a puzzle game or something fun, but it has the potential to leave something behind, something to think about. And that makes it a great game. Did I mention the fire extinguisher? Wait till you find out, what a Mini Soda is!

_childDocuments_.review: I wish more studios would make games like this. Story & GameplaySuperliminal is a perspective-based puzzle game where the player is in a supposed "dream therapy" but things go wrong. You start entering rooms and areas that aren't supposed to be open to you, the dreamer (or are they?). You start to solve puzzles by grabbing something and changing it, whether it is its size, shape, dimension, or quantity, to move onto the next level. The entire experience seems extremely intuitive and provides an, as my friend describes it, "trippy" experience.GraphicsThese graphics, especially towards the end, is unbelievable. The fact that the devs were able to make something so  mesmerizing and beautiful really amazes me. I truly hope, that with this game as the pioneer, more unique and special games like this one comes out, instead of another lazy fps cashgrab. Pros:-Visually mesmerizing-Intuitive gameplay-Overarching story-fun puzzlesCons:-Some puzzles you may need to look up since they are so difficultOverall:91%
