Explore a fantastic handcrafted world across multiple unique islands, meet curious characters and creatures, and uncover the archipelago’s secrets.
short_description: Explore strange and wonderful islands and dark labyrinths below in this narrative puzzle platformer. Guide young mechanic Mo on her quest to repair a world on the brink of collapse. The powerful Omni Switch at your disposal may not be enough to fix the damage that hides beneath the surface...

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, as long as you look for an easy, slow going platformer where the main challenge is to find your way (and some secrets). Yes, if you enjoy narrative games in an interesting, dystopian setting. Otherwise, no. No challenging action sequences, no convoluted puzzles. You don't even have a real inventory. Minute plays a bit like... Loom.You play a girl with blue hair and yellow shoes, tasked with keeping vital biological-mechanical machines running in a devasted - and mostly deserted - world. Four giants power the machines, and when the game begins they have stopped working. So you grab your Omni Switch and look for the reason, which starts a long, linear journey during which you have to travel between the islands to get everything in working order again. The world is mostly deserted, covered by poisonous spores that kill unprotected humans (and animals). You'll encounter withering plants, animal carcasses and the the story is told by the calming voice of the narrator, while the few humans you meet don't talk that much.You can run, jump, crouch and climb, but the game is designed to be playable by everyone. Even if you miss a platform, there is no fall damage when you glide down with your dress that works as a parachute. The spores might eat humans and animals alive, but you are quite resistant and are only in danger in areas with a high concentration of spores. In such areas the spores might poison your mind and induce a little delirium - but you know how to escape back to reality.The game autosaves every now and then, savefiles are stored in the cloud. Playing with a controller works fine.Narrative game with easy puzzles and simple platforming. The story in a polluted, abandoned world is quite interesting - like a good book, even though there are not many texts to read. It is mostly told by visuals, and memories you find, and the narrator who explains this or that.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Minute of Islands is a hand drawn narrative puzzle platform game set on a collection of islands once inhabited by giants.The lands have been ravaged by The Blight, a poisonous gas filled with toxic fungal spores. Inhabitants scurried to safety but the giants used their ingenuity and saved the world. Four giants were relegated to underground caverns where they power machines that purify the air and keep it fresh and breathable.Mo befriends the giants and they make her their apprentice, rewarding her with the Omni switch, a powerful device that can control the giants and the machinery that drives the purifiers.One day the machines stop working. All the inhabitants’ lives are at risk if Mo cannot get the engines turning and the purifiers working again.Minute of Islands excels in the looks and sound department but it’s sadly lacking a little in gameplay.The gameplay on offer is very repetitive. You will perform the same actions, in the same way on each of the four islands. You will need to find the purifiers and find the blood vessels of the giants, and although there are a couple of other distractions, that is about all you can expect from gameplay. The challenge, however, is in finding them.Environments can be quite tricky to navigate. I did get lost quite a lot. There is no map, but the omni-switch will point you in the right direction. I quite enjoyed navigating the mazes of ladders and ledges to begin with but it does become a little tiresome later in the game. There are some small puzzle elements but mainly it’s about finding the correct path to your destination. This can become unnecessarily awkward sometimes. It’s not always obvious what you can and can’t jump on. The hand drawn art looks incredible but it doesn’t always translate successfully into a decent platform experience.The story develops as we progress through the different islands and this is the part that is done very well. The atmosphere is so unique; The wonderfully hand drawn art and the the eerie music play an important part in creating an unusual experience. It reminded me of Norse mythology, especially as the narrator has a Scandinavian twang to her voice.What will keep your interested throughout the eight hours of gameplay is the story. The narrator does a wonderful job of describing things. It is almost poetic in nature but never sounds pretentious. It just oozes class and sophistication. The narration is extremely clever. Not only does she act as story teller and relay different character’s thoughts and words, but she also acts as Mo’s consciousness. Whenever Mo is experiencing hardship, the narrator becomes the voice of doubt telling her she’s not good enough. It is scathing and critical, painting a disturbing and depressive picture of how Mo is feeling. The weight of expectation on Mo’s shoulders is tangible and that comes across so clearly in the story. I found the whole premise very interesting. I’m starting to wonder if the repetitive nature of the gameplay reinforces the notions of duty and sacrifice emphasized in the story.Mo can run, jump, crawl and traverse ledges in the underground caverns or the surface of the four islands.A biomechanical boat takes Mo to each island. As custodian of the islands, she is familiar with each of the characters. Her sister and grandmother live on neighboring islands as well a handful of other characters we meet during her quest. Mo is able to talk to these characters briefly. Very occasionally, they will ask her to perform tasks for them or they will have objects needed to access areas. Scattered throughout the islands are a number of purifiers which she needs to find and engage using her Omni-switch device. Once these have all been activated on the island, she must travel underground and reawaken the giants who have collapsed under the strain of arduously turning the mammoth cranks providing power. Mo must perform a recovery operation by finding and stimulating their hearts and getting the blood flowing again.The Omni-Switch can act as directional guide and it points towards any open objectives. Mo must find her way through the maze of ledges and ladders and find each purifier on the island. Often your way is blocked by locked gates and broken pathways. Pressing switches can bring down bridges and call for lifts. Sometimes, you may need to talk to a character to get a key to open a lock. Mostly, you will be jumping around and climbing ladders trying to find the path to your destination. There are a few logical puzzles to complete, mainly from tasks initiated from other characters.We share the journey with the narrator. She comments on things we examine, indicated by an eye symbol, and narrates all of the character’s voices when conversation is initiated. A text box is also present during these events. The narrator also acts as our conscience. Although this voice is brief initially, as the quest becomes more strenuous, we hear the dark and scathing voice of Mo’s mind, questioning aspects of her work and relationships. Dispersed throughout each island are memories which can be caught, showing scenes of past events. Often, her conscience will remark on these too. Each island has a set number of memories to collect indicated by a counter.Mo is able to breathe in the toxic gas but occasionally she gets overwhelmed by the poisonous spores in the air and enters a delusional state. In this state Mo must wake herself up by remembering the order of musical notes and then find them and play them in the correct order. The game took me eight hours to complete.Even though there are counters for the memories collected, and your memories are carried over, you will need to restart the game from the beginning to pick up any missed ones.The visuals are stunning and original. Hand drawn art and imaginatively drawn locales provide plenty of special moments and impressive vistas. The sound is amazing too, with excellent voice acting by the narrator and a wonderfully atmospheric soundtrack and special effect noises. It really sounds unique and creates an eerie but suspenseful atmosphere which is memorable.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing this game for less than two hours and I already love it. The transitions between doing things sometimes makes things a little slow, but for the first time in so long I feel like I am playing a game that delivers exactly what it promised. The world manages to be falling apart but beautiful at the same time, and the controls are simple and intuitive. I haven't had issues with getting on or off platforms and everything is really smooth. The game has crashed once or twice but the way that it saves made it almost not even annoying. Both times there have been crashes I could load into almost exactly where the game crashed which is HUGE for me - I hate doing things twice. I often also struggle with puzzle games being too difficult/too easy but Minute of Islands does a good job with helping you find your way while still forcing you to think a little. I love how the dev's chose to help you out figuring out where to go next, and even the lore has caught my attention. It is definitely story-rich and doesn't have much "action", but if you like this sort of game it is easily something I would recommend.I was so sad when this game got delayed again, but it was totally worth the wait. I am excited to finish the rest of the game!
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: To be informed as humanly possible, I completed this game. In fact, I got 100% completion just to ensure I was as informed on this review as humanly possible. I would like to break it up into two parts, as my opinions on them clash wildly.The visuals and audio in this game are simply stunning, and my main draw to the game when I first saw the E3 trailer for it. The world seemed very unique and reminded me of a children's book, and I quite enjoy this aesthetic. And once I started playing, I found that the music and sound design was simply stunning. It's clear that a ton of work went into making this facet work (See the headphone recommendation every time the game is booted), but sadly some more time should have been spent on other parts of the game.The gameplay of Minute of Islands is some of the slowest and most tedious I have encountered in quite a while, on top of the game being quite buggy. I had it hard crash and boot me out of the game during one of the early cutscenes, and was softlocked out several times requiring me to return to the main menu and reload a save. For a game I spent roughly 6 hours on (15 total from my partner playing it as well and an error forcing me to restart halfway through since the game only has 1 save slot), I should not have had the game effectively be unplayable for me at a rate of about once per hour. Whether clipping through floors or objects getting frozen in places that block progress, this game definitely needs some cleaning up around the edges. Besides the glitches, the minute-to-minute gameplay left much to be desired. For a puzzle platformer, this game only really had two puzzles that each take about thirty seconds to solve. I ended up holding shift and sprinting everywhere to just move along the story rather than appreciate the gorgeous artwork every island had. The story was entirely fine. Nothing too crazy happened, following the Hero's Journey fairly closely is almost always a good bet.My biggest comment I feel should be made about Minute of Islands is that it's a good cartoon but a bad game. I mean this in a way similar to Danganronpa, which has the same issue of having decent story and art but horrendous gameplay. The beauty of video games is they let you interact with the world, and it never felt like I was really interacting. My choices as a player never mattered because I was never given the opportunity to make a choice. Every NPC seemed to have a moment where it would have been cool to make the choice of stopping to smell the roses or continuing with your duty, but that never happened and it was really unfortunate. This game had stunning visuals and music, but so does a game with oddly similar overarching stories and themes: Hyper Light Drifter. The main difference between these two games, however, is HLD is actually fun to play. I don't regret my time with Minute of Islands, but I'd only really recommend it if it's on sale or the aesthetic is *that* important to you. To add insult to injury, the final achievement for 100% completion of the game is bugged and the only one I do not have.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: I am Belgian and we have a very large comics and graphic novels tradition in our country, I have read and collected a lot. The beautiful, hand-drawn art style reminded me of comics and that's why I bought the game.The second biggest plus was the narrator's voice. Warm, sympathetic, with venom in her intonation at just the right moments.The story gives you just too little information to place all the events. I don't always think this is necessary, it tickles your imagination, but I did go to the Steam discussions to see what others thought.  The moment when the title of the game was mentioned was a highlight for me. Suddenly my eyes became as moist as the island environments.As for the gameplay: abysmal. A number of negative reviews already indicated this: the flow is constantly interrupted by cutscenes that are much too slow. The world often requires climbing in heights – which is a plus - but you cannot easily climb the obstacles. Sometimes you have to make a series of short, little jumps up or down, other times you have to make a big jump to be able to cling on an edge with white blobs of paint. Why can't I always do the big(ger) jump? Sigh... That also interrupted the game flow. And the endless walking back almost sent me into a frenzy. Why didn't the devs choose fast travel when a certain point was reached?Yet another shortcoming was the lack of a manual save. At one point I found a memory, after which the save symbol appeared. When the symbol had disappeared, I closed the game. A day later I wanted to continue, but my game was not saved at that point! Very disappointing.The negatives weighed too heavily in the end - it was a chore to move on - which is why I don't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: The ending was nice and I liked the main protagonist, but other parts of the game could have used more refinement.It really should have focused on the story, visuals, music, and experience over its attempt at gameplay. It could have been a really good and sweet 3-hour narrative game with a beautiful atmosphere. So much fluff with reused or similar places to explore that have tediously plain platforming making up about 4 of the 5.5 hours of the game. The other 1.5 hours are so unique and interesting it makes me wish more of the useless stuff was cut from this game.Inconsistent visual cues of areas that can and cannot be used to platform. The most egregious part of the fluff has to be the super slow and repetitive animations and the camera pan cutaway shots. So often you are stopped and forced to watch a slow camera pan. Sometimes it happens right after being forced to stop and watch one just a literal half-second ago. It doesn't value your time, and I don't value it.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent art, superb narration, and most importantly, incredible atmosphere. This game is oozing atmosphere from every pore and the world-building leaves you hungering to know more.Unfortunately it's all shackled to some godawful gameplay, a mixture of poor platforming and weak puzzles, all of which appear to exist as a bit of an afterthought to make this a game. It feels like something that would be so much better suited to being a point & click, or just fully accepting that it wanted to be a mood piece and become a walking simulator.Somewhere along the way the narrative gives up pretending that it's really anything other than a metaphor, or just a generation of mood, and the ending may well leave you feeling empty for it. There's also a slightly clunky "this is the message" moment near the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: I have very mixed feelings about Minute of Islands. It is an exquisitely crafted game that moves very S...L...O...W,,,L,,,Y...You guide a girl named Mo. With blue hair and yellow boots, she lives underground and awakens to discover silence. This means that the machinery controlling her islands has come to a halt. Poisonous spores are no longer being filtered and her people are at risk. Mo's quest is to visit various islands to troubleshoot and fix the problem. The art work is, in a word, stunning. It is all hand drawn with an incredible level of detail. The scenery is diverse and marvelous. The sound track is soothing with a story told by a very talented female narrator.  Although the game is a platform side-scroller, you move in all 4 directions (right/left/up/down). Objectives are clearly noted and your progress with collectibles is easily accessed. You will find and use a handful of inventory items.My problem with the game is that it is incredibly slow to play. Although Mo can run, you cannot move during narration or any slight animation in the environment. This means that you will be 'waiting to move' at regular intervals.  I would not describe myself as impatient, by nature. But, the waiting for Mo became very annoying.Mo travels through multiple islands, collecting memories, and restarting equipment. She also goes underground to restore power. There are interludes in between where she collects musical memories. The first iteration of these activities was delightful.  However, gameplay soon becomes very repetitive, with the underground segments being almost identical to each other (including some tricky timed sequences which took me multiple attempts to master).The game auto-saves at regular checkpoints and asks for confirmation before leaving an area. This allows you to complete collections or tasks before passing a point of no return. The game is very linear, with optional memories to collect and a couple of optional tasks related to achievements. Paths are clearly visible and it is almost impossible to get lost.Without venturing into spoiler territory, I will say that the story takes a turn at the end that I did not quite relate to. It moves from heroic quest to 'deep thoughts' which I found jarring rather than heart-warming. I recommend this game to those who are more patient than I am and can slow down to appreciate the artwork and the charming narration. Be aware that you will not be able to move through Minute of Islands at your own pace.An added note - Completionists should be aware that there is no going back for something missed. Your only option is to start a new game. Also, this game is not considered 'finished' until after the credits have rolled by, in full.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings so...Pros:-Beautiful world, design, and animation.-The narration is well done.-Sad story with a good message.Cons:-I found the game very slow, it's more of a story than it is a game. -The puzzles are not challenging and make up a small part of the game time. -It's all just a bit too straightforward with very long cut scenes and repetitive puzzles.-I had a hard time connecting with any of the characters, the narration was well done, but it kind of took me out of the experience.Does it look and sound great? Absolutely. Is it a fun game to play? Meh? I'd recommend getting on sale, it is a very interesting world to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: so... After completing the story after 6 hours (with taking it slow and trying to explore) I can sadly say im a little disappointed. It really weighs heavy on my heart that I can't recommend this to people as much as i wanted it to be good.For the people that aren't gonna read a detailed review I'll list pros and cons really quickly:pro:- excelent visuals- awesome soundtrack- interesting world setting and backstory- pacing and overall feeling are goodcon:- level design wasnt great (paths and areas were very linear and a pain to navigate through)- exploration wasnt encouraged enough- puzzles are way too easy and seem very repeaditive except two- blockpuzzles were uncreative- main tool of Mo (Omniswitch) is wasted potential especially when mechanics for more creative ways of handeling are there- hallucination worlds are wasted potential. most of them are just cool looking fetchquests. there could have been some creative puzzles in there due complete freedom in physics but all of them are just straight forward.- story ends up way too short. In fact it feels like you establish a setting since most of it is backstory and then end it soon after. I would even go as far calling it a bad conclusionFirst of all I'm a huge fan of both parts of "The Innerworld" that Studio Fizbin produced a couple of years back. On the basis of those two games I was hyped when i read Studio Fizbin had released a new adventure game.After checking the trailer i was impressed by the visual artstyle and the soundtrack. I didn't have to think beforethe game and the OST ended up beeing in my libary.My experience while playing:Everything started out quite compelling, by giving me simple instructions how to play the game. The eerie atmosphere drew me right in and I enjoyed backgrounds while climbing in the first couple of maps. I was hooked and wanted to know more about the world. I thought the base idea was actually quite nice: making me search for memory fragments that could be found in various locations on the maps. It spiked my sense for exploration and i couldnt help myself looking forward what else this game would offer me. Sadly this excitement soon fell off. The Maps are mostly linear even though, they have stacked layers of paths, for  the player to run onto. Most of the time is forced to take an up or down zig zag route throughout the game without  branching paths for exploration. Most memory pieces are handed to you while you tavel on the main path. It bummed me out since I really wanted to search for them and maybe get rewarded for doing so. I found myself often blocked by an invisible wall or just walking into one direction. sad.The next part I want to talk about is the hallucination worlds (not sure how to call them). I thought they were a really nice idea. You could have done some very trippy puzzles in these, since the devs were pretty much free what to do in those. To my surprise that never really happened. Most of the worlds were almost identical in what to do. Its really all similar to a fetchquest with low efford. Its just pure estetics, which is cool and all, but I'd like to mention here that it was a lot of wasted potential to me. you could have done a lot with it but all of them were tutorial difficulty.Another wasted potential was the Omniswitch. There practically were only 4 uses for it in the entire game. activating airpurifiers, making the same underground object float, connecting to various objects that need a charge and showing you the direction of the next objective. Why was it wasted? because you only used it, when it told you to use it: "press button to activate". there were no other uses (besides the compass) that were of any significance, even though the mechanics were there. Like: why didnt you make mazes for navigating through with the connection beam? its almost always just straight to the energysource and thats it. you could have used it to scout areas, you could have used it to open hidden doors or for example in the halluzinationworlds you could have implimented entire puzzles surrounding these things. but nothing of that sort was done in the entire game.Now to the weakest part of the entire thing: the story. Its supposed to tell the story of mo, but to me it felt only half told.A story that ends after it established the setting of a journey. I was invested into the story from beginning to the end but it never felt like there was a curve to me. There was never a turningpoint that i anticipated. In the end I ended up not connecting with Mo. I understood her story but i ended up not liking it because it felt to me like a child throwing a tantrum and never getting corrected. Its a pitty because i expected so much more from this game.Hopefully Fizbins next adventure ill be more fleshed out story and characterwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful artwork and interesting story but this is supposed to be a game and it fails horribly at being one. The platforming is awkward and the puzzles are not challenging at all. Just go where you have to go and pull your staff out. That's it.I couldn't bring myself to finish the game because of the CONSTANT stop of flow for camera pan or naration. And when i say constant, i mean every ten steps you made. Steam says i played for 1,5 hours and i feel like i played for 10 minutes while the rest of the time i was waiting for the narator to talk or the game showing me something which i didn't care about. If it was skippable i think i would enjoy it much more. If you try the game and feel the same way as me in the first 15 minutes of the game, my suggestion is that you stop and get a refund because it isn't getting any better afterwards.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely spectacular visually. This game looks absolutely beautiful, like a french animated movie or a comic book. The plot is okay, even if it's laid on thick at some points. The game play however, oh the game play. I haven't played in something so soul killing and mind numbing in a long time. It consist of walking from a narrator monologue to another monologue, during which the game is paused and you cannot move. The platforming is boring, badly made and all together unpleasant to go through. The challenges are repetitive if not all the same. Every time you crouch you're stuck in few-seconds animation at the beginning and at the end, unable to move and having to watch it over and over every time. And that's only one thing of many. The beautiful backgrounds do little to distract you from the fact that you're sitting still doing nothing and watching almost nothing. All in all this game should have been a movie or a comic book. It doesn't have any qualities one looks for in a game. There is neither a choice nor an engaging and challenging game play. We are simply taken on a ride and told to do tasks over which we have no control. And this would've been much more pleasant and valuable in a different media form.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: The strong points of this game are its art and story. (The music and ambient sounds go well with it, but they're not anything I'd listen to on their own.) Those were engaging for most of the game, but I don't recommend it because the story doesn't wrap up very cleanly. The unanswered questions leave me unsure what to think or feel about not just the ending, but the whole journey, and the overall tone is so depressing that I can't enjoy that as food for thought. It's like not knowing whether something that's lost is gone permanently, and thus being unable to grieve properly. This game could have benefited greatly from an extended epilogue.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: This is a strange combination of point and click adventure (barely!) and puzzle platformer (also barely!).....okay, that's not quite right either.....think of it as a narrative adventure, filled to the brim with gorgeously grim, bio-organic artwork that would feel right at home in a Heavy Metal comic, where you try to collect certain memories, hook up ancient, dying giants that toil away in biomechanical dungeons trying to cleanse the atmosphere of floating fungal spores that will do terrible things to the world if allowed to proliferate.  You, the protagonist, have been chosen as the custodian of these tired, possibly dying gargantua and thus have a special magical/techo staff that allows you to shift energy beams, crank-start generators, and point the way to your next location of interest.    All the while you'll be interacting in a point and click fashion with old friends and family, while your inner demons rant and rave about how they're all jealous of your responsibility and trying to hold you back.  Oh, and occasionally indulge in voyages to fungal induced hallucinatory landscapes to try to solve some simple puzzles and "escape" back to the real world.Positives:-Artwork-  Holy crap, this is just excellent, and even if everything else about the game fellated dead dingoes, it would still be worth the price of admission.  From the characters to the mind-blowingly detailed and disturbing environments, this is just top bloody notch!-Writing-  Yeah, it's a little pretentious, and a little on the artsy-fartsy side of things, but damn it all, it works!-Voice acting-  At least in English, the Tilda Swenton sound-alike narrator was very good.Meh:-Gameplay- It's a little on the walking-simulator, move-right-to-win side of things, in so far as none of the puzzles are truly mind-shattering, and grabbing the memory based collectibles isn't all that difficult.....bottom line is, do you mind relatively simplistic, not particularly challenging gameplay?  If yes, then don't bother, but if exploring the world and fleshing out the story matters more than nail-biting difficulty, then you may have found hog-heaven.Negatives:   None.I really quite enjoyed this game and can unreservedly give it a recommendation; this one was pretty special (even if a little on the simple side).  Noice!!

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: story, art, music and voice-acting are fantastic and work together in a way few games manage. The "game" side feels superfluous, and calling it a "puzzle platformer" is something of a misnomer. Recommended with a caveat.PROS+ stunningly beautiful hand-drawn art. Kept running back and forth to get a better look, and I took so many screenshots. The penultimate island, specifically, + mood is a perfect blend of "oo, pretty" and "DEEPLY DISTURBING" that very few games meet (see again: the penultimate island)+ great narrator, well-written and acted+ music matches everything+ character-based story that hits hard without sliding into sentimentality, especially for anyone who has ever struggled with issues of guilt or self-worth. (I see some reviewers were expecting more plot, adventure or lore, but Minute of Islands is very firmly a character-based story. By its nature, it is very open-ended, and this is a good thing.)CONS- not... an awful lot of game going on. This feels more like an interactive comic, and while the comic itself is, as mentioned above, absolutely gorgeous, this leads to my next point:- the "game" elements are very simple and linear, with most puzzles consisting of "follow the linear path to the next location where you press the appropriate key when prompted".- the three underground areas are almost indistinguishable, disappointing after the rich, varied backgrounds found elsewhere. The puzzles within are equally indistinct.- lots of backtracking: end-of-level shortcuts are noneexistent, a problem exarcerbated by the frustrating platforming. One should not have to consult a video walkthrough to find which part of this beautifully-drawn platform I am allowed to climb / drop down from. It really doesn't help that the control for dropping down (down + space) also reads as the control for climbing (space).- memory cutscenes force Mo to stand still while an audio plays. Why not let me move? It feels like the designers wanted me to stop and look at the art, which .
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Dark, despite all the ostentatious brightness, chronicles of a slowly dying world. The main character is desperately trying to save what is already impossible to save, trying to breathe life again into giant creatures, who themselves are tired of rolling a constantly falling stone up the mountain. The atmosphere in the game perfectly conveys the oppressive feeling of the inevitable end, which has long come, but not everyone understood it. The world is dead, the survivors do not take off their masks so as not to inhale a dose of deadly spores, human emotional ties are destroyed at the deepest level, all that remains is to turn the lever and walk to sail on your bizarre boat among the dying whales. Even despite the shortcomings, which I will mention later, I would like to hope that this universe will become the basis for a large number of subsequent games, there is definitely room for movement, developing the scenario in the most unusual directions. In some places here, you really feel the thrill of how competently the moments of unity with the world of the game are worked out.You can endlessly admire the visual, magnificent in its ingenuity, a very solid literary foundation on which the local world stands, but after the final credits one question does not leave the head, summing up all the shortcomings that are present in it - “Why is this not point-n-click quest, but a puzzle platformer? " This is all the more relevant because these guys in the past made the wonderful adventure "The Inner World", where the rhythm of the action and the depth of the surrounding world were perfectly combined. Here we are faced with a calm and even slow pace, characteristic of a point-n-click quest, but in a game, that positions itself as a platformer. This creates a certain dissonance, much more inclining the genre of the game to a narrative adventure, where you slowly move around the world, touching the millions of stories that it keeps. Does this critically break the connection with the game? Not. However, the feeling of understatement arises, forming a whole spectrum of strange sensations."Minute of Islands" is imperfect in its gameplay, but it makes up for it with the uniqueness of the world and the integrity of the story told. I really hope that this is not the last game in this setting, and we will see many more stories from the world of bright colors and fading.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Like one of the purifiers on the island, Minute of Islands has restarted an engine of child-like wonder that I was unaware needed a resetting. Thus far I have only played a couple hours, barely wetting my feet, but I have already been moved to such a degree that I had to write. This world has a sense of uncanny fantasy unlike anything I have experience before, my curiosity spikes like walking through Mark Twain's estate when I was a child, but at the same time there is a sense of unnerving from the unknown... the world feels familiar yet I can tell something unseen, something possibly forever unknown, isn't right, I am once again in elementary school exploring my grandparents basement. I must applaud the developers ability to walk this thin treacherous path to this peak of eye opening engagement - avoiding cliffs of cliches and tedium on either side. As the overabundance of my late night metaphors might suggest the beginning of this adventure is very angled toward setting the scene, tone, and mechanics, but there already are hints of some more complicated mechanics and puzzles to come. I can tell that they wont be force fed though, they have all fed the narrative whilst allowing side exploration and stopping to smell the flowe...fungus? The small cut scenes and narration is just the right amount, its like the waiter describing your beautiful dish in front of you before you begin to dig in and taste it. I really look forward to my next bite of Minute of Islands, an adventure that I must force myself to put my fork down between bites to ensure that I savor every morsel.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game, I really do. The art is beautiful and engaging. The story is sweet, sad, and heartfelt. _childDocuments_.review: This game has very pretty art, great atmosphere, fantastic sound design, a very enticing premise and hints of a rich world to explore. Unfortunately, that is where the positive aspects of the experience that is this game end. While the art is pretty, the animation leaves something to be desired, but isn't bad by any means. In my view, the main failings of the game are that it falls completely flat on its face in the two most important (at least to me) parts of this sort of game: gameplay and story.The gameplay, if you can call it that (honestly it felt more like an interactive cutscene), is stiff and clunky. Another (positive) review compared this game to a short film, which I found to be an apt comparison, but not for the same reasons. Short films are at most 40 minutes long, usually, and this game stretches what should take about that long to 6 hours of tedium. You have 8 buttons in theory, but only 7 in practice since if you're anything like me, you'll always have left shift held down in order to sprint. Some may object to this practice, claiming that I'm missing the wonderful art this game has to offer by constantly sprinting. There are two reasons this isn't the case. For one, even sprinting is unbearably slow, making navigating certain long, maze-like sections of the game very frustrating. For two, the game will  wrench control away from you as the narrator lectures or insults the character you play as, leaving you plenty of time to appreciate the pretty colors. Ascending or descending  ledges is vital to navigating the world, but often times it is not at all clear where you can drop off a ledge, leading  to frustrating mashing as you try to position yourself over the exact right spot along the 20 foot long ledge where the game will finally allow you to make the 2 foot drop.The story, as I mentioned earlier, starts off with a very promising premise and a solid hook. What are the giants, what do they want, why are they helping, where did this fungus come from, are there other survivors somewhere out there? The game halfway answers like one of these questions by the end, leaving all the others hanging. Don't get me started on how frustrating it was watching the protagonist do the exact opposite of what I wanted her to do in several key moments. The "story" is an obvious metaphorical vehicle for the message, and the game pretty much blatantly tells you "this is the message" at the end. I found the ending to be very unsatisfying, personally, as it brought up yet more questions that weren't answered.  and left me with tons of questions that I found more interesting to think about than the story the game presented me with and expected me to be satisfied with.This is not a terrible game. I don't think I'd even describe it as a bad game. But it is certainly not a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Only made it past chapter 2 before I got tired with it. It is very slow.I understand having slow moments in a story, I understand wanting the player to linger on an emotion. But forcing the character to stand still, rather than letting the player decide o do so themselves to take it in is NOT the way to do it.When your game has no gameplay, basically no puzzle aspect, nothing to engage the player other than some decent visuals here and there and the story, then I want to progres the story.Frankly I dont understand why the creator didnt make an animated short, or a comic, instead of this game. Everything is so on rails, no decisions can be made, no doing things out of order, no benefit gained from collecting memories and no secrets to explore as all the "hidden" areas are pointed out with glowing little white lines. In short when the only thing this game has of any value is the artstyle and the vibes, this would have fared much better as an animation as instead it comes across as a game that does NOT respect the players time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, and has some lovely writing as well! I completed it all in one stretch while getting over a cold, and the story caused me to reflect on a recent experience I had working a thankless and life-destroying job. That being said, I can't recommend paying the full $20 for this game. I have some minor gripes about the controls and feel of the gameplay, but mainly I can't recommend this game because of its core design. First, the small potatoes: The controls are... weird. I started with my keyboard, but quickly swapped to my controller because I found the keybindings confusing. The controller was certainly better, but the game really makes you work for every task. For example, almost all  actions start by equipping the PC, Mo, with her Omniswitch. To do this, I had to hold down RT, or Mo put the omniswitch away. To actually use it, I mashed buttons or used the joystick with one or both triggers held down. It strained my fingers, and the overuse of the rumble pack didn't help. Movement is also strange. Sometimes I couldn't jump on cue, or I fell because the platform's edge wasn't where it appeared to be. Going down stairs is janky, and more than once I missed part of an island because I didn't realize there was a place I could step down to. There are also some glitches with the shimmying animation, one of which made me reload a save to fix.I could look past those issues to a certain extent, if they were the worst thing I could say about the game. However, the game has a couple of big flaws in its design that I want to address. First, it breaks the "show don't tell" rule in a way that feels condescending at times. The writers obviously loved the story they made, and they ensure there's no way for the player to miss a bit of it. There are pop-ups that remind you how to use your omniswitch everywhere you need, and there's a narrator who tells the player everything about the world around them. I'm not against in-game narration, and it's a part of some wonderful games like Hades and Disco Elysium. However, the narrator in Minute of Islands gets in the way of the truly beautiful game world that the artists made, and that was disappointing to play through. There are a lot of clever scenery items that would have made for excellent environmental storytelling, but the narrator ensured that I understood them exactly as the designers intended. The narrator also serves as the PC's inner monologue, which is a bit of a double-edged sword. At times it adds to the game, by revealing her feelings or memories in a scene. At other times it takes away from a scene, by declaring the PC's intentions, rather than leaving that to the player.That brings me neatly to my second complaint with the game's writing. This is the most on-rails game I've ever played. I can hear my pimply DM from high school squeaking "No, you can't do that!" whenever I try to explore the world on my own terms. There is only one path to take. Literally, there is only one path to follow in order to progress, and only a few side rooms that aren't part of the main path. Also, I wasn't in charge of the choices Mo made. There are five specific scenes where I had a clear choice between Mo's two priorities, and every time I was not allowed to make the choice for myself. It really damaged my ability to engage with the game, because I felt like I was just a spectator to the story instead of a part of it. The game also uses a lot of cutscenes, which exasperate the problem. I was literally watching the game happen without me in some of its most important moments. I don't want to be too hard on the game, though. It's clear that the designers put a lot of love and effort into it, and as I said earlier, it tells a very touching story. The team fell for some common pitfalls for new designers, but that doesn't negate all the great things about their game. I wouldn't be writing this Moby "Richard" of a review if the game didn't mean something to me. This game is beautiful. Seriously, Tim Gaedke and the art team, hats off to you. The art is almost worth getting the game just to look at it all. They also do a great job with visual storytelling, even if the narrator kind of spoils it. The world has a beautiful, cobbled-together look that hits a sweet spot between Fallout-style post-apocalypse and magical high fantasy. I haven't seen anyone do it this well since Adventure Time. I also really enjoyed the story. Without spoiling anything, I'll say that it speaks to the very human conflict between our duty to our work and spending time with our family. If any of that speaks to you, wishlist the game and get it when it's on sale. I paid $8 for it, and I feel like that was money well spent. I hope this studio learns from this game and has the opportunity to grow. They have some good bones, and I'd love to see them reach their full potential.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a cute art style a la Adventure Time, and one aptly designed soundtrack as well as ambient sounds. HOWEVER. The game is also glitchy as hell, making it basically unplayable for those with keyboards (Who the hell decided on this control scheme too? At least make it remappable). That being said, I came across a game-breaking bug during Chapter 3 while trying to leave a specific area. After looking into it, the devs told another player they would look into said bug...a year ago. Even the beta build they added had the same issue. I have not seen the devs communicate anything else with players in six months. Waste of time and money, which is a real shame because there are some shining aspects to this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: It's sad to not recommend this game, because I actually enjoyed it very much before I was stopped at a puzzle glitch at Ande. I tried everything possible to get passed this point, including attempting to contact the developer to perhaps get a save file to go from like was offered by a different developer this happened with. But all attempts were not responded to, and it feels like the developers are not available to tend to this game anymore. If I am wrong about this, and somehow am eventually able to finish the game, I would change my review to positive. For although the setting and story is grim and strangely somehow echos the past three years of weirdness and isolation for us all and the aftermath of such a thing rippling through the world; there is heart in this story, character, and game. And I really wanted to see it through. All the best to the devs and hope I can finish this game some day, whatever fate Mo decides for herself and the sad world she tries to assist.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Minute of Island is a walking simulator - platformer, where playing as a little girl called Mo, and island and nearby lands are in danger, because of a deadly spore and you need to stop it at all cost.I'm not gonna lie, the game's first 2 and half hours were hard to playthrough, because it was uninteresting and boring. Truth to be told, the game looks amazing, caught my attention from the very beginning, the sound design is marvelous, especially the soundtrack and the controls were easy, but this was not enough in my opinion. The game was boring, because you basically activate towers to clean the air and get energy to underground giants, who can keep supply energy, meanwhile you travel around the islands, meet with different characters and learn your past, which Mo seems to forgot. This sounds interesting on paper, but it really is going, searching, do some things and move on, and this won't change at all. Also, I got annoyed from the platforming, especially when there were parts, where I could only get up to a small ledge, even though from my point of view it was available from anywhere basically, but the game really limit these options.What kinda saved this game for me, was the second part of the story and the morale of the game. I won't spoil it, but it has a nice meaning at the end when you realize what is going on... well kinda as I said, because there are things which unexplained in the story and I wasn't quite confident in the whole thing, after thinking about it more. I think the game had a  great idea, but the writing in the end wasn't quite right about the morale and how things should have ended.Minute of Islands looks promising and unique, starts well too, but it lacks gameplay at first half of the game and the whole story felt bit disappointed, after I realized how the game really ended. I can still recommend this game, although it's more mixed for me, but get it on sale, maybe for 6-7€.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Played it all the way through. This is basically a "walking simulator" with some jumping and light "puzzle" solving sprinkled inbetween.The story and world is interesting, the art is well done and fittingly strange, especially towards the end.But that cannot remove the feeling of being incredibly BORED while waiting for animations to finish so I CAN GET ON WITH IT.If the animations were about 20% faster and the WAIT between everything didnt exist, this would have been much nicer to play through.Without exaggerating I would assume about 30 minutes of this game is just WAITING for animations and transitions to be done. Animations and cameramovements which should have been at most 10 seconds long stretch on for 30+ seconds.Example of annoyance:Each time you crawl through a crawlspace, you wait for her to go into the crawlspace, then wait for her to move through, then wait for her to look around, then wait for her to jump down, then wait for her to dust herself off, then wait for her to insert her arms through her tunic again.You do this at least 20 times if you want to find all the secrets and finish the game. so about 3-5 minutes of playtime.I would like to recommend the game, but I just cannot. Which is a shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: While there isn't much player agency and the puzzles are very simple, Minute of Islands tells a short, charming tale about finding one's purpose that's best experienced firsthand. The visuals are stunning and graphic in an Adventure Time meets Double King kind of way, and they do a surprisingly good job of storytelling without becoming the center of attention.That said, at $20 the price is set rather high for a game that will last, at most, 4-5 hours even for achievement hunters. It's much better picked up on sale, or when the whim strikes for a delightful, bittersweet tale juxtaposed against stark, psychedelic, candy gore visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Hello! I really loved the artwork of this game! It was super visually pleasing! I was reminded of Adventure Time! Big fan! I would say the game play is was pretty straightforward with little to no changes in the mechanics. I enjoyed the puzzles found within the game as well. If you like platforming, this is for you! I did get stuck on one puzzle (and received help from an online source), but overall, really enjoyed collecting all the memories and taking in the amazing art. One negative of this game is the story line and ending, mostly the ending. I felt like it was lacking. As I finished the game, I didn't even realize that I was at the end. I was disappointed when the credits started to roll in...  I thought it was extremely abrupt and wished there was more dialogue as the game finished. It felt like I had played this game for no reason, other than to enjoy the cinematic feeling. Regardless, I loved the simplicity of the mechanics, amazing art, and the overall message. Just beware that the end as it might not be what you were expecting and feel super abrupt.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute masterpiece of a game. Would recommend from the bottom of my heart. As someone who has struggled before with depression, family stroke, loss of friends and family members and even suicide attempts, I was able to really feel and understand the message that this game wanted to share. Really good sound and level design, and, as a graphic artist myself, I absolutely loved the art style this game went for and the character design of choice. Not many games make me go out of my way to write a review for, even thought i really enjoyed said game, but this one.... this one is something else. Great work developers! Amazing story, amazing gameplay, amazing style. Cheers y'all and dont forget to take it slow and enjoy every moment of this life, for we only got one.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Essentially a 2D walking simulator, which kind of surprised me as I thought it might be more of an adventure/puzzler. The game is beautiful but incredibly slow. Anytime there is any narration, control is taken from you and you just watch. Movement is slow, especially with the crawling animation taking far too long. The story sets up an interesting world but doesn't really capitalizes on it. The ending make things a bit better but admittedly if the game wasn't as pretty as it is it would be a skip.As an aside, Steam Deck performance is great. The game is rated "playable" for showing PC buttons, but the second you hit A to start the game, all the rest of the button prompts show correctly.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a nice art style and a beautiful story. The game's theme would justify a slow pace, but not one this excruciatingly slow.This by itself would not be bad enough for me to warrant a bad review, but there is more: The keyboard controls / bindings are horrible (why do you do arrow keys to move *only* in 2021...).I immediately switched to a controller, but alas, those controls seemed to glitch quite often.In a game that involves a lot of jumping to move around, it is not much fun, if that particular button press is not recognised reliably.Sorry Studio Fizbin, I enjoyed your other games but this one... can't recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is for you if you are looking for something:- slow/story paced- narrative focused, less puzzle and minimal platformery gameplay - beautiful visuals and sound combo- like dogsWhen in doubt, wait for a sale.I highly enjoyed it, though not all was perfect. It also ran well on my system and I didn't encounter any bugs.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: The art style is probably the only thing good about this game for me. I didn't enjoy the rest. The gameplay was weak and too slow. If it was a bit faster you'd probably just fly through the game. The puzzle scenes were just so boring. Again, I think they were only there just to add more time to the game. Everything is very repetitive and there is no imagination to the puzzles. The story also didn't click with me.I guess, judging by the reviews, there are plenty of people who liked the game. I'm definitely not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Game frequently freezes and crashes at loading screens. Can't even really play it.Considering this appears to be a sprite-based platformer without particularly intensive graphical effects, it seems poorly optimized in general. Hope the dev makes more technical improvements with time.I was honestly looking forward to it as the art and animation reminded me of the kind of striking work Pastel Games did back in the flash days. However, I can't recommend the game based on my experience trying to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, the art work, soundtrack and story are well executed, just keep in mind that the gameplay feels more like an interactive narration than anything else, i am completely ok with that, as it makes for a relaxing and laid back experience, if you expect a platformer full of action, challenging puzzles and complex mechanics.. this is not it.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Saw a decent interpretation of the story in one of the discussion threads so I'll keep my gripes there to myself. Visuals are nice, but the gameplay is awful. Jumping down from platforms tends to require being in a very specific spot, which often is unnecessarily strict, and there are a lot of repetitive animations and 'cutscenes' that constantly slow things to a crawl.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully drawn characters and world! Unfortunately the game is poorly optimized and the graphic stutters on my system -- one that has no problems on other high-performance games.The puzzles are really easy. Navigating around feels slow going and there's a ton of back tracking, so quite tedious.On the other hand, visually it's very pretty.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: A game that's barely there - if a walking sim would be made into a 2d platformer, that would be Minute of Islands.That, by itself, is not really an issue. The issue is that it's done poorly. Making the "gameplay" of a couple of jumps and assorted keypresses without any particular point is just bad taste. "Puzzles" are not really puzzles (there's 1 and a half across the entire game that can qualify as such, the rest require zero thought), platforming is not really platforming (has no difficulty and requires absolutely no thought). Everything that's done for the gameplay is detrimental to game's impression simply for how plain and lifeless it is.Okay, but if it's a "walking sim" kind of game - why it even matters? Because it's still the main filler. If the "gameplay" took only an insignificant part of time with the rest left to other matters - that would be great. But it is not so.There are other games that used a similar approach, but did it considerably better. E.g. The Cave did puzzles right, and GRIS did platforming quite nicely.So what's for the story when? The story fares much better than the gameplay, of course. Might not be terribly deep or have mindblowing delivery, but it's nice. However, as most of my gameplay time was spend on extremely bland platforming, I'm basing my total score mainly on that. And that total score turned out pretty disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful game. The game-play itself is very simple which works with the game. It is more of a story-based game rather than a puzzle game . The assets clipped occasionally but overall it was smooth. While it is a good game I don't think I would spend the whole price for it, I got it for 5$ on sale and I would recommend waiting for a sale since its such a short game. Overall, enjoyed it
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine and I did enjoy it, but there's a handful of issues that I have with the game (some more trivial than others) and Steam doesn't have a "thumbs middle" option so:1.- I ran into two different softlocks, the game has a Reload button on the menu which solved one of them but it glitched the music, the other softlock was more serious and only fixed itself after several restarts, there was a report about it from a year ago but it hasn't been fixed it seems.2.- The game doesn't have any form of frame limit nor vsync, so it will just run at hundreds of FPS for no good reason, don't you love toasty graphic cards?3.- The keyboard controls suck, and there's no way to change them, all games should have remapable controls. Controller bindings are ok though.4.- The credits can not be skipped, but the post-credits cutscene will be skipped if you are mashing buttons when the credits end.5.- Despite being tagged as a puzzle game, there's only one real puzzle in the game, which also isn't particularly hard and can just be bruteforced if you miss the hints to solve it.6.- The animal that appears in the artwork of the game doesn't really play a role in the story, it's only there in the transitions and at the very end.7.- The art style, while great, does make it hard to distinguish which platforms allow you to go down, not the biggest issue but still something that happened relatively often.I liked the aesthetics and the world is interesting, the music fits nice and the atmosphere is great.The story feels like it could be taken further, more explanation of the world would have been nice. There's some interpretation about what's going on the main character, but regardless, it makes it hard to put yourself into her skin after some stuff that happens in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Almost Perfect.After beating the game, I came to the reviews to see if other people felt the same way I did. From what I can tell the general consensus is more or less the same: atmospherically, visually, and narritively this game is outstanding, though the gameplay and actual story (particularly the ending) are lackluster.I'll be describing many of the flaws this game has, but this is by no means an outright bad purchase.Mechanically, the platforming can feel frustrating as there are times where you have to be very particular/precise with movements and jumping/dropping when it's truly unnecessary. More forgiveness in this area would make playing the game require less time and deliberate planning and effort to complete simple movements. Reducing the headache here will better showcase the definite strengths of the game. It certainly isn't outright unplayable, but it detracts from the experience.The game does a good job of not explicitly giving the solutions to every puzzle, leaving the satisfaction of their completion for the player. That said, the puzzles in this game aren't terribly complex or thought-provoking. This isn't necessarily a good or bad thing, but I would by no means consider this a puzzle-focused game. There just isn't that great a sense of satisfaction upon completion of any of the puzzles. It's more of a narrative experience that has some simple puzzles present.The story through most of the game is interesting, compelling, and complex with themes of anxiety, trauma, family/loss, and moving on. But this brings us to the biggest issue with the game: the ending. The ending, in no uncertain terms, is bad. It's a real shame too, because it's the only part of this experience I would outright call poorly executed and the only thing keeping this from being truly great. Put simply, it feels terribly rushed. Until the very end, the game maintains a consistent, satisfying pace that maintains suspense, feels rewarding with each milestone, and feels like a well crafted buildup to something bigger. Then, once you reach the conclusion, it feels more like it was dropped in as an afterthought by someone who didn't realize their deadline was coming up. It's like they had to give up and figure out a way to shoe-horn in their first draft for an ending. I felt confused by the sudden shift in tone and quality, and unsatisfied with the ultimate outcome.The game only takes about 5 or 6 hours to complete entirely, but had they made it closer to 9 or even 12 hours, I'm confident they could have more fully fleshed out elements they clearly wanted to and created a more satisfying and cohesive experience as a whole.All that ragging aside, the elements like the art, concepts, lore, etc. in this game are second to none and a play-through of this game is a good way to spend a free afternoon or two. TLDR: I'd give it a 7-ish out of 10. I'm happy having been able to experience this game, but it's disappointing knowing how much better it could have been and deserves to be.

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed exploring the world created in Minute of Islands, and while I found the universe the game is set in to be fascinating and wildly creative; I sadly can not recommend this game. Firstly, I find the tags used by the game to be misleading. I get that the main character of the story is going on an adventure, but 99.9% of main characters in story based video game are also going on adventures, that does not make a game an adventure game. Being an "adventure game" implies that your game has a level of interactivity directly related to the story/adventure your character is undergoing, which Minute of Islands does not. The player in no way interacts directly with the story, there are no items to find and use, very minimal environmental puzzles, none of which tie into the story in any capacity or are even referenced by any characters (they're just there because something needs to be there), no dialogue choices, no deductions to be made by the player, nothing. You start the game with every ability you will use from start to finish (and it's really not a lot: walk, climb, drop down, interact with staff. That's it.) I normally wouldn't complain about something like this, but I found out about Minute of Islands from an adventure game forum, so I can say personally I was at least to some degree mislead. Even something like Jenny LeClue is astronomically more of an adventure game in the traditional sense than Minute of Islands.I also think I should say here that I don't believe you can accurately label Minute of Islands as puzzle platformer either. Being a platformer requires there to be some kind of fail state, whether your character falls and dies and you have to restart the level, or you miss a jump and have to restart the series of jumps you were working on. The "platforming" (which is horrifically clunky and unresponsive) in Minute of Islands is so rudimentary that I'm hesitant to even call it that, it's really more like go here and just walk along this path that requires you to climb up parts and drop down parts. I can pretty much say the same thing about the "puzzles" in the game as well, just go here and move this thing onto this other thing that you've done 8 other times the exact same way. Did I mention Minute of Islands is also painfully repetitive, to the point where I verbally said "oh, come on!" on I believe 3 separate occasions? Minute of Islands took me 4.3 hours to complete. I left it running for a while after beating it. Really, the point I'm making is that Minute of Islands should really be advertised as a walking simulator, because it does little as a game to warrant any other genre description.Ok, so Minute of Islands is a walking simulator, is the rest of the game good? Well, not really. I said the universe the game is set in is brilliant earlier, and it is. It's great, and I would honestly really enjoy a second honest attempt to make a game, hopefully something a little more on the adventure game side of things, in the same universe. The art is for the most part very gorgeous, though some of the less in focus landscape animation looks strangely like flash animation, idk, maybe I'm just being critical. The problem really is the story. Minute of Islands pretty much gives away the whole, I struggle to say point because the whole thing's so convoluted, but I guess what the game's supposed to symbolize, right at the beginning as a disclaimer (which is completely unwarranted and to some degree spoils the game). On top of that the dialogue or I guess points of view and actions from all of the characters in the game, the main character Mo included, are nonsensical. No one would rationalize things the way this game has its characters rationalize things, and it really just removes any empathetic response you may have had, while spoiling the game's attempts at making meaningful symbolism. The story is also really, really predictable, and all of the main plot points are overly hinted at to the point that nothing succeeds at catching you off guard or at the bare minimum, invoking an emotional reaction. It's just not a good story, and not a good game, unfortunately. 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line: This is not a game. it's a simple story with nice drawings that progresses too slowly while forcing you to go through the motions.I'll start with the good: the drawings & animations are amazing! There's a story, but it's pretty flat, and it's told on a level that resembles a children's book - although this game is certainly not intended for children. The story is extremely linear. It might look like a point-and-click adventure, but you can't interact with basically anything (which is a real shame with all of the intricate artwork) and the forced linearity ruins any feeling of adventure. The tasks themselves are very basic, it would be a stretch to call them puzzles. Meanwhile, the game also tries to be some kind of simple platformer, but it's a very janky one with weird controls.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok I have a lot to say so I'm gonna break it down and there will be like a tldr at the endThe game play was simple. Mainly the emphasis was light exploration as you visited all the different islands in the archipelago searching for the next air purifier to turn back on or the next giant to wake up. One thing that maybe does feel a little tedious are the hallucination phases Mo has when she enters areas with particularly high spore count. They just feel kind of annoying to go through, but maybe that's personal opinion. They do have some really clever platforming though and that was a big plus for me. What the game mechanics lack in complexity, it made up for greatly in art style and atmosphere which enhanced the experience an incredible amount. The grotesque, mechanical-organic technology and the contrast with the incredibly vibrant (and destructive) fungal blooms was *chefs kiss* and it completely immersed me in the word of minute of islands. The surrealist art style of the hallucination phase was also just brilliant, and only added to the immersion.This is where I start to have issues with the game. For one, the story writes itself as something that should proceed with some haste. The giants are suffocating, the spores are taking over, we should be moving with relative consistency... and yet... there's so many times when the game grinds you to a screeching halt with useless "cut scenes" that merely sweep the island, and narrative pauses that cut off your movement capability for the narrator to simply read your inner thoughts on the situation. Many of these moments could either be completely cut from the game, or done in conjunction with the character moving to their next location. For example, there's always like a 45 sec cut scene of the character leaving the island, which is nothing but the boat pulling out of the dock for an egregious amount of time. We've already seen this scene in reverse when Mo first makes her appearance on the island, and it's much more impactful then because we're arriving at a new place and taking in our surroundings. We don't need to hold focus on her leave of the island because again, it grinds the pace to a halt to watch our protagonist linger on a scene that neither adds to our understanding of our surroundings nor does it advance the story or game in any meaningful way. I took so much issue with how many times the game would shoot its own story in the foot by forcing the player to stop when the story was continuously pushing this sensation of urgency. It contradicted itself and made me increasingly impatient with the narrative they were trying to lay down.***THERE WILL BE SPOILERS*** ( I marked when they start )The story of minute of islands really is what kept me coming back to this game despite certain frustrations. They really write Mo's struggle and her trauma very well and in a way that was super relatable and empathetic. As someone who was diagnosed with PTSD, seeing it depicted so accurately in this game was really important to me and quite touching to feel understood by the people that made this game.  My one major complaint was the ending. The story was so masterfully set up for the vast majority of the game. I understood Mo so completely as a character, and empathized with all her actions regardless of how futile they were. And then we reach the climax. The fourth giant is dead, and probably has been for a long time, Mo is devastated, her failure to save him comes crashing down on her, and she falls into the sea, washing up on a small island to mourn by herself. And then?? The thing that brings her out of her depression ??? is the axolotl dog that has contributed absolutely nothing to Mo's character growth? He's just been in the background as a cute thing and legit (to my knowledge) meant nothing to Mo. And he's the one that aids her at her lowest point? It made no sense and was deeply unsatisfying after such a brilliant build up to this point. What would have maybe made more sense is if the spirit of the old giant visited her in one of those hallucination scenes to comfort her (especially because there was something akin to a giant's grave already on that island), or even the spirits of those totems she brought to the cemetery, of whom we never actually get to learn the identity of (to my current knowledge). Both of these options would have made way more sense to Mo's established relationships and the story as a whole. And the fact that the dog-not dog was catalyst for acceptance just really dampened the authenticity of her moment of character growth. Afterwards, Mo places the omni switch on the grave and goes to relinquish Safan of his duties and then just??? Jumps on the arc that was the antithesis to her pride, her control, and her self-identified purpose and the game is just???? Over???? It was hard to accept. I would have much rather this acceptance period have been longer, as you back travel to the rest of the giants letting them go one by one, and finally, you yourself as the player choosing to get on that boat. It would have completed her phase of grief and acceptance much better than just abruptly cutting to her being on the boat she previously so despised and I don't know, I guess it was frustrating to watch such an important part of the stages of grief be so quickly skipped over when the whole story seems to revolve around Mo's grief and trauma. I have a lot of frustrations with minute of islands, maybe because the topic hits close to home, but it doesn't mean I recommend others don't play it. There's a lot of really well made aspects of this game that kept me coming back to play more and more, and was the reason I played through to the very end. If the premise interests you, it still deserves your unbiased play through, because (and I can't say this enough) it's a beautiful game about important things. It's far from perfect, for all the reasons mentioned above, but I believe, it's still worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one to review; Minute of Islands is among a category of indie games that is remarkably beautiful and deep AND is held back simply by being a game rather than a show in several spots.If you're feeling moody and reflective and can tolerate a slower paced game with some janky parts, I recommend it.If you're someone that is looking to play a well-polished, smooth-playing indie game, I'd recommend watching a Let's Play; there are some immensely clever symbolism and themes that left me with some satisfying questions to chew on. It was just too bad that some frustrating moments and inconsistent platforming held the experience down for a lot of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game about anxiety, trauma, family, loss, and moving on. The art has a lovely if occasionally grotesque style to it that was always exciting to see what the game would show me next. The writing was moving and struck a good balance of leaving things for you to fill in some blanks but also being blatant and telling you what you need to hear when you need to hear it. It never once felt like it was clumsy or being too mysterious and I really appreciate that. The platforming is pretty simple but I think that serves the game's goals well. The puzzle solving is similarly simple but, once again, I think that's for the best. If either of those aspects were too difficult it would just make the game a slog to get through and no one would want that.It does drag a bit in the middle but for a game that's only five hours long what that amounts to is a 30-ish minute section in the middle somewhere that should've been 15 or 20 so overall that's a pretty minor complaint.I love Mo and I want her to be happy.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game is very pretty, and I in general  the artstyle, as a game it is terribly designed.Controls are frequently unresponsive until you get into just the right spot, like being exactly beneath a ledge. Walking is also somewhat "lurchy".Many simple actions are based on key combinations that are inconvenient in terms of hand positioning but none of the keybinds can be changed.Simple things that would speed up gameplay, like walking off of ledges to avoid ladder-climbing animations, aren't even allowed (and, in the example case, the ladder climb animation is inexplicably ridiculously slow, as are the ledge-grab-and-climb-up/climb-down animations).You can't fast-forwards through the annoyingly "nature documentary narrator" voice describing even the simplest of actions despite the subtitles being perfectly capable of conveying the information near-instantly.Said voice describes actions with constant references to the main character's name, Mo, rather than ever bothering to use pronouns, in a manner that detracts from feeling immersed.You can't skip past the animations of doors opening up either, which for some reason also takes forever.In general, many features of this game constantly makes me feel like yelling "get on with it already!". It feels like the developers got super insistent at making the players only experience the game with a certain pacing and were unwilling to allow players to adjust it in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy games that take patience to play this is your guy. You have to wait for everything and everything is slow. You'll solve puzzles before you're finished moving through them, you'll have control constantly taken away for boring screen scrolling, you'll wait for unnecessary pauses over and over, and god help you if you wanna backtrack for missed memories or achievements. If you missed anything you'll just have to repeat the entire game. The message is great and the art is beautiful but it genuinely is not worth the slog. I often had a major sense of anxiety that I would be wasting my time given how slow everything was and unfortunately I have to say I am not better off having gone through the effort to 100% this game. Easy game with the biggest challenge being of your patience.
