_childDocuments_.review: Minute of islands has a bunch of minor flaws that unfortunately make the experience unbearable.The good stuff is obviously the art of weird biomechanical underground and partially destroyed overworld. But at times it feels empty. Not because it lacks detail, on the contrary, the game is bustling with small objects scattered around larger scenes. The problem is that these details don’t really add anything most of the time, they’re just visual noise. But overall the art is amazing, although art alone isn’t enough to warrant the given price.The gameplay wouldn’t need much explanation if it was a simple walking sim. Unfortunately, there is some ‘gameplay’. First off, the game has some puzzles, but they aren’t anything great, just some basic iteration of, I’d say, sokoban. You can interact with background objects to get some info about them. Does it provide some interesting insights into their history or how the character feels about them? No, it just tells you exactly what they are.Some things you intereact with will spawn little memento-creatures you have to catch to remember something from the past. Now this sounds interesting, if not for a few details. Basically the game is still a walking sim, and the islands you travel to are fairly big. But the game locks you in place after you catch the memento to tell you the memory. The catching game itself is also just a pointless time waster with no real reason to do that. It’s not hard, it’s not a puzzle, you just have to jump at a certain moment.The walking itself is filled with some rudimentary platforming, it's not really a problem in the overworld as it has some things to look at and collect(although the game does it’s best to discourage you from exploration). One thing I don’t get is that every time you encounter an elevator, you have to first call it to you. Every single time. Maybe it would be a good time to tell us some more of the story, but the game does nothing, you just have to wait.The so-called ‘powerful omni-switch’ includes one type of action. It’s cumbersome and repetitive and is needed with every mechanism you come across. You plug it in and mash a button. Then you plug it into a different spot nearby and mash the button again. EVERY TIME.The underground has more of the ‘move object’ type puzzles, but is for some reason filled with unnecessarily long hallways and ladders. And again, we travel them mostly in complete silence.But the game calls itself a narrative experience after all, so maybe the story can save it.Well, this is all subjective, but I don’t get the story at all. The girl’s behaviour and character doesn’t evolve much, at least on the two islands I’ve been to. She’s this extreme introvert with some self-harm issues, as I understand it. I’ve completed two islands as I cannot bear it any longer. Nothing’s changed. We are just shown how she dislikes everyone. I was hoping for some worldbuilding and lore, but it does not exist, at least not at this point of the story. Everything just is as it is, the narrator says this is post-apocalypse or something and that's it.The narrator. I personally hate this narrator. She does a good job, but the script is kinda bad. It’s really condescending, explaining the most obvious things.Ironic, seeing as this game was published by people behind FAR, it just makes me want to play that game instead with actually clever and wordless environmental storytelling.Overall, you can give this a shot, but don’t hesitate to refund if the beginning feels kinda eh. It's like that all the way I can imagine. I’d buy the artbook, if they had it, instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty tough to recommend, but I'd give it a 5/10. This is a story game, the puzzles and platforming are secondary. Really, they're only there to be a break from the walking simulator the main part of this game is. Not a criticism, just saying that if you're looking for interesting platforming or puzzles, you won't find them.The story of this game is wonderful, the art style is really impressive too. It surrounds themes of death, life, work, family, and insecurity. I'd say it's worth buying on a 50% or more sale.There's so many bugs, poor design choices, and unaddressed issues. There is no chapter select, there is no keybind change, all cutscenes are unskipable, overly long cutscenes, the crawling animations are so godamn slow, the animations stutter, the textures changing before and after animations are inconsistent, textures will appear on the wrong layers, there's a tree that will not stop blinking out of existence, etc.I enjoyed it, but the amount of problems it has that have gone unaddressed makes it hard to recommend. Buy it on a sale, and use a walkthrough if you want the achievements without spending another 4-5 hours of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: A really pretty narrative game, even when it uses that prettiness to depict very ugly things! XD The gameplay elements are fairly simple and rudimentary, and honestly most of that didn't improve the experience much for me - I did like the button combinations used to activate various aspects of the Omni Switch, but the more gamey parts of the game like the platforming and the puzzles, didn't super engage me much.That said, I am recommending this game despite that because the narrative was generally pretty compelling and evocative to me. Combined with the artstyle and imagery of the world, as well as the little sweet and sad lore details you can pick up around the world, and overall I found it a positive and interesting experience. Don't get this game if you are looking for complex engaging gameplay, but if you want an interesting world and story, you might enjoy this one. :)

_childDocuments_.review: The game  It is extraordinarily pretty and the worldbuilding is interesting, but they seem uninterested in exploring the psychological aspect they introduce or the effect of the fungus on Mo (who pointedly never wears a mask and yet seems completely unaffected). I'm left wondering why they felt the need to make this a game. The interactive aspect drags down nearly every part of it, from the fungus visions to the abrupt ending to the shallow exploration of culture and psyche. Virtually every aspect of this game would have been improved if it had been a film. Several really, really interesting elements go unexplained or unexplored over the course of the game. How Mo  Unexplained. The whole body horror aspect? Unexplored.  Unexplored. Any time I thought "Oh, that's interesting, I wonder if they'll go into that", I knew I wasn't getting any answers. It's so weird that they chose to set it in a dystopian, apocalyptic bioware environment and then didn't use any of the most interesting elements aside from aesthetic choice. Overall, the game just feels like it was too busy trying to figure out how to get to the third act to realise how many much better concepts and catalysts for story it was ignoring.The price tag, as well, just means I can't justify giving this game a positive rating. $30AUD for a game that takes 5 hours to 100% complete is a little absurd. The fact is that almost every aspect of the About this Game is wrong. The archipelago isn't pastoral, wasn't once inhabited by a race of giants, the threat isn't almost forgotten (I mean, come on. The first appearance of the threat happened at most 15 years ago. Probably less considering ), the engines aren't hidden, the Omni Switch isn't powerful, you don't wield it, there's exactly one puzzle in the entire game, there's no dark truth below the islands' surfaces, and there are no secrets to the archipelago. Sounds like a great game, but it isn't this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Minute of Islands

_childDocuments_.review: A game about what it can mean to be "The Chosen One". What does this impression of carrying the fate of the world on your shoulders do to yourself and how does it affect the relationship to the ones you love? Minute of Islands tries to answer these questions and aims to put an antithesis on the classical hero's journey.Gameplay-wise this is more or less "just" a walking simulator with some light platforming and puzzle elements. The focus is definitely on the narration here. And the stunning and quite unique visual style is where this game really shines. I enjoyed this a lot, but be warned: This is definitely not for everyone and might not live up to more conventional expectations in terms of gameplay as well as story.

When giants really are the saviors here. They made the system which helps to dispel the toxic and save people who live there. They bind themselves to this system, so they made a sacrifice.The ending is even more stupid)))). Mo hits the woman with the Omni Switch and breaks it. I don’t even know what to say here. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of the few times I wish there was a button between like and dislike. I give this game 3/5 stars. I absolutely loved the wonderfully hand-drawn and detailed settings and backgrounds, and the Adventure Time-esque style. Visually this game is stellar, my gripes come with the game style, and most of all the heroine herself. First off this isn't really a puzzle game, there is only one "real puzzle". Second there are sequences that happen between islands, that at first are interesting, but become awfully repetitive and I began dreading them. Lastly but most importantly, Mo is very unlikable. She is rude to her family, is a terrible hypocrite and actually hurts people to further her own needs. There is a situation at the end where I was supposed to feel sad for her, but I felt nothing. I didn't care about her, I wanted her to fail. One more detail, we get a cute animal companion, but we don't... we only see it on the short rides on the boat, I felt robbed.

_childDocuments_.review: is a "narrative puzzle platformer" in which you guide a young girl, Mo, through a devastated world that is about to be even more ruined because of a poison that seeps through the air. Fortunately, Mo is a mechanic and wields the Omni-Tool, a powerful artifact that can activate mechanisms and reactivate air purifiers as well as an ancient race of giants...What is most striking about the game is its very strong setting. You get some glimpses into the world's history during the course of the story, but as the player, you're mostly thrown into the heat of things - the story takes place after some possible apocalypse that you were not here to witness, and your task is simply to fix some air purifiers. You do this by travelling between islands filled with the ruins of a dead world, occasionally meeting old acquaintances and collecting optional memories. These are littered through the islands and are a short recollection by Mo, which can be about that time she got stuck in a cave or the lingering taste of burnt jam on her fingers. They're very sweet! It's interesting to not know much about the world and its characters, only getting some small glimpses of their past through these optional memories. This is a great motivation to explore in order to get them all.Unfortunately, the way you explore in itself isn't that interesting. As I said earlier, the game is a "narrative puzzle platformer". While it technically ticks all the right boxes, puzzles are rare, simple and repetitive while the platforming is basic and mostly serves to get around. , then, is more of a narrative walking sim with some light platforming and puzzles sprinkled throughout - which isn't a bad thing! But I wish that instead of being a half-baked puzzle platformer with repetitive sequences and boring gameplay, the game either had less gameplay and mostly walking, or more interesting puzzle platforming. The worst offenders are the dream sequences that occur when Mo breathes in too much poison. This happens four or five times, and while these sequences aren't too long, they're very repetitive and don't bring much to the table. Fortunately, the game doesn't feel boring at a 5-hour playtime, and it's very accessible thanks to this basicness which lets about anyone experience what is has to offer... but it gets close to it, which is a shame.And it has got a LOT to offer. You can't really talk about  without mentioning how amazing it looks. The hand-drawn style oozes personality, with a huge amount of variety between places. You start underground, in a strange area that seems to mix machines and anatomy, but then set out on a little boat to an island filled with animals, a jam factory, a broken down theme park... It's wonderful to look at, and every single corner of the world is filled with environmental storytelling. These ruins that tell stories without words are the strongest point of the game, and the way they accompany the simple but somber narrative of Mo's adventure throughout the islands is something that feels both sad and humbling. Every single word is read by a narrator who does of wonderful job of communicating emotions.Despite not telling an incredible story full of twists and turns or having fantastic gameplay,  feels like it's way more than the sum of its parts. It's not mind-blowing, but it isn't meant to be. It's not fun, but it isn't meant to be. It's an emotional romp through a dead world, walking through atmospheric set pieces and trying to piece together Mo's memories in order to understand her better - in a way, it's about the story of Mo as a person, and the whole adventure is just a way to tell that story.  is a wonderful game that is beautiful to look at, and I hope we will get to experience more of its world in other titles.

Finally got around to playing it a few weeks ago, and all of that initial excitement was gone. All of the gameplay I experienced the demo, that was it. I got most of the plot, I was left with one big question: . _childDocuments_.review: Minute of Islands is a short, slow-paced and narrative game that wagers entirely on the visual and artistic side, with beautiful backgrounds heavily reminiscent of Moebius-esque echoes mixed to a bizarre and unsettling creature and bio-mechanical design, in open contrast to the very stilized and cartoonish design of human characters. All accompanied by a remarkable soundtrack alternating nostalgic and melodic tunes with oppressive and creepy ambiences that bring the memory back to the distinguishing soundscapes of the Silent Hill series. In this interactive adventure there's little to interact with and a lot to walk, with some simple puzzles sprinkled here and there, so if you're not into this kind of experience you should be advised.Despite being an entirely narrative-driven title, this game suffers from a somewhat lacking execution: the story and worldbuilding are very interesting and captivating, but some of the most implied aspects should've been expanded more, the ending is somewhat abrupt and the psychological implications of a protagonist suffering from the consequences of a lifetime spent in isolation, which made her paranoid and self-destructive, haven't been elaborated deeply enough in my opinion. A lot of the material could've been developed more, it's not a bad result overall but it lacks that certain something that could've made this game a real gem. It doesn't deserve a thumbs down, but it still left me with the sensation of a project developed in a bit of a contrived manner, perhaps due to the original concept being more suited to a graphic novel or an animation than a videogame. I've also encountered some minor bugs, mainly the arm of the protagonist going a bit haywire when crawling in narrow passages, but nothing too bothering. With all this said, consider Minute of Islands as an intersting experiment that may or may not be worth the deal depending on what you're looking for; if you put visuals, atmosphere and untold lore above all else you might just love it. Otherwise, you'll probably be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is definitely not for everyone, but if you've ever been stuck in a mental health spiral with a strong amount of intrusive thoughts...damn does it hit hard. (So Content Warning in that sense, I guess)I played it in short intervals over a few weeks, letting every part sink in a little before I continued on and I'm sure there is a lot of subtext I will slowly come across when I eventually revisit it.I adore the artstyle! A friend, who was playing it at the same time as me, and I called it "H.R. Giger's pastel phase" and I haven't found a better description quite yet.There is definitely a lot of strange, alien imagery and some pastel gore (what a weird combination of words honestly) going on. I loved the moodlighting and general color palette! Very nice!The controls are sometimes a bit clunky, but if you play it in short bits and let the whole thing breath it becomes very natural to climb, jump, descent and use your tools without much thought.Again, I really enjoyed this game and I could easily emphasize as soon as I caught on to the metaphor they were going for, even if it is viewed through a very peculiar lense and world. It also is a very different and interesting look at the heroes journey, "heroism" and martyrdom.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy! Where to start with this game... Finally finishing it after the long excited wait for Fizbin's newest game, I was left with quite a few lingering thoughts and emotions. I'll try to arrange them as orderly as I can below.First of all - I'll get to the mainline review with its pros/cons, but first I think a bit of an insert is needed for this game in particular:THIS IS A VERY PLOT-HEAVY GAME where the progression, emotions, and weight of the story take precedence. I certainly wouldn't call it a walking simulator by any means, but if you are aiming for a gameplay challenge and would rather pass on story/lore, then I expect you won't like this game too much. Most of the other negative reviews I see are on this subject, so I want to get that out of the door.Anyway, onto the actual review!-----Pros:- The game has a consistently wonderful and immersive hand-drawn style that is equally as beautiful as it is in parts horrifying- sometimes both at the same time. Every scene is a delight to not just pass over, but pore over every little detail of.- Without spoiling anything large, the story deals with mature themes in a very responsible, engaging, and satisfying way, without ever becoming *too* mature itself.- The soundtrack is arguably one of the best parts of the game with many moving moments when the story calls for them, but still giving you time to breathe in between.Cons:- At some times, the movement can be mildly clunky - a bit of an unpleasant combination with the occasional platforming challenge. Still, I wouldn't say any of it is exactly bad. Probably my smallest gripe, to be honest- During my entire time playing, one of the largest interests in the back of my mind was "What's the story behind this place? Who are these giants, where did they come from? What was the history here?" and while there were definitely tidbits to stave off my lore appetite, I never truly felt 'full' by the end, with a fair number of questions of the world's mythos left unanswered and unresolved. I know exposition dumps are usually seen as a drawback for many games (and rightly so!) I can't help but feel a game like this, whose own forte is its storyline, could have done with a bit more cosmology and background as I wandered through its many twists and turns.- I know I said at the beginning that one should come into this game expecting heavy plot more than heavy gameplay, but even so I still can't ignore some pacing problems that come with it. Nearly every piece of unique gameplay you can perform is already set in stone by the time you get to the first island. Nearly every other action (with some welcome exceptions) in the next several hours is some simple combination of these mechanics, which would be fine if this arsenal wasn't so small. I wish Fizbin would have innovated slightly more with these mechanics in the moment-to-moment gameplay, especially towards the end, because it just begins to feel stale as the story is nearing its climax, when your investment should be at an all time high!-----Overall, I think I would rate the game a solid 8.3/10, with major points for the engrossing story and sheer environment, and some detracted for the mildly repetitive gameplay and small worldbuilding loose ends. At any rate, it is, and will almost certainly remain one of my favorite titles of 2021. Definitely recommend for anyone who's looking to play through a fantastic story in a fantastic world.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has some elements that are emotionally moving, but on the whole the game design seems a bit haphazard. Most of the scenes have puzzles that don't require very much coordination -- a little bit of working out where to go to and what to push/press/move/etc., but mostly not tricky in terms of keypress coordination. So those sections are action interspersed fairly evenly with memory cutscenes or other emotional details. Whereas the vision sequences require quite a bit more coordination, as well as a lot more irritating backtracking if you get that coordination wrong repeatedly. So I HATED the vision sequences, which totally spoiled their impact for me. The physical coordination and timing required for those bits, let alone all the backtracking, added NOTHING AT ALL to the actual emotion/story of the scene, and just made it IRRITATING instead of moving. In all the bits underground, I found it extremely tedious that every time Mo crawled through a tunnel she spent a few seconds at the far end cautiously stepping out and brushing her dress off etc. That was probably meant to be a cute mannerism, but unfortunately after the first time it just ends up interrupting the flow of the player-controlled movement, and so it took me out of my feeling of immersion every single time.The bit on Graba I got quickly bored of and just looked up the walkthrough to find the solution to the puzzle, because there weren't any useful graphical clues to the solution without doing a hell of a lot of tedious running and jumping around and backtracking, so rather than completely give up out of BOREDOM I just used the walkthrough to skip through that bit.Overall, I think the game designers should have thought a lot harder about what kind of game mechanics would actually serve the theme rather than being randomly tacked on because they felt like it. A lot of the time the game could have shortened a lot of the jumping and running around sequences without impacting the game story at all, and that would have made it a more fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't go as far as to call it a 'game', as it's more of a narrative art piece which requires you to perform deeply tedious work in order to experience. Moving around is tedious at best and deeply frustrating at worst. Your character move glacially slowly, and the platforming is without doubt the most aggravating I've ever experienced, requiring you to position your character in precise but unmarked locations in order to successfully execute jumps or drops.I can only think of one puzzle, which was itself so frustrating and arbitrary that I just googled the solution. The principle conceit here is of the compelling narrative, which is one of urgency - so throwing in timewasting elements such as a 'rotate the wheels' puzzle is a really bad idea. On the subject of time wasting, there's a lot of that - including tortuous dream sequences which contribute nothing except slowing you down. And it's constantly taking away control from you so that it can sloooooooooowly pan over to show you something that you've already seen a bunch of times. And often when the narrator comes in to talk at you - you have to stand stock still and listen. There is stuff to like here, don't get me wrong - the art, sound, and music are incredible, and form a evocative and compelling backdrop, and there are glimmerings of a fascinating story, the payoff for which is regrettably anti-climactic. You're forced to drag this unlikable protagonist through actions that you don't agree with just in the hope of receiving some snippets of story, only to be slapped in the face at the end by a 'moral' that's so unsubtle it's one step away from being presented in flashing lights.If it were edited down to remove the time-wasting aspects then I'd probably have to reservations about recommending it, but as it stands I can't feel like it was time I enjoyed spending.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first review on Steam after owning and playing over 200 games. This game is so unappealing that I feel it is necessary to leave a review to try an dissuade anyone else from purchasing this game. I, like most people, I imagine, were drawn to this game by the hand drawn art style. It is very nice. It reminds me of a children's story book. That is the sole highlight of this game. Everything else is either pointless or outright not fun. You play as Mo. A, probably, teenage girl who has been entrusted with some alien technology to help take care of the archipelago. Mo has some mental health issues. She's insecure, anxious and isolates herself from her friends and family. And that's the whole theme of the game; overcoming or at least managing insecurities. The story I find wholly unconvincing. Firstly, Mo is a teenage (probably) girl. Every teen girl is depressed, anxious, insecure about something. That is not an interesting story. Mo is only unique because she was chosen over everyone else to safeguard the islands. And the game gives us no reason to wonder why she is that way. No insight into a past life which may have caused her to be that way. She just is. And because she just is, she comes off as a brat and not someone to sympathize. Oh, the narrator will try and flesh Mo out from time to time. The narrator will say things like how much Mo enjoyed the mulberry juice her uncle made. The thing is, the game gives no reason for me to care about Mo. So I don't care that she enjoys her uncle's Mulberry spirits.Secondly, and I realize this is not germane to the game's story, but being a millennial and the first generation of humans to embrace social media, I am more than familiar with the flaunting, pin it to their chest, outwardly showy behavior girls and women make of their anxiety. As if it is a badge of honor to be mentally broken. Except we all know most of those girls and women are not suffering from debilitating mental issues but rather a rough patch in an otherwise normal life. But damn if they won't try to milk some likes and shares out of it. The point I'm trying to make is that I've become desensitized to it. So when someone is trying to tell me a story about someone's depression, insecurity, et cetera, I find it trite and unconvincing. Celeste had the same story and I found it equally trite and ridiculous but at least the game play was spectacular. Which brings me to the game play, which this game has none. It's four to five hours of moving up and down ladders, walking left and right and pulling out your magic staff once in a while to activate a machine. And it's so slow. Painfully slow. Nearly every room you visit the game with enter a cut scene to show you where you need to go. I think they did this to force you to appreciate their art. Every time you active a machine the game will pull you into a cut scene to show it's working. As if the developers want to assure you that you're not being lied to. You can walk or jog slightly faster. There is no reason to walk. You climb and drop off of ledges but not just anywhere. You can only drop down where the ledge is painted with gull guano. Thought you could jump off that ladder to get down faster? Think again Buck-o.  Mo's parka expands like a chute and you will descend so slowly, so gracefully slowly. You may even wish to take a nap. Do not buy this game. If this game was given to you for free, do not play this game. It has no redeeming qualities outside of the art style. If you want to play a "game" about an insecure girl then play Celeste. Again, the story does nothing for me but at least the game play was good. If you want to play a "not-game"  about an insecure girl then play What Remains of Edith Finch. It's a walking simulator like Minute of Islands but with a phenomenal story that doesn't waste your time.

_childDocuments_.review: "Minute of Islands" is yet another of literally thousands of console ported 2D retro platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.  It's a handheld (Nintendo Switch)/console game that's also been put on Steam as a bit of an afterthought, as it's very much designed for the handheld/console gaming audience.This one has slightky production quality than your usual Adventure Game Creator construction kit job, but not much.  It carries a story about a young girl who has to deal with various psychological traumas and other problems as this game attempts to be more "art" than "game".  And it's true, games can be art, but only when they exceed the sum of their parts... when "artists" try to just dump their work onto Steam without pairing it with an exceptional gaming experience, this doesn't make art better, it just makes gaming worse.Trying to address social issues through the medium of video games is misguided and can be harmful.  While it's plausible to suggest the intention was noble, this can do more harm than good.  Game developers are not professionals in areas of mental health and social problems, and when they use video games to pretend they are, this can cause far more harm than good.  It's my opinion that it's improper to use video games to push political or social agendas.  Apart from the harm such hamfisted attempts at addressing social problems can cause, this offers zero benefit to PC gamers.  People suffering from health issues or other social problems should seek out professional help rather than going to crap shovelware video games attempting to get sales by exploiting such problems for their own benefit, as is the case here.There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style cutscenes in this game.  The developers failed one of the most basic, fundamental requirements of game design.. "Show, don't tell."  So you'll spend a huge amount of time not playing the game, but clicking through endless lines of poorly written VN text cutscenes because the developers couldn't work out how to relate their narrative through the game mechanics, and decided instead it would be better to compete with reading a book for your time.We're here to play games, not read through hours of garbage intersituals.  My gaming rig is not a Kindle.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The game is comprised of somewhat mediocre hand drawn 2D illustrations instead of professional looking 3D game assets.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget to arrange someone who can create graphical assets properly, or lack of talent.  Regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is very low, beneath what PC gamers have come to expect in this era of cutting edge photorealistic 3D graphics.  At least it's not pixel "art", but if you're looking for contemporary, immersive visuals, this game is a fail.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.Arrogantly, the developers demand you should find a way to plug headphones into your gaming PC to experience the craptastic audio they shovelled into this terrible game.  I run a 9.2 surround sound system for my gaming rig, I'm not interested in downgrading just because the developers demand I experience the game in a compromised manner.Developers must never dictate to gamers how a game should be consumed, it's their JOB to ensure a game is experienced well on any gaming rig.  Failure to do this is a failure on their part, and not the gamers.The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just point and click stuff like a browser/Flash game.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?"Minute of Islands" has the farcical price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "Age of Empires IV", "Yakuza 0" or "Red Dead Redemption 2".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.
