_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Andrew Hulshult, the little Retro FPS Goblin that lives in the bottom of a discarded oil drum, only coming out when a Retro FPS needs a badass soundtrack, told me to buy this game and so ofcourse I did, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥' Andrew Hulshult!But yeah, this game is incredibly fun, there's alot going for it: Weapons all feel and sound great, movement is serviceable at the beginning, but upgrades improve it tenfold. The upgrade system of needing to play little platformer levels in order to gain your upgrades is a pretty genius idea honestly, and again the implementation is spot on too!Ofcourse Andrew's soundtrack is fantastic as always, dude is like the Mick Gordon of Retro Indie FPS' games. Admittedly before purchasing and buying the game, the thing holding me back from doing so was the Art Style, as I wasn't a fan - but honestly, it does grow on you: so if that's what's stopping you from trying this one out, give it a chance!As Civvie (#FreeCivvie BTW) said in his video for this game, the terms "Procedural Generation" and "Rouge-like/lite" does signal a couple red flags, but this game implements them in the best ways possible, so again - if that's why you are not buying this thing as we speak, give it a chance!
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: The game has certainly improved. It is miles better than it once was. With interesting additions to the weapon variety such as the Trap Puzzle Cube (basically a Pokeball). I still don't quite enjoy the game. But I definitely feel like it deserves better than a negative review now.OLD REVIEW (no longer relevant, but available for posterity)Very bland. The weapon variety is very low and mostly uninteresting. They just all feel very standard for an FPS. For a game where I am an asylum patient living violent and fantastical dreams, the weapons are quite ordinary with the exception of the chained-saw (and, to a lesser extent, the spellbooks/staffs). The quantity may be high, but nothing makes me care about getting weapon X vs weapon Y when there are no significant changes to how I would approach a room. Desert Eagle vs. shotgun? Aim roughly at their head and fire. Didn't work? Repeat the process.The chained-saw can significantly change how I approach a room, because it adds something new and interesting. In fact, it adds a high level of movement and speed making gameplay feel briefly exhilarating as I zip around the room tearing high priority enemies apart before mopping up the riffraff. I'd almost say that ditching all other weapon choices in favor of refining the chained-saw to a higher degree and adding various additional mechanics around it would lead to more interesting and  gameplay than it currently has.Though, then again, maybe my issue doesn't necessarily lie around the weapon variety. Because, there seem to be frequent lulls in gameplay (with the Sulphur mines being the biggest offender because of the slow and necessary elevators). The majority of the game involves walking through hallways/small rooms with 1-3 low-tier enemies in them. The few times where I've come across a massive roomed filled to the brim with enemies to deal with were quite enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Bit of a mixed bag ultimately, I personally vote yes rather than no but it could go either way. Go for sale if you're interested.+ Lots of levels not counting new game +(+)[+]+ Huge weapon variety+ Satisfying effects, feels good to get that ultimate weapon that takes out fifteen enemies at once+ No need for peekaboo around corners to avoid hitscan which is something I appreciate myself+ Has enough ammo going around that I actually don't feel the need to preserve it like a madman which is my usual go-to, I really like that. You can't keep most guns with you between stages so it encourages using them, ones you don't take with turn into currency* Roguelite progression, become stronger as you play, good or bad depending who asks* Getting the permanent upgrades has you play different minigames to get them (which can be toggled off to skip them), leaves me a bit confused but I suppose having a toggle pleases everyone, although arguably you get several hours less if you skip them. That being said, their gameplay is limited to say the least. It's weird, ok?* Game is grindy, possibly too much so depending who asks- Procedurally generated levels so sometimes that key item is in that random corner you don't realise to check- Permanent upgrades require currency, lot of it being in secret areas, which are kind of a pain to find, especially lategame when maps get even bigger. Not STRICTLY required but seeing that treasure counter not be 0 is going to be a dealbreaker for some, could have been for me- Once the weaponry expands enough there's going to be so many particles on the screen when you fire you won't see a thing, which in one hand is fine since everything probably got obliterated, but I can see this being a pain in higher new game tiers where things supposedly get even more punishingAll in all I liked it but there were several grievances that took away from the experience, so I would suggest trying the demo first to get a feel for it if nothing else.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: You are a paranoid schizophrenic who kills hoards of enemies in her nightmares... what more do you need?In all seriousness, this is a fanatic shooter. The movement is fast and frantic with very tight controls. As you unlock upgrades and find better weapons, your rampages become bloodier but you never fee *too* overpowered. The weapon system is somewhat reminiscent of Synthetic: Legion Rising where there are many different weapons, but the are dozens of attributes they can have making them all feel and function differently.Great lineup of enemies with differing attacks and ranges that can swarm you in seconds if you are not careful.I'm 18 hours in at the time of writing this and only about 60% finished with the main story. At some points and can feel a bit repetitive and sluggish, but each level is relatively short (10-30 minutes) which is great for playing one or two levels and stopping for a bit.All in all 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me of old school doom but with more complex controls. The action is super fun and it get more and more difficult as you progress. The skill progression system is playing on a gameboy in a Mario-like video game to unlock more and more abilities. The weapons are so awesome. I can see why this game got overwhelming positivity. New Favorite!
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: -Satisfying Weapons ? Check-Kickass Soundtrack by the one and only Andrew Hurshult ? Check-A minigame system that rewards you with skills to boost your character(like double jump/Dash/Extra heath etc) ? Check-Graphics inspired by top tier Boomer Shooters ? Check-Secrets(some with some neat Easter Eggs) ? CheckOne of the more creative Boomer shooter inspired games curently available  EA with full release around the Corner(28th of March) but even then i would still recommend it,you are getting so much value
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being early access, this is one of a handful of games that has managed to actually do procedural generation right. The devs seem to have added enough level pieces that repeats aren't too noticeable and each different area has some different mechanics and level structure, so they never feel like a recolor of a previous area. The only pieces that do get a bit stale are the challenge rooms that appear in each level since there only seem to be 2 or 3 of these per area, adding a couple more of each would probably suffice.The weaponry is procedurally generated in the same style as the Borderlands series, but there is a large enough arsenal of melee weapons, firearms, and magic weapons that it doesn't suffer from the sameiness that Borderlands weapons often would. Combat feels extremely satisfying and is on-par with Dusk and Blood. The Grapple-Saw is the best thing ever.The skill tree is a neat idea but suffers from its minigame which ends up feeling like a chore as it is pretty janky. It definitely can be salvaged though, and the dev has already expressed interest in doing so.I've had some stability and performance issues. Game gets crashy when the player is in water and oddly enough my performance tanks when I'm in the hospital if my graphics settings are maxed but runs decent in the actual levels, whole game could definitely be better optimized for performance.It's like if Dusk, Borderlands, and Rogue Legacy were the delusions of a mental patient. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This the best doomlike I've played. The random level generation keeps runs fresh, and the sheer amount of content to discover is fantastic. I have one solitary nitpick that the level design sometimes leaves you wandering around without a clear picture of what you need to do to progress, but it rarely hurts the joy of melting demon faces off.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I hate it! That is why I played it every day for two weeks.I saw someone complain that it is too long, which is just.. the strangest complaint. So much effort was put into this game. I'm at level 75 or so, I'm not sure how much is left. If I were to hazard a guess, I would say it's 100 levels, but I didn't check. The one bad thing: It's ugly, looks like minecraft. But you do not actually care, do you.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome, and you should be playing it now.It's a little on the easy side at first, but gets much more challenging as you get along. However, it isn't brutally unfair like Blood or anything.Very fun. Think a rogue-like Wolfenstein meets Quake physics as a looter shooter.Also, the shotgun is perfect. Seriously. I'd marry this shotgun if I could.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: The idea of a roguelite doom intrigued me, the unique level up system then provoked me to wishlist it. I've already spent 11 hours in this seemingly small game and can't wait to spend another 11 hours exploring every nook and cranny for more content.There are many weapons to choose from and you get to keep one each level, all of the unique weapons for this game have their normal use and a secondary use. Most level 1 items consist of guns and a few magic staffs and some melee weapons. level 2 has more unconventional weaponry like chainsaws with a grapple hook and katanas with a blood slash. Level 3 items have cannonballs and a chainsaw you can ride on.What still keeps me playing is the unique level up system that is enacted through GBA style game cartridges. The idea of playing the main game just to progress this minigames to help you further in the main game is something i wish more games would do.I would recommend this game for those with short attention span or those that don't wish to feel the vastness of some of the new AAA games, this game has variety set as the focus and achievements every step of the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how this game isn't more popular than it is.  It takes just about the best aspect of roguelite, along with randomized levels, filled with the beauty of gorey doom style graphics. It's just amazing in every way.  My ONLY gripe is some of the "secrets" are a pain in the butt to find.  EASILY a 9/10 and worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: It took me 27 hours to reach Episode 2. Not because of the difficulty or anything but just because how much there is to do in this game.And then it took me another 70-ish hours to get to New Game +3 (which would be the 4th walkthrough in a row, yes) and complete the achievements.I regret nothing and the game is more than worth its buck.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been a blast, oozing with boomer shooter feels and references.  Weapon diversity is fantastic, there's something out there for every play-style you could imagine.  Hulshult knocked it out of the park with the soundtrack (as usual), keeping things feeling intense during every shootout.Can't wait for the future chapters, keep up the outstanding work Blazing Bit!
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is very solid, that's the best part. If you're expecting anything beyond that....look for any of the other many many retro FPS games. Roguelike mechanics are fine, and the minigame upgrading is a neat idea, if a bit too long when you just want to get more maximum ammo or whatever. The story starts getting a little interesting, despite it's presentation just being notes you get after every level, after a while. But...it just ends without a real resolution or explanation. Trying to find NG+ is also bafflingly confusing. Overall not a bad game at all, but try the demo out first. If you like the gameplay, you might like it. But it's *just* gameplay.*Much later edit:  Changing it to a recommendation for this game, actually, but with the caveat mentioned above that you should not go into it for anything *but* the gameplay. Play the demo, if you like the shooting and the roguelike stuff, you'll like it. The grappling hook you get later on was very fun. But don't go into it for anything but fun gameplay. The most notable thing is that there's a promise of a story and it completely falls flat with the really bad ending which left a notably sour aftertaste.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely good sprite-based FPS game. Just the rolls for guns alone drive a deep replayability, but the procedurally generated maps and the skill system ensure every save slot is a little different. Act 2 was just released, adding 18 new levels that play differently than the first act, as well as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of new guns. I have no doubt that the developer will add an interstellar third act. My only gripe is no New Game + option.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Keep a chainsaw with you whenever you can because the alt-fire really helps navigating the jumping puzzles.The ghost head trap might look inescapable at first since it follows you around and it doesn't look like you have enough time to find and destroy the orb generating it, but there's a way to deal with it. The 8-bit bonus levels are a bit of an afterthought right now (early access, 2/3 done), like a basic Flash game (RIP). This means you won't be blocked from upgrades for being bad at platforming, though...
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I like 95% of this game a lot. The only thing I really hate about this game is the screen shake when you get hit by an explosion, that is absurdly excessive, what it does is just wildly fling your view around in random directions and there are enemies who spam homing explosive weapons at you. It feels like deaths related to this aren't because I'm bad at the game, it feels like somebody sitting behind me is slapping at my mouse hand and if I get hit they WILL NOT STOP.This also applies to effects that don't actually damage the player like one of the powerups and it just sucks to look at.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game, I've played 30+ hours and it kept me entertained for the entire time.Overall I'd give the game an 8/10 at this point - it is a well made, enjoyable roguelite FPS with great promise if it continues to improve and expand in the same way as it has in the first two chapters! I would highly recommend playing it even though it is in EA because it's as good as any other 'retro' FPS out there at the very least.There are a few improvements to be made in my opinion, the monsters are quite samey (even if they just changed cosmetically to fit the level-set they are in that would be an improvement) - they do change per chapter, but then you have an entire chapter of essentially the same 3-4 enemies over and over.The random level idea is great and I like the way to switches up the maps each time you play but after finishing a 3-4 level 'episode' or dying a few times, you've probably seen all variations of that episodes levels - it would be great if the rooms were a little more random (it picks from a pool of prefab rooms which are the same but in different orders) but maybe that's just because I binged the game so I was used to it quite quickly.Another point on the randomisation idea is the weapons, I seemed to encounter the same 10-12 weapons out of the apparent 58 available (as of episode 2) so it would be good if there was more common variety. I found a quad shotgun at one point, at the end of a level and never saw it again in the 30 hours!Difficulty really depends on what weapons you get and their quality and stats. I died a few times but the majority of deaths were me blowing myself up with a fun explosive weapon - the skill tree really makes the game get better over time, you start quite slow paced and are quickly able to dash around, double jump, move much quicker, ignore your own splash damage and fall damage etc. which makes for many different ways to approach a battle.Bosses are all different and hard but entirely doable. I did all of them without finding anything particularly fantastic or using powerups, but they took a few tries! Don't be put off by dying once or twice, you'll soon learn the mechanics and if you're lucky you might find some better weapons in the next playthrough that'll make it a breeze.I was disappointed when chapter 2 ended and so did the game - my only option now is to wait or create a brand new save slot and start from scratch, if there was some way to play endless maps from the various chapters and episodes but keep my skill tree progression, that would have kept me playing much longer. I assume this is because otherwise I would have unlocked everything before chapter 3 arrived!
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: All you have to know is that this game is about a woman in a mental hospital or asylum of some sort where she has badass dreams of being the main character in an FPS styled nightmare.The graphics of the game looks retro as hell with a few modern splashes here and there, The soundtrack is nice (Which really got me jamming, not gonna lie), and the gore is just...Oh it's bloody brilliant (I'm not sorry).I also like the fact that upgrading makes you play minigames, and THANK GOD they patched a checkpoint system in it.You can also just check the minigames to off in the settings if you don't like wasting your time, but...Why would you want to disable a time waster that's actually fun to do?Overal, this game is quite nice, however sometimes there's so much crap going on I can't even see. It's just confusing. But I guess that's done on purpose. The game is challenging, but rather not impossible.I'll give it a solid 8.5/10.But you'll be the judge yourself once you bought this masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best retro shooter IMO. Trying out different weapons and modifiers is half the fun, and there's an overwhelming variety to keep things interesting. Also has some decent exploration mechanics (not on the level of Painkiller games though).Biggest con was that it becomes somewhat grindy towards the end, and the NG+ doesn't really offer much replay value. But by the time I got that far I was already very happy with what I got.Also I had some performance issues initially. Even though it uses pixel art, the sheer amount of sprites and effects that can accumulate on screen can bog things down. In particular, turning off shadows make a big impact on performance.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: 100% one of the best boomer shooters on the market. Definitely the most chaotic.PROS:- Huge arsenal with an array of modifying properties that are randomized, like decreased reload times, explosive rounds, health leeching, etc.- Extensive character upgrades, ranging from simple things like more health or ammo capacity to useful abilities like a grappling hook or double jump. Plus the way you upgrade these things is through mini-games based on classic games like Mario or Pokemon.- Lots of unique enemies, including elite enemies which are regular enemies but bigger and with some kind of modifying property.- Unique power-ups to pick up. Time slow, movement increase, etc.- Randomized level designs. If you die on a specific level, the next time you play it will be entirely different (aside from a handful that seem to always be the same on every playthrough.) Unfortunately, this feature also brings some of the games bigger cons, which I'll mention.- Varying levels. Every few levels, the arena type changes. The woods, a hospital, city streets, a space station.- An arena mode with different preset themed arenas. Always fun facing off against hordes of enemies, and they tie it in to one of the upgrade systems to make it a little more important.- New Game +CONS:- A lot of the upgrade systems and how you access them are confusing. The game would benefit greatly from some kind of in game compendium that explains how certain upgrades work or what certain terms mean in regards to modifiers and what not. Hope you know exactly what a "soul orb" or "tornado dash" is/does, because the game sure expects you to!- Randomized levels bring about the issue of a lack of consistency. Multiple times I would have difficulty finding the right place to go or thing to do because the game randomly designed the level poorly. A small handful of times I had to just let myself die because it seemed no matter where I looked, I couldn't find the right thing to progress. One of the more consistent problems I found.- "Find X and place in Y to proceed" obstacles. I'm all good with finding keys, but as the game progresses they introduce levels where you have to find an object and insert it into something else so it will open a door or drop an item. These items tend to be harder to spot than the keys, making them often a pain. Sometimes I would find levels unfinishable due to the randomization seemingly putting the item somewhere I can't obtain it.- There can be some frame dropping and sound issues when things get hectic, but honestly it kinda just makes the chaos you can create feel even more insane. Like you're gonna break the game by blowing things up too hard. You're making so many explosions and jibbing so many enemies that ♥♥♥♥ slows to a crawl. A con, but is it really?- A lot of the best old school shooters or boomer shooters have a memorable main character, but this one is pretty dry and unremarkable. Probably better than being annoying and a loudmouth, though.Highly replayable. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I don’t normally do “this game is X meets Y” reviews because they can often be kind of reductive, but there’s no avoiding it here.  Nightmare Reaper basically broadcasts its influences in bright neon lights; it’s as much an homage as it is a game.  Luckily, it’s a fine example of both.  The developers took three parts Doom, two parts American McGee’s Alice, and sprinkled in some Borderlands and classic Nintendo titles to make this delightful cocktail of carnage.Retro FPS games are a nickel a dozen, so it can be hard to parse why some of them work and some don’t.  This one definitely does, though, repeatedly tickling the blood-crazed part of your lizard brain that just wants to see monster giblets fly.  A huge part of it is the game’s enormous arsenal of weapons, which range from melee gear to conventional firearms and all the way up to magical items that evoke classics like Heretic and Hexen.  A game where your potential loadout is a katana, Molotov cocktails, an ice spell book and a staff that summons hornets is a good time where I come from.  And this is a looter shooter, so each weapon type can have special abilities and modifications based on rarity.  And the game isn’t shy with drops, so there’s always a fun new toy to try out.The game’s story is minimalist, told in brief journal entries and from context clues found while exploring the hub areas.  You play an unnamed brunette girl in a mental health facility (who is not named Alice, in case American McGee is litigious) who explores procedurally generated levels full of monsters every time she goes to sleep.  The game strikes a good balance, as levels are long enough to feel satisfying but don’t drag on past their welcome.  And if you die, well, a whole new level will spawn this time, so maybe your fortunes will improve.  A lucky early weapon drop can make a stage a cakewalk, while bursting into a room full of ranged murder machines with nothing but a sword can be an early grave.  RNG giveth and taketh in equal measure.Do note that despite all the rogue-like trappings, this game is not meant to be played in one sitting unless you’re a speedrunning machine.  There are dozens of levels to blast through, along with exploring the hubs and powering Not-Alice up via playing minigames on her off-brand Gameboy Advance SP.  There are multiple games to play on it which mirror Super Mario, Pokemon and Gradius.In fact, it’s here where the game hits its first snag.  Spending all the gold and shinies you collect to permanently power up Not-Alice is perfectly cromulent design for titles like this, and doing this by playing takes on old classics is a creative spin on the idea.  However, execution is lacking here.  The Mario game is fine, as the design is solid and the stages are short.  I rather enjoyed the brief change in gameplay.  But the Pokemon and Gradius games get old and repetitive very quickly.  I bought this game to shoot demons  with improbably designed shotguns, not fly the same Gradius stage 73 times.  Mercifully, the developers got the hint and sent out a patch, so you can now just buy the power ups without the hassle.My only other quibble is the music.  The DOOM METAL GUITAR OF DEATH is great, yes, but it plays literally any time there’s an enemy nearby, no matter how feeble.  The ROCK OF CARNAGE is perfect for a slaughter fest with dozens of baddies, but wears on you when it revs up 14 times per stage because stray rooms had a bad guy or two in them.But these issues have either been remedied or are fairly trivial.  This game is a blast and an easy recommend if you like the genre.  Honestly, this game made me realize how boring a lot of overly-codified modern game design is.  I had forgotten how fun it was to simply drink insane boost items, kick open doors and go bananas with a deranged Mad Libs arsenal of mayhem.  Thanks for the reminder, Nightmare Reaper.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is loads of fun. To start off, I'll get the negatives out of the way. The secret hunting gets a bit tedious since its a bit RNG related so it's hard to really give any contextual clues as to where a secret could be. The minigames for the upgrade system are a neat creative idea, but doing em too often distracts from the game a bit.The good stuff is basically everything else. I love the frantic chaos, the satisfying pixel gore, the wacky weapon variety, and the music. The art is pretty dang cool too, it fits the chaos of the game pretty well. Overall, it's an addictive game with lots to enjoy. Some may count this as a negative, but the RNG makes the games difficulty vary immensely, but I find that unrpedictability to be enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun. The music is incredible, the enemy encounters can be absolutely brutal, and the gun variety rivals Borderlands.It has some problems. Performance is spotty. The procedural level generation creates some truly dumb levels sometimes. You can hit a wall with a tough level and feel trapped by your weapon choices and RNG. Once you unlock enough upgrades, it's incredibly hard to start a fresh game file because you feel so handicapped and slow and weak. NG+ modes crank the enemy HP up so high it can become tiresome. The grapple hook, especially in the later parts of the game, can feel a little loose and more like a rope you swing from.But man, there's nothing better than getting some hilariously OP shotgun that fires canon balls or a burst fire orbital canon and watching whole rooms of enemies get obliterated. This game has that classic "one more level" feel to it, you know what I mean? You'll finish a level and RUSH to start one more. You'll die and RUSH to try again. Always wanting just to play just one more level.It's also a fairly long game. The length allows for incremental progress in power and difficulty, as well as providing a lot of time to experiment with different weapons and approaches to combat encounters.Overall, this has become one of my favorite games. It really rides the line between "wacky randomness" and "balanced design" for enough of the game to make its shortcomings forgivable. Plus, it has some fairly unique takes on upgrade trees by turning them into fully functional mini games. It also makes the hub world a narrative puzzle that you progress between levels. Despite how over saturated Steam is with roguelites / retro shooters / pixel graphics, Nightmare Reaper stands out by providing a novel concept and exceptional gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Cool weapons, cool atmosphere and lore/narrative, smooth shooting, fun gameplay loop. It's a solid game.It has a lot of issues though. First of all: Make pickups inventory items of sort that you can activate throughout the level. Most of the time when you find a power-up you'll have no enemies nearby to kill with it. One of the downsides of randomly generated levels.Second of all: walk option. As you increase your movement speed it makes it harder to do platforming or trap sections in the levels, and there's not much you can do about it. Add a button that we can press to go back to a slower speed. Third: the platformer minigame you play to increase your skills. The hitboxes are busted. It's like your character has a big invisible box around them which doesn't make any sense and makes some levels and sections frustrating.Fourth: Kinda minor, but sometimes some curse bubble thingy will spawn in the area you're in and start pelting you with BS. They're pretty annoying and don't add much to the gameplay since they mostly spawn after you've killed everything. Then it's just a game of running back to it and shooting at it until it goes away, and then dealing with the health loss. I might be missing something with this mechanic since the game came out literally today, but still.Fifth: bugs. It's completely playable, but I've had one crash so far and another weird bug where a room full of enemies killed themselves while I was on the other side of the map, having never touched that room. I guess they somehow touched some barrels? I got a 16x combo notification out of nowhere and a bunch of gold, so I'm assuming that's what happened. I'm confident some or all of these issues will get fixed, as the devs do seem to care about making a good game. So far, it's quite enjoyable, so I recommend it. Just keep in mind it's in early access.Edit: after playing for a longer time, the platforming minigame gets REALLY frustrating. Especially when you just wanna get an upgrade and shoot at more stuff. Spending 15 minutes trying to do a challenging platformer level is just not as fun as going around shooting stuff. Please add an option to deactivate the minigame! It's cute and all, but a lot of people just wanna play the shooter part of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I deleted my previous review since I wanted to write a new one with a new perspective since my original review was made back when only chapters 1 and 2 were available.So where to start...Nightmare Reaper is a pixelated fps looter shooter type game with roguelike elements. You play the role of a woman who is trapped in an mental hospital for unknown reasons but you will come to understand her reason being there as you progress through the game and read the notes from a doctor who is in charge of her care.Your time will be divided between exploring the hospital and after going to sleep, fighting through randomised dungeons and the enemies who inhabit them. You earn currency as you go through the game to buy skills to help through the game, this is added on when you unlock the 'Topaz' and 'Jade' trees. All skill trees are gotten via minigames you play on your what looks to be a knockoff GBA SP like device and will help you in various ways.Weapons available vary and come in 3 varieties of bullet, magic and explosive weaponry. These can range from pistols to spellbooks to grenade launcher to the extra heavy stuff like black hole launchers and flamethrowers.I found it to be an enjoyable experience if a bit drawn out though this is me playing it the normal way rather than the shortened game mode that released a bit ago. If I had to really nitpick anything it would probably have to be the pain of finding secrets.Secrets are important if you are looking to gain that moolah for buying skills both via the treasure they hold and from the end of stage bonuses but they can be a pain to find. You do eventually get tools to make finding secrets easier but even afterwards they can be a pain sometimes since I have sometimes spent like 5-10 mins looking for secrets if only to make sure I get that 100% stage completion for maximum cash and the lack of a secrets counter can make it hard to tell if you have collected absolutely everything in a level.But that aside it's a good game to play and is a recommendation from me, there is a free demo too if you want to have a look and see if it's the kind of game you want to commit a purchase too so go for it if you think you will like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: A quality retro-style shooter with good weapon feel and tight mechanics. The procedurally generated levels don't feel repetitive since the game changes level themes (and thus room designs) frequently. _childDocuments_.review: When seemingly every game coming out now is aiming to be the next big sensation, pushing boundaries of graphics and stuffing games to the brim with pointless filler, it's nice to play a game that's trying to be none of that and is all the better for it. All the elements of the game just work and it's genuinely fun to play and entertaining. Many AAA developers take notes - I play games to enjoy myself, as I'm sure is the case for many others. This game is well polished and will remind you of the times you just turned on a game and had fun.Despite some randomness, it never feels over the top or unmanageable. The difficulty curve is a bit high at the start of the game, expect to die a lot until you unlock some upgrades. Performance could be better, even if I use the lowest settings I experience frequent FPS drops on a 3070, they're not game breaking but it would still be nice if this could be fine tuned somehow. Your enjoyment of the mini games to unlock skills may vary but I found them a nice simple distraction from the main game, though they wouldn't carry a game on their own.There is a demo which is meaty enough to know if you're going to like it enough to purchase to continue playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I am having a worse experience playing this than I would have had if I had just modded Doom 2 and used a random map generator. It may have potential, but it has so many design problems in every aspect of it that there's no way I can recommend this.This is a long review, so that's your warning.It starts out seeming fine, but I realized that, for myself at least, the random weapon mechanic is actually making the game worse. It gives the player more variety, but you have to throw out all but one weapon at the end of every level. You can't build an arsenal you can use to handle different situations. You're also much less likely to pick the neat fun weapon over the boring and practical one that is ammo efficient.The enemy design starts out simple if boring, but starts introducing frustrating nonsense around chapter 2, with the worst offenders being that multiple types of enemy introduce a variant that has a decent chance to just swooce right out of the way as soon as you click on it, causing you to waste ammo with very little actual ways to play around it. The only way I can think of to consistently deal with that is explosive weapons and aim at their feet, but following that advice would just mean you would have to narrow down the one weapon you keep every level even further. Also, some of them fly, meaning that won't work consistently.The music is actually rather repetitive, which I hate to say because Andrew Hulshult has done great work on other games. It is dynamic, but not well done; I once went through an entire level with it on, and then while i was scouring the level for secrets it kept going until a tiny enemy that was hiding in a small maze of barrels in one of the first areas finally made itself known and I killed it. It was a good 15 minutes of that song, and it lasts maybe 1 minute. The rest of the sound design is alright, aside from the secrets.Speaking of secrets, the game rewards you for finding them with goodies, but also gives a big multiplier to how much gold you earned at the end of the level if you found them all, incentivizing you to find them all. This is a problem because the secrets are both tedious to find and difficult to make out sometimes, as the wind sound effect used to denote them is similar to sounds used in level ambience in several instances. I have problems with seeing things directly in front of me sometimes, so these sounds are very important to me.Graphics aren't going to be why you get this game, but nonetheless I feel compelled to mention them. They don't have much in the way of charm. I personally especially don’t like that shiny surfaces such as glass can’t be turned off, as the glare is distracting.The story is something I hesitate to touch on, as I haven’t finished it yet, but so far it seems like another cliche “You’re mentally ill, and a danger to yourself and others” story, with the levels being nightmares you’re having. Not all protagonists in these games need stories that’re in depth, but this particular theme can be stereotypical, if not outright eye-rolling, if not given the proper care. I myself have family members with histories of mental illness, so this is a topic I’m especially unforgiving about. What does this narrative add to the game? Could this story have been told outside the confines of a mental hospital? Could someone not have just been having bad dreams, maybe even from a supernatural source? Wouldn’t it be more effective to hint that you’re insane, instead of confirming it? The story isn’t done, but I have little reason to look forward to more.There are challenge rooms that have a bunch of traps to navigate, and there is a single treasure at the end. You’re not doing these for the treasure but for the end of level bonus you get for getting all the treasure. They’re not really very fun.The skill tree has a mini-game attached to it. It’s a tedious platforming game. If you play this, I think that it’s important for your enjoyment that you know you can turn it off in the options.Overall, this is a game that is less than the sum of its parts. Many features the game has, especially the random weapons that the game has as a selling point, actively make it more tedious to play. I would be having more fun with Doom 2, playing a random weapon mod, with oblige made maps, and I can’t really recommend an experience that doesn’t add anything a game from 20 years ago can’t do better.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a unique playstyle and atmosphere that really makes it stand out from the rest. The RPG/looter-shooter system combined with the RG zones rivaled to that of Diablo 2 is top notch, and the gameplay overall is pretty fun. But like all games, it does have it's faults. The main deal breaker for me as to why I stopped playing this game is the lack of replayability. "How is that possible?" you ask? Well, after each completion of the game, the enemies scale higher in stats. After about 6 playthroughs, the game becomes a 1-shot fest relying completely on luck to complete rather than skill or gear. There is no way to toggle the scaling you want, so after a certain amount of playthroughs, you are forced to erase all progression and start fresh if you want to make it easier again. IMO, there should be a hard cap of 5 and a way to scale the game to your liking. The reason for this is not only to curb the insta-gib fest, but to also be able to find and loot the dream weapons you want. Weapon stats are locked behind playthrough completions up to 4 or 5, so in order to find the best weapons in the game, that is how many times you have to replay it.Maybe sometime in the future the creator will revisit this game and add more content and adjust some things, or maybe even make a DLC or start on a sequel to give more options. The game's setting offers a lot of potential, so I'd hate to see this be a one and done game.TL:DR: The game IMO is only good for 1 or 2 playthroughs, after that it becomes repetitive due to lack of features.

_childDocuments_.review: The game from the start is a fun, rougelite experience with progression thru themed stages with randomized layouts. Guns are random and have specific tiers of rarity that give an extra stat to your gun per rarity level; up to about four extra stats. Enemies feel like standard enemies of a shooter: melee oriented rushers, grunts that gun you down, and demon-like flyers that chase and spit out at you. I found the main loop of getting guns and going thru the levels rather fun, but was truly intrigued by the mental ward hub the main character ends up after every level. If this game stayed like this for the entire game I would have enjoyed it a lot more than experiencing the rest of the game.However by the time you get halfway thru chapter 2 the game slow downs considerably. The randomly generated levels get longer and introduce new door systems that require a different kind of key to fetch and unlock. It wouldn't be too much of a problem, but the map is as basic as it gets, and features nothing but walkable surfaces, walls, and doors. The fact that there's no way to see anything beyond that is a travesty, and really hurts this game. By chapter 3, there are various other "put thing into other thing to get into another thing" that makes the maze-like levels a pain to traverse at best, and a frustrating nightmare scouring every inch of the level at the worse.Enemies start getting much more stronger and spongier, and new types that are "upgraded" from past enemies. While this wouldn't be much of a problem, these new enemies tend to have abilities that explode, disable you, or deal loads of damage without much warning with little counter play other than make lots of space and kill them from afar. With the amount of melee weapons in this game, I find it a little disappointing that the game discourages me from using an entire weapon class because the amount of damage every single enemy can deal at close ranges.Clarity in general seems to be lacking as well. Clutter, explosions, and other particle systems make things hard to visually understand. Enemy sprites get lost, and on death fly off in a pseudo rag doll instead of having an animation collapsing to the floor. Map and level clarity get worse as the game goes on with each new renamed key and keyhole item is introduced, clutter that adds to the visual chaos, and confusing paths created procedural and not handcrafted. With the amount of weapons and stats, it almost would be paramount to have some sort of encyclopedia of weapons and stats that could explain what thing does what. Weapons in general feel good in the first chapter, and you can genuinely make choices on which weapon to keep and which to leave behind. When you reach chapter two you start seeing weapons that feel straight upgrades from their previous counterparts that you probably can't keep yet, and the interesting weapons you come across start feeling gimmicky compared to the one weapon that can reliably kill all the annoying tanky enemies as soon as possible. Weapon rarity only affects the amount of extra stats you can get on a gun, and the sheer amount of guns and stats makes it feel like you get barely usable or under performing guns against the enemies that are constantly growing in strength. These are my main complaints with the game, and I feel these are big enough to not truly recommend this game. The first chapter of the game is super engaging and interesting, but from the second part to the end I couldn't help but play to see it through. If you do still want to get this game I highly recommend getting it during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Is "Nightmare Reaper" a good shooter? Yes. Is it a good rougelike? Not really. The best and worst parts about this game are in fact its main selling point: that levels and loot are random for better or worse in ways that equally rule and suck.The problem is for every awesome moment of kismet, there's 2 or 3 other insane design choices I truly don't understand. I would like to see a more linear version of this, maybe as a DLC, or perhaps some curated seeded runs. Pros:- Weapons feel awesome to shoot, enemies are varied and fun to annihilate, the game moves so fast, it's like it fell out of 1996. - An absurd, bonkers arsenal that kicks so much ass. There's some truly hall of famers in here. Looking at you Post Driver and Scrap Launcher. Weapon balance is truly messed up, though. I would like the ability to improve a weapon with more deterministic choices, rather than just a random slot machine.- Lots of level variety, from spooky dungeons to outer space to under da seaaaaaaa. (Not any real cohesion and city levels are bland.)- Tons of upgrades and minigames to playCons:- Game is extremely punishing and you can die before you even know why. Feels not good sometimes.- Maps needs improvement. Keys, locks, batteries, teleporters, and special mechanics objects need to be highlighted.- This game is long as hell. It's 3 times as long as it needs to be. Only needs 1 level per world, not 3.- Bosses can be some real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.- Levels can be either a cakewalk or a maze. Later levels suffer from sometimes needing special keys to progress or just unlock a secret. This needs to be way more clear.- Random enemy placements, especially in big open arenas, can be a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. It has moments when it can feel a little broken (mostly mid-late game) but there's a surprising amount of depth to it. Also certain "upgrades" aren't upgrades, but basic skills that you'll need to get through the game. So always try look ahead in the skill tree and get things like "dash" or "mantling" as well as starting ammo increases. Starting off with only 1 gun that inevitably runs out each level before you can find another gun is disappointing but I guess it forces you to be resourceful and look for breakables even though the breakables typically contain treasure (money) and not ammo or guns.Anyways it's a great game. I am recommending it to all my irl friends. Apparently it's even going to come out on console. I'll probably buy it there too.

_childDocuments_.review: A rogue-lite FPS that combines the best of both genres and dials the result up to 11. If the graphics hold you back from trying it out, there's not much I can say that will sway your opinion I guess (even though also that aspect is way more intricate than you might think).The FPS part is fast, satisfying and full of mechanics that come naturally and are immensely enjoyable. The rogue-lite aspect is unpunishing and brilliantly realized. And don't get me started on meta-stories and meta-games. There is way more to discover in this game than you'd expect.Speaking of things not to get me started on, the sound design is top-notch and the soundtrack by Andrew Hulshult is... well, when you know, you know. This man can do no wrong.There's a demo, so you don't have to shell out your coin on my word alone - and if the price seems steep to you for an indie retro-FPS (we're just spoiled that way), apart from it being on sale really often, it's also got a hell of a lot of content and is definitely worth every cent.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a ton of fun for a while. I put like 20~hrs into it and beat a lot of levels.However the difficulty scaling is poor. I'm at a point in the game where even with 180 health enemies kill me in less than 3 seconds, the area is that awful subway area where the doors always close behind you and there is ZERO area to move around, and enemies spawn in groups of 10-15 that can kill you in a few hits. It is just frustrating, losing your guns every level, running out of ammo, and the only way to beat levels is by random chance and getting lucky. _childDocuments_.review: Normally I love boomer shooters, and when they add gimmicks that work well together to make it more unique it should be perfect right? Not for me personally, at least not in this game's case. I'll admit that I haven't finished this game and don't plan on doing so in the near future because after 4 hours I felt no incentive to push through till the end, not even out of spite like I do with other games. It's just so middle of the road for me that I can't marvel at how good it is nor can I laugh at how bad it is. My main gripe with this game is the level design. This is one of the key aspects in every game, let alone in a retro shooter. All levels feel the same the play through, sure there's some variation in environmental hazards and other stuff but it wasn't enough to keep me engaged. Especially levels that are in the same environment have the same couple of preset rooms copied over and over, making it such a slog to get through because you fight through the same room a couple of times. Maybe the randomly generated levels are to blame for this but I don't feel like this can be used as an excuse.There are also some other problems I have with this such as that all the gimmicks don't feel like they work together well enough, especially the RPG one. It's a neat idea (not a unique one, but it is implemented the best way I have played so far), but it doesn't work for me. It should feel like a change of pace but it kinda felt like a slog, also the 'upgrades' you get are simply +X% which is boring.Another one is the randomly dropped weapons, it feels obsolete once you get a good gun such as a legendary double-barrel shotgun. Also, the 2 or 3 bosses I've encountered were stronger versions of normal enemies with one or two new moves which is lackluster, to say the least.Some positives however are for example the gunplay, because of the visuals and the audio design it feels amazing and impactful. Another one is the soundtrack which is simply great.Overall it's not a bad game at all, and I do recommend giving it a go if you like the look of it (and if you enjoyed the demo). But mainly out of the experience that I've had with it, I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man, so much would I recommend this game.  The shooting is verrrrry solid.  The roguelite game design is very forgiving (you don't lose level progress when you die).  The roguelite system in regards to weapons is brilliant and allows you no choice but to embrace the multitude weapons thrown at you, letting you to keep one weapon with you throughout level changes.  The weapons are very unique from each other and so fun to use.  The randomly generated special, rare, and legendary variants of weapons add even more variety to the 80 distinctly different weapons.  The random level generation has been a blast and when I die and have to redo a level it's super refreshing and less of a slog to find the layout vastly changed from the last time- it's another way this game keeps it's simple and satisfying formula endlessly fresh.The music is fantastic and quite varied- on par with Doom 2016 which is unparalleled. So ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool.  So ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun.  So ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ GUN.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the graphics put you off.This is old school doom with diablo loot, and the gunplay feels great. A huge amount of weapons, with almost infinite variables and stats. _childDocuments_.review: Nightmare Reaper is a retro shooter that claims to be inspired by roguelites and looter shooters and random levels aside it's mostly a retro looter shooter. And it's rough around the corners, yet it works and offers some intense action!First thing's first, starting with negatives, I must say: this isn't the prettiest and real janky game. The enemy sprites are good but they clash with really mediocre blocky environments. And the environments don't suck solely because style, there's some Z-fighting of level geometry, and not just randomly generated locales at that, but fully handmade ones which is lousy! And there's some moments where you may get stuck or experience some physics or gameplay oddities, not to mention a lot of procgened level geometry can be exposed in more open aired levels and it looks lazy. You could have had some cool spires or whatever, sheesh... Also I imagine Hushult isn't the cheapest composer but wish there were more fitting tracks here, similarly to Dusk, as as-is they all felt samey.Now, the good: It gameplay is actually good, starts off slowish but real quickly gets intense and you constantly unlock new fun things, and the plot that drives you forward is solid enough to grip and motivat eyou when a hard level demotivates you. You gotta beat a locale three times, each local having unique level elements each area gets built from every time, the levels are relatively small so five to twenty minutes time depending on how through you wanna be with one, and there's like almost 30 of them or so? The enemy variety switches with levels, they kinda do get reused but at certain point the weaker enemies disappear and get replaced by new enemy variants, so there's a pretty nice growth of challenge even as core aspects of game, usually, remain the same. Gun variety also grows with progession but there's gonna be plenty of unusual firearms from early on, there's staple guns, magic spellbooks and staves, scifi and pop culture references, and some genuinely original weird stuff like triple naval cannons that shoot out a barrage of shots after a delay.One thing why this is much closer to a looter shooter or action RPG than roguelite? Progression is persistent but also crucial, so it's like Diablo or whatever, gotta grind skill trees. Except here they're represented as... minigames? There's a Super Mario World-like main tree divided into "worlds" where you gotta beat a simple brief paltformer lebel to unlock an upgrade, these are usually creative enough and short not to get onto your nerves, then there's Pokemon-like pet game which I fully neglected, and a bullet hell spaceship exploration where you can unlock unique attacks and bonuses, but which instead of regular currency has a separate you learn in arena, a more close to regular game gameplay mode where you fight off enemy waves. There's a lot to unlock, seemingly tons of content still to unlock in new game plus or so??This is definitely worth a try if you enjoy a retro boomer shooter and some randomness and don't mind rough around the edges visuals and jank.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but this is not the case. I love shooters, but Nightmare Reaper goes to the hall of shame.Some issues:- The minigames. Thankfully you can disable them, but they feel out of place, samey and just a bad version of the games they're supposed to emulate. Just go and make a Mario, Pokemon or Gladius clone instead?- The platforming. , the platforming. Platforming like that has no place on an FPS, especially if your movement feels like you're on rollerblades.- The level design. Sure, it's about it being a roguelite, where you have random levels and lose almost everything when you die. But the levels are all the same, the enemies are all the same, and the weapons are all the same. 8 hours in the game, I'm hoping to find a weapon not present on level 1. It doesn't help that it takes a lot of upgrades to reach a point where you can keep better weapons. Which leads to...- The permanence roguelite mechanic: you keep your favourite weapon from level to level. Since for the majority of the game you'll only be able to keep level 1 weapons, what ended up happening is I had the same weapon saved for all of my playtime. It also meant that the best thing to do was to keep upgrading the skill related to that weapon. Very boring.All in all, it's a bad shooter, with bad roguelite mechanics and bad minigames to get skills. Cannot recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to overstate how good Nightmare Reaper is. In short, buy it, especially at the price point.Yes, it's a 'boomer shooter' in a tide of similar games, but the polish is incredible and the devs obviously put mountains of work into the final product. The first main standout is the overworld hub progression. Each level is a Doom-style ten-minute bite, with every few punctuated by some change in the hub. Each of these feels revelatory and it's a blast unlocking new sections of the hospital.The second is the weapon randomization. Granted, this is often a negative as you end up lugging the same gun through most of the game once you get a particularly satisfying roll, but it's a welcome change to the formula and it's incredibly gratifying when you do find 'the' gun to suit your playstyle.The last is the breadth of different systems. Again, this could be a negative, but the minigames and different systems are a breath of fresh air in roguelike permanent upgrades. Tying the upgrades to Mario-esque, sidescrolling shmup, and Pokemon-style minigames is a unique and novel choice. The best part is, if you hate them, you can turn them off at any time.But these are all icing on the cake and underlying the whole experience is an extremely fun retro-shooter with visual polish (to the extent it's possible) and unique mechanics like a grappling hook and dash. It's a blast to play and even more of a treat if you're into roguelike progression. I can't sing the praises of Nightmare Reaper enough. If you're on the fence, just get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Weapons - I don't think I've found half of them, but most feel vastly different and require a learning curve to master. The RNG modifiers on weapons can make or break the usefulness of that weapon, which is great for grinding out that "Best" weapon, but for the most part the modifiers offer some generic bonuses. Weapons all feel great and most feel fairly balanced. A lot of love went into these.   Solid roguelike mechanics - The level length feels perfect for me. Wiping on a level leaves me wanting to try again. Enemy variation isn't too crazy, but the enemies each feel unique and have patterns to learn/master. Level variation was great, secrets were rarely easy to find even playing the same level over and over. Progression - Yea yea, the minigames are kind of eh sometimes. The upgrades and options start off basic, but when the others are unlocked it's addicting to want to grind out all the upgrades, some of which are pretty game changing. I turned 2 of the 3 minigames off after a bit simply because the length required to play them was more than I wanted to deal with. It's still a cool option, and the fact that you can easily turn it off makes it a non-issue. Graphics - I thought they'd be annoying, but the everything varies enough that each level/weapon/enemy gives off it's own vibe. It looks great honestly. Replayed a few levels that I got stuck on and scoured every level for secrets. I never got bored of the graphics. Movement - You unlock many additional movement options, which add a lot of skill to how you move around the level and  dodge around enemies. I don't think I ever mastered every element of movement. Challenge - Perfect for the roguelike genera, but I've been playing FPS's for a couple decades now. If you've ever enjoyed a fast paced single player FPS (Or any of the retro games this emulates like doom/Hexen/etc) it's like that. Get it. Verdict - If you like FPS's, get it. I'd instantly buy a sequel. Note to the dev: GET CO-OP INTO THIS GAME OR A SEQUEL! I could dump 100 of hours into this game if I could play it with the homies.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start of my review by saying that this is not a 'Don't play this game' Do not recommend, more of a cautionary tale.The game describes itself as a looter shooter and roguelite, but I would say it is neither of those things, or at least not very well designed in those aspects. The game feels like it was designed with a lot of care and had some very good ideas on paper, but when those ideas came to implementation and didn't hold up, instead of being scrapped the devs doubled down.The game is not a Roguelite in the usual sense of the word, you don't lose all progress on death, you just get put back at the beginning of the level, pretty much like Doom or any other FPS game. There is meta progression, but it is lacking the most important part of a Roguelite game. There is also not much progression within the space of a level, you will most likely be as strong at the beginning of the level as you are at the end.As for the looter shooter part of the game, if you are expecting Borderlands levels of loot you will be disappointed. The quantity is definitely there, but the quality isn't which means you will be left with a sea of awful guns to sift through. The overall implementation of loot is very rudimentary, with most guns of the same type feeling exactly the same. I ended up playing the around 80 levels with 3 guns in total, that I kept bringing to the next level and ignoring most others. A shotgun you find on the first level will do the exact same damage as the shotgun you find on the last level.The narrative of the game is another example of sounds good on paper, but breaks down when it meets reality. After every level you get a page of a notebook that explains the overall narrative. Well, page is pushing it, you get a sentence. Since the story the game is trying to tell is very simple lot of these notes are just padding, and you can feel that the developers struggled to come up with enough notes for the 80+ levels the game has. Despite this at the end of the game I still was left kind of confused on what the game was trying to tell me through the notes.The progression systems in the game also fell victim to the same consideration. There are 3 separate progression systems, that are all their own minigames and are also explained in the story. Sounds good on paper, but they end up being a drag as they are understandably rather rudimentary and not well balanced. The upgrades you can unlock are also uninteresting, with most of them being +2 max ammo or +2 starting ammo (not sure why these are separate). I ended up mostly ignoring them in the last 30 levels as they felt like they were not implemented to the core gameplay loop properly.Overall if you are looking for a fun boomer shooter with a creepy aesthetic you won't go wrong with this game. But if you are looking for a roguelike or a looter shooter with good progression you won't find it with Nightmare Reaper.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I share some thoughts:- This game is incredible and needs more love.- Although Nightmare Reaper is pixel art styled, it has a collection of modern shaders wich enhance drastically the visual experience... No need to use Reshade, it would be redundant.- The gameplay is among the best I've experienced in a retro shooter. It is as good as Brutal Doom.- Don't expect a Rogue like game, it's absolutely not that at all. The only two "rogue" elements I've seen so far it's that you can only keep one weapon of your choice at the end of the level and the level maps seem to be randomized (I'm not even sure of that).- Nightmare reaper is more a RPG retro shooter featuring a skill tree and a puzzling but interesting story between each level. I would have liked to have more story elements but it's an Early Access game so maybe it will make sens later in the game.- The skill tree is funny. Whenever you buy a skill, you have to complete a Mariolike platform level. It's very well made and sometime tricky but I don't understand why the devs put some efforts in such a dispensable feature, lol.- The armoury features classic guns but also magic wands, chainsaws, katanas, broadsworsd, spellbooks and knives. All with randomized attributes and rarity level. Really cool.Conclusion :I really love Nightmare Reaper and again, I don't understand why it doesn't have the love it deserves while others retro shooters like Dusk sells hundreds of thousands copies. Really, that's odd considering the pretty low price tag and how the gameplay and atmosphere have nothing to envy to Dusk.PS : To be played in the dark and with headphones !

So if you love Dusk's soundtrack, then you'll love Nightmare Reaper's soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: The game is still filled with bugs with the 1.0 release. The most frustrating issues are unbeatable levels due to the semi-random level design. Some of the level pieces simply do not fit together, rendering the levels impossible to complete.EDIT for the dev response:The two main bugs I had to deal with playing this game last night:1. Weapon not firing. I ran into this one a few times. It appears to resolve itself when you pick up another weapon. But there were times where I could not locate any other weapons to fix the bug (do to being unable to fire) and had to reset the run.2. Enemies appearing behind the walls. This MAY not be a bug technically, but it feels like one. I had multiple instances where I could not find enemies that I could clearly hear. That's normally not a big deal, as the only consequence is that you will miss out on the end-level bonus. However, I had to deal with a red orb that endlessly generates exploding green orbs around the player until it is killed. I dashed through the entire level multiple times looking for it, could never find it. A slow, miserable death for that level. Again, maybe not a bug, maybe just really poor design?3. Level design in general: Perhaps the issue is not the procedural generation creating literally impossible variations (that was simply my guess, dev says it's ABSOLUTELY FALSE, so alright). A few times, I found myself trapped in the levels with no clear exit. This IS due to the procedural design. The pieces may technically fit together, but the variations do not present a visual language that the player can consistently interpret for navigation. The map does help to an extent, but the game starts introducing verticality and alternative zones (e.g. under sewer gates), which makes the map less useful. There were times where instead of running through the entire level looking for what I missed for the 20th time, I just restarted the level to save time. Was it a bug? Or is it simply bad design? I will let the dev decide.I have enjoyed the game to an extent, and love the very creative concepts employed. However, the end experience was simply too frustrating for me to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: I guess. Its addictive. If you are into rouge-lite games sure. I do really like it. But I think more of a tutorial is needed. I admit I am not used to this type of game. But I am getting really frustrated at level 2. I think overall I recommend it, but as much as I want to find out the whole story, the gameplay is turning me off. _childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game...Rouge like looter shooter where the you play through biome after biome of randomly generated maps and pick up and random weapons with random modifiers etc. Think Deadcells but mix that with old school super twitchy FPS like Blood, Hexen, Duke 3d, etc. Music by Andrew Hulshult! Nightmare Reaper is a GREAT homage to what has come before it. You are very likely to trip over cultural references to other DOOMER shooters and their communities while playing this. Even Civvie11 and his sewer count are in there somewhere. The way a standard gameplay loop goes is you jump in your bed, then have a fever dream about Kung Fu Woo Johnning Bunny Hopping Rocket Jumping Double Barreling a map of nightmare demons who explode like candy into coins, ammo and random weapon drops then, at the end of it all when you find the exit, (which may or may not have a boss fight), you get to keep your favourite weapon and pawn the rest for more coins that you can spend in the "skill tree" for character upgrades. Movement is really good and responsive, gameplay is very satisfying. But also... like...I bought in during the first early access and by now I've played through all chapters multiple times, and every time I've done so, It's been very very different. There are times when I see myself defaulting to my reliable well curated weapon selections or other times when I end up with that "what the hell is this thing?!" kinda weapon just making it work. And It has always been fun.Nightmare Reaper isn't a high commit game either. I mean if you want to go deep, you can. There are many different biomes and chapters, mechanical depth, side games within games, even exploring the hub hospital is an adventure in itself. Personally I'm happy just booting this up 20 minutes at a time every now and then blasting through a map or two looking for that golden unicorn best in slot totally not a Belmont whip or w/e weapon I have my sights on. This game will never end, yet it simultaneously respects my time. I really like that.So yeah, great game so far, very much looking forward to where it will go.PS: Yes, you can pet the dog.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Whereas most other modern boomer shooters take after the genre staples, i.e. the Doom-, Quake-, and Build engine games, this one is an unholy bastard child of Rise of the Triad and what feels like half the bloody homebrew DOS game scene of the early 90s. It's a chaotic, densely packed pandemonium of ideas and mechanics that range from janky to surprisingly refined, but always come in short enough bursts to not outstay their welcome, and whenever the inevitable sense of repetition starts to kick in, there's usually a new mechanic being introduced. The result is stupidly fun and addictive.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

If they marked those items on the map it would be a welcome improvement.

_childDocuments_.review: Buying into this wave of retro-fps games, I've played Wrath: Aeon of Ruin, Ion Fury, and this. _childDocuments_.review: Retro FPS meets looter shooter, with roguelike elements, a metal AF soundtrack, and a skill tree you unlock by playing a mario-like minigame on "totally not a GBA" you pull up on the pause screen. _childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to like this game during the hours I played I just can't recommend it. It promises rogue-lite x boomer-shooter elements but it fails to deliver on both ends. The overall gameplay loop is also pretty annoying: complete "nightmare" or arena levels, play mini-games to level up, repeat. This dragged on for too long in a fast-paced shooter.On the rogue-lite side, we get to carry over one level-1 weapon after each "nightmare"; you can upgrade this in the skill tree. Each world consists of 3 levels, but these "randomly generated" levels felt boringly cloned with few differences. I would've preferred to play uniquely designed levels instead. There are also some events that occur based on RNG but it doesn't really make things more interesting. That's it. Did you notice that I didn't mention perma-death or difficulty options? Unfortunately, these don't exist in the game.On the boomer-shooter side, it can actually be pretty fun and fast-paced. I enjoyed the weapon variety. The 2D horror art design and visuals are on point. The puzzles and backtracking elements are also pretty interesting, but they get super repetitive when you're playing the same level layout 3 times per world. If a difficulty option was available I think I would've really, really enjoyed this game: I was super disappointed when I melted the final boss.All in all, Nightmare Reaper fails in its attempt to marry the rogue-lite and boomer-shooter genres together. The level design suffered heavily due to the "rogue-lite" elements. The mini-games interrupted the fast-paced shooting gameplay. And the lack of difficulty options is a BIG negative for both shooter and rogue-lite genre fans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review:I came back to this after the latest update and...I want to like this game so much.  The style and presentation are excellent.  It's an amalgamation of my favorite genres.  But it's just...Not very fun.  Not very good.Maybe it's me.  Maybe I'm doing something wrong.  But I die A LOT, for really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reasons.  I play a lot of roguelikes.  I play a lot of challenging FPSs.  I can rock most hard DOOM WADs on UV no problem. I have 50+ hours in Elden Ring.  I've got most Isaac bosses down to an artform.But Nightmare Reaper kills me in ONLY frustrating ways.  I never ever die by my own error.  I always die because the randomization or blatant design of the game didn't give me anywhere near enough resources, decided to throw insanely tough enemies at me with no weapon options, or decided that a jumping puzzle with instadeath failure consequences in the middle of a level was a good idea.Ammo is far too rare.  Weapons are usually worse than useless.  There's no system to recover if you do run out of ammo and haven't found more weapon variety in a mission yet.  And, as noted in my original review, below, monster health is just out of control nonsense.  Why do some mobs fall to a single bullet but others can soak your entire ammo supply including an entire arena's worth of pickups for 3 weapon slots?  There's also extremely poor telegraphing of where damage is coming from.  Is it a monster right above me?  Is it across the map sniping me through 4 doorways that aligned for 72ms?Also, the ONLY time I get power ups is in the back corners of obscure hallways exactly 95% of the duration of the power up away from the nearest enemy.  Pretty fun.The game basically doesn't give you any tools to succeed and then dumps monsters on you.Which would be fine if:A: the weapons were good relative to monster health B: There was a resource balance that allowed the player to control the pace of combatC: Every other arena wasn't the equivalent of shotgunning 7 Barons of Hell and a Cyberdemon.  It's just NOT FUN.  It's tedious.  When I go bone dry on ammo on ONE mob, EVERY OTHER ROOM, something is seriously, massively wrong with the balance.  It's just not fun. It's not a challenge of skill.  It's not an obstacle you can overcome by practice and persistence.  It is tedium as a shooter.And I have to get back to the weapons: man they're underwhelming.  Sometimes you get one that really feels like it has half a ping pong ball worth of punch, and it's Blue or Gold, and you start to really almost get a combat flow going.  Then you run out of ammo, or you die.  And you lose the weapon.  Or you manage to win and you STILL LOSE THE WEAPON because it's not crappy enough for you to keep yet.  But the crappy weapons you can keep can't take down the mobs that appear in the first room, so you never make any progress.Roguelikes work by setting up a set of very clear rules and giving the player tiny opportunities to use their knowledge of those rules.Nightmare Reaper's rules are nonsense.  It's impossible to enjoy progression in a game where it feels more like luck than skill.  I'd rather fight a pack of 600 Elden Ring dogs than one arena in Nightmare Reaper.It's just bad.  I keep going back to it because the recipe tells me it should be fun.  And every time within 5 minutes I'm angrier than I have been at any other game in decades.Original review below:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Nightmare Reaper is a lot of fun.  It's got the bite-size, high-variety aspect down, but it also uses the flow from dreams to waking to skills minigames to break up the repetition. I love the weapon variety, the art style is great, and movement is sharp, responsive, and fluid.I only really have two complaints with the game:1: Gamepad autoaim is far too aggressive and takes over horizontal control to an intrusive degree.2: Most enemies have WAAAAAAAAAAAY to much health which really harms the pacing of actual combat.  Even good rare weapons take 3-4 hits to take down many fodder enemies, and 4-5 high-damage rockets to take down bigger common enemies is pretty rhythm-shattering, especially in rooms of a dozen enemies.  Hitscanners in particular either need a lot less health or much slower fire rates as a small group can take you from 150hp to 0 in seconds, while you'll spend several times that whittling away at each of them.  I'm not saying I want a DOOM clone (plenty of those) but the balance between zombie, shotgunner, chaingunner, and imp is a great example of how to use hitscanners vs projectile mobs without sludging up the pace.
