_childDocuments_.review: You're a psycho, alone in a ward. There's nothing to do, so go to sleep and dream up some monsters to shoot. An insane asylum is one of the best worst settings for me. Worst because it triggers flashbacks, best because those add some spice to whatever's at hand, I guess. Besides, from a visual standpoint, the place is spot-on. Even the sheet colours are the same as I remember! The ward I was committed to a couple of times looked almost identical, although we had more soul-sucking ceramic tiles everywhere, covering both floors and walls. Maybe also ceilings, but who has the strength to look at the ceiling while injected with horse doses of neuroleptics? Sometimes I felt like I was on them here, especially when the framerate began to dip out of the blue in certain places. I started playing while having a relatively old PC (that could still run Doom Eternal without a hitch), so I thought I deserved it. But recently I got a new powerful rig - and it still dipped! Seemingly at random. Even if not as consistently hard. Someone screwed up, this game doesn't look like it should stutter on anything but a complete potato.At first, without squinting, NR reminded me of Project Warlock (in regards to performance as well). But nope, the quality here is way below its level. And don't get me wrong! When stars align, NR looks fine. You make hordes of demons, warlocks, zombies, biomutant tanks, guys who are circles and guys with televisions for heads go boom in a spectacular manner. It's a diverse bunch that goes along with the eclectic theme of mostly occult insanity. Oh boy, you should see what a clusterf#ck some Desert Eagle with explosive ammo type 2 can create in its midst! Yeah, in theory, there's nothing gorgeously juicy gore can't compensate for. When you can see it, that is, or anything but it. The randomiser doesn't always give you optimal rooms for encounters, squeezing crowds of foes into tight spaces with little to no cover, putting you in situations where you can't even see what's happening behind all the giant pixel particles. To boot, I think the pixel art is just sloppy. The pickup sprites are well-made and recognisable yet enemy designs look messy. Not bad, just incoherent, and they get smeared when piled up. Coupled with excessive particle effects, it turns the game's visuals into pixel porridge during massive fights, which is every fight by the end.Whatever, not a deal-breaker (in moderation), I think NR starts out fine and developers did a great job at improving the look of its environments over time. I suppose I'm in the level design elitist camp when it comes to shooters, hence that Minecraft for office drones didn't entice me enough back when I tried NR a year ago. Do my eyes fail me or do the levels look better now? So bright and sparky, with lovely lights dancing in the air! I didn't appreciate the beginning still, but then the game descended into madness with its insane skyboxes, relentless gigagore, and vibrant lights. These colours out of space make it the Dario Argento of video games. Seriously, though, did they make so much progress since I last looked or was I simply more depressed than usual? Having said that, I still think that generated maps, despite the periodical cosmetical changes, lack the heart and eventually become a blur. I'm also not a fan of NR trying to replace the lack of level design with a stupidly unnecessary amount of lock and key types. I get it, I get it! I need to find a thing, then open a door... uh, right, put that thing into another thing, then open a door? No? Ah, now you invented a new thing that doesn't look like the previous thing... keep it simple, for f#ck's sake!Should I be impressed? Overjoyed? It still feels like playing the same four levels twenty times over. Manufacturing steps and changing appearances doesn't change the fact or add a lot to the gameplay. Now, for the features that definitely add... something, or at least add up to something unique. After beating a level, however annoying it may be later in the game due to thoughtless automated encounter design and inconsiderate ammo placement, you're allowed to keep one gun of choice. I think they should've moved the perk which allows you to keep one more gun closer to the beginning rather than making players wait for twenty-something hours to earn it. I still haven't! It gets old since most generated weapons are trash, so you might get lucky or get completely screwed over for a whole level. It helps that failing isn't too bad when you're plopped into a somewhat new map every time. Nitpicks aside, I liked the system. It forces you to try newly-generated stuff instead of sticking to the same comfortable arsenal. I can see the value in that line of thinking yet the implementation could be less restrictive. In my eyes, one should be permitted to muster a custom arsenal after a certain point.To take a break from whining, let's say I loved the challenge rooms with hazardous trials and tight-timed puzzles! And I enjoyed killing stuff, chaining combos, flying around using a grappling hook with fun physics, exploring the levels to find treasures, spending them on incremental upgrades. Initially, I didn't mind dying, too. You wake up in the ward after death, losing all progress in a level except for treasures, usually worthless without the multiplier. Then go back to a new one, partaking in an engaging gameplay loop, which sometimes breaks for a while. I kept selling my best legendary weapons, the deals were too lucrative in terms of coin. There's nothing I wouldn't do for coin since it means fresh perks. And sometimes I did it without thinking in the middle of a level. Don't die if you do this or you'd have to partake in a new slaughter map with nothing but a trusty kick, desperately throwing yourself at hordes of monsters in hopes they'd drop something useful quickly. Ah, the suffering! There's nothing like cornering yourself for no good reason, am I right? Persevere or get lucky. And I did, sticking with chewing that stale loaf until I gagged.But I can't drop a shooter just because I can't see sh#t, most guns are unusable garbage, and the levels are sort of insipid, can I? Besides, NR kept throwing me curve balls... of varying quality maybe, albeit, they were enough to make me expect positive changes to the formula. I gave it my all and hoped for the best. So what if I hated a few enemy types, the islands in the void, and spawn crystal rooms? It was bound to happen due to the game's atypical girth. NR experiments and makes mistakes, knowing full well no annoying feature would last long enough to completely discourage you from pressing on. For a time, it worked like a charm. However, pacing matters. There's simply too much of the same in NR, it kept going until it began to drag. After a certain threshold was reached, little problems I'd shrug off before got magnified tenfold. Upon playing for 15 hours, I considered this game a masterpiece, but I was spent after 20, wishing for it to be over. The late-game difficulty spikes are nothing short of obnoxious and its simplistic level design doesn't leave room for tailored encounters. NR plays itself out like almost any other shooter would in its place. It was disheartening to see it dip like that by the end, disappointing not to be able to make myself finish it.  ahem. In the end, it was a fine 15-hour game. But can I really recommend it by saying that one should drop out in the middle? I don't think so.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Whoooooole lot to say about this one.Nightmare Reaper is... a game. You can play it! It is one of the games of all time.I'm very middling on this. I'm not very far in, but there are things that I have loved and things that I have hated. I'm just going to list some (what I think to be) pros and cons, and give my conclusion so far. You take it as you like.Pros:The shooting feels incredibly good!The looter-shooter aspect is held up by an astonishing variety of weaponry that, based on the rarity, has even more variety through modifications, eg explosive ammo, lightning damage, etc.The story seems very intriguing so far.There is a Pokemon style mini-game to level up.Randomised levels automatically creates a level of replayability.I love the main character and her design.Cons:Levelling up requires you to play a 2D platforming minigame, with at least 3 screens, (PLEASE READ EDIT)Levelling up even more requires you to play ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ POKEMON, including all the grind that comes with that game.The level design feels uninspired, partially because they're randomised (i don't really mind this all the time, but the randomisation feels... idk Bad) and partially because the textures are very VERY pixelated, to the point where I can't tell what some things are supposed to be (although this very well could be a me issue)There are a lot of very small, tedious little details that add up, like how you need to kick a cracked wall multiple times before it opens, and the kick is very slow, or the fact that you return to a bedroom every time you die or complete a level. It's a fun novelty at first, but gets old.My final thoughts:If you go into this expecting a pure Boomer Shooter, Bunny hop-at-mach-12, quad barrel shotgun toting experience much like I did, then you're going to be slightly disappointed. The demo also doesn't really help with this, either, as it shows only the first level, which doesn't have much of the tedium in it quite yet. (READ EDIT) I can't bring myself to  recommend this, though. The core gameplay loop is lacking and there's a lot of little annoying things here and there, but honestly I have a lot of respect to the devs for sticking to their vision. They made this game however the damn well they pleased, and it shows! It was also a pleasant surprise to learn that Andrew Hulshult composed the soundtrack, and Gianni Matragrano doing some voice acting, too. If you're after a somewhat unique experience with some satisfying shooting, broken up by 2D platformers and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Pokemon Blue, then first off, why? but secondly, Nightmare Reaper is perfect.EDIT: Thanks to a response from the Dev, i've since learned that A: The demo is way longer than I thought, I am just INCREDIBLY stupid and B: The levelling minigames can be disabled, again, I'm very dumb. With that in mind, I still very much do recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed old school-style shooters like the entire Doom franchise and Dusk, or looter shooters like Borderlands, this was definitely a treat to play. I first heard about this game because I heard Andrew Hulshult, my favorite video game composer of all-time, has worked on its soundtrack, and the soundtrack was beyond badass. All the guns were fun to use, I had no problems switching out my previous gun from time to time. All the trees felt satisfying to progress through, especially the skill tree which I looked forward to unlocking the next extremely useful skill, not to mention that the level design in the platforming was superb (it's just a minigame btw lol). The story is nice and simple, portrayed through single sentences which is appropriate for a old school-style shooter.It's a game that isn't faultless, however. Had performance issues throughout the game. Ran at 1440p, epic settings on a 3070. At-times I was able to at least nearly match my high refresh rate with FPS, but some areas or even maps dipped in frames. Stuttering came along, too. Games like Doom and DUSK I didn't have issues like these, especially Doom which is an AAA title in comparison to Nightmare Reaper being an indie, and is overall more demanding. A handful of enemies like the auto-shotty skeletons and the grappling hook demon felt downright cheap and unfair, you die instantly to them the moment you make a single mistake and is ultimately unsalvageable. I thought that the randomly-generated levels could have been handled better, at-times it just felt like a mess especially in comparison to levels that are made with precision.Those few cons aside, this game is a spirited effort and became one of my favorite games of the year. Definitely give it a go, guys. Can't wait to see you guys in the Game Awards, if that'll ever be possible.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE 2: So the game got updated again and personally I thought many of the changes were excellent and exactly what I would've wanted coming from the older versions I'd played. What I wasn't prepared for was the new content that blew my expectations away.Aside from many many quality of life changes and general functionality improvements that, I as an older player, found scratching every itch, the new chapter of the game surprised me. From the get go, the map design fully broke out of whatever confines it had impressed in the previous chapters, and immediately lent much credibility to the otherwise stifled movement options available prior. Already large and open arenas fell away to totally open platform-based map design. Despite the occasionally strange situation encountered due to the doorway restrictions extending all the way through the playable map, the new areas introduced let you really fly around with the grapple, creating many scenarios yet unseen.As the chapter progressed, the encounters also did a good job of reflecting the chaotic, hectic nature of a nightmare nearing its conclusion. Cohesion and recognizable features give way to more illusory and imaginary environments. Paired with the narrative beneath, as well as more adventures in the hospital, the atmosphere was maintained and nurtured properly. The updates to the gameplay, such as NG+ and Survival, also served to improve the overall quality of the game. The survival mode became a small obsession of mine as I started getting more used to the new movement options, as well as providing a much needed increase in enemies to slaughter. The NG+, on the other hand, went out of its way to scale in such a way that I didn't feel like I was any more overpowered than usual. All in all, the game is in a very good place.-- Older Reviews:UPDATE: PLEASE PLEASE ADD PLAYABILITY AFTER YOU REACH THE END OF CHAPTER 2. I finished the boss that marks the end of Chapter 2 and immediately hit something tragic: I can't play! I can't use my upgraded perks or my saved weapon or anything! While I can start a new save and repeat the grind, I must admit, I'm spoiled. Especially so soon after my first run, jogging around the early levels and replaying the perk minigames isn't enough. I need the carnage! I NEED THE SLAUGHTER! Devs your game is amazing but I can't help but lament my inability to play more.My best suggestion is, as a placeholder, just let me sleep and go back to the hub area, with all of the portals open again. Whichever I run into starts that string of levels again, until I beat the boss. Then, return to the hub as usual, of course with every portal still active, and do it again. I beg of you. IM PLEADING. PLEASE. PLEASE. YOUR GAME IS SO GOOD.Also some optimization might be nice too, but I just want to play. If I see an update in the next month or so with anything like I suggested above, I can GUARAN-♥♥♥♥♥-TEE I will hit 50 hours EASILY!!!!!!! I LOVE THIS GAME!!!!!!!!!!Since I like this game I wrote a lot, TL;DR below.It's insane how fluid this game feels. Despite the art style and presentation, this game is a fully functioning 3D game. The movement feels tight and responsive, which matters in the multiple puzzle platforming sections that appear to give you a shot at better loot, and offers many maneuvers to help aid in level traversal as well as combat. The platforming as well, unlike what you would expect from a 3D platformer/shooter, feels very fun to perform, and is almost always optional save from certain level areas. I had a lot of fun beating the variety of courses I encountered, and it served as a nice mixup to the normal gameplay of shooting and running, alongside the perk minigames.Enemies are exceptionally well done, and feel challenging and chunky to attack without being too overwhelming or bullet spongy on their own. Again, this is where the 2D sprites belie the 3D functionality underneath. Enemies path properly, never get caught on geometry where you'd expect otherwise, and boast very pleasing headshot hitboxes. The variety of enemies is also well done, and progression of more advanced enemy types flaunt more varied attack patterns and styles rather than a simple palette swap with increased health. I especially love how when you kill enemies, their 2D sprites become 3D models, kinda like cardboard cutouts, and fall over. It's immensely gratifying. The bosses too aren't exceedingly challenging, but provide just enough variety to satisfy that feeling of progression. The weapons are also a treat. While the roguelite stats occasionally feel useful, they are more often than not underwhelming aside from blood ammo, which is a great detractor. The actual variety between weapons, however, is fantastic. Each weapon offers something unique, and while I found myself with preferred choices, every weapon I tried had a clear cut function that felt interesting and useful. My favorite so far has definitely been the Consecrated Whip: that thing blasts EVERYTHING for the low cost of 5 magic ammo. The game mechanics as well feel great. The procedural level generation, while occasionally giving me some templated rooms that I definitely recognized, is stable. Likewise, as the player unlocks more and more movement techniques, the overall design of arenas really opens up, creating opportunities for really exciting fights. Dying never feels punishing either. Sure you have to replay the level, but you lose nothing else besides that single level's progress. All the gold you collected remains, and while you don't get to sell the other weapons you collected, you still hold on to the last weapon you picked to keep. This leads us into possibly my favorite feature of the game, weapon retaining:At the end of every level you must decide what weapon to keep. This selection is limited to a level 1 weapon, however, unlocking additional perks expands the level cap of what you can select. As long as a weapon is under a certain level, you can keep it, regardless of what tier it is. This results in many quirks to gameplay, each of which I absolutely adore. For starters, it forces all us kleptomaniacs into a more comfortable headspace. Knowing we can only pick one weapon to keep has saved me from obsessing over what I'm carrying. It also limits the sort of firepower that you can bring between levels, as you may find higher level weapons but be unable to carry them over, preventing you from steamrolling the game due to one lucky find. That one weapon you pick, however, allows you to confidently approach the next level knowing that the one weapon you DID pick is there to have your back as you progress. (GO CONSECRATED WHIP!)I haven't explored the game nearly enough to have opinions on everything, I haven't even beat it yet, although I'm four bosses in. I wish the reroll stats seller was a bit more varied, often it feels like a stat is locked and the reroll only changes the specific value. Other than that, I really haven't found anything that really bothers me beyond better optimization. Fantastic game, feels amazing to play. TL;DR Movement and shooting feels very very good, and very very fun. Enemies are exceptionally varied and all have unique threat patterns, as well as appearances and sounds. The level generation is slick as hell, and the weapons are all super duper fun to use. As far as Early Access titles go, this game is essentially finished, so I cannot wait for the degrees of polish and new content that will continue to come as time proceeds. My only real gripe is that when you gain the chance to reroll stats on weapons, it often times feel restrictive, as you cannot roll a malus into a bonus (or vice versa, fortunately), and most rerolls seem to only change the numerical value instead of the actual bonus (i.e. Pull 250% will get rerolled into Pull 315% etc.). Likewise you cannot reroll Blood Ammo, which kinda sucks, cause some weapons really, really do not like blood ammo.

_childDocuments_.review: I was warned about this game. But the draw of playing through recommended Steam boomer shooters was too great. This game is not for the faint of heart. The visual style and repetitive puzzle solving will almost certainly drain even the lootiest of loot goblins. Combat CAN be satisfying and a lot of the guns can be fun to use. I found myself maining a legendary mini gun for the majority of my play through. It is absolutely not enough to warrant a play though. Movement is actually very satisfying, especially vertical movement with the grapple. I was very surprised to see this mechanic worked consistently. But yes, you can abuse it to bypass a lot of puzzles. Good riddance. I'm not sure if it's the procedural generated levels or the broken ways in which you traverse them, but I found myself hoping that it would be over as soon as possible. I feel like all of the little nuances that make this game "quaint" end up adding hours of tedium. Talking specifically about the 8 bit mini games for your character upgrades, and the "complexity" of the treasure hunting puzzles. You can turn them off by the grace of god. I would say if your able to get this game dirt cheap and enjoy the first few parts - or even the first chapter - you'll like this game. But if you're like me and you LOVE a majority of the retro shooters on steam and you're just not sure - stay away. This game was just straight up not for me. The only reason I played through this game was simply to say that I've completed it. I realized it wasn't going to get any better after chapter 2. I hope in future games (possibly a sequel?) is able to improve upon its world and be a much more personalized experience minus some of the power ups and occasional cameos art. A lot of questionable design choices made by a very competent development team. I wish them all the luck in the world!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fantastic blend of the boomer shooter and looter shooter genres, the meta story is interesting enough if not a little cliche but still fun to follow along to. The over all design of the levels and the hospital are super fun and very atmospheric (Hospital is super spooky when it wants to be). Almost all of the weapons and weapon stats are awesome though there are definitely some duds and bad combos that are not fun or not worth using which creates a problem when you decide to hold on to one for a new level (Looking at you blood ammo P90 T_T).My only gripe with the game is the level layouts on new game. They're just not that fantastic. New game+ layouts however, are absolutely amazing and I wish some of those layouts were in the initial new game instead of being gated behind new game+. In the base new game the rooms are fairly linear, small, and not with that many enemies (Especially in the earlier chapters), I feel like the base new game, while great already, would have been even better with more to run around in and more enemies to shoot at per room.Overall the game is fantastic and if you're a DOOM fan or twitch arena shooter fan you will definitely enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much inspired by Doom, nightmare reaper is an FPS game where you fight weird as ♥♥♥♥ monsters. The set list of guns found in Doom have been replaced by a more looter-shooter style pickup, where you find an assortment of stat-randomised weapons around a level, and are allowed to keep one to carry onto the next. Contains strange mini-games used to unlock buffs in the shooting part; a pokemon clone where you level up creatures and fight enemies, a mario clone where you choose a "world" (an upgrade) jump on blocks and collect coins/powerups, and finally an bullet-hell style minigame where you fly a space ship around and kill enemies while dodging their attacks.The plethora of weaponry feels great and is very varied; lots of close range melee weapons mixed in with guns and an explosive arsenal.There are some environmental story telling elements, your safe-hub is a hospital room that you can later explore in more detail, with some notes written about the games lore, but nothing that ties back into the actual action part of the game.One of the few games to keep me interested in it after a few hours of gameplay, and I do recommend to anyone who likes the old Doom games.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR 7/10 DOOM shooter with fun tight shooting, but suffers from over length for the content offered.  It's fun for a time but couldn't bring myself to finish it. Core elements are great, but it definitely overstays it's welcome after about 12 hours of gameplay. Would have preferred Unique level design with premade levels than the odd randomly generated thing they went for. Everything feels like the same level with a new texture. Pros------Fun, DOOM like combat that feels pleasant.-Unique weapon variety to use each stage.-RPG level up elements are fun to do.Cons-------Stages start too blend, far too much of the same thing throughout the game.-Weapons are unique, don't feel like they get much stronger as you go, and you end up sticking with the same thing level after level.-Most enemies are just recycled with minor changes and reskin.

_childDocuments_.review: I've purchased and played this game on the PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. I LOVE this game for the non-stop action, great music from Andrew Hulshult, diverse enemies, insane weapons, and finally a really good random level generator. I'm not big into rogue-lite gameplay but Nightmare Reaper does a really good job of it. I've came across weapons that fires poop with fire damage or a minigun that fires cannonballs. Want a gun that fires rubber chicken? You got it! I insist every one to try this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the lovechild of a quality gzdoom based mod and a rogue like (this is a good thing).  A few things I wish I had been aware of at the start: you can turn off any of the mini games that you don't like.  The skill tree is huge with more than enough buffs, skills, and talents to keep you busy.  The mid game is merely okay - once you acquire and upgrade the dash, the grappling hook, and the wall sliding you become a nigh unstoppable tornado of destruction (more akin to a flying wood chipper than a person).  Negatives include repetition, the opaque nature of what you should focus on upgrades wise (read a guide - it helps), and I found that I had to cap the frame rate to keep my graphics card from getting pegged at full blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Right off the bat I don't generally care for Roguelikes/lites and super crunchy pixelated graphics can be hit or miss with me.But I love this game! The shooting is fast and satisfying and the aforementioned roguelike elements are not overly punishing. The graphics are easy to read and the levels are short enough where you get that "just one more level" feeling and lose 3-4 hours. I am not even through the EA content on this one yet but in the current boomer shooter craze if you like great combat, procedural generation on levels and lots of randomized guns then this is one to pick up!
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: Nightmare Reaper is a fantastic game. A beautiful blend of upgrades with impact, visceral gunplay, and a story that left me playing the game for a couple more hours every night - after 22 hours, I've managed to finally get to NG+!The movement can feel a little unusual at times, with guns that you'd expect to have more knockback not... really giving much knockback. But with the arsenal that there is, you're bound to find something that'll make your job easier.The new upgrade systems, being the Topaz and Jade carts, seem unusual to me. I know that since we're in NG+ territory, it makes sense to have extra upgrades (and may as well have new gameplay loops for those upgrades!) but I've not really found much pleasure in playing the turn-based battler, or the space shooter. Perhaps they'll grow on me.The game also has a few hitches and stutters when loading big areas - but this could just be my issue.Nitpicks aside, this game is wonderful. Most of the guns have a beautiful sound and design to them, and combined with the gore, makes dispatching enemies SO cathartic. The homages and easter eggs are a cute touch, and it shows that the team at Blazing Bit Games wanted to make this game worth every cent. $30.99 seems like a fair hike for an indie game, but it's worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: From the trailers you can expect the same type of action- there is downtime such as when you clear a room, you can mostly path back and get drops that you missed or were full on before.Overall pretty fun, I enjoyed the levels and enemies, it could use more varied types.  The current amount of weapons could do with more but still enjoyable.I found a rare ice tome early on, before the first boss, and that thing made the game a cake walk, continued to use it up until the end of the available content – makes me thing the game was too easy, but when I tried to not use that weapon I would have trouble.The minigame could stand to be reworked so that when you are in the overworld you travel to nodes in one click instead of grid based movement or for that area to use the arrow keys as well as wasd.As what seems to be becoming a standard for unreal engine game, it will unfortunately lag randomly and stutter in parts.Got my eye on the game for future content, hoping the ending does not turn out to be herp derp ‘so sad too bad, you’re crazy’, that will change the review from positive to negative as resolution plays a large part.
_childDocuments_.name: Nightmare Reaper

_childDocuments_.review: This game's truly a little gem for what it has to offer, but there's been a few points where I felt fatigue from playing through it. Some points felt like the length was just getting stretched out with mixed hub-world levels of sorts (it's a bit odd) but again overall very enjoyable time and if you think you'd like the game I'm sure you would.

_childDocuments_.review: Take the Borderlands loot system, mix it with boomer shooter gameplay that only gets better the more you play, a protagonist who resembles Alice from Alice Madness Returns, add procedurally generated areas (which are way better than I thought), then to top it off make it roguelite with skill points you can buy and lots more.It was a blast to play through and I'll most likely start new game+ in the future for sure, my only issue is that RNG took a big role in terms of difficulty and drops, that and technical issues which got fixed halfway through my playthrough! I was so pleased to see it run great after the update, not perfect but smooth enough.Highly highly recommended

name: The Red Lantern
detailed_description: The Red Lantern is a narrative, dog-sledding game about survival. You play as the Musher as she makes the rash decision to start a new life in Alaska. Along with her best friend Chomper, she assembles a dog sledding team and embarks on a journey to find her new home. Unfortunately, she isn’t quite prepared for this adventure. She must learn to adapt so she can take care of herself and her dogs as they try to find their way through the wilderness. Features In this trail-based adventure game you must manage your resources, care for your team, and learn from your failures to find your way home. Choose the 4 dogs that will complete your team, each with their own unique personalities and stories to discover. Learn from your failures and become better prepared for your journey. Explore the wilderness of Alaska as you choose how to approach the various wildlife you’ll encounter. Take care of your dogs by hunting to collect meat, caring for them at camp, and making sure to rest. Unlock upgrades to your sled and find tools that will help you and your team on your journey. Continue to explore and train your dogs after you reach the cabin. And adopt your remaining dogs! Relax with Zen Mode (unlocked at the cabin) where you can sit back and let the dogs run. Thank you for checking out The Red Lantern. We appreciate the support!

_childDocuments_.review: So reading over my review I guess this a review for people who are buying games because they want something to occupy them and work their brain a little.TL;DR: The Red Lantern is like a visual novel. It's completely point and click and every action is made through text choices. You cannot move with WASD. You cannot steer your sled in any way other than saying "Haw"(Left) or "Gee"(Right) when you reach a fork in the trail. You can pick which sled dogs you have at the beginning but that's about where the choices that make you feel in control end.A lot of games I find tend to be very beautiful- and this one is no exception. However, when it comes to beautiful games that are below $40USD, I tend to triple check the reviews. The Red Lantern's reviews were a bit of a problem for me so I didn't buy until it went on sale. I bought it for 50% off aka $12.49USD and while the game is pretty, the dogs are cute, and the idea of it is nice... the gameplay is just.. boring.I've seen it dozens of times with games like these where they're really short and lack anything to keep the average player's attention but still have Mostly Positive rating because they're short games with beautiful artistic graphics that some people can replay over and over because they're imaginative enough for it- so this is a review for people who want a game to entertain them all the way through instead of a game to assist in you entertaining yourself through imaginative roleplay. There's no shame in a game like that, it's just not what I- and whoever this review may assist- are looking for.It's a pretty game, but it's boring. You start with 1 dog, your sled team leader, Chomper, and pick 4 to sled behind him- the order of the dogs' positions does not matter though. You visit 8 dogs or so to pick your 4 and go through them one by one until you have a full team. Each dog has their own unique set of events as far as I'm aware. All of the dogs are adorable and/or pretty. The world looks pretty too- snowy landscapes tend to be that way after all and the art style is appealing. However, once you make it past the intro you may become quickly disappointed by the fact that as I said before this game is basically a visual novel. You have no control over the sled until you make it to a fork in the road where you can then choose right or left. The dogs will then drive right or left. At no point can you use WASD or arrow keys to actively move (off and on the sled). Everything is point and click and a lot of the cutscenes are unskippable and too long to be repeatable... and yet they are. You are not able to skip them even after seeing them once before which is kinda annoying to be honest for the longer ones. You can press "c" to set up camp at the next safe spot. At camp you'll have full view of all the dogs chilling about you can pet each one of them, check and light your campfire where you can then cook food, feed the dogs by clicking on their bowl, click your sleeping bad to sleep, or click your sled to go back sledding. All of these actions involve the screen going black and teleporting in front of whatever you're interacting with other than sleeping and sledding. You can not use WASD within camp either. I didn't expect a giant open-world experience but I was hoping to be able to at least steer my sled and walk around and explore different areas without the game doing it for me. Honestly, if I could have control over my own movements and skip cutscenes that I've already seen, I'd probably be totally fine with going through the repetition just to unlock everything in the end, but unlike other games, I don't feel like I'm actually in control. I feel like I'm just watching a movie where I can't even skip the parts that I've already watched- cutscenes and gameplay itself.If this is something that you're interested in then good on you, but it's just not something I'm looking for and I'm hoping I can help other people like me who didn't know that this was completely point-and-click and also solely randomized while seemingly not having too many events in itself..
_childDocuments_.name: The Red Lantern

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended with *huge* caveats.**Do Not** buy this game if you are expecting an action-adventure game similar to The Long Dark or Green Hell or another other Survival genre game out there where you actively explore, loot, hunt, fish and craft. This isn't that kind of game.Roguelite- expect to die often. Food does not go far, and you will die of starvation over and over, as your hunting opportunities are all scripted encounters. The hunting mini-game kinda sucks too- you will have few bullets, and some big critters like a caribou may turn out to be bullet sponges- leaving you with no food and no bullets.  You'll die, and you'll start again.The game is more of a Visual Novel with a "Survive in the wilds" flavor to it."Choices Matter"- well, yes and no. Some situations and encounters seem to have scripted encounters or results, no matter what choice you make, while others have differing results.You only get to choose what direction you "explore" in at forks in the road- you choose left or right. You do not get to explore the entire world- which is a shame, since it is a beautiful world.The audio is quite good, as is the voice acting. You can pet the doggos.The music is quite nice.I really like the stylized art style of the game.But it *is not* a survival game, It is a guided story, linear, with some differences in what you will find and where you will find the,m based on "Gee" and "Haw" choices at forks in the road. You are not going to be fist-fighting a wolf, or killing every yummy-looking animal along the way. You are going to find new things, meet new critters, learn new things each time, then die, and start again with the new items and knowledge.There are no good guides for the game, and it looks like the developers may have abandoned the game, or run into development interruptions. They were active on the forums when the game first released, but there has been no response to player questions in some time.It's still a beautiful game that runs well pn my older machine with an 19 9900K/ 2070 RTX Super/16 GB DDR4 RAM- though it does not run at a steady 144 fps (setting it to a max 61 fps via the NIVIDIA control panel does make it run smoothly at 60 fps). It is a chill game- not high action. Knowing what you are buying and not expecting it to be a TheLogDarkDogSleddingSim is key. I recommend it only at a deep discount, since any bugs or technical issues may or may not be dealt with if the devs have ghosted. But I can see sinking 10-20 hours into the game trying to complete the story and the journal, in short-ish sessions- so 50% off or more, maybe, if hours/$ matter to you. I don't love it all (only parts of it), but I don't hate it either- just a bit frustrated with the hunting minigame and lack of food availability for you and your dog team if no hunting situations come up in your travels. Expect to die and restart a good number of times.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this game. Because it's definitely overpriced, and even if it wasn't, it's definitely too short for my taste. After just 4 hours, it seems as though you've already seen the majority of what the game has to offer, barring teeny tiny (and grindy) pet stories that require you to go through the same content over and over again just to get 3-4 or so events related to a given pet. But the 4 hours that I played were really fun and relaxing. I really wish there were more maps to delve into once you beat the game once, as that would more than have motivated me to keep going. New events, new dangers, perhaps a sort of resource management game with the cabin where you actually have to live in the cabin, I would've loved that. But once you've reached the cabin, it seems as though that's just kind of it. You can go out onto the same trail or adopt a new dog, only to go out into the same content again. Which is too bad. A great concept, definitely. But I personally thought there'd be more to it. If you want something to chill out with for a few hours, fine, go for it. But I wouldn't pay full price for it, wait for it to go on sale!

_childDocuments_.review: I see dogs I buy. 10/10Can you pet the dogs?  --- YES! <3But in all honesty it's a wonderful atmospheric game. You need to decide which dogs will join your journey. Choose wisely since it will affect your encounters. You decide about breaks and how you want to ration your supplies. If you are brave or take some risks you can find some useful stuff. But be careful depending on your decisions it can mean losing one of your good boys. (you can actually turn off possible death of your dogs in the settings)This game is about trial and error. You probably won't make it in the first run. But that's ok. Since it restarts from the point after you chose your furry companions. Every useful item you found in your playthrough will be packed on your next try. It can get pretty repetitive with each run. It‘s possible you will witness the same events multiple times. At first it‘s gonna be charming and sweet but I‘m sure there are people who don‘t enjoy seeing the same sequence times and times again. I actually didn‘t mind. You will definitly listen to the same monologe of our protaganist. That was the one thing which got me sighing. But it‘s still worth the experience. The scenery is beautiful.It‘s so satisfying starting more and more prepared for your journey.And making it to the goal feels great.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly, it's not the idea of seeing a dog getting hurt that is making me turn away here.  Sad as it is, while this game has loads of charm thematically, it is just awful mechanically.This game suffers from the same issue that made me throw away a number of other games that use this particular mechanism.  You are presented with choices in the form of prompts and a list of possible responses.  However, those choices often don't make any sense, and ofttimes the little 1-2 word options don't really tell you what's on the far side of them:Prompt: There's an owl.  Response: Owls are cool.  Result: Nope, owls are bad.  Me: What?Prompt: There's an owl.  Response: You said owls were bad.  Don't follow.  Result: *run over by an elk*  Me: What?Prompt: There's a caribou.  Response: Let's hunt it.  Result: It didn't immediately keel over like this is some sort of video game.  Secondary prompt: Do you want to shoot it again?  Response: I guess I should preserve my bullets by tracking it and waiting for it to bleed out, like hunters do.  It'll probably use time/energy, but I have enough to spend a point and this should be a lot of food.  Don't shoot it again.  Result: Choosing not to shoot again means leave it alive and wounded for some reason, wasting the bullet and leaving it to die pointlessly.  Me: What?  Why is that an option?Even the little hunting minigame suffers from a similar lack of control.  The only thing you control is one button to change the relative rhythm of a pair of UI elements and then you click when they overlap.  It's just obtuse.  What could be more controlled than using a long-barreled rifle to shoot something that's less than ten feet away?  Is the bouncy circle my aim?  Am I so drunk/inept that I can't just line up some sights on something at damn near point-blank?The other issue is how it handles the roguelite element.  You don't start out with all the tools to succeed and learn to use them, putting the onus on you to get better as a player.  You are supposed to go through repeated failure from lacking tools and earn the tools through your pointless pain.  This is just bad design.It's one thing for a game to be difficult, but a game where the biggest difficulty lies in its intentional obscurantism is just annoying.  It's like learning to play monopoly, but you have to lose enough times to start with money and you aren't allowed to read the properties before buying them.  I can't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was dreading playing this game. I thought it would be hard and I would get frustrated playing it. It was such a nice surprise when I first tried this game!+ gameplay is very simple - most of the time you just make choices - basically only other thing to do (at least that I found so far) is timing the shoot (I hate you, dev, I am awful at this) and holding the line in place when fishing.+ I love how there is an option to make dogs not die! I would be devastated if they did.+ on the same note - a nice touch to be able to continue the same save with more items/experience - and how it's explained by "waking up from nightmare"+ graphic, atmosphere and aesthetic - amazing. Loved just checking my surroundings between stops because it looks beautiful+ very relaxing because gameplay is pretty simple (except the shooting but that's a me problem)+ good music, sounds, narration/voice acting+ nice, interesting story; nicely made characters; and funny jokes (I am sorry, Barkley who doesnt bark? XD)+ did I say you can pet the dogs? YOU CAN PET THEM and they are good boys.+ someone said it's a negative thing, but I like how you have basically no help or explanation through the game. I liked the learning process, made me get more immersed into the story - I had to pay attention, take mental notes which animal is the best to hunt, which route to take, how to act to be safe etc.... My first run lasted like 15 min max maybe? I didn't know what to do, how to do it, soon I was gone and guess what? _childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art style and functioning gameplay, but not for me. The idea of rogue-like survival runs like this is actually pretty cool, but instead of letting you try your best to chose a loadout that you can afford, dealing with your own choices, it puts you into the shoes of the main character. A girl in an existential crisis who thinks that it's a good idea to pack 3 bullets in a rusty old gun for an adventure like this. Let alone from enough meat to not starve a day. I know this is the gameplay loop and makes for a quick end of runs, but I had preferred if that quick end came because of other means that don't have you sit in front of the screen and shake your head on the level of irresponsibility the protagonist puts her dogs into in order to "find herself".I'm not a fan of this premise - it's the typical american luxury life problem type of person who lost herself in consumption and now thinks that pulling six dog lives into her struggle and just go fully unprepared into the wilderness is a good idea.Like... how am I supposed to empathise with that? The description reads "learn from your failures to find your way home" - but they aren't my mistakes. It's not my mistake to get run over by a moose regardless of whether I keep going or check out the owl. It's not my mistake that I can't hunt for food anymore because I brought 4 bullets. It's not my mistake that I didn't bring a fishing pole, nor that I didn't bring an axe right away.For the gameplay loop this works, as you iteratively "automatically" learn from these mistakes. But it's a bit like a rail shooter. I just have to die often enough to get the good stuff, and there's no way around it. There is nothing to "survive" in this game. You can't make the right choices to survive because the character that you play, or rather watch running into her doom with little participation, has already made the wrong ones before you even start the run.For whom it's fun to spend hours on watching someone else make absolutely bonkers levels of stupid mistakes (Like who doesn't bring an axe. a fishing rod and a gun with a few packs of bullets with them?), just to live them out and be rewarded by the character iteratively realising her stupidity and incrementally "changing" them, then this game is for them.Like "Oh, in my "bad dream" we died because I just brought 3 bullets. Maybe I'll pack 4 next time" - sorry, this just doesn't work for me. Pretty visuals and lovely theme and setting set aside.
_childDocuments_.name: The Red Lantern

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful, immersive, and genuinely emotionally engaging game that will speak to your heart if you're feeling lost or looking for meaning in your life. On top of that, it's also a pretty fun resource management game for your first few runs. However, after those first few runs the game's Achilles Heel becomes prominently on display, which is that the game is very easy when you figure out how to allocate the few different kinds of resources necessary to survive. And because of how easy the game is when you learn its rules, it also becomes extremely short, especially for a game of its price. Despite only having 1.8 hours on this game I have beaten its main campaign, sure I haven't beaten all side content or discovered all encounters, but I've seen a vast majority of what this game has to offer and beaten the entirety of its main campaign in under 2 hours. After two runs where I failed early on, the last run I made through very easily, not because I'm a god gamer or anything, the game's just hella easy, which would be fine if the campaign wasn't so short.I actually do really like the concept and execution of this game, and there's a ton of aspects of this game that I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loved, but there is just WAY too little for the price. sad not recommended
_childDocuments_.name: The Red Lantern

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I'm bad at words so perhaps I won't be able to capture how good this game is, but honestly its a real treat!! :'DI'm a sucker for any games with dogs in it, and especially about the sport of sledding, so when my brother sent it to me I had to try it. The dogs all have unique personalities, the journey has beautiful sights to see with the graphic style, and overall I adored it personally! Pros:- Dogs. Do you need more- The more attempts you take on the the runs, the better your next chances are. I appreciated the fact that any gear you found carried over! It feels rewarding being able to make another attempt and actually feel like you know what you're doing- Back on the dogs; they do all have their own personalities and perks to the team, learning about them is really sweet actually- The graphics and music are gorgeous and I love the stylistic choices the team made! Cons:- As stated in another review; the runs can get a bit repetitive, and the monologue's do replay sometimes. Luckily mine actually muted so I didn't have to hear it again, not that I minded though, but keep this in mind if you're easily annoyed by repeated things.- You won't always get chances to bond with your dogs. In my run I picked up Stilton, Barkley, Fin, and Noodle. While I had chances to learn more about Barkley and Fin.I actually bonded with Fin enough to pet her hehe. I didn't get as many chances nor prompts for Stilton and Noodle. Perhaps they come later on, but it seemed a bit strange to me- Another note about bonding with the dogs; this does not carry over on new runs, which is understandable, but can be a bit annoying- especially if you become dependent on some of the things they can do once bondedOverall, I really enjoyed the game, and will definitely play it more as a relaxation thing yknow?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lovely little game about leaving your old life in the city to start a new life in the Alaskan wilderness. You are traveling to your new home with 5 sled dogs. This is a survival game built around making choices that determine if you will survive and reach your destination. You are also unlocking the stories of each dog (you travel with 5 at a time but there are more dogs to choose from). This game has rogue-lite elements where you learn from each failed or successful run so that next time, you start with more resources which aid in your survival.The game is visually gorgeous, the main character is voiced by the talented Ashley Burch, and the dogs are adorable and you can pet them as much as you want to. There is some replayability with regard to unlocking all of the dogs' stories, finding the best items and completing the journal by making different choices but it's still a fairly short game even with all of that.I really enjoyed my time with it. Recommended for people who like survival-lite, rouge-lite and/or choice-based adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: Venturing into The Red Lantern felt like embarking on an Alaskan odyssey, with breathtaking scenery that almost distracted me from my mushing duties. Gameplay, while solid, unfortunately suffers from a touch of repetition – I found myself barking orders like a broken record. 'Haw (left), Gee (right), keep moving, ignore that squirrel.' It's like a canine Groundhog Day.Graphically, the game is a snowy spectacle, and the hauntingly beautiful soundtrack had me questioning if I was playing a game or starring in a wildlife documentary. The story, much like a determined sled dog, pulls you along but it's not deep. If only the gameplay had a few more tricks up its fur-lined sleeve.In the difficulty department, The Red Lantern is a bit like the Alaskan weather – unpredictable. At times, it felt like a leisurely stroll through the snow, and suddenly, it hit me with a blizzard of challenges. The learning curve is akin to teaching a dog new tricks – you'll stumble, but eventually, you'll get the hang of it.Comparing The Red Lantern to other games is like comparing sled dogs to racehorses. It's a unique experience, but it may not have the same universal appeal. There's no denying its charm, though; the canine companions add a delightful layer to the journey. But make no mistake, this is no "The Long Dark."In the spirit of constructive howling, The Red Lantern could benefit from injecting more variety into its gameplay routine. Perhaps a surprise encounter with a mythical Alaskan creature or a quirky dialogue option that makes even the toughest sled dogs crack a smile. Unfortunately, you're ultimately reliving a varied experience trying to mark off items in your journal. The rogue-lite element feels a little weird for this type of game.In the end, The Red Lantern is a subpar sled ride through the Alaskan wilderness, and more often than not stumbles in the snow. It's an adventure worth leashing onto if the game is on sale, just be prepared for a few bumps along the trail.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I completed all of the dog's stories, I'd like to share my thoughts on Red Lantern.The positive first:Going on a journey with your chosen dogs is very relaxing.There is no way to take full control of the sled and all you can do is to select if you want to go right or left.For me, this was relaxing just to watch and press a few keys here and there.The dog's stories are very entertaining and it seems natural how the protagonist bonds with them during their journey to their new home.Collecting and managing your food and other resources is fun and challenging for your first runs.The voice actor did a great job and I can never get enough of her calling her dogs pups.Now to the negative:The encounters with wildlife are completely random and you are up to luck if you get missing ones for the journal.This makes it hard for people who want to complete 100% without getting burned out due to bad luck.After collecting all the gear it stopped being challenging and I never felt like it was difficult to get to the cabin anymore.It seems like the game locks you out of certain encounters after finishing the dogs stories, so you have to start a whole new journey and try to avoid completing the dogs stories for the completed journal. The encounters have a chance to fail even if you pick the option that would've led to the outcome that you need for the journal, so you might end up missing out on an entry just because the encounter gave you the bad outcome, and who knows how many times you have to try certain things to get what you want.For example: I tried to pet the elk 4 times, but every time it ran away, or something else happened.All in all a good game to sit back and relax for a few hours, but not recommended for those who want to complete it 100%.I'm not sure if I would recommend it for the full price either since it took me 8 hours to finish all the dog's stories and I'm sure you can complete it faster than that.I spent a few hours after completing the stories, trying to complete the journal, but it is frustrating and I think I won't be able to, even if I start a completely new run due to the sheer randomness of the encounters and their possible failure, even if you chose the right option.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was not was I was expecting when I first read the description and started playing it for the first time. At first, that unexpectedness was a bad thing. After the second or third run, it was a good thing. Or, more appropriately, what was there was charming enough that it made up for what expectations had been disappointed and I was now definitely appreciating the game for what it had to offer.For those who just want a quick review, this game is a solid 7.5/10 with definite room for an additional point with a content update. - It has lovely music and visuals, some solid moments of interaction if you're into the snowy wilderness and dogs and a surprising amount of replayability. - I would criticise the lack of variety in the music, some weird choices (or could be mild visual bugs) in the art style consistency and a few corny lines of dialogue. It is also very overpriced but this is an indie team so if you want to support them, buy at full price, and if you want a great experience for a bit more of a reasonable price, wait for a sale a buy for closer to $12-$14. - A definite recommend for a casual, chill game that provides more of an experience than a gameplay challenge.Now for more of a detailed review, with a more accurate rating out of 20. In no particular order of positive or negative, here are some thoughts:- While it is admitedly a  good track, it's completely baffling to me that the entire game essentially only has a single track to play for the entirety of the playtime experience. Unobstrusive and atmospheric as it is, there is no excuse for a game that relies so heavily on your immersion and investment into this experience to only have a single track running on repeat for runs that can last 20 minutes.- I really like the art style. Its cell-shaded look will make it age like fine wine and it really brought me into the world and made me feel like I was in Alaska. But the snow on the dog houses and the cabin at the end, as well as the blocky, grey, single-color clouds in the dark sky look completely unfinished, as if the game was missing textures in some areas.- Not a single bug to be reported, impressive (well, it shouldn't be, it should be the bare minimum, but given what games look like nowadays, it's impressive for an indie game to have literally zero bugs when million-dollar game studios are incapable of shipping functioning games)- The journal was an excellent idea and by extension, the numerous and varried events you can encounter based on the dog or the wild animal selected is impressive; the events are enjoyable, sometimes fascinating, and all the time at least interesting enough that I would sacrifice a hunger slot just to check out what my dogs had sniffed out or what this glint behind the hill could be- On the same note, I wish there were hints or an official guide on how to get some of the rarer events or how to deal with some of them. For ex, meeting the bear between the two rocks has always, every single time, resulted in injury for either me, my dogs, or even both I'm pretty sure. It seems utterly impossible to avoid, which makes it feel like the numerous options have zero impact and I may as well just pick whatever is fastest and will let me get back on the trail to use one of my precious one or two medkits. Now, whenever I see the bear, I'm like "here we go, another run lost" half of the time if I only had one medkit. It does feel unfair and renders the options meaningless. Even if having a particular dog could help, because there are no hints and, as far as I can tell, no part of the journal where you can see what each dog is good/bad at (given the number of dogs, it's hard to remember each dog's particularity), it makes it feel like I'm picking at random rather than make tactical decisions- I think it should be made clearer that getting to the cabin and the red lantern is not the end goal of the game, because when I made it to the cabin on my literal fourth attempt, I was pretty mad and disappointed that I had paid so much for a 1.5/2h game. It was then a good surprise that there was in fact more, but I was still bitter enough that I refused to play the game for over a month because I felt lied to. - In general, I feel like the marketing and descriptions of what the game is are rather poor and don't match well with what the experience ends up being. You don't control the sled at all (I don't even understand why the button controls are there given that they don't do anything) and there is nothing waiting for you at the cabin, no lore or story or cutscene, just more runs. The game is very good IMO, but it is described and advertised as something very different than what it actually is and if I had not been charmed by the music and some of the events on my second run, I would have given up and asked for a refund because that first run was so wildly different from what the game made it seem it would be, and I was honestly disappointed. The description should be changed to match the sort of roguelite feel of the game, with a clear disclaimer that you are, in fact, not piloting the sled at all, and that the main goal of the game is to get to know your dogs, manage resources and encounter charming events with northern wildlife. Nothing more, nothing less. I'd be willing to bet you're losing quite a few players in the first 30 min because you're doing a very bad job at managing expectations.So again, as a summary, a very good game that I enjoyed a lot, with a few minor internal issues and a few major marketing/expectation issues, that I would absolutely recommend for a casual time with an atmospheric experience. A solid 16/20

_childDocuments_.review: As hard as this may sound, it has to be done. I have watched many people play this game on YouTube, and I was intrigued. It seemed promising so I got my card, hopped on steam, and bought it. There is a reason I have only played 7 hours of this game. This game just can never cure my boredom. This game is kinda just a one time thing where you binge the story then leave it for dead in your library. If the storyline was longer, I wouldn't be this upset, but this is probably the shortest storyline I have ever seen. What I recommend to make this game better, is to give us more freedom at the end of the story. For instance, make a town where you can go visit. _childDocuments_.review: 27h (26/27 achievements, finished the game) Yes (~2 achievements). Yes (~24 achievements). No. is a narrative-based rogue-lite where you have to manage resources and choose between several options in each encounter to reach a house. Some choices will have their result determined by RNG, determining whether it'll be beneficial or unfavorable for your playthrough.- Different events played out in each run- Extra resources after each death- Some choices rely too much on RNG- Can be boring after several runs- Sometimes you are forced to remember the beneficial answers to finish the run effectivelyIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650The dogs look cute and simple. Despite the simplistic look, they still look realistic to some extent, just with fewer details. You won't see much in the background since it's mostly snow or trees, but they don't look that repetitive to me.There might be a lot of dialogue, but it's mostly about the encounters that you face and how you choose to respond in that Alaskan wilderness. There are also some encounters where your dogs go through character development, but I found the story to be quite simple. As for the narrative value itself, I found none - there isn't anything else apart from what the main character is going to do and why she's doing it. It's not a story-rich game and you won't find any story with depth in this game.Your dogs will carry you to the Alaskan wilderness and you need to direct them. Say Haw to go left and Gee to go right. It doesn't matter whether you are going left or right, though - you'll eventually reach the end regardless of the route that you take. The only difference will be the events that you encounter along the way.You have several resources that you need to maintain: meats for you and your dogs to eat, bullets to shoot animals for meats, bark to set up fire to cook the meats, and med packs to tend you and your dogs' health. At first, you will be severely lacking in resources. In fact, I don't think you can finish the game in your first run unless you are very lucky. However, your initial resources will be upgraded after dying several times. Moreover, there are also other tools that you can find in the wild to make the run easier - I found the lighter to be the most useful since it's hard to get bark. Once you unlock them all, it'll be hard for you not to reach the end unless you are doing it on purpose. Events will happen from time to time. You can choose to engage or not, and the encounter might be beneficial or unfavorable to you. It's all determined by what you choose - there will be several options, and although some options have a guaranteed result, others have several results that will be determined by RNG.This makes your run to be purely reliant on RNG. You might get bad runs because RNG doesn't give you a favorable result - heck, the events that you got might even be lined up in such a way that makes it impossible for you to finish in your first few runs. Sometimes, you will fail to shoot an animal even though you finish the minigame properly, or you might even have no chance to accurately shoot it because the cursor in the minigame won't line up to guarantee the shot. Yes, hitting an animal will require you to do a minigame where you have to press a button when the moving cursor is lined up with a target.I reached the end at 4.4h after dying several times. I hadn't unlocked some journal entries at that time, so I continued playing to get the rest of the achievements, including the journal entries. The latter one is the worst. I have been playing for more than 20 hours since then, and I still haven't got the last few known encounters for the journal. Everything is just purely RNG and it doesn't seem to go in my favor. I won't recommend it to achievement hunters though since there's hardly anyone that really knows how to unlock 1 achievement. And yes, it's the journal entries again.Despite promoting replayability, the game isn't meant to be played for the long run. There aren't that many events in the game, so you are bound to find the same events after playing for a while. You need to deal with how slow the character is talking, waiting for the next choice to come up, and most importantly, waiting for the delay between each action when you are in the camp. It's so annoying to wait for the latter one to finish. was an okay game at first. The gameplay was unique and it was nice to see what happened from the decision that you made. However, the RNG is just too much. You need to remember the correct choices to finish a run effectively, especially when you don't have a lot of upgrades. Moreover, some results are also too reliant on RNG, and if you are going to play for its replayability value, don't. It's not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an adorable game with stunning art direction. If you like the concept and don't mind the choose-your-own-adventure-book style gameplay, it is fun for about 5 to 10 hours depending on how much of a completionist you are. HOWEVER the normal price of this game ($25 at the time of this review) is a bit too much imo for the amount of content you get. I got it on sale for about $5 and I feel pretty happy with it, but I would be a bit irritated had I paid full price.The graphics may be simple, but the colors, lighting, and shadows make it all look stunning, especially at night. I wouldn't mind the dogs having slightly higher-quality models, but they are adorable as they are.The narrative reminds me of Firewatch in some ways, but it doesn't quite manage to hit that level. I'd like to hear a bit more about the protagonist's previous life, and/or have some interactions with other sled dog owners/mushers (currently there are no interactions with other humans in the game, which works for what's currently here, but more on that in a moment). The conversations with the dogs during their storylines are well-done, but you run out of new dialogue quickly.Unfortunately this is where the game kinda falls down, and might be a deal breaker for some people. You need to manage food (for both your character and the dogs), birch bark for lighting your campfire, ammunition for your rifle, and medical supplies for tending injuries. As you go along the trail you run into various random events that are triggered by a few things - the terrain, how far along you are on the trail, the dogs you chose, and probably other factors as well. You can choose to ignore most of them, although some of encounters are unavoidable and have to be dealt with (mostly predators). However, you have to do most of the encounters in order to get more food, ammo, etc. Unfortunately not all of the situations and choice prompts make sense. For example, in the encounter where your sled team runs into a bear, your character gets off the sled, and walks up to between your dogs and the bear BEFORE you get to make any choices. Your options from there are: Shoot It (if you have ammo), I'll Distract It, and Run? Planning a route is also completely unimportant. When I initially saw the map I assumed I needed to aim for the cabin that was roughly in the middle of the far side of the map, but you can choose to go left (or right) at every single turning point and you will still end up at the cabin. In fact avoiding the middle of the map by going only left or only right seems to avoid some of the more dangerous encounters, although that may have been luck.The roguelite structure is also an odd choice imo, because it means that for your first few runs you have barely any starting supplies and no tools, because your character didn't think to bring a firestarter, an axe, etc. I did almost manage to win my first run anyway but accidentally ran the dogs too long because I thought you had to wait for a prompt to camp (you don't, you just hit the button to camp and your character will stop at the next available camping spot).I think the game would massively benefit from the option to go on races after you've gotten to the cabin at least once. Most of the systems for tracking the passing of time seem to be there (after all there's a day/night cycle) and you could use time to determine your place in the race without having to show other sled teams (although simulating the progress of other teams could allow for interesting interactions and events). This could allow for new maps, more questlines for the dogs, and interacting with other sled teams between races and during events without massively changing the current gameplay loop. Failing that, even just adding more events would be welcome, especially weather events and other environment-related events like thin ice or avalanches (it seems odd that it's always clear without so much as a snow squall). More terrain and weather events might also make planning a route more important, especially if you want to actually win a race.

_childDocuments_.review: So... it's cute. Extremely cute. But the actual gameplay is.... severely lacking. You are playing a young woman who has decided on impulse to go to Alaska, adopt some dogs, and sled out to a cabin in the wilderness to live. Your goal is to get there alive. You have to find resources as you go. These resources are presented to you as random encounters--and they are not well optimized. I made three runs and only was presented the chance to collect firewood twice, which resulted in spending most of the game eating raw meat (and suffering a status effect for it)... despite being in a forest, filled with trees. Among these random encounters include opportunities to bond with your dogs, or fulfill their "quest". This is the bulk of the game, since once you reach the cabin, all you can really do is go on more runs to complete each dogs quest. After that... that's the game. So essentially you are repeating a bunch of random encounters over and over again, hoping you get the ones you need for some doggy questing, while eating raw meat because the game won't give you any firewood to cook with.It took me about 100 minutes to get to the cabin (three runs). By then I was so bored with the gameplay that I really didn't want to bother trying to unlock each dog's story, as cute as the dogs themselves are. I was really expecting something more fully fleshed out given the price tag this game comes with. Sure it's pretty, but even walking simulators have more content in them.

_childDocuments_.review: I got Red Lantern after watching a couple videos of people playing through the game, and as I had initially expected, I really enjoyed it! The graphics and atmosphere of the game are absolutely breathtaking, and I love all the dogs and while the voice-over is constant, it adds so much content that players like myself, can really relate too. The dogs and their stories are all very unique and engaging, and while most of their stories can be easily completed within one run, they certainly kept me hooked. On a bit of a different note, one thing I had to point out for it's excellence is the way the game handles failure. Sometimes, you hit a few too many bears or starve, and you die on your run. Instead of throwing that run to waste, the game sets it up as a nightmare which further prepares you for your next attempt. I think that makes the game so much less frustrating, and improves the flow of the storyline so well. I totally recommend this game to anybody who loves dogs and a bit of a challenge. P.S. The soundtrack is top-tier.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this game. Because it's definitely overpriced, and even if it wasn't, it's definitely too short for my tastes. After just 3 hours, it seems as though you've already seen the majority of what the game has to offer, barring teeny tiny (and grindy) pet stories that require you to go through the same content over and over again just to get 3-4 or so events related to a given pet. But the 3 hours that I played were really fun and relaxing. I really wish there were more maps to delve into once you beat the game once, as that would more than have motivated me to keep going. New events, new dangers, perhaps a sort of resource management game with the cabin where you actually have to live in the cabin, I would've loved that, especially as a fan of The Long Dark. But once you've reached the cabin, it seems as though that's just kind of it. You can go out onto the same trail or adopt a new dog, only to go out into the same content again. Which is too bad.Sooo, this is a very tentative "recommended", or rather a "I recommend this game if it goes on a 50% or more sale".

_childDocuments_.review: The Red Lantern’s charming premise, colorful visuals, and simple gameplay make for an entertaining ride through the cold, but it lacks the depth and replayability of other rogue-lites. Your canine companions help liven up the experience, and I fell in love with each of their different quirks and personalities. And don’t worry, you can pet them.If that’s all you're looking for, then this game will keep you entertained for one or two playthroughs. But if you’re looking for the next addicting rogue-lite to sink your teeth into, you're better off searching elsewhere. Either way, I’d recommend picking it up during a Steam sale. _childDocuments_.review: This game has lots to recommend it - beautiful visuals and soundtrack, and an interesting and unusual premise - you are a sled driver (musher?) traversing a frozen wilderness with a pack of sled dogs.  You do get to choose the dogs.  Yay for dogs!The whole game plays like a visual novel.  There are choices but also many unskippable cut scenes.  The story feels a bit sparse.  The game reminds me of 'in the long dark' but there is much less content.  You drive your dogs through the wilderness (on a path, occasionally choosing left or right) and events happen, both good and bad.  You decide what to do.  You must also look for various things to keep you and your dogs in good condition to continue.The game is good, but repetitive.  I've played for about 1 hour and 30 mins (2 partial run throughs) and I'm bored.  I would say that the game is better suited to people who enjoy repetitively playing through the same game (with some different procedural events) in order to win.  I feel there could be more content - the price tag even on sale is too high imo.  I doubt I will play this again unless there are more updates.
_childDocuments_.name: The Red Lantern

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult not to praise this game after playing it. + It won't make you feel depressed like other games that "lure you in" with cute animal characters to push someone's nightmares on you. It's quite relaxing.+ You have an option to toggle dog death off. Thanks for that.+ The game gets even more enjoyable after the main storyline. Cudos for that!+ No stress gameplay. Fair, out to teach folks not to give up. Well done! + Dogs have different personalities, you get to choose your team that fits you the best. Like!- Is there any? Probably the limited gameplay, but that's how the game was made, so no complaints here just wishes for some more adventure. - I really hate the graphics. With nowadays technology put yourself out there and animate correctly. Please.Overall it was totally worth the purchase and I give my heartfelt recommendation to anyone who loves dogs. I will keep playing it and hoping for a musher game with much better quality graphics and animations, some open-world adventure, maybe a bit of competition in the end to show off the great team I put together. I'd totally keep the gameplay elements, it is fun and surprising. One can dream. Anyways, thanks for the game, I really enjoy it.
