_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps stands as a masterful testament to the brilliance of 2D platformers, intertwining breathtaking visuals, emotionally resonant storytelling, and an enchanting musical score to create an immersive gaming experience. Developed by Moon Studios, this sequel not only lives up to its predecessor but surpasses it in every aspect.One of the game's standout features is its awe-inspiring artistry. The meticulously crafted environments, characterized by vibrant colors and intricate details, elevate the game to a visual masterpiece. Each frame is a work of art, bringing the mystical world of Ori to life with a sense of wonder and magic. The level design is equally commendable, seamlessly blending beauty with functionality to deliver a platforming experience that is as challenging as it is visually captivating.The emotional depth embedded in the narrative adds another layer of richness to the game. The poignant story of Ori's journey, filled with moments of sorrow, hope, and friendship, resonates long after the credits roll. The nuanced character development and the connection forged with the spirit companions, the Wisps, evoke a genuine emotional investment from the player.A standout aspect of Ori and the Will of the Wisps is its evocative musical score. Composed by Gareth Coker, the soundtrack complements the game's emotional beats and atmospheric nuances flawlessly. The music serves as a guiding force, intensifying the impact of key moments and creating a deeply immersive experience. The synergy between visuals, narrative, and music is a testament to the meticulous craftsmanship behind the game.The challenging platforming elements, coupled with demanding boss battles, contribute to the game's overall excellence. The decision not to grind for skill upgrades adds an extra layer of difficulty, enhancing the sense of accomplishment when overcoming obstacles and defeating formidable foes. The finely tuned balance between difficulty and reward keeps players engaged and invested in Ori's journey.While some may find the game's level of difficulty daunting, it ultimately adds to the sense of achievement when conquering each section. The commitment to a challenging platforming experience sets "Ori and the Will of the Wisps" apart in a genre that often relies on nostalgia rather than innovation.In conclusion, Ori and the Will of the Wisps stands as a testament to the potential of 2D platformers in the modern gaming landscape. With its mesmerizing art, emotionally charged narrative, and challenging gameplay, Moon Studios has created a masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of the genre. It's not just a game; it's an emotional journey that captivates players from start to finish, solidifying its place as one of the finest examples of gaming artistry in recent years.

_childDocuments_.review: 2/5 stars. Disappointing despite technical improvements.If you liked Ori and the Blind Forest, man was this game a disappointment. Storytelling is cheesy and the kind of silent companionship you felt in the first game is just gone.It gets 2 stars instead of 1 because the developers clearly put in a ton of effort and fixed a lot of problems! They made the map more explorable, improved combat, improved movement.But what made Ori and the Blind Forest so special was the storytelling and the silent characterization. You even hear Ori speak. It's like....hearing Pikachu speak for the first time ruining countless childhoods. There were quite a few bugs this late into 2020 but honestly I don't even care about them. The biggest problem is they just ruined Ori's story. And to be clear, I'm not mad at the ending, I actually think this ending should have happened in the first one. This game should have just been a standalone title in the same world, not a sequel.I finished the game, 100% completion, for those that are curious how far I've gotten.
_childDocuments_.name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, overall, the experience is the same as in the first one.  Its not for everybody though.  Even at the hard difficulty, its a pretty easy. Its a relaxing game, there's not much challenge.   Its not like Hollow Knight where, when you die, you go back to the checkpoint and have to trek back to retrieve your currency you lost.  Here, you die but you respawn at the same area and do it again, no lost shards.  So in this game, you can try and find out if you can make the jump and die trying with no consequences.  Its pretty relaxing.  As an adult, there should be no excuse to not be able solve the puzzles and obstacles in your way.  Its a children's game. I prefer to use the game pad over the keyboard for this game,  just feels better for me but the KBM controls work fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for amazing visuals and breathtaking music, this is the game for you. If you're looking for interesting gameplay that is challenging, fair, and rewarding, I would recommending checking out the first game by Moon Studios, Ori and the Blind Forest. Will of the Wisps falls flat in a way that I can't quite put into words. I think the biggest flaw to me was the shift to a focus on combat. Ori 1 was such a fun game to platform around and bash about, but Will of the Wisps feels like too many things were slapped on at the last minute. It feels like the members of the team played through Hollow Knight, and then decided the next Ori game should be exactly like it (even the story). I loved the original Ori and the Blind Forest, but I can't say Will of the Wisps is a satisfying sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rare instances we all know and love, where the 2nd is much better than the first. Ori and the will of the Wisps is an amazing game by itself as well. _childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, the game is not really that bad, it's just a downgrade from blind forest because it feels like they  forgot what made the original excellent just to make it more generic.- Platforming: platforming in Ori 1 was excellent, Platforming in Ori 2 is excellent. You gradually get upgrades to improve it which are well spaced out allowing you to reach new collectibles. The bash is such a fun movement option that also helps in combat. In addition, there are little race challenges scattered around which are fun extra content. Basically they just did again what they did so well, and I'm glad because it's the best aspect of the game by far- The combat: My biggest complaint. Yeah Ori 1 had very bad combat but that was definitely not the focus of the original. This one has a greater focus on combat and it just fails in many aspects. You will obtain a sword and bow around the beginning but can later buy a varaiety of weapons (such as a hammer, lance or shuriken) but you only get 3 slots to equip them, slots also taken by movement/utility abilities like your heal, so you effectively have 2 slots, likely 1 for melee and 1 for ranged. The only thing about the combat I adore comes directly from Ori 1, that being Bash.My biggest complaint tho is the bossfights: there are ONLY  6 BOSSES in this meteroidvania, one of which is a tutorial boss with essentially 1 attack and  2 are bosses in par fun-wise with some of the worst in Hollow Knight. the third one has pretty bad hitboxes, the 4th one has a cool aesthetic and a mid-battle chase scene but spawns adds which are not fun. In contrast the final boss is excellent, mainly because it heavily makes you use the parry + an endgame movement ability to create a really fun challenge. For the lack of bosses there are some chase sequences (simmilar to Ori 1) which are  really cool at first but once you die 2-3 times all the impact is already gone.The enemy variety is good enough, but while they work differently many enemies are just reskins of each others which makes you feel like there's less variety than there actually is.- Core mechanics: Another major gripe is how linear this game is. The structure is simmilar to base hollow knight where you first reach a specific area, then you have to obtain the 3 things to access the final boss, but unlike hollow knight there is very little variation in how subsequent runs will go. the only real 'fork in the road' is chosing which part of Seid you get first. One good thing is how they add hidden areas with upgrades which makes the exploration more fun.The interesting yet flawed 'set your spawnpoint' mechanic is fully ditched and replaced with a checkpoint mechanic, but checkpoints are a bit too close together. This might be really good for some but for me it made dying not punishing enough. Finally, there is a map guy npc (simmilar to hollow knight), but instead of giving you a map for you to complete it just sells you a filled one. I generally tried to ignore the guy because it's just more fun to discover stuff yourself.- Story and ambient: The game looks amazing. The environment are expertly and beautifully crafted, baur's reach and Luma pools stand out for me. The music is beautiful and atmospheric as the first game. The story is perfectly serviceable yet not as deep and epic as they try to portray it and it hit the right emotions, but it is also NOT DISTINCT enough to Ori 1's story. The world is not aesthetically distinct either (world engulfed by darkness where everyone is sad) and the main enemy is again a big bird. Finally, if you buy it dont play it on hard it sucks they just improved enemy damage and health every boss just turns into a damage sponge it's just not enjoyable at times.In a nutshell, I feel like the game would have been a lot better if they just doubled down on the platforming that made the original so fun, greatly expanded upon it and polished it to perfection insted of making the game more generic by adding combat and a charm system the game would have been amazing, but I cant just overlook how flawed and undercooked the new mechanics are.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is improved and much better than the predecessor but there are still several bugs, frame rate drop and game crashing. _childDocuments_.review: Will of the Wisps is a beatiful and smooth platformer. Just controlling the character and running around in the gameworld with all these awesome and fluent movement options is pure joy.Yes, it also comes with some metridvania elements and a new combat system. But the focus is clearly the platforming. And this game does that so freaking well. The control are precise and responsive. The different movement abilities compliment each other so well. Let'S be honest. Once you got all of your abilities, running through the game to collect stuff for completion is the best part about it. Using your skills and literally flying through the zones like it is nothing is AWESOME.This game is an evolution of the first one. It takes everything the first game did well, improves on it and adds some fun new things like NPCs, quest, an actual combat system and bosses.If you loved the first Ori game, you will love this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, visuals and soundtrack are some of the nicest i've seen/heard.Always felt some kind of emotion while playing, whether good or bad. Flow of the game is a nice wee change to most things, but.. i found that the combat while still being pretty solid just got boring after a while. What i mean by this is by the time you have accumulated more energy and health you can just brute force past things, bosses become a breeze and the walk to the next location become a dawdle. I found myself blasting through new regions easily and if i took a bit too much damage from being over zealous i would have a full tank of energy to just heal back up to full then hit a few monsters and crystals to regen back everything. Certain bosses could also just be overpowered like this.I would give it a 7/10 if i had to give a numeric rating, while a bit drab combat wise the game looks actually unreal, and for the hours i put in for just a blind 100% run i had fun during all of it. Once i've delved a bit more in my library i WILL be replaying this as it's such a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a few insurmountable issues that make it frankly not fun to play at certain points. With Ori 2, they added more emphasis on combat, and introduced boss fights - something that was intentionally ignored in the first one. This was a poor decision.If you're familiar with Ori 1, you'll recall that "Boss fights" were escape sequences. These are still present, to some degree, but most are shortly followed (or preceded) by actual boss fights. These actual fights have some rather significant problems. The choice of difficulty level makes no difference in what you're fighting, what moves they use, how fast, or anything of the sort. Hard mode simply inflates enemy HP and damage dealt to high levels. Even despite this, it gives excessive amounts of energy restores which couple with a healing ability to present no relevant threat when the game plays well.Therein lies another problem. There are new abilities which share keybinds with existing abilities. There are instances where I concede damage because instead of bashing the projectile within range, Ori grappled onto a plant - simply because I was facing towards its direction, on account of spacing myself for safe and comfortable bashing.Even if such a bash of a projectile back at an enemy (or boss) is successful, the hitboxes (and hurtboxes) of some enemies (and  boss fights) are at the best of times obscure or broken. On a certain 8-legged boss, only 2 legs are hurtboxes, but only during certain animations, they are never hitboxes, and it can be a real issue keeping track of the two relevant legs due to the visuals and swift movement causing a sensory overload worse than many other games - even those that had adjustments specifically to reduce visual clutter or enhance clarity.There are even abilities that straight up do not function on these bosses: an ability that reflects a portion of received melee damage back at the attacker will not function. There are regular enemies whose attacks go out despite being visually staggered after you hit them with a full combo, on the whole the combat (and associated difficulty level) is simply deeply flawed, and this emphasis on combat is the only new thing brought to the table by Ori 2.  As long as these issues remain, I cannot recommend this game - the first Ori game is better, and this game is not similar enough to be guaranteed enjoyable if you liked the first one. If you do purchase, note that the only reason to ever play on Hard mode is to obtain an achievement for beating hard mode - and combat will take at least twice as long.

_childDocuments_.review: You will buy Ori and the Will of the Wisps, you will start it up, and before you can check the clock 20 hours will suddenly fly by.  Watching the credits roll down the screen, you're left with a sense of awe, of accomplishment and a nod to the developers for a good job done.  Not to mention the soundtrack is now in your collection.  If only that urge to play it again wasn't so strong, maybe you can get to other games on your steam library.  One day.Ori and the Will of the Wisps is the second installment in the Ori series, and a shining star of a game as a whole.  It comes off like the love-child of 'Ori and the Blind Forest' and 'Hollow Knight', with the vibe, living art backgrounds, abilities, and story of Ori and the charm system and sword-slashing fighting feel of HK.   Unlike the previous Ori, this successor has a full world of talkative NPCs to support you on your journey. This game is a fun jaunt to 100% completion.  It's well worth the money.  Get the soundtrack because that's also gold.  And don't fault yourself if you find yourself replaying Ori over and over again for the thrill of it.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels a bit shallow.I never have to think much, or have any difficulty. I can just brute force everything and all unlockables are kindly sitting on my map waiting me to get them.In this game, it is impossible for me to feel smart or skilled. It's almost like watching a movie, since my thinking and executing abilities do not matter.Even if I pull of nice movement tricks to get into places I shouldn't be able to reach yet, I am never rewarded.There is always an annoying barrier to greet me.Something like "Oh, you need to go from the other side, this is the return shortcut of some place, dummy ;)"!The order I face certain challenges is even gated. There is a door that says you need to complete basically "all other main objectives" before you can open it, but I went there 2nd. It was a slap in the face.I have no attachment to the characters or story (generic and forgettable), so it's not a reason to stay.The mechanics of moving around are mostly good, so that's the positive, but it's not enough to keep me playing the game. Also, the animations and graphics are good as well, it's a beautiful world, I just don't care about it.I really tried to like it, but I couldn't. I felt it tried too hard and copied a bunch of things from Hollow Knight, but this didn't help it much.

_childDocuments_.review: Just bought both of these games on sale about a week ago. Played Ori 1 (definitive edition) in a single weekend and loved it. Did not feel compelled to go back for 100%, but was happy to start the second game a week later.So far, Ori 2 is an improvement over the original in a lot of ways. Animations and controls feel smoother. Platforming is more challenging right from the get-go, as in, there are way more jumps that require your maximum distance with your currently unlocked movement abilities. So it's just more consistently engaging to navigate the environment. The combat is way more interesting and satisfying, especially having unlocked the stronger hammer-like attack as my first unlock.PSA - I was experiencing a ton of choppy visual and audio issues, regardless of which graphical settings I had selected. Moving my install from my HDD to my SSD solved the problem immediately and completely.

_childDocuments_.review: Feel free, like a leaf in the wind.Another masterpiece from Moon.Another gem, another diamond.Same tight and intuitive gameplay, beautiful soundtrack, amazing graphics and art style as before.More of the same awsomeness in a new adventure, could've we asked for more?We can see that a lot has been influenced by and borrowed from Hollow Knight in this one, from the Spirit Edge similar to the Nail and the Shards just like the Charms. These aren't bad additions, it does add more flexibility in a build you could make with the Charms and where as the Nail in Hollow Knight allows you to bounce off of enemies by attacking down, in Ori, a hit resets your jump count so if you're hitting and jumping right, you can keep being airborn, which feels -so -good.You'll find most of the shards exploring or from some NPCs and this is where you'll get to select your double jump, your wall grab as well as other buffs and other helpful benefits. You unlock more shard slots the more you go.  The main abilities are now in a wheel that you can access with LT, stopping time, allowing you to select your skills and put them in your shortcuts (X,Y,B). This is where your main attack, Spirit Edge, is as well as Recover for life recovery, fire orbs, a spear and such.It feels a little too much compared to the simple and effective way the first game was built around, unlocking your abilities felt more natural without having to select them, but it's well done still, I got used to it without much issues, everything flowed well because the game got great design in overall. Differently from the first game where you had a skill tree where you would spend the Spirit Light you're collecting, all the shards and abilities can be upgraded with Spirit Light at certain NPCs now.Talking about NPCs, they now also give some side quests and we got a Trade Quest like in A Link's Awakening. The throwback.So, one more time, one of the best Metroidvania.A third game would be more than appreciated because there's nothing like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a beautiful 2D Metroidvania. A direct sequel to Ori and the Blind Forest, it follows on from the plot of the first game. In the introduction to the game, Ori and his little family help to raise Ku the owl. She is an adorable little thing, but has a bum wing and so has a hard time flying. Fortunately, you figure out that you can use one of her mom’s feathers (an item from the first game) on her wing as a sort of prosthesis, and she can fly after a fashion.Naturally, this cuteness can only last so long, and it isn’t long before Ori and Ku fly into a horrible storm over a nasty, shadowy forest. You get separated from Ku, and it is up to Ori to venture into this scary new world to rescue his friend/daughter.Visually, this game is pretty spectacular; it makes excellent use of light and dark, the enemies are menacing but have a certain glowy aesthetic appeal to them, while the various allied creatures are cute or cool looking. Everything in this game looks really good.On top of that, the game works quite well at pulling at your heartstrings. Not only are characters emotive, with Ori holding and hugging Ku, and sometimes getting hugs back, but the world has problems and the game does a good job of making you want to protect the people in it from them. The darkness is forboding, and bad things are happening to good people who are helping you out – or just trying to survive.As such, the game does a really good job of making you feel bad for the characters, and while it doesn’t always hit, it generally does, even if it ends up making the game a bit predictable at times. Still, these developments work well, and we do feel bad for various characters – even the villains at times, as we understand the origin of their dark feelings.If I had a quibble with the aesthetic half of the game, it is that the narrator is a bit of a weak point. The game probably would have been more powerful if it hadn’t had one, and while there IS a plot-related reason for their existence, I’m not sure that the payoff from it was ultimately worth the exposition.The gameplay, too, is really good. Ori’s movements are really fluid, and his command set is quite solid – you eventually gain the ability to double and triple jump, air dash, “bash” (launching yourself off of enemies or projectiles in mid-air, which will also send the enemy/projectile flying in the opposite direction, making it useful both offensively and for mobility), float (which isn’t actually that useful by the time you get it, but still appreciated), climb up walls and walljump, and generally get all the abilities you’d expect to. But what makes the game work well is that Ori’s movements are really smooth, and it feels good to control him – Ori is highly responsive to your commands, and easy to control and get to do what you want him to do.There are a number of interesting environments to go through, with a variety of mechanics; these include not only interesting platforming puzzles, but things like darkness that closes in around you and which requires you to dash from light to light, or icy areas that you need to thaw out by manipulating projectiles and getting them to the right location.There are even some very interesting timed segments, where you are trying to escape from some big horrible monster, or a catastrophe like an avalanche or flood, and have to keep moving as the environment disintegrates around you. These are really cool, and end up taking up the space of most of the boss fights in the game – they actively test your platforming skills, and are long enough to be exciting and present at least some challenge while short enough not to be obnoxiously long. This extends to some “spirit races” as well, where you race a ghostly spirit to some destination for a reward.Ori also does something else important – it actually has good pacing. Many Metroidvanias are a bit lame at the start of the game, but Ori manages to engage the audience with an unfamiliar landscape, excellent visuals while carrying around only a torch as a weapon, and getting the player some extra movement abilities early enough to avoid feeling stale.The game’s only real weakness is the combat, but it is a rather significant one. Ori’s own abilities are actually pretty cool – he has quite a variety of combat powers, and there’s even a “shard system” that allows you to modify them. The problem is, the game fails to make interesting use of them. Almost every enemy can be beaten with your basic attack, the few who can’t can be beaten with a hammer smash ability you buy, and… that’s about it. None of them really present a significant challenge, and only one type of standard enemy even remotely represents any sort of mechanical threat, and even they are pretty easily bypassed or defeated.As a result, the enemies in the game end up feeling pretty samey after a while, something which isn’t helped by a lack of variety in them – there’s not that many enemy types, and none of them do anything particularly interesting. But they’re all over the place, and the game seems to think they represent something challenging – even though they’re very easy and not super interesting to fight.The game is also lacking in interesting boss fights. While there are the “boss escape sequences”, the game still has you fight a half-dozen bosses – but these aren’t tremendously interesting. The bosses almost all have very basic attack patterns, and the only real dangers from them after the very beginning of the game (where your resources are very limited against a beetle boss, the second boss in the game) is falling off into bottomless pits and dying during sequences where you need to escape from them.On top of this, while the game has mostly quite good pacing, with reasonably sized areas, the bosses are not very well spread out; you fight two at the very beginning of the game, but the middle part of the game has none that you fight. There is a point where the game opens up and you can choose which area to go to next, and I went to literally every one of the bossless areas first – resulting in me facing two bosses at the very start of the game, and the other four at the very end, with none in-between. This felt kind of weird, doubly so as one of the bosses runs off rather than being “beaten” and felt like it was going to return, and then never did.As such, while the game excels in most ways, it ends up falling short in the area of combat – something that the game gives you a ton of skills to use in, but which you have little cause to use because there’s just no point in doing so.The shard system, too, was a bit of a disappointment; in theory, there were a bunch of different shards you could equip, but in practice, because some basic movement abilities were equippable (like the triple jump and wall cling), and others were just really big QOL improvements (a magnetic ability that sucks in the spirit light that is the game’s currency, and another ability that caused enemies to drop more spirit light, making it easier to buy more upgrades), you often didn’t really have a lot of slots to play around with, resulting in basically equipping and keeping the same set of mostly utility shards for most of the game.Still, that is but a minor quibble.In the end, Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a very good game, which is held back from greatness by its weak combat. But the fluidity of Ori’s movement, combined with the game’s excellent aesthetics and ability to engage the player with the game’s plot worked to make this a very engaging experience on the whole. I had fun with the game, and the ending, while bittersweet, was a nice bow on the series.Overall, I’d recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Metroidvanias, especially if they like the look of the game, but know that the combat is not the main attraction of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty late to playing the first game (finished it only in summer last year) and was left incredibly impressed. This game, however, I bought at release, and what can I say, it still met all my expectations and was an absolutely amazing experience. Just as good as the first game, really. Here's my in depth opinions on my easy mode playthrough:Positives:~The joy of movement was present in the first game, and it certainly hasn't gone anywhere! Along with some of the classics like bash, there are many more fun movement abilities in this game that are an absolute blast to use. Not only that; you also get cool weapons now which, if used alongside your abilites, can make you feel really epic and strong. Ori is no longer weak and fragile; he's a cool warrior now!~Speaking of "no longer weak and fragile", Ori really has become stronger. It was probably also the fact that I was on easy mode (and that I played the first game fairly recently), but, my death count really paled in comparison to what I ended up with on my easy mode playthrough of the Blind Forest. That would be about 100 deaths compared to 700, and during my first two hours of the game I didn't die once. It's pleasant, really! Beginner friendly and much less frustrating. Getting caught in a spike hazard or among a group of enemies no longer means certain death, and insta-kill is less common. Though, there definitely were still a select few difficult parts that took a good couple dozen deaths for me to get through.~In the previous game there was an area that took away that joy of movement and was a total drag for the first time player. I am proudly announcing that this game did a little better in that regard. There is still one part where you have to ride the owl for a bit and it prevents you from using a chunk of your skills but you can still run and jump and glide, so it's not that bad. In fact, the developers probably knew that no one was gonna wanna spend too much time without their cool abilities, so the owl section was short enough for it to not get boring and tedious.~Story is still beautiful and emotional; a great sequel and end to a 2-part series. AND I can appreciate the continued straightforwardness. Leave all the cryptic mysteries and secrets to stories like Hollow Knight.~Speaking of HK, the game seemed to have taken a few pointers from it, which I think is awesome. Gameplay wise? Those little skill badges you can choose from are useful, and boss fights are fun and engaging. Story wise? It's really cool to be talking to other living creatures here and there, some of which are recurring, and help them build their little sanctuary. The side quests are a fun little addition.~Visuals and sound are still just as incredible. Awesome art and music; in fact, I found myself immensely enjoying and listening on repeat to even more tracks than I have from Blind Forest. Character designs are also as enjoyable as ever. ~Ku is adorable. The Moki are adorable. Ori is adorable. Everything in this game is so CUTE AND WHOLESOME. (except for Shriek, and that one Moki family side quest. I am still so mad about that quest. How could they do that to me)Like with the previous game, I still have some nitpicks, however:~Technical issues here and there. My playthrough was fortunately free of any game breaking bugs but there were some audio glitches and performance drops which were a tad immersion breaking.~The ability/weapon system is a bit limited in my opinion. You get a whole lot of them but can only use 3 at once. And yeah you can switch them pretty easily at any point in time, but for the sake of convenience, a 4th active ability slot would have helped a lot. I found myself almost never using up all my energy because of the lack of energy consuming abilities I was able to freely use at once. ...though, I guess that's easy for me as a keyboard user to say, having access to a lot more buttons than a controller does.~no more stomp! spirit smash is its successor but dang, stomp was fun. RIP stomp.~Not enough lore for the owls, honestly. Maybe there will be a definitive edition sometime that adds an area that tells of the story of the owls much like there was one for Naru in the first game? I sure do hope so. I wanna know aaaall about them!Long story short: this game is great, worth every penny, and every minute you spend on it. Even if story games and/or side scrolling platformers aren't your thing, it's still totally worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted game across the board. The environments feel alive, and the game provides a terrific sense of control and movement as you gain more abilities. The platforming sequences are punctuated by spectacular, interestingly designed boss fights, along with occasional high-intensity escape sequences. A forgiving checkpoint system and near-instant restarts after dying means the frustration factor is kept under control. The music by Gareth Coker is another highlight, adding emotional weight and a mystical feel. While the story is quite simple, the animation is stunning and creates some genuinely heartfelt moments. I didn't feel compelled to explore every square inch of the map, and enemy variety felt relatively limited, but the variety in locations and overall quality more than made up for these small issues for me. While Metroidvania-style games have a high standard thanks to games like Hollow Knight, Ori and the Will of the Wisps is way up there -- and you'd be hard-pressed to find a better-looking game.

It requires a lot more exploring, due to the spirit light now being more of a currency than experience. I cant even believe that there are negative reviews. For those who say the performance is bad, I run this game at 144 fps on a 2080 Super, and a 3.2Ghz Processor. If you are getting bad frames on a 3080ti like ive seen people complaining about, the problem is clearly on your end.100000% recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles, and having fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It very much lives up to the legacy of its predecessor, and even expands on it significantly without losing any of the original spirit. _childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is an incredible feat of artistry! I was drawn in and blown away by its emotional storytelling, satisfying movement, vibrant and diverse world, and its many little heartwarming moments. I would highly, highly recommend the game to anyone who likes metroidvanias, platformers, RPGs, and beautiful and satisfying games in general. However, I feel like it's important to note: don't come into this game expecting Ori and the Blind Forest but improved, or Hollow Knight but with dynamic lighting and 2.5D graphics. Combat makes up a much greater part of the game than it did in Ori 1, but while there is certainly a lot of variety in how and when you deal damage, none of it is really necessary when you can complete all the content with just the basic, required skills- very much unlike the simple but nuanced and actually versatile combat in HK. It's ok though, as even though many of Ori 2's combat skills do feel unnecessary, the game, much like Ori 1, shines in its complex, satisfying platforming and movement, and in- of course- the iconic Ori chase challenges. Therefore, even though it might have content more akin to HK in the form of bosses, vendors, map collection, collectibles, ect., it's its own thing, beautiful and incredible! But by virtue of all those additions, it may feel more complex and more combat focused than Ori 1, which might turn you off a little bit if you liked the simplicity of Ori 1. Regardless, Ori and the Will of the Wisps is probably one of my new favorite games- just please add a boss rush/rechallenge mode!Sorry for the rant- hope this helps!

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is another visual treat of a Metroidvania bringing a lot of improvements over it's previous entry such as overhauled combat, a skill system, and more varied map.Ori's second outing borrows a lot from other Metroidvanias of recent years to improve upon the original. In particular Ori 2 adds skills, similar to Hollow Knight's charm system, where you can pick and choose certain bonuses, abilities, and/or buffs to Ori. The combat has had a complete rework compared to the previous entry. You know wield a melee weapon, that coupled with positioning and direction inputs makes for more engaging combat encounters.  Just like the original, the highlight of the game is the visual and audio art. The game's look is a major improvement over it's predecessor, mostly due to it's better lighting. An issue I had with the original was how some foreground and background elements blended in too much. That is not an issue in this entry; As part of the combat overhaul, it looks like there was extra care to make sure enemies and their actions can be recognized easier. Ori tells a great story in the new land of Niwen. This time around there are more NPCs to interact with throughout your journey, even going the route of having a "home-base" in the middle of the map. This entry is somehow even more emotional than the first and is masterful in the way it tells it's story through set-piece and quiet moments alike. Ori 2 stumbles in some of the same areas as the original. The map design feels very similar, possibly with even more hand holding than before. Another complaint is that the power-ups don't feel as impactful as before. New abilities either supersede previous ones or are more one-off, only used in specific environments. I would have liked to see more varied abilities.Overall, great game. One of the most artistic platformers I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game with flaws.It's in 9/10 ways a complete upgrade to the first game.Combat feels great, can get a little confusing with too many enemies, though.Buttons having multiple uses can sometimes be irritating, but it's very rare.Some sections of the game require precise aim and timing - some people can find this bothersome.Story is, as the first game was, sad, yet uplifting. A ray of hope in the dark.Soundtrack fits the game perfectly.I can't really say much more, I don't want to go in too deep with this review. I just want to give anyone liking good platformers a very, very, very strong recommendation to buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed , you're going to love . Heck, even if you haven't played the first one, you're probably still going to love this. -The world map was already pretty big before, but this one is huge. It's absolutely jam-packed with secrets and collectibles, and every screen is a work of art. -There are noticeable improvements to the lighting effects as well as the overall level of detail. Textures have additional dimensionality to them that look great with the dynamic lighting. Visually, this game blows the first one out of the water.-Bosses! There are bosses now, as well as additional escape sequences. And worry not - the escape sequences are much more fair this time (so no cheap shots like the huge falling rocks in the Forlorn Ruins from the first game). You can also re-fight bosses or re-play escape sequences using the Quick Access feature from the title screen when selecting your game. -The combat mechanics have more of a focus now - and they're great fun. Ori gets a samurai sword thing for a main weapon, and it's incredibly satisfying to chain together several hits and take out a bunch of enemies in one continuous rampage.-The three-pronged upgrade tree from before... gone. Now you collect and spend Spirit Light on Shards (think buffs/abilities) and weapons. You also have the abilities that you gain from the spirit trees like before (double jump, dash, bash, etc), and I was pleased to see that a lot of the navigational ones are earned early on in the game. -In each major map area, you'll also encounter these Spirit Trial racing shrines where you can compete and compare your replays/performances with your friends. It's not required for the main story, but I thought it was a fun little side-game.-There's also a Backup Save feature, which is a very nice convenience. If for whatever reason you need to return to an earlier point in the game, you'll have some past autosaves to choose from.-As for the Steam achievements, I found them to be easier than the first game's. They did away with One-Life mode, though I can't say I miss it, myself. There is still an Immortal achievement for not dying, but it's not as nerve-wracking now that there are fewer things that can one-hit-kill you in this game. Overall, I really have nothing to criticize about . Everything is competently done and very refined. If you enjoy Metroidvanias, don't miss this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first one, I loved the sequel as much. Now, I'd recommend this to everyone who obviously liked the first game and to anyone else who's into a beautiful jump 'n' run game.

_childDocuments_.review: There are no words to describe how good is this game, you have to experience it first hand in order to appreciate it fully.The graphics are amazing! While in the first game the visuals were in the same league as this one I feel that in this one there were a lot more diversity in the different locations.Each time you enter a new location you can't stop looking into the distance and appreciate the scenery.I'm not gonna lie, there a few sections in the game that made me take break before I start breaking stuff. While I don't consider it as a "hard game" ( though I was playing it on normal ) it's quite challenging.By the end you need to use multiply skill you acquired just to traverse the different locations, not counting the boss fights and maybe my favorite sections "run like hell".Just for comparison I've played Hollow Knight and that game was challenging as hell, so much that the the biggest enemy was the environment itself and not the mobs. That's why each time you died you got more and more frustrated, to the point you just drop it. ( well that said I had to pull out Cheat Engine just to finish it... so no, I don't like too much challenge at an expense of my sanity )That's why I say that Ori is challenging but not too much, since I finished it fair and square... except when I got stuck at a few places a few walkthroughs helped there. :DIf you played the first game you know how the story is presented in this game. Pretty much the story as minimal as possible while still staying relevant to the game.The dialog is straight to the point and it doesn't stretch so much that it becomes a filling for the total hours of the game.I found it very interesting, while it could've expanded a little more in regards to Gumo and Naru point of view, it's delivered a fine conclusion to the story.Here hoping for a DLC that provides a Gumo and Naru as playable characters. ( even though Naru is not very... gymnastic )I think that this is the main selling point of the game, no matter how obvious this sound.While the gameplay is similar to the first game, the skills you acquire are quite different and they provide a very interesting way of fighting and traversing in the game.Each move flows very nicely and the response is quick and on point. There is no animation to wait for or something else that take away from the fast pace moves you need to chain.The progress feels very natural and each time you get  a new skill you can't wait to tray it out and gather the items you couldn't before.Most of the enemies were easy ( at least on normal ) and the bosses... not gonna lie my favorite part was running from the bosses compared to the actual fights. That said the boss fights had really interesting ways to interact with the environment in order to defeat them. On normal the boss fights were pretty easy even if took a lot of damage, since you could heal your self, but on hard... I assume that it will be hell to beat.So yeah the gameplay stay fresh throughout the game with new skills and locations and it will hook you. I stayed up two nights on a row until 1:00 AM when I have work tomorrow at 8:00 am. It hooks you and you lose track of time.The music is outstanding! I can say for certain that this is my favorite game when it comes to music composition.Each area has it's unique music and every one of them fits the scenery very well, so well that you forget that it's there. I will probably have a new work playlist mainly taken from this game.Once again props to the compositor!Someone mentioned that the game had too many bugs, for me everything was OK with a few exceptions:And that's all, by all means there are no breaking game bugs and the present bugs are not affecting the enjoyment in any way or form.For me the game lived to it's hype and delivered more than enough.If you liked the first game you will definitely like this one as well.

_childDocuments_.review: "Ori and the Will of the Wisps" was a colossal disappointment. From the very start, it felt like a game desperately trying to recapture the magic of its predecessor but falling flat on its face. The first thing you'll notice is the lackluster graphics, which are a far cry from what was promised in trailers. The once vibrant and enchanting world of Ori feels dull and uninspired, with muddy textures and choppy animations that make it hard to stay immersed.But it's not just the visuals that suffer; the gameplay itself feels like a step backward. The controls are clunky and unresponsive, making precise platforming a frustrating chore rather than a joyous experience. Combat is a dull slog, with repetitive enemies and uninspired mechanics that offer little in the way of challenge or excitement.Perhaps the most egregious sin of "Ori and the Will of the Wisps" is its story, which is a disjointed mess filled with clichés and predictable plot twists. Characters lack depth, and their motivations are never fully explored, leaving you feeling indifferent to their plight.Overall, "Ori and the Will of the Wisps" is a prime example of a sequel that fails to capture the magic of the original. It's a lackluster experience from start to finish, and one that I wouldn't recommend to anyone looking for a truly memorable gaming experience. Save your money and stick to the original Ori instead.

Why rubber band enemy movement?!Lack of gameplay polish in this one almost made me throw controller few times. Also commonly used movement skill somehow warped the camera to other side of the screen everytime and was fixed only by restarting the game.Ori and the Will of the Wisps has lot of heart but still can't recommend in its current state.I very much liked the first game better overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember watching a YouTube video that compared this game to Hollow Knight—their conclusion was that these games have many similarities, but rather than copying from Hollow Knight, the leader of Moon Studios (team that made Ori) thought he could do better than Team Cherry (team that made Hollow Knight). Ironically, throughout my experience playing this game, the thought of "Hollow Knight did this better" was usually at the back of my mind.Hollow Knight doesn't have 3D models; instead it has fantastic artwork, tight controls, and challenging gameplay.Ori's aesthetic is similar, but it's more 3D and your character has inertia: I literally spent a good 4 or 5 minutes trying to jump onto a small platform because of this.Ori also gives you a lot more text to read. In Hollow Knight, you can collect a Mask Shard, Vessel Fragment, or other important item, and there's little to no descriptive text, because none is needed—everything in that game is intuitive. By contrast, every time I got an item in Ori, they gave me a lengthy explanation about what it does and how I should get ready to collect a bunch more of them. I'm sure not everyone will feel this way, and I'm probably making a huge deal out of something that's not very important, but for me it felt like I was being patronized.I can respect the opinion of anyone who enjoys this game (and/or its predecessor), but it wasn't for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps

_childDocuments_.review: Rarely ever have I found a game to be this beautiful and exciting over the last few years. Ori and the will of the wisps becomes one of my favorite games of all time, not only because of the stunning and art-like graphic but also the phenomenal soundtrack. The studio did a great job in capturing the mood of  each individual environments using a variety of color combinations which is eye-pleasing of course. But I have a difficult time at the start trying to distinguish Ori and the surrounding/ enemies because they all glow quite similar. For gameplay mechanics, it is an overall improvement compares to Blind forest with additional skill tree and shard spirits! (which are quite fun looking for after finishing the story). Although I completed all the achievements, I still comeback to this game daily re-playing some parts or taking screenshots of the world. This game is a must-have for any artists who are struggling in designing the environment of their own world, it looks visually-appealing and one of many top inspirations that I can look at. All in all, can't wait another 5 years for another masterpiece coming from Moon Studio.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are using mouse and keyboard then don't play this game. If those part are within the first 2 hours, I would have definitely ask for a refund.In the sand part, ori swim through the sand but it is too damn fast, plus I use keyboard to play so I only have at most 8 direction but not more continuous angle using controller so I keep bumping into wall. This also makes the whole movement kit of ori useless, which is not why I came for.In the dark part, if you are in a place without light you die within a few second, which then relies on some glowing bud to guide you to through the map. However, the bug spawn in some fixed spot and go through some fixed route within a fixed period. If you don't follow close enough, you die. If you try to go alternate path, you can't. If you are looking for fun, you won't. It is the stupidest design choice I have ever seen. Instead of showcasing the fluid movement, it restrict you to a point of no room for error. Instead of encouraging you to explore the world, it tells you to follow a path.Thanks I hate this game

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with the first Ori game and bought the second when I had money to spare. I love it as much as the original. Even with trying to mock dark souls or whichever else, honestly I'm enjoying it. My only gripes with the game are the poor optimization, constant frame drops, getting stuck in walls, maps not loading and almost walking down into a void and the occasional gray screen during cutscenes. There's a lot of technical issues with this game. My computer was built to be able to run and play Witcher 3 for hours without issue, and can still do so reliably to this day. I bring this comparison up because the Witcher 3 is a massive game. If my computer can handle the Witcher 3 no problem, Ori and the Will of the Wisps shouldn't be having any of these issues at all. Please make sure to fix this or let the community make a patch if you wont fix it. Something. When the game does work however, it's really good and worth playing. _childDocuments_.review: There are few games that hit home like the Ori series and Moon Studios knows what they are doing. I preferred the story of the first one, but this one does not slack in any regard. In fact, this one wrapped me up on the edge of my seat. The new method of fighting was a bit irritating at first but once I got used to it, I preferred it, as it provided more freedom to not only explore different methods of fighting but also countering the different enemies. The movement system for the game, while slightly more complex still has that smooth and exhilarating feeling that makes searching for the secrets one of the best parts of the game in my opinion.The only complaint I have for this game is that some of the speed trials seem to stretch some of the movement mechanics too far, mainly the one for the silent forest as the burrow was finicky in whether it would work or not.Other than that the game was amazing and I hope that whatever they come up next contains as much love as they put in this one.9.9/10 Will play again!

_childDocuments_.review: Unpopular opinion, but I didn't enjoy the game. My first issue is the unskipable cutscenes that really don't have to be there. I like to play a good platformer, but when every minute I get stopped to watch an unskippable cutscene, I start to wonder wether I'm playing a metroidovania or an interactive movie.My second problem has to do with level design. I found this game after completeting Hollow Knight, a game with where you can feel how much time has been put into adjusting room layout to make it clear what areas you can access and which ones you can't. Then I played the first Ori game, and I don't remeber having any unpleasant experiences. Then I played this game. I don't know why, but I feel like the creators just assumed people knew exactly where to go. I constantly noticed areas where I technically can access, but in such obscure and sometimes cheesy ways that I wonder if I should be able to get there. I usually try to look at the map to find any areas I left unexplored, but the problem is there's no way to tell the difference between currently unaccesable and unexplored areas, so in the end I'm running from one side of the map to the other like an idiot and finding a wall every single time, even though the map shows a path there.The graphics are great, I'll give them that. My gaming laptop sounds like it's about to fly to california whenever I force myself to play this game again, but I guess that's my problem. These people can make amazing art an animations, but video games aren't their strong suit.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very similar to its predecessor.  Unfortunately.The graphics, music, and sound are amazing.  The platforming is quite good as well.  The combat is better than the last game, but still very weak.  As I said in the last game, they should have made a platformer rather than try and be a metroid-esq game.  The last boss is the best example of that.  First, there is no enemy anywhere near as hard as this at any point in the game.  You go from decent combat with abilities you can work with to the mess the last boss is.The game shows you where an attack is coming from, but never shows you what the actual hitbox is.  I kept getting his by the ground stomps because I would move just outside of the where the head would be to get some hits in.  Neither the head nor the marker on the ground are anywhere near the size of the hit.  That head is another example.  I could stand a full Ori width away from the head, but still get hurt when I tried to attack it.  The last phase shows the really bad design.  The projectiles come at you with pure RNG.  This means you can use them to keep up, but suddenly, the direction you were moving in from them becomes empty and the nearest one is literally on the other side of the screen.  This will kill you through no fault of your own.Really, if they left out the combat and only did platforming, it would be a truly amazing game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first game, this is more of the same, but with better combat and combat customization. The game is slightly more difficult in the start, but once you start gaining upgrades, the difficulty lowers. I would recommend playing this.The story is good, but I felt that each area lacked in the lore department. Most of the time, the bosses were unexpected, and only after defeating them did you understand why you had to defeat them. There were lore NPCs in each area too, so the only thing missing would be fleshing these out slightly. The main story also continues from the first game, so if you want to understand what's happening, you have to play or watch the previous game first (at least the intro and ending).Combat is much better than in Blind Forest, with multiple skills and abilities to choose from. However, a few of the abilities become obsolete extremely fast, and some of the shards are either vague or obvious bad choices. There are also some risk/reward shards, where you deal/take more damage, or give enemies more health against better rewards, and these can be fun to mix things up. The "race bosses" are still present, but even on the normal difficulty, the margin of error on these are infuriatingly slim. Combined with deforming terrain, you can't guess the path in some circumstances, so you're stuck redoing the same sections over and over again until you see exactly how it will deform, and what paths will open.A lot of the mechanics from the first game, has been replaced by NPCs that you buy things from, and the "experience points" has turned into a currency. I did like this change, and also that they had a small town that gathered these NPCs, but I felt like the prices were too steep. I ended up getting 100% on collectibles in the game, and despite farming for light, I wasn't able to afford all the upgrades before finishing the game. In fact, I was not even close to affording them all.Overall, the game felt very similar to the first game in what it wanted to convey, and at points this became a bit too similar for me. I expected things to be shaken up in more ways than just the combat system. While Blind Forest is a hard 10/10 for me, I would probably rate Will of the Wisps at an 8.5/10. It's not much worse than Blind Forest, but it lacks some polish and didn't differentiate as much as I had hoped.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing. I usually find video game sequels to be worse than the first game, but Moon Studios found a way to do otherwise. The game's graphics and artstyle are beautiful, the story is charming, and the new features such as new moves, new abilities, and others are a really nice addition to the sequel. The secrets are fun to find as always, and the game is just... fun! It feels good to control Ori (except when swimming), and the side quests are also a nice addition. The only problems I have with the game are the autosave feature, the HUGE difficulty spikes, and... the ending. I understand that they wanted to end the Ori series so they could work on new games, but that ending REALLY made me think of Darling in the Franxx. Anyway, I strongly recommend picking this game up if you like metroidvainas, and I'm sure you'll have a lot of fun with it. I did. Good job, Moon Studios.

_childDocuments_.review: This has hands down been the most disappointing sequel I've ever played. The first game's platforming was smooth, the progression made sense, and I encountered absolutely zero bugs in my three playthroughs. I understand that most bugs in this game recently got patched out, but that didn't help me as I had already suffered through them all and gotten to the final boss, which I was stuck on for a week because the final phase relies on complete RNG.       Something that plagues the experience of this game from the very beginning is the fact that Moon Studios added so many new moves that send you in drastically different directions, but they mapped them all to the same button. This makes the chase sequences, which were the best parts of the first game, completely unbearable in this game since half the moves rely on proximity to certain objects. If you're even a millimeter too far away it's game over.       To make matters worse the developers felt the need to completely reinvent the wheel in terms of combat and saving mechanics, which were the two biggest selling points for me in the first game. Not to mention that they don't even explain what happened to Sein and just brush him off like he never existed. Furthermore all of this game's promotional material is plastered with that baby owl, who gets 5 minutes of gameplay and then you never see it again until the final cutscene and then the game just ends. No post ending content either so get ready to be reset to your last save before the final boss like it's 2009.      Lastly every single boss is the same, the enemies are just reskins of enemies from the past game, the songs for individual areas are forgettable (except for Luma Pools) and the boss themes are all the same. Not to mention that they basically just ripped off Hollow Knight for the combat mechanics.      Overall a complete and total letdown. I looked forward to this game for three years, as Ori and the Blind Forest is one of my favorite games of all time. Do yourself a favor and just stick to the first game, this one isn't worth the frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute gem to play. I don't write reviews for things often, but I figured it was necessary for this game.To start off: I hate 2D sidescrolling games in general. This game managed to be be the exception to my usual hatred of the genre.Pros:- Visuals, SFX and music are all absolutely stunning (favorited the soundtrack on Spotify :3)- Movement is like butter and is extremely satisfying to pull off, especially later in the game when you can chain so many different movement options together- World is extremely visually appealing and a lot larger than you'd expect, with many different areas to exploreCons:- Story is kind of lackluster (the spoken bits at least). A lot of what it tells is through visuals with some minor dialogue just to make sure what's going on is understandable- A little short on playtime. In Normal Mode, I was able to 100% the game in about 20 hours. That's still quite a bit of play time, but I guess I'm just kind of greedy when I say I want moreIn summary: I would highly recommend it to anyone who has the $30 or so to play it. It's got a pretty emotional story to it and definitely left me feeling the feels by the end. Haven't played a game that gave me the chills as much as this one did in quite a while.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where the developer made a great game (Ori and The Blind Forest), which while great, was not perfect. But then they took most of the not-so-great parts and fixed them in the second game (Ori and the Will of the Wisps).  Somehow they also improved heavily on already great parts. Huge emphasis on the fluidity of movement. It feels really good, better than the first game’s. This has also been accounted for in the level design.The game is still not perfect though. The main negative I have has to do with the game sometimes forgetting it is a game and not a movie. How is this bad you ask? Well, if the game 99% of the time gives clear indications of what you are supposed to do/where you are supposed to aim etc. but then suddenly there are these seemingly random situations where there is absolutely no indication whatsoever and then you die. And then you respawn at the very beginning of the level/boss fight, have to do the clear part all over again just to die to the same part again. And then you repeat this until you by pure coincidence realize what you actually have to do. Please, either always give me guidance or never give me guidance, the sudden change is the problem.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review off saying that I did not particularly like Ori 1, but I enjoyed this one a lot. I played for around 17 hours for 100%. I'm a veteran platformer and a fan of metroidvanias. I decided to play this game bc I read a review that said this was hollow knight in Ori world. Let me say that that person has NO IDEA what they are talking about. This is definitely not hollow knight even remotely. The only similarity is having a sword and having a selection of "notches" to equip. The game is mostly linear.It would've taken a lot less time to beat if I didn't try to sequence break every second of the game. "Oh, you want me to go in this direction? ♥♥♥♥ you, I'm going the other way" the entire game. That's how I missed the healing spell... And also met with disappointment bc I can't progress another direction because of said linearity. In hollow knight my 4th fought boss in the game was a dream boss. Just saying.I played on hard mode, had the take more dmg/do more dmg item on maxed upgraded, and apparently didn't collect the healing spell and heavy attack until the literal end of the game and I still didn't use them other than to get 100%. That honestly might've been the reason I enjoyed the game so much otherwise would complain the game was too easy and lose interest.The boss fights were really fun and required me to learn their attacks to a T because of said no healing and getting basically 2 shot all the time. There were arena combat challenges that were fairly challenging early on. The bosses had checkpoints for a reason...but honestly glad there were under the conditions I was playing in. The game shouldn't be hard at all for normal people.Metroidvania wise, it's not that good of an experience, but still way better than the first game. It is somewhat nonlinear but mostly still linear. There is an area in the game that is completely optional. And there are easily missable side quests. If any non linear part of the game exists it's when you have four different places to go, and you choose where to go, but still you'll need to at least collect some upgrades to bypass certain areas of other zones.I also enjoyed the mechanics in the game a lot. Movement for the most part was really fluid and sequence breaking/puzzle skipping was very possible with triple jump + bashing mechanics. I got several upgrades/pickups I wasn't supposed to with my current equipment that felt satisfying.The game near cutscenes were laggy af for me and during bootup my GPU goes crazy. I streamed and played the game, so I had 50% resolution on all the time due to the severe lag spikes I encountered early. Probably poor optimization - I have an above average rig.There were some game breaking bugs I discovered...especially early on. I was super close to skipping the game altogether. In the prologue, I got stuck into the wall, so my choice was either restart and watch prologue all over again that would take 5-10 min at that point or skip prologue. I did the latter. Redoing keybindings are the most frustrating thing ever if you're a keyboard only player like me. I had to unbind everything except the keyboard. AND if you bind those buttons that have two separate bindings for the same button by default, you will be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ when you try to move rocks. There was one rock near the beginning of the game I could not grapple onto. I spent about 30 minutes trying to figure out why. That's when I figured out for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason I needed to have glide and grab binded to the same button. WHY GOD does it have two separate bindings when you could write Glide/Grab onto one line in the controls? I don't know if it was those two bindings specifically, but it was something like that. There is a sound bug that either requires dying or restarting the game altogether to fix.  There is a control bug where ur character is permenantly pressing up, glide, or similar that requires a quick alt tab to fix. Otherwise, the bash mechanic stops working and you die. Oh...and you can't bind V to the keyboard for some reason, it always sets B instead lul.Also, during the last boss... The first time I died AND killed the boss. It put me in a glitchy area with no boss but can't leave the boss area. Upon suicide - I had to restart the entire fight over. THANKS.The game could've really benefited if it was longer as there were so many mechanics introduced not utilized. More boss fights would've been nice.Overall, great game. Would recommend to anyone - even those not a fan of the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, in visuals and the message it sends is truly something special, at least for me it resonates a lot. _childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely stunning game.- Gameplay is super fun with many enemies to fight, abilities to gain, and creative puzzles to figure out. - Great replayability, even if you beat the game there's so many more parts to discover and side quests to complete. This is basically a free world, although there are many parts you can't access until you get specific abilities.- Story line draws you in and is fun to follow, although there are some times that it really hits your feelers. I do recommend that if you have not played the first game to do that before you play this one, because while it is not needed to understand story, Ori and the will of the Wisps builds off the first one, Ori and the Blind Forest, and either way they are both fantastic games.- Visuals are by far some of the best I've ever seen in a game and absolutely gorgeous! Great opportunities for screen shots. (guilty :D)- The sound track and specifically the Orchestral score is just amazing to listen to.- I really have nothing negative to say. _childDocuments_.review: A great game, and in my opinion an improvement over the first installment. I only have one complaint. The game becomes far more open-ended partway through, which in itself is not a bad thing, but it unfortunately leads to many of the abilities you collect beyond that point barely being used outside the area you get them from, with one ability legitimately having no use beyond its home area and a single optional room elsewhere, and even in the area the ability comes from, it becomes useless beyond a certain point. It's only in the final sections of the game that you're really given a chance to use all your abilities in tandem, and it's a great feeling that I wish more of the game would tap into. Compared to the vast amount of things the game gets right, though, it's problems are insignificant. The soundtrack, as in the previous installment, is masterful. The visual design of the game is phenomenal, to the point I'd wager any random screenshot would be right at home in an art museum.I didn't find myself particularly invested in the story, but I hardly ever do. The set pieces, as in the first game, are tense, high-energy, and challenging. The game strikes a balance with collectibles and sidequests, enough to be engaging, while not being so much that it ever feels like a slog, which is owed in part to how good it feels to traverse the world.As for performance, I can't speak one way or the other. My computer is ancient, so of course the game did not run very smoothly, but for more modern systems, I'd assume it runs far better.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the 1st Ori, this game's a visual treat. The music is also amazing as expected, and the various addition of NPCs are a welcome upgrade to this type of game. Environments doesnt deviate much from what we saw in the 1st game, but all of them are very breathtaking to look at. Its very calming when its needed to be but can also turn quickly into a nerve racking affair when it wants to. I've died most of the times due to environment than the enemies (just like the 1st game), but I did feel that few of the platforming section wasn't well thought out as they needed memorization of the layout/map rather than reactive decision. Game's best played with a controller. The game's addition of quests and sidequest is another welcoming affair that turned this metroid-vania type platformer of a game into more of a side-scrolling action adventure game. The npc's are also fun to interact with, although some of the side-quest are the ones you end up doing automatically without even accepting the quest before hand, few of them do need the player's attention though. The game also added few optional challenge sections this time around; from combat trials where multiple waves of normal to hard enemies spawns like a survival/horde mode, to platforming race challenge at various spots on the map. The game also has improved on the combat system significantly by adding few melee attacking options. Aerial combat is the main deal this time around, also you can juggle enemies and do combos once you unlock enough abilities to quickly swap back and forth. The auto attacking wisp from the 1st game isnt available from the beginning; you'll however do unlock a sort of similar auto attacking ability later on in the game, but it doesnt function the same as the 1st game especially considering the new aggressive enemies. The game improved on the rpg aspects of the game by adding ability upgrades and slots. You can equip 3 abilities at a time that can be quickly swapped even during combat, You can also equip ability modifiers that would either improve your chances of survival or make it harder to turn the game even more challenging. Enemies have been significantly improved this time around, they are harder than expected and comes in multiples. The enemy projectiles track the player a lot more than it did in the 1st game. There arnt that many boss fights but the game does indeed have atleast 2 good/worthy bossfight that isnt just the usual ori style run-away-and-survive sort of stuff. There are a lot of those water-run section in this game, some being straight up frustrating , but most of them were a breeze to go through if your fingers are quick to react to stuff.  The Story was a bit led down towards the 2nd half (especially the ending). This might differ from player to player, but I personally have seen this sort of ending a few times from other media and game's itself. Wish the game did approach a different ending.  The game is amazing to play, especially if you are a fan of the 1st Ori, but the game isnt a great recommendations if you havnt tried the 1st. This is mainly due to the story it tells this time around and not the gameplay itself. If you are fan of a side scrolling action game, then definitely get this. You can also get this game just for its art. Just dont get the game right now as of posting this review (4th day of release). The game has some annoying bugs on PC/steam that affects your experience. From keyboard input bugs that interfere with gameplay, to fps issues in certain sections or while using a mouse, to minor ui bugs, to major audio bugs that happens quite a lot. Keep an eye out to see if the devs have fixed these issues.

_childDocuments_.review: This is what happens when someone loses confidence in their own formula.The previous title, Ori and the Blind forest, was superb. Fast and fluid with platform mechanics that were on point. This is just a bloated mess....Why did they lose sight on what made the first game so successful? Why add a bunch of mechanics that were not needed? Why rip ideas so blatantly from hollow Knight? Why add annoying loops in the map? All of this mess even got in the way of the one thing you are supposed to be good at.....platforming!This title shifted away from what it was, a fast paced platformer, with a great story and sound track, to a title with too many poorly introduced mechanics and broken pacing to boot.So sad to see a sequel perform so much worse than its predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: This might very well be the best game ever made.The mobility and fluidity of this game is unmatched even by Celeste. An extraordinary complete Metroidvania, with amazing escape sequences, memorable soundtracks, stunning visuals, and unparalleled gameplay.The game continued to surprise me until the very end, with endless upgrades and mobility options that never become obsolete (with perhaps the exception of one), and amazing combat system that I could never expect to be so fluid. Not even fighting games have such an arsenal of combos.The game has a neat feature that highly encourages speedrunning, and is incredibly fun to play with. Comes with a in-game scoreboard and live replays, even!I recommend this game to be played by every person that picks any interest at all.I cannot think of anything of negative to say about this game. Maybe only one: it has a few bugs, that you might likely encounter on a explorative gameplay. If you are like me that tries doing stuff kind of out of order (although not on purpose), you might stumble upon a few. Not that they break the immersion of the game, they don't. There were also two cutscenes where my fps dropped to 25, but this might be my computer fault.I highly recommend playing with an XBox controller, as the game deals really well with controller vibration.I recommend recording your gameplay, as you won't want to forget your first experience.Don't forget to put on full screen and disable V-sync for no input latency!This quickly became my favorite game in just a few hours, and I haven't even completed 100% yet.I am looking forward to getting all of the achievements for this game, and maybe even speedrunning it!I congratulate every person that participated in the creation of this game. This is the masterpiece of this decade so far, and I think it will take a lot to surpass this!Good job, Moon Studios and every single worker!

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a pretty fun game. It's a metroidvania with a high focus on platforming and this is done really well. You get lots of platforming abilities quickly that are really fun and satisfying to use. It's also satisfying when you pull off some minor cheese, which can happen a lot due to the varied platforming abilities and the fact that at least one attack gives you a small amount of extra height. The game also has frequent checkpoints, so you don't spend an absurd amount of time walking back to the hard part just to die and repeat the process again. Combat is alright too, though a bit repetitive. The focus definitely feels like its more on platforming. As for other aspects of the game, the story is alright (it mostly just kind of exists, but it is pretty unintrusive), though I enjoyed the ending, the art style and graphics are brilliant, and the soundtrack is also very good.However, there are a few downsides. My biggest issue with the game is that there is no minimap. Having to press the map button instead all the time is really annoying, and I found myself wanting to see the map a lot. Also, this may be an issue unique to me, but I found the default keyboard controls quite bad. Luckily the game lets you rebind everything, which I did several times, so this isn't too much of an issue. The game is also a bit buggy. Nothing too huge, but I occasionally had to exit and re-enter the save. Examples include the game freezing during black screens (for example in cutscene transitions) or Ori disappearing. These are rare, but did happen often enough for me to notice. The difficulty is not changeable mid-game, which was a shame as I basically had to guess what difficulty might be right for me, and game's often have very different interpretations of what is easy or hard. The enemy variety was also a little bit disappointing.The issues in the last paragraphs are a bit picky and definitely not too bad. Overall I really enjoyed my time with this game and would recommend it to anyone who is interested.
