_childDocuments_.review: I had planned on skipping this because I played the first one already, and didn't feel the need for more Ori. This looks pretty much identical. But I underestimated how much fine-tuning of the fundamentals here would improve the gameplay. This elevates a game that was loveable-but-janky into perhaps the best platforming experience ever crafted. It takes the handful of ideas that made the first game work and polishes them until they shine oh-so brilliantly.Once you have all the tools of movement at your disposal, it feels incredible to zip through the terrain at lightning speed. The controls are tight and intuitive - I rarely struggled to execute any maneuvers. The pace of learning is just right - they give you just enough time to master your current tools before adding more complexity.Perhaps most importantly, it's flexible and forgiving. You can smoothly cancel out of nearly any animation, which gives you this incredible dexterity with a low barrier to entry. Most challenges can be accomplished using a variety of methods, allowing you to develop your own style. An extremely forgiving checkpoint system encourages you to fail and experiment freely.Combat still isn't great, but it's totally passable - especially early on where enemy design is simpler and more focused on encouraging dynamic movement. Similarly, I didn't care for the bosses (and the boss races make an unfortunate reprisal). Attack animations, particle effects, and hitboxes are just too loose and hard to interpret to make the combat feel anywhere near as tight as the movement. There are also unclear rules around when you can bash through enemies, which leads to a some frustrating moments in late-game battles.But most of my time with this game went towards exploring the map and time trials. I'm dedicating an entire paragraph to the time trials because they're so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. The length is perfect - each course can be easily completed in under 40 seconds, which is just long enough to feel like a satisfying journey, but not so long that it's a struggle to keep the whole course in your head. Each one teaches you how to master a new mechanic, and by the end you'll have that skill fully incorporated into your toolkit. They're easy to learn and difficult to master - they're finely-tuned, dynamic, and just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of fun.Easily one of the best metroidvania platformers ever made. It's hard to go wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps

_childDocuments_.review: The best metroidvania/platformer i have ever played.Superb atmosphere/artstyle/music/gameplay/level design. Unlike the previous iteration, this Ori actually is formidable in combat, which is needed in all of the boss fights (which are mostly really good). The escape sequences are an absolute blast as well. Collecting upgrades and solving some minor puzzles from time to time is also a nice treat (which is to be expected from this genre). One thing stands out, however, and that would be the movement system. It is sublime. The movement in this game is S M O O T H. You have so many traversal options that it gets overwhelming at some points in time, but that is not  a bad thing in my book. The story is also neat, i really liked it.I love that there are devs who still make these ''passion projects'' which are not your typical AAA soulless trash. Moon studios is definitely on my preorder list.I love the game, and  I think you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a perfect example of more being less. The game gives you plenthy of new powers and trinkets, but limits you to three of each, making them mostly pointless. You end up either spending most of your time switching these around, or just getting tired and sticking to 3 for most of the game. This is made worse by the upgrading system, which also incentivizes you to not switch things up. Other upgrades also don't feel very rewarding or impactful, other than just advancing the story.The quest system is mostly a giant mess too, where you talk to one person to start the side-quest and randomly at a later time talk to another person to finish it, or randomly find quest items here and there which you can't do anything with until you randomly find the right person to give it to! It's bastardized fetch quests taken to their limit.While this sequel tries to spice things up by introducing a more complex fighting system, the game still remains primarily a platformer, which really is where it shines the most. This is best illustrated by the fact that most "boss fights" are still escape sequences, having you platform your way out in time.So all in all, this is trying to build up on the success of the first game, but ends up diluting what made it great in the first place and feeling like a confusing mess. The best parts of this game are the parts that were in the former game, so you may as well just go and play that again instead.I had high hopes for this game, and don't get me wrong, it's still far beyond most indie games out there. The art is better than ever and the music is fantastic, but it simply is a step down and is an unnecessary sequel to a perfect game.

_childDocuments_.review: So my PC runs Crysis 2 but not Ori and the will of the wisps...?disclaimer: I am well aware, that I cannot blame the developers for my low spec PC (Thinkpad from 2015, Intel i5 5200U, Intel HD Graphics 5500, 8GB RAM, Win 8.1)...but the fact that high-end games (Crysis 2, Mass Effect 2 and the like) work flawlessly on my PC - even in medium range settings - and the new Ori game does not leaves me a little speechless :)I know that these mentioned games are "old" but still they have quite a heavy graphic engine running, with a much higher complexity than Ori.For me, this leads to the conclusion, that Ori has a lack of code-optimization. This is especially frustrating for a game like this, since a lot of folks out there play metroidvania-style games on low-end hardware.For all of you who dispose of "up to date"-software, I wish you a lot of fun and heartbreaking moments with the game, for all of you who don't - sadly I CANNOT recommend buying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished it yesterday. It hurts me becouse I enjoyed a lot of things in game, probably if not for aticlimactic ending I wouldn't felt so negative towards it. I really don't want adventures of ori as a franchise to go in that direction, that would be huge waste. I do not advise against buying it, especialy on sale, since its still a good game. Good game but a bad sequel to something that to me felt unique and magical.The graphics are beautiful, level design is great, I enjoyed the hell out of platforming through this charming world again. The story is alright, not great tho, feels like microwaved something from last week. There were moments in it that were just plain wrong like e.g. when badly placed controller shakes ruined immersion of game ending cutscenes. But the main offender for me is combat.Oh I know that fighting feels better in this one, but its only as far as controlling ori is polished, so you can do a lot of cool stuff. On the other hand I don't vibe with the idea of this nimble forest spirit slashing bugs to pieces with a sword, or why is he even wielding arsenal of weapons invented by mankind in firs place. It still feels good to slash, smash and shoot, couse moves are responsive and well animated. But really, due to enemies being boring and sometimes a little spongy, I think I had fun only when doing environmental kills.And then there are enemies... I cant stress this enough how hopeless they seemed against ori's new abilities. With them having only 2 or 3 moves at best, and not being particularly aggresive, I rarely felt in danger. A lot of times on my playthrough gorleks just stopped moving entirely, becoming passive punching bags. Overall, this combat system got stale pretty fast.So here is one idea how to make it way better: if only devs focused on environmental kills. Ori was never defenseless, his platforming skills can be frickin deadly. I'm saying lets add more trickery like a feather that blows enemies away, maybe a different kind of lasso that would allow player to switch places with enemy etc. And then make fights as a combat puzzles, in which you have to think quick how to get rid of mobs using  only environment with fun (and not stupidly violent) mechanics. People who designed levels are so talented, I think they may create a masterpiece if core mechanics of the game will be more connected to their ideas. For now, I cant say what was the idea behind will of wisps, its eighter just a mess, or ripoff of mechanics trending in all modern metroidvanias...Bosses... are awful. They are dissapoiinting, softly speaking. The thing with games that rely on combat experience like dark souls or hollow knight is that they are trying to make you feel like youre fighting for real. Enemies are aggresive, they have decent move pools (with moves that usualy make sense for what those enemies are), and their attacks are aimed at you (very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ important). In will of wisps bosses are just patterns, with animations slapped on them like no one cares. Why the hell owl is shooting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ laser from her mouth, and always doing so from left to right, no matter where player is. Why every time its about to hit the ground with claws, there is an air flowing from it to make sure you wont get hit.Telegraphing attacks is fine if done properly (like e.g. in Furi) but oh god these bosses are like uncle playing with children, inventing some flashy epic punches that are aimed at air, so the kid will think hes agile or whatever. Only chases were cool, and maybe the last phase of final boss (but that also felt wrong how he went from cruelly boring to very challenging only for one or two minutes).Another dissapointment was that little sister from boxart was barely itegrated into gameplay. Seing trailer and all I was really hoping that this will be the biggeest mixup - ori is not alone anymore, means new moves, completely different way of experiencing this world. Well no, you controll her in only one level if I remember correctly, and she is lame. She cant do nothing that ori can with feather, so this level is just being slightly slower and more limited.Also, why did they drop one of the most interesting mechanics from blind forest - placing chekpoints as a skill, that costs mana? I was good, felt unique to me, I liked it a lot, it made me way more invested in game. It was also corresponding with worldbiulding. So they had something going for their first game, which was creative and absolutely working, I consider it amongst the best mechanics like showering in blood in ultrakill for example, .... and they dropped it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is overall a good game. I like the atmosphere and the music. It is a platformer with some combat elements in it. So yeah I played the game in hard mode and was expecting some tough fights. In general hard mode is really weird because the difficulty doesnt feel balanced. From my experience the hardest part is the start when you are not used to your movement and dont have movement abilities and die to 2 hits from the environment. After finding some additional life cells on the way it becomes way easier and you dont really have any difficulties at all. Dying doesnt set you back and since the game saves all the time you can just try again. The combat vs normal enemies feels way too easy on hard mode, there are even some combat shrines where you have to fight a couple of enemies in a row but they are hardly a challenge. Boss fights are in general ok - in my opinion the last one is a bit strange. Not because it is too difficult, it is just weird that there are two save points in between the fight. So I took in my firsts attempts some extra damage because I didn't know the boss abilities and what i was supposed to do and then I got with very low hp / energy to the first save point which made the following parts of the fight unnecessarily hard because I got always two shot without really knowing the abilites.In conclusion there are a lot of things that could be better for sure. _childDocuments_.review: There's not a whole lot to say about this game, it's simply an incredible experience that I think everyone should get the chance to try.Will of the Wisps makes Blind Forest look like a prototype - an amazing and beautiful one, but a prototype still. This game manages to turn its predecessor, which was essentially just an adventure-platformer with some combat, into a fully fledged action RPG with quests, NPCs, boss fights, challenges and an in-depth abilities and upgrades system. WotW is a gigantic step-up from BF's basic skill tree, adding a lot more complexity and diversity to the gameplay, while also making important changes for balancing.Since this is an Ori game, it goes without saying that the visuals are on another level of beautiful, and the music perfectly hits the tone in any situation. It's really clear how much love the devs put into building this amazing world that makes you want to explore every nook and corner. Combined with the emotional story and great characters, this game is an experience unlike any other. Yes, it is  difficult at times, but in the same way as a Souls-like that gives you the feeling of achievement and reward in the end. I deem this game well-worthy of the title of a classic, do yourself a favor and play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Blind Forest is a masterpiece and the developers somehow managed to make an even better game. The graphics are gorgeous, the attention to detail is just crazy, the music is just as good as in the first game if not better, the gameplay mechanics are fun and new, and the ending was just incredible.This game is much harder and longer than the first one. First game took me about 12-14 hours to 100% complete for the first time, this game took me 21 hours and I enjoyed every minute of it! When I said the game is harder than the first one, I meant it, seriously. I've completed the first game on one life difficulty multiple times, but there were still sections in this game that took me a lot of trial and error to complete. That is not a complaint by the way, I loved the challenge!I really like the new combat system, it's a lot like Hollow Knight, and while I had no problem with the combat in the previous game, I think fighting in the new game is a lot more fun! I was really happy to see that we still had some of our abilities from Ori and the Blind Forest, and that despite the fact they have added a lot of new game mechanics, the good things, like the escape sections, were still part of the main focus of the game.I only really have a few complaints. As I'm writing this review, there are some minor performance issues with the game, and no, it's not my computer, I've seen a lot of people reporting this problem. Occasionally there's a little bit of lag or a sound glitch, but only for a brief moment. It doesn't ruin the experience luckily, and I'm fairly sure it will be fixed soon (hopefully).The Spirit Trials was a nice addition to the game and I already know I will spend hours trying to get the best score I can. I just wish the people on top of the leaderboard weren't all hackers (it's possible that they are just using glitches to use abilities you weren't supposed to be able to use during the Spirit Trials, but I find that REALLY unlikely).Now, my main complaint (gameplay spoiler alert):  The idea is cool, but it could have been executed better. This was the first time ever I almost started raging while playing either this or the previous game (if we don't count the time when I tried to complete the game on one life difficulty, that's a completely different story). I'm just glad I was able to get past that area relatively quickly, I honestly can't imagine how bad that section must have been for people with less practise. Overall the game only has some smaller issues, otherwise it's a work of art like the first game. If you like good platformers with fun fights and the occasional smaller puzzles then you should definitely give this game a try!9.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps really tries to be better than its predecessor. The game is far longer (judging by completion %, I did not/will not complete it), the world is bigger, there are more characters, more movement options, more attacking options. As a result, the game comes across as bloated, lacking polish in favor of having more for the sake of more. My biggest complaint is the combat. There are no redeeming traits to Ori's combat. Blind Forest's combat works because your attacks auto-lock, allowing you to enjoy the fluid movement mechanics, cleverly ignoring the imprecise and floaty nature of Ori's movement. In its sequel, however, you are forced to move with a precision that the game does not afford you in order to make use of a lot of its combat mechanics. Many of the enemies have weird animations without telegraphs, and even the ones that telegraph correctly aren't any fun to fight. This is immediately apparent when fighting the first boss, a wolf. You'll know when you get to it because it sucks. This doesn't mean the combat is necessarily difficult, but it is unbalanced and unfair. The various attacking options you can buy later on did not look like they would remedy the problems either. I recommend just getting the big hammer attack, its upgrade, and plowing through everything along with spamming arrows. The bloated nature of the game really exposes the tediousness of combat. WotW sends you on boring side quest after boring side quest, introducing backtracking but not in a manner that makes you actually want to explore the world to find new things. Rather, it's "go give this to x" or "go bring y to me", and off you go, at the mercy of more poor combat as you wind through the ever-growing world of WotW just hoping it will end.The main plot is uninspired. I did not finish the game, but from what I've seen it's simply a fetch quest where you rescue the baby owl from the end of the last game. The amount of emotions Ori tries to pry from you while proving in the Blind Forest that they will literally revive dead main characters if they need to reveals a lack of understanding about what makes stories have tension.  There are a lot more cutscenes in this game, breaking up the flow about every 5 minutes. Some are skippable. The art is very good. Character designs range from cool to amazing, backdrops are beautiful if a bit high on the contrast.3/10I don't know why people like this game.Edit: I forgot to mention they removed the one unique idea they had in choosing where you save your game as an in-game mechanic. Now you get checkpoints like everyone else.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Version: Whether on sale or not, this game is totally worth it. If you liked Blind Forest, this will continue that love. Honestly, I have to give Will of the Wisps a 10 out of 10. Right now at the time of writing, this is on sale for $10??? BUY IT. Long Version: There's so much to love about Ori and the Will of the Wisps. Let's dive into it. Mechanics: The powers you get this time around, are fresh and interesting. They make sense, though you may struggle for a bit to get a hang of some of the powers in the beginning. Story: Seriously, just a kick in the feels, right from the start. In our last game, Ori got a family. In this game... well, Ori's family goes through some hard times, including some serious loss. The characters experience pain and loss differently, and not just once, but several times. However, this really does wrap up Ori's story very well. I really enjoyed, though I was struggling from time to time, this story. Though I was sad for the one who shunned the light. New Characters: There are some great new characters in Ori, and some of our old faves. Some of these characters are really well done. Some are just functional, but I really liked some of the bosses and their stories. Not everyone has a happy end. Controls: Precise and Intuitive. Ori does what you want, when you want. No issues here. Combat: It's Ori! Combat is seriously fun and well thought out. There are some annoying features when it comes to some enemies, but even on my last play through for a speed run, I figured out some new tricks to make them easier. Experiment, experiment, experiment. Music & Voice Acting: Ori has brilliant music that seems to match each and every scene perfectly. Fast paced beats with heavy dark tones when you're running for your life to mellow sad notes, that seem to tug at your heart... Whomever composed this really did a great job. The voice cast is small, this isn't a dialogue game, however, there is effort and it fits and is done well.Graphics: Honestly, I didn't really expect much going into Ori. I mean, we're talking about a side-scrolling metroidvania with our lovable Black and White Hero, Ori. But, boy was I wrong. There is loving detail put into each and every area. The added effects everywhere in the game, will just blow you away. For extra oomph, go into settings and just run everything up to max. Seriously, why would we need max in a game like this? It allows the game to bring the background and extra effects to life. It's pretty amazing. It's no wonder the game won for Outstanding Visual Style. Achievements: I've got 35 out of 37 and I'm done and lazy at this point. Perhaps I'll go back and get the last two, but just needing a different game at the moment. Most of the achievements are fun and help you enjoy a second play through. Some are annoying in that they push you to be perfect, but some people love that. Save System: Well that's weird, there are auto-backups which you can access if you need to, so that's helpful and annoying if you're trying to do a flawless run. Knowing which save is actually the save you want can sometimes be hard to tell. Overall: This game is really amazing. I got it on sale but I would have paid full price had I known what I was getting. It's come out to just around $1/hour and each and every hour were jam packed with entertainment.... Except maybe the speed trials. Seriously though, if you liked Blind Forest, you're probably going to love this. I don't know why some people thought this was worse than Blind Forest. Makes no sense. Though it does put a cap on the story. I spent hours exploring beautiful landscapes brought to life by gorgeous backgrounds and awesome music, all while helping Ori and the Wisps.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is masterful just like its predecessor, however, there are crippling issues that made this game way less enjoyable than the first one. Keep in mind that this review is coming from a KBM perspective, and while my overall opinion of this game is positive, I have highlighted (or 'nitpicked' if you would like to consider it that way) several major issues that I take with this game that greatly contributed to my frustration and detracted from my enjoyment of Ori 2.Don't get me wrong - Ori and the Will of the Wisps is an absolutely beautifully crafted game, with extraordinary soundtracks, breathtaking graphics, an stunning visuals. The introduction of the weapon system is a breath of fresh air, and the animation in-game is just as captivating. Nevertheless, I cannot help but be disappointed by how much this Hollow Knight-esque combat system detracted from its original format, and that is the platforming aspect with Ori's signature "Bash" at its core.While working just like it did in the first game, the Bash's charm has lost its entire purpose other than serving the sole goal of solving platforming challenges. In the first game, we had to redirect projectiles as our way to deal with hostile mobs, and and juggle between many projectiles (or one multiple times) in order to solve the platform puzzles. Here, the weapons take up much of the combat, and while it is masterfully animated, there are major issues which detracts from my enjoyment.Firstly, while the main weapon can lock onto a target and executes the full combo when connecting the first hit, the direction of your attack is determined by the direction you are facing, and not the direction of your mouse. Of course, this is coming from a KBM player, and thus I am sure the system works well for controller players. However, as Ori is, at its core, a platformer, players should be granted some form of combat forgiveness that would make the combat system more fun rather than frustrating to be hit because you are locked into an animation when the attack goes the wrong way.This auto-target (or lack of) system brings me to my second point, and that is how the game treats your movements - in a game that is overly encumbered by it. There are way too many different movement commands in Ori, and not only does the game not tell you the extent to which you are execute these moves (namely, dashing through dirt platforms - which ultimately is a minor discomfort once learnt, but still), it tries to predict your move by auto selecting objects within range to facilitate the flow of actions. Now, when it works, it works great, however, when it doesn't, it creates major frustrations where the game will pull you in one direction or force you to dash in mid-air when you are trying to dash through a platform or grapple to a different object that your cursor is covering over.Lastly but not least, the story is decent, but not outstanding, and the game-play pales in comparison to the first game. The section with the bird-riding is short and could have been explored a lot more if not for story purposes, while the platforming difficulty is significantly lacking in creativity as more attention is given to mob-fighting and not solving puzzles. In the end, this creates a shallow Hollow Knight feel with a shadow of Ori's former platforming greatness, as Ori 2 tries to accomplish both but fails to do either one great.In the end, Ori and the Will of the Wisps is still a great game that I would recommend picking up for anybody who enjoyed the first game. The nostalgia factor is strong, and I applaud its attempt at integrating something new, even though the execution of said system could have been done a lot better in favor of player satisfaction rather than artificial difficulty over poor combat optimization.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: The 3.1 patch has addressed many of the performance issues I described in my original review. The game now runs much more smoothly in many places where it used to chug quite heavily, and I am able to play mostly without the game suffering much slow-down or input being dropped. Thanks so much Moon Studios for the update! <3Original review retained below for posterity.--I really want to like this game. I really do.Ori and the Blind Forest is such a masterpiece, and I was patient enough to wait for the Definitive version so I could play it at its best. I loved that game; I cried so much during the story, and enjoyed both the variety of the game mechanics and the flawless level design that made every feature useful in some tangible way. I've played the game through four times and still I find myself going back for more!When I heard that there was going to be a sequel, I was so excited that of course I immediately put it at the top of my wishlist so I could keep up to date with news! I even almost bought the game on release day - something I have only ever done one other time in over 25 years of playing games - and I only didn't due to having real life commitments requiring my full attention at the time. I've been looking forward to playing Ori and the Will of the Wisps for over a year now, so it is with a heavy heart that I have to write this review about is.Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a stunning game, with beautiful scenery, a deeply emotive musical score, and such wonderful attention to detail that has produced a rich and dynamic environment for Ori to explore. Sticks, logs, vines, fungal growths, and so many other things in the environment respond to Ori's passing, making the world feel malleable and alive in a way that few games of any genre have achieved.The addition of peripheral characters with their own agendas, and side quests that encourage exploration of this enchanting world, provide a sense of continuance that was, by contrast, missing from the game's predecessor. On top of this, the game is full of gorgeous visual effects that further add life to the game, and which also serve to highlight Ori's distinct, luminous nature in a world so filled with gloom and shadow.Unfortunately, it is this last feature that causes the experience as a whole to come crashing down. There are regions of the game where one can run through an area and experience only minor, if any performance hits due to effects. And then there are places where performance is hit so hard that the framerate can drop as low as 5 frames per second, sometimes with a suddenness that can tear a chasm in the flow of the game, and subsequently ruin the immersion. And all this even when the only application I am running is OatWotW.Even worse is when the game begins to miss input events coming from my controller, especially when in the middle of a combat challenge. There's nothing quite like the feeling of impotent frustration one experiences when watching Ori, in slow-motion, sailing gracefully, face-first into the sharp end of a Skeeto, despite having pressed, held, or repeatedly tapped the button assigned to an attack in the hopes that Ori will do.. something, anything.In contrast, the performance issues in OatBF were relatively minor, and could be mitigated by reducing quality settings. As with many other players, I first encountered flow-breaking performance issues in the Ginso Tree's escape rush, but a quick tweak of the AA setting was all that was needed to make the level playable again, and with the exception of the other rush sequences, the rest of the game played just as smoothly. In OatWotW, the only graphics settings that look like they might help are already switched off, so I feel powerless to mitigate the performance issues with adjustments on my side.These issues combined make parts of the game unplayable, and ruin my experience of the game enough that I'd rather stop playing it and wait for the Definitive Edition in the hope that it will have some performance improvements, as well as more player control over quality settings.Moon Studios: I really love what you have done with Ori as a franchise, and I will definitely be back once these issues have been addressed! For now though, I just cannot play this game in its current state and be able experience it as you would have intended. Please keep us apprised as to how and when these performance issues will be fixed, and when we can expect to be able to experience the game as it was meant to be experienced! :)

_childDocuments_.review: If you're fortunate enough to have a QD-OLED HDR panel and can play this game at 4K, prepare to be absolutely blown away. This game is, without a doubt, the most visually stunning experience I have EVER encountered. The graphics are nothing short of breathtaking, with vibrant colors, deep blacks, and incredibly sharp details that bring every scene to life in a way that few other games can.But it's not just the visuals that make this game a masterpiece. The soundtrack is equally phenomenal, perfectly complementing the stunning imagery and immersing you even deeper into its world. Each track is thoughtfully composed to heighten the atmosphere, whether you’re exploring serene landscapes or diving into intense action sequences.And then there’s the story—compelling, emotional, and layered with unexpected twists. The narrative pulls you in from the very beginning and keeps you invested until the credits roll. Combined with the top-tier visuals and sound, this game offers an unforgettable experience that will leave a lasting impression.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:-That same level of glorious art and music from the original game.-The combat is greatly improved from the original. Instead of a lock-on ranged attack, you now have a melee weapon, which makes combat much more satisfying. -The addition of a charm system similar to Hollow Knight adds a lot of variety to the gameplay and also makes exploration much more rewarding as a bonus.-There are now NPC's speckled throughout the world that breathe a lot of life into the game, it's a really nice touch. They also have side quests which give you all sorts of new stuff to do.CONS:-The game is a little buggy in its current state. I had issues with periodic audio farts (for lack of a better term), a bugged rumor that never went away even after completing it, and a collectible that showed on the map, but wasn't actually there, which unfortunately prevented me from 100%. I'm told that some people have had much worse issues than these, but I have confidence that they'll get ironed out, since it's still early into the game's release.-There is a currency in the game that can be traded to friendly creatures for various items and upgrades. I (basically, due to the aforementioned collectible bug) 100%'d the game, and even still was lacking several thousand Spirit Light worth of upgrades. These upgrades fortunately don't count towards 100% (as far as I can tell, anyway). It is entirely possible this intended to give the player some sort of variety on a 2nd playthrough, encouraging you to try out different playstyles, but to me it was frustrating, since I wanted to finish the game with everything unlocked.It's a little buggy, but somehow they did it, they made a game that far exceeds Ori and the Blind Forest.

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is almost certainly a better game than its predecessor by most objective measures. Everything that made the former great is still here: Bash is back, as satisfying as ever, and the game thankfully knows to return it to you much sooner than the first game did; it comes alongside a host of well-executed improvements to the combat system, and a host of new abilities to complement Bash, with Grapple and Burrow being, for me, the standout additions.     The game is also bigger than its predecessor, with more areas, a grander and more expansive soundtrack, and a larger cast of characters; Ori can hardly turn a corner without bumping into some new NPC to bestow a quest upon him. Usually these quests require Ori to travel to some designated location to pick up or deliver a trinket, and some minor reward accompanies it.    This, for me, is the first sign of cracks in Will of the Wisps’ armor. If I could describe Blind Forest in a single word, I would use “elegant”. It is focused, streamlined, and tightly designed. Will of the Wisps, for all of its mechanical enhancements and improvements, sacrifices this elegance for scope, and in my opinion not usually to any real benefit. The quests are mostly busywork; they provide you with currency, which you might use to buy a shard or a new weapon technique or an upgrade, but you can complete the game while disregarding almost all of these. What do they add to the experience?    Much is said in the world of game design these days about so-called player expression. “Play your way!” the marketing engines howl, but the problem with accommodating multiple styles of play is that each style is diluted as a result. The game cannot run the risk that I haven’t bought the spirit hammer, or whatever, and so it can never require me to use it. I have a giant palette of paints to choose from and many styles of brushes, but no real painting is demanded of me; what, then, is the paint for?    Sadly, this same dilution occurs in the structure itself at the midpoint of the game, where Will of the Wisps seems to take a cue from Breath of the Wild and tells you to complete four areas in any order you like. Again, play your way: nice for marketing perhaps, but this means that the previous game’s elegant progression of Ori’s abilities cannot be replicated. The game cannot risk that I haven’t acquired the Burrow move, so I can never be required to use Burrow in any of the other three areas. Gone is the buildup of powers, gone is the designers’ ability to weave them together in increasingly complex and interesting ways; you get a flashlight here, a burrow or a fireball there, and none of it meshes, synergizes, or works together. This, to me, is a colossal missed opportunity, and cuts against what made the first so satisfying from start to finish. The final area of the game provides a token nod to the kind of cumulative design that might have been - but too little, too late.    The platforming is still pristine, arguably improved from the first game. The combat is undoubtedly more engaging, challenging, and fun, if bloated with excessive options and unnecessary fat. Once again, I think it would be fair to say Will of the Wisps is the better of the two games, and will find a wider audience than the first. But the elegance has been lost in the process, and the focus. It seems a shame. 4 stars out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this review is going to be heavily edited from its original after I convened with a friend on Steam (thank you Ladosia, for - likely unintentionally - giving me some new perspective) who played it and talked with me about it just over a month ago and I restarted with new button-mapping to test if it was actually as bad as I thought it was. I've been wrong about this before - the Misty Woods in the first Ori being a prime example - so maybe I was just over-exaggerating?Scroll to the bottom if you want the TL;DR, but keep reading for more in-detail explanation.Now, I absolutely love Ori and the Blind Forest and the ability to explore a new world with the same fast, energetic, and bouncy controls I love using was amazing overall. Once you get the movements down, it really feels like you're flying through the environment. The new mechanics in this sequel are fun and unique - if juggling your abilities can occasionally be a little awkward, though it's rare so no real complaint there.The new boss fight mechanic is incredibly well done and I relish the occurrences in which you get to fight something bigger than your average enemies. I feel like Moon Studios took a lot of inspiration from Hollow Knight and other similar games with the shards, abilities, and fights. Which I'm content with since I love Hollow Knight to pieces!The introduction of characters you can talk to and side quests make the world feel much more alive than just doing the main storyline and gives a good excuse to explore the map in its entirety. As usual, the soundtrack is amazing and I may end up buying it at some point.Now, why aren't I changing this review to a positive one/recommended if I'm happier with the game now?Minor spoilers for game mechanics, but none for the main story except the vague mention of the existence of a chase scene.When I first wrote a review I was immensely frustrated by the keybinds for the dash - its default is ctrl, but I'd moved it to alt in the hopes it'd be easier to use. This meant I had to move my thumb off the spacebar. Evidently, this wasn't the case and I was unable to complete one of the end-game chase sequences.After talking with Ladosia on her first delve into the game and its mechanics, she didn't complain about very much and had no issues with the dash in its original place on ctrl. I moved around a few things so my dash was now bound to -shift- and, as a result, grab was now on alt (ended up launching myself off a platform a few times due to reflexively pressing -shift- on a lever, but I digress). Was finally able to complete the game entirely using these bindings, but I bet it still doesn't explain why I'm keeping this review as negative.I'm not changing because there's a lot of people who struggle with the controls since there's so many buttons and keybinds in already-more-convenient places. It's hard to find a place to put things if its original bind isn't working.Additionally, there's a new mechanic called grappling that I still find a little finicky since its introduction. This is bound to the right-click for keyboard users and depends entirely on the direction you're pressing -wasd. So, if it's in the upper left you have to press -w- and sometimes -a-. This sounds simple, but if you even so much as tap in a different direction it'll deselect the lantern/blue moss. Not to mention, it's incredibly easy to fly in the wrong direction or fling yourself into spikes, since the grapple on a lantern simply launches you in the direction you're facing the lantern (if you're on its direct right, you'll be flung left; upper left, it'll shoot you toward the lower left; etc. Hope that makes sense). It's very difficult to get used to and I still sometimes fly directly into a spike wall because I wasn't in the right spot when i grappled.This game overall feels like it was optimized for controller use, though it is definitely possible using a keyboard if you've got some patience (though that was true for the first game as well). I don't own a controller myself, but others have also mentioned that it's better with a controller. If you prefer using a keyboard, go right ahead and use one. But if you don't care or prefer controllers, I'd say use a controller.  A good game and worthy sequel with a beautiful soundtrack and fun combat, but a few controls such as the grapple and dash require some struggle/practice or moving the keybinds in their respective places for smoother gameplay. Don't have a controller myself, but it feels like using one would be astronomically easier with how the game is oriented/played. Though it is very much possible so beat/play with a keyboard+mouse.For those wanting to know who just scrolled down, I put my dash on -shift- and grab on -alt- and it helped a lot.If you decide to buy this game or are reading reviews after already purchasing, good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps is an action platformer and the sequel to Ori and the Blind Forest.Having played the first game a lot, and most of it quite recently, I naturally couldn’t wait for the sequel. I was a bit worried that it might be too different, yet not different enough to feel good - but nothing of that mattered anymore the instant I started playing: It felt great!Ori and the Will of the Wisps has lost nothing of what made the first game so good, meaning the platforming and the movement mechanics, basically. At the core it’s still the same, with some additions, mostly more complex combat than in the first game, and a much bigger map with more content. There’s more variety in a lot of things, and I want to mention the soundtrack specifically for that aspect: The soundtrack in the first game was great too, but it consisted of variations of the same theme for the most part. It feels much more diverse here. The gameplay is fun, as well as as the overall world, the boss fights, escape sequences (although there was one I had quite some trouble with and I ended up kind of hating it, as the most important mechanic didn’t feel very precise. I’m not sure how much of that is my fault, but the other escapes felt rather easy, so it was weird). The NPCs are well-designed, there are side quests and other activities you can do, apart from collecting stuff throughout the map - and completing the main story, of course.To me it feels like most of the additions and changes compared to the first game really were aspects that people didn’t like so much or would have wished for in the original Ori, so that’s a plus, too. Many of those changes feel similar to Hollow Knight, but to the right extent: It definitely is still an Ori game, but it might appeal a bit more to fans of Hollow Knight who didn’t like Blind Forest so much. Many have said it before, and I was no exception: I had some minor bugs and glitches, as well as one game crash. I was lucky, it didn’t happen very often, and there was nothing gamebreaking for me. Also, all problems were solved after I restarted the game, but still a bit annoying. Things are probably going to be fixed soon, so it might be a good idea to wait for a few more days if you’re not too eager to play right away.Not taking this too much into account for the overall experience, I do recommend the game - very much. Compared to Blind Forest I wouldn’t necessarily say it’s better, it’s a bit different and it offers more (personally, I think I prefer the first one as I think the level design is better in Blind Forest). But in comparison or on its own, doesn’t matter, because I do think it’s a great game!

_childDocuments_.review: 9-10/10 Game. Easily.The Soundtrack is phenomenal. I never get annoyed of hearing it. Will likely listen to the soundtrack while I work.The world is beautiful. The art style no different than the first game, but wildly expanded upon.The combat is... well its intentionally a little lackluster here and there. More on that below.The movement is super nice. It feels really good and crisp. You have so many ways to traverse and I love it.The story compelling if you're willing to listen. Even then, it's pretty visual so it's hard to miss whats going on unless you skip the cutscenes. I almost teared up at the end.On combat:The Ori Franchise is part of the metroidvania genre, but it takes a scenic route approach. It's beautiful and easy. Even when made hard, it's significantly easier than other games. Because of this, the combat is not as moment to moment intense and sharp. If you're expecting fluid and amazing combat from Hollow Knight, you will most definitely not get it here. It is however smooth. The movement is great and makes up for the lacking combat. Befitting of the story and atmosphere, you don't have to fight everything, you can smoothly move (schmove) around them. And it feels really good.I adore this game and look forward for more from this developer.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Ori and the Blind Forest; it sits proudly as one of my favorite metroidvainias, and it's safe to say to Moon Studios has completely knocked it out of the park with its sequel. As well as making everything Blind Forest got right even better. And it goes without question but the game's art style and soundtrack are stunning. If I had to give out some criticism I would say that the map can get really cluttered at times and that there's way to many different weapons and items in the game, most of them being useless compared to others. But overall, this game is a gorgeous masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Great game with interesting gameplay and captivating story.Ori and the Will of the Wisps has everything that made the first game so great. Well optimized, interesting puzzles, beautiful colour and atmosphere, with a story line weaving the levels together.the Will of the Wisps does all these things right, and added a couple of little extra features that makes it just that tiny bit better that its predecessor. These little extras are: -Friendly NPC's you can talk to, that are fun to have short little interactions with, which helps with the world building. -The introduction of side quests, forcing you explore the world more, instead of only going for the main story. What made the first game so good is how as you progressed and learned new abilities, you can reach new places in biomes you've already been in. Making you go criss cross from biome to biome, rather than a straight linear path. These side quests initiate that behaviour and give a little of incentive of exploring all the corners of the world of Ori. - A well writen story that continues where the first game left off. With genuinely engaging moments. Both happy and scary.All in all, it's very similar to the first game, with the same vibe, same abilities and type of puzzles. but with a little bit extra, making it different enough to be enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR A disappointing and mean-spirited cash-in on the brilliant and beautiful first game. Gameplay is more of the same with some bells and whistles, but everything that made the first game exceptional is just gone. If you liked the first game, save your money and your time. There's nothing here except a soulless glowy-cat killing everything on screen. Oh except there's merchants now.Wow. I have never played a worse and more mishandled sequel in my life. And I played Duke Nukem Forever. I am utterly shocked and overwhelmed by how much of a disappointment this game is after the first one.So petty stuff first. The graphics optimization is HORRENDOUS. The graphics are identical to the first game, but this one runs considerably worse. Tons of clipping, stuttering, and major sound glitches. My computer is pretty old, but the first one runs flawlessly and there's no apparent reason this game should run any different than the first one, so if they have updated it only shows in the issues, not the product.The real issue though is the game itself. The first game was a powerful, emotional story with deep messaging about loss, forgiveness, healing trauma both personal and generational and hopefulness in the face of adversity. I cried multiple times. It also had thoughtful gameplay that reinforced the message. This game has a throwaway sappy plot comparable to a Hallmark commercial, and right off the bat, it's just senseless violence against random woodland creatures. Last time they had me healing the forest. Now in the first moments of gameplay I'm burning it down. Before I fought corruption and disease. Now I'm fighting animals in a forest where I don't belong.It's a shame, because some of the new gameplay elements are really fun, but they're tied to a game that has ZERO respect for itself or the player. Ori and the Blind Forest is a MASTERPIECE. Ori and the Will of the Wisps is just another game in an endless sea of Metroidvanias.There is absolutely nothing special about this game. It just exists to cash in on a predecessor it's not worthy of. Oh also, there's no more making your own save points, and the wells are WAY further apart than the first game. So make sure you have lots of time on your hands before starting a play session.

_childDocuments_.review: I am 32 years old.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps was an amazing experience. They fixed all of the issues of the prequel, like combat, the skill system, save system and some minor enviromental/level design problems. For some of those aspects they clearly took some lessons from Hollow Knight. Everything else is as good as it was before, or in the case of the music, even better. Sometimes I got pissed off though. While the combat looks and feels fantastic, they achieve that by sacrificing clarity sometimes. Bosses were the biggest issue. One boss has a stupid "getting stunned" animation, which makes it flail around in the air and touch you with its limbs, while you are trying to attack it airborne (the game is punishing you for stunning it). Another boss has extremely unclear hurtboxes. Normally any enemy you touch anywhere will damage you, but this boss is not like that (cause then it would be impossible to deal with), but it's not clear which parts are hurtboxes and which are not. Other bosses have problems too.Despite the issues, this game is easily one of the best games of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the only games that left me almost speechless.I'm not going to spoil anything, but oh my gosh that was the most emotionally powerful and beautiful ending of a game I've ever played. I was watering my eyes out for a solid 5 minutes.The art in this game is exceptional. The environments feel so alive and colorful, and match perfectly with the gameplay. All the characters are so well designed and Ori and Ku are downright adorable. I love how even though this is a 2D Metroidvania, it feels like you are interacting with a wonderful 3D environment.Next up, the gameplay is INCREDIBLE. I personally had way to much fun in Ori and the Will of the Wisps. The controls feel amazing and very smooth. The combat is also extremely fun to mess around with, which pales in comparison to Blind Forest's... Combat? Platforming also flows way too well. I could just get mesmerized from grappling, Bash and double jumping all over the place.The story? Exciting, EXTREMELY EMOTIONAL and very polished. The way it ties in to the first game's story is just... *chef's kiss*. Fair warning though, as you are bound to shed a tear or two at some point. What ties all these fantastic elements together is Gareth Coker's exceptional musical score. Every soundtrack in Ori and the Will of the Wisps is memorable, and it adds so much to the atmosphere. (Luma Pools, Baur's Peak and Ori, Embracing the Light some of my favorites)All in all, you absolutely have to pick up this game if you can. It's more than a game, it's an experience. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ori and the Will of the Wisps takes lessons learned from the first game (Ori and the Blind Forest) and builds on it to create a more expressive and interesting combat system while expanding on the already beautiful art style to create a visual masterpiece. While playing I wanted to explore every nook and cranny the game offered, discover every collectible and just experience the moving painting in front of me. The gameplay itself is terrific as you fly through the air moving from one enemy to the next, bashing off of plants and using your hang glider (Kuro's feather) to navigate through the terrain. The soundtrack deserves every award ever, sweeping orchestras mixed with soft compositions which fit each environment perfectly and had me listening to the soundtrack on my own for weeks after I finished the game. The mechanics and puzzles included were satisfying without being too hard or easy, and each new ability you unlock somehow manages to change the way the game is played. It can be challenging at points, but stick with it, it makes the moments even more rewarding and the game is well worth tackling a few obstacles. The characters are loveable, the story is compelling and environments are diverse and brilliantly designed. On release the game had some performance issues, but playing it a few months after release after playing it on the first week of release these issues have been fixed. Buy and play Ori and the Blind Forest if you have a pulse, even if you don't have a pulse the wonderfulness of this game is proven to revive the recently diciest. TLDR:Gameplay: Satisfying and rewardingVisuals: Any screenshot could be put in the Louvre Story: Captivating and tear-jerking Soundtrack: Stupidly amazing Performance: Runs fine for me, and I mean its on the switch so... (1070ti, Ryzen 7 2700)Price: This game is a 100% worth it at $30, it is a %10000000 worth it for $15 when it's on sale

_childDocuments_.review: (If you don't care for a long written review, just scroll to the bottom for the summary). My first review, here we go! Overall I sing my praises to this game. I do adore the prequel "Ori and the blind forest", and have sunk numerous hours into that one, but there are some definite improvements here. The movement in particular is amazing, so many different positions when jumping and running around, not to mention subtle details like the wiggle of the tail or flicker of the ears really drives the package home for me. The boss/NPC sprites are also improved a lot upon, although that perhaps comes more down to taste. In general I'd say the whole game is visually stunning, and has beautiful music to accompany it. The story telling is simplistic, and follow somewhat the same route as it's predecessor.Combat and general enemies has also received a lot of love, perhaps the biggest drawback of the first game Ori and the Blind Forest. In Will of the Wisps there are loads of new enemies with their own attack patterns and themes. There is also tons of new weapons and skills for Ori himself, which really allows you to pick and chose what fits your playstyle.There are however a few drawbacks/notes. The leveling tree of Ori and the Blind Forest has been swapped out for a "talk to NPCs for upgrades" system. Now, whether that's a good thing or bad will be entirely subjective, but I'll admit I feel a little nostalgic for the leveling trees Blind Forest used. That said, most of the NPCs are easily located at any time so it doesn't pose an obstacle.I have encountered a couple small glitches/bugs that will instantly kill you, so beware of the snapping plants of the ice area. You  want to get caught standing on their side when they're opening, especially during a death free run. Some of the long necked plants can also push you into the walls or bite a hold of the floating log you're standing on. Else from that, it does at times take a really long time to start up.-Visually stunning-Simple, yet tear jerking story-Engaging enemies and combat-Responsive and simple controls (gets a bit harder as the game progresses)-Minor glitches (non game breaking)By now I've played through it a good four-five times across two accounts, and I still find myself returning to it time and time again. What it perhaps lacks in the deeper meaning department, it definitively makes up for in the emotions it provides. Not to mention the visuals, gameplay and music is top tier. I highly recommend Will of the Wisps, it was worth every penny for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Great sequel to a great game.This game is everything I wanted it to be, and it also has many things that I didn't know I wanted, but like none the less.The world is once again huge and full of wonderful gameplay elements, hostile creatures are very interesting and challenging. What is really sweet is that during the main portion (2nd act of the game, which represents about 80% of the time), you will experience deja vu to the first game - there's once again a quest to purify waters, to unleash the winds, to deal with scorching hot land... but the areas are sufficiently different and can still surprise you with their mechanics.Boss battles and "escapes" are just as challenging as in Ori 1, which is part frustrating, part awesome.Perhaps the only point of criticism is the convoluted way for switching SKILLS. Now, you need to set (up to) three skills to three predefined keys, and can only use those; if you need a different skill, you need to reassign it, but that means you'll temporarily lose access to the one being replaced. This is further made worse by the fact that one of the keys is the Interact button (with which you talk to people or place objects onto other objects), which means Ori regularly "attacks" friendly creatures, Keystone gates etc.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Ori and the Blind Forest but this time it's almost exactly the same?You may balk at this negative review, given the overwhelming praise and adulation that's flowing this game's way, everywhere you look. But I'm sorry, it's not worthy of that of universal praise. Nothing is. This game has its flaws, and I want to draw attention to them, because I don't want to see them repeated another time around. There is a good game buried in here somewhere, but it is spoiled by careless execution (as well as enough bugs to feed a hungry tarantula). My complaints about this game's prequel are as follows: - the art style came, too often, at a cost to the gameplay- the autosave system was a bastardI am going to essentially copy-paste those comments because, in many respects, this game is a copy-paste of its predecessor. I'm not saying that's an entirely bad thing! If you enjoyed The Blind Forest, you will probably enjoy this too. But it's not anything like the radical evolution I was expecting. Like before, while the backgrounds are gorgeous, they are often too bright - especially considering your character is a luminous little star-gremlin. The camera movement in this game also leaves something to be desired - especially when you transition from one medium to another. If you are burrowing through sand, then leap out into the air, you will notice the camera struggles to keep track of you. This problem becomes acute, because there is an entire chase sequence *built* on this mechanic, which need not have been so frustrating if only it had been slightly better executed.Like before, while the autosave system is usually "adequate", for the purposes of exploration, it often forces you to relive your most frustrating moments over and over, because boss battles and chase sequences are usually quite long, and they offer you no respite whatsoever. These encounters tend to be quite long, and by the end, they overstay their welcome. And fundamentally, that's my parting thought with this game. While it's beautiful, it overstays its welcome. I'm only going to give passing comment on the story, because it's clear that that's exactly as much effort as the writers put into it. It's amazing what meaningless, pretentious trollop you can get away with when you use an artistic filter to make every character sound like they have a bassoon lodged in their trachea. This is a game which thinks it's deep, when really it's just very pretty. Before I sign off, a word about the bugs. I have encountered multiple performance issues with this game, despite having a pretty solid gaming PC:- Framerate drops- Audio tearing- Outright crashesI hope to goodness that if there is a further sequel to this game, that at least *some* of these criticisms can be addressed. There's a good game buried in here somewhere - but if I could make one change myself, I would not have a glowing protagonist in the next one. I would much rather play as one of those delightful little Moki - they're irresistibly cute and also, they don't give me eye strain...
_childDocuments_.name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost it is important to state, that Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a good game in its own right, yet I don't recommend it to anyone who played Ori and the Blind Forest, as I found it to be a poor sequel in every regard.TL;DR:Rant. Rant. The game feels like Hollow Knight dressed as Ori. It's an OK game, but not a good sequel either in regards of mechanics or story.Atmosphere and aesthetics:- Let's face it, these are defining components in the Ori games. I personally admit buying the first game because I came across its OST while listening music on YouTube, and I just got THAT hooked on the pure awesomeness of the music (the only other game I purchased for the same reason was Nier:Automata, and no I did not regret any of these decisions).And to jump to the problems: the music in Ori and the Will of the Wisps jus wasn't appealing. Great ambient music, but lacked the impact of the first game, felt generic. Even the recycled melodies from the previous installment felt meh.- With the graphics, I had a similar feeling, the old designs carried over looked great, but most of the new enemies for example felt off. I has been years since I have played the first game, so I can't tell exactly, but the new models did not fit the hand-drawn visual style of the environment.But what's worse, many graphic designs just felt like things were changed for the sake of changing it... I can't say it any better. I mean, what was the point of changing the light of the soultree from blue to yellow? It sure looks awful. Like, really awful...- And the last one, the NPCs. I include them here, because they effect the gameplay less than the atmosphere.  The first game was mostly about Sein talking, with some rare interactions with dead spirits and the absolute minimal number of alive NPCs, all of them critical to the story. This was completely overturned, as random interactable NPCs litter the whole forest of Niwen, the player never really feals to struggle alone. The narrative is splintered, interactions are often absolutely pointless and the inclusion of side-quests just make them even worse (especially considering the minimal compensation).Gameplay:- There is a set of new movement skills in the game, which allow for even greater freedom of movement, but their control scheme is just awful. Both true for the lasso and the digging dash (or really any aimed skill), that aiming them can cause more frustration than joy. Speaking about mouse and keyboard controls, the aim is truly deceiving, as it is sometimes but not always towards the mouse pointer and what's worse, not at the mouse pointer but just at it's direction. Fighting multiple enemies at once or being near multiple similarly interactable objects can randomize the result. The player can try to catch an incoming projectile just to grab a dangerous enemy instead taking damage for both, or can try to flee just to jump into the fray instead... I recognize this as a moderately well though out conversion of controller controls, but still...- The most fun parts of the first game were the chase sequences. Well, here they are gone... not really, but almost. They are shorter, much less dramatic and bring more frustration than challenge. Originally they could be done on the first try just by quick thinking and situational awareness, well, not anymore. While in the first game there was a clear way through the obstacles, here there are often multiple footholds offered, but if the player decides to make the jump a bit longer or shorter than the lenght intended by the developers, it could mean the loss of the round. Floors crumbling as soon the player almost lands on them becomes a thing, or just the boss catching up randomly if a wrong location is chosen for no apparent reason. It's trial and error finding out which plant to hook, which platform to land on, etc, while much less emphasis is placed on the precise execution.- But instead of chases, we have boss fights. And God why? The player has to fight several of these bosses, really meaningless large creatures we barely get to know (main one included) and we are thrown into an arena to bash them until they move. Yes, I played this game on Hard (I played the first one on the same difficulty as well) and as far as I know, the bosses are more reasonable on lower difficulties (not easier, just more reasonable, and I'll explain what I mean) so take my complaint as such. The bosses have MASSIVE health pools. And they are just that, sponges. Incredible variety of spam attacks combined with small windows for damaging them, while retaliation is almost certain retaliation. They are still not hard though, there is always a skill setup (heal+meele+utility and energy rec.+conversion) that makes them relatively easy (yet still time consuming) to defeat. It just feels like abusing the game mechanics, while I'm fairly certain that's how they were ment to be defeated.There is no terrain awarness or creativity involved, as the arenas are absolutely empty and bland. These are just lame attrition battles with some trial and error to learn the attack patterns and sudden terrain changes.Ok, this was much more of a rant than I intended it to be. I have played Hollow Knight a year ago, and I'd say this game had many similar features, but not all for the best. They should have stayed closer to the original design.I'm not sure the first game was ever in need of a continuation, but this definitely wasn't the sequel I was expecting.If this was the first game, I might would not consider playing the sequel. (Kinda like with Hollow Knight). Generally it was a ok-goodish game, but compared to the expectations, brought mostly disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Game isn't fun. The story makes 0 sense once you see how exactly you ended up in the situation you're in at the beginning of the game. You end up so strong to the point where you don't have to worry about taking damage and most mobs end up being more like decoration instead of actual mobs.The final boss battle was actually pretty terrible considering the conditions they had to put you in to go around how strong the game makes you towards the end.Basically, this game just seemed a bit rushed and it feels like my enjoyment is supposed to come from looking at the environments and playing as a character I've grown to love back in 2015. _childDocuments_.review: Progress: First pass hard, 100% (I decide to finish this anyway).Storyline: 8/10Very predictable (-2), and so far so good. Some of the side quests are fairly attracting, like . The main storyline is semi-sandbox.ART: 10/10Masterpiece, more charming than the previous title as the hues are diversified this time.Music: 9/10So far the music renders a bit sadness mostly, which suits the story quite well. But the music alone is not recognizable. Masterpiece when blended in, excellent if played alone (-1).Level Design: 8/10Most regions serve a meaningful aim. There are too many secrets, which makes it a bit tedious (-1). Similar to the previous title, Metroidvania style of secret placing is kept in some degree, which I personally dislike (-1). The overall flow is smooth.Puzzle Solving: Literally no.Combat: Overall 7/10Non-boss Combat: 8/10The default melee and the hammer are fantastic; they are shiny, and the feedback is awesome especially the hammer. But Bash from the previous title is still a thing, which actually means these melee attacks are not that important (-1). Besides, I personally don't like any flying foes to be charging at me if I can't dodge/parry or dash/bash, thus giving an extra (-1) here just for this. All in all, non-boss combat behaves like a normal platform game as previous title does.Boss Fight: 6/10Introducing real boss fight into this title is something I don't like that much. Meh, this signals a transition from platform-adventure to a mixture of platform-action-adventure, which is an acceptable try; how to properly balance is not properly handled in this title tho.Platform style of boss fight is more like running and dodging, and leveraging environmental interactive to defeat the boss; action style focus more on fighting and dodging. They are born to be conflicting with each other: Action style design usually forces the player to fight a boss in limited area says a small chamber, to exert maximum pressure and excitement on the player. This makes it extremely hard to blend in platform elements - the scene is so limited in size.I would say, honestly, remove the collision damage as a whole for bosses, you will grant more space for player to operate, to leverage the platform to gain an advantage and to organize the attack sequence and timing. This way, you can still have a huge boss thrilling the player, you potentially can further limit the scene as player becomes relatively more agile. Otherwise, the boss is yet another giant monster requires you to do hit and run which will promote ranged attack naturally. To be honest, I hate it much when there is collision damage in combat-heavy platformers or Metroidvanias. Save Mechanism: -2/10I am sorry but I want to control when I save the game (-1). I want to save when I have done digging out a secret. I want to save when I am ready to take a risky move. I want to trigger a save just like the previous title as it blends in so well (-1). Escape Sequence: 6/10Overall I don't like these sequences: I am not here to practice the muscle memory (-1). Burrowing thru sand is just a disaster; it's like driving on ice, dancing on butter (-2). Is this title a good game: 7/10 YES, this is still a decent game.Do you recommend this game to your friend? NO, I have had terrible experience regarding the autosave and some escape scene, thus will not be the preacher this time.Edit on Mar. 16: Fix a few typos.Edit on Mar. 17: Complain about desert escape, and drop to 7/10 from 8/10 due to some tedious escape sequence.Edit on Mar. 18: Add more complaints and finalize the review after beating the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that are a hidden gem, the quality of... well everything really is top notch! If you love Metroidvania games, this is a must grab for your collection! Especially if you loved the previous title, Ori and the Blind Forest.But lets see the game itself:Ori and the Wave of the Feels, I mean Will of the Wisps plays smoothly. The story itself - without spoiling much - has the similar feels train as the previous game, but cranked up a notch. While nothing groundbreaking, but the music and well made animations will give you an amazing atmosphere for sure. You are introduced to mechanics in a nice pace and the abilities are flowing well. There are some that are better than others, some are forgettable, you get a few choices (6 abilities, I mostly used 2). The game also upgraded its difficulty compared to the previous entry, the puzzles, enemies and environment is a lot more complex and can be challenging! While its not around the difficulty of Hollow Knight or length, its a solid, well built game. Platforming can be a challenge sometimes as well.Controls (I played on mouse + keyboard) are solid, though you can't map it which may be a downside to some. Though the layout was quite easy on the hands and logical, got used to it rather fast.There is more emphasis on dexterity and speed (like chase scenes and traversal in general, like speed races, difficult places that need timing, etc.), amping up its difficulty as the game progresses. You may find these hard to pull off, I had difficulty myself at some parts, but nothing game breaking.TL;DR: Aside of some minor nitpicks like abilities  (most of them are forgettable) and some annoying fight sequences, this game is a true gem with an excellent experience and atmosphere. A real treat for players who enjoy Metroidvania games for sure!

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to love this game because I loved Ori and the Blind Forest. But after a while I realized: loving the game comes with enjoying to play it ... and I truly don't. Ori and the Will of the Wisps goes out of its way to annoy its players. The mechanics established by the original game are still there ... kinda. But they got buried under so many more moves, abilities, powers, and whatnot, that playing this game and trying to internalize its ridiculously overladen gameplay loop is more a nuisance than entertainment. It literally feels like a chore. And I am saying that as someone who escaped the Ginso Tree and had fun doing it.Ori and the Will of the Wisps is still utterly gorgeous, the story is once again beautifully sad and the world design and character art is amazing yet again. But playing the game becomes farcically hard within the first couple of hours, and once I reached the desert part with its silly pinball mechanics, I just didn't want to do that anymore. It's probably a good game, but it's not for me. For one thing, they changed the formula on combat. The original wasn't really all that concerned with fighting enemies as it merely used enemies as parts of environmental puzzles. The Will of the Wisps however, gives you a hammer and suddenly everything turns into nails.And does a  game like Ori really need lengthy NPC dialogue in gibberish, side quests about finding a stick or a flippin' teddy bear, and (and that's the clincher): who the heck asked for LESS focus?Ori and the Blind Forest struck me as a game that always led me into the right direction, even though it never felt like I was being guided. Progression was a very natural thing in this game, you always ended up where you were supposed to go but it felt like good luck or happenstance.The Will of the Wisps will just let you explore a dungeon for hours only to let you know "Yeah well, you can't go here until you found XYZ!" at the very end, with XYZ being buried somewhere at the end of some other dungeon on the opposite region of the map. That's not gameplay, that's frustrating.I don't like being angry at a game. My cat doesn't like me being angry at a game! Anyone now saying "Well, git gud then!" will only receive a heartfelt F*CK OFF!! because no ... I want to enjoy the game, I want fun! I want rewarding platforming and a sob story, that's it. And dying every 8 seconds because I didn't perfectly nail that jump - dash - bash - double-jump - glide - bash - dash sequence peppered with a little randomness to make it even harder is not fun. Quite the opposite!So no, it's sad to have to admit that this game broke me. Maybe I will try again later, but so far ... I do not feel entertained. I feel punished and I am not quite sure for what
