_childDocuments_.review: The first time I played this game, I thought it was only okay. But that changed once I got past the mediocre story mode and got into the Arcade and Mission Modes.My god, this game has a lot of single player content. If you go for the 100% achievement status, you're going to be at it for about 40 hours, by the looks of it. (I'm 34 hours in as I'm writing this and have 9 semi easy achievements left). The biggest downside is that online is dead because nobody plays this game, especially on PC, so don't expect much online playtime. There is some online achievements (you have to play - not win - 30 matches to unlock them all), and while online with random players is mostly dead, you can likely find another fan that'll rock out a few matches with you to help with that.A smaller downside is a number of developer oversights. You can't use custom outfits in Mission Mode, for example, even though all the opponents use unique outfits. You can use them in Arcade mode, though, so it's not too big of a deal. Also, the textures don't load properly. They just don't. It's a mistake in the PC port. The steam discussions have a link on how to solve the issue though, and it's a 30 second process.The highlights of the game for me is the nice presentation, the manual combo system, and Arcade and Mission modes. Arcade may get repetitive (especially for the 50 routes achievement), but at the same time, it gives you a chance to play all of the characters and try out their different combo structures. Mission mode is interesting as well, because as you play, you get better abilities, and it gradually gets more fun and you get to do a number of different things. Early on it can be an aggrivating mode, because you're so weak, but after an hour or 2 it should get better.Overall a good anime game. Definitely worth 30 dollars on sale, or even 60 if you're a big My Hero fan and know you're gonna sink a lot of time into it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a My Hero fan, I just wanted an anime fighter style game that had split screen on PC. Because of that I can provide a outsider's prospective.SUMMARY:Solid gameplay for an awesome and cinematic anime fighting game with full quality English voice-over and a full layer of polish, love, and attention to detail. All with multiplayer on one computer.Buy it when on sale. The full price is for fanboys/girls.FULL REVIEWFirst the negatives and there's only two. The game assumes that you just got done playing the previous title a few minutes ago so you will be completely baffled for plot. It was kind of annoying to try to piece together what happened in the last game. The second is that online play can feel the ever slight bit laggy. My internet is top notch but it might've been on the other end. Finally the AI is decent but the difficulty ceiling is a bit too low. These are just small critiques.Now the positives and oh boy aren't they big ones.3 Reasons why this game is great.1. Solid gameplay:The gameplay is smooth and dynamic. Absolutely solid. Hits connect; blocking is effective but has it's counters; and the Plus Ultra moves are well balanced to not be overpowered and you have to be set up the situation so your Plus Ultra move hits rather than it being a mere "Press X to lower enemy health by 15%". This game is good at being...well...a game.2. Lots to do:The game has a variety of different modes and such that take that fantastic gameplay and gives it some direction. Customize character appearance; unlock cosmetics through gameplay; a fun story for both the Heroes and the Villains and they both get a full story too rather than anything half-hearted. A agency mode which is kinda like the Galactic Conquest mode from BFII (2005). They even added a simple way to practice against an AI that does nothing so you can get used to the controls and test things without getting hammered.3. A fine layer of polish:It's an anime fighting game that has a full English voice over and man does that add so much charm. The characters will make remarks to eachother; they will make comments and all kinds of different interactions. Even so far as telling you which cosmetics they personally like and dislike. The main menu is beautiful. They could've just done a regular menu and it would've work but my they made perhaps the coolest menu I've ever seen in a game. Each menu option has a character who voices over it and a little animation. The comic-strip/manga style cutscenes too even will shake or move depending on the scene. There's been so much love poured into the little things of this game to make it an enjoyable experience. Even adding that awesome and calm guitar piece for the menu theme rather than some battle theme adds so much.

_childDocuments_.review: For people who already have the first game: I recommend waiting for a sale. The improvements that come with My Hero One's Justice 2 make it a vastly better game, but they are improvements that should have been part of the first game (which was sold at full-price and then abandoned after rollout of the DLC). Bamco doesn't deserve your $60 if you already paid them $60 for the privilege of beta testing their engine.This is basically the same game as My Hero One's Justice, with additional characters and QoL changes that was vastly needed by the first game - particularly tweaks to the combat (movement is less floaty now) and CPU AI (cpu-controlled enemies are no longer passive bunny-hopping gits that only occasionally fight back).Performance-wise, there's no real noticeable improvements. It's still a light install (around 8GB on disk) and will run at high settings even on a modern low-end build (1080p/60FPS smooth on a Ryzen 3 2200g + GTX 1050 non-TI) .

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, floaty, and buggy are my top 3 words for this game. this is the only anime arena fighter ive ever played, but ive heard globku say its one of the best ones out there. the characters are diverse and fun, and its clear that at least some passion was put into making the game. but the support is lacking from the devolopers, as the only updates so far have been silent, small updates that only do things like sometimes give you 500 coins as a bonus after the online match. hawks is going to finally release soon, and we all hope that we get some good balance patches to accomodate his release. overall id say this game is fun if you enjoy your character(s) that you play, and can tolerate the mass amounts of bugs and poor netcoding, becauae this game has often disconnections or poor internet moments. The community is small, but close, and there some awesome people in it. the lack of crossplay means that you can only play players of your same console, which is both good and bad, depending on how you see it. this does breed little "subcommunities", like the small pc community ive become a part of, which is close-knitt and sick to be in. you can enjoy this game if your tolerant of its issues. also network play is arguably the best part of this game. the story, per usual with most fighting games, isnt going to knock your socks off. mission mode can be an annoying grindy mess, and is bad. arcade mode is an improvement from last time. character and hero card custimizations are also better from last time. UI is cleaner. Ranked mode in online is a definite upgrade as only winning or getting oone round for a loss will get you points, the latter only giving one point. disconnections/ragequits also give one point, so a game in which you've won one round already that was cut short will give you 2 points, which is a good idea. events arent super special, but is no harm to the game or anything really. i could see it maybe being enjoyable for some people. I have one last note to end off with: the best part of this game is the fact that Mineta is now in it.

Animation, model quality, arenas, ultimate moves... it's all kinda flat.But for MHA fans--and ONLY MHA fans--it's a pretty good time. _childDocuments_.review: My Hero Academia is one of my favorite manga series- I think the characters and powers are a lot of fun to look at, I like the designs, and I enjoy the story; it feels like a video game adaptation should write itself! Unfortunately for me, the One's Justice series does not do it justice (huehue) and leaves me wanting more.Maybe this is all just a skill issue, in which case I'll accept my judgement as a scrubby, sweaty trash-tier gamer, but it never felt like I was truly able to do what I was intending to do as any given character. The special moves felt over-costed so I couldn't use the ones I wanted in each fight, and the characters felt weirdly heavy as well. Running felt more like plodding and the combat felt "sticky" in the sense that each input was tied to a long animation versus a specific action; I felt like I was stringing together a series of mini-cutscenes instead of performing a combo of sorts. That's not to say this game didn't do some things right- the character roster is sizeable and has plenty of fan-favorites to play as, as well as a suite of DLC characters to add if the initial selection doesn't quite fit your bill. Even when I was struggling to properly play the game, I was having a bit of fun just watching my favorite characters do their thing. On a similar note, the visuals are great and the game expertly adapted the anime's style to a 3D environment without sacrificing the show's originality.It might be that this game is just more directed towards fighting-game players with a slower, more tactical approach to combat, but I much prefer the fluidity and speed of arena-style fighters like the Naruto Ultimate Ninja storm series, and this felt like a weird hybrid that didn't quite pay off to me.Cinematic playthrough here:

_childDocuments_.review: This was my original review after playing the game for 12 hours:     "Pretty fun, quick arena brawler. :)"TL;DR: DO NOT BUY. This game is a cheap, loveless cashgrab!I have now spent 128 more hours in this game and am, at the time of writing, ranked among the Top 20 players on PC.My original point stands - it's a fun, quick experience. Just don't expect any mechanics, that, even as shallow as they are, hold up to scrutiny. Let me give you a few examples:The hitboxes are wonky as ♥♥♥♥ and you regularly can experience characters just clip through each otherBalancing is non-existant, with some characters having literal touches of death (meaning they can kill you from full health in a single combo - the worst offender is Gran Torino) or are simply unpunishable through their mechanics (Mirio, again Gran Torino, 100% Deku) yet deal outrageous damage. On the other hand you have characters like Kirishima and Muscular who are completely useless.There are tons of technical issues like the game dropping frames or inputs(!!), frequent disconnects in Multiplayer or the game starting to stutter if you have a video player open at the same time. Seriously, if you have a Twitch stream or YouTube video open on your second screen the game becomes borderline unplayable. And no, this is not about insufficient hardware, I have a 1080ti and a i7-8700k.While we're using the word unplayable:If you're using a keyboard to play, you literally can't play the game if you're assigned the "Player 2" slot. The game won't recognize your inputs. Player 1 and 2 are assigned more or less randomly online. So you literally can't play Quick Matches, only premade lobbies that YOU opened. This bug is in the game since release and has not been fixed.There is literally no communication from Bandai Namco or Byking about the game, its future or even the DLCs.This game is a mess. AVOID!

_childDocuments_.review: My Hero One's Justice 2. A brilliantly well needed breath of fresh air from many other survival games. It isn't some run of the mill stranded somewhere deal, it isn't trying to be realistic, it isn't trying to be gimmicky, it is simply, fun.The idea of making a fighter game based of Hero Mythology is a brilliant idea, something I've not seen before, and its done to great effect. I will admit, i am somewhat biased as i have a great love for the mythos, but there are few games that are truly built around hero Mythology in the way this game is. It isn't just Vikings who believe in the heroes, the gods are a relevant part to the lands, the enemies, and why you are fighting to survive in the first place.The combat is surprisingly fun and interesting, it seems at a glance extremely simple, but it has depth thanks to a few key mechanics, such as, types of damage: there is Pierce, Slash and Blunt. Each of which being effective, neutral, or ineffective to certain enemies. Making it so you don't just go into a single weapon type the whole game and encourages you to explore and experiment with different weapon types. Same with armour, at certain levels, there can be a couple different types of armour you can make, giving different stats or effects.The food mechanic is also fun, letting you explore certain combos of food items to see what works best for you, and letting you go more health based or stamina based depending on what you prefer or need.The difficulty scaling of this game is pretty solid, nothing is ever unfair in difficulty, unless you bite off more than you can chew. Each area you move on to starts off difficult, but a fair level of difficult, making it fun to explore and progress through and past them. Even now, i am 83 hours into the game, and I'm probably only just over half way, having only beat 3 of the current 6 bosses. Usually, in a situation where it takes that much time to progress that much, it's due to tedious grinding or annoying difficulty scaling, My Hero'es one justice 2 has neither. There is grinding, but it's resource grinding, rather than grinding weak enemies or something mind numbing like that. That, as well as a lot of other fun mechanics, such as building, cooking, terraforming, sailing and just the general exploration, make it so even though i have progressed slowly, i have still had plenty of fun doing so.Visually, this game is absolutely stunning, but not much due to the actual graphics. The graphics are simple, somewhat retro, with them being low poly and low detail, although basic, it is stylised really well so it isn't too bad. However, on their own, the graphics wouldn't be that much to boast about. The lighting. The lighting and shaders, when combined with the stylised graphics, make this game look stunning at moments, and tbh, those moments are pretty common.Overall, this game is a win, and i would highly recommend it for anyone who enjoys fighter games, a challenge, and doesn't mind a bit of resource grinding, to give this game a go

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming from someone who's a MHA fanboy, to the point where I have: 3 All Might action figures, 2 All Might plushies, an All Might hat & t-shirt, All Might pajama pants, a MHA blanket with All Might on it, a framed picture of All Might with an autograph from the English VA, and who has set my morning alarm clock ringtone I wake up to every day is All Might's theme. I'm probably gonna buy All Might slippers, gloves, and sweatshirt too. In other words I love MHA.So from someone that in love with MHA, I genuinely have to say this game isn't worth the buy. If you're buying this game for the fan service, and wanting to play as your favorite characters and have wacky fights with them for a little while with your buddies? Enjoy yourself, this game is most likely for you. Are there improvements from OJ1? Definitely! It'd be a lie for me to say this game hasn't had some improvements from its first version. Though in the long run, if you're looking for a game with genuine compassion and quality poured into it? It's something i'd have to avoid.OJ1 is such an abandoned game that if you go to its update page on the date i've made this review: It's empty. This game is no better but in its own special way.The code is so rampant that people have not only been able to find out what all the upcoming DLC characters are, but have been able to construct some of them together; aka these assets, textures, animations, models, etc. are all in the game already to the point where a minor amount of DLC characters are able to nearly be fully playable within the game, not lacking much else besides voice lines and a character picture on the screen near their health bar.I had high hopes the addition of DLC meant that this game would be given support, though the fact that DLC has already been imbedded in the game to that extent? My disappointment is that all this is already in the game. Like, cool yeah they did make it - but let's say with smash bros releasing a 10 fighter dlc pass, they actually work on it as time goes on rather than having it 100% ready to go, just behind a release date. That keeps them attached to the game and community, allowing them to know what needs to be fixed, balanced, etc. etc. The fact that all this stuff seems to be so ready and only behind a wait wall makes me feel the 5 fighter DLC pass was a ploy to fake dedication towards the game, and get more money from players who aren't active enough in the community to find out the details i've mentioned about DLCThere's more that I could rant about, though there's better things I can do than giving more time to this game. Like I said: Searching for fan service in the form of fighting as characters you love? Sounds great! You'll like the game. I don't know for how long, but you'll like the game for a good bit. Could this change? Yes, of course! Though I can't say you would like it for anything beyond that if you're hoping for support & updates for anything beyond DLC additions.I said to someone i'm refunding this game to buy the new Doom, and was told that it's not worth it cause i'll finish the game in maybe 20 hours and be done with it. So I took a moment to think, and I realized something. Even if I magically finish it in 10 hours, i'd rather support a game that delivers to their players and cares for the game, rather than the games that undercut and cash grab from their players - think about it. If all someone does is support games that cash grab, why be surprised when the next game cash grabs? I supported the 1st game which was a cash grab, and I got cash grabbed again. So with that said, i'm refunding, as i'd rather boost up games that push initiative and support towards their fan base.Could this review change? Yes, if OJ2 actually evolves to a game that gives care to its community and helps it succeed, rather than keeping it at a 100% cash grab. - if otherwise? I'm afraid i'll have to leave this game in the dust; hope I get my refund. Worst waste of 65$Update: I got my money back!! Time to support a real game

_childDocuments_.review: Literally got me into the entire franchise as a whole, saw a couple clips of this game and on the very same day i declared i'd buy it full price because what i saw was good and the gameplay seemed interesting, safe to say i do think it is absolutely worth full price, although waiting for a sale is never a bad option and you should be wary of what characters are extra dlc and what ones you get as standard if you care about this, though not like thats not a part of any other games in similar styling. Some notes that i thought were important to mention are:Movement is fluid and camera work is (usually) pretty co-operative, characters are *very* fleshed out and have insane amounts of dialogue, animations, and visual effects (characters like dabi and endeavour completely transform a map just by being on it)Customisation is amazing, featuring pages upon pages of cosmetics to unlock (99% of which are using ingame currency, meaning other than specific dlc characters the amount of purchases you make after buying the standalone game is small) and more than enough characters to turn into monstrosities beyond your imagination, although some aspects of the system are lacking in imagination from the developers side of things, endeavour is completely cloaked in flame permanently, but no customisation options allow you to change the colour of these flames despite it being such an obvious move to make, meaning his customisation is quite stifling seeing as you pretty much have to work with the orange fire colour to make anything on him look half decentStory isn't great i'll admit, it cuts *a lot* from the anime and the final mission from the villains side of the story can be a real pain in the neck (although being able to play as a veritable kaiju in a game like this is pretty fricken sweet) though if you like ooga booga big jiggly jogglers in your face the story cut-scenes tend to offer a decent amount atleast where toga and camie are concerned.The optional modes Arcade and Mission are pretty interesting too, arcade is by far and away the bread and butter of the game in my opinion, letting you go through multiple environments and enemies while sticking by a particular character to achieve a good score and bragging points as well as the aforementioned ingame currency, which can be obtained through any of the modes in the game including the story, mission introduces too much to explain in a steam review but the general gist of it is that you control your own hero (or villain) agency and take contracts and jobs to beat out whoever your aligned against and protect the area from harm (though be warned, its probably the grindiest mode in the game but once you get used to it, its pretty fun).Overall im not gonna do a stupid number/10 ranking for this because that is incredibly subjective in our modern day video game rating society, but in my personal opinion its well worth the buying price and offers hours of content to immerse yourself in and is a must buy for any big time MHA fan (or in my case, served as my introduction to the franchise alongside the help of my SO's) so sod off this review page and go add it to cart X)

_childDocuments_.review: My Hero Ones's Justice 2 is a interesting sequel to the first game. It was interesting to see the legacy characters are basically the same. Same plus ultra moves . . . but a tad different move sets here and there. One pet peeve I have is that the combat system seems to be a tad broken and one sided. I had a match where I was juggled by a Shigarki with two side kicks that seemed to just not allow me to have a turn to fight. As well as another peeve I have is that to continue your combo you have to use a gauge bar or whatever it's called that gives you ultimates. Apparently when you break your current attack string to mash a different type of button you can just have a match where you just never see a bar of 1 ultra gauge. Which I don't believe was in the first game at all. As well as it seems that sidekicks are now just going to instantly guareented a combo break. Oh you finally get a hit on your opponent? Nope. Trying that combo string you practiced? Nope.I mean overall this is a great game to start with if you don't have the previous game. It has even more characters and some new combo's. And I am suggesting this if you like fighting games and MHA, but at the same time, it just seems to be very one sided sometimes. I really wish that there might've been an air breaker that doesn't rely on sidekicks and could use a gauge of meter if you have it. Otherwise you can, again, get put in what seems like an infinite loop if your opponent if playing a juggling comp and playing super aggresive. The only real counter that is given that is ground based is a counter move while blocking, otherwise you get no real help other than timing a hit during a combo or learning the mechanics that are given to their best potiental.

_childDocuments_.review: There's alot of thoughts i've been wanting to jot down here, so lemme set a sort of precedence cuz i find that this is a very complicated situation. So mixing that being confined to "Yes or No" doesnt fully interpret my thoughts accurately. Please bear all this in mind before reading.This game is meant for me, but in the worst way possible. It has many characters that i look forward to playing as, & as a My Hero fan, that means alot (especially as a Tsuyu main since OJ1). If only all this wasnt dampened by the lack of quality assurance that's plagued this game, making me hesitant to come back. With the recent reviews, im getting the impression that they're not the type to structurally look into this game as a whole, not nearly as much as i am here & i dislike the thought of putting myself into the shoes of more casual trains of thought, who this would appeal the most to (if not My Hero fans). Since OJ1, i've seen streamers say the games're for My Hero fans, & they're on the right track, but nothing else in-depth than that. Bad enough i've seen most say this is an expansion pack DLC of the 1st game, which they're not off either.What's saddening is that they could've improved on all this from OJ1, but it appears they didnt, so let's get into it.Gameplay:There's a number of factoids that i need to make clear or one may get lost pretty easily, so walk with me on these points.- Controls: The controls for movement and attacks have not only been the same as OJ1, but for most, if not all characters've had their movesets expanded upon. What's this mean? This is a fundamental problem, because even though you can get used to the controls, doesnt mean it's a good thing in the first place. Giving us up to 4 Quirk moves, with two being loose directionals is such an off design choice & they should've simplified this by having us hold another button opposed to directionals. This wouldnt be bad at all for a 2D fighter, but for an Arena 3D Fighter, it's a very awkward thing to implement for this game. - Unintentionality: This spot is mainly for the tag system. Though its used as a balancing mechanic instead of doing what they did in the first game, they took the liberty to make it where if you're being attacked, knocked down AND getting up, then you tap on one of your teammates, that person will knock down the opponent, letting you get back up safely. The end goal looks attractive on paper, but this is three instances where you need to make sure you dont press the support buttons or you lose that support, depleting their gauge. I've seen this be essentially abusable, where one can just make sure they combo the hell outta the opponent after landing, say, an unblockable, causing the player to potentially lose their support twice in a row. Could've been alot more sound from a design standpoint if it was OJ1's system, where you call out support & they use a special to help you after closing in (which still needs work).- Meter: This is the same problem i had in the first game but it's marginally worsened here. Getting a full 3 bar feels impossible to do in the first round of a match, & now it's arbitrarily depicted as PLUSULTRA, starting from A to fill up. This can be hard to keep track of & not all that smooth to get used to from the OJ1's bar depiction. It does tell you how many full bars you have but semantics. - Normals >>> Supers: Supers are virtually shafted in this game as well, where if the opponent's close to you and their Normal's animation is in start-up, they'll stuff & interrupt ur Super at least 90% of the time. In fighting games Supers very often have things like invincibility & come out faster than Normals, which is rewarding when pulled off. In this game, distance or comboing into Super is needed, which could've been on purpose, but it wouldnt be so bad if this wasnt for all characters.- lvl1 & lvl3 Supers >>> lvl2 Supers: This is very backwards, but the damage output for lvl1 Supers supersede lvl2s, which again is across the board. This puts lvl2s on a pedestal, from a spectacle standpoint. Even worse is that they're often smaller moves & lack tracking unlike most moves, so this game discourages you from really using this. Which really really sucks if you miss it & you gotta get all that meter back. No one wants to do that.- Cancels: Now this would've been in the game's favor if meter wasnt so dam hard to gain in a match, & to do one Cancel, it takes 1/2 of a letter, which if it weren't for the game itself fling the opponent away from you eventually, you have the potential of 18 Cancels. I know its for balancing reasons, but it limits the fun factor.- Normal >>> Manual control: Normal control is the modern fighting game system of "mash to complete the combo", but Manual, you have to do your own attack inputs to fabricate your own combo. This wouldnt be bad if it weren't for the following.- No OTGs: What's this you ask? It's something that helps separate good fighting games from bad ones, & this stands for "Off The Ground". Meaning you can still hit and the opponent while they're knocked down. OJ1 didnt have this & unfortunately same for this game. Many times someone cant get combo'd & you cant continue ur string of attacks in Manual mode, further hindered upon loss of floatiness. This other aspect wasnt nearly as bad previously, where Manual combos were easier to do.- Story Mode, Arcade Mode and Mission mode are worse: Story Mode's far too long like in OJ1, and didnt improve on it at all. It's still "Watch this Powerpoint. Now fight" & gets old real fast upon the 5th time. Arcade Mode is way longer to get through with having more opponents to fight, which would've been fine, but this is a total of 18 fighters you can fight per character, opposed to OJ1's 6 fighters per run. Mission Mode is a no-death run & there's over 20 of them, and gets worse than old fast, it gets too hard around the halfway point. No one wants to solo run thru 10 characters with one character's ever-decreasing health, losing characters in the process. Even worse is that the CPUs power-stack & some can revive themselves, so they're way ahead compared to ur lesser power-stacking. Literally no one wants to 100% this. It's a massive slog.- DLC characters take too long: Not for gameplay, but we're waiting far too long for two more characters that we already know of. There's no word on this situation, but for the three we have so far, that's 5 months of waiting & that honestly isnt good, nor does it look good.- Dialogue Clutter: They always say something when doing ANYTHING, in battles and for menus. It dampers the experience, & cheesy one-liners dont help either. The 3-man lvl2s are the worst with this.- 4-player: Online-only. Can be hard to get folks together to play with for this.- Bad Post-Game: Customizing, Online, Arcade & Mission Mode, and getting all the trinkets. Guess what, players wanna do 2 out of 5 of those, so congrats on your 40% success rate, Bamco.- Tags and chip-damage cant kill.- Hawks is a slow character: Self-explanatory. Really doesnt help when he hypes himself up for being fast, and characters in-game know him for his speed- Swimsuit DLC (w/ Miruku): it'd help.As you can see, there's many things that aren't truly in the game's favor from a gameplay standpoint, which is why i stated the conundrum that reeks and comes back up for our game here, OJ2. Good concepts, poor executions. Here's a list of the good: Polish for giving quotes, good voice actings, Online Mode, big roster, tons of customs, Tag Supers, armor vs quirks vs normals vs red moves.Music: The tracks are too middle-of-the-road to even remember anyVisuals: Some (mostly) very competent modeling & animationsVerdict: This is the roughest 5/10 in history, 6/10 on a good day., 3/10 otherwise. This could've been the next Storm series, but misses many marks & opportunities. It's alot to swallow for 60$. I'll still play this, but man it's sad Bamco cant give this series proper justice.

_childDocuments_.review: So I've watched My Hero Academia again recently with my girlfriend and absolutely love the series. I have no problem with the story or really anything about this series. But I will be the critic in a sea of praise of this game.I usually try and not criticize games too harshly since I certainly couldn't make one and I know people put a lot of time and energy into them. But this game just feels very lackluster. The "video" cutscenes are merely snapshots of the anime stylized into comic book strips. It reminds me of those old PS2/PS1 games of movies where the cutscenes are literal imports of the movie clips themselves. But even those were more interesting than a picture with a speech bubble in the corner. It's just lazily done.The combat is REALLY good! The flow of movements, the diversity in character quirks, the interactive battlegrounds, all of it is really good. However the battles are usually over within a minute or so leaving the awe of some iconic battles out of the picture. I would have liked to have longer battles that have more depth than a glorified Tekken/Soulcalibur simulation.This game isn't bad. But it isn't good either. It's very 'meh.' Not worth the $60 or even the $30 I spent on sale. I'd say a solid $20 for the base game is appropriate. Maybe it's because I don't play a lot of anime games, but this game just feels like it could have been more in terms of gameplay and cinematography.

Online pvp is fun if you don't mind getting your butt kicked by cheap shot combos until you figure out your own cheap shot combos.Basically, if you like anime fighters and you like My Hero Academia, then it's a good time. You will probably spend a lot of time waiting in online pvp lobbies though.Also there's a voice language option so if you're a dub hater like me you're in luck! It doesn't work on the opening screen for some reason but you can have most of the game voiced in the original Japanese if you prefer.

_childDocuments_.review: Better than most copy/paste anime arena fighters. Animations are gorgeous. The characters are really fun to play. It's everything the first game had but better. This review will specifically be explaining the key differences between OJ2 and OJ1 as I feel they are important.One's Justice 2 doesn't rely on cheesy combo strings, unlike its predecessor. You are punished for extensive combos by having your special gauge depleted if you dash cancel mid-combo. If you want to deal some damage, you're better off conditioning yourself by using your gauge as a stamina meter. I appreciate how they wanted to go against the grain a little with this, but it is a drastic change compared to the first game nonetheless. While it was the smarter choice to make, it removes a lot of the hilarious chaos that OJ1 had.It's definitely worth mentioning the the philosophy of Assists, as they operate completely differently in this game. In OJ1, you could call in Assists during your combos to fully maximize your damage potential. These were incredibly smart plays because it calls for incredible skill and timing to be able to pull off. In OJ2, however, Assists are used for escaping combos rather than extending them. It is quite literally the embodiment of a "get out of jail free" card. It's completely lousy and negates high-level plays.Another general issue is the usage of armored attacks. If this were OJ1, you could counter an armored attack with another armored attack, avoiding the initial punish. The flaw in this feature was that if your armor was countered by an armor, you could retaliate with another armor before you received the blow. This would result in 5-10 second, drawn-out armor battles. It was silly and quite honestly a half-baked mechanic. They removed a lot of chaos with the release of OJ2, which is where most of the fun was usually had. The game is solid fun regardless, but it definitely misses that charm the first game had. But if you never played the first game, these changes shouldn't bother you! This game goes on sale quite a lot due to Bamco's endless publisher sales, so I only recommend picking this up if you're a fan of MHA  when it's discounted. The replay value isn't that great (arena fighter moment) and the community is so dead you have to request battles via discussion threads.6.5/10 hands down most enjoyable arena fighter I've ever played.

Moves also see a huge upgrade, shoot style Deku is an absolute beast, with his 1st Plus Ultra see WAY better hit detection! 100% Deku is a total monster! Honestly this game is a ton of fun, even though it has some copy and paste elements, like story mode and some character moves. Wierd quirks like, Bakugou's 1st Plus Ultra needing his gauntlets, even in his NEW UA uniform is just awful, making the move very glitchy looking. Almost like a bad mod. I have only played this game a short time, and I can already say I love it! As an offline casual player, who bought this for classic offline usage, I am VERY happy with My purchase! Though I hope the dlc gives Us 100% Bakugou, Nine, and other characters. The game feels a bit light in the villan department. Either way I'm satisfied. Pay full price and regret nothing!

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: -Nerf Hado's damage, it does as much as an ultimate when using a combo attack. -Fix match timer or allow the option to turn it off in all modes. -Tone down the AI on One Justice fights ___________________________Reason for NO, I put no but its mainly mixed. I like the show and am glad about there is a second game as well as more characters being added to what already exist but...there are a few things that ruin this game for me. -Nejire Hado is broken at the time of posting. She combo locks you and deals a third ( or more ) of your HP in a single combo chain with no way of getting out of it without a usable sidekick, she can even reflect Plus ultra moves back at the user with a basic attack. Even if she is part of the big three her damage out put and combo locking ability is insane. There are youtube videos of this if you don't believe me or haven't see it. -During arcade One Justice fights, the AI difficulty jumps greatly, that's normal for a fighting game but what i'm referring to is the 'perfect counters' - the CP will only act most of the time if they can perfectly dodge or counter what ever attack you're currently doing or get an opening to combo lock you. Otherwise it will just run around the map until it gets that chance and stay out of range endlessly running, using ranged attacks, or if you dash in to close the gap use an attack that usually gets you locked in a combo since your guard is down the second you dash. -The match timer resets after hitting zero if you're going to win by time running out, but will run out if your going to be considered the looser. Obviously most matches don't last that long regardless of the outcome, but when they do how is that even remotely fair to the player?

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who watched the anime and read the manga... I regret the purchase, even at a $6 discount. Why? Cause it took me 6 hours to beat the story mode, and I feel like that was a waste of my time.This games story mode added nothing to plot. It was a hasty regurgitation of everything up to overhaul. This wouldn't be bad if the story made you feel like a bad ass the whole way through, but it doesn't at all. In fact, the game play itself just feels lazy, making it constantly feel like your fighting the fighting system rather than the enemy. All the fighting feels stiff, some moves are just brokenly overpowered or absolutely useless, alternate attacks feel incredibly wonky to use, and a majority of combos all link down to one or two moves. It's honestly seems like it's better to mash X then it is to manually combo. Some of the super moves look cool, and some of the aesthetic design in the game is neat. But even those start getting annoying when you realize they are all un-skippable and take 10 years to finish. An incredibly annoying game as a fighter, and a skippable game as a story.I'm really hoping the offline multiplayer will at least be fun as a drunken party fighting game but somehow I anticipate us going back to Smash, FighterZ, MvC, Guilty Gear, BB, or any of the other better fighting games.

_childDocuments_.review: My Hero Ones Justice 2 bursts onto the scene with a dazzling display of vibrant colors and beloved characters from the popular anime. It's a visual feast for fans, capturing the essence of the series with its flashy special moves and dynamic environments. 🤩Beneath the surface, a *janky* and  fighting experience awaits, but there's also a spark of fun and potential waiting to be unleashed. 😉While the combat might be repetitive due to shallow mechanics and limited move sets, there are moments of genuine enjoyment to be found. Some quirky interactions and unexpected combos can lead to hilarious results, and the game doesn't take itself too seriously. 😂 The inclusion of fan-favorite characters and their unique interactions provides some amusing fanservice, and the potential for creative combos and strategies keeps things interesting for a while. 🧠However, the overwhelming amount of overpriced DLC remains a major drawback. 😤 It's a greedy practice that locks away a significant portion of the roster and features, leaving a bitter taste in the mouths of many. 😑 My Hero Ones Justice 2 is a mixed bag. It's a visually stunning brawler with some fun and quirky moments, but it's ultimately held back by repetitive gameplay, a lackluster story, and an abundance of overpriced DLC. If you're a die-hard fan willing to overlook its flaws and invest in the DLC, you might find some enjoyment. 👍 However, if you're looking for a deep and balanced fighting game experience, you might want to explore other options. 🤷

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly?It's fun. If you like the Anime then I'd say WAIT FOR A SALE and pick it up then.If you are NOT a fan of the anime... Its okay, but you probably won't enjoy it too much.- Characters are done WELL (Better than I expected tbh.)Keep in mind, some characters feel a LOT more powerful than others, and that is by design. Some quirks just dont match up well with others, and some match up really well against most others. It makes things interesting tbh.- Graphics are okay. You get used to it.- Story is decent, feels a bit weird playing through and needing to do a mission as the canon loser and WINNING the fight...but then losing in the next cutscene. For the most part, I didnt care. BUT playing as OVERHAUL in the villains storymode felt really, really, really bad. Why? The last fight as Overhaul in his Ultimate form is a HUGE PAIN and when you eventually win, Overhaul just loses in a cutscene.- Mission mode?... I like it.Most people don't. Difficulty curve is wild starting on "Dragnet" and "LOCK FEST" with those two missions feeling borderline unfair. Once you are past those two it feels better again...but you need to grind for good cards to actually do well in this mode so keep that in mind. (That, and lvl up your characters.)- Arcade? Quite fun. I like it.- Overall, get it on a sale.Hope they make a third game. This was actually really well done save for the weird story (Though I can forgive that.) and the weird difficulty curve that relies on having cards or flawless fights. Those things aside, this felt like *some* passion went into making it, which is surprising in gaming these days.

_childDocuments_.review: So i was going to say dont buy it on steam due to not being able to play it again but i found a fix online.  If you like MHA, i recommend it. sure its not perfect and maybe quirky ( pun wasnt intended but it works ) but it i find it fun. If you can't play My Hero One's Justice 2, here's a solution I found with the help of the communityStep 1. Open "Control Panel" by searching for it in Windows search bar, by pressing the Windows button or key.Step 2. Go to "System & Security"Step 3. Go to "System"Step 3. Press "Advanced system settings"Step 4. Press "Environmental Variables"Step 5. Create a new "System Variable" (NOT USER VARIABLE)Step 6. Enter the following into the Variable name box: OPENSSL_ia32capStep 7. Enter the following into the Variable value box: ~0x20000000Step 8. Now press OK.

_childDocuments_.review: About the Story Mode (which you may not care about. Skip this section if you don't care):DBZ fighting games have spoiled me: this game's story mode is not a complete rehashing of the entire series, but instead specifically starts and ends with the Chisaki arc. WIth 50+ missions, this means there are a lot of filler fights that didn't happen in the original story, most of which are against a generic thug character. They clearly knew you wouldn't be coming to this game for the story, which is IMO a mistake but maybe I'm just not the Exhibition Fighter genre's target audience.Each story mission comes with three objectives for unlocking cosmetics (most of which are for your multiplayer card). The first objective of every story mission is complete the story. The second one is usually win with 50% health, or within 60 seconds. Both of these are non-brainer objectives it will be difficult not to get. The third will then be either survive with 80% HP left (which is actually difficult sometimes) or finish with a special move (which is easier than getting the 50% health requirement).What this means is you can Gold-rank, S-rank every story mission in one try, just about.---Outside the Story Mode:The combat system has a nice level of complexity, with unblockable attacks, blocking/dodgeing and counterattacks as part of the base combat abilities of every character. Some characters are actually faster than others, while some have a Sturdy-like effect, or custom counterattack moves (which differ from the standard "can attack after successfully blocking" attack all characters have). All in all I can tell each character has their own "flavor" based on their Quirks.Each fighter feels unique in their animation, and their personality comes through. I wish there was a little more variation in the voicelines that play when you use certain moves, or that the character didn't say something every time you used a move (once every 3-5 times would be better, IMO) as it can get repetitive. I assume there's a way to turn these voicelines off in the settings, but I haven't looked because that's not the point: it should be possible to have them happen *sometimes* not *every time I hit Y*. It's amazing how quickly you get tired of Sir Knight-Eye saying "Heavy, right?"Despite the unique animations and Quirk abilities, the vast majority of fighters can easily chain from their melee combo into one or both of their Quirk combos, which can make for a repetitive-feeling attack if you're being aggressive. Additionally, there is a mechanic where the milisecond a character starts falling due to gravity (as opposed to being launched somewhere by an attack) they become invincible until they land and have finished standing back up for about 0.2 seconds. This means it's very difficult to chain combos beyond the pre-built standard-combo->quirk-combo chain, as the moment you finish recovering from any combo finisher your enemy is already in this invulnerable state.Overall, I give the game a 7/10: It's fun to play, but at 3 hours in I'm feeling the game's mechanics needed a bit more polish, and the story mode was definitely neglected which is a downside for me but may not be for others. The Aesthetics and attention to the combat style of each character though is very nicely done: Deku's Shoot Style feels legitimately more mobile than others. Red Riot feels unstoppable. King Murder Death Kill :tm: feels like an explosive powerhouse. Etc.I recommend getting the game while it's on sale, as it's probably not worth the full $60. It feels more like a $40 game to me personally.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't an in-depth technical fighter like Blaz Blue or anything. If you are super into the anime, this can be enjoyable, but it is not challenging, and it introduces nothing new from a story perspective. The story mode can be fully completed in less than 12 hours from the very beginning to the finale. Lots of customization options to unlock, and costumes you can dress the heroes in, though again - not much that is particularly unique, simply reclolors of various accessories the characters wear, which can be mixed and matched to your will. This can be enjoyable if you prefer a simple fighter that follows a familiar story (Or a way to introduce yourself to MHA, though you'd be far better served watching - or better yet, reading it), but do not look for a challenging and technical fighter you can get truly masterful at, here.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, the combat mechanics are quick, fun, and responsive. With the variety of characters, you can experience the diversity of amazing combat skills. I recommend using a controller to get the best experience. You can also customize the characters' outfits and accessories, which is pretty cool.This game also does not require a powerful PC, you can already enjoy the game with lower-than-average PC specifications at 60 FPS.About the downsides, the overall system seems too repetitive. There are actually no other combat mechanics besides 1v1 battles, so it is very likely that you can get bored after a few hours. You also cannot run the game over 60 FPS, which is kind of disappointing.Next, there is still one unfixed major issue about the game. If your PC happened to use Intel 11th gen CPU, you would probably be experiencing the issue of the game not starting. As of the time I am rewriting this review, there are no official fixes from the developers, but there is a fix found by the community on 22nd August 2021, which you can find in the discussion section.This truly shows the ignorance of the developers. They did not even address the problem or showed an effort to try to fix it. I was not able to play the game since I upgraded my PC for around 4 months. Steam would not let me refund the game either, so I gave up on this game. I have just found out about the community solution right now, so I am rewriting this review.To summarize, this is overall a good game, I recommend this game to people who love the anime and the characters. If you do not care about experiencing the story that much, let alone the first game, just buy this one, it is pretty much an upgraded copy. You can just experience the story by watching the anime. Purchasing the game at a discounted price is also recommended as I personally do not find the content to be worth the full price.All that being said, I am still downvoting this because of the ignorance of the developers and I doubt if I will be buying any more games from this developer or this publisher.

Sadly, this game doesn't have remote play (when I got it) so your friends need a copy too.TLDR: I do like it, it gives me the feel of the show, but it's a typical anime fighting game with a few issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I was someone that fell in love with the first game, and coming into the second I can tell you that over all the changes were mostly positive.Castwise, the game was changed heavily to favour a rushdown meta with highly aggressive gameplay. Learning to master skills like guard cancelling and using your supports only on combos that are overextending what you can take are the key to becoming a master of this game.Both on this and others, the majority of the negative reviews on this game are complaints about the publisher (Bandai Namco) or whining about their main getting nerfed because they had things that were too broken for the new combo system, so please be wary of that; however there are some about missing one more time the crossplay feature on a Bandai-Namco game (and I agree with them).The fact of the matter is the game is new, as with any fighting game it still has to be discovered the whole way through. They made lots of changes to the system to make it run more smoothly and tying dash cancelling to meter was a positive change with how much damage characters can do using them if they're smart. A good Shigaraki player could do 75% of your health without any meter cost otherwise.This game is a solid experience if you want an arena fighter with more depth, if the NUNS games left you like they did me where you felt it was just too much mashing circle. This game is fun, well put together, and an overall improvement from the original.The only problem about this game is the camera angle (not bad like the first one but not the BEST I've ever seen) and the Multiplayer. As i said, there isn't the crossplay, so on Steam is very difficult to find someone but not impossible so remember about it during the purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything that was great about One's Justice 1 has been expanded, reworked, &/or improved. An excellent game which somehow got even better! For these reasons, I'd bypass 1 entirely & get this one.An expansive roster, healthy mix of modes, & a gigantic selection of customization options provide this game with an insane amount of longevity. As of writing, I have finally cleared the story mode, but have maybe played merely a whole 1/3 of the characters & have only even seen maybe half of the available customization items (let alone picked up & played with them). One's Justice 2 has made a few significant changes from the last one, for the most part, for the better. In particular, no more ridiculous ring outs from the previous game that the AI is ridiculously near-impervious to. Some characters have suffered serious nerfs in some areas, but strong buffs in others - making them almost new (where other characters are more-or-less the same). Mission mode, while fun, is still ridiculously difficult & not explained well. A co-op mode exists, but I haven't been able to make it work - I'm also far from the only one, unfortunately. Despite these weaknesses, the game is still a great time.An eclectic cast that all feel unique with particular styles & focuses are engrossing to learn & try out. The previous title was creative in how some characters worked while this title continues that even further. Some characters are an even mix of close range & distance attacks while others lack one or the other entirely. Others are powerhouses that crawl across the level. Others still seem to work best by goading nimbler opponents into attack range. Some characters are extremely nimble strikers, others revolve around defense & parrying, some almost exist just to bounce around the stage & keep you guessing. That barely scratches the surface of what you can do in this title. While something so asymmetric can lead to bad match-ups, practice & observation of your opponent can still make victory possible. The attention to detail is also expanded upon, which continues to be a treat - especially if you come from the anime or manga. Conversations between characters, unique animations depending on match-up (allies or combatants), a plethora of voice lines & triggers for them, appearances of even more side characters (be they customization items or gameplay elements). The entire Photo mode can speak for itself.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best anime arena fighters we have ever gotten and it vastly improves upon the first game. There were a ton of gameplay and mechanic changes that overall made the game more competitive and feel a lot less floatier and faster than the first game. The roaster nearly doubled, and the characters that have returned all got tweaked a bit to make them better than their previous iterations. Each gamemode got revamped and there are a few new ones to play around with but they aren't the main focus of the game in my opinion. Another thing that is quite irksome is you can tell which characters are overpowered, so sometimes the fighting isn't fair, but once again, not impossible to beat. Overall, the game is good. Different from the first one, but in a good way. Haven't tried online yet, so can't say much there, but if its anything like the first game, online mode will die off quickly since no one will be around to play. But story mode, arcade and free battle mode are fun. If you aren't a fan of offline battles or one on one battles, this isn't the game for you then.  Overall, 8/10EDIT: So I finally tried online battles because its fun to go against actual people and the whole game glitched out. I couldn't move, I couldn't fight, I couldn't leave the match. I just stood there and took a beating from my opponent and there was nothing I could do about it. I just had to take it. I don't know if this is a one time thing or not, but its now got me not wanting to go anywhere near online battles if I know that I won't be able to fight. They should have checked for these glitches sooner and this should have been fixed before the game was released because it makes it less fun. 7/10

name: Signs of the Sojourner
detailed_description: TRY THE FIRST TRIP FOR FREE About the Game Signs of the Sojourner is a narrative card game about relationships and connecting with people. Your deck is your character, reflecting your experiences and shaping your relationships. Make decisions about who your character is in this world, pushing forward with the cards you’re dealt. You take over your mother's store after her death, traveling to diverse locations in order to acquire goods for the shop. Along the way, encounter optimistic stories, compassionate characters, and delightful surprises in a world where travel is difficult and climate change has made life hard. Key Features Forge new friendships, rivalries, and connections through card game conversations. Play cards to match the tone and perspective of your partner or disregard their feelings to sell your own point of view. The story continues either way. Venture forth to find rare and useful goods to aid your town. Make difficult choices along the way. The consequences shape your character’s deck and every conversation that follows, en route to many possible endings. You'll explore the world, but also explore what it means to return home. Meet and grow alongside unforgettable characters. Will you hold on to your childhood friendships? Will your adventures on the road lead you down different paths? Who will you become, and what will you leave behind?

_childDocuments_.review: Mono no aware. Life is fleeting and ephemeral. As you wander the landscape of life, people enter and leave your social sphere -- some good friends you'll see again and again, other friends you'll lose touch with over time, and yet other people will make you wonder if you could ever have been good friends with them and how life might be different if you had just said something differently or attempted to reach out to them. And not just how they might have changed your life, but how you might have changed theirs, too.You're not going to find the next Mass Effect here or anything like that, but this is the sort of imagination-driven game that will sweep you off your feet and transport you to a magical land that time forgot about. The setting and the amazing music feel very cowboy-Western, just with the actual cowboys replaced by little villages and towns struggling to eke out a tenuous living on the back of a gritty, dying world as tumbleweeds roll by.Something which I feel makes Sojourner stand out against the backdrop of other deck-builder games on Steam is the narration -- specifically that not only do you not have to "win" every battle in order to "win" the game, but that thematically speaking, the game encourages you not to by building a story based around your cards and the outcome of your matches, win or lose. This is a step away from your typical roguelik/te card battler where you are the hero looking to defeat the villain and one lost battle means death.In reality, life and people are more complex like that -- everyone wins some things and loses others, and it's how we react to both the wins AND the losses that shape the story of our lives. The game reflects this in that there's a lot of unique speech that you'll only see upon losing a conversation "battle", and some opportunity doors that open only when others close. It's all somewhat abstract, but the game in a nutshell talks about the fragility of friendship, and how, while on one's sojourn through life, friendships can break apart and shatter even with the best of intentions if one doesn't think ahead, but yet sometimes can be rescued with enough effort.That being said, there are still a couple negative points one should be aware of. The major one for me is that the game is light on the conversational details on a moment-to-moment basis, so you won't ever find walls of text or even complete conversations between characters. You will get the start and end of each conversation, from the NPC's point of view, with every conversation ending you get being contingent on how the conversation minigame itself goes -- and even beyond winning or losing, sometimes *how* you lose (or win?) affects what the NPC says as well. But it can certainly feel one-sided, because responses are never forced upon you, the player.In tandem to that, while you do get a decent feel of this region of the world and the things going on in it, there is a lot of vagueness in detail in terms of world-building, and even after multiple playthroughs it feels a lot like I'm a fish trapped in my own little glass tank, while being dimly aware that there's a much, much larger world out there that I cannot set out to explore.  I can sort of understand it, because the interconnections between the NPCs are nuanced to the point that they can do vastly different things from one playthrough to another, but it can leave one wanting more information on this or that. Which might or might not be a bad thing.But still, you are expected to fill in the in-between parts with your own imagination, so if you are the type of person whose thinking is really structured, and you are unable to trust your imagination to fill in the gaps of things left unsaid, then I don't think you're the type of player that the game is aiming for, and you might have a problem with this game. Similarly, if you expect to win every conversation "battle" and will get upset if you do not, well I'm not actually sure if it's IMpossible, but you would be completely missing the point and it's probably not the type of game for you.It's also not a terribly long game, each playthrough will take maybe 3 hours if you're not purposely rushing through things. But it does require multiple playthroughs to see every ending, and you need to take different routes to see what people are doing at any given time, since some things are "time-sensitive" in terms of the in-game calendar. There's no "combat," no "speedruns," no "daily seeds," or any of that sort of thing, thinking of it as a short visual novel wrapped around a cardgame would be a better way to go about it.Still, overall, I kickstarted the game and I don't regret it. I do recommend the game, as it's a fairly compelling story that respects your imagination enough that it doesn't hold your hand through it, and with a minigame that's easy to pick up but has more nuance than it seems at first glance.But overall, I'm a sucker for a good, melancholic story about the struggles of friendship. Dare to dream big and wander far, but treasure your friends, as they are the most important currency in life!PS, <3 Klaus!!!(Note: There was a demo and a backer beta and that's where most of my hours were.)
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Signs of the Sojourner puts you in the shoes of a silent protagonist, with a cat-like hood, that lives in a world where traveling between towns isn’t the easiest. As a kid, your mother was a part of a traveling caravan group that traveled around to the surrounding towns where she talked with various citizens and receive various items or food that represented their town. Then, once she arrives back home to Bartow, she sells them in her store to other Bartow citizens or anyone from other towns that decided to drop by. Since you were a kid, you had to stay in Bartow, but you’re best friend Elias kept you company. Not to mention hearing your mother’s stories about the various places she visited that ultimately fueled you and Elias to dream about traveling with the caravan when you’re older.However, the future doesn’t always go the way you expect it to. After your mother’s death, you inherit her store and all the responsibilities that comes with it. Though, there’s even more bad news. If you don’t bring your mother’s store back to it’s former glory, the leader of the caravan, Nadine, is going to take Bartow off their route. After all, if Bartow has nothing to contribute, why stop there? Given only 5 months to turn the shop around, you leave Elias and Bartow behind in hopes that your conversation skills is enough to save it.  Signs of the Sojourner is all about having conversations, which is where the card aspects come in. Instead of picking dialogue from multiple choices, it’s based on what cards you play. Each card has a symbol on the left and right side that’s supposed to represent different ways of speaking, like empathetic or diplomatic. When you first arrive at a town, you’ll see who you’re able to talk to along with a short description on what they’re doing and what symbols they primarily have before starting a conversation. From there, a board will pop up and you and the character you’re talking to draws five cards. To connect with them, you have to successfully chain match cards with them. However, if you or them plays a card that doesn’t match, it’s a disconnect. How many cards you have to chain, and how many successful chains you have to do or how many unsuccessful ones you have left before they end the conversation depends on who you’re talking to. Successfully connecting results in you learning more about them, the area around you, and perhaps something about your mom; while disconnecting distracts them as you did/said something wrong and ultimately will cause them to shut down the conversation if you disconnect too many times. After each conversation, you have to learn a new card you saw your conversation partner using to replace one already in your 10 card deck.To spice it up, card abilities are introduced. One that you’ll always have is Accord, which is activated when four or more of the same symbols are connecting in a row and in response a sort of shield appears on the last card played to protect your progress. So instead of a mismatch causing a disconnect, it won’t. The others are connected to the cards themselves and can be pretty helpful when you’re in a pinch. Like Clarify (lets you insert the card in anywhere as long as it matches), Observe (lets you see the other character’s current hand), and Prepare (which lets you choose what card you draw next).Making sure your deck lets you connect with others isn’t the only thing you have to worry about. As your map gets filled out more as you visit more areas, you don’t have to follow the caravan’s usual route if you don’t want to. There are a couple events that a town will host that you won’t be able to see if you follow the caravan and there are towns that aren’t on the route. Occasionally as you’re traveling between towns, you’ll also come across mystery events where you’re given a choice to go along with it, or continue on. If you do, it’ll grant you a bonus like putting a temporary Accord or an ability on a card. Though, you can’t get out of it if you don’t want it.Every seven days, you’re also given a fatigue card. Fatigue cards basically clog up your deck with a card that can’t match with anything and makes it harder for you to have successful connections. These cards won’t only make you fail the current conversation, but the next (which, is also true if you play a card with a right symbol that they don’t have). You can be extremely unlucky and just have a hand full of fatigue as the max is 10. The only way you can get rid of them is by returning home and unpacking, conversing with Thunder the dog (though, you can be unlucky and have Thunder appear at an early town), or the rare chance that you get an opportunity on the road.Signs of the Sojourner encourages you to play multiple playthroughs as you won’t be able to connect with everyone and get all the information you’d want. With how this game is designed, it theoretically has limitless replayability. Not only will you not be able to connect with the same people or be able to connect with characters you weren’t able to before due to having a different deck, but certain story elements do get changed around. Like early on, I had one of my items stolen from me, but in my second playthrough, the shop owner was stolen from. I also heard about new areas and got access to new routes that I didn’t know about in my first playthrough. There are also multiple endings, with each ending having different variations. Of course, this does mean that you’ll be facing the same dialogue most of the time and it can get frustrating if you’re just getting essentially the same ending.There are some aspects that I didn’t like and probably kept me from enjoying it as much. First of all, I wish you weren’t forced to replace an old card with a new one. I know it's supposed pushes players to take on cards and change up their deck when they probably wouldn’t have, but at the same time, not having a deck that’s not prepared for connecting with certain people is enough. Often times, I did replace a card with the same card to try and skirt around it. Though later on, it does feel a tad punishing once you have cards with abilities as it makes you downgrade a card. I know you can just skip these conversations, but the story is tied to the characters and all of them are just a delight to talk to.While I do like what the fatigue card represents, I certainly had times irl where I placed a fatigue card, but it’s not fun to play around. I’m fine with not connecting with characters due to having a poor deck for that area, and not drawing the one symbol you need (though most times, it’s already on the board), but not when I failed due to having fatigue cards in my deck. Even worse is when you failed not just once, but twice in a row because you had to play a fatigue card.On that note, there seems to be a bug where the character you’re talking to won’t play a matching card. I know this happened to me at least once as I was able to see that they had cards with a circle on the left, so I played a card with a circle on the right, but they mismatched with me instead.Flat out, if you’re looking for weird and unique card game that isn’t obviously somewhat inspired by Slay the Spire, Signs of the Sojourner is going to appeal to you. I certainly knew this was a weird card game, as I did get the chance to play the demo last year, and I’m still in the middle ground after playing the full release. While I did like how conversations were represented by a card game, enjoyed talking to the various characters, listening the music that represents each town well, and the wonderful art style, some aspects does have a chance at bringing the experience down.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. Cozy vibes, engaging characters, a unique and interesting deck building mechanic. Unfortunately everything about the gameplay ruins what would otherwise have been a game I would be happy to engage with and sink time into.It feels like the game punishes you for engaging with it. You need to match symbols on your cards to the other person's in order to move conversation in a positive direction. But you only ever have 10 cards and with 5 symbols out there to match to that makes it very tight and hard to build a deck that can cover your bases without constantly drawing a dead hand. But even if you do get a set of cards that works for you, whenever you talk to someone you HAVE to replace one of your old cards with a new one based on what they played. At first this feels like an interesting mechanic but it quickly turns into a jumbled mess as your deck is bogged down with cards that are only good in one or two locations out of at least a dozen. Forcing you to always replace a card makes me feel like I'm being punished for wanting to talk to new characters and engage with the story and world. To say nothing of the fatigue system which bogs your deck down with nothing cards with little to no way to mitigate them. It's rare the game gives you a chance to remove a fatigue and when you play one you almost guarantee yourself to fail twice in a row in a conversation. Which again disincentivizes you from exploring and traveling around as much as possible because you likely won't be able to successfully accomplish anything due to all the fatigue in your deck.I was on the final section of my run and it felt like the game was just sitting there telling me how bad I was doing and it felt like I had already failed and gotten the bad ending but at no point did anything in the game make it feel like I could have done things better. The one really good trip I had in the run an earthquake happened and removed half my stock of items. Overall the game feels stacked against you and if you could build your deck up instead of being stuck with only 10 or refuse to take new cards instead of constantly being forced to switch stuff out it would have been a less exhausting and frustrating experience.I wanted to finish one run, get one ending before stopping. But I was so exhausted and just waiting for it to be over and realized I could be using my time on something more enjoyable instead. So I cut my run short on the last trip. It's a charming game with an interesting premise but definitely isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: So first the things i like: i like the art style and music, i also like the idea of telling a story with a deckbuilder.But here's the issue, the deck building is extremely frustrating as the protagonist seems to be the only person who seems to be affected by the massive changes in character and or unfortunate miscommunications. Both the caravan leader as well as the mother shouldn't be able to communicate well with many people, thus not being good at their job, yet they didn't have that problem. Only we have that problem.It's frustrating that no matter what you do you can't really have more than two proper styles and that a lot from character interactions to card gains to card draw is random.having traveled a lot in my life the difference in communication should either be less extreme or the deck should slowly expand. This game gives the idea that the only way to learn a new way of communication and culture is to forget something you already know. while sometimes of course one comes back changed it never feels as drastic as in this game,Things i'd like to see: 1st. at the very least there shouldn't be any downgrades when gaining new cards2nd. the deck size should be able to grow it's annoying and not at all realistic that one would forget how to talk to your best friend in a couple of months. maybe make a sort of main deck/ side deck deal. Many people switch into a different mode when abroad but mostly switch back when at home. You could limit the amount of times you can change your deck or make you gain a fatigue when doing so etc.3rd. there should be at least some explanation to how other people on the caravan are able to communicate with people who are not circle and triangle heavy but we aren't4th. to the topic of fatigue. While i think the concept itself is neat i feel like you gain too much fatigue too quickly. It's so frustratingly punishing for a game that has such a chill vibe. there should be ways to get rid of fatigue like spas or a park etc. maybe have it cost a trait on a card or use up a day making you fall behind or so, let us choose. So less fatigue gain and ways to lose it would both be niceover all right now it's a nice looking and sounding game with neat ideas, just for my taste way to punishing for the theme it's going for.
