_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever written a bad game review before, I rarely write them as is, but holy ♥♥♥♥ no game has made me more made than any other game I've played in the last 5, maybe 10 years. I'm going to talk about what frustrates me with this game so much, and maybe more experienced players can tell me that I've simply been playing the game poorly, but after constant and repeat failure, I feel like I've got some room to critique the game design. So as you've probably seen from some of the screenshots, you get a hand of 5 cards with symbols and you must match them with whatever your conversational partner has in their hand. Seems simple enough, even when they add traits to the card to shake up the turn order or allow you to manipulate their symbols. Cool stuff? Yeah it feels that way for the first two trips. Around trip 3 is when I started getting frustrated. As the game adds more symbols it becomes harder to work with your deck, after all, your deck only has 10 card slots and you get five cards in hand. So if you draw a bad hand, there's nothing you can do other than literally close back to the main menu and reload the encounter. Oh, and the person you're talking to can also fail the conversation FOR YOU AND THEN THE DIALOGUE HAS THEM CHASTISE YOU FOR MESSING UP THE CONVERSATION. I had a situation where an AI played a card with a trait that allowed them to play another card in succession, they mismatched their second card because they had nothing else in hand and the entire conversation had to be scrapped. Now, the answer to this is "build your deck better" but that isn't so easy since you only get cards *after* a conversation. So if my deck didn't have enough diamonds going into it then I can't really have a productive talk with them until I acquire enough cards of the right type to make that conversation. So by the time your deck is filled with cards that would be relevant to later areas, you wind up back at the beginning where the early game cards are useful. So notably you're forced to swap your cards out, as someone with an interest in game design I understand the purpose of this, you're making me adapt to later encounters by trying to blend your encounters so I'll be able to progress in an easier fashion. But it's genuinely the most painful experience to throw away cards that feel good, only so you can get a traitless diamond-diamond card and then watch that card be worthless because when you go into the next encounter your hand is filled with fatigued cards. OH YEAH DID I MENTION THERE'S A FATIGUE MECHANIC???These cards are horrid even for a mechanic that's supposed to punish you because they cause you to fail BACK TO BACK. So fatigue cards have no symbols meaning if you put them up in the stack they'll fail the card you played them against AND THE CARD YOUR TALK PARTNER WILL PLAY RIGHT AFTER. Obviously the solution is just not play them right? Yeah well it's pretty hard when you draw multiple of them in your opening hand, which remember when you're drawing 5 cards out of 12? That's a pretty fair chance you'll draw 2 fatigues right as you start (did you expect players to save scum conversations?) So with the fatigue mechanic you can only remove them through a few ways, return home (ending your trip and progressing the story), by patting your dog (sporatically available), or through random events (Unpredictable and can effectively undone by another fatigue card being added to your deck just by traveling). I don't know if there's a limit to your fatigue cards but without trying to hard I've gotten 3 pretty easily early on into my 4th trip. It's rough, but let me tell you about my last play session on the 4th trip. Light spoilers ahead. The fourth trip introduces a 5th symbol, spirals, now your deck of ten cards needs to balance 5 symbols.... In a deck builder where you have to constantly replace cards, and you can only get new cards by having conversations with people who have the spirals in their deck already. I wanted to punch my monitor after failure, after failure. after failure. Because I didn't draw the right cards, because my talk-buddies couldn't draw the right cards. I wanted to scream. I wasn't mad the first couple times I failed because it's a new experience and comes with the territory, but facing nothing but so many defeats just makes me bitter. This is a game where I would have liked a progression system, more trips lets you draw more cards or have a bigger deck as time goes on. Something that makes me feel like I'm getting better at talking to people in this game rather than getting worse because the challenges have diversified but I'm limited to how I can approach them. Dev, please explain to me what you want the player to do when playing your game. I tried sticking to the cards I knew worked, I would fail conversations outright. I tried to adapt and bring in other card types? I draw my fatigues and the wrong symbols or my opponent just so happens to only have 1 symbol time in their hand and it doesn't make to any of the cards that I was told would help me prep for them. I wouldn't ask for a refund if there was just a way I could play the game without feeling like the losses I experienced were my fault, but right now it feels like the game just decides to throw me a middle finger because I got unlucky. Honestly, if there was an update that increased the deck size to 15-20 and hand size to 7, I will delete this review, because that's ultimately what irks me about this game. This is a deck builder game where I don't feel like I have control of what can happen. I have played hand of fate 1 and 2, I play magic the gathering, I love deck builders. Right now I cannot love Signs of the Sojourner because I don't feel like it wants me to play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really torn on this.  On one hand I really enjoyed the beginning of the game.  I bought this immediately after playing the free prologue.  If I had played any amount of the third day's conversations prior to owning the game I don't think I would have bought it.The introduction of a fifth card type (not including Fatigue's blank sides) combined with the 10 card maximum, forced card swapping, and fatigue system doling out useless cards, I kept returning home and personally being distressed and frustrated that I couldn't communicate because I had wild amounts of fatigue cards. I thought I was signing up for something more relaxing, but I genuinely had a bad emotional response throughout most of day 3 due to a combination of the story, and what felt like me being punished for just playing the game (starting hand had 4 fatigues three times in a row, wild).I was sincerely enamoured with the game at the beginning and I stuck it through to the end, I didn't do amazing but I did well enough. I don't think every conversation in the game needs to go your way, at that point it would just be a visual novel. But literally any amount of control over my cards would improve the experience so much more.I think if you could either collect communication cards and had to pick and choose 10 when you started out the next month, or increasing the amount of time before receiving fatigue cards, would have made things so different and much more enjoyable. For a game about communication, the further in I played it felt like I couldn't get my voice across, even when I was well prepared.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: During my first play-through of this game I got frustrated multiple times because I "failed" several conversations. But as I continued to play I realized that each "failed" conversation also had opportunity. Opportunity to see the other side of the conversation, to witness events which may not have unfolded, and to learn. How often in life do we "fail" at a conversation, only for it to bring something positive later in life? It's what we do with every moment in our lives that allows us to grow or stagnate. This game about relationships and conversations is refreshing in a world of finger-twitching shooters and daily-grind questies. I crowdfunded this game, and am happy I did. I look forward to more from this studio.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game a while ago and yesterday I remembered it and how much I loved the vibe and art style.I remembered that I'd stopped playing it because I'd gotten frustrated, so I decided to give it another go.As lovely as the game is, the card mechanic feels incredibly punishing. I personally love seeing all a game has to offer and, as some other reviews pointed out, the smartest and most successful way to play the game is to adapt your deck (of only TEN) cards to specific locations and leave out the ones that don't match your deck.The game itself is about the fact that you can't please everyone. But in trying to give my deck variety, because I wanted to interact with everyone, my deck was essentially built for failure. The cards themselves would actually work, but the fatigue cards you get from travelling can block 3/5 cards that your hand can hold. In that case, you're destined to not get anywhere...Love everything including the idea of the card mechanics. But how it works feels counterproductive to the relaxed vibe it's aiming for...

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to like here, the idea is interesting in principle and the world is quite an interesting one to investigate. Sadly, its let down by the fundamentally poor implementation of the deckbuilding core of the game.Essentially the idea is that you carry on conversations by laying cards down with people that have symbols on the right and left, if all the symbols match you successfully move through the conversation, if not, you don't. Most the people in your home town, and you, use the same set of symbols, while those further afield use different ones, so to communicate when you go out into the world you need to update your deck with new cards and new symbols, but when you return home, you'll not be able to talk to your old friends. Its an analogy about how broadening your mind with travel is a good thing, but often you can never go home again.At least, in theory it is. In practice, in your home town your best friend regularly uses a card "accommodate", which automatically copies both symbols of the previous card. 90% of the conversations in the game can be completed by pretty much just spamming this one card. You don't really need to learn and grow, you just need to parrot back what people said to them. This is exacerbated by your deck being locked at a static 10 cards, so rather than growing your vocabulary and then needing to use card abilities to pilot through your deck and negotiate through a conversation, then thinning the deck back down as you learn to better talk to strangers, you can pretty quickly reduce conversations down to a set of simple non-choices. Worse, this means that most of the time when you're forced to take a new card from each conversation, its just junk that you cycle in and out of your deck, that's to say, most of the time you don't want to learn from people and grow, but you're forced to whether you want it or not.The story of the world is interesting and quite involving, but the execution of the central game is so fundamentally banal as to suck the life out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: If you are the type that likes to please everybody, this is not your game. You are mostly at the mercy of the RNG for successful conversations, and there are no mechanics in the game to make you feel less bad about not being able to have a successful conversation. There are also missing basic QoL features like multiple save slots and the ability to interrupt a chat with somebody even after you exit the game.The dog was cute but overall the game stresses me out more than it soothes.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: A interesting card-based convo game where the MC travels to different towns for trading and talking to unique individuals who tell their stories. I remember looking at a short review of the demo several months ago but I actually played it just a few weeks ago when I saw that it would be released soon. I’ve played through the demo and comparing it with the full game it’s pretty much identical except for that you will be at the mercy of the RNG. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve felt frustrated when I had the right shapes but the hand that I’d been played was just unlucky.The full game is pretty short and I managed to clear it 4x in a few days but there’s no ending gallery so I’ve only gotten 2x variations of the same ending. It starts out as a calming and chill game that has a great OST but quickly I felt railroaded as there’s a lack of certain square/diamond cards and I found that halted my progress. So far I’ve made a mixed, circle/triangle, and circle/diamond decks so I’ve spoken to most of the NPCs at this point and visited different towns. Although I found it very relaxing there’s definite moments where I felt lost and the overall plot is mixed. We’re searching for clues about our late mother but I’ve only gotten brief convo and so much of is just filling in the blanks using my imagination. For a story-based convo game I’m baffled at the lack of a main plot details and even when I found out the answers they were lacking.There are mini-stories along the way but they were also pretty open-ended with the details as I followed different NPCs around town. I didn’t feel like interacting with them changed much of their stories and even I didn’t get any sense of closure from their final outcome. There’s so much potential in the game but it’s just oddly empty or obtuse. The silent MC where we don’t see their replies is just a mystery and I prefer any kind of personality vs nothing at all.I would say there’s some replayability with the different towns but I felt that if there were most options they were locked behind some serious RNG and it didn’t help that there’s only one save slot so no real way to try again w/o starting over each time.Do I recc’d the game? Maybe just for the colorful artstyle and OST but only for a few times since I’ve been stuck on the 4th playthrough for few hours w/no progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: To give you some idea of how much I've enjoyed this game, I got it practically for free as a part of The Bundle, but after playing through it 4-5 times I decided to "buy" it separately just to support the developer.At first, the conversation system feels like it's all about luck, but there's actually a lot of strategy in how you build your deck and what cards you play - e.g. if you know you're going to play a mismatched card, deciding on the "safest" time to play it. It's possible to make it through the whole game with only a handful of "discordant" conversations. But, the fact that things will sometimes go wrong and there's nothing you can do about it, or that you'll be forced to trade a good card for a lesser one, is part of what makes the game so emotionally engaging. I'm not sure I've played any other game where failing to connect with an NPC left me feeling quite bad and wondering what could have gone differently.Also, the art: such whimsical backgrounds, and such evocative character sketches. I love the color palettes. I also love the world-building, where things keep getting weirder the deeper you dig. It's not a huge or complicated game, but it's a game that knows what it wants to be and achieves that goal perfectly, with no extra fluff getting in the way.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the Pros and Cons:PROS1. I love innovative deck building games that aren't about microtransactions and P2P battles. This game was right up my ally.  You'll love the clever and deep card-to-polygot conversation mechanics overall.  2. I LOVE the art style, all of the different characters, variety of outfits, their slight poses, the world itself is really captivating. I could feel and love and care that went into each character and their respective voices. It's something I feel came right out of my own mind.  The characters (when you can communicate with them) are all believable and interesting.3. The music is so amazing.  You'll be tempted to get the soundtrack.CONS1. It's a shame it's largely one track for city, I would have loved that the instrumentals begin to drop away as you fail a conversation/or perk up if your crushing a conversation with resolve at each turn.2. Resolve (I forget the exact name) is buggy. I'm referring to the ability when you match four items, you get a barrier that provides you with an extra chance to get a situation right. Here's the issue, it works about 90% of the time--but sometimes when you play, say, Duplicate to make a 4-tile combo, you also aren't rewarded with Resolve. When this happens you go, "oh, so it must not work if it combos into other cards. I won't try that anymore then." Then in other times you do it and it works--you get resolve--and you're like "Oh, I must have did something wrong before? I guess I'll remember that this works." Then later on in the same campaign you try it and it doesn't work, and you're like. "Tch. This games got bugs.  Either that or it doesn't even play by it's own rules."3. Character AI should ALWAYS attempt to make a four tile combo whenever possible. I had a crucial conversation with Mimi at the Long Gate where I could see her hand, saw she had two Squares, saw the board that could definetly gain resolve if she played that card, and instead she played Square-Triangle, which caused the entire conversation to fail. That's literally the AI undermining itself and my progress because any other player would make the more optimal move. I've taken screen shots of this--but what's really frustrating is that it's a failstate that's out of my control as a player.4. Fatigue cards should either be accumulated less frequently (say every 15 or 30 blips instead of every 10 blips), or you should be able to play them immediately after Resolve has been achieved (as in playing one fatigue card into a Resolve barrier will eat up both the fatigue AND the barrier. You lose your extra chance but you optimize your deck. It's a good balancing mechanic).5. You should be able allowed to keep your roadmap at the start of a new game. Listen. This is the one thing I desperately wish would be implemented in the game. It's a single player game, let us have the player choice to have us start a new game with our map (at least). Having to reforge the same roads again and again is tiresome.6. The tone of Elias when you can't communicate with each other is such a left turn from when you try to be friends that it's hard to like him as a character. He's your best friend if you can communicate, and when you struggle to have a conversation with him--he literally chews you out and storms away. I've had encounters where he flips me off and walks off. The writing on here needs to be toned down just a bit--the last two days I didn't even want to bother having a conversation with him because it puts such a sour note at the end of each chapter. I think you can still communicate the difficulties of talking to folks when you come home from a journey AND tone down his attitude a bit--so that you can still like him as a character. "Elias looks confused, there's a lonesome feeling separating the two of you as he walks away and goes back to work." Vs. "Elias shakes his head, flips you off, and heads back to the cafe."7. I've said this before, but please let us keep at least the map + roads from previous playthroughs.8. I've said this before, but please reduce the degree of fatigue accumulation or give us a better way to remove fatigue cards.9. The whole game seemed to be setting up for a single conversation in Hana (sp) which I failed--easily. As a result, the entire set up about the mystery locket fell flat. The constant fighting against the game mechanics is tiresome.10. It certainly feels impossible to travel and adopt your cards to speak the varied languages such that you can visit most of the cities in a single month. Likewise, many characters if the game seem to imply that "you won't please everyone, don't try to" and "there's only so much you can do" so big swaths of the game feel largely untouched.11. It's silly you can play fatigue cards. They're in an instant "fail twice" card. Why even have that be an option? Why not have fatigue cards turn into "Thunder the Dog Match with Everything" cards when you get to do those mid-road Pick A or B decisions? This would at least keep the dog more as a agent in the game (I think he only popped up three times and disappeared forever in my playthrough), give fatigue cards potential strategies other than (Play/Collect to Fail).12. I feel like, overall, fatigue card collection was leaned on too much. Conversations should just require more card chains to be successful as the month progresses. Being inundated with fatigue is like playing Skyrim with being encumbered. Yes, you're character is fatigued, but the mechanic is extremely frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: A major challenge of story-driven tabletop games is bridging the gap between players and their characters. Though some might immediately feel  comfortable improvising and conversing in-game, in my experience it takes a significant investment for players to internalize their characters. Often the burden falls on the game master - which, depending on the game, might act as a moderator, narrator, or just be the one person in the group who read the rulebook - to help players ease into their roles and become comfortable playing in the space the group creates.Video games often attempt to emulate this experience, but without the flexibility of human-to-human interaction it can be extremely challenging to adapt something as abstract as a conversation into static systems. This is not inherently an issue, but it does create a situation where few games feel reactive enough to hide the binary input/output of their story engines.In our post  (Telltale Games, 2012) and  (Bioware, 2007) world, games overwhelmingly lean into the transparency of their narrative structures by highlighting even before an interaction has played out how it will sit with the other party, and then emphasizing if the character will respond to that response later on. Liam Esler’s talk at the 2016 GDC Narrative Summit does a good job illustrating the draw and challenge of implementing these systems, but the key take away is balancing the illusion of agency and the realities of producing a branching narrative. (Echodog Games, 2020) hacks this model by layering a card game on what would typically be a choice of responses. Conversations play out as call and response monologues, wherein the player’s ability to successfully match a series of card symbols determines if the conversation is “successful.” These symbols, theoretically, correspond to different conversational tones: direct, logical, empathetic, grieving. Actual play is much less articulated - play is not disimilar from a stripped down, linear version of dominos - but these symbols do help flavor interactions which typically last for only two or three exchanges.I don’t think it’s fair to judge  on the versatility of its conversation system, as a card game which attempted to model the impenetrable complexity of actual conversation models would be overwhelming. But like  and its derivatives, the emphasis on conversations  systems also calls to the surface all the ways the system begins to break down when it tries to diverge from a perfect chain of events.  describes itself as “a narrative card game about relationships and connecting with people,” but more accurately it is a card game about unlocking the history of its characters.The protagonist speaks only through the cards they play, leading to conversations that are effectively one sided. These stories can be delightful as even with only a few sentences to spare at a time  characters are remarkably well drawn, but I kept wanting a version of this game that traded its card mechanic for a system that let its characters speak more. I want to learn about the secret art society, The Circle, and how its members are confronting profits versus artistic integrity. I want to help the robot that can’t find its home and is stuck working as a farmhand to a vintner. I want to talk to my dog.To its credit,  is deliberately structured to allow these stories to trickle out over repeat visits to the same areas as you meet more characters and get into their good graces. But this always requires a successful game of cards, something which becomes highly stressful given how many symbols are in play by the end of the game and the limitations put on controlling your deck. Ideally, this would still allow for interesting conversations when a conversation falls apart or the protagonist is too tired to keep up, but aside from a handful of interactions a failed game of cards stops the conversation cold. And this is what I find most frustrating about : it wants to be both a game about conversations, but only allows for mutually agreeable ones.A lot has been written about the dynamics of conversations, much of it too academically dense to be worth reiterating here, but one aspect which is directly analogous to  is . Building on the speech act theory of J. L. Austin, Airenti and co. define two elements of interaction: conversational and behavioral goals. Put simply, the difference between what is being said and what is being done. “One can be noncooperative from a behavioral point of view, for instance, refusing to comply with a request, while still willing to maintain a correct conversation: 'Could you please help me prepare dinner, dear?' 'Sorry, Bob, I’m busy.'” (Airenti, Bara, Colombetti).In , every interaction is strictly over conversational goals. Either you meet a character where they are or the conversation ends. Austin would describe these as perlocutionary acts - conversations designed to do something without being explicitly about that thing. But even in describing these acts, philosopher A. P. Martinich recognizes the issue of having them be the basic form of a conversation. Writing in his book , Martinich says that “persuading, angering, inciting, comforting and inspiring are often perlocutionary acts; but they would never begin an answer to the question 'What did he say?'” The effect does not explain the cause.As Airenti and co. highlight, often conversations introduce behavioral confrontation without immediately disrupting the conversation itself. Without a distinction between conversational and behavioral goals, arguments are impossible and the subtext and history underpinning a conversation is flattened into oblivion.Again, Airenti and co. articulate this problem well, writing “a model of communication should account not only for standard, successful, and sincere uses of language, but also for failures, deceits, and parasitic forms of communication, like irony.” I said earlier that I didn’t want to judge  purely for how well its conversation game maps to actual conversation dynamics, but the ability to fumble interactions in interesting ways seems so fundamental as to be necessary for the system to have any resemblance to the things that make conversations interesting.Had  allowed the player to fail without having the door slammed in their face, it would be easier to forgive some of the flatness present in its card system or the brevity of its script. But by framing conversations as games to be won without anticipating how often they’d be lost, huge chunks of the game become sequences of frustrating nonsequiturs.I adore the world Echodog has invited me into. I want to live with these characters, travel aboard the caravan, and try to keep my hometown from folding under economic forces. But the game only ever caused me to feel as I was being talked at rather than conversing with. I feel no control over the tone or substance of these interactions despite having to invest heavily at every step. Maybe I’ll get lucky and draw the card I need, maybe not. But surely there is a better way than coming to a fork in the road and being told it ends here because none of my cards have triangles.///

_childDocuments_.review: I think in order for people to really appreciate what this game is, they first need to understand that there is a difference between games that expect you to win and games that want you to learn something from losing. In Signs of the Sojourner, the game wants you to sit in the discomfort of loss. The choices you make between either keeping your current hand and choosing new ways of communication will never lead to you 'winning' every conversation. In fact, this game tries to gently disabuse you of the notion of 'winning' entirely, as conversations with people never tend to end the way you want them to in real life. Do not treat Signs of the Sojourner as a game with a 'good' or 'bad' ending, as those are not concepts that this game wants to reinforce.This is a thoughtful, and beautifully composed experience of learning to live with the innate humanity of not always getting along well with everyone, and how despite that, there will always be people who will share the same ideas and beliefs as you do. I highly encourage people who get frustrated after 'losing' a conversation to stick it out and continue on their journey, because they will find that the people who understand them are often times just a town away.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short (about 3hs per playthrough) but amazing game. It manages to tell a nice coming of age story, with dozens of quirky characters and A LOT of choice & consequences based on your actions and decisions.The core of the game is traveling with a caravan and talking to people you meet using a deceptively simple card game, similar to deck building roguelikes like Slay the Spire. The genius of the game is that it manages to convey feelings like familiarity, sadness and tiredness with this card game, making you experience things like growing apart from a friend or talking to someone you have no affinity simply by playing cards.Moreover, it's a game were failing these card encounters is a vital part of the experience. You can't see everything and win every time. Sometimes you don't even want to win. And the narrative of the story adapts to that, leading to multiple endings, side-quest stories and hidden areas.It's not a long or deep game, but it's a really interesting experience that delivers a lot in a very short time.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Ahh, where to start? With myself, I suppose--I'm playing this game in the midst of the pandemic quarantine and what a perfect time for this game to come out. It's a relaxing, hopeful, but slightly melancholic game (I think I read that exact term in the marketing literature and they nailed it). This game is soothing to play and is exactly what I needed. First off, the soundtrack is amazing. AMAZING. I always, always turn off game music. Don't need it, don't want it, get a headache. I kickstarted this game on a level without the OST, and I just went and bought the soundtrack today as well. It's stunning. Get the game if only to listen to the music. I also really enjoy the small sound effects within the game. This is like an ASMR snack. The art is gorgeous-I don't need to wax on about that because you can see for yourself on the store page just how fantastic the art is. I will start with my favorite things: the game play is fast, and I never find myself waiting through loading screens, forced slow conversations, or cut scenes, which are the worst things in the world. Oh, and NO TUTORIAL. Hell, not having a tutorial gets five stars from me.The other things I find fantastic about this game are things that some other players will not like. I'm not going to give major spoilers away, but stop reading if you don't want to know anything about game mechanics.First off, the narrator is silent. In this game, you build conversations with a diverse, eccentric, sometimes enigmatic cast of characters, and you are the main character--but as the player you're just playing cards trying to develop some sort of conversation, you don't get to read the main characters responses. I find that absolutely stunning and refreshing---I'm developing the main character in my imagination. Her attitude, her responses, her attachment or distrust of each character, etc. But, some people will find the silent narrator frustrating.This is an interactive visual novel, and people who come into this game looking for a card battler will leave disappointed. I do think the cards as a metaphor for conversation and connection with other people works, but it's a bit muffled, and I find myself more often than not forgetting that I'm building a conversation and I'm just trying to match symbols so I can get to the next snippet of conversation. I know it sounds tedious, and for some people it may be just that, but for me, uncovering each tidbit of conversation is a delight. The writing is good and several times I found myself quite taken by a turn of phrase--I didn't write it down but something like "the dogs tails whirring as fast as fans"--really fantastic imagery. I sometimes feel that there's a missing connection between the cards and the story of the game but, I can't verbalize what I'm looking for. There are special cards that include conversational tactics like preparation, or clarifications, but I don't know if they're actually having an effect on the story/responses. Ahhh, and the piece that I'm not quite sure how to write about. In the game someone tells me this about my recently deceased mother: "Just because she had friends on the road doesn't mean you do. You don't inherit connections." I stopped short for a second when I got to this line because I realized this game isn't about a girl going on a road trip to fill her store; this is about people and the connections we make and dissolve during our lives. I mentioned in the beginning I'm playing this during the pandemic quarantine and this game hits all the feels. In this time of social distancing, here is a game about making connections to people, and the bittersweet realization that when you start to fit in better in some places, you start to lose pieces of the old you that fit in better somewhere else. The main character has a bit of a whoa moment when someone talks about her mother in a way that she's never heard her mother talked about before, and as the player we realize that this game is not just about people but also about our understanding of who someone is being challenged. This game is unintentionally timely and I cannot recommend it enough, for the people who are looking for that chill introspective moment in our current whirlwind climate. If you're expecting the next Slay the Spire or Undertale that's not what you'll find here, but for those who go in with an open mind I think you can find something especially poignant in all the things unsaid in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: "Signs of The Sojourner" is a kind of baffling game. From the pleasant graphics to the beautiful soundtrack, everything about this game seems to promise that this is going to be a pleasant and relaxing alternative to the typically punishing card battler. However, lurking beneath this pleasant facade is a pretty steep difficulty curve. While the card plays never feel unfair, the game often does with the way it ties your decisions in game to the success of these cards. For instance, let's say you want to give the old man's son a ride. Or help someone out. If your play is wrong, you can't complete these tasks. So often if you have made errors in your strategy, you'll be fruitlessly travelling around unable to make progress . This game feels like it has a nuanced but ultimately black and white view of human interaction. Like for instance, my neighbor may rub me the wrong way but he also might win me over by agreeing to mow my lawn.  If human interaction were the way the game sees it, I would refuse to let him do me this favor.Another issue I had is I really dislike the way the game seems to want you to feel bad for not connecting with certain people. Maybe this is just my own self-preservation talking but I don't believe that having an awkward interaction necessarily will spoil someone's perception of you. At times, this aspect of the game felt like it added insult to injury. Overall I would recommend the game as a fascinating but ultimately flawed exercise. There's a lot to like here and it's worth checking out but I do think it has some core problems in it's design.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an incredibly good idea, and I encourage everyone to try it on the merits of that idea alone: the entire game is you talking to people, however your conversations are abstracted as a card game. Cards have symbols that represent the tone of your speech, and you have to match the tone the other character is going for. If someone plays cards with a circle (meaning emphatic and observant), and you try to play a triangle (diplomatic, logical), the conversation doesn't develop in any useful way. And since you're a traveling salesman of sorts, getting on the good side of people is how you progress. So that's awesome. And I wouldn't even say the game is not awesome. It is. It's very charming, the soundtrack is incredibly soothing, and it does interesting things with its mechanics. For example, some cards have unique conversational properties such as allowing you to redraw your hand ("reconsider"), matching whatever symbols were in the card your conversation partner has just played ("accommodate"), or even to play the card retroactively in a previous point of the conversation ("clarify"). This is just the tip of the mechanical iceberg here, and I am not kidding when I say the game is remarkably industrious with how it unfolds. However, some of the things it does, regardless of how mechanically creative, just rub me the wrong way. For example: after every conversation, the game forces you to change one of the cards in your incredibly small 10-card deck for one that was used in the conversation you just had. At the start, these feel like upgrades to how much you can express yourself. And it makes sense: the more you talk to people, the better you get at talking to people — especially if they're the kind of people you just talked to. However, as you go along, the size of your deck doesn't increase, but the number of different symbols you need to effectively juggle in order to being able to talk to people in new places increases a lot. At the start everyone just used the same 2 or 3 symbols, I could be sure to almost always have the right cards to ensure effective communication with all of them. But later on, there's twice as many symbols, but my deck still only has 10 cards, which means talking to everyone is harder — including those people at the start that used the first 2 symbols in the game. It doesn't make sense that the more I talk to people, the worse I got at talking to people, especially to the people I was already good at talking to! This only happens because the game mandates that I substitute one of my cards for one used by the person I just had a failed conversation with. Anyhoo. This relatively small thing was enough for me to drop the game. I'm not sure this means this "flaw" is that heavy (and I'm sure some people wouldn't even consider it a flaw) or that I'm just eager to drop games since I've been juggling so many at the same time, but the truth is it happened. Creative, nice, and soothing as it is, Signs of the Sojourner failed at communicating with me.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I would make the case that as of writing this, Signs of the Sojourner is probably one of the more under recognised games on steam, at least based on sales and review volume. It's a game that is particularly unique in its mechanics and therefore, quite hard to market - though the trailer does do a good job at selling the core appeal of a narrative focus.The design that abstracts conversation to a token based game is very fresh, and the writing quality is excellent. Conversations felt natural both in the way they read as well as how they progressed based on the card game. With some conscious and active imagination of how characters talked, it was very easy to see conversations develop as consequences of the right or wrong cards being played. It's a little high minded but I personally enjoyed it a great deal. There are also other elements of decision making involved, primarily in journey planning and management. These remind me a bit of old visual novels that used calendar based events, though they're not so tedious in this game. Briefly on the subject of the writing itself- the story is fairly loose and seems to embrace some vague genre themes of an adult slice of life. The focus is not drama necessarily, but on transience and change. This thematic tone is also very well accented with some lovely art and excellent music. It's rare for a game to hook me in on narrative alone for the multiple hours stretch that I played through in one sitting and I very much enjoyed my time. I certainly recommend it to anyone interested in an exploration of some interesting game mechanics to tell a story.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually played a bunch of this on itch and then got a steam key for it in a charity bundle. It's a pretty neat little indie that tackles trying to portray conversation as gameplay. So the way it works is that you play a card game where you and the NPC take turns playing cards to try to match one another's "language" which is represented by different symbols. Your deck is quite small, and changes every time you succeed an encounter (you discard a card and gain a card from the NPC's deck), and every NPC speaks with two of the symbols minimum, so the challenge of the game is trying to manage your deck to be able to speak the right way to all the people you want to make happy.But what I like about the game is that it uses this system to tell a story. "Winning" a conversation is not necessarily winning at the game. Because they are conversations after all, not competitions, and not combat. When you "win" all it means is that you are in accord with the person you're speaking to. Is it good to be in accord with every person? What if they're a bad person? What if you don't agree with what they have to say about the world? With what they're asking you to do? You might wanna speak circles to their squares when they're being horrible. But it's not just about agreement and disagreement, sometimes you are interested in a person and you just don't speak their language. Sometimes you come back to a person you were once in accord with and your experience has changed you so much you can't connect to them anymore. I think being able to create these experiences in this extremely abstract way is a measure of really intelligent game design. So I think this is worth a look for anyone who's interested in that meaning making side of gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. There's hardly a negative comment I could make upon it.Story-wise, your mother passes, and you're responsible for keeping your hometown alive through her story/trade caravan. You meet a variety of people and learn about/influence their stories, learning hidden stories about your mother's past on the caravan route and ultimately finding an appropriate ending to the caravan problem (the town relies on the caravan for business, and your store needs to be successful for the caravan to justify coming around.)Gameplay-wise, the gameplay is a deck-building card game with folks you encounter, with the unique twist that the cards represent a dialogue, the goal being to have cards that match with theirs to reach concordance (make a successful connection.) Interacting with characters will allow you to take one of their cards and swap out one of your own for it, and traveling will give you 'fatigue' cards that don't match with other cards. Some cards have special powers that allow you to change your deck, see their hand, or change the order that you draw in.SotS really shines in the atmosphere and story-telling mechanics. The music and graphics convey feelings appropriate to the setting and situation, and each character is complex and interesting enough that it's easy to form an attachment to them-I remember that I allowed myself to be robbed by a known thief just because I wanted to hear more about her story, and I legitimately shed a tear in the later part of the story when a character I was very fond of passed away. I really appreciated how the story-telling was integrated almost seamlessly with the gameplay. A character's choice of cards really captures their style of communication: the special cards they have correspond generally to their communication style/how they interact with you, characters that have traveled will have a mix of symbols to correspond to places they've inhabited, and characters that oppose each other in some way will generally have opposite output/input sides. Tips/gameplay advice are, because of this, integrated very cleanly into the interactions you have with other characters, as advice that works on a story and gameplay level. I noticed on several occasions that a character telling me how to travel to another location had their own reasons, but that it would also assist either in a task I need to accomplish or in changing out some of my cards in interactions there to better communicate with them in the future.There's a lot to be learned in this game in the meaning of each symbol and how different communication styles don't necessarily dictate the whole of a character's personality. To give an example, I remember a discussion how the art city of Pachenco used mostly empathy/logic symbols, but not the creative symbol. Thinking about it more, I realized that the Pachenco residents present a logical approach to an otherwise creative endeavor, whereas the people of the west approached their trades, mostly making food and spices, in a creative way. There are many other examples of this and how people can still be warm and fun to connect with despite having different communication styles that might seem cold/difficult at first.I also learned a lot through the discord/concordance interactions. I saw a lot of messages during discord that seemed at first to be regular responses given the conversation. I spent time reflecting on this and believe that I learned a lot about how to empathize with other people and make genuine connections through conversation, as I learned how these responses weren't as constructive to making a connection.The only thing I'd want to warn you about: The game is short (a couple hours), but don't let that or the pricetag dissuade you. There's loads of replayability as you seek different endings or focus in certain areas, and the lessons the game can teach you are well worth the 20-dollar price tag. I know that some people might want to wait for a discount, because it's a single-player game, but I think it's important to support these developers and keep them well-financed/encouraged to make more awesome games.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely like the concept of the game - gradually learning new languages while traveling to different places, but realizing soon enough that trying to focus on all conversation topics will cause you to fail, so you have to balance your options and make tough choices. _childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: For me, this is a near perfect game and has automatically made it onto my favourites list. I'm currently on my second run and fully intend to do a third. It reaaaally spoke to my experience of leaving home and subsequently struggling to 'speak the same language' as my friends who remained local. The story tells itself inherently through the design, which for me is the mark of a masterpiece in game and narrative design. Some aspects of the design were frustrating, but in the way they were meant to be, if that makes sense. For example, I didn't always want to swap out cards at the end of a conversation, but that's the choice you make both in the game and in life... we are the people we surround ourselves with, so think carefully about who those people are. Doing different things in your life will change you, so carefully about what you want to do. I do kinda wish we had New Game +, but I also understand that that would detract somewhat from the message so... it would be nice maybe to have that as an extra option? Maybe unlocked after a few different runs with the places from all your runs unlocked? Idk. Anyway, obviously I loved this. The only people I wouldn't recommend it for are those who prefer games that can be 'optimised' and 'won'... that's not what this is about. Just enjoy the ride and let it speak to you, no matter how things turn out. Then play again and do things differently and enjoy that too. Just... enjoy it :)
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Inkle-like quality, narrative originality and magic. Game about leaving, travelling, changing and returning. About people you meet and stories you witness. About getting close to someone and/or getting far from them. With great cards "battle" system awarding long-time planning as well as clever choices in the heat of a moment. _childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I very much wanted to recommend this game, and completed it once (there are likely a wide array of endings). I love the concept, and the mechanics are extremely interesting.Unfortunately, your ability to have narrative input is limited by your cards, and you really need to specialize in a few symbols - this sharply limits who you can successfully talk to. There's a lot of awkward between-specialization phases where even folks you should be able to talk to have failed dialogs because you drew too many cards outside where you're trying to get to.The world is not well explained, which kept me from any level of immersion. Interactions with characters felt like implied depth, rather than real depth - again, possibly a result of unavoidably failed checks.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super cute. I've never played a card-based game like this before, and am very pleased that this was the first one. The graphics are aesthetically pleasing, and the soundtracks are great too. It was a little difficult for me to get the hang of the gameplay in the beginning (probably just a me thing), but it got easier as I continued the journey despite the incoming card attributes. I have just finished my first playthrough and "failed", but was pleasantly surprised that the ending wasn't the typical "bad ending". These types of endings encourage the player to start again, and I am grateful for that.This is a game about navigating life. You're going to find people that your ideals and beliefs line up with, and others that you have little in common with. You won't always get your way, so it's time to move on and find what brings you happiness. These types of stories make you think of your own--who you're going to be, and where you're going to go. Life's a journey. I think that's what this game is trying to tell me. I am looking forward to trying again to continue the story.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: One of the games that I keep coming back to, because of its unique premise, mechanics and overall atmosphere. Just rewatching the trailer again reminds me how well its graphic design and visuals fit with the music, and how, despite the cute art style, it can be an extremely stressful and challenging game to play. Signs of the Sojourner's strongest suit is the ludo-narrative harmony represented in the deck building. Of course, you can choose to stay on the same wavelength as your childhood bestie, but you would need to sacrifice your ability to open to the outside world, which is, unfortunately, directly tied to your financial success. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everyone interested in the game mechanics as tools for storytelling, and also enjoys when game looks and sounds amazing. It's the whole package!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Non-combat deck-builder based around communication and growth? Incredible. Honestly such an amazing game! _childDocuments_.review: The experience of Signs of the Sojourner was completely unexpected. As with most games, I attempted to hold no preconceptions of the game, instead opting to engage in a very reactionary way. I was moved by the music, captivated by the atmosphere, engaged with the strategy and puzzles intertwined within the dialogue. There was no adverse impact to the gameplay due to exhausting exposition or obtrusive loading screens; everything was fluid and paced intelligently.I also found that within the mechanics of the game, there was a dearth of clunky mcguffins or afterthoughts. The tools given to you served only to enhance the playing experience, without overloading your brain with choice. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I have to recommend in the category of "there is nothing else like this".  I'm not sure that I personally find the game "fun" but it is an amazing narrative style with completely unique gameplay.Signs of the Sojouner is a deckbuilder where the cards represent portions of a conversation, and symbols on them are different emotions or communication styles.  You play as a supplier for a store and have to go around with a caravan collecting items to sell to keep the store in business, so modifying your communication style allows you to work more easily with different people along the route.  Most of the people you encounter near your home are empathetic and logical, but the further out you go, the more you encounter creative or direct communication styles that the initial deck has difficulty with.  As you adapt to be able to handle those styles, going home becomes harder and harder.

_childDocuments_.review: This was very close to being my favorite game of 2020! My only complaint is that the game is really crying out for you play through it multiple times (you can take completely different routes each time!), but the length was just a touch long for me to immediately want to jump back into a repeated attempt.Highly recommended if you like deck-building games, or games that try smart things with how they tell their story!

_childDocuments_.review: "Signs of the Sojourner" is a mobile app-like CCG/deckbuilder game.  Great, right? We all love Hearthstone, Magic the Gathering, Slay the Spire... aha, but wait.  This is not like those games.  See, the developer saw how popular card battlers were, because it's cool to use cards to summon minions and fight your enemies and stuff.  So they dumbed the whole thing down, and ripped the cool combat/minions part of it and made it so your cards reflect "conversations".  Ugh.  Talk about throwing away the banana and keeping the peel. This doesn't work on pretty much every level.  Playing a video game about conversations is not fun.  Playing a video game where you can't have conversations properly because the right cards didn't come up in your crappy little deck is the video game equivalent of a Tourette's simulator.  Why is that going to be enjoyable?  Yeah, it's not.  This is a bad idea implemented badly.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.The game features simple, cartoony 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort mobile apps.  3D graphics programming does require a degree of skill and competence and unfortunately not all developers have the budget or talent to deliver this, despite 3D graphics cards hitting the mainstream in the 1990's.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.Because this is designed for consoles/mobile phones, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).Regardless, for all intents and purposes "Signs of the Sojourner" might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game."Signs of the Sojourner" has the preposterous price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  Because this is the kind of game you can just play for free on mobile phones, it's impossible to recommend anyone should pay money for the same experience on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: a fresh take on deckbuilders is really exciting, and the deck-as-personality system in SIGNS OF THE SOJOURNER is really clever and leads to some great moments (like that first time you come back home after a long trip, and try to have a conversation with your friend...).the writing and characters are really fun too, but that also leads to one of the game's weaknesses - it makes repeated runs feel like more of a chore, as you have to click through all of that dialog every time. _childDocuments_.review: A great game.... if i find a way to mod out fatigue.really really enjoyable, ignore what everyone says about the story or the mechanics they are both wonderful! it is a shame this one feature (fatigue) is in the game. exhaustion adds nothing but increases difficulty to an absurd degree, you can have the BEST deck, it doesn't matter, you will still gain fatigue the same as everyone else. I was half way through my second trip and i have 5 fatigue.... the hand size is 5.... you cannot do anything and auto fail every conversation. so in summery, the game is great IF you can go into the game files and remove the fatigue mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I have not yet finished this game but so far I feel that this game managed to do something really special with how the narrative and gameplay intertwine. The way where the game is conversation and the ai is trying to play with you as best as they can rather than against you. While the game might start off simple it quickly grows very difficult and it becomes a struggle to stay on top of everything. There is a undeniable, clear and severe scarcity in the resources you have at your disposal to engage with the diverse array of cards people and it really adds to the narrative weight and tension of the journey's you go on.With such simple mechanics it really manages to capture a sense of Anxiety and unease at what the future could bring. Will the store survive? How will your relationship with your friends, your home survive the distances you travel? Will the world be able to yield enough to feed it's people. This uncertainty is so excellently captured by this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Beat the game, or at least got one of the endings, it's very fun and there's so much todo, therte's so much I don't know even after beating the game. The game at its core is a deck builder where you talk to NPCs with your cards, the stories of the characters are so good and I related to many of them, I haven't got so invested in a game's NPCs for a long time but this game made me actually get so immersed, I would get mad if RNG messed up a conversation or got annoying at the few NPCs I couldn't help BC my deck was built to help other NPCs, very good game with amazing art and soundtrack, the characters are amazing and it seems to have a lot of replayablity with what appears to be multiple endings and routes
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: The plot & world-building: The need to try and keep the shop in Bartow open and along with the mystery surrounding the nameless main character’s dead mother are fantastic and the main reason why I kept playing. I want to try to keep Bartow on the caravan route! I wanted to know more about whatever the hell my mother got up to on her caravan trips (and she got up to a lot apparently)! The game allows for multiple replays and there’s an option in settings to turn off the tutorial so you don’t have to go through it every time you start the game again. The gameplay: I love deckbuilding as well as story-driven games and Signs of the Sojourner is the perfect combination of the two! I have described it to my boyfriend as Slay the Spire, but instead of defeating enemies, you’re trying to make a good impression and hold a decent conversation with the people you meet. I think this is why some people I see in reviews and myself find the game stressful – it’s too much like real life, I guess! It can be difficult to decide which cards you should add to your deck. I would recommend deciding what routes you would like to unlock and/or people you want to please after you’re familiar with the game and aim to get the cards with which to gain a positive conversation with them. Art style – so cute and original, I loved the variety of designs for each character and places. I would love a graphic novel drawn in this style. Music – incredible! I love how each place has its own unique tune. My favourite is Bukam Boro’s funky guitar. And all of Elias’ musical solos. Yes, all of them. Dog: 10/10, very good dog.Verdict – if you love deckbuilding, strategy and/or mystery games, I highly recommend Signs of the Sojourner!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if this is worth full price but the soundtrack is absolutely insanely good. I didn't have any complaints about the balance of the game difficulty or having to swap out cards or anything like that. I thought the buffs like  made it very possible to do what I wanted in one playthrough, but maybe some experience with other strategy card games helps. In fact if anything, I felt like since I got to do most of what I wanted, I have little reason to go back for another playthrough. Maybe in a few months. And seriously that soundtrack is *everything*. Congrats to the composer, and the whole team. Lots of fun flavor and stories throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning game! The artwork, music, and overall vibe are lovely. And the gameplay is a very interesting, challenging (but not very hard) deckbuilding mechanic. It's worth it to play through it several times to explore all parts of the story and the various endings, but I do wish it were possible to skip over the intro conversation whenever you start a new playthrough.Bonus points for being able to pet a dog! And more bonus points for the fact that petting the dog actually helps you in-game :D
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Genre mashup of roguelike deckbuilder and branching-path visual novel, which turns out to be a hugely effective combo. I made choices I regretted and had to deal with the consequences. I had to figure out who to be able to befriend, and how best to make that happen. A true roguelike, not roguelite, but each replay gives you something new and different, and reason to try again and see if a different path is more your taste. Very emotionally introspective and grownup, looking at the consequences of actions and how hardships change people. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fascinating take on the conversation simulation genre by incorporating deckbuilding as a central mechanism. The deckbuilding works by representing elements / approaches to conversation (for example: empathy, aggression, distress, logic, etc) using symbols on cards, in addition to card modifiers or effects.What I find really interesting (and some find frustrating) is when you first leave your little village to set out on the trail you will inevitably encounter people who converse using different card symbols than you currently have in your deck. At first, this results in complete failures to communicate but as you travel and refine your deck you make it easier and easier to travel and have successful conversations all over the map. After each conversation (pass or fail) the game forces you to throw away a card from your deck and replace it with a card you've encountered in that conversation, making your deck this morphing thing that remains limited but ever-changing.My only complaint is that once I've completed the story it's daunting to restart fresh to try new pathways. I would like to see a New Game+ mode that allowed you to carry over a limited number of cards. Signs of the Sojourner is an interesting game with a good and fitting soundtrack, a pleasant art style, good execution of an idea, and doesn't overstay its welcome. Play the demo!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: A chill card game where winning or losing isn't really the point, just different outcomes.I enjoyed my time wandering that world and meeting its protagonists greatly, loved the environment / character art by the way, and great storytelling. The interesting thing is that your playthrough can lead you in many different places and there will be a bunch of story beats you won't be able to follow your first time around, it seems there are actually a good number of endings depending on what you do and it's all the more reasons to specialise your deck and eventually go in a completely different direction next time you'll play the game, to experience it entirely.To sum it up, if "losing" a few times doesn't scare you, you'll discover a beautifully drawn game with a nice story about connecting with other people and might even vibe hard with it, give it a chance !
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Signs of a Sojourner is a really beautiful game I would recommend people to experience at least once. It manages to be a cleverly original deckbuilder, which is a tall order to be in a world deluged in card games of all shapes and sizes, and a good narrative game filled with simple, yet poignant moments. It's difficult to find many other games in which mechanics and narrative meld so well, sometimes to its (forgivable) detriment. The writing succeeds in delivering characterizations and moments in short, bite-sized sentences carrying only half of the conversation (because you, the Player Character, is a silent protagonist). There is so much to say about card games being analogy of communication that warrants separate article, but I believe Sojourner delivers what it set out to be. Even when conversation breaks down, it still seems meaningful. The worldbuilding is atmospheric. The card game part is just as clean and simple, but in no way lacking depth. Cast is literally colorful, with distinctive art style and evocative illustrations. It's a chill, non-punishing game of cards, which is refreshing. This seems to be at odds with a lot of comments I find on Steam. Be forewarned though that chill as it may, it IS a proper deckbuilding game, which mean you can't jam everything in your deck willy-nilly and expect it to be functional.I don't find the deckbuilding aspect punishing at all, even charming. The idea of an ever-evolving deck influenced by your experience, the people you meet and the places you visit, is wonderful and encourages people to adapt. The randomness of ability acquisition means you cannot rely on the same strategy every single time. It is better to focus on card composition. Yes, ten cards are enough. The very first thing you have to learn in Signs of the Sojourner is to learn that you cannot have everything, that there is no winning/losing (and consequently, being in accord with whoever you meet on the road does not guarantee positive outcome). You may not always please everyone, but it is very possible to construct a deck which allows you to talk with generally everyone unless you get bogged down with too much fatigue (which is also an on-theme, interesting concept for me). While you can choose not to visit places or refrain from talking to certain people, I managed two successful runs with a balanced deck and talking to everybody I could visit in every trip (I used all 50 days). My playing style, if anyone is interested: I find that 2-3 Accommodates work best, followed by 5-6 'core cards' comprising of multi-symbol cards. Make sure all symbols but grief are distributed as uniformly as possible. Whenever you can, put useful abilities on these cards. These cores could stay till the end, largely unchanged. Then 1-2 utility cards that might not be very good but have useful abilities (Prepare and Elaborate are my personal preferences, or a single Reconsider to sweep away pesky fatigues). Then designate one slot as the 'chopping block'. Whenever you are forced to take a card that does not fit your deck (not an upgrade to your cores and is not an useful utility), use this slot. You may sometimes get useful card in this slot and have to rewrite it with not-so-useful cards, but that means you only have to deal with changes in this one slot. I find my deck mostly settled by the second or third trip. Between Accommodate and Elaborate, you can even handle wild griefs while not sparing a single slot to grief at all. Yes, you do have control over your cards to some degree. Like any other card games, you may have to rely on the luck of the draw at times, but that's what the abilities are for. Honestly, the abilities are well-designed and mostly useful, so feel free to tinker on your own. The only real liability is Fatigue, and even that can be mitigated by planning the route to make sure the place/people you really really want to visit is earlier in the trip, before you get too tired. However, while it does make sense thematically and I still appreciate it, having only a single save slot (and an autosave at that) hinders people from seeing all the game has to offer. The prospect of having to replay an entire playthrough for specific things missed might deter people from trying at all, because despite randomization and variety of scenes, the repetition shows after 1-2 runs. Ultimately however, I can respect the theme of life going on, you can't have everything, etc... but it makes the game feels divided. It's too long for people who wants to replay it for completeness, and too short for people who just wants to play it once and savor the experience. You can rewind to the beginning of a conversation, but your hand and the cards you draw will stay the same. It is often enough to save you from ruinous decision should you feel so compelled towards a specific outcome, though.Echodog has something special on their hands. I hope they will revisit this title in the future, maybe add more locales or implement some QoL features (such as actual save slots. I would like to see and compare how my endgame calendar looks like in each playthrough!). It would also be nice if you get a checklist of things you have done in one playthrough at the end (e.g a list of recap: you reunited the twins, you found your mom's secrets, etc) not just at the end of the separate conversation sequences.

_childDocuments_.review: Signs is a tough game to navigate (pun intended) during your first run. The symbol gameplay can leave you unequipped for a given path and ready for failure at the hands of a conversation style you had no idea you'd encounter. It is also a work of beautiful art with engaging design, gorgeous music, a lovely theme about community, and some of the most heartmelting writing I've seen in a while. Well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered Signs of the Sojourner through the bundle for Racial Justice and Equality on itch.IO and then re-purchased it here along with the superb soundtrack. This game is truly a treasure, and I keep being drawn back to it.  There are all sorts of little dialogue details that change from run to run, and the newly added characters are challenging and fun to converse with.  The story overall is a mixture of wanderlust and melancholy, with moments of tenderness and joy throughout; I highly recommend exploring different choices as you play (it's true that it's best not to try to please everyone!).I think the only gripe I have with the game is that runs can take a lot of time, and may require savescumming to explore certain routes.  Dialogue savepoints aren't the best place to pick up from sometimes, so you really have to plan out what actions you want to take in a run...but it's honestly a minor inconvenience.Anyway, it's great!  Give it a try :)
