_childDocuments_.review: Overall: B+ Most games fumble when trying to make dialogue feel natural. The much-maligned dialogue trees are fine for a more utilitarian bend to communication but would fall completely flat when attempting to make a game about communication. So, Signs of the Sojourner takes a different approach and abstracts conversation through cards to great effect.  The gameplay revolves around building a deck of cards which all represent a small interaction in a larger conversation. Each card has at least one symbol on both its left and right sides. To play, one just matches the symbols on the left side of the card to the same symbol on the right side of the previous card which builds the conversation. Your entire deck of playable cards is limited to 8 and after every conversation you add a card from the conversation you just had and forget an old card. Choosing how to build your deck is like dwelling on certain parts of a conversation more than others. Each interaction changes you slightly—each new experience causes growth.  Trouble arises when you talk with people who are farther away from your quaint hometown. They have new symbols and you can’t communicate with them as easily. Sometimes, even with the right cards, you just get unlucky and the conversation doesn’t go your way. The simplified card system allows for conversations to, ironically, feel more natural than in almost any game I’ve ever played. You can adopt the culture of far-off cities but then you might have trouble connecting with the people in your hometown, now too changed by your journey. Assembling the deck and talking with the characters quietly builds a rich extra narrative through the mechanics.  While on the topic, let’s talk about the characters. Each one is fairly simple. Few characters get to speak much when you talk to them and every conversation only results in a paragraph or so. While these brief interactions do build over the course of the game, I would have enjoyed getting to know the people a little better. When traveling, the colorful locals are complimented by the wonderous score. Music makes every location feel alive with their own culture and in a game about just that, the soundtrack does a lot of heavy lifting.  If you want a fresh take on a narrative-driven game the delightfully paced Signs of the Sojourner will show you how mechanics can build a story. Clocking in at only ~4 hours, it’s not a huge time commitment either. If you have any interest in non-traditional storytelling, give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's a simple set of rules, but the various card types make it interesting to strategize. I will likely play at least 2 more times as there are other paths and places to explore. It's cozy and has a lot of heart. It's interesting to live in a video game world that moves on with or without you.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my relatively low playtime here, I've beaten the game several times through Itch.io and I regard this as one of my favorite games of last year.Signs of the Sojourner is a piece about gamifying conversations.  But what does that actually mean?  If conversations were a game, it wouldn't simply be about picking the right option in order to please everyone, because that's not really how people work.  People say silly things, they make mistakes, they meet people they don't like, they meet people they hate, they meet people they love but who have no interest in them.  A real simulation of conversation has to include forced and unforced error.  That's the beauty of something like Signs of the Sojourner.Using the underpinnings of an anti-capitalist quest, this game explores feelings of loss and legacy, asking questions about how important memory and "truth" are in relation to it.  It swirls these into a nomadic story, bouncing from place to place meeting characters fascinating, funny, and intriguing all the while.  There are countless games that allow the player to manipulate conversation the way they wish.  There are even games that play with that expectation and withhold the things players want anyway.  There are very few games in counting that accurately simulate the sense of knowing you have to say something that is going to damage your relationship with someone.Signs of the Sojourner does this with its mechanics.  It uses the actual gameplay to instill in the player the emotions that are being felt by the characters.  You feel the hesitation when knowing you cannot match with another character's cards.  You feel the excitement when you say something risky and it pays off.  You feel the relaxation when you engage in a conversation with someone whose deck matches yours.  You feel the fear when you are about to have an important conversation and you aren't sure if you're prepared enough.Another quick note to make is Steve Pardo's absolutely phenomenal score!  Bouncing, distorted violins, moving acoustic guitars, shakers and gourds.  It's filled to the brim with life and emotion that highlights the utterly beautiful art direction of the game and its writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game's mechanics are such an elegant metaphor for lived experience and human interpersonal interaction, especially in regards to travel and how every place you visit or live, and how this impacts the way you approach the world. I had no idea a game could express such concepts via simple and straightforward card-drafting mechanics, I'm truly blown away. I also love how the dog's mechanics are implemented :)The art style and writing and top notch too. The card-drafting requires a decent amount of strategy and playing hands involves potentially complex tactics - I'm still unlocking stuff and getting a handle on all the special mechanics though. I'm sure I'll update this review as I play more (I also played through the free demo prologue which took about an hour and leads directly into the full game).
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: absolutely gorgeous game. the atmosphere evoked by the music and visual style is the big draw for me, but the characters and world-building are what keep me coming back. while the mechanics are simple, the challenge builds in a way that allows for very satisfying strategic forethought after the first play through. not a stye of game i'm usually drawn to, but so very worth it in this instance! quite excited to see what echodog does from here!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: As I usually do when I buy a bunch of games, I fired this one up to see how it was. I didn't close it after twenty minutes, though -- I kept playing until the end. And the next day, I did it again.This game has successfully managed that elusive balance of gameplay, story, and aesthetics. I mention gameplay first, as  is trying to be more than just a visual novel. I personally think the game mechanics have been carefully designed to give some inkling of the trickiness of human interaction. Quite often, quests and side quests can be derailed by conversations that go sour in maddening ways... as in real life. Thankfully, with some forethought, you can limit the extent of such setbacks.The setting and story seem to be post-collapse. What we have here is as far away as you can get from  within the genre. If our current civilisation croaks, I do hope this is how we end up.The art is sketchy in a pleasing way, and this, combined with the varied musical themes for each location, fills the characters and environments with life. The music is really, really easy on the ears, I should add.I've done two playthroughs so far. As regards replayability, I've had different outcomes each time, with a bunch of threads left unexplored.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I think the core game mechanic doesn't work (due to its narrative explanation having implications on how people work), but this game is noteworthy for how well put together it is otherwise.The only flaw with the entire game's UX is that it doesn't indicate who played a card when it matters for one mechanic.The only flaw I found otherwise is that in one specific instance it's unclear if you are trying to succeed or fail as a player, as it gives mixed messaging (Convincing a painter to leave a town)
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great little game! It's pretty short, but quite deep. I played it through the first time and immediately started it up again for another go. I'll probably play it at least one or two more time before uninstalling it.The main gameplay is pretty simple, but subtle enough to be engaging and challenging. After playing for a while, when things were going well it really felt like engaging with and being on the same wavelength as someone else. Likewise, when things weren't going well, it actually felt like two people struggling to communicate.The art is great, the character design is varied and well thought out, and there are a lot of different things going on in the story. Definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Played it originally on itch.io when I got it in a bundle and it's a game with a lot of heart. It's a strategic deck-building game that is strongly focused on story-telling which is done through matching communication styles with the character you're talking to. Your interactions with each character influence their story lines and the outcome of their life. Additionally, the characters are also likable and have very real issues making them all the more interesting. It's also realistic in the sense that you can't be friends with everyone, conversations will not always be so smooth, and befriending certain people can upset others as well. Aesthetically, it has a unique art style with very soothing colors bundled with a relaxing and fitting soundtrack. Highly recommend this game to those looking for a chill game that is story driven.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great narrative adventure in a unique and interesting post-apocalyptic setting. But the way the game integrates the mechanics into its storytelling is what makes it a must play for any RPG fan.The whole game is dialogue, but you aren't making dialogue choices with a traditional branching dialogue system. You're playing cards to match them with the NPC's in order to have "concordant" or "discordant" conversations. Every time you have a conversation, you replace a card in your, rather small, deck with one of their cards. New abilities, such as seeing the other person's hand or forcing them to play two cards, are introduced overtime to add to the simple matching of shapes. I don't want to say anything more and risk spoiling the narrative or the symbolic significance of the mechanics.And hey, the tutorial is available as a free demo. Go for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: In times of COVID 19 and all its restrictions and imposed limitations I enjoyed heavily to have an experiencing of traveling, meeting new people and bonding via 2Signs of the Sojourner". The game is very easy to play and a mixture between a card game, exchange with different personalities and the challenge to pick out your own way from different possibilities. The best feature of this game experience is the way you interact with others: collecting experiences from past interactions you are able to learn and accommodate to new situations. Placed in a context of trust and relationship building I enjoyed highly this way of "playing" communication. (Differently from what one might think, this is not always easy). I am about to play the game a second time and from while I started, I saw that I probably want to play it a third time as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This is the sort of game that makes me wish Steam reviews had a "Maybe" option.On the positive side, this game has everything a good indie game needs: charming visuals, a compelling storyline, simple but solid gameplay and beautiful acoustic music and sound design.On the negative side, because gameplay is deck-based, it feels very luck of the draw sometimes, it starts to feel very frustrating as you play it, especially considering your deck is limited to ten cards at a time (not excluding 'dud' Fatigue cards that do nothing but hinder you). A lot of the time I felt like, because of the nature of the cards I had, any move I made would put me in a bad position.Then again, the very chance-based nature of the game could be said to be a central theme of the game - that sometimes nothing you can do can change who you or anyone else becomes.That being said, it also feels like sometimes you get Fatigue cards a little too often and the ways to get rid of them are also based on random chance.And while the game is fairly short for a $20 game, the game seems like its designed to be played through multiple times to get multiple endings. But I'm also not sure I want to play through the game multiple times after I was finished with it?That's just it. My feelings on the game are... complicated. My recommendation would be to just play through the demo and see if you like it. It's a very unique, definitely love-it-or-hate-it kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Ecstatic that steam recommended this game to me. It's a literal gem of a game, and I love how much life and personality is in here! Actions do have consequences, and my little (BIG) detours end up being so meaningful to the overall story that I end up playing. I highly recommend this game, as there are high replayability in the game and multiple routes/mini stories to explore.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: A creative and charming game about relationships and the ways our travels change us. There are interesting mechanics and more content than can be discovered in just one playthrough. Both the art and the music are fun and the UI is polished.My only critique is that there should be a new game plus mode. Because there is more content than I could get through in the time limit (often due to failing a conversation due to bad luck), I would appreciate the opportunity to bring cards into the next game, and to retry certain days within one playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: incredible, now one of my favs of all time. the core mechanic of deck building conversations just really works for me, it's engaging and challenging but it feels fresh, great rhythm between the card roudns, getting dialog / items / story beats for playing your cards right, balancing your deck, and then popping out to the map screen to uncover new roads and locations and decide where to go next. the character designs, environment art, soundtrack, and setting/themes are all absolutely ace. and there's a lot of story/character threads, and different endings and achievements, for multiple playthroughs. with the playtime short enough that you'll want to go at least a second time. i got to 3 or 4 playthroughs before some of the flaws started showing. most of them i think are just consequences of a different, interesting design and couldn't really be patched out, just don't binge on the game super hard and you prob won't get frustrated. but i do think it could be improved with some kind of New Game+ mode that skips or changes some of the more repetitive early-game content, and maybe allows you to keep some cards or map routes from your last playthrough. because some of the story lines you'll want to chase down don't actually start until your 2nd or 3rd caravan, and you still might fail a critical conversation and have to start all over. all in all though, i just love the heck out of this game for its incredible style, heart and innovative engaging design.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Biggest surprise of 2020 for me. I was genuinely shocked by the amount of content, replay-ability, story, and what it can teach people about real world communication. You can play this dozens of times and still find out new things about characters. I'd recommend anyone who wants to become better at communication to give this experience a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore my play time; I already fully played through the game when I got it on itch.io.This game is extraordinary. I'd recommend everyone that likes innovative gameplay ideas to play it.The way the game uses a card game and different modifiers to abstract a conversation is just genius. It changes the focus from  to It's easy to imagine how a person ticks just from seeing what cards they use and how they use it; Without even taking into account what they say.It's a game of consequences but also about moving on and not looking back.A serious contender for game of the year for me - and it might be the same for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I think a lot of the people who gave this game negative comments and reviews don't really understand the point of this game. Signs of the Sojourner does an amazing job of simulating actual conversations. It took me a bit to realize that it's okay if I don't 'win' a conversation. Just because you can't please everyone doesn't mean you've lost.The more I played the more I started to appreciate the design of the game. The 'annoying' mechanics were actually really well thought out to simulate real life. The deck count limit is annoying but it's there so you can't just stock your deck with everything you would need without stretching yourself thin. It forces you to decide what you want to focus on. This means that some conversations aren't going to go your way and that's okay. No ones good at everything after all.Another annoying mechanic is fatigue but that's another good simulation for real life. Constantly traveling and meeting new people is going to be tiring and will effect how you interact with people. You can find little joys to lessen that but it's still going to be there. I found that some of the card abilities were helpful with dealing with fatigue and actually influenced the type of character I created. Alternatively, I could have decided to ignore those and risk it.This game is meant to be played multiple times. It's impossible to see everything right away because some things require a different type of deck build. It's short though so playing it again isn't really a problem for me. After my first game ended, I closed the game only to start a new one a half hour later. I love all the different paths you can take and the different characters you meet. I can't wait to play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game with a unique take on language and card skills. There are a couple things I would like added. First being a mode that is randomized. Starts you off in a random town working for your own shop would be cool. I also feel like there needs to be a way to redraw a hand occasionally. Maybe allow your character to obtain "relics/artifacts" that you can sell or keep but they can do certain things in game. Such as drawing a new hand, applying a card mechanic, removing a card permanently, etc. I feel like as it is now its only replayable a few times.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite game of this year so far, Signs of the Sojourner resolves around understanding each other in dialogue despite having different characters. The card game might looks to lack depth, but don't be fooled: it's the perfect metaphor for what it tries to accomplish. At the start of the game you are surrounded by like-minded people and dialogues are easy. But the farther you travel the more otherwise-minded people you'll meet. Even if you talk past each other they'll have an impact on you. So by the time you return home, working things out with your long time friends might won't be that easy anymore. The story is personal and compelling, and the music is great as well. It's impossible to visit all places and meet all characters during one play through, so I'll definitely come back to this piece of art once more.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Seemingly simple game, but more complex than it seems and weirdly addictive. I just don't want to stop playing. And I'm pretty sure I'll play it several times.I love the idea of the game, the atmosphere, the music and the graphics. However, there are some annoying things about it. For example, the idea of learning new ways of "talking" as you travel is great, but it is annoying to lose all the old ways at the same rate. My experience from actual travelling is that you learn more than you forget :) But even though this game isn't perfect, I still recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: It's a calm, meditative game that makes you think, but doesn't force you to. The story goes its way whether you put effort into it or not, and only your experience depends on it. The music is pleasant and nice, the characters are lively and easy to get attached to. The gameplay is unusual: playing cards as a huge metaphor to speaking in different languages and manners. It's all about making connections, in the end. I loved it. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: When Echodog first contacted me about trying this game, I wasn’t sure if I’d pass on it - I don’t often play puzzle games and I definitely didn’t know what to make of this one.  I think the unique presentation won me over (and that awesome trailer theme - which also appears in one of the game’s locales).The card-based conversations are amazingly clever - trying to figure out what symbols to play (representing your tone and choice of words) and how to use abilities found on some card (which help resolve conflicts and offer a change of direction) create a ton of interesting scenarios.  The differing amounts of cards required to win each round, the last card played affecting the next round, and the varying amount of matches required/mismatches tolerated does a fantastic job of both setting the difficulty and fleshing out the mood (Is the character especially chatty? Are they on your side?  Are they blunt and standoffish?).It seems that there’s a ton of choice for where to travel, who to talk to, and ultimately where you’ll succeed or fail.  As far as I can tell, you can’t please everyone (the game strongly alludes to this), and having to earn/discard cards with each conversation means your toolkit (and who you’re best at interacting with) will change over time.  Should you stay in the good graces of the earlier and nearer characters, or take bigger risks and expand outward into unfamiliar territory? - at the cost of alienating close friends.  I think there will be a ton of variance in each run, and I’m looking forward to seeing how things go with others’ playthroughs.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game that combines a super interesting mechanic with its narrative flawlessly. Feels frustrating at first but trust me, you can get the right cards to really feel like you're learning to communicate. The story and worldbuilding are very well done, and it's the perfect length for a game - any longer and I would have gotten fatigued, any less and I would have wanted more. Can't say enough good things about this game. If you like TTRPG, Text Story games, Card games (or any combination of the three) I heartily recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favourite game of this year so far. I was honestly close to just quitting within the first few minutes, but once I got used to the concept the whole thing became weirdly addictive. I got drawn into the game's world and was excited to plan my trips, explore all the places, meet the people, solve the mysteries, find out about all the subplots... The first playthrough took me about 5 hours, and apparently the other ones weren't much shorter because there was always new content - and admittedly also because I've spent quite some time figuring out which cards to collect and to play and on retrying conversations... I'm almost done with my 5th playthrough, all of them lead me to a few new places, people and stories, and there are still some left to explore. The card thing does get a bit challenging, though the difficulty seems to vary depending on where you go, who you talk to, what mood they're in and maybe more. You'll be able to make decisions about which regions to explore and which NPCs to deal with. If you're not good at or invested in figuring out the mechanics, you'll have more conversations go badly and fewer options, but the least "successful" ending you can get (afaik) isn't terrible. You do get more out of the game if you plan and strategise for more exploration and storylines. Content-wise, there is (sometimes frustrating) conflict, there are tragic events (some topics dealt with: , , ), but there is also hope, and your actions can make a difference if you think strategically and literally play your cards right. The identity of your character is left very vague and the NPC cast is really diverse in a casual way ("even" including someone in a wheelchair), which I guess feels "political" to some people who are used to being represented just about everywhere. To me it's a very clear plus. Anyway, I'm glad that I chose to go on this journey. If you're still on the fence, there's a free  (actually the first part of the full game). * * * For more recommendations of chill and story-driven games, check out my curator .
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely charming game. It gives off a lot of the same vibes as 80 Days in that it's a game about exploring the world through text and there's this pressure to be economical with your time, but whereas 80 Days is this grand globetrotting adventure, SoS is this intimate little regional travelogue where you get to know the locals. In terms of writing it really manages nail sentimental without being overly sappy. The music and visuals are gorgeous. The world itself it wonderful to explore and the characters interesting to meet and get to know.The deckbuilding, dominos-esque conversation mechanic at its core is a frankly amazing representation of conversations. The basics are simple but there's just enough variation in symbols that need to be matched and special abilities that most conversations can feel weighty and meaningful. Even the somewhat annoying aspect of drawing a hand full of useless cards feels thematically appropriate.It also has a good and extremely helpful dog, so if nothing else you've got to hand it to the game for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of the itch.io Social Justice bundle, and then rebought it on Steam because I liked it so much. If that isn't enough of an endorsement, here goes:This is a beautiful game with a lot of replay value. I love the characters, and I always want to find out more about them. The constraints of the game mechanics mean you can't uncover everything in one playthrough, but every playthrough (except my first when I messed up big time!) feels whole and satisfying. Each one (4 so far) has had a different spin on the ending, and I think there are several I haven't uncovered yet.The music and the art style are as enchanting as the writing. When I play Signs of the Sojourner, I feel immersed in this world in a way a lot of games with bigger budgets can't match. On the cons, there are a few quality of life features that I feel are missing (an ending gallery would be great, as would a way to skip tutorials on subsequent playthroughs). Honestly, though that's not enough to keep me coming back to this game. Definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed my time with this game. Card-based conversation mechanic had a fair bit of strategy to it without being overcomplicated. A neat idea. I liked the narrative best of all though—it has an excellent mix of personality, levity, and gravity. Comes with good replayability as well, given that you likely won't resolve all characters' storylines in a single playthrough. Definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game in The Bundle for Racial Justice on Itch.io but then I fell in love with it and wanted to support the devs in addition to my donation so I bought on here too. Just wanted to start by clarifying my low play-time numbers. I did 2 complete loops on Itch and I can honestly say that this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. The way that the card system symbolizes conversation alone is great, but the deeper you get into the game, the more that it plays with your expectations for playing a game. I was trying to "win" every conversation, and I was struggling. I would return home from a long journey and my best friend could barely relate to me anymore because of my experiences with different groups of people. I was becoming a different person and I stopped to think, is this a good thing or am I losing touch with who I really am. Who do I want to be? Which of these varied cultures did I relate to and want to ingratiate myself with over the months/years to come? These concepts alone make for an incredible and unique gameplay experience. But then you add in the fact that the writing is excellent across the board, the music is amazing and varied, the visual style really adds to personalities of this great cast of characters and locales, and then you have a masterpiece. The high highs of having an awesome conversation with someone who i forged a relationship with over multiple trips to their town, paired with the low lows of not having the words to talk to someone you care deeply about are both incredible and emotional experiences that I am hard-pressed to find in games. Truly one of my favorite games of all-time and I can not recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: this game is utterly fantastic! the story, theme, art, and soundtrack all conspire to create this charming, wistful game that works in the tonal registers of cheerful and melancholic. it's gentle in a way that's perfect for right now, and it's also quietly science fictional in ways I won't spoil. highly, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This is legitimately one of the best card game based games I've played. The dynamics of how the cards work not only with each other but in the context of the story make this game as cohesive an experience as you can get from a game like this. I've played through the campaign twice now and got two very similar endings. It has very high replayability because every time you finish a game, you want to start again. It's like a rogue like without death. The failure state is mistakes you make during each of your five trips. Dialogue options toward the end of the game hint at things you could have done better and ways to improve. After two whole playthroughs there's still a lot to the mechanics of this game that I still haven't figured out and places I haven't gone. The art style is remarkable, I love the design of each and every character and it makes you want to spend a real day in these gorgeous towns. That coupled with a soundtrack that is comfy when it needs to be and intense when it calls for it makes the experience of playing this game unique and fulfillingI seriously can't recommend this enough. If you're sitting on whether or not to but it, do yourself a favor and spend some time with it. you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: The true sign of a good game is wanting to play again immediately after finishing.   I did and the went ahead and played a third time as well. And I still look forward to playing again.  Lots of replay value as you try to explore the nooks and crannies of the map.   Great Art, a unique card based communication model.  Lots to love here.  Characters you hate and characters you enjoy.Buy Signs of the Sojourner, you wont be disappointed in this truly unique game.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Chill deck-building game with a weird sort of freedom -- conversations generally end one of two ways, but the order in which you go to places and the times you visit people matter in a way that's really interesting. There's a clear suggested route to always take, but you can deviate (and that also affects how some characters think of you). The game's short enough that replaying to try to find a new combination of stories feels really possible, too, and I'm planning on doing that -- I wasn't able to visit some locations, even by the end of the game. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Phew, this is a tough game. Anyone who's left home knows the difficulty of fumbling through a conversation with someone after you've grown apart, but Signs of the Sojourner steps it up a notch: conversations are a card game, and you're going to lose some of them, no matter how hard you try. Should you stock up on new knowledge in far-away towns, or try to stay close to the home you've left behind?  I'm going to have to replay to see if I made the right choices. Honestly, losing card game after card game did get a little frustrating, but I figure that might be part of the point. I still recommend it, just...play it on a patient day.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: It's a unique take on how a story-based game should function. The card-building aspect of the game very well symbolizes the way humans evolve as a communicate with others, and how we sometimes can't vibe with everyone on the planet. The different abilities are also a clever substitution for the subtle ways human speech can be adapted on the fly and be interpreted in multiple ways as opposed to just linear conversations. The story and the lore is deep and requires multiple playthroughs to even start to connect the dots, increasing replay value. The art is beautifully done and the transitions are clean, even on a high refresh rate monitor. Well made for an indie game, especially a team of three.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing a little but of Signs of the Sojourner over the last couple days, and although I'm only two hours in I'm really liking it. The premise is that you're traveling to various towns talking with people to build relationships and gather the goods you need to stock the shelves of the shop you've found yourself in charge of after your mother's death.The gameplay consists of the conversations you have with the residents of these towns, which plays out as a card game. You'll have a hand of cards with symbols on their edges that you have to match with previously played cards as you and the other person alternate turns. It's basic to begin with, but as you venture further and further from your town you run into more and more people who speak entirely different languages (symbols) than you, which makes success more difficult. At the same time, engaging with these people is the only way you'll get better at speaking their language (win or lose, each conversation gives you the chance to get a card with the symbols they're conversant in) and the only way to learn about routes between different locations and events that are taking place. There's also a system where the more you travel, the more "fatigue" you acquire, which manifests itself as junk cards that you can only get rid of when you return home at the end of a trip. It's a really carefully thought out system, and one that maps well to the game's themes. The writing is pretty good too, funny but also melancholy at times as you try to reconcile your new life on the road with the friendships you're trying to maintain in your hometown.The only thing I'm not certain of is the longevity-- when the game starts you can only make five trips out of town, and I've only done three so fast. Still, for as well thought out as everything else has been so far, I'd be surprised if the developers dropped the ball in that regard. It's twenty dollars right now, but I think it's definitely worth it based on what I've seen so far.(edit, now that I've played for longer)I've run through the game twice now, and although I like it, I'm not quite as hot on it as I was originally. Despite uncovering information about my character's mother's backstory in the second playthrough, the ending was nearly identical. I feel like there's a "true" ending in here somewhere, but it's only after playing twice that I feel like I have a grasp on good strategies, and I'm not sure I feel like restarting and going through the opening sequence again. The other complaint I have is with the fatigue card mechanic. The longer you're out on the road, the more fatigue you acquire-- fatigue cards are automatically added to your deck every seven to ten in-game days, which results in your deck getting cluttered much more quickly and feels like it encourages you to cut your trip short. This ends up limiting how many alterations you can make to your deck, which consequently limits the areas that you feel that you can travel through successfully. It's a fun game, and I enjoyed the eight hours I've spent with it so far, but a few adjustments here and there would make it easier to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly moving!! The writing is phenomenal. I adore how the narrative is so intimately linked with the mechanics. It's tender and beautiful in all the right ways. It really sums up the difficulties I have with conversations and communication in a profound way. The art and music complements it perfectly and it's a lovely world to become immersed in. I adore the characters!!! Elias!! Tomas!! Alexis!!! (YAY non-binary rep) Klaus!!!!! and even XN-220!!!!!The beginning learning curve is gentle and it feels very natural to learn the systems, but like all good deck builders it's actually a very complex and difficult game to master. The narrative kept telling me that I need to not worry about doing everything or pleasing everyone but I didn't take it literally enough. It really means that! Strap in and expect several play throughs because you really can't do it all at once, it's impossible!
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: What a delightful game!! The artwork and soundtrack combine to create a whole afternoon of chill vibes. Gotta say a game about roadtripping around a satisfyingly barren landscape is the perfect quarantine game. The gameplay is more of a puzzle game than an actual card game, BUT it is addicting and sometimes you get screwed by RNG so you get the same feel of losing a hearthstone or M:TG match.All of the story lines are fun and positive and very well written. Sure there's some obvious elements that could be improved or expanded on, but it's an indie game on a shoe string budget and it will make you feel good about gaming. Also there are optimal loadout discussions to be had. Personally I  have a Chatter in my EDC, but I find the card that allows you to see your opponent's hand to be a trap card. Just learn how to do hand reading.TL;DR: yes you can pet the dog.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: The modelling of conversations works very well. There's something refreshing about how every encounter with another character has a conflict, but that conflict is like that of a cooperative game. Although some NPCs seem to try harder to achieve a concordant outcome than others, which is itself interesting (not sure if the case or just a feeling; effective either way)
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, finished my first campaign in about 4 hours, clicking through some of the dialogue. I restarted once on expedition 2 and got a different set of NPCs in the first couple locations, so there is definitely some replayability, so i gotta see what else i can uncover and how to visit the locations i haven't managed to reach. Fatigue mechanic can get a bit frustrating, especially when you come back home after an expedition and your buds want to talk to you when you still have a mostly blue/purple deck and 7 dead cards that burn not one, but 2 lives. Otherwise a very nice chill game you can play one-handed with no rush or focus.
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: In this narrative card game about relationships and communication, navigate conversations in a colorful world reminiscent of our own. Learn and grow through the cards you choose to play. Who will you become? What will you leave behind?
_childDocuments_.name: Signs of the Sojourner

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so awesome. It is in early access but there is a pretty good amount of content available currently. I am a huge rhythm game fan but this game is different enough that it feels really challenging and it's really satisfying once you get better and start to knock out some hard sections. Developers plan to add a ton of stuff too including an even harder difficulty! I think this is well on it's way to being one of the best rhythm games on the market.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: I loved DJ Hero 2 when i was a kid, or rather the concept of it, but it just wasn't much fun to play except for a couple of songs like Replay vs. Rude Boy or, well that was about it. But Spin Rhythm XD is nothing like DJ Hero 2... in the BEST WAY POSSIBLE.Only 7 hours in and this game is amazing! I love rhythm games, I've always wanted a type of game that can feel more connected to the entire song rather that just a part of it. I grew up with games like Rock Band and Guitar Hero so I know a thing or two about rhythm games that revolve around a particular part of the song. And as much as I love playing plastic guitar and my pro drums, this game's take on connectivity towards the songs is on a whole other level.This game feels amazing to play because the charters have the whole song to work with rather than just splitting a part of it. You feel so connected to the music when you play it. You're always in a flow state with the song, and the things you can do feel so smooth and fun. It may take a bit of time to learn the language of the game and build the muscle memory to hit the right buttons to do the job, but once you do its extremely rewarding. I only have just over 2 hours of song play time (7.6 hours is mostly being afk in menu and learning to chart songs for this game) and I can already do half of the Expert Songs in the game, although its probably a bit easier for me to learn since I already play a lot of other rhythm games so take that for what you will.Best of all, custom songs. Unfortunately this game is still 'relatively' new so its hard to find a bunch of custom songs, but if you do find songs that you like you get to play them! I've found a couple of custom sonic songs that are a lot of fun to play. Some of which insanely difficult for measly me with only 2 hours of experience :(, but its still cool that I can play them! (Yes, there's no fail and a practice mode)Oh one more thing, there's multiplayer but for what i can tell its only local multiplayer. However since this game is on steam I can almost feel that one day they'll be able to add online play. And also remote play exists so you can play multiplayer through steam remote play even with friends who don't have the game so that's pretty cool I'd say. Or at least I can assume, I've never done it before so take that for what you will.Summary: Game play is smooth, fun, expertly crafted and extremely interconnected towards the player and the song. 100/10 recommend this game for people who want that kind of experience. Even if you don't typically play rhythm games I think this one is worth the try. I can almost guarantee you will be in a trance-flow like state when you play. I know I do. [p. s. --  This game is half off by the time I'm making this review, but only for the next 6 hours, so if you want to consider it definitely try the demo for a bit. I personally believe its worth full price, if not more! Even though I did get it for half off.]- JrKirby

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing Rhythm game. I can't really stress enough how fun this game is, and how it feels to play to the music. The key word I think that describes this game best is flow. There is an incredible feeling as you move the wheel, hit notes, hit beats, and match the colors. I don't play very many Rhythm games, but SRXD has gotten me to take a closer look at the genre. It takes some gameplay mechanics from Vertically Scrolling Rhythm games, and makes them its own. As well as introducing entirely new sets of gameplay systems and mechanics, which I will try to explain below.The game has a fully customisable keybinds system, where you can bind basically any ingame action to whatever key and button you like. I play by moving the mouse to move the wheel, and having 2 keys for hitting tap notes. As for the gameplay you have a wheel in the center of the screen with 2 colors. You can move the mouse, use your keyboard, use a gamepad, or use a MIDI Wheel (yes it has full MIDI device support) to move the wheel. Throughout the different difficulties they introduce new game mechanics. Easy starts with just the fundamentals of moving the wheel, and understanding how it works. You match the notes to the indicated colors. There are also tap notes, where you match the note to the wheel color, and hit the Tap key to clear the note. There is also the spin mechanic, where you flick your desired input method (mouse in my case) to the direction indicated by the Spin Pad. Normal  adds sliders where you follow a path with the wheel to the best of your ability. Hard adds Beat Bars and Lift-offs. Beat bars are green notes that you clear by hitting the Beat key (space by default), and they are often on a kick drum or bass kick. Liftoffs are at the end of a slide note indicated by an arrow. Let go of the Tap key at the end of slider to clear the Liftoff. Expert is basically Hard but more difficult, introducing more complicated placements of Beat notes, and more complicated matching patterns. Finally there is XD difficulty. It's intended to be the farthest the game will be pushed difficulty-wise officially, and is meant to turn the game up to 11. It adds 1 new mechanic, the Beat Hold. It is like a hold note, but you hold the spacebar and release it at the end. XD is meant for players that have mastered the game, and it is not really recommended to start with it until you are acquainted with all the mechanics.The main mode is Arcade mode, where you play charts that were designed by the developers, in 5 different difficulties as I explained above. There are online leaderboards and friend leaderboards, so you can compare your score between your friends and other random SRXD players. Currently the game has 30 music tracks by many different artists, in many different genres. There are more planned in the future, and there is a level editor that is in Beta as I will explain further below.SpinFM is this game's implementation of Online Multiplayer, where you compete against other players for a high score on a track that the game's server rotates between. Currently there isn't a mechanism to choose upcoming tracks, but that is something that has been discussed as potentially coming in the future.The level editor lets you import any music track you want into SRXD, and chart it. The file has to be .ogg and you have to put it into a specific directory for the game to read it. Currently it seems you can do everything that the developers can with mapping a chart, and the limitations are just your understanding of the tool, and your imagination. I hope to see many different charts and mapping styles in the future from this amazing community, and I look forward to what the future holds for custom mapping. In order to share your tracks, you have to manually give them to other players. This is an unfortunate limitation to the game costing money, the developers can't give you a mechanism to share the music and charts without it being illegal. Currently you can export everything as a .Zip, and players can extract that to the game's data directory. If you join the SRXD Discord, lots of players are already sharing their progress.The game features an extensive options menu where you can customize everything to your liking. Currently there are only a few graphics options, but the game is fairly easy to run anyway, so I feel like what is there is adequate. As I stated before, there is an extensive keybinding system, where you can map basically any function to whatever you want, on any device you want. It's really quite impressive. There is a calibration tool, which allows you to change the delay on the notes to match your audio and video setup. I recommend running this as soon as you get  the game, to calibrate latency to your setup.Overall, this game is extremely fun to play. It looks like Guitar Hero mixed with something like Sound Voltex, but it's much more than that. It's hard to describe the feeling of the game unless you play it. It looks complicated from the outside, but once you actually play it, the game is very intuitive. That being said, if you want a challenge, once you understand the game's mechanics it can be pushed very far in difficulty, and it is. For $23 CDN, this is honestly one of the best games I've ever purchased on Steam. It's only going to get better, and it's already huge value for the money. The level of polish for an Early Access game, I have to say is unprecedented. The developers are very vocal and active in the SRXD Discord, and they try to check the forums often. If you have been considering the game but haven't pulled the trigger, do it. The level editor adds huge value, and they are adding new songs in patches on a nearly month-to-month basis. This game has an extremely bright future if enough players pull the trigger and decide to join the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Had this game for years through its early access period. It was good when I first played it, then it kept getting better and better with every update and right now it's the best it's ever been. And the best it's ever been is really really good. The controls are responsive and feel good, the song-list is really good, the latency calibration is best-in-class and the presentation is super-slick.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably my favorite rhythm game up to this point just because of how unique its mechanics are (and how based its music choices are). The difficulty curve from Easy to XD difficulty is very well done and progressing to higher difficulties feels incredibly rewarding. And if the 50+ songs in the game aren't enough for you, the myriad of custom levels have you covered. Also having a friends-only leaderboard for every song is great and a feature more games should have.I just wish they had kept the multiplayer mode from early access but hopefully something comparable will be added in the future. Also kinda wish Final Boss wasn't so hard to unlock but I'm like 10 levels past that now so whatever.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: It has an extremely intuitive feel; I love how you can use your own controller if its supported (which it generally is). This is the DJ Hero we DJs were looking for, and enthusiasts deserved. "an Homage" is an extremely humble understatement. Not only is it a great tracker with some extremely pleasant runs to ride. There seems to be a frustrating curve until one day. It clicks. Its a rewarding nostalgic feeling. Great set lists as it is straight out of the install.. but you can also program runs for responsibly curated songs. Very cool community who to this day are still very excited to be involved and extremely open to fresh faces and people to run grooves with. Im really happy to have found this experience. _childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Spin Rhythm XD has impressed me in less than an hour. There's already a lot of songs included, if they increase the library, it'll be well worth it for full price. It runs great on Linux, not one hitch, no delay, very snappy. I haven't tried online PvP yet, but getting my friends to buy games is always a hassle.The Steam Controller really shines with this. Flicking & rotating on the trackpad feels so responsive, intuitive, & most importantly: doesn't tire your thumb like classic controllers. _childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Spin Rhythm's uniquely analog design makes even lower levels of the difficulty curve feel satisfying. The tracklist mostly isn't styles of music I'd listen to on its own, but there's few real duds and it's well chosen to be rhythmically fun to play. Really can't recommend this enough for at least casual to intermediate rhythm game players.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: The game has plenty of ways for it to be played, either with the keyboard alone, mouse alone, a controller, an actual turntable, a mix of everything, etcetera etcetera.It has a hefty amount of different mechanics you have to time accordingly, so the game isn't entirely just "press button at correct time" like most other rhythm games. Because of that, it can be very difficult to ingrain into your muscle memory what your hands should be doing for what when it gets really hectic. And also because of that, I can only play comfortably on the game's "Hard" mode; above "Hard" there's "Expert" and "XD" mode, which mix up and combine the mechanics of the game to really ramp up the difficulty even further.In terms of its music, half of it has a bunch of dubstep, which I don't really like when they kick in, but they do make the gameplay fun.The game also uses the entirety of their songs, meaning they're not 60 or 120 seconds as per many usual rhythm game standards, so you have to be prepared to endure a few 5-minute tracks.It's very fun, and very difficult.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've ever actually bothered to do all the achievements for. It's like if Thumper and DJ Hero had a child and I cannot understate how much fun it is, and I've been playing since early access.The first dozen or so hours were spent rewriting my brain, but now I am hunting Perfect Full Combos on XD difficulty. I would definitely recommend you don't skip the tutorials for the mechanics introduced in each difficulty level, as you'll most likely not understand what the hell you are looking at for a while. You need to learn to decide how you're going to play a section so you don't run out of desk/arm/mousepad. The new addition of RemiXD difficulty has fixed a very minor gripe of some songs being ever so slightly undercharted, especially with beat notes. But the added difficulty adds that and more. However, the full release took away the daily challenge mode which I was actually trying to maintain my own little streak on - this is because not many people were actually using the feature, which is a fair comment. However I would like to see the Weekly Challenge make it's way into the full release at some point, as I'd like to try out the modifiers that were going to be in it. The loss of the SpinFM is not so bad, as I was mainly using it to randomly go through songs as a sort of queue - which is now solved with the What's Next randomiser - but it does remove the only multiplayer aspect, which should hopefully come back in another form at some point.The developer support for custom songs also means I can cry desperately trying to finish Crazy Frog in an insane difficulty. With full release and RemiXD difficulty now, I only expect the quality and quantity of custom charts to increase.Overall, I love Spin Rhythm, and will continue to hunt for those PFCs.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: The devs are really trying to make it better every patch. It's super tough and I needed to play a few sessions before I really started to be able to wrap my head around it. But it plays so smooth on my 144hz display and it looks and sounds so good. Once you get a feel for it, it becomes super natural and just incredibly satisfying. I feel like a lightweight mouse is an asset for this game. I also can only play in short bursts at a time because it requires such intense concentration, but that's not a knock as far as I'm concerned.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Typically do not write reviews. Fell in love with this as soon as i played the first track. I love the old similar music games like Amplitude and Frequency. If you like beat game please buy this. I like the new release compared to other games. The controls feel very natural. The music selection seem to be very nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: I've played my fair share of rhythm games over the years: Dance Dance Revolution, Stepmania, DJMAX, the various 'Hero and 'Bands -- Spin Rhythm XD is an absolute blast and may just be *the* best rhythm game within the dexterity (hands) subgenre.I mean holy hell, I was not expecting the game to be as razor sharp and adrenaline pumping as it is. The music is banging, visuals are engaging, mechanics are wholly original, fluid and precise, and the five difficulty modes are guaranteed to make you sweat. To top it all off, the game supports over a dozen various controllers including MIDI turntables.Spin Rhythm XD is flipping magical and absolutely worth grabbing at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:If you like Rhythm games, this is for you!Spin Rhythm brings a unique SPIN to the rhythm game genre. No turntable required. This works so well with Mouse & Keyboard it's mind blowing. You feel the beat and it's extremely challenging.Cons:I;d very much like to see a "reward system" in place here. It's just the menu, play songs, repeat. There COULD be more. Simply an XP system with in-game achievements. Complete x songs on x difficulty. Complete all songs.CONTROLLER SUPPORT: Would not suggest the game to users using a controller. The way the analog sticks shift your "record" is a snap-to method instead of free. DEVELOPER: PLEASE enable an option to toggle this. I'd love to sit back and use controller. The locking makes it too blocky. Possibly add a sensitivity for it was well so we can spin super fast with our sticks!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, of course I absolutely love rhythm games! When i saw the videos for this game I couldn't quite understand how the controls would work, with what I was seeing on screen but I decided to give it a go as its very reasonably priced.I am happy to say the controls work absolutely perfectly and are incredibly smooth. You can use a controller but i would say mouse and keyboard are better as it gives you a better range of control, and just feels better overall. You literally do feel like some sort of DJ spinning decks it's brilliant!The music tracks are excellent and you can even import your own music to create your own tracks which is fantastic!  Overall a fantastic rhythm game and I shouldn't have waited so long to press the buy button.Highly Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, for those who don’t have very good rhythm~This game is going to get you started on the right footOr the leftLet’s begin-Let’s begin with a simple rundownTo get you attunedTo the sound and feelOkayClick to the rhythm (cha cha!)Match to the rhythmSlide to the rhythm (to the rhythm!)Spin, and do it all over again!Sound and feel, Spin RhythmThe game with a simple rhythmSlide to the rhythmSpin, and do it all over again!Ok, I had to get that out of my system. Hah, this game is so fun, so fun. I want to play this game all damn night, man.So as above, Speen Rhythm XD is all about clicking, matching, sliding, and of course, spinning to the rhythm. What makes this game so great is just how amazingly slick the controls are, because this is probably some of the most fun I’ve had controlling a rhythm game. It takes a little getting used to, but once you are, this is seriously one of the best rhythm games out there.Also helps that the customs editor is pretty great (made my first rhythm game maps!) and that the soundtrack is full of right bangers.STEPTOTHE RHYTHM!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an awesome rhythm game experience in itself. The spin mechanics feel awesome, it's got great tracks and their map are great. The progression isn't that hard but can lead to some good challenges.If you're looking for an intersting game you can play with a mouse and your keyboard (but also other devices) this is a great choice for it's price
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a game you want to play with an actual jog wheel or trackball controller.  This is a fun rhythm game whose soundtrack and emphasis on analogue mechanics makes it stand out from the crowd.  I'm not sure it'll have the staying power of other controller-focused games due to it essentially being a two-button game, but at the asking price it's a good deal anyhow.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the best rhythm games I've ever played.Holding down long notes while moving side to side and tapping to the beat feels INCREDIBLE.Difficulty wise there's easy, normal, hard and expert. Each of them getting harder within reason.Then there's XD difficulty, which provides a nice challenge and once you're able to play the songs, it feels nice.Unfortunately there's no "official" custom song support, so you'd have to create your own custom songs, which is a chore with the current editor to say the least, or find them elsewhere. Also not  having a hotkey for selecting a random song feels weird, but might be implemented in future updates.100 % recommended for rhythm game enthusiasts.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: A GOOD GAME WITH UNIQUE CONTROLS! very fun to play!- i just wish there would be an track generator for costum tracks and not an editor you need to days for to finish one track for playing... why not a map generator that would make this game perfect.the ingame music isnt bad but just not my thing and im to stupid and lazy to sit down on and study how to get that editor to work..... still 10/10 and worth playing and YES I DO RECOMMEND!

_childDocuments_.review: Spin Rhythm XD took rhythm games to a whole new level. This game is beat saber but as a spinning wheel. Using the spinning wheel, you switch between 2 colors while matching the notes to the associating color. Each difficulty adds an element to levels each time which definitely makes the game challenging and lots of fun. The music selection is great, I've added a couple of songs to my Spotify playlist. I've had no issues with controls or bugs, the game runs perfectly. If you're an expert player at beat saber, it's easier to progress up in difficulties and start to become a pro at the wheel.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely solid game, the gameplay is without a doubt the most fun I've ever seen in a rhythm game and IMMEDIATELY had me hooked after the first couple levels! It does an incredible job of getting you into the groove, and is unlike anything else I've played. The gradual curve from easy to XD difficulty is great, and I'm a big fan of how mechanics are separated by difficulty - it means that with each difficulty, you have more to keep track of. And the soundtrack for this game is absolutely INCREDIBLE - it might just be my music tastespeaking, but seeing Camellia, some Rushdown color bass, Teminite, Douglas Holmquist, Lena Raine, Hyper Potions and more in here seals the deal for me. The customization options for the wheel that you unlock alongside the wealth of settings related to the HUD and accessibility and colors for the notes are perfect additions to round it all out into one complete package.Also, Jim Rhythm is such a good name for a mascot. Thank you for him. His existence is great.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing and unique rhythm game - the closest comparison I can think of is Sound Voltex. I'd still like to see more songs, but what songs are already there are all amazing fun to play, and so far I haven't gotten tired of any of them. There's an official discord and the devs are pretty active in chatting with the community and tackling any bugs or issues people have on there.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

My favorite franchise of all time is Guitar Hero and I play it every single day since I've discovered GH2).If you want a really cool and addicting game, this is great suggestion. You'll be thanking me tomorrow. I hope they keep updating this game, because I'm speechless how awesome this game is and how much I want them to get this game bigger!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Holy crap, I am so in love with this game.  Right from launch it has that classic arcade feel to it, and for an early access title it plays so damn smoothly.  I never had enough money to go and spend in arcades when I was younger and was always eagerly watching other kids play the DJ rhythm games, and now I can finally experience it from the comfort of my own living room!The track list is pretty meaty even in EA, with more on the way.  It's pretty modern EDM with quite a few notable artists and very much suits the style of the game. The fact that leaderboards are already implemented is both a good and a bad thing - great because it's a highly demanded feature in rhythm games that some are only getting years after release (looking at you, Groove Coaster Wai Wai), but kind of disappointing as a new adopter because I have no way in hell of catching up to the veterans.The controls on a controller feel REALLY good and I can't begin to imagine how satisfying it would be to play with an actual turntable controller.  Easy is not too much of a snooze but also doesn't drop you in the deep end when you're brand new.  The tutorials are swift and effective in conveying the mechanics.I'm really glad that the tracks each have all of the difficulty levels, so I don't feel like I'm missing out on half of the tracklist just because I'm not good enough to play on higher difficulties yet (*cough* DJMAX *cough*).  There's TONNES of accessibility options to customise it as you like and from what I can tell, there are no penalties on your score from lowering the speeds or making the visuals less explosive.I can't wait to see what else is to come, and already I'll happily whale for DLC track packs because this ♥♥♥♥♥ all over DJMAX and other similar games on Steam.  It's also a bargain, given how many features are included!  If you love rhythm games but need a break from the tappy tappy tappy, give this one a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Spin Rhythm XD is a music rhythm game with a very neat mouse control scheme.But I didn't enjoy the game much. To me the gameplay felt worse than e.g. Avicii Invector, Crypt of the Necrodancer, Beat Saber, or Bit.Trip Beat. Or even obstacle dodgers with a great soundtrack, like OlliOlli World. I don't quite know why that is, but contributing factors were that a) I didn't love any of the music, and b) I didn't really feel like I was playing the music.The game has a really generous track list, featuring 64 tracks à 2-5 min, or >4h altogether. But I didn't particularly enjoy most of them. I'm not familiar with the main music genres used in the game, but I did notice that many tracks have dissonant parts in the middle, or otherwise almost seem to change genre partway through, which I found aesthetically unappealing whenever it happened. There were several tracks I liked in the beginning, only for them to turn weird partway through. I completed all tracks on Hard, and ultimately there were barely any songs I found good enough that I'd be motivated to replay them.Other than that, I also didn't like the game's highscore system. There are many achievements, but when I got a Full Clear (beat a song without missing a note), that somehow didn't warrant one. Instead the game's achievements and leaderboards seem obsessed with "Perfect Full Clears" (i.e. missing no notes and hitting all notes with perfect timing), and that's the typical "counting down from perfect" attitude that makes many highscore games rather unappealing to me.Verdict: I recommend playing one of the aforementioned music rhythm games instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: super fun and the controls feel super nice to play with even just with a mouse and keyboard. _childDocuments_.review: So as far as to what I was looking for in a rhythm game this nails it and I am sorry I slept on it.It combines every I loved about Guitar Hero and DJ Hero into on cohesive experience and; IT'S HARD AS HELL!For my masochistic side I love playing this and for my chill creative side I have FUSER. You can look them up on Spotify too (there is a Spin Rhythm playlist somewhere) to see if you will enjoy them.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: The song list is quite small at the time of this review, but the current songs are pretty good and more are added over time. The gameplay mechanics are extremely solid and satisfying, with well-designed beatmaps and a wide range of control options. I've been looking forward to this game ever since I first saw it 2 years ago, and it does not disappoint! It's unlike any other rhythm game I've played and despite being in early access, it's already very polished. It could become my new favorite rhythm game!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game with some interesting mechanics. As a rhythm game veteran (I started with DDR back in the 90's) I'm really enjoying the new "spin" on the mechanics of this game. However, it isn't without its problems, which you'll need to know if you're thinking of playing this.Do I recommend the game? Well yes of course I do. It's a very fun game with a low barrier to entry and a decently high skill ceiling. It's amazing how much they seem to be able to squeeze out of the seemingly simple mechanics of just 2 buttons and the spinning.Should you buy it? If you have the money, yes, go for it, especially on sale. It's well worth it. The only thing I'd be aware of is the seemingly slow development especially when it comes to adding new songs. Like I mentioned earlier, the song selection is often what determines whether a rhythm game lives or dies, even more than the mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty much what I wanted out of DJ hero and I dare say beatmania also (don't hate me pls veteran rhythm game ppl)  I'm only geting into expert level right now, but when stuff starts clicking, it just feels so smooth.  I use an old Numark DJ controller, and would honestly only recommend this using a DJ controller personally.  I don't feel like Mouse does this game justice!  Super fun stuff, can't wait for the full version so I can plug my own music in and make crazy charts for 'em too!
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: This game did something that I wasn't sure I was going to see again. It re-invents the rhythm genre. Whilst your classic games we all played as kids (Guitar Hero, Rock Band, Donkey Konga etc.) are all about hitting each individual notes and not falling that half second off beat. Spin Rhythm takes a different approach.Whilst the beat is still important, and there is a couple of great mechanics to support it (especially on Hard difficulty and above), I feel as though Spin Rhythm is more about FLOW. From the micro-movements to catch all of the smaller notes, to the full spins there is an amazing sense of feeling the song, and moving with its builds and drops.It's almost hard to put into words how uniquely pleasurable the feeling of doing well in this game is.I would 100% recommend this game for both seasoned Rhythm gamers, and newcomers alike. Something gives me the feeling we'll all be starting from a similar page with this one.(Also, getting a 2Mello track for this game was a big draw for me as well. Whoever sourced that is a legend.)
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: This is a sublime rhythm game. Probably my favorite I've ever played, especially because I don't have to slap facebook goggles on my face to enjoy it. I wish I could pay for extra songs but these gosh darn devs give them away for free, how dare they.Update: Original review was written while at <1 hour, so, have my thoughts changed? Heck no. Game still bangs. Absolutely criminally underrated. I'll reiterate my desire to spend money on extra songs.Update 2: Devs let me pay for DLC. Thanks! Glad to see the game still chugging along.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: I pretty much never leave reviews but needed to as this game filled a void in my heart I didn't know existed.It's a simple game to play, but a hard one to master. It's a fantastic rhythm game, and the UX/UI is just as fantastic. The ability to create your own tracks is great, and if you're not great at making your own tracks you can download and import custom tracks that others have made - making the game as infinitely re-playable as you would like.A 10/10 I go to whenever I just want to relax or play more competitively - even though I suck. If it looks even mildly interesting to you: give it a go.EDIT: I realized I missed one of the more crucial elements about your decision to purchase the game - the music itself included in the game is great to play along to as well. Again though, you can make/download your own tracks as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Rhythm game echoing the awesome beats of DJ Hero but with its own spin on it. Supports a very surprising amount of control options including Actual DJ mixboards through midi, even OG DJ hero controllers! but if you don't have any of those laying around you could always go for the more traditional Mouse keyboard or your gamepad of choice. I myself tried out MKB and Gamepad both felt fantastic to use, though i found the gamepad(i use a PS4 one) a touch easier to use especially for the left right swipes which require you only to tap left and right with the analog stick instead swiping left and right with the mouse, its not a complaint per say as the mouse motion does feel more satisfying but for us more competitive types that try to go for the best score(or try to barely get through expert) there are definitely advantages to other control types, can't even imagine how many types of actual DJ controllers there are out there and i bet it would be real fun to use. Visuals are a very clear, clean and colorful spectacle of motion with quite a bit of variety of different visualizers that elevate the experience while playing, never too distracting though as to become a hindrance in gameplay, atleast from what i have seen so far. Soundtrack is absolutely fantastic though ofcourse limited a bit by being early access, 15 songs for now, 30 expected on full release. Also its mostly Electronic, chiptunes, dubstep  and other song genres fitting the DJ aesthetic which is understandable as its the most suitable music type for the controls. So if you are not a fan of this type, well this wont be for you.......... atleast until the custom music tools come out!All in all i think you get my point, if you have any sort of love for the rhythm genre (especially DJ hero) get this damn game and support these fellows for keeping the Rhythm genre alive because not a lot of people are doing it right now(aside from the whole of Japan, but exclusively to japan dangit!)Only 17.99€ to feel the  bless your soul.
_childDocuments_.name: Spin Rhythm XD

_childDocuments_.review: One short last review for the Rhythm Fest (I guess I definitely also have to at least write something about Spin Rhythm XD). Probably everything already has been said before, great innovative concept, the whole spinning feels really fresh, good difficulty selections with new elements, precise controls, regular updates yada yada yada. The game-play itself is pretty flawless in my opinion, can’t really make it any better, progression feels rewarding, many songs and variations to play. In this regard my review is completely superfluous. Anyway, one thing though to note, for my taste, music-wise over time the tracks were a bit too similar, mostly Dubstep/Electro mixes, and quality-wise the first quarter was phenomenal (even vocal tracks), but later most of the songs felt kind of shallow in comparison (not bad, yet kind of forgettable, at least for me). Maybe the DLCs are stronger, can’t say, and it’s definitely a matter of liking, but hmm, maybe you know what I mean. Still, hearing myself talk too negatively again, nahh, this isn’t meant that way, not at all. It’s just some old man rambling that the cherry on top of that super tasty cake faces the wrong direction, errr, or something like that. Just try out the demo, and if you like rhythm games I don’t think you’ll regret buying this one, because in its core it’s really really good, right on top of the genre.
