_childDocuments_.review: Short form: Langrisser I & II is fine. Not amazing, but good and in a genre this niche where most games range between tedious, meh, bad, and ok, fine is good. The commander/merc system is unlike any other SRPG I've played (at the start of each mission, you pay gold to give each commander a number of mercenaries) and it's actually quite efficient to allow the AI the move the mercs for you so even though the board fills up with units, you only have to move a couple. The gameplay is solid and deep enough to make things interesting.I have many criticisms (see the long form below), but all-in-all I think this is a worthwhile experience, though more so if one can pick it up on sale than at full price.Long form: I wouldn't blame anyone for assuming this is the first game they ever made. Chara-Ani, a company more known for anime figurines and merchandise is listed as the developer, though in-game credits suggest City Connection Co., Ltd., a company more known for its music label than games. Yet references to Langrisser are missing from their website  so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯The overall lack of features missing from this game that really aren't hard to implement and questionable decisions suggest poor quality control. For example, the lack of warning when you pass a turn without moving all your non-AI controlled units and the lack of damage prediction for spells despite implementing it for melee attacks. Also, you can't move a character and have them attack in the same motion. The credits only list two programmers so missing features in the engine are almost expected. What makes most of this forgivable is the strength of its source material.Langrisser I & II is a tactical RPG centered around the micro-decisions such as strategic placement, planning, and deciding who attacks what. While a good deal of planning happens outside combat, shopping for equipment and changing character classes which allows assigning different skills (pick 2), it's a minority of the gameplay and that's a nice change of pace for a genre moving more towards a Persona/Three Houses style of getting to know your soldiers and building relations. Fans of that style may find a little missing here, but the combat is deeper and requires more planning. In Fire Emblem, you just tried to keep your units from getting one-shot while one-shotting your opponents, but Langrisser demands you enact multi-turn plans and makes you watch in agony as your unit is surrounded and slowly killed.That said, even though maps are large and full of units, combat is fast. You can pretty much just move your commanders and let the AI move the mercenaries. In most TRPGs, this would be a tragic error, but it makes sense here, both because it values the player's time and because you generally want your mercs hugging your commander and that's what the AI does by default. When taking out enemy units, most enemy mercs fall in one or two hits, but just taking out the commander is faster. While this does lose you a bit of potential EXP, it can save your unit and commander's health pools and can at times be a necessary strategy based on the scenario. When this happens, all ther mercs attached to that commander also die so one might do it, at times, purely to create space on the board.Those who've played Langrisser Mobile will probably notice that combat animations are not what they should be. In the original, combat was simulated with units physically moving towards the enemy and striking each other. Ranged units always hit first, but melee units hit harder and it was easy to visually see this in how combat played out. The mobile game did much the same and animations were clean enough to see their cause and effect. In Langrisser I & II, units just sort of flail at each other and at some mysteriously-chosen time, the game might decide to take a portion of the enemy's health. After sufficient observation, I realized this happened when the attack animation finished rather than when it appeared to hit. This throws off the balance in a big way. For example, spears should always beat the generally more powerful horses, but since damage comes in much later the horse units have more time to attack spear wielders than they should.Though, the pacing of Langrisser I & II definitely is improved over the original. In the original game, even the first level was a long, grueling bout that can last about half an hour's investment [2], but matches in this remake never feel like they take too long.This is a bit par for the coarse in SRPGs, but Langrisser is not difficult. The developers added tips on how to approach each encounter, but one can honestly just power through and generally win without a unit dying. Part of the issue seems to be that the player acquires equipment that is too powerful and even though gold is a resource used to buy weapons and mercs, the player is never constrained enough on gold for this to matter. By the end of the game, my mercs would die easily, but my commanders couldn't be killed. In this sense, Langrisser falls into the same issues as Fire Emblem and similar SRPGs where stats can play a much larger role than strategy.To be fair, there's a sort of ascension system where you can run through the game multiple times and perhaps the real challenge starts there. You can choose to not import your XP and gold into the new run, though you also get achievements for completing the skill trees which encourages the player to do the opposite.While Langrisser I & II offers a plethora of content, in theory, this lack of challenge and encouragement to explore each branch in the story and the achievement for fully exploring the class tree ultimately caused my interest to wane.In terms of balance, magic users are incredibly OP, but have a major setback of not being able to move and cast spells on the same turn. This often makes them impractical as offensive weapons since they always arrive one or two turns late, but they make for a very good defense, setting up a strong wall while enemies close in before unleashing strong AOE. This is something I'd like to see tried in other games.The story of Langrisser isn't too much of a selling point and no single path down exemplifies terrific writing, however taken as a whole it does offer a slightly more philosophical angle than what players might expect. For example, one path of Langrisser I takes the hero through a journey where he sets a goal to fight in order to end all wars while another has him aim to end inequality (but still allowing for war). Through their juxtaposition, we can see these ideals to their logical conclusions. The last thing I want to touch on is the music because it's a big deal. The original megadrive sound track is doesn't seem that amazing at first glance, but hearing the soundtrack as arranged for the mobile game reveals these songs are actually great. It is mind boggling, then, why they chose to rearrange all these songs once again, but such that each song is boring and lacking in energy. Compare "Thought Of The Holy" in the remake  vs the mobile OST . The use similar instrumentation and many listeners may even think they are identical, but audiophiles should be able to hear how the remake uses more muted orchestral sounds, less chords and arpeggios, less notes in general. The original is jammin', too .Despite all the missed potential in Langrisser I & II, it still offers a good experience and I look forward to seeing it to the end.[2]

_childDocuments_.review: I played langrisser I back in the day which I why I bought this. I've noticed some things that are different from what I remember. _childDocuments_.review: I played Der Langrisser (Snes) many times in the past and I never expected that we would have a remake of it and of the first game.Overall, it's a very good surprise and a great remake.It's such a pleasure to hear the memorable OST of the game once again.This is quite a unique tactical RPG with it's mercenary system. Each "hero" can recruit several troops at the start of the battle and depending on the type of mercenary it can be more or less efficient depending on who they fight (spearmen counter cavalry, etc...). Each hero also has a set of classes they can choose from with unique skills and spells to deal damage, support their troops, heal or even summon unique units. Overall, the whole gameplay system is brilliant and fun.As a JRPG if you focus the "main" story, it will feel mostly generic similar to stories from Fire Emblem games and most RPGs. However, what's great with Langrisser is that it has a unique story system with a lot of possible routes and endings. It's based on actions performed (or not) by the player during some missions. It means that the story can drastically deviate from the "good" one and you could choose a route that is more evil, neutral, special, etc... Regarding the characters and the overall stories and lines during battles, they are much more developped in Langrisser 2 than Langrisser 1.Some issues with the remake is that it probably lacks some tutorials and the onboarding for both games could have been improved. Some information are also missing from the UI like the magic resistance of mercenaries for example. It's also a shame in my opinion that they didn't remove/reduce negative stats from some skills and items. It heavily limits the choice and make some skills/items useless.If you like tactical RPGs, it's worth trying (I think there is a demo on Switch). Now I hope that they will release a new Langrisser 3 with a very different story. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game series with some modernization improvements and issues.I played Langrisser I on Sega Genesis in its original US version, Warsong, roughly 30 years ago. It is one of my favorite games of all time. Even playing through this iteration, I’d call all of their characters by the Warsong version names: Garrett, Mina, Sabra, Thorne, Baldarov, Calais, Tiberon, Carleon, and Lance. This was nothing like anything else in video game history at the time: a turn-based tactical war RPG where you recruited your soldiers and found and equipped powerful items to fit your playstyle. There was a ton of strategy, from which units were strong and weak against others, positioning your soldiers next to your commander to heal them every round, and even the commander treating for their turn to heal themselves. I would often cling to mountain ranges and castle walls to get the added defensive prowess and maximize my experience points by killing every soldier. It was difficult, there was permadeath, and you had to strategize which soldiers to bring because you had limited funds and could only pick one type of unit per group.I can’t tell you how much I loved everything about the original Warsong. The character sprites were amazing and, other than a few of your last commanders all being knight masters or magic knights, unique. The promotions were meaningful and powerful. I was addicted to leveling my characters and optimizing my army for the next battle. The story weaved itself throughout the game, with the characters talking before, during, and after the battles. The characters were developed with backstories and personalities that showed up in their dialogue and their professions. And the fact that you could literally choose your own promotion paths was amazing. I ended up going Grand Knight for Garrett because it was the only one of its type in the game, looked so cool, and had higher attack than the King. After all these years, I remember getting to buy the only copy of the game I could find at the rental store and then beating the game after the last level was super-punishing where your soldiers were borderline useless and you needed your strongest commanders and tactics to win.Fast forward to playing this modern remake of the game and its sequel in 2023. I made sure to get all of the achievements and play through all endings before giving this review, and there’s way too much to cover in the short space here…but I’ll try, anyway. Let’s start with what is awesome about this game: there are more branching pathways than ever (the first game only had one path), there are many different unit types, items, and promotion paths, and there are so many different scenarios and storylines going on. You definitely won’t be bored through the first run, as every 10 minutes or so a new plot point or change to the battle conditions pops up. It is quite a fun ride, and it’s also one that you can track because the game provides an amazing graphical interface of all of your promotion paths and storyline progress, even allowing you to backtrack and change your path without having to replay the entire game to do so.The negatives are that the graphics were updated to what most people call “mobile quality” because mobile games use them. If you combine that graphic design decision with the overwhelming amount of reuse happening across the two games (items, levels, character designs, enemies, storylines, promotion paths, and plot twists are used repeatedly—and I mean repeatedly), it feels like this must have had some budget or schedule constraints. For example, my favorite part about Warsong was that all but 2-3 characters had their own unique character sprites for their promotions, and every promotion felt like a significant upgrade to the character. In this one, they literally take the same base character sprite (you can tell because when you flip between soldiers, their faces are all the same) and maybe, if we’re lucky, change the weapon or armor a little bit. In many instances, a higher level looks identical to the previous level, and that really ruined a lot of the fun of getting the upgrade. I was torn on the “anyone can become anything” aspect where most characters had 4 or so paths, but it wasn’t a big deal since I usually picked the path where there was a level 5 version of it (only some have that). Because of this overlap and reuse, Langrisser II—which I played for the first time in this version—felt more like an encore of Langrisser I, which is both good and bad because it was essentially the same game but through a hundreds-of-years-later lens with callbacks. Ledin (Garrett) is now Elwin, Taylor (Tiberon) is now Lester, etc. You get roughly the same items at the same time in both games, and the paths are nearly identical for the characters. I will say, however, that I quite enjoyed playing both games in parallel since they had the same structure, kind of like the “Machete order” of Star Wars, where I played II and then played I and it felt like I was making my own movie with flashbacks. It was pretty awesome.Because there’s so much to say and so little space, I’ll conclude with as many interesting thoughts that I can get through here. I played every version, and I’d recommend that no one do that unless you want 100% achievements because branches at the end for a few of the endings are near-identical. For example, one path you’ll fight Chaos, and in another you won’t because you’ll have stopped him from getting summoned. Again, I loved the choices-have-consequences element, but it made playing all the paths a chore for the achievements because nothing else happened. So just play it once if you want to keep the magic alive. Also, every major path split (known as “light”, “empire”, “independent”, etc. among gamers but not in the game itself) was completely different and amazing to experience. I felt like I was playing an entirely different iteration of the game—like a DLC—sometimes, the difference was that stark. It was heartbreaking to go through an opposing path and fight the people I fought alongside in the previous run, and that was brutal. The slow descent into madness (through your lens, it was simply wanting to restore order and end war) was fascinating, and the dark path where you basically align with the dark lord was cool because you fall into it under the guise of human-demon peace. Yes, there were occasional bizarre plot contrivance moments like when Aaron just decides to retire so you don’t have more than eight characters if you allow Lana to join, but otherwise every path was pretty solid. I wish there were some better triggers for the paths, however, as while playing optimally for Experience gets you path A as it should, some conditions (like joining Lance/Leon for the empire path) are disconnected so that it feels like the player did not really choose an option that took them down that path. Like letting certain enemies escape or grabbing Langrisser under certain conditions not tied to the path were not as much of a conscious player choice as to what they were doing but rather sometimes luck or based on the first-time-run-through battle plan.Overall, I liked the game but would prefer it if I had the OG graphics options completely (including character sprites) but with the new items, story paths, and quality-of-life improvements like the graphical visuals of the promotions and storylines. I loved the classic art style for the characters (which I used) and the classic music (which I also used—it’s an amazing soundtrack), but I didn’t like the classic map art, as it wasn’t from the Genesis version of the game and so I didn’t care for it. I, of course, turned off the battle animations. 90% of the stories and paths were excellent, with only minor WTF moments like Betty being Lance’s sister and you both turn into lunatics. I still like the original Warsong better, but playing the various paths was an amazing experience that’s not in the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played Langrisser 1 and 2 for Mega Driver, Der Langrisser for Snes and Langrisser 4 for Playstation 1, this was a natural buy.I confess I was a bit skeptical because of the sheer amount of bad reviews but thank god I had the courage to buy it. _childDocuments_.review: I have played through the first couple of missions and so far I like it well enough. The game is very user friendly and the option to freely move through the scenarios and classes is a nice forgiving feature. The issues I do have with the game are that the  combat strays too far from the original content for my tastes in a numerical sense.  The main grievance I have with the game is that the combat numbers are bloated. Originally everyone had 10 HP. Now the numbers go into the hundreds for a very bloated feel.  I do not personally like this change however I feel that the change may appeal to a much more broad audience. I have only played Langrisser I so far and perhaps once I play Langrisser II my feelings might change as i was much more of a Der Langrisser fan. Rating 8/10 bit pricey for a remake/remaster but it feels like new game entirely so perhaps its justified.

_childDocuments_.review: There's permadeath in this game, but it's kind of subtle about it.  Characters will "have mortal wounds" and be "too injured" at the game's end, and you won't know about it until it's too late.So pretend you're playing Fire Emblem Classic Mode and you'll probably be fine. _childDocuments_.review: Langrisser 1 RemakeTurn based strategy game where your commander units are like normal characters in games like this but each one can spend gold to hire units of soldiers before battles start, with the options available to them and the quantity available depending on their class and promotions. Hired units will be much weaker if they leave the command range of their leader and if they are adjacent to their commander they will heal some of their health at the start of each turn. Hired soldier kills will give their commander experience and if your commander or an enemy commander is killed all of their hired soldiers are lost with them. It's one of the better games on the Genesis and the sequel's Super Nintendo upgrade Der Langrisser is one of the best games on the SNES.This version adds new branching paths with multiple endings and new stages to the original Genesis title. New CGs and added JP voice acting (not translated though when out of plot scenes). You can use old character and map art and music (except for combat animation), new art is hit and miss depending on the character but the new style is pretty generic. Hero characters now fight with whatever kind soldiers instead of awkwardly by themselves. New opening questions like in the sequel give equip/skills but effect little as they are mostly just going to give you equipment and skills that are soon to be replaced anyway. Missions can have some objective changes, usually being easier as the first map has an easy escape and time limits are removed. New health system is less intuitive, in the old game everyone just had 10 health with each representing a soldier in the unit. Too easy to level/promote, and you can go back to past areas in the story to follow branching paths with your levels kept. The battle animations are much worse, even in the old Genesis version it would show the soldiers meeting in combat where melee units could be killed by archers before reaching them leaving bodies on the ground, the terrain of each side effected the look of the fight where units would have to charge up or downhill if you had elevated positions, this follows more of an Advance Wars style where all units just stand on a side of the screen and attack at nothing towards the middle of the map while damage numbers show up. Maps look like a bad mobile and no longer have as many terrain differences. About halfway through the first playthrough it becomes so easy that you don't even need hired soldiers to easily win, defeating the main mechanic of the series. They also removed the treat command which was used for commanders to slightly heal themselves (and in some entries recover some MP) and replaced it by having everyone fully heal when they level up, making the game even easier and magic overpowered.The new branching paths are mostly terrible (now that I've played Langrisser 2 I see that some of the branching maps are just random copies of maps from Langrisser 2 with different enemy placement). There was never much story to begin with in the first entry outside of a very simple retaking of your shortly inconvenienced Kingdom followed by holy sword defeats chaos god plot, and the paths add mostly nonsensical story turns where you will often end up playing on similar or the same maps as before fighting very short battles. There are five paths with each having two variations. To get a branching path you reach mission 11 of the 20 and then can start doing or not doing things that can put you on another path, a few missions after that it can split again. The two alternate options on each of the five paths could change very little, on one actually effecting nothing but a few random lines of dialogue.Screenshots: Langrisser 2 RemakeLangrisser 2 holds up better than the first but that isn't at all thanks to anything the remake does and is just from it being a better game. The story path splits are a bit more logical and can come from a wider variety of actions, there are more characters that get a bit more backstory, there are more characters to use on route splits, 75% of the playable cast doesn't primarily promote to the same horse mounted unit.It did feel much more balanced throughout where I never would have had an easy time never even hiring soldiers once I reached the midpoint of the game (though just nuking everything with the Meteor spell about 3/4 of the way through causing the mage to level up and regain their full MP so I can do it again was still massively overpowered).Neither game is ever really bad but there's no reason not to just play the original on the Genesis/Mega Drive and the sequel on the SNES (or both of them on the Saturn if you read Japanese). The new additions to the main game aren't good and make an already poor story even worse if the paths are followed, battle graphics don't hold up in terms of how they visually play out, the new art isn't awful but looks like a by the numbers mobile title, it's all less balanced, and the price of the game is higher than it should be.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: This is currently a review of only Langrisser 1, as I haven't played the second game yet.This is a very basic remake of the original game. It comes with new character and battle art, and interface modernisation. That is pretty much it, I think. You can choose if you want to use the new or the old art, and you can separately choose if you want new or old battle sprites. I personally liked the old artwork more for the sprites, but found the new battle art cleaner to look at.The story is... very uneven. First of all, bulk of the info is hidden under summary button in the map screen. I didn't realise it until about 16th or 17th mission, so I often didn't quite know the context for what is happening. The game is 20 missions long. Furthermore there are 8 routes you can take, and some of them are rather well written, while others are pretty much "what if" scenarios with huuuge leaps from mission to mission in both war and character development. You might be best buddies with someone in one mission, and next mission they are the enemy boss.This game has a concept of leader units, which are surrounded by regular soldiers. Each soldier can be controlled separately, but if they move out of the leader influence they will be pretty much useless. If you only move the leader the rooks will follow him automatically at the end of your turn (unless you moved them manually). This seems fine, but the path finding in this game is AWFUL. It doesn't help that the maps are designed in a way that specifically break the pathfinding. So even though in theory you can leave rooks on their own they will only mess up most of the time. Instead of moving trough the corner they will go back, because the shortest way to the leader goes trough the wall. The wall the unit will not be able to pass trough. The rooks will also automatically attack enemies if you let them, but only if they can do so by staying in the leader influence zone. That works pretty fine usually, but sometimes they will just suicide without doing any damage to enemies.Many areas also have very thin corridors that lead to the main battle. The AI is also very bad at passing those. Usually you can just forget about any of them passing trough there and are left with just the leaders. There are some ways to fix it, for example by using teleport spell(later on, when you unlock it), but overall it's pretty bad.That said, the game is very easy, at least on normal difficulty. You can also start with some starting gold to make the initial missions easier. I took the gold, but I actually never found the reason to use it.Remember the story was written in 1991, and is presented here basically with no changes. The cutscenes between missions are only few sentences long, and they don't really build much of tension or emotional punch. People just die off(all the time), and sometimes they don't. Now, the thing is, the game has some very strange design decisions. The first mission where you can change your "route" in story progression is 11th one. So first 10 will always be the same. Once you beat the game on your route you can make a final save and then start from 1st mission. But you also have an ability to jump to missions you already did on progression tree. It makes much more sense to save before mission 20, beat it, load the save, and jump to the mission where you can make a decision, instead of replaying first 10 stages. When you jump back you actually close out access to the future missions, and they change back to "?????" on the tree. I don't see a reason why they did it. Allow the players to jump freely to any mission they already unlocked!The other thing is, there are 8 routes, but in reality there are 4. Each of the 4 main routes has one more split that does nearly nothing. At most it changes 1-2 sentences in the following events. But it means you have much more missions to replay if you want to see it all. And really not all of the routes are worth reading trough. Once you beat the game few times everything is so easy you can just AFK half of the time, while the CPU is moving your and their troops.  Unfortunately first time given general is moving they have to comment about it, first time each combination of commanders are in combat they comment on it... it adds to character development on your first run, but in future runs it's just tiresome, and makes AFK harder to do.That said despite all the problems the game was quite enjoyable. It had strong moments. It plays very fast, and you can make it even faster by focusing on generals (killing a general kills all his subordinates too). Later on you get overpowered spells and summons which wipe out half of the enemies in one hit. The characters are enjoyable. But I wish there was actual romancing or something. RIght now who your main character ends up with depends purely on the route you finished, and there's really no reason why he ends up with different woman in each of them. Except for the Betty route. I suggest completing only 1 route and moving on. Ideally one of A-D routes, as they feel most canon.

_childDocuments_.review: Langrisser I & II are originally from the early 90s, so one shouldn't really expect very in-depth gameplay mechanics. I preferred the original sprites with the remastered soundtrack in my playthrough. Voice acting is great with renowned voice actors and the sequel is slightly the better game of two. One thing the games suffer from is how repetitive they are with more than 15 different routes and endings, and how most of them really add to or change the outcome of the story. If you are a completionist like me, be ready to spend more than 80 hours.Rating: B

_childDocuments_.review: Lifelong Langrisser fan here. This game is a must-have for any Langrisser or SRPG fan. Shows a lot of promise as it breathes life into a nearly-dead franchise; is easily the best Langrisser game of the past 20 years and I want nothing more than for this game to succeed and pave the way forward for more Langrisser remakes in a similar style. Of course, this game isn't perfect, and is a bit rough around the edges at some points with its SLIGHTLY clunky controls, some QoL changes, and lackluster graphics when it comes to the sprites. So for future remakes, I think there's certainly room for improvement.If Langrisser 3 is ever remade, I think I can die a happy man. There's still so much to be done with this franchise. I'd be ecstatic to see it rise from the ashes and come back bigger and better than ever before. For anyone unfamiliar to Langrisser, this is a superb place to start, and the money you spend on it will directly support efforts to take the franchise to even greater heights.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I'm a keyboard and mouse user, this game doesn't natively support that, so I got upset and would not recommend it to other people like me who are tired of lame porting companies pulling this sort of idiotic move.If you are a controller user, it might be a good buy. The strategy part of it is solid. What little story I saw was completely forgettable. Maybe if I'd sunk 10 hours into it I would have gotten to anything interesting, but I didn't, so there.I will say that if Steam rejects my refund request, I wont be too upset. I'm sure I'll go through and play it eventually... and try to get used to the crappy controls.and if I see it on sale for the Switch, I'll probably end up buying it. :XReview:Saw someone stream this on twitch a couple days before launch, thought it was neat, wishlisted it. Bought it the day it came out. Installed. Fired it up. And... it doesn't respond to a mouse??? Odd... arrow keys work. Okay! Does not respond to the enter key... wtf? WASD does nothing. Oh... great. Kill it with taskmaster. Go to forums. Official pinned developer post saying that mouse is not supported, official keyboard buttons are like... zxcv. Other posts are saying that there is spotty support of controllers, but that controllers are the intended way to play it. I relaunch the game and plug in my windows-xbox-ish controller and it works! I play for an hour or so before heading off to bed.Next day I play it again and... the controller buttons are now reversed, the menu button is no longer the menu button (never did find where it went to...). The button I used yesterday to assign things is now the cancel button and vice versa. I get back into a battle and discover that the little up and down arrows on my controller no longer do anything, while the left and right buttons are now the up and down buttons. Great! Great. I beat a map, then I shut it down and submit my first ever refund request. I've been on Steam since the Orange Box, own too many games, including a few I should definitely have refunded because they are crap, but this... this is stupid. It's 2020. The developers did an honest to god good job of remastering their old game with new art. They had to have paid multiple people thousands of dollars to work on this port, but they cant invest in standard issue windows control schemes? Is this one of those weird Japanese society issues where they just expect customers to 'deal with it' to save a few dollars? Because I'm sick and tired of crappy control schemes and if I don't have to put up with it, I'm not going to. Get over yourselves developers, and give us good control schemes from the start. Windows gaming on keyboards has been a thing for like 2 and a half decades! It's not new or hard.end of rantGood:Tactical gameplay is interestingI liked that the little battles between individual units have little hordes of dudes attacking other little hordes of dudes. Its fun to watch.You can go after elite units and knock them out to wipe out whole groups of enemies, which leads to options for strategy and weighing the chance to grind a little extra xp vs knocking out a bunch of enemies at once (note: unsure if killing the elite is worth the same, more, or less xp as compared to killing the whole group of enemies). There is also a couple of loot spots hidden on the battlefields. You can get them, but usually only if you play everything right and you set out to do it from the get go. The first time I hit the second map, I didn't plan it quite right, and accidentally lost the fight because I moved my hero unit out of the way in order to stretch the battle one more round so that a different unit could grab a piece of loot. This let the enemy into a vulnerable building where they were able to kill off some poor innocent villagers, causing me to lose the battle. Turns out self-sabotaging to get phat loot has consequences! Neat!The mediocre:I only played 3 missions, but the story I saw was super generic and pretty bland. Didnt give me high hopes for the rest of the game's story. But it wasn't any worse than, say, Disgaea 5's story, or something you'd see on like the Disney channel. And we're here for strategy and murdering things, which it does well at, so I wouldnt keep this from selling the game on you, if I were you.The bad:Control scheme. If you are a keyboard and mouse player, just skip it, unless you have somehow adapted to use the zxcv keys (how? why?), then go for it. The developers say they dont have any plans for supporting the mouse. This is stupid. See rant above. See the threads on the discussion form.Alternatively, if you are dieing to play it and patient, there are forum threads for working around it and using exotic configuration software to finagle things. But I do not have that patience.If you are a controller user, and you have patience, by all means, go for it.The AI. In the aforementioned 2nd mission, you are supposed to try to save villagers in a village from rampaging bandits. Well half of these villagers run straight to the bandits. Straight to them. Didn't even try to not die! The enemy also exposed their elite units to me multiple times, even when weakened, making it easy for me to wipe out whole groups without having to work terribly hard for it. So if you want your enemy units to be smarter, well, I don't think that's going to happen.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent remake. Runs great, top-notch presentation, superior to Fire Emblem in every way.The ability to deploy generic units without fear of having anyone die permanently opens up a barrel of tactical options and approaches. Levelling up is even and there are no "empty levels" or Random Number God curses. Class changing is clear, intuitive, and meaningful far beyond "ooh, extra stats."And the branching story is amazingly well-written. This game is a gem.

_childDocuments_.review: While the story is pretty straightforward and you have to find out on your own how to play the game effectively, I still consider this a great tactical RPG. The Commander & Mercenaries mechanic gives a spin to the otherwise simple gameplay these types of game have, deciding whether you want to attack with your commander or support your units with magic is a tough decision sometimes.The AI is not completely stupid like in most other tRPG's, they usually don't attack if they would die and almost never respond to a single unit stepping into their threat area.I place the quality of this game right beside the Fire Emblem saga.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolutely my style of game, so obviously I love it. The mercenary mechanic really sets this apart from other strategy games of this type.Critique, like many classic games the AI lacking. The difficulty (no setting by the way) can be greatly reduced by taking advantage of silly things enemies do. Try to fight fair!I love switching back and forth between the classic and remake art/music. Tiny critique, this is done through settings, where as I've played other games that let you do this with one button press.

_childDocuments_.review: An OK remake for casual players, but too plain for veteran players, and certainly doesn't worth the price tag (I picked up at 50% off, after playing it I think it worth 10 at most).Pros: Arts (yes I like both old and new), music, simple and intuitive tact game play. The story tree is really a good thing that saves time.Cons: Gameplay is too easy and no depth. Plots and characters are too plain. Those two really kills the game for me.There are many steam games that are far superior. Gameplay-wise, I would go for XCOM 2 and Battle Brother. Plots and character-wise, Persona 4 and Utaware are far better.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: It's very cool that this exists; the Langrisser series (especially 2) is a textbook example of a hidden gem, similar to Growlanser which had the same original developers. But this remake is, unfortunately, not 1 to 1 to the original... some of the subtleties of the combat system have been lost in translation. The aesthetic also veers a little too close to 'mobile game', though I think the new character art looks okay, and you can switch to the classic (and I mean 'vintage anime' classic) character art at any time. The music (which is frankly fantastic) also gets the same treatment, with pretty good remastered tracks and the option to use the original Mega Drive versions.I don't love this remake as much as the originals, but I want to support the series in the hopes of seeing more of it. (And Growlanser, maybe? ... ... Growlanser 2+3 remake when?)
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Warsong on the Sega Genesis, I was excited to play Langrisser I and II (Warsong = US version of Langrisser). However, the difficulty of this game and the overall game play are much weaker than the older/original versions of Langrisser games. The unit balance is bugged on many of the missions, making them a cakewalk on even the hardest difficulties. The different gear and hero upgrades are effectively meaningless stat buffs that have no measurable impact on battles. While the story branches make it easy to roll back to prior paths as you play through, given the busted battle mechanics and lack of meaningful character progression, repeating similar fights and side paths to see the alternative storylines turns into a chore. Overall not worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: Just a piece of my thoughts.I've played the original version of the game, mobile version and also been into quite some chapters in this remake.For those diving into this game as their first, it is a decent turn base tactics game, though not much of a challenge thanks to the back tracing of story line so that you could grind. (You can go for the challenge after completing a clear save game)While comparing to the original version of the game, the changes in commander stat especially HP (original use to have max 10 HP for all commander, mercenaries includes) and also the fact that commander now cannot rest to heal up their HP&MP during the skirmish put importance into your use of MERCENARIES.Mercenaries use to be like a useless lackey or just fodder for your commander to last hitting most enemies in the original but this remake changes this. It is now equally important.Now about the unable to regain MP which I myself had complaint about when i venture into this remake turns out to be a good mechanic.Overall MP pool is increased in the remake but the cost of spell mp requirement remains fairly low. This introduce a new element of carefully handling your MP but still you don't have to be too careful (i've tested by using a skill each turn since turn 1 and MP pool lasted until the end of skirmish.) Personal advice : use spell when it matters, you won't ran out of MP unless you played your strategy wrongly.Original battle effect is better. Remake version of 2 troops fighting each other is like they're hitting at air. This sucks.side note : AGI affect miss rate, DEX affect critical rate.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally I don't like it. I recommend trying out the demo tho if it might be for you, as I can see other SRPG fans liking it.Think of Fire Emblem but you get to controll mob unit alongside your heroes, that sounds good at first as the battles become bigger, but at the same time battles also get slowed down by the unit blobbing. Additionally the game has many endings 8 in the first one and 13 in the 2nd.  Which is cool, HOWEVER the way that the timeline jumping is implemented is questionable, instead of just making maps playable to from wherever you are in the story once you have beaten them the game sends you back (tho your stats and items carry over) and locks the missions after the map you selected leading to you having to replay all of them up to the point you want to reach later on.Now that wouldn't be so bad if you got a guide to what switches you need as especially in the 2nd game you might need to jump back to mission 2 of the game multiple times if you made a mistake or want to see all endings.

_childDocuments_.review: The old Sega Genesis/Mega Drive versions are still the "best" (speaking from nostalgia), but this is very good, IMO. Being able to play with the classic BGM and original artwork is killer. The reworking of game 1 using game 2's options for troops/mercenaries and shop for items (which you can equip 3--weapon, armor and accessory) is pretty neat, too. I haven't played Langrisser II in quite some time, so I don't know if the class progression tree is new or revamped from that game. In any event, being able to effectively choose _all_ of the classes (after earning enough CP to "purchase" them) is interesting and also attainable since you can replay completed maps (with caveats; game progress is reset to the selected map--all XP, gold and items are kept, but game progress is lost. Also, any items already claimed later in the game cannot be acquired again, so no exploiting treasure and gifts). Pro Tip: if you're interested in the game, play the Demo first. If you do, there's the option to receive bonuses at the start of the full version. A nice touch that reminds me of the demo days of old.I have the full set of Langrisser, I - V, Japanese. My Japanese isn't what it was 15 years ago, so it's great to see these games translated and released is the West. NIS America is also a great company, as they've published/developed the Disgaea series, La Pucelle: Tactics, Labyrinth of Refrain and others I should probably look into. But, I digress. It would be amazing if NIS translated and released updated PC versions of Langrisser III - V. If they had physical versions of these games I'd definitely get them to put next to my Sega Saturn versions.(Now, if someone could just do Phantasy Star I - IV to the tune of Generation 1...)

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable, simple, and straightforward tactics game!The battle system is very simple. You have a few Commander units and every Commander can deploy some Mercenary units. The Mercenary units are kinda weak, but they're disposable and useful to whittle down enemy ranks. Choosing when to attack using a Mercenary unit and when to strike using a Commander unit is really fun.Commanders can change class, and unlocking new classes will grant you new spells and skills that you can use in any class. There is no exploration, but you can replay story missions if you need to grind. The difficulty is quite easy though, so you probably won't need to. Various factors can affect a unit's strength, such as terrain or the enemy unit's type, so even though it's easy it still provides some meaningful decision-making.Some negatives about the gameplay are that the battle maps can sometimes be too large, and you can't cast spells after moving. This makes spellcasters difficult to utilize, although when you are able to do so their spells can easily turn the tide of a battle.The graphics and soundtrack are nice. You can use the classic artworks and BGMs. The dialogues are fully voiced by famous Japanese voice actors, they are really enjoyable to listen. I highly recommend this game if you're a tactics game fan and you want a game that's simple, fast-paced, relaxing, but still rewards strategic thinking.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: Langrisser I and II are sort of weird design artifacts when you compare them against modern tactical rpgs, but they're not bad.Their big feature is that each character can bring a half dozen disposable mercenary units into combat with them. The mercenary units can die without impacting gameplay, and they heal and get stat buffs when they're close to their commander. They also cost gold, so you have to juggle getting new equipment for your characters vs shelling out to give them small armies.Of course, having to control fifty or so units during a map is kinda grindy, and the game's exp system (which rewards pointlessly casting buff spells whenever you have a character not doing anything else) kinda contributes to the problem.On the other hand, if you like the feeling of just slamming formations of units together, Langrisser delivers on that in a way most other tactics rpgs don't.Story-wise, there isn't much here. The games take place in a bland, Record Of Lodoss War-y fantasy setting. However, the plot can branch wildly, and as a nice convenience feature you can easily revist and replay past scenarios.Overall, if you want a meaty, moderately difficult, plot lite fantasy tactics game, this is a fun way to kill time. It's probably not going to redefine your life, but not every game needs to do that, and I'd love to see the other Langrissers getting remastered.Edit: Langrisser II is definitely the stronger game in terms of storytelling and design, but it's also a fair bit harder and more random. The AI is breathtakingly suicidal, and enemy formations like to spawn and then immediately take a turn while in your back row, making it so that if you have an isolated character and you're doing no-deaths sometimes you just lose. These are mostly things that can be played around (sometimes a neutral formation just charges an enemy and gets blown up because the RNG skews the wrong way), but missions are long and it's a little annoyed to reset and waste an hour of gameplay because forty guys just teleported in on top of Liana.

Repetitive music, but it reminds me of the "good ole days" so I'm okay with it. :) Fans of tactical RPGs will definitely want to pick this up - great value for the price!

_childDocuments_.review: The story and characters of Langisser are likely hit or miss for the masses. If you are a fan of classic JRPGs, they will be right up your alley and very familiar to you. If you’re looking for something that’s unique and not entirely soaked with anime inspiration, it might not be for you. I fall into the latter camp, so one again ‘being a prince who experiences the death of his father in a last stand battle followed by the death of his overleveled mentor before marching forth to face an ancient evil with his new friends’ wasn’t the most appealing to me. There were few surprises and anyone who’s played a JRPG in the past will see the twists and turns coming from a mile away. That said, the narrative isn’t terrible if you can get past those points, even if some choices in its design seem like odd ones. Yes, I’m looking at you, first few scenarios that forced me to watch the AI fight itself.While the story and setting never pulled me in, the party management system made the playthrough more than worth it. Every character in your party has a class tree with a unique setup, attributes, a set of skills, a batch of spells, and an inventory. Classes stand out for being a bit outside of the norm as, although there are mages and knights, there are also serpent riders with a knack for combat at sea, lords with a talent for buffing their associated mercenaries, and so on. As your commanders perform admirably in combat and gain experience, they’ll level up, increasing their attributes and gaining class points that can be used to unlock new and superior classes. It’s important to note that character progression is more akin to something like Shining Force or Vandal Hearts than it is to Tactics Ogre or Final Fantasy as you’ll mostly be using it to upgrade from your current profession to a superior one, carrying over previous abilities while receiving new ones and a nice attribute boost as well. Classes are by no means unique to any one character, though each character’s class tree is organized differently, no two have the exact same setup of professions available to them.Your commanders won’t be going into battle themselves. Instead, they’ll be hiring mercenaries at the start of each combat based upon their current class and those that came before it. These units come in a wide variety, differentiated from one another by their role, attributes, and cost. Roles tend to be classifications such infantry, spearman, cavalry, flying, and so forth, and each has something of a rock-paper-scissors relationship that makes them ideal for countering another type. If you see flying units incoming, for example, ready your archers, if you see a squad of marine units, lure them onto the land. The price to hire these mercenaries is based on their stats, they aren’t created equally and many units are simply superior to others in their category. You’ll have to gauge on a case-by-case basis how much firepower you need prior to each scenario or risk losing plenty of gold on units that never draw their swords as they’ll be disbanded at the end of a scenario either way.Spells and skills are somewhat similar to mercenaries as they are determined by the class line that you’ve progressed down. You’ll unlock plenty of skills that offer passive benefits, either directly to that character or to the mercenaries that they lead, though you’ll only be able to equip two of them at any given time. As with classes, many of these are simply better than previously unlocked options, but there are plenty of exceptions where you’ll have to decide what you’re focusing on in that character’s build. On the other hand, all spells that you’ve learned on the class branch are retained so your magic-focused characters will have end up having hefty spellbooks at their disposal.Managing your inventory is surprisingly deep. Characters have three slots: weapon, armor, and accessory. There’s a significant variety in each of these and characters are free to equip any item that you’d like them to. Different types of equipment in these categories can be divided up into tiers and those of a similar tier are rarely straight upgrades. One weapon, for example, may simply add a sizable bonus to your attack, while another may offer less attack but more defense or a nice buff to your mercenaries. This system succeeds at keeping you invested while you tweak your party between scenarios.Chapters in Langrisser are defined by their battles and, unlike most tactical RPGs, this title has large-scale battles. In what might be compared to Wargroove, almost every unit is composed of a large group. A berserker, for example, isn’t just a single person but a sizable squad of similar-looking berserkers and every hero in your army has a unit that fights with them in the zoomed-in battles. As you’d expect, commanders tend to be the units that have the most impact on the battlefield, but they also hire several mercenary groups to accompany them and a number of them tend to be quite powerful themselves, particularly when their associated commander is specialized for leadership.I was quite impressed by the variety found in battles. Many games fall into a repetitive pattern that feels like something of a grind but Langrisser manages to avoid that particular trap. Battle maps differ significantly from one another and objectives follow suit; nearly every combat encounter is unique and memorable in some way. However, as unique as they may be, the same villains show themselves multiple times, sometimes even in a handful of scenarios consecutively. There’s a nice variety of classes and units, but characters are in short supply and frequent encounters give the overall setting something of a Dynasty Warriors vibe where your foes just won’t die.Langrisser II is an improvement over the first, but just barely. The mechanics are the same, the units are the same, and the overall style of atmosphere is the same. The story is a new one though, and with that comes a new cast of characters for you to become acquainted with. Though you’ll have strikingly similar equipment, skills, spells, and classes available to you, the most significant improvements are on the skill trees. For the most part, the sequel manages to enhance character customization by making more end tier classes available for them, thus cutting back on a clear best option for each character that was prevalent in the first title.Langrisser 1 & 2 are surprisingly strong entries in the tactical RPG genre for titles that were originally released nearly three decades ago. Their presentation is spot on for modernizing the old visuals and audio and the flow of the story and combat is surprisingly fluid and superior to many modern releases. The braindead AI can be a bit of a downer at times, but fortunately, it never gets in the way too much as long as you make sure that you give your most important orders manually. All in all, these are two fantastic titles that show that if there’s one genre that is truly timeless when done well, it’s strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really brings back memories, but it's not really what I expected in a remastered game. After some hours playing, here are my opinions about it:- Character arts look great!- The remastered music is great! But some of the old tracks from Der Langrisser are better.- Some conversations are a bit odd and need more polishing. They should have kept some jokes from the original or make better ones.- Voices are good. But demon and ghost voices are terrible, they just used human voices without any modification and that really kills the mood (especially werewolves voice, it's like wtf?).- Magic animations are great! But they shouldn't end with a freaking white screen, it really hurts my eyes.- Magic casters say some magic words when casting magic and that's so magical!- Buff magic has no visual effects on units and that's just lazy.- Magic range is too short, it really kills the desire for having a good offensive mage.- Items has no image! At least in the original I can have a feeling about how awesome an item is just by looking at the tinny image, and I totally expected that in a remastered they would let us see an item with full HD quality.- Hero's aura looks terrible.- The maps are a bit small.- Bad support for playing on PC.- Great game feature: you can move back to any battle in the story line with your current characters level, items and money, or start a new game from a cleared save in challenge mod as many times as you want.- Combat animations suck. I mean, looking at two groups charging at each other and suddenly stop midway and then doing air slashes are just too disappointing. At least I can see the soldiers clashing in  Der Langrisser. And the air units are just hovering above the ground instead of actually flying.- Special events should have animations instead of just poorly draw pictures.- Units from different countries should have different colors like the original. And units from the same squad should've had special animations when pointing at one of them so it's easier to tell which squad it belongs.I really hope there will be patches for this game in the future, because there are so many things could be done to make it a really great game. Especially when it comes from Japan, where product quality is something really important that I already see in many Japanese games.Despite all the negatives, I still recommend this game, for both people who have played the original and ones who haven't, because its game play and story lines are really good and it totally worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: A remarkably awful remake that doesn't offer enough positives to outdo the negatives.First off, the art. Ryou Nagi's art is terrible, plain and simple. The Satoshi Urushihara art option is included which is the only thing even making this remotely playable, but it's lazily implemented. You get options for using the new or classic art, and using the new environments or old NES-style environments. But no matter what you pick, you're still stuck with these ugly new sprites, which makes me wonder why there's a classic environments option at all. I cannot understate how horrible the sprite work in this game is. I'd call it phone game tier, but that would be insulting to the actual Langrisser phone game, which has significantly better visuals than this, along with much better new takes on the character designs, so this remake fails to beat a phone game on two fronts. Also, there's no lip syncing to speak of with the classic art at least, characters' mouths just flap open and closed in an ugly tweened animation for as long as the voice line is playing.Langrisser 1's story was exceedingly simple even for its time, and the only thing this remake did to change that was adding a new route to it (consisting of five stages), neglecting to do anything to flesh out the ridiculously sparse story content throughout, so the entire thing remains shallow. Langrisser 2 had more story to it in the first place, with the first stage of 2 having more dialogue than the first four stages of 1 combined. There's not much to say there really, if you've played the originals it doesn't seem like you'll find anything new here, and if you're new to it, the story of 1 isn't going to grip you in any way.Compared to the old PC port of 1 the single biggest point of improvement in this remake's favour is that it made the game progress at a significantly faster pace than before. Whereas in the old version of 1 I would be hesitant to hire mercenaries at all simply because of how much of a chore it was to move them around every turn, this remake makes it easy to do so with simple orders to give them, and the controls all being quick and snappy. The menus are functional, but good lord are they ugly, I can hardly think of any game I've seen where all the menus are so utterly devoid of any character. Maybe you'll like looking at them if you love white text on black backgrounds everywhere, but I sure don't. And as far as gameplay goes, that's about where the positives end. The gameplay is just braindead easy; the only difficulty you'll find here at all is in having NPC AI act idiotic and enemy reinforcements appear to kill off NPCs that need to be protected, so you might fail from that if you don't know what's coming. And guess what happens there? The game sends you back to the set up screen for that stage with all the EXP you just acquired attempting it kept, without even asking you if you want that kind of cheap bonus. So if you want any sort of challenge at all you can't just start over quickly, you have to exit back to the title screen and reload your last save instead. The game also showers you with money to buy equipment and mercenaries with, even if you reject the offers at the start of the game for a help bonus and demo bonus, so money is never a consideration. Compare that to the old PC version of 1 where hiring mercenaries actually needed to be weighed against how much money it cost, and you could easily end up dead if you didn't think things through. This game is just braindead, and the early stages are all that are needed to compare to see that.Additionally, you'd think equipment would be restricted by the characters' class, but nope, anyone can just equip whatever. Which then makes it absurd how you can buy Armour A which gives +10 defence, or Armour B which gives +9 defence and +10 magic resist, when both of them cost the same amount of money in the shop. Without any restriction on what gear can be equipped there's no reason at all to buy the A item in that example, and the shop is full of blatantly unbalanced options like that.The new soundtrack is probably the game's best point, but it can't save how much of a lazy, ugly, mess of a game the rest is. If they ever revisit the series in the future I hope they can get Urushihara back on board, never let Ryou Nagi near it again, and try putting more care into it than the Chinese phone game got.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Fire Emblem-like games, I really like this one so far. In these types of games, casualties always bother me, because you get invested in characters on different levels. (Pun intended.) In this game, your characters are commanders, surrounded by troops. The troop units can be lost without loss of the character or any other penalty. (Dark Deity did a good job changed that FE permadeath feature.) The game scratches the itch without being as stressful under this system. It makes me wonder why the genre changed, since the original Langrisser was one of the first of its kind on Sega Genesis. Anyway, once you get used to the mechanics, it's a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really well done remaster of the Langrisser games. If you are into the Fire Emblem series, you will love this. The remake now shows you were branching paths are, so you can make the choice explore a different path for an achievement. You can switch between old school graphics and music to the remaster in the menu.The only 2 issues I had were: I need to use MSI Afterburner to keep the FPS at 60; it was jumpy without using it. And also, the Hard Modes are unlocked behind beating the game at least once. This kinda sucks for a first playthrough because the game is super easy on default (at least if you are used to Fire Emblem).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is extremely addictive once you get into it. I played the original Warsong when I was a kid and this new version still has me playing hours on end into the night. For newbies, you don't want to finish off the enemy commander first. You get more experience killing off all his personal soldiers first. The game play is really addictive and something I haven't really seen been successfully duplicated after all these years. Definitely try out the demo and at least play through a whole scenario.Here are my cons:I think they could of made the new battle animations better. I also prefer the old art style of the characters. The new music is also a bit forgettable. The nice thing about this is they let you customize it to have the old art style if you wanted to.   A terrible choice that you can't really customize. I had to figure out what the keys by trial and error. It's not listed in the menus. This game was designed for the old consoles. Mouse support just wouldn't work with the way the game is designed when moving commanders so I wouldn't expect that to be added in. The game got a face lift, but it's still the original game play that was designed for a controller.Final thoughts:I wish they would add an option to remap the keys, but its not that big of a deal with this type of game. Its a turn base strategy game. It's not like you need precise key strokes to play the game better. So overall, I do recommend this game as the game play is very fun. Other games have tried to imitate some of Langrisser's mechanics, but nothing has come out that is quite like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: Langrisser(both games) are a classic of SRPGs and were an enjoyable foray into the beginnings of the genre. The story might be overdone by current standards, but the fact both games have a lot of endings, means that if you find the general "dark lord' story generic there are other routes you will enjoy. The battle system is also interesting compared to other games of the genre because the main unites have with them support unites that are actual separate units in themselfs and not just ingame battle animations as say in Fire Emblem games. The games also have difficulty modes that are not chosen at start but each time you begin a New Game+ the new run is harder than the last. It also is not the same game every time because you would be going for different routes each time.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: I would first like to start this review by saying that I am huge fan of tactical RPGs. I am new to the Langrisser series, and after seeing some of the screenshots and trailers to this remake of the first two games in the series, I was immediately excited. Anyways, I have put about 2.5 hours into the game (also spent some time in the demo before I bought the game) at the time of this review, and I have nothing but positive things to say about the Langrisser I & II remake.To begin, you have commanders in which you can recruit troops too. Commanders gain exp, level up, and gain cp (class points) which you use to unlock different classes. You can also change your class whenever you want to.Combat is fast. This includes movement on the battlefield, AI turns, and the battlescreen when attacking. I personally like this myself because when turns take too long or when movement is slow, it just drags the game on. So, you don't have to worry about that in this game.There are plenty of spells and skills based on what I have seen so far. You can buy weapons, armor, and  accessories in the shop before each battle. There are plenty of classes to unlock. You can replay missions to grind for exp.Another thing I like about this game is that the dialogue is not bloated or overwhelming. The story gets to the point with the right amount of dialogue. Sometimes in these kinds of games (JRPGs etc), the dialogue can just drag on and on. It's not like that in this game. Also, the story is really great so far. I am totally enjoying it.The music and graphics are awesome. I am playing the game with the remastered graphics, and it really makes the game shine in my opinion. Of course, others would have different preferences, but each to our own.One thing I would have liked to see in the game is a character creation system where we can create our own characters. However, it didn't stop me from using my own characters. With a little bit of editing, I was able to rename the characters in the game to my own preferences.Anyways, I am really enjoying this game. It's worth every dollar spent. Although, I haven't purchased any of the DLC yet, I will be purchasing it soon as well because of the soundtrack and the art. So, if you are fan of tactical RPGs and JRPGs, I would highly recommend that you pick this game up. I give the Langrisser I & II remake a 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics: 8/10Music: 8/10Replay Value: 7/10Bang for the Buck: 6/10Pros:- Ability to choose from original music and graphics, or the remastered ones;  Original artwork has more personality but the remastered ones will allow for cutscenes;- Japanese voice-overs for pretty much all characters;- 5GB in size but plenty of replay value with many endings;- Ability to go back to previous chapters in the story in the menu to allow for easier unlocking of all endings.  Players used to have to use a code on the Sega Genesis to do this.- Game is not chopped up into 100 DLCs like most games (Can you say Total War?)- Nostalgia!Cons:- Pretty pricey for a 5GB game, though less so considering it is a Japanese game- Poor keyboard and mouse support- Almost no tutorial or general info in game; Resources on the internet are often for the previous versions and can be poorly translated or just wrong/outdated.(29-03-2020) Cons- no option to quit the game unless you return back to the main menu, or force-stop it from Steam/Windows.- Joypads have to be connected before you launch the game.  The game will not recognize them if you connect them after you start the game, even if it is still loading.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this is a really good strategy RPG.++Original art by Satoshi Uruhshrara is goddess-tier. Like there are some sexy waifus ;-) and ridiculous but awesome shoulder pads for either gender. Great color contrast and thick dark lines...+...but if you're a pleb who doesn't get art and the concept of color contrast, you can always use the new crappy designs if you want ;-p++Character personalities are mostly likable and believable. Many of the "bad guys" aren't that evil when you learn more about them++Select any music style from any release of Langrisser. ++Deep strategic combat with huge armies to manage. Of note is the mercenary system.+1 battle save (I would have preferred 2 but 1 is way better than none)++Branching storyline with differing objectives in battle depending on which faction you side with.+You can grind if you want...--...but there is WAY too much grinding to get the perfect epilogue for all characters. 100 kills is doable but hard, especially when some characters join late game.-Mercenary AI is bad. Troops move in order of commander, but this often leads to Commanders that join later getting their troops cut off due to crowding. Also they can't understand things like walls and other unpassable roadblocks. This can be solved by manually moving all mercs but that takes a lot of time.-Minor Characters/generic troops don't have the option for Urushihara art.As of this review, I have cleared the light path in L1 and Light/True Light paths in L2. I am hoping to continue with Empire/Independent in L2, but considering I have clocked in over 100 hours, I figured I would write this review to show my appreciation. Edit: I have since completed the Empire/Independent routes in L2, and they are also great.

_childDocuments_.review: I could see the screenshots, and videos, and I went in for the purchase anyway expecting the game to be a nice trip down nostalgia road.  It wasn't.The voice acting is only Japanese without any way to change that.  You can change the art styles but then miss out on cutscenes that are only available in the new style.  The music is fine enough, and allows you to change it to the old chip tune version which is better.The new class system is much better and the game is way easier.  But the graphics are so jarring and terrible that the game was simply not fun.  The names of characters have been changed and the second I saw Taylor, not Tiburon, as a regular guy not a Crocodile Knight, Volkov instead of Baldarov, and Ledin instead of Garrett I knew I was going to be a gamer sad boy.  All the graphics are cutesy little mobile game looking, almost chibi.  For a game that was so difficult and dealt with darker and interesting storylines, this chibi look aint it.  Not to mention the battle system has been reworked to be simplified and more boring.Overall I bounced on this game hard because its like that ancient painting restoration at this point.  Took something that was incredible and memed it.  Submitted for refund.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic turn based strategy game setbin a fantasy kitchen sink. It's fairly easy, got a level and class system, combined with multiple endings. This time around the gameplay has been rebalanced, changed around a bit and now has better scaling and more magic to pick from.Levels can be replayed, without losing exp,  money and items. And losing a scenario is just a slap on the wrist, since exp gained during the match is not lost. Speaking of items, the hidden squares now have a sparkle effect to mark the spot. Music  style can be switched during gameplay, between retro and hair metal style. The dlc adds more options.Anyhow, if you enjoy a simple story and moving units around on a grid and optimization of stats a bit of grinding, it might be the one for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Langrisser I & II

_childDocuments_.review: Most of my time with this game has been from langrisser 2 as that was the game that introduced me into the franchise. Overall the game is similar to fire emblem but often feels like it's on a larger scale with upwards of 50 units on the screen at once. Both games have multiple story routes that invite replayability to them. From some of the reviews I skimmed at, I am seeing that the controls could use some work as there is no keyboard mouse set up, which I think should be added in the future. However, if you can get past that, the game itself is a fun srpg with lots of replay value.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't play through the story yet, but as a fan of snes/gba/megadrive strategy game like Fire Emblem FFTA and Shining Force, I couldn't be happier.This remake does everything one would hope for a remake of their favorite game : voice overs, dual graphics using the original and a more modern artwork, dual audio with original and remastered soundtrack?Sign me in !Many people want mouse and keyboard support for this game and I can't blame them, but if you have a controller and are used to play games from that era, you will fell right at home.The gameplay is very close to Fire Emblem, except you are able to buy disposable goons for your generals at the start of the battle. Those soldiers will actually be separate contollable units around your general which works like a Fire Emblem character.Looking forward to play it more, as the first few missions are very good.

_childDocuments_.review: The nostalgia value of this game is worth picking it up.  I remember playing the old Warsong port of this game on Sega Genesis back in the day.  The remastered art work is really nice.  The only downside I have with the game is the controls.  There is no keyboard/mouse support which is fine for me.  I use an Xbox controller plugged into my PC anyway so no loss there.  The problem is that the button mappings on the settings screen don't match up with the controller.  I have not looked at a switch or playstation controller, but I am wondering if they are modeled of of one of them.  There are 4 button setting options and none of them match up.  Most wouldn't be too bad because you can figure it out on your own with trial and error.  After a while you get used to the config layout.  The only one that causes issues though is the left analog stick.  This is what moves the cursor around the screen and highlights characters.  For some reason clicking the stick simulates pressing the start button.  More than once I was moving the cursor around the screen and the start menu would pop up.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, technically, I DO recommend this game to a very select group of people; people who like strategy games, but don't care about the strategy aspect all that much. I personally don't always care for strategy games because I find alot of them too finicky; move one guy one square to the left, and he'll get killed and the whole battle goes downhill, that kind of thing. But even I find this game to be a cakewalk--the only challenge is usually late-game enemies with spells that obliterate half your army at once, but even those end up not mattering because your hero characters become god-like beings capable of shrugging that off with a simple heal spell. So ultimately, the only joy is that of getting stronger, becoming OP, and beating your opponents into the dirt, which gets boring fairly quickly. What about other elements? Story and characters and all of that is paper-thin, so basically irrelevant flavor text. There's not a ton of depth to equipment and skills and what units to hire, so long as you're not completely brainless about it--generally, as long as you equip stuff that makes numbers go up or hire units with bigger numbers, you're golden. I played the game for a while as a time-waster, the way folks used to play Farmville, and that's about all it's good for. Outside of nostalgic fans, I think the game would most appeal to boys not quite old enough to feel bored with the simple combat, but old enough to appreciate the, ahem, "artwork."

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just writing this as a PSA:The chibi sprites are similar to the original games (Sorry DL kiddos, there are more goofy chibi fights than there are normal fights in this franchise.).The gameplay balancing absolutely is not similar to the original games. There is so much different that this game cannot rightly be called a remake of Langrisser 1 and 2. It is a new product with L1 and 2's story brought back. Core mechanics simply are not there and the gameplay is changed around considerably.It is my argument that L1 and L2 did not have particularly interesting gameplay to begin with, so I do not consider this a huge loss. I'm almost certain most of you just used the level select to grind your troops up and create overpowered combos. Baaw you can't start your hero as a sea unit big deal.You may not agree with that argument and I have not played either game to mastery, so it is possible I am just wrong and stupid. (I am certain the number of people who played Langrisser 1 and 2 to mastery number probably a couple dozen at best, though I'm also certain a few of you have fond childhood memories of the DL patch or Warsong which this product does differ from, so you may be invested in those and disagree with me.) I make this review as a PSA.What is here is slick and pretty all the same and worth at least a try at the demo if you have a taste for old school fantasy TRPG type games.
