_childDocuments_.review: Lair of the Clockwork God is extremely frustrating. The whole schtick is trying to take the piss out of "modern" (circa 1993) gaming trends like puzzle platformers, so it complains about everything that sucks in platform games - you have to keep repeating the same bit over and over, you keep falling down a hole and you need to play it again, you waste half the day sitting around waiting for moving platforms to reappear... But instead of subverting the tropes, it becomes exactly the sort of game that it (rightfully) was dumping on.Do not be fooled. This is not an adventure game. This is not even the skeletal remnants of an adventure game. It is a platform game with all the terrible parts of platform games, but it's even worse because it tries to shoehorn in some vaguely adventure-ish mechanics. The control system is designed for consoles, I guess, which means you can't just point at something and click. You need to walk over to it with WASD, then hold down Q, then grab the mouse, then click some icon while you're still holding Q, then let go of Q, then some incredibly slow dialog starts, which you can't skip with the mouse, but there's another obscure key for it, but then you miss an important hint because the dialog doesn't work like an adventure game where the first click reveals the sentence and the second click moves to the next one, it just skips the whole thing, then you need to hold Q again, or maybe right shift, I don't even know. At some point you can use T to teleport, or maybe it's tab, and E does something too, and at this point I'm starting to think this is some kind of cruel meta-joke about flight simulators or something.It is the most infuriating control system ever. And I suppose it might be alright if the jokes were really funny, but - just like the previous Ben and Dan games - they're mildly amusing at best. A few mildly amusing jokes definitely do not outweigh hours of falling down holes and landing on spikes and holding down Q. I rarely give up on games, but this was such a chore, I couldn't go on. To quote the characters: harrowing.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Half point and click, half platform, completely funny. It took me about 10 hours to beat Lair of the Clockwork God and I feel completely satisfied by this little indie gem. Puzzles are mostly surreal and hilarious, just like the ones from the LucasArts era, the platform sections are ok (I'm not a huge fan, tho, I mostly wanted to play for the adventure stuff), but the game completely works as a whole. If you already played "Ben there, Dan that" and "Time, gentlemen, Please" you know what to expect in terms of writing, if not: a witty, funny, crazy, hilarious story, as you probably didn't see in a while. Maybe a little bit patronizing at the end, but overall a FANTASTIC GAME. Just to see if it was possible I went through the whole game using a gamepad and the experience was almost flawless.

_childDocuments_.review: This is very unusual, albeit with certain questions about the implementation of some gameplay moments. Combining a platformer and a classic point-n-click quest in one game already looks like a rather unusual undertaking, but this is only an introductory part of what the creators have prepared for the players. In some chapters, the relationship between genres is so perfect that you don't even think about the genre orientation of the game at this particular moment, focusing solely on sensations. The main characters of the game - Ben and Dan, known for past projects of the developers from Size Five Games (Ben There, Dan That! And Time Gentlemen, Please!) are back in a new adventure. Ben is so old-school in his love of classic quests that he flatly refuses to jump (in general), to perform actions that require at least minimal muscle tension (except for pushing other characters on thorns into death pits, collecting things in inventory and their stupidest combination, of course), and Dan is a typical platformer fanatic who can jump a huge chasm and taunt the boomers and their love of collecting items in bottomless pockets. Most of the puzzles and locations imply that the player will have to combine the abilities of both heroes, sometimes even in the most unexpected sense of this possibility.The humor in the game constantly walks along the edge, often deliberately crossing it. I can't say whether this is good or bad, for me personally, most of the jokes are quite good, although some have caused the feeling that this is too much. The puzzles here are something completely different. The creators bombard the player with so many new and interesting ideas that it is difficult to even count them, often requiring the player's mind to get out of the box of obvious solutions. To be honest, many of them are incredibly difficult to solve on your own, but you can be sure that it is worth it The limping component of the game becomes platforming in the final third of the game. My God, he almost made me throw it almost at the very finish. Places where you need to go through large sections with inverted gravity, with rather inconvenient character control, and many obstacles, each of which kills the hero from the touch is pure torture. And I can understand why this was implemented in the corresponding chapter (anger from the inconvenience of control and idiotically placed obstacles became the essence of this chapter, and it was monstrously funny). But why do it in usual places, I don’t know. And this despite the fact that for most of the game, the platform part does not raise any questions inThe project turned out to be very bold, unusually daring and experimental. And for the courage in implementing their own fresh ideas, I am generally always ready to only praise any creators, no matter what genre they do. Fresh blood in the veins of ideas in the gaming industry is always needed, so I recommend the game, you will get a huge amount of new impressions from it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is buggy, kinda janky, with poor mechanics and poor level / game design. Most of the puzzle is far fetched and I did not enjoy the five hours I spent in it. It does a terrible job as a platformer and a bad job as a point and click (the whole gimmick is that you control two characters, one platformer and one from a point and click, each with their playstyle)

_childDocuments_.review: I really like platformers. I really like puzzle games. As soon as I hear enough good news about a game from either genre, I dive in instantly. I heard a lot of great praise for Lair of the Clockwork God, and seeing that it was a puzzle platformer, I picked it up without doing any further inspecting so to prevent spoiling the experience.I didn't like LotCG. Not even enough to get past an hour or so of gameplay.Here is why it didn't work for me:- Glitchiness: 20 seconds in I got a glitch where Ben got stuck underground and popped up after a couple seconds. After a few more minutes, this had happened several times, sporadically. Then I got to a section where a NPC is supposed to interact with an object. Instead, the character glitched out and became invisible. I could only solve the puzzle by finding his invisible body.- Controls: I started with mouse and keyboard, but it felt really awkward by default and the "look" function felt naturally suited for a joystick, so I switched to controller. Some of the buttons were assigned wrong, and by default showed up in game incorrectly (the game would indicate press the left button on the pad, but that would be incorrect). I'm not sure if that is just on my end with my controller, but I thought I'd mention it. The real issue was actually understanding what the function of all the controls was. Ben (or whichever the puzzle one is) has a typical set of point and click controls, but set to a quick menu where you can choose basic functions (Look, Talk to, Use, etc). The weird thing is, you can also always look at things with the joystick and hear a description. Not sure why the "Look" feature is doubled up like that. Otherwise the quick menu is a bit strange at first but then feels pretty natural.- Platforming: It's hard to make a platformer with good feel, but this just doesn't have it. There is a strange snapping action that happens when Dan (I think he's the platforming one) jumps into the corner of a platform. It doesn't feel natural at all as can even hinder movement. This also became an issue with a bit of the platforming in the first couple areas where you had to make a surprisingly tight jump to a object that wasn't very visible (I think? I had a hard time navigating some areas, the background is very samey and I got lost within even smaller areas). - Puzzles: Think "Secret of Monkey Island" but with nothing to actually piece together. This game doesn't explain anything to you - which I'm fine with! This game is clearly an homage/parody of those older point and clicks. Yet, the beginning puzzles are ridiculously simple while also being convoluted. For example: There is a cloud of poison smoke. "Ok, I guess I need some sort of tool to get past this, or maybe I just need to platform cleverly?" No, "look"ing at the smoke tells you you could use a make a sort of periscope/snorkel with a pipe you obtained earlier. And it just tells you that, so nothing to solve anymore, just do what game says. Maybe this was supposed to come across as a sort of aping on the ridiculousness of early adventure puzzle games, but the joke shouldn't have to replace fun gameplay.- Humor: This is the last thing I wanted to address, because humor is very subjective and I don't think it's worth arguing about what's funny and what's not. But for me, it just didn't click. From very early on, it's apparent this is a meta-commentary on video games, specifically indie puzzle and platforming games from recent years. But it just keeps digging into these topics without any relief, and I personally dread that sort of 4th wall breaking introspectiveness, at least when it comes as constantly as it does in this game.I gleaned from only a bit of gameplay that this game just wasn't my cup of tea, despite this being my favorite flavor. Oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not as if point-and-clicks haven't been seen since the Lucasarts days. They've even seen something of a resurgence - seeing constant, albeit often under the radar releases or an otherwise bleeding of their influence into existing or emergent genres.  It's joyeous. - imprinting implicit criticism on everything from walking simulators, microtransactions, the internet, Twitch/Mixer streams, etc -  In part because it's written with such professional comedic precision, but also, it's clearly done in the spirit of self-ragging. First rule of comedy - punch up or, preferably, your own face. Lair is not only about aging genres, but also the real-life writing pair, Ben Ward and Dan Marshall who star in the game. That the process of aging, unbeknownst to you, irrevocably contains you in a time capsule as the world keeps spinning is pure comedic tragedy that Lair leverages fantastically. It straddles the line perfectly between being 'sincere and inspired' and 'absurd and lewd.' The jokes hit at the pace of a British hyperloop. Despite a script of corkers, nothing can beat the joke at its core - that Ben and Dan cling to their respective genres - point and click  and platformer - with such fervour that Dan can't interact with anything or anyone and Ben can't be convinced to raise himself an inch off the floor, let alone jump. Such is the basis for a cavalcade of puzzles where the two enable each other's deficiencies. One limited by genre parameters of the past, and the other the current trends of 'emotional platforming.'  Whilst I'm eminently cognizant that a few standout moments shouldn't overwhelm my perception of the experience in its entirety, it's hard not to keep coming back to them. Call me a particular fan of their antics with bug lists, an in-game store and coffee. Whilst consistently great, these really do come to mind as puzzling at its most creative and are worth the price of admission alone.Otherwise, Lair offers spectacularly solid 'walk and click' and platforming fares to freely switch between -  And making it work! Whilst platforming sections feel like the weaker component (inevitably for being the harder to execute the game feel of), gravity manipulation and a good dose of shooting certainly trend-up Lair in an especially entertaining way. Platforming also contains decent accessibility options otherwise that essentially scrub its presence away if it's the clicking and pointing you're slavering over.  It helps that the walk and click UI is the most intuitive and fun to use I've yet seen. It's hardly surprising hopping around isn't quite as entertaining as trying to use your bladder on every interactable.  Its story is thoroughly fun - seeing you play out themed levels to add emotional components to an ancient computer as the apocalypse(s) rage outside. Not only does it make every section feel refreshingly focused, but it's an excellent excuse to get constantly inside the heads of our protagonists. By the end, these two bastions of humanity feel like fully fleshed-out flesh bags.If I had to level any criticism Lair's way, it would simply be that despite its more than reasonable length, longer levels seemed to give way to shorter and shorter emotional representations. It felt like it was in a hurry to end! And I suppose I didn't want it to.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: As a die hard fan od the point and click games of the 90s, I was quite intrigued by the premise: mixing an adventure game with a platformer?  How could that possibly work?  Well, I don't know how, but it DOES work. It works really well.  Maybe it's the charming cartoonish graphics. Perhaps it's the hilarious humor. Maybe it's the endearing characters.  Perhaps it's all those things.  Regardless, I cannot recommend this game enough, it's just so much fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure there's an audience for this, but it isn't me. "Lateral thinking" puzzles, where you end up having to try every combination of items in your inventory to "brute force" it and land on whichever obtuse nonsensical combo the writer thought would be wittiest, is just too much of an effort. It's *very* well written and *very* amusing game, with *great* attention to detail in all the dialogue options, but man, I just can't with the lateral thinking, especially given the UI is a tad too clunky for all the repetitive crafting attempts involved.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since I played the hilarious point & click games that brought Ben & Dan together for the first time, I've been waiting for more goofy adventures of these two. I didn't expect to get any, because I feel the devs didn't see enough profit in that genre anymore and then one day... they gave us this! By combining point-and-click adventuring with platforming and mixing them just in the right proportions, they breathed some fresh air into the idea and presented this new wacky adventure!The key element that I've always loved about the old games is also present here: it's packed with humour! And this is the kind of humour that makes fun of everything, including itself and the people who made it and it's not afraid to take the jokes pretty far, where others wouldn't dare. All these platformers and point-and-click games are just way too nice, while here you get to embrace being a couple of pretty terrible (yet strangely likeable) people and there's great satisfaction in that and heaps of laughs.The game really cleverly splits the platforming and point-and-clicking parts by making each of them a specialty of one of the two characters, but they need to co-operate to make progress. Neither of these sides of the game feels overly difficult. I feel the balance is just right to just sink in and enjoy the adventure. And what an adventure it is. It's gonna take you through several very different clever ideas through each of the parts that represent different kinds of emotions and it will all come together as one really good story with the ending making a very surprising connection to the beginning of the game.I also have to say the solutions to some parts of the game were very unusual and unexpected, especially that the game played me for a fool since the moment I started it with one of its quirks, confusing me throughout the gameplay until finally I reached a point in this game when I just thought: "WHAT?... Oh... Okay. You got me there." I can't explain it any better without spoiling it for others, but I have to say... There were things that I simply did not see coming. That also includes a certain visual novel. I don't regret being caught off-guard with any of them. Being full of surprises is one of this game's biggest strong points. So give it a chance to see what it's got in store.Personally I can't recommend this game enough. It was right up my alley. Give it a try and support great indie devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe the hardest bit of this review will be trying to explain what Lair of the Clockwork God actually is, at least in a compact, competent manner. So I guess I’ll try and get that out of the way early. It’s a pixel-drawn point & click that openly wants to have existed back in the 90’s adventure game boom, though, at the same time, it’s also a modern-day indie platformer that wants to be both a Super Meat Boy die-a-thon and a pretentious Braid warbler. It shouldn’t work, but it manages to pull it off by forcing the two halves to coexist while still keeping them somewhat separated. For the most part, Dan will have to do a bit of platform chicanery until he reaches an obvious dead end, wherein Ben then takes over to try and find progression by way of mashing random items together and being really smug at his accidental success.This bizarre hybrid is fuelled mainly by a light pummelling of the fourth wall, as is the style of the times. The resplendent Ben and Dan are virtual caricatures of the two lead developers behind the game, which casts Ben as a stubborn traditionalist longing for the golden days when Lucasarts were still a thing and Tim Schafer put out fully completed releases. Dan’s over all that noise, and desperately wants to be an indie platformer darling, waxing metaphysical about obscure symbolism while mindlessly collecting all the shiny objects that make a bing sound. They’re up for making fun of each other’s contrasting preferences. Or indeed, their own. Or just each other. Or just about anything else.While a lot of Lair’s humour is to be found in the borderline obsolete practises of retro adventuring or the oft-ostentatious overtones of today’s self-important indie scene, it paints its targets for mockery with liberal brushstrokes. For example, it’s quite happy to make its opening stages revolve around trying to find a cure for cancer because it knows that bad games will always get good press while weaker-willed critics are scared to put the boot in lest they be seen as attacking the message rather than the product. But rather than get hung up on some grandiose podium, it’ll then make a series of events based around a refusal to urinate in public, or how best to use the noxious fumes of a rotting corpse to complete another one of those so passé switch-flipping puzzles.Humour is a subjective little bastard, but I’m not afraid to say that the game had me the moment it took sliding tile puzzles to task (I hate them with the eternal fury of a million desert suns!). The gags and one liners are so frequent, though, it’s unlikely you’ll not find anything to appreciate during its ten or so hour lifespan. Perhaps its biggest selling point as well as its biggest detriment is just how meta-based some of the puzzle solutions can be. Maybe you’ll be like Ben and grumble about every instance of bending the genre back on itself in order to find unexpected results. I just thought a lot of it was bloody clever.

_childDocuments_.review: Tedious, tedious, tedious, tedious.Many years ago, when I was just a kid with no money, I saw a bundle on sale on Steam with two games in it: "Ben There, Dan That!" and "Time Gentlemen, Please!". While a little clunky and kind of annoyingly obtuse at times, they were still enjoyable, and today I look back with fondness on these two little gems. When I heard that Lair of the Clockwork God (LOTCG) was another, similar game by Ben and Dan, I put it on my Steam wishlist and impatiently waited until I could purchase it. Unfortunately, I should've waited for another deep sale.Here's the thing: when I purchased and played the two original games, I had zero interest in puzzle games. It was the clever writing and the lack of actual game mechanics or real challenges (except, well, literally point and click) that made it work. The puzzles could become annoying and yes, as a last resort I had to try everything with everything, but this eventually worked and also meant not much else could go wrong. When I play LOTCG, all I can think of is how hard it must be to make a game. The devs tried to splice platforming and point-'n-clicking together but it just does not work well in practice. Dan glitches on every edge of a platform he tries to jump on and constantly falls in the world. This falling can either result in a death, or you getting back on your feet, it's a roll of the dice. This can be a right pain in the ass when you're trying to do every achievement, which is another annoyance with this game: the achievements make you play the game in a way the game wasn't meant to be played. One requires perfect platforming precision while the precision is nowhere to be found. Super Meat Boy this is not. You'd think the developers would be aware of this and wouldn't lean too heavily on it.A few years ago I tried to get into programming and discovered very quickly how frustrating it can be due to being punished for making an incredibly small mistake, be it a missing letter, a symbol like a semicolon, whatever. LOTCG constantly reminded me of those classes because the solution is often found in the smallest of details, or where you exhaust every single possible option on the game field or try every single item in your inventory with every single object in the game, while the solution is staring you right in the face, but requires moon logic to connect the dots. Not only is this highly annoying, it also means you wasted a lot of your time trying to think the puzzle through in the normal way.In one instance I was stuck in a room for a very long time, blocked between a door with an "obnoxious puzzle" (no really, that's what it's called) and a chamber filled with deadly gas. - A room above me had a keg of powder which I already managed to interact with by punching holes in barrels and making sparks but nothing to set them on fire. So: no real results.- The chamber with gas had a lever that made one door close, but after plenty of searching no other consequences. Dying in this room provided the opportunity for the characters (the stand-ins for the devs) to pat themselves on the back how immensely clever they are. - The "obnoxious puzzle" I tried to solve on my own, but my character verbally argued many, many times that there had to be a better solution to it. As my options dried up, I tried everything with everything, taking into account that both the main characters are pathetically, obnoxiously lazy, almost selectively lazy, and in most cases refuse to so much as jump or exert themselves at all. It turned out that all the switches and things I could tinker and touch were all red herrings because all I had to do was to jump across a very small, hard to see gap, and USE A ROLL OF DUCT TAPE AS A WHEEL FOR A CART.The final nail in the coffin for me was in a level aboard a space station where a death caused me to not be able to progress anymore, thereby softlocking the game.  My kingdom for a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a fantastic and unique experience. While other games have attempted to mix the gameplay of platformers with that of point and click adventures, the resulting gameplay loop is usually an awkward mish-mash which compromises the core of both of these game styles. Lair of the Clockwork God instead fully embraces the dissonance between two wildly different genres both in its gameplay and its clever meta deconstruction of these genres' tropes.The platforming in LotCG is more than serviceable, but I imagine most people who play this game will be doing so to solve the ingenious puzzles of its point and click half. These puzzles are phenomenal both in their variety and their execution. I would go so far as to say that they mostly supersede the puzzles of the Lucasarts classics to which the game is obviously paying loving tribute, insofar as the developers never fail to eke out as many novel puzzles as possible from the game's unique mechanics. This, to me, is what I imagine Lucasarts games would be like in an alternate history where point and click adventures didn't die a death in the early 2000s.All in all, I would really recommend that anybody try this game. The difficulty is not so high as to make the game frustrating, the writing is genuinely really funny (and showcases British humour in a medium where that humour is somewhat underrepresented), and the game is generally just a huge breath of fresh air.

_childDocuments_.review: A platformer-adventure mashup that was a delight from start to finish. Even the occasional breaches of the fourth wall, which don't always work for me, hit the spot here. Some of the puzzle solutions were just ingenious enough to make me feel very clever indeed for working them out on my own without ever making me reach for a walkthrough.The episodic, level-by-level structure works much better in my eyes than the overly open nature of Ben and Dan's last adventure, Time Gentlemen Please - at any time you can be fairly confident that you've got everything in your inventory that you're going to need to solve the puzzles in front of you, which makes it much harder to get stuck. Levels are varied too, with themes that hang together very well, and the sort-of-pixel art style is a big leap forward from previous Ben & Dan outings.Also as you'd expect from Size Five the sarcastic, smutty British humour running through the game is straight out of the top drawer and a constant joy. One of my favourite games in ages, definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, makes me terribly happy. Not just because of the shotgun humour, but also because as a long-time fan (my antiquated netbook still has the other two games by these fine fellows on it) I can appreciate the joys of getting old and watching technology melt into a morass of bleh, as well described and lampooned in... well basically, the whole of this game. Also, because of the level where a very rude word was said. A lot. A lot a lot.In essence this mash-em-up of disparate genres and themes should not work, but very much like the music for the opening sequence, lumping together a bunch of things that should not go together and giving it a steady beat, somehow produces magnificence - the beat in this strained analogy being two cranky blokes just wanting to get on with things and sup some beer and not have to suffer the indignity of the world ending pants going on around them, but having enough savvy to make us laugh at it.And I suppose that truly is, and has been for decades, the best way to make bad things go away, is to laugh at them. Or use a big gun. that's good too.Good gods though, that one bloody arsing platform level. Guh!tl/dr - Dan+Ben= Awesome, Game=Awesome, Music=Sublime, Big Gun=Mess.End Credits=Horrifying.

_childDocuments_.review: Dan & Ben are back with a hilarious, self-aware, genre-bending masterpiece that goes far beyond their previous point-and-click efforts (Ben There Dan That, Time Gentlemen Please, both recommended). I won't deny that this game has its flaws, especially in the first third or so as you get used to the complicated control scheme (it ain't easy being a p&c adventure and an indie platformer at the same time) and gather the power-ups needed to even get around the maps without feeling irritated. And yes, I got frustrated and stuck a number of times-- occasionally the "what do I next" signalling could be better.Even so, it's an incredibly funny and well-designed game throughout, and it really starts to pick up steam by the halfway point when you've settled into its rhythms and it keeps building and building continuing jokes and themes. There are a couple of payoffs in the later chapters where I had to set down the controller between laughing and wanting to literally applaud their skill at building up to some of the most brilliant slow-burn punchlines (some embedded right in the platforming gameplay) that I've ever seen in any medium.The writing mostly runs on a very cynical and very British sense of humo(u)r that longtime Ben & Dan fans will be familiar with, and that I personally find consistently hilarious. But there's real heart here as well. Even Ben grows up a little bit at the end (although the Final Emotional Lesson goes a bit differently than he probably intended). I wasn't expecting a tough but affectionate critique of the entire video game industry and online culture when I fired up this game, but they delivered that too in their own unique voice. If you like point-and-clickers and/or platformers, enjoy British humor, and you've got the patience for a few gameplay glitches, this game will reward you immensely. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Hilarious and very well designed hybrid between a platformer and point & click game, and much more than another puzzle-platformer. There are two guys to play with: Dan loves platforming but hates solving puzzles, while Ben loves puzzles but even refuses to jump. Yet they have to work together to reach the end of each level in many creative ways. Each level in the game feels unique and there are plenty of clever ideas and funny situations. In fact this is one of the most funny games I've ever played! :)Be warned though: the game is rather difficult, both the platforming and solving some of the puzzles. The devs really like trolling the player so you'll need to think out of the box from time to time. Strongly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Lair of the Clockwork God is exactly what a says on the tin: a wholly unique combination of classic point-and-click adventures and late '00s indie platformers. After introducing this dichotomy in the opening hours, the game quickly finds new and interesting ways to combine the two, though it's always the marvelous wit that is the star of the game. It starts meta and gets more so as you play, but in ways that lead to clever and often brilliant puzzles, rather than navel-gazing. There is no way to pitch these here without spoiling them, but suffice it to say that the attention to detail is fantastic, and it rewards lateral thinking while always giving you all the information you need to solve a puzzle.It's also hilarious, and probably the most consistently funny game I've played since Jazzpunks.As an adventure game, it's top notch, one of the best in years. And a platformer, it's solid, but unremarkable, and the platforming segments are going to be the sticking point for a lot of people; fortunately, the game has fantastic accessibility options that not only change the difficulty of platform segments, but provide everything from colorblind support to different fonts. If a tiny indie team with one programmer can do this, there's no excuse for all the AAA games who don't.Each new level is a breath of fresh air, and I found I enjoyed the game more and more as I played through it; I was sorry to see it end, though it's always good when a title leaves you wanting more.Definitely one of the best games of 2020.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: A sweet and (very) funny love letter to classic adventure games and those trendy metaphorical platformers you get now. If you've liked previous Size Five games, you'll love this, and if you enjoyed those Lucasarts adventure games in your youth there's a lot to enjoy.Lair has some of the best puzzles in any adventure game I've played, none so hard that you're frustatingly stuck (though Ben has written a hint guide that should get you out of any tight spots), and several so elegant I started laughing even as it dawned on me what the solution was. The jokes are good, and while there's always a piss joke to lift the atmosphere (and lower the tone) when things get too serious, there are moments of genuine self reflection in there... Nothing is mean spirited, and even the jabs at the modern video game experience are done with love.It's also just about the perfect length (6-8 hours ish) and is delivered in manageable chunks which keep your inventory down and the puzzles a case of thinking rather than trial and error. Also a godsend for those of us with adult lives to contend with... That the platforming isn't *super* smooth is really my only criticism, but honestly none of the sections last long enough for it to become frustrating (well, unless they're meant to). Absolutely recommended to any fans of the genre!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really really fun. It is a platformer but not the hard one, more a kind of exploration one. Then it is a point and click adventure but without a mouse, and without many areas to revisit. Puzzles are contained in levels, and while the inventory is big enough, a little bit of thinking can be used to solve any problems. Finally, it is really really fun, the script is great, monkey island level or even better. A very polished experience and one of the best games i played
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Will update review once finished, but am really enjoying so far. The mix of genres is really refreshing, and they mesh well together. The puzzles are interesting and make sense in the context. The writing and humor are great, which should not be a surprise considering the team's previous games. And the pixel graphics have so much character.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This game is much smarter than it looks, works really well because of (and despite) its weird Frankensteining of genres, and is the most affectionate parody of adventure games as a whole I've ever seen. The jokes also somehow appeal to both my inner twelve-year-old and my outer crotchety old man, so that's certainly something. Does a lot it shouldn't be able to, dunnit? Well, yes. That's why you should check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I was a big fan of "Ben there Dan that", and "Time Gentlemen, Please" - and so was very happy and surprised to find a followup came out many years later. Thanks RPS!Like the entries before it - this is funny. So very funny. I would even say I have been made to chortle and possibly guffaw.If you are a fan of adventure games (and cannot let go of the past), play this.If you enjoy humour, play this.If you like games, play this.Half the fun is being surprised and caught off guard by an unexpected joke. Combine, (sorry craft) every item combination you can, examine every item, use everything on everything and just have fun with it.Thanks for making this guys!
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: It's as if Douglas Adams arose from the dead, played a bunch of indie platformers and decided to make a video game. It's a fantastic mix of puzzle solving using both platforming and adventure game tropes while thoroughly taking the piss along the way.It's of course very Ben and Dan humour, which is to say very British and silly, just look into Behold the Kickmen to see if their style is up your alley or not.PS. I'm yet to finish this but having such a lovely time I almost don't want it to end. And I haven't even touched the bundled, free game yet!Massive congratulations to Dan, Ben and the rest of the staff who worked on Lair of the Clockwork God. It's proper brilliant.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: My full review is up here , but what I'll excerpt here is this: adventure games, especially comic ones like this, always revolve around particularly convoluted workarounds for what would normally be simple problems, if only you had the right items for the job. Here, by splitting the game not just across two characters, but across two types of playstyles--classic adventure and modern platformer--you get a gold mine of comic scenarios. Dan’s refusal to interact with even basic objects like a light switch means that Ben must find a way to use his inventory to send Dan an assist. A lot of very funny (and sometimes very crude) jokes follow--as does a lot of punching-up at games (and human emotions) as a whole. Particular highlights include the Super Meat Boy-mocking "Anger" as well as the walking-simulator and virtual-reality spoofs.I'll say no more; just check it out!
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly this is a narrow recommend. The game does a lot of neat stuff that's worthy of attention, but its let down by a few things:- The control scheme never quite gelled for me (I used keyboard + mouse), I got used to it, but it wasn't that fluid switching between characters to do different things. Part of me was just pining for the two character to be merged into one, so you could platform and point & click without switching.- The ending. I don't want to spoil, but I found it disappointing and damaged a lot of the game for me. I wanted more of a cullmination of all the themes of the game, and it just doesn't give us that.But there are a lot of positives.- The puzzle solving can vary and be a bit unintuitive at times, but other times it's super creative and just fun. Good point and click puzzles are a pleasure when you finally realise what you need to do, and this game touches on that a lot, doing truly perverse and crazy and creative stuff. The use of  was fun for instance. - British humour and slang. I have not heard the term "John Thomas" in years, and "standing around like a lemon" is a term a British friend I have uses a lot, but don't really hear anywhere else except for this game. It's just nice some of the more understated turns of phrase are used.- Ocassional pontification. Sometimes the game dive in and discusses some theme or other. As I said above, I felt there could have been more done to build up on the themes, but the discussion they do have can be pretty fun. The  level for example has a couple of good observations mixed in.I liked playing this game for the most part, and apprecaite it's doing stuff that's different, just sadly not overly enthusiastic about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games, you should play this game. If you have played games for a long time, you should definitely play this game. If you are a game developer you should definitely *definitely* play this game. If you are a game publisher you should play this game and then send these guys some work.Not only is this game hilarious, but many of the puzzles have solutions that subvert tropes and expectations in the most wonderful ways.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that a game makes me literally shout "NO...!!!" in elated astonishment because something so absolutely bonkers and yet absurdly brilliant happens that it utterly breaks me. This one managed to do so twice; three times; four... I lost count by the end. There is one bug I encountered where if you as Dan jump on Ben's head, you sink partway into the ground. Strange that this hasn't been fixed yet; otherwise the devs have been very good about maintaining their game.Anyway, if you enjoy games, then play this one. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Finally gave Lair of the Clockwork God a shot after avoiding it. It's a slow burn at first and I didnt immediately click with the humour, but once it got going? I can see why people rave about it so much, especially with the not so subtle nods and the credits.  If you've been trying to justify buying the game yourself, honestly just buy it if you have the money. Take the leap and give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: The follow up to the previous  Ben and Dan games: 'Ben There, Dan That!' and 'Time Gentlemen, Please!' which as well being great for having punctuation in their titles, are also really good and very funny tributes to/pastiches of Lucasarts era point & click adventure games.This game is pretty different. It sets its sights on indie games in general, drawing from a wider range of influences.Ben is stubbornly sticking to his 90s point & click roots, and is all about looking at things and solving puzzles by combining items from his inventory (which is DEFINITELY not crafting!). Meanwhile, Dan wants to get with the times and be an indie platformer because that's  what's cool these days. The result is a hybrid point & click/puzzle platformer, that surprisingly works very well. The writing and humour is by turns clever, silly, perceptive or biting as required, and works well for me as a fan of the previous games.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Generally very amusing, although not always to my tastes. Lots of funny custom responses to commands, and the overall story goes places.I have some issues with the platforming controls, but the platforming itself is rarely difficult enough that they become a problem. Mainly with walljumping (which wants to work a particular way) and shooting while midair/on a wall (not helped by playing with keyboard & trackball).
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Every bit as funny as its predecessors, Lair of the Clockwork God is a genuinely enjoyable adventure game alongside a rich and affectionate mickey-take (in the British-est way) of indie platformers, point and click adventures, and games in general.Come for the jokes, stay for the fiendishly designed puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Its a clever, sweary journey through human emotions, with loads of gloriously funny moments. It's the third game of a trilogy, following on from "Ben There, Dan That!" and "Time Gentlemen, Please!", but doesn't assume you've played them (instead acknowledging their past adventures with small dialogue references and easter eggs) and stands on it's own merit. The gameplay is a mix between a platformer (while playing as Dan) and old-school LucasArts point & click adventure (Ben) game, and fits a niche I've personally missed in video games. It doesn't take itself seriously, and even has a separate standalone game, "Devil's Kiss" included for free which covers Dan's first day at school, and can provide useful character exposition in Lair of the Clockwork God.All in all, I loved it, and I think you should definitely check it out. Easily recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic and very funny puzzle platformer/adventure game hybrid. Although it's a sequel to the Ben There/Dan That and Time Gentlemen, Please adventure games, it only very vaguely references them, and serves as a standalone game (aside from coming with Devil's Kiss which you shouldn't play before this game).My only issue is that the game's framerate was inconsistent (or sometimes consistently 30fps) despite exceeding the system requirements and telling the NVIDIA control panel to use dedicated rather than integrated graphics. Although the platforming was serviceable in the brief sections I had 60fps in, the drops made it much worse than it should have been. Oh, and the game generally doesn't look as good as its predecessors but I adapted.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Lair of the Clockwork God is an extremely funny and well written game. It features dialogues, an inventory system, pointing and clicking and more willy jokes than you can shake a penis too. There's also some ham-fisted bloke with fists the size of hams running and jumping about but I think we can ignore him.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Properly fantastic.This game will have you scratching your head and then laughing at both the solution to the puzzle and any number of jokes told in the interim.It also has a dog, that you might be able to pet - currently unsure.A few bugs but Size Five have always been exemplary at post-launch support and bug-fixes, and the game being on 1.04 already highlights this.If you have ever played any of the other Ben There, Dan That games then you owe it to yourself to play this - Size Five have given us years of quality games and this is the best yet, so support them.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: So you remember how sometimes game devs in search of inspiration would just mash two completely unrelated genres together to see what happens, like that "Baby Pac-Man" arcade game that was half Pac-Man, half pinball game?You do? Seriously, you remember that weird coin-op monstrosity?Well you're definitely old enough to get most of the jokes in this one, then. But either way you should check it out. Fun game, packed with good gags, and has slightly fewer bugs pretty much every time I play it!
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: So far it's great and Dan said on Twitter it doesn't suddenly get ♥♥♥♥ at the end so I'm gonna review it now in case I forget later.I can't seem to find a way to upload my Sonic/Dan/Ben crossover fan art to this review form.[UPDATE]I just finished the game. It's great! Dan didn't lie, it really doesn't get ♥♥♥♥, it stays good. In fact I think some of the best bits are near the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game!Switching between platforming and puzzles is fluid, best enjoyed with a controller.Writing/Characters are fun as alwaysWhile the puzzle parts aren't too mysterious, they certainly made me swear because I didn't expect THAT.Platforming works alright, the gravity seems a bit much to me - you accelerate really fast downward - but I didn't get that angry.If you liked this game, check their other point-and-click adventures!
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I love this. It's funny, thoughtful and inventive, and playing it is a series of delightful little experiences one after the other. It's not gimmicky, though it would probably still be awesome if it was. The two sets of disparate skills complement each other superbly thanks to some inspired level design and some utterly ridiculous sets of circumstances. You can feel the love and care in every step of the design of this, from the jokes that are laugh out loud funny  and pitched just right, to the little tweaks along the way - like the fact that before you start to consider that operating both characters one after the other could prove to be a chore at times you get the ability to 'piggyback' them. The designers know their stuff, and that is a crucial part of the game. What it isn't at any stage is annoying, fiddly or *unnecessary*. This is a game for those of us who remember point and click adventures fondly, sure, and if you like your Lucas Arts you will love this - fact.  But it's also a game for anyone who just wants to be entertained by whipsmart dialogue, fun game mechanics, clever little puzzles and lots and lots of proper laughs.Get this. It *is* big, and it *is* clever.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this for the most part. Well written, funny, and a nice art style to it. I enjoyed the puzzles and didn't find myself getting stuck on them much, because when the game dropped hints it was clever about them. I admittedly found the platforming a struggle though, especially the bits that play with gravity, where the controls seemed to be counter-intuitive.edit: Since posting this review the developer has adjusted the difficulty of the part i found frustrating, which means I basically consider the game flawless.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Having thoroughly enjoyed the first 2 games (not counting the Devil's Kiss, which was also pretty cool though), I was a little worried about this one not being primarily focused on adventure-style gameplay anymore and the overall shift to a more platformer-style experience. Well it turns out the game itself is worried about the same thing too, with one of it's main themes for me being "keeping up with the times" versus "staying content with what you know". And this theme is incorporated beautifully with the game itself, the two main characters representing and constantly arguing about those two opposite views. It also hits pretty hard at times, but still stays humorous (like that one level sigh).For me this is a much more mature work than the previous games, but I am now more mature as well, so it works out I guess. Besides, the humor is still there, albeit a bit adjusted for the times, which is fine. It's still funny and clever, as are the puzzles, which I do not want to spoil, but do not know how to otherwise comment on. The same rule of "examine everything to get additional clues" from the previous games applies here as well. It's great.In the end, I was not disappointed. I was very much entertained and had a little bit to think about. Which is more than I could ask from a videogame these days.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of P&C Adventures - indeed, anything by the likes of Ron Gilbert and Tim Schafer - you'll be at home with LOTCG. It's funny (you'll be grinning like a loon even before the title screen appears), witty, clever, charming, very British, and loaded with neat references and nods to pop-culture. The game design is also staggeringly clever, and plays on the genre differences between Dan and Ben in really interesting and unique ways. Puzzle-wise, there's a few moments where you'll be scratching your head, but there's no major show-stoppers - everything's within your grasp. Simply, LOTCG is an utter gem, a delight to play, and loaded with belly laughs. Buy it forthwith, and wallow in its goodness like a cat lying in a patch of sunlight.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a heck of a cool thing. Love the clever, witty dialogue, and the mix of platformer and point and click adventure is surprisingly effective (though I'm sure that's helped by my love of both genres.)Graphically it's a total delight and wonderfully charming. Fantastic animation. The music perfectly sets the tone and mood of each area.Also I really love the amount of accessibility options. I don't think I've ever played a game with the option of a dyslexic friendly font before. All that inclusivity is just awesome.So yeah, pretty enamoured with this game. Deffo recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I love adventure games and I find some light platforming to be fun as well.Somehow this combination of game play styles doesn't work for me. The platforming is a bit unresponsive using keyboard controls. The adventure game puzzle elements, at least in the very early part of the game, are quite simplistic.Given the unresponsive platforming controls I know there will be sections where I'm not sure I'm facing a adventure puzzle or a platforming section that is unresponsive. I experienced this very early in the game where I was unsure whether I should continue trying to make a certain jump or it simply wasn't possible and I should consider the current obstacle to be a puzzle. Maybe using a gamepad would solve this issue for me, but I much prefer keyboard control in adventure games.Update - I have updated my review to provide a bit clearer feedback for the developer. Also, I think I was too harsh. I haven't changed my mind about the game, it isn't for me but if you are more patient or better at the platforming sections than I am, the game is probably fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first two Ben & Dan games ten years ago while trapped in my flat by the worst gastric event of my life. They had me laughing so hard and so often as to pose a severe threat to both my own health and that of my trollies.When I heard Lair of the Clockwork God was coming out early this year, I was looking forward to enjoying a Ben & Dan game in happier, non-housebound circumstances. So that went pretty well.There are two possible conclusions to draw from this unfortunate squits/COVID coincidence, other than that it's a coincidence. One is that Ben and Dan are the bearers of a powerful curse and their games should therefore be avoided in the interest of personal safety. The other is that their games are so relentlessly splendid that they make even the worst times that bit more bearable. I lean towards the second conclusion.Quick gameplay summary: it follows the point and click, collect and combine model of the earlier games (as ever, it's worth exploring every possible action/combo for the reliably funny, situation-specific text they've taken the time to write for most of them). The introduction of a platforming element helps break the potential monotony for point and click sceptics, as well as preparing the ground for some excellent genre interplay and in-jokes. Mercifully, though, there's a platforming difficulty slider so that uncoordinated lumps like me can get through the game without hurling the controller through the monitor in frustration.Ben and Dan are the cleverest, funniest writers I've come across in 30+ years of gaming, to the extent that I was shaking with laughter before I'd even clicked a single button. I don't really play this as an alternative to other games, but as an alternative to reading the Viz, watching Taskmaster or listening to I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue (Humph era, obvs), when what I need more than anything is a proper, snort-tea-through-the nose laugh. I'm nowhere near finishing it, partly because I'm bad at games but mainly because I want to stretch out the joy of reading the jokes for the first time.If you grew up in 80s/90s Britain, it's near enough essential that you buy this game. If you didn't, you really should buy it anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Great diversion, very distracting. Basically it's Chucky Egg meets Level 9 adventures and Space Adventure / Leisure-Suit Larry... Pixelated but challenging and fun (more so, once you get into it). Be warned it has a lot of click-to-acknowledge-someone-just-said-something going on. Get past that and it's a great, inventive, far-fetched, ludicrous, 80's-video-game-revival with a lot of humour that wouldn't be out of place in Big Trouble in Little China, Evil Dead or Red Dwarf. Brings together platforming joy, social-angst and dystopian comedy with some great story-telling. As a hard-core gamer I've been entertained playing in spare time all week - only made it 10% of the way through. Solidly-written with a clever back-story and endless plots / twists and a clever progression of 'power-ups'.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I was in stitches from the opening credits. It's rare that a 'comedy game' can stick the landing with such confidence and sincerity. The humour is genuine, warm and yet never saccharine - and while Ben and Dan will frequently pick one another apart, their conflicting worldviews and attitude to gaming can't hide their obvious affection for one another. Seems a daft thing to focus on, but their friendship makes me a little nostalgic for something I can't really put my finger on. Gameplay-wise, Lair of the Clockwork God's alternating styles are executed with such efficiency that it's easy to forget that the entire concept hinges upon a joke - and a very good one at that - simultaneously mocking two genres while elevating them.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This game has good nostalgia-fueled intentions and some truly awesome artwork, but the repetative dialogue and seeming inability to skip the lines means the jokes and quips run thin very quickly. Some of the puzzles are also wildly unintuitive wherein the game works on its on laws of physics that constantly seem to change. Instead of point and click feeling like problem solving, I found myself asking what sort of convaluded solution the game wants be to find. Puzzles shouldnt feel like I have to figure out what the dev was intending because it just took me out of the game. Specifically, one puzzle in the space section which requires you to time one extended platforming action with a point and click action that is very difficult to gauge. I wanted to throw my laptop after attempting this many times until I finally gave up and quit. While the commentary on the gaming industry and platform/point and click games is appreciated, save yourself the headache and pass on this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This game is rather good.  I debated writing a haiku to describe my feelings about it.But I suck at poetry.Then I decided, mmm....I could write some lyrics in a sort of sing-a-long game review to let's say....the tune of Wake Me Up Before You Go Go.  I mean, I've got rhythm.  Could knock that out in short form.But that song has a lot of finger snapping and I've got carpal tunnel and all.  So, scrap that.Next I toyed with the idea of writing a lengthy almost article looking review about the variety of game mechanics, wit, and finely tuned pacing. That would be nice.  I could carry on about the juxtaposition of two opposing game styles coexisting in a seesaw of platforming and adventure game genres.But not many folks read long reviews anymore.  TLDR you know.  Life is short, make it quick and get on with it.So, I would like to say this:Buy this game and be happy.  It is very very clever. The jokes don't make you want to roll your eyes, and the platforming is surprisingly fun.  The adventure gaming parts make you do things you would never dream of doing too.  Probably the best indie game I've played in a few years.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: It was never my intention to complete the game before writing a review. In fact, like many of us, I rarely complete games I own on Steam. However this was just too good all the way from start to finish *not* to see to it's conclusion.I'm going to keep this brief-ish because you're all busy, but please believe me when I say this is something special. Its blend of "point and click" style adventuring with platforming mechanics works way better than I expected. The puzzles were almost all intuitive and the moments I got stuck led to some very rewarding "Aha!" moments in the end. (For instance when you steer a remote probe and there's a password and...ah well, you'll figure it out).There are times with the platforming that can drive you crazy, The mechanics that switch the direction of the action in particular caused mild rage. In fact this is poked fun at later. But generally the platforming is great fun especially when you gain further powers. Also you can give Ben a piggyback.Story wise this feels more coherent than what I recall of the previous game (I didn't bother to replay it and it's been...what, a decade? since I have). The calibre of the humour is top notch, but do I think that because I too am British and a small portion of the dialog based jokes are very self depricating towards current British society? Hmm, nah, that can't be it. I especially enjoyed the digs at walking game simulators.I'm going to mention a single thing that caused me problems:The game camera mucked up about three times during my play through. By the time you read this it might be well sorted. But if you ever think there's a moment where you can't see everything you should be able to see I recommend just quickly restarting the game.(Oh but that other thing that keeps happening? You know the *thing* yeah? Well, don't believe everything you read in the updates for the game, that's all I'll say)All in all then I'll be surprised if you don't enjoy this. Ambitious, eclectic and hilarious, I'd recommend it to anyone. Don't let this end up being one of those games that you end up getting at a massive discount, or in a bundle later on and think "Gosh, I would have paid full price for this..." Get it now and be proud of yourself for supporting it before everyone else knew it was amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to get a refund based on how it ran on my Macbook Pro (6-core/16 GB RAM/Radeon graphics) and it seemed very glitchy/buggy. My refund was denied due to purchasing the game a few days more than 2 weeks ago. So keep that in mind when you buy games on Steam, you have 2 weeks to play UP TO 2 HOURS before your refund will almost certainly be denied. Happily, I did try this on my PC, and it works a lot better. Surprisingly resource-hungry for what you see/what you get though. I don't think this game would run well on low-end PC's. Also, it is pretty funny.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: My experience with this game was really bad. I liked the platformer and point and click adventure combo but graphical glitches ruins a lot, I had to restart a couple times because the platformer guy got stuck underground and game crashed. The platformer bits are pretty casual, but keyboard and mouse controlls gets frustrating. It felt like some sort of input lag you wait for the guy to realize you pressed a button. I think it was designed with controllers in mind and I don't use a controller, so sucks for me I guess.It's not a bad game and the bugs I experienced might be an issue on my end but I ended up uninstalling in the early game, the graphics style I love and decent humor doesn't carry the game for me. Honestly I regret buying it but it might work for you, who knows?
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: If you like mashups of point and click adventures and 2D platformers, as well as funny jokes and works that star their creators, this is the game for you.Okay, maybe that isn't the best sales pitch. Uhhhh...Look, this game is thoroughly great. Somehow, through great design, it takes two completely opposing styles of game and makes them work together, with absolutely minimal clunkiness, in a way that fans of either genre can understand and be able to play this game with little confusion. Like a more extreme version of Lost Vikings, Ben and Dan interact with the game world in completely different ways. The dialog is funnier and more meta than that game too, with lots of dialog, including much lovely bickering between Ben and Dan and a unique, funny response for almost every action the player could take as Ben. Not to mention that the puzzles are cleverer and better put together than LV too, pushing the game to its absolute limits and requiring the player to seriously think outside the box, yet I was still able to go through the entire game in one sitting without needing any hints, and without having to use the in-game store at all. Thoroughly wonderful game, the few negatives (like a bug where Dan briefly glitches into the ground when he jumps on Ben's head) are outweighed immensely by the positives, and the creators are working vigilantly to improve the game until it's the absolute best version of itself it can be. Wonderful game. Heartily recommend.As a, ahem, bonus, the game comes with a visual novel, absolutely free, no way to get the game without the VN. Yeah. Ugh...
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: This may quite honestly be one of the most well thought out, well planned, creative games I have played my entire life.From apocalypses to hacking to 3d to...I don't know what to say beyond:If you love point and clicks OR platformers, this is a must play.If you get stuck, just be sure to talk to people.This is the most amazing game I have played in the last five years.
_childDocuments_.name: Lair of the Clockwork God

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game a long while and honestly it was definitely worth it! I also had to wait a little longer to experience it as the launch window fell the week I was moving house - sods law!After finally playing and completing the game, I can honestly say that it's the best Point-And-Click game I've ever played, and certainly up there in the top few Indie Darling platformer games I've ever played too. The unique way in which the two genres are combined sounds weird at first, but Size Five achieved effortless synergy of the two in this game (no doubt through A LOT of trial and error during development). The end result was certainly one for the ages, perhaps we can hope to see more genre-mashing in the future!As for the game - it's incredibly funny, emotional in parts (What, you're telling me a Ben and Dan game is going to make me FEEL things? pffft) (yeah, one or two parts got  deeper than I was expecting), well thought through, and generally executed to a fine tee.The puzzles in the game have well designed solutions, some were silly/easy solutions (as mocked by Ben), and some solutions hit Hideo Kojima mind-blowing levels of design (not really a spoiler ahead but tags out of respect) . I'd love to see more of Ben and Dan's puzzle design in the future, it's only gotten better with age... like a fine wine!The sheer amount the game achieves in terms of variety, mechanics, polish (such as lines for a considerable number of random interactions for Ben) is honestly impressive considering how small the core development team is - primarily Dan Marshall and Ben Ward. Their experience from past titles is clear as day with ever evolving adventure game tropes building on BTDT, TGP, and the old adventure games they're such big fans of; smooth platforming mechanics with inspiration from The Swindle, Gun Monkeys, and of course the many indie darling platformers the game regularly pokes fun at (as well as highlighting some of it's best qualities and testing our assumptions of well defined linguistics of the genre a couple of times).There are a few jokes in the game I missed out on, either I'm not old enough to get the reference, or I've not seen the particular game/film/tv show to truly appreciate the punchline - but that's okay, not every joke is going to land with everyone, and the number that stick the landing vastly outweighs those that flew right over my head! I genuinely found myself laughing out loud at home alone to some lines I'll remember for a long time!As a quick round off of some other features - the accessibility options are thorough, clearly a step above from their past titles and even most other games on the market. Whilst the humour might be immature in parts (plenty of poo, bum, and penis jokes) it's never distasteful, and sensitive topics are treated with the respect they deserve (a reflection of Ben and Dan's own growth in the past 10 years no doubt) and poke fun at the negative sources of these remarks rather than the subject matter itself (for example - racists and sexists are the butt of the joke). Whilst the overarching themes of the game might touch upon gloomy, the journey along the way is light-hearted and memorable. There are a couple of aspects of the game that people might not "get" or could cause them to think of the game in a poor light (big spoiler in the following tags)  but people should give it a chance, there's always more under the surface you're not aware of! Everything has purpose, and Size Five have not overlooked that one bit.Overall the game is an absolute blast, well deserving of all the positive critic and user reviews coming it's way. I would expect in the future this game could become a milestone we look back upon to see where adventure and platforming games are at in the early 2020's. Hopefully we don't have to wait another 10 years for a sequel, but equally if it's as polished, well executed, and consistent as this then I look forward to the sequel in 2030!P.S. If you're reading this and still have any doubt in your mind about whether to buy it, you REALLY should - it deserves a lot more recognition. Plus the additional sales will (hopefully) bring us more of that Ben and Dan design, humour, and fun that we all love.

_childDocuments_.review: Tags: Adventure - SidescrollAdditional Tags: RefundTLDR: Gobliiins style platformer puzzler hybrid with mixed polish, fun writing and a somewhat unfun gameplay loop. Wait for a heavy sale.I've completed these dev's previous adventure games and really found the writing and the main characters endearing. I was attracted to see a new game come from them, especially since after launching I noticed that the game was in unity, which is definitely an improvement over Adventure Game Studio engine. 4K support and controller support were well handled. The ambiant audio track was relaxing. The graphics looked very unity-like but were acceptable.I took special notice of a heavy use of tooltips. The activated character is shown as activated with a subtle overhead arrow and contextual hotspot menus with appropriate gamepad binds are shown and updated smoothly bottom left corner of the screen. The handling of more complex operations or choosing dialogue is done through a radial menu using the analog sticks. Works nicely overall. Smooth.The quality of the platforming was a tad strange... with the character not quite falling when walking past ledges, and some odd quirky behaviors in the momentum at times. It is possible that this is due to the "platformer assist" feature that aims to correct results of user inputs to make the platforming easier but I have not spent time testing that theory out.The writing is still interesting but leans heavily on gaming mechanics, and the fact that the game uses two different conventions, one from platformer one from adventure games. It works nicely and perhaps it opens up as the story progresses. There is also quite a bit of meta commentary which in this case works but that I am not usually a fan of. There is only so much comments about how adventure games combine inventory and how platforrmers can be gimmicky that you can handle before it gets redundant.The deciding factor in my decision to refund is that I simply do not find the gameplay loop fun. It always boils down to moving forward with a character, hitting an obstacle, swapping characters, moving that character forward, and starting to mentally map out if a combined action of the two can progress. There is also the environment navigation aspect where a useful trigger might be hidden somewhere around the multiple platforms. It's not the worst and it's not often done. It has... *some* originality. Because of the laid back mood and the humor I would probably play this to completion too. I just have only so much to spend money on in terms of my gaming library and other concerns that offering five dollars for an experience I know is part of a niche I dont belong to is not really something I can do at the moment. I could rebuy at same price later if I ran out of things to get, or preferably get this for an even heavier discount or as part of a bundle. But for today I would like to be credited back. Especially since it is likely that I will get stuck on a puzzle and go past the 2 hour refund window without really getting a chance of assessing more about the game. I might be in the  minority but a in-game hint system might have swayed my decision here.My compliments to the dev on all the progress they've made in terms of offering a decently executed product and their brand is still, in my eyes, attractive... I'll just have to skip on this temporarily.

_childDocuments_.review: Cross a point-and-click adventure, a platform game, and comedy about game design and the result  be truly awful.  It isn’t.A brilliantly realised title that never stops laughing at itself and the world we live in, Lair of the Clockwork God (almost) seamlessly yo-yos between point and click and platforming, with a very knowing nod to the joys and horrors of each genre, against the background of our planet succumbing to the apocalypse.  It’s testament to the skill and sheer imagination of the development team that whenever the shtick feels on the verge of getting tired, they pull a rabbit out of the hat and switch the gameplay mechanic, spinning things in a different, completely unexpected direction.  One minute you’re shooting at possessed pinatas, the next you’re contemplating the meaning of existence in the world’s most hilariously overwrought walking simulator.  It's anarchy, in the best possible way.Pretty much the only issues I’d point to are ones that aren’t bad enough to ruin the experience.  First, a few of the platform segments are on the too-difficult side (but the game knows that well enough to include regular checkpoints and not to let them outstay their welcome).  Second, some of the controls take more getting used to than they should, namely interfacing with things (a fiddly affair that requires you to use keyboard and mouse at the same time while standing in the right place and too often leaves you accidentally repeating the same dialogue for the fifth time when you wanted to twiddle with your inventory), some of the switching between characters, and the jump / wall clinging mechanism, which can be frustrating beyond belief because it works the opposite way to what a keyboard user would expect (don’t hold down the jump key).As problems go, they’re minor, and put it this way: any game that manages to condense into three minutes of hilarious dialogue -- played out while a building is collapsing around you and monsters from outer space do their utmost to devour you -- the very same points that it takes a game like Disco Elysium its entire play time and a million words of po-faced gibberish to articulate (badly) has got to be a winner in my book.This isn’t just smart, warm, very funny writing.  This is seriously good game design that breaks every rule of how computer games are supposed to work and leaves you with a big smile on your face.  It’s worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played about 3 hours of the game thus far. Will be updating this review as I play more. Also going to keep it spoiler free.To start off, I am not the biggest fan of the platformer/point and click format. That being said, Layer of the Clockwork God is a game that oozes personality and creativity. It doesn't feel much like a game but more like a journey of two good friends who enjoy making each other miserable at times (I'm assuming that is how Ben and Dan are in real life) and are bringing you along for the ride.So think Deadpool and Negasonic Teenage Warhead going on an adventure with you.Now let's get into the ACTUAL review of the game thus far at 3 hours played.The gameplay is relatively simple, in terms of the platforming mechanics (from what I have encountered so far). The puzzles on the other hand are a different beast...it could be that I am not used to using my noggin while playing games anymore (thanks EA), but man some of them are tough...I am currently at one where I have to solve an ACTUAL puzzle. The silver lining, there may be a way to bypass said puzzle, which in itself is a puzzle...so there in lies the dilemma, which puzzle is easier to solve??????This in my opinion makes the game fun, you actually have to think and all the while you have Dan and Ben making quips about the going ons around you.The game is also FULL of references to the genres of Platforming and Point and Click that poke fun at or use the tropes as mechanics of the game. It is genius level game development. Tying in mechanics to the dialogue and making it seamless and extremely entertaining. SO basically nothing is forbidden and everything is permitted in Lair of the Clockwork God.So far I have no complaints. I will update the review with more details as I play more.As of right now, definitely recommend buying this gem...if you like point and click or platforming, or have a sarcastic sense of humor, you will love this game.OH AND THE VISUALS AND ART STYLE ARE AMAZING! I have died multiple times because I was too busy admiring the background and what was happening there...
