_childDocuments_.review: Conan Chop Chop is a mixed bag that will give back plenty if you put a few hours into it, but the quality of what it gives largely depends on what you want from it to begin with.Room to room based combat and meta progression are a genre staple at this point, and the core gameplay of this one in particular is fun, but not without a few problems. First and foremost there is no option to rebind keys. I personally had an issue that only happened in online co-op (more on that later) where the game decided I was using a controller while I had none plugged in. This lead to me not having a cursor on the screen, making aiming with my sword and/or bow interesting to say the least. Speaking of the bow, it is naturally bound to left CTRL. Oof for some.There are two currency based progressions in the game. One is your character's skill points. Each character has multiple skills to unlock that range from basic +max health starts to unique traits. The other form is unlocking items such as weapons, armors, shields and charms (perks such as having a pig or chicken follow you around, or coating your weapon with fire, etc.) So here's the thing about co-op. I couldn't find a single game online, and the community created Discord is more dead than not. Luckily a friend snagged this game, so we played it to completion together. Inviting people is simple, as is connecting. Remember the meta progression? Well, if you are a visitor, you can't unlock weapons, charms, etc. This was done on purpose. This is fine though, because the currency will carry over if you fire the game up in single player. The bigger issue is that sometimes enemies die, but.... they don't. Only one player can see them. The issue is that the rooms lock until they are cleared and if there is an enemy that has no health bar and can't hurt you and you can't hurt it, well, that's a soft lock. The first few times we thought it was funny, but the further in we got and the more it happened, we got annoyed. I have many theories as to what causes the bug, and mind you it didn't happen SUPER often, but that is a huge buzz kill, especially later in the game when we built our characters and had decent items.Despite all this, I got my money's worth. I had more fun than not parrying slimes, understanding boss patterns and making builds. Personally, this one gets a yes from me because I had fun and I got decent play time out of this. I mentioned all of the big things that could potentially put people off to make this as informative as possible. I looked for a fun game to play with a buddy, and that's what I got back.

_childDocuments_.review: It's... okay. It's a poor man's  . It would be a lot better if it didn't suffer from so many issues.  In particular:• Something is seriously wrong with the hitboxes, causing you to  take damage when you shouldn't.• The game doesn't do a good job of telegraphing when you take damage, so you won't even know that you've taken unfair damage until you look at your healthbar and see that it's low.  This leads to surprise deaths.• It's possible to take damage (and even die) during cutscenes, when you can't move. I lost to the secret final boss in this way.• The invincibility frames after taking damage are way too short. If you get caught inside a continuous attack (such as a spin attack, which all the bosses have), you go from full HP to 0 almost instantly.• The boss design is lazy. Every boss (except for one) is a small variation of the same fight. The secret final boss is literally just all the previous bosses copy+pasted into a single fight.• There's a "waiting for players" softlock bug that can even happen in single-player. Fortunately it only happened once to us, but it causes you to lose  progress and have to restart. Even your experience gets reset.• There's only a handful of viable builds. All the weapons are same-y, and there's only about 30 or so trinkets. A few of the trinkets don't even work right.• The devs have known about all of these issues since launch, but have apparently abandoned the game.If you are a zealous fan of  and need something new to scratch that itch, this is a fun one to play with friends. But for everyone else, go play Heroes of Hammerwatch first.

_childDocuments_.review: The game clearly has potential and the classes and weapons I tried were very fun to use. Overworld movement is too slow, even with the dash abilities.Unfortunately, I've encountered several game breaking bugs in roughly 1.5 hours of playtime. Reading through the community discussions, it seems there is a lack of communication from the developers. On top of that there is a large list of fixes already and the game is still very buggy. I'd say wait and come back to it after you've checked if there are improvements. All in all I have to rate this negatively, despite the potential and really liking the gameplay so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I admit this review is kind of biased, because at the moment of writing I and my wife have played this game for only 5 hours in local coop. But aw man, what can I say, seriously, how this game handles progression is kind of unnerving. To get things straight, yeah, I get it, Conan Chop Chop obviously is meant to be more in a traditional Roguelike spirit (sorry for my non-purist view, but it just didn’t feel very Roguelite to me like the game description states). My biggest gripe, even if you beat any or several area bosses, in the next run you STILL have to start all over again if you die. But in my opinion actually this concept completely ruins the overall fun. Really, the game would have been SO much better if you could start in the next area after beating a boss, like so many other famous Roguelikes and -lites do (e.g. Children of Morta, Crypt of the Necrodancer etc.). But I guess they didn’t implement that because the game only features 4 areas, and then you’d probably rush through it too quickly (and the content is lacking). Anyway, the leveling system (to alleviate some minor aspects) sucks as well in local coop. You see, you only get the same XP as in single player after a run, but you have to pay for 2-4 players to level up, which of course is super arduous all in all (multiple the grind so to speak). Sigh, everything just costs so much, while you get so little experience in the first levels, which means either you get lucky by getting the perfect items in a run to reach higher areas and get more XP, or if not (because chests/keys, hearts dropped and items sold are extremely unbalanced), repeating and repeating the first levels over and over again. Tedious, boring and grindy over time, especially if you keep in mind that you have to level up all 4 characters for all achievements. Add to this that weapons, charms, armor etc. also always start at early tiers in the hub shops (good advice, don’t buy too much, you’ll get better gear in the chests afterwards soon), and also with few varieties, because the other currency needed for better unlocks is super scarce in the first levels as well. Seriously, everything is just so horribly und unnecessarily time-consuming, this just drags everything down in my opinion.Long story short, under the line Conan Chop Chop definitely could be really promising, but the state it’s in, I don’t know. Some other reviews say it’s supposedly based on 4 players, which would explain why the bosses are so darn hard (you simultaneously always have to fight off a wildly moving boss and other quick, re-spawning, area-damaging enemies, way easier with several partners). But for me, urg, my experience is just a negative one at the moment. Sure, I might get back to it once in a while, just to see how much we’re able to progress, but it’s definitely not my favorite pastime right now. And I seriously wouldn’t pay full price for it (got it in Humble Choice, so at least that’s nothing I can complain about).Edit: Meanwhile we played it a whole lot longer, and guess what, we found out that you can practically save everywhere (even inside the dungeons). Just quit a game when you got a good load-out and managed some levels/rooms well, backup your file, and if you fail after that, just exchange those files and use ‘Continue’ (if you’re wondering, the save is in AppData-LocaLow-Funcom_Oslo_AS). At least then the game definitely is slightly more fun, and you can easily test out new attacks/rhythms of bosses in the later levels. Keeps your mind saner ;) But I still hate the area 4 boss, and the fact that in some levels the map just scrolls too slowly so that enemies shoot you from outside the screen is stupid. Nevertheless, my first-impression negative rating still stands, because all those workarounds shouldn’t be necessary in the first place. And even then you’ll probably need a lot of super grindy re-runs to achieve all achievements and upgrades, not speaking about the balancing issues all over the place regarding the player number and item spawning. In my opinion especially the levelling system needs a SERIOUS makeover, because meanwhile we also noticed that the higher you max out your overall profile level, the less experience you get in future runs for the skill points, which means the 3rd to 4th character got horrific costs (just for an example, in early runs you get 14 skill points when you reach boss 4, but in the next run only 7, next 5, and later obviously like someone reported only 1). And like I said, in local coop (where 2 players are mandatory after all) this equals to hell incarnate. Urggh, I don’t know, this game is just so unpolished and got so many issues (the damage telegraphing that other reviews speak of also annoys me a lot actually, you never know what really hit you). Seriously, everything considered, under the line this game just feels like a kind of hate-love-relationship which is bad for you in the end. I mean, as good as the game looks and feels at first glance, and even if you just love the Conan trope, but who in the world would replay a game like this (with only 4 levels) hundreds of times, just to unlock everything, when there are lots of fair, modern and clever scripted Roguelites with extremely high replayability value and lots of variation?

_childDocuments_.review: We got some fun out of this game, but it's severely lacking in variety and needs some gameplay/balance tweaks.  Overall game feels too easy/grindy/irrelevant, and it's hard to want to push through it again and again to get another try at last boss.  Whether you "have a good run" comes down to what charms you get (90%) and what weapons/armor you get at the top tier (10%) - as the weapons you get earlier are mostly irrelevant/outclassed.  Both are completely out of your control.  If we could get a good set of charms (eg. the one that gives you an extra dash and the one that lets you hold more meat) I think we'd probably beat the last boss.. but we've got mono-trash (you don't see that many charms in a run) the last couple times and I don't have the patience to try again.In terms of gameplay: the game seems to work best at 2 players - 1 player would be lame, more makes the screen to crowded.  Lots of the damage you take feels cheap (eg. projectiles from off-screen enemies, getting snagged on the corner of scenery bits).  The simplest approach "dash and kite" is pretty bland, but seems way safer/more-effective than trying to time parries and what not.  Again, the levels/enemies/bosses all feel way too similar to each other, making the overall game feel super repetitive.To be clear, it's not a terrible game, and I really like playing a simple co-op action game with the kids.. but it's close to being something much better.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for January 2023, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before February 7th, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A multiplayer rogue-lite. Conan Chop Chop is a fresh take on the Conan character, using the style of Cyanide & Happiness, as well as the gameplay of Binding of Isaac, though without the darkness of either of those.  There’s an ability to add in up to four players including couch co-op which is a nice touch.  The story has a bit of solid humor.  The combat is good, though parry heavy, and there’s different equipment you earn.However, the first boss was brutally hard, to the point that we only took off less than a third of his life bar on the two chances we got to reach him.  It feels like the game wants the player to master the encounters more than anything else.  There is unlockable equipment, which might help, but that boss felt like a major skill or grind wall. Pick this up if you have a group to play with.  I don’t know if I’d enjoy this as much solo, but it also was more interesting with multiple people.  I played this game alongside my daughter and we had a good time with it though it’s probably not going to be something we will rely on.  Still, it felt like a fun and unique game that I wasn’t expecting. _childDocuments_.review: It is okay for the money,  I should start off by saying that the game is fun, and it is more fun with friends. The rest of this review is showing off game issues that impact me as a player.the game does have a few problems such as: -hit detection problems on bosses (although they seem to be rare)-the game likes to jump down to 29hz with vsync on for some reason, which makes the entire game feel choppy and unresponsive. I have to force it back to 60hz frequently in settings.-the game plays relatively poorly on keyboard and mouse, you need a controller to really enjoy it, but-there are no key rebindings in game, you have to do it through steam or scripts-collision detection on bomb arrows is poor and they frequently get stuck on the wall you're standing next to while firing your bow-there's a synchronization bug with traps where traps will be active in an already cleared room (they are supposed to be disabled) for everyone but the host when you revisit the room.-some doors do not appear on the map or minimap in dungeons (these are regular doors, not secrets)and the core loot mechanic is pretty bad because it is based on unlocks which add items to the loot table, but then all of the loot is randomly dropped in the world.  This means that you are less likely to get what you want as you unlock more items, leading to a regression in getting what you actually like.It seems like a weird design decision because the starting town has random loot you can buy with starting money, so you can restart the game over and over until you get what you want, but that leaves you with the question, why not just let players play how they want to? Try different builds? etc? The random loot throughout the world is great, but forcing players to play builds that they don't like "because RNG" isn't very fun.XP in the game is universal, which means if you build up the wrong character, and then want to switch to a bow character for example (because melee with the keyboard and mouse feels bad), you then have to slowly level up the higher universal levels to get points to distribute in your second character. There are no respecs, and it's saved in the cloud so you can't fix it by starting over.The game has a number of unskippable screens when you start it, and when you begin a new game. If you want to emphasize that you need a controller to play, do it in the steam store and not every single time we start the game.Overall it's pretty fun for a cheap game, only get it on sale and if you have friends who want to play with you. It reminds me of Castle Crashers a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: Conan Chop Chop is a rather charming take on the titular REH hero.  Players can choose from Conan, Valeria, Bêlit, and Pallantides and play solo - which is challenging at first and requires some grinding to get a solo character to survivable level - or together in groups of 2, 3, or 4.  Despite the comic strip style, Conan Chop Chop is full of the mayhem that one might expect from killing lots and lots and lots of enemies.  The comic art is actually rather endearing, and there are lots of little cosmetic touches that can be appreciated once the frenetic combat has stopped.  Thoth-Amon is trying to resurrect Xaltotun, but only has one half of The Heart of Ahriman, so Thoth-Amon decides to trick the heroes into competing in a battle to find a strong enough sacrifice to complete the ritual.  (This is all explained in the intro, so I'm not divulging any spoilers.)Players can customize weapons (melee and ranged), armor (suit and shield), and charms for lots of different interesting effects.  Each hero has certain special abilities that change how each is to be played - for example, Conan is good with all weapons, but great with swords, while Bêlit really excels with bows - and at the end of every adventure (and you will die many, many times) - your stats are summarized (e.g., time alive, damage dealt, gold collected) that awards you experience which is converted into points used to unlock new abilities or bonuses.  Leveling up not only helps your character but also your base village, which in turn unlocks more powerful weapons, armor, and charms.Players will quickly figure out how to play the game, although I do recommend going through the tutorial as it was helpful.  Mini-bosses in each level are appropriately tough, and each end level boss is rather daunting if playing solo and requires wise planning.  (I won't spoil the surprises of these bosses, but one is clearly visible in the promo art, and if you are familiar with "Rogues in the House", it will still bring a smile to your face when this boss appears.)  Each area has its own style related to its geography in Hyperborea, and new opponents will deploy some new mechanics that will keep you on your toes.  The audio is very well done with some great dynamic/adaptive music.Overall, I find Conan Chop Chop to be very true to the spirit of Conan and a fun take on the days of high adventure.  I would like to thank the fine folks at Funcom for gifting me with this game after an extended, informative conversation about all things Conan.  I think Conan Chop Chop is a good twist on the rogue-lite genre and the developers wove in a lot of great Conan references.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good little game, I enjoyed playing it. The combat is smooth and well paced. The art is pleasant and somewhat whimsical. The music, sound and particle effects are well suited to the game.That being said, I am a bit disappointed in the lack of content. I'm not a big fan of rogue-like games, starting over after every death is frustrating as a player, and shows lack of resources/commitment by the devs. The public multi-player match making does not work at all, so I was forced to play through the game solo. I had to play through it over a dozen times before making it to the end boss. I finally beat Xoltun and was hoping to fight Thoth-Amon, but instead I am forced to fight shade versions of the 4 bosses from the previous zones. I found that upsetting and a lazy move by the devs. To top it off they don't even drop you any health hearts in-between fights. I'm sure all that would be a lot easier if the multi-player was working, but as a solo player I'm done with that nonsense.In conclusion, it's a fun game that was cut short due to lack of content. A non-functioning public multiplayer made for a somewhat frustrating solo experience. With the current price the game is worth every penny, and I would really like to see more content added.

_childDocuments_.review: Editing my review after extensively playing the game (mainly on console).Huge amount of Fundamental design flaws with this game: - It's a roguelite yet it doesn't respect your time at all. It forces a lot of backtracking (especially with keys and dungeon exploration) instead of keeping the moment always pushing forwards.This is made worse by the fact that a lot of mechanics such as the boss' spinning attacks are almost always = instant death.- The success of your run isn't determined by your choices, because there are none. It's always the same. You never think, oh I should've gone left or right, or I should've gone with the HP buff instead of dmg. When you die, it's only due to overpowered mechanics that force you to grind out character power. The developers don't even understand the principles of a game like this and what makes them good.- Boring repetitive music. - Uninspiring enemy design and lack of variety.- Dungeons all feel and look the same.- You can't create "builds" because the forced power increase from tier to tier means you have to change all your equipment after each boss or you don't do enough damage. There is 0 reason to double / triple enemy hp after each boss. No idea what the devs were smoking.- Boring / uninspiring progression systems. - Forcing you to level your character to reach unobtainable chests is bad design, especially when you don't explain it. - Lack of dev support and communication is disgusting.

_childDocuments_.review: Played about 90 minutes, refunded.The thing is, I'm totally going to buy it on Switch for $20 to play with my wife and 11-year-old. As a local multiplayer light action RPG romp, it's great. But as a computer game, it falls short. Technically, it's an action roguelike—same genre as Hades, Dead Cells, etc. The combat lacks heft. You don't "feel" hits, explosions, blocks, and enemy deaths. Numbers float above their heads until they die, at which point they just ... disappear. All of this is kind of okay when you're playing on a big screen, but when you play on a computer monitor the lack of effort put into the combat tactility is really evident.There is some mechanical interest in the form of different characters, weapons, and skills, but not enough to justify this game's existence in a genre crowded with landmark titles. Recommended as a fun and relatively simple multiplayer diversion on your Switch; not recommended on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review:
The treacherous wizard Thoth-Amon has devised a plan to resurrect the ancient evil that is Xaltotun. If he succeeds, he will condemn the world to an eternity of darkness and enslavement. Only you can stop him, but in order to do so you must use all your cunning. All your guile. You must summon all your courage and swordsmanship. You must Chop Chop!

Conan Chop Chop is the most epic and realistic stick figure game ever to be set in the world of Conan the Barbarian, thus there will be an excessive amount of gore and flying limbs. Be warned that this may in turn lead to uncontrollable outbursts of joy and/or profanities, usually depending on which end of the sword you are on.

1-4 players
Play solo for the ultimate thrill of a roguelike or have your buddies along with you in online or couch co-op mode.

Become Conan or someone else!
All brawns, no brain? No worries! Choose between a diverse cast of badass warrior gods, and add weapons and items to match your style!

Embark on quests of pure epicness!
You are about to save the world! The merchants are still going to charge you for their wares, and some townsfolk may even pester you with tasks of their own. But fear not, some of them will make it worth your while.

Explore in every direction!
Brave the shifting sands of Koth, explore the dark woods in Darkwood, move valiantly through the searing land of Hyperboria and see the icy world of Vanaheim. Conan® Chop Chop lets you explore to the left, right, up and down! A skilled player may even find himself jumping, dashing, or moving diagonally, resulting in the ultimate 3D experience.

Loot, loot and more loot!
Master the fine art of delicately bashing your enemies' heads in with a broom and turning them into chop suey with a bastard sword. Conan® Chop Chop contains a wide variety of different weapons, trinkets and legendary items, each suited to tailor any kind of violent playstyle you can think of.

Master astonishing combos!
Perform the breathtaking 360° spin-attack to crack skulls all around you. Dash forward with the speed of light. Swing your sword both longways and sideways in a game that will have you gasping for air as you struggle to grasp the pure awesomeness of your fighting moves.

Ruthless bosses!
Before facing Thoth-Amon, you must defeat bosses such as The Giant Sand Worm of Koth and The Frost Giant of Vanaheim, neither of which are particularly sympathetic to your cause. Instead they will attempt to destroy you with killer moves like Lava Reflux, Tail Whip and Loogie Glob.

Infinite replayability!
Completely random maps and tons of weapons and abilities to try out ensure that every new game will be a whole new experience. You are bound to die more than once, but you can unlock new weapons that will be available for your next play-through.

name: Metal: Hellsinger
detailed_description: Reviews About the Game Part human, part demon, and bent on vengeance. Become The Unknown, and fight through the fiercest domains of Hell on an infernal ride to face the Red Judge herself. You have a score to settle. Metal: Hellsinger is a rhythm FPS, where your ability to shoot on the beat will enhance your gameplay experience. The more in sync you are with the rhythm, the more intense the music will become and the more destruction you will cause. Defeat the demon hordes with your skull-clad blade or range of murderous weaponry. Once your ultimate is ready, unleash havoc with the weapon ability of your choice. Enter the Leviathan game mode, where you must defeat increasingly challenging waves of demons in hellish arenas. As you progress, make brutal decisions about what upgrades to choose, and forge yourself into a true headbanging machine of death. Every track has been created specifically for the game by composer duo Two Feathers, with vocals by metal icons such as Serj Tankian (System of a Down), Randy Blythe (Lamb of God), Alissa White-Gluz (Arch Enemy), and many more! Play through an epic storyline, narrated by award-winning actor Troy Baker. Unlock special challenges and conquer the realms of Torment to become more powerful and get a leg up on the leaderboards. Although commonly known as Hell, The Infernal Planes is in reality a union of a thousand Hells, all of which are terrifying and diabolical in their own way. In order to dethrone The Red Judge, you must fight your way through the fiercest corners, from the icy world of Voke to the maddening world of Stygia. Metal: Hellsinger is created by an experienced FPS team at The Outsiders and is the passion project of David Goldfarb, Game Director on Payday 2 and Lead Designer on Battlefield 3 and Battlefield: Bad Company 2. For content creators, we have done everything from our side to make sure strikes won't happen.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely a recommendation. Takes the ideas that BPM put forward as a game, and expands them into a narrative-driven experience, with insanely talented musicians on board. Lets you score chase and everything, too. A fantastic rhythm game, a fantastic soundtrack, and a fantastic experience.Even if you aren't musically inclined, beat assist mode is available, too.And if you think the music in this game might turn you away - trust me, try the demo, give it a shot. It's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: A gem of a game. So you understand how good it is -  my potato pc ran this game at 15-30 fps and I still rushed through it like an adrenaline junkie and had an absolute blast playing it. Only bad things I can say about it is that the performance isn't super great and the bosses are a bit meh, besides the final boss which is just awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome hellbound FPS game with an insanely perfect metal soundtrack. The gameplay is like a mix of Doom and Crypt of the Necrodancer and though it isn't really a revolution in the FPS genre the rhythm-based shooting gimmick is enough to carry you through at least one playthrough. I do wish there were more weapons and bosses (you only fight one OVER AND OVER... why?!). Not only that but I was kind of hoping the story would be a bit more linear instead of just quick arcadey levels. Its also, incredibly short clocking in at 4-6 hours depending on your skill level.Gotta say though Hearing Serj Tankian from System of a Down and Tatiana Shmayluk from Jinjer made this an incredible experience from a sound front.Overall, its a pretty decent FPS that didn't blow me away as much as I had hoped. I believe it is carried by a cool mechanic and expertly crafted soundtrack that do little to cover up the shortcomings no matter how unique the game itself is. I hope this series continues in the future going all in on the idea of rhythm-based shooters, but just goes a little more in depth in terms of scope.7.5/10 - A fine entry in the over-saturated PC FPS genre that is sure to stand out among others. Just don't expect it to completely blow you away too much.

I thought the mini bosses where going to be repetitive too but i was mistaken(Other than the similar design). If there ever is a heaven DLC ill be on stand by XDPS. Stygia's theme is an absolute blast.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game open minded, and it was so much better than I thought!The game play was smooth, the sound track was epic, the battle mechanics are not to difficult, the game is challenging enough and the story is solid.The stage bosses needed a bit more variety, but all in all, a good couple of hours worth of play!

_childDocuments_.review: omg this is so fun. pros: * it's a rhythm game, and it is really accurate.* it's like Doom, but Doom gives me motion sickness, this does not.* so far, the plot is interesting* each weapon seems to have its own strengths and tactics- your starter sword is just as good as "insert other weapon here".* the challenges to unlock perks are very challenging, but satisfying when accomplished* excellent choices in music that should satisfy any headbanger, metalhead, or hessian. cons:* there is (so far, to my knowledge), only one boss, but you have to fight her in different situations* Paz is really specialized, and probably won't need to use it unless you're struggling to find the area's exit* my wrists hurt now. lol

_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredibly fun game! The music is amazing, of course. Aside from that, the gameplay puts me into the flow state and I barely notice time passing. The art style and overall graphics are high-quality, especially for such a small team. The bestiary is a nice touch, offering a little more lore and flavor to the world they're creating. I only have one complaint. There isn't enough of it! You can clear through all of the content in just a few hours. There are small challenges to unlock passive buffs, but they're quick to complete. Aside from story progression, they are the only unlockables. There is no incentive to complete stages on higher difficulty. Adding some weapon skins locked behind higher difficulties or punishing challenges could help extend the experience without much dev time. And endless mode would also be a welcome addition, perhaps rotating between songs. I really love this game. I can absolutely recommend it, but be aware that it's not a very long experience. It's a good thing that the game is priced at $30. If it were fuill-priced at $60, I would have a really hard time recommending it despite how much I enjoyed it. I would absolutely buy some DLC, and hope that this studio can make more games like this. They would be insta-buys for me.

_childDocuments_.review: just go play Bullets Per Minute instead. It does the rhythm shooter angle so much better than this. It does it so much better I even have a list.1. You cannot fire on half-beats. This is by far the biggest mistake this game makes. By counting half-beats, BPM feels like it has a faster pace and makes it more forgiving as you can just hop right back into the beat instead of having to wait and ultimately missing it. BPM even counts quarter beats at some points depending on your equipment.2. Reloading feels much slower than BPM because you only need to hit the reload button once. In BPM, you MUST hit the reload button multiple times (more or less depending on the gun) in order to complete the reload. In this you just hit it once on the beat and you can't fire for a couple beats until your character is done. It does allow you to hit it a second time to make it go by faster, but that doesn't excuse it.3. You can still shoot off-beat, albeit with little to no damage. It's good that it does almost no damage, but simply being able to fire off-beat at all will cause the player to make more mistakes, as instead of frantically trying to get back on-beat you just wait until your slight difference in beat catches up.4. The music is MUCH worse from a rhythm standpoint. I did not say it's bad, it's pretty good all things considered, but it did not have as strong a base as BPM's. In BPM, I could count every beat by the song alone no matter the situation. In this, I often lose track of the beat because the game is too busy screaming into my ears and playing guitar riffs (not like I'd find the beat anyway when the drums are going so fast). I'll also add that the enemies not attacking on-beat makes this even worse because I can't follow their actions to get on-beat either.5. The beat tracker is sometimes hard to read. This may just be me being stupid, but I find the beat tracker to be way too busy. It shows the shadow of my shots so I know how far off I was, but it just ends up confusing me due to their size and length. BPM did it right by making it so that the beat tracker just turns red and continues if I make a mistake. It's so much simpler and easy to read.6. The narrator can be annoying sometimes. This isn't related to gameplay, but I find narrators interrupting the game to tell me exactly what the character is thinking instead of what I think she's thinking is just a dumb decision. There's a moment in the second level when a mysterious monster flees behind a corner. I thought to myself "I wonder what that was, guess I'll follow it to find out", and then the narrator chimed in to tell me the exact thing I was thinking. Just let me think for the character please.7. BPM has much more varied gameplay. It has many different characters and difficulties to pick from, and adds their own challenges that change how you have to play. Hellsinger does nothing of the sort, but I guess that might just be because BPM is a roguelike. At least you can start with different loadouts.8. I could tell that from a pure enemy and level design standpoint that this game is easier than BPM. This game has a long tutorial that explains super simple mechanics (for a person that's played rhythm games and shooter games before), and BPM has no tutorial at all outside a practice mode. Most of the difficulty comes from how frustrating the controls are compared to BPM for all the reasons listed above. I died within 5 minutes in BPM, and soon got good enough to beat the next couple of bosses within 15-ish minutes. I got through two stages without dying in Hellsinger, and I didn't improve by playing these stages.This does not mean the game is without its perks though. Here's a couple I could think of in the small span I'm writing this.1. The inclusion of melee weapons is such a no-brainer I'm surprised BPM didn't include it at all. I'd prefer if it was bound to a single key like borderlands, but this works perfectly fine.2. The weapons are pretty nice. I always like dual-wielded revolvers and was pleasantly surprised to see them in the trailer and game. I'm sure there's many more interesting weapons later in the game that I didn't get to see.3. It's nice that it has an actual story. BPM never even attempted at a plotline. You just go through a dungeon and kill a dragon. I especially like the narrator's voice, even though he often rudely interrupts the gameplay so I can hear what the character's thinking. If the voice was confined to just cutscenes it would make it much more tolerable.4. The graphics are much more refined than BPM's. Obviously this is due to the game's budget and the it looks much better, but I don't think it feels as inspired as BPM's. BPM's graphics are very stylized with it's cell-shaded high-saturated look. Hellsinger's looks much better, but it mostly feels like a rehash of doom. This isn't helped by it being a journey through hell.5. The player character is much cooler looking than most of the valkyries in BPM. I'm a bit of a sucker for demonic character design and this character really hits that for me. Still not as good as Gery though, nothing is.I will say that this is not a bad game. As much as I rag on it, I think it's a worthwhile game for many to play seeing it's a much more mainstream approach to a rhythm shooter. I mostly criticize all this because I think BPM is more worth your time than this because of it's much more fun gameplay and better-integrated rhythm mechanics. In some ways this feels like the comparison between Doom Eternal and Ultrakill. Ultrakill is a much more fast-paced and skill oriented shooter than Doom, and BPM is a much more fast-paced and skill oriented rhythm shooter than Hellsinger. Hellsinger even has glory kill animations

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly a game for the metalhead gamer. Incredibly fun, fast-paced gameplay, phenomenal soundtrack, fantastic visuals, I was hooked immediately. + Obvious thing out of the way, the soundtrack. As a metalhead, such a soundtrack is highly enjoyable. It SLAPS. It just makes you feel pumped and ready to kill. Each song features a famous metal vocalist and seeing all their names always filled me with excitement to keep playing on.+ Gameplay feels smooth. Controls are responsive, maps have smooth clipping, no invisible things to get caught on. You have incredible control over your character movements which is essential in such hectic gameplay.+ The “rhythm game” aspect might be a bit hard to get used to at first but once you’re past that initial hurdle, it eventually becomes second nature when you’re in the zone. Getting the sound effects (gunshots, reload) to sync up and play in tandem with the hard hitting music is incredibly satisfying. Even your footsteps always play in time with the music. All the sound design is a huge plus in general.+ 4 different guns (5 with DLC) that all handle very differently to one another. You’re sure to find your favourites. You are only allowed to take two guns at a time with you into the levels so you have to pick and choose. Bonus levels (Torments) don’t allow you to pick your weapons so you’re forced to have some time with each weapon so you have the chance to learn how to use all of them.As for the negatives, I really don’t have too much to say. These are far from the most concerning issues but they are still things I'd like to note.- Lack of the traditional quick-switch button is highly disappointing. It’s such a universally used control in first person shooters so I really wonder why it wasn’t included in this game. There is a button to quick-switch to Paz (a specific weapon) which I do find useful but I don’t see why both controls couldn’t be included as separate bindings. Relying on scrolling or pressing number keys is hella annoying and always risks you switching to the wrong weapon when in a critical situation. Really miss it.- The game’s performance really dips during high activity moments. The range of fps is quite large, it can drop from a comfortable frame rate really quickly which gets distracting in a first person shooter. It didn’t hinder me too much while playing, but it is something to note if you’re worried about your rig's ability to run this game.- (Incoming salt) Everything was pretty well balanced up until the final boss. I didn’t die a single time in any of the previous levels during my first playthrough on Goat difficulty. Come to the final boss and it’s an absolute train wreck of a fight, if you can even call it that. It’s a chaotic first person bullet hell. I did manage to beat on my second try (like months later cuz I'm lazy) so it is doable for sure. But it might catch some people off guard if they didn't find the rest of the game as challenging. Yes, it's the final boss. It’s supposed to be challenging. But I expected it to be a little more intuitive than just running and dashing around randomly in hopes of not getting hit. I feel like the main issue is the lack of healing opportunities in the first section of the battle. If you deplete the available health crystals too quickly, you’re kinda on your own. You don’t get the opportunity to slaughter fodder (which also heals you) until much later.I intentionally avoided making comparisons to the Doom series but there is no doubting that they are very similar games. If you enjoy Doom and are interested in adding a little rhythm element to your gameplay, I can pretty much guarantee that you will enjoy this game as well. And for everyone else, there’s a lot of fun to be had in this game. It’s not the longest game, but you’re still sure to get your money’s worth with the 8 - 10 hours you’ll put into completing the campaign, and the all Torment levels.

_childDocuments_.review: As a metalhead, this is the perfect game for me, well almost.A combination of Doom-style shooting and rhythm-based mechanics... to the beat of ONE OF THE BEST SOUNDTRACKS EVER WRITTEN. HELL ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ YES. The concept is fantastic and executed mostly well.My main issues are the visual clarity and some of the enemy design.There are an insane number of projectiles in this game, especially in the latter half, to the point that it is difficult to tell what's going on on-screen. The lighting in some areas just seems off in some way and makes it hard to notice enemies at times.The green bug things and stalkers are often very frustrating to deal with, the former because of what feels like extremely janky hitboxes, and the latter because of the constant teleporting that clashes with the rhythm-based shooting. I understand what they were going for with these enemies, but it doesn't work in the context of this game.The bosses consist of repetitive bullet hells and the final boss is especially poorly designed as close range weapons don't even work in its second phase, which I think is a huge oversight.The story is there, but I got tired of the narrator with the cowboy accent pretty quickly and he just narrates for so long without any substance in the writing. I wish there was less focus on the story. Other than that, the gameplay is fantastically exhilarating and all the songs are absolute bangers that are stuck in my head. Highly recommended for any metalhead gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Metal: Hellsinger is a great, metal music based game that any metalhead will enjoy. Also, I believe those who are not metalheads, or into metal at all, may still find it fun. The game has some shortcomings, but for the most part, it is solid, fun and well made.Pros:+ Superb, memorable, dynamic soundtrack created by real metal musicians, including but not limited to, Lamb of God's Randy Blythe, Trivium's Matt Heafy, and the legendary Serj Tankian, most famously known from System of a Down.+ Engaging 'shoot to the beat' mechanics+ Visuals are nice to look at+ Comes with plenty of settings for controls, graphics and game play+ Side challenges are available for additional skill testing and will reward you with optional perks+ No false or fake metal, such as post-core variants. Features only true metal and true metal artists.+ Reasonable price for the provided game length and contentCons:- Has an ok story with cut-scenes consisting of off-putting, simple animation. A plot seems unnecessary overall in the grand scheme of things.- The narrator's western-american accent seems out of place. Luckily, volume controls can remedy this.- Frequent and consistent frame drops on high-end machines note poor optimization, when playing in 4K.Debatable:~ Noticeably heavily inspired by other games, such as Doom and Beats Per Minute. This is not necessarily a bad thing overall, as the final product turned out to be a good one. However, some mechanics and enemy designs are clearly taken from them.~ The 'shoot to the beat' mechanic is too simple and wastes potential to some. I can see where players are coming from when they see this, and maybe it should have been more complex for the final boss or Beast difficulty.~ The soundtrack is not currently available separately by any means. I cannot hold the game itself against this, as it purely comes down to licensing and extra work. However, the devs say it is still a possibility!In conclusion, I will recommend this game, mostly because it is fun and brings to life something I had envisioned and wanted in a game while playing Doom. There is an added bias on my part, due to the fact that a handful of my favorite artists joined this project. However, if they had been substituted by other artists that I do not know or follow, I would probably still recommend it.Overall rating: 4 of 5
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: The demo for this game really hooks you in with "Stygia" sung by Alissa White-Gluz from Arch Enemy. The final game properly saves Serj Tankian from System of a Down to end the whole affair with "No Tomorrow". The other songs are all very good, but those two stand out the most. Matt Heafy's song was also really good. All of the music was written by Two Feathers, and they did a splendid job tying the game together with its soundtrack. For a game about being a metal rhythm FPS, they kept the game soaring high. Definitely think it should've gotten Best Music at TGA 2022, but glad it got some recognition at least.I think that without question if you love metal and FPSes, you owe it to yourself to play the game. It's really short, yet replayable. Has things to unlock and is at a decent price for what's on offer. I appreciated the different weapons and their abilities, keeping it relatively simple. However, there is almost no reason to use the sword and arguably 2 of the weapons, which brings it down to 3 weapons to choose from (besides wanting some variety, you'll quickly realize what's the best). Despite that, the weapons are properly chunky and satisfying to use. The performance for me was kind of a low point, but good thing the visuals are highly stylized and still look good at medium settings.Gameplay-wise, the game felt slightly off with beat timing. I messed around with calibration, but could never get it quite right. I did get better over time, but there was something odd about the offset. Thankfully, the timing is fairly generous, so I think if you stick with it you'll get used to it. The animations accompanying the music and guns are all very smooth and satisfying. Enemy variety was fine, just didn't really like one of the tanky enemies as they had a strange hitbox on their attacks. The bosses themselves are fine bullet-hell segments, but the designs are really weak. Just the same abstract angel look across all of them - the exception being the final boss. Level design is also fine, it just kind of flows from one area to the next with nice backgrounds that remind me of Doom Eternal. Speaking of, the game definitely feels a lot like Doom Eternal but with the twist of rhythm. You NEED to shoot to the rhythm more than anything else, or else you will not be effective at all. "Glory kills" restore health, and you have movement that feels a lot like Doom Eternal. Besides that though, it heavily differs - particularly in the rhythm focus and unlimited ammo. The story was more interesting in the final parts, but it serves as a vessel and plot device to move the players forward enough. Hearing Troy Baker and Jennifer Hale were nice though, you can immediately recognize the former's voice nowadays.Overall, I really like the game and plan to play more to unlock more skins and get better scores. I think there is a lot for them to improve on in another title. I think performance and enemy variety would be welcome improvements as they have solid core mechanics, plus the metal music was top-notch. On top of that, I would love to see some beat variations rather than a consistent beat the entire time. Above all, I hope to see another title! Thanks for reading and hope you support the guys by grabbing this game if you love metal music and you already played BPM - another metal rhythm shooter.

_childDocuments_.review: The Metal album you didn't know you wanted that comes with a free game.No, seriously if you're into beat matching games and FPS like Doom, this is a great game to buy. This single player game is great just as, but factor in the leaderboard and you've got some great competition. The character performs fluidly and movement in this game has an excellent balance. Weapons in this game aren't plentiful, but unlimited ammo is beautiful. This isn't a game that's build around conserving ammo for boss fights, just use the one you prefer to engage the mobs in that moment. They all have different attack cycles to match to the beat (Revolvers shoots a faster rythem then the shottie can), so it all plays a part in the fun.The whole reason for this game is the music, and it delivers with a unique track list that is streamer friendly, so no one has to worry about getting a strike on their channel. The tracks themselves have a great line-up with the levels having their own vocalist from other bands. Seeing how this is a game based on firing off the beat, rewards for being consistant and accurate will make the track come to life. When you hear the singers really going off, you know you're in a high fury state and the battle is burning hot.There is nothing in the terms of customization other then combat related choices. I haven't came across any cosmetic choices and that's fine. Unknown is perfect in her own. Options for personal optimization can be earned early into the game.Overall, it's a very unique and well designed game. It's not a long title, but the learning curve and improvement rate is serves well to let you replay levels as your skills become more natural and combat becomes more understood. For $30, I didn't mind grabbing it. I actually saw the price first, then played the demo version. 30 minutes later after starting the demo I was uninstalling it to install the retail version, not something I normally do.Metal: Hellsinger: 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Since the dawn of time (the 2000s), man has striven for the one video game that allowed him to partake in a battle of glory to the drum of triumphant music. Perhaps the most successful of those attempts came from Tango Gameworks' Hi-Fi Rush, but there is another attempt from a year earlier that ought not to be lost to the tides of time. That game is none other than Metal Hellsinger. Truth be told, this is a pretty darn good shot at this concept, if not without its fair share of hiccups.Metal Hellsinger is pretty straightforward as a concept: it's a retro-style first person shooter with simple mechanics and the one defining feature that is shooting to the beat of the music. You get a double jump that is not tied to the beat, a dash that can be chained together if your timing is perfect, and a mild bit of depth with the ability to utilize them in different combinations or ways for different effects, such as long jumping by jumping and dashing at the same time, or star-falling by aiming towards the ground and dashing. All of your guns shoot with the left mouse button, and your right button is your ultimate that is charged with use. Your weapons may have an infinite pool of reserve ammo, but they do still require reloading which can be significantly shortened by timing the reload button to the beat that is shown on your on-screen cursor. Speaking of, your on-screen cursor will help you keep track of the beat at all times, and there is a score multiplier at the top of the screen at all times to help you keep track of how you're doing, with more elements of the background music kicking in the higher your multiplier goes.That's pretty much the game, and onto my biggest complaint that I feel is holding it back: how brief it is on content. You have a total of nine levels, the first of which is a very short tutorial level. Most levels will last you about 15-20 minutes for a rough estimate of 4 hours to finish the game. There are some additional challenges in some of the levels and a separate mode from the main game known as Leviathan mode, but they all utilize the same levels and don't alter the game in any significant meaningful way. Even the rewards from doing some of the challenges aren't even necessary at all to completing the game. The enemies are very simple to a large extent, with some later enemies standing out as especially annoying, but nothing too difficult for the player on the normal difficulty. I don't mind the enemies being simpler than usual given how much is being asked of the player to aim, move and match all of that to the beat.Barring the two default weapons of the game, you have a total of six weapons in the entire game, two of which are locked behind individual DLCs. Even if all but one of those weapons do feel incredible to use, this is the one part of the game that delivers below expectations that I am bothered by, especially with the fact that you're only allowed to take two of them with you. The shotgun, revolvers and rocket launcher are all vastly more well-rounded and better than the other three guns (yes, the DLC weapons are in fact the weakest in the game despite having to spend more real world money to be able to use them) that have far more situational uses. I could see myself resorting to the bow and arrow when having to confront any of the heavier enemies, but to be asked to give up a slot to it for an entire run is obnoxious, and will simply push me to never use it. It makes far more sense to save up the shotgun's ultimate for big enemies and to only use costumes that boost your ultimate bar build-up at the x16 score multiplier. Speaking of which, three of the costumes you get as part of one of the DLC packages have abilities locked to them that I found less fun than simply being able to use the ultimate abilities of my weapons more easily.Now onto parts of the game I dislike that aren't related to length. First is to do with the Coat of Arms, the only collectible in the game. Not only do I think adding collectibles is a disadvantage to a game as fast-paced as this, but it's also completely inconsequential. Collecting them only unlocks skins, and not only are they hardly any different from the default, but beating the game once and collecting every emblem along the way only unlocks skins for the sword and skull, the two default weapons that are always on you that you barely ever use regularly. There are also some odd collisions here and there with the terrain, and I'd suddenly find my character moving a lot slower than usual or not at all for no reason or even enemies standing on thin air. The technical aspect of this game is also not great, where you have to recalibrate your audio and video input delays at every boot and maybe a second time while in-game once you realize it's still off with how you're missing beats you normally should have hit perfectly.The story isn't much to write home about, and the aggravating repetition in the design of all the boss fights will get on your nerves, even if they all have different attack patterns. The level design can also get a tad repetitive, and could have benefited from more objects that would help with maneuverability, such as bounce pads. I also wish many of those levels didn't have tall pillars or walls in the middle that made it feel as if I have to run around the arena to locate the new batch of enemies spawning in, or even just the last remaining fodder enemy I need to take out so that I can progress. I also do wish that enemies moved to the beat as well, especially given how some are frustrating to deal with and are made far more difficult if you happen to have a slow song playing that would allow you to react less frequently. I have not yet tried Leviathan mode as of writing, but I am not confident given the sentiments echoed by various people who have.Now after spending four paragraphs criticizing the game, you would think that I would recommend against this game, but far from it. I do admit that I took a lot of time explaining just one point in one of these paragraphs, but even so, this is still a game with a rock solid concept that also comes with a lot of flaws. The concept itself works amazingly well and is backed by some incredible music and visual feedback that only enhances the experience further. The excellent sound design trickles down to the guns too, and having a game that lets you shoot with the shotgun on one beat then pump with the next is so satisfying, or even using the burst-fire rifle that will shoot additional bullets if the guitar in the song revs up and will throw up its hand attachment in the position of metal devil horns once activating the ultimate ability. I appreciate how much care went into various aspects of the game's design to pay tribute to metal culture.Metal Hellsinger is a very promising albeit flawed attempt at the concept of "Rhythm FPS." Perhaps the decisions and focus on content around the game rather than just making new content for the core game itself was not exactly the best call, and I understand that the price point of this game isn't the most attractive given its brevity. There's a lot working against this game that would normally have me thinking far less of it, but it has a core concept that is genuinely very fun and unique of which I would love to see improved upon in a potential sequel, if not other franchises tackling this idea with better success. Definitely recommending this game lightly for most folks, but certainly a stronger recommendation for metalheads. With that said, absolutely buy this on sale and try to aim for the deluxe edition with everything included. If there is a chance you might keep playing beyond your initial playthrough, you'd want to have access to all the additional songs you get from those DLC, especially the Essential Hits pack.

_childDocuments_.review: this game is a complete missed opportunity to make something wholly unique, given the complexities of metal drumming compared to many other genres. i fully agree with this comment:  . the game rewards you by following a 4/4 beat, which is FRUSTRATINGLY SLOW, much slower than you'd normally shoot when enemies are coming at you from left and right. what's even worse is that the 4/4 beat does not always match whatever else is going on in the music - where the emphasis is, so i'm forced to play an unintuitive beat, pulling me out of the zone to search for the beat that the game thinks is the correct one.  whyyy have the devs chosen metal as a genre, but not focused on the beat pattern and emphasis that makes metal as a genre unique?  at this point the game is like every other beat matching game, only slower and with a metal skin. pointless! ironically this makes the game less suited/more annoying for metal fans/musicians, as they are more likely to follow the intended emphasis, more than a slow 4/4 beat. the "correct" beat feels artificially applied, and as the commenter in the link above says, you'd be better off turning down the music and putting on a metronome. if this appeals to you, i recommend the game. if not, at least know what you're getting. glad i got this in a bundle.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: The game is unique and fun enough to get a strong recommendation. Music is great, mechanics are solid and the points made in the positive reviews are all valid. But I do want to highlight some areas where the game falls short, as constructive criticism for devs if nothing else.- Enemy AI is very underwhelming. There is reasonable variety, but don't expect Doom Eternal level of mature/intelligent AI.- All levels look same-ish. The only memorable/different arena was the bossfight on the rotating gear things.- Torments could have been used better to explain the game/movement mechanics better. By the time you figure things out, the game is over already.- Leading in from the previous, the game is only about 5 hours long including all torment arenas. But I'd rather have a short and entertaining game rather than a long game that gets repetitive and boring.Having said all that. Still a solid game, worth a playthrough, priced very reasonably, and I have no qualms about paying full price to support the studio and the musicians involved.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: I love the concept of the game, and it can be a very cool way to train your rhythm. It has different difficulties and even a mode in which your actions are always automatically on beat (the leaderboard is turned off for that). The soundtrack is awesome, I loved hearing some of my favourite artists in the game. The visuals are stunning, and the animations are smooth and very fluid. There are also some really cool weapons, and it's so satisfying to hear them shoot and reload in beat. The developers also made sure you'll feel like a badass doing all these things in beat. The game was a bit short though, and almost all the bosses looked the same. I would've liked to see some differences between them, even if they have a certain something in common. Overall, I'd recommend this game to metalheads who like shooters \m/
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: I will likely come back to elaborate on this review when I am less angry. But, to be brief, this is one of the best video game soundtracks of all time attached to a game that is very difficult for me to enjoy. The combat is aggravating and clunky. I wish there was a mode that allowed me to listen to the music at full intensity irrespective of my combo meter, because I cannot seem to avoid being hit at all. Movement does not feel smooth, and no matter how much I adjust video/audio latency I can never seem to hit beats on time. I'm really, really, really frustrated by this. I want to enjoy this game so badly but every time I try to, i feel rejected. This is not fun. I would like to say that you should just enjoy the soundtrack, but, well, there's no official OST. So... even in that regard you're kind of screwed. BPM is a much simpler game, but I have a lot more fun with that and find myself a lot less angry.

_childDocuments_.review: Right away. It is a good game. I enjoyed playing it and recommend it to you. But speaking of cons, it's a little more complicated. If you've played BPM before, then you know the rules. Shoot to the beat, preferably hitting enemies. And on paper it works, the music is great, shooting is comfortable. But something is wrong. Either a small variety of weapons, or a small variety of enemies, or the general slowness of process. Dodging and generally moving around the level is quite pleasant, you feel control in all directions. But something is still wrong. Once again, the game is great, but it feels very strangely short and lacking in substance, as if it were a prologue to something larger. At the very least, you should definitely try this game for the music. It is simply beyond praise. The gameplay may be average. But the music is great.

_childDocuments_.review: There is another similar game called Bullets Per Minute. The developers of Metal: Hellsinger are probably heavily inspired by overall gameplay and style of BPM. The problem is that they copied the gameplay and adjusted the graphics but lost the soul (sort of). The game does not have a repeatability, sure there are modifiers and challenges, but you will grind the same levels again and again. Weapons does not feel that great, animations are chunky and its hard to land them on bit. You can forget about making shots every half bit - the game does not reward you for that. Each level does not have its own music theme, since all songs are similar (if you are not hardcore metal fan). Enemy variety is missing as well and on maximum difficulty they are just super fat. Long fight are boring, there are enemies that just don't allow you to keep the tempo and enjoy the game. Guess why? Game does not keep the modified when you land hits in bear, but only when your hits deal damage.Finishing mechanic is what actually makes the gameplay horrible. Instead of dodging damage at all costs you can face tank hits and projectiles because you can just press one button heal for all missing HP and warp to a different part of the arena. If you are a beginner (sort of) then can recommend as a first game in this genre. For any other player - mediocre.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. It's clearly inspired by DOOM but with the addition of rhythm mechanics. Everything you do has more impact if you press the button to the beat of the music. My only issues are that the game feels a little short, and sometimes enemies spawn in an unreachable location and I have to restart, but it's only an occasional annoyance. Overall, great game that I'd recommend. I might wait for a sale if you aren't sure you'd enjoy it. It's pretty re-playable for higher difficulties and challenges to complete. I'd also recommend a game called Hi-Fi Rush, it has a very similar mechanic to this but it's more of a beat-em' up kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: If DOOM got together with a rhythm game like Guitar Hero, Beat Saber, or Pistol Whip and F*CKED, this would be their offspring.To simply put it, this game ended up being way more amazing than I expected. The sound track goes hard, and so many more things in the game are in sync with the music besides just the shooting. As a drummer, this game is insanely fun. Once you are locked into the beat, everything is smooth sailing and fun.My only negative is that I hope they release some DLC soon as there are only several maps at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: + Fantastic rhythm shooter. + Fantastic music.+ Fantastic visuals.+ Basically you feel the rhythm just pumping out of your controller.+- Listen, we don't came here for the story, but anyway there is a story (and it's quite interesting overall), but quite simple and nothing special about it.+- I'm not a big fan of competition in single player games, but as I see, every story-rhythm game adds some sort of scoring system for their games, I just think that exactly this type of rhythm games do not need it- Some weapons don't feet well integrated for the gameplay for me, especially Hellcrows.- Every boss fight feel the same, firstly because it's basically a same boss every time, and also nothing special happen. It goes something like this: Boss appear -> you shoot boss -> boss disappears and enemies appear -> you shoot enemies -> boss appears and so on. They could take BPM approach with this, they have more unique fights for every boss.

_childDocuments_.review: It has around 7-8 Levels called Hells. I needed 2hours to complete the campagn. Spend 2 more hours finishing some challanges to get all the passive boni. If you want to train up your highscore, there is some replayability. Except that it might be a fun past time to replay a hell when I have only 10-20 minutes to play.The Music is very good, quite catchy. Graphics look decent. I like the Artstyle, there are quite a few weapons, which all play differently. Didnt quite warm up with the skull or the crossbow, but in large the gameplay is good. The story is neglectable, but still, its nice to have it. Dont go in expecting a triple A production. Its not on par with Doom Eternal. Its more similar with Bullets per Minute without the roguelike elements. It is however a good time if you like Metal, Demons and Guns.

_childDocuments_.review: Metal Hellsinger is REMARKABLE.It's not a long game but, despite being linear and limited in exploration, it's incredibly well done.I have zero talent with rhythm and beat, but this game was such great training and fun. If you like games to music/ a beat, something new and novel, FPS's, or just the future of gaming, you should give Metal Hellshinger a play, your way of viewing games will be changed for ever.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: At the time I'm writing this, I haven't put that much time into this game. That said, without a shadow of a doubt, this game is phenomenal. I recommend this game to any fan of heavy metal and of first person shooters. The gameplay is so much fun, and the soundtrack is easily one of the best soundtracks in any game I've ever played. I'm constantly finding myself headbanging as I'm trying to time my attacks to the beat, and it's pure satisfaction when you get a good enough hit streak going and the vocals come in. Please, if the premise of this game sounds remotely interesting to you, buy this game. You won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: However, Metal: Hellsinger is just too good not to love. I think my dislike for rhythm games is just past experiences with other games like Osu, Geometry Dash, Beat Saber, etc. They have been so quirky, and I have never really enjoyed them too much, but Hellsinger just feels good. When I'm playing, I'm not trying to match the rhythm, it's just automatic for me. The music is great, and there is actually a story here that is interesting enough. Bosses are great and feel like a challenge, it's not a walk in the park or just torture like other rhythm games. It's just a good time, you feel like you are in hell, you feel the pressure and it feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great to beat it.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: Like DOOM but BETTER! I say better because there is no exploding candy when they die. Definitely a rhythm game that is reinforced by punchy tunes fitting the environment that engage your actions very harmoniously. Graphics are quite polished everything I've seen so far has looked very high quality. Audio is literally tailored for the game featuring some rather LARGE vocalists, when I say large I mean well knows bands. Story... So far has me interested in more than one aspect as it is not just a mindless rhythm game to music such as ITG/DDR or PUI, there is actually a story which at this point seems decent. After completion of said story I feel a sequel is in order, also with that ending looks like they may incorporate a co-op somehow.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% Worth the hype and the buy. A fun game that continually challenges you, with achievements that aren't extremely hard to get but does show some form of skill in the game. The game is enjoyable on all the difficulties I've played so far and I am eager to progress even more.The music is absolutely phenomenal and stays true to the sound I'd expect from the well known artists I recognise! Two Feathers did amazing composing while keeping the artists in mind all while keeping the music enjoyable to play along to.It is sad the storyline is as short as it is in the game and it does leave me wanting more, however I hope to see a sequel to the story (The company would be insane not to carry on with this as a franchise, every metal fan would love this game, and many bands who are gamers might start showing interest in being in the game as a featured artist). But finally a rhythm game with a story that makes me want to know more and more about the characters, and isn't just there for the music alone. 10/10My only gripe I have with the game is that it has crashed on me a few times during my play out of the blue. No error message or stutter beforehand, just outright kicks me out of the game along with a windows tune and I find myself back on the game page in steam.Other than that, the game is worth the buy if a FPS with Doom vibes along with some kick*** music and a good story told extremely well is what you're looking for!Thank you to the dev team and everyone involved for delivering such a masterpiece to our collections!

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome music, great gameplay, lots of fun.Don't be put off by "short" game time, the game is absolutely amazing and definitely worth its money even if it's not on sale.I thought I'd suck at rhythm related games but even though I was not that bad and I am having a great time with Metal: Hellsinger :)

A simpler Doom clone but great fun in a casual sense, made with metalheads in mind. Anyone can enjoy but I highly recommend a FPS rhythm game to anyone who wants to try something new and exciting.

My one gripe is a lot of the bosses look a little too alike but other than that this is totally worth a buy undoubtedly. And now you can put your own music in which is sick!

_childDocuments_.review: While the concept and gameplay of this game are pretty amazing while you are in the groove, I can't in good conscience recommend this game with the sheer number of soft-locks I'm encountering. Nihil boss fails to re-materialise in most runs, even after the supposed fix in Jan 2023. And I've never been able to get to the Acheron boss because I always get soft-locked and unable to proceed by an enemy being out of bounds. Back on the shelf for now.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: Metal: Hellsinger is basically the answer to the question: "what if you turned DOOM into a rhythm game?" Its an incredible idea that you know would work well before you even see it. Thankfully, the devs nailed the execution too. The gunplay is very satisfying, the music is amazing, and it all comes together very neatly. The only real negative I can come up with are that it is a little short. Sometimes you can be fooled into thinking this is a AAA game, and that's a testament to how well made it is. However, it is made by a much smaller team than the game it draws its inspiration from. i hope this game sold well so that a sequel can really up the production quality. Not that its bad in this game, but that's realistically the only area they need to improve.If you like DOOM and metal music there really is no reason you shouldn't be playing this.
_childDocuments_.name: Metal: Hellsinger

_childDocuments_.review: Killing demons? ♥♥♥♥ yeah. Games set to music: Hell yes. Despite how it appeals to me, Metal: Hellsinger has a few shortcomings. The creature designs are mostly unique visually and gameplay wise, but the bosses are a let down. They're just variations of the first boss sans one (granted they try to write this off with game lore). The music is superb. When comparing it to a similar game called BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE, I prefer the metal of this game but both have great OSTs. The problem is unlike BPM, Metal: Hellsinger doesn't support mid-beats. It would be nice to hit the mid-beats especially when enemies tend to be very aggressive.The game is still mostly well-balanced. Also the challenge modes reward you in the base game. Maybe the BPM devs can collab with The Outsiders in the future to hash that out. They have their own strengths.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is hard and extremely punishing, but unlike DS it's not fair or reliable. When you are in the flow, it's great. But sometimes it makes it impossible to stay in the flow. Combat design is undercut by level design more often than not and vice versa. Vast majority of the levels don't support sideways dash (you either fall into your death or dash into a wall), but that's the most obvious counter for a lot of enemies.Some enemies can shoot you across the whole map, even at distances where you can't even see where the projectile is coming from. (I'm playing on a standard fullHD monitor)Some arenas are so big I lose by combo bonus by the time I finally find the last enemy remaining of the current wave and start the next one from a disadvantaged position. When a wave starts enemies can spawn right onto you and break your combo without giving you the chance to react. Some enemies are just poorly designed, like a invisible-longrange dashing-teleporting enemy who can also shoot from extreme ranges. And its projectile looks almost exactly like its teleportation effect. The enemy with a shield is like... WTF for me. This enemy archetype is usually for harassment of the player if it's not careful, here it will turn the map into a bullet hell almost always breaking you combo while it's relatively hard to deal with.But at least enemy AI is terrible, they get stuck everywhere (Especially jumpy ones have the tendency to get stuck on the environment), they move in a semi random pattern (looks like a pathfinding issue, not a design choice), sometimes freezing in one place when you dash or jump and they are recalculating then just jump at you at a random distance or time interval. About combos, it's a really important game element but practically all enemies and all enemy attacks are designed in a way that will inevitably break your combo. All enemies have a gapcloser, a dash, a jump, sometimes at absurd ranges, I was constantly dashing backward which makes  the game feel like an anti-doom where you feel like a pansy trying to save your combo. My favorite issue is when the usual low health "heartbeat" sound is directly conflicting with the music's rhythm, it's not synced up, but it's somewhat louder than the basic rhythm, making it extremely hard to recover since you'll miss every single beat. Engagement design feels random, I didn't find a pattern that I can learn, the game just throws a bunch of basic and 2-3 special enemies at you all the time without taking into consideration the current arena design or the rest of the enemies in that wave. Sometimes it feels trivial sometimes it feels a lot harder than most of the bossfights. I could list another dozen issues I have with the game, I think it's inconsistent from a design perspective, there are a lot of conflicting concepts and elements. I want to love it, I want to play it forever but it's just too damn annoying. Please save the "git gud" comments, yeah, I think think I could be better, but I can play Doom without any problems or frustration (that game has nice level and enemy design). This is not Dark Souls as I mentioned, I have no problems with hard but fair games, I have issues with unfair random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game so badly, but no matter what I do to calibrate it the beats just don't work properly for me. Rhythm games are my bread and butter, but nothing I do seems to line the visuals up with the audio in this case, which is a shame because the mechanics at play would be perfect if it would just sync up. I've done my best to research this issue to no avail. Most threads just explain how to calibrate at all, rather than the most effective approach to calibrating. I've tried sitting and down and messing with the settings manually and through the quick calibration of the game, and I tried waiting to see if maybe an update would address my issue. Alas, I'm forced to leave a negative review for what's probably an incredible game. The music, the visuals, and the plot have all clearly had a good amount of care put into them, but it's far too tedious for me to see those things through when I can't get the game to function as intended. I'm running a 4K 144HZ HDR Monitor with a Ryzen 9 and MSI 3080 12 Gb for reference
