_childDocuments_.review: Pros: -Excellent combat-Nice pixel art-Interesting time limit mechanic-Some of the dungeons were fun to explore-You can feed your dog an appleCons:-Some of the dungeons were not fun to explore-I didn't feel like I had enough of a connection with the NPCs to prioritise extending their lives over my own, other than my fairybot companion. I wish that had been a more difficult choice-The story felt pretty generic, I didn't feel like I really cared about what was going on most of the time-At the beginning you're told that you can tackle the dungeons in any order, but you really can't, because pretty much every dungeon requires that you have a tool from an earlier dungeon to progress-The game takes control away from the player a little bit too much, especially in the middle of combat (e.g. in the mecha-bird boss battle, when minions spawn, you lose control of your character for a second, and it really interrupts the flow of the battle). Overall it was a really nice experience with a few flaws, but it didn't outstay its welcome. If you can grab it during a sale, I'd say give it a go, especially if you're a fan of games like Hyper-Light Drifter or CrossCode.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. I've seen it compared to all sorts of titles, all across the genre spectrum - Zelda, Souls, HLD... - which, I believe, speaks to its true uniqueness. Though you will find familiar elements in exploration, graphics and combat to things you might have played before, believe me: the ensemble is something altogether different. The combat is amazingly fan and incredibly fluid - quite honestly, I believe it has the most satisfying parry timing/feel of anything I've ever played. Exploration is awesome: from the get-go you can go pretty much anywhere, and though the sequence you get the items affects your progression, it never stalls it. It's a very clever level and world-design that encourages exploration and makes revisiting earlier areas a joy and not a bother.The "time limit" was, I must admit, something I was a little bit skeptical about initially. I'm more of a chill gamer, and I was afraid it'd make me anxious - but it surprisingly didn't, not at all! I think the way the time limit works (which I will not say because it's a plot spoiler) is VERY unique and it ends up serving more as a plot point (and a very engaging one at that!) than as a true limitation. It forces you to make decisions and manage time and resources, but it is very fair and forgiving (I've been playing in the standard difficulty - I'm sure the highest level offers a more unforgiving and challenging experience for those who seek it).The art is something else. Some of the prettiest pixel art I've seen in my life, and it's unbelievable it was all done by such a small development team. The cutscenes are moving, the parallaxes are out of this world, and all the tiny details (the reflections, the rain drops, the bounce-back frames) are a feast for the eyes.Finally, the soundtrack: it is at the same time widely diverse and incredibly cohesive and consistent. There are many earworms which will be stuck to your brain for hours after you've stopped playing, but there are also many chill, ambient tracks that perfectly match the post-apocalyptic setting. All in all, UNSIGHTED is an INCREDIBLE game that you should pick up right now.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED is by far the best game that came out in 2021. The game is a blend of 2D Zelda and (a finely paced) Metroidvania, where each gameplay element is finely tuned and never overbearing.You play as an Automaton who is trying to stop the sentience of all Automatons from withering away: as each day passes, the Automatons are losing their sentience, becoming "unsighted". This affects both the plot and the gameplay: NPCs will permanently die as time progresses and they become unsighted. Basically, the whole game runs on a timer. This might seem a bit oppressive at a fist glance, but the system is actually implemented quite intelligently. It's not as depressing or brutal as it sounds like, it just adds some somberness to the game. This time mechanic can be disabled at any time, but by doing so you would do a huge disservice to the game. UNSIGHTED is balanced around this time mechanic, and by disabling it you would take away more from the game than gain.The world is structured like an open-ended 2D Zelda, and it is one of the highlights of the game. The world is crafted in such a way that there is basically no big distinction between non-dungeon and dungeon areas, everything blends naturally and seamlessly; this makes the world truly feel authentic and interconnected. Obviously there are areas that are a bit more dungeon-y, but they do not feel disconnected from the rest of the game.In the game, you can tackle each objective in any order you want, as any route is possible, with plenty of chances to sequence-break out of the intended itinerary. Each element in the world is placed with care, making it enjoyable to explore around and trying to find new ways to exploit all the tools at your disposal. Contrary to many 2D Zelda-like games, the tools you obtain can be used with purpose basically in every part of the map, giving this game a sense of flexibility that is missing from many games in the same genre. Also, each tool has a hidden function that is not explained directly by the game, but that you can find out by experimenting: this knowledge can then be used to explore the map in new and unexpected ways. In short, the level design is truly excellent, and for sure the best part of the game.The movement of the character is snappy and fluid, and this, combined with a parry-based combat, makes just moving around and fighting enemies never dull. This is also one of the few parry-based combat systems that works well when fighting multiple enemies, as enemies always attack in a staggered way, where parries can be executed rhythmically, almost like a rhythm-game! Ranged weapons can also be used in conjunction with your melee weapons, but I found only a few actually viable in combat. As a downside, there are only two types of melee weapons. Having more variety would have helped in making different playthroughs play differently, at least combat-wise.There are other systems in the game, such as item crafting, weapon upgrading, NPCs trust levels, but all of them are kept quite simple, as to not overshadow the “meat” of the game, which is exploration and combat.The pixel art in the game is quite beautiful, everything is recognizable at a first glance, and I had no trouble at all with depth perception, which can be a bit problematic in some pixel art games that make frequent use of verticality (e.g. CrossCode).Many games have tried to be either good Zelda-likes or Metroidvanias, and most of them fail. UNSIGHTED does not fail, and it actually manages to be one of the best in both genres, which is an achievement by itself.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? YES, it is an action RPG with an interesting, post-apolyptical story and polished gameplay.You awake in a lab, without any idea who you are and what is going on. It just looks a bit... abandoned and damaged. As soon as you find your first melee weapon, the first enemies appear. Little robots that attack you on sight. After escaping the lab, you rescue a little flying robot, who becomes your companion. It is soon revealed that you are Alma, a sentient automaton.You are fighting humans, who sealed away the source of Anima - a large meteor - required for all automatons to stay conscious. If an automaton runs out of Anima, he becomes UNSIGHTED, losing his mental capabilities and running around like a zombie. The city is full of those zombies, and you only have around 500 hours until you run out of Anima, too. Some of your friends have considerably less time left until transforming into an UNSIGHTED. You can find meteor dust to prolonge the time a bit, but will you use it yourself or give it to your friends? So your aim is to find five crystals and then free the meteor, the source of unlimited Anime.You run around, using melee weapons (but mind your stamina) or ranged weapons (aiming with twin-stick, having unlimited ammo but the need to reload), collect ressources, kill zombie robots (the UNSIGHTED), find your way around the isometric maps. You can jump, climb, push crates or activate levers. Grab chests and throw them at your enemies, this inflicts serious damage. Parry enemy attacks to stun them and inflict critical damage in a counter attack, parry enemy projectiles to send them back. Your life is represented by health points, when they are all gone you respawn at a checkpoint, losing some money which can be regained when you find your corpse. You can inject yourself with a healing syringe or use a recharging point to completely heal you. Using upgrade chips you improve your health, strength, stamina and other abilities, when you find blueprints (and the required ressources) you can craft new equipment. Cogs can be used for temporary buffs. You have a map available, and can relax in a hub (Gear City) with shops, training and upgrade possibilities (and also most of the last remaining sentient automatons to talk to or get sidequests from). Besides fighting mobs and bosses, you also have to search the decaying city, some ressources and upgrades are well hidden.The visual presentation uses nice pixel art, inspired by 16bit games. It is re-using visual assets a lot and also not very high-res. The isometric view is annoying, even after playing for some hours I still didn't easily recognize (bottomless) chasms or was bumping against walls. At least there is no fall damage when you fall down from a house, or any punishment when you fall down a bottomless pit - you just respawn without any losses. I played in a resolution of 2560x1440 (with black borders on the sides) on my 3440x1440 monitor, controller support was fine. Even the PlayStation Dualshock 4 is supported. A well-implemented local 2-player mode allows you to play the game together with a friend. You then play Alma and another, similar looking automaton - with its own health bar and inventory.One of the better action RPGs, using classic 16bit graphics. Fight your way through a destroyed city overrun by zombie robots and collect five crystals to save the sentient robots.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: first caught my attention as a tale about automatons, one of my favorite science fiction staples, often diving into deep themes such as what does it mean to be alive. When I sat down to play, I realized that the game is described as a metroidvania, a subgenre I was familiar with by name and not much else. Historically I have avoided games with that tag due to my belief that they would be too difficult for me, but I tried to go into playing  with an open mind and have had a thoroughly enjoyable experience despite the challenges. That said, this is essentially my first experience playing a metroidvania game. borrows from classic Japanese fantasy games as well as cyberpunk manga and anime to spin its own story. The character awakens in a lab with no memories of who she is or how she got there, only that she is looking for Raquel. Eventually the player meets other characters and learns she is Alma, an automaton created by the human Doctor Zeferina to be perfect to fight the humans who are attempting to run out the clock on all Automatons. Automatons are given consciousness by Anima from a Meteor which landed on their world some time ago. Humans at war with Automatons have sealed away the Meteor and begun stripping Automatons of consciousness, as Automatons who run out of Anima become UNSIGHTED, mindless killing machines. Alma sets out to recover five Shards that will allow her to access the Crater Tower blocking the Meteor.  is not a 2D side-scrolling platformer like some classic metroidvania games but contains key elements of the subgenre, such as a large interconnected world map with areas that become explorable as the player gains the right abilities or equipment. The game can be played as both single-player or shared-/split-screen co-op and provides full controller support as well as remote play on phone, tablet, and TV. As of the time of this review, I’ve only explored the single-player mouse-and-keyboard options on PC. There are three levels of difficulty to choose from: Explorer, Action Girl, and Robot Apocalypse. Action Girl is the recommended difficulty level, but as an inexperienced metroidvania player, I opted to play on the Explorer difficulty for my first playthrough. The Explorer mode offers additional customization, including invincibility, although I refused to enable that particular option.One of ’s key gameplay features is the limited amount of time each character has left before they become UNSIGHTED, which is indicated by a timer near their name. This time can be extended 24 hours by using Meteor Dust, but since there is a limited amount available, the player must decide whether to use it for Alma or whether to give it to someone else. The player can see which Automatons they’ve met and how much time they have left in the Contacts List. In Explorer Mode, the Character Timers can be disabled, but I hope to have this feature on in a future playthrough once I’m more familiar with the game’s mechanics in order to fully experience the spectrum of choices as far as storytelling is concerned.The game saves at Terminals, with only one save slot per playthrough and three save slots total. Dying causes Alma to lose half of her accumulated bolts (the currency of ), but they can be recovered once she returns to the location where she died. The player can choose to respawn at the last Terminal or Gear Village. Fortunately, ‘dying’ only applies to combat and not to falling off a cliff or in the water; in those cases the player simply respawns where they were before falling. The Terminal is also where the player can adjust Alma’s chips or teleport to other visited Terminal locations on the map. Chips are effectively equipment that increases Alma’s stamina, health, or other attributes. There are a limited number of chip slots, although additional slots can be purchased with enough bolts (up to a point). Crafting Tables can frequently be found near Terminals, and with Blueprints Alma can craft better weapons, chips, or cogs. Effect Cogs are a consumable resource that can temporarily enhance Alma’s attack, defense, stamina, or other attributes. Crafting isn’t the only way to get weapons, chips, or cogs though, as they can also be picked up during exploration.Alma has two weapon slots available. The first one is activated with the left mouse button, and the second one is activated with the right mouse button. It’s important to use the mouse cursor to help aim Alma’s attacks. For me, it worked well to have a melee weapon in the first slot and a ranged weapon in the second slot. Some of the weapons effectively become part of solving puzzles; for example, the shuriken is a guidable ranged weapon that the player can navigate around curves to hit switches that are otherwise out of reach. The art style and graphics nail late 80s/early 90s arcade games, with a retro comic book color palette, pixel art, and anime character attributes. Alma’s hair in particular is very dynamic, waving as she walks. Day and night visually cycle to show the passage of time. Death calls to mind classic arcade games as Alma flies in the air and the background fades to black, leaving Alma laying defeated in the center screen.The sound effects are an homage to late 80s/early 90s video games, and the soundtrack is clearly inspired by that era as well. The music uses industrial and electronic elements to create a cyberpunk ambience with notes reminiscent of MIDI.In addition to the Main Story,  also has Dungeon Raid and Boss Rush challenge modes. There are 42 possible achievements, some of which are definitely going to make the player work to earn them. offers a high-quality gameplay experience with plenty of content for variety throughout multiple playthroughs, well worth buying at full price ($19.99 USD at the time of review). Fans of metroidvania will find plenty to love here, and for players like me who have been hesitant to give metroidvania a try,  offers an engaging story and characters, fun puzzles, ample gameplay customization options for the inexperienced, and an artistic retro feast for the senses.

_childDocuments_.review: Big note before starting the review: Unsighted has a time limit. All characters are under this time limit, and even important NPC's can turn into enemies if they are left unattended. HOWEVER, this element of the game is completely optional. The difficulty of the game can be changed to completely remove this time limit, and allow for a slower and more laid-back adventure. Too many people are unable to read this and are unsatisfied with the game. On to the review.Unsighted is one of the best games, indie or otherwise, to be released in the last few years. Everything from the combat, to the exploration, to the story works so perfectly together to create a vibrant and somber world. Combat is fast-paced and dynamic, with the player needing to manage multiple elements that all blend together perfectly. The world is massive and open-ended, allowing the player to explore around as they please if they please. Dungeons and puzzles have interesting design and make exploring the world even more rewarding. The time limit keeps players on their toes, and adds a ton of replayability to an already great game. Seeing your favorite character's time slowly tick down gives a feeling of urgency that I've never felt in a game before. I've already put in about a dozen hours on the switch version, and decided to support the devs with another purchase and a review.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Unsighted is a top down metroidvania that takes inspiration from The Legend of Zelda, Hyper Light Drifter, Dark Souls, and Hollow Knight.  This game has gorgeous pixel art, a really large, elaborate, interconnected world to explore, sports fast, fluid, and dynamic movement and platforming, and has a top notch parrying system.  The learning curve is quite steep, but if you are willing to invest the time, this is one of the best metroidvania's you will play all year.What's Good:-The devs were able to achieve something really special w/ Unsighted.  That's probably the most impressive thing about this game - the devs ability to mix so many different genres and influences together and create such a well designed and fun game.  This is the first metroidvania that I have ever played, and it changed how I viewed this genre.  I love when devs take really innovative risks and it ends up all coming together in the end.  -Almost every upgrade in this game has multiple purposes.  The double jump makes it easier to avoid enemies but also let's you gain access to previously inaccessible areas.  You will gain a frozen shuriken which can be used to damage enemies and create frozen platforms on water, allowing you to walk across water.  The hookshot will be vital in late game for traversing the world, but also can be really nice for moving around enemies.  I love how the devs found clever ways to add functionality to every item or upgrade.-The best games in this genre have massive worlds that are so exciting and rewarding to explore.  Unsighted crushes that aspect of the genre.  There's always a sense of wonder as you explore the map.  It feels great finding a secret, opening up a shortcut, or stumbling upon a new biome.  -The parry in this game is really well designed and fun to execute.  It will take some practice, but it's very much worth your time.  Since this is a top down metroidvania, you will need to be really quick w/ your timing b/c you may have to parry 4 or 5 enemies that are surrounding you.  Some of the battles can get really intense, so memorizing every enemies telegraphs, and mastering the timing of the parry is crucial toward defeating late game bosses.-The pixel art is top notch in this game.  This game reminds me a lot of both Hyper Light Drifter and Dandara.  Every biome has a distinct look, feel, and specific colors that make it unique.  All of the enemies are very detailed and have a really cool robot-monster look.  The bosses are big, badass, and intimidating.  The attack animations are some of my favorite visuals in the game.  Could Use Some Changes:-You are going to get lost a lot in this game.  This is the biggest downside to a top down metroidvania.  It's hard to understand how the world functions early on and the map is really hard to read.  I think the map could use some work to make it feel more practical. During the first few hrs, I kept falling off of ledges, getting lost, and was backtracking constantly.  It took about 6 or 7 hrs for me to start feeling really comfortable w/ exploring the world.  Every time you turn around, you run into a locked gate or something that you can't cross w/o an ability.  -There is a "Nemesis" like enemy that is really irritating.  I lost track of the amount of times I would accidentally run in an area near him, and then he would kill me as I tried to run away.  To make this more agonizing, you will lose half of your currency and you sometimes are sent very far back to a checkpoint.  This is especially defeating early in the game b/c you haven't unlocked any of the shortcuts.  I'm not sure I found this creature added a lot to the game, other than more frustration.-The race against the clock is one of the hardest things you will face.  I wish I would have turned it off for my first playthrough.  I eventually got the hang of things, but by then, almost every vendor had died.  This made my life far more difficult b/c I couldn't add ability chips.  The defense cogs became my best friend, b/c a lot of enemies could 2-hit w/o any cogs.  I think the timer is a great idea once you have a good understanding of the game, but it's really tough for first time players.  The timer adds a layer of tension (probably the point of the Nemesis) but it's a massive challenge for players that are new to the game.Consensus:-Excellent Game (Tier 2 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  This was one of my more polarizing gaming experiences in a while.  There were hours where I was convinced that this was the best metroidvania I had played in years.  There were other times, where I was so frustrated that I questioned if I wanted to continue.  I'm really glad I saw it to the end, b/c this is a really well designed, satisfying, and fun game.  It's one of the best metroidvania's I have ever played.  I think it goes right next to Blasphemous, Dandara, and Guacamelee 2, which are three of my favs.  The learning curve is extremely steep, but it's worth the patience and effort.  I'm excited for more devs to try their hand at top down metroidvanias.  This is a really good one, and one every fan of the genre should check out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is criminally underrated. It's like 2D zelda with lesbian robots, what more could you possibly want? I'd personally recommend giving the game two playthroughs, one where you play with the imposed time limits, trying your best to save everyone, and going for the regular ending, and then once again without the time limit, giving yourself the chance to explore everything and find all the secrets, and pursue the true ending. If time limits really aren't your cup of tea, the game still absolutely holds up on its own, and is still for sure worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: The quiet footsteps of Unsighted still resonates in the grand cathedral of metroidvanias.I'm going to be pretty direct, it's a shame that Unsighted hasn't received more lights upon it.— The gameplay works incredibly well & keeps you constantly satisfied by the smoothness of Alma's controls (+ the feedback in terms of sound & impact is so addictive).— The musics are soothing & thrilling at the same time (pros for the dynamic themes in some dungeons).— The level-design keeps reinventing itself (through the various tools the game throws at you), the various dungeons are efficient, polished & the amount of interconnections between areas will remind some of the best hours of Dark Souls 1: I just wish that puzzles used more the mechanics given by your equipment. — Almost all of the bosses are well designed (which make even more relevant the fact that you have a Boss Rush) and you'll have a pretty high playtime if you're ever interested by the latter, NG+ & the Dungeon Raids (they are procedural dungeons played through a game mode). Honestly, in a contest with Hollow Knight: I would ultimately choose the latter as my favorite of the two, but I would still feel guilty of choosing it since Unsighted shined in so much ways. It does have his flaws & some things could have been better polished, but damn: that's a lot to put one of the best games I've ever played & that "little indie game" on the same platter, and Unsighted highly deserves it.Thanks for the trip Pixel Punk.

_childDocuments_.review: This is technically a decent game, and it's very interesting in a lot of departments, but some essential things feel neglected to me.Nearly all the puzzles are so basic that it made me question why they're here in the first place.And enemies, well... They're interesting in the first few areas, but eventually, they're failing at their job, because of how easy it is to trivialize every fight (including bosses).You can very easily, and very early on, come up with a build that will let you either :- boost the damage of an automatic weapon sixfold and kill anything before it even gets a chance to attack you, or- boost your physical damage, and just parry and hit with a charged attack. The damage output from both the charged attack and the multiplier that comes from hitting a stunned enemy is absurd. Every boss (besides a couple optional ones, that are like, 10 leagues above everything else) CAN BE 2-SHOT doing this. For real. And ultimately, all it requires is succeeding at a QTE.Now I did enjoy how you don't get punished for skipping on secret hunting, as there's nothing in all the hidden chests across the game that can't be bought or crafted elsewhere.Basically, you won't miss out on anything if you're not willing to engage in tedious tasks. And while it's not stated clearly, the game does manage to make you understand that.(Unfortunately, there's a couple exceptions to that rule, if you want to get to the true ending, but still, that was very refreshing. After all, I've never heard of anyone being happy about having to look up a guide to know where stuff is hidden.)I also thought it was very interesting how the game is built to be sequence-broken. It's unlikely to happen in a first playthrough, but knowledge of advanced mechanics enables you to skip on so many things it's definitely fun to experiment with (and probably made early attempts at speedrunning the game very stimulating). That even applies to the keys, which can work on any door in the game, and can even be bought!Now both these things were probably motivated by the fact that the game revolves around a time limit (as your character will eventually "run out of battery" if you don't beat the game fast enough). Similarly, all the NPCs' days are numbered, and you will eventually lose access to their services.That's certainly an original idea, and it did feel like it could have opened a world of possibilities. But at the end of the day, it barely changed anything, as far as I'm concerned. I had more than enough time to get everything I needed from the few actually meaningful NPCs, even with no prior knowledge of the game, and I never felt personally threatened either, while I did take my time to explore as much as I could.In a nutshell, artificial pressure, and a lot of unexploited potential.It does add something to the game's identity though (notably a lot of dialogues can be altered), and I suspect it did push the developers to make cool design choices that I mentioned earlier.Ultimately, I just wish the game was better balanced around all the things you can abuse, and didn't push you so much towards the "stand still, parry, attack, repeat" playstyle. Few games manage to make something out of it, and this is not one of them.I'll end with a quick word for the AD, which is definitely fine work, and especially the soundtrack that I found quite inspired.

_childDocuments_.review: is a pretty unique blend of different elements: stamina-based melee combat, Zelda-like structure of interconnected dungeons with non-linear exploration, and a timing gimmick that builds a form of scenaristic urgency into the gameplay mechanics. It is also, hands down, one of my absolute favorite 2021 releases, despite the (inexplicably) little attention it has garnered from the press and the public thus far.The first thing you'll likely notice is that the game just  great, right from the get-go. The move set is simple enough to pick up in a matter of seconds, but the numerous enemy types will keep you on your toes throughout. Combat puts heavy emphasis on a deeply satisfying parrying system, which is accessible enough to use and rely on but requires precise timing. Landing a perfect parry stuns the enemy, giving you a great opening to attack.The exploration of this beautiful pixel-art landscape is also a treat, with a clever use of perspective, numerous secrets hidden behind simple puzzles and very neat little pieces of equipment that you'll pick up along the way. There's hardly a dull screen in the entire game. The devs went surprising lengths to allow for non-linear approaches, going so far as to integrate numerous little tricks than can allow you to deviate from the standard path. also comes in with a gimmick that sounds like a terrible idea on paper: the player as well as all the NPCs have limited time left to live, which counts down in real time (x60) in the game. You  are running against the clock to save the world and all of your friends, and as you find limited supplies of an item that can extend someone's life span for 24 hours, you will face crucial choices regarding who to sacrifice or keep alive. This unique (and rather brave) little twist plays out just fine in practise: you will likely lose some NPCs on your first playthrough, but the time pressure is not high enough to deprive you of the pleasure of exploration. You'll likely want to try to save everyone on a second playthrough, and notice that the game is finely balanced in order to allow you to do just that. And if all else fails, you are also free to activate "Explorer mode" at any time to enjoy the game at your own pace without this mechanic.If any of this sounds like it might just be your sort of thing, please give  a chance. You won't be disappointed. On my end, I'm happy to do my part to spread the word and I'm definitely looking forward to whatever Studio Pixel Punk has in store for the future.

_childDocuments_.review: An adventure with relentless forward drive, in which you and your robot pals face the loss of consciousness once your individual timers tick down -- with a few items found along the way which can extend this time.  Will you use your meteor dust on yourself?  Your friendly fairy bot Iris?  Some other bot who just  give you a nice upgrade if they stick around long enough?  With everything designed around speed and sequence-breaking, with a bitter note of impending  to goad you on your way, you'll never stay in one place long.  Fittingly, all combat is lightning-quick.  It's based around parries; no matter your loadout -- which is really just garnish, as about any set-up will work -- a last-instant rebuff and the vulnerability that ensues will always take you farther, faster toward victory than .It's a good game with a good story -- pared to its essentials, without meandering filaments to clog up the race track -- better puzzle-dungeons than some Zelda games, and an interesting world in which lesbian android warriors strive, with blade and blaster, for the right to  freely.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't beaten it yet but you should consider this if you enjoy metroidvanias at all. Selling points:- Its a good metroidvania- Good combat- Gorgeous graphics- Big ladies- REALLY cool mechanicsAs a metroidvania its quite competent with gates being communicated well in memorable places and the upgrades and new ablities feeling quite powerful. Its a bit on-rails in terms of which larger area you go to next, but you can go off track a little once you're half way through. What should bring you to this game though is that the NPCs (AND yourself) all have death timers that are ALWAYS counting down, you only have so much time to save everyone. So many games go through so many hoops to bring out the immersion that time is running out to save the day but this game says screw that, you LITERALLY are running out of time to save ANYONE. This alone adds this unique urgency to everything, as unlike in Majora's Mask, you can't rewind time, the clock is always ticking, giving this real finality to EVERYTHING you do. Its honestly so incredibly cool, and if its not your jam it can be disabled, but I'm determined to experience whatever results from such a cool system.You CAN extend the amount of time that you and others have by giving them an item. This mechanic of being able to quite literally give people more time puts you in a strange reflective state of mind when running between rooms, where  you're considering the value of the time others have left and the heaviness of that choice, and how unfair it is. Which for me only became motivation to save everyone so I wouldn't have to, but I have a sneaking suspicion this game is gonna make me cry a ton.Absolutely buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very special, and I do mean it, it's genuinely a wholesome combination of souls-like combat, metroidvania exploration, top-down platforming, smart puzzles, good controls, lots of optional content, decent weapon selection, and just a really fun narrative with enjoyable characters - kinda gives me HLD and EarthBound vibes too. It's almost like the devs tried to combine the 10 best indie games in the last 20 years, and you know, it worked, despite all of the features, it's very rare for something to feel out of place, and for the most part, I didn't see any technical issues or control problems, actually a very complex and polished game. Even the art style, you would think with all of the game mechanics they would have to cut corners on the visuals, but it actually looks very good aside from a few enemies, and there are many cutscenes even for insignificant moments. Overall the combat is very fair, I think most people that are familiar with the genre won't find it too difficult, plus the game has build-in assist features, so if you really having a problem, you have on-demand cheats in the exploration mode - which is admittedly a strange feature.Despite the game having an open world and a lot of places to get lost, I think they did a good job helping the player without actually forcing you to do things, the navigation, the map, and the markers are very useful if you don't ignore them like me.Combat is pretty good and not too punishing, it has that basic souls-like formula to it, you can rely on a dodge, parry if you want, watch your stamina - or be a **** like me and use ranged weapons, it's slower, but it does the job. Enemies drop some currency for the "bonefire" upgrades, and if you die you have to pick it up, unless you have a special upgrade that lets you keep it. I will say there is a decent amount of interesting weapons, they feel different in the application, plus some of them have cool interactions with the puzzles. Personally, I don't have any issues with the controls, for the most part, the game is responsive and you will recover your stamina or parry frames very fast. My only small problem with the combat is that when you get the timing on the counter, sometimes the enemies bounce away too far, like you would need to do a running jump attack to cover the distance, and sometimes their hitbox will clip you, with some bosses anyway.Now the game does have a timer for narrative and gameplay reasons, but you can change it into exploration mode that will extend the time significantly. For clarity, once you change it to the 'exploration mode', it essentially won't run out fast enough, so you can take all the time you need, too bad the game treats it as the lowered difficulty, even though you don't have to lower other aspects of the game with it - so it mostly affects a few achievements that are unique to other modes. I like the idea behind it and what it does for the narrative, like gifting your life energy to someone else, for example, you can sacrifice your time to the smith, and he will give you an awesome weapon at the end. I guess if you really wanted to replay the game, it would add more complexity, balancing your overall time for what is more useful for the run speed, but again, I don't really care personally so it's not something that I wanted in a first place.I guess I just don't like the game telling me that I am playing on the easy mode just because I don't like the timer, I don't need other assist tools, I just don't want the ****** time limit on my first playthrough, I don't care how generous it is. (+) I do think the level design is a highlight of the game, it has that spider web feel to it, you can navigate the map in multiple ways, there are secrets, shortcuts, alternative solutions, and just fun exploration all around. Pretty good map systems, not too confusing if you pay attention. I also like the implementation of the perspective, obviously vertical design in a top-down game is pretty cool on its own, but also like jumping between the different floors.(+) Solid narrative, enjoyable characters. I like that you can use time that you need yourself and gift it to others for unique items and upgrades. Again, not sold on the timer overall, but I like the idea behind it, at least from the story perspective. I thought the hub town was really cool, many places to visit, some fun dialogue here and there.(+) Pretty fair combat, not too hard, not too easy. Solid controls, lots of weapons to try, several upgrades. Good enemy variety, decent boss fights.(+) Overall good visuals, good music, good content, intuitive hints. I don't think I need to elaborate there, you know it, I know it. Plus, good achievements support. - I don't want to invent problems just to put something here, objectively I think the game is solid, the devs know what they doing. The timer, I just don't like that it lowers normal difficulty, I don't want the timer to be a part of that personally, if you telling me the run speed is part of the game, then I feel like I am not playing the game properly. Who cares about my first run speed, why do I need to care about it, I can't take advantage of routes I don't know anyway. Some of the enemies fly away too far after counters, sometimes I have a hard time actually getting 1 hit in there even when I do the dash attack.I don't think the game was made for me, but I loved it anyway. Look, I think it's an amazing game in terms of content, story, and gameplay, I just find it a little strange that devs are playing both sides, it's clearly a game designed to encourage finding faster paths, and yet, it's only as hard as you want it to be. It took me about 10 hours to finish the game, I decided not to play on the normal timer early on so it would not annoy me, and I only got 13/42 achievements despite not really trying to skip content, so it has plenty of things to do if you enjoy the exploration. I understand what they wanted to do with the expiring characters, the idea is cool on paper, but it's just not for me. Overall, probably the best indie game that I played in this genre, I wish the timer was not part of a 'mode' difficulty, that said, not the end of the world, I can dislike a feature and recognize that everything else was really good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolutely phenomenal experience. Between, the combat, the music, the atmosphere, and the pressure of not having enough time to absorb it all, there is so much to fall in love with about this game. The variety in customization is also amazing, although I wish I could have accessed full customization sooner so I could better define different builds.My only qualms with the game would probably be some of the dungeon layouts, which felt a bit confusing at times. While some people might not be a fan of the timer mechanic (and it can be disabled), I think the urgency it adds to the game definitely makes it worth experiencing.The story was interesting, but I also didn't find myself getting too attached to any specific characters-- which unfortunately lessens the impact of the timer mechanic.If you're a fan of Hyper Light Drifter, CrossCode, or honestly just want to play a DAMN good game, then please do yourself a favor and play UNSIGHTED. I greatly look forward to what Studio Pixel Punk puts out in the future :)

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted Wow, what a game...was not expecting a Metroidvania/souls/whatever the hell this actually is to be this good.Unsighted plays like an amazing little explorer side scroller, puzzle, platformer and it feels really well made and plays awesome! This is unlike most anything I have ever come across, it's amazingly unique and fresh! Unsighted starts you off alone in the dark and no idea what the hells gone on or is going to happen and you instantly get pursued and have to run away or you die regardless of the difficulty. Kinda gives you the idea that the meteor creatures are too be runaway from where ever you encounter them but this is all a ruse!Unsighted is a very very hard game to play and master, I am playing on the absolute easiest difficultly and I die in 3 hits! with no upgrades to my chipset. It is about as unforgiving as games get, however upon death similar to the souls franchise you drop half of your resources if you do not have a chip that prevents loss on death.The story - overall seems solid, I can't fault it for the most part. It is very unique and I haven't come across a story like this one just yet. It's a bit on the Anime-cyborg-LGBTQ scale a bit but I'm ignoring that as that stuff doesn't interest me in the slightest.The Combat - I haven't played many games of this style and the only one I have seen is HADES and having not played it I can't compare but ♥♥♥♥ me this is hard! Even on the easiest difficulty this game has a skill curve that I am hella lacking. The volume of equipment and chipsets is insane, you can design Alma however the hell you want really, it's pretty insane.The platforming and Puzzles - They get the little noodle thinking, the level design so far is fantastic and with a little bit of exploring and note taking or even dropping a pin on your map can help you retrace your steps for when you find the items that enable you to access those hidden paths. Just the type of game I like. The sheer volume of puzzles and opportunity is beyond anything i've come across.Choices - Unsighted comes with a ton of choices, playing to a death timer and become a soulless automatron you have to find meteoric dust to give you or someone else an extra 24 hours before losing control. I find this a very interesting game mechanic as it is forcing me to look everywhere to find as much dust as possible to save myself aswell as the others in the Village. This approach also helped me to save a large quantity of the Village allowing me to get access to alot of devices, weaponry and blueprints such as portable crafting tables, weapon upgrades and even changing my chips on the fly, really handy hidden feature that I appreciate!The Combat - Like most of this genre this is where the game can be make or break and to me Unsighted has definitely been made with this combat system, using the different chipset and different weapons such as fire or ice weapons, you can string together some chunky combos or even just be a parry master depending on playstyle. It's very interesting.The black meteoric sentinels, I thought these were to just run from because you die in one hit and deal 1 damage to them, however without realising I countered one and managed to kill the damn thing....they're not all that the game makes them out to be, they are just dangerous early...Overall - Unsighted to me seems to be one of the strongest releases within the Metroidvania genre and it's a shame it isn't heard of more, it's such a slept on title that deserves to be played and a sequel be produced for the game is an absolute gem and I am so glad I found it somehow.I'd give this a flat-out 9.5/10 I absolutely can't fault Unsighted at all, It plays beautifully and whilst there are huge learning curves with parry timing and combat development (for me) I can't get enough of this game, I actually want to replay it over and over and do things differently, as the game sets you 5 targets but you don't have to do them in that order I just did this time around to see what the crack is and going again i'm gonna try mix things up. Really awesome game, really impressed. Hopefully we'll be looking at a sequel given the ending I got. Fingers crossed for more unsighted!

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this game is fantastic, it does Zelda better than modern Zelda games, and has a unique time limit mechanic that keeps you on your toes and forces you to make difficult decisions your first time through (unless you are extremely skilled and fast). This is one of those Knowledge Based Games, so I highly recommend going in blind and this is an easy recommend to pretty much anyone who enjoys action games. There are tons of secrets, items, and routing logic to find. The game reocommends an order to the dungeons, and I wasn't able to find the hidden ways to do it in a different order, but its pretty clear they are there just difficult to find on your first playthrough. I think thats awesome, because different players at different skill levels will have different experiences.With that said, I want to point out a few issues I think you should before playing, so you don't put the game down halfway through. There is an annoying "navi" like companion that has a tendency to talk about literally anything in the game world, often multiple times, and does. not. stop. As far as I know there isn't a way to turn off her "hints", but some of them legitimately spoil puzzles and progression. She straight up tells you how to complete areas, and for that reason alone I wanted her to die. If you let her die, you can't upgrade your character, and I don't remember this being communicated. I really thought the devs were screwing with me.There is a "True Ending", and to get it you have to enter several rooms that are not marked on the map, and there is no indication whatsoever that they are there. No hints anyway, no riddles or puzzles. Nope, you just have to slam your face into every wall until you just happen to walk through one of them to get a mcguffin. This is really irritating, and it seems like you aren't supposed to find it without a guide. I'll change this review if someone points out how you are supposed to know which walls don't exist. There are secret rooms like this already in the game, but they all have a noticeable out of place feature, like the walls not aligning properly, a sound effect, or a scratch mark on the ground. The true ending progression rooms don't, and I do not understand that design decision.Finally, they make you fight the crab boss twice, and that was kinda lame.Those three points aside, I really enjoyed this game, the movement and combat are very fun and satisfying. There's a good deal of customization, and there constant tension from the story time limit that pushes you forwards and forces you to make consequential decisions. Fantastic game.

_childDocuments_.review: A cute little metroidvania whose story is focused around a timer (optional) and saving your kind from an unknown mutation and fleeting life juices.Every character in the game has a certain amount of time to live left, which you can extend by gifting/using optional collectibles, different characters give you different kinds of services and goods, making each use of these collectibles strategic and important and reminding you that you can't save them all. (unless you speedrun the game)The game's graphics are absolutely wonderful, beautiful pixel graphics and a unique 2.5D fully vertical playfield makes platforming in this game extremely unique and satisfyingrThe soundtrack in this game is decent, nothing that'll really stick in your mind but nothing to scoff at either.Not much to say about it, it's very middle of the road.Weapon and utility variety in this game is insanely good and satisfying, you can mix and match chips, cogs, weapons and elemental damages to your heart's content to fight enemies and traverse the terrain in unique ways.I cannot recommend buying this game at full price, 20$ is too pricey for the content this game has, but I would definitively recommend buying this game on any sale, even 15$ is very much a fair price for the experience this game gives for sure!

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED is phenomenal. It's my GOTY, in a year of impressive games (for me, Beast Breaker, Riftbreaker, Death's Door). UNSIGHTED's main gimmick (death timers) is optional, and it is a creative and intense adventure even without it; it goes as far as to try to be mechanically accessible, allowing you to make combat more forgiving. When playing on its default mode, though, it allows for extra meaningful player expression. You can even TRY the mechanic and turn it off later if you decide you don't like it. It's a must-play game for lovers of action-adventures/action-RPGs. At LEAST try the demo. The temptation to describe UNSIGHTED as an "topdown metroidvania" comes from how shortcuts are tied together with your movement options and weapons.• It has Legend of Zelda blood (its frequent puzzling, its dungeon structure, its playful bosses).• It has Dark Souls blood (lethally punishing but fair, with tactical and weighty stamina-based combat).• It has Metroid blood (an immaculate atmosphere, dripping with attitude, tension, and bullets).These games do have things in common. But ultimately it FEELS most like a metroidvania, what with how you frantically platform around its world, stopping to beat things up or hunt secret goodies... also, what with its jazz-fusion soundtrack. :)However, before you commit to a quick romp or completionist journey through UNSIGHTED, you are confronted with a question: What if everyone around you is dying, on a visible timer, and the survival of those you find useful or lovable hinges on how efficient you are? If your answer is ♥♥♥♥ THAT, well, you can simply turn those death timers off. If you find the premise interesting though, it'll add so much more tension and many more options for player expression.It's is partly inspired by "rando" mods, like the ALttP Randomizer, and while it's not a particularly random game, when you don't know what lies in store, you view everything you have in a utilitarian way, doing your best with what you have, as if you were playing a randomizer or roguelite. It invites you to discard your perfectionism, or put it away for future runs. Those who really value randomness may even find its bonus Dungeon Raid and Boss Rush gamemodes scratch their itch.UNSIGHTED is so full of ambition and the emotional energy of its two indie devs, you expect it to stumble over itself. Sometimes, it does stumble, briefly, but, before you can be embarrassed for it, it does a combat roll, stands up, and grins.• The balance of the weapons available seems iffy, like you're railroaded into an optimal combination. But, the combat mechanics  intricately designed and you'll find later you've just favored weapons because of your playstyle!• The writing must falter, the gorgeous presentation crumbling, at some point. But, there  organic and heartfelt explanations for things you might think are strange. The characters are good and the story wraps up solidly.• The beats of exploration and puzzle-solving may feel tedious, an oversight. But it  deliberate, to make you intimately familiar with rooms. When you backtrack or replay, you have epiphanies for how to better navigate the world.The game may at first just seem so spunky it's clunky, but, as it turns out, attitude and intelligence can coexist in a package. Try to recall when games have felt that clever and cool to you, when your love for gaming-- overcoming challenges and discovering new things-- is raw and rewarding. UNSIGHTED is genius, it's beautiful. It's sick, dude.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is quite the hidden gem. The game sets you in a world once ruled by humans, now populated by automatons (made alive by the life source Anima). After the humans tried to contain the Anima, the Unsighted started showing up. You play as Alma, who awakens after being asleep for some time; it is your job to investigate these Unsighted and help save those who are still alive.I started playing the first 4 hours (out of 30) or so of this game in 1-Player mode. I wanted to play this game with my brother, but I had to make sure this game was up to snuff first. My initial thoughts were somewhat critical - this game is damn hard early on, and I respect that. I was able to button-mash my way through some encounters, but not /.every/ encounter. Upon fighting the first boss, I was punished over and over until I learned the parry mechanic. That tough love set me up to use an incredibly useful tool when fighting beefy enemies backed up by some minions. After getting past that, my brother seamlessly joined in the fray. The two-player experience felt equally balanced, with the added bonus of having your bro there for couch co-op :)As we explored further, rewards were consistent. There are some fishing and digging mechanics available later on that helped a little bit (much more than just breaking containers). This game plays as you'd expect out of a high-quality metroidvania. Slowly but surely your character develops a /battery/ of skills (pun intended), eventually making her a force to be reckoned with in any scenario.Unsighted employs an interesting time-is-running-out mechanic that adds some pressure to tackle the main storyline and not just wander about. I call this interesting because the effect it has steers the player in the right direction without pulling them along. That said, the time limit gives enough space for you to run off the beaten path and go treasure hunting. My brother and I got through the whole story with enough time to spare that we felt we'd had to make both sacrifices while following our goals. The game forces you to make life or death decisions, but what will you do for "the greater good"?My main gripes are these:- 1. This one dwarfs the rest by a long-shot. Not sure if I didn't pay attention enough or missed something, but Iris almost perishes WAY too quickly. The issue is that you can't get no chip slots without her. Lord how I wish I know that. Not having those certainly made the later parts of the game a fair margin more challenging.- 2. Unfortunately, not many of the shops are that useful. It's became hard to decide who should get Meteor Dust (for their longevity) and who wouldn't.- 3. Travel felt kind of slow sometimes. It was usually hard to swap out a combat chip for a running chip.And that's all those really are, gripes. Not anything disastrous. I recall speaking to my brother on this after playing with him for several hours. "You know what man? This game isn't just fine. It's good. Like, two thumbs up kind of stuff. This is a fun game." He agreed, Unsighted certainly deserves high marks, and much more attention. And as a special mention - many games insert diversity in their games not because it's a natural part of our everyday lives, but because they want to push an idea. What Unsighted thrives in is /representation/ WITHOUT /politicization/. Many of the characters in game are given for the world; hell, even a few of them you can tell are queer in some fashion (whether in their style or expression) without them even saying it. This makes the characters represented in-game feel natural in their world, and relatable. And this is what many queer people want - to just be treated like everybody else. I think the developers and artists of this world have a strong and confident vision of the future, and have keen emotional understandings of relationships. There is one romance in the game that certainly made me misty eyed in its conclusion.As you might be guessing, I highly recommend Unsighted. It's an engaging, atmospheric, and fun game that should be in any seasoned metroidvania player's back pocket. Top notch stuff, and a sincere 8.75/10. Oh but wait, I forgot, there's dogs!!! 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED is an amazing experience, from beginning to end. You start in a world you barely know anything about, but progressively becomes more familiar and you get personally attached to the characters and locales.The game delivers snappy, impactful action where you're always on the edge, but overcome whatever the game throws at you, with a mechanically sound combat system.The story is simple to understand, but compelling thanks to the world building and unique characters.The game also boasts a robust crafting system that gets explored as you progress through the game, and gives the game high replay value, as you can pretty much craft all important items in the game to sequence break.THE SOUNDTRACK IS A BANGER AND I CAN'T STRESS THIS ENOUGHOverall, it's a very solid recommendation! I hyped this game for a long time and got to play it 2 weeks early. I couldn't wait to see people playing on live streams and enjoying it as much as I did. I couldn't see everything it had to offer thanks to my relatively tight schedule, but I did get 100% map completion, which says a lot! Definitely a game I'll replay many times!

_childDocuments_.review: One of those rare games with combat that is challenging to master but easy enough to pick up that the difficulty doesn't immediately turn you off. The parry mechanics have a gratifying feel once you get them down and the bosses all feel unique and interesting in their own way.The variable difficulty options aren't the most fleshed out but there is enough there to make the game range from a cozy exploration of the world that you can take your time with to a challenging race against time as you slowly lose NPCs and every death means that extra bit of time loss that can be the difference between a character's loss or survival. Secret bosses and challenging achievements add to the ways you can approach the game and I found myself doing back to back runs just to chase some of those challenges. New Game+ and New Game Extra make sequence breaking easy and fun to try and optimize and end up making the speed run achievement that seemed impossible in my first run an easy task to overcome.The story and world building are interesting in their own right. They might not be for everyone but for me it scratched an itch that I've been having a hard time finding a game for lately. So go recover your memory, save your girlfriend, hell save all of robot kind, and look badass doing it!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: B- Unsighted sells itself on a unique premise: time is always running out. Every character (including the player character, Alma) has a finite amount of time left. You play as a robot who hopes to avert the inevitable extinction of their kind. The pressure of the clock provides an interesting motivation for a metroidvania since the genre prides itself on allowing players to get lost in their worlds. With the looming threat of time, players will be forced to not dawdle. The narrative reason why everyone’s lives are so short involves anima. Ever since a meteor crashed and humans craved that power for themselves, the supply of anima has been dwindling. Think about anima like a life force for robots.  You might think this game disincentivizes exploration which is partially true. On paper it certainly seems that way, but because the time span given to each of your robot friends is very generous, exploration can still take place without worry. Even more so since you will occasionally find meteor dust, a consumable item which grants any robot an additional 24 hours. I didn’t exactly use my dust ‘optimally’ and I still only had one person die despite my heavy exploration and general messing around. I will commend the game for intertwining its narrative so thoroughly with its mechanics. Very few games pull this off in a way that doesn’t feel forced, and Unsighted does a fantastic job. Unfortunately, this mechanic falls short in one major way: the characters. For a game which puts so much of its effort into the mortality of its cast, it forgot to make any of them really likeable. The interactions you have with most of the game’s characters are short, transactional bits of dialogue. You will get a short scene with all of them the first time you meet, but that means each character gets only a few paragraphs (if that) to endear themselves. Thus, I didn’t feel any connection with these characters which deflates the main mechanic more than a little. The narrative, in general failed to grab me. Humans supposedly started to turn against the machines for…some reason and we hear some bad stuff they did. Crucially, we never actually see anything the humans do directly and during the time the game takes place in, all the humans are gone. As a narrative pro-tip, if you plan on making humans, as a whole, the villains, you should give a good reason why we shouldn’t like them. I am biased towards favoring humans since, you know, I am one.  Beyond that, the narrative boils down to collect the five things which will allow you to beat the game. Nothing too special. The non-narrative bits are pretty good. Dungeons contain solid puzzles (though some are annoying to navigate) and the combat feels decent. The combination of ranged and melee options feels nice. Even without doing much exploring, the main path will take you over most of the map. I don’t have much to say about the game play itself, its good but not enough to really wow me. I wish I felt more strongly about this game. The gameplay is fine but the narrative leaves me feeling a bit cold. A lot time gets spent on the story, one which I don’t think is particularly good—not outright bad or anything just falls short of carrying the game. It tries to carry the experience and that’s why its flaws feel more noticeable. In a vacuum, the story is fine but when so clearly highlighted it falters.  In conclusion, Unsighted plays like a Zelda metroidvania and thus, if you enjoy either of those, you will probably enjoy the gameplay here. However, if you really crave a great story in your games, you will probably be left unfulfilled.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not fear the timer.It took me 11h30 to beat the game, i took my time for the first run, obviously. You can remove the timer if you feel like it, but it adds a bit of tension in your every move. I think it was a good idea that needed maybe a bit more polish. Anyway, the game is made to be ran faster and faster on each subsequient playthrough.Combats are fine, i would have like a third melee weapon, but it's okay between fast sword and slow axe, and a dozens of ranged weapons. The metroidvania formula does wonders : being able to not only craft weapons, but also having, multiple ways to get around obstacles, or tackle the world in the order you want.Graphics are perfect, i do not mean the most beautiful, incredibly breath-taking, no : just not too coloured, not confusing. Not even "downtown" area, where lots of people speak bad on the reduced visibility due to the rain, was a bother. Every hints or hidden areas are displayed just like it should be.Scenario-wise, it is okay as is, not really talkative though, i would have prefered a tad bit more interactions with npc.Where this game needs optimization is MENUING. There are lots of weapons and chips to switch, sometimes during a harsh battle, it would have been more "organic" if there were a button (maybe the directional arrows?) to change our load out, and switch them on the fly without pausing.i had a blast, and if you like fast-paced metroidvania formula, you definitly should check this game

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- Big dungeons with well designed themes and layouts, varied mechanics, neat puzzles, and very good boss fights.- You will learn all there is to the combat in 30 minutes: parry until the enemy is stunned, then attack back. Most enemies have the same timing and the attack windows are telegraphed very clearly. If you master the parry quickly, you can even defeat seemingly unbeatable enemies. Same with boss fights, which feel very balanced because the only difficulty comes from when to expect an attack and them sometimes spawning multiple smaller enemies.- The story makes sense immediately (even if you don't care about stories) and actually explains most mechanics in the game.Neutral:- The characters look cool, a bit like action figures. Some may also find the dialog and relationship aspects appealing, but it didn't interest me that much.- There is the option to play the game out of order, but they really push you in the direction they laid out with the obligatory annoying emotional pet companion telling you what to do and the numbered dungeons. You can e.g. play the game in reverse order, but you may need knowledge from a previous playthrough to make it possible and at that point the game has nothing new or worthwhile to offer.Negatives:- Why does this game have Dark Souls elements? It doesn't need Dark Souls elements. Stop putting those in every game that has combat and exploration. No, I don't want to walk back to the boss room from the last save point for like 2 minutes and do the same platforming section for the 10th time. Just put me right back in front of the boss door and let me try again. And I also don't want to clear enemies but never fully heal because they will respawn (which is completely inconsistent anyways). I also want to keep running without having to waste an upgrade slot to remove stamina usage. And i bet losing half your currency on death unless you collect it again is just there because they found it on some "how to make a Dark Souls game" checklist online.- You can't see very well in this game. Most areas are tunnels or buildings with barely any lighting. Otherwise, the colors are kept very muted, so you can't easily distinguish enemies and projectiles from the background, especially when there's also rain on the screen.- The game really likes wasting your time (even when booting the game lol) because it's the only way to justify its main mechanic, which is the timer that is constantly ticking down. So when you respawn miles away from where you were, when you have to backtrack though dungeons, redo whole combat arenas, check back with the characters in the village, do simple puzzles to open doors, accidentally explore in the wrong direction - all of that is just to keep the clock ticking down so you probably lose a few characters on your first playthrough. And then you find out that the characters are meaningless anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a phenomenal game that echoes 2D Zelda and Metroid design. There's a generous playspace that spans 3 elevations and you're tasked to net 5 macguffins before you can enter the endgame. Right off the bat, I loved the game's difficulty. The weakest, smallest foes you start against do more than just 1 HP worth of damage, meaning you normally can't play sloppily, especially in the early game when you're pretty weak. Also, there's a time-limit mechanic whereby both you, but more importantly, the NPCs will eventually die if you don't offer them a unique item found in the overworld that extends their lifespan. Some NPCs hoard unique items/weapons that only become accessible if you turn in 3 of these items to them. Thankfully the game makes it clear what kind of item each of these NPCs holds, so you don't waste that precious resource. I noticed that the time mechanic made me focus on acquiring the macguffins and not dawdle about. I never felt like it hindered my curiosity to explore. You may not be able to "save" every NPC on your first playthrough, but I really do appreciate this extra game layer whereby you have to think about whose lives to prioritize.Another special element of the game is the utility of your items. Much in the tradition of Zelda, you acquire new tools and weapons that grant you new verbs to use in exploration. A gun can be used to shoot down foes, or activate switches. A shoryuken may be just another projectile, but you soon learn that it can also catch fire and burn objects that are only immune to fire. The game has several of these wonderful surprises that trigger your memory into recalling playspaces you couldn't navigate before. Also, the game does a great job of letting you know whenever you reach an area that you aren't equipped to engage with. Yet another tiny way the game does the player a service so they don't waste any time. It removed the frustration of hitting your head against a wall wondering if you aren't progressing b/c you can't figure something out or if you're actually missing a critical item that's needed to proceed.The combat is also excellent. As mentioned, the game's enemies hit pretty hard, so you'd do well to learn their movement and listen/understand their tells. Your dodges and attacks are governed by a stamina meter, if depleted you leave yourself open to attack as you can't dodge or parry. Your firearms are not affected by the stamina bar but do utilize the Gears of War reload mechanic. It's great fun weaving between attacks and letting your stamina nearly drain completely, then follow up with the firearm to let the stamina charge back up. In terms of dense, time a block right and enemies are left in a staggered state and susceptible to a critical attack. You can best most enemies with just two of these critical blows. Some enemies require multiple consecutive parries to enter a stagger state, so don't think this makes things too easy or trivial. Thankfully, the boss fights not only make use of this system, but many encourage the use of the tools you find in their respective areas. In sum, this is a fantastic continuation of the 2D Zeldas and Metroids. The game nails exploration, item acquisition that deepens your means of engagement with the playspace, and satisfying combat thanks largely to enemies who are NOT pushovers. On top of this, there's the interesting time mechanic that encourages you to think about the NPCs and who you're going to prioritize to take care of. Things I didn't mention: a breezy soundtrack that reminded me at times of The Seatbelts (Cowboy Bebop) and the Vampire the Masquerade soundtrack. I loved some of the moody, electro-jazz tunes and will be adding them to my collection. There's also a pretty expansive arsenal that I have yet to fully experiment with as I was quite happy with the default loadout. The art is easy to read and nicely detailed, same goes for the sound effects. I must also commend the game's map, as it provides you with sufficient hints as to where to go or where a necessary dungeon key lies. Replay value: the game lets you attempt any of the 5 dungeons as you see fit, though you really should require a movement tool that's left nearby the "first" dungeon the game encourages you to attempt. I'm on my 2nd playthrough now (I liked it so much on GamePass that I bought it on Steam) and I'm already noticing new ways of exploring the map by buying weapons that give you access to an exploration verb I didn't have on my first go until much later. Lastly, I really dug the Fallout-esque epilogue which details the fates of all the NPCs. I loved that it doesn't just omit the NPCs who didn't survive, but when it shows the shot of the cemetery it includes all the new tombstones of the folks you didn't save. Fantastic detail, surely one that may encourage folks to do better by the NPCs should they want to replay the game. I definitely am, not just to tackle the dungeons in a different order, but to see if I can save everyone, and also planning a third run to check out the hardest difficulty that needs to be unlocked.minor complaints:(1) when selecting weapons, I wish reaching the bottom item on the list would send you back to the top if you hit down one more time(2) the game is so well detailed, it seemed odd to me that there isn't a sound effect for when you hit a stop block when grinding on the rails(3) there are so many systems to help ease your travels, that I felt like the game may be too balance in your favor by around halfway point of the game. Not only can you upgrade your weapons, but you can stack permanent buffs on yourself, and even activate temporary buffs.(4) I wish the enemies encouraged the use of specific tools to make them vulnerable. perhaps an enemy could wield a shield that needs to be pulled off with the grappling hook. or perhaps there could be elemental enemies that need to be countered with a different elemental weapon of your own

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted certainly has good ideas, and solid foundations. It's the details where things fall apart. The basics of the combat system are fun (though unoriginal) but any semblance of balance is lost due to rampant power scaling on the player's part, and ranged weapons being way overpowered but also necessary to prevent you from tearing your hair out. One combat "upgrade" just makes it hard to dodge because if you try to spam it a little too quickly it activates the move which you don't want to do.Another failing of Unsighted is that it doesn't try very hard to make you care about the characters. You need to save them because... that's the plot. The game advertises itself as making you get close to the characters, and then forcing you to pick and choose between them but then most of the NPCs I only talk to once every hour. With 7 hours of play time I have not a shred of emotional attachment to any character, and just gave meteor dust to the ones that were most useful. Also, the whole thing about picking between characters you dislike that are useful and characters that you like that are useless? There are very few actually useful NPCs, and half of them have built-in lifespans that exceed what you would take to beat the game.
