_childDocuments_.review: Beaten the game in co-op via Steam Remote play, we have completed all achievements, which includes the true ending.Steam has a very binary way of recommending games, which is very important with the case of Unsighted. In terms of overall score, I feel a strong 5 out of 10 for this game. Depending on what you personally look for in games, I may either recommend or not recommend the game. If you like rock-solid gameplay with lots of things to explore and uncover, I may somewhat recommend it.If you expect to have a good story with well-written characters, this is not the game for you. I put “Not Recommended” because I value storytelling the most and okay-ish gameplay doesn’t redeem the game. Why you might be interested in playing the game aka gameplay review section: The main gimmick does wonders for gameplay of the game in my opinion: having a global timer ticking down puts emphasis on decisions you make, which is important considering that exploration is a huge part of the game. In a normal playthrough you would not be able to explore the entirety of the map without NPCs or the main character dying, you need to know when to take risks and how to be efficient with your resources, builds and the way you play Unsighted. Combat has good flow to it and accounts for different playstyles, depending on the way you build your character and what weapons you decide to utilize. The game doesn’t take too long to beat, first playthrough taking around 5 hours to complete with some of the issues beginning to appear somewhere in the middle of our session. Namely, with players becoming stronger both in terms of mechanical skill and equipment, the game doesn’t do much to try and catch up with the players in terms of difficulty (I acknowledge the fact that it is done in such a way so that players could pick any dungeon to start with and continue in any order, but the game could have used dynamic difficulty or introduce enemies that require unique combat approaches, the same is applicable to bosses, who go down rather easily). Outside of combat, the game has an interesting variety of movement options, which is helpful, considering that you want to go fast in this game (for Anima reasons and for speedrun reasons), puzzles are adequately puzzling and the world is very much explorable. Playing in co-op was a good experience (even with Remote play being quite laggy at times). If aforementioned things sound interesting, you might want to try Unsighted, especially in co-op. And here are the reasons why you will be disappointed playing the game aka story review section:Gradually diminishing Anima is a driving force not just only for the gameplay, but for the story as well. If player’s life force runs out, lights out and it’s game over. If NPC’s life force runs out, you will not be able to access them anymore, which sounds like a huge story-altering tool. Having a key NPC or multiple of them go missing from the story could open up gates for very interesting events and whatnot, but that simply is not the case. All characters in this game are disposable blank slates with no redeeming features. Factory robot Haylee undergoes more character development than any of the featured automatons, including main ones. The writing is absolutely horrid; every dialogue adds nothing to the story or makes characters involved sound dumb. All pieces of lore scattered around the map boil down to either “human bad” or “automaton mad”. There are no different endings that could have depended on choices made throughout the entire game (like letting certain NPCs live or die) and that applies to true ending content as well. There’s more, but since I could have gone on and on about the story, I will leave a condensed list of bullet points that underline my issues with the story (spoilers, naturally):  -	Main love plotline falls flat  -	Main protagonist is very boring and shows little to no redeeming character traits besides going “ooo Raquel” every cutscene-	Only a single dungeon boss gets some sort of lore backdrop (aquarium area), and it was incredibly underwhelming-	Other bosses just exist, they’re not story-relevant in any way and only exist to guard the shard (the idea behind Prometeu was cool I guess, but it could use more)-	Village NPCs have extremely limited amount of dialogue, every single line of which is agonizingly uninteresting-	Iris is incredibly unhelpful, annoying and should die-	I let Iris die and I wasn’t satisfied-	None of the automatons gone-unsighted are actually plot-relevant, ex-NPCs change to an enemy type and that’s it (except for Granny’s corpse found outside of the village, that one was neat)-	The ending sequence is not good, the concept of fighting against the godly embodiment of life force, winning and having said God be like “wow you’re gay? okay then, do whatever” is incredibly stupid-	The ending itself is a load of nothing, showing NPCs doing things means nothing to me if throughout the entire game I didn’t care about any of them-	The entire true ending sequence from narrative standpoint is disappointing (the dungeon itself was fine)-	M gets no character development outside of a single log fileIn the end, the story suffers from poor writing and desperately begs for cool interactions of the main gameplay gimmick with the world and its characters. Instead of having an NPC turn into a generic Dumbbot upon Anima running out, have said NPC turn into evil-self and have a unique fight with the player, or, have said NPC die and have their robotic corpse remind the player of consequences behind our actions. Have these changes reflect on our dialogue, story events and the ending in a meaningful way. Have dialogue that isn’t written like a stereotypical exchange of anime character clichés and have more environmental storytelling, I enjoyed these. I do not write reviews, but the developers of this game seem to actively follow the community, which is a good thing. I’m writing this in hopes that said criticism is going to be taken into consideration in order to develop a more refined gaming experience. The team behind the game is very talented and it shows that a lot of care has been put into making a great game, but I can only wish Unsighted had a great story to tell too.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game on Gog, bought the game twice to write a review here.As a person who's mostly bored of single player action games nowadays (last ones I enjoyed were Nioh 2 and Doom Eternal and that was like a year ago) and play mostly fighting games, I was genuinely surprised by Unsighted.I tried the demo and the first thing that lured me in is the feel (kinetics) of the action. A lot of action games fail at this - like 95% of action games on market are unplayable for me because of this (recent Aeon must die is the perfect example of kinetics hell). Here everything you do feels really satistfying and when you hit an enemy, attacks are so JUICY and MEATY (like in my street fighter haha). The second good thing I noticed is the combat itself. I really liked the fact that you can't just mindlessly dash around, I like that you have several ways of defending yourself, I like the healing system, the stamina system, the fact that you can jump over enemy attacks, etc.Speaking of jumps - the third thing that got me really interested is that you can jump and even wall jump in a top down 2d game (!) and it's well implemented into the gameplay. But the game didn't stop here - the are a lot of REALLY interesting mechanics that I don't know much coding knowledge one should have to implement. And they are extremely fun to use too. This point alone is enough for this game to stand out.The fourth thing is the time management. This is just brilliant. And combining this mechanic with things like passwords that you can use on the subsequent playthroughs to save time is even more brilliant.The fifth and the final thing is the general gameplay pacing of the game and the quality of puzzles. The mix of combat, exploring using fun abilities and puzzle solving works perfectly. It reminded me of the 1st dungeon in Cross Code when I was really excited about the game, but the grindfest that followed killed the game for me. Unsighted on the other hand is the embodiment of that 1st dungeon from Cross Code. The puzzles and exploration are all well done and don't require intensive youtube consulting (the only puzzle I didn't have enough iq to solve is the 3rd puzzle in the ruined catacomb before the super-crab boss).Not to sound too fanboysh, I should pinpoint minor gripes - -Making additional slots for equipping weapons and weapon switching button (DMC-like) would save a LOT of time spent in menu.-Factory boss (mecha) is a bit lacking - I think it focuses too much on timing attacks (parries), and not enough on positional attacks, not utilising your mobility and positional play enough.All in all, it's a 9.5 game on my list. If you compare it to similar modern games, it's 10 times better than Hyper Light Drifter (HLD may have a more solid graphics and ost, but that's it) and it's what Cross Code should have been.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is one of the best metroidvanias of the year - and you need to play it. Here's why:The PlotThe plot is intriguing from the off. You control Alma, an automaton who awakens with amnesia at the start of the game. After you escape from an underground laboratory, pieces of the past start to come back to you, as do familiar faces, and the woman you love. In a neat subversion, sentient robots, or the ‘sighted ones’, are the good guys here, with humans cast as the antagonists. They have crafted a weapon to turn the robots into mindless killing machines – known as ‘unsighted’ and it’s only a matter of time before all anima (the resource that provides sentience) runs out.A Beautiful Mix of the ClassicsUnsighted features a bit of everything. The top-down pixel art style, and combat, is similar to Hyper Light Drifter, the level design reminiscent of classic Zelda games and the upgrade system is typical of the metroidvania genre. There’s even a sprinkling of Dark Souls in there; you drop resources on death, but can pick them back up if you return to the spot of your demise on your next run. Yet, I never once felt the game derivative. In fact, it pulls all of its inspirations together into a super cohesive experience.The GameplayIt’s hard to cover everything I like about the game, but here’s a few things. Unlike HLD, verticality is added to the top-down areas, which open up when you get a high jump and wall climbing ability. Combat is slick and satisfying. Enemies are not a push over, and require timing and precision to defeat. You have an easy-to-use parry move, that pushes foes back and opens them up for a critical strike. There’s a neat crafting system where you can forge new weapons, upgrades and the like. The Countdown TimerAnd then there’s the potentially divisive enforced time limit given to complete the game. Early on, you are told all sentient automatons are on borrowed time, and will turn unsighted when they run out of anima. When talking to NPCs, you get to see how long they have left before they mechanically croak  it – so to speak. Anima can be harvested. But will you give yourself more time, or those your meet? It’s not often I play a game that really poses such a moral dilemma.I imagine some will definitely be put off by the enforced sense of urgency, as you really can’t be wasting time exploring every nook and cranny of the world. Luckily, the developers have included an ‘Explorer’ mode, which removes the time constraints and allows you to play at your own pace.The Wrap-UpThere’s also additional challenge modes, a boss rush, a dungeon raid mode, as well as local co-op. The developers have really thought of everything – and considering the game is primarily the work of two people, it’s some achievement. If you want a super polished metroidvania with an engaging story, I really can’t recommend Unsighted enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is an action adventure game. Play as Alma, players find themselves awoken in a war-torn city named Arcadia. In order to save her friends, Alma needs to traverse through the land to find answers and solutions before before everyone loses their consciousness, thus becoming Unsighted. This is a well-polished game,  sporting beautiful pixelated artstyle, an inter-connected world full of secrets and treasures waiting to be found, a simple yet satisfying combat, and more or less a good story. It does have some minor issues and other questionable design choices. There are still more rooms to improve for Unsighted, yet I still consider it a wonderful experience. If you are a Zelda fan or a metroidvania enjoyed, please don't pass on this gem.The standards for inter-connecting world of metroidvania grow larger and demand more variety. I am glad Unsighted not only passes the grade but also adds some interesting interactions to enrich player's experience. You are free to roam most of the world. Every area contains secret hidden in plain sight waiting for the keenest eyes. From time to time you will encounter some areas where you need specific tools to go on. Classic. What I love about how Unsighted does the trick is that some of those hidden treasures are blueprints for guns that can double as traversing tools. The best example is the cryo gun. It can be found somewhere in the underground aquarium, but its blueprint can be found in other place if you explore enough. This design choice marks the difference for my playthrough. Getting the cryo gun early on opens up so much more water areas for me to explore.The one in previous section is just one of many ways Unsighted allows you to optmize your adventure in Arcadia. The game has a countdown mechanic as a race-against-time challenge. I love this challenge, but I love it even more when the game lets you turn it off. The world is rich in detail and totally worth your time to take it slow to explore every nooks and crannies. As a soul-like, Unsighted has its fair share of difficulty. Besides weapon upgrades and chips, the game also introduce cogs as temporal buff. Their introduction is early and is a great way to ease the pain of dying over and over again. Cogs can be acquired by buying from merchants, crafting, and fishing. Yes, Fishing. Fishing is another way to improve your gameplay. It's one way to get bolts, materials, and random cogs upon perfect timing, as well as a moment of respite from the fanatic combat.→Wonderful pixel art.→Soundtracks slap.→Interesting and unique bosses.→Lovable NPCs.→You can pet four dogs and a cat in Unsighted.→Quite generous parry window.→Iris is really cute.Most of the bosses and their dungeons are quite balance and entertaining in their own way. However, the final boss and the boss in ruined catacombs up their ante way too much. They have become the very definition of damage sponge. I know the dev justify this by expecting you to have a powerful corrupted weapon. And yes I do have a +33 axe but it still feels really underwhelming.→You can't craft or upgrade multiple items at once. You need to reopen the menu every time.→Upgrade cost can be really grindy.→Axes consume way too much stamina.→Some secret area can use just a little more hints.→Wish there were more weapon types rather than just swords and axes.→Why can't I use Morgana's great scythe????中文小簡評→向薩爾達致敬的類銀河系惡魔城。→充滿驚喜且互相連通的世界設計。→遊戲擁有許多直接和間接手段讓玩家能夠渡過卡關的痛楚。→多多探索能夠先行解鎖好用的道具。→音樂好聽。→架招易上手。→四隻狗跟一隻貓任君摸頭餵食，如果你找得到牠們的話。→後兩隻王坦度高得不尋常。→製作跟升級道具都只能一個一個做，做完直接關頁面，想多做就得做一次開一次。→升級武器要的錢很多、很農。→斧頭消耗的體力太多了，砍兩下就累了。→很希望能有多點武器類型。→為啥不讓我用M的大鐮刀QQ。

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 Game.Pros: Music and graphic slaps. Combat is extremely smooth and the parrying system very satisfying. Decent enough explorations and a variety of environments.Has New Game + which allows you to inherit all items.The game rewards you for sequence breaking, very nice.Cons:The timer mechanic is a hit or miss - unfortunately it's a miss for me. I much prefer to have all the time I need for exploration which is my favourite part of any metroidvania games, and the fact that the timer forces me to forfeit exploring and just rushing bosses and ending stories is extremely frustrating. Good thing that the devs allowed you to turn off the mechanic and play on - maybe if I do an NG+ I will have the timer on.Low variety of boss fights. It's gets quite similar towards the end and has a very similar pattern for every boss. Personally dont like some of the sprites, the ratios feels a bit off. Not particularly a big fan of some designs either.Very singular fighting style. There's little to no variety between different weapons for playstyle and the equipment upgrade mechanic is basically not useful at all. This game heavily relies on parrying and that's about where all your damage come from. Upgradng doesn't matter at all.NPC are very, very flat and bland. They have little to no stories and it's hard to develop any connections with them. Also, a lot of vendors has overlapping items which makes some completely useless (like 3 of them sells the exact same kind of craps - and you can never run out of craps because they have a decent drop rate, so i never had to buy from them at all).Some weapons are also used as a travelling method to get through obstacles, and it's quite often that you need to switch between them. Switching between off hand weapons is a gigantic pain in the butt and doesnt feel smooth at all, especially when  you have to do it so much.Final area wayy too small and trivial. Definitely not enough thoughts put into that.Overall, though I did write a lot longer about the cons they are all minor details. It's a very fine game. Majority of the time, I had a great time. Main problem would just be story and NPC developments - which are at best mediocre, which is quite a shame because there are potentials. Still, would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I have just defeated the first major boss and I can already recommend this.What made me like it at first is how well put together it is. Everything feels right so far, the sprites, the sounds, the parrying, the dialogue, the music kicking in when in combat, the little roll after dodging while sprinting... it feels very good to play and feels even better when you start to play it well and fast.One of the things that might be more divisive are the time limits, personally I really like them. Also, If you don't like it, you can just disable it by using the explorer mode. I don't think the game depends on the time limit to be great so I recommend you give it a try even if you don't like time limits.I like the idea of an exploration game with a time limit, it turns exploring into a decision that costs the resource of time rather than something with no cons. And since it's a time limit for each character, including you, and that time can be extended with items, I really like the layer of having to choose whose time to extend.It's uncomfortable when you watch your timer go down a little every time you enter a new area, and when you see how much time someone has left when you talk to them. But it being uncomfortable is why I like it, it made me feel the urgency of the situation instantly. I also feel it's long enough for you to take your time sometimes, but short enough for you to feel it's really there.The game is very open-ended. It gives you a recommended path, but it gives you a lot of freedom to do things the way you want to! I don't know how long the game is, but I really hope it's just the right length so that I can feel good about replaying it multiple times and trying different routes and outcomes.also the robots are gay so 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted isn't here to re-invent the wheel.  Metroidvania's have been around for a while and so there are a lot of lessons to be learned and the devs for Unsighted LEARNED.  It pays homage to those before it, elevating the aspects from each it has borrowed and provides it's own flair in just the right ways.Definitely put it up there with Hollow Knight in terms of setting an atmosphere, telling a story, and doing it all with engaging gameplay that never feels boring or like you "just have to get through this one part and it'll be fun!"

_childDocuments_.review: Equally puzzle/combat metroidvania. The game requires some crazy creativity with the movement options you get. Solutions are never simple and sometimes tedious. Combat, crafting, chip (perks), cog (power ups), weapons, and loadout systems are typical and straightforward. Despite a very complex map, the game does a decent job directing you, as it should considering the time constraints. The environment is detailed, animation is very fluid, music also caught my attention a number of times. Characters are likable, but most don’t do much.The most interesting decision this game makes is to give you time limits for every character, including yourself. You can easily disable them but it was clearly intended. Being on the clock made me consider not talking to everyone I met or breaking every rock I saw, especially in the second half. The stress did a good job immersing me in the story but also retracted from the fun. You will have to make decisions that test your morals, doing something or nothing to prevent the death of yourself and others. This system is why I will remember this game.Overall, lovely. Quick tip: when in doubt, parry.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't played the game enough yet to make a full review, but after the three hours I've put in so far (I'VE BEEN BUSY), I can give you at least a description of what the game is like.Imagine a mix between CrossCode, Souls and old SNES action RPGs like Secret of Mana. That's the main gameplay loop you'd sign yourself up for and it works amazingly well. The combat could have a little more depth BUT I'm willing to bet that there's a lot more that I just haven't gotten to yet.Story themes are nice. So far nothing too out there, characters are written very well, believable and likable. At the time of writing this, I cannot go any deeper into the story, but have a little spoiler for the very early bits: The artstyle of the game is amazing if you're into the 16-bit aesthetic. Character and enemy models have very unique designs, which makes combat readability very easy. The music is fantastic and I can see myself jamming to some of this during work. The environments look intriguing and flat out gorgeous.Something I've seen a couple negative comments about and I'd like to clear up: The game features a time mechanic. Basically, every character you meet on your journey has a clock that is constantly ticking down. This might put pressure on the player, but the devs have been super nice about it, by including an exploration mode, where you can slow time down to a "crawl" and not have to worry about it, giving you more freedom overall. Don't be afraid of using this mode on your first playthrough. It might not be the intended difficulty (WHICH STILL CAN BE TWEAKED IF YOU WANT HARDER COMBAT, BY THE WAY), but the game is intended to be played multiple times anyway and starting out with a slow exploration playthrough instead of a stressful first experience sounds pretty ideal to me.I can highly recommend this game, even after only playing for a rather short amount of time. I've only spent 3h on it so far and already feel like I've gotten my money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is meant to be played multiple times. In the first time you will most likely fail, lose a number of character due the 'time limit' they have and so on - but everytime you gain map knowledge and defeat the bosses quickly, allowing to beat the game faster and save the most of them. It is challenging and rewarding.That said, Unsighted is a GREAT metroidvania with gorgeous visuals, fluid combat and an amazing dystopian sci-fi world. It is definitely worth for the price and if you like the genre you should give it a try.Edit: you can also active the Explore mode in the menu which 'removes' the time limit. Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Me when my whole village dies because i didn't feed them space fentanyl, i'm just a girl!pretty cool time trial-esque zelda souls game. they took zelda's exploration, souls-like combat, outer wilds time limit (OUTER WILDS MENTIONNED?!?!) and blended and twisted it all into a short but content dense game. the art in game is great (although i'm not a too much of a fan of the character sprites in cutscenes, they look uncanny), the world has a ton of variety and interconnects decently well a bit like in DS1. combat could be a little faster, i found that the main character walk speed was slow even with speed upgrades, but even with that being said parrying is still a fun mechanic, but the enemies could use a bit more attack variety as most of them just have two moves. the OST has some MAJOR hood classics and i'm confused why no one talks about it, crystalline made me not want to leave the caves. with all that being said, the highlight of the game is definitely the time limit mechanic. basically you and every NPC in the game is on a time limit and if you want them to live longer, you have to give them space fent. problem is, space fent is limited so you have to decide if you want everyone to survive, give more space fent to a certain NPC to get special rewards or just take it all yourself so you just don't die. this sounds rough, but it is pretty forgiving so as long as you take some of your time exploring you will get your desired outcome. this pretty much encourages you to do multiple playthroughs and the fun part of it being a knowledge based game is you can sequence break it. alot. if you take your time to learn what everything in the game can do, you can break the game and just skip to one of the last bosses or even get busted stuff in the tutorial. it's hard to do on accident, so don't worry if you tend to "over-explore".overall, solid game with a few things that could be changed. sequence breaking is cool. 8/10, would deprive my loved ones of space fent again

_childDocuments_.review: + unsighted has a great world building and overall setting - the setting itself is nothing too exciting, but well made nonetheless. loved the atmosphere while exploring the vast, abandoned and unsighted infested cyberpunk city.+ the story was well written and engaging. quite emotional as well at some point. told over the course of the game with simple dialogues and gorgeous cut scenes. + characters are adorable and memorable throughout the game.+ combat feels polished and plays excellent. the whole combat is more or less built around parry. the parry windows are fairly big and the payoff for a successful parry is huge. the mechanic itself works kind of like in sekiro, so if you whiff it's still a block in the end.+ metroidvania aspects are well made and fit into the game. honestly they're actually fun and some of the "tools" are useful outside of standard "metroidvania"-progression and mostly based around  all sort of range weapons.+ bosses are unique and somewhat challenging. may need a couple of tries (or not if you abuse cogs [consumables]), but nothing too fancy except two bosses tied to the secret ending. + exploring the areas is quite enjoyable and feels rewarding at any point in the game.+ the difficulty settings. difficulty isn't built around a simple mode like "easy", "normal or "hard". you have certain settings and option at the start of the game and while playing, for example: deactivation of the time limits (robots going rogue), easier combat, some combat power ups called cogs and more. kinda like the build your own difficulty kit.+ the puzzles are decent. crosscode comes to mind even tho the puzzles in unsighted are overall easier and less complex. i personally liked it that way, but that's preference.+ top notch pixel graphics and a well crafted art style in general.+ soundtrack is quite good and atmospheric.+ unsighted just wants to be part of the speed running community from the core of the game.~ sequence breaking the game is easily done even in the first play through and can potentially be done in many places all over the game. for me this one's a huge positive, since such things always ad up for future runs and speed running in general. could be a bad thing for some people getting stuck cause of it tho.~ unsighted mechanic - every single character (the main character is no exception to this) has a given time next to it's name. if this time is over, the character goes unsighted and is basically lost for the rest of the play through. it's definitely not a negative even if you dislike permanent loss and / or time limits, since u can simply disable it at any point in the game. on the other hand it does add a lot to the atmosphere and plot tho, so keep that in mind if you're planning to deactivate it.~ there could be overall a bit more text and dialogue for my taste.~ you can offer "meteor dust" to the named npc's, increasing their live span and affection to you. this whole thing itself isn't a bad feature and i kinda liked the idea. sadly the npc's answers are the same after every single gift, with an exception after the last one, yet kinda disappointing. this could be so much more in terms of character development.- iris talking bs about parry after every single death. i do love you little one, but it starts getting annoying quickly. add an instant skip button for this dialogue or a disable option in the settings.- the "wind" in the upper level wasn't that great. it didn't add anything to the quality of platforming and is constantly slowing you down for no reason.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid metroidvania of decent length. It'd probably be longer, if not for the time pressure the game puts on you.The time-dependency mechanic on the characters, including the player, really leads to a sense of urgency when playing the game. You're constantly trying to find items to extend their lifespan, but it's never in enough supply to save everyone - especially since you need to save yourself. I really enjoyed this, honestly, as it made me think hard about which NPCs I wanted to save and how far down I would let my time go to extend the lives of others. As an experienced Metroidvania player, I managed to get away with only a handful of deaths, but this could easily spiral out of control for newer players. The game is also insanely sequence-breakable, on the level of Rabi-Ribi. It downright expects you to crack it open, and really lets you explore freely if you're clever enough. Combat is fluid and smooth, albeit a bit lacking in variety. The art and story are also pretty good, although figuring out height and depth is a bit funky sometimes. Boss battles are a bit too basic but still provide a meaningful challenge. My only complaint is that .All in all, a very good metroidvania that I'd highly recommend checking out. 8/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I did all of the challenge achievements I cared to a while back when I played this. Pretty fun and challenging, with a lot of potential diverse paths. The time mechanisms for triggering Unsighted might be a turn off, but you're meant to make choices of whom to support, and whom to save--up to and including sacrificing. Your resources for saving your friends and allies is effectively limited, but there's perks to each person you invest into, receiving permanent upgrades, special items, or weapons, etc.The game is appropriately challenging, with an emphasis on parrying. You're also highly encouraged to further combine in your ranged and melee, particularly for the challenge dungeon and boss rush (and something additional). Overall, combat has options in weapon choices for both melee and ranged, as well as your actual utility with mobility (a strategy I didn't personally use, but have seen a lot use it).The art and animation is very good, along with the sound effects. Soundtrack varies, cementing the bleak atmosphere, or having some pretty nice boss battle music. Some of the dreary ambiance can be kinda dull if you're slowly exploring an area, but I'd say only one specific zone comes to mind for me.This game seriously supports speedrunning, up to and including the developers being aware of possible skip straight to the end with an in-game interaction. lol As a standard, you can do all sorts of wild skips and speedrunning tricks, but you should absolutely play the game through your own way first.Overall, I enjoyed going for the challenge achievements later on. I didn't do any of the speedrunning things personally, since I enjoyed the combat enough.Great game, and I highly recommend if you're into the genre. I did get lost in a few areas until I learned the maps better. I might replay this at some point.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good. There's a few annoyances like save rooms being too far from bosses, weird default controls and for some reason you can have 3 weapon sets that you scroll through with the d-pad when they could've just let you bind every direction to 1 set and leave 1 for healing or whatever. Also making several weapons necessary traversal tools that you have to then switch to between combat isn't ideal. The game also shoehorns you into parrying and counter-attacking which in turn makes strong but slow weapons way better than faster weapons even though those feel much better and look cooler. It also makes combat very janky if there's more than 2-3 enemies attacking you.Overall I still like it enough though. More games should implement the Gears of War reload timing minigame. The art is very good and the style reminds me a lot of Hyper light Drifter. Music and writing are nothing memorable but they get the job done. If you love metroidvanias definitely get this one on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Felt like I was playing Zelda: A Link to the Past on SNES all over again, in a good way.Picked this game up cheap, with some hesitancy, but I was convinced by the incredibly positive reviews. And the game earns them well. It's a solid metroidvania with stellar combat, exploration, puzzles, and genius map design.The graphics and music aren't amazing, but they get the job done. We're here for gameplay reasons, right? And Unsighted has that in spades. Yes, you will look forward to every combat encounter. You'll squeal with glee when you get ambushed by 5 enemies. And in between you'll be engrossed with progressing through tricksy, puzzle-laden rooms, and rewarded often with unlockable shortcuts that make navigation easier, not to mention all the loot that allows you to customize how you like your combat.And yes, you will be using both melee weapons and guns and damn, it just feels so chunky. So finely-tuned and so satisfying to decimate big foes after parrying them. Which in this game, is easily attainable - not some skill to be skipped over because only the perfect-timing-elite can handle it. Or you could build your character to pelt enemies with bullets and grenades from afar. The game gives you 3 loadouts to play with, and lets you change those loadouts instantly, even in the middle of battle, without having to slog through slow menus or long character animations.I won't comment on the story since I don't play games for story, but it seemed fine to me. The dialogue is quick and the cut scenes are skippable (many thanks to creators who do this). And it's always nice to see characters treating each other with kindness, whenever you take a break from the unspeakable violence.I kinda cheesed my way through my first playthrough, playing on the easiest difficulty, and using the minecraft-style crafting system to make myself a bunch of late-game items at the beginning of the game. (As long as you know the recipe to make an item, even story items like the hookshot, you can make it in the first few minutes of the game.) But even with all that, the game was challenging and the bosses had me sweaty. The game is designed such that you can conquer the areas and bosses in any order that you want, so even with mild cheating, you won't find yourself stuck in an area that you're completely unprepared for.The bad:Not anything major, just a few nitpicks.-First of all, although the controls are good, it might take you a few attempts to find a control scheme that works for you. Perfectly doable.-You'll end up spending a fair bit of time in the menus. Crafting things, adding chips to slots (like the Hollow Knight charm system), swapping out weapons, and turning temporary buffs on and off.-the name. Is so Unsightly. So much that I kept failing to notice that I actually had this game installed and it sat dormant for a month. But this downside can be overlooked.You need it. Buy it; play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is best described as something like a topdown Zelda game with a particularly fulfilling combat system with its parries and dodges. Good thing blocking and dodging hits is so very fun and rewarding because most of the enemies here will hit real dang hard.There are multiple ways to adapt combat styles in Unsighted, from getting new weapons to modifying Alma’s chipboard. New chips are easy enough to find or buy if one has the credit, but the problem is space for more chips. To buy more chip-space, we need the currency of Unsighted – which is where the game turns into Dark Souls in some ways. It follows the typical formula of “kill badguys to get dosh! If ya die, gotta pickup dosh before ya die again!”Unsighted offers a large futuristic city to explore, interwoven with a variety of ways to explore. The game promises that the way we choose to traverse this world is up to the player.  The clock that Unsighted’s city of Arcadia runs on is slowly ticking down with every moment wasted dying or spent exploring. As time progresses, every character in the city will eventually run out of Anima – the energy keeping them from turning into kill-crazy robots. This pressure made it hard for me to enjoy exploring the game once I realized it was there – but there is an Easy mode, as well as an Exploration option for the game.The developers did a good job putting a variety of options for different playstyles in the game, while maintaining their vision. In addition to the story mode of the game, there are two additional ways to play: Dungeon Raid, and Boss Rush. I was able to get somewhat far into the first Dungeon Raid I attempted, but it was pretty difficult – my abilities at these sorts of sword-fighting games are certainly lacking. Dungeon Raid was a neat remix of assets from the main story with a sort of rogue-like element where in between each level the player picks upgrades to their character.Unsighted is objectively a good game, with its quality art, clever level design, and satisfying combat. I think a lot of people will really enjoy what Studio Pixel Punk and Humble Games have brought us, especially those people that enjoy games where the exploration is sneaky and cunning with its path and reward placement. I’m really looking forward to returning to Unsighted on Easy or the exploration mode to get a fuller look at what Arcadia has to offer – apparently there’s even fishing!I totally recommend UNSIGHTED, especially for those who consider themselves skilled in games with this sort of combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this game multiple times! I'm going to just do a quick rundown cause it's older and on sale so... you know... read this, and then buy it! Just to start, the presentation is great, the art has a lot of personality and the character designs while fairly basic robot fare overall are varied and well animated. While the story isn't hugely complicated, the writing is decent and the characters are endearing enough that you care about what happens to them.The time mechanic is really intimidating at first but as soon as the game introduces it you can turn it off if you're really concerned (though not only do you as the player start with plenty of time to clear the game a lot of the important NPCs have more time to start than you do so unless you're dying a lot or backtracking a lot to explore you'll probably never risk running out of time), and there's a fairly abundant item in game that you can gift to NPCs/use yourself to extend your time so there's plenty of ways to deal with it.The combat and the movement is just... top notch. In both combat and movement the game feels incredibly responsive, and combat feels really rewarding as you are incentivized to keep up the pressure by the combo system but the stamina bar means you can't just mindlessly mash buttons. Parries are a nice mix of fairly forgiving if you miss the "perfect" timing but also challenging enough to keep the combat engaging. The movement feels incredibly smooth and many of the puzzles in the game have multiple ways to solve them depending on how comfortable you are with the movement and traversal.There's also a few different difficulties and some accessibility options to make the game easier if you're struggling with the combat but would like to experience the game, which is a nice touch, as there's a lot of hidden stuff to find and even just running around the world filling in the map is super fun when you've got all the movement options unlocked.Overall, if you were a fan of something like Hyper Light Drifter, definitely give this game a shot. It's an incredibly solid game, especially when you consider that the dev team is two people, and there's tons of extra content to explore even past the first playthrough (new game extra/new game+, extra super hard difficulty, boss rush and dungeon raid modes)

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. The timers are a divisive mechanic. A lot of people don't want to play under the "pressure" of constant timers. But really all the pressure is entirely psychologically. You have 300 hours to live and an in game hour is more than 1 min. So you never actually need to extend your own live time if you beat the game in ~10 hours which is basically the normal game length anyway. And most important NPCs have more live time than you anyway.I actually was kinda disappointed in how little the timers actually matter. And even if a npc turns, they don't actually get a cool fight against unique enemies but only a generic enemy you have fought before already. The other merchants also do not comment on how their friends are suddenly gone. That part should have been fleshed out more considering how core to the game its supposed to be. Weapon variety could be better and especially the stuff the npcs offer is kinda useless after a while, which is a deliberate choice since the npcs can die but again its a diminishing factor on the timer mechanic. But the actual game play and metroidvania map are phenominal. Any fan of metroidvanias should play this game, even if they are sceptical about the isometric aspect. The platforming is very tight and you don't constantly have depth issues like in something like Cross Code.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is unbelievably slept on. Fantastic and incredibly dynamic combat, engaging puzzles, beautiful art direction in both the visual and musical departments. Endearing story and lovably characters (to a fault honestly). The timer that's constantly ticking for each NPC adds an even more stressful and engaging aspect to the game. You have to make some hard decisions sometimes in order to keep certain people alive. You can also turn this aspect off (I did my first playthrough because A) I wanted to explore the world at my own pace on my first go around and B) I didn't want the nice old lady to die. Once you finish the story the first time, there are multiple new game modes (including a dungeon crawl which works beautifully for this games combat/item system as well as a fast paced boss rush). Well worth the money. More people need to see this game. Thanks Iron Pineapple!

_childDocuments_.review: It's easy to bite off more than you can chew when making a video game. You can dream up a bunch of features and mechanics that you've seen in other games that turn out to be way harder to develop than you thought. Most of the time, the game ends up never being finished or just being an unpolished mess.Unsighted is not one of those. Instead it's one of my favorite games of the year.Movement is fast and fun, combat similarly so; and the game invites you to play it multiple times and see how much you can break it open. The entire map is jam-packed like an intricate clockwork of shortcuts and puzzles, always giving you a new fastest route to where you want to go.The time limit, while stressful, is respectful of the player inevitably struggling on their first playthrough and further encourages breaking the game to finish it faster. You Will Master This Game.Please, please please play it if it looks interesting to you. It's a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: This... is a really good game. The constantly ticking timer on you and all the fantastic NPCs contributes beautifully to the plot's tension without being so tight that you can't save everyone (as long as know what you're doing). _childDocuments_.review: I do not think this game is getting the proper attention it deserves. I got this game as a gift from my brother for Christmas, and at first, I thought, "What the ♥♥♥♥ is this? Meh, Thanks bro!" then I booted it up. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, was I surprised, wrong, and humbled. Call me slightly bias, but Metroidvania's are my favorite genre, and this one hits the nail on the head. The pixel art style is some of the best I have ever seen out of any generation. This title has a combination of some of the best tropes from several different games, while this game does not reinvent the wheel in any new gameplay style, as long as you have a captivating narrative and the gameplay to back it up (which this game does). This game was just solid fun from front to back! Pick this one up. You will be glad you did!

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED is a brilliant blend of Metroidvania and Zelda, with gorgeous pixel art, jiving soundtrack and touching story. Perhaps the biggest highlight is it's combat, which feels fluid and satisfying, especially the parrying mechanic. It helps that you have a surprising amount of customisation at your disposal.Exploration in itself is fun but also intense and sometimes anxiety inducing depending on what mode your running. Yet, I'm referring to the time mechanic tied to both Alma (Your character) and other NPCs. Yes, for some, this can dappen the experience, but the game makes it clear you can turn this option off if you so please. However, for me, I rather loved the mechanic, as it added to the story and gave me a sense of urgency that other exploration titles just haven't.Also, I said it before but I'll say it again, the pixel art and animation in this is absolutely jaw dropping. There's so much art and detail put into, which makes the world stand out along with the banging soundtrack.If I did have one caveat, it's that once you acquire a lot gear and chips, it can be bit of a slog to scroll and sort through them. I'm hoping future updates will add a sorting element to the UI as a QoL improvement. There's also sometimes the need to switch weapons, which can be cumbersome sometimes.However, the above are very minor issues for what is really adrenaline pumping experience. It helps that the game can allow you to sequence break a tone in future runs, which really ups its replayability a tone. Bottom line, if you love metroidvanias and zela and pixel art, you definitely need to give this game a try

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, this game has everything you should want from an isometric metroidvania. There's a lot here to enjoy. (Unless you're horribly turned off by adorably pixel graphics and and awesome soundtrack, in which case, that's a personal problem.) Then you get into the nitty-gritty and...the game is still good. Really good. Until about 3/4 of the way through. Then it's...boring.And it's boring for a few reasons. Reason number one. This game does NOT get more difficult in a meaningful way. Enemies just do more damage. You see every single attack pattern in the game in the first hour. Then you learn to parry. Then the game gets easy. Unless you mess up the parry. Then enemies deal more damage. And the game throws more enemies at you, stretching the limits of your stamina bar. Which isn't inherantly bad. But it does lead into the core issue with this game.Reason 2: The maps are confusing. Its super easy to get lost, and sidetracked, and then you have to backtrack. A lot. It reminds me of link's awakening. Which was good...when it came out. But the map design in that game is based around the game boy's very limited memory. Which means the dungeons are about 70 percent backtracking to extend the game. Which is understandable on a game boy game, but not anymore, when PC games have basically unlimited memory to work with. But this deliberatly obfuscating level design does get tedious. Add this to busy-work puzzles, which are remarkably basic and easy, but do serve to take up a bit of time, and ONLY to take up a bit of time, and you'll start to see a pattern. This game. Wants to take up a lot of your time.Because everyone is constantly dying. In the game. In real life, too, but also in the game. They have a literal death clock. It's a main selling point of the game. And it would matter if...if literally any of them had anything resembling personality. But they don't. I never cared about any of them, except what I could get from them. Even your little fairy companion, which is like Navi if Navi was even MORE obnoxious, so, Fi, basically, has a death clock. And you know what? I wanted it to run out. I wanted that little, annoying, flying box of trash to die. It made me happy. I was happy right away. And that's the game's core problem. It is busy work for the sake of busy work, to elongate the playtime, so that the deathclock every NPC has is meaningful. But. It's only meaningful if you care about them. And perhaps it's the translation, but the writing in this game is the equivilant of a 1980s fan-translated anime made for edgy 12 year olds. Meaning. Awful. I simply don't care about any of the characters. Life, or die, 99 percent of the game will be the same for me. Sure, I can't upgrade my weapons, but I keep getting better ones, so that doesn't matter. Sure, I can't buy upgrades, but I get free ones all the time. Sure, I can't buy items, but you don't need them, so who cares? It's a good idea, wrapped up in a decent package, that turns into a slog of a waste of time towards endgame. Is it worth it? Maybe, if you're more patient than I am. And I'm pretty patient. It's by no means a bad game, it's just a horribly flawed game. Consider yourself warned, and, I hope, enjoy.TL/DR because your brocheal region is underdeveloped:Game doesn't work good because boring characters remove emotion impact of core concept, leading to slog of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like the game; however, there were a few things that really made the game difficult to enjoy as-is. The positive: I enjoy the open-world aspect of the game, the map system, and learning that certain abilities can be used in different ways that was not expected (wall jumping, spinner on lava, etc.). The puzzles were a nice touch as well. The negatives: this game is WAY too hard with too much of a focus on parrying. Only 40% of users beat the first boss - so it is difficult to say the least. Your fighting style has to be parrying or you won't make it. I have no idea how people beat the crypt boss or the last boss without explorer mode help. Also, the 'secret boss phase' is literally impossible to do on your own without a guide for the ancient clockwork pieces. I really wish I could have gotten into the story more or more into the lore/backstory of the world. I felt that the story was lacking and pretty generic - you only got a few sentences of information at the last boss for his backstory and that was it. Also, the 'secret boss phase' didn't add anything of substance to the plot/ending. Lastly, the whole 'love' concept with the lesbian androids felt forced.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a deeply satisfying and memorable labor of love that will stay in my thoughts for years to come.The combat and parry system is greatly satisfying to master, the time limit instills every moment, every encounter you face with a sense of weight and urgency and the soundtrack was masterful in both it's quality and use. Finally, the graphics are packed with a mind boggling amount of detail considering the small team that worked on this game.That is to say this game isn't without it's faults. The English translation is a bit rough around the edges. The scenes and general plot conveyed what they wanted to convey; but I always felt myself taken out of it by some of the stilted dialog. Beyond that, I wish the supporting characters did more throughout the story and got some more development. Still, this is hard to do with a small team and the nature of the game's mechanics.While the game is deeply satisfying and challenging, I found it a little too easy to break once you get the hang of things. By the end of the game I could craft an near infinite amount of healing items, even in the middle of combat; and the last meteor shard boss died very quickly to a +5 thunder blade + a full suite of attack boosting chips.Still, I highly recommend Unsighted, because it is the best kind of game; one made with love, determination, and craft. A personal piece, one that makes me feel like I've really gotten to know what's important to the developers. I also highly suggest you play with the time limit on.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing metroidvania with excellent artstyle, enjoyable combat and very fun bossfights in amazingly done dungeons. I really wanted to like the game and almost enjoyed my time with it - However, the negatives outweigh the positives too much to choose this game over other metroidvanias:- NPCs are too bland and one-dimensional. They are irrelevant at best and mostly annoying.- Time mechanic, the premise of this game, is not relevant at all. It's actually the opposite, I was looking forward to have some NPCs die to no longer deal with them. However, even with plenty of backtracking, major NPCs do not get near their time-limit.- One of the most annoying companions I have experienced. Long, unskippable cutscenes to trivialize new puzzles before you even get to experiment with them take away from the more enjoyable parts of the game. Despite the dungeons being fun and rewarding to explore, you only feel annoyance everytime the companion chimed in.- Story is decent but gets worse the farther you go - utter mess in the end unfortunately.- love relationship is forced, they actively dislike eachother at first and continue to dislike eachother until the story/flashback tells you they actually care deeply for eachother? Simply because the story wants you to? It's lazy, either flesh out their relationship more or leave it out

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a hack-and-slash that has a unique time pressure paired with a limited resource that makes you decide which robot friends you want to keep alive and with that, also their benefits (gear, healing, powerups, upgrades)There are two problems with this:So I turned it off, and I’m glad they had that option. I would have refunded it otherwise.The combat and overall feel of the game gave me hints that it’s a hyper-light drifter but at home.Aka, Unsighted is overall too easy. You have an open-ended world design, where you can go to any of the 5 required areas in any order to beat the game. If you don’t know why that’s bad, you don’t know how important a challenge curve works. Speaking of, you have a parry that is required like sekiro, and it’s too forgiving. Enemies are too readable and most fights are won by just parry than slash. Nothing to really mix it up.Because of this open-endedness, each new unlock is mostly tied to that zone. You need this bayblade in one area to grind rails to get around, you need a grapple hook to traverse large gaps. But outside each zone, it’s rarely used for some reason, beyond one or two secrets. You can ride your bay blade to move faster, so that’s nice.It’s a weird choice to have this time mechanic, a parry system, and open freedom to tackle bosses in order, but none of it felt right in execution. Unsighted is an easy game but hard to recommend or not, because it’s not a bad game, it has so much potential if they further refine the combat and find a way to make choices but not tie it to a timer. Maybe let me choose a friend to save over another; it has the same effect but doesn’t ruin the gameplay. You have variety and a cool mech section that requires powering it on and off in a fun minigame.But the core game and story overall got less interesting as time went on and it’s mystery was revealed. So I’d have to give an overall thumbs down. Hope to see the improvements on your next game, as it’s not that bad for a first game made.

_childDocuments_.review: i feel really bad leaving a negative review under a game that was worked on by only two people, and i seem to be in the minority when it comes to stuff i didn't likenonetheless, the biggest turn-off with this game for me was the lack of polish when it comes to... just about everything the music and character art is a bit goofy, environment art is often too overloaded making it hard to parse what is even going on on your screen, lack of any pixel grid makes all art look wobbly, there is for some reason a very glaring plot hole in the ending, the speed at which you push blocks during puzzles is abysmally slow, the game does not respect the player as an intelligent being, most visual cues that are in place get huge red circles and arrows around them in form of your pixie companion pointing them out, it is also extremely mechanically complex and drops all that complexity on you within the first 30 minutes but then all the combat is just "wait for enemy to flash red, guard in time to stun, hit, repeat" and enemies/bosses almost never get more interesting than that. and speaking of bosses, they feel stretched out, considering they all have very simple attack patterns, and that *your* only attack is parry and hit, it really feels like you're just stuck doing the same boring thing over and over again dozens of times in a span of 3 or so minutesi don't feel like i'm qualified to talk about the story or writing but i've seen a lot of other people say they're not good and i'm inclined to agree - i found it hard to get attached to, care for, sympathise with, any of the characters in the story at all. which is a pretty big flaw imo considering the game's main gimmick is the lifespan (time limit) all these characters have. it has its place on a technical level because the intention (i guess) is for you to prolong the lives of characters that you find useful (that you buy items from etc) and if you reach max friendship level with someone, they will give you some special item or ability (but you don't know what kind, which makes it even more intriguing). but to me, that just feels like i'm befriending them only to gain something from it. as if i am doing it with an ulterior motive. as someone who would never do something like that in real life, it felt off to me.i could go on, probably. these are all small things but they add up and as a result the game was a slog to play through because almost none of it felt good or satisfying. there are a few gimmicks it introduces along the way (in the suggested order) that are actually pretty fun, but they're underutilised and as soon as the game got at least somewhat enjoyable, it was over. it feels like a collection of small neat yet unpolished ideas that were put together without giving how they'll interact with each other any consideration well, that's just my opinion, anyways. based on the rating and the lack of any negative reviews in this vein online, i guess most people aren't as pedantic about what they play, so maybe you'll enjoy unsighted. i didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Brazilian indie devs taking the world by storm! Heck yeah! I really love this game, not only because it was made in my homeland (by a studio founded by two very talented girls!) but because it is genuinely amazing in (almost) every way.The game is a top-down pixellated Souls-like, set in a futuristic sci-fi city inhabited by robots. There was a war against humans in the past, and the remaining robots need dust from a special meteor to retain their consciousness, as otherwise they'll go "unsighted" and become mindless machines. As the protagonist Alma, you must venture through a post-apocalyptic city in search of crystal shards to penetrate the ominous tower at its center, so you can save all robots from going usnighted, and rescue your girlfriend Raquel, who was kidnapped by the humans. Both the post-apocalyptic sci-fi story and the intense romance are extremely well executed here.One may be excused for thinking the whole "unsighted" thing is just a stand-in for the concept of going "hollow", but unlike hollowness in Dark Souls, going "unsighted" holds more gameplay impact. See, in Dark Souls, NPCs only go hollow if their particular story reaches a certain point where that is supposed to happen. Case in point, Sigmeyer going hollow in Ash Lake, Laurentius going hollow after trying and failing to reach the witch of Izalith, etc.In Unsighted, on the other hand, there is a ticking clock associated with every character, showing how much time they have left before going "unsighted". Once they do, they're gone forever. Every single friendly NPC is subject to that, including helpful merchants and your adorable fairy friend. The amount of meteor dust items to extend NPC's lives is limited, and they're also kinda hard to find, so you have to spend them wisely. That mechanic holds upsides and downsides for both gameplay and narrative. For the narrative, the upside is it forces you to choose between helping the NPCs you like the most, or only the ones you might need. I, for one, find that to be a significantly more interesting form of "moral choice" than the usual "good vs bad" we see in so many RPGs. The downside is most characters remain in one place, and interact with nobody but Alma herself, making some of them a bit one-note.For the gameplay, the upside is it keeps you constantly on the lookout for more dust, and the decision to help one NPC over the other affects what kinds of upgrades you'll have access to in the long run. There is also a ticking clock associated with Alma herself, so you might need to use dust on her as well. The downside is that the developers created this amazing, large world full of cool secrets, but the ticking clock over everyone's head discourages you from exploring it too much, since people's lives are on the line.The more you progress through the game, the more friends you lose along the way, and the more desolate and cold the world feels. I find that a brilliant way to create a sense of impending doom. If you don't succeed on your quest, then everyone will just die out, and if you take too much time to finish it, then almost everyone will die out.You may also choose to turn off that mechanic altogether. I don't think you should, at least not in a first playthrough. I advise you to beat the game once as intended, then turn on exploration mode to finish exploring the city on a new playthrough. Without that mechanic, the game is still pretty good, but the impact of the narrative is almost entirely killed.Okay, so let's talk about the other aspects of the game, starting with the presentation. The pixel art is absolutely stellar. Every character animates with a ridiculously high amount of frames, and the environments are always spectacular, sometimes even too detailed. I swear the first time I walked out of the tutorial area, there was a bit of information overload before my brain adapted to all the details.The music goes for simple ambient tunes that get pumped up and extreme when you're in combat. I quite like it when games do that, and it works well here. The sound effects are good too, the shooting effect being particularly visceral and satisfying, to the point where I defeated most bosses using almost only ranged attacks.Speaking of shooting, how about the combat? It's also pretty good! It's fast-paced, challenging, and very fun most of the time. There are two different types of melee weapon, a few different types of ranged weapon, and almost all feel good to use. There are parries, dodgerolls, quick weapon reloads if you time your button presses right, and all very well implemented. The combat favors fast decision making and quick reflexes, and some fights are absolutely epic. I quite like the boss fights in particular, as they elevate the challenge without being overwhelming.Without spoiling much, the final boss was AMAZING. I remember saying this OUT LOUD at least five times while fighting it. "THIS BOSS FIGHT IS AMAZING" I said, and my wife, who was asleep at the time, told me to tone it down a tad.Another thing this game does quite well is the movement. Just running and jumping around is extremely satisfying. There are some decent platforming sections where you must hop across chasms, and sometimes you might need to wall jump to reach some ledges. You eventually unlock this spinning top thing, like the one from Twilight Princess, but actually satisfying to use. Later on, you also get a double-hookshot which is even more awesome.The level design is reminiscent of both Dark Souls and Zelda. From Zelda, it takes its abundance of puzzles and usage of dungeon items to open paths, and from Dark Souls, it takes the interconnectedness, the way we open new shortcuts as we explore, and the ominous dark atmosphere. It is incredibly well executed, to the point where it rivals actual Zelda dungeons.I do have a small gripe with the way parts of the world are designed, however, and that may just be a me problem. It makes sense for a dungeon area guarded by an ancient protector to have tons of puzzles and platforming sections, but I really don't understand why a ruined city of all things has certain, for lack of a better world, video-gamey parts to them. Like, someone just left this block puzzle here in the middle of the city? It just doesn't make sense to me. Heck, even Zelda strays away from including puzzles in the "overworld".And since we're mentioning Zelda so much, I think I need to address the elephant in the room: the fairy character, Iris. I, for one, adore her, but I bet she's going to get on some people's nerves real quick. She's adorable, and her character design is really precious. I love her face-screen and how expressive it can be, and I also like how she actually adds a bit to the narrative aside from being "the tutorial character". She has this really sweet and emotional backstory that got me invested in her.However, she has this REALLY annoying tendency to pause the game to explain the obvious. Everytime you encounter an obstacle which requires a key item you don't have, she says something like "I don't think we can get past this with our current equipment," and sometimes she says stuff like "oh, look, those blocks we saw before!" - EVERY SINGLE TIME YOU SEE THE DAMN BLOCKS - so by the end she was trying my patience a little bit. I still love her, though, because I find her absolutely precious, but I perfectly understand it if some people just let her go unsighted. A friend of mine commented that Iris has... jiggle, but I think he needs to stop being horny all the time.Overall, I think Unsighted is an absolutely excellent game. It has many amazing qualities and very few flaws. I recommend it to all fans of action adventure and action RPGs.Also, please don't deactivate the unsighted mechanic unless you absolutely can't play the game with it on due to anxiety or some other problem, or if you've already played the game and want to see what you missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid enough combat, environment design, and variety of ways to progress that I still mostly enjoyed a style of game I'm not usually much of a fan of even without finding one of its main features interesting enough to not turn off.Top down action adventure with Zelda like elements and a timer that can be turned off where the other characters you meet and your own character will eventually lose their minds and become like the game's enemies unless you give them a limited supply of items you can find that will add to their time limit. The story involves your character waking up with some memories missing in a destroyed city where the remaining robots were at war with humans. Years ago a meteor crash left a crystal-like object on the planet that gave the machines sentience by giving them anima. During the war with humans they did something that blocked the anima from that object from reaching the remaining robots and over time they started to lose their minds and become violent. The main character is told to retrieve five fragments from the meteor that were given to powerful robots that they had lost contact with in order to forge a weapon that will allow her to enter the structure blocking the spread of anima while also attempting to find her girlfriend she had been fighting alongside before being damaged.You can equip your character with three loadouts of two weapons that include swords, axes, grenade launchers, shuriken you can control after throwing (more useful for puzzles than combat), and guns with some having fire, lightning, and ice elemental effects. You can slot chips into your character with stronger ones taking up more of your limited space to influence the damage you do, your health, stamina, reload speed, and to add a variety of other helpful effects. Combat is fast paced as you can quickly run and dive and turn those moves into quick attacks but your strongest source of damage comes from parrying an enemy attack right before it hits you which will put them in a stunned state where a hit will cause massive damage to them. The ranged weapons make use of a Gears of War style reload system where you can reload much faster if you hit the reload button and then hit it again when a fast moving meter is just over a notch in the middle of the UI.The game gives you a variety of ways to sequence break or to take different paths as they are multiple ways to deal with certain kinds of obstacles with what you have available, skills you might not know about at first like wall jumping or attacking while jumping to gain extra distance. You might cross over water by finding switches that make platforms, use a single or double hookshot to swing across, use a spinning top you can stand on to bounce over the water, use an ice grenade to create temporary platforms of ice, etc. Your ability to do things like that are further enhanced by being able to craft most of the games items from blueprints even if you haven't found or bought the blueprint by remembering what items and configurations craft what. The environments and enemies are typically well designed and animated.Usually I am not a fan of this kind of Zelda like genre. I normally find combat and combat options too simplistic, which is improved here, but what I didn't find any better is the environment and puzzle design. There is a lot of fairly useless things to find, you'll run into multiple puzzles where to need to push blocks around or slide them over an icy surface in ways that will land them in the correct slots, you'll run back and forth to activate switches to make the right blocks appear or platforms to rise or lower. There are a lot of dungeon design choices and side activities that are little more than time wasting busywork to run the clock out for yourself or other characters, a timer which I just ended up turning off as it both added nothing to the game for me and I wanted to take some time to test things out. New game plus and new game extra modes allow you to start a game again with different things carried over from your last playthrough and that combined with the knowledge you have of the game now is the main way you would be expected to be able to save the majority of or all of the game's characters if you are playing with the timers. Most of the game's characters are pretty low on personality and likely due to the mechanics of the game most aren't able to do much for you when they are alive as what they provide can often be earned in other ways or just isn't important at all. It gives you very little personality to your existing enemies and most bosses and that seems like a place where more of the narrative could have focused. There's some small moments with characters like the one that just uses the last of his time fishing to clear garbage from the water for the remaining fish but I can't find much use for the timer when you only vaguely care about like three people and the game would just be set up to say, "ok just run through it all again but faster now that you know exactly what to do and start with an advantage." It's not Pathologic where you have to make some hard choices.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be discouraged by the "negative reviews". The game is extremely well polished and the combat mechanics were executed exceptionally.The negative reviews are misleading, and often done by misinformed people: the game has a "global timer" mechanic in which the player and friendly characters have an expiration/death timer. Your objective is to try to save them and yourself, making this is a crucial part of the narrative. The game gives you the proper tools to deal with this timer. For those who don't like the idea of a time limit or the consequences involved with it, the game also offers an "explorer" mode which gives you more time than you would possibly need.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game.However, it has one major flaw, the game is on a time limit. All the friendly NPCs and even the main character have a timer constantly on them, reminding you that they will die soon. When NPCs go, so does their shop, or whatever services they offer, if the main character goes, well thats the end of your save. In a game that plays like a metroidvania, where you get new powers to reexplore old areaa, this seems like a major design flaw, there is no fun in exploring when there is only anxiety.To the games credit, there is an option to disable the timer, however, the game warns you this is not the "intended experience". I like intended experiences, and I like a challenge, so I played with the timer running. As I got further into the game though, I found myself not wanting to play a game I had been enjoying. The anxiety of exploration was too much for me to want to enjoy, and my instinct was just to stop playing. Eventually I gave in, I turned off the timer.Suddenly the game was truly fun again, I could run around and do things and die in fights I had no chance against, I decided playing the game without the timer was the way to go. Soon however, the problem showed itself. The games world is portrayed in  a certain way, and suddenly it lacked the tension. The intended experience was correct, it was there with good reason. Without the timer, this games atmosphere, and a few of the mechanics, make no sense.The game needs the timer, and that is a problem. Left with the choices of a timer with all of the stress and unfun exploring, or no timer with the game lacking the bite the story wants to present, there seems to be no solution. There is one clear solution: play a different game.

_childDocuments_.review: I just cannot complete this one. This is my second attempt and I've left off where I did the first time - right after completing the Highways boss. It starts out feeling as if it'll be interesting, exciting, and unique; however, it ends up with extremely middling combat, okay exploration, and very very flat characters. In a game so focused on time being against you, you'd think a single character would have personality but that is not the case. No one has a unique voice or storyline and the flashbacks are wildly boring.On top of this, the controls are just odd to me. So many buttons are used when combinations or context-specific buttons would work far better. The puzzles and exploration are not hugely difficult to figure out and there's no point where you're like "Oh! I can do THAT?" You're limited to two items per loadout, which is fine, but puzzle specific items take up this space when they could be hotkeys or trigger combinations. This really slows the pace.Unfortunately, the combat is dead simple and never gains more complexity than the first fight. I seem to be an outlier here, but I really don't think this one is worth the money when there are so many other fantastic Zelda-likes out there.
