_childDocuments_.review: This is gonna sound very exaggerated, but for me it's not.Unsighted is probably one of the best games I've ever played. I grew up alongside flakship IP's and titles such as early Zelda titles or Final Fantasy. I am vastly aware of the significance of many of the titans that have influenced and formed gaming as we know it. I also hold many of them dearly and "dearly" doesn't even remotely scratch the significance of just how deep I care for many of those games. For me, those games weren't just games - I identified with them and have profoundly deep emotions for them.Sometimes, games are just good. You play it for the first time and you like it. Sometimes, just sometimes, it its you so deep to the core that it just isn't some videogame anymore and it kind of becomes your friend or family. I'm sure most if not everybody has that one game they played that is so important to them on such an elevated level that saying "it's a really good game" doesn't even begin to cover it.This is where Unsighted, for me, comes into play. Gameplay-wise, It's basicly a fast-paced SNES Zelda with metroidvania-like platforming. You know, the typical loop of coming across obstacles that you can clear later once you have the right tools and such. In that regard Unsighted doesn't do anything groundbreaking or new. The thing that makes it so unique and incredibly good is the world, the real-time consequences, the secrets, the possibility to express skill and the overall presentation of it all.Without spoiling, the world all around you lives and dies in real-time. Characters can actually die and you have to make a lot of decisions. (If this freaks you out, you can also turn it off so characters "don't age and die" anymore. There's also new game plus and because of the mechanic above, it integrades so damn well into the flow of the game. You can do so many different things depending on how you handle the dying world around you and get all kinds of different outcomes that actually change some things. (I'm being vague on purpose)New game plus also does one thing really well and that's you having tools and power you'd usually not have. (duh) and apply them very smoothly. You can do things completely out of order and the game just does fine. You don't feel that linear restriction anymore.There's also a lot of customization to your character and choices for how you play and decide to build it up.The game also looks just incredibly gorgeous and the ironic part is, yes I have mentioned this JUST now all the way at the bottom of my review, but the truth is, the visuals go hand in hand with everything else. It fits so well together. The game can also be really difficult and you have a lot of control over it and I'm not talking about artificially restricting yourself like those challenge runs in others games like "no magic no guns just melee" or whatever. I'm talking about the raw difficulty of the game. You can somewhat control it and it's kinda baked into the gameplay. (Being vague on purpose again). Of course you also have the traditional options for difficulty, but that's seperate to what I'm being vague about.Honestly if you're down for a world that feels very immersive and significant and you enjoy fast-paced action combat and skillful mobility and map movement within the genre of adventure and metroidvania, then I can't recommend this game ENOUGH.One of the best 20€ you'll ever pay for a game. In fact, if it's on sale it should be straigh up illegal NOT to buy it. It's just that well done.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: This game was interesting to say the least. I found that this game has some really good highs and some shallow lows. There was a lot, that I felt, kept this game from being top tier. The area exploration was great and it was really fun traversing the whole map and finding secret areas and shortcuts, it was really refreshing to get to areas I was not supposed to due to the movement system and the jump slash giving you extra distance. One thing I should add is as soon as you get the hook shot (granted it is much later in the game) it makes every area really easy to traverse, which can be taken either way, that being good or bad.I felt the combat was very awkward at times and when playing on controller at least it felt like I was accidentally did something I didn't mean to, it is not the games fault for that but something worth mentioning. Along with the combat it felt a little repetitive at points but it was a rare feeling. The bosses were lack luster for the most part. _childDocuments_.review: gladly drops you in a world you know nothing of and say “good luck champ, go getem” before putting you on limited time to complete this metroidvania title based on exploration and route-finding.Robots and humans had a big conflict over one of the only energy sources left, that left the world torn asunder and with humans keeping the robot consciousness-giving resource for themselves inside an impenetrable tower.It’s up to an amnesiac robot-girl to find a way inside to stop this madness, collecting five artifacts that will help you achieve your goal.You are dropped in an overworld and let free to explore.You can equip up to two weapons of your choice, both long and melee range, to face enemies with, along with a 3-loadout system swappable at the press of a key to expand your available arsenal even more.Attacks are simple and functional, parrying also makes an appearance as a great way to dispatch of enemies as almost all attacks can be easily parried and reposted for a lot of damage.There is no traditional leveling in favor of a “chip system”, opening upgrade slots to receive specific bonuses from chips you can swap in and out anytime you’re at a save spot.in true metroidvania fashion unexplorable areas aren’t gated behind progress but movement options, maybe the gun that freezes water can pe used to traverse that area you’ve seen some time ago, or a high jump letting you jump between those two blocks you didn’t know what to do with.During exploration you’ll be doing a bit of puzzle-platforming, using the tools you have to navigate towards the next area or to receive rewards from treasure chests.And now to talk about the mechanic that’s also in the title: UnsightingEvery robot in this world is given consciousness by an alien meteor, and this meteor being sealed away means you, and everyone else, are on a timer before reverting into just another enemy you’d see in the overworld.Time ticks down every second you’re not in a menu, dialogue, or cutscene meaning there’s limited time you can complete the game and even less to interact with the many NPCs that have a gameplay impact like chip sellers or blacksmiths.Even better as you can find a resource during exploration that can extend this timer by 24 real life minutes, and as on your first playthrough it’s a trial and error experience where to go and what to do first, you’ll have to face the choice of who to give this precious time or if to keep it for yourself. I don’t like some art choices, like the use of mixels (basically pixel size inconsistency or rotated), or the heavy contrasting colors that sometimes fill the whole screen.The wall-jump mechanic is implemented abysmally, and even worse it will be required in some sections.Many weapons that have a use to activate switches and needed for exploration see almost no in-combat use, restricting your arsenal as these are a must have to travel around the map.But the strangest offender is the main Unsighting mechanic itself, as you’re pushed to never stop moving to take in the world Unsighted paints as NPCs will die left and right if you do so as well as shortening your own character remaining time.The devs made this optional however but enabling infinite time for everyone would go against the narrative and artistic choice this game went for in the first place.Unsighted has the misfortune of coming out in recent times but with a design philosophy of the very early indie game scene, making it unable to soar the heights others enjoyed by simply having their title release in a different timeframe.Doesn’t do anything too different but it’s really enjoyable nonetheless, I recommend it, but I’d say wait for a sale of at least 50%.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a flawed masterpiece - some things it does extremely well, while a few poor elements stop it from being a fully satisfying experience. Firstly the good - the non-linear exploration is great, with the player unlocking new abilities that enable them to reach more and more previously blocked areas as the plot progresses. This strongly encourages backtracking and secret hunting - you can easily spend 20-30 hours on a playthrough if you're a completionist. Gameplay mixes elements of Zelda, Medroidvania and Soulslike to great effect - challenging skill based combat and puzzles, minimal hand-holding so you actually have to deduce where to look next or what you might have missed to find something you need in an previously explored area. This blend of influences in combination with a refreshingly unique art style, buttery smooth pixelart animation and tasteful atmospheric music makes for a really impressive and at times inspiring experience. Some of the subtle details clearly show the game is a labour of love - for example, the pause menu is so well designed and animated that I often found myself opening it just for aesthetic enjoyment. Now for the bad - unfortunately, the devs made the baffling decision to include a countdown timer as a central mechanic of the game. It does make sense for the story, but in practice a mechanic like this fundamentally undermines the style of gameplay everything else is built for. It's the kind of world that takes a lot of time to explore, requires backtracking, has you losing time figuring out puzzles - everything about the gameplay screams slow and methodical, so throwing a death countdown in the mix just makes things too stressful and implies that you should be speedrunning as the optimal approach. THANKFULLY, there is the option to turn this mechanic off, which is absolutely essential for this game to be worth playing. It would have made so much more sense for the devs to make non-timed the default game mode, then to offer the timed one as an extra challenge for NG+. The timed mode could actually be fun for players who already know the game well, but it absolutely will not be fun for anyone's first run. The other worst aspect of this game is the story - the plot is wafer-thin and just as water soluble. The dialogue and characters are equally one dimensional. No depth whatsoever to be found here, which even further highlights how silly a choice it was to implement that timer mechanic in such a central way - it was purely for the sake of plot, but the plot isn't strong enough to merit a core mechanic revolving around it. In conclusion, some parts of this game are truly excellent, while other areas haven't been given enough thought. If you're into challenging combat, exploration and aesthetics - it more than delivers on these fronts; just make sure you play on exploration mode (non-timed) for your first run and don't expect too much in the narrative department. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a thrilling adventure game built around an apocalyptic setting and puts pressure in the player in the form of managing real time as a resource.The visuals of the game are smooth, beautiful and more often than not dim colors which fit the setting like a glove, along with helpful animation clues to tell what actions are the enemies doing in the middle of the combat screen, which can get cluttered with projectiles, slams and slashes.Gameplay-wise is super responsive, with options to tackle enemies from long or short distances, play with the enviroment to kill enemies quickly and use various tools that can turn the tide of the combat, along with a Combo multiplier which rewards flawless execution by the player.The dungeons are intricately built to provide various challenges in the form of platforming and puzzles using the environment, while also being able to connect to various areas of the map, allowing the player to visit areas through multiple routes either by speedrunning or exploration.The soundtrack while simple and fitting for the game, it changes along with the enviroment of the dungeons and when the player goes in and out of combat seamlessly.My only complaint is that it can be kind of hard to change to a new weapon in the middle of a playthrough, due to the upgrade system requiring materials and the time needed to grow accustomed to the new equipment, I would rather stick with the practical weapon I choose at the start of the game, time is running out after all.In my first playthrough I couldn't save everyone, but I was able to make the best for those who were still there with me. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. If you love metroidvanias and top-down Zelda-likes, this ain't one to skip. Similar to CrossCode and Hyperlight Drifter. You gotta rescue em first, but there's like 4 of em, and they're all good boys. They'll sic the baddies, but also bug you for food and naps. 3hr naps. Which may not be worth the time wasted bc everyone you meet in this game is on a doomsday countdown timer. X amount of hrs (in-game, not actual hrs) until they turn "UNSIGHTED," rendering them useless monsters. You can find meteor dust which will extend a life-span by 24hrs, so you can give it to NPCs or keep it for yourself, but it's unlikely you'll be able to save everyone. Not on a 1st play through at least, especially if you're slow as me, exploring every nook and cranny of the map. Thankfully, you have the option to turn that stressful in-game timer off, which I did. I couldn't deal with the pressure of letting potentially useful NPCs expire bc I'm slow and there ain't enough meteor dust to go around. But I'm definitely gonna play it again with the timer enabled, as intended, and probably on the max difficulty bc I got WAY too OP on my 1st play through. Beating the game unlocks New Game + and New Game Extra, which I assume one is a continuation where your progress carries over and the other is not. But yeah, great frickin game. I wish there were more just like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a great top-down action game that wears its influences on its sleeve, but is willing to put its own unique twist on things. At its core, it's structured like an old Legend of Zelda game: you have a bunch of dungeons you need to get through before fighting a final boss, and while you can theoretically do them out of order, that takes a lot of know-how and on your first playthrough you'll likely be doing them in the recommended order. As such, I view the game as a Metroidvania, but purists may disagree since it's not a sidescroller like the classic examples. The game does a lot very well, but also has its fair share of flaws, both of which I'll cover here.The combat system is pretty simple to understand but somewhat hard to master. It's very parry-focused, in most fights you switch between whittling down the enemies with your gun and then parrying to set up a charged melee attack for huge damage. It felt very satisfying and meaty which is a huge plus in my opinion, but I know some people don't like parry mechanics and it is important to note that those are absolutely the focal point of the combat here. In my experience, a few of the bosses were difficult, but some were easy and none of them were as difficult as something like Hollow Knight. One of the game's biggest selling points is the concept that the way you spend your time really matters, as each character has a finite lifespan and will eventually die. I thought this was a cool concept, but I should note that it can be disabled, and in my experience it didn't make a huge difference anyway. I had a fair number of deaths (each death progresses the world forward by one hour) but still managed to beat the game before any NPCs I really cared about died, though several minor characters were long gone by the time I made it to the end. Of course, I wouldn't fault anyone for disabling the system if you don't want to worry about that at all. Speaking of NPCs to care about, there weren't many of them. One of the flaws I feel obligated to point out is that the game's plot is pretty thin. There's an explanation for why you're doing what you're doing, and there are a few characters, but there isn't much to get invested in. The way I see it, the lack of a deep plot isn't a huge downside for a game like this which is heavily gameplay-focused, but a really strong plot and characters I cared deeply about absolutely could have elevated the experience. Another flaw is that the game has some very annoying segments in the dungeons. Out of the five main dungeons, I found one of them to be a pretty bad experience overall (the aquarium, which has a lot of sliding ice physics and some very annoying enemies), and I mostly liked the others but there were several specific rooms or encounters that frustrated me. Overall, though, I really enjoyed my time with Unsighted. From landing a charged attack on a boss right after parrying it to take a huge chunk out of its health bar, to finding a grappling hook and feeling the world open up, it's a really satisfying game to play through. I'm looking forward to Studio Pixel Punk's next game, and I'm sure I'll come back to Unsighted in the future too.

_childDocuments_.review: IMO this game is really good. It's basically a top-down 2D Metroidvania style game with Dark Souls (lite?) esque combat. It sounds weird but it really works! The game has a lot you can do to essentially specialize your character build to your liking/needs which I love and made heavy use of. The upgrade chips are one of the best examples but there are also a lot of weapons that you can obtain in a variety of ways and you can upgrade them. Overall the game starts off incredibly strong with all of these systems and a really detailed world that invites you to explore. Going off the beaten path is really rewarding.Regarding the timer system: I played in Explorer mode and honestly would recommend it (this mode disables the timer system). The game is built around this timer system that limits character lifetime and it's integrated into the story but frankly I feel that having it enabled would discourage exploration too much for my liking and would prefer to have it turned on in a future playthrough.The game starts to suffer from some bloat and annoyances towards the end of the campaign. Some of the user interfaces really need better ways to scroll through them faster with a controller to find the items you want. The chips screen was the worst offender especially since I wanted to vary my build for certain situations (exploring, farming for money, boss fights, etc). This game REALLY needs some sort of chip loadout system and some tweaks to make navigating the interface better when you get a lot of chips (at least on controller). I also thought the factory area was pretty annoying honestly but it was not all bad and the puzzles were interesting.The upside is that this is the sort of game that seems to have a lot of replayability and I really look forward to future playthroughs and going for some of the achievements. I discovered some awesome secrets on my first playthrough and ways to obtain some weapons early that I am excited to use in the future, and I want to see how fast I can beat the game, and on hard mode with the timer on. I also plan to go for 100%. The core gameplay of this game is frankly incredible so there are lots of things to try. I highly recommend Unsighted especially on sale. The aesthetic/music is very good, the gameplay is super rad, and it's overall a great game that isn't too long to get through.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted:Base price: £15.49Price paid: £7.74EST. Length (hrs): 8-11.Time played: 9.25 hours.Roll credits?: Yes.Rating: 4/5 Great.Reasons finished:Unsighted is a very charming game. It’s fun to play, has a decent story (that does, granted, take a bit of a backseat to the gameplay) and has several side activities to play through. The games fun, simply put, if you enjoy the general flow of Metroidvanias you will enjoy Unsighted. With that out of the way, the game has several mechanics unique to it. Some argue that these mechanics bog the game down, despite the controversial nature of them I have no qualms with any particular choices the developers made as I felt everyone of them enhanced my experience. To give you a good idea without spoiling any of the game, the main attraction/controversy that has the game stand out is the choice to have a game long timer constantly ticking down. This is true for your playable character, but also for the npcs. Every character in the game has a timer counting down continuously until they die, or as the game puts it, they go “unsighted”. The reason for controversy surrounding this core feature of the game is due to the limited nature of the time you have with certain characters or just to explore the map in general. My personal take on the mechanic is that I felt it wasn’t restricting until the end game and even then I had accumulated plenty of “meteor dust” (a time extender) to get by just fine. That said meteor dust doesn’t take away from just how limited everyone’s time really is. In your playthrough someone you like will die, for me it ended up being most of the npcs as I really took my time with the game. Unsighted genuinely brought with it an emotional kick everytime I got the alert that an npc I liked had gone unsighted. I came into the game with the mindset of saving everyone but that was not physically possible and so I left only wanting to keep two alive no matter the meteor dust cost. My favourite thing to come out of the time limit was a moment during the final dungeon where I had no meteor dust and one of the two characters I wanted to keep alive had less then 8 hours remaining. In real time this only amounted to around 8 minutes and as such I believed they were going to die. Within the last remaining hour of their time I finally picked up a piece of meteor dust but by that point it was too late. I went to their store and was forced to watch them go unsighted. It’s moments like that really make me love this mechanic, it’s new and it stands out sure but metroidvanias don’t typically put many eggs into the character basket and as such when one finally did I loved it. The timer is limiting, that is absolutely true but if the disheartening nature of watching npcs you’ve been trying to keep alive finally succumb to the games world is something that won’t have you upset to the point of dropping the game you will like it. For me I felt it made my playthrough my own and it made the game feel more real, emotional and it made the stakes higher. Moving past the timer I feel my only criticism of the game is that the story felt undeveloped in certain places. While I appreciate that it was added to layer by layer with each dungeons completion I felt there was context that could have been added pertaining to the core events of the game. Minor spoilers here: To give an example I would have loved the added development of the beginning of the war between the humans and the automatons. How did it begin? Why did the doctor take the automatons side? Why did the father of Iris start creating fairy bots? I had some unanswered questions and while it’s nothing major even in a text log the additions would have been appreciated. All in all though the game is great, it’s core mechanic while controversial makes the game stand out and made my playthrough feel unique in a way not many metroidvanias can do. I felt the characters and stakes were both fun to interact with and work around respectively and I felt the game overall was a very fun and enjoyable package. I would certainly say it’s with the £15 price tag, especially considering the 8-11 hours of content. If you have the option to buy the game on sale then you’d simply be remiss to miss out on it provided you are a fan of the metroidvania sub-genre. While I appreciate I’m quickly sticking this at the end I’d be remiss to ignore the soundtrack. The game’s soundtrack is amazing. I even told a friend “I hear people rave about different games soundtracks a lot but I don’t really feel I notice them. They don’t typically stand out to me as anything extraordinary but Unsighted’s soundtrack is so genuinely good.”  With the obvious exception of Undertale this in the first time I’ve found myself listening to a games soundtrack of my own accord. In particular the track “Anima” stuck with me. The music sounds pretty similar to One Shot’s soundtrack and as such it’s an automatic ace of listen. I can’t way to replay the game and achieve the true ending.Summary:Unsighted is a fun game, it’s time limit for each and every character can absolutely be constraining but I feel this adds a layer of depth to the games stakes and to each characters presence. I wanted to keep characters alive but sometimes I simply couldn’t and while each death was a kick in the balls it added to my playthrough in ways no other metroidvania has done for me. My only criticism is the story feeling like it took a big backseat to the gameplay, which while not necessarily a problem for a metroidvania, some extra logs adding to the core part of the story the same way as with each of the five major bosses would have been appreciated. If you like metroidvanias and you’re willing to pay the price of the timer killing off most npcs you’ve come to appreciate during your time in the world then you’ll love it and for the general 8-11 hours of content the base £15 price tag is worth it in my opinion. Soundtrack is also amazing please minimum listen to the track “Anima”. I can’t wait to replay and see the true ending for myself.

I enjoyed every minute of this game.It definitely reminded me of the SNES times and older Zelda games and Unsighted pays huge respect to those.Gameplay is fluid and seldom Boring and it scratches the old explore x dungeons to get x items to do something else ItchPros:- Great Music, that changes in and out of Combat and areas as well as night and day Rythm- Fluid Controls and simple combat System make this a joy to pick up- Interesting Core Mechanic (original Mode has a timer on the Lifetime of every NPC that ticks down.   Lifetime can be refreshedwith certain items on oth you and NPCs- Good take on progression items, but not too boringly the same as in other games- Logical and Easy puzzles- for such a short Title, surprising wealth of gearCons:- i don't really see any. It sure is no Triple A product but it's great for what it costs. -Could be considered on the short side of things (12 Hours for standard gameplay with 96% map Completion), but i think they thankfully didn't make it longer than it should be herePlayed on Normal difficulty, will probably not replay due to other games existingcheers

_childDocuments_.review: This metroidvania comes highly recommended. The story so far is excellent and the characters are really cool. It is a top down with the look of the old DBZ games for GBA, that plays sort of like cult of the lamb with some excellent anime type NPCs. _childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a fun game and has all the pieces of a good metroidvania, but I cant help but feel it never tuned all those individual pieces quite right.I played the game on Action Girl difficulty. The game suggested it as "Intended challenge level, recommended for experienced players", but I found it to be very easy. The stats screen at the end of the game said I had died just 11 times and I didn't even use items like the revive cog and other stuff that felt too game-breaking. Just about every enemy can be defeated by parrying it 1-2 times and all of the parries are heavily telegraphed. Even the big endgame bosses that your companion warns you against fighting are pretty simple to beat with tutorial weapons (Steam even shows 35% of players have beaten them with a non-endgame weapon, compared to 56% who have beaten the tutorial boss).The timer also fell flat. Meteor Dust (the currency used to extend the timer for each character) is abundant and you'll only hoard it early when you don't realize just how plentiful it is. Meanwhile most NPCs have timers that are more than enough to complete the game without you ever needing to extend them. I only lost 3 NPCs total thanks to their time limit, but I had more than enough dust to save them anyway. I just didn't bother because they were useless and I couldn't be bothered to backtrack just to extend their life.I will give it credit. Unsighted is a fun game to play. The enemies are quick and movement is fun. Even if its not very difficult, I still enjoyed the moment-to-moment feel of the combat. While I would have enjoyed it more had the challenge been a fair bit higher, its far from a bad game as-is. Maybe Robot Apocalypse is a better fit for challenge, but I don't care enough to replay the game to find out. I'm happy with what I got to experience and that's about it.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. Very Link to the Past inspired. Cool puzzles, fun bosses, a lot of freedom to sequence break if you enjoy that kind of thing. The story's pretty meh, in my opinion, and I don't really care about any of the characters, but the gameplay alone is enough to keep me playing. Good for a playthrough or two.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful mix of 2D Zelda and Hyper Light Drifter combat. The world is beautifully realized with gorgeous pixel art and the sense of progression as you collect new abilities is as good as any metroidvania. The pressure of keeping your robot friends alive with meteor dust reminds me of Majora's Mask, where a ticking clock is hanging over your head. While not my speed, I think the fact you can speed run the game and complete dungeons out of order is a cool feature. I also thought the 2d platforming was done in a way I hadn't seen before, with ledges to grab and even some wall jumping moves.Highly recommend if you enjoy 2D zelda games and metroidvanias in general.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game for around 3 hours now, and I can say without a doubt this is a very, very, very good game. The music, level design, and combat are all very good. Anyone who likes 2D Zelda games, pick this game up. It is difficult at the beginning but the systems get easier once you get used to them, specifically the parrying system. The only real downside is I get anxious with the timer but that's something that is intentional, and there is an option to disable it.

_childDocuments_.review: An underrated top down Zelda-like/Metroidvania.One can easily see that the world and story were crafted with a lot of love.The combat mechanics are intuitive and navigating the maps is never frustrating.I personally disabled the time limit thing, as I don't think it should be enabled for a first playthrough and according to certain review it's not that important, though I can't really be sure.The first hour or so of the game has a bit of a slow start, but one you beat the first objectives, new movement options and satisfying combat upgrades make everything extremely enjoyable.And also Good music too.Oh and it's about lesbians so BRAVO LES LESBIENNES!

_childDocuments_.review: We've all been sleeping on Unsighted, this game is awesome! I love the Metroid-Vania-ish world, and the combat that's really fun to master! The mechanic of spending your time wisely and choosing who's lifetime to extend adds so much tension to everything you do in the game, to the point that every time you make a mistake or have a setback, it becomes a strong form of motivation to push forward that most games can't capture.I only lost two friends on my journey, and I was only minutes away from losing several more before I finished the game. The guilt of letting those lives slip through my fingers weighed down on me on the same level as AAA games like RDR2. Unsighted is just REALLY frickin good guys, y'all need to play this!

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a gameplay-centric action adventure with a permadeath timer.pro:- The death clock. It is a relatively unique feature. Every character has a permadeath timer (unless you play on easy mode), from your main character to the shopkeepers and so forth. This generally limits you to ~10-20 hours of maximum play time per playthrough.- The level designs are good. Lots of useful hidden loot, enemies aren't too bothersome and there are plenty of shortcuts. Has a decent amount of environmental variety too.- Open exploration. There are multiple ways to overcome obstacles and/or multiple ways to get the tool that you need to overcome an obstacle.- Fast movement, especially once you've unlocked some exploration tools. You can get through levels very quickly if you know what you're doing.- A rare type of item (usually acquired while exploring) adds time to the death clock, but you have to choose who to give it to, which adds a layer of gameplay relevant, mildly story-related decision making to the game.- Has some ending variations and a little bit of secret content.- Combat is skill intensive.- The game is challenging, but not unreasonably so. My first playthrough was on the recommended normal difficulty ("Action Girl") and I finished it with over "100 hours" (= ~3 hours in real time) left on the clock. It gets easier or harder depending on how many npcs you want to keep alive.- Has a NG+ mode where you may carry over all equipment (including exploration tools), which makes consecutive playthroughs much faster. - Has alternate game modes (bossrush & rogue-like) that unlock after you beat the game.- Has an easy mode where the permadeath timer is disabled, for completionist who want to do everything in one playthrough.- Only a 2GB download, the game is compact.- Has 2 player local coop.- Very fast load times.- You can skip all cutscenes and dialogue segments, another thing to speed up consecutive playthroughs.neutral: - You often have to think outside the box to reach the end of a level. Clever exploration puzzles are good in isolation, but losing death clock time while running around not knowing how to continue doesn't feel great.- There is a little bit of gameplay customization through different equipment, but it is primarily just picking between axe or sword and then whatever ranged weapons you need in the current environment.- Bugs, but only rarely. I encountered one where a sound effect kept playing on a loop, but restarting the game fixed it.con:- The overarching story is bad. I don't mind the characters, but there is very little to them, so they don't make up for it.- Bosses aren't very interesting and there aren't many of them. Especially the final boss was a bit disappointing to me.- The music sounds like random royalty free samples from the internet.- The art. Characters look off somehow, especially the heads and faces. Also, the low minimalistic shading makes it hard to judge elevations in the environment. Conclusion:Unsighted's poor story is a major flaw, but I think the gameplay makes up for it. It is not an expensive game either. An especially good pick for speedrunners and experimentalists.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with Unsighted a lot. It isn't my favorite 2D action game ever, but I did find it much more unique than I was expecting. It doesn't do anything particularly new, but it combines so many elements from different games it couldn't be called a copy of any of them IMO. You can call it a zelda-souls-jrpg-vania if you really really want to I guess, but why? What does that even mean at this point? Which parts of those games is it taking? Do I always need to explain that it takes Zelda and JRPG camera angle and level design, Zelda and souls combat, JRPG and souls story, metroidvania map, 2D metroid/zelda-ish artstyle and progression gated by puzzles using unlockable skills, but it also puts its own twist on all of it and feels cohesive? Can we just go back to calling things action RPGs and stop all this madness?It does everything it's trying to do very well. The combat feels great. There are tons of different ways to play with different items and weapons and upgrades. The chip system is very cool. The bosses are fun and challenging. There are puzzles and dungeons and they're well done.But I have a bunch of little problems with it that kept me from getting hooked enough to finish it. The art and animation are beautiful, and while I like the character designs, I find the design of the world and most of the enemies a bit forgettable so a lot of what I'm seeing on the screen most of the time feels wasted to me. I can't put my finger on it, but I found the world annoying to traverse. There's a lot of backtracking through repetitive areas. The story also got kinda tedious.BUT overall the gameplay and polished visuals easily carry it. I do recommend it and think it's worth twenty bucks for the right person. You need to be really into creating fun builds and upgrades and managing things, because you also need to decide which NPCs to save and they each provide different services that will eventually be taken away so that adds a layer of complexity.I say buy it. Especially if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE Unsighted. Stumbled onto this game when it was on XBox GamePass. Loved the combat, the relationships I grew with the NPC, hated saying goodbye to the ones I couldn't save, loved the new weapons that added mechanics that exposed me ways to explore. The aesthetic is awesome. Just purchased it on Steam but haven't made it to a full second playthrough yet, but it's on my list. Environment and combat reminded me of CrossCode which made it easy to fall in love with this game. If you enjoyed CrossCode or any of the isometric Zelda games, then do yourself a favor and grab UNSIGHTED!

_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: this game is really fun. probably 8-10 hours to beat the main story and totally worth your time.the combat feels awesome and the exploration-based puzzles feel interesting and satisfying.You have a lot of options on how you progress through the game, which is quite cool (look through the in game achievements for a sense of how much freedom you have) but it also means YMMV with the sensibility of the mechanics. That's my only real criticism of the game. You should absolutely go play it, but now I am going to whine about this one thing in the game that bothers me.There are some fun, hidden techniques you can do. Some of them are reasonably discoverable and it feels like the interaction design guides you into finding them. Others are pretty obscure, and for those the game has (missable) text logs explaining that they are possible.Mostly that's fine, but in my playthrough, I burned a lot of valuable time because I didn't realize an item you get early on can do a hidden technique that is required to enter a level way later (I'm sure it's not REQUIRED because you can progress through the game in many ways, but i didn't find another way). The text explaining it is in a completely optional area that you go to as part of an optional side quest that I had put off doing because I thought the main story was more pressing due to the game's time limit. That felt pretty frustrating and I actually ended up searching up how to progress, where I saw an offhand comment saying "btw it's possible to do X technique"It turns out there was even a small tutorial room in that optional area that you can't get through unless you figure out the technique in question and it really made me wonder, "why didnt they just serve you this really good tutorial right after giving you the item?"Similarly there's a fun technique you can use to manage stamina that has a good risk/reward tension to use in combat, but it's on a pretty non-obvious input and the tutorial for it is literally hidden and i can't help but think, well that sure sucks for the players who didnt find the clue telling them about the fun gameplay they could be doing.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I thought this was a metroidvania, as that’s what I kept hearing. This is closer to a Zelda game. A 2D Zelda with some souls-like elements thrown in.The combat in this is very satisfying. I really enjoyed the parry system. You lose a bit of stamina when you swing your weapon, just like Dark Souls. Your guns function kinda like Gears of War, even with the crazy satisfying perfect reload sound effect. This game’s sound design is absolutely fantastic overall.The music is mostly okay. I can’t remember any songs after beating the game besides the final boss music and the music that plays in Gear Town. It mostly goes for atmospheric and calm sounding music, which is fine enough. I liked how some songs would change depending on what was happening. Like on the fire dungeon, the music getting more rock-like when the lava was turned on.The story was nice enough, and the characters are cute. I especially like the dog and the fairy bot. Super cute. There’s a crafting system that seems to be inspired by Minecraft. I’ve never played Minecraft as I’m not 10 years old, but I think it’s similar enough from what I’ve researched. You do get blueprints you can buy or find so that you don’t need to remember the patterns. Nice.With all that said, about the worst part of this game is the time limit. The moment the game introduced this system to me and told me I could turn it off, I did so immediately. I never want to engage with such a stressful mechanic. Especially in a game like this with so much exploration to do. Every robot NPC has a time limit, and you have to give them “Meteor Dust” to keep them going a bit longer before they become “Unsighted” which is like a robot zombification. Even the main character has this time limit, but I’m not sure what happens if the main character runs out of time. Do you lose your save file in that case? If so, I’m glad I noped out of this system.Even with turning off the time limit, you see references to this system everywhere. Under each character’s name you now have this useless frozen time limit. You keep being told Meteor Dust will add to their time, even though it’s not necessary anymore. You keep hearing “Time is running out” even though, no, it’s not. I turned off the time limit, I don’t need these constant reminders.Plus, with such an exploration focused game, even if you do play with the time limit, you’ll be doing so rushed. Maybe some people find this fun, but not me. I’d rather take my time and explore and find new gear. Plus, I don’t want all these cute NPCs to die just because I took extra long to collect more treasure chests.Still, it’s a good game, and I want to come back to it to get more achievements. I recommend it to anyone that likes Zelda games or souls-like elements.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10. Map has some annoying parts and stamina management is constant. But it's a good game worth playing. Not too hard. If you are a completionist type of a gamer who wants to comb every part of the world, but don't like NG+ or repeat playthroughs, just enable explorer mode right away to disable the stressful timer.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the games that I was happiest to double-dip on. The Metroidvania has always been a formula to be broken by the player. Whether these are intentional skips built in by the developers or glitches and tech hammered out by the community, sequence breaking is key. Unsighted is a game that not only has tons of ways to break it, but also hands the methods out with a wink. But that heart is not just mechanical... or maybe it is, in its robot centered narrative. Themes of colonialism and the resistance thereof, sacrifice and loss, are channeled through its weaponized protagonist. It's about what may have to be given up to halt genocide and empire. And it's also about what we can cling on to. The world is a specific way. It is bleeding. Some of those wounds are still being actively sawed open. Cultures die to make way for the cold and indistinguishable. But the pumping heart of Unsighted tells us that it doesn't have to be that way. That a better world is possible. It's just a matter of finding out what we have to break.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: A classic formula with a heart wrenching twist, this adventure didn't let me put the game down. Every time I thought this game couldn't impress me anymore, it surprised me again with a fun mechanic or lovable NPC. Highly recommend to anyone who enjoyed Cross Code, Death's Door, or any other top-down RPGs. As for the twist to the traditional RPG gameplay, I guess you'll have to play to see!
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to like this game more but it ended up just being alright. The combat is solid, even if the parry can be a bit finnicky for reading attack timing. Theres a decent variety of weapons and guns and gears and chip upgrades and complexity. Theres also the dust you can gift to different vendors with different bonuses. The map is also pretty decent in length and theres a lot of secrets and side things to do. Then theres the problems. I turned off the time limit because its pretty dumb for a metroidvania, i hear people blabbering about meaning and characters and story but honestly the story was kind of meh for me, was mostly just about a bunch of robot lesbians and other LBGTQ stuff, which although I have no problem with, didn't really compel me and was a bit heavy handed. The main problem is the map and the amount of puzzles. The map has 3 different levels to traverse and all over the map there is a ton of verticality. This creates problems as its common to be lost and have no idea how to get to a certain place. That's because although you are aimed at a certain room to go to but 3 out of 4 entry ways are blocked until you have to solve a bunch of puzzles to get one thing to go through 1 room to go back around behind something to be able to get something else to get past another thing. Ive never played a game with more constant obstacles and having to constantly solve a puzzle or flip a switch to get anywhere. Normal metroidvanias have you getting new abilities and then backtracking to go a different way, but this game just puts a ton of unnecessary work just to get around. I constantly had to look up what small little room or ledge or thing I missed, and judging from how many other constant threads there were on reddit I wasn't alone. It just created a ton of frustrating and time wasting and running around looking for where to go. So although I enjoyed some of it many other parts brought it down, but overall it wasn't too bad. 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: B: Good metroidvania. Best feature is the world layout and items, providing satisfying feeling of exploration with each new acquisition. Really appreciate the versatility of many of the items which provide interesting ways to sequence break/speedrun. Lots of exploring to do with hidden chests and objectives abundant. Customizable playstyle via chip and cogs system that introduces opportunity cost since chips compete for limited slots that themselves have to be purchased with currency. Cogs are temporary powerups that can be crafted, which allows for player choice in how and when they need these powerups. Satisfying parry combat, not too deep but you get the options of jump attacks, spin(charge) attacks, and basic attacks along that interplay with the stamina system. Fairly unique premise regarding the timed lives of every character, though this theme is never fully utilized. Heard second hand that there is little effect on the story, and personally there was always enough dust to go around that only at the end of my 8 hour play through did I feel a little nervous. Still, is a fairly unique concept that stresses the player while forcing choices on who gets more time, and who you let wither away. Regular enemies throughout the world remain threatening and provide challenges with different parry timings.I appreciate the artstyle but didn't mesh with it and wasn't blown away by the animation or the art detail. Effects and music are kind of flat, somewhat trending towards boring and unimpactful, at least for me. Bosses have really cool designs but gameplay wise are fairly dull. Due to the strength of followup attacks post parrys, any non parry-able attacks from the boss feel like a gap in the action where you are simply avoiding hits. It wouldn't be so much of an issue if these attacks were engaging but many many of them can be avoided by simply walking. Plot and writing are bare bones.Achievements are mostly manageable, if not monotonous for how many playthroughs that need to be done (by the final few I could do them in 45 minutes to an hour via sequence breaking). There are a few exceptions which were quite difficult to obtain, namely achieving 100 straight parrys in training, completing the final boss without taking any hits, and boss rush in under 10 minutes. These seemed overly harsh but that all depends on player skill.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Very satisfying combat, super smooth traversal, fun (if a bit easy) dungeon puzzles, and a good soundtrack. The main conceit is that all the characters, including the player character, are on a time limit, which felt odd. Normally a big part of a metroidvanias is exploring and backtracking to find secrets once you get new abilities, but the time limit encourages minimal backtracking, ignoring side quests, and just bull rushing to the end. The time stress added a fun component of pressure because it gave the main quest some high stakes, but it's definitely weird that the game simultaneously encourages and discourages you from poking around to find secrets. Overall recommend though, worth playing for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: The parry trivializes every fight pretty hard, but the timer on every character was enough to keep me engaged even if most of the puzzles and enemies were dull. I'd say the biggest disappointment is that the timer on characters is never toyed with in any way (play Fallout 1 for an example of this being done well). There's never an acceleration on people's time, dying doesn't hurt the timer much to matter, and you'll likely beat the game without anyone dying from the disease. The only reason I'm not giving this game a thumbs down is because 3/5 dungeons are pretty good, with the fire and ice ones being the standouts.Overall, its a well-made game that you'll probably enjoy, but there's not much to love about it.Also, if any of the developers read this, please remove the ability to turn off the timers, its the most interesting part of the game and almost everything falls flat without it. I know it makes some people uncomfortable, but the timer IS the game and it made me feel certain emotions I haven't felt in a while.This might be a bit of an extreme suggestion, but I think every character's timer should be halved or be the same across the board so you have to choose who to keep alive. I never had to make a tough call because the times are so generous. Maybe new game plus or hard mode fix it, but that first playthrough didn't give a great impression on how I think I was supposed to feel.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: This is amazing. I just dove into this game for a few days, and it was hypnotizing.First of all, the mechanics make it delicious to just play around. The different kind of weapons and equipment, plus the movement freedom, allow you to develop your own style of play without overwhelming you with excessive variables.Second, even though the story is short, it is engaging. And it has quite some replay value (it is awesome they put a "newgame+" option.Third, the graphics are simple, but a delight. Well drawn characters, involving scenarios and cool effects make it easy on the eyes.Fourth, the music is very nice.For a 80s born gamer, this was also a very nostalgic experience, with the game reminding me some of my favorite 90s games, like 'A link to the past', the 'Megaman X' series, 'Chrono Trigger', 'Seiken Densetsu' and, of course, 'Metroid'.It is not perfect, but I highly recommend it, not only for fans of the metroidvania genre, but for everyone who likes simple, but well thought games.

Easily one of the best games for your dollar.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Just now finished this game and man, how do I even start?This game is GORGEOUS! The characters look incredible, the level of quality of the pixel art in this game is just unbelievable, there were times I'd just sit around in Gear Village just appreciating how gorgeous everything looked. That's not to say that things didn't look incredible in motion, Alma's movements feel very smooth and real, and that makes the combat feel great to do.Since I brought it up, the combat in this game is very fluid and freeform, you can play the way that you want, be it using longer combos of many fast hits to rack up that combo meter, or you can disregard the meter altogether and just give enemies one big whallop! The combat itself is very simple and though it might be a bit rocky at the start, once it clicks it's just very pleasant to take down the monsters that roam around Arcadia.The soundtrack is top notch, every different ambient that you go into in Unsighted has a delightfully unique tune that really sells the vibe of the location, like the more intense metallic symphony of the factory or the more soothing ambiance of the aquarium. The sounds in these tracks are very unique and are something that I'm not going to forget anytime soon.I'm not going to touch too much on the topic of the game's story, even though in my opinion it's one of the aspects where Unsighted is at it's strongest, because I don't wanna run the risk of spoiling anything in my post-clear hyped-up review, but at the same time I really have to say that I adore how this game handles it's characters and the relationships between them, it really pulls you into Alma's shoes and makes you care for the world around you, and that's something that only truly special games can do, this is one of those games.With the story out of the way, I think it's about time I talk about my favorite thing about Unsighted, and the one thing that is going to draw me to my second playthrough probably the day after this review goes up: The exploration.The map is surprisingly large for a game that takes less than 30 hours to fully complete the main story, and there are SO many secrets just waiting for you to find them, it's crazy, you can really just get out there and lose yourself just going from area to area looking in every nook and cranny, and you will find that there is always something to discover. So you might be wondering, how come a game with this many things on it's relatively large map manage to not slow down to a slog or take a long while to full clear? The answer is the MOVEMENT.Unsighted's movement is smooth like butter, fast like the northern wind and incredibly fun. Once you fully grasp all of the different types of movement that you can pull off, you'll understand just how quickly you can zoom from one screen straight into the next one AND IT ONLY GETS BETTER THE MORE UPGRADES YOU GET. I'm not kidding, this game's movement will get you hook, line and sinker into the ride that it offers. Fast travel? Oh no thank you, I'm already traveling plenty fast.I could go on and on and continue singing this game's praises like the neat progression system and the really interesting mechanics, but all things must eventually come to an end, so I'll wrap this up with one final thought:GO BUY THIS GAME AND TRY IT OUT FOR YOURSELF, IT'S ON PROMO AS OF THE TIME I AM POSTING THIS (I THINK???), YOU WON'T REGRET IT.

_childDocuments_.review: Combat feels great, weapons are unique, puzzles feel fun to solveReminds me of CrossCode a lot which I also enjoyedEdit after beating the game:This is more like a old-school zelda-like (non botw) game. If you're a fan of those games you'll like this game.The story is serviceable, it's not really the highlight of the game imoNegative-ishs:There's a time mechanic in the game that is part of the story that I don't think really adds much. Instead it sort of makes you want to rush through the game instead of exploring side paths. Fortunately you can turn the time mechanic off, and that's how I played the gameThere isn't a screen that shows your current objective, or side objectives. If you get lost or stopped playing for a bit, it's pretty hard to know where you need to go exactly. I think it was made this way because technically you can finish the dungeons out-of-order, but it just makes it a bit confusing for a first time playthrough

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best indie Zelda style game. Period. It ranks among the greatest games ever made, with just a couple of things holding it back.The puzzles are on par with Zelda. The game progression feels quick. The combat is the best overhead action combat I've played BY FAR. It's fluid, fast paced, controls are responsive. You can parry attacks, reflect projectiles, jump, dash, and use fun gimmicky weapons. One of the key features though is melee weapons have a Dark Souls style stamina gauge, while projectile weapons have ammo that needs refilling each clip, but is otherwise unlimited. Since melee weapons don't use ammo, and projectiles don't use stamina, this encourages the player to effectively use both. While your stamina is recovering, you fend things off with your gun until your stamina recovers. When you're out of ammo, you fend things off with your sword until you can reload.Where does it fall short? Well, it has a gimmick where the player, and all NPCs die after a certain time limit. You get an item you can share with anybody to extend that time. But honestly, I never felt any attachment to the NPCs, and never felt like giving it to any of them, aside from my companion fairy. I enjoy this type of gimmick when done correctly to apply pressure, but honestly, this just didn't do it for me. It also didn't help that once you have a certain amount of time left, you can head to a specific place on the map to get as much time as you need, with apparently no *significant* cost, but this seems to lock you out of the bonus boss. I played on the standard "Adventure Girl" mode, but I recommend just playing the game on explorer mode. You won't be missing anything, and you may actually find some more use out of the NPCs. Sadly, you can't play with the toughest enemies without the time limit.Now the other issue is much bigger, and doesn't seem to have a fix. It's just really hard to tell the difference between walls and bottomless pits, and sometimes between regular ground and walls. No joke. A lot of the areas in the game are very dark, and the walls and pits are both near black. I'll try to jump across a pit, just to run into a wall. Or I'll try to circle around an area, looking for a path through, just to figure out I was on the road, looking for a way around the sidewalk. This gets much, much worse when it's night on the world map, or in areas where you have limited field of vision. Fortunately, the dev team seems to have kind of addressed the issue, in that you don't take damage while falling into bottomless pits. But that's extra insulting, as it seems to mean they were aware this was an issue, and didn't bother fixing it properly.The visual issue should be just a minor nuisance that you occasionally see pop up in games. But honestly, it was kind of a big deal, and for me, costs this game the 10/10 it would otherwise deserve. We're still looking at a 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed it! I slept on it for a while because the timers scared me a bit, haha. But they weren't as tight as I feared, made for a memorable driving force to keep going. The fighting is fun. There's dogs. I also enjoyed the art and the overall atmosphere. _childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite games of all time, and also probably one of the metroidvanias I feel has the most replay ability. Exploring the world is a lot of fun with many different tools to move around the map, and the stamina/parry system is accessible yet still challenging. It's also a really good intro to speedrunning game, as sequence breaks are built into the achievements, and there are some neat, easily accessible tricks you can learn by watching runs from people like Symphonian. Definitely check this one out.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really great game which has strong replay value. Super tight combat and very interesting, open exploration. I think a lot of games suffer from aimless exploration. A lack of clear direction and no big rewards in an open plane. In this game though, there's a frantic momentum to exploration in the game because of the meteor dust system. In my first playthrough, blind clear at high difficulty, I managed to save everyone but one poor character. There is so much heart in here, and everything is very well thought out. Very often, there is more than one solution to a problem, so if you didn't understand a puzzle the first time you saw it, you might come back later and find a different way to do it with a different set of items. This is a very speedrunnable game, and that sort of play is encouraged.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: It's Mega Man X, except X and Zero are now girlfriends.  It's as awesome as its sounds!A post-apocalyptic world filled with sentient robots, electro-swords, and alien meteor monsters is the backdrop as you play in as Alma, a robot girl searching for her lost girlfriend Raquel.  The inspiration from games like Mega Man X seems obvious, but Unsighted does enough with little twists and alterations to make a world that still feels unique and worth exploring.  Tiani's pixel art is among the best, with environments that are a true sight to behold, and characters and creatures that are well animated and beautifully detailed.  Add in Fernanda's excellent, moody music for an awesome OST, and you've got an aesthetic with a unique flair that shouldn't be missed.Where Unsighted shines, though, is in its design and mechanics.  Dodge rolls, timed reload gun play and hack n' slash melee combat combine with straightforward but rewarding upgrades and environment exploration to add up to a game that feels just plain good to control.  Mixed with thoughtful puzzles and excellent dungeon design, and Unsighted comes out as one of the most well designed games I've played in years!And, hey, this game is gay as hell.  Alma and Raquel's relationship is blunt and unmistakable, and watching their relationship progress throughout the story is incredibly endearing.  You really feel how much these lady bots love each other, and I adore this game for that.Do not, under any circumstances, miss out on this truly excellent experience.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED reminds me a lot of classic adventure games from the early 2000s; lots of enjoyable challenge, a good amount of replayable value, classic style pixel art, but somewhat light on the narrative beyond what's necessary to push the story forward. I was initially hesitant to play this due to the time limitation mechanic, but found in my main playthrough that it provided an excellent impetus to push forward and try to finish the game, rather than get caught out trying to find every last secret. Once I had done that, I ended up turning off the timers so I could explore and find what secrets there were. The combat is varied and satisfying, very reminiscent of Hyper Light Drifter, but with more complexity (i.e. with parrying, active reloads, and equipment with status effects). The story is an interesting concept, but I found the characters and dialog somewhat flat. Beyond the main character Alma, there's not much character development or exploration of the themes this world sets up (what makes a person? how do you choose who to save when you can't save everyone?). The story also fails to engage with the disturbing implications of the ending, ). I honestly would have liked to see the devs at least engage with that in more depth, or flesh out some of the other characters further. That said, I think the story is enough to motivate a playthrough, but not enough for me to play through again. Overall, if you enjoy souls-like adventure games with challenging combat I think this is absolutely worth the time. However, you may find that the timer mechanic is frustrating if these types of games take you time to pick up. I encourage you to try to get as far as you can, and if you get to a point of no return, simply turn the timer off (that in itself, a great concession by the dev team).
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic little metroidvania. Combat is crisp and fluid, feels close to Hyper Light Drifter. Exploration and traversal are very satisfying. The constant awareness of time running out is an excellent narrative device that isn't too mechanically punishing. Also there's an excellent cast of hot robots.Postgame update: There's a lot of value for subsequent playthroughs. It is very fun to run through the game with the accumulated knowledge of maps and mechanics and tackle the optional challenges you probably didn't have time for the first time through. Boss rush and the roguelike dungeon run mode are both solid if slightly rng dependant. Excellent candidate for speedrunning if that's something you're interested in.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Hyper Light Drifter + Crosscode + LTTP + Super Metroid. Yes. To all of it. Will need a few playthrus(EDIT) My first playthru was 8 1/2 hrs with 100% map completion. There's more beyond that. This game is an amalgamation of the games I've listed, and turned up to 11 in most cases. This is the most complete example of any given game I've listed as influence. It does justice to each area, and then some. One of the best games I've ever played. Easily among the best of it's kind. What a ride

_childDocuments_.review: really good game, nice gameplay, tight controls, fighting is fun and you can adjust your skills for your preference, also the menu and your items are really fun to use to give yourself an extra boostthere is crafting in there but it doesnt overwhelm you at all, the activitys like fishing etc are also really coolthe characters are also really likeable and the premise hits you hard, once you see the timers running lowbossfights are really cool, soundtrack is good, art is really nice to look at

_childDocuments_.review: Very good. It's very impressive that only 2 people made this game!It's a mix of ideas from previous games, mostly Zelda, Metroid and Dark Souls. But there are mechanics taken from Minecraft, Stardew Valley, Call of Duty and others. I personally loved the combat. It wasn't super simple nor super complicated. But it did force me to focus with almost every encounter to win. I couldn't just mash away. Also the graphics and the music were super appealing to me. Retro-futuristic and jazzy. The puzzles were also difficult without being impossible. I wasn't super convinced with the time limit mechanic. What really bothered me and actually left a sour taste in my mouth was that I let my guardian fairy die, and then I found out that I couldn't update my chips count for the rest of the game. At least if that would have been clear to me I would had taken an informed decision. Also I didn't like that very often it's very hard to determine the depth of a platform, since internally this a 3d game projected on flat 2d plane. It's also hard to se exactly what you can walk on or fall in. But at least the developers made it so you don't take damage when you fall off a cliff, making it less frustrating. (At the same time for the boss battle that happens in the sky this mechanic works against it, because you can just jump off to avoid attacks, which makes the boss super easy.)Also there's a bit of too many things that don't add much. Fishing and digging for example. Also crafting is unnecessarily complex in my opinion (You can set ingredients on a grid like in Minecraft).But overall even with these negatives this was a very nice experience. I've been playing games for over 30 years now, and most games I try these days don't excite me very much and I abandon them after a few hours.This one definitely did. I finished my run in regular difficulty but I don't think I'll do another one for now. I look forward to what the developers make next!
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted has some truly impressive pixel art/animation that goes a long way in making even the basics of swinging your sword continuously gratifying. It's worth noting that the more you play, the more parrying becomes a necessity. Usually, this would be an issue for me, but the visual/auditory telegraphs are perfectly readable. Parrying itself is fun enough to where my typical distaste for the playstyle vanished over the course of the game.I'm thankful for the option to circumvent the stressful time-dependent character lives. It's a neat idea, but seemingly overwhelming for a first playthrough where you spend a lot of time learning the map.Even though the game offers plenty of variety in secondary ranged weapons, keeping certain key items equipped led me to neglect ranged combat almost entirely. Having such an emphasis on parrying and there being so many enemy lunge attacks that close the gap for you essentially excludes the need to do less damage at a greater distance.Despite collecting a hoard of materials, I rarely ever used crafting or cogs. This was disappointing since those systems felt like an underutilized hole in an otherwise well-balanced stat system. And on the subject of stats, I enjoyed how little of an individual edge the chips or weapon upgrades give you. It’s a reminder of how your individual skill has grown. It also means that, with a little prior skill and knowledge, you could tackle the 'dungeons' in any order.Unsighted was an absolute joy to play through. The difficulty is well-balanced and improving at the combat feels great. I was constantly immersed in the process of finding new paths and practicing the stamina-managing dodge, parry, and attack process. The option for local co-op sounds like a lot of fun too. Even if the prospect of plenty of parrying potentially puts purchasing Unsighted a non-priority, I’d implored you to consider otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted grabbed my attention right away in the first couple of hours, with its level of polish and lovely pixel art. Within that time I could already list many good things about it:- gameplay is smooth, with loadout changing in real time adding a good dose of flexibility- combat feels satisfying with a simple but juicy parry system- good customization with chips and cogs lets you cater to your playstyle, and more or less alter the game's difficulty on the fly- traversal is fun- puzzles are light enough to add another layer without bogging down the pace- the overall level and world design is a delight- at first, the time mechanic which gives NPCs a death timer keeps you on edge as you start to consider who you're going to care about and try to keep alive.Did that magic feeling last until the very end of my play-through? Not exactly, and probably for two main reasons. The big letdown is that the timer mechanic doesn't culminate in anything interesting, and doesn't play into the story. Sure, you might lose some NPCs along the way, but the game doesn't do a good enough job of making you care about most of them, and you're gonna use all your Meteor Dust to keep a few important ones alive and get shop discounts. The only ones I grew somewhat attached to were Iris and the blacksmith robot BB42. On top of that, the story itself is kind of generic (humans bad! consume and destroy everything!), and as good as the character designs might be, the writing doesn't deliver.And second, the game is pretty easy. Now I haven't played it on the harder Robot Apocalypse difficulty yet, but on normal I died 19 times over the course of an 8 hour play-through. Probably half of those were outside of boss battles. Very few bosses give any real challenge, even if they are still enjoyable.I'm not a big Metroidvania fan by any means, but I would still easily recommend the game, as there's a lot to like. And if the timer mechanic really worries you or stresses you out, you can play the game in Explorer Mode which lets you disable the timer and / or make the combat easier.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Fluid combat, encouraged to explore, ENCOURAGED TO BREAK INTENDED PROGRESSION - all can be found in Unsighted. The gameplay is great and I'd recommend it to everyone. The major con is the time system. Not cause of the stress, cause the game asks you to care about characters without giving you enough reason to do so. Story is servicable. Nothing too complex. It sets the mood and gives you goals to achieve. To summarise: I love the moment to moment gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is very satisfactory, with fluid combat and rewarding exploration. The timer adds just a bit more of intensity to the journey, but ends up not being that much of a hassle. I enjoyed it in the end, as the setting justifies its presence in a meaningful way.The pixel art is also gorgeous. Every character is expressive and the animations are really good. The only gripe I have with it is that the game is not "pixel perfect", so sprites rotate and scale in ways that I find kind of weird. I reckon it is just a matter of personal taste, and the sprite work itself is superb, so it wasn't that big of a deal.The music is so good, it really makes for a great ost. The sfx are lively and cohesive. The noise that enemies make, in particular, is very in place for a cyberpunk game, with those robotic pitches that you naturally associate  with corrupted androids. In sum, everything in terms of sound is amazing, very nice work done in that department.The story and its tones sounded a bit repetitive for me. There is a little twist that I found clever but, otherwise, the plot didn't catch my attention that much. The characters are charming, though. The fact that each one has a reward for you if help them is good, even though I did not care much for the development the game displays when you get them.Be it for the gameplay alone, or for the amazing soundtrack and beautiful artwork, I'd really recommend this game. It is a labor of passion and it shows, so check it out if you can.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Initially I bought this game because the mechanic of NPCs with limited lifespans intrigued me. After completing it, I think I can safely say that mechanic was a near-complete failure - the game does very little to make you care about whether characters live or die beyond the threat of losing whatever service they provided. They're generally one-dimensional and unresponsive - they don't have much dialogue variety and didn't so much as bat an eye when their comrades died (at least in my experience, though I didn't let any important characters die so I might have just been too good to see any mourning). However, even if these characters  written well enough to be worth getting attached to, the resource to keep them alive is so deceptively plentiful that keeping essential characters up and running is a non-issue. The lack of good character writing also extends into the overall plot - it's not outright bad, but certainly nothing special.That said, nearly every other aspect was handled well, especially the metroidvania and Zelda-like elements. The game world looks great, has a ton to explore and is full of puzzles ranging from trivial distraction-difficulty to genuinely difficult. Combat and enemy design are pretty alright -  there's a Souls-ish focus on stamina management, dodging and parrying, and it generally feels good to make use of every option available to you. I will say that parrying is so important to general survival and damage output that you might not enjoy the game if you intend to not make use of it. Enemies were generally creative and pleasant to fight, though in my experience bosses were a bit lacking in terms of difficulty - first boss took two tries, every other boss took one. Difficulty aside they were mostly well-designed.However, in my opinion the most interesting thing this game does - and I heartily recommend this game to speedrunners solely because of this feature - is that it actively facilitates sequence breaking (  ) through an incredibly generous crafting system - you can put items into a crafting grid and, provided you yourself know the recipe, you can get nearly every item in the game, be it a melee weapon, a gun, or even a progression-critical movement item. You can reliably create all the items you need to beat every primary dungeon in reverse order, all without acquiring the blueprints for any of them! That's a huge amount of freedom!But yeah, if you're into metroidvanias and/or the Zelda formula you'll probably like this. Overall it's pretty good with a handful of setbacks.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: UNSIGHTED is a really good game that could've been a great game, but a few annoyances held it back. As much as I loved the world and story, certain aspects took away from it that couldn't be ignored. I cannot stress enough how much I enjoyed the boss fights.Pros -Multiple endingsUnique lifespan mechanicSome very interesting charactersGreat storytelling/world buildingSimple but clean combatAmazing boss fightsRewards player for being curiousUnique character upgrade mechanicTime pressure elevates gameplayWide variety of enemiesBeautiful art styleCons-No checkpoints right before bossSome exploration puzzles are very tediousNot much incentive to talk to many charactersOnly two types of melee weaponsNot enough checkpoints in generalIf you are into Zelda-like puzzles, and think the combat looks interesting to you, this is a game you'd most likely enjoy. I personally would rate this game a 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a very fun game. Once you get the hang of the controls and the mechanics, which admittedly can take some time, the game is a joy to play through.
