_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is incredible in pretty much every aspect. The graphics are simply amazing, the combat is extremely smooth, the characters are some of the best and most memorable I've ever seen, and the exploration & puzzles are always fair and satisfying. The music is also excellent, and the story is very good too.The time mechanic, the main gimmick of this game, gives it a very unique feeling of pressure that many other "Chosen One" stories fail to generate. There are actual stakes here: you can fail, and if you do, everyone could die – your friends, your loved one, and even yourself (and the world with it). While it can be quite stress inducing, it's also an incredible & memorable experience – each loss, and every win (saving someone at the last minute), is so much more impactful.There is also a lot of post-game content. Replaying the game and trying to find sequence breaks is really fun, and there are a ton of secrets hidden in the game world. There’s also a two-player co-op mode, and boss rush & dungeon raid modes.Unsighted may be amazing, but it isn’t perfect. The ending is a bit too vague, and generally the story has a confusing timeline. Also, finding the “true ending” basically requires a guide, and it doesn’t add much to the story (only another phase to the final boss). The game’s world is incredibly rich – I just wish there had been more story content in the game (then again, it may just be my preference for story-rich games).Nevertheless, Unsighted is still the best game I’ve played this year, and one of my all-time favourites. And I don’t usually like metroidvanias nor Zelda games – Unsighted is just that good.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted's timers makes this game very stressful sometimes, so make sure to be aware of that when you start. For me, this made this game one of my favorites. The pixel art is beautiful to look at, and the controls are tight. The platforming in this game is surprising good considering it's a 2D game. The timers ticking down to you're and you're friends deaths is a constant reminder of your goal and it encourages you to keep moving, But there are ways to increase the timers for certain characters you like. My only real complaint about this game is some of the items. Certain items like the ice grenades, shuriken, and a couple others are required to get past certain areas, but since they count as weapons, they need to replace one of your two weapons. When you have a specific combination of weapons you like (for me it was a sword and a shotgun) having to switch them out constantly is tedious and frustrating. Other than that, Unsighted is a great game I would recommend to anyone

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great action metroidvania that is definitely worth the price.  It has some great sequence breaking and there's points at which there are multiple solutions to the problems encountered during the game.  The action flows well, the RPG system is fine, the sound design is good, the music is fine, the art style is great, the story is fine, and all around I'd give this game a 7/10.  Well worth it.Also, the faster movement mechanic (that is present in practically every metroidvania) is super cool in this one.  The character whips out a giant top and spins to win while speeding off.  Love it.  Easy to pull out, easy to hop off, makes moving around a joy.  Super unique.There are, however a few draw backs.Every NPC (including yourself) are on a timer.  When that timer runs out, they die.  You can find meteor dust and give it to NPCs to extend their time.  This meant I did not dawdle and do idle exploration in any area.  How could I, after all?  The game is on a timer.  I kept every single NPC alive (at least, the shortest one still had 40+ hours going into the final tower), and as a reward got ... nothing.  Not even an achievement.  Literally did not matter.  So, this hurt both from an acknowledgement side and the fact that it really does affect how you enjoy the game.  Taking time to enjoy things, whether it's music, the art, or exploration, now comes with a drawback.The story is serviceable but didn't feel great.  It's not bad, but many of the characters are pretty cliche.  Strong big woman who doesn't admit her feelings is hard on the small newcomer who is secretly more powerful than anyone but is emotionally a weakling.  It's practically an anime trope at this point.  Then she's gotta go around and collect the final fantasy crystals and save her big strong lover.  There were many topics in the game that would have been phenomenal to go into, because the issue of robots gaining consciousness is a pretty philosophical topic, but it just...doesn't.  Humans bad, humans kill planet, humans fight robot, we kill humans.  We innocent.  Humans bad.  It's very young adult-y.Post-end game doesn't exist.  Not necessarily a draw back, but with the main game punishing drawn out exploration (you are on a timer, after all), it would've been nice to explore things without rushing.  There's a secret area, but upon looking it up, you have to play through the game a second time and it unlocks a slightly harder final boss.  Yeah uh...no.The RPG aspect is nice.  I do like that it lets you experiment and figure out the best solution to things and allows different playstyles.  I didn't really use it, however, because the game pushes parrying pretty hard, so I just parried and killed stuff with the lightning sword.That said, the actual action part of the game is fine.  It's not great, but it's not bad.   There are a few enemies and a few situations that are incredibly hard, and then the rest of the game really isn't that hard. Those situations are ones where there are multiple hard hitting enemies.  You do not have a block - only a parry, and thus two enemies that are overlapping and staggering their attacks can become a blob that's very difficult to parry or get attacks into.  Out of my 12 deaths, I'd say most were to these situations where the game throw 2, 3, or 4 hard hitting enemies at you at once.  I actually didn't die to the final boss a single time because by that time you're shoe horned into the one style that the game wants you to play - parrying.I collected dozens of each of the items in the game that you can use to craft things.  Weapons, cogs (activateable buffs), chips (permanent buffs), and extra health.  I crafted all the weapons I could, and that's it.  Didn't craft a single cog, chip, or extra syringe, because the game just wasn't difficult enough and didn't really put me in situations where those would had a massive effect.  I did use a few defense cogs and one revive cog, but that's all.  I died roughly once every 50 minutes.For all of these negatives, if you enjoy metroidvanias, it's worth experiencing it, just go in knowing that the timer means your enjoyment may suffer.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I'm very cynical about game releases, especially indie ones.However Unsighted is down right fantastic.The story for me is sort of 'whatever'. What's there isn't terribly deep, complex, or nuanced, but it's also not terrible. It does what it needs to do.The gameplay is phenomenal. The combat is super fluid, chaining combo's, parries, and your various abilities feels super natural and responsive. The movement is super clean.On top of that, there's myriad 'chips' which you can equip to augment and enhance your preferred combat techniques and styles.One gripe is that later in the game, switching between certain mobility items and your weapons can be a bit of a nuisance as you progress through certain areas.Game has various modifiers/enhancements/features which you can toggle on/off depending on your preferred gameplay experience. (i.e. increased stamina, turn off time-limit, etc)You can progress through the world in pretty much any form or fashion you prefer, in fact there's even an achievement for killing the main bosses in reverse order.I played this game 10 hours straight the first day I had it.Hands-down one of the best games I've played all year, without question.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Easily in my top 3 games of 2021. Absolutely perfects the sense of exploration that the best Metroidvanias offer, while also delivering on some of the best combat I've played in the genre (Dare I say better than Hollow Knight's...?). But what I think surprised me the most was the story and the attachments I made with the characters. Far too often the games are coming out without any heart...this one soared in this area. So, if you want great combat (OH! and it's completely co-op viable, too!), an awesome world full of puzzles and beautiful pixel art, AND an amazing premises...Unsighted is a must buy. Can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: The good:- Tough but fun gameplay for the most part- Lots of exploration and collectibles- Many intended (and unintended) sequence breaking options- A fairly generic story, nothing to write home about but it's well done for what it is- Amazing sprite art- Tons of customisation- Fun/interesting puzzles- The looming threat of NPC extinction- An option to remove the above, options are never bad- Gay robots in loveThe bad:- Every boss has adds, even the final boss and everything does high damage- Unfair deaths due to ganking, this only applies to bosses and fighting the big beasts- Lots of little unskippable things here and there like waiting for the title screen- Not enough teleport/checkpoint consoles in some areas, resulting to a lot of unwarranted backtracking- Slightly cringy dialogue sometimes, and the message about humans being butts is mehOverall:I'd say I still recommend this game, it's very fun and while not terribly unique it's still an impressive little gem, just happens to be rough around the edges. Easily the weakest part of it is the bosses, and not through any fault of their own. The bosses themselves are very cool and fun to fight, but having such a fixation on them being able to summon enemies is bad design and makes them unfun. When everything hits you that hard having to keep track of tons of projectiles, varied enemy timings, your stamina, on-screen warnings, and the arena itself becomes very taxing and frustrating. Especially with the final boss, but they're all plagued with this. If a boss HAS to summon enemies it should be nuisance fodder to distract you from the big attacks. This game is still worth your time and money, but it comes with some baggage.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a good metroidvania. The first playthrough chances are you will play in the right order, and that's great, you're experiencing the story how you should, but as with any metroidvania, the game doesn't end when it ends.Firstly, the successes and the 100%. (I want to emphasize on the fact that I did not 100% the game as of now, but I am working towards it.) There are a couple parts of the game giving a lot more lifespan to one save files, if you're trying to do as much as you can before going for NG+ (I'm coming back to it a bit later), some hidden zones leave you looking for them, puzzles are great, and the honing your skills with its gameplay is another fun way to pass time.But now, the NG+ and speedruning. There is a LOT you can sequence break in NG+, or simply in NG if you know the game, in fact, there's some successes just for that (RBO, sequence breaking your way to some items in the prologue, the such.) Your first playthrough might be long, but once you know the game there is a lot of puzzles you can skip, shaving off HOURS on the time spent.One last thing though, the timers are in fact stressful, especially for a first playthrough. It's no big deal once you start speedruning the game though.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: A fantastic entry into the action-adventure library full of smooth combat , epic boss battles and satisfying puzzle solving.  Thought there are some awkward animation moments and a looming death clock, the game delivers a beautiful experience.Full Review: From the first frame, Unsighted draws you in with an eerie pixel art aesthetic reminiscent of other major action adventure games gone by (Hyper Light Drifter).  The further you get into the game, the more you discover just how deep the inspiration from Alx Preston's masterpiece runs within Unsighted's veins.  You have a sword, you have a gun.. you dodge, hack, and blast your enemies.  Even the targeting reticle draws inspiration from HLD.  It may seem an unfair comparison to pitch this pixel art underdog form Humble Games against the Zelda-like giant, but it's asking for it.  And truth be told, once you do stack them up, Unsighted comes away several rungs over it's inspiration.  There's dialogue (!!).  You have more weapons and guns at your disposal.  There are challenging puzzles to solve, and unique items that unlock new areas, drawing inspiration from the Zelda series, the grandfather of the genre.  Action in the game is incredibly smooth.  There are no cheap shots, no controller-chucking moments that make you question the developer's abilities.  Each weapon has it's strengths and it's drawbacks.  Bosses feel epic, and give you a challenge.  The well-composed score for for the game evolves to fit the tension of combat as you explore.  The environments feel intriguing, pulling me into a dystopian world where I need to know what happened.  Honestly there is really so much to love about this game, it's hard to be reminded of it's faults. For all of it's strengths and good points, however wrongs do exist within Unsighted.  Pixel art animation, while beautiful in some areas, feels awkward and rushed in others.  Boss animations are fantastic yet Alma's walk/run feels just... off.  Explosions are beautifully done, yet Alma's close-up in the pause menu reveals some cheap sprite rotation tricks to get around the tough animation work, and comes off as rushed.  I even paused to ask myself "if they couldn't animate Alma's hair.. why have the portrait so huge or even have it at all?".  Another pain point I have with the game is the choice for a world-ending clock looming over the entire game.  NPCs, the Navi-like mechanical fairy guiding you through the game, and even Alma herself will become "unsighted" if the game progresses too long.  I'll put it very bluntly.  This type of mechanic does not belong in an action-adventure game that promotes exploration.  Now I feel rushed to get to the next area as quickly as I can, skipping chests and other small rewards I normally would have taken the time to get.  Sure, you can turn off the timer mechanic, but I want to play the game as the developers intended, and I'm afraid it just doesn't fit. Don't let the bad pull you away from this gem, however.  Unsighted is easily within my top fives games of the year, if not number one.  You will not regret buying this game. Funny observation:  Why are there no males in the game?  I think I met one the whole time I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that exceeded all of my expectations. Worth replaying even a day after beating it, and I say that about very few things. Probably some of the most intuitive parrying I've gotten to use in a game; especially important given how absolutely core it is to the combat system. Master parrying early, you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Very well done for a top-down exploration based action platforming game! Combat and exploration both feel very polished. The stamina system for melee combat with dodge rolls and parrying feels really good, as does the active reload mechanic for ranged attacks. Exploration and progression upgrades are handled well, and secret hunting and sequence breaking are very rewarding!The fact that you and all the friendly characters you meet have limited lifespans makes for some uniquely interesting and painful decisions in a playthrough. You need to give away a meaningfully limited resource in order to give your friends more time to live, a resource you might need to use for yourself. This encourages the player to engage more thoughtfully with the other characters in the game, which I really like to see.The game's design really lends itself to replayability, I had a great experience with my first playthrough and I could see a lot of quality time could be spent experimenting with different builds and routes to see everything Unsighted has to offer. A lot went into making this game what it is, and it shows!
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what to say about this game? I absolutely loved it. Really tight controls and great combat, fantastic art, and THE MUSIC! Absolutely fantastic soundtrack. They threw in really interesting mechanics. I played on very much "default" kind of settings, but I love all the accessibility and difficulty options. I didn't try them out much yet but I am glad they are there.It's a really really well done metroidvania that feels fresh and different in a genre that can sometimes feel stale. If you're a fan of these types of games, you really owe it to yourself too check this out. I hardly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: A most excellent Metroidvania/Soulslike (as far as I can tell, these are practically the same genre but with different combat difficulty expectations, which is kind of funny when keeping Metroid Dread in mind).The story is good stuff, both for its dark sci-fi setting and for all the queer robots. The way Anima (the source of all the robot characters' sentience) both drives the story and aspects of the game mechanics is really interesting.So, yeah, early in the game you find out that because the Automatons have become isolated from their source of Anima, they all have limited amounts of time before their sentience runs out. So that means the game is constantly on a timer. It quickly became clear that this was too stressful for me, and kept me from actually being excited to play the game. Thankfully, I could just switch to Explorer Mode to pick and choose between a set of accessibility options, and disabled that gameplay feature.There's also a [SECRET] that ties into the mechanic, which for sure will make it easier for me to replay the game without Explorer Mode features later.One of the other accessibility options is invincibility, in case you want to lower the stakes in combat. To be honest, I think Metroid Dread could have used that feature more, as its combat felt much more difficult to me than UNSIGHTED's, but it's obviously still a good feature to have. UNSIGHTED has a few different flavors of swords and axes available to fight with, as well as a larger variety of ranged weapons, allowing for a few different fighting styles. I spent most of the game mostly hitting and dodging, and only needed to really master the parry mechanic towards the end when fighting some of the heavy-hitter enemies just became unfeasible otherwise.Anyway, I'm not sure where else I should be going with this "review". It's a fantastic game, handily beating Metroid Dread in my book, and I've been a Metroid fan for about 20 years now. For UNSIGHTED, the combat felt more well-balanced, the story was a whole lot more interesting, it was super gay, and there's apparently a randomizer update in the works.There's one point where UNSIGHTED stumbles, though, and that's in that it's almost cruelly difficult to find some of the secret items stashed all over the map. There are a fair number of hidden rooms with no real signalling to indicate that they exist, and the map does very little to clue you in on where the treasure chests you're missing are located. (All you get after finishing the final boss is a list showing you how many chests you're missing in each of the map's sometimes expansive sectors.)It's really good stuff. Get it, play it, and cheer on those funky little gay robots. Don't know why they took away the demo from Steam, but if you have a Switch or any of the other consoles I'm pretty sure it's still there if want to give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Really awesome game, feels like a mix between Hyper Light Drifter and Zelda, especially some of the equipment feels right out of Twilight Princess.Very friendly towards every kind of player, character time limits can be set off, theres even an invincibility option.Im not sure if thats intended, but having two grappling hooks lets you literally bypass every kind of platforming section and water bodies/ravines. If you were to craft two at the beginning of the game you could go virtually anywhere, theres no hindrance anymore aside from rocks lol. I appreciate that freedom a lot, but it also feels like this shouldnt be in the game like this, because the levels of exploitation you can do is ridiculous with two hooks, and it makes ice weapons obsolete.

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest thing you'll probably see brought up in reviews and videos of this game is the time system:The game is timed, in the sense that there's a day/night cycle, and the game tracks what day it is as you play.  Oh, and each of the NPCs you run into have a certain amount of time allotted to them before they .  At first, this mechanic turned me off and I immediately began to wonder if I had made a mistake in buying Unsighted.  Thankfully, I decided to stick with it.  Time limits are scary, but Unsighted offers more than a few ways to alleviate it ignore the mechanic altogether.It took me about 5 hours to complete the main story, during which I managed to keep everyone alive.  As it turns out, the game has a finite resource that allows you to add 24 hours onto the clock of any NPC (or yourself) you talk with, and there's more than enough of the stuff to keep everyone nice and sane unless you leave the game on unpaused for extended periods of time.  Or if you're really bad at the game, since dying doesn't cause you to "game over", rather the game skips ahead one hour (one hour less on everyone's lifespan) and allows you to restart at the nearest checkpoint or at the hub town of the game, while also making you drop your bolts, the currency of the game.If you really don't care about the lives of the NPCs, there's also a mechanic in place that lets you kill off an NPC and adds their remaining lifespan to yours, letting you have all the time in the world to explore every nook and cranny, as long as you don't mind a completely empty world where all your friends are dead.If all that's not enough though, the game allows you to check an option to either slow down the time mechanic or turn it off entirely, so if you absolutely must play the game without the feeling of being timed, you have the option of it.If you like metroidvanias and action games, Unsighted is definitely a game you don't want to leave unsighted.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is reminiscent of the classic action adventure games like Legend Of Zelda: Link to the Past with tight, Souls-like combat. a heart wrenching cyberpunk story and awesome queer characters. It forces you to make tough decisions throughout. The developers clearly are fans of some of the classics but they've refined them and, in my opinion, made some better. I wasn't exactly a fan of the day/night cycle, occasionally making things hard to see for me but it is necessary to illustrate the passing of time, a key part of Unsighted's Plot. The game is really about as hard as you want it to be, giving you options to play it on the developer's terms or your own. This game is likely my GOTY for 2021. I cannot recommend it enough!!!

_childDocuments_.review: (Disclaimer, my play time is low because I played this mostly on Nintendo Switch, but bought it again on Steam to show my support and to review it!)This is a top 5 game of the year 2021 for me. It's SO GOOD. The game takes design inspiration from so many games, but combines them in a cohesive and satisfying way in an original universe. I did my first play through in "Explorer" mode, but I'm curious to play it again in the future in the intended fashion so that the time I spent has more meaning and integrates into the story.I love the metroidvania map structure, Hyper Light Drifter style third person perspective with great melee combat and parrying. The active reload, the multi-purpose weapons/means of traversal, the flexible upgrade system, finding secrets and of course the story. This game was one of the rare ones where I try to squeeze it in every spare moment of my days and nights because I just have to keep going. There's a staggering amount of bespoke art and animation not limited to cutscenes and the wide cast of characters reminiscent of classic SNES JRPG villages.So so much good stuff taken from lots of classic games with modern design choices. I forgot to mention Legend of Zelda style dungeons and puzzle solving which can also be done in any order like in "Link Between Worlds" and I can tell there are TONS of sequence breaking possibilities. I'm sure speed runners are going to have a lot of fun optimizing their runs with this game.Highly highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: - Zelda a Link to the Past: 4.5/5- Hyper Light Drifter: 3.5/5- Cross Code: 4/5 if you enjoy old Zelda games (top down view), Hyper Light Drifter, Cross Code, overall enjoy Metroidvanias, this game is a real treat. It does almost everything right!Unsighted is an indie top down action game. It focuses on the story of a world which changed completely because a meteor landed on it and spread around an energy called Anima, which gave true sentience to robots and automatons in the world. Which is pretty cool except the humans didn't like it and started a war. Oh, silly humans.At one point, the humans managed to seal off the meteor using a gigantic spaceship and secured it completely. It also halted the spreading of Anima, which causes all the remaining sentient robots to have a very limited lifespan before they become the equivalent of zombies/wild animals, called Unsighted.And that includes you, because you too are a robot. You start with a few hundreds of hours to live and do your main quest which is explore the world (!), get upgrades (!!) and defeat the super ancient Unsighted bosses for meteor shards. Get all 5 so you can craft a super weapon strong enough to raid the meteor and bring back actual infinite Anima to the world.This is super brutal for a game like this, paradoxical as well but also super fun. The time limit varies per person and over the course of your journey you're forced to share your precious Meteor Dust (the only EXTREMELY SCARCE resource you can find that extends your lifetime) with those who need... or save it for yourself because your quest is super important. Its very tense and very fun to play with this kind of limitation. Stressful as well but really really fun.But if this isn't your kind of fun, the game allows you to turn it off at any time and explore at your own pace, which is also wonderful. Big thanks to the developers for putting this option in the game, and kudos for the commitment for implementing it well and making the player aware of the importance of it!The game does all the cool things about metroidvanias (or more accurately zelda-likes in this context?) correct! The movement is super fluid, there are basic and advanced techniques and the game very correctly teaches you with superb level design so you know what to do and how to do from the get go. Its very intuitive and pleasant and keeps the action going very naturally.Combat is very cutthroat as well. You can hit enemies repeatedly, parry and counter with devastating critical hits, but also you have little room for mistakes, a few hits are enough to kill you. Pick your fights correctly and learn the enemy combos, you can feel the increasing efficiency of your navigation and combat growing over time in a very natural and satisfying way!Finally, the story, expert level design and gorgeous pixel art ties this all together. The game is fun, challenging, mysterious and doesn't overstay its welcome. Its made to be fast, it makes you stand constantly on your toes and really rewards you for being daring and precise.

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is such an amazing little gem of a game that it's a shame it's so overlooked. It looks and feels like an old school Zelda game with puzzles, unique tools, and platforming elements, but spices things up with an immensely satisfying combat system. There is a surprising variety of enemies and the bosses are so, so fun to fight that I don't even mind dying to them. While some elements feel a little lacking in polish such as the crafting system and the Navi-like character being a tiny bit too handhold-y for my tastes, I can happily overlook that in favor of everything else the game does so well. The timer element of the game can be intimidating, but you can effectively disable it as soon as you create a save file, as well as turn it off later. I'm doing my first playthrough on "Explorer" mode so I can play at my own pace, and I don't feel like something is lacking from the game as a result of nullifying that element. If you're on the fence, I highly encourage you to at least check out the demo and give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 wwould save cute automatons again. I can't recommend this gem enough!I don't normally play metroidvania titles but there was something special about this game that made me give it a shot and I am so happy I did. This has easily made me more interested in the genre and I can say that this is in fact now officially my favorite metroidvania title to date so much that I even started a new game+ for the first time in any series ive ever played. _childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is probably one of the best games that you haven't played this year. It's a genuine contender for my game of the year. The story is great, full of well realised characters with lots of heartfelt, believable dialogue. The world design invites exploration and makes traversal a joy (mostly, more on that later). The combat is meaty and challenging, but still give you plenty of tools to manage the challenge. My favourite part is that the "Explorer" difficulty gives you a ton of options to customise how you want the game to play out. You can turn off the time limits while keeping the combat challenging. The time limits are admittedly a big part of the game's narrative, but if you just want to explore then it's a good option to have.There are a couple of minor issues however. You will sometimes get lost, especially because there are times when the game doesn't tell you about an ability that you have which is key to progression (hint: once you get your boots, did you know you can wall jump?). The 2.5D platforming in a 2D screen is sometimes frustrating, you'll find yourself missing jumps you think you should have made, or not being able to reach certain platforms that look like they should be climable. The menu and inventory is pretty clunky, but it's not a dealbreaker.So, definitely pick this up. It's a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: UNSIGHTED

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a fantastic game. I had a ton of fun on my first playthrough and expect to get many more hours of enjoyment out of it as I replay it on the highest difficulty and go for more of the achievements!Exploration is a core part of Unsighted, with a huge, multi-layer map with beautiful, pixel-art environments. The the feeling of anticipation of what I'll discover next is what I love about Metroidvanias and Unsighted does not disappoint. As you explore, you find new weapons and abilities that allow you to access new parts of the world. There are all kinds of hidden treasures, weapons, and upgrades to unlock, and each new area feels distinct from the previous one, with new hazards and enemies.The combat system in Unsighted is what cemented it as one of my favorite games. A major part of the combat is a parry mechanic that allows you to block attacks, which stuns the attacker and rewards you with an opportunity to hit them with a critical attack for massive damage. Parrying is optional for some enemies (you can also run and dodge to avoid hits), but pretty much required to make some vulnerable. You also have limited stamina (depleted by running, dodging, and attacking), so you need to be careful not to run out and be left open to attack. The game has only two types of melee weapons, but they both are fun to use and can be supplemented by a variety of ranged weapons. Overall, the combat is just immensely satisfying, which is what drove me to start a second playthrough on the highest difficulty.I'm not the best when it comes to reviewing a games story, but overall I enjoyed the world building and found the characters to be endearing. The limited amount of time each character has before the perish was tragic, but I was able to beat the game without disabling it.Anyways, I can't do this game justice without tripling the wordcount of this review. I highly recommend trying the demo for Unsighted to see if you like it! It's definitely one of the best games of 2021 and it's incredibly impressive that it was developed by a team just two people!

_childDocuments_.review: : Unsighted is a fantastic game. If watching any video of the game made you think "why not", there is a very good chance you will love it.Unsighted is a top-down action adventure game (think Zelda A Link to the Past or Hyper Light Drifter), with a very cleverly implemented exploration and a solid combat system (more on these below). The structure of the game is fairly classic - you navigate main character Alma from dungeon to dungeon, while upgrading your character or weapons, or crafting items to help you in the process. There are various NPCs throughout the world you can bond with, which can unlock new stuff to equip on Alma. Both Alma and her friends have a time limit before they lose their conscience and turn to mindless automatons, but you can postpone that limit using meteor dusts scattered around the world.Let's address that elephant in the room right now : yes, the game was designed with a time limit in the game. If you read the negative reviews on this game, many of them focus on that point alone. But the time limit can be disabled whenever you want - before even beginning a game, or during one if you start one with the default setting and regret that choice afterwards. Disabling the time limit is in no way an easy mode, and won't lock you out of any content, except for  three achievements (). With all this in mind, I find it unfair to discourage other people from playing this game, even though it's so good gameplay-wise.EDIT : I thought the "explorer" mode prevented only one achievement (pertaining to the hard mode), but a friend playing on Switch informed me there are a total of three achievements he cannot get in his playthrough, all related to a specific way of playing through the game. Nonetheless I stand by my conclusion above, but I'm sorry for not double-checking that before writing that paragraph.Regarding gameplay then, let's first talk about exploration. Compared to the aforementioned games, Unsighted borrows some ideas from metroidvania games, in that there are some roadblocks, or "out of reach" areas that require you to have an item to go through. But the way in which Unsighted manages this brilliant, and I wish more games did this. I sincerely advise you to go in blind and discover this for yourself, but if you need some more convincing, I'm detailing what I think is fantastic in spoiler text below - you can skip to the next paragraph if you'd rather experience it first-hand. Also, the exploration is not necessarily linear. Early in the game, a NPC will suggest an order in which you can do things. For the first playthrough, it's easier to follow these guidelines, sidetracking occasionnally to get some items or upgrades. But as you understand the game better and better, you start to see options to explore areas in vastly different ways (and order), and this enables you to be quite free in your exploration. Aside from some "overworld" areas, there are five main dungeons in the game, each with a specific gimmick to make it stand out, often tied to a specific item you get in the dungeon - rings any bell ? All of them feature both puzzles and some "combat zones", complete with a boss at the end. On to combat : at any time, Alma can have two weapons (either melee or ranged), a number of "chips" (passive upgrades) and cogs (consumable boosts) equipped. The weapons in the game are not insanely varied, but they more than get the job done. If you want some details regarding the weapons you can find in the game : . Alma has a stamina gauge, which feeds both melee attacks an invincible jump/dash you can use to evade enemy attacks. To top that off, add in a parry (which stuns enemies and open them up for big damage) and a chargeable strike with your melee attack for big AoE damage. I wouldn't say the game is hard, but it's not easy either. At the very start of the game especially, it's easy to forget about the stamina and get stomped by enemies for instance - Alma only has so much life. But much like the exploration, you progressively get better during the course of the game, and soon enough the various tools offered become a second nature, making managing the threats that much easier - not to mention satisfying.There are only (and I mean only) two complaints I have with the game :1) During the course of the game, you often need to swap weapons, because some weapons double as progression tools. At the time of this writing, this requires opening the menu to do the swapping - there are no "quick change" options. Now, the weapons menu is ordered in a "last-used first" fashion, which means it's not  of a hassle. Also, the devs are aware of this and might tackle this in the future .2) There is a "true ending" of sorts in this game, and some of the necessary steps to access it are IMHO quite frustrating. For just about everything else in the game, there are nudges or subtle hints to point you to either interesting directions, or even to learn new gameplay elements. These might exist for the true ending and I missed them, but at any rate I confess I eventually looked them up on Youtube so as not to spend an absurd amount of time on this. The game two other modes : a boss rush, and a "dungeon raid", which has you moving through procedurally generated dungeons reusing the "main" mode's assets. Both are serviceable (and each has two achievements), but the meat of the game is the standard, "main story" mode. It's also possible to play the game co-op, but I didn't get the chance to try it out. If it's par with the rest of the game quality-wise, I have no doubt it's a fun romp.I hope this review made it clear how much I love this game. For what it's worth, I rarely go trophy-hunting for games, yet I was unable to play anything else until I had done exactly that for Unsighted. This does not necessarily mean this game is for everyone. But if the genre or gameplay appeals to you, you owe it to yourself to try this game out. It is honestly one of the best of its kind.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. Great art, great gameplay, good level design, good music, good worldbuilding, and so much replay value.The movement and combat feels a lot like an evolution of what Hyper Light Drifter did, and I'm very happy to have found a game that expands on these mechanics so well. And it really has a lot of stuff going on, mixing a lot of concepts from various games and genres with intention. Top down platforming, several types of movement, a large variety of weapons, a chip system, effect cogs, crafting, upgrades, etc. The devs did a good job introducing the mechanics over time, so it rarely felt overwhelming.The game also has a promising amount of extra challenges. I'm really looking forward to trying the hard difficulty. It also seems made for speedrunning, with so many opportunities for optimization and sequence breaks.There's a lot of talk about the timer mechanic. I found it refreshing. So many games attempt to instill a sense of urgency while simultaneously providing a hundred distractions, the world waiting patiently until the hero is done playing blackjack. This can really strain suspension of disbelief. But when UNSIGHTED tells you that time is running out, that is the truth, and you'll have to make some tough decisions. I recommend giving the timer a chance before enabling explorer mode.Nitpick 1: The writing is pretty good, but it felt a bit off at times. I think sometimes the dialogue sounded more like text messages than an in-person conversation, in a way? Most characters also remained somewhat static throughout the events of the game, not reacting very much to the events unfolding. The world, story, and characters are well-made, but the execution lacked something for me.Nitpick 2: There's tons of options for replay, but it's a bit overwhelming. There's New Game, New Game Extra, New Game+, a hard difficulty, Boss Rush, Dungeon Raid, maybe more? You'll probably want to do that second playthrough where you try to save everyone with the knowledge and skills that you gained. But maybe New Game+ allows for some sequence breaks that unveil new secrets or change the story? And what's the deal with New Game Extra? A clear, recommended choice for the first replay might help.Nitpicks aside, it's still my favorite game of the year so far. Just give the demo a try if you're unsure.

_childDocuments_.review: I just completed my first playthrough and this game is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece.  The art is gorgeous, the gameplay is TIGHT and super fun, and the level design is extremely intuitive.  There's a perfect blend of action and puzzling and platforming, and there's lots of ways to customize your arsenal too.  It really just leaves so many possibilities, and there are even other difficulty settings and extra gamemodes to try out (which I have not at this point).This is basically the Cave Story of the 2020's in my opinion.  Don't miss out.

_childDocuments_.review: Main Points:* Very good art and animation* Dynamic music feels rewarding* Very tight controls and gameplay, feels great to play* Music, graphics, and gameplay blend very well to enhance the environment* Creative and fun mechanics keep the game fresh* Well written story that makes you care about the characters and world* Difficulty options make the game accessible even if you're not up to the default challengeIt's hard to explain to someone what UNSIGHTED is. The best way I could explain it to people who ask is "top down Zelda-like with Metroidvania and Souls elements". I don't think that does the game justice though. UNSIGHTED is very much aware of its influences, but it still feels fresh and exciting compared to how other games can feel like they're rehashing what has already been done. It's a game that wants you to care, beyond the superficial aspects of having an engaging story. It wants you to engage with the world, to explore it and to challenge it. The power curve is very satisfying, with not only your combat abilities growing, but also your movement options. By the time you reach the endgame, you feel your full growth from scrappy underdog to powerful warrior. Highly recommend checking it out!

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game that on first instinct would call zelda-like, but I feel would be short changing unsighted with that comparison.  There are several dungeons that you platform, puzzle solve, and fight your way through against several ticking clocks where if they run out you lose one of many npcs or you die.  The ticking clock portion of this game may turn many people off and although I didn't hate it and appreciated the physical reminder of what would happen if I went slowly there were times where I was annoyed that I had to stop my progression to run back to town and re-up someone's clock, and by the end of the game I had just stopped caring about anyone outside of my character and fairy companion.  The music in the game was a high point for me, with one track in particular reminding me heavily of the police station in parasite eve.  The music was not the upbeat frantic music I have become accustomed to for dungeon exploration, but I enjoyed this so much more than if it had been.  I will say that a couple of the sound effects (receiving an item) are "homages" at best.  The visual portion of the game is a mixed bag.  The gameplay portion looks great, some cutscenes look great, but the character portraits vary wildly from acceptable to just bad, if you enjoy the gameplay or story then this won't matter, but I feel like not pointing out such an obvious thing would be disingenuous.   Gameplay as previously states revolves around puzzles, platforming and combat.  The puzzles are enjoyable though not overly difficult and certainly nothing more difficult than you would find in a zelda game.  The platforming is enjoyable once the player unlocks the jumping boots that allow wall jumps (explaining that you can perform this maneuver comes hours after getting the boots), long jumps, and running up walls.  Platforming mostly boils down to creating platforms to run on before they disappear or break apart, using grappling hook(s) to move between moving platforms, and physically moving platforms into position so that you can use them to jump to your destination.  Combat involves having two weapons/gadgets equipped at a time, a stamina bar that depletes based on the weapon or gadget used, a charge attack that I used once just to see what I could do and promptly forgot about, and a counter button that starts as overpowered and becomes more required as the game goes on.  There are items to boost you temporarily, healing vials and temporary versions, and chips that alter your power/health/stamina/extra abilities, but those are all supplementary to the meat and potatoes I have laid out.  The combat is fun, the stamina bar can feel a little limiting, and the counter as stated goes between massively overpowered to acceptable, but in the end I enjoyed the combat anyway.  I played the game to completion once, but apparently there are alternate endings which I did not care to go get as I found the ending satisfactory and didn't feel like raising affection levels or speeding through the game to keep everyone alive.  Solid game, good length, recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: We were prepared to like UNSIGHTED from the second we first heard of it, but we were not at all ready to fall in love with it. From the moment you take control, the finely tuned controls and movement stand out. The graphics are amazing, the story and world building are top-tier, the music is beyond impressive, the combat fluid and satisfying, the gameplay mechanics all precisely balanced...You get the idea. There's no way to do this game justice in a couple of paragraphs, but let us make one suggestion: don't miss out on something truly special, give this game a try! 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unsighted is a brilliant exploration action game. It most reminds me of the Legend of Zelda games. Most of the game is about navigating the gameworld, exploring the unknown and unlocking paths using the different equipment you find along the way. The combat is very fluid and services to create tension, though the combat did grow a tad repetitive for my tastes.An absolute stand out aspect of the game is how it enables players to explore freely and find less-than-obvious routes. You can always follow the mission pointers to get an enjoyable well-paced experience, but don't be feel like you must follow the obvious path. There are almost always alternative routes to even reach end-game areas fairly early in the story. This mastery of the game world and navigating through it  felt excellent. Another spicy element of the design is how every NPC (including the player) has a timer ticking down towards their death. There are ways to extend this time, but it does create an element of tension and unease to exploring the game world. This enables another layer of meaningful choice - who do you save and who will you sacrifice?

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Great story, characters feel so authentic, the flashback scenes and interactions with all the characters you meet take you on an emotional ride that's quite rare in gaming. You'll smile, you'll laugh, you'll frown. If you're as sensitive as me you may be moved to a tear or two. I don't think I'm out of the woods on that yet from where I left off, lol.The graphics are absolutely GORGEOUS. Incredible pixel art, which GOSH I appreciate. Something about pixel art just does it for me, especially in a game with this kind of combat style and general feel. The cutscenes are so visually pleasing, so much love and care went into this. Games like this, Blasphemous, and Death Trash (Great, but in Early Access) have given me so much life lately with the gorgeous and unique pixel art. Combat is fun and satisfying. The RPG mechanics are decent, not overwhelming, not overly simplistic. I'm loving it, I've barely put it down since I bought it. This is a must buy for action rpg fans, for metroidvania fans, post apocalyptic/cyberpunk dystopia fans, it is an absolute masterpiece so far. Going through it slowly in Explorer mode, because that's just how I play RPGs, I love to explore every nook and cranny. I am excited to play through on Action Girl and higher difficulties now that I've gotten the hang of it and feel of how it all works, and have a good idea how the time limit will work when it's actually ticking down faster.Buy it, gift it to your friends and family, spread the word. This game deserves to be trending big time and get some eyeballs on it. Don't believe me? Play the demo. I knew ten minutes into that demo that this was gonna be amazing, and it's lived up to every bit of what I thought it would after trying it. I will absolutely be first in line for the next game or any sort of DLC or expansions in this universe. Studio Pixel Punk deserves to go straight to the top! I love it. I won't shut up about it to all of my friends and followers on twitter. Thank you so much, ladies!

_childDocuments_.review: Game of the year, for me. This game is super-fun from start to finish; it's like a top-down Dark Souls, where you have to juggle reading an enemy's pattern with dealing with many of them at once. There's also how the game progresses; you and your friends are all running out of time to live, and the lack of a manual save means that you are constantly on a clock. That sense of urgency really added to the overall feel of the game! Having said that, there are great accessibility options, too; you can turn that timer off completely, and instead focus on exploring.The dev team also nailed it with the sound and art direction. I love how most of the enemies in the game can be simultaneously unsettling and ADORABLE. My only real complaint is that the plot itself is a little mediocre. For a game that has so much to explore, and with such lovable characters, the actual story just boils down to "humans evil, robots good". After progressing through the game and powering my way through so much insanity, the actual background of this amazing little world felt... shallow.Either way, the game was great! Had a lot of fun with this wonderful cast of LBGT robot women!

_childDocuments_.review: Uniquely awesome.There are a lot of great games out there that make us feel and think about stuff; about life, the world and ourselves. But this game also made me think about how I play games. It's one thing to play something that has specific moments of decision making (usually you have to decide between 2 or 3 options the game presents to you: "now, choose: do this or do that"), but it's a whole another thing to feel that every step you take in the game is a decision you' re making naturally, between various others possibilities. And that all of your choices have consequences, for real.Unsighted is, without a doubt, one of the best games I've played in years. It was open for me to be myself, to play in my unique way—and made me question and think a little about it too in the process. It's beautiful (the art, the music!), thrilling, FUN — and was all made by 2 people!Just play it, it's awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still working my way through this (dungeon 4 of what appears to be 5) but I already know this is a game of the year contender. I'm playing on Explorer Mode because I want to get familiar with the game before I start racing against the clock and let me say, there's more than enough time to do everything. There's just enough of a subconscious tug to encourage you to finish quickly, but you won't sit there getting stressed about time if you can't figure out a puzzle or you're going for 100% items/map. Other options that explorer mode offers include more forgiving combat and invincibility, but if you just want less time pressure, you can turn off the other options.The search action/metroidvania genre is so saturated that any newcomers to the scene need to focus on making a good metroidvania first and foremost, and Studio Pixel Punk absolutely pull it off. Weapons have multiple utilities, and little touches like aim assist for your blaster or hookshot really help with the platforming. Combat feels extremely fluid once you get into the rhythm of it, especially the parrying mechanic. I noticed enemy groups will start attacking one after the other so you can keep a parry chain going instead of getting overwhelmed.So far, NPC personalities do seem a little thin, which could be a detriment if you're trying to play favorites with who you save. If you're the kind of person who just wants to save everybody, though, I don't think you need too much more incentive than the ticking time clock. I will also be up front in saying that I haven't been making liberal use of Meteor Dust, so it could be possible that these NPCs grow more the more you help them out.I think the studio has crafted a great story here, one with real stakes for everyone in the world. I'm learning more about Alma's past at the same time she does, and there's some conflict between her and Raquel that I'm very curious to see the resolution of. I think the nature of the game also means that I have an immediate desire to see through the goal of removing the control tower and freeing the flow of anima. If I can pull that off, the energy crisis is over and I get to spend more time in this world.And the world really comes to life with music from Fernanda Dias, showing off a breadth of styles that all work together in service of the whole. Combat music weaves seamlessly in and out with environmental music, and every time I hear the emotional, Erik Satie-echoing piano in a cutscene, I know I'm in for something good.Bottom line, absolutely hard recommend this game. If you're intimidated by the premise, try it out on explorer mode and I promise you'll do fine. Main NPCs all have hundreds of hours on their timers to begin with, and I've barely cracked 48 in-game hours even while exploring. You've even got time to take some naps with some dogs.

I'm intrigued by the quite unique setting and very curious and diverse cast of characters.There is a lot of platforming so far and I love how vertical the levels are, it's great to figure out how to get to a chest you saw an hour ago but couldn't get to yet or stumble upon a sneaky, hidden away chest, it makes so that exploring every nook and cranny is rewarding.The combat feels very good and fluid -love the parry mechanic- and it is possible to change and adapt how you approach each area to your taste through different character builds, which can be modified at will at specific spots, so you could easily experiment and see what suits you; there seems to be something for everyone's preferred fighting style here.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the demo with zero expectations Unsighted really hooked me with the great atmosphere, art, and gameplay. Parries and the fast reload speed encourages carefully timed button presses incentives learning your enemies patterns. The game is on a timer and encourages replaying the story, so for those who enjoyed playing games like majora's mask or any game with movement in mind this game is for you. name: Garden Story
detailed_description: A chill game set in a cozy village Traverse the four seasons in this wholesome world inhabited by quirky fruits and vegetables! As the newest guardian of the Grove, it is your duty to rebuild the village and uncover the story of its hidden past. Grow with the town Complete daily requests to defend, restore, and improve the town. As you progress, you'll unlock memories that allow Concord to harness the power of their predecessors. A satisfying journey of rebuilding and collecting Listen to the sweet and catchy music of the island, relax in The Grove’s cozy and inviting atmosphere, cultivate gardens and libraries, and enjoy the delightful personalities you’ll meet along the way. You can even collect adorable hats and backpacks in every village! Play at your own pace Only have 12 minutes to spare? That's just enough time for a quick gameplay session. Looking to stay awhile? Take your time rebuilding the Grove. Either way, there’s always something you can do to help your community— they’re counting on their new guardian! Accessibility Options For those who prefer to progress the story without the stresses of combat, you can always turn on “perish prevention” mode in the gameplay options. This setting is also helpful for getting past difficult enemies or boss fights. Explore a lush, living world: Immerse yourself in The Grove’s vibrant, organic ecosystem with four distinct (and adorable!) regions to enjoy. Foster community: Take on requests, complete favors, and work as a role model to provide inhabitants with the confidence to support one another. Don’t be afraid to ask for help: we’re rebuilding together! Combat Rot: Solve puzzles and fend off Rot as you delve into particularly infested locations of The Grove. Take caution: especially formidable Rot have taken residence in the depths of these areas! Experiment with equipment: Utilize a variety of items to help gather resources, grow gardens, stave off Rot, solve puzzles, and indulge in the occasional musical interlude! Cultivate your home: Care for garden plots, gather resources, curate libraries, upgrade your tools, and rebuild structures.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite whatever the thumb says, the verdict of this review is "mixed" or "neither good nor bad".This is one of those games that's difficult to give a definite yes or no to. Steam forces you to choose up or down, but honestly it's really a coin flip with this cute little grape man.First of all, if you're expecting a game that scratches your Stardew itch, this aint it. Watch or read about the gameplay before you buy. There is no farming or mining or decorating or anything like that. This game is NOT a life sim. There's nothing like that. At all. So beware any game journalism articles you may have seen claiming this game will "give you your Stardew fix". It might or might not. Depends what you think that means. Maybe in terms of how cute and colorful it looks, but in terms of gameplay, it's not even close to that kinda game. So let's just say that up front. This is not a review where I just neg on the game for not being Stardew. I'm just saying, those headlines are out there, and they may give you wrong ideas about what Garden Story actually is, so you should look into it first.First let's talk about the good stuff. This game is overflowing with outstanding pixel art and and cute happy characters. This is the kind of pixel art that makes you buy up an indie game on aesthetic alone. It looks fantastic. And you have to love all of the cute little plant people who have names related to the kind of fruit or vegetable that they are. It's just hard not to feel happy when you are looking at these cute little sprites and their cute little faces living in their cute little town. The wholesomeness in the visuals is carrying a lot of weight in this game. It's on point.Second is the soundtrack and audio. The game has great music tracks that fit the happy visuals of the game perfectly. Not only that, but the sfx are pretty good, too. I loved every time I woke up in the morning and was greeted by the sound of rain softly hitting the roof of my little house.When all is said and done, if what you prioritize most in a game is art or music or just general character, then this game has all of that in droves.Gameplay, though....? I gotta say it leaves something to be desired.First thing to know is that the vast majority of the gameplay is pretty much all all combat and smashing vases. The obvious comparison everyone is gonna go for is the old top-down Zelda games, but I think even that comparison might be a little too generous for our little grape man. There are some issues.First is that the game seems to have some kind of low or locked frame rate issue that makes it feel like it's perpetually stuck in a state of stuttering or lagging. So if you're sensitive to frame rates, this game might give you a little bit of an eye twitch. Even on top of that, the combat controls just kinda feel stiff and locky in a way that makes combat not that enjoyable to perform. Fighting enemies is just not that fun or satisfying at the best of times, and it feels like you're dropping frames at the worst of times.Putting even the feel of the combat aside, the core loop of the game also doesn't really have too much going on that's interesting either. If you were going to compare any part of this game to Stardew, the one thing they do have in common is the "job board" where requests are posted for you to fulfill. Only with Garden Story, fulfilling those requests is literally 90% of the gameplay, and you get the same three or four requests over and over, to the point where you almost don't even have to read them. You fulfill them mostly by defeating enemies or by smashing various types of vases. (I say "vases" as a zelda comparison, but "vases" could be boxes, rocks, or plants. Just various static "smashables".) This kind of "harvesting" is a little more rewarding in Stardew where you have a wide variety of options, a variety of tools, a variety of locations, and you're free to decide what you want to harvest and why, free to prioritize, free to use the rewards you receive in ways that let you customize and be CREATIVE and EXPRESSIVE and really forge your own path as a player. But here, you're not making any decisions, not expressing yourself, not investigating or exploring. You're just doing what you're told. If you try to go off path at all, the game just yells at you to stop it. (Literally, it does this. It won't let you.) You're just mindlessly and obediently smashing vases with your sword in order to get rupees so that you can give them to NPCs who want them. That's all. It's just kinda shallow when it all shakes out.So it's tough to give a definite yes or no. On one hand, I want to give this game a yes. It's beautiful and adorable and the soundtrack is great and I find being inside this little garden world to be charming and a place I like to be. I think there are people who will just find it relaxing in the same way as games like Eurotruck, which could also fairly be described as "mindless" and "grindy" by many players and yet tons of players find it relaxing. So the grind of it might be appealing in that way to some players. And for players who are extra sensitive to stuff that is ridiculously cute, you might not be able to resist its charms. It might still work out for you on that basis. So thinking along these lines, I kinda wanna give it a yes.But at the same time, I want to say no, because the gameplay really just does not measure up for me. It doesn't have the adventure, or decision-making, or self-expression that I really want in a life sim or in an rpg. It's not really relaxing in a mindless way like Eurotruck, because it's almost all combat. And yet the combat doesn't feel that good. And the rewards for the combat feels about as exciting as the rewards of playing a clicker game. After several hours and multiple towns, I still just don't really feel like I'm having that much fun.I just can't decide. Thumb extended not up nor down, but exactly sideways.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished 100%ing Garden Story for a second time since the game first came out. I do not enjoy this as a game, rather I engage with it as something to numb my attention. It's provides me the emotional sensation like that of accidentally slamming my elbow against a hard surface making my mind go fuzzy in a way that could be described as interesting and fun. Garden Story is part of a trend I refer to as "chore games", or more amusingly "sanrio productivity software" which were sparked from the seed of Stawdew Valley and exploded in the wake of Animal Crossing. You're a little friend and you're in a place where things won't get done without your tedious repetitive efforts. It's just like real life except you don't have to stand up. You can talk to other cute little buddys to read their lukewarm agreeable thoughts about The Crushing Distress eating away at the world. Such are the classics of emotional game in displaying Theme and Allegory, it's not subtle or particularly deep but considering how lackluster video game writing can be it's pretty nice and mostly unintrusive.I am magnetically drawn to any game that looks cute and lets me pick stuff up off the ground. I will play any game like this even if I actively dislike it. I played 300 hours of Animal Crossing on the Nintendo Switch in the span of 2 months and then I never touched it again because there's something wrong with me.Garden Story is not a game I have spent 300 hours playing because it was not meticulously designed by a tightly focused team with millions of dollars. I am grateful for this. I maxed out every status and upgrade I could in about 25 hours so I am once again free. I liked looking at the bright colors and seeing all my little meters slowly tick up. I liked running around and tending to all the little plots and resources. I liked that the combat and puzzles are easy so i don't have to think too hard and risk waking the demons. i liked buying the final powerful upgrade that are completely useless because by the time i've expended the effort to get them the game is long over. I do not like how certain rare resources are a huge pain to collect. I do not like having to resolve every puzzle dungeon a dozen times to even access certain resources or to get them the most efficiently. I do not like how almost all the places I have to backtrack to aren't on the screens that fast travel connects to. I do not like how spread out the farming plots are and how a game that lets you craft decorations only has tiny sequestered plots for them that barely fit any of the things you can build and even then you'd really want to use that space for the quest and storage objects. I don't like that I have to go to sleep and wake up hoping I get the more rewarding daily chores and then having to speedrun the day to try again.Despite my many annoyances with this game I have somehow ended up completing all its chores and taking out all its metaphorical garbage instead of doing something actually fulfilling with that time. If that for you as it did for me sounds more achievable than doing something actually fulfilling you may also like playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited for the release of Garden Story since I played the demo last year.So far I've played through Spring Hamlet (maybe 20-25% of the game?) and decided to write a review. The story seems rather average, but gameplay reminds me a little bit of older The Legend of Zelda titles-- which is a good thing, in my opinion.So far I'm having much fun and can recommend Garden Story for anybody who likes Zelda-like games and has 20 bucks to spare.

_childDocuments_.review: Couple things I want to start with. 1. This game is ok. 6/10, where 5 is neither good nor bad. It's better than nothing.2. I really appreciate developers putting in all this hard work into games. I think it's easy to write a review and talk about things I did or didn't like. It's much harder to create things that delight, and remove things that don't.Something that's a first for me is that I actually started taking small bullet notes when playing along with this game. That doesn't mean this review will be any better than normal. It'll just be more documented.I'll start with the 'bad things' and move on to the 'good things'. But more accurately, they're just things I didn't like and things I did like. Not all things I dislike are bad. Additionally, these notes were taken more as someone who was playtesting a game, and less as someone who's trying to write a review.Things that I didn't like (no particular order):* You can't access daily requests from anywhere. If you have the memory of a gnat, like I do, you'll constantly be rushing back to the request board to remember what the requests are and where they are. * Combat isn't really fun. I'm afraid I don't know exactly how to describe it or what I would do to improve it, but combat kinda seems like you just have to rush in there and just start swiping, then extract yourself once you're low on HP.  For shelled creatures you have to switch between two weapons to attack, which kinda sucks (switching isn't immediate, and the rod tool is slow to use). Additionally, leveling up tools never seems to make you strong enough to make your life easy. I was hoping by the end of the game that I would be strong enough to merc simple slimes in a single swipe, but that's just not how things work. They ALWAYS form these 'second-phase' small slimes that have to be defeated, and that sucks: They can't be swiped at immediately, and they usually end up taking a chunk of health away from me or slowing me down with their slow-down-goo. I might just suck at this game though.* Resting. I feel like I should be able to go to sleep as early as I want, or be able to skip forward to a specific time of day ('nap' or 'wait'). Then bench mechanism is ok, but if it's morning and you want it to be night, you have to do a lot of waiting and moving between zones in order to make it so in a timely fashion. However, I did think that the time mechanism was unique (time advances until it is about to transition between, say, morning and afternoon, at which point it pauses until you move to a new screen).* The controls really suck. For keyboard, it's basically impossible. For controller, it's not impossible, but it's very unintuitive. Like, why does left bumper open the map but right bumper doesn't open the inventory. Confusing stuff all around. I'm not foreign to learning new keymaps, but this broke my brain.* Memories. Which memories are currently applied are not denoted in the memory selection menu, making it a guessing game (or a memory game, not my strong suit, see above) as to which ones are already applied. Also, I didn't find memories particularly useful except for min-maxing my resource gathering towards the end. They were perhaps a bit heavy handed with the 'cons' vs the 'pros'* I can't think of a reason why filling at a well shouldn't automatically fill you health to max* You need to get 'main story' quests done, or the game won't progress, but not doing the 'daily tasks' gives little 'guilt trip' messages (oh, you didn't clear out the gutters so the towns people had to spend all day doing it). Nothing BAD happens, but this kind of message feels tonally inconsistent with the aesthetic of the game. And like, hey. I'm busy with other things y'all.* There's a split second after having a conversation but before receiving a favor request/item where you feel like you're going to resume playing the game but then it pulls you into a 'thing-get!' animation, which is jarring and a bit annoying.* Waking up, the vignette effect stays around you too long. You can be moving around with it still clinging around you. Makes me feel like it's a spotlight on a stage + being myopic at the same time. Not in a good way though.* I didn't really see the point of getting clothes. Also the clothes were visually bulky. Some people might really like it, but it just wasn't for me - it kinda seemed like a waste of money when I had to spend it on a bunch of other stuff. I think I would have preferred mixing the buffs of memories with the clothes, perhaps. * I don't know if I should include this or not - it may come across as insensitive. This game is vehement in its they/them use of pronouns. In one hand, this is nice because it sheds the complications of gender that many people may be struggling with on a day-to-day. Also, it makes logical sense: Why should we care about the gender of a grape?? At the same time, its vehemence makes it very obvious that there was intent in the choice of pronouns, which makes it feel...I don't know. Forced? Disingenuous? It also makes it slightly more confusing (and I know this is a tired argument used by 'anti-pronouners') since they/them can refer to multiple people. I feel like variety (he/she/they) would add a bit more color to the game (since we're already making sword-fighting grapes, giving them genders isn't too much of a stretch). I think this should be considered more of a null point than a positive or negative just because I can understand how socially charged changing it one way or the other might be.* I don't think I should need to confirm audio changes in the settings after I've made them.* Many structures exist solely to break and become chores later. This makes villages feel a little hollow - just as task hubs rather than centers for habitation. Villages themselves feel a little hollow - houses that never open. Villagers that never move. Making villages that feel alive is tough: I have played a fair number of games that have done it poorly. It's tough because we, as humans, habituate so damn quickly with everything that we need an immense amount of variety to make it feel like things aren't static, and that requires an immense amount of programming and content. So I kinda get it.* Inventory management is kind of a bear. Things don't stack, and often you have to run back to a supply bin to be able to make a particular transaction or fill out a request etc. A small but significant improvement would be to allow shops and such to pull directly from your supply bins. Also some kind of indicator as to how much I own in the supply bins would be nice (perhaps accessible through an inventory menu)* It would be nice to be able to zoom out on the map* I feel like some of the tools were never really used except in very edge cases, which is weird. Sometimes I feel like it would be better to just add abilities to tools already given rather than make an entirely new tool.* You can enter doors by walking 'across' them rather than into them, which sometimes triggers entering/exiting doors when you don't want to.Things I like:These are very general because honestly there were a lot of good things going on. Don't confuse the size of the section with its importance* Cute artstyle (this encompases a LOT of the game)* Nice music - each time and environment had a nice song to fit with it.* Names of characters are cute* Nice ambient sound. One of my favorite things about this game was the stillness of night. No music played, it was just the stillness of nature.

_childDocuments_.review: The art and music are great. But the game part of this game leaves a lot to be desired.- Combat is the main focus of this game. Absolutely. If you came here thinking you were getting SDV, oops. You don't get the ability to garden until 3/4 of the way through, there are only four plants, and the only reason they exist is to be something else for your weapon upgrade tracker and/or library upgrades.- Combat is the main focus, but it's clunky. The beginning of the game is way harder than the end, because having low stamina is extremely punishing. The first weapon you get has a minuscule hitbox, so if you want to get close enough to kill the only enemy in the game that deals contact damage... you have to get right up in its face.- The enemies are weirdly balanced. The only one that will consistently cause you trouble is the mini-oozes that jump around, because they're the only ones that deal contact damage, and they're hard to hit. Sometimes the game seems aware of this, with the first boss, where you're better off letting the mini-oozes combine into their slower, less-threatening, second form. But most of the time, it doesn't.- What I wouldn't give for an attack that has an arc shape. Seriously, mini-oozes are the worst part of this game. My favorite weapons were the sickle and the parasol, but since attacks can only be in the four cardinal directions, you still miss the mini-oozes a third of the time.- You have the ability to build structures at the halfway point of the game, but the world is already so populated with stuff that you'd only be changing out existing things, not really adding new ones. There's only a couple unique structures available, so it's not like you have a ton of options for more interesting/cooler stuff, either. The only thing that you really want to build everywhere is a village storage box, so that you don't have to run three areas away to get the items you need for whatever upgrade.- Just because Stardew only saves at the end of the day, doesn't mean this game needed to do that also. For better or worse, when I started a new day, I asked myself, "do I really want to play out another full day of this game?" Sometimes I just wanted to do 1-2 things and then come back later. But having to ask myself that question meant I just turned the game off more often than not.- The story is... ehh... it's aiming for something bigger than what it could accomplish with a short game. Too many characters we're expected to care about with too little development on them, an iffy third act twist, a Dark Souls-y theme of a dying world that needs you to turn the lights off when you leave, but then everything's magically fixed with no downsides when the cycle ends... I don't know. I didn't connect with it.- This is a niche point, but the dialogue boxes are handled weirdly. There's no character portraits in the dialogue boxes, so the boxes are typically in the upper right or lower left corners, while the facial expressions are happening on the character sprites in the center-ish of the map. So you wind up having to either constantly look from one to the other, or (in my case) just read the text and ignore the sprites.
