_childDocuments_.review: A cute game where play a guardian you have to gather resources, complete quests, defeat enemies and restore 4 different villages each themed after the 4 seasons. The game started a little slow and very confusing to me but once I got the hang of things I was actually enjoyable. The combat is pretty basic but it has a few different weapons types (all melee) you can pick from (however for some enemies you are forced to use a certain one) and 6 different enemy types to fight not including the 4 different bosses.There is a few things I definitely disliked about it however:- The controls are not great on keyboard (there is no mouse support at all). It was very obviously made with controllers in mind and it shows badly. I mostly got used to them by the end of it, but for the love of god, if you release a game on PC make sure it has decent keyboard and mouse controls. It almost put me off the game completely at the beginning trying to figure out the confusing control scheme and I had to rebind some stuff because it was unusable how it was setup by default.- Everyone just speaks way too much. I get that the game wants to tell a story, but at some point you actually do wanna play the game and not just go through a bunch of text.- This is only an issue if you are a completionist, but the last few achievements were painfully grindy. I don't generally mind grinding too much, but the tool/jar upgrade and kill 50 X enemies (except the Acorns which I got before I was done with the story) felt just awful to do for me, ugh...Works without any issues on Linux with Proton (7.0-6).

_childDocuments_.review: The art style is cute and the music and sound effects are good. But this is not a farming / town restoration game, it is a "walk around a specific area, pick up resources in the same spot every time, and fight the same enemy over and over in slightly different locations" game.I've been playing the game for 20 hours and still haven't unlocked farming, which is very disappointing for a game called Garden Story that is being compared to Stardew Valley.NPCs are similar to characters in an RPG like Pokemon in that they have one or two lines of dialogue that they repeat over and over - there's no relationship building. Completing the daily quests does not seem to have an effect on this. I think this was the most disappointing part of the game for me.The game advertises "restoring the town", but all you're actually doing is pressing "a" on a broken fence or other item to complete a daily quest. There is no true building - just placing items in very restricted areas. You cannot customize your house or the town.Foraging is extremely simple because all resources spawn in the same spots every morning. You end up going on kind of a daily jog. Enemies are not very fun to fight, especially for the first hour or so when your weapons are particularly weak. By the time you upgrade your weapons, you know the enemy's movement patterns well enough that they're not challenging - and almost all of the enemies are slime variants.I quit playing just now when I reached the sewer in Autumn Town - I lost to the boss three or four times and had to redo all of the same block puzzles each time. It's just so much repetition that the places where the game really shines - exploring new areas and learning about the world - don't stand out. The best part of the game is at the very start, when there's a lot of cute dialogue and cutscenes, but the game holds back its core mechanics for too long.I think the first two areas are worth playing if you know what you're getting into. I would not pay full price for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Garden Story is perhaps one of the cutest pixel games I've played on Steam. The story is rather simple and doesn't try too hard to be more than it is. It begins with Concord, a small greenling (grape) who is now tasked to save his community from an entity known as the Rot. If you're looking for a game with stunning pixel visuals and aesthetics; calming soundtrack(s), simple puzzles, occasional gimmicks in boss battles, and a decent amount of grinding for customizations and weapons - then Garden Story is up in your alley.It's definitely more combat heavy than games of similar nature (think Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, etc) but nevertheless very calming. I found it to be a rather relaxing game for my anxiety ^___^ My only complaints about the game are that it's not as customizable as it may seem: there's very limited variations to townscape architecture, Concord's outfit(s) sometimes are hit or miss, how low rate and exclusive some item drops are, and the game banner can be a tad misleading (I initially thought you would get to have travel companions such as the frog and the tomato guy they advertise). Definitely a 10/10 in terms of pixel aesthetics and cuteness, but overall a solid 7.5/10 for game-play and everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a cute grape named Concord who has resided over at The Kindergarden ever since he was born, looking over a vine and waiting for a new Greenling to be born, mostly due to the exit being locked. Even if he wanted to, he couldn’t go out and explore The Grove. One day Plum, one of the Guardians of the Grove, decides to visit you and finally notices that you were locked in there this whole time (or well, finally took it upon himself to unlock you as it seems others mention watching you). However, there’s a catch. It seems that The Rot, goopy enemies that threaten to destroy The Grove, has become even more out of control and Plum needs another Guardian to help shoulder the responsibilities.And from then on, your responsibilities are widened to defeating the Rot and help the towns rebuild. You first start in Concord’s hometown Spring Hamlet, but you will visit the other seasonal themed towns (Summer Bar, Autumn Town, and Winter Glade) in due time. One of your main responsibilities is to help rebuild the four towns and connect them back together. Every day you’ll wake up to a little weather forecast and 2-3 help requests up on the notice boards scattered around the towns. The help requests fall under three different categories (you can only get one from each) ranging from defeating a certain amount of Rot, gathering a certain amount of a specific resource, and fixing something like bridges or fences. These requests takes the whole day (there is a day-night cycle but it won’t switch over to the next day unless you sleep), but completing them will level up that aspect of the town. Which in turn gives you more items and upgrades available in shops. But don’t fret if you can’t complete one as it doesn’t seem like you take a hit on incomplete requests other a blurb on how it affected the citizens. In addition, some characters also have favors (or side quests) for you to do which can grant you a reward for your trouble.Though, the help requests do get tiring after a while and it’s really just best to do them when you’re going to be there anyway. This is mainly due to the same tasks being repeated, which also will likely have you traveling all over town. I also did wish that you could see the requests somewhere other than just the notice boards, like maybe have a toggle on the map screen between story quests and town help requests.While you’re traveling around or when you’re not doing requests, you’ll often come across the goopy enemies called Rot. When they catch you in their view, they’ll start going towards you to attack. There are different types of Rot, mainly dictated by the time of day and which town you’re at, and their attacks differ from one another and may even have more health compared to their basic Rot. Along with some requiring you to use a tool to take off their protective covering. Not to mention that when defeated, you’ll still have a tiny bit of Rot left behind that can still hurt you or combine with another to make another Rot. Thankfully, you get a weapon early on, a pick that acts as a sword, and will be able to buy other weapons as you progress. As well as getting a jar, with more becoming available as you visit the other towns, that you can fill with Dew that gives you back your health (or give you a little boost depending on the type you filled it up with). You’ll also have a shield that you can block attacks with, though I honestly forgot about them until I met an enemy that launches projectiles. The combat takes a while to get used to, as it does feel pretty clunky at the beginning, which is mostly due to the stamina system. Each swing of your weapon takes a whole stamina bar, each dodge roll takes one too, and the shield you get needs at least one stamina bar to be filled. Considering you only start with 2, it is a struggle. But when you get more stamina to work with the combat does feel better.Each town will also have their own dungeon and completing them are the last story request for you to do in the town you’re in before you get the blessing to go to the next one or be able to go back to previous ones. These dungeons aren’t that long, but to continue to the next room will require you to solve a puzzle or defeat all of the Rot. And at the end, you’ll be granted with a challenging boss fight. The hardest boss for sure is the first one though, due to not having as much stamina at that point and the extra jars do come in handy as it does give you more Dew to drink.Here, you don’t really level up, but instead use the systems in place to help you out. When you first start, you’ll notice these strange orbs varying in color, but when you try to interact with it, only a notification appears. This is due to you needing a specific tool or a stronger tool to break it, which you’ll eventually get as you visit the other towns and take the time to gather resources to upgrade your weapons. Breaking them will grant you more stamina, health, or Mind depending on the color and it certainly helps in keeping you alive longer.Mind, in particular, feeds into Garden Story’s interesting mechanic of Memories. When you lay down to sleep, you can choose to look at the Memories you collected by doing various different things and see what you need to do to get more. These Memories are actually used to alter your stats or grant you a helpful ability or boost. However, a lot of them do have downsides by lowering another stat. So one may give you more health while lowering your luck or you can have one that just flat out gives you a special charge attack. Don’t worry though, as you can freely switch out your Memories depending on what you need at that time and you will get more Memory slots as you raise your Mind stat. Though, I do wish the game showed you the effect your Memories are having on your regular stats, a before and an after, just so you know what effect it'll have before equipping it.Other than completing help requests and defeating Rot, there are a couple of optional things you can do. Considering that you’ll be picking up a lot of different resources, there are libraries in each town that have lost their books. You can replenish them by donating resources that its missing, though you won’t know what exactly they need other than a black outline of them. There is also some farming and building here too, but it’s introduced pretty late in the game. The various soil plots you see can be watered with Dew and have a seed planted there, which takes a couple days before it fully grows. It also seems that the seeds will grow differently depending on the town you planted them in. Once you unlock the toolbox, you’ll also be able to build various things that can be functional (like another storage box or a bench) to purely cosmetic (like a glass tank or an umbrella), though you have to contribute to the libraries to be able to build more things. However, I never really got into building stuff past the repair boxes needed to continue and a few other things as you are only able to place things in small designated plots and more often then not, they are already occupied with something else that is more helpful.Overall, I really enjoyed Garden Story. While it was a struggle in the beginning when I barely had any stamina and the daily tasks to build up the towns got tiring after a while, I liked going through the vibrant world, talking to the other characters, and looking forward to what the next town looked like. I would recommend picking up Garden Story for anyone that wants to fight as a cute grape and want to help these towns rebuild.

_childDocuments_.review: Garden story is a mediocre game about rebuilding towns by doing repetitive fetch quests and defeating the rot. I wanted to like this game but it is falling apart at the seams after just a couple of hours so I can’t recommend it.Let’s start with the good things about garden story, first of all I really like the pixel art. While the style is simplistic it is very effective and especially the characters look unique and adorable. Occasionally they reuse the same sprites a bit too much but it is still a charming world. The story is okay, it is about small organisms fighting back against the rot. The music is chill and relaxing and fits the game perfectly.The last thing I like about this game is the weapon design. The sickle ended up being my favorite but pretty much all of the weapons are usable or at least interesting. Tools such as the fishing rod doubling as a weapons is a welcome surprise.Now with the good things out of the way the gameplay is a catastrophe. The combat is so easy and boring that it is impossible to die but you will be forced to fight a lot of enemies. There is almost no variety as the only enemies in the game are acorns, roots, tentacles and 6 variants of slimes. If you think the bosses are any more interesting or challenging they aren’t. The worst thing about this game is the daily quest system, every day you get 2 or 3 different requests and by completing them you level up your towns. Quests are usually repetitive small fetch, repair or combat tasks. If you don’t level up your towns you cannot buy any upgrades as the villagers will simply not sell them to you. I do believe that the quest system only exists to stretch the playtime because without it there is maybe 3-4 hours of content in total. Out of the 14 hours I have played this game 10 hours was doing repetitive quests because leveling up your towns takes forever. I didn’t even max out a single village because I got so bored towards the end that I just wanted to finish and stop playing this game. Another problem with quests is that once you hit the resource limit in the area there is nothing else to do, you might finish both quests in a minute and then you have to wait around for 5 minutes or however long a day is until the game allows you to sleep and start a new day to get new tasks.The resource collecting is fun at first but your inventory and storage is too small so you have to do a lot of backtracking, it eventually feels like a chore to collect things. Farming and fishing are both superficial and basically just different ways to collect a resource.It also worth mentioning that the ui is terrible, you will spend quite a lot of time shuffling items around manually and transferring items 1 by 1 in and out of your stash. They wasted an entire button on the controller so switching weapons and tools is more cumbersome than it needs to be. I also don’t know why you have to manually select your repair box or seed bag instead of them being activated by context.When you first play this game you might see a beautiful flower but upon further inspection you will realize the flower is growing on a nasty compost heap.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really addicted to Garden Story when I first started playing it. The design is lovely and I really liked the environment. As time passed I started to become less enamoured, but I'm still happy I experienced this game.The music and art style are the strongest parts. From start to finish the developers really nailed the themes. The music is still playing in my head, especially the summer tracks.The story itself was decent and made enough sense; nothing amazing but it was fine.The gameplay loop of daily tasks and upgrades is a neutral point for me. I don't mind doing daily missions, and I like upgrading items. But as each in-game day went by, I felt myself rushing through some of the tasks. I didn't like leaving them incomplete! The days don't last very long, and if you want to do other things (like advance in the main story) it can be a bit of a chore. I can see why some people think it's monotonous, too.Completing tasks will level up the village you're in, which in turn gives you more options for upgrading your items. But some of these upgrades require grinding for materials. A few are not that convenient to collect, which is a drag.To be honest, you don't have to do all of these daily tasks and upgrades. You can get away with keeping it simple. As I was playing, I didn't feel like I could hang around and focus on those extra things. It's a shame, in hindsight, because I think more value could be placed on the items. Later on I did a couple for the achievements; luckily they weren't too bad. But I did it after the main story was complete, so I didn't really get any benefit from stronger weapons!I thought the favours mechanic was fun, though. Certain characters will give you a little mission to do. There is no "deadline" and you'll get a reward for helping them.Even though Garden Story didn't quite hit the mark with its gameplay, I'm not upset that I bought it. The atmosphere and story kept me satisfied. Now that the main part is done, I think I will go and finish all the extra stuff, but with a more chill mindset.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Stardew Valley. Not gameplay-wise, not spirit-wise. Forget about it. Ok? Ok.What is it then? It's a foraging community maintainer. The gameplay consists of doing tasks to keep things running, fighting, and progressing the story. You get to collect resources by smashing them, fishing, some minor farming rather late in the game... but it's mostly about maintenance, combat, and the general feeling of connection with the world.And the last thing is why this game is so great. It *spoke* to me. I *was* Concord, and Concord was me. And it hurt when it was time to leave this world.Not many games manage to cultivate this feeling. It's possible you've never experienced it. It's also possible this game won't make you feel that. But it did for me.If I had to explain what exactly made me feel that way... well, there's great worldbuilding - the plant people aren't just plant people, there's a reason for how things are how they are. The world has its history, its past heroes, its own divinity. And the characters present have relationships with each other, yes, but also with the world. And with you. The game excels at making you care for each and every character you meet. They're all endearing in some way, and you really want to make the world better for them. I can't possibly express how much I loved playing Garden Story. If you ever played Wuppo, and liked it, then maybe you have an idea of what sort of emotions I'm talking about here. If not - let's just say that after finishing it, I immediately rushed off to my friends to get them a copy, and every day the bittersweet feeling of longing to be Concord again stirs within my heart. Maybe one day there will be a DLC, or more content, or I don't know. I will return then.Until then, I will stand on the shore, waiting. And I invite you to explore those lands. Chances are, you'll fall in love like I did, and you'll stand with me.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to be short and to the point for those who are interested in buying or playing this game.Pros:-Very cute and relaxing to play-Good Soundtrack-Very similar to turnip boy-Good Story and Characters (Rana is my favourite)-The bosses are well made, not very difficult to beat them -The graphics are very good and run perfectly if you have a potato PCCons:-Too few bosses and content in the balance with too many weapon upgrades. This is the worst thing in the game, to do all the weapon upgrades and complete the remaining things in the game after finishing the story takes about another 10 hours. But in those 10 hours you won't do anything new, you'll just collect resources to max all your weapons and unlock special abilities on them which are useless because there are no other bosses to beat. Of course, you can beat the same bosses again (which are only 4 anyway) but it wouldn't make any sense because with the upgraded weapons it will only be much easier to beat them and you will get bored faster.-I would have liked the game to have more different difficulties or more content after finishing it, with new missions and more dialoguesIn conclusion Garden Story is a very nice game that is worth playing if you liked Turnip Boy, a game that needs more content like a dlc and updates to be balanced in terms of difficulty, upgrades and quantity of content offered together with missions and story.One or 2 dlcs would complete this game properly. For example, a new story to play with Rana or young Plum or why not a prequel with one of the guardians and their adventures. Something to add content with new areas, bosses, enemies and new characters for more story where you can use your upgraded weapons and plus one or 2 new ones. This is of course just an opinion because the game seems to need a continuation in the form of an update or dlc, or both from my point of view. It gets an 8/10 from me because I liked it and it still has potential

_childDocuments_.review: The best part of this game is by far the visual aesthetic and sound design. It looks just like a DS game, but in a higher resolution. It's reminiscent of 2D Zelda and Pokemon. I like how the towns are based on different seasons. Each town is a real visual treat. The character designs are also great; they are simple, yet reflect each character's personality well. I also like the various hats and backpacks you can equip Concord with. The soundtrack and nature sounds are good & relaxing, and the other sounds made when interacting with the world & UI are satisfying. I enjoyed the story, especially at the end of the game. Overall this is a genuinely wholesome and kawaii game.The worst part is the gameplay itself which is why I don't recommend it. It is combat heavy, yet the combat is way too sluggish. The boss fights were also too long and tedious, and I found them exhausting. Also, pulling up the menu to switch weapons doesn't stop enemies from attacking. Their attacks interrupt you in the menu, and then you have to attempt to open it to switch weapons again. Rolling around is also very inconsistent. And the 30 FPS lock makes no sense. It does not add to the visual aesthetic or immersion. It just makes the gameplay worse. If this game had gameplay improvements and no framerate lock then I would recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lately, I've been in the mood for a cozy-style game, and it wasn't that long ago when I got a copy of Garden Story (GS). Although playing as a grape sounds a bit odd, I was charmed by the screenshots and trailer. Of course, the real dilemma comes from having farming components in the game. What would a grape grow for food, and would it be sentient too?In most games like this, progress and leveling up comes from clearing dungeons or earning XP from enemies. However, the most important objectives in GS are completing daily tasks the villagers have. They're organized into different categories, so you won't be doing the same tasks on any given day. You're able to do up to three a day, and can include things like clearing enemies, gathering and depositing resources, or solving a puzzle to make something such as a bridge functional again. This system does draw your attention away from exploration, in favor of completing these tasks and reaping the rewards from it. Because of that, it can feel repetitive, since you'll be in the same area and doing similar things quite a few times. Finding a new location will alter the gameplay to an extent, but not this basic loop. For those who stick with GS, your character will grow stronger and obtain more items, but it feels slower and more methodical than other games I've played. Fruits are more patient than doggies, I guess.I'm glad that GS worked with my controller, but I'll admit some of the controls seemed odd to me. For instance, the way certain menus are accessed, that some tools are unique and function differently than others, or how some actions need to be held down before they'll work. After getting used to it, I had a better understanding of the system, and liked it.Concord, a fitting name for a grape, has been designated as a guardian of the Grove. It's his duty to protect and help the good vegetation of the land, but while performing his tasks, he'll learn more about the disjointed village's history. You might not think there's much hidden amongst the garden, but as they say, you never know what you'll hear through the grape vine. Cutting-edge graphics have never been the way to my heart, but I'm a sucker for a spoonful of sugar and plenty of charm. That's a big aspect to the design in GS, as NPCs look cute and cuddly, while Concord has some adorable facial expressions! Even with globs of the rot terrorizing the villagers, the locations still look quaint and a nice place to visit. With the day/night system, each area also comes in four shades to match the rising and setting sun. Also, because of the plant motif, green is used abundantly, but there's enough breaks in the environment to not over-saturate the screen.Appropriately enough, the music in GS is on the calm, relaxing side. I think it might be a bit too subtle against the sounds of combat, as those sound effects dominate the softer notes in many of the game's tunes. It was an especially pleasant soundtrack to listen to on YouTube though, and I'd recommend it for easy-listening. An aspect I enjoyed about it were the various instruments that were used, such as an accordion, sleigh bells, and steel drums. One noise that irritated me was when the mailbox had money in it, but that's easily dealt with. I'm a bit surprised there wasn't one for Concord's health dropping to a single sliver.🌟 As you get new tools from other areas, it'll open up earlier sections and give access to new resources. Patience is rewarded in this title.🌟 After getting used to how the game works, going through daily tasks and gathering resources becomes an enjoyable cycle.🌟 It's not a hard game, and the options menu allows you to alter some of the mechanics for more accessibility.❌ Since Concord was nothing but a farmer previously, it seems odd those mechanics are introduced so late into the game. I'd think that'd make up his early duties as a new guardian to boost his confidence and build off what he already knows how to do, “You're a pacifist, right? Thankfully the bulk of your new job isn't combat. No wait, it's primarily fighting. Oops.”❌ Movement can feel clunky at times, especially if you get stuck on something in the environment that doesn't seem like a barrier. For instance, little clumps of grass.🔍 Stone and wood come in different forms, but cannot be withdrawn later in the village storeroom. Unless you need a specific version for an upgrade or library, and you've already stored 100 or more of each, you can sell the excess without concern.🔍 Even if you had the necessary items to upgrade a weapon or item, you have to improve the village through daily tasks first. That'll raise the cap on what you're able to level up.🔍 I wouldn't fight every enemy I see, but you'll want to fight many of them as a convenient way to make money.Many action games involve helping people, so I'm not bothered by the tasks I'm assigned in GS. What they ask for isn't any more demeaning or frivolous than other titles have come up with. I think the aspect that threw off my sense of rhythm was the way days pass, as I'm required to end each one going to bed and restarting the system before I can get new tasks and keep progressing. Instead, if each completed task immediately opened another one, I could play through a constantly rotating day/night system. The ability to continuously make progress and not needing to wait arbitrarily would help me not feel so tied down by the game. Plus, I could save at any time this way, able to pick up and leave GS at my discretion. Worst case scenario, sometimes a game will crash, and it'd suck to lose progress because of something like that. This theoretical alternative would suit me more, but I still enjoyed this game as is. It plays differently than I might want, but still offered a fun system. That's why I earned every achievement. Generally speaking, I do recommend GS, and suggest that anyone who's interested should give it a few in-game days to get used to some of its quirks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely lovely. Very cute artstyle, nice music, lovely atmosphere, decent gameplay. But it is missing one thing - variety.The gameplay mechanics have a very solid foundation, but once you've played a while you notice exactly how repetitive it is.TLDR: The following is a rant of how the game is repetitive and wastes your time.The main culprit is the "requests" system. Every in game day you are given various requests that you can do to level up your town. The requests are: kill X of monster Y; use resource X in area Y to repair a thing; do a puzzle to fix a thing; move a box from one area to another; donate X of resource Y in a donation box.This might be fine until you realize that there are only a few monster types and all since all the tasks and puzzles are hand crafted, you are doing the same few tasks and puzzles over and over. Every time you have to fix a specific thing, it has the exact same puzzle. Every time you have to collect a specific resource in the 3rd town, you have to enter the dungeon and do the same puzzles every time in order to get to where you can collect the resource. Every time you need to move a box, it has to be moved along the same route every time.Initially, I had fun doing these tasks and didn't mind how repetitive they were. This was because I knew that there were multiple areas in the game and expected some variety as I progressed. But sadly once I got tired of the first town I has already seen most of what there was to the requests system.At that point I decided to skip the requests and focus on the main story (which was only possible since I could do all the dungeons on the first try - other reviews mention dying in the dungeons, and they would have to do the requests to gain upgrades). But then the game starts introducing arbitrary limits. Sometimes you _have_ to progress the town to a certain level. Sometimes the story involves talking to a person and then waiting until the next day. And at one point you need to use a specific resource to progress - a plant that requires four days to grow.This brings us to the time speedup mechanic: The bench! If you have had enough of the tasks and want time to progress faster, you can sit and wait on a bench. You cannot sleep until night time, and by sitting on a bench you speed up the time. This however clashes with how the game splits the day into five parts (morning, midday, etc.)and only progresses to the next part once you move to a different area. This means that to skip a day, you need to wake up, walk to a bench, sit on it and wait, walk to another area, walk back to the bench, walk to another area, walk back to the bench, walk home and sleep. And when you are far in the game and simply want to finish it, being forced to wait four days for a plant to grow quickly becomes annoying.So yeah. It is a great game, but it feels like they spent too much time on designing the areas and ran out of time when they needed to fill them with things to do. It therefore becomes a 10-20 hour long game with enough gameplay variety for 5-10 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very plain game. There's not much to like and also not much to dislike, the gravest sin I feel this game has is just how insubstantial it is.You start the game harvesting stuff, rebuilding the town as you go a la the Rec Center in Stardew Valley, but it rapidly becomes apparent the tasks you get every day to fix the town are busywork to pad out the game. You'd think given this is the game's major gameplay loop that it would be more involved than the game just randomly rolling 2-3 jobs from a list of about 4 of the same jobs each every day, but nope that's all you get. And you know the worst part? The longest and most involved parts of these jobs is the walk to them.The plot is... decent. It's nothing spectacular, but it's fine. Apparently all the characters are never referred to by gender, which I never even noticed as instead everyone is referred to directly by (still fairly gendered) names, but besides that odd writing choice are fine. Again, the issue is one of substance-- plenty of interesting things are brought up by characters; old rivalries, history, conflicts, etc, but there's extremely little actual substance to it. Everyone, even characters who supposedly have long bitter history, just give up and abandon it with no celebration in favor of TEAMWORK! Really fails to sell me on the characters.The gameplay itself is weird, with the meanest enemy in the game being one of the most common: small slimes. They're small, fast, deal contact damage, and have extremely annoying i-frames while spawning and jumping. Oddly enough, the game seems partially aware of this as the first and third boss largely consist of spawning them to bother you, which raises the question of why they didn't make the other enemies more threatening, or the small slimes less so. Because ultimately, the only thing the game does to make the later enemies any threat at all is... render them immune to damage besides from the area's weapon, like it's Zelda. Unimpressive.Ultimately, the game's okay. It definitely won't win GOTY from anyone, but it'll pass the time... at least before you realize how vapid the request board is.

_childDocuments_.review: Wholesome Games' Wholesome Direct is a sort of mini E3 for fans of indies and cute aesthetics, and a perfect place to discover new gems to play. It was in one of these streams that I saw Garden Story for the first time, and I was completely captivated with the cute style it radiates, and the peculiarity that all the characters are fruits, vegetables, plants and animals. Now that I've played it, I can say that it's more than just visuals, since it offers a story with funny, serious and even emotional moments in equal parts, as well as a deeper gameplay than it seems at first glance.Perhaps it's a bit redundant to mention it again so quickly, but the game's art is simply adorable, although it isn’t only that. Garden Story boasts pixel art with meticulous attention to detail, from little things like grasses getting squished as we step over them, to the different facial expressions of the character. It seems like a small thing at first glance, but it fascinates me to see how the developers manage in such small sizes, where changing a couple of pixels gives a different result.This, added to the different areas and villages that share the beautiful aesthetics, contrasted by gloomy dungeons, and a varied cast of characters of all kinds, from mushrooms and frogs to various vegetables, generate a great visual section, especially for fans of the pixelated style like me. Although I'm very biased about this, it goes without saying that I loved the graphics. And I want to make a special mention to the music, which is a beautifully crafted section. The sound effects in general are super satisfying to listen to, and the songs masterfully accompany the story.But not everything is colorful and vibrant, as the story also takes more serious and slightly dark turns, although it does not touch bottom so to speak (fortunately). We follow the adventure of Concord, a grape fruit in seclusion who spends her days tending the vine that saw her into existence. But beyond this small garden, rot, a kind of corruption of nature, threatens to completely destroy the balance. Appointed as guardians of the village, we will be in charge of helping the inhabitants of this beautiful world, and try to solve the mystery behind this enigmatic danger.The gameplay of Garden Story is extremely entertaining, since it offers several systems apart from the typical exploration. First of all, we’ll be able to navigate through different areas surrounding the village, travel to other towns and collect materials along the way. These resources will be used to unlock upgrades, fulfill community assignments and eventually build some stuff, both useful and decorative. Do take into account that the building aspect is quite limited, but it is appreciated anyway.The assignments go hand in hand with the upgrades, since fulfilling these objectives raises the levels of the facilities, and this will be reflected in the options that we’ll have at our disposal in the stores. At the beginning we’ll have a pickaxe, both for combat and for collecting materials, a dew-jar to heal us, and a shield; and it is in the stores that we can improve the effectiveness of these elements, either by raising the attack level of a weapon or increasing the charges of our flask, for example.Touching on the subject of weapons, Garden Story has several types of tools for combat and other mechanics. For example, a parasol that performs quick thrusts but does not reach the strength of a hammer, or a spade that is a little slow to fight with it, but necessary to dig plots where to plant seeds. I like that the systems go hand in hand and that everything has its use, although some things certainly serve more than others, like a musical instrument that I barely used, mostly to amuse myself.In combat we can attack, defend ourselves with the shield, roll and run, and all these actions will consume energy, illustrated on screen with a yellow bar. At the beginning, I admit that the confrontations were very slow for me, since we have little energy when we are just a budding grape. However, as I got more power-ups and abilities, the progression started to feel strong, and being able to perform several actions before getting tired was very rewarding. It's worth noting that the combat itself isn't difficult, but it's a crucial addition and one that really entertained me.In addition to the upgrades in the store, we can get permanent power-ups as we explore, through some orbs that we can break if we have the right tool, and the necessary level. These benefits usually grant more health, energy, or special parameters such as mind. And what is mind? It's a stat that allows us to store memories, another type of bonuses that we will unlock as we interact through the world, from fighting a certain number of enemies with a particular tool, to sitting on a bench or spending time in a specific town.This addition left me pleasantly surprised, as it adds a lot of customization to our character, allowing us to choose what kind of passive upgrade we want to have, and thus assemble a kind of build according to our needs. Some memories even give us special attacks! Undoubtedly of great help for the bosses of the dungeons, which although they are not very complicated, they bring a somewhat more interesting challenge to the combat. The dungeons themselves are short, with a few unique puzzles and resources inside, and little else.I really thought Garden Story was going to be a "cute" and relaxed adventure, but I was taken by surprise by the variety of mechanics it hid, and the amount of fun it provided. It's full of cute details, like being able to customize Concord with different hats and backpacks, or being able to decorate some parts of the towns. The story is entertaining and easy to follow, the gameplay is accessible, engaging enough even if it doesn’t offer a difficult challenge, and the audiovisual section is simply wonderful. It earned a place among my favorites of the relaxed and wholesome vibe, with little effort really.
_childDocuments_.name: Garden Story

_childDocuments_.review: This game is kind of a trojan horse: when it was first teased, it seemed like a game that would fit into the curious genre "Stardew Valley" seems to occupy. But in reality? This game is more Zelda-like with some interesting twists than a RPG farming sim. And it's charming and pretty polished; it made a stronger plot than I ever expected, with an adorable cast of fruits, veggies, frogs, and fish people to meet and help out. The controls are reasonably responsive, and there's a wide range of weapons to choose from for combat. It's not a super long game, but nor is it "Onion Boy Commits Tax Evasion" short. The music was extremely soothing and very wholesome. Overall, this game is super-duper wholesome. If you love wholesome games with decent plot and cute pixels, this is your game. I wanted this since it was announced, a friend bought it for me for my birthday and gifted it. It's a fantastic, light-hearted adventure. As for my criticisms... I completed the entire achievement list and reached the ending, but for post-game, there is nothing. You don't lose your save file or anything, but there doesn't seem to be much of a reason to keep playing it unless you need a few unstressful hours of helping some cute pixel fruit people with errands. But if you're me, and you're wondering if there's any post-game content: at the time of this review (which is only a few days since the game launch), no. Also, there are some bugs? It's impossible to completely finish any of the museum collections (yes, there's museum collections) because there are items I can't ever manage to forage. And, there's a mystery attack/weapon that I have yet to solve despite the fact I have filled all my weapons slots. It doesn't seem possible to max-out upgrading all the weapons, and the hats/backpacks? I was under the impression they'd give stat boosts and things, but they are entirely cosmetic. You can't unlock all of the stat/memory slots; I'm one short. So seriously... unless the developer later releases some post-game content updates, this is basically a "play once and only revisit when nostalgic" kind of game. The ride was great, but there isn't anything after it ends beyond the ability to finish off the Steam achievements for the 100% complete.Edit: They fixed a lot of stuff! So there still doesn't seem to be much post-game content still, but I did come back and discover there's tons more building stuff to do with little hidden places to find. Also, they fixed the museum collections. You can complete them with no issue, and get a special cosmetic hat/bag as a reward! Still don't know how to gain my last memory slot. Started and played through a new save file and it's still charming as hell.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the whole game, have all the achievements, and almost all the memories and upgrades. I've seen a lot of reviews online giving this game high ratings. Its not bad, but not as good as video reviews from The Escapist and Noisy Pixel make it out to be. Also, this game is NOT Stardew Valley, Garden Story is much more combat oriented and has much less building and farming. There are some things this game does very well, but Garden Story fails overall to be a great game. Start off positive.  good music, cool and creative theme, cool cosmetics and great artI liked adding memories to improve my character, completing the libraries, and creating shortcuts via repair kits.however...story is basic. Basic save the world story. everybody (except Ledidi and Rana) strokes you off like you're the best. The ending is insightful into the true purpose of rot, but everything else still sucks gameplay is repetitive. Literally do the same quests over and over again. Need to do many of these to upgrade town level to max and get weapon and storage upgrades. Driftwood is needed for a lot of upgrades and you can only get it by spending 5 minutes in one of the dungeons (with the same rooms every time), and you can only do it once a day. Not to mention how repetitive it is to get every other resource in the game. The game basically becomes a point and click adventure for meaningless upgrades because the game is easy.building and farming are dumb. Not introduced in the beginning so you don't have much time to use these features. farming takes way too long and is only for resource gathering and upgrades. there is hardly any room for building in the game, which limits functionality and decor of the game because you can only place so much. Not to mention you can't even rotate the buildings lmao. too easy and straightforward. this game is so easy, and I could have beaten it so much faster if I had realized how hollow this game was. There isn't much to do besides what is required to beat the game besides find a few hidden areas and create shortcuts to walk through. Wished they could have added more to the dungeons since this game is so combat oriented.stamina and combat. the beginning is very slow since you don't have a lot of stamina which limits how much you can run and attack. The combat is very clunky on a keyboard (probably much smoother on a controller). The creativity with weapons like the scythe and parasol are cool though, especially when paired with their respective memories.I have a lot more nitpicks with this game, but ill just mention one. Why did this game default to arrowkeys for keyboard users? its not 2006 anymore. It sucks to see a game with great art direction have such middle of the road gameplay and overall content, but I guess it doesn't matter because the art lured me into buying this game. If you really don't have anything else to play, then buy this. If you want a good combat oriented game with great art and an immersive world, play hollow knight.

_childDocuments_.review: For some reason, adventure games in the style of Zelda never clicked with me: I have been trying to finish a Zelda game for years, but I simply abandon them after the first one or two hours: I simply stop playing and don’t pick them up anymore. Like a lot of other players, I noticed Garden Story because of some apparent similarities with Stardew Valley, even if it is a completely different game. Don’t get me wrong, the two games have some aspects in common, but the core of the game is completely different: for starters, you’re a grape. Then we can also say that, instead of managing a farm, you are instead the guardian of a village in the Grove, where some animals and different fruits coexist peacefully. But a sneaky evil is damaging the Grove: you will have to protect your friends against the emerging menace of the Rot and, in the meanwhile, fish and grow a library while you’re at it!Garden Story can be a pretty confusing game at first: watching the screenshots and reading the description in the Steam Store page could mistake someone into thinking that this title is something on the lines of Stardew Valley. While the two games surely have some mechanics in common, Garden Story is instead way more similar to an adventure game to the likes of the older Zelda titles than it is to a management one. While you will travel in the same areas a lot, throughout the story you’ll be able to move to other villages and you will fight a lot, whereas the completion of objectives like the library and farming will be fun activities that will always be in the background.As guardian of Spring Hamlet, you’ll have to listen to the request of the villagers and work towards fulfilling them: each day you will find new requests on a notice board. These are made by the villagers and divided into three different sections: Maintenance, Forage and Conflict. Completing these tasks each day gives experience to the respective category of the village where we complete it, while a failure to fulfil them before the end of the day means that the village won’t level up and a short sentence will describe the consequences.While this is a fine distraction from the not very active villages (especially at the start of the game), the requests become repetitive in the matter of a couple of days. At the third or fourth day, the probability of finding a request you already completed the days before is really high and, after something like 8-9 days you will remember them all by heart. Why? Because they not only are really simple activities, on the lines of “Kill 7 enemies” or “Repair the bridge in this portion of the map”, but they usually take very little time to complete and there are simply not enough of them. The ones where you fight are simply not challenging at all, while the ones that have some sort of puzzle linked to them never change.Even worse, there are no real consequences for not completing a request: if I don’t destroy the rot invasion in Treepath and the game tells me that it grew stronger, why doesn’t it? I could find stronger enemies the following day, making it harder for me to use that path, but instead it’s like it has always been. The consequences of not completing a request are simply not there, besides the fact that the village is not levelling up.Protecting the Grove is not an easy feat: not only you have to help the villagers repair buildings and gathering resources, but you also have to protect them against the Rot! The Rot can manifest under different forms: being giant Glomps or pesky Acorns, you will have to know your way around a sword. Garden Story’s combat can be a little clunky and requires a little bit of practice at the beginning. This is due to its stamina mechanic, which is required to use the shield, attack with your sword and roll. While this is pretty standard, the initial amount of stamina is 2, which means you can only attack two times in quick succession before having to recover. Luckily, you can get stronger by using memories, which grant different bonuses and can be changed at the start of the day, or breaking some special orbs that you can find around the world.Usually, after a few days of completed requests the story advances, opening up a dungeon that has a boss fight in the end. Each village has its own dungeon with its own big, Rot monster in the end: boss fights are more on the easier side, but some situations can prove challenging and personally I died to each boss at least once. Once you remember their (rather simple) attack patterns, though, these big monsters can be easily beaten without getting you stuck. Beating these fights means that you will be ready to move to the next village, for a total of four: Spring Hamlet, Summer Bar, Autumn Town and Winter Glade!In the end, I finished up enjoying Garden Story despite its faults. The colourful graphics, the cute characters and the vibrant world have bested the repetition of the daily tasks and the initial clunkiness of the combat. If you’re interested but not completely sold, I would suggest to get this title on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: A really cute and fun combo RPG, Exploration, and sim game.  It  has cute characters and pretty easy to use interface, but you really need a controller to play it.  The boss battles are challenging, but not ridiculously hard and it's easy to manipulate your buffs to do certain tasks.  The only thing I would criticize is having to collect massive amounts of a resource (namely driftwood) to level up your tools. You have to delve an entire dungeon to get to the resource and you can only get 4-5 per delve.  Really frustrating when you need over 30 pieces to get a level up.  It's not that the dungeon is hard, it's just tedious that you have to re-open every door every time you delve.I spent about 28 hours getting all the achievements and I could still spend some more time to get all the power ups, etc.  But don't think I'll bother.   It was enjoyable and on a good sale, you should pick it up if you enjoy these types of game.Edited to add:  I tried to play this on  the steam deck and it is playable, but for me it was too tiny on that little screen for me to see what I was doing.  The pop-ups with resources, etc are small pictures already and putting it on the tiny screen made it virtually impossible for me to see what was needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Garden story is a super charming RPG about (mostly) fruit and vegetable based characters. I won't lie that when I first booted this game up I was daunted by the stamina bar and how breaking materials worked but after getting more used to how the cycle works this game is a wonderful way to unwind and sometimes just turn your brain off to collect and do small tasks for the villages you become part of!I was pleasantly surprised to find myself actually caring quite a bit for the other characters as well as the main character throughout this small journey to the point of dropping all the smaller tasks the moment something big happened to other characters as well as the feeling of belonging in these small groups of people just trying to make it by another day.This game's cycle can be a bit boring sometimes, and there's never a 100% chance that the jobs you'll get will be ones you can even finish depending on what they ask of you, and the space you have to play with even with some of the upgrades feels a bit restrictive but all in all these are rather minor issues when everything surrounding it is just dripping with love.If you like comfy adventures, characters you can care about, adorable art style, and don't mind a little bit of that framing grind cycle. I highly suggest giving this game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: 15h 2/10 1 Not really, but you don't need a guide No No Not really, maybe the different enemies if you did avoid them. The achievement for rolling 100 times is quite fast when you focus on rolling a lot.  No No No No No NoThis game is such a gem. It has a wholehearted story and I enjoyed it so so much. You play as Concord, the youngest guardian of this island and they let you free from "kindergarden" to help save the island, as it gets invested by rot. It is your task to help all the lovely and not so lovely people from this island. A lot of people won't believe in your abilities at first but maybe you can change their mind? The gameplay isn't that hard, except maybe from some bosses, but it doesn't punish you when things don't go so well. I believe that you have even an option so you can't die, but I didn't use it. While going through the story and having story quests, there is also this bulletin board on which daily 2 or 3 requests from villagers pop up, it is no problem if you don't complete those, but they will help out with the main story. They can become boring after a while since it recycles through a limited amount of quests, but I just did them if I was close by the area or if I needed the points they gave in some way. This game is mostly a resource management game, you will collect all kinds of resources but have a small backpack. Gladly there are a lot of storage boxes placed throughout the world which will be your main way to store the items. Don't expect much gardening in this game, it unlocks lately and I only used it in that area because of some quests requiring the materials. This may sound bad but it isn't. _childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this by saying that despite how the screenshots look, it's  something like Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon with sapient fruits and stuff. The closest I can think of is a "social simulator", in that your primary function is to go around helping people/towns out while also periodically smacking down enemies.A second note, though not terribly important, is that the game repeatedly says "sentient" when they almost certainly mean "sapient" - aka ♥♥♥♥-sapiens - because these are intelligent, tool-using creatures and not simply self-aware lifeforms like horses or birds. I'd elaborate more but the game does enough that I won't spoil anything else.Garden Story is one of those games whose visual style is what appealed to me almost immediately, though I confess when I originally bought I wasn't entirely sure what the purpose of the game was. As is often the case I got it on sale cause it looked neat and was on my wishlist, but was distracted by something else like life or another game I was already playing. So it's been in my library for  before I got to it.The first thing you'll notice when playing is that the game is going to walk you through a bit of what you do, and this is important cause it's establishing the basic gameplay loop. Which is largely going around and doing odd jobs from the community message boards for the town you're staying in. A lot of that is gathering resources, such as wood/stones & misc other goods for repairing broken objects in town or purchasing upgrades. Don't worry too much about coins because you'll quickly find yourself with a large surplus - especially if you get the fishing = money perk about halfway through the game.That's another semi-vital aspect of the gameplay. Both the fishing (or dowsing, as they call it) and the acquisition of "memories" by performing various tasks. These include making Tap Dew (healing water) restore a  more health, which makes it a vital one, and giving you stat bonuses. You'll no doubt see the game comment on "Concord has made a connection with an unknown guardian" as you play, because you need to find their monuments as you go. Most are in plain sight, but a couple are easily missed if you're not mindful of more obscured paths. For instance, in Winter Glade there is a patch of snow you can cross near the place your can rest in. It doesn't immediately look like an actual path cause of the snow, but it's there!The gameplay is fairly straight-forward. You slowly acquire a variety of tools which can be used as weapons but also function to interact, such as the aforementioned Fishing/Dowsing Rod, or the shovel. Although it's received fairly late, and is nearly useless for combat, the shovel is vital for growing seeds which can become a number of different resources depending on where you plant it. The first seed is a Cobble Seed, and in Autumn Hill it grows into mossy looking cobble bricks for trade or in a few cases town quests. However, every where else it will become a handful of large stone blocks; there is one that becomes wood, as well, outside of Spring Hamlet.Enemies are frequent, but rarely aggressive except at night. Ambling acorns will often rush towards you and spit a few bullets, and jump Glomps will charge at you doing damage if you don't dodge or attack first. The most common enemy, though, will be the mostly docile Oozes, and there's a unique one for each of the four areas. Fair warning, when an Ooze dies it leaves behind a tiny lil' Rot ball that bounces around and can slap you or give a speed debuff if you're not paying attention.All in all, I found the game to be very fun and delightful with a fascinating little world it was building for itself. However, I'd be lying if I said it doesn't eventually wear out its welcome. One of the secondary goals is raising the towns up to a maximum level of 5 in three different categories. Combat, Maintenance, and Foraging. This is accomplished by doing quests from the town message boards, and they rank from 1-3 stars. This does not represent difficulty most of the time, though it can be more  at times. The key problem is that it takes ages to get all the way to 5 in order to unlock the last of the upgrades and personally I didn't find it worth it by the time I was done. The best two tools are your Pick and Hammer, the former being quick and effective while the latter being required for a number of resources and jobs. The third most important tool is your fishing poll, which is used a  in Summer Bar but also useful for resources in other locations. Everything else is entirely situational, so I kept those three on my hot bar with one of the jars. You can get a number of jars over the game and each is a little different, but all can be filled with different kinds of dew.My log of about 40 hours is how long it took to finally get all the towns up to max level. Maybe I could've gone a little faster, I dunno, but you do spend a  of time doing little tasks every day. Oh, and despite their being a daily time bar, once it reaches night it's just infinite time, so don't feel like you need to rush unless you want to. You can't sleep until at least evening, so make use of the benches if you're like me and bored stiff trying to get the towns finished.If you just wanna get to the story's end, it's probably half of that time, and outside of the final boss the game isn't going to be a huge challenge. If you do have problems, however, there are accessibility options for disabling death. I did have it turned on myself, but honestly I never really needed it, and one memory actually requires you to revive yourself with Amber Dew 5 times so you'll need to switch it off for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Garden Story

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a hard no but just enough about this game made me annoyed to recommend against it, but it's a tentative enough no that it's worth considering if you're a die hard fan of cute, casual games.Note: my playtime is artificially bloated because I forgot to close the game before I did a bunch of errands. Twice. Oops. Knock maybe eight hours off the time to platinum. Pros:- Beautiful to look at. Some sick boss battles.- Some really interesting mechanics (having all the villages level up separately was a great choice, and having levelling up tied to how well supported your villages are has some fun themes tied to it.)- Some really good music. Like, I went out of my way to look for the Summer Bar themes on Spotify because I enjoyed them that much.- Concord is cute. I like that guy. Cons:- The combat system is slow, unwieldy, and annoying. It's not difficult, but it's never satisfying. Every battle feels like a chore and most of the damage I took was stray globs smacking Concord around unfairly. The way it's connected to stamina was unbearable.- Material collecting was only marginally better in this regard. Also you have to pick up every single item manually one by one. This was such a bad choice.- The amount of back and forth was unbearable. One really brutal example is that the shops in the first area initially have no nearby resource box, so if you wish to purchase something with a resource in storage you need to walk a whole loading zone away to the nearest box. Later the library opens with a box, but that too is a separate loading zone. later later you can build your own resource box, but you can only place it on the other side of the map from the shops. Huh??? Why was this a choice made. There's rarely loading boxes beside the merchants you can sell to as well, and you can only sell to some merchants. It's just so unnecessarily tedious, especially considering the next issue.- For like 90% of my time with the game my backpack was just so tiny!!! It was awful!!!- This is very YMMV but the dialogue annoyed me. It's clearly trying to go for a cute and cozy vibe, but everyone talks the same way--even old and weathered town leaders talk like sassy twenty year olds. Every time a character would accent their texts with something *sooooo* emphasised I felt my bones wrinkle in distaste. - The story also did nothing for me. Very tell don't show and very toothless. The themes are half baked, and whatever story it wants to tell about loss and preservation is muddled by it's clear ethos of Good Vibes Only. A cozy game can still have something to say, and Garden Story clearly thinks it does, but god does it let down. You know actually looking at this now it isn't actually that hard of a no. This game is a beautiful piece of hot air, and I think you could play something better.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start this review off by saying this game is Stardew Valley (The OG GOAT), mixed with Ittle Dew, Littlewood and Moonlighter. If you loved all those games you will adore this one. I'll also say this game is chill and fun and as satisfying as a slot machine hitting the jackpot for seretonins and dopamine. So much so that this is one of a rare handful of games I don't turn the music off, not even 3/4 through the game. It's that good. If you're ADHD/autism like me and always have something on in the background when you game to help you focus, like youtube or spotify, you'll know that is very high praise. I'm scatterbrained and ADHD AF and have trouble focusing on everything, even with meds. So, all that out of the way, you know when a game and you  Like a game you fw hardcore fr bestie? Cozy as ♥♥♥♥ and comforting to hop in and play? A game that gives you zero stress and yet still has massive stakes that feel super rewarding to chip away at? For me that's this game. There's dopamine around every corner, in every nook and cranny of this charming ass game and it caters to my specific cocktail of neurospiciness like a kind friend or a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lover. Every feature I could want, it has. Every utility, every QOL thing I want in a game like this is there, right were I need it to be, when I need it, every time. This game is your comfiest pair of old shoes. This game is wearing a pair of yoga pants resting on the couch after Christmas dinner. It's zoning out at the beach enjoying the sound of the waves and movements of the water. The rain lulls you along late at night as you toil contentedly, burning the midnight oil as you strive to complete tasks and hack away at your list of delightful little gathering chores. They don't even feel like chores, it feels like... being a squirrel, hoarding up nuts and fruits for winter and then that squirrel donates the contents of his hoard piece-meal, to help fund the rebuilding of various community centres. You can take care of your little villages (and they do become so very yours in the nicest most satisfying ways). It feels so indescribably rewarding to find the hidden little bursts of serotonins hiding in plain sight (I'm a bit of a dunce sometimes and sometimes don't see/ forget a shop keeper exists for a while, its an ADHD/object-permanence deficiency brain thing) like when I realize "omg `O-O' there's been a shop there this whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time and OH HELLO I can UPGRADE THAT TOOL? WAIT, WHAT!?" that happens just often enough, doling the sweet sweet brain chemicals out in generous packages wrapped in cuteness. The doctor is in and has just what your brain needs to feel goooood. Juuust when the game starts to feel grindy (and that isn't often), like, when I start to crave more progression rewards, the game seems to just...know that I need it and "Voila!" there it is. And the cycle continues. I hate using the word addicting but my god is the loop sweet in this game. The game is giving to an endless degree. The music lulls you along as you do your chores. The characters are adorable and say just enough to get what I need to know across and that's it. Perfect. The sound effects are pingy, beep boopy and all over very thuddy and tactile and rewarding and...appropriate? The combat is smooth as silk. You glide effortlessly through battles that feel complicated enough to be challenging but not too hard and the animations ooze charm. You pirouette through the combat and dungeon diving portions of the game feel so rewarding, challenging and satisfying no matter how many times you delve into the depths. And wanna talk satisfying, snappy combat? Just WAIT until you unlock the sickle. Never before in a game have I wielded so fine a piece of artisan-crafted agricultural badassery. The entire game oozes satisfaction and bursts with charm.If all that weren't enough to sell you on how perfect this game is, it also has a feature I found amazing and innovative! When I found it I was like "omg this is very different and rewarding in a weird way (That being the inventory upgrade system. You only get a set number of bag slots to start and each slot can carry one item. You can have as many stacks of sandstone in your bag that you want, for example, so long as the stack only goes to 1 that is unless you upgrade your bag so that each slot lets you carry 2 items, then 3 and so on. It feels really neat to me for some reason. (That might be the zaza or the autism talking) If you are on the fence about this game, don't be. JUST BUY IT. Do it right now! Seriously. If you love what I call "town rescue games" like this, where you collect resources, do tasks, fish, listen to the music and just vibe all while getting the satisfying, rewarding,  brain chemicals that come from helping cute af chibi fruit and animal homies get back home safe/ fix their house/ live in a nicer town/ increase their levels of local tourism/ just live a better life in general? A simple game where you get to enjoy a fine variety of magical drops of the finest aged Dew--only little drops, you're tiny after all-- enjoyed from an array of handcrafted, upgradeable, jars, jugs and vials? Then this is the game for you. Look no further. Welcome to your new life in the Garden, Guardian, your new job at the dopamine mine awaits. Here's your hardhat and pickaxe, now get to work having so much damn fun.PS.: C O L L E C T   A L L   T H E   B O O K S   A N D   C U T E   A C C E S S O R I E S  <(UwU);>

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this a lot and have completed it. I don't think it's so much a Zelda-like, as Kotaku described it; it's a 2D adventure game with a top-down perspective, but it doesn't feel like Zelda, dungeons are simple and linear affairs, there are only a few of them, etc. But it's a very cute, very pleasant game. While advancing the main plot, you'll do people in the towns a solid, causing them to level up and therefore offer you more upgrades. Bunch of different weapons, mostly you can choose what to use and upgrade, occasionally things are only vulnerable to something specific. I do have a couple notes. Combat can be finicky; your starting weapon has a wide sweep but doesn't hit as much as you'd think. Upgrades can be expensive in materials, forcing you to farm items with low drop rates if you want to upgrade weapons. I completely ignored the Dew system, using nothing but basic free Dew for healing, because the others didn't seem worth it. There's an entire category of Memories (buffs) that I never unlocked because I didn't find the statue of the Guardian that unlocks them; I still have no idea where it is. There's a fast travel system, but it unlocks quite late and many of the warp points aren't conveniently located.I quite enjoyed it and I'm glad I played it, but there are too many design decisions I don't care for and I think the team should have reevaluated some of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I just got 100% of achievements in this game. I've enjoyed playing it, although I have some criticisms as well, so I thought I'd list those here. Light spoilers ahead.Pros:-The core gameplay is fun. Exploring new areas, the variety of weapons and the little busy work quests all feel satisfying and the combat feels rather unique and solid. The game even reminds you about what you did at the end of the day and gives you an experience bar to help make it feel worthwhile. It would be nice if there were more areas to explore, though on the whole it's a pretty good game if you just want to walk around and explore some pretty areas.-The achievements don't require you to do absolutely everything in the game. I really appreciate this because it gives you something to go back to later on and discover new things even in a second playthrough. Apart from the "Kill this" quests, there isn't really much filler in there either, which I appreciate.-The soundtrack is really nice. It's relaxing in ways like Pikmin and such - it's just pleasant, calming music befitting of each area. It can also get really dramatic at key moments at the story as well. Whoever made these tracks, I commend you!-The enemy designs are fantastic. They feel well animated and the focus of quality over quantity makes each enemy stand out as unique and memorable from the first time you see one. The bosses are all very distinct and are interesting fights in their own right.-Some of the little details are really appreciated. I believe after going into the last area of the game, Concord's leaf gets a little bit paler and they made it possible to catch items with your fishing hook if they're too far away from you, which is mostly pointless but feels very satisfying. I also like how the plants are affected by the climate they grow in.Cons:-The NPCs feel lifeless for the most part. Excluding cutscenes with major characters or quest dialog, all the NPCs will stay in the same spot for the entire game saying the exact same line, even if it doesn't make sense. Why not have some of the characters like Rana or Elderberry move around from day to day or at least say different lines of text? The writing in the cutscenes is usually pretty charming, there just isn't enough of it to fully flesh out these characters. A better but more costly way of adding some life could be to show some of the characters actually doing something for their towns, like maybe seeing Rana out talking to Goldie or planting seeds while complaining about all the hard work.-It almost runs contrary to a pro, but the game almost guilt trips you if you don't do a quest. At one point I had to get 6 tombstone for quests, but I believe I only got 5 after exhausting all the tombstones in the entire town. When you miss a quest, the game tells you about how the townsfolk struggled that day. I understand that this is to encourage the player to do the quests, but it just feels bad if you don't want to do that particular quest. It's a minor thing, anyway.-The building system. This is the only part that I feel went pretty disastrously. In the game there are run down buildings and areas here and there. The NPCs hint at some areas once thriving as well, but even with the architects in the game you can't rebuild anything meaningful. In fact, you actually can't really build anything useful at all. There are 'functional' items which you can build, but they really aren't that useful, like a request board for example. Most people will just choose to memorise the requests or go back to the previous board. There's technically no real-time limit, so it's typically just a waste of resources unfortunately. I see the potential in it though.Overall, Garden Story is a fun and relaxing game which feels a bit rushed. I'd say as it stands, it's a game worth picking up on a sale as it feels unfinished right now and there's just better value games out there but if it gets a few updates, it could be something really special.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I received Garden Story as a birthday gift.I am really enjoying my time with Garden Story- while it's not a perfect game by any means, and could use a bit of polish in some minor areas, overall it's charming, addictive and well made. I'm not done yet, but I'm looking forward to finishing the game- it's basically a cross between a zelda game and a basic farming game. The game tends to lean much more heavily into the adventuring than the home-steading, so play with that in mind.Things they did well;-The art and design: The art is cute, simple and expressive. There's a good variety in terms of the character design and environments, which makes it fairly easy to learn the map layouts and remember specific npcs-- they are all different.-The sound: Overall the music and SFX fit everything excellently and loop really well. Zones generally have one song that loops until nightfall, but I haven't found any of them to be annoying or obtrusive.-Combat: The combat is fun and fluid. The memories system is a good way to tie in the idea of guardians with stat upgrades and provides a good amount of customization.-The loop: The gameloop is fun and addictive- doing the village quests and gathering resources for the item upgrades doesn't overly distract from the story and encourages you to keep moving forward and not get too bogged down. (more on this though when I talk about skipping days below)-The story and writing: I find the story to be really interesting! I enjoy the new beats and sequences as they pop up and I'm looking forward to binging the library info once I have them all filled out. The characters are also pretty distinctive, and each area has it's own flavour, which is something I appreciate.Things they could do better are pretty minor in application, so they don't really detract too much from the overall experience, however it would be nice if the devs were able to update them at some point. I'll say upfront I'm not a person that expects devs to work on a game endlessly or that people should wait in hopes of this-- as far as I'm concerned, devs can wipe their hands of a product once it's released and start fresh with a new title (other than to fix big bugs, which I would hope most address). These are simply suggestions.Limited keyboard or controller functionality: This will be a bigger issue for some, however it is a bit of an inconvenience. You do get used to how things are laid out for the controller, from what I can tell you can't change the button functions. You can change the keyboard keybindings, but there is no mouse functionality so it's a bit finicky. If you try to remove the arrow keys from movement to use them for something else, you get told it's still bound to "undefined", so not sure what's wrong there.The building system: I like the idea of having some customization with the towns, however the way it's implemented doesn't take advantage of the full potential. Items only have one orientation, and many items that have some sort of function must be accessed from the front. This severely restricts the way you can use the building spaces, to the point that at least some of them may as well not even be there. In many instances you will be collision blocked. It would be helpful to be able to rotate items with functionality (benches, storage boxes, forage boxes etc) in order to maximize the spaces that can be used. Yes, I know this means extra art and implementation, but as it stands the feature seems half done and very under-utilized.Being forced to wait to skip days: As time goes on, and you get further into the game it becomes less of a time sink to top up resources and complete tasks for the area you woke up in (as well as the other areas), but you cannot move onto the next day until at least sundown. This can lead to a lot of wasted time, just wandering around, waiting for the time to shift. You can adjust the speed of the day, but it seems like a better option to simply let Concord sleep whenever he wants to move onto the next day.I started noticing this once I hit autumn town, especially since some areas are blocked with things that require at least a bit of time to go by (waiting for crops to grow, repair boxes etc.)Maybe you could have the option to gather quests for more than one town at a time? It seems like right now the system is set up to increase game time arbitrarily.It may seem like this is weighted towards the cons, but I can safely say that is more because of the need to explain the issues, as opposed to them actually being ever-present.This will definitely go onto my "replay" list, and I hope to see more from these devs!Edit: Changed my section in regards to the keyboard/controller after taking a more thorough look.I've now completed the game, and other than some parts that seem bugged or removed from functionality (but still look like they should work), I found the overall experience to be polished and enjoyable.
