_childDocuments_.review: Suck it Nioh 2. Eat it Sekiro. Get ready for the TRUE Samurai action game!Okay maybe not.People love Way of the Samurai but they forget Akiba's Trip, Shinobido, etc. Acquire makes a lot of games where you grind at short, repeatable systems, and that's really what Katana Kami is, too. Only this time it's a dungeon crawl, well, sort of...Describing Katana Kami is very difficult as it is certainly unlike anything you have played before. Sure, the combat is straight out of Way of the Samurai. The movesets and weapon variety are lifted verbatim from that game. But those were mostly one-on-one affairs with the slightest flavor of a versus fighting game. Once you were done with the stories of the mainline WotS games, collecting swords and building an ultimate sword was the main long-term goal if you intended to stick around to grind or play for mastery. Katana Kami gets you a lot closer to the swordfighting and collecting. Probably closer than most of you ever got in WotS3 or 4.Katana Kami takes this combat, adds a dodge button complete with cancel properties, and shifts the perspective into a top down dungeon crawler with just enough "traditional vidya" style enemies so not everything you're fighting is an enemy samurai like in previous WotS games. Your movesets are mostly the same, the focus is still pretty one-on-one, but now some enemies are dogs who have tells before they pounce.The basic gameflow is you running through this dungeon, starting with a 20 floor dungeon but you eventually get a couple more, fighting a bunch of baddies, looting the place, maybe completing a side quest for rare blueprints or something, and emerging with a whole rucksack full of looted swords and mats, and you repeat this every day. It's.... kind of a roguelike? Your level resets, but the level just impacts your max health and stamina. Your sword, the source of your attack stat, stays with you. If you die, you lose everything, but the game provides SO many ways to get that stuff back or just avoid dying at all it's almost not worth worrying about*. You can save and quit at any map to restart the floor, and if you do it before you actually die, you can avoid the consequences of a terrible run. The dungeon maps are all the same (And, insultingly, often repeated. You couldn't do 20 floors without a repeat, Acquire? Honestly!), though the entrance and exit are randomly placed at opposite ends. But they're devoid of puzzles or anything to interact with. Just enemies to fight or run by, stuff to bust open for loot, and the exit. Even the side quests are just "Kill this thing on this floor." It's all straightforward. There are monsters, you have a sword, they have loot, you need money.Money, right, see outside the dungeon there is a day phase of the game. You are here to help the local blacksmith get out of debt. Swords are the currency here. You consume them to repair your swords, and you sell swords to the game's factions to amass large piles of money. So each day you hit up the blacksmith, repair the swords you intend to use, fuss about ditching the rest of the swords you don't want into the "to sell" pile... if you spot a boss sword worth a lot, you have the smith fix it up and upgrade it a bit to fetch more money, you then hit up the orders book and round up 20-40 swords to feed all the orders there and ship the factions some items as gifts, and then you're ready for the next night. The rest of the day is you wandering around the one overworld screen outside the shop to talk to various members of the factions walking through to advance side stories, buy dungeon crawling gear, or even fight them for no real reason. Now one of the side goals is to try to exacerbate the war between the various factions so you can sell more swords (Or loot and re-sell some of your works from the corpses caused by said war), but this part of the game tends to play itself. I strongly suspect they hint you should wink, wink, nudge, nudge, murder a few people to really get the fight going or ship all the best swords to one faction but I could not for the life of me figure out what impact my murders had if any, and wars broke out all the same.This game would be a pretty brisk and quick dungeon crawl if not for how fiddly the day phases are, despite how little meaningful stuff you actually do during them. But the dungeon crawling isn't the goal. You can beat the dungeon as often as you want but your goal is to make money to get out of debt. Defeating the evils of usury unlocks an actual final boss and a new dungeon... and an even HIGHER cash wall. Clearing all THAT unlocks a 99 floor post-game dungeon and model swap.The port runs beautifully at 60 FPS, too, while not doing too bad for eye-candy or music. The controls need some work though. You have to draw your sword each fight like in traditional Way of the Samurai, but this draw action is ridiculously unreliable and prone to input dropping. I have to mash LB CONSTANTLY to get the sword out, and for this being one of the most important actions of the game, it's utter incompetence to let it be so unreliable. In addition, late game dungeon runs get to be fairly tedious. Monsters get tankier but they seldom drop anything worth the extra effort, so often you are running by them to get to the next floor to avoid having to fight two dozen tedious HP walls. Some enemy sword movesets are perfectly capable of trapping you in an endless knockdown loop if they attack you while your sword is not drawn and thus you don't have a wakeup attack, as I have had happen multiple times. I've had a few invisible walls across normal terrain and a few dialogue bugs too, but nothing too major.I enjoyed this game quite a lot, but because it really does not hew to any action RPG, dungeon crawler, or loot farming game convention, it's a weird frankengame. You are not going to find a rare +2 haxblade. The named boss will always drop the same sword of a modest range of stats, you have to build your OWN game-winning sword through farming and grind. It's very focused on a few specific mechanics and fairly straightforward in that regard. It's certainly no Way of the Samurai game, but I have enjoyed it as Yet Another Acquire Grindfest.*(In fact, I will add that there is not much point in worrying about anything in this game. If you can't pay the debt collector, you can just apologize and he will come back next week. If you lose something actually WORTH getting back, you can still retrieve it from the dungeon. If a faction hates you, you can eventually woo them back with gifts. Katana Kami will not force you into a failure state at all. Just a temporary setback state.)

_childDocuments_.review: There's some outright falsehoods in the negative reviews for this game so here's my take.First, this is Way of the Samurai, through and through. The camera perspective may be different, but the combat is very similar. You slash at enemies with your swords, you learn sword skills by using them, you can perfect parry/dodge to do an instakill move (WOTS3), and you can kill enemies to charge a gauge that drastically increases your strength when activated (WOTS4).Enemies can be fought with or without lock on. Without lock on, enemies freely charge and attack you, so it's easy to get overwhelmed. With lock on, you and the locked enemy enter a duel and you can freely ignore nearby melee enemies (ranged enemies still attack). This is identical to how combat works in previous WOTS games so it felt intuitive to me. You can also cheese the game by sheathing your sword, running around until it builds up steam, and then unleashing a screen-clearing AOE, but that takes a lot of time so it's mostly useful for thinning a herd rather than actual combat.The first dungeon is 20F and constructed of pre-made maps with random items and enemies. It's repetitive - budget game, remember - but has some interesting complications as you play that make the game either harder or easier (depending on how good at the combat you are).During the day - when you're not dungeon crawling - you have to help Dojima the Smith fulfill sword orders using swords and materials you bring back from the dungeon. It's like a very stripped-down Recettear. You get an order from each of the three factions, and can fulfill it how you like. You can either manually select the swords to send, or you can make Dojima pick. The quality of sword impacts the strength of that faction's fighters, who come to the pass and fight from time to time, as well as their behavior towards you. If you keep sending them awful swords, they'll insult you! You are encouraged to anger factions and make them fight each other, which I did by getting everyone drunk and sending them way more swords than they needed.Speaking of swords: the most important and impactful thing you can do in Katana Kami is invest in a sword. If you see someone complaining that you do no damage and the enemies are way too tough, it's because they went into the dungeon without enhancing their sword. At the start you won't be able to upgrade much - maybe 4 or 5 enhances if you're lucky - but that changes as you progress and get access to higher level materials and smelting. Eventually you'll be able to fully upgrade swords you like. I'm only 8 hours in and I already have some near-maxed swords that have trivialized the dungeon up to level 14 or so.Oh, and death basically doesn't matter. As long as you store higher-quality swords in your chest in case of emergency, you'll be fine. But even if you don't, this game is quite easy, at least in the first dungeon.I came into this knowing exactly what I wanted:* A goofy, tongue-in-cheek plot full of absurdist caricatures.* Combat that emphasizes crowd control and character action in equal measure.* The grind to acquire swords with titles and attributes that make you happy.Katana Kami delivers on all fronts. It's not WOTS5, but it should keep you sated.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the Way of the Samurai games, and I recognize that this is trying to be different than the main series games, but I think this is overall a failure.First, the good:  I actually like the idea of a rouglike WOTS game.  When I stopped and thought about it, the other games in the series have these type of qualities as well, so it's actually a pretty good fit.  The combat is pretty good, with an emphasis on parries and dodges leading to very powerful counter attacks that can be chained if they kill the enemy.  The storyline is funny, and watching the residents of the Pass randomly fight each other is amusing to me (I saw two people bump into each other leading to a brawl that killed 4 people).Then, the bad:  I'm 15 hours in at this point and there is no town to explore.  Every once in a while you will see some characters from the first WOTS game come by and say something to you but there is no meaningful interaction there.  The story doesn't seem to be explained all that well, either.  There are a few cutscenes in the beginning to set up the scenario, and there is a cutscene after clearing the 20th floor of the dungeon.  I'm assuming there will be something else after paying off the debt, but I haven't reached that point quite yet.  The game winds up feeling very repetitive with the lack of the branching storyline you get in other entries.  The dungeon doesn't have enough variability to be compelling for long.  I've encountered dogs, snakes, rats, skeletons, demon women, and oni in the dungeon thus far.  Only six types of enemies, plus a boss have already gotten dull, and the only way the game knows how to generate difficulty is to throw ridiculous waves of them at you.  The other games in the series broke up this monotony by shortening each playthrough, giving the player a town to explore, and having branching storylines.Overall I kind of at a loss with who this game is for.  A fan of the other WOTS games will miss the feeling of being in an old (and kind of wacky) samurai film as they just grind a dungeon over and over again.  Fans of rougelikes will wonder why the dungeon only allows you to explore 20 floors, has trash loot, and not many types of monsters to fight.

This absolutely misses the point. Maybe the game opens up into something different at 30 hours or something, but I'm not sticking around to find out.after some more playing:The combat plain sucks, it's way too slow but tons of enemies are thrown in your face anyway. It's hard to call it risk vs. reward when the game doesn't really reward you with anything for going deeper. Your inventory is just filled up with garbage and at 20 levels I got some barely story cutscene.There is some attempt at roguelike elements but again it's kind of pointless because you're not going to even care about the dungeon, the combat, or your loot. Even worse if you use the life insurance to get back the items you lost any traps you can't fit in your inventory will fall on the ground auto-trigger and just kill youNo matter how many times you've played the other way of the samurai games you're better off just playing them rather than this piece of crap

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, this is a SPIN OFF game of the Way of the Samurai franchise.Now, continuing with my review..Katana Kami is a roguelike-way of the samurai game. Instead of the usual semi open world map, youll be killing monsters and looting in different type of dungeons which features characters/items/weapons from the previous games. The story follows a ronin who meets the blacksmith Dojima (wots 3), whos daughter is being taken away by some loan sharks as collateral, so you offer to help him pay up what he owes in exchange of marrying her.The reason why it gets a lot of hate/bad reviews is due to not following the formula of the other way of the samurai games but instead, it takes a complete different approach, its a well done game tho, but a spin off will usually get some hate.The gameplay is fun, similar to wots 3 but much smoother. The story and dialogues are very goofy, just like any other wots game, the characters have better interactions and they even fight between themselves (one of the shop vendors gets into a lot of fights and usually ends up dying lol). Runs at 60fps and the overall performance is good, a controller is HEAVILY recommended tho (the game autosaves after every interaction, so if you ever encounter some kind of issue you can safely close the game).Since its a roguelike, youll be doing the same routine again and again: explore the dungeon, loot and kill, decide to keep going further or go back to the village, manage your inventory in the village, sell, upgrade, check your current quest and repeat, its fun if you ask me since its all rng so no run will ever be the same, theres TONS of different possibilities. WOTS is one of my favorite franchises ever and i absolutely love this game too, just like anyone else i want a wots 5 too but this is what we got and im having a lot of fun with it. Spike chunsoft: you guys did a terrible job advertising this game, you could have even done it through steam without spending a single dollar but decided not to which is a shame, -1 point to SC (also, fix the Acquire corp developer steam link).If you have any questions post them in the comment section!TLDR; If you are a way of the samurai fan: Its way of the samurai gone roguelikeFor roguelike fans: An action roguelike based on the japanese meiji era.

_childDocuments_.review: Day 30I appeared in the local newspaper this morning as a mysterious unknown serial killer, alongside a note of appreciation for my gift of an exploding boiled egg, sent to my kidnapped love by a man who accusedly s***s in the bush outside my house.Night time came and I entered the dungeon for the final time before I pay off the debt and free the brat.What a fantastic time I had harvesting the best weapons and loot available from the corpses and smashed crates at my feet, whilst kicking dogs and beating snakes to death with a sword I acquired from a kind of  post dungeon dream sequence at the end of a previous run through.As usual, it was a rewarding gauntlet and I climbed to the final boss ready to slice him up and get the hell out of there with a load of bunce (£).Entering the final stage I was welcomed by another real time player, however like a cowardly dog, they stayed hidden away from the monster and me, leaving me to tackle it solo and do most of the chopping before signalling to play co-op."Great" I thought.Together we went in and attacked, but I took a hit and got struck to floor.Immediately as I hit the deck, my fellow Samurai turned against me and took the opportunity of my momentary weakness to slice at me in the hopes of  killing me and taking my heard earned loot!Not today.I managed to ran away, drink a Miracle Potion and cut him and the beast down, proceeding to steal all of his money and kick his corpse until I earned the title "Sadist". I escaped, paid the debt off, got the girl and unlocked a new dungeon.What a great game.PSYou can't go there!

_childDocuments_.review: Short answer: Fun game, it seems slow at the start because it uses the first few dungeon attempts to ease you into the gameplay loop, but it does open up and give you a lot to do.This game is kind of like a mix of Way of the Samurai and Animal Crossing. Instead of paying off your house debt, you're paying to save Dojima's daughter from a life of slavery. That's also only the beginning of it, cause once you upgrade your house then you have to pay for even more expensive "add-ons" and the only way to do that is go fishing for more swords and upset all the villagers. I don't think you get to teach them naughty words to say to you though, they know those on their own.It's not quite way of the samurai since it's got the top down action dungeon hunting thing going for it, but the most rewarding way to murder is still awase baiting for massive damage. Gathering money is a chore if you stick to trying to gather it directly in the dungeons, but the true moneymaking skill is in disrupting the harmony of the clans and then peddling problem solvers to anyone who wants to bring back peace forcefully.I guess that means the long version of this review is that it's fun.Also I want Way of the Samurai 5 and you should too.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, this is in no way a match up to the original WOTS series. It has less depth overall and no huge branching stories or side quests.It is however a simple light spin off from the original series.Most of the negative reviews also stated it being repetitive. Somehow i don't particularly agree with that. In the end, the core gameplay loop is to go in to dungeons and see how far you can get before choosing to either play it safe and leave earlier or risk death for nicer rewards.Another thing, a staple of the WOTS series is the sword/skill customisation/learning as you play. This should encourage you to try for different styles and builds overall. So far, combat is not particularly demanding or varied but that could be due to me being still very early in the game. There are at least some mechanics that make it stand out from a generic fighting game.Considering the game is also pretty much 20$, it really isnt such a huge asking price for the content it provides.

_childDocuments_.review: Dont let the simple appearance of this game fools you. Its actually a LOT more than that! But you have to be patient. This game opens up slowly to you. At the beginning, it seems like its just you, a weird dungeon inside a tree thats kinda repetitive, a blacksmith and an empty field. But then slowly the game unveils your role in all this:To help free the blacksmith daughter from debtors and marry her, you have to help her dad sells sword. In the late samurai era where swords are starting to get prohibited by the law, nobody ever bother to buy them anymore. so what can you do? You troll and instigate the sh*t out of the 3 available factions in the game into killing each other - and then you provide them with the tools to do it!Thats right, your role in all of this is as the Merchant of Menace. once tension among the factions is high enough, it will soon kick up an arms race. people will be lining up for your swords and youll happily farm the dungeon to fill their demands. that peaceful field near the blacksmith where you started soon becomes a battlefield, bodies will be piling up as passersby cut each others guts out. (hilariously the factions will set up shops next to each other near the blacksmith and even the shopkeepers cant keep out of the action) and youll be standing on the side, counting your profits.Overall a good and comfy game to pass up time. Always a fan of the WoTS series. If i could pick something wrong with this game, it will be that the interface might takes a while to get used to.Its a budget title so i recommend it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I seldom write reviews, but... when I was younger, I loved Way of the Samurai 1/2, they were an interesting sort of open world game with branching stories and it was honestly my first run in with this type of game.  Unfortunately, outside of character references I've not seen too much of this style of gameplay yet but as of right now I've only ~2 hours in the game.  What I can say, is this is a pretty damn fun dungeon crawler though.If you're in the market you for something you can relax and waste some time in, while still offering some sort of challenge from time to time, I would say this is it.  I'll revise my review as I get further in, but as a knee-jerk reaction?  It's worth it.  The price may be a little steep but I can see myself sinking enough time in to it to justify it as a fan of the series.  If you're not really a fan of the series, waiting for a little discount may be worth it.The combat seems to lend itself better to a controller but is completely passable on KBM.  I've not seen any sort of bugs thus far.  The graphics are... there, nothing to write home about but it's not going to make you want to rip out your eyes--if you've played older Way of the Samurai entries it's actually pretty much like a shaped-up 2's graphics...  Story is pretty basic thus far but enough to keep you going.  The, as of this point, limited shop management mechanics are a fun diversion and give you a little something extra to do--maybe this gets more in depth later, I feel like it will, but it's limited to someone requesting an item to be crafted and fulfilling the order as of this point in the game for me.I

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game going in with the mindset that I'm going to get the WOTS experience. I was definitely proved wrong, but that wasn't a bad thing.The story was simple enough. Go through dungeon, collect loot to make swords,make swords to sell to pay off debt. You do this for quite a while and I was honestly confused if anything was going to change. I can't say what happens after you pay off the debt (spoilers).PROS:- WOTS universe. The weird whackiness from the series continues with the vulgar grunts and the comical iconic characters.- Fighting mechanic changes. The series wasn't known for it's cancel-heavy gameplay (unless you used the right moves in Iai style, WOTS3 &4, plus a few other off styles). The dash/dodge now acts as a much needed cancel-move to get you in and out of combat since enemies will no longer fight you 1-on-1 like in previous games.- Dungeon crawler. Hit or miss if you like dungeon crawls or not.- Sword upgrading is fairly easy. Just need the right materials and you're set. It's a bit of RNG and you can blow through mats fast if  you're trying to get the best sword possible. The title system is interest but I don't mess with it very much.- A collect-a-thon gone crazy. There's a ton of unlockable stuff, swords to use, farming to do. This only applies if this type of game interests you. CONS -- NO CHARACTER CREATION. You play as the protagonist guy. You get to name him, but that's it. (SPOILERS: You can play as other characters when you under the correct conditions, though through the majority of the game you'll just be protagonist guy)- NO SWORD CREATION. There are only pre-built swords, and they don't come apart. You can't make your own masterpiece.- There's no town to explore. I was really disappointed at how limited you are on where you can go outside of the dungeon(s).- The sword move list is a bit nerfed. Very few moves compared to other titles, though it's not a big deal considering how combat feels in t his game.- A LOT of text errors. From the get-go, Sound is labeled as "MUSIC", the game starts off in Japanese even though I bought it in the states. Percentage values are listed as "#NUM",- A.I. of partners are a bit wonky. They'll freely step into your path when fighting.- A.I. of enemies are a bit weird as well. Some enemies will just stop fighting and space out.- Tension system not explained as well as it could be. It takes a bit for clans to start fighting.- With the isometric view, there are still some foreground obstructions when going through dungeons.- NEW - Controls are just ... weird sometimes. Sometimes buttons won't register, other times you'll be stuck traveling in one direction for no reason.I'm pleasantly surprised with the overall experience of the game and will keep playing. It just barely scratches my itch for the WOTS series and I hope to see it continue after this entry.EDIT: I've finished the game up until unlocking the final dungeon. I have not yet beat the final dungeon but am planning to.The Pros and  Cons of what I said before still stand, though it seems a lot of the blacksmith shop running is a lot of learning through experience. It becomes easier to understand once you're over 30 days in (in-game). There seems to be a lot more Cons than there are Pros, but the Cons don't detract enough for the game to become a negative experience. After a good 50+ hours I can say that I enjoyed my time playing the game and would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is strangely addicting. This game is a real time action mystery dungeon game. The beginning starts off slow and gradually more options open up for you the lower and lower you progress down the dungeons. The game itself is themed around the Way of the Samurai series. But the dungeons are based on Shiren the Wanderer which is a mystery dungeon game. A mystery dungeon game is like a randomly generated dungeon with a different layout every time. Each dungeon has different items and different enemies. When you die, you lose all your items and start from above again. But when you return above ground without dying, you get to keep all your items. There are various ways to mitigate the risk such as buying insurance or being extra prepared with items before you go into the dungeon. Which brings me to my favorite part of the game: the swords. You upgrade your sword the same way you upgrade them in the Way of the Samurai series. You bring materials to the blacksmith and you make your sword stronger. Each sword has a different upgrade limit and a different fighting style. Finding a sword that has a fighting style you like and making it stronger is quite fun. This game is released on the PC but actually, I feel that this game was more meant for consoles because of the controls. I rebinded almost all the buttons to fit a controller layout by having the buttons on the controller mimic the buttons on the keyboard. This makes navigating through the menus and controlling the character much faster and more natural. The story itself isn't much to write about. Save the damsel in distress from a group of loan sharks. There are three different factions in the game and their relationship changes, but at the beginning they don't actually do much. This game is quite fun among the mystery dungeon types, but temper your expectations because it is still a relatively simple game with chaos thrown in.

_childDocuments_.review: Katana Kami is a dungeon crawler version of the Way of the Samurai series. You will be going through consecutive dungeons to earn money and pay the debt to free Dojima's daughter. Compared to the original series where you mainly fought humans, instead you will be fighting wild beasts, skeletons, and japanese demons.This game takes place during the events of the first Way of the Samurai game. In the first game, two gangs are competing for territory while the citizens of Rokutsu Pass get caught in the crossfire. In the original Way of the Samurai game (for PS2), your decisions affect both sides and you get a different ending depending on the decisions you made.In this game, however, you play a smaller role, and your main focus is to free Dojima's daughter by paying off her debt. By going into a mysterious dungeon fighting monsters and demons, you obtain better weapons, and gold to spend on whatever you please. You pay Dojima's debt through increments, and the collector arrives every few days. Later on, you will be able to accept quests, give gifts to Nanami to earn her affection, and ship out swords or send out gifts to either of the gangs to affect the tension of the entire town and control the war.Pros:- Combat is fun and feels like you're playing Way of the Samurai in an isometric view.- They brought back the Kiwami system from Way of the Samurai 3. Blocking or evading at proper times will allow you to parry and one shot most enemies or do massive damage. Killing an enemy with this will continue the streak. It feels exhilarating killing a group of enemies with this.- I appreciate seeing characters from the first game as well as one from Way of the Samurai 2.- As of this review, I got as far as the 3rd type of dungeon, and encountered an insane boss that almost eliminated me. Kept me on my toes, and fighting that boss felt exciting.- Dojima's daughter is cute as hell.Cons/Differences:- Performing certain moves (ex: like the forward plus light/heavy attacks) require a certain precision and are slightly difficult to do. This can be overcome with some practice, but I feel like this will be a hindrance in future areas where you're just trying to survive.- In the original series, you discover moves for your sword/style by executing and experimenting combos or fulfilling certain conditions (ex: kicking someone, eating during battle). This is changed slightly in this game. All swords have levels and will only learn certain moves when you reach required level.- There is only one map when you return from the dungeon. That map is just an open field where Dojima's smithy is located. Several NPCs do walk around during the daytime, and you will be able to interact with them. Shops may set up from each faction for buying/selling. I was expecting more exploration, at least being able to visit the town or either of the gang headquarters.- Buried Fire and other traps become annoying when you're fighting or running away.- Dungeon is fairly short.- Storage is limited. This was not a issue in WotS 4. You may buy upgrades for an expensive fee.A spinoff of the Way of the Samurai games, Katana Kami is a unique take on the franchise. I'm enjoying it currently, and I appreciate that Acquire released another game in one of my favorite series.

_childDocuments_.review: KatanaKami is like a mix of Diablo & Nioh, it offers online co-op but sadly only random players. There is no friend invite menu as far as i know. I managed to push through basement floor 11 on my first try but was killed by an unexpected challenger (most of the players i met before was helping instead of challenging to a fight so i wasn't ready). At daytime you live as a merchant helping the blacksmith owner to settle his debts in exchange to help reclaim his daughter held hostage. When night comes, you go forth to the land of jikai through the tree portal to slay oni to get bounties and rare weapons. The dungeons of jikai are randomly generated so each playthrough will never be the same. There you'll met other online players who might help or challenge you instead. The deeper you go the harder the enemies and the better reward you'll get. You might even stumble upon a secret blacksmith in the land of oni's. At the end of each stage there are two portals for you to either leave to the surface world or descend even further. Your hero can hold up to 3 active weapons which you can switch anytime, but bear in mind once it breaks you'll need to have a similar pair in order to fix it. Other types of sword can only strengthen the weapon before it is broken. So make sure you level up your secondary and tertiary weapon as well. Once you decide to return to the surface the many bounties you hold can be used to buy loss insurances in order to decrease the risk of item loss if you die in jikai world, albeit very expensive. So try to play safe in your first & secondary journeys and come back to save some money before you go all out in those dungeons because you still need to help the blacksmith owner to pay his debts else you'll lose his beautiful daughter.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not what you might expect, it is set in the Way of the samurai universe, no doubt, but it is an alternate timeline if anything. You will see characters from the main games, but they are merely NPCs or appear briefly in the form of the game's newspaper. It does have a story, but it is very short. You will have dialogue options, but don't expect branching endings or being able to join factions. Your role is to help the blacksmith, while things just kind of happen around you. The main meat of the game happens in an alternate world, where monsters, demons, and magic exists, and for you to utilize. You go in, you kill things and level up, collect materials, and return to the real world to give it to the blacksmith. At first it was slightly off-putting, but eventually as the in-game nights and days went on, it became addictive and very hard to stop. There are a few secrets here and there for people to discover, in a different way to the main series, but still good. It is different, but not bad. I wouldn't mind playing another one of these games, if a sequel came out. However, I would absolutely prefer one of the full story, fleshed out main games of "Way Of the Samurai".

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good stuff.  But, it is somewhat limited. The best thing about it is the combat.  The sword play is fun and there is some variation between all the different swords.  And there are LOTS of swords.The story is ok and the rogue-like nature of the quests and dungeon diving will keep you interested for a little while.Now for the bad......The controls.  They are just bad.  Very bad.  Not the worst out there...but pretty bad.   You will die because your character decides the put away his sword.  Was that due to hitting the wrong button??  Not necessarily...but it should be, and that's what is majorly wrong with this game.There are only 20 floors to the dungeon.  Most are small floors.  Sometimes so small everything on the floor aggro's you as soon as you spawn in and start fighting.   You'll blast through them over and over again.There are around 15-20 different enemy types.   The game is good. I wouldn't recommend paying more than $15 for it though.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a huge Way of the Samurai fan like me, then I think Katana Kami is a welcome addition to your collection. Yes, it's not Way of the Samurai 5, but Way of the Samurai 5 was cancelled. However, its cancellation eventually led up to Katana Kami.The game isn't perfect but sets up a nice foundation for improvement. Classic Way of the Samurai game play can be found here, along with the nostalgia the series is known for.Diving into the cave is fun, but paying off Dojima's debt will require a lot of cave diving which may grow repetitive and tiring for some. All in all, Katana Kami is an interesting spin-off from the mainline series that will leave Way of the Samurai fans hungry for Way of the Samurai 5.P.S. A message to the publisher/developers. Please continue making the mainline Way of the Samurai games. Don't feel discouraged that other companies with more money are able to put out prettier looking games. The Way of the Samurai games have a lot of heart and charm to them, that can only be found in a Way of the Samurai game. I grew up playing this series, so the series means a lot to me. Everyone has a game they resonate the most with, Way of the Samurai is that game for me.~A western Way of the Samurai Fan

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like a step backwards in many ways compared to WotS 4 which sucks.Mouse and keyboard controls are just awful in general and when combined with the fixed camera angle, make for an annoying time trying to move around when not in combat.SPEAKING OF WHICH, I'm saddened to see sword-specific stances and moves making a comeback. One of the best parts of WotS 4 for me was messing around with all the different styles and being able to switch between them on the fly. This also means that if you're going to invest resources into a sword, you're going to have to be sure you like that set of moves/stance the most out of everything or you'll have to grind up another one.And the death gods.. god, no thanks. They feel like a punishment for playing badly or not having high enough numbers, which means you're probably going to die if it's your first time running into one and you better pray it's not on a floor too deep or you're guaranteed to lose everything. At least when you get started (spoilers, it happened to me and I just started over at that point)Not being able to explore the town is also just disappointing. I've loved going around and just starting random brawls with people in town square or somewhere on the outskirts, and whatnot.In spite of this, I'm still excited for Acquire's future releases. Just wish this one wasn't as.. bad I guess

_childDocuments_.review: Katana Kami is easily one of the worst games I've ever played, and that's saying a lot. From what I understand, Acquire (the dev behind Way of the Samurai and Octopath Traveler, along with a couple of the modern Japanese-made Wizardry games) is low on cash and doesn't have the money for a full Way of the Samurai 5, so they're releasing this as an interest gauge ala No More Heroes: Travis Strikes Again. Katana Kami is a Shiren the Wanderer/Mystery Dungeon clone, easily told by the fact that Shiren's outfit is available as a preorder DLC. The premise is simple: you're a wandering samurai trying to help a blacksmith get his daughter back by paying off his debt. You do this by going inside a magic tree at night that sends you to the realm of the blacksmith god Ippon-Datara (who you may know from the Shin Megami Tensei games).The dungeon itself controls a lot like that one car in Daytona USA that has a handling stat of 0, which is to say that it doesn't. You start with one sword, and are immediately put into the dungeon against a bunch of enemies. From there, you start getting bombarded by tutorials for esoteric mechanics that don't matter (things like frame-perfect parry chains). The keyboard and mouse controls are awful, which makes me wonder why Acquire even bothered to release this piece of crap on the PC. Your sword has a durability meter that constantly needs to be refilled, in addition to your stamina gauge (read: hunger meter, because every roguelike has to have one of those, except all the ones that have forsaken it because it's a bad mechanic) and your HP meter.The game isn't based around simply attacking, but a system where you're supposed to keep your sword sheathed in order to build up power. By itself, your sword does next to no damage. When you sheath it, you eventually build up power that allows you to either do a few hits with increased damage or an "iai explosion" that hits a very small radius around you for high damage. The problem here is that the game is in an overhead view and the animations are so bad that it's difficult to tell what's going on. On the keyboard, the iai explosion is "hold F and left click" but half the time when I tried to do that I'd just pull the sword out, as F is also the key for drawing your sword. Worse, if you're ever afflicted by a status effect, your character gets locked into a single animation that makes it impossible to tell if your sword is even drawn or not.Otherwise, the controls are still bad. Attacking locks your character into a single-direction animation that cannot be cancelled and is usually very long. Your character is very slow, the enemies are very fast and don't get locked into place when they attack. Trying to use the guard breaker moves is even worse, because half the time you'll be facing an enemy, go to kick them to break their guard, and then have the enemy move while you're locked into your kick animation causing you to miss and them to hit you several times.I think what made me decide to refund it was a single chain of stupid events. I picked up a sword that had a title on it, which gives the sword extra power or something. The sword turned out to be cursed even though I had identified it and it hadn't mentioned being cursed. Cursed weapons force you to use them, so I did, figuring that when it broke I'd be able to drop it. Only... nope! If you try to use a cursed weapon and it breaks, you are now effectively dead: you have a weapon that does 1 damage and can't get rid of it. Dying, by the way, removes all of your items and money.The game is on a time limit (you have to pick up money from the dungeon to pay the debt collector on time) and dying basically means you've rendered the game unwinnable because you won't have enough time to recover, even if you stored all your money away. Overall, I'd say this game isn't worth it, unless it's on sale for like $5 or something. Definitely not worth it at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Complete trash game. Despite a pretty good feel to the combat, everything else which surrounds that is cheap AF. It's a proper amateurish game which just feels tacky, and the biggest deal breaker of all is in here for me, one of my pet hates - huge damage numbers being displayed with each attack. Honestly, it's downright insulting when a game feels the need to tell you how much damage each blow does, I'm not an amoeba, I can figure it out for myself you know lol. But it's far worse when that display half covers your character and/or enemies, as it does here. In a turn based game where thought is the main drive behind the combat? Fine, but in an action-based one like this it just gets in the way of the action. I want to see my blows land and the enemy recoil, and visa versa. Did none of these devs ever play Gauntlet, Smash TV, The Chaos Engine etc. or any of the other many amazing overhead action games which trusted the player to figure out damage as the went themselves? A game made for low-level gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: I figured I'd give this a positive but with the asterisk is it's not entirely for me, but I do enjoy Way of the Samurai and I think this is a good microcosm of the franchise.The game is a roguelite dungeon crawler where you're on a timer to get money to get somebody's daughter back. I'm aware that it isn't world ending if you don't and it's probably intended you play multiple times to unlock everything, but the time and roguelite elements add a bit of stress over the whole thing which kinda lessens the appeal of the game for me personally.  All that being said, it does seem pretty easy, I actually haven't died in my 9 hours playing, it just isn't my favourite format for a game.The graphics are very reminiscent of Way of the Samurai 3, which wasn't a visual powerhouse when it came out, though the view distance helps with the ps2-esque modeling quite a bit. A lot of the accessories and character models actually do seem like they may be from that game, but there is a lot more to the game itself than that, so that doesn't bother me. If Yakuza and Elder Scrolls can recycle animations for like three gens of games I'm okay with a couple character models being recycled for what is a much more budget game.The action is... good? It's a lot more simplified and snappy probably due to the viewing angle, but everything is easy to grasp but nuanced enough to have fun with. I enjoy games with parry systems, and I always thought WotS swordplay was a bit too complicated for its own good anyways. A lot of staples are still present in the game such as the micro-story that you have a number of influences over, the bizarre humour and the over the top characters. I think it actually brings in some of the best aspects of WotS 3 and 4 in that sense, having the interesting grounded designs and the absurd garish ones. The introduction of overtly supernatural elements is a nice touch.At the end of the day, roguelites aren't an enticing game loop to me, but it did get me back into replaying WotS 4 and trying to make a bit more headway into WotS3 which I gave up early. I also think I got more than enough enjoyment out of it despite the deck being stacked against it.I think I got this for 5 usd, but I think it would be well worth four times that, particularly if you're a fan of roguelites or Way of the Samurai.

_childDocuments_.review: Why you should play this game:- Dungeon crawling- Fun and satisfying combat mechanics- Because you played Way of the Samurai 1 and you liked it- You are a fan of Way of the Samurai games- Several references to the Way of the Samurai games. Many swords, movesets and one boss from Way of the Samurai games- Like with Way of the Samurai games, getting your favourite sword and strengthening it is tedious but fun, at least for me.Why you shouldn't play this game:- It's not Way of the Samurai 5- Somewhat repetitive- Some of the things in this game are VERY counter-intuitive, coupling with translation errors, which I addressed in my guide- There are still several rare but annoying bugs, and they are not going to patch this game anymore- Terrible save system. One slot only, autosave only. Autosave I get, but one save slot only is really terrible- Bodyguards are more often than not, worse than useless- Some quests, some places just take too long to reach- Lack of story- Punishes new players very harshly. There are many ways to die and some are just cruel and unfair.I thoroughly enjoy it and still come back to it once in a while. I think it is not a game for everyone. It might not even be a game for some Way of the Samurai fans because of the lack of story. If you're looking for a dungeon crawler with satisfying combat mechanics and exploring hundreds of swords and movesets, you might enjoy this game. For other people, I'd just recommend getting into Way of the Samurai 3 or maybe 4 first if you're looking for some game to do Samurai-y things in. You'd still get all the good things Katana Kami offers. And if you decide to get into this game, I'd recommend reading guides or discussions about it due to how things can be so counter-intuitive or the game's description is just wrong at times.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of WOTS, I didn't think I'd like this top-down, isometric style; but it's actually not bad.  The only problem with it is that sometimes trees and terrain features can block your view.  The game itself is very fun.  There is a rhythm to the combat.  Once you get in the groove, it's very satisfying and fluid.  I also really like the faction conflicts that you get to influence; it has a surprising amount of depth.  Another cool feature that is often overlooked is the game's liveliness of its NPCs.  There isn't really a town to explore, but there are NPCs constantly walking through your hub.  Their A.I. isn't the best, but they interact with each other and react when they see one another.  It's interesting.  I don't have a lot of negative things to say about this game except that it can be repetitive, and I wish there was a town to explore, and I really wish more people played it.  I feel like it really flew under the radar and wasn't advertised very well.  Overall, I love this game.  It's one of a kind, and that needs to change.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm not even close to being done with this game but I've put in quite a few hours by now and since it atm stands at a mixed review score I just have to give my opinion on it. I think this is  a great game. But it's important to set your expectations straight before going in. It's not a way of the samurai game. It's more like a mystery dungeon wots crossover and being a fan of both series I just have a blast. I'm into rogue lites. I'm into samurai. I'm into arpgs. This game is all of that and while its not a perfect game by any means it really gets me. The graphics are a bit outdated, the game is still pretty buggy, it can be utterly frustrating, it's quite repetitive the mechanics are barely explained and the "cutscenes" are so barebones I would've preferred they if didn't include them at all and just made it regular game dialogue. But the moment to moment gameplay is great, the voice acting (while in typical wots manner rather sparse) is good as is the sound design as a whole and honestly this soundtrack really is a bop!The story so far is okay I'd say on par with other wots games but obviously stripped down with this being a rogue lite with just a little hub world and all. I like some mechanics like the whole gifts and sword selling stuff. It just feels very wots. So does the whole store your loot in the base and upgrade it etc to get stronger. It's not only a clever but also very WOTS way to do rogue lite progression and paired with the gambling of "will I be able to survive another 5 floors or should I get out rn" it can get very addictive. I really like the enemy designs. I like the boss designs and the fights can get pretty tense my main critisizm regarding the bosses would be that they are hard because they have ridiculous amounts of hp and that just feels a bit unrewarding and boring. Most "stages" (or whatever you wanna call it) are okay looking but a lot of them are lazy reskins.There are not quite enough different weapons imo I miss yuris and naginatas and while it is enough to satisfy me most weapons are just katanas (fair enough considering the name of the game) .Overall theres a bit of a lack of content. Also please give us more than one savegameslot wtf?Overall a great game thats right up my alley but a flawed one nonetheless. Know that you're not getting a "real" WOTS game.Get it on sale.Enjoy the satisfiiying sound the enemies make when you kill them7/10ps. Hey chunsoft pls give us a mystery dungeon collection on steam. I know most games aren't translated but that can't be that expensive right? I mean the series is on of the OG roguelikes I think it could sell pretty well. Also Way of the samurai 1 &2 ports would be greatly appreciated.

_childDocuments_.review: While it's not the "way of the samurai" I wanted, it's one I'm still enjoying.    A bit of a slow burn as it drip feeds additional features/mechanics/content to you over the course of playing, but it also fully embraces the zany nature that the series it's spun-off from is known for.As a side note for series vets, the combat is only slightly simplified to what you would expect, the skill trees on weapons is still there, but the amount of skills per weapon seems pared down slightly to the usual offering. Also the fights are a bit more frantic as enemies can and will assault you in mass instead of the usual one on one or two on one that the series usually incorporated with any additional enemies circling you, and you might have to endure upwards of a dozen enemies trying to take a piece of you on the higher floors.

name: Inkbound
detailed_description: Inkbound is a turn-based roguelike set in a world where the dangerous magic of the written word comes to life. Go on a quest to save the stories of the Atheneum, unlock new classes, and master the challenge. REINVENTING TURN-BASED GAMEPLAY Within the unique turn-based combat system players move freely, act simultaneously in multiplayer, and can rapidly use abilities. Go fast when the decisions are easy, go slow when the threat amps up and you need to strategize more deeply. DIVERSE BUILDS AND CLASSES Explore a varied set of character classes while adapting your strategy during runs to craft powerful builds. With draftable abilities, ability upgrades, and hundreds of items to find there are many possible ways to play. 4 PLAYER CO-OP The Atheneum acts as a social hub where players can meet with friends and strangers to party up into groups of up to four. Take on challenges as a team and strategize together to determine the most synergistic builds. SAVE THE STORIES The magical Atheneum contains all stories ever written. Each book becomes a portal to another world where you will face unique threats. Inkbound’s stories are unraveling due to an unseen threat and the inhabitants of the Atheneum need your help.

_childDocuments_.review: I think you're probably going to enjoy Inkbound if you like:1.) Tactical Roguelikes2.) Evolving abilities3.) Deceptively simple mechanics that come together in exciting waysIt has a strong co-op element, to the point where I think I prefer playing this game with friends. The ability upgrades do feel like they have an honest impact on the gameplay experience, and the runs are just about the right length for it to have a place in a gaming group's nights on Discord. Additionally, this doesn't appear to be Vaporware - there's an update in the wings already adding a new hero choice and level to go trough(and it's scifi themed!) and the developers seem genuinely passionate about what they're trying to go for, here.It's a hard recommend for me, this game does a lot of things right and combines them in new ways. Give it a go if you like a game with that "going on another run" feeling but want it in a co-op setting with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the greatest games I have played this year! takes a well known genre and adds new and unique gameplay to it, as well a beautiful art and great online multiplayer. In addition, the devs are active in the community, and have made some great choices for the sake of the game, such as the removal of a paid battlepass. 100% worth the money if you enjoy this type of game, or want to try something new with friends!
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Great simple rogue-like. Turn based and free moving but the system is really good about making sure you aren't wasting movement or moves unintentionally. The characters all feel very different but not incredibly deep. Most of the depth comes from self imposed changes to the new abilities you take so if you find that fun or enjoy chasing achievements and small story progression bits then you will enjoy this game. My only complaint about game play is the lack of explanation on some of the power values and what they do the first time you see them. Other than that the always online aspect is bothersome but not a deal breaker for me personally. In game shop and battlepass are for cosmetics only but I guess that bothers a ton of people into making a negative review. As long as it stays for only cosmetics who cares, just don't buy stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible! From the devs of Monster Train, another fantastic roguelite game that has you feeling so incredibly powerful and rewarded for decisions you make, throughout the game. I played a good 30 hours during the demo, and 13 on the day it dropped - it's incredibly fun, and easy to play with friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Game: 9/10MTX model : 6/10 (after update)I played this game about 20+ hours in the February demo and back then this became one of my most anticipated early access titles this year. Now the game is finally for sale. More content, more loot, more fun. This is a strategic, free movement, turn based roguelike from the makers of Monster Train. It can be played solo or scaling up in difficulty with friends. Having seen a few dev streams, I know how much the team loves the game they are making, and it shows. Yes, the game has a cash shop and a battlepass. Well, actually 2 battlepasses. One free, and a paid one. They only deliver cosmetics. And once the BP is gone, you can still get the cosmetics from the shop. Devs plan to use the money earned from the shop to deliver future seasonal content (maps, heroes, themes, etc.) for free. I feel that it is fair to have the option to only pay 20€ for the game and free content. If you are into cosmetics, it is your choice wether to pay or not, as there are no lootboxes. Everything is transparent. EDIT: Recent changes made the monetization model less shady. Coins can now be bought at 0.5€ value and shop is no longer rotating. I just mentioned this as I feel some folks on the forums blowing this out of proportion.Hope you enjoy the game as much as I do!
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Inkbound, even as it is still being worked on. already has an amazing game with lots of replay ability. i'm not the biggest fan of the season pass as i believe it is a shoddy way to add extra monetization to the game. but outside of that, i believe the core game play is amazing, easy to pick up, and very nice to experiment with. and as long as the season pass stays to just cosmetics, i believe the game is worth every penny. and very interested in what it'll look at full release
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Update 11-02-2023:All in-game monetization has been removed and Shiny Shoe continues to update the game with new content and gameplay improvements. I think this is probably the most hours played I have put into an early access title. Highly recommend buying this game right now as it will only continue to get better!-----------------------------------------------Really enjoying this game. I haven't found another game quite like this one. The blend of roguelite and tactical turn-based combat works really well, and I find myself wanting to start a new run as soon as the previous run is finished. A few of the issues I had with the game seem to have been addressed with the most recent update. The movement system has been improved, solo ranked mode is far less frustrating now, and the daily challenges are a welcome new game mode to change things up.While I'd prefer not to have any season pass/microtransactions in a game, I have to say that the way Shiny Shoe has implemented the season passes here is very good. You don't lose out on a previous season's rewards that you paid for, and during the current season you can earn enough currency to either pay for your season pass or at least get it at a significant discount. I hope other developers take note and start offering season passes that don't expire. That alleviates the FOMO aspect which is what I hate the most about the seasonal model.I'm not the biggest fan of how the story is delivered in the game, but I guess I am not really playing this for the story. It's the gameplay that is keeping me hooked, but it would be cool to see the previous season's books and stories chronicled in a journal or put someplace where you can review past stories and see how they tie into the bigger story narrative.Don't let the early access label deter you from playing this. There is already a full and well polished (and continually being improved) experience here for fans of Monster Train and other roguelite and turn-based strategy games.

_childDocuments_.review: Not in the mood to write a long-winded review, but the positive ratings are baffling. The game is very shallow and every run feels the same. There's little enemy variety and builds always end up same-ish with little synergy between different paths, so you are forced into the same build every time or you end up with skills and stat distributions that literally conflict with each other. And even if there was more synergy, the game wouldn't even force you to make hard choices, because you get enough rerolls to always get what you want. Also, while there might be a few more to unlock, there are only like 5 generic skills shared among all classes, which only differ by their passives and 3 unique skills. I've played Monster Train for hundreds of hours and am very disappointed, that this doesn't even have enough depth to keep my attention for 7 hours. It's so bland.

_childDocuments_.review: Changing my review for a third time. I wasn't sure about the rank system and how it would achieve what they wanted it to. It is far more detailed and in-depth than I thought.There are cosmetics for only ranked milestones (number of bosses defeated). This ties in to the ranked system, which is cool is cool because you can't go back in level, so the number of bosses defeated is directly tied in to the difficulty of the runs. I have found some broken combos that make the runs blow up, which didn't matter in the early ranks but now you basically need a broken combo to win a run (solo).Combat is creative but I still think the builds are lacking in flare, particularly in solo mode. Basically half the builds are unplayable in solo mode, and here's why: stacking debuffs are unplayable in solo, because you need to kill at least half the spawns in a single turn, otherwise you take too much damage. This means that although DoTs can blow up an entire screen easily (ie. spreading poison), they apply after the enemies take their turn, meaning you are forced to take all of the damage before you win. I have given up on trying to make DoTs work but may circle back now that I know the game mechanics a little better.I guess it is fair that some builds aren't useable on solo mode, since there is an emphasis on multiplayer. Maybe I will try to convince some friends to play with me.

_childDocuments_.review: Since buying, playing this game non-stop!Having all these different classes, skills, items and a similiar progression system like slay the spire, is an absolute blast! Although every build seems to be quite viable, there are certain builds that clearly dominate within all classes, Nonetheless, key mechanics, rank and ascension system for skills are perfectly in sync elevating the satisfaction from run to run. _childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best co-op turn based style roguelite/like I've ever played.  Me and the boys had been searching hard for something to scratch the itch after Ember knights, and although Inkbound is different in many ways- we love it.  Initially it felt like the game pushes you to build a certain way, boy was I wrong.  I have successfully had high level runs with smite, burn, poison, blur, crit, etc.  The build freedom is great.  Inkbound also has free cosmetic rewards that you constantly get currency for if you're into that.  The difficulty scaling may feel rough when you first start grouping with a party because it ramps up the enemy damage/health pretty significantly.  Just stick with it and you'll figure out its all very manageable.  One gripe is that the attack numbers above the enemies health bars don't always show the actual damage they will do in higher teir multiplayer matches.  I assume this is due to difficulty modifiers, but it just makes things a bit confusing after you've learned to depend on these numbers in previous runs.Alas, Have fun and scoop this one up - you wont be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: From the creators of Monster Train, one of the best deckbuilding roguelikes you could buy, comes an incredibly unique roguelike turn based dungeon crawling rpg. That's a whole mouthful to say that this game is AMAZING.Typically in games with so much randomization, the luck of the draw determines quite a bit. The measure of a good game in this genre is whether or not they allow you to consistently pull out a win, (with enough skill), but to always be fun in doing so. Inkbound's unique combat feels like a speedcore rpg run; start weak, with very basic abilities... Level up, or in this case power up your build with unique items, and gain new abilities. Enhance and alter your abilities to create truly broken combos and destroy bosses in a few hits. All in about 20-30 minutes. Bask in your glory, fill a few more quests out in the logbook, and go back to do it again. If it sounds formulaic, it can be at times; but the loop is so fulfilling that it's difficult to put down.The sheer variety of things to do is absurd. There are eight classes, dozens on dozens of 'Vestiges' (items which enhance your build), multiple secondary abilities, and many more factors that could turn your run into a dud before the first floor, or trivialize it within moments of starting the game. It feels amazing to constantly march forward, and part of that is the fact that there is ALWAYS something else to do. The logbook full of quests is so thick that it could take one weeks to make a dent in it, and when you finally do there is still even more to do. You could cruise the whole story mode and come out the other side with barely a third of the book done.Not enough? There are a huge variety of cosmetics unlockable in game. It should be lauded that this publisher realized that their old, abusively monetized model was no good, and saved this game from the unfortunate cash grab it might have been. And if you somehow find yourself unable to find a fun combination of hats and costumes, don't fret! There's even an in depth character creator! It's limited to the face, but it's remarkable what can be done with it despite its seeming simplicity! I hope the developers add more to it; specifically the ability to see other peoples' faces, and to save separate faces to use on different characters. That should say a lot; I do not want anything changed, I just want more!And of course, all this is already well worth it. Now throw in online co op to let you run with your friends, and you have a near perfect game to grind.Unfortunately I do have to begrudgingly admit to 'near' perfection. There are some odd balance decisions, the occasional graphic hiccup or stutter, and you will lose at least one run you thought you had in the bag because a boss decides to crush you at the same time his minions decide to unleash THEIR big attack. But none of it is off-putting enough for me to drop this game. Maybe it's just something that clicks for me, but it feels like the natural evolution to the multi hour rpgs I used to play as a kid, only compacted into a short session.On top of it all, the team made a very strong effort to make the story and world worthwhile and engaging. Like Monster Train, the developer took time to put real thought into their lore. Whether it is a hit or miss is up to you, but so much of it is fully voice acted, and at least well written enough that whether you enjoy it or not it should be respected. And it's pretty much skippable anyway, if you just want to go around bashing faces with co op buddies.This is a 9/10 game. It might be more. It is worth every penny and then some, especially if you do it with a friend. If you enjoyed Monster Train, if you like turn based rpgs, if you enjoy roguelikes at all, give this one a spin and you will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is terrible. Here's an easy test: Don't join a party, don't look up any guides, just go in to the game and once you get to the hub (the Aethernum), see how long it takes you to figure out how to play a run. No peeking.What a miserable failure of game design that they *failed* at getting "Play Game" right!The rest of the "game" is filled with style over substance - the hub is a big anti-design pattern, there are a ton of NPCs that serve no purpose, and maybe you're willing to endure all of that because the flavor is interesting? It is not. It, similarly, is a closed empty coat, hinting at something big but actually just nonsense and air.There might be some interesting mechanics in terms of drafting and destroying gear, to boost a talent tree by any other name, but you wouldn't know it because the game spent all of its time on pointless NPCs with pointless dialogue.Edit: I did it! After *80* minutes of play time, I found the PLAY GAME button! Are you ready for this? It was buried under a stack of other players, because hub design is a bad idea. It's easily missable, because prominence wise, the pointless Borekeeper is where one would expect "play game" to be, and going to the left or right end up leading you to character (re)customization (clearly more important than playing the game), some lore nonsense, a daily quest board, and no PLAY GAME. You have to go one of those directions, and then up and the OTHER, to get to PLAY GAME.This should go down in textbooks as an example of what not to do, and why.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I have found my new addiction. This game is a lot of fun. You choose a class (which you can swap around as you like, outside of runs) and you are trying to make a strong enough build to make it through and defeat the final boss. Your build consists of your class abilities, which includes a passive and three abilities that you will get to augment. Vestiges, which are like relics that grant bonuses and have keyword traits. The more of those keyword traits you stack, the better the bonuses you will get. You also get to add two more abilities during a run which can range from buffs and debuffs, to damage, and they also gain augments. There are consumables and you also get Trinkets, which essentially grants an extra passive. It's a lot to manage at first, but it clicks after a run or two.There is a multiplayer aspect to it, but up to this point, I've only played solo and it has been enjoyable. There are only a couple of negatives that I have at this point. 1, I'd like to see more variety in the abilities given during runs. This may actually be addressed via unlocking them over the course of the game, I just don't know yet. 2, a "quick delve" can take about an hour, which isn't too quick. This isn't a major issue, but it has stopped me from starting another run, because I know I don't have the time to dedicate for it.Overall, this is a solid game with satisfying build construction, combat, art/graphics and surprisingly great voice acting.

_childDocuments_.review: Really great, fun game with focus on getting immediately into the action. Great class variety, great encounter variety, grouping is very optional, great development team which is extra communicative on their official Discord.First game of this genre I have played, in many years, and did not disappoint. Season pass is 100% cosmetics and entirely optional.To get the most of the game, I would recommend joining their official Discord and playing with others.Few cons:No PvP - at allRanked does not seem to increase rewards, just makes the game harder for those that like the challengeThere are some cards (upgrades) that seem like straight nerfs to your runThere are no run history logs available, at least none that I can seeNo guilds / emphasis placed on being grouping. For the socialite gamers, this may make the world feel smaller.With that said, the game is worth the 20GBP price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Weaver is one of the most unique classes I've played in a turn-based game in ages (and might I say they pulled it off far better than Bu*gie ever could...). Very unique way to play a turn-based tactical RPG and I'm enjoying it a lot. Co-op is an excellent addition. I'm not understanding the negative reviews about monetization - sure, there is a premium currency/battle pass, but you can accumulate the currency without ever paying money again so...what's the big deal. Battle pass and currency unlocks cosmetics only. This is clearly a passion project for the devs and one I will find worth supporting in the future for more content.Edit: As I play more - the builds are intricate and the strategy is deep. You unlock new combinations as you progress the story. I thought I had a good build for my weaver until I unlocked the ability to pull NPCs together and a whole new game opened up before me. Highly recommend if you're a fan of turn-based and want to try something new.

_childDocuments_.review: not quite as deep as monster train but lots of fun just the same. fomo-free season structure too, so you can go back and pick up cosmetics using reasonable amounts of in-game currency you'll get just from playing. as a lover of traditional roguelikes I've always been surprised there isn't more innovation and risk-taking in a genre that is literally indies-only, so I had my eyes on inkbound from the start. hoping they add more content in the future - the current classes are all super unique from each other but for me my builds for any given class don't vary as much between runs as I'd like.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: I am having a great time playing this with a group of friends. I can't speak for endgame, but so far, the journey is a blast!Update: I am level 100 plus now, and at rank 14 group runs. Game is actually more fun at that rank in my opinion. Totally worth buying and playing.Update: I played a lot of this game, and the gameplay and mechanics of the game are awesome. However, after completing just about everything worth doing in the game I can tell you why it was a failure.1) Aesthetics: Visually, the game is pretty ugly. The graphical fidelity is fine for an indie game, but the art direction, color palate, and look of the cosmetic items is pretty terrible. I was able to look passed the aesthetics of the game and focus on the mechanics and gameplay (which are excellent), but most people won't, especially when the replayability of the game is designed around chasing cosmetics.2) Writing & NPC Characters:The overarching story and plot points are mostly fine. However, the dialogue in this game is horrendous. Its the typical infantile Millennial writing I have come to loath wherever I encounter it (and it seems to have become the norm across the game industry). The "jokes" don't land, and all interactions are overly expository. Most of the conversations sound like an NPC just word vomiting their stream of consciousness at you. Its the type of interaction that would compel you to make an excuse to go to the bathroom or get a drink if it happened in a real social setting. I eventually started skipping it. The NPC characters you interact with are not likable, and almost all of them are annoying. Honestly, I can't think of an NPC I liked. The best ones are the ones I can't remember at all. That should tell you something. Not to mention, that visually they all look some combination of ugly, silly, or stupid.3) Content:This game needed a larger variety of bosses and boss fights. The variety of encounters in the game is severely lacking. If you played one run through a particular book you pretty much saw everything that book has to offer from an encounter perspective.TL;DRI still recommend this game as a fun party game if you focus on the mechanics, teamwork, and gameplay.As a single-player narrative the game completely fails and I would never recommend it to someone who plans to play it for that kind of experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid game, especially given that it's currently in Early Access. There's an absolute ton of progression and ways for "numbers to go up" which I thoroughly enjoy. There's four player co-op as well (though I've found it very hard so far!) which is nice since I mostly play games with friends these days.I played during the demo/beta/before it launched period and had it on my wishlist with the intent to pick it up in due time. They also eliminated any form of FOMO (again, much like DRG) and I felt very confident in my purchase knowing that the devs really acknowledged and cared about their players and the long term success of their game. Looking forward to what the future holds for Inkbound! Also the story is neat it's getting weird it's sus I like it

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true gem and with another unique concept from the studio that brought us Monster Train. The game is a "Turn Based" RPG Roguelite  game, but it is not as turn based as one would think. Solo or Coop, there is only a Player's Turn that can do actions equal to Will (Action Points) and an Enemies' Turn where they carry out their Intents (Just like in Monster Train) all at once. This is really good in my opinion as with Turn Based Coop games the thing that takes up the most time is every single turn the game has to go through (Each Player Character, NPC, and Enemy NPC). There is little to no AFK time like in those games which is good.Combat wise it is great as you have your turn to do read the field find your most dangerous enemies based off their intents and figure out the most efficient way to take out the threats while trying to avoid damage. Some enemies will cast AoE attacks, Some will hit the whole Arena you fight in, and some will try to attack you directly (Indicated by Arrows drawn from enemy to you) which you have to mitigate by killing that target or finding some way to tank it.With the game being a Turn Based RPG Roguelite you have 8 Aspects (Classes) to choose from (4 at the start) that each play drastically differently with each having a Major Mechanic to play around and 3 Abilities that you will be able to Augment/Alter throughout the run to fit your desired build/playstyle. In addition the game has Vestiges (Items/Artifacts) that you can have up to 7 of that can influence your build/playstyle even further and do things like make "Anything you hit, inflict a stack of Bleed" to "On the start of your turn, Smite (Deal Magic Damage) to all enemies." and to add to this you can stack these effects with multiple copies of the Vestige (Item/Artifact). And on top of that Vestiges (Items/Artifacts) also carry these things called Sets which are like another system where if you have enough points in a set you can unlock bonuses like Extra Physical/Magic Damage etc. In addition there is a mechanic where you can find these grinding machines that allow you to destroy one of your Vestiges (Items/Artifacts) and you will be given double its Set Value Permanently for the run which frees up slots as you will be getting better ones later.All in all this game has a lot to offer and you will get well over your money's worth if you love RPGs and/or Roguelites. It is fun to play with friends as the game doesn't take forever to take turns like Baldur's Gate or Divinity Original Sin 2, etc. I cannot recommend this game enough and to all the reviews saying there isn't anything to do after unlocking all the Classes, it is literally a Roguelite game. You pretty much challenge yourself and try different things out.
