_childDocuments_.review: Kudos to Shiny Shoe for producing a brand-new style of roguelite tactical RPG. There's a lot here to like even as a solo player and I would highly recommend. I have a long list of pain points since I'm a grizzled roguelite veteran but don't let this discourage you from picking up and playing this great game!Pros:1. The vestige system takes some inspiration from Vivid Knight; When you sell off an item in a vestige set you get a permanent count towards set progression. This gives the player a fair amount of agency to optimize the synergy of their build in the future at the cost of damage. The game becomes extremely fun once you get a grasp of what each vestige set does and you figure out what are the best synergies to pair together.2. Combat encounters become complex to navigate especially at higher ranks. Each act contains its own modifier, bosses gain unique modifiers, and individual mobs spawn with unique modifiers.3. Combat is brutal at times if your build does not come together in time to scale in higher rank difficulties. Health can be used as a resource to get more powerful loot early to provide a foundation for future success.4. The trinket system is a fresh way to play each class. At the time of posting I have 50H all using a single character (Magma Miner) but having played every trinket as well as (almost) every difficulty. There is enough variety here that pushes you in different directions between each run.5. Players get to draft from a shared pool of skills (bindings) early on in the game that gives a direction on what build (vestige set) to work towards. There is a fair amount of variability when upgrading each binding to unlock powerful combos later into the game.6. Multiplayer co-op!Some noticeable cons which could be easy to fix:1. For as much story as there in the game it attempts to be told through multiple characters all at the same time and becomes a jumbled mess. Much of your first few runs will have you running through the Atheneum talking to various characters one after the other. You have to do very specific quests in order to unlock specific things (no spoilers) but it's not clear what is the 'main' quest that requires progression. It also is not clear what are the quests needed to unlock other characters. The unlock system seems far too contrived for this reason and should unlock more naturally.2. Ranking up difficulty is BRUTALLY time-consuming. Surely we can do better than introducing players to difficulty by making them play Rank 1-20 in sequence. It's quite honestly a waste of my time because there's a great game with a ton of replayability that doesn't need to gate my progress so linearly.3. Current build influences future options too much in the current patch in my opinion. If you are heavily into one build (vestige set) you are somewhat disincentivized from investing further into a set when you already have a full set bonus (8 of 8). In the mid-game this is a crucial way to make RNG favor the player to help them bring their build online but late-game this amounts to overkill as a single vertical trait isn't often powerful enough to carry you throughout a higher rank late-game.4. Enemy positioning and targeting can be downright frustrating. Perhaps the AI is sophisticated enough to know exactly how to position 1 unit away from being in range for an AOE attack but plenty of time is wasted by the player trying to figure out if they're bad at targeting or it's just not possible to hit both enemies. If there were some sort of option to allow the player to rotate through possible targets (optimized for AOE) and then allow them to fine-tune their movement it would be an incredible quality of life.5. Early-game fights in higher difficulties can be run ending. Battle 2 and 3 can be complete death traps if you choose the Hard Battle after having drafted a utility/defensive Binding or utility/defensive items/vestiges. This point of the game feels worse than it should given that the fights afterwards don't have the same sting.6. Early game builds are a coin flip. There is very little variety of choices to start with (current patch but being addressed in the next patch). As the devs have noticed, the limited starting points from a build drastically impact the branching decisions that one makes over the course of a run.7. Clicking on destructibles to pick up gold (kwillings) is a dumb mechanic. I'm sure I forgot to click on gold at some point since it is disguised as a random object in the surroundings. If gold was literally gold on the ground and it was picked up as I walked by it that would be fabulous. I also found out that in a Sea Breach event *sometimes* you'll find gold in a random alcove NOT immediately obvious on the character's screen. Lastly, when choosing paths between encounters anytime you're offered an event to speak to someone it should specify that what rewards you get other than potentially being able to progress the convoluted story. Please tell the player what kind of vault they will get and if they will Kwillings (Gold).8. The branching roguelite map somehow takes a step back here in favour of world-building. As a player, I should know how many encounters/paths am I away from the Carver and subsequently the Boss. This influences my decision on whether or not I visit an early Carver to heal or if I pick up a vestige that grants me rewards after X rooms of combat. This is not something the player should have to remember.9. Items disappearing on the ground after picking a branching path seems like a poorly designed mechanic. It is optimal to pick a path first (let's say a Vestige Collector) backtrack to your vestigial (item) draft, and then make a selection. It is also optimal to wait to use the Vestige Collector until AFTER combat (a held vestige is often better than a vestige set bonus) or after selecting your next path (Sea Breach, Encounter, Carver). Potions are a bit awkward as well because some potions allow you to drink them prior to combat (some should definitely be done as this is optimal) in order to let you pickup a potion/fish in your two-slot inventory. If you forget to juggle your potions and you begin combat, too bad the item dissolved away into the ground! For these I would encourage the ability to archive dropped vestiges so they can be rotated in/out of inventory or recycled at the vestige collector anytime while in the same act. For potions, instead of dropping it automatically when clicking on it the player should be given a prompt that their potion/fish inventory is full. If combat starts and I can see that on Turn 1 I need to use a potion (let's say +1 will reserve per turn or +10 crit chance) those effects should be applied immediately. I don't automatically know which Hard enemy is going to pop out of an encounter and in what positioning.10. The combat preview on enemy health bars could use some additional clarity. If I don't have any Will leftover but I want to figure out if a skill I have will defeat that enemy there isn't a way to know what the current HP of the enemy is without applying damage-over-time effects that trigger at the end of the enemy's turn. It's not even a question of my ability to do math to compare my binding damage to the enemy's health bar, sometimes you just can't know what the enemy's current health is.11. Later difficulty levels gain complexity by placing modifiers on a handful of regular enemy mobs on each turn. This is cumbersome to understand on Steam Deck. Some of these effects could use arrows drawn between the enemies. For example, support mobs will spawn and buff a character with a barrier (damage resist) or heal all allies on turn end. Some arrows would be helpful to make it obvious to the player that while the support mob doesn't do damage, it's probably wise to focus them down first. I'm not asking for overlapping arrows of different colors but instead some way to indicate this upon hovering over the skill that is being casted.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game to play with my friends as an interesting new roguelite with a cute, pleasant art style. For a week, while I played other games, I kept asking myself: "Why aren't I just playing Inkbound?" I really liked this game before the Vestige Set system, but after that system and everything that came with the Gods + Relics update, I fell absolutely in love. From the totally free battlepass, to the solo and group balance, to the plethora of both earn-able and purchasable cosmetics (using currency from the battlepass), to the surprisingly unique and varied vestiges and their sets, everything makes me want to play more both alone and with friends.I know I mentioned both a battlepass and cosmetics, but there is no way to spend money in-game at the time of this review- everything can be earned through gameplay, even cosmetics that released on previous battlepasses. If you like turn-based tactics and roguelite/likes to any meaningful degree, give this absolute gem a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to see some reaction gameplay and some honest first impressions, I did a let's play that I posted on YouTube, you can check it out here: This is pretty good as far MMOs go in my opinion, especially indie. I think if you like magical RPGs with fantasy themes, you will probably like this. I enjoyed the color and graphics, as well as the expansive skill and ability system, which compensates for the initial difficulty of the game. Don't expect an AAA production for an indie MMO, but do enjoy the effort given to the environment, story, and characters of this indie alternative to some of those big games. It is clear from the Steam page that they are working on fleshing out this game long term, noting a major update soon. I did notice a little bit of oddness in early access with lag, and the party system was not very active for me--though the co-op seemed functional, but the combat sequences and interaction went pretty mush undisturbed--plus I saw tons of players running around the library area. If you don't like rogue-likes, and you want everything to cost a million dollars to produce, then I guess maybe you won't like it, but even then you might because it's pretty good. I really like Inkbound and am happy with getting it.

_childDocuments_.review: Shiny Shoe does it again! While being set in a different genre, the fundamentals that made Monster Train a fantastic rogue-like are present here with the added bonus of being co-op! Playing with friends and family is a blast. Genuinely one of the first turn-based co-op games that I found fun to play with friends. It solves the issue of "waiting for the other person's turn" by letting you both take your turns at the same time, and it works wonderfully. Developers are involved with the community, already tons of content, and lots of system mechanics so the game feels fresh every time. You're given the freedom to explore builds and it feels great when you character is simply OP. If you liked Monster Train and aren't locked into the "deck-building" aesthetic of rogue-likes, you'll love this gameI am grateful for the developer's response to initial criticism. It is commendable of them in a world where game devs don't take much ownership for poorly received decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game that more about skill than meta progression or luck. It could feel like luck based in the beginning, but it is far from that. And usually it is not a one mistake but several that leads to that end.On a side note - kudos to developers for abandoning paid battle pass model in favor of cosmetic DLCs. I am not sure if I can remember a single other game where that happened, usually it is other way around, unfortunately. And, while there are seasons, none of the content is gone. _childDocuments_.review: The changes from the previous iteration of the beta to this are very poorly thought out.This game used to be centered around the player's ability to position themselves and conserve their resource in order to do so, while also using the resource to deal enough damage to outpace the shrinking arena. However, the vast majority of the enemies have been given an absurd amount of attacks that will just hit you no matter what you do, no matter where on the map you are, no matter how far you move, and this is overall unfun and unsatisfying.In addition the removal of several enemy mechanics that were fun to play around, such as enemies attacking in the middle of your turn, or enemies turning to do their large AOE attacks towards you whenever you hit them, these mechanics really made you balance your movement and combat in fun and interesting ways.Sadly the game is now basically just. "Man I hope I RNG into enough sustain items/upgrades to survive the unavoidable health tax that I will take from every other fight"Its important to note that these changes mainly affect singleplayer, as in multiplayer its significantly less taxing as the unavoidable damage is not only split up, but your overall ability to kill specific targets is significantly higher, and while I do LOVE playing this game in multiplayer, making the singleplayer experience significantly harder/less satisfying is not very healthy for the game.If you really wanted to add more unavoidable attacks to the game, presumably to up the difficulty level, they should only be given to fodder tier enemies that can be dealt with in the single turn they exist. Walking into the second fight of the game and having 2 enemies with 500 HP each both aim straight at you with an attack that will hit you no matter where on the map you are is not only not fair, but not fun at all to deal with.All the complains about the microtransactions are just not that important, and I'd much rather have the actual gameplay issues fixed, rather than to deal with those.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly lacks replayability for this type of game. Once you've unlocked all of the classes there really isn't much variance to gameplay as the main RNG difference between your runs then becomes "vestiges" (accessories that add stats or some modifiers) and the 2 extra skills you can use, but there are only a handful of extra skills.Unlocking additional cosmetics is not really interesting to me, as I'm not a huge fan of the game's aesthetics but YMMV. Unlocking vestiges is also not really exciting, as they are stat pads and minor modifiers. It's not like unlocking a new skill to use on your next run (like Fights in Tights Spaces or unlocking new monsters/spells in Shiny Shoe's other game, Monster Train). It's just unlocking stat changes and affixes, which is not really fun.Since the only progression in the game is unlocks, and trinkets (there are only 2 pages of trinkets, you get to pick just one, so unlocking more is not really important), the game gets stale since vestige unlocks aren't fun here.I did not try MP. They also have a leaderboard but I don't care to chase scores either. Again, up to you to decide if that's something you like or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a turn-based Hades with the graphics of Torchlight and strategy of Slay the Spire. If you like those games, you'll probably like this one. It's got a decent variety of aspects (classes), each with their own niche style of gameplay and unique abilities (called Bindings). Variety is found in drafting secondary bindings, augmenting and ascending your bindings, and picking up vestiges (items) along the way, making each run a little bit different.I have only played solo so far, but it's a big plus that you can play in a pickup group or with friends. In its current state, it could probably use a few more variety in bindings, perhaps some new augments and/or ascensions. If you've got enough resources to reroll your drafts, it's certainly very easy to get a godlike build.This has promise, and I've had a great experience so far. Apparently there used to be microtransactions so I'm glad that's not a thing I've had to experience. Keep the good stuff coming, devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic roguelite game for solo or a group of friends. The simultaneous turns makes the combat much faster than a traditional turn based game which is great. Currently there are 8 different classes I believe so you have a wide range of options to choose from. I wish the game had more classes/aspects or had a blank class where you drafted your starting skills to add more variety to starting loadouts.Apart from your chosen aspect and its skills you have Vestiges which are items that will give you passive benefits. These Vestiges belong to Sets, in most cases more than one set, and when you have enough of a set you get an additional bonuses fitting the theme of the set as you increase how many of the set you have. For example, collecting multiple Vestiges that apply posion to enemies allows you to increase your poison damage when you have 2 of the set. Once you get 3 of the set you get more poison damage and you do additional attack damage to poisoned targets. Most, but not all, Vestiges sets have more items apart of the set than the number of items required to get the max set bonus. For example, the bastion set bonuses maxes out when you have 3 items from the set and there are 15 items in the game that are included in the set.One complaint is that I wish there was an in game glossary or compendium. Having access to a list to see what all keywords do would be nice. Being able to easily see the different skills and their upgrades would be fantastic as well. (I believe the 1.0 update in April is including some sort of function that let's you see what upgrades skills can get and the upgrades affects, but I am not certain on this).Other than that the game is a blast. The Vestiges sets system really let's you pick a niche and build your character around it. This makes playing one character/aspect feel different each time you play them.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Not reviewing this would feel unfair to the devs.Amazing gameplay, very nice and colourful visuals. Like a lot of games of this genre, the story is nothing to write home about, but it more than compensates with the rest, my only gripe is the coop's balancing. The game can be played with a party of up to 4, but enemy HP grows WAY too much for every player added, don't get me wrong, runs can still be completed in multi, but it is A LOT harder and requires a lot more thinking behind each move.With 17h in, I haven't unlocked all characters yet and missing a lot of achievements / artifact unlocks, so for it's price, it's an incredible buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I only started playing post the major "Gods + Relics" update, but it based onthe patch notes, many of my favorite features were only just added, for context. The psuedo-"always online" requirement is interesting, albeit seems to have made it impossible to save/pause runs (maybe you can do it solo? I haven't tried). That is the only thing I'd like to see added, that isn't already on the road map. Excited to see how this develops as we head to release, but seems like it's a perfectly reasonable time to jump in!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most fun games that I have played in my life. From the same developers that brought my favourite deckbuilder Monster Train, we now have a new rogue-like with great mechanics and absurd build options.In Inkbound you play as the Needless, a sentient ink creature that was just born and is pushed into a cruel and dying world. The people of this world struggle to survive because their world, which is made up of books and stories, gets ruined by monsters and villains who take the ink from the book, basically erasing parts of the world. Your job is to defeat those villains and take back the ink and maybe find a more permanent solution to this problem. Or not.The gameplay is centered around turn-based combat. Your character will open up different locations during his run, alternating between a battle location and an event location. Battles happen in circular arenas with new enemies spawning in each round. Your character has access to five different skills, three are exclusive to his class, the other two are drafted from a random selection each run. Using an ability costst energy, some abilities cost more than one energy point. Additionally, everything except your most basic ability will have a cooldown, so you have to manage both cooldowns and energy costs. Movement however is free up to a specific limit and is not tied to energy. Each ability also has thre upgrade slots which you can fill with all kinds of improvements exclusive to each ability. Some upgrades simply improve damage or they might give you shields, apply debuffs and much more. There are some great choices here and upgrades are dividied into three different rarities, with the rarer ones usually having very strong effects.You can also "ascend" abilities. Each ability has three different ascensions, from which you can pick oe, usually after kiling a boss. These ascensions completely change how abilities work and help you to specialize your build. For example, one ascension could focus on pure physical damage while another instead reduces direct damage but adds fire to the attack.Additionally you can aquire a collection of passive items, which will usually increase your stats but also have all kinds of extra effects. Items are divided into different item sets and collecting enough items from the same set will give you an additional effect as long as you have items of this set. You have however an item limit, so you cannot hoard everything you find. After beating a boss, you have access to "shredders" which will destroy an item of your choice but give you double the points to the relevant item set. This allows players to think carefully which items they don't need but want to keep the special effect for the set.The game has 8 different classes, from which you start with 4 and the other four have to be unlocked through gameplay. Each class is incredibly unique not only in their abilities but also their passive effect, which changes completely your strategy. Each class also allows for a wide variety of builds, which is great and gives the player many hours of experimentation and gameplay.Just like Monster Train, the game expects you to break it. The base difficulty is hard and gets even harder with the extra challenge ranks, which add all kinds of nasty modifiers and challenge buffs to enemies. Understanding the game helps you to create insane builds that let you feel like a god. The high difficulty can be off putting for more casual players however that struggle with these types of games. The soundtrack is okay. Personally I liked the music of Monster Train better but it's alright. However, there is one thing that I should mention since it could bother people. The game was designed as an open multiplayer game in mind. This means you will have an open lobby with other players running around until you jump into an actual run. The game features a lot of cosmetics, emotes and other stuff that you usally wouldn't see in a rogue-like. You can play the game completely alone, even offline but the developers main focus is the online art and the game feels like this. If you are the kind of person that does not want to interact with other players at all, skip this. While you can play offline, you will notice how empty the actual lobby is, which was designed to hold many players at once but barely has any NPCs to interact with. If you like however to customize your character and show it off, then you will love this kind of thing.But of course, the main reason to buy this game should be the gameplay and I have to say, it is absolutely fantastic. And I still haven't tried out all the things the game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, nearly 30 hours so far in playing multiplayer with friends (and some solo) and I still feel like I'm far from discovering everything. In atypical-to-roguelites fashion, you have quests that give you some variety in how to play, for a while. The classes are fun and different, and their abilities have plenty of ascensions and augments so they don't feel too samey across several runs. The turn-to-turn "puzzle" of figuring out the right order of operations for you to balance your damage output versus staying out of harm's way at the end of it all, is very enjoyable. Not everything is perfect, but we have a fun game here that's certainly worth its price, though whether it's "just" worth it or WAY worth it may vary from person to person.Plenty to say about the gameplay: it's fun, if you are a fan of positional turn-based combat to begin with. There's a mild puzzle which I mentioned, which is the phase of your turn where you think about how you are going to utilize your movement, your cooldowns, and the orb spawns to reduce said cooldowns/provide extra movement, in order to get the most damage out while avoiding being hurt by the end of it. You are given all of the information for what each enemy will do on a turn, and it's up to you to choose how to react to this—I believe a strong factor in your success in this game is having good target selection. Not every enemy on a turn will be directly attacking you, so you may want to focus on the ones that are. If none are, you might just want to pick off the ones you know will be directly attacking sooner than others while removing yourself from in the way of their indicated attacks.As far as enemies go, they are all predictable. I've noticed that they behave the same way (aside from where precisely they move) most if not all of the time. Each enemy, from the turn they spawn, will perform the same order of actions on a loop, so part of learning how to improve as you scale to higher difficulties is recognizing which enemies are most dangerous right away and which aren't going to be for a couple turns, and acting accordingly. The biomes are similar. After enough experience, you can acquire the knowledge for what kinds of enemies are going to appear in a biome, similar to Isaac. If you think a specific biome's enemies or boss will be difficult for your current build/run/team composition to deal with, you have two other options for where to go. I think all of this works in favor of the player and is a positive for this game, because the difficulty would certainly spike if 6+ enemies could suddenly be attacking you directly and unavoidably in a way you couldn't have predicted, given the limitation on actions. Thankfully, that isn't the case here. Learning the enemies and their attack patterns is massive, especially as difficulties ramp up.All good roguelite players understand that there is skill to mitigating the randomness of your run or simply being good enough to make even subpar item combinations work. Plenty of people have complaints about the RNG of the game, but personally I believe that these players rely too much on tactics and not enough on strategy. Time will tell, though, and as of right now I feel confident that it is very much in the player's hands to decide whether they'll succeed or not.The audio is pretty good, but to me, not memorable. I don't mean to say that the audio or art or voice acting is poor, it just doesn't quite stand out. The background music feels just like background music and not something I'd ever pay attention to, the sound effects are quite good but lack an individualized punch to make you feel like you're engaging with something unique. They're just sounds and songs that play while you do stuff. I'm somebody who adores great soundtracks and loves when a game's audio compels me to keep playing it just to have my eyes and ears further blessed, but I don't see that in this. Thankfully, the mechanics and combat, which is the meat of playing the game for me, pulls it right back.The voice acting is great and I am glad they chose to go with it for a game like this, because is genuinely feels like anything less than every line being fully spoken wouldn't quite fit with the rest of the effort put into the non-gameplay aspects here. Huge props to voicing it all.The story is... I'll be honest, I don't really know, nor do I terribly care for it. The settings are nice to look at, and the characters say a lot of stuff, but I've gotten to the point where most of it seems like worldbuilding without a definition. We don't really know what's going on aside from the fact that we're a being who was inexplicably spawned out of the ink ocean and immediately serves the greater good of saving the world. It seems like a shame to me that they chose to dress up the narrative so much without actually having a story to tell. I find it to be entirely ignorable. The characters talk a lot about themselves and their surroundings, but you're never really drawn into anything greater than quests, which are fine, but can get annoying if you just want to unlock stuff but need to go through potentially several runs of just not getting what you need in order to complete their requirements. All-in-all, money well spent, and I see no point soon where me or my friends will stop playing it. Eventually we'll get there, because the runs do seem samey due to a lack of... well, variety content. What's there is good and what's there is enjoyable, but there could stand to be a lot more there. Six biomes (of which you go through two in a single run) and three final bosses just seems sad, I guess. Here's hoping to more content in the future, because more content along the lines of biomes, enemies, bosses, classes, draftable abilities, and vestiges, would do a lot for the game. Borrowing a page from Risk of Rain 2 and offering an alternative binding or two for each slot of an aspect's base kit that you can choose between would be stellar. I believe that the game needs that kind of choice in fundamental gameplay of aspects to keep things fresh and keep players experimenting.

_childDocuments_.review: As a reference, I started this after burning out on Monster Train.Pros-The graphics are good, -The concept is interesting,-There are easily enough variables to keep me invested for 40+ hours.Cons-There is no map of the home base meaning if there are new quests you spend minutes running around trying to find them.-Settings routinely set to different values after game closes.-The game is not as easy as some people say. There is a lot to learn, this becomes significantly detrimental if your builds during your earlier runs goes poorly.-Some builds are impossible, or so situationally dependent on a certain piece of gear that your run is done by the time you reach the first guardian if you're unlucky with drops.-Certain skills like Poison Vapor and Incendiary can be built to drag any character and nearly any build of vestiges to win the run. There is almost no other skill that can do that.-Stats like Crit are split effectively into two vestige lines (Precision, and Reaver.) This effectively means you have to collect or sacrifice twice the gear to run a crit build as both are absolutely necessary. I have failed runs with 10 points in precision and 1 point in Reaver, because it was the only piece of Reaver vestige that showed up in the whole run. I lost roughly 10 straight runs reaching just shy of level twenty before my first run win. The game automatically pushed me to rank 1 when this happened, and I likely lost another 4 or 5 runs in a row until I noticed this. I lose roughly 75% of my runs, with the overwhelming majority of my wins being Burn or Poison builds. I haven’t won a single crit run, same with spiked, frostbite, bleed, and smite. The game becomes disappointing when you realize the amount of luck you need to make the majority of the vestiges have any value.And that is what it is, luck. Nothing you can do. So many builds are dependent on one or two vestiges that you can build 6 amazing vestiges in, but without that 7th that operates the other 6 you sit there getting curb stomped by the boss.More than likely these cons mostly disappear when you play with a group. I did just solo and hated it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does the Hades-but-turn-based idea really well. Particularly, I enjoy the ranked system being an increasing difficulty challenge. In most rogue-likes we've gotten to the point where they get easier as you unlock and progress. There are minor things I'd want to see upgraded, like very minute positioning requirements that force you to make very very small movements back and forth to fit into an area with no damage. The main playable classes all look quite poor in my opinion, visually, and their gameplay is the only reason to pick them. There are cosmetics that kind of help remedy this, but at the end of the day I think  the visual style is great, but the playable character designs are visually poor. The final "villains" (what this game calls final bosses) are all somewhat tedious to fight and start to feel like a slog. I feel this is because nearly no fights require you to defeat it in certain ways, or interact with enemies to weaken others, etc. so when bosses do it, it suddenly feels like a loss of freedom and a constraint, and you no longer get to fight freely and optimally. With all that said, I highly recommend this game to fans of the genre

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of the negative reviews are focused on a few areas that I would like to address because, after 10 hours, I disagree with them. With that said, there are some valid criticisms that I will cover after. 1) Cash Shop/Battle PassPeople still live in a fantasy world where they believe that games are made for the sole enjoyment of the players. Games are created to make money, and cash shops are proven to make money, so developers will continue to add them to games. End of story. It's purely cosmetic, so I do not see anything wrong with developers trying to bring in additional cash to fund the development of the game. Am I a fan of cash shops? No of course not, but I am not going to stop myself from enjoying an otherwise fun game for the faint sense of justice from sticking it to the man.2)  Live Service/Always OnlineI love roguelikes. I would go as far as to say they are my favorite genre. Despite that, I eventually hit a wall where I have unlocked everything, and simply ask myself "what is the point in another run?". The idea that this game might have a steady flow of content that I can experience with others is actually a plus for me. Unless someone lives in a country that limits their access to internet, I am still baffled that people care when games require internet access. 3) Unavoidable damageI don't really understand what people want here. They want to be able to avoid every attack? They are upset that some areas are a DPS race? They don't like having to use defensive options? This approach has been common in the roguelike genre since...forever, so I am not sure what the issue here is. Unironically, I feel like this could be summed up with "git gud". With those out of the way, I want to highlight some actual criticisms that I have with the game:1) Balance There are some skills in this game that are absolutely broken (burn), and others that are entirely useless (frostbite). Build diversity and viability in a roguelike is key in replayability, but right now the game is just not in that state. Hopefully this gets ironed out with time. 2) Story and characters Entirely too boring. I do not feel connected to the cast whatsoever. They are a vehicle for me to obtain and hand in quests, and that is all. I tried reading the dialogue, but now just skip through it since every quest boils down to "we need this from this place and then you get this artifact". There are a ton of characters in the hub, and I just do not gaf about any of them. 3) Art/GraphicsNot a fan of the aesthetic. It feels extremely dated. I feel as though they might have benefitted from going a more stylized route, since the graphics are....bad. Now that the negatives are out of the way, I want to call out why I am giving this game a positive review, and it is as simple as this. It is fun as hell. I love tactical turned based games, and I love roguelikes. If you do too, you will probably like this game. The combat could use some tweaks and balances, but overall it has a great foundation. I wish this game nothing but success, because I really think they have something unique and scalable. I will definitely be checking back in to see where they take it.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Train devs know how to make a pretty competent roguelite at this point. This one has an interesting topdown perspective for the combat, and it kind of feels like a turn-based Hades. Allows the player a lot of freedom in executing their movement and abilities on their turn, and you have to prioritize not having your character stand where impending attacks are going to be when the enemy takes its turn. Some of the classes (Clairvoyant in particular is fun - plays like a slightly deeper version of Orianna from League of Legends where the ball and its vectors/landing spots are the medium for all its abilities to act) are really neat and you can do some cool builds on. Some of them end up feeling pretty straightforward though and sometimes the runs can blend together because you're picking the same items or abilities that feel like they're universally good.I think a deeper item pool and more abilities makes this one a really solid play in the future. For now it's still a little early but I've already gotten a fair number of hours out of it. There's some good creativity on display and the daily challenges have been surprisingly enjoyable with actually impactful modifiers. I can recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real gem of a roguelike with seemingly endless replayability.As far as the game itself, I would say the combat gameplay has a lot in common with 'Into the Breach,' though not nearly as rigid and unforgiving, as well as typical turn-based RPG combat (Divinity, etc.). The run structure, build diversity, and even art direction feel very reminiscent of Hades. The build diversity of this game is extensive, and despite what some may say, nearly any style is viable, as long as you have synergy. There are definitely some absolutely broken builds, which can, at times, make the game feel trivial, but the RNG nature of in-run items and upgrades make it hard to replicate a style 100% (which I think is a good thing!).It should be noted that this is the kind of early access game that is always changing. This isn't to say it doesn't feel like a complete game, it absolutely does, but rather that pretty major features and gameplay mechanics are semi-regularly added or changed, making it feel at times like an entirely new game. The tweaks and changes have  had a knack for fixing issues that weren't even that apparent until you see what the game feels like without them, so any lamentation over what was lost is quickly replaced by excitement over what has replaced it.  I do think this game is better than it has ever been, though I have loved each iteration.Tldr, This game is a steal even at full price, very creative, surprising depth, super-engaged devs.  If you love tactical RPGs and/or roguelikes, then you will love this.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a beta tester but life got busy so this is my first time playing in a few months and I'm really enjoying it! _childDocuments_.review: Game is really good. You get rewarded by planning your moves and focus on your character building. Most of the bad reviews right now are made because of the cash shop, and while I totally understand where this come from, keep in mind that to get a game online in 2023 you have to be able to sustain a regular income of money. But please, before complaining :- The game is <20€.- If you play regularly, and I don't mean intense gameplay (the levels in the battle pass are really fast) and IF they keep being as generous as they are right now with the currency, if you play 2 battlepass you will be able to buy the next one for free, and then won't need spending a penny ever again to get it, or you can spend ~3€ once the pass done to buy it. Yes, it is FOMO. Yes, it's an early access. But i'd rather pay that way for good game made by a small company than...- AAA studios nowadays release unfinished games for 70€, games that are artificially extended with repetitive task, boring gameplay and online mandatory for a game you can only play solo, and still they will put battlepass, cash shop and a lot of cut content as later DLC and are taking more positive feedback than this.- The cash shop is not intrusive as some reviews are telling. There is a small button on the bottom of your screen, next to other character/quests/options icons. If there are more that I missed, maybe. But if I missed it, maybe it's not as intrusive. I sincerely believe the game will age like fine wine. Right now, as an early access, game is already full of content.Give Inkbound a go. At least if you don't enjoy it, there is no 2hours long tutorial so you can't refund once you get a grip of the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be clear, I've played Inkbound since the early access and the early sneak peeks. I adored the game back then and thought it was the right combination of fun, random, and tactics. Ever since the vestige change and the marked modifications to balance; I find that I can't even enjoy a casual playthrough anymore.If I wind up with the right concoction of vestiges, it's a breeze. If I run into a grouping of enemies that simply can't be overcome with the luck I had in a given dive, there was no counterplay for me to explore or attempt. You're either fiercely overpowered (and with far less frequency than originally possible) or slowly grinding away to wasted time and frustration. The aspect designs are wonderful, the variance in gameplay is often times exciting since you get to try new things. But the current balance is just simply far too overtuned. I come back every now and then to see if things have gotten better, and as I have for the past few times, I leave scorned and feeling like I should have just played something else.There's challenge, and then there's the amalgamation of RNG intermingled with more RNG finally topped with another dash of RNG before spraying it with a heavy mist of RNG. I want to feel accomplished for overcoming a tough situation, not thanking my lucky stars I got the right vestiges early enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a superb game loop. It gives you more control over the builds YOU want to make even though it's a roguelike. Turn based combat is fast and fun, but complex and deep. For that I recommend it.Where this game fails miserably is the overarching narrative. All the dialogs look the same: take one of the made up words: "inkbound", "bindless", "needless", "binders" add some empty phrase, like "were here for centuries" and finish up with "it's not what it seems" to add mistery. It doesn't help that the only time you speak as a character, you speak in weird symbols (that player is expected to decode himself?). The narrative is obfuscated for no reason and there's no reason for me to want to understand it. I feel sorry for the amazing voice actors and character designers to do such a good job and then be put in such a poorly written story....

_childDocuments_.review: After knowing they dropped the in-game monetisation(the reason that I gave up on this game in the first place), I bought it straight away.I don't think I had played any turned based rougelite game and this game is my first. _childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun roguelike with deep buildcrafting and unique character abilities! I loved unlocking the different characters and mastering the item set bonuses. I played exclusively Solo and for the most part once you start to understand the combat mechanics it becomes MUCH easier of a game. The "Inkwell Dive" Rank system adds difficult modifiers into the equation, so those looking for a more difficult experience will find it there.The only aspect that hurts this game is the Quests and Story which are repetitive, long, and requires a lot of restarting for efficiency. I can't count the amount of times I had to restart a run with a great build because it required me to talk to a character in another "Book". The Story really picks up at the end of the game and is very interesting, however it took a lot of time, restarting, and frustration to get there. Overall I enjoyed my time with it and am looking forward to mastering the higher difficulties!

_childDocuments_.review: well, I really like never write reviews, but this game just deserves it.I love:the different archetypes you can playthe rising challenge of the deep dives (the mode you rise a rank and face off more and more challenging affixes)the daily challenge dives with funny setupsthe great way to play solo OR in a groupthe wild setups through bindings and their ascensionsthe vast amount of items and the new item set systemthe relics that can change the way, how you playand of course the possibility of broken combinationsthe soundtrack is neat, I like the graphics and the humour.In short: I really can recommend this to everyone liking roguelikes, broken builds and/or turn based battles.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reluctant thumbs down.The game has a decent core with the potential to be an enjoyable turn-based tactical roguelite, but fails to deliver. As it currently stands, there is no real tactical choice or player agency. You either memorize the correct route/choices and win, or you try to play it your way and lose.A good roguelite will let the player figure out how to win with a randomized assortment of upgrades. Inkbound instead forces you to save currency to make sure you re-roll the "correct" upgrades, thus completely negating the point of a roguelite in the first place.The "tactical battle" layer of the game isn't tactical, and it's completely subservient to the roguelite progression. The battles are just boring stat-checks without engaging tactics. The game is won or lost entirely on the decisions/RNG you get inbetween fights, not based on the battles themselves. Once you get to the battle you either win or lose based on your stats when you went in, not based on in-battle play.

_childDocuments_.review: I love it. It took me a few hours to lock it in, but yeah, I love it.It's not as easily approachable as Monster Train was, but I also very much loved Monster Train, so I wanted to give this a go. Seriously, it's going to take a few runs to "get it", but once you do, if you like rogue-lites, TBS, and Monster Train, you're going to like Inkbound.There's only one negative, and that's the quest system can be unclear on what you're supposed to be doing sometimes. For example, there's a questline where you're supposed to bind a book with a Birdie and I'm like, "What the heck does that mean?" Yeah, one of the end of run bosses is a giant bird. Duh. But I figured this out completely by accident. But if they firm this up a little better over time, I think it's a minor quibble.As a pro-tip, When working on unlocking everything, there's an icon on the bindings and upgrades to show you the ones you haven't chosen yet. It took about 15 to 20 hours of gameplay before I noticed this. I keep having to scroll through the awful quest book to look every time I got to an upgrade. Yeah, it was there the whole time. So they thought of things, they just didn't make it clear they thought of it.That's the Inkbound experience. You're knowledge of the genre will get you up and running pretty fast, and then you'll eventually figure everything else out. I'd say half of this playtime was fumbling around getting better and better at the game. OH, and there's a challenge rating for the Aspects (Characters) you can choose from at the beginning. Choose the Magma Miner. Trust me. It's just easier to learn the game with that character. Once you got it down, try the others.Anyway, YES, buy this game :) It's REALLY fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun, albeit super tough, rogue-lite.  The change from the demo where direct attacks aren't able to be outrunned has made it supremely hard (I'm yet to win a run out of about 6 or 7 so far, whereas in the demo I never failed one), but at least it's not an absolute steamroll.A lot of reviews mention the MTX & Battlepass being available the second the game hit early access, which I semi agree with, it's never really the best when a game that's not even fully developed & released, and is fairly buggy (which thankfully Inkbound isn't, that I've seen at least) has a fully complete working in-game shop, but comparing to some other games the MTX and Battlepass is extremely unintrusive & cosmetic only.  You won't get better at the game, or even have xp boosts or anything for buying anything from the store, nor will you get popups non-stop saying "wow you could have earned these wings if you paid for our battlepass!!", and it's not asking you to pay $20 for a single item piece while charging AAA prices for the base game *coughlastepochcough*.The progression is great, you get a boatload of quests you can complete whenever, and that'll unlock relic-style items that can show up in future runs, as well as there being a good amount of skills, that have multiple augments, and even ways to upgrade them to act differently (you can make a spell either more AoE focused, or more single target focused, or make a leap slam skill set enemies on fire, or daze them so they deal reduced damage).Definitely a recommend, not an insane price for an early access game, lots of content to get through, fairly difficult, and as long as they don't put classes, skills, relics, or anything like that in the battlepass then that's a big plus for me.Edit: As much as I praised it originally in the review, they've had a patch that's MAJORLY changed how the game plays, and it's for the worse.  Before this patch you could slightly move and use a skill, sort of stutter-stepping around the place, which was mechanically hard to do, so why not reward us with the ability to do it?  Not only that but you could use Will (Action Points) to move further than normal, but they've completely changed that.  Now you get a set amount of movement, and that's it, you can't spend extra Will to move, which is an awful change, what happens if we've got spare Will, but no movement left & aren't in range to hit enemies?With the movement being changed and made worse in such a massive way it worries me that no part of the game is off-limits to these sorts of changes, so probably wait until full release to pick it up, and hopefully by then they'll have stopped with the major changes that make the game feel worse to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Great gameplay, solid art, quest design is a bit ♥♥♥♥, music's fine, thumbs up, blah blah blah, but... I just need to rant for a bit.About half of the NPCs you'll meet are generally inoffensive, if sometimes a bit obnoxious - some are even neutral or pleasant to talk to! The other half, though, are INFURIATING BEYOND DESCRIPTION. They will NEVER tell you ANYTHING about what's going on, INCESSANTLY act demeaning and disrespectful to you, and INSTANTLY blame you whenever ANYTHING goes wrong in your general proximity. This might not rankle me so much if I had either ANY idea what the results of my actions in game would be before I did them, or ANY alternative option to take besides just... not progressing the main storyline at all. This ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game will pretty much repeatedly have a character tell you (very rudely) what to do next, then once you do it it'll give you another objective in that same quest chain, and then once you do that it'll have you go back to that same first character so they can tell you what a stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dimwit you are for doing such an idiotic thing and that you should just go off and die in some hole so you won't get in the way of the (generally useless) real smart people solving problems. And that's the end of the quest. Nice job dumbass.This is exacerbated by the plot already having chronic DLC-itis despite the game not even being released - characters will sometimes violently whiplash in mood between runs as they bounce between different questlines, and I still have no bloody idea what's actually going on in the story - there's a purple ink dude and a cyborg guy and a weird gardener lady and an incredibly pretentious old man and the titular inkbound who never actually shows up or does anything besides hide in their room and throw a tantrum when you knock on their door but is supposedly working very hard on... something, because... something is wrong... somewhere... There's an ocean of ink involved... and some kind of weird shapeshifter blob monster too...I am still unbelievably pissed that a quest had a dude tell me, (Spoilers, but who even cares,) "Hey, can you go get that traumatized orphan's favorite doll for me? I just need to borrow it for a bit, I promise." And then after you give it to him, he fusses with it for a bit, then suddenly stops and refuses to acknowledge it ever existed without giving it back. I don't even know what the point of that whole thing was!And then MULTIPLE other characters tell YOU "Hey, that was kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, taking that girl's doll from her. Why would you do that?" Like you had any bloody agency in the matter! You literally saw HIM tell me to do it and say he would give it back, why are you mad at ME?So yeah. Fun game, but I don't think I have ever hated a fictional character the way I hate some of this game's NPCs, and upon finally completing all the available story (as far as I can tell) and basically getting "I hate you, your efforts to help are pathetic and actively detrimental, and I'm going to try to have you executed, bye." As my reward, I may have lost a wee bit of my temper. Still a good game, but... Grrr.

_childDocuments_.review: 💠💠 Inkbound is a decent rogue-like game. You go into various mini-worlds/dungeons and you defeat minions and bosses. Simple enough! The game offers in-game purchases and seasonal awards but they're mostly all just cosmetic save a few titles and whatnot. Aside from the rogue-like dungeon progression and picking up a variety of skills and buffs along the way, this game had fun and funny tones to it!✅✅Granted I only played for a few short hours, I did enjoy *SOME* aspects of the game. Creating your character is always a fun part of any video game I play, and this game had some decent options. Not many, mind you, but still decent. Editing placement of various facial symbols and designs was in-depth as well! I enjoyed the artistry, paint-like graphics of the game. It was new and something I don't recall ever having seen in other games before so that was a nice change of pace!⛔⛔After having played for three hours, I definitively knew that the game wasn't for me. The game itself wasn't "horrible", but I found that I couldn't really find many "pros" to write down in my review here. The game was next to impossible to party up with anyone. Nearly the entire time I was in the main lobby area of the game (before you went in to the dungeons, or "worlds"), I was attempting to queue for teams. I searched and searched and couldn't find anyone willing to join up with me. Aside from the lack of a multiplayer community, the actual game was difficult to say the least. I could not for the life of me get past the second "world" after you beat the final boss in your first round of battles. The difficulty spiked heavily, thus my need for team mates.  I tried all variations of strategies, and various classes, which are switched through the aspects apparatus in the game. No matter how hard I tried, or what new abilities I found in each run, I couldn't get further. ❇️❇️ Not a game I would try again. It was a shame because I had looked forward to buying it and playing it for some time now and I waited for it to go on sale to invest in. Of course, everyone knows that all of us gamers have our own opinions. Take what I've said with a grain of salt of course. Happy gaming all!

_childDocuments_.review: The game has improved drastically since its early access release. In game micro-transactions (premium currency, battle passes) are now gone. All cosmetics were placed into a Vault, which you can buy from by leveling up your seasonal level and gaining a currency (which can be farmed seemingly infinitely past 100). Additionally, every time you kill a boss, you have a small chance to gain a random item from the Vault. The battle pass was replaced by Victory Road, which is akin to a "to do" list, but you get rewarded a cosmetic at certain threshold. It is seasonal, but the moment the season ends, the rewards from it gets thrown into the Vault. Monetization aside, the gameplay has changed a bit too. Movement is different: you can no longer abuse the radius around you to move for free slightly after every action. Now you have a set amount of movement points to use each turn. Vestiges have set effects and can be dismantled at shrines to get permanent set points. I find the new characters interesting as well.The only thing that's left that's negative for me is the lack sorting/categorizing feature for the Vault and the inability to see what the seasonal level rewards are outside the next one. That aside, it's a visually pleasing and fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit overwhelming and confusing at first with a lot of narrative elements I just cannot imagine caring about, overall its a fun package and despite the limited options and enemy variety you definitely don't feel like any run is like the last. The 3D isometric turn based gameplay uses movement within a defined area as part of your turn and most of the gameplay is about playing out your abilities, moving around, and then letting the enemy have their turn in the way that deals the least damage to you but its hard to explain without seeing it or doing it yourself - definitely not as dull as it sounds.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good coop roguelite. I'm not sure if I would want to play solo, as having multiple characters on the board makes it a lot more strategic and interesting.A few things to note:-There is a lot of dialog IF YOU WANT. You can skip it and quests get completed rather passively.-There is NO metaprogression.-There are class unlocks that take a reasonable amount of time... I'm 17 hours in and haven't unlocked the last one.-You can take a single trinket into each run that gives a small boost.-There are a reasonable amount of cosmetics if you care about this stuff.The game is easy at the start until you "rank up" and it gets a bit more difficult, but I didn't mind the easy phase like I usually do... it was fun to find the OP builds and wreck things. It felt good, and ranking up felt like good progression in conjunction with the quests getting completed.This was definitely a sleeper hit for me. Didn't expect it to be as good as it is.

_childDocuments_.review: When Inkbound’s early access 0.1.0 dropped, I put in plenty of hours both in solo and multiplayer. First impression, I was worried about the game’s future. Unbalanced characters, unbalanced difficulty, a FOMO rotating cash shop, a battle pass, an always online connection needed. It was like they wanted to check every box for what is trending in gaming, and what is killing gaming. I gave up and uninstalled the game.Time went on. Then one day I saw in my steam library of “What’s New” Inkbound patch 0.2.0. I morbidly took a gander at the notes. Color me surprised! The developers started to unchecked a majority of those pesky boxes. There was a re-balance to characters and encounters. They even added things to make the game more interesting. I wouldn’t jump with joy just yet, but I will give the developers their dues. Nice work! Please keep this positive momentum going. Would I recommend getting into Inkbound right now? Let me pose a question to you. Do you want to experience an incomplete game? Are you fine with spending money on an incomplete game to which god only knows when it will truly be done? Are you going to be fine with certain ‘standard’ features still missing? I already paid for it and I’m finally enjoying my time with Inkbound. Though it still has a long road ahead of itself. Here is hoping it doesn’t trip in fall.

_childDocuments_.review: "Roguelike" The GameEdit:Now that I have more hours in this game I can put a bit more of my opinions here.Its been a long time since Ive got insta-hooked on a game and this is even rarer cause I knew nothing on it going in other than "colorful roguelike from Monster Train devs".Game feels like it did its research and picked up a lot of good ideas from other games to combine something more than the sum of its parts.Visuals, camera perspective, choices between combat and story-telling and narrative progression is very reminiscing of Hades.Charcters and Cards/abillites very Slay the Spire (but what turn based roguelike isnt?) And have a unique spin on its own (unless I missed the roguelike that it inspires from).And the "MMO" aspect and (the elephant in the room) monetezation is very much like TemTem.Now, the monetezation is why I see a lot of negative reviews here and frankly I dont think its justified. In this day in age I think season pass and cosmetic microtransactions are just the nature of the beast.Sure, it would have been great that game companies would have ban this practice, but its far easier to expect for world peace.With that in mind, the season pass is very cheap (and half refunds itself for the next one) totally optional and does not impelment anything game releated other than to flaunt a bit, and your charcters are not humanoid and detailed like in big name MMOs that putting money on this aspect does not invoke much FOMO and is not predatory IMO.To me, its more towards supporting the game and ita active development which I already want to see more of!So dont be swade by negative reviews towards this aspect, only if its gameplay critical and the likes.The devs put a lot of love here and its shown (Esepcially for an Early Access!)All in all, this game is beautiful, voiced act in a lot of places, amazing art style, highly replayable and addicting gameloop, solo fun, co op is a big bonus, and the amount that there is in here is way more than the 0.1.0 version tag they put in the top bar.Im excitied for the future of this game very much.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkbound is excellent. It is a lovely mix of deck building and turn based action RPGthat I would not have purchased if the Micro Transactions were still present.Inbound is a run based "deck builder" in which you draft abilities and items. It features a hub you return to after each run with NPCs that flesh out the world with lore and provide additional goals for unlocking additional stuff to find. In this way it feels a lot like Hades. However, it features turn based combat that allowsfor planning synergies between group members or tactical handling if you are solo. A build is a combination of your base class/skills, two drafted abilities, and a series of items that provide passive benefits. These items are part of sets which when combined provide additional benefits. These sets are what really stands out to me and I really enjoy it.To explain, each item is a part of one or more sets. Each set has a distinct bonus that grows in power as you collect items that belong to that set. However, there are opportunities during the run in which you can discard an item while retaining the sets that it is a part of. Since inventory is limited this adds an extra layer to the strategy. For example, when drafting a new item I might pick something exclusively for the sets it is a part of. I might also find myself asking "Which items have effects I can live without to make room for the stuff I will get during the next act". This system is one of the big ways Inkbound sets itself apart and, as noted above, I really enjoy the way it does so.Lastly, I want to touch on the monetization. Games are expensive to make and I believe the industry needs additional routes to support the studios for people that have the means to do so. However, the MTX (Micro Transaction) model that many games are adopting from the mobile market is not okay. They are designed to make people more willing to purchase something. Inbound recently removed all of the MTX in favor of support pack "DLC". This means you can still throw extra support to the studio without all of the trickery the MTX systems use to convince you of a purchase. Whether it was a simple marketing ploy or not, I hope the feedback from players both in terms of sales and sentiment is one that moves the needle across the industry. We as consumers should be open to additional funding for games, but it is also important we try and show the industry that it can be supported without the trickeryand exploitative systems used in those MTX models. This patch led to three sales of the game (myself, and the two others in my regular gaming group). After spending the entire weekend playing it and having a blast while doing so, I plan to buy one of the supporter pack "DLCs" because voting with my wallet and writing this review will hopefully move that needle just a little bit.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is interesting and I would strongly recommend the game based on its actual gameplay loop. There is great fun to be had with it, and its complexity is sufficient to keep one entertained for many hours.The story, however, is thinly spread and uninteresting and the characters are so annoying that they are actively detrimental to the experience. Most are very one-dimensional and condescending and their stories are really not fleshed out (they are more like outlines for what should have been developed into actual stories). The gatekeeper is patronizing, the carver is needlessly aggressive, the counselor's lack of self confidence (copying Dusa from Hades much?) while she is called amazing by the stigmatist becomes old really fast, and so on. Pretty much the only characters I did not feel grated by were the stigmatist and Nib & Bin. The main mystery of what is actually happening and why has little emotional impact, partially because of the unlikable characters. I trudged along the unrewarding questlines hoping there would come a point where I actually care for them, but ended up feeling utterly unrewarded. Another reason for my disappointment is that they certainly try to tackle deeper themes such as altruism, duty, emotional manipulation or child neglect, but the superficial treatment makes the attempt fall flat. I feel it would have been better if they had stuck with a smaller cast and told a more focused story.As a final grab bag of complaints: Tldr: the gameplay is nice, but it mixed with a very unsatisfying narrative experience.

_childDocuments_.review: After the awesomesauce of the Devs first game, I was really really hoping for another Monster Train, even if it was to be in a slightly different rogue-ish genre.  This isn't it, at least not right now (I tried 7/23, still very Early Access).Remember Quest 64, or another old RPG (or MMO) when 3D was new and fancy?  Running around in a circle field to position yourself during your turn, then stopping to choose what spell to cast?  This is that, but stuffed into a multiplayer rogue-like package. Free roam movement before stopping to use abilities, then ending your turn outside of the enemy attack zones.  The 'free roam' movement really seems to slow things down more than make them enjoyable (you have to place your characters juuuust so to make abilities hit right while minimizing movement points used), and multiplayer bogs things down even more so.  On top of this, the multiplayer focus really doesn't do it for me, especially when devs really seem to want to focus on it simply to sell cosmetics (yes.... there's already a cosmetic BattlePass.)With a *lot* of love Inkbound might be a fine game someday, and I do hope it makes it there.  I won't write off the game fully, out of my love for their first well polished hit (Oh Monster Train, how I adore thee).  Unfortunately, without a great deal of care and possibly a few redesigns, I doubt that this will be a game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I was eager to playtest this game after the Nextfest demo. I recieved a copy for free due to playtesting and I'm playing it now.My only gripe with the game is the same gripe I had when I played it during playtesting - unavoidable auto attacks. I never once thought this was a good idea and was vocal about it. These still remain to this day.There is nothing tactically engaging about soaking up unavoidable damage every round from multiple sources. Some things - like bosses - could have unavoidable autoattacks. The problem comes when you have 5+ sources of unavoidable damage incoming with the next wave spawning more.Simply, this needs to be toned down. You've increased HP from 20 to 50, with healing offered after every combat. If that doesn't tell you the damage is too damn high, I don't know what will.At this point, monster HP seems to be an arbitrary number as well. When did normal mobs have 5k hp? With certain book modifiers, this can honestly become a bit insane with a mobs staying power.This game was loved when damage was dodgeable with proper positioning, HP was low but manageable, and mobs actually died from a round of attacks.Somewhere along the line, this game lost that spark. It's what lead me to put this game down for a while and stop participating in live streams. Things change but this fighting system does not even resemble what it was when I first found the game.I personally don't mind the monitization in this game. I find it fair, especially as you get more than enough currency to buy the next battlepass if you complete this one. Especially as its non game defining, cosmetic items.But if things are not addressed in the combat system, I fear you may not have a playerbase by the time this is out of early access. People want a fair challemge, not the feeling of putting their ♥♥♥♥ in a doorway and slamming a door.

_childDocuments_.review: With over 100 hours of Monster Train logged on multiple platforms, it saddens me greatly to write this negative review: I really had high hopes for Shiny Shoe's next game!The core gameplay of Inkbound is promising, channeling both Transistor and Slay the Spire in a satisfying gameplay loop. The different classes offer cool building strategies, and it's really enjoyable to craft a devastating build with the tools the game gives you. This is hands down the best thing about Inkbound, and it's disappointing that everything else gets in the way of gameplay, as opposed to enhancing it.The game's Hub feels like somebody's first attempt at an MMO/service game, in the sense that it clutters the UI, but doesn't actually add anything to the core experience. I think Inkbound is an odd choice of game for some co-op sessions with your friends, but perhaps I'm wrong. Regardless, Inkbound is a bit of a niche title with an uncertain lifespan, so the developer is taking a risk with this approach: few things are as discouraging as an empty, lifeless Hub.The art direction is decent enough, although the 3D art is a little basic, and can't hold a candle to the great 2D art. The serious problem comes chiefly from the very unexpected Battlepass system, which means you need to pay some money and grind like hell to get any of the decent character customisation options. Now I get that Shiny Shoe needs to keep the lights on. What I can't get behind is the FOMO of timed content and the quantity-over-quality flood of cosmetics.Again, besides the gameplay, everything else feels like an afterthought. You're going to click through dialogues overloaded with exposition and unnecessary terminology, just to get your XP rewards for quests you also didn't bother reading. Let's face it, this is not Hades, and I can't possibly think of anyone playing this for the witty dialogues and character development. Just click through text, and go pound on monsters: at least that's enjoyable.I'll keep this short: Inkbound is much, much less than the sum of its parts. It feels unfocused, as if it attempting–and failing–to be different things to different people. I am aware the game is in early access at the time of writing this, but I can't imagine a universe where the final product compares to the laser-focused, zero-bloat offering that is Monster Train.

_childDocuments_.review: First let me give a clarification on some of these negative reviews as I was confused how anyone could rate this game badly. Almost all of them are complaining about micro-transactions/season pass which I was extremely confused about because it's a cosmetic only shop.ALL Micro-transactions and season pass are 100% COSMETIC ONLY. There are no annoying pop ups, no menus telling you to buy the shop currency (shinies). Everything is in the background the only time any of the menus pop up is when you are getting free cosmetics from the FREE track on the battle pass, it's very behind the scenes, and completely optional. There is no pay to win, there is no pay to unlock characters, there is no pay to unlocks skills, or powerups, It is PURELY ethical and cosmetic. Beyond that there were a couple people saying the balancing is off or the game is too difficult but I have already won complete runs with 3 of the 5 characters (There will be 10 total eventually) and I think I've only done 5 runs so far so I've won more than half while still learning new mechanics and synergies. In addition this game is a Roguelike, like every other Roguelike you will unlock additional powerups as you progress thru the quests and the storyline, these offer new build synergies and I'm sure will offer more power as you continue to unlock them. So for anyone struggling early I would suggest you continue forward and try to unlock more items that will help your builds feel complete and add synergy giving you an easier time at completing runs. OK on to the much shorter review of the actual game. Overall - 9/10 Fantastic game, unique take on turn based combat mechanics, art style is really well done I don't usually like cartoony styled games but this has a vibe and a theme and does a fantastic job of creating a original world and characters. Voice acting is incomplete at the moment as the game is in early access but every character with voice acting and fully fleshed out dialogue is a 10/10 the narrator is also really good. Music is original and well done, sound effects are great. The characters are really well done some one of a kind classes that feel like a ton of work was put it to make them stand out from one another and seem extremely well balanced for an early access game. Tons and tons of achievements, quests and unlocks, the only reason I don't give it a 10/10 is it's still early access and some things are not 100% complete. Great game which is only going to get better over time, 100% recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright singleplayer game, instantly want to turn that voice acting OFF. If you like the new age of turn-based games (Slay The Spire, Into the Breach) where you're solving a sometimes cryptic order of operations I can recommend. But I bought this for co-op. Scaling is utterly broken for co-op breaking most synergies you would be use to from singleplayer such as "on kill do X". Normally trash mobs would have something like 10 hp and you can dome them with one hit, in co-op they're marching around with upwards of 100 hp robbing you of a lot of the traditional thinking you would employ in this generation of turn-based RPGs. Imagine Gremlin Leader elite from Slay The Spire but all the gremlins he summons are 50 hp. Yeah there are 4 of you but you will never feel like you're making a difference the co-op scaling is just too insane.For a better co-op roguelite experience go play Hellcard instead, they're patching out those annoying modifiers on endless as we speak.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game, there's a lot that's good about it, but in the end there's just not enough variety. In many ways it's modeled after Hades but with a different combat system. The difference is it's too easy to win a run. You will accomplish this fairly quickly. Then there's nothing to do but keep repeating it over and over again... literally you're given a quest that says just do the thing you just did 3 more times. Okay, now 5 more times. The gameplay just isn't engaging enough for that to be fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Game was great before 1.0. The RNG was huge factor in going through the run, or not, but it was manageable and you could try different builds. I had no problem finishing runs and going through first chapter or two, depending on the build. Now, they buffed the enemies, nerfed sets and made the first chapter much more harder. Difference is now I struggle to even get first boss down, cause in first chapter its super rare to get your build finished, or even started, due to the RNG nature of the game and runs. Previously the game was challenging, but fun, now it's tryhard and very not fun. I don't see why would devs go this direction. Are there no casual players playing this game? Or do they want to only appeal to the hardcore audience that get to level 500+ every season?
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: I wish this game was good. When you lose it feels out of your control entirely. When you win it feels like you high rolled and no amount of misplaying would have changed the outcome. Enemies that do direct damage have unlimited range even though you don't on almost any ability for any character. Random effects as difficulty scales up are annoying to keep track of rather than fun or intuitive. Monster train will always have my love, but this game leave so much to be desired. 3/10
