_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable if you liked Monster Train. Good amount of content and balance for the start of early access; there are multiple viable ways to build each class during a run and the options keep on growing as new items are unlocked.Five classes included now that are all fun to play, five empty slots for future additions.Party play is fun but not necessary unless maybe for doing ranked runs on higher difficulties - hopefully that will be better balanced for solo. Some classes will have an easier time solo than others, but there are many balancing changes ahead. Cosmetic-only season pass currently costs $6 in premium currency and returns 3-4x its cost. There is a cosmetic shop as well which is no longer rotating after initial backlash.The game is reminiscent of Hades in that there are multiple character stories to progress, but I end up skipping through it all whereas in Hades I would listen to every line of dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: A great roguelike with Transistor combat. There are eight playable classes that all feel very different from one another, with a ton more variety added by the draftable abilities and items. The story is nicely presented, but can also easily be skipped for players just looking for the mechanics. There's an easy hundred+ hours here with great difficulty scaling, and the game is on a seasonal model (with no microtransactions) so new items and cosmetics are released each season. 1.0 marks the beginning of Season 4, and all previous seasons' items are available. I played solo, but up to 4 player coop is available and seems like it would be a ton of fun for a coordinated group. The game is online by default but can be switched to offline mode at any time. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, this game is addictive.Feels like more action-packed Hellcards. It's a great coop roguelike.Rogueikes have good replayability and catch me for a long time often. I'm a huge fan of coop, to the degree of dismissing lots of games just because it doesn't have the option to play with friends, generally spending more time in coop playthroughs.I've longed for the roguelike coop for a while, and here it is. And boy, does it deliver. The gameplay feels fluid, allows you to not just play along with your pals, but really strategize and cooperate, and has incredible aesthetics and a big variety of biomes... The game started incredibly, reminds me of Valheim in terms of readiness when going into early access.It's already a good product as-is, and I hope they will improve and add more content.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing since before 1.0 (not sure when) and can say that this game is a lot of fun in what it has to offer. However, there are two gripes that I have with the game that I will now list below. I'm not entirely sure about this one. I see people saying that single player is easy, but I seem to have difficulty even on the first rank and I'm not entirely sure what I'm doing wrong. This gets amplified by the fact that me and my two other friends can clear (so far, we don't play that often) up to rank five. In single player It just seems overwhelming in some fights and my movement constantly feels limited, so I'm forced to go for certain builds to get far enough to get anything accomplished. This might be entirely a skill issue on my part. Yet, if the only way that I'm going to progress in a run is by having a semi-specific overpowered build, I feel like it removes the fun of trying new things unless I'm playing with other people. Again, I don't really know how to approach this gripe, it just feels like you need too specific of a run to defeat the villain in single player and that doesn't feel good to me at all, I guess. I'm going to start out blunt and say that this story is all over the place in my eyes. There just isn't one thing that I can focus on since I'm getting dialogue and quests from 3-5 different people in the span of five minutes and things just seem to blend together. So, I end up being confused and just uninterested in what's going on. Speaking of quests, wow, there is a lot, and they can be quite specific (and sometimes quite difficult) to the point that I was checking back to my book to make sure I was taking the right items and getting to specific areas to complete them. I can't tell if the idea was that these were supposed to get done naturally as you played runs or if you were supposed to have a session where you were just starting runs to complete quests and then abandoning them so you could complete the next part of that same quest. The biggest problem that I have with this idea is that, with the 1.0 release, there is a new endgame villain. To the best of my knowledge, you have to complete a lot of quests to get to a specific questline in order to unlock this villain. I personally don't agree with this strategy as I was really excited to fight this boss with friends, and now more time has to be spent just for us to unlock it? I just don't understand what the move was there. Hiding the main villain of the game behind hours of quests just feels like bloat in my eyes. These are just my opinions, and I could be completely in the minority with my issues. This game is fun and has good variety and I don't think it's bad. I think I just either misunderstand what I'm supposed to do and the grand story that's going on in this game or maybe the game needs more time to rough out the edges and I'm just hitting said edges.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a tester for Inkbound for a few months and I've absolutely loved it and played the heck out of it. _childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly pretty great.There's not a ton of content out there about this game, and the trailers/screenshots don't really do a great job  of conveying what this game is about and what it's like to play. The visuals themselves also don't really remind me much of anything like it, if anything at all. The closest visual comparison in games that I've played would probably be the original Dungeon Defenders game, which isn't anything like this game. And being compared to that game for visuals wouldn't necessarily be a trophy I'd be extremely proud to show off in 2023.But then when you give the game the benefit of the doubt, and you sit down to play it for a bit, it's really quite special.At first, I just kept dying. It felt fun to play, but somehow I couldn't quite build the required momentum to get beyond the first boss.And then at some point, by what was honestly just sheer coincidence, I had a run where my build magically steamrolled the challenges in front of me and only kept snowballing harder and harder. I didn't even understand what was happening, but it was incredibly fun to watch the fireworks and made me excited to start biting myself into the game proper.I could ramble on, but it's late and I'll spare the good denizens of the webz an incoherent essay.My takeaways from the game so far, in short, are as follows:1. The game isn't a looker, but it looks pretty good while you're playing. In my opinion, the visual side really needs some work still. But it's pretty much the only side of the game that isn't bang on.2. If you enjoy roguelikes, especially ones that play on the power fantasy of snowballing a build into oblivion, this game is incredible.3. The co-op is really quite fun, and in my opinion harder than solo play. The difficulty scales quite well, and even though you have access to the resources and skill of multiple players, coordination is the real challenge here.4. The gameplay loop feels incredible. Just awesome.If you're on the fence, but you can afford the asking price with some ease, I'd urge you to just try it.Even if it ends up not being exactly what you want, you'll have put that money towards a project made by devs who care and you'll probably get at least some hours of fun out of it.Very much recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun rogue-like and an interesting take on turn based combat. I have played both solo and in a duo, and I think where this game shines is in the multiplayer. Unfortunately, I believe the biggest issue with that is that it is exceedingly important to coordinate and talk about your moves and order of moves, which is not really great for a random party type thing. But, if you have at least 1 friend or more who would be interested in partying, you can do very interesting and fun combos. Overall worth the pickup and I hope there is plenty more to come.

_childDocuments_.review: The ink is finally dry now that Inkbound is entering 1.0, and having sprinkled in a few hours throughout early access and about 20 more this past week; I’m confident that Inkbound is an acquired taste. There is a deep strategy roguelite here, but you do have to wade through some tedium when it tries to wear other hats. I did eventually grow to accept and love its unique flavor but that onboarding was weird–especially because of how unique it is.Inkbound is a run based strategy game with a strong emphasis on build crafting. Though not a card game itself, it does inherit a lot of deckbuilding principles owed to this being developed by the same folks who made Monster Train. Start a run, pick synergistic abilities and enhancements after combat rounds, and hopefully make it to the final boss so you can do it all over again.But Inkbound is also a long term progression game. Massive cross-run quest chains, a persistent avatar, and annoyingly required story stuff are the scaffolding that support those runs: and they’re not always a positive inclusion.A lot of Inkbound makes more sense when you recall its early access launched with a battlepass and in-game cosmetic shop. Somewhere along the way the team did respond to all that anti-microtransaction pressure and removed them, but what’s a little harder to remove are the gameplay systems that were designed around their presence.Your rogue home base is an online hub where your little dude can walk around and gawk at other avatars. That visible and movable character is a design ethos outside of the hub too: even though the game follows a fairly standard “pick one of three lanes” roguey path system, you actually walk those paths instead of picking them from a menu—which also means there’s lots of little doodads you gotta click on as you travel the short but completely superfluous walkways.But where these systems go from headscratchingly weird to actively detrimental is long, grindy quest chains whose long grindiness feel like they were designed for the game that Inkbound used to be—not the one that it is.Some are passive kill quests you’ll accumulate in the background of regular play, some are cool incentives to try a build you may not have otherwise, but the bad ones are corny RP quests and mandatory story deviations.I once bottlenecked my progression because I didn’t realize a main story quest demanded that I play a particular class, go to a particular zone, then use an emoji. Other quests force suboptimal runs by having you spend one of your path choices on talking to someone and getting a random boon rather than piloting your run the correct way: and the story just is not interesting enough to warrant forcing you away from a perfect build. I frontload all of this criticism because I do love Inkbound, but it’s despite and not because of its whole. It’s got a serious case of Marvel Midnight Suns Syndrome where a superb core gameplay system gets its attention diluted by a story and subsystems that are boring at best and bad at worst.When the game isn’t getting in its own way, you get a fast paced turn based battler with a strong building emphasis. Think of a roguelite version of the second Mario and Rabbids game and you’re on the right track: you get free, gridless movement where locations and movement points ‘lock’ into place after you attack, rather than treating movement as its own discrete action.It feels great: you get the strategic benefits of turn based but when it's time to start hitting things, the rules and animations allow you to quickly navigate and spam attacks. Your opponents all resolve their turns concurrently so you’re only ever not in control for a few seconds at most, and when you’re in control you’ve got a bit to think about.Whichever class you pick comes standard with three starting moves and a starting passive bonus, which you can accent with two additional moves and seven additional passives via items unlocked mid run.Those hard limits are where Inkbound gains a lot of texture compared to some of its peers. Whereas many rogues will treat the acquisition of a new passive as a permanent and uncontroversial addition to your power, Inkbound forces you to make trades and lateral moves on your way to a great build.A small sprinkling of autobattler inspiration exists here in the form of numerical set bonuses, where reaching certain threshold of like passives will give all of them a boost. They’re both an incentive to chase on your road to power and they also fold into the limited slot strategy: one of the most powerful boons you come across on your journey are ways to free up item slots but retain the set bonuses of that item, which takes some of the sting out of all the swapping and dropping you’ll have to do.The late-run encounters always give a great feeling of a build coming together, and that feeling is exacerbated by how tangible the combat is.There’s also a lot of interesting class design here. There are loose approximations of archetypal warriors, rogues, and mages but also a spear wielding gladiator and a brawling fisticuffer and more. They vary in their damage patterns and mobility, but they’re all flexible enough to take advantage of any build and item that may drop.The added layer here is that they can also interact with each other: maybe the one benefit of Inkbound’s weird online priorities are that it gave us a half decent co-op system with its own stat tracking and progression.The trickster area damage class is fun on its own but get someone to compliment it with the relocation focused “Weaver” to suck all the foes together and you’ll really see its potential. Relying on matchmaking for a party can be kind of a bummer though, as there’s no protections against people leaving you mid run—I was really dying for a way to convert a half finished run into a solo when the random I was playing with disconnected. Inkbound is all over the place. You don’t need to look at old reviews or read articles to learn about how its vision changed during development; it’s manifest in the text itself through lack of focus and vestigial systems that supported something closer to a live-service than the final game ended up being. At times it feels like a better combat system than it does a game.Despite that inelegance, the rogue core is great fun with tactical yet fast paced combat and the thrills of stitching together a powerful build. It’s created an interesting middle-ground between a pure action roguelite and a turn based strategic one; even if it spills too much ink on everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: When this game was announced I perked up right away, having logged a lot of hours into Monster Train and being drawn to a coop experience in a similar rouge-like vein. Having enjoyed playing throughout the early access phases of Hades, I figured Id enjoy what Inkbound had going on and I'm thrilled to say it lived up to expectations. If you're like me and are very into all the tags and genre influences of these kinds of game, rest assured, it's gonna be great.There are already a healthy amount of options in terms of powers (bindings), power modifiers (augments), major changes to the power's mechanics (tunings? honestly I lose track of the specific terms), vestiges (items I guess?), aspects (classes), status effects (so many and p unique), and enemies to keep it spicy, and knowing the genre and Monster Train I'm certain that we will see more as the game develops. I suspect I'll be very happy to play throughout development but people like my partner will probably want to pop in every few major updates for a sip before drinking their fill when the game is released.I'd say maybe the only critiques I have are p pish-poshable and extremely subjective: I'm not a biggest fan of the writing/world building per se. I felt the same about Monster Train, but the game play loop was so fun I never cared and the way story/lore/writing was reflected by game play mechanics satisfied me enough. Also sometimes it tickles me anyway, shout out to the Gardener, love her, and you know what I love the Kwill too tho obviously it doesn't have a lot going on thus far.As for the critiques about the season passes and cosmetic stuf... I don't understand how gamers resent a totally optional non-pay-to-win way to support game makers... the season pass amounts to about what, six or seven bucks? which then rewards you p frequently with lil cosmetic doo-dads to decorate your Needless avatars and more in game currency if you really want to buy, say, pink head flames. Not only will this encourage the game makers to introduce new content (cosmetic and otherwise) it also encourages an active player base since... you know... its a coop multiplayer style game. I feel like if I'm enjoying the fruits of their labor for hours at a time (which I already am for an unfinished project) i dont mind tossing the game makers like two cups of coffee or whatever.

_childDocuments_.review: As a solo player who likes roguelites, this one's a lot of fun. Combat and overall design reminds a turn-based Hades, but with nice personality and ideas of its own. There's a decent number of classes and items to unlock and try, and many different in-run upgrade paths leading to that real fun "OMG how overpowered I became" feeling. In short, the basic roguelike formula works well here.It is missing some variety in enemy types and boss battles; I hope that future updates solve this. As the game stands now it has great potential, but it's not completely there yet, although at 17 hours in I'm really enjoying myself.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Monster Train, you'll most likely also enjoy this game. :) It's a really addictive mix of Roguelite, Deck-/Skillbuilder and turn-based strategic combat in an arena with free movement. The learning curve is steep but super satisfying, even more fun in a party when you can synergize together and experiment with different builds and characters. Story is kind of generic, but the setting definitely has some uniqueness. The game looks and sounds beautiful as well. Not much to say on the negative side, except that sometimes I wish I had an in-game glossary and that quests are a bit strange to track and RNG dependant. Battle arenas can look a bit confusing with all the area cones, arrows, numbers and status effects being tossed at you. There's tons of QoL updates announced for the official release though and development has been super transparent so far, so I'm confident all of that will become so much better. Any micro transactions/season pass mechanics from the very early days of this game also got removed completely, so it's safe to play in peace without any "buy this! buy that!" crap and still being able to support development with cosmetic DLCs if you wish. Inkbound is really fun, I hope to see even more characters, worlds and content in the future, so best of luck and success with the release!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is okay. There is some build variety and several classes are available at this stage in early access. Honestly, as far as early access goes, it's not bad. A lot of things are not really explained super well so there you're just gonna have to experiment to learn a many things. If that were all, I'd recommend this game if you're into rogue-lites.The problem is the monetization. I guess I can see the appeal for developers to implement something to keep players engaged and milk them beyond the asking price, but it just doesn't sit right with me. I guess it's good that the devs were forthcoming about the greed and not waiting to add in monetization after release. I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest; I was really looking forward to playing this one. It might be acceptable if it were free to play, and this game isn't. I just can't in good faith recommend a game that does monetization in this way.

_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: Co'op and turn based combat, can't check anymore boxes for me initially.I find this game to be overall very intriguing, I really, really enjoy the implementation of co'op combat they created. You can, realistically, just throw abilities out in at least a somewhat sensible order and not pay attention to your parnter(s) (at least in unranked, and we haven't done more than a single ranked run yet). However, the fun for this truly has come from figuring out the different combinations of builds. Playing duo's like we have so far, having one player take augments that gives debuffs like shocked that make the next hit do 50% more damage can be huge when that person has a large hit lined up to use. The simultaneous turn is pretty neat.With Inkbound currently being almost a month into it's EA release, it feels extremely well put together and a bit more of what you'd hope an EA game feels like. We've ran into a couple of small bugs, had an item disappear we dropped once, looked like an ability was gonna hit then didn't, but nothing too major. There feels like there's enough content to get a good feel of the game. Graphics are solid, personally I'm a fan of the art, there hasn't been any lag or co'op desync and I'm running 200+ FPS without a cap on pretty smoothly. (5900x, 3080 specs).Character wise, they feel fantastic. There's multiple builds you can run with each Aspect, our initial 3 runs we tried each combination of the 3 base characters and played them wildly different from each other. My friend is more of a tank/support type of player generally where in these types of games I like to roll damage out. I played the mage as a burn build, he played as a shield/heal tanky lad. Solid concepts here. Big fan of the way you can evolve your bindings/abilities in different ways to make massive changes to your skill set.I'm not entirely sure what's on the roadmap for the game, but here would be our wishlist as we've discussed while playing. I'll break it up into "new content" and "current content". I'll clarify that most of this I'm sure is stuff that's coming, but it is within the wishlist.Current Content: - Customize your deck. Even about 6 completed runs in, we've really started feeling the item bloat. Spending a *lot* of rerolls just on items. I'd like to see some customization for the Font of Wisdom (character augment) abilities as well possibly but perhaps not needing as many rerolls for items would make that better? - On this note, it'd be *fabulous* to have "sets" or "builds" or whatever you could create to hot swap between to change the current deck layout. Maybe I want to go in and run a tank build, so I want to swap out items that are going to give me ability power, or maybe I don't care about spiked damage, etc... - Some item balancing. Items like Paradigm Shift seem ridiculously powerful and almost a mandatory grab for a couple of the characters, but it hugely changes the playstyle of the entire game. Some people may not like that, and it also just feels bad if you *don't* get one.New Content:  - Based on the character select screen, there's plans for at least 5 more "Aspects" to be released. Neat. - More variety in the actual content itself. After doing a few runs, you've pretty much seen everything. The replayability is in the randomness and combinations but I'd assume they'll eventually double the amount of mobs/areas/etc. - More bindings/abilities, and ways to customize which ones you are offered once there is more of them. There's only maybe... 8? Or so? Plus or minus a couple, and at the moment, only a couple of them feel truly impactful to us on each run, some we grabbed once to try and doubt we'll touch again. - On that note, I'd rather the difficulty be overall a bit harder but we get access to more binding upgrades. Customization is the name of the game with a game like this and I do sadly feel a bit limited on our selections. I'd like to see more evolves, more upgrades, harder overall. - Difficulty seems a bit weird atm. Most of the ranked "mutagens" which is what increases the difficulty just baseline increase mob health/damage. I was hoping for more varied things. Perhaps traps on the battlefield, gain X stat but lose Y stat, whatever it is, just not "mob has more health. okie gl."If I was forced to make an actual complaint about the game so far, it would be that last bit. It's a bit of a stretch to call it a complaint with the game being this brand new, but, I hope that Shiny Shoe will continue to develop with that.The only other thing I have on my list to mention is the "unranked" and "ranked" feels odd to me and might scare some people off who generally avoid anything with "ranked" or "competitive" or whatever in a game. I don't know what to change the names to by any means, I went into ranked expecting this leaderboard to pop up and us be timed and be forced to compare ourselves to others when in reality it just meant you add difficulty. Maybe there's plans for there to be leaderboards eventually.Right. TL;DR, great game. Hugely love the implementation of co'op and turn-based combat. See a lot of potential here, probably my first roguelike game I'm looking at as a potential to play long term as generally I'm not a massive fan of the genre. Here's to further development!

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Monster Train, I was initially very interested in Inkbound. I tried the beta, saw how the design was geared towards monetization, and lost all interest in the game. I totally forgot about it until I saw that it was on sale and that the monetization had been removed. I decided to give it a try, based on how positive the comments were. Having done so, I feel like I need to provide a counterpoint from an experienced roguelike player who only played the game in single player.The game's main problem is lack of depth in builds and encounters. Regardless of which of the characters you play as, there are a few avenues to victory that you can take every time in order to win. The pool of possible items you can get is small, so you'll definitely be able to find the necessary items to have a god run each time. That means that the build choices you're offered along the way ultimately aren't choices at all: when you're offered different options, there's generally a correct answer if you want to win. You could choose options that make your build worse, but that's not very interesting when the impact will generally just be decreasing your damage and ability to survive. This is the key thing: choices will generally only impact how much damage your skills do. The only exceptions are the debuff system, which allows you to pile on various virtually identical debuffs (poison, frostbite, etc) that cause the enemies to take damage on their own turn instead of yours. Either way, runs will mostly be about getting the right artifacts (which you will) and making numbers go up. That could be fun, if not for the game's sloppy communication. More on that later.Unfortunately, enemy and encounter variety also lack depth. The enemies are all designed to be compatible with the fact that virtually every move in the game hits for damage and then applies a debuff. That means that while there are enemies that you'll want to defeat earlier than others or wait a turn to take on, you won't run into enemies that test the flexibility of your build or really change up your playstyle. That's by necessity, because builds in this game just aren't very flexible and there isn't an alternative to the playstyle of getting healing, getting extra energy, strengthening your debuffs, and then just applying damage. There are three final bosses in this game and I remember two of them. One of them has an interesting mechanic where you attack tentacles instead of the main body. It's not much, but it's the highlight of the three options.Finally, the Sea Breach encounters, which are this game's equivalent of question marks in Slay the Spire or Caverns in Monster Train. They're a way for games like this to give you a more unconventional choice, typically one that can potentially transform your run but has a temporary downside. There just aren't enough of these in the game. I honestly think there may be five different ones. You see the same ones each time. Some are interesting choices and some aren't, but after a few runs you'll have seen them all and they'll never surprise you again.Roguelikes, especially the ones that aren't action-oriented, are all about choices. That means the player needs to be informed about what their choices mean. On each turn, the player needs to know what exactly is going on so that they can make informed choices. Inkbound's UI isn't very good about this. It doesn't tell you what turn of battle you're in. It doesn't tell you how much damage each enemy is doing to you, only how much you're taking. Unfortunately, the game's communication of how much damage you're doing is far worse. There are so many enemies that the hp numbers that they have are de-emphasized. I never had to worry a single time about how much damage I was doing in number terms in order to win (even on ascensions). Why not? Because it's way more efficient to simply point your attack at an enemy, see visually how much of their health you'll be hitting for, and decide that way. You can just figure out which enemies are on lethal or soon will be, without ever thinking about the damage numbers you're doing. The only exception is the damage debuffs you'll be applying, which the game doesn't visually represent at all (unlike games such as Slay the Spire, where poison damage is clearly visually communicated). Furthermore, it doesn't always explain its keywords to you. Sometimes you'll receive an explanation, but not always. I didn't find a glossary, either. Ultimately, however, it doesn't matter very much because most of the debuffs apply damage on the enemy turn and so their differences are mostly negligible.The presentation of the hub world is annoying. You're slammed with uninteresting scraps of story, unremarkable voice acting, and generic characters that give you fetch quests. You can customize your character's appearance, but I didn't enjoy the game to want to do that. Ultimately, the game feels like it was designed for children. Runs are short, designs are simple and generic, and as long as you take the obviously correct choices you can win every time. The game doesn't want to trouble you with difficult choices or exact numbers; it wants to trouble you with fetch quests and cosmetics. The UI itself demonstrates this design philosophy. The hope, I guess, was that children would dive into the cash shops and indulge in digital fashion to show off with their friends. I don't think the cash shop was removed because developers responded to community complaints. I think it was removed because developers responded to their community not spending money in it and not buying their game because of it. That may be cynical of me, but putting cosmetics behind a cash shop in a $20 game is pretty cynical too.+ You can have some fun with the game while it slowly dawns on you how shallow it is+ Becoming OP is fun the first few times- It's shallow- Poor presentation

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some if not the best multiplayer turned based strategy game play mechanics out there. No one is forced to afk for 10 minutes while another player min maxes their turn. Everyone takes their actions simultaneously and you can interweave actions. The classes have both internal and external synergies so you can combo off of yourself but also set up crazy combos with your teammates.The only downside is that if you play with people who aren't interested in cooperating, it's pretty easy for them to sour the play session. Definitely a game to play with friends you know and trust.The monetization seems to be a big point of contention. All of the game play is accessible without any micro transactions and I have never been pressured to even look at the shop. You're able to see the premium track when you level up but that happens so infrequently. If you want a fun game and you don't care about cosmetics, this is an instabuy.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkbound is a turn-based roguelike that can be played in teams or solo. Each run should take roughly 45 minutes to complete. There are a handful of aspects (classes) to choose from that each have a fairly unique skill set and you can change between them without restriction. While Inkbound is still in early access with much more in the works, it's still fun in it's current state. There are a ton of vestiges (roguelike buffs) that carry additional thematic buffs in the stlyle of Teamfight Tactics where stacking multiple vestiges that share a theme provide set boosts. Each aspect has three skills by default and throughout the run you will be able to acquire two additional skills that aren't restricted to an aspect, and all of them can be upgraded.Combat takes a unique perspective on the turn based system. The enemy will prepare an attack and then your turn is spent dishing out your combos and assuring you have enough movement that you don't end up in the way of an enemy's hit. Each run you complete unlocks the next run with a slightly enhanced difficulty. Completing a run isn't difficult to do and you'll easily start snowballing after a few warm up runs.The storyline is charming but I found myself skipping through a lot of it. The characters are all eccentric and unrelatable, but they provide interesting things to say every now and then.I hope to see many more aspects in the future and to really dive deep into customization of my character outside of the run itself. I'd also like to see longer game modes with the possibility of looping the run. If you're on the fence about this one, it will keep you entertained for a few hours at a time. I find that I can't binge out on it in its current state. I highly recommend it for fans of roguelike tactics games.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkbound

_childDocuments_.review: So many people complaining about a battle pass and cosmetics, when not only are they cheaper than most other games, but you can also just not buy them altogether? It's 6 euros for the battle pass, and even free if you use the currency they give you in the free pass and the code EARLYACCESSTHANKS (see their discord). The pass itself contains about 10 euros worth of currency for future BP or cosmetics, so it's really not that bad. It's not like they sacrificed gameplay to make the store anyway, the game is great!The gameplay loop itself is very refreshing, I love the dialogues and the various quests you can do. Really makes you feel like you progress and invites you to try different builds and paths every run. I also like the ranking system although I haven't gone that far in yet, it's like an ascension system.I'm okay with the always online part of the game, the chat actually makes you feel connected a bit to the other players, you can chat if you want or hide/ignore it if you don't. Makes a small community, it's interesting!I also very much enjoy the various builds and classes, pretty diverse once you unlock a few things and they all feel quite different.As noted by others, I'm not a fan of unavoidable damage on some of these enemies BUT it mainly happens when you don't know the game, at first. Later on, as you get more knowledge and unlock more gear it actually gets a whole lot better in my opinion, as there are more ways to evade, move the enemy or shield yourself. Plus knowing which enemies to focus first, their attack patterns, etc is part of the strategy.Overall I would say it's well worth the price now, and it will only get more content anyway. The game is very good as is (possibly not as good as Monster Train, but does it have to be?)I'd be mad if they had sacrificed gameplay to make a shop, but they really didn't. So don't listen to the haters too much, developers have to make money and they don't force you to buy any cosmetics, it's much more bearable (for me at least) than most other games. Just try out the game and refund if you really don't like it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game continues to improve through early access, and the devs do a good job at listening to player feedback. The newest expansion, Gods and Relics, expands upon the strategy and depth of the game tremendously. If you're looking for a fun turn-based rogue-like, give this one a try.EDIT 5/2/24 BELOW:The game has improved through and through since I started playing in early access. The game has since officially launched, added tons of new content, listened to the community relentlessly, and has made the game genuinely fun to play each run.The difficulty scales up each time you win a run all the way up to tier 20, which is currently the highest. I have made it to that level each "season" and have felt good the scaling each time.Each character feels fresh and it feels like they're releasing a new one each major patch."Vestiges", which are passives that grant you various bonuses (even more so if you have multiple of the same set) keep the game fresh and add in a HUGE variety of builds. There is basically "anything" that can win you a run if you spec into it well.Monster Train was a home run for this company, but Inkbound truly is a fantastic game that is best enjoyed with a partner/group. Definitely a win for rogue-like enthusiasts.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving Inkbound an optimistic thumbs up, but I think it's important to understand exactly what the game is before diving in. I thought it was going to be a procedural co-op rouge-lite Transistor or a turn-based Remnant: From the Ashes. A lot of the talk has been about the combat, and while it is innovative, and the world you're thrown into is interesting, at the moment there isn't as much content and gameplay as you might be expecting.Not to sound sassy, but it does feel a bit odd that a game focused entirely on books and stories doesn't have much of a narrative going on beyond the surface level. A lot of it is being teased out slowly. This is probably because, as polished as it looks, Inkbound is still very Early Access. The story and quests are mostly just talking to the same few characters and doing things that aren't very out of the ordinary. I've completed a lot of quests already without realizing I was doing them. There are also only a small handful or worlds, 3 bosses, 5 classes, and a few dozen abilities. It's easy to see most of the content within the first 10-20 character levels.Everything also feels very on theme to an almost irritating degree, while also seeming a bit too far removed from that theme. The different books you go into are pretty, but ultimately feel empty and lifeless. The repetitive nature of the gameplay loop makes it easy to start ignoring what world you're in altogether since they mostly just serve the same purpose as the map does in Monster Train. There's no exploration or anything to discover as far as I can tell. The path you're travelling is just to get to the next arena to fight and collect your rewards, with the occasional shop or goodie along the way.If I were walking through and fighting characters from some public domain works of fiction, that’d be pretty neat, especially if each run had you crafting your own hero's journey, or just had something of a three-act structure. Right now the settings you visit are a few steps removed from wallpaper without much purpose. Imagine if Bioshock Infinite were ONLY the large fight arenas.It's definitely clear that Inkbound is still fleshing out a rough draft, but it's hard to shake the feeling that there's something missing. There isn't much to convey why we're meant to care about the characters or why we're fighting at all. There are properly named "guardians" and "villains" but nothing is really holding them all together, especially compared to Monster Train's captivating "what if heaven won the apocalypse?" premise. Obviously this will change, but Inkbound is leaning heavily on the unique combat right now.Also, the hub world feels unnecessary. I wish there were a way to limit it to just friends, but it seems to be everyone in a particular region or server. It's a bit hard to take the Gatekeeper's dialogue about this very dire situation threatening his books at all seriously when hordes of players are spinning and jumping around him.Again, these are just to highlight where Inkbound needs work, but I'm still finding myself really enjoying it. I just worry that without more content or care put into aspects of the game outside of the combat, it won't have much of a long tail in its current form. If you're interested in the game, understand what it is, and are excited to see it evolve then I do really recommend it. I don't blame anyone who want to wait on it for now, though.Being a $20 game, that's fine. If I were going to compare it to another game, I'd actually say it's more like a co-op turn-based Stories: Path of Destinies. There's nothing wrong with that, I loved Stories, but the inclusion of a Battle Pass in Inkbound has me incredibly worried that this is being set up as a paid live service game, and I've already gone through a lot of server closures recently because developers with great ideas are chasing an unattainable goal.Update 6/21/2023: I've come to realize that ranked runs and multiplayer are the real meat of the game. If you're only interested in unranked solo, I would also wait for now.Update 8/2/2023: I'm now 100+ hours in, Platinum 3 in Ranked (mostly done solo), and done with every quest except for 6 of them... so ya, Ranked is definitely the way to go!

_childDocuments_.review: I dont like battle passes and mtx in non f2p games, but this one at least has a 6€ battle pass where you can gain enough currency to then get the next one without real money. The game is really fun, it hits several points i love in games and i just have a blast playing it. I understand part of the players dont like the always online, but i really enjoy the lobby where you can see the other players run around, socialize and party up. I just did that with people i never met before, we ran in and won by defeating everything and the boss, it felt fluid and fun. I also like the turn based combat where you can still move and adjust in a more precise way, its difficult to explain but it makes it fresh compared to some other games. I liked the solo runs i did, but in group it really shined. I dont like the fomo-timed shop tho, i think it could be organized differently without using these tactics.I also really enjoy the art style and vibe of the game, the interface is good enough to understand things without the need of guides/videos for me, thats also a plus.What can be a bit weird maybe is that some classes can feel much harder, the weaver for example is very fun but it requires way more thinking than the Magma Miner... I guess it can be both a good and bad thing as there is no difficulty level (aside from the "ranked" mode which adds an increasing difficulty to runs), so you can move to other classes as you learn more - this could be pointed out by the game tho.I couldnt find a game i wanted to play for more than 30 minutes lately, but Inkbound really captured me so thats something.

_childDocuments_.review: After 82 hours I have finally beaten the story. Inkbound is a turn based roguelite that to me was pretty unique and one i fell in love with. it definitely takes a few runs to get the hang of it but once you understand the base game and how it works, its fun creating different builds to see how good they can get. it does get very challenging as you go up the ranks up to rank 20, ive only managed to beat it on rank 20 with 1 character since i have perfected the build on that one, but every character has the ability to get there. Also the game being multiplayer adds a whole new layer to it, as i feel like not many roguelites have that feature. My only downside is the questing can get repetitive and sometimes you cant always work on getting to higher ranks and work on quest at the same time, but there is no rush to do either.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a ton of fun both solo and with friends. A lot of people are complaining about the battle pass, but its one of the cheapest battle passes that I have seen, and it is also the most generous. It only costs 6 dollars if you buy it out right, and you can earn 3 dollars from the free part of the pass. Which means you could spend only 3 dollars. They give you enough of the premium currency in the premium battle pass to buy TWO more in the future if you don't spend the currency on something else.The game play itself is very tight, and fast based even though it is turn based, and there are plenty of build varieties to try, loads of quests and challenges to complete for those 100%ers too. The MMO aspects such as seeing other players running around the hub is a nice addition and helps give it something unique that other roguelikes don't have. It also makes it way easier and faster to find other people to play with if you want to do a group run. Ranked runs are also a fun addition. As you improve your rank by completing runs, they get harder and harder. Who doesn't love a challenge?Overall, I do not believe the people leaving negative comments just because of the in game shop gave this game a fair chance. Even with the shop, (which is 100% cosmetic) there are in game cosmetics to earn. Here is another crazy concept: If you don't want to buy digital cosmetics, then don't. The game is a lot of fun and you can make your character look cool without them.Please give the game a shot, its fun, and if you are really worried about the in game shop, you always have two hours to try it out and get a refund if you don't enjoy it. I hope to see you in the hub!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tactical roguelike and you can see that it takes a lot of cues from Hades, with a neat twist of being all turn-based. There's a solid, 20 hour game in here. Unfortunately, it's buried in a 40+ hour experience. If that middle 20 hours of grinding were cut out, I would be able to recommend it, but that's a heck of a slog.All the other things I would say are very much secondary to that. Combat system is kinda cool - but you have to spend 20 hours trying to do very specific things in it, which is annoying. The story is good - at least, the story arc that starts at 30ish hours. There are lots of options for character builds, but during those middle 20 hours you see so many samey unlocks that it loses it's charm (and becomes harder as each random pool of items gets so big).If you like roguelikes it's still maybe worth a play, but even if the ending is pretty solid it isn't really worth getting all the way to the end.
