_childDocuments_.review: They made an already hard game less accessible.  They seem to be catering to the smaller amount of Top Players Who Had Already Beaten The Majority Of The Game With OP (Overpowered) Builds that they felt made the game too easy so they made it harder.  Instead Of Nerfing OP Builds, They Made The Entire Game Harder In Response Which Made "Okay Builds" Garbage, And "OP Builds" Almost Required To Progress.I thought the game was too difficult, sad to see that it got more difficult. I have yet to complete a single run as I have never gotten past the last boss and I won't look for special builds just to progress, it should be balanced so each class can finish it without having to grind away to find that special build or played via googling tips...It's too bad they are catering to a few hard-cores and not to A wider audience...Some say there is a learning process that goes on, that you learn to play the game,  if that is the case I haven't seen it and what I have seen is frustration and insufficient rewards and progression which does not go well with a good learning process.Overall I am not recommending it as is, unless you really like to find OP Builds or keep trying over and over to find a path to success.  It is a shame as it is a great game otherwise with interesting characters and game-play mechanics.  If they start to cater to a wider audience with the difficulty and made an easier mode then it would be a no brainer to recommend until then only get if you are into the torture.

_childDocuments_.review: Game was enjoyable before the latest patch already, albeit a little repetitive at times. Since the 0.2.3 update it's absolutely incredible. So many more choices when drafting abilities and items, a whole new movement system, a new class, new area and many, many reworked abilities and items. No two runs are the same anymore. They're also much more challenging now, which I consider a good thing.Fair to say, this game *has* a season pass. However, importantly, there is one free and one "premium" season pass which you level up simultaneously - and the free pass holds enough currency (Shinies) to eventually unlock the "premium" pass. Also, all the rewards from the "premium" pass are cosmetics only and they never go away, meaning, you can switch between old and new passes at will and get the rewards.

_childDocuments_.review: (Playtester here, got the game free a little early to help search for bugs and the like. Also, this review is like 90% jokes so don't take it too seriously, besides the fact that the game is good).So, imagine for a moment that you are reading a good book, sitting in a nice, comfy armchair, perhaps sipping on a nice warm cup of hot chocolate or a latte, basking in the warmth from a nearby fire on a cold winter's night.That's the Atheneum, or the hub of the game, a book-lover's paradise.Threatening that paradise are a bunch of inky bois, dead set on making you set to dead.Your mission is to dive into that and weave a story, getting to pick which zones to travel through on your way to the big bad inky guy (BBIG) AKA "Villain". _childDocuments_.review: Inkbound represents a great execution of co-op turn based strategy, with some rogue like progression and gameplay elements.  In terms of progression, players complete quests and objectives to unlock more powerful relics that can then be looted (at random) and equipped to the character.Each delve into an inky dungeon brings a randomized path, set of rewards, and choices for the player (or team) to make.  At the core, Inkbound has a solid system with a relatively responsive dev team that seems dedicated to polishing the game in early access through to a successful full launch.* There's great item variety for building out various builds.  You can focus on physical, magical, a hybrid -- poison, fire, ice, AOE, Single Target, etc.,  Truly, the diversity of builds is amazing and will stand out to most players that enjoy custsomization.*  There's a well executed system to allow for turn-based multiplayer combat.  Essentially, players act first and spend their energy - the enemy NPCS, then retaliate attacking players through GTAO targets and direct attack indicator lines.* Controls are simple (be it good or bad, con on this later for camera movement) - WASD to move your character, click interactions, and keyboard shortcuts all within easy reach of the keyboard hand.* Graphics are charming for this genre, and character creation is quite fun.  It's reminiscent to Spore colorizing, though not as in depth.* Like many games today (sigh...), the price you pay isn't all inclusive.  For ~$20 USD, you get the game; cool.  Then, there's a battle pass that offers Shinnies (Premium Currency) and various cosmetics throughout its 100 leveling tiers, and an in-game cosmetic store.  If you plan to invest any time into the game, and enjoy a variety of looks, plan to shell out another ~$6 USD to get your battle pass.* A disconnected player can mean disaster.  Dungeon scaling is certainly a thing, and I've encountered a lost group mate in a few matches where the mobs didn't re-scale to accommodate our smaller size, resulting in lost runs.  * Dungeons can become a slog at higher difficulties with a full group, and a single delve can take well over an hour to complete.  * Item variety is both a pro, and a con.  As you unlock more items, you add to overall pool of items that can be rolled for.  Initially, finding the item you want may be a 1 in 5 chance, but as you unlock additional items, your probability may drop to 1 in 50, making an optimal build for each one near impossible.* Camera movement is limited on the battlefield, and you can't always see your team mates or their intentions.  You can hold Shift + moving the mouse cursor to see some of the battlefield, but not all of it.  NO free camera movement is bad in a strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: The turn based combat is fresh, and I enjoy planning for moves that I know are coming. There are unavoidable attacks, but you are given ways to mitigate them with shielding or healing. Other attacks are telegraphed AOEs that are easily dodged. Without the unavoidable attacks, this game would just be a red circle simulator with little challenge.DIFFICULTY: Seeing reviews that say this game is too difficult. Like Monster Train, the game is balanced around the fantasy of making a  broken character that does a ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. One of my characters crit the final boss for 12k health and the final bosses generally have 10-20k health (and it scales up with number of players). Even if your character isn't giga broken, you can still win with a decent build.I generally play solo ranked, and unranked co-op. This game is not that difficult for solo players. I have no idea what is up the reviewers that say this game is unbalanced for solo play. Reminds me of the reviews that trashed Wildfrost's rating.SEASON PASS: the rewards are just cosmetic, and you make more than enough currency back. The season pass costs 600 shinies, and you receive 1600 shinies back so you can purchase the passes by just playing. Even if you don't want to pay for the pass, you will be given enough shinies after 2 passes (each free pass gives back 300). If you don't want to pay for the cosmetics, you don't have to.This game is really great, and it pains me to see the negative reviews :(

_childDocuments_.review: (I purchased a $32 pack of in-game currency (shinies) to offset having received a copy of the game, so I can leave a fair review.)Inkbound is basically a turn-based Hades.  Choose which events to take, draft power-ups for your character, make decisions to navigate combat, repeat.  There's a bit of a "grind" in the beginning to add new vestiges (gear) to your pool, which can then show up in later runs, but that's the only meta progression.  I have over 400 hours in this game and I'm still learning new combinations and how to make the most of mechanics.  Season 1 starts you with 3 characters and has 2 to unlock, and offers 13 ranks of difficulty (more of both to come in the future).The store is pretty well done; don't let those "battle pass" and "live service" buzz words scare you.  You have a box price of $20, and you can play forever for free after that if you choose.  They included $16 worth of shinies in the pass, and the pass costs $6 (will cost $9 after early access), and it's their intention that you can chain these from season to season just by playing the game.  Owning the pass doesn't give you extra exp.  They recently removed the ability to buy season levels, and added a 50 cent option to the store so you can avoid ever having leftover you can't spend.  They also removed the rotating shop, and are working on filter/search features to help players find what they're looking for as the shop grows in the future.  You get "rested" exp if you skipped a day or few.  Items in the premium track are "cheaper" to get by earning them through the pass, but they will be available for purchase after the season is over.  They're also discussing how they can make previous season battle passes available for anyone who missed a season and still wants to complete them.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend you to look at this game as something distinct away from Monster Train.  It's a completely different game but by the same awesome devs, you probably would have not liked Into the Breach at first if you were expecting something like FTL, right?  But Into the Breach is one of the greatest strategy games ever made, and you'd do yourself a disservice to just write it off entirely because it was "different" from FTL.It's the same thing with Inkbound.  It's a truly unique game, just erase Monster Train from your mind and experience this game for what it is.  The devs are super active and making adjustments constantly, it's still early access as well but they could list it as fully released and I wouldn't bat an eye - it is very polished and I have yet to encounter any bugs.  Game is definitely geared toward multiplayer so don't go into this expecting the single player experience to be what it is designed for.  Don't be afraid to queue up with randoms if you don't have any friends that play it, it's still quite fun even with randoms!Also - there are a lot of negative review bombs because the game has microtransactions... but they are purely cosmetic.  You get the full functionality of the game when you purchase it for 20 dollars USD (less than the price of a takeout meal).  Harping on indie developers for trying to support server costs with cosmetic only microtransactions is a pretty wacky complaint in my opinion.  Have you seen how many indie developers make a great game and it just fails because it can't keep up with the server costs?  It'd be one thing if it game in game advantage but it doesn't... not sure why people are so up in arms about this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot to love.  My husband picked it up, as it checks a lot of boxes for him- strategy, relatively turned base, interesting narration, really pretty environments.  Once he did, he realized it ticked a lot of boxes for myself, as well.  I'm not a big fan of roguelikes unless there is some sort of meta progression.  I'm building an empire, damnit! I can't just DIE and be left with nothing!  It also is repetitive enough to be entertaining and help you get the hang of things, but has enough differentiation between runs so it doesn't get boring.  There's a decent number of classes to play, and a lot of room for customization. And some of the builds are truly, entertainingly busted.  Until you get to a boss with a weird power that can sometimes just erase you, depending on the customization you choose.  There's a lot of replay ability, and the difficulty really scales depending on which game mode you choose and if you're playing multiplayer.  For an early access game, it's remarkably polished.  I look forward to many more hours of playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is written while keeping in mind that the game only just released in early EA. I do believe that some things will change for the better, but judging from what I'm seeing at the moment, I'm very sceptical. The gameplay is alright. It's fairly fun, although, for the moment, extremely one-dimensional. The possibilities of the open combat arena are underutilised to the point where there wouldn't be much difference if every unit would just stand in a row. Content is very limited. Balancing is all over the place - the difference in power level between lateral choices really made me scratch my head often. Archetypes are heavily enforced, items and upgrades that aren't your archetype are mostly useless, and half of the choices you're stuck rerolling, hoping you find something remotely useful. There's a tedious amount of finnicking every turn to find the exact optimal spot to stand/launch an attack from. Enemies and areas have next to no variety.All this being said, I can see how these things aren't of much importance to a more casual audience.Apart from the gameplay, neither the setting nor the metagame are appealing to me in any way. I found myself very quickly clicking away both, npc dialogue, and weird quest popups that seem totally out of place in a roguelike. Daily Quests, Seasons and Battle Passes are way too reminiscent of all the garbage cluttering the games industry today and paired with the fairly poor asthetics - graphics as well as UI - give the game a very cheap, low quality feeling.Although it seems that microtransactions will only purchase cosmetics, their very existence together with some aforementioned aspects gives the impression that monetization was a major factor in the game's design.

_childDocuments_.review: I just can't stand season passes; this one feels pretty egregious. 6 bucks for one season pass (not a horrible price as season passes go, still hate the practice as all it does is introduce FOMO in my opinion. Does nothing to motivate me to play more so it's just a list of rewards I'll never grind to get anyway.), and you'll need to buy two of the 300 shiny packs to have enough. This is on top of the 20 dollar price tag of the base game.No option to just buy 600. Some of the later shiny packs are marked with the standard bonus shinies for spending more money; advertised as 1000 shinies for 8 dollars (200 bonus!) Comes across as a little scummy; just list what's going on in the amount (800 +200 bonus!) and don't separate them. Sure, the customer should just be able to do the math but I don't think that's an excuse for a lack of clarity, especially when it comes to charges like this.A lot of fun cosmetics are of course locked in the season pass rewards. Yeah, they're just cosmetic, uh huh, I can hear you, shhhh. I want to wear a silly little wizard hat. And I don't want to spend 6 dollars and grind to season pass level 12 or whatever to get it. I want to do a funny little wizard quest to get it. Ok? Ok. You can unlock some through class achievements and story quests and such but they require a good degree of grinding.In multiplayer games like these customization is important to many people and companies know this. That's why they hide their funny little wizards hats from me behind a six dollar charge. 26 dollar charge if I'm being petty. The tools you are given at the start of the game are quite limited and come down to picking a base color for the model and slappin' on some stickers that look like eyes or other bits along with some alright hair models. Cute; but kind of annoying to use properly. Mr. Potato head without the satisfying pop of the joints. Lemme put a 3D rendered nose on that bad boy or something. C'mon.Also put a color wheel in that thang.

_childDocuments_.review: So, instead of improving things for 1.0, they nerfed them and made them way worse.-The bosses thought of as problematic and in need of a nerf (Janus, Promenade boss) before got buffed to have enemies spammed alongside them (including a random buff of three, one of which leaves a PERMANENT gunk pool every time it attacks, one that spawns eggs that spawn even more enemies, and another that spawns bombs on when you hit them twice per turn) every turn, so now those bosses are more about killing minions and healing/shielding every turn than about, you know, hitting the boss??? Shoutout to Rhunstone to now no longer being beatable with most builds because his fight now requires 2+ movement bindings, buffed movement, and constant positioning to take out the otherwise-invulnerable adds he has. I vastly prefer the beatable pre-1.0 version.-The area right before the run end boss is literally just a dps/healing check, which makes the necessity of Heal/Shield/Crit even MORE needed than it was before, limiting winning builds even further.-Most of the added vestiges are interesting, but... the issue of having too few Vestige Slots to really care about growing a build/making one more interesting is still present, as is certain set bonuses not being better than the items that give said bonuses (example: the magic-centric one has a buff of +25 at 2 , then +10 on 3, and another +10 on 4, but ALL of the items that give said bonus give a +25 base, so there's no reason to recycle any of them; example 2: you have a full set of vestiges that give specific roguelike interactions between various aspects of your build, but the set bonuses are not those interactions, and the buff from the bonuses isn't worth losing the interactions in the slightest, but since you're not getting the DPS ups from the sets, you're probably about to fail, which seems completely wrong given how harsh the newly-more-difficult difficulty curve is, it almost feels like Stat Wells need to come back to even things out again...)-Magma Miner, a class that was regarded as being already weak, got a nerf via removing the shields on heat gain, and now can only be played by getting more heals and shields than any other class. What the heck happened to make this change occur?-They buffed the overall difficulty when the curve was already a bit steep.... WHY?TLDR, everything that was fine before 1.0 has now been made moot by non-tested points in 1.0. They had it in early access before the 9th, I don't know why they didn't test the difficulty and boss changes before 1.0, but, here we are! Untested changes making the game worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good experience. Any gripes I had with the game during beta (which weren't many) have all been addressed. Inkbound is a quirky little "tactical" roguelike? "Strategic turn based roguelike?" A roguelike that is turn based but has some free movement and important positioning? You know, it is just a great little game with a ton of unlocks, a ton of quests to keep you busy, and some of the most unique class designs I have ever had the pleasure of messing around with. Weaver and Clairvoyant, along with the new Star Captain, are by far some of the most original class designs I have seen in a game like this, or any game with a class-based system. Loads of build options, loads of things to do. The game is just a lot of fun.Now to address the tiny elephant in the room: the battlepass. Everyone complaining about it has a point in the grand scheme of new games with premium battlepasses, sure. But what Inkbound does different, especially in EA, is that you can get a free code from the devs for 300 of the in-game currency, and earn the rest pretty quickly through the free battlepass side of things to get enough to buy it the full thing if you want. And it is pretty easy to do it too by just playing normally. It is probably one of the best, if not the best, uses of a premium battlepass I have seen. Spend money if you want the cosmetics now, or just play the game and you will get enough currency to pick it up anyway. Also, an obligatory "They are just cosmetics. If you don't want to pay for them, don't pay for them." Except, unlike games like Halo Infinite or Diablo 4's (two games I have played extensively) battlepasses, you can actually earn the in game currency to buy the damn thing just by playing the game. All in all, 10/10 game that is just getting better as seen with the newest major content patch. Keep going, devs, you got another gem on your hands with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkbound is another roguelite from the developers of Monster Train. Its not a deckbuilder, but it has a similar focus on turn based combat. Unfortunately, while Monster Train is one of my top three favourite roguelites (alongside Slay The Spire and Balatro), Inkbound doesn’t come close to that high quality level.•	During combat, enemies will spawn over a few turns, within a small circular arena. Some enemies have area of effect attacks which you can move to avoid, while others have attacks which are unavoidable because they’ll follow you anywhere in the arena like a heat seeking missile. Some enemies also have special effects, such as redirecting their attack to your current location when you hit them.•	There are eight playable characters who each have three unique starting abilities, and you’ll be able to select two more abilities during a run. These abilities can be direct attacks, area of effect attacks, or defensive abilities such as healing, gaining shield, or teleporting to another location within the combat arena.•	You have a limited number of action points to spend each turn, and each ability costs action points to use, while some abilities take multiple turns to cooldown between uses. Abilities can be upgraded during a run to deal extra damage, be cheaper or quicker to activate, or apply extra status effects either to the player or an enemy.•	Each turn during combat, an orb will spawn somewhere in the arena, which gives you an extra action point and reduces ability cooldowns when collected. Orbs also restore some of your limited movement points for the current turn.•	Over time, the combat arena will shrink, as a circle of ink gradually closes in each turn. You’ll lose health if you activate an ability or end your turn while standing in the ink, so ideally you need to win each combat encounter quickly. Each turn feels a bit like a puzzle, as you try to figure out how to deal as much damage as possible to enemies, while moving to a safe location to avoid losing health.•	The UI is quite helpful and clearly shows how much health you’ll lose if you end the turn standing in your current position without killing any more enemies.•	Each run follows a node structure similar to other roguelites, including normal and elite fights, random events, shops, upgrades, and locations where you can visit NPCs to progress story quests.•	The other type of upgrade you can acquire are vestiges, which provide passive bonuses that can synergise with your abilities, similar to relics in other roguelites. You have a limited number of vestige slots, but at certain nodes you’ll have the option to destroy an equipped vestige, which lets you upgrade a different type of bonuses, while freeing up space to equip another vestige. This does provide a lot of options for how to build your character during each run.•	A full run should take around an hour. There are two acts which end with a boss fight, followed by a final boss fight. The first two acts have five different bosses, depending on which zones you choose to visit, and there are three final bosses, which provides some variety to each run. There are also daily runs, and extra difficulty levels which add modifiers.•	The biggest negative relating to gameplay is that the boss fights can be annoying, especially at the end of the second act, which I often find is much harder than the final boss. The bosses have lots of health, but also constantly spawn more minions which have unavoidable attacks. Its not unusual to start a turn in a position where the potential incoming damage is more than half of your maximum health bar. So you have to spend action points on killing the minions just to stay alive, which means you can only chip away at the boss’ health bar slowly, and eventually the ink circle will get so small that there’s just nowhere safe to stand.•	I don’t necessarily object to encountering difficult fights, I’ve beaten Slay The Spire, Monster Train and Balatro on their top difficulties (and I kept coming back after losing many runs). But while I’ve beaten Inkbound’s third difficulty level, its just hard in a way that isn’t fun, so I don’t have much motivation to keep going.•	There is some kind of story that progresses during and between runs, but I’ll be honest and say that I don’t really understand what is happening, because the various NPCs just ramble on about nonsense. Something about villains stealing ink which means friendly characters can’t write stories anymore.•	The presentation of the story doesn’t help. Many quests ask you to talk to several NPCs, and because you only visit two zones during each run, it will often take multiple runs to complete a quest, so the story doesn’t flow properly. Also, the player character is unable to speak, so I feel disconnected from events.•	I don’t know how long the story is, but I don’t think I’ll finish it. I’ve read that there are a lot of quests, so I don’t think I’m close after 20 hours.•	I also don’t like that the hub area where you start each run and where you’ll find some other NPCs, has other players running around like an MMO, which I find distracting.•	I didn’t have any problems with framerate, bugs or crashes.•	Controls are fine with mouse and keyboard.Inkbound is one of those games where I’d prefer if Steam would let me give it a sideways thumb. Its not terrible, and the first few runs can be fun, but long term replayability is hurt by annoying boss design and poor story presentation.

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is cringe and the voice acting is bad.  It really sounds like the devs read the lines themselves or got friends and family to do it to save money on good VAs.  And unfortunately, there's a *mountain* of cheeseball dialogue given clumsy life in this way as part of an excessively convoluted and tedious quest system.  In the first few hours it feels cool how it encourages replayability and variety, but now that I've finished the game, I can say on balance the quest implementation is atrocious.  To sum up, you are a blob of ink and everyone calls you Needless.  There's an enormous amount of fluff added to that because it dedicates a ton of real estate to the story, but it's all extremely skippable.The core gameplay saves it.  Despite the quest system being what it is I still finished the entire thing because the gameplay loop of the runs is fun and varied and is always just a chill thing to relax to.  There's a ton of stuff to unlock as you go, which can backfire as it makes you more and more reliant on good RNG the more you progress, but OTOH it enhances the variety of the runs.  I like a turn based roguelike and overall this is a solid choice.

_childDocuments_.review: For context I did all of the challenges available in 1.0 (played the game a lot) This isn't even the same game after the 10/27 patch. The update with the two new aspects is effectively v2.0. They removed MTX, so that's cool, maybe shouldn't have been in a EA game in the first place, but they're self publishing this title so I think it's more excusable.   You used to be able to slowly increase your stats by choosing a certain room when available. So if you wanted to do a fire build you would pick up fire damage when available (often). Now, if you want to do a similar build, you just have to get lucky picking up items with set bonues. The pool of items is large and gets bigger as you play. There is no way to remove items from your pool like in other games in the genre. They had a well thought out system that worked well and then just removed a bunch of those systems to add in more randomness. Before you could lose runs to bad RNG for sure, but you still had a lot of agency over the course of a run and could counteract a good amount of bad luck. You could also force a build you wanted to run and support it with stats. The current version of the game is just worse than it was. The last few balance updates have been focusing on the item sets they added. They just adjusted a set that basically let you ignore a ton of damage with minimal investment. I bet there will be an uptick of people upset about item sets now that they can't cheese the system. Item sets are a cool idea, they just can't replace the depth of the old system. Since the major update, Inkbound falls into the trap of runs being both long enough for them to drag in the early/mid game while you try to piece a build together, but short enough that you don't get to spend very much time with a 'complete' feeling build. If you want a turned based rogue-like this game is a solid 6.5/10It just used to be 9/10I'm sad that the version of the game I enjoyed was just a phase of development.

_childDocuments_.review: Not one to write reviews often but honestly I'm baffled by some of the negative reviews here. I've had zero issues with clarity or understanding what's going on and when. The game has tons of unique features and a well thought out design that I'm already loving. I've had a blast figuring out the best ways to handle each level, exploring how each class plays and the different ways to build them,The "microtransactions" are purely cosmetic items which is essentially saying "Hey if you want to support us more you can!" Not only that but it's probably the most fairly priced Battle Pass (and generally all the cosmetics) in current gaming. The premium battle pass gives you 1000 "Shines" while only costing 600 itself, so with consistent gameplay you could perpetually maintain it in the future. Cosmetics are basically priced at 2.50 for a weapon or 8 dollars for en entire outfit which compared to most games that's nothing. Furthermore the free pass + questing and playing give you tons of free cosmetics that look just has good as any of the current pass items IMO. Not to say the pass items look bad but rather all the items have clearly had love and attention put into them.It feels disingenuous to see the negativity directed towards this game when the shop model has zero impact on the game itself. The game itself plays really smoothly, has been enjoyable in both single and multiplayer, and has a ton of potential to continue growing into something amazing (while also already being incredibly fun!)Edit to address another common complaint: I keep seeing that the game is either "too hard" or that every ability is unavoidable and the only way to win is to burst enemies down/shield spam. The first of those arguments is subjective and the second is just patently untrue. To the first point I've tried about 8? runs now mostly in ranked so that includes consistently scaling difficulty and I'd say I've won about 70% thus far. The difficulty feels to be in a great spot and I've been playing a variety of classes and builds.  It's okay if this game isn't your cup of tea, despite being from the same developers and a similar genre it is quite different from Monster Train and I think that's a wonderful thing.Secondly there's a room wide AOE maybe once every 3 rooms from a single (usually boss level or at least floor boss level) monster that typically does meager damage. Other than that the minor mobs tend to do a targeted attack every other turn (although many have different patterns!) and after one run it's fairly easy to identify which monsters you should focus down first. There's also numerous mechanics outside of shielding and healing for handling them. You can use CC such as Daze to reduce damage, you can use Damage Resist potions or have stacked for vestiges that reduce damage, most importantly in co-op sessions you can juggle aggro as the targeted attacks will focus the person who most recently damaged them leading to some very fun and intricate comboing and planning with your partners!Overall many of the complaints towards this game seem unfounded and I'm frustrated more everyday by the harshness of Steam Reviews attempting to tank new games with misinformation they've either heard from their favorite youtuber/streamer or generated themselves from their whopping 1 hour of playtime 🙄

Inkbound reinvents turn-based gameplay in a fluid online-only co-op roguelike from the creators of Monster Train. Play solo or party up to dive into the magical, dangerous books of the Atheneum Library and fight to save this rich, ever-expanding world.

Inkbound is a fluid turn-based roguelike that brings the best aspects of Shiny Shoe's award-winning title, Monster Train, to an online world where the whimsical and dangerous magic of the written word comes to life.

Inkbound requires an internet connection in order to play.

name: New World: Aeternum
detailed_description: NEW WORLD: AETERNUM GAME UPDATE A major update has arrived for New World! New World on Steam is now titled New World: Aeternum. The New World: Aeternum update includes a fully revamped storytelling approach with enhanced dialogue, in-game cinematics and pre-rendered scenes, the first-ever large-scale PvP zone, a challenging 10-player raid, new end-game solo trials, and more. For players on PC, access to the content in the New World: Aeternum update will depend on what New World products you have: I have the New World base game and the Rise of the Angry Earth expansion. If you currently have the New World base game and the Rise of the Angry Earth expansion, you will have access to all content in the New World: Aeternum update for free. I only have the New World base game and not the Rise of the Angry Earth expansion. If you currently only have the New World base game, you will have access to only some of the updates and content that launch with New World: Aeternum. To get access to all of the content like the new Raid, you will need to purchase the Rise of the Angry Earth expansion. I don’t have New World yet on PC. New PC players will want to get either the New World: Aeternum Standard Edition or New World: Aeternum Deluxe Edition. NEW WORLD: AETERNUM - DELUXE EDITION The New World: Aeternum Deluxe Edition comes with: New World: Aeternum Corrupted Mauler Bear Mount Corrupted Soul Armor Skin About the Game Explore a thrilling, massive and beautiful world filled with danger and opportunity where you'll forge a new destiny for yourself as an adventurer shipwrecked on the supernatural island of Aeternum. Endless opportunities to fight, forage, and forge await you among the island's wilderness and ruins. Channel supernatural forces or wield deadly weapons in a classless, real-time combat system, and fight alone, with a small team, or in massed armies for PvP and PvP battles—the choices are all yours. KEY FEATURES: DISCOVER THE ISLAND OF AETERNUM For thousands of years, Aeternum has been the source of fantastical legends—and now you've found it. Shipwrecked and without supplies or allied, you'll need to make your way in a dangerous world where supernatural power has changed all the rules. PLAY YOUR WAY Play solo or use cross-platform play to team up with others, or compete head-to-head in a variety of PvP battles. Customize the look, skills, and abilities of your character, and experiment with different builds to suit your play style. SWORDS, GUNS & SORCERY Arm yourself with brutal melee weapons, ranged artillery, or supernatural powers and jump into New World's classless, real-time action combat system. As you progress you'll be able to determine what you want your gameplay experience to be like—will you act as a protective shield on the front lines of battle? Will you sling spells to support your allies from a safe distance? Only you can decide. CHOOSE YOUR PLAY STYLE Choose from seven unique starting archetypes. Each archetype has its own play style. From the Destroyer, a mighty slayer, brutally executing foes with a massive great axe and war hammer to the Mystic, a scholar-warrior who seeks to master the forces of life and death. Choose and change at any point in the game. SUMMON YOUR MOUNT Master horses, dire wolves, and lions, each with a unique look, dyeable equipment and a name you can set. Level up your Riding Trade Skill to earn upgrades like increased speeds, buffs and higher tier consumable food for your mount. Customize your experience with accessibility settings before game play. Tailor audio to your preferences with settings for volume controls, mono sounds, stereo sound, and surround sound. Personalize camera comfort settings, subtitle settings, and alter game inputs via key binding options. Finally, ensure no message is missed with chat text-to-speech and speech-to-text. ACCESSIBILITY FEATURES: Customize your experience with accessibility settings before game play. Tailor audio to your preferences with settings for volume controls, mono sounds, stereo sound, and surround sound. Personalize camera comfort settings, subtitle settings, and alter game inputs via key binding options. Finally, ensure no message is missed with chat text-to-speech and speech-to-text.

_childDocuments_.review: Hit 60 and this is what I experienced:   This game seems to do a lot when it comes to the crafting and gathering portion but heavily lacks in the PVE/PVP department. I have enjoyed my stint thus far, lvl 55 as of writing this, but the closer I get to 60 some issues are starting to stick out to me more and more. Factions are pointless, Endgame is gated by select companies/factions (invasions/wars), economy is bad, bugs galore, innate money generation tappers off to nothing and relies on running invasions/outpost rush which you can’t even participate in until 55-60, PVP is company focused not faction focused, Toxic companies will extort taxes from the player base on smaller servers resulting in it basically dying due to mass server exodus with server transfers, world PVP is really hit or miss depending on the server and typically requires a full group or more. The current endgame is basically locked out by whomever the controlling companies/factions are and if you aren't among their coveted members you will not participate in Wars (controlled by company leader) or Invasions as they will just kick you until it's filled with the people of their choosing despite the fact an invasion is supposed to be 10 people of the Governor's choosing and 40 randomly selected. But AGS says that is an unintended but acceptable mechanic so w/e I guess. Sell only starter materials to make money Iron Ore/Ingots will sell more than Starmetal/Orichalcum/Platinum/Gold etc. Lower tier resources have a higher demand because they are the base of all higher tier resources, but higher tier products require an abundance of lower tier resources and reagents, require more time and effort and will sell for less than the lower tiers.  Hit registration for some weapons/moves does not work, I have experienced this with the Hatchet, Fire Staff, Musket and Ice Gauntlet to date. (Biggest aggravation for me personally). There are literally so many, just check out their bug list forum.  Innate income generation tapers off. Mainly make money from quests, but quests taper off so the only way to make any significant renewable money are invasion/outpost rush. Currently dealing with a money duplication exploit so all trading of any kind is disabled. If you are going to push factions as a thing their needs to be an incentive or gameplay elements that effect factions. As it stands it's just a group identifier and participating in any "faction" related content is simply to benefit a single company (guild). This game looks like it took some heavy inspiration from Albion but with a halfhearted/non-committal approach to the faction PVP side of things. There is very little overlap between PVP/PVE unlike in Albion where there are gatherers/crafters who need to move material through PVP zones so they will be escorted by their faction or hire players to protect them etc. It gives it some life and melds the two. Doing protection runs, transporting secret documents, holding multiple forts for influence, having to take down PVE bosses in a PVP zone allowing for factions to ambush and protect their PVE VIP, player bounty hunting etc. Something more than Wars/Invasions that a company can practically gate keep the community out of. Functionally, factions only exist to benefit companies as in people see they are of the same “faction” so will help/contribute to that company but will ultimately receive little in return after said company has seized territory. There are faction benefits and the only one that really matters is the ability to move items between storage from different locations if the faction controls those territories.   You will be taxed for everything in this game with little to no say in the matter this is literally the embodiment of taxation without representation. Those taxes which go to the ruling company mind you, which on my last server were actual extortion. The largest faction Syndicate with largest company held 3 to 4 territories (all of the servers crafting hubs) and raised all taxes to max. My 5k house would have cost me 2k in taxes every week requiring me either to pay, abandon the house, or transfer…I chose to transfer.  Azoth is a currency needed to fast travel or imbue crafted gear with perks, it caps at 1000 and you will never have enough. Everyone’s biggest complaint is fast travel cost of azoth as it is based off distance to travel and raw weight, which the gear that you are wearing will factor into. Even if your faction controls a territory it will likely still cost you anywhere between 100-300 Azoth to fast travel. Best way to farm Azoth is to run invasions/outpost rush as you will get like 150-300+ Azoth. You can also farm open world portals but that only nets about 20 Azoth for the little ones and 40 for the 5-man ones.     Quests come in 3 flavors find item in chest, kill mob for item, run to place interact with an item standard affair. However, they need to stop giving me one quest at a time to go to the same location to do a different thing over and over and over. This got to me when questing in Brightwood and having the same quest giver, give me one quest at a time to go to the Green Defile like 8 times. This was the worst offender and made me stop questing outside of the main story quest because I was done running back and forth to do essentially the same ♥♥♥♥ for a seemingly “different” reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointment is the best word to describe this game. We all had high hopes for this game. Meaby we did not expect it to be just as good as World of Warcraft but let's be honest... a lot of people were hoping for this game to become the new MMORPG to spend countless hours in but the reality turned out to be harsh... This game is literaly the new Destiny,,, For those who don't remember what was destiny like. It was more less like: on ?Wednesdays? - Patch day devs would happily announce that they fixed for example "infinite money bug". The day after youtube would be full of guides on how to become immortal. Week later devs would proudly release patch fixing immortality but the very next day youtubers would release guide on how to do milion damage with each bullet oneshotting everything. and so on and so on for the next few months....Now lets look at New World... My guild was commited to playing fair and not using a single exploit. As you can expect this was a huge mistake. We lost capital city due to enemy team exploiting ice gauntlets generating server lag to cap our base without doing any real pvp. Than there was the duping bug. All of a sudden the biggest guild on our server started flooding the market with duped gold. regular players were struggling to pay 1000 gold on house tax while cheaters were buying for example jewelcrafter chest piece for 190k gold... Did any1 get banned for doing that? No. Not a single ban. Than there was the infinite orichalcum node. 24/7 there were always players from this biggest guild mining it endlessly. Result being -> now they all wear semi bis gear while those who played fair have trash gear with trash perks. I could keep going on with this list but that's not the point of this review. The point is -> This game punishes people who tried to play fair and rewards players who exploit every single bug they can.   No1 is getting punished for exploiting and cheating. Whats even worse devs trying to fix one bug, break 3 other things.  Right now when i am writing this review 2 out of 3 fire mage spells dont deal any damage. in pvp fire mage deals like 1k dmg to enemy player with heavy attack. At the same time, person who would equip trash hatchet and unlock specific perks would deal 4k damage every half sec with light attacks. Broken armor.... stacking food to get massive hp regen... armor perk decreasing incoming dmg by like 60%.... the list is extremely long.There are activities in this game that could be considered fun. The game itself is not that bad. Unfortunately the game is broken to the point that it probably will never be fixed and unless ur going to exploit evey possible bug, you are simply not going to achieve anything in it. This game is never going to replace WOW or any other mmorpg  that you used to play. At most, this game should be considered as smth to try, to play for a week or two and than to forget it and never come back.== Update after 1 month ==As i expected, over last month we experienced multiple new ways of duping items or exploiting bugs to gain advantage over other players. Right now the servers are off again because almost everyone was given for some reason few hundred thousands gold and people who were online at the time literaly bought everything off the markets.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start, firstly 6 out of 10 is what I would give this game. Would I recommend this game... not to new MMO players, there are way better MMO's to start with. Remember "Reviews" are opinions and stories of what player experience and can vary from player to player. So take what is being said with a grain of salt.  So for me I love MMO's and as I got into NW I come to learn that this game doesn't feel that good as an MMO. It feels more like an RPG with MMO features. Honestly if they went the route of Guild Wars with zones designed for just your party it would play a lot nicer. As for PvP I tried it for like 20 mins and it was just boring, didn't have a real combat feel to it. So over all it's better solo PvE game with multiplayer aspects that could be tweaked to make it fun.  As for the community, it's very toxic and dangerous. I never recommend not asking for help but with this community I do. They kept trying to take advantage of me when I would say I am new and needed help with getting stuff for armor and bags. But I read enough to know it was cheaper to craft then buy but they offer to sell me thing to help me. And people would be like here's a staff you can use I'll sell it to you for 40 gold or so. These players would gang up on you and from other reviews I can tell that they would report people that would call them out on their BS. Lore wise I got so confused by what the story was or was supposed to be. I will play through with another character to see if I can keep track of it by ignoring other players but from what I can tell the story feels unfinished and what is there leaves a lot to be desired. It's almost like Destiny 1, pre DLC, where you are just left asking what happens, what's next and never get an answer.  So with all that said, if you are an MMO fan but also love resource management games and bland combat, then yeah this game will be fine for you. Everyone else, I would recommend something else but feel free to try this game when it has a free weekend. Remember "Reviews" are opinions and stories of what player experience and can vary from player to player.

_childDocuments_.review: Journey to 60 was fun.  Once you get there, you're supposed to focus on gear progression, dungeons, crafting skills, and PVP - but these are all broken.There's a monotonously grindy system in place at 60 to improve your gear score, where you have to gradually get better drops by fighting 61+ monsters and getting lucky on drops just to increase by a point or two, per slot, per armor/weapon type.  The gear is just a linear progression of RNG stats - if you're lucky enough to get an item with the stats you actually want on it, you need to advance your gearscore to eek out another few points of armor or another attribute point boost in "strength" or whatever else.  There's nothing unique about any of it, and it's very cookie cutter.The crafting system is cool and has a lot of potential, but as implemented is just a ridiculous grind to make a bunch of crappy gear that nobody will ever buy or have interest in, just to make a few select items at the top end.World control system could be cool, but needs work.  Actual PVP is a mess - the war system is a lagfest and no real strategy, just pigpiling and AoE attacks, played in Powerpoint.  World PVP is largely just chasing each other over the map, doing quests to run from place to place or kill wolves, while flagged.  The combat system needs a lot more depth, it's rather boring without much skill involved.  For PVE, shallow strategy in general, threat management is completely broken, and "push" on monsters and players is like everyone is wearing ice skates.  Doing dungeons requires grinding dungeon keys, and grinding crafting to be able to make those dungeon keys.  Why does everything have to be a chore?At least on the server I played on, a few big streamers have multiple "companies" assigned to them that they try to control as a block, and all the PVP feels like an epeen contest between streamer fanboy groups as a result.  You get all the normal PVP toxicity mixed in with that.  I don't know who would want to deal with the drama.World is huge and while that is good in a sense, they also clearly want people to walk everywhere because while there are some fast travels, they have a pretty significant cost where the resource has to be grinded back up.  Mounts would help a lot, but understand from the dev communications that they are not currently in the plans.On a positive note, the game is beautiful, and great sound.  It's too bad they didn't spend more time to polish this up, probably another example of a game with extreme potential that was ruined by a hurried rush to market, driven by dates.Lazy reuse of same monster models with minor tweaks for monsters from level 1 to 60, and even entire villages and towns. There is no variety in quests, though the town boards help a bit with that. It's a good distraction for a few weeks, which is all you can ask for from most games, but for an MMO I'd like more staying power, and that just isn't there.Town control and housing systems are intriguing and have potential but seem to be a constant gold bleed at the level cap, I'm not sure sustaining multiple houses is realistic at all.Story quest is a bit broken, you have to find other people to help you on some of the non-soloable fights towards the end of it and they have to be on the same quest step as you.  People who have already been through it can't go back to help others.  This sucks worse than it should.Amazon has been terrible about any communication on any of these widely acknowledged issues, and people are leaving the game at this point.  Me too.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever notice that with MMO's how rabidly people will defend the indefensible? They will tell you basically, "YOUR TOO DUMB TO KNOW HOW TO ENJOY THIS GAME!" or similar tripe. The more people post about how bad a time they are having in a game, or why they are quitting, the more vitriolic the posts become from those that stay. That is because EVERY SINGLE person that quits potentially puts at risk the fun the person that stays in the game is having. MMO's by definition, thrive when many people are playing. New World is even more susceptible to this because of the territory control/pvp system they have. Let me state my opinion about this game unequivocally, New Word isn't worth your time or money.  Save your yourself a disappointing wake-up call a few weeks from now by just scrolling on to something else. if you must know the reasons why this game isn't worth your time, just go over to YT and search "New World - Timeline of a Failure". He highlights every single issue the game has had since its launch. Even though it has only been out a very short time, the video is 47 minutes long. So there is no reason for me to restate what he has so eloquently organized.      I have been playing MMOs since starting EQ right when Kunark was released (early 2000) and I can tell you that I haven't been this frustrated with a game since Wildstar. Wildstar basically banned both my wife and my account roughly two weeks after we started playing, for using what they said was a "Stolen credit card" (It wasn't of course). They made it even more fun to try and fix the problem by limiting access to their forums to 'subscribers' which we weren't anymore because of the ban. Yeah, New World is THAT kind of fun. For those out there that are still enjoying the game, more power to you. I am not saying you shouldn't enjoy it, only cautioning people that might be interested in the game to seriously consider all the problems the game has before setting fire to 40-50 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Astounding visuals, a wonderfully crafted world, and a surprisingly interesting story. The gameplay itself is basic, but better than most MMOs I have tried. I would liken it to a watered-down Souls-like but with a good levelling system. The crafting is perhaps one of the best parts of the game and truly feels rewarding.Cons:It seems every time they fix one thing, another thing breaks. And on top of that, there are countless duplication glitches for money and items. It seems, at least on smaller servers, faction balance is not as large of an issue, but that could also change at any time. Meh:The game is not the most supportive of solo players and really does benefit those who play with friends and even more so those who join Companies (guilds). It's not impossible to play alone, but will require you to join randoms for Expeditions (raids) and occasionally ask for help (in the convenient Help chat). And obviously, as with any MMO, the game can at times feel like a bit of a slog with the numerous repetitious quests.Verdict:The game has immense potential, but will require an incredible amount of effort through back and forth updates from the devs. If you are truly skeptical of the game, wait until it is heavily on sale or free to try before you give it a go. Otherwise, I would recommend it for both veteran and new MMO players alike.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazon Games refuses to listen to the true fans of the game! Despite countless mistakes, they still ignore us!Most of the content feels completely pointless—factions, replaying dungeons, a ridiculous amount of gear that just gets salvaged, and crafting that serves no real purpose.But now, they’ve gone and ruined the one thing that actually made this game great—the combat system. Instead of building on that strength, they added an aimbot, turning what was once a skill-based action combat system into a lazy tab-target joke!There’s no skill cap anymore, no room for outplays, no chance to develop your own fighting style, and zero opportunity for real skill expression. You can’t be the best when the game basically plays itself!When you first announced New World: Aeternum, you said aim assist was coming—not a full-blown aimbot. It’s completely unbalanced right now. Almost every shot lands perfectly. It locks on at 25 meters and only untargets at 50 meters. It practically covers the whole arena, even tracking enemies behind obstacles so you can follow them without even knowing where they are!In the arena, 90% of PC players are using it because if you don’t, you lose as a ranged DPS.This mechanic is fundamentally broken. The tracking is way too aggressive. If projectile speed is fast enough to hit moving targets, it becomes overpowered. If it’s too slow, it’s useless—except for the tracking, which stays OP no matter what. You’ve killed skill expression entirely, and this makes the mechanic completely broken. It needs a total overhaul.Right now, this aimbot (because it’s not just assist) is turning the game into a tab-target grind. The only things that matter in PvP are your gear and skill timing, not actual mechanical skill. You've destroyed the one thing that worked in this game.Amazon, for once, do the right thing—REMOVE THIS AIMBOT FROM THE GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: I think New World is a fun waste of time, but at the current stage of the game, I can't recommend it. It is beyond broken.Now let me preface this so readers can understand how I play New World: I am a healer primarily (Life Staff in-game), and have participated in at least 20 wars on attacking and defending sides exclusively as a healer while also progressing the PvE section of the game as a healer as well, so my experience is not going to be the same as others. I am part of a company that owns land - the zone being Ebonscale Reach. That being said:It's a vast, empty game that has pockets of engaging content that are probably ruined by game-breaking bugs and exploits.Let me break this in to PvP issues and PvE issues:--PVP--Healing is beyond boring in PvP wars: run Beacon (an AoE healing-over-time), Sacred Ground (an AoE healing-over-time), and a third healing option of your choice (I use Orb of Protection, which is a AoE healing-over-time), and just throw all of that at a ball of 50 players on a capture objective. If you want to bring any single-target heals, you're purposefully stunting your healing effectiveness in wars. The congestion of almost 100 players fighting in a ring that probably has a diameter of 20 meters combined with every single AoE in the game lags the game severely, which just turns it into you hitting statues and taking hits from invisible enemies. This has been an issue since day 1 of release. The end-game of NW - PvP - is just unplayable and not engaging.Territory ownership is hit and miss. If your company does not own one of the three major central zones, your company will most likely never earn enough money to cover territory upkeep, leading to a downgrade of work stations you've upgraded. As mentioned, my company owns Ebonscale Reach, a non-central zone, and there is no reason for many players to go there to put items up for sale or craft unless we have higher tier workstations. However, to upgrade workstations, we need money. This leads to a cycle of we can't earn money to upgrade unless people go there, but people won't go there unless we upgrade.Open-world PvP is nonexistent unless somebody organizes a zerg rush through a zone in order to throw it in to conflict in order to further declare war. Countering a zerg is possible, but there is little reason to. Usually attackers get a massive leg up in influence gain (influence needs to be at 100% for attackers to throw a zone in to war), while defenders do not get this benefit. In my experience, this disparity of influence gain just leads to defenders giving up, letting the attackers declare war, then going to the 50-on-50 PvP battleground. Countering a zerg is almost always a waste of time because even if you kill everyone and they give up, they can log in late at night and finish the push with no resistance.Since the main focus of the game is PvP, PvP naturally attracts more competitive players, which isn't an issue. However, what IS the issue is that a lot of PvP revolves around abusing bugs and exploits that are still not fixed. Lagging the war to prevent people capturing a point, abusing invincibility exploits, taking advantage of broken armor effects, and using meta loadouts (in my case, 3 AoE HoTs) is the norm for PvP warfare. These causes compound into a feeling that I didn't win a war because of skill, it just makes me feel the other side exploited less of the game than we did.--PVE--PvE is noticeably bolted on as an afterthought. The early leveling experience is acceptable, but as the player reaches level 40 and beyond, the quest structure is all the same: accept everything you can, go to a copy-pasted town, kill 15 of the same enemies you've seen in 4 other zones, and loot 8 crates for an item, then return to town. Rinse and repeat until level 60.Dungeons are interesting sometimes, but access to dungeons is restricted based on if you have a tuning orb (read: key) into the appropriate dungeon. Tuning orbs are time-consuming and cost a fair amount of money to craft, and up until recently, the end-game level 60 dungeons could not be crafted because players could not clear the PvE content necessary to get the crafting parts for the key. It wasn't a case of people being underleveled for the content: it was simply that Amazon Games didn't allow players to because the PvE content was bugged for weeks.Gear score is infuriatingly hard to increase. To increase gear score, players need to endlessly grind level 60+ content in hopes a higher gear score piece of loot drops. When that happens, the game bookmarks what was dropped and increases the chance for something to drop later that is even higher gear score. This is known as the "watermark", which is not explained anywhere in the game. This "watermark" is also gear specific: you can get a metric ton of fire staff drops and get your fire staff drop watermark to 600 gear score (600 is the max), but your watermark for life staff will still be 500, which is the bare minimum for player level 60. This gear watermark dissuades players from running the end-game dungeons until they're maxed in gear score because they run the risk of getting legendary equipment that is not 600 gear score.Corruption invasions are completely overtuned for what the game asks of you. A corruption invasion happens in a zone when enough corruption portals spread in a zone, and corruption portals are passive spawns in the world that spawn monsters that players must cleanse. Rewards for cleansing a portal include dungeon key materials and chests to increase gear watermark. With the explanation out of the way, the bare requirement for participating in an invasion is the player is level 50+, but the tuning of the invasion feels like everyone needs to be decently coordinated, level 60, and at least 550 gear score. This issue is compounded by anyone who is 50+ can sign up, including opposing faction members who, in my experience, purposefully troll by stealing siege supplies (necessary to repair the fort) and don't participate in killing enemies. Why would they throw the game, you might ask? If an invasion is failed, the zone will lose up to 5 settlement upgrades, costing the owning company up to 50,000 gold if everything is upgraded to max.Azoth is very clearly put in as a future moneymaking scheme for Amazon Games. Azoth is necessary to fast-travel, craft, AND respec your weapon talents, and the player can only hold 1,000 Azoth at a time. Crafting one item takes up to 60 Azoth, traveling is based on player encumbrance and distance teleported (at minimal encumbrace, a teleport across the map will take about 200 Azoth), and respecing a weapon at max weapon level is 200 Azoth. There is simply no way to store enough Azoth to keep doing everything that is expected of a player, forcing the player to just autorun everywhere.There are many more issues I could add, but I feel that talking about my personal issues with the fundamental games are enough. To reiterate, I think that New World has potential to be a good game, but at this stage, I can't find a reason to log back in and grind. The only reason I have left to log in is to help in wars my friends organize and to defend my territory. Once I lose my territory, I have a feeling I'm just going to deinstall until I can find a reason to come back.

_childDocuments_.review: Hmm, where should I start? Well after spending 100 hours into New World I can confidently say that it's definitely a time sucker and a grind fest. But I'm guessing that's how most MMORPG's are, since I've only played 1 before New World and that was quite a long time ago which was a not so popular MMO called Drakensang Online which I sank a lot of time into. So take my opinion as you want since I don't have that much of a background with this types of games but I do have a lot of background with RPG's, which I'll probably talk the most about that side of this game, also considering that I mostly played solo up till now. So after all that being said let me actually start this review. I'll first start with the World considering the name. Aeternum Island is the name of the world you've been stranded off to, and to be honest... It's pretty plain... Though there are some really beautiful places out there, it's nothing too spectacular for the most part. It mostly looks like a combination of a survival game and a medieval RPG, nothing more to it but it's alright. I can also say that a minimap would've been much more better the a compass, but I guess I can live with that. The classes. Pretty standard, it's the basics for almost all MMO's. You can choose between DPS, Mage, Tank and Healer. Really not a lot to talk about, although I have to admit that it feel pretty nice you can always switch if you found a weapon that better suits you or for a role you need to cover since it's all depended on the level tree and you can always respec your character if you have money. Really sweet! Now let's talk about the thing that annoys me the most in this game, the combat. God, it is just deplorable and it leave a lot to be desired, like literally it pisses me off so much. I don't know much about the ranged combat, it seems a little better but can't say for sure. But I can tell you how bad the Melee combat is! It tries to mimic the combat of Dark Souls and... It fails horrendously. It feels so clunky to maneuver, you can't even cancel your basic attacks to dodge or anything else for that matter, the attacks are slow with a big pause between depending on your weapon and the special abilities barely make up for it, they're not as bad but could've been better. I think the best abilities are on the War Hammer, though I'm not using it anymore because I like the more AOE attacks on the Great Axe and the faster Hatchet. Overall I really hope it gets better with time. I quite like the mobs and the bosses, although most of the mobs have the same attack pattern and the same looks only with slight differences sometimes, and the bosses with not so many different attacks and spells. The mobs are really easy to tell what their attack is gonna be next but at the same time it's really hard sometimes which I quite enjoy that about them and the bosses look pretty damn good, most of Dungeon bosses have 2 fazes with some interesting catches or some new cool attacks which are fun to play around. I think this might be the best attribute of this game so far. Pretty good stuff. Now lastly just to share a piece of mind without subject, I don't know why I like this game after I've read everything I've said, like it looks like I hate the game more then I like it, but I guess I like the core of it, all the grinding, the leveling up, the attribute tree, the raids and all that stuff. Even though it has a lot of flaws it's just a really fun game to play around and it's even better if you have someone to play with. Guess I'll just sink even more hours into it until Lost Ark launches, then it's next for that game to eat my soul, haha. Anyways, if you got this far thanks for reading my review, I know it was long but I hope it helped you in the decision of buying the game or at least enjoyed what I've said. :DOh and I forgot... ADD SOME ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HORSES IN THE GAME!!

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways, a stark break from traditional MMOs, and yet in others it's comfortably familiar. While it still suffers from the core/fundamental issues of MMOs - namely; a lot of slow walking back and forth from quests, generic fetch quests to pad out the story, and the threat of other players stealing your gatherable resources - it stands far above other MMOs in many ways. The UI is absolutely top-tier, the combat is punchy and meaningful and has more to do with strategic positioning and timing instead of just juggling skill cooldowns, and the crafting system isn't saddled with obvious time-wasters like class/character restrictions or arbitrary wait times.In short, this is very likely the best MMO I've played, but it's still an MMO. Once the honeymoon period is over and the novelty of the setting wears off, I'm sure the grindy nature will become more apparent to me. I have high hopes that the combat system can stay engaging enough to keep me playing, but I imagine this will eventually end the same as any other MMO for me - reaching a point where the grind outweighs the fun and I just stop playing. (That's not necessarily a bad thing, though)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a big fan of MMOs. I've tried several through the years (FF11 and 14, WoW, Aion, Bless, Black Desert, Blade and Soul, LotR Online, Wildstar, and a few others), but I've never been able to really get into them, usually it was the combat being an utter grind, and I absolutely loathe tab-targeting now and refuse to play any MMO that uses it, but New World....it's a different story. The combat is very action forward and engaging. You only have 6 skills total, but the game plays like an action game with an MMO skin on it, which is fantastic. Haven't made it to endgame so I won't speak to the quality or length of the content there. The biggest thing about the game, aside from the combat, is the crafting. If you enjoy gathering and crafting then this is the game for you. I've spent hours and hours just running around smacking trees and rocks, fishing, cooking, etc., and it's all a blast...for some reason. I'm loving the game so far, and would recommend it over any other MMO if you're like me and hate tab-targeting. The graphics and lack of a sub fee are another highlight for the title!Update: Endgame content is fairly lacking and turns into a grind, which isn't a bad thing, for me at least, but if you're not expecting it, it may throw you off. The game has continued to be updated often, however, there are still many issues with the title. There have now been two separate occasions in which the AH was taken down for a full day or more due to a gold duplication glitch players were exploiting. Other weird bugs here and there, but the game is mostly stable now, I've only experienced one crash in my playtime thankfully. Still would recommend the title as long as you know what to expect.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is rather barebones from what I can tell? It lacks any real customization aside from a few preset faces. The game itself feels more like a store to sell you things, rather than a game. A list of complaints would be;-No races outside of human, and very little customization there as well with about 8 preset faces per sex.-No mounts at all and a lousy fast travel system so you'll be walking alot. And I mean quite alot. -Stiff animation and little build variety. The whole combat system is clunky and feels like a cheap asset flip in some scenarios. Cooldowns are shared on slots so you don't swap weapons in a fight, or do much thinking at all. It's mostly mindless mashing.-It's slow. The grinding for cutting down trees, mining, etc, is tedious and has long gathering times tied to your gear and where in the world you are. This may be a bonus to some who like a good time sink, but it isn't for me.Only fair to add a list of pros+It's pretty. In the areas that aren't barren. Though I haven't seen the majoirty of the map, so I'm sure there's more than just the beaches and jungles I've been running through...+There's an auto run button. Which is useful, because again, you will be spending a good portion of your time running from A to B, or tabbed out as you wait for a gathering node to finish.+Its an Amazon game, so there's frequent giveaways of select armor cosmetics and the like. Usually purple from twitch drops, but a freebie for those who spend money on prime. Or watch twitch a bunch.+Game keeps going when you Tab out. So you can start one of the gathering animations or autorun in a direction and tab out to watch a video or do something else. So it's got potential for a simple side-game or time sink like one of those mobile games, or if you're in que for some other game you play.That's all I've got from my brief exposure. Maybe the PvP and later on progression is more engaging? It's early game was a slog that put me off from continuing. Thankfully I won this in a giveaway, as I couldn't imagine spending 60$ on this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game presented itself as a "New World". It was exciting, beautiful and seemed to fill a gap in the MMORPG world. However, it filled the gap with disappointment.Until I hit lvl 60, I wasn't aware of how broken this game is. It is a waste of time to even repeat what players all around the world are saying. Every time there is a bug or exploit going around, all the decent players suffer: closed trades, closed trading post. After countless of players leveled up their trading skills buying resources from bots, speedrunning elite zones in BIG groups, the new players have to spend more time and more resources to even TRY to catch up with the lvl 60 players.The map system is completely badly designed. When there is a war, only the company that owns the territory will choose the players to participate at war, leaving the other players without activity and waiting for their fate to be decided by a company. Faction influence never resets, full companies are leaving servers because they can never win back their lands and all their work was in vain, players are too disappointed to even try to win the lands back, they go to wars just for the rewards and refuse to move. Once one company owns a big part of the territories you can't even transfer to that factions. Azoth costs are quadrupling, players don't want to do the missions for influence, don't want to take lands, can't earn money because the azoth costs prevent them to run any business model. With the new PVP flagged buffs, is even harder because the lvl 60 players of the faction that owns a land, don't let the other players do anything and so, the winning company will always be winning. Who falls under, is dead forever.Also, this game is based around the idea that ALL players will play PVP, all players have gaming experience, all players will participate in all the faction activities, BUT that is entirely not true. The game marketing included skills like harvesting, furnishing, fishing, a whole another game environment than it is actually asked from the players.More than that, the game has repetitive content all over the place, same missions, different territory, mobs with higher lvl. And if this wasn't enough, once you hit lvl 60, you have to grind your watermark. This wouldn't be a problem if you had to do this grind with friends and company members, but when they are all disappointed they have no land, they don't have a reason to fight for their watermark anymore.  Also, some players are playing only during the night or only during the morning, so can't experience a big part of the game because they can't find parties with 50 people for elites or Outpost Rush at 3 AM or 7 AM.The Trading Post is another horror story. The prices are made by no rules, they fluctuate too much from day to day. Also, the servers where there are resources bots, they sell everything at low price. If I want to do mining, I have to sell at bot price. If I want to do cooking, I can't sell anything because people are buying resources from the bots and don't see the need for foods. If you want to make some gold, you have to engage in pvp activities, or go to elites runs with other players(which won't even take you with them because your "gearscore is too low"). And when you finally go to elites and find a good piece of equipment, you find that it costs almost nothing on the amrketplace because there are not enough lvl 60 players to buy them or they already have voidbent armor and don't need your loot. Overall, the game has a good potential which a lot of gamers around the world hoped to find inside the game. It was nicely wrapped and sold to hopeful gamers who wanted a New World to explore and keep their gamer flame alive. The developers may not care very much about reports, bugs or player opinions, but this review may help someone to not be fooled by a nicely wrapped beta game whose structure in crumbling under bots, bugs, incompetence and ignorance.

_childDocuments_.review: 90 hours in and this is my two cents:Combat is objectively fun. It's fluid, there's some fun skills to use and it's fast paced. No standing still and waiting for your character to queue up a skill. Albeit if you get ganged up on by anything, you are gonna go down pretty much instantly.PVP is bad. Especially for new players. If you aren't slotted with top tier gems and gear bonuses, don't bother. You're going to get slaughtered in two hits from anyone who has been playing for a long time. Severely favoring ranged DPS spam or melee stun locks, no in between. That's it. Either you run a really strong snipe build, or you get in the enemy's face and lock them down indefinitely as you smash their face in with your dual hammer/axe combos.The world is beautiful, but sucks to traverse. Game needs mounts with how large the world map is. It's a crime to force people to rely on teleport pads to get around effectively. There's only a handful of dash skills and half of them are glitches (Void blade lunge + Oblivion). This game involves your classic "kill 10 wolves" or "collect 5 materials" and then having to manage which town has an Inn for you to be able to effectively get back to where you are.All in all, it's a decent game if you're not looking to do PVP. If you prefer PVP, prepare to spend a ridiculous amount of time playing catch up, or buying your way to the top. I have more gripes with it but these are the major issues I have. It's another generic Tera-like MMO with a ridiculous gear ladder.
