_childDocuments_.review: 12.7h (based on Steam, 100% achievement, 2x playthrough) No. Yes (8 missable achievements). No. tries to emulate the look of retro games while combining modern elements at the same time. It is a platformer game that will make you think as if you are playing a retro game while not playing it, with combat and puzzle as its focus.- Bosses with different attack patterns- Unique puzzle where you have to find hidden symbols to unlock doors- A lot of power-ups that help you with combat- Character doesn't respawn in the screen where you died- Tutorials blend well with the background, making them hard to notice- It's hard to differentiate between walkable platforms and hazardsThe game tries to emulate the look of CRT displays, but instead of presenting the screen with scan lines, it uses a blur effect instead, making it hard to appreciate the detailed pixel art behind the filter. The game offers an option to disable the said filter, although it only changed the display into a flat-screen instead of a curved one with a slightly reduced blur. Some tutorials are hard to notice because of this, especially since buildings tend to have a similar color to the grey-colored button.The visuals also make it hard to distinguish between walkable and dummy platforms - both look similar apart from a white-ish line that is added on top of it. Although I noticed the difference eventually, some areas are also not very clear when it comes to hazards and platforms. Fortunately, it is only happening in the first area with its blue-colored theme. Dialogues tend to give more information than necessary. Everything that you need to do will be told right after you enter a new area, giving too much information to process. Moreover, characters tend to mix their dialogue with coding terms - people who have little understanding of the subject will need more time to process the dialogues. Luckily, the game offers a shorter, more concise version of the dialogue from the objective list so you don't have to worry about not understanding them.Another story tells about what was happening before the game starts. However, the writing is too bland to my taste, and the weird ending doesn't help either. It seems to be made that way to leave room for a sequel, but I'm not sure if I'm interested in the continuation at this point.Exploration is mostly linear with minimal backtracking as long as you know where to go next. However, some platforms tend to be very small or far from each other, making them hard to reach with the character's fast walking speed. The lack of power-ups to control your landing also prove to be problematic at the beginning of the game. Fortunately, the game is more focused on combat later on, and the power-ups that you'll learn as you progress the game can help you to pass through these areas quickly.Despite some problems, the game does a wonderful job in this aspect. The fast movement speed turns to be more suitable in combat although controls need some improvement - it is easy to press the wrong button by accident with the current setup. Some skills are also tricky to execute, making it hard to finish some enemies.Some areas will lock you out, forcing you to defeat hordes of enemies before you can proceed. Your skill will be tested since the game is quite stingy on heals - you can only heal after you hit the enemy a lot of times, and trust me, you can't exploit the healing system to get out of this. Enemies are varied and come in waves, with some being more annoying than others. You need to prioritize which enemy to kill, all while making sure that you dodge their attacks in the limited area. Bosses have varying attacks that you have to dodge properly. One of them is also clever enough to take advantage of your newly learned skill to beat. However, they tend to be repetitive with their bulky HP and different phases, which doesn't mean much since it usually just becomes faster. This turns the final boss to be a punching bag with its bulky HP and little variation of new attacks - you can even tank the said attack as long as you avoid the rest of its attacks.The game offers puzzles in the form of hidden objects. Colored symbols will appear in the previously explored areas, which you must take note of somewhere outside the game, to unlock a new area. The symbols are not that hard to find as long as you are attentive enough although the symbols for secret areas are more tricky with their subtle hints and placement.  I finished the game for the first time in 8.6h. The game doesn't support backtracking so I had to replay the game to find secrets that I missed. I had more difficulty navigating the area at first, especially since the tutorial isn't so intuitive. The J button in the tutorial looks like a clockwise button and it was hard to figure out where to go next due to how platforms are designed.The difficulty is shifted to combat after I understood how the platforming works. Some areas are challenging to clear because of the enemy variation - some even more difficult than bosses due to the enemies' composition. However, some enemies have too many HP, making them boring to beat in my second playthrough.The game has a weird respawn system. Instead of respawning on the same screen where you died, the game will respawn you at the latest checkpoint. It can be problematic when you are exploring secrets, especially if you die far from the checkpoint. The first area also has too many "pixel-perfect" exits where you have to stand on a specific spot just to exit the area.Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650Despite the promising look, it proves to be problematic at the start. It's hard to know where to go next due to how walkable platforms are designed and the decision not to allow your character to move to the next screen because you are not standing in the right spot - even though you're on the edge of the screen - also becomes an annoyance. More and more problems keep on appearing and I wasn't having fun in the first few hours.Everything changed after I moved to a new area. Some problems are fixed while others become more bearable. The new power-ups also help to ease the problematic platforming elements while increasing the variance in combat. Although some skills tend to be hard to execute with its button placement, it's still possible to finish the fight with basic dodge and attack. New enemies and bosses also keep on appearing to make the game more lively - it proves to be an enjoyable game in the end despite its odd design choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I don't feel like I can recommend Narita Boy, even though it has a lot going for it. Here's my thoughts on the game:The good:* The game has a really well-executed aesthetic. It looks AMAZING.* Soundtrack - the music is banging.* The story. The game tells two stories simultaneously, and so far I think it's pretty decent. Compelling, more than I thought    it'd be.The bad:* Level design / interactable objects: I almost ragequit the game before finding the first key to the first door, because it    required a leap of faith from a place where I couldn't see (hence, leap of faith) to find it. I feel like the game could've been    friendlier about signposting that. The thing is, from where you have to jump, you can see a platform...That leads to    nowhere. You have to jump the other way to find the first key.* Combat / controls. A few hours into the game, you unlock an uppercut move that's pretty important both for platforming    and for boss fights...The only problem is, the game is REAL finicky about when it'll acknowledge that you performed a    successful uppercut. Which leads to situations where you're standing around like a goofball, swinging your sword instead    of jumping. It wouldn't be too critical, except the uppercut becomes an important part of boss fights, which makes it    super frustrating when you take damage because the game didn't like the way you clicked up + attack to perform an    uppercut.* Signposting. It's fair enough to have to find clues to solve puzzles, keys to open doors etc, but... Especially early on, I    spent a lot of time running back and forth on levels, trying to remember where I needed to go to finally unlock doors    after I found the keys to them. Sometimes, the game will literally point arrows at where you need to go, and more often    than not...It won't. I feel like the game would've benefited massively from having a map, which could've been where hints    and quest markers could've gone, to make navigating the digital world a bit friendlier.I don't think, all in all, I can recommend Narita Boy in good conscience, which is a pity. It was clearly made with a lot of love, but there's some misguided design choices in here. Hard combat encounters are only as fun as their controls are responsive, and continually losing to a boss because the game doesn't correctly register an input is not fun. I think there's a reason less than half of all players (48% at the time of writing) have even gotten past the first boss of the game.I think there's a fun experience to be had here, especially if you don't mind harder games. There's a lot of 80s nostalgia, if that's your thing (but not to the annoying levels of Ready Player One).I hope that Studio Koba makes more games, and that they improve on what they have here - the base is solid, but unfortunately marred by some key annoyances with design choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: In this case it would be a very cautious thumbs-up rather than a heartfelt recommendation but, for me, the positives ultimately outweighed the negatives. Beware though, it might very well be the opposite for you, depending on the type of player you are.While the artistic direction of this Tron-inspired 2D platformer is top-notch, it is sadly marred by the slippery movements of Narita Boy, the titular main character, and an uninspired, somewhat linear level-design, with no ability to revisit earlier segments to look for missing collectibles.Yet, the story it tells is touching and the beautiful world of the Digital Kingdom is intriguing enough as to make a player look past these issues, as long as they keep their expectations in check and treat the game as a somewhat action-y walking simulator rather than a full-fledged action-platformer or a 2D metroidvania.And the mesmerizing OST, full of fuzzy synth tunes and callbacks to the 80's, will linger in one's head long after the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes. And quite a strange one.You play a young boy in the 80s, who is sucked into his computer after playing a simple action game for the whole day. You have been summoned by the priests of the Digital Kingdom, a kingdom in the digital realm inhabited by thousands of programs and threatened by HIM. It is a world with quite a few similarities to the world of Disney's Tron. HIM is an evil program, who sends his minions to enslave the whole Digital Kingdom. Noone is able to fight the minions of HIM, only you, Narita Boy, the wielder of the Techno-Sword, can kill them.The game consists of exploring the kingdom, talking to its inhabitants, fighting the minions of HIM. You fight, jump, climb and try not to get lost. Fighting starts easy, but the game continously presents you with new enemies, who all require a different tactic to fight them. Most are easy to dispatch, but when you have to fight more of them at the same time it can get a bit more challenging. Not really difficult, though, until you have to fight the large bosses. They are all completely different, and they do require a bit of thought, sometimes the use of the environement and of course a few retries. Or many retries, as in my case. Apart from the bossfights, the challenge in the game comes from some jumping/climbing/dashing sequences, and from finding your way. Sometimes it can be hard to find a platform or climbable wall and you run around in circles until you see where to continue. The kingdom certainly is not handicapped accessible. Your character downloads new packages to learn new abilities, like a dash or the ability to heal. Actually, there are a lot of upgrades for your hero to find, and you will need most of them to beat the game. There are pools of data to mediate in, and you need to know the correct symbols for each pool. They are hidden in the world, if you keep your eyes open. Apart from that, there are not many puzzles to solve. You receive Techno-keys to unlock the many doors, but there is are no other interactive spots. You just fight, find your way and listen to the inhabitants of the realm.The story is simple - defeat HIM and his minions - but the Digital Kingdom and his inhabitants are presented in a very creative way. A kingdom based on the sacred source code which was designed line by line by The Creator, inhabited by sentient programs that pray to The Creator in temples, with holy relics and Tech-Priests, the beam of the Trichroma as the foundation. When I met Motherboard, supervisor program and protective mother of all the programs in the Digital Kingdom in the beginning I thought what a creative idea, but to my surprise this creativity goes on and on during the whole game. HIM, the former manager of the data dumps, his generals like Lord VHS or the Inquisitor, the Synth-Sensai - Bard of Trifurcation playing synthmusic, a priest who mediates in the mists of the code to connect to the Creator's oneiric flow, the three Houses of the Trichroma... there is a lot to see and read during the game. Knowledge of the Holy Bible, the inner workings of a computer and coding experience are helpful to understand it.HIM destroys the memories of the Creator, and you have to find and preserve them to save the world. You learn about the real-world creator of the Digital Kingdom that way, and have to visit the real-world later in the game. Perfect controller support, a memorable dark synthwave soundtrack, no bugs (that I found).Great surreal techno-religious action platformer in a bizzare digital world.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy always intrigued me with its banging soundtrack and stylistic visuals. So I was delighted to see this in a bundle earlier this year and quickly picked it up. Having played it for 2 hours now, I can say that Narita Boy is an unbearably poor video game. Quite frankly, the only reason I was even able to stick with it for this long was because of the soundtrack, as it is impeccable. Almost every other aspect of this game is, at best, dull, or at worst, excruciatingly insufferable.I think anyone who has played this game would agree that the kind of backtracking present in Narita Boy is one of the worst implementations of it ever seen in a game. The 'mission' structure revolves around entering a brand new area with branching paths and coming across several locked doors randomly scattered everywhere. From here, you have to hope to get lucky to find the one path that has a thread you can pull on which will reward you with a key to access one of the several other locked doors. At this point, you repeat the cycle by backtracking through the entire area - sometimes all the way to where you started and hope to find the one door that you can now open. Repeat until you enter the last locked door, fight a boss, slog through some slow and painfully boring exposition, and then enter a brand new area to repeat this whole cycle. I believe I got halfway through the third big area before I realized I could not spend another minute in this game. Never have I felt like a developer has so adamantly wanted to waste my time as a player than I did during my short time with Narita Boy. Even the starting (unskippable) splash screens take over half a minute to get you into the game.The combat is fine enough, I like the slow but steady introductions to new abilities and movesets, but what I liked the most was the high enemy variety they threw into this game. Coupled with the music, this is by far the best part of the game even though it's so sparingly used in between the tedious walking and jumping and dialogue.This brings me to the story and dialogue. There is simply far too much of it and it was not able to hold my interest for any significant amount of time. Maybe there's an exemplary story that's waiting to be discovered in this game, but I just don't care. Especially since there's someone or something willing to deliver you paragraphs of text every step of the way. I can't recommend this game to anyone but I hope to see big improvements in Studio Koba's future projects. Rest in Force, Narita Boy.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I got the game after watching a glowing review about it but unfortunately have to conclude that it is just not for me. Narita Boy is all about style and theme and it does look glorious in its pixel art splendour.  If the presentation and nostalgia hit your heart you might be able to enjoy this game because I cannot deny it is a really beautiful coat of paint. However, if it does not, I don't think the gameplay or storytelling hold up on its own and the game is not fun to play.Up to the point that I played the game the gameplay consisted of moving from one hub area to another and within the hub searching for keycards and symbols to unlock doors to advance fighting enemies on the way. It is a bit like Metroidvania in this way. This loop is however really repetitive. You have no map to see where you should go so you need to memorize the doorways where to go. Often all you are doing is getting a key item to open the next door which leads to the next key item and this often keeps you running back-and-forth between the extreme ends of the area. It does not help that that traversal often contain precise jumps and the control are very floaty and the character overreacts to the slightest input. It's just plain frustrating. It feels like this design serves no purpose other than pad hours to the gameplay and if there were no better ideas then the game might have benefitted from a more linear design especially because for me the only fun part in the gameplay was the combat and I did enjoy that.What should keep you wanting to advance in the game is the story but it, unfortunately, falls flat for me. The biggest issue for me is that the main character has zero stakes in the plot and because of that I cannot connect to it at all. As far as I understood the player is just someone who gets pulled to the virtual world, is told that he has to save it and slowly unlocks the memories of the world's creator. This in itself is a cool mechanic of revealing the backstory of the world but because I cannot see any connection between the main character and the world or this backstory I found no engagement in it. The main story beats were just snippets of a person's life and I didn't know why I should care about them. And when the gameplay nor the story would drive me to play further, I finally gave up.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: An addendum to my original review: If you have the slightest sense of doubt within your refund window, get a refund. This game starts out pretty cool and turns into a joyless slog. The worst part is the combat. Fight sequences are based around gauntlets and feel like they are crammed in to remind you that this is supposed to be an action game. The ideas and the story could make a good point and click adventure or even an animated movie or series. Narita Boy is a prime example of style over substance. As a stylistic piece, it is great. As a game it is OK at best. Overpromise and underdeliver, the indie way.Original review: Fellow Metroidvania™ enthusiasts, heed this warning: Do not be fooled by mentions of Metroidvania™. If this is Metroid or -vania, it is Castlevania II. Putting a lot of doors in your game and filling it with obscure directions does not make it a Metroidvania™ game. I hate to say that I wanted to like this game just because I wanted to like this game, but at around four hours in this game sure feels like style triumphing over substance. The game looks good, sounds good and plays ... ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game so much. I even came back to it a year later and gave it a second chance. I gave up now.Pros:- The art style is unique and truly extraordinary. It shows a lot of effort was put into it.- The lore has all the potential to be captivating.Cons:- Extremely bad controls all around. Ticks all the checkboxes from “How to create the worst platformer experience 101”.- Lots of upfront lore before you can even do anything. Way too many names and terms dumped on you, and you need to pay attention as a few of them are actual key references to gameplay goals, but it’s not clear which ones.- Unclear progression. It’s very easy to get lost in rooms where to go or what to do next.- Unsatisfying combat.Overall feels like a hugely missed opportunity to create a legendary game. Instead, it’s a combination of the extraordinarily good and extraordinarily frustrating. How did it ever pass early play testing?Without an enjoyable gameplay experience, it’s a visual masterpiece with a sad excuse of being a game. The visual artists would’ve had a better use of their time creating this as an animated series.

The trailer hooked me immediately and I thought, “Wow, this is going to be a banger”. Excited, I bought the game during the winter sale and a month later finally found some time to dive into it. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Gotta be honest, I feel cheated. I was promised a Metroidvania with a cool aesthetic and instead I got a frankly by-the-numbers platformer-beat-em-up which abuses padding to increase its game time. Every single step in your quest is a Fed-ex quest. Go to the guy, get the key, stick it into the thing. I'm serious, every single step is like this. It gets old incredibly quickly and no amount of cool animations or impressive spritework will let you look past how utterly boring this game becomes.The writing kind of has the same problem, it starts out charming but it quickly gets bogged down in its Proper Nouns and, seeing how you're gonna be sent on a Fed-ex quest by the end of the conversation anyway, quickly becomes tiresome white noise. Which is a shame, because I did enjoy the whole "computer terms as fragments of power" aspect of the writing while it lasted.I also hated fighting bosses in this game. It's nothing but waiting for them to actually appear and become vulnerable, buuuuuut you can't really use any of your cool techniques reliably or else you take a hit, so you end up just pecking at them with basic slashes during the vuln phases. Again, it's padding. The whole wait...attack...wait...attack is a sign of bad design.On the whole, I cannot recommend this game. I have about 2 hours of playtime which got me through 1/3 of the game and it was a chore. I have no desire to pick it up again.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy has a great artstyle, some swanky music and an interesting premise, but it's all held back by the fact that it hurts to look at, is clunky to play and makes no attempt to have the player care about its story.Set in a digital kingdom, you set out to restore peace as Narita Boy. The story is a bit more complex than that, also centering around the creator of the kingdom, but it's told very haphazardly, with frequent walks down memory lane (literally), but it's told in a way that makes it hard to really care about what's happening, with prose that doesn't stick in your mind no matter how hard you try. No matter, the core gameplay remains to travel through several kingdoms, vanquish foes and fight back the invaders trying to claim the world as their own.The gameplay is clunky; you learn a lot of different moves throughout your adventure and meet even more enemies, but in the end, you mostly attack with your normal sword attacks and a shotgun which, like most other abilities, has little range and a small attack delay, meaning you get hit more often than not when using it. Fights get somewhat hard pretty quickly and while there is a dodge, you still seem to get hit during it and especially bigger fights often devolve into chaos. Even with a somewhat big arsenal of moves and enemies, fights get boring very quickly because there just isn't much variation. You clear out an arena, move on to the next. New enemies get introduced very frequently, but there's almost too many of them, so you barely have time to get used to what one enemy does before a new one enters the fray.The other part of the gameplay is platforming. It works, for the most part, but there is a small delay before movement stops and you also slide across the ground shortly when you stop moving, which makes precise platforming more clunky than it needs to be. Later on, you also learn an uppercut move that gives you more height and is mandatory for platforming, so instead of jumping, you often have to do an uppercut move that only works from the ground, which just feels awkward.The worst part of Narita Boy though, in my opinion, is just how much the game is designed around wasting your time. It's not really a metroidvania, and yet you have to constantly walk back and forth the kingdom. Go to Task A, then get told you can't do A until you do B, then go to B, then get told that B won't work until you do C, and so on. You walk past tons of locked doors and find keys for those as you progress, but since there is no map(!!!), you have to remember where those doors are and areas get pretty expansive later on, so not providing a map is a game design sin to me. Instead of having a nice, linear game where you progress step by step, you are instead just walking back and forth the same areas, interrupted by fights, to open up doors. Sometimes, you have to solve a small, super easy symbol puzzle, but that barely breaks up the monotony.The last problem is with the artstyle. It looks great, it really does, but the game uses a CRT filter. You can turn it off, but the edges remain blurred and the game continues to look strangely washed out. Every session I played this game, I could not play longer than twenty minutes at a time because my eyes were legitimately hurting from looking at it, which almost never happens. Why mix such an interesting and unique artstyle with a terrible, pain-inducing filter?Overall, I think Narita Boy has very little to offer aside from it's interesting, unique premise and the cool artstyle and music. With clunky platforming and repetitive combat gameplay, I quickly found myself very bored and only about two hours in I realized this would never change for the remaining 7 or 8 hours I still had to go, so I stopped there. On a big sale, it might be worth a look just for how unique it presents itself, but don't expect stellar gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't have a great aesthetic, it *is* a great aesthetic. That is the entirety of the game. It's very apparent where the time and effort was spent in development. There are reams of word-salad exposition, alongside genuinely spectacular art, and it's all very creative. But that's the whole of the game. The combat and platforming feel absolutely awful -- floaty and unresponsive to the extent that I never once, in the 7 hours it took to complete, did I enjoy exploration or combat.If all you need from a game is a 'remember the eighties??' retro aesthetic then great, go for it. But if you need your art to be backed up by an actual game, there's nothing here for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short and sweet.Narita boy was a sensory marvel, with some of the best character designs, illustration, animation, music, world-building, and some spectacular writing.If there are any misgivings in terms of game design, they are overshadowed by everything this game does right.A treat from beginning to end, a true reminder for how games are an art form.Best of luck to Studio Koba for the sequel, and high hopes for improved game design, and some recurring fantastic art and sound in that one!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: + Narita Boy has style in droves-- the world, the visuals, and the music are outstanding. - However, the gameplay is sorely lacking and I found it too shallow to compel me onward. What I experienced in Narita Boy was one giant chain of fetch quests, consisting of tedious backtracking and looking for doors and platform that blend into the background. This combined with floaty, imprecise platforming resulted in a lackluster gaming session for me. - The combat sprinkled throughout the game actually felt like annoying interruptions, and it somehow detracted from the rest of the fetching and the platforming rather than enhancing the game. On top of that, the combat had no sense of challenge or depth. While the enemies vary in appearance and attacks, the method of dealing with them doesn't change in a significant way. If you happen to lose all your health you will be conveniently re-spawned nearby with full health restored.In conclusion, I really wanted to like Narita Boy, but in my opinion it's all style and no substance.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: ABSOLUTE FAVORITETLDR: If you have no patience, this game will own your ass. But if you listen, learn and persevere, you'll get to experience a jaw-dropping, one of a kind world.Not so TLDR: I see a lot of rage about the game mechanics/fight system or having to search around a bit for the way forward, but my peeps, it's just your genuine retro game that seems simple enough but you really have to get your ♥♥♥♥ together and, if need be, repeat everything over and over again until the movements become muscle memory and you don't even think before the combos anymore. It's maybe because I started gaming in the nineties that this piece felt like coming home in many ways. For me, nothing felt clunky, there was just the right amount of delays, heck, even the slight sliding when you land on a platform felt so familiar the creators couldn't even deny they aren't copying an era but lived the original. It was like I played this long ago and now got to visit the world again. Was I lost occasionally a bit before getting through a part? Definitely. Did I have quite malicious thoughts toward the developers at fighting certain parts and bosses? You don't even want to know. (If I ever hear the word "glaucoma" again, I swear...) But heck, it was worth it. Beating the game feels like a real achievement, and when you realise how the movements and hitboxes work, everything gets easier. Just give yourself time to get the rhythm. This game is about getting shocked AF when suddenly out of the blue it throws literally everything at your head at once, but if you don't chicken out and keep trying then in the most unexpected moment you'll notice that somehow you have done it, right before your brain would decide to simply explode.So don't give up!I loved the story snippets too. This game doesn't have to be more to be extraordinary. It's an obviously very personal project and I am glad to be someone who was able to peek into someone's soul this deep. The music is also absolute perfection, and in the world of images being so sharp they are close to damage your vision, the blur and chromatic was a very welcome addition too.Narita Boy is a forever favorite for me for sure. I hope one day I can continue this adventure.Honorable mention:As much as Glaucoma shortened my life with a few precious years, I just loved the Glove fight for some reason. It might never happened before that I laughed more than I cussed during a fight this crazy. And holy hells, Black Rainbow design just blew my mind. A real eyegasm, all of it.Thank you, Studio Koba! ,\m/
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a very charming game with an immaculate aesthetic. The surface of the story is nice and all but the dialogue in the game really gives TMI, personally after 2-3 hours I got tired of reading walls of text and I started reading through the lines mostly to save my time and sanity, the controls feel kinda bad, yes you get used to it but it might get a tad bit frustrating especially on platforming sections and areas with a lot of enemies since your character won't really listen to your inputs and will cause you to get a lot of damage in the process, there's also like an animation for some of your skills that lock you into place, leaving you vulnerable which felt really bad at times.Narita Boy is not the most polished experience you'll have but for the aesthetic, the amazing soundtrack it has and the content it offers for its price I think it's worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I have not ever been this conflicted on whether I enjoyed a game. I am quite glad I experienced it, and I will remember it very clearly (even fondly), but I never want to touch it again. So here are my thoughts, from most positive to most negative.The visuals are excellent. Jaw-droppingly perfect. I played Gris recently and thought it was the most stunning game I had ever played, yet Narita Boy blows that one out of the water (albeit in a very different style). Every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ location, character, enemy, etc. is dripping with details. It's nearly over-designed as some of the most detailed settings and characters make up about ten seconds of your journey. This is the single strongest aspect of the game, and not once in its seven hours did the visual quality drop for even a moment. It's the biggest reason I'm recommending the game, as (alongside the stellar soundtrack) it transforms the game into an otherworldly experience the likes of which I am sure I won't see again for a long time.The story is fine. I've heard people say it was the best part of the game for them, so I really don't think I got it. Within seconds of existing in the world you're given several paragraphs of Proper Nouns that you've never heard of, and this never ceases. The narrative was at least interesting enough to make me want to see the end. I'm sure it would make more sense if I replayed the game, but as I said I have no desire to do that.The gameplay? It's... complicated. At best, it's serviceable, and even a little fun. There was one really great boss fight, and several of the minor enemy encounters tested my skills in a satisfying way. I'd occasionally find that even if a group of enemies ambushed me really quickly, I would respawn and take them all out without taking a single hit, which is the mark of a well-designed combat system. But the game only felt this good to play some of the time. It's death by a thousand cuts, where there are too many tiny problems:-enemies are absurdly tanky-some attacks are barely telegraphed and have unclear hitboxes-some bosses (the Koifish and White Noise spring to mind) are just awful-there are too many instances where whatever your doing is randomly interrupted by mediocre combat, or worse yet a random boss fight with no build-up-player controls are not satisfying and make all instances of platforming a choreI suspect these problems all could have been fixed by more thorough playtesting, but none of Narita Boy's flaws were as preventable as the one which made me the most sick of it:Save points don't restore your health. Unless I'm really dumb and missed something obvious, the only way to fully replenish health outside of combat is dying. This meant I would frequently enter encounters with only about two bars of health, do well enough to almost see the end, then die, only to have all of my health restored for the next attempt. I'm willing to bet that most of my playtime was wasted fighting enemies I'd already fought before, because even the easy ones have too much health. You learn their patterns, you fight them, you eventually kill them, then one of the difficult enemies in the next wave takes you out with its inconsistent and poorly-telegraphed attacks, and you have to suffer through all the easy enemies again for so, so long. That's how most of this game feels to play. Why not simply make health fully replenished when the game saves, like so many other games have the sense to do? It's not more challenging due to this problem, it's only more tedious. This one issue destroyed my momentum so many times and I have no clue why it works like this when there has been so much care put into making the atmosphere the best it can possible be. One simple fix to this system and I would've come away loving this game despite its flaws, but I just can't remember my time here as fun.I still absolutely recommend this game for the experience it provides, but please be warned it is all-too-often a slog to play as it fails on so many levels when it comes to game design.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: What happens when you turn programming into a religion?You end up with .Watching the trailer and getting this on a discount I expected it to be some generic hack and slash with interesting visuals, and a story just to excuse it.What I got instead was a trip into mysticism and crisis of faith, all repackaged into the context of self-aware programs and a world that has been developed by them to reflect where their faith brought them, following the lore of its world and the Creator’s backstory was a delight.It takes the “chosen one” trope and really makes it work within the story instead of being a random dude with no reason to be suddenly important.Combat is intuitive but some battles will require to be quick on your reflexesI wish that the combat system stayed as basic as possible over introducing mechanics you’ll use in a very specific scenario and never again, or redundant powers that feel the same.While I would have liked a higher intensity ending, and one that wouldn’t need a sequel to work, I’d still consider this to be a great game, and is a shame that the 25$ price tag has scared so may people away from this.(Message for the dev, please for the love of the Trichroma, make this title cost around 5 to 10 dollars, what you would lose in a single sale you’ll make up in more sales, especially since this game deserves to be played by a wider audience)
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I’m giving the game a negative rating mainly due to a game-breaking glitch that forced me to quit halfway. I tried Googling for a fix and searched the forums, and eventually found a post on Reddit from two years ago mentioning the same issue, with another player replying having the same glitch and was looking for a solution, yet no answer was ever provided. I can’t expect the developers to fix it.Game art style is imaginative. I especially liked the electric sheep with monitors displayed on their sides, they reminded me of a book I read as a kid: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? A classic. The giant electric frog with a glowing belly that lights up when it breathes was both crazy and cool.The combat mainly involves basic attacks, but the enemies aren’t too tough. The most frustrating aspect of the game for me is the lack of an area or mini-map. Player is constantly required to backtrack to retrieve cards and then place them into card readers. Without a map, the game quickly becomes a test of memory. I had to focus and keep in mind the locations of the card readers because if I exit and return the next day, I wouldn’t remember where to go.The most disappointing part goes to the game-breaking glitch. In the second totem area, I got a hoverboard for surfing but suddenly my character froze. I exited the game, when I got back the hoverboard was gone and nowhere to be found.I can't rate a game positively when there’s a glitch that breaks the main story, regardless how good it performs in other aspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: A 2D action platformer with an awesome retro aesthetic.Pros:* Music's great! And the theme song is pretty catchy.* The pixel art and CRT soft filter look good.* You get to ride a 3.5" floppy disk, how cool is that. Cons:* The controls didn't feel as responsive as I would've liked and having to use your uppercut attack to reach higher ground instead of a typical double jump was odd.* You can't revisit areas which means if you miss a collectible for an achievement, you have to start a new game.* The boss fights were mediocre except for a few.* Max resolution only goes up to 2560x1440, no 4K option.It's a decent game but I didn't really feel engaged in the story and the gameplay itself was a bit of a letdown.I'd only recommend picking this up if you want that nostalgic feeling and when it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy disappointed me. I expected and wanted a full action combat platformer. But action combat and platforming are minor aspects of this game. What this game really is about is the story...and running around already visited screens searching for that one damn door where this key you just got belongs to.I said ok, I don't get what I wanted/expected, but maybe I can enjoy this too. I took a walkthrough video to skip this dull searching for that one door you have to find and additionally went with an achievement guide and this saved me from some frustration.This is not a metroidvania, but a linear game letting you search in much too open areas. Also you cannot revisit older areas! Achievement hunters beware! Once you reach specific points you cannot return to the visited areas. Not found achievements will require another full playthrough! But what this game really shines at is its dope pixel art, sci-fi computer world and its heartfelt story. The story really got to me and made me feel for the characters. Though I thought, this whole "we're in a computer world" thing was too made up and got old a bit while progressing, as well as the NPCs trying to tell you to pronounce it more heroicly as Naaritaaaaa Booooooyyy! But overall it's a good experience if you let yourself be gripped by the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Okay the music and visuals are really beautiful aside from the rapid flashing, but the writing is so terrible and seems so proud of itself. It sounds like technobabble from the worst episodes of Star Trek, stretched out over multiple hours, every level is just backtracking from one key to another, and combat is barely-passable button mashing. And then it uses the exact same storytelling device as Code Vein, right down to the cheesy sad piano music, to explain the story rather than letting you figure out the themes on your own.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The obvious things this game does well are almost immediately overshadowed by everything it sucks at. It's a really pretty experience, despite its own best efforts to blur the screen constantly and obfuscate its own hard work. The sprites were clearly a labor of love, as was the entire game world, but it's all impossible to appreciate under the horrible vignette filters and faux CRT blur. There is an option to remove said filter, but it's pointless, as the blur and fuzz remains either way. It's a terrible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. Absolutely a drag to play. The bosses are uninspired and dry, like three-days-past leftover turkey. The general gameplay loop of fetching a ton of runes from pretentiously esoteric and violently bland NPCs (all of whom have the *exact* same design, making the entire game a veritable house of mirrors) is only briefly broken up by incredibly disappointing views into the "creator's" history and slapdash-at-best combat sequences. You're given a small handful of tools to approach combat, but why bother when you could just turtle the corner and baseball swing like a Little League kid on the losing team? All this is compounded further by the *absolutely depressing* ice-surface momentum of your jumps. For a pixel-art platforming adventure, there's not a lot of fun in the art, the platforming, or the adventuring aspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: are sensational & give off an almost melancholic feeling at times. For the most part It wears it's influences on it's sleeves and is self-aware. Actually playing a game of a game is an inception of it's own ordeal. Quite a fascinating concept that is utilized quite well in the story and gameplay. is very fitting and sets the tone well, the main menu and end credit songs were especially certified bangers. is multilayered and very thought provoking at times, expressive and interlinking with subtle meanings and hints to things that you might not notice at first. is top-notch with varied abilities that flow seamlessly together thanks to the high-quality animations. It's a deep and engaging system. Moreover, I loved the way the difficulty ramped-up as the game went on. Though nitpicky, fights at first were a *bit* tedious and took a long time, with later abilities this gets resolved for the most part but still happens here and there. that lead to an extra cut-scene. I *HATE* missables in games, it adds nothing to the experience and only sours it when you miss just one item out of the whole, it also makes you constantly worry if this is a point of no return or not and if you've missed anything. The game already allows you to backtrack a fair portion of the map, so adding that tiny bit more would just give the game a feeling of contentedness and would solve missables. goes opposite to the way your character is facing, while a directional dodge will move toward the way you want but it will rotate your character to face the opposite side. This is, to me at least, opposite to the way I have been conditioned in every other video game I have played. It has got me hit way too many times and seems kinda backwards to how your brain thinks. The gap-closer/stinger/pierce in the game also needs to be input after a dodge so you have to: 1- Face the enemy, 2- stop. 3- dodge, 4- move toward the enemy while simultaneously attacking.One nitpick I have connected to this is, all directional attacks require you to input a direction with the attack simultaneously and not already have your analog in a direction and then press. This might be a non-issue to you but for me it interrupted my flow sometimes.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I don't see what I can write that others haven't already. The art and the music are great, but the control feels bad and eats your inputs, general movement feels bad, the fights don't feel good and are very basic, and so far the story feels like a journal turned into a walking simulator. That is, when the paragraphs of nonsense words convey actual story information. Pretty as it is ( with the blur filter off anyhow), the story isn't interesting enough, and the gameplay controls poorly enough, that I can't go on. I'm not alone in this, as at the time of writing only 30% of players have made it this far into the game, and from the other achievements about 13% of players have finished the game. From the reviews I'm betting it has a devoted following but I'm not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This is yet another example of what happens when a studio puts too much emphasis on artistic style, and forgets that games are supposed to be fun. If I were giving this a score based entirely on the audio / visual experience, it would be among the best of the 2D nostalgia set. But since it's a game and not a movie, gameplay matters. And the gameplay, to put it simply, sucks.I won't rehash what the other critics have said; every negative point mentioned is a valid criticism and collectively, it's just not keeping me interested enough to keep playing. If I have spend an hour looking for some generic key-like-object because the on-screen objectives make absolutely no sense in English, and the level itself is designed to obscure anything that would make navigation tenable... well, I've just got better things to do with my time.It's sad because that game this almost was, would have been really really wonderful. We can only wonder what might have been, if all that sound and graphics were put into the hands of a capable producer.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: They fixed it now (Developer commented and I confirmed it).Which probably means I should write an actual review.Well to put it bluntly the game is good.  You play as a chosen one destined to save the Digital Kingdom from HIM.  Even though the story is just a bucket of tropes (that even ends the same way  does), if you actually play this you won't care about that because a. that's more fun and b. the worldbuilding is absolutely NUTS.  The best way to describe it is imagine Tron and Japanese Shinto had babies and threw them at your dad's apple macintosh.So how does it play?  Well, it plays like a 2D sidescroller that starts with sword combat that has a basic 1-2-3 combo, a charge strike, and a cooldown-based shotgun move that can either fire 3 individual shots in melee range or use them all at once for a beam attack.  This then expands with a heal, dodges, an uppercut, risk/reward polarity matching, summon attacks, and some other surprises I won't spoil here.  And as you get these upgrades the game does a great job of adding new things to get you to use them and mixes things up with some well done boss fights.However the only problem with the gameplay is that it doesn't control as well as it should.  General movement feels a bit slippery and sometimes dodges and jumps don't occur right when you push the button (and one of your dodges is super stingy with I-Frames).  However since the game doesn't demand THAT much precision from you AND since it's ludicrously generous with checkpoints the worst you'll have it is restarting A combat encounter or boss fight.  (and complaints about the servo horse segment are complaining about a bug that has been fixed as stated above.)Asides from that though I have three other complaints:1. This game is begging for a chapter select feature awarded when you beat the game so you can go back and grab the things you missed.  (And it would've made verifying the servo horse being fixed a lot easier.)2. It would be nice if you could swap the d-pad and left analog stick for summons/movement.  YUP, that's right fellow d-pad brethren, the superior mode for movement for this game was sacrificed on the altar of summon attacks.3. going by the other reviews it seems like button prompts for keyboard controls aren't working.  (If you are using a keyboard, you're supposed to mash the attack key when you're trying to meditate and the prompt is telling you to press a button that doesn't exist on your keyboard.)TL;DR:This game's main strengths are presentation, soundtrack (did I forget to mention the soundtrack is AWESOME), and combat.  There's a few control ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but they're more annoying than anything.  It probably isn't going to win Game of the Year anytime soon but it's a good time, particularly if you're into the aesthetic.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: There are a number of player inconveniences throughout this game. Full animations for mundane tasks play throughout the entire game instead of cutting it short after the first one. The interact area for using doors, talking to npc's etc is small and can be annoying to get to with the in game movement. The font used made it hard to tell they wanted me to mash the "J" key. Some npc's give you actual information while some say a paragraph of absolute gibberish. I stopped reading any of the text pretty early on. Some of the visuals are just hard to see compared to the rest of the game. I accidentally stumbled upon an opening early in the game after looking around for a while because I couldn't tell where to go next. It was below me and the same color as all the cliffs and platforms around. The memories are pretty bad as well. It forces you to slow walk through a story that is really hard to care about. I started "speed" running these sections pretty early on. If I could jump or move at the normal speed I wouldnt mind it as much.. but making it a slow slog through this other world just made me want to get passed it. I didn't finish this game. The visual noise on the top of the train finally made me rage quit. There are much better games out there. Play those first.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Think of a pixel-art TRON but with more techno, more computer-babble and a far better storyline and you're close to . Journey through the digital realm to piece together the memories of its Creator, so he can erase the scourge that has fallen on it. Very good pixel art graphics and an exceptional soundtrack encompass an above average hack and slash game. It desperately needs a map, better controls (no D-Pad controls at all, seriously?) and the combat and platforming get stale fast. But it’s a solid game and well worth the money for the few hours you'll get out of it. Just don't expect anything mind-blowing. is a 2D, pixel art hack and slash game from Studio Koba and published by Team 17. Set in the ‘80s, it places you in the shoes of the titular protagonist and tasks you with ridding the digital realm of HIM and the stallions, an army of corrupted entities who want to rule over the whole digital realm and try to merge with the real world. Armed with the trusty techno-sword, you will chop your way through three worlds while re-assembling the fragmented memories of the Creator so he can restore balance to the digital realm and eradicate HIM. Starting off, the visuals are excellent. The graphics in pixel art games are improving rapidly and  continues this theme. The area landscapes are rich and vibrant and a joy to look at. The retro ‘80s aesthetic is in full effect here, from every level being coated in layers of neon to the screen having a slightly curved and blurry CRT effect (which can be switched off if you hate it). All of the NPC models are really well detailed, the enemies are quite distinct with superb animations while they all die in a nice, interesting fashion. The bosses, in particular, have a health bar that's represented by a beating black heart that gradually pumps faster as they absorb damage until it bursts in glorious fashion. In fact, the worst designed character model is that of the Narita Boy himself, who's just a grey stick figure with a glowing symbol on his chest and a yellow block for a face. Pity more detail couldn't have gone into the lead character.  The visuals are not the high point of ; however, it's the soundtrack by Salvador Fornieles. It's an explosion of synth and techno excellence that compliments the gameplay and surroundings perfectly. Subdued and simple during the story and exploration sections while pounding and complex during the combat, it carries you along at just the right pace. It's a real show of how a soundtrack can enhance the gameplay so much; Studio Koba and Salvador Fornieles deserve so much credit for it.  Storyline-wise, there are two distinct layers; Narita Boy’s quest to defeat HIM and liberate the three worlds (or houses as they're called) and the journey through the Creator’s memories. Each house’s quest objectives are vomited out at their beginnings in jargon-laden walls of text that seem almost designed to be difficult to follow. It gets easier outside of the starting sections but not by much; there's just far too much text at times. You'll wind up just pressing the button as quick as you can to speed through it, and you'll only take in one word in every five. It doesn't make the game worse, but means that it takes a bit more effort to enjoy. By contrast, the Creator’s memory sections are absolute gold. Soundtracked with a gentle music-box style melody, the memories give the game a surprisingly emotional tone. Detailing the Creator’s life from his early childhood to the present, each sequence expertly links the digital realm you're fighting through to the real world you're trying to save. I genuinely got excited every time I came across one of these memories and thoroughly enjoyed them all.  The gameplay and combat are where  starts to let itself down, though. The controls are really floaty, and you never really feel as if you're in full control. Even the gentlest push of the analog stick will produce huge, exaggerated movements, and the lack of D-Pad controls is a frankly incomprehensible oversight - especially seeing as the D-Pad isn't used for anything else. This lack of control really becomes apparent in the game's platforming sections. You'll routinely overshoot ledges, and it gets very annoying - especially in the odd boss fight where platforming and combat are combined. Trying to land on a small ledge at full speed whilst also dodging an attack will have you swearing at your monitor in frustration. It feels like this is a game that calls for precise platforming but doesn't have precise platforming controls. It's an element that gets stale fast.  The combat is a little better but suffers from the same staleness as the platforming. At the outset, you're given a standard set of moves: a three-hit combo and a shotgun blast that can be powered up into a screen-length beam attack. To this you'll add your standard fare of an uppercut attack, a downward strike, a shoulder bash and a dash attack...and that's it for moves. None of them evolve over the course of the game in any way; most aren't usable on every type of enemy. They're only usable on the enemy they were designed for, making them seem less like a proper combat technique and more a kind of gimmick. In fact, they’re mostly used for platforming, not combat. The shoulder bash can break through certain walls, the downstrike is used to get through floors and the uppercut’s chief use is as a higher jump. Combine this with most of the enemies having only one attack and one method to dodge that attack and you've got a combat mechanic that's shockingly short of ideas. There is a "wildfire" mechanism where you power up a particular colour symbol above your head and can deal and will also receive extra damage to enemies with that same symbol, but it doesn't make the combat any more fun and can be totally ignored if you like. Having said all this, the combat in  is quite a lot of fun until you hit this nadir. The problem is you'll hit it pretty quickly.  It’s also the exploration element that suffers massively from this lack of ideas. Ignore anyone who tells you this game is a metroidvania, it's nothing of the sort. In those games, the back-tracking and exploration are worked to form part of the core game design. In , it's tacked on just to stop the game being a linear progression from one end of the map to the other. Running back and forth looking for a particular door without a map will test your patience, and the fact the keys have no identifying text is baffling. They're only identified the moment you pick them up, so if you miss that, you'd better hope the mission objectives state what they're for (they don't always), or you're stuck running around a pretty labyrinth. This doesn't bog the game down much, as the maps aren't that large, but it's another puzzling design lapse.  In the end,  is a short game and benefits from it. It doesn't overstay its welcome by much and is enjoyable while it lasts. Its main attractions are the gorgeous artwork, banging soundtrack and an emotional story. Its main flaws are repetitive combat, loose controls and a lack of any innovation outside the audio/visual elements. It's gorgeous, flashy, fun (for a bit) and completely hollow...hey, what could be more ‘80s than that?

_childDocuments_.review: I've bought this game because in the first trailer on the steam page somebody says that Narita Boy is one of the best metroidvania games in recent memory.....well that's a lie.One of the most boring games I've played in a while, go from door to door getting keys to a different door. To just get a key again to go to a door next door. I feels so pointless. The story also didn't do it for me, and combat is basic at best.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game. Not a metroidvania in the slightest, I dont know why I thought it was going to have some elements of one. Its more or less an adventure game.. with some combat. A lot of the game is in the story and environmental story telling. Its essentially Tron. If you are interested in the art style, a Tron-like story and a banging soundtrack, definitely check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game, or so it seems. Ultimately it overstays its welcome and has little to no variety and some irksome shortcomings in quality of life and controls. I really like the aesthetics and the subject matter, story and overall design. However these cannot make up for sometimes unnecessary stale controls (instead of a double jump mechanic you have to uppercut to gain access to higher places as only one example) which can really spoil the fun. Not only are they sometimes unnecessarily complex but chaining movements and attack moves feels unresponsive and annoying. On top of that there are little things like the lack of a map screen (in a Metroidvania type game) that give the player a feeling of disorientation and make the world feel smaller than it actually is - not to mention there is little to no exploration or impetus therefore. I liked the storybit and the technobabble the lovely design but sadly for me at least the games lacks substance to keep me playing all the way through, I may return to the game one day but for now I can't say I feel like spending any more time on it after about 9 hours and 75% of the single player campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic artistic direction, great music. People seem to dislike the combat. It wasn't that varied but you could do things like cancelling mid-combo to switch into other attacks. I enjoyed it enough to finish it. The story was interesting, but it left me feeling there was something more to be desired from it.I did not like the lack of the map, and that you could not backtrack to find the rest of the memory fragments.I was oftentimes lost and had to walk around back and forth till I figured what it was I missed. It was still quite enjoyable. I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: your classic PC adventure game with some modern twists, it is slow starting and very unnecessarily wordy.+ beautiful art and designs all around+ fun and well done animations+ amazing music+ huge variety of enemies and bosses+ the game keeps itself fresh with new mechanics and enemies every 5 min +\- the story is ok nothing special- the dialogue and "lore" in the virtual world is really long and unnecessary it made my first half of the game hell trying to read it all, as soon as I learned to ignore it and skip it I ironically found myself much more immersed in the world and the game.-  with so many bosses you sadly run into a lot of designs that needs a lot of tweaking- I know it's designed to be a classic adventure game but the game could really use a map, even if it is something that you can trigger from the options if you don't want the "classic" experience - the game could be shorter by an hour or so, as much as the game tries to keep things new at the end, I felt the middle to be somewhat badly pacedthe game in general is good with amazing aesthetics and pretty solid gameplay, if after the first 30 min you don't enjoy the dialogue just skip it and your experience will be much better.can't wait for the continuation! it ends on a really interesting point and I'm excited to see more
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I understand what Narita Boy is trying to accomplish. It seems to borrow some inspiration from TRON to a degree but brings it's own flare to the table. There's other inspirations I'm probably not connecting the dots on but I do feel a vague resemblance of them through this game.I do dig the music, it's got nice synthetic electronic ambience and beats that are worth a listen.The gameplay is okay but nothing intriguing, just the basics of do this and do that. I will say Narita Boy has that obnoxious method of combat where your momentum is so continuous that it opens you for hits which can be annoying.But the one fundamental flaw about this game which is not going to see me play it again is the flashing effects. I don't have photosensitivity, but my eyes will get strained fast if there's enough flashing bright colors and lights to see. It's like glitch effects, I just can't deal with it anymore and this game has some of that.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for September 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.This is a game trying to base itself on an eighties game and it’s really obvious from the video, Narita Boy has a ton of style in its art.  It’s just a shame that the gameplay and the experience are so underwhelming. The story is about a player sucked into a game and then fighting to save it from its creator and an evil force named the Stallions.  As I played it, I couldn’t help but think about how many missed opportunities there were here.  One character is named the Motherboard, but there are not that many other references to computer hardware or software.  Even when the game tries, it just makes up words like Trichroma instead of giving players something recognizable.  I kept thinking of how Tron did this idea so much better, even in a movie. The gameplay is also lacking, while the combat is acceptable, there’s also a lot of walking, and a ton of backtracking.  Directions aren’t always clear, but even then the battles are mostly easy to dodge attacks and then punish enemies, nothing that deep.  The platforming is merely ok.  There’s just nothing beyond the art that I clicked with. Pick this up if you love the art style here, this is really what it looks like, but the gameplay is pretty rough for what it is.  What a shame, because I love the concept here.  Traveling into a computer can be a rich experience, but this one just wasn’t that enjoyable.  If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough of the game and overall I can definitely recommend this game.In my opinion the visuals are absolutely stunning and one of the best uses of detailed pixel graphics I've seen in a long time.Similar to that the gameplay feels pretty nice overall its a 2D-sidescroller with heavy empathize on close engagements with the enemies, you start with only a handful of moves and in true metroidvania fashion unlock more and more moves over time. The introduction of those moves is overall pretty well done and I found use in basically all moves till the very end. The inclusion of only one range attack is a very good choice since it always forces you to get close to enemies in order to battleSome downsides to this system however is that certain hitboxes can feel weird sometimes and from time to time the game has some problems with enemy visibility especially in areas where there is a lot of movement While I would say this game falls into the metroidvania category compared to other games like Hollow knight it is far far more linear and less build on secrets and hidden paths so for people who look for a true metroidvania experience like Hollow knight I cant recommend the game in that sense. Most of the Boss fights in the game are mostly well done, they all follow their own scheme and are never crazy difficult well all of them except one (Warning story spoilers ahead)Overall I enjoyed this game a ton it always felt engaging and I can only hope for a DLC or next game in the future(Also one last note this is kinda my first ever review so I apologize for any grammatical errors or hard to read parts)

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a game that takes such a strong influence from so many past works, it can often feel a bit derivative. However, that doesn’t stop the game from being enjoyable, as there’s plenty of unique challenges to overcome as well as some solid lore-building. It’s gorgeous visual design and soundtrack will be enough to entice anyone familiar with 80s pop culture, and could prove irresistible to those that have a fondness for the era.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Since I don't want to give a NEGATIVE rating, I want to start with what I DIDN'T like for readers to know this is not a high-praising review. Steam does this positive/negative rating which I always found extremely misleading and inaccurate.This is a game for people that loves a story and appreciate art, not someone that enjoys complex mechanics and character evolution. The game mechanics are extremely simplistic, I certainly didn't enjoy much either the combat or the platforming. There's also ZERO secrets to find, which in these kind of games, really keeps my curiosity for exploration going, I really missed that.This is a VERY linear sidescroller, with a satisfying weapon stroke feel, but (as far as 4 hrs in) almost nonexistent attack variety. The jump and landing are the kind of sluggish, sliding, which will keep you missing (the many) tiny, unnecessary platforms along the way, which will certainly make you waste time, but not stop your progress, as the continuing is unlimited pretty much from where you die.I wish all these aspect were more complex, the game could be way more addictive, interesting and fun to play, but as it is, it's just a VERY beautiful game, I really mean it, the art design, backgrounds and animations are absolutely amazing and it's definitely what keeps me playing the game.There's some good retro music, good but nothing you haven't heard in the thousands of games following this retro trend.The story seems deep, due to the long texts and dialog, but I find them at many times boring and unnecessary, some times skipping them. Recommended for story-telling fans, not for combat or platformer enthusiasts.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Amazing pixel art.✔️Great universe and intriguing atmosphere.✔️Decent level design.✔️Good synthwave soundtrack.✔️Nice gameplay with satisfying combat.✔️The techno-sword.✔️Cons:Lot of backtracking.❌Lack of minimap can be annoying at times.❌Dash stab ability is not very intuitive to use.❌Probably doesn't offer much replay value.❌Narita Boy is a great indie game and you should play it.Well done Studio Koba.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy!  Narita Boy!  Save the world!!!Narita Boy is one of the best games I have played in a long time.  I was blown away.  It is a 2D side scrolling action game.  It's non linear, but not a metroidvania or anything like that.  You don't even get, or need, a map.  I am always skeptical when approaching games with retro graphics, especially when they lean into the whole "retro" vibe very hard.  It not that I dislike that kind of stuff, in fact I love it.  It just seems that games will sometimes use it as a crutch, to hide crappy gameplay, or poor production values (I'm looking at you, Retro City Rampage).   Narita Boy could... usher you into its world a little better than it does.  After a short cinema, you are seemingly pulled into the digital world of a computer.  The digital characters you meet inside speak english, but their vocabulary leans heavily into "computer speak" and especially at first, it can be difficult to figure out what the hell is going on.  Adding to the trouble, the first area is a little boring graphically, and even worse, somewhat generic.  While the fighting is pretty good from the start, you don't have a lot of moves yet, and therefore it is not nearly as dynamic as it will become.You just have to get through that first bit though, because Narita Boy is incredible. The music and sound are astounding.  PLAY WITH HEADPHONES ON!!.  The music (by Salvinsky) is so good, and so varied.  While it incorporates electronica and chiptunes, it is not held back by any sort of retro limits.  There are voice and instrument samples, etc.  The graphics are equally astounding.  It is a pixel art style that reminds me of old pc adventure games, or a more recent example, Superbros Sword and Sworcery.  The pixel art is lovingly and expertly rendered, and also incredibly animated.   Like the music/sound, the art never lets itself be held back by any devotion to retro limits.  Every area is beautiful and varied.  There are a number of memorable, beautiful moments, but I do not want to spoil much more, especially because Narita Boy is brief in its brilliance, clocking in at about six hours.  The story that ends up being revealed is nothing too groudbreaking, but is certainly interesting, and seems personal to the developers.Narita Boy is a work of art.  All of its parts are crafted with equal amounts of care and expertise.  I can not say enough good things about Narita Boy.  Play this game!!!  (with headphones)10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Play it to slash stuffs, go on an adventure and pay little to no attention to the actual storyline and pretend you're having an acid trip, with an awesome soundtrack and honestly very cool enemy/boss designs, and areas.Admittedly very confusing at first but stick with it.V gg, I enjoyed it, buy it during a hefty sale
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This is a mixed bag. Narita Boy really feels like it wanted to be an album+short story, then remembered it has to be a game at some point. The movement feels too loose, and combat feels like it was added in as an afterthought. I died a lot, but there was never any real punishment, maybe because the devs knew it was a bit of a slog already.That being said, the best part of this game are the visuals and soundtrack; some of the best pixel art I've seen in a while. Unfortunately that does end up meaning that telling what is and isn't a platform can be an issue.Also, whoever wrote the story needs to learn to show and not tell. I eventually ended up just mashing through textboxes.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth it at the moment.
