_childDocuments_.review: This game is something else, this is what art in video game format looks like and it really goes to show in the visual sound and storytelling department, all of them are splendid, now that brings me to the one downside of this game, the gameplay:-The world while built to look expansive is quite linear (not too big a deal this is a metroidvania after all and most of the time I was losing myself in the aesthetic of the world)-The controls are quite irritating sometimes, most frequently with dashing some of the attacks (THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ FORWARD SLASH DASH IS A SKILL YOU HAVE TO MASTER) -The story is rather short beat it in 8 hours 100% (which you might have to do a second run on )Otherwise great game GREAT JOB
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: It's a well made game for sure, for me the story is overwhelmingly the most captivating aspect of the game, almost Tron but not quite, laden with 80's references including that old staple the DeLorean.What I would say though is as a tagged "metroidvania" it's lite on that aspect, it introduces power ups and enemies at an alarming rate then you never see or need to use them again. As an example colour / elemental matching is a nice idea but it's completely unnecessary for completion of the game. At one stage your a horse, then it morphs into a robot and then all of that is never to be seen again. In specific areas, even across the broader game that thick and fast approach comes across as muddled, less is more at times when you make a comparison with something like Guacamelee (and two dozen others) where every power up has a clear purpose game wide...dimension switching, colour matching which is a requirement to beating enemies and just more refinement generally and certainly more refinement to the platforming and combat.Nitpicking aside however it's an enjoyable playthrough with the casual approach to difficulty allowing the story to take centre stage.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Cool style, nice music, pretty good combat animations.Yet even the first hour of the game is so overloaded with text that clearly interested the writer morethan it does the player, full of absolutely nonsensicle technobabble that would be fine as a little joke,but seems to take itself so serious that it's only a pain to read through.That, combined with the fact that the level design gives absolutely NO INDICATION OF WHERE ONE CAN GO or what is possible to interact with, unless you're already standing directly in front of it.And because there's also no map, I had absolutely no idea where to go once I had reached the first cul-de-sac that the game seemed to guide me to.So I quit after the first memory of mister bearded man. Which was in itself absolutely pointless. Good to know that some bearded guy had a mother. Who'd have thought.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation, visuals, audio, story and stuffs are stylized really well and delivers what they wanted to deliver.But the gameplay is really hollow, not much really going on, especially the level design which contains a lot of backtracking that feels like chores, sure the visuals are eye-candy but the controls are floaty and horrible, the combat is also plain. It feels good punching those red digital thingy but it gets boring p fast :(Idk how to rate this, but I don't want to recommend this for those guys who prefer good gameplay over presentation :(
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Choices that made this game not enjoyable:- Bad jumping mechanics. Different isn't always good. Can be VERY frustrating and clunky. Half the challenge of the game is the controls. Maybe keyboard is better than on controller.  - No backtracking to completed areas in case you missed something. No given reason why, but you can soft lock out of getting the optional memory if you leave one of the three color areas without one of the back up floppies. Can't reload a save either: you need to start a new game. - The auto save points can be pretty inconvenient and lead to unnecessary back tracking when getting to a boss. - Many bosses are just not that fun. A lot have tedious patterns where you have to wait for an opening. They are often so simple its frustrating when you die to your own jumping mechanic rather than the boss design. Some bosses were great, but its not consistent. The good: Aesthetics are great. Love the artwork across the board. Music is great. I really wanted to like this game, but I really don't like the control scheme. Even something like a double jump would Greatly improve the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Music is amazing, it forces you to play more or just sit back and relax on techno style. Gameplay is really cool with animations and battle music to indulge into the game. Graphics are truly fantastic and its a small game of 4-5 hours, but if you take the time and just relax it will be a different experience.

_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: While Narita Boy is lovely to look at, it's mostly a chore to actually play. It introduces too many mechanics and enemies and requires mastery of almost none of them, is insultingly easy and quick to finish, ends on an obnoxious cliffhanger, and takes itself far too seriously. Regarding the game's self-seriousness, I want the characters within the game itself to take the ridiculous plot seriously and certainly don't crave something cutesy-pie or tongue in cheek which always ends up making me cringe. But the writers seem to think that what they've created here is a self-reflexive, post-modern masterpiece, when what they've really done is awkwardly mash together Tron and Krull. I love both of those movies, but I was really more hoping for vaporwave Dark Souls. Definitely stay far away if you're expecting anything like a Metroidvania or any kind of open-ended play whatsoever. Progression in almost all cases is boiled down to point A to point B key hunts, or one-off runner sequences to get between areas.Unfortunately this is fairly casual trash meant to wow hipsters and journalists who don't really like games, and I would recommend watching someone else's playthrough for the gorgeous visuals rather than actually paying for it and wasting your time. I would say there are literally two to three fights in the late game, none of them boss fights, which even begin to approach being fun or rewarding to play. And even when watching someone else's playthrough, fast-forward through the pretentious 'creator's memories' bits. I wish I could have been more positive because I wanted to like it, but this is ultimately just nothing of any substance.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend as a game? no.  Recommend as a mind-blowing audiovisual narrative work of art? YES. An 80's nostalgia game in style-only. Magnificent grandiose retro style... but with gameplay so weak it mocks the 8-bit era games from which it draws inspiration. Cons:- Platforming and combat mechanics feel sloppy and unresponsive with input lag + poor collision, lacking any meaningful depth.  - Level and puzzle design are shallow, inconsistently vague / obvious, with needless backtracking - there is no "Metroidvania" here.  - Tapping through long prescriptive story/dialog texts gets old quickly and detracts from the experience which is actually pretty cool without the need for so much dialogue - the entire production is just an excuse to admire a world of awesome pixel animations and sublime sound design, which for some is worth the price of admission.Pros:Style over substance? The rule of cool *is* the substance, if you're patient enough to wade past the gameplay flaws.- A ton of passion clearly went into everything besides the gameplay- soundtrack and audio design is an abso-@%&*^-lute masterpiece- worldcraft and backstory are a surreal 80's pixel fever-dream worth exploring- feels like walking through enormous virtual art-installations filled with lovingly crafted detail and symbolic nuance... if only the crap gameplay didn't keep marring the experience.Sorry for the harsh review - if digital art & sound design are your jam, I heartily recommend watching someone else play it and skipping the tedious bits.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: A true retro feel with in every sense of the way, with hypnotic atmosphere and stunning visuals backed up by one of the best fitting soundtracks ever, and that is what really sets this game apart. The combat is simple and precise and the story is surprisingly deep and well written. A joy to play and a true reminder for how games are an art form.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This is one hell of a presentation, the esoteric techno religion motif is beyond well done. If this is not an Amazing game, I don't know what is. This animation, this atmosphere, this art style; all top-notch.  The people who made this game know where their strong suits lie. The world and surreal palette of colors and shapes keep you entranced in the game. Narita boy doesn't try and have you press complicated button combinations. Nor is it imploring you to finish the level faster than the Flash trying to escape Darkseid's boot up his rear. Studio Koba wants you to get lost in the splendor of their Digital Kingdom You are the digitized anointed of the Trichroma; an ascended techno being working on behalf of algorithmic heaven. The game doesn't say this in so many words, it instead allows you to traverse this world's setting and experience the prayers of programs, the wisdom of amalgamated algebraic expressions of life. Even when it does give you text, they are more the musings and theorems of theories on how different life functions, than plain exposition and narrative.  Beings of encoded light ask you to save their world with a chromatic blade of power. That is the premise of this game, and it is pulled off brilliantly. The game is accompanied by an amazing soundtrack. This is easily one of the best games this year.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game and it's obvious that a lot of love was put into it, but I can't recommend it. The good: The visuals and the soundtrack are awesome and super stylish, I've made more screenshots than with any other game. The meh: - The story is ok. Creator's story is touching at times, but Narita boy's story is soo convoluted. The game just spams you with tons of text and lore, which is fun for the first five minutes, and then you just learn to distill it to essential messages: "Ok, so I need to fight an enemy there", "Ok, so I need three keys for three doors". - The gameplay boils down to "talk to NPC - go and get a key to the door - open the door - repeat" and becomes boring and repetitive waay faster than the game ends. The bad: - The fighting is downright awful. Controls are clunky, the key binding for combos can't be changed and there are far too many attacks in your inventory. To give an example: you have two same attacks which are bound to different keys, but for some reason only one can be used against the enemy. There are a couple of attacks that can only be used against one particular enemy. Most of the time you'll just need "evade" and "basic hit": you won't have time or space for "big hit" or any other attack types. The battles moves are not always registered if you miss a pixel and are overall clunky, plus sometimes the screen is shaking or having visual glitches solely for aesthetic reasons, which would be fine if the battles were easy and not demanding, but that's not the case here. I had no problems with Hollow Knight, Ori or Shovel Knight: these games aren't always easy, but they are just and attacks are balanced and precise. In Narita Boy the battles are unnecessarily long, attacks are sluggish, most of the attacks are useless and the "evade" button doesn't always work as intended, so battles, especially boss battles, become a tedious exercise rather than fun experience.    - This game is not a platformer, it's hack'n'slash with occasional jumping on platforms, which is a good thing, because the movement controls are slow and not precise at all. Precise jumps were already difficult and platforming would be a torture. - The level design is boring and there isn't much to do. It's not a metroidvania, you can't really explore the world: you get to a level, go left, right, up and down, get all the keys, open all the doors (which are always closed for some reason) and move on. No way to revisit the previous levels and frankly speaking nothing to do there, which is a shame. It's visible that creators though of a whole world with its own mythology, but the only thing you do there is open doors. Overall, I finished the game because I wanted to complete it, but the experience wasn't fun. If creators fixed the combat, cut down the unnecessary parts and added more content to explore, the game could really shine, so wishing best of luck to the developers with the next game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an investor in the Kickstarter. This game delivered on every single promise, the soundtrack is perfect, story is great, and there's more than just nostalgia.Control of the character, as well as getting good at some of the special moves, definitely takes a little time, but that's not to say you feel powerless in the meantime.10/10 highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I almost put the game down after the first hour or so, then I followed a guide, I had just no idea where to go and I kinda got the hang of it I thought, but then it got annoying again. The art style is amazing! But that is not holding my attention when I have found 10 locked doors, then find a key and have to check all the 10 locked doors, because the 16x16 detailed pixel art of the key doesn't really tell me much.I'm also fine with dying, but outside of combat it should not deplete your health bar and when starting a fight should always start you with full health. It is so annoying to fall in water for you to fully die and then get put back at the start of a portal or to start a fight with one health notch for you to die in the first hit and then again putting you back in the last check point.This is more some general gripes I have with games. I'm going to put hours in your game. I'm not going to finish it in one sitting, so if I want to quit the game let me just quit the game! Also have booted your game for the sixth time, please let me skip the splash screens I already know you've used gaming tool X and gaming tool Y, I just want to play the game!Also for any game developer out there, I know you’re game has a style, but please readable text should be in a readable font. Go nuts with titles, but text that you want people to read put it in a font that is readable!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Really awesome side scroller. The story is surprisingly good and well written. Stunning visuals, the pixel art and animations are well done. Combat is simple yet fun, with new moves being added constantly as you progress through the game. Some of the later bosses get a bit challenging and may require a few tries to beat.Probably the coolest part of the game was getting a floppy disk surf board, there's a lot of cool moments in the game.The only negative is the level design: you often get lost and forget where you are supposed to go and end up backtracking a lot. I wish there was a map of the areas.Completed the entire game on a Steam Deck. it plays great on Deck, 60 FPS and low 7-8 Watts power draw.Looking forward to the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: In one Sentence, Narita Boy is a Metroidvania in a world where 90s MacOS is an Alternate dimensionI've got 4 or so hours in the game so far and I'm still not sure if I would recommend this game. Not that my opinion matters much. looking at all the accolades this game has received so far instills me with doubt. Let's get the obvious things out of the way: the art style  is nice. the music is okay if you like that sort of thing but it certainly compliments the setting of the game.Is the game hard? no, the enemies are a bit dumb and basically just hammer at them till they die is a pretty good tactic. Does it play nice? No, The controlls feel loose and thats not a good thing. Are the puzzles challenging? No, The puzzles/levels are repetitive, go there, get key, come back here, do quick time event, get key. Is the game fun? Sometimes, all of it is covered under a big warm blanket of retro pixel nostalgic 80's synthwave. The story is served with a large helping of Programming technobabble, which fits the settings nicely offcourse. Writing this I've decided, not to recommend this game. If you want to play a metroidvania, get Blasphemous or maybe Carrion.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent action platformer, with a great art style, sound design and music. The story is simple and relies too much on exposition dumps to make it engaging, and the lack of invicincibility frame on the dodge was consistently frustrating. Still good fun, but not really worth full price when it's only 8 hours on the first playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: From the artistic point of view Narita boy is beautiful. But this is poorly made game design, specifically combat design. The art is cool, but this is a platformer. It can`t just be pretty. The narrative design is also too clumsy. Why is there so much text? The game has some interesting ideas, but they are badly implemented. For example the fight with the red knight. You and your horse transform into this big heavy robot to fight the big heavy boss. But this piece of can just doesn`t respond to commands properly, huge delay. The fight is too freaking long and honestly I don`t understand why the complexity growth curve is so pointy. Also the long fight on the top of the train is pure disaster.  This is a frustrating game, which will probably damage your nervous system.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly linear action platformer with the best pixel/retro visuals I have seen.So many cool and trippy ideas here, definitely took me to another place while playing. CONTROLS - feel a bit floaty at the beginning but you'll adapt quickly especially after unlocking dashes. COMBAT - gets progressively more interesting and feels fluid. Besides art/worldbuilding, slashing with the technosword is definitely one of the best aspects of the game.Great variety in enemies and there are some awesome boss battles towards the end.Pacing is also well thought out. Didn't feel repetitive at any point.Would have loved some newgame+ features like skins, hardmode etc. Other than that, awesome experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a beautiful pixelated artstyle, but the rest of the game has several minor annoying quirks: - Roughly thirty seconds of unskippable logos before the title screen, - Unintuitive keyboard controls, and the option to customize them doesn't work, - Flowery dialogue, - No real map, despite this game having metroidvania influences, - The elaborate pixelated backgrounds make the platforms blend in with each other sometimes, - And the game has several flashing lights (which the game at least warns the player about when the game boots up)In short, unless you love 80s nostalgia and programming in-jokes that badly, I would not recommend playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Really quite enjoyed this one. It has an absolutely unique style and it's really worth experiencing. It's not a long or complicated game. The combat is probably average, though a bit clunky or floaty. Encounters are generally quite easy. I think there were only one or two fights in the game that were a real challenge, even after you work out the simple pattern to follow. Some are calling it a metroidvania, but it probably really isn't. You don't go around collecting anything. There's not much backtracking, apart from needing to use you new abilities to progress an area further. There's only one "side-quest" you can miss during the playthough.There are some issues, mostly in the beginning. You need some time to work out the rules of the platformer. Sometimes it feels like a real jerk because and kills you instantly, but it's not a big issue further on. Auto-saves are quite frequent, so you neer lose too much.Going back to the art style and the world - that's the bit really worth exploring. There's so much unique stuff here. No two rooms feel anything like each other. They really went all out to flesh it out and it all feels like a lot of love and effort went into all of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I tried really hard to like Narita Boy.The visuals are astonishingly original. I love the character designs. I also think there's something bizarrely charming about how in love with its own lore the whole game is. Every box of dialogue overshares and overexplains in long techno-fantasy ramblings, and somehow it comes across as funny and sincere more often than annoying.Maybe it's just too long or demands too much precision from its floaty combat, or maybe the whiplash is too strong between enjoying a goofy Tron fantasy world and piecing together the depressing life of a Japanese-American celebrity dev savant. I kept feeling worse and worse about coming back to the game.You do get to mash a button to meditate, which rules. The puzzles were interesting at first but got repetitive. The main quest is just a chain of confusing fetch quests. But wow, the atmosphere and animations are something else!I don't know. Broadly, I don't recommend this game, because I feel it has taken more from me than it has given back.  But if you're looking for a vibey experience and some truly transporting visual design, even though you're probably not going to see everything it has to offer, maybe give Narita Boy a chance.Edit: I finished the game and ended up really hating the direction the story went. I found it far too literal and heavy-handed, which really changed my positive feelings on the tone of the whole game, which I had been perceiving and enjoying as more ethereal or abstract. Soured it even more for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a tough one to review. I would love to be spoiler free but it's a bit hard, so I'll try to be careful.On one hand, it's a cool retro-style with good (but slightly repetitive) music. The bad though, is kind of a long list. - Every character interaction is an exposition dump of made up 'techy-sounding-words'. - The fights are both fun in one hand, and a slog in the other. Enemies have unavoidable moves, you get flying bats above, a guy running across screen on the bottom, and a floater inbetween summoning mobs in the middle. - You get three main summons that are all the exact same thing with a different look, but same thing otherwise. You get a 'damage buff' that also gives 'damage taken increase' - three of those as each summon gives you one, all look and act the same way. So that's boring and kind of pointless. - Controls are slightly floaty and I kept running into issues due to have two 'dodge' buttons that did the same thing but different directions based on how you were looking. This made dodging a constant pain in the butt.- Some of the buffs were cool, but used for minutes and never touched again, things like a horse and "big mode." So there was literally no point adding them as "buffs" and adding them to the power-up menu.Then there is the 'story': The entire game could have been avoided by simply having the creator seek professional psychological help at any point in his life, and as you unlock memories it just becomes more and more apparent that he should be on some medication. Again, I don't want to spoil it, but the ending was twisted. Narito Boy (the character) was .. stupid. So stupid. The ending was like the worst "after credits" moment I've ever seen. "She's just sleeping"... what kind of stupid person would believe that? The entire story was nullified at the end. I will NOT be buying any follow-up game that should be a sequel.All in all, the cons really do out-weigh the pros. If the game had less data dumps and more actual platforming/fighting, it would have been better. I enjoyed a good portion of the fights, but sadly the fighting wasn't the main focus of the game. The main focus was running from point a to b and talking to people, you fought to get keys and then stopped fighting once you had them. You'd then fight a huge wave of enemies on a single screen and nowhere else on the map.

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is one hell of a trip. A style-heavy combat-slinging platformer drowning in 80’s kitsch and Tron-tinted neon that asks you to battle through the personified innards of a prototypic console in order to unlock the stolen memories of its creator. It’s a lot of things at once, and there’s always the concern that this top heavy atmosphere is going to topple over at any second. In order to avoid that, it props everything up with even more things; pseudo-religious undertones that mimic Shinto and tie in with the relaxed flashbacks of the creator’s memories of growing up in the Japanese providence of Narita, juxtaposed against high concept 16bit violence and CRT monitor grain overlays. It’s not an invitation to get lost within the chaos; it’s a promise. You will spend time wandering around, hoping to stumble across the Techno Algorithm Hall or The Stable of the Servo Horse because you’ve found a digital key with that name on it, and have some memory of a previously bypassed pixel priest mentioning it briefly within several paragraphs of technobabble. It flirts with metroidvaniaism, making you backtrack because you’ve discovered a new key or a new ability that lets you circumvent a previously unpassable object. But the stages are linear, enclosed and small enough to get from one end to the other without due concern. They’re never static; nothing stays the same long enough to get stale.Learning new moves is often the key to accessing new areas – you learn a leaping uppercut that gives you more air than a regular jump so you can reach higher platforms, or a ground pound attack that can smash through wonky floors. But you’ll also need your constantly evolving moveset to deal with the ever-expanding enemy roster. Shuffling digital zombies begat hulking footsoldiers with man-sized blades begat screen-filling behemoths with oversized clubs who, even if they miss you, send dangerous shockwaves racing through the ground. Cackling electronic witches pelt across the sky, casting trails of neon napalm. Cocky guards tap their shields with their blades, mocking your impotence against their airtight defence. Except you’re given all the tools you need for wholesale slaughter. Frontal attacks are useless against shields, so you learn a running shoulder barge that can knock armoured opponents off balance just long enough to land a few choice blows. Witches might feel safe, lounging about above you, trying to roast you with digital flames, but they can be reached with your new uppercut. They’re not so fond of that. The footsoldiers need little prompting to swing their huge swords at you. Time your dodge dash to either scoot out of the way, or slip straight past them, leaving their undefended backs completely at your mercy.You do all this with your Technosword, which you wretch free from an altar like the one true king, because of course you do. As well as everything else it has going on around it, Narita Boy invests heavily in the ‘chosen one’ trope, granting the sword only to the fated hero who will save all from the twisted disposition of HIM. This isn’t a bit; the main antagonist is called HIM. He used to be a supervisor program from the Red Beam before he decided that Red was much better than both Yellow and Blue, the three programs that made up the Trichroma which power the console. It’s these three colours that the quasi-religion of the electronic world is based upon, and this is reflected through the game’s pixel-plotted landscapes. They’re often dominated by these three tones, except for when they’re not, wherein Narita Boy does its best to be an LSD-powered heavy metal music video.To that end, Narita Boy is never above ridiculous spectacle. Galloping at speed through a desert on a robot mount that later transforms into mech-like heavy armour, allowing you to pummel once formidable foes with spiteful indifference. Conversing with fifty-foot-tall oracles with CRT monitors for a head, cradling their bloated, pregnant stomachs. Delving through a monochrome wasteland before being assaulted by a nightmarish siren, often only distinguishable by her hugely distorted face panel, flickering between static and trichrome. Being temporarily transformed into a stag-bot so you can traverse a scared woodland. Peacefully meditating in front of an army of pulsing speakers and hard-rocking disc jockeys, or surging across the roof of a crumbling runaway train. Taking on a wireframe carp made solid in the midst of a flooded bathhouse while you surf on a 3.5” floppy disk.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: It's an OK game: the first thing that comes to my mind, right after the amazing art stile and title track, is boredom. I still recommend to try it: its artistic side is really incredible.The main problem of this game is that most mechanics are quite dull. - Exploration: note that his game is not a Metroidvania, don't expect any actual exploration. You find a closed door, go forward a bit, find a key, minor backtracking, open door, repeat. The backtracking is always limited to few rooms before and never branches out meaningfully. Once an area is cleared you cannot go back.- Movement/exploration: feels stiff; jumping feels floaty. Old trailers showed ledge grabbing, which is not there anymore. Moving across levels offers little satisfaction; the platforming sections are barebone. - Combat. Suffers from the same rigidity of movement. Despite the additional moves you learn through the game, it never gets really snappy or completely satisfying. Enemies get diverse over the game, but it always feels like you can't be as fast and effective as you wish. It feels like some attacks were stripped of features in development: e.g. the charge attack looks like a home-run and from a previous trailer it seemed capable of deflecting fireballs; now it's just a stronger attack. Eventually all fights are dodge-attack-repeat, with minor exceptions of some enemies requiring a particular ability to be defeated which really does nothing on other type of enemies. In other words, some abilities are there to vary the combat, but fail to do so in a meaningful, fun manner.- Narrative. There's a great central narrative that you discover in specific spots; I really loved that one. In parallel, NPCs literally flood you with LOTS of text that could have been pruned. The aim of this was to build world characterization, but I personally found it very lacking, and soon decided to skip most of the dialogues. This is because it uses too much pseudo-philosophical nonsense, and long, pretentious expositions that I found very boring and failing to add meaningful characterization. On the artistic side:- Visual art is incredibly good. - World building: quite incredible, set aside from some writing I personally disliked, see "Narrative" above.- Music: the title track is great, the rest is very good but with many missed opportunities: for example, the combat music starts great but never climaxes, remaining flat; same for most boss fights. Some environmental music feels uninspired. However, in general the quality is EXTREMELY high.Overall, despite the problems, I quite enjoyed the experience, and I encourage anyone to at least give this a try. I'm really looking forward to Studio Koba next game, as I'm sure they've learned a lot from this project and have a great potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: From the outset Narita Boy is a feast for the eyes and ears. It's absolutely gorgeous and chock full of little nods, references and love notes to '80s and retro culture. The gameplay is pretty tight and while some of the fights can be a little tricky to master and the controls can occasionally be a bit finicky, I never felt "cheated" when I died. It took me, a clumsy gamer, about 13 hours to complete live on stream and would probably take a skilled player much less but I think the game is a good length. The story is well paced and can be genuinely moving at times. I have had a lot of fun with it and will definitely be playing it again soon!EDIT: I started speedrunning it. Narita Boy is a fantasic hidden gem for speedrunners!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the atmosphere and aesthetics of this game, the story has potential, and the combat is passable, but the level design is tedious at best and way too boring most of the time and the movement is just... bad. It feels really floaty and delayed and isn't fun to use. The game also just throws 'lore' at you all the time but it's intentionally cryptic and doesn't really make sense. I ended up ignoring most of the NPC's dialogue because it was essentially gibberish technobabble.There's potential here with the artstyle, music, etc. but the actual gameplay side of things makes this game not fun to play at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I kept with Narita Boy right up until the last area. Even though my appreciation for the god-like pixel art that’s on display and the strange, alluring retro/alien world got me this far in, I think I’ve had enough.A lot of time in Narita Boy is spent retracing your steps to find/use keycards or talk to NPCs. If the backgrounds you run through weren’t so dang appealing and detailed, this would’ve been more of a hassle. Combat gets more interesting with enemy variety and new unlockable attacks, although this means that it starts out very dry. When all the red-palleted enemies in an encounter start to pile up, the amount of retro distortion, particle effects, foreground elements, and screenshake make success more of a visual challenge than a reflexive one. Bosses rarely find a middle ground between grade-A BS and chump change. Exploring the game’s elaborately painted environments consists of choosing which of the two paths isn’t the one that needs the key from the other. While there’s not much of an emphasis on it, the platforming doesn't feel quite right. I can't put my finger on why, but it doesn’t help that the camera is usually a bit too close to the character. All that said, Narita Boy is still a short meter away from a recommendation. It’s visually remarkable (when it’s not testing your photosensitivity) and the combat is tactile and largely enjoyable (with the right setup). If only the structure of the levels was as equally creatively choreographed. Ultimately, it was the smaller things like the backtracking with keys or the more annoyed boss battles that slowly killed my motivation to push through to the very end.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Great Style - no substance?  Wanted to love this game, but nope. And on a second try, after some time: Still Nope, just Nope.While the art style is awesome, the controls feel extremely sloppy. I'm not fighting the enemies or the environment - I'm fighting the controls. It makes you miss simple platforms even while having all the time in the world - but it also throws platforming at you in the arena-style combat encounters - so there's a good chance you die, because of missing platforms,  in the otherwise unspectacular/dull combat.Add a ton of lore before you can even begin to play, dialogues that make little sense (at least not yet), confusing progression (where to next?), confusing level layout (invisible walls - sometimes truly invisible, sometimes just obfuscated by fancy stuff in the parallax foreground) ... and I'm out.Perhaps the game get's better later, but as it's just no fun upfront - I won't pursue it any further.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Got the game on sale and i would 100% recommend it. Flat out fun game with a mix of "arcadey" fun, references, comedic relief, and a deep story if you can bother to read all the dialogue Gameplay is fun with a variety of moves and enemies to keep you busy. Parts can be challenging but its not gonna take you more than a couple tries.Visuals, holy s*** one of the best looking games ive ever played, artistically speaking. Just the pixel art design mixed with the lighting is top notch. Story has alot going on and reading it all can be a pain. The in-cyber-world story can be alittle weird and wacky but its okay. However the story based in the real-world involving the creator is much more consumable  Cons: No new game plus, cant back track in saves, visuals can sometimes make it hard to see things that'll hurt you, intro is stupid loud.Just get the Game
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I pledged for this game on kick-starter and unfortunately am not happy with it.The game LOOKS AMAZING!, it has a beautiful style and the animations are fantastic, but the game-play quickly became frustrating. Not because of the difficulty but due to the lack of (in my personal opinion) necessary info given to the player.Some examples:- At the beginning of the game, the font used to tell you to press a specific key to pick up the sword is so obscure and unreadable that the Devs literally needed to post in the forums to say what button to press.- No visual feedback to show how much health a boss has.- With the amount of backtracking needed to navigate the world, there is no map or any way to know where you are and how to get where you have been before. It gets very confusing very fast.I sadly would not recommend this game to anyone. Watch a play-through on YouTube if you have an 80's nostalgia itch.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, it took me about 9 hrs to beat the game and unlock all the achievements. It's a bit short but I enjoyed every moment playing this game and feel that this is a high quality work so for me it's worth it.I really like how this game stands out among other 2D adventure games and brings back the 80's retro vibe with its stylish visuals, great music and story is a plus. So far I haven't seen backtracking as an issue as some of the negative comments said, my only issue with this game is more towards the controls though. Unable to use a mouse plus weird control keys, it took me quite some time to get used to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Love the presentation, graphical style and music. Unfortunately, so far, that's all the positive I can lay upon this game. The story is far far far too bizarre to easily follow, and even someone who has a reasonable grasp on the english language, has to say that it uses far far far too many 'big words' for it to just to come of as a bit pretentious. Gameplay-wise, so far, i've got the sword, admitidly i'm not a huge way into the game yet, but I'm finding I'm doing a hell of a lot of running around the same locations as I'm not 100% what I'm supposed to be doing right now (despite having a list of 'tasks' of what i'm supposed to be doing.  Opening random doors by pushing buttons some distance away, not even knowing that was supposed to be something i had been tasked to do. I'll prob give it another chance, maybe even look up a walkthrough just to get me past this bit (not sure why i should be stuck on a platformer game, though). and maybe, hopefully it gets better and less ridiculous story (guessing the latter doesn't change).
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a game with excellent execution in some areas, but simply terrible in others. I still do recommend playing it, this game left me with a very good impression.Art in all of its forms is simply excellent. The backgrounds, enemies and Narita Boy animations are just brilliantly made. Music is excellent, almost all tracks are bangers and used properly throughout the game. Sound design overall is also quite good.Combat is great, starts simple as just about every game, but once you start getting upgrades feels awesome. Controls can be a bit sketchy though, as there is a bit of a delay in some moves, mostly noticeable when jumping.Enemies are generally good, and with a lot of variety. Bosses are kind of a hit and miss. Some are terrible, some are good.The lore and backstory is quite good and satisfying. The story that takes place during the game, unfortunately, not so much. It's poorly implemented with an ocean of mostly meaningless dialogue that could have found another way into the game with other methods.The true shame of this game that, in my opinion, holds it back from excellence is its level design. Or, to be precise, its lack of it. There is no dedicated level designer in this game and it shows. Go from point A to B, most of it backtracking, get a key from someone with no real explanation, use the key and repeat. The game barely uses its movement options to create interesting levels or platforming sections.After seeing the ending of the game it seems that the developers want to expand on this IP with either DLC or a second installment. I think that it's a fantastic idea, as they really have struck with something special with this game. Just, please, hire a level designer before doing so and we're golden!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Fantasy, science fiction and electronic music mingle in this 80's neon drenched adventure. The visuals are striking and the presentation is top notch. On the other hand, gameplay and exploration fall more on the servicable side and that's a little disappointing because with more care put into them, Narita Boy could be a classic.Read more on:

_childDocuments_.review: keycards keycards keycards keycardsbut very good art.(edit2: soundtrack is phenomenal, if you guys make a vinyl I'll be the first one in line)I do regret backing this game (update: actually I do not, I chipped in for an art book and art here is all the worth, it's fantastic, and hopefully devs get to make another game after this which I am sure will be great after all the experience on this game)- controls make you wanna quit- tons of text and back story is nice, but I feel I might rather read a book. this is a game, games are supposed to deliver story through gameplay and immersiveness- some (actually pretty much all) bosses are incredibly easy- one boss is all of a sudden pretty hard (but incomparable to other bosses, no gradual progression)- art is good, but it's kind of... doesn't really have any impact if you think about it. it feels kind of all for show, but without any substance, it's just kinda there. But it is great.- "J" doesn't look like "J"- pc controls aren't particularly great - why z,x,c and not c,v,b? or at least x,c,v? Why not use shift? Why "F" and not "E"? Why would you have "K" for shooting AND fast walking (in a specific location)? I bet a lot of people fast walk though that location and when they leave that area they're confused with button maps for a second and shoot instead.I feel like this could've been a quite an incredible point and click adventure game with this world. Dunno. I really wanted to like it. I don't think I did.2017 trailer still feels bigger, richer, more in depth, has better art style and sound design, looks like a movie with a huge world. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: compared to hollow knight & blasphemous its a very basic metroid style game, in terms of exploration; the areas are very small, extremely linear with no side paths or secrets, with a huge amount of backtracking between empty rooms. combat is very irritating and while the graphics and setting looks cool at times, most often it gives me a headache with how often it flickers and strobes. cool concepts & characters appear for one scene and are never revisited or expanded upon, they just exist to give you a key to a locked door, for example you get an upgrade to transform into a stag; this ability is used to cross three empty rooms and is never used again

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a stunning retro hack 'n' slash game with a glaring, old-school vibe that seems like it was made in the 80s and travels in the model present as a classical game. We play as the chosen one selected to go on an adventure to save the Digital-Kingdom by restoring their master/ memories corrupted by a malware program known as Stallion. From that, with each memory we recover we learn a lot about the creator's backstory from birth to the present, revealing some touching events. Visually, this game is ambitious, mixing religion and early upcoming technologies into making a cool atmospheric cult, like an altar with a computer in the middle of a sculpture of the motherboard. There is also a lot of interesting things that happen in the background, even during combat like a rock band playing behind the scene, NPCs just chilling in a café, or the creator morphing in and out of themselves, chilling. All of that just made this game aesthetically pleasing and in-depth, seeing all the chaos that occurs from pausing it for a second and immerse yourselves in the scenery you're seeing. Furthermore, there are some interesting stylizations like the fog and glow-up visual effect or smashing a single button during a medicating QTE (if you could call it that). As for combat you get to use it as a baseball bat, a surfboard, or a shotgun, I don't know about you, but for me, that's just wacky, but that's a cool interversion to use other types of weapons rather than just relying on swords and shields like in some other game. Finally, most of the boss fights are fair, well not the last 2, 'The Glove's' and 'The Core' are quite extremely difficult, I believe it had taken me 40 tries combined to defeat them, other than that, each of them has their own style and theme OST making each encounter from them quite epic and memorable with one of my faviourite being 'Black Rainbow'.Here's a 2 minutes short example if you want to check it out:Saying all these positives, there are still some problems with this game, starting with the language barrier as it is spoken in scripted technical terms along with a lot of info dumping which could make it quite hard for some people to understand it or know what's going on. Even though like mention the main quest is quite standard and most of the objective goes like this: The premise is quite basic, it just takes a few decoding the message like maybe by taking notes to keep up with the terminology, for that, if you're planning on playing this game I suggest try not to have a big gap in between playtime as it can be quite easy to get lost and forget on what to like I did. Onto another problem, this game is not quite a Metroidvania game, more so a linear one with a lot of backtracking and believe me there's a lot, that's why I recommend to those to try to play it within a condensed timeframe so you don't lose track in what you need to do.  Another, you can say nitpick now, is the dodging on the ground and midair feels a bit awkward, only moving the opposite way you're facing, making it tricky to navigate from avoiding upcoming attacks, especially in a tight corner whilst there's a swarm of enemies. Narita Boy is not perfect by any means, but at least it's playable and fun to play overall. I still can't get over the fact of how visually impactful this game was, it stuck the landing with its presentation. I see it as a testament to how art style captivates world-building with a lot of soul and depth sprinkled in it. A game with styles I'll truly miss and be anticipating what the sequel may turn out to look like.The main game, along with the soundtracks is quite pricey for what it is, so I did you stranger a favor and posted this review a week before the discount expires (not like it matters), so get this game now while you can if you’re interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The art is amazing, the combat is well implemented, I missed a bit more vertical gameplay to me that is key for 2d games, the music is very good (the synth guy and the theme just came straight from Yellow Magic Orchestra band), I missed though dpad controls and I didn't like that I could miss achievements :/I finished the game on a day, it's so beautiful and hand crafted that I couldn't stop playing!It's a love letter to japanese culture.It's not a metroidvania game though, it has some metroidvania features.. but it's more linear.That makes me a bit sad because there are a ton of assets that are created for just one use. I think this game could benefit from less paced progression and a more reuse/revisit approach dungeon system.I can't wait to see what the developers do on their next game!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter because of its beautiful art and I got what I wished for. Estetically speaking, it is truly a marvel. Alas, all the rest is bad.The story aims to show Narita Boy as a saviour who needs to protect the Digital Kingdom from the Evil. In practice, the Evil barely does anything, you are running from one closed door to another, because everyone closed everything everywhere. It is completely absurd, you are running hours in circles to get a key to a key to a key to a key to a key to a key to a door which which has something to do with your actual goal. This is not an exagerration, I've counted.Because of this the plot is nonsense. There need to be reasons for all this running left and right and they are completely absurd. At one moment you learn that a whole city has been build in order to help you with your  current goal. After a while you learn that this goal was to... wake up a man who overslept.Both platforming and fights are very very basic, they are serviceable at best and often just bad. Mobs have one attack, bosses two attack max and there is always one and only one way to deal with them. There are no interesting interactions. You are just running on a flat arena and killing mobs one after another. Near the end and with all the perks this game starts to have a complexity which games like Ori have after a first hour or so.Buy it if you want a visual spectacle and you feel you can ignore the rest, and only in this case.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing visuals,great music,decent combat with a pretty big moveset that can be combined if you're good enough. Unfortunetaly you cannot change controls so I had to use WASD+GHJKL keys on my keyboard which often made me press the wrong key causing me to die during combat. Thankfully you get autosaves before fights so you can quickly retry a fight and memorize enemy types and ther timing of attacks. However,even though there is not a lot of backtracking with fights,you have to spend the majority of your time backtracking from one place to another and collect floppy disks and symbols in order to go to other areas,and since the game isn't always clear about your next objective you can get lost for a long time,unless you watch a YT guide to realize where you must go (I did it after first 3 hours as I got lost quite frequently). Story is quite good,however the lore is put in vast infodumps,and I would have preferred if they did it similarly to Skyrim,where the majority of the lore is put in books that are scattered across the world.I think it's a 7/10 game,would have been higher if the game was a bit more player-friendly.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a very forgiving action platformer with light puzzle elements required to unlock all of the secrets and achievements the game has to offer. In my approximately 7 hours of gameplay, there were only a handful of times I felt frustrated at the combat, and even then only for a few attempts as I learned the patterns for the enemies and bosses.Combat and puzzles are not the main reason to play this game, however. Narita Boy is a story first and foremost, albeit a slightly opaque one in the beginning. Some of the motifs are a little unsettling, especially since one does not expect to see them take such a prominent role in a game about technoswords and digital worlds. It is difficult to discuss the plot without major spoilers so forgive my cryptic brevity, but be prepared for a story of love, loss, illness, broken homes, triumphant returns, and the pursuit of balance. How much of the story is supposed to be complete metaphor or dream and how much is really happening is not clear to me, so enjoy the wild ride if you do play.I would give Narita Boy a solid 8/10 as a complete experience. If you do not like strange stories, you will likely feel a 6/10 is more appropriate.

_childDocuments_.review: Without giving too much away, I love that this game not only invokes the usual nostalgia but makes it apart of the story. It's a love letter to nerd culture, equal parts corny and tragic. The techno babble-infused dialogue is absolutely unabashed, unloading paragraphs worth of immaterial fluff that initially turned me off, but eventually warmed my heart. Again, it's hard to get into the why's and how's without just spoiling the crux of the narrative.There's a bit of an irreverent detail towards the end that I wasn't a fan of, but the story is an overall winner. Visually speaking, it's gotta be one of the most beautiful games I've witnessed. Animations exude oomph and personality, the unique architecture is just as alien as it is contemporary, and there's a l-... lot of shiny things! Sadly, the time spent existing within each gorgeous hub is spent sprinting from NPC to NPC in a usually contrived fashion. Find person [x], person [x] says they lost [item] but person [y] has a copy, person [y] was captured, find person [y], person [y] hands you [item] to access a door all the way back at the start, meet person [z] who needs a favor done before they do [the thing], person [z] gives you [item] to access a small room housing [item], trek back and person [z] does [the thing], final door opens. Not a whole lot of it feels natural. Locked doors inside locked doors that have items that unlock locks to other locked doors isn't particularly engaging.One could argue there is justification for this, albeit incredibly loose. Like a broken record, I can't comment any further without spoilers.Thankfully, the music, visuals and combat tend to obfuscate that lone major gripe. The most latter of which is pretty damn fun! New enemies are constantly being introduced, each new ability is sufficient and plays off of new and old enemy types so satisfyingly, and that former most aspect, the music, will make the moment feel right if your laser blast or uppercut combos won't. Not since Hollow Knight or Undertale have I heard a soundtrack of this caliber. Call me a sucker for melodramatic synthwave, but it's epic. Truly epic. Like, in the old sense of the word and not in the butchered sense. I will say, though, your mileage may vary on the dialogue and some are even saying the combat is not up to their tastes. All I know is that I, personally, can't wait for the squeakquel.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: An action-platformer that has a polarizing mix of good and bad points.Although I am on the fence, I have to lean away from recommending it.Pros:- Amazing synth soundtrack- Varied levels and well-paced introduction of new abilities- A wide array of enemy types and plenty of unique bosses- Gorgeous pixel art if you are into that aestheticCons:- This normally doesn't bother me, but the flashing lights warning is no joke with this game.  Had to put it down a few times since it would give me a headache- Clunky controls that cannot be rebound- The dialogue, while at times can be touching, is often esoteric and incomprehensible- Quite a bit of backtracking required- No good way to heal outside of combat (although dying is hardly punishing)

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic Action/Platformer that wears it's inspiration from TRON and Japanese culture on it's sleeve. This game has a fluid combat system that isn't super difficult to learn but is extremely fun to master and string together combos. The standout parts of this game are absolutely the music and story. The music is across the board incredible, evoking a synthwave/techno style that is so good, I would sometimes put the controller down just to listen. The story is a tear jerker, the way it's integrated into the gameplay is super clever and the twists it takes are genuinely shocking. That being said this game isn't perfect, do note that you cannot revisit areas so if you missed one of the few collectables you do have to replay the game again, which I could see annoying some, especially those going for the 34 achievements. Most are story progression but some require finding cleverly hidden areas that can be missed, requiring a full game restart. In addition, they did rely a little too heavy on "enemy halls", areas where the action stops and you have to take out a certain number of enemies, bogging the pace down. The boss fights however are awesome and have fun patterns that teach the player to effectively use their abilities. Overall, if you like the aesthetic of TRON, or love 2D Action/Platformers, pick this game up, it's a great 7-8 hour ride.One final note, this game goes very, VERY heavy on multicolor strobe lights and flashes. While I love this game's graphical style, do not buy this game if you are susceptible to seizures or otherwise have adverse effects to strobe lights, this game has them throughout and I couldn't find a way to turn them off.

_childDocuments_.review: As you'll see in another review, I ran into the same issue with the horse part. It's WAY too fast and difficult to complete. It hurts my eyes to the point where anyone with the mildest of seizure issues wouldn't be able to play this part. I looked up someone else playing this part on Xbox and it seems like console in general plays this part very differently, so I believe it's a bug.Believe me, I am really enjoying this game so far. Amazing visuals, amazing soundtrack. The story is intriguing. I like the combat too. But until that horse part get's fixed I can't even play the game.IMPORTANT EDIT: After doing some research, it turns out that you can fix this visual bug by lowering your refresh rate. Kinda dumb but it's whatever. Mine was at 144hz. I changed mine to 60hz and was able to complete this part first try.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game! Old school is the vibe!Has some teeth to it which I am a fan of but certainly not super difficult or anything.The soundtrack... ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ THE SOUNDTRACK IS AMAZING!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! That truly takes this game from being just pretty dang good to being really freaking great!!!!The controls are great, really tight and precise. Although, as some other people have mentioned (complained), you are a little slippery which takes a little bit to get used to with the platforming, but that takes like a few minutes lmao and it's certainly not a deal breaker like some would say.The combat is so fun and feels very good with the tight controls (except for the damn bats lmao) and it's quite varied with all the different abilities and moves you get and different forms you take based on the things that happen in the story.One thing I have to complain about that I agree with from others is that they do text dump a Lot of story on you early on before you get into the gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: First heard about this game about 2 years ago, been on my radar ever since. Finally played it and it was definitely worth the wait. From the world, lore, and everything in between, it caught my attention and never once did I feel bored through the game. The combat is pretty simplistic although you get new moves and mechanics to help you through your fights. I would say the game is not too easy and not too hard as some bosses took me a few tries before I bested them.     I came in to this game knowing about "issues" with the controls and certain portions of the game like the horse riding segment, so I was expecting frustration to some extent. Personally, the controls are fine, they are responsive and there is a little weight to the jumping (mostly the start of the jump) which is probably why some people are having problems. After the first 30 minutes, I got used to it and it became second nature. The horse riding segment is NOWHERE as frustrating as it is made out to be. Sure I got hit by several obstacles but I never died once in that part. You just got to know how long to hold the shoulder bash move and jump.    Unless you miss the secret (4? or 5?) collectibles, there really isn't any reason to replay the game besides experiencing the game again. The ending had me wanting more after I completed it and the soundtrack is really good...that is if you like synthwave etc. I'd recommend this game no doubt and glad this game finally got its release.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: My scores/reviews are almost always based on having bought the game at close to the "lowest historical price" on steam at time of purchase.Quick score: 4/5Notes:-In terms of presentation the game is amazing.-Combat is a bit simple and button mashy but overall fun, a couple boss fights are really good, but most of them are pretty underwhelming mechanically.-Movement feels good but unfortunately the game doesnt really ever introduce any kind of real platforming sections. Which is a shame because they could have definitely made some interesting platforming with the current movement mechanics-The story and world of the game are pretty interesting, but the games dialogue tends to be VERY dense and long winded for no apparent reason. Overall I would say the game is definitely worth checking out, but be aware that it is much more focused on presentation and story rather than gameplay. The gameplay isn't bad, but it does get a bit repetitive and is overall underwhelming compared to what it could be.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many action platformer/hack n slashes/2d soulslikes that could learn a LOT from Narita Boy.What you need to do is always conveyed in some way, clear enough that you can figure it out, subtle enough that it doesn't hold your hand.The story is straightforward, but how it's presented to the player is incredible- there's a lot of worldbuiling packed into what amounted to a 7 hour playthrough.But where this game excels is the visuals: beautiful pixel art, masterfully animated. The colors used where always just right to make everything that needed to stand out do so JUST enough to convey your surroundings and enemies at a glance. Overlayed effects were never too much and help to blend everything together into one package.Overall, Narita Boy is a great game with a lot of skill behind it, and I can't wait to see where it goes next.

_childDocuments_.review: A cool-looking game with a great soundtrack - evoking feelings of nostalgia.You'll be exploring a digital kingdom (within the program), and you need to save this realm from evil corruption."Narita Boy" is not a classic Metroidvania but a platformer with traditional combat mechanics (dodge, power-ups, special moves).Decent game. I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I don't necessarily agree with the "Metroidvania" tag, it's easy to see that this was made with a lot of love and creativity.  Instead, I'd classify it as an atmospheric adventure along the lines of Flashback, Out of This World (also known as "Another World"), and Blackthorne.I went in with different expectations but had fun nonetheless.  At first I was expecting 80s reference silliness, but then found a coming-of-age story and a loss of innocence.  Things get weird.  But hey, the synth-heavy fight themes rock.The backgrounds and characters teeter just on the friendly side of the uncanny valley, but it's a major part of the journey.  Though it gets more linear the farther you go, it never stops being finely detailed.It's not a long game--nearly all players could beat it in under ten hours, so it can make a nice present to a busy middle-ager who might get some of the eighties oeuvre.One caveat, though--if you have trouble with fighting, you might find yourself stuck in some places.  There are no levels or stats, and you can't skip ahead or go back for powerups.  Bosses, especially, straddle the line between riddle and twitch play.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Game starts off slow and sort of maintains a soft jog throughout the playthrough. The gameplay you probably want is stretched out slightly via the back and forth you're forced into when retrieving technokeys. I don't think I would have minded this as much if the "Big fights" were more challenging and memorable.Personally I enjoyed the diverse enemy population that gets revealed through the game. However regardless of the enemy, and most of the time even bosses, the strategy of just mashing basic attacks and ignoring incoming damage proved to be a successful way to progress. I want to adapt my combat for the fight, I want to learn their moveset to win, I want to feel like I deserved the victory. Instead Narita Boy coddles you with the health/life system allowing you to get away doing the bare minimum as death serves 0 regression penalty once the fight is over.I will mention while I didn't find the combat challenging, it was still interesting to a degree.I really wanted more from this game, and constantly found myself looking for that great moment I really enjoyed. As a whole I can appreciate the project, but I couldn't find that individual moment I thoroughly enjoyed. I'm recommending it as a nice casual game with a well done soundtrack and beautiful art style.5.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game in the Steam Sale and got sucked into it immediately. The atmosphere of this game is hypnotic; both the style of the graphics and the music really add to the game. I can't compliment the music enough as every track is a banger. It's not a particularly long game, however. I beat it in about 10 hours but every one of those hours was packed with content. The combat system is really smooth. The movement feels a little floaty at first but you get used to it. I can't wait to start my second play through of the game and can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it more than I don't. Here's some pros and cons.Pros:- Soundtrack is pretty serviceable. I liked it for the most part.- Combat and platforming are intertwined in an interesting way, and there's times where offense is literally the best defense.- Probably some of the best 2D graphics I've seen a Unity game. Animations were clean and fluid. Environments were varied and interesting to look at.Cons:- The dialogue can be confusing sometimes and often just a little boring when actually understood.- The story is... alright, I guess, but mostly uninteresting. The combat and aesthetic make up for this a bit, though.- Sometimes, the enemies feel a bit spammed, which cause unnecessary deaths. Speaking of unnecessary deaths, taking damage from falling off the edge or into specific hazards probably shouldn't happen.- The dodge mechanic seems a bit too precise/short, and sometimes dodging simply doesn't mitigate potential damage or allow you to pass by enemies.- The ending was a bit lackluster and also kind of undercuts a few things with a sudden shift in feel.Overall, it's not bad. I'd be interested in a sequel, but the implications at the end make me a bit hesitant to put my full support behind it. 6.5/10.

_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: My limited vocabulary won't do it justice but, suffice to say, Narita Boy is a fantastic game! I particularly enjoyed the aesthetics and world-building of Narita Boy - using top-tier pixel art to create a fantastical landscape that seems heavily inspired by film titles like 'Tron' and 'The Never Ending Story.' Narita Boy does an incredible job of keeping the visual imagery fresh from start-to-finish with each in-game 'stage' boasting its own unique scenic flavor and personality.Gameplay-wise, Narita Boy is fun, fluid, and intuitive. The player-character is easy to control and combat feels 'weighty' while allowing significant freedom in how you dispatch enemies. My only complaint with controlling the player-character is that jumping can feel a little 'floaty' which is a minor grievance since it rarely impacted my ability to push through a section/battle that required tight platforming-like movement. Narita Boy does a fine job of balancing difficulty and accessibility - the game doesn't hold your hand in-regards to puzzle solving or level navigation but is fairly lenient when it comes to player death. One of the most surprising and memorable elements of Narita Boy is its story! **Possible Spoilers**  The narrative felt unique and the accompanying visuals and music during the 'playable cutscene sections' make for quite the emotional experience. My only complaint story-wise is that the 'techno babble' dialogue that some NPC's use for passive story-telling/world-building purposes can seem a little jarring and difficult to digest but that stuff is mostly superfluous in-regards to the larger narrative and I got used to it quickly enough.If you are a fan of linear story-driven games with a unique atmosphere and tone, then Narita Boy is a must-have! I  highly recommend the game and look forward to the next game from this developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really should love this game. It feels like it was built for me from the ground up: pixel art, action platforming, techno soundtrack. However, the level design and combat severely hold it back. The levels feel overly "linear" in that there is really only one objective at a time. Sometimes you move left to get there, other times right, but it really doesn't matter, you aren't actually making a choice in exploration. The level design would have been better if they just had you move left to right every single screen. Shoe-horning in backtracking doesn't count as exploration.The combat is very flat. You get "power-ups" that don't really add any extra complexity or skill expression. The Dodge ability should have been given by default The best way to heal is to die since the checkpoints are so forgiving. The bosses have 2-3 moves and feel lazily designed.I will probably force myself to give it another replay to get 100% achievements. I would have gotten them all on my first playthrough but I stepped through a door unknowing I could not go back so I was locked out of an achievement. Only get this game if you are ok with a very linear and shallow game, but that looks great.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: is a wildly colorful, unapologetically unique, 80s-inspired action/adventure platformer with a bangin' soundtrack and  animation. Highly recommend, particularly if you enjoy similar games such as , , and .
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita boy is a journey in the mind and hearts of a dev team that has a lot to say.It would be presomptuous to believe I can summarize this title in a short review.I would say the following about the positive aspects :+The artistic direction, soundtrack and pixel art are absolutely mind blowing. This is seriously in the top 5% that's available out there+Some of the environments are simply stunning. The team gives incredible depth to certain parts that match perfectly with their respective soundtracks. Just really mindblowing.+Combats are fast paced and the controls of the character and the various augments you will unlock through the game are satisfying+Deep lore, it's seriously completely unique.I did have some frustration with this :-the level design would confuse me at times, I got lost several times and used a youtube playthrough to advance at times-While the lore of the game matches its amazing art, getting into the story can be really overwhelming, added to the fact that the level design of the first 15 mins can be hard to get atoned to, the beginning of the game can be a bit of a turn down due to its complexity.-The team has poured its hearts and souls in this title, sometimes too much (texts can be at times heavy)All in all, Narita boy is an exceptional title, there is no doubt about it. The team behind it also basically has its specific touch. It's a touching tale, it has serious moments of awesomeness  but it might turn down casual players that won't dig into the 80's vibe while they might find navigating the game as too complex and confusing.Narita boy is a tribute to games in their primal essence before it all turned into billions and influencers, it is an extravagant journey into a fictive digital world articulated around profound analogies and metaphors, but also foremost a reminder of how we all grow, and that the events we remember the most, as insignificant as they may be, are often the most important ones.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is AWESOME!I waited years to play this game and now I finally had the opportunity to play it till the end.If you are a 80's lover like me you will love it too.I need to highlight that the art direction of this game is gorgeous! The pixel art, music, level design, characters, story are so well balanced, it feels like playing a masterpiece that the team from Studio Koba created with lots of passion, you can feel it!Narita Boy will have an special place in my heart and I can't wait to continue this adventure in the sequel!May the Trichroma bless you!10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an action platformer that fails at both. You go through each section usually by reaching the far right of the area, getting a key and coming back to the far left to open a door. There's only one puzzle which is repeated throughout the game, and in between that there's combat and some platforming. The good:- The art and animations.- The music is pretty good.- The flashback story is emotional.The bad:- The combat comes down to hitting "x,x,x" and sometimes dodging. The hits don't have any impact to them. There are no combos. The dodging mechanic is badly executed. - The platforming constantly requires you to hit "up+x" which can't be performed airborne.- The checkpoint are totally random. - Massive amount of useless expository dialogue.- The environments are beautiful but have no impact on gameplay.Worse of all, I never had any fun playing it. It's a damn shame because the art is so great.

_childDocuments_.review: OMG - so this game was exactly what I expected it to be; the pixel art what made me try this game. The huge sale sealed the deal. The rich atmospheric music made me stay. _childDocuments_.review: Slight spoiler alert.It's a metroidvania with a "hidden" ending. There are a number of problems with this and let me start by saying I am not some platforming god so take that into reading my review. I will start with the combat. In general the combat feels alright, the sound, animation, and the swings themselves hit nicely and leave an impact. At a basic level it's pretty entertaining. You have dodge, swing, and jump which make it straightforward. Then they introduce weird gameplay mechanics that complicate the combat. Then they introduce enemies that are meant to be killable mainly through these new mechanics that become regular enemies. Obviously this is a staple of metroidvanias but it just felt like a wet noodle slapping around to me. None of the abilities felt interesting. At some points they even introduce form changing (you turn into a horse person at one point) then proceed to force you into boss battles with the new forms. Very jarring.The world is cool too. It feels like it belongs in some retro universe, like the one it was written into. But the world is kinda... complex? The characters talk a lot about the world they live in, in ways that just confused me. I'd say 99% of the time I was asking myself where I even was. You start in a garden but then walk into some weird hub world... I didn't even know it was a hub world until i came back after world 1. That same non-sensical-ness is everywhere. I had no idea what the world was supposed to be most of the time, like world 1 is apparently a medieval world what with the horses, stables, kings, knights. But they've twisted it into a Narita boy way as to just kind make it look like a mishmash. When it works it works well but the other times it's a neon mess.Movement was perhaps one of the worst parts. I dont know what it is but there are some places where movement sucks. The dodge skill helps cover the walking simulator bits but sometimes it just makes you get cardio for some reason.  At one point you have to avoid puddles formed by the rain. Not discolored puddles or something, just puddles that are maybe a line of pixels on the screen. You unlock the ability to "surf" on all water/puddles (no matter how tiny) but I had more issues discerning what was and what was not water. Then, if you surf onto land and dont manually dismount, you are forced through this animation of your character eating ♥♥♥♥. Why does that exist? I want to keep playing, it was cute once. By far the worst part is the story. I played for 32 hours and still don't exactly know what I was doing. The entire plot of the story is to unlock memories of the old man that is (isn't?) the main character about how sad his life has been so far. Just so we're clear you are not the main character and as far as I can discern none of this is relevant. It's just a bunch of black and white cutscenes with sad music. There is no character development outside these cutscenes. "Narita Boy" is just some faceless, nameless, kid who got kidnapped by a creepy old dude into his digital dungeon. You are then expected to just go to the right for a while to move forward. The absolute worst part was theres no backtracking. If you miss a part of the hidden ending, it's gone forever unless you restart from the beginning. Why? This basically is the entire premise of the game: "why?". Why is this save point back here? Why do bottomless pits deal damage when there's a save point adjacent to them? Why does this boss not let me dash through them sometimes? Why does the horse suddenly become a mech? Why are the hidden ending collectibles in random, totally nonsensical places?Why should I bother spending 20 dollars on this game when it's less than 5 on ♥♥♥?If you want a metroidvania, play Ori. If that isn't hard enough for you, download Dolphin and emulate some older games.
