_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow. One word to sum this up - F r u s t r a t i o n.I saw the gameplay, saw the visuals, read the reviews. Only one person mentioned a problem with the floaty jump controls and thus I dived in to see for myself. Spent these past 40 minutes giving chance after chance wanting to like this game, manually troubleshooting the terrible framerate optimization (I have a 16GB Radeon playing a pixelated game ffs, like how even?), getting frustrated with the seemingly non-responsive jump controls, terrible UX choices left and right (you wanna transition to a new room? where you going? how about you return back here at the middle of the door and press up? oh you wanted to do the charged attack? how about we give you a FALSE visual indicator first and then give you the exact same one but it will work now, and don't you DARE wait a millisecond after that second one cause the attack is no longer charged now.)I mean seriously this game has literally brought me more pain than pleasure. _childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a straight forward side-scrolling action platformer taking place in a gorgeous pixelated digital world.The game combines a simplistic combat system with probably the most beautiful pixelated world I have ever seen, and sends the player on an adventure across the three different digital worlds and defeat the bad guy to clear the system of any corruption. In other words, you are an anti-virus/anti-malware program. The story and the plot is honestly not important at all. The combat is a bit on the easy side and the bosses are a breeze.Whether or not you will like this game depends entirely on how much would you enjoy exploring a pixelated digital world. I was very happy to do so. Despite the simple combat, I enjoyed my time with Narita Boy. It doesn't have anything innovative in terms of its narrative or gameplay, but it excels at just providing stunning locations for the players to just take some time and look around. The team went out of its way to make a memorable world and they accomplished that without a shred of a doubt.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Great visuals and good story. Gameplay is hack and slash, but you still need good timing in scenarios. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Good game.  The combat is responsive yet deliberate, punishing overextension and mashing.  The encounters are well planned and don't simply dump a bunch of enemies on the player.  The aesthetics are fun.  It's got that synthwave 80s neon styling, but combines it with a fantasy-type setting, and the result is like "Tron by way of Studio Ghibli".  The music has a few really stand-out tracks, with good grooves that don't wear themselves out, and the more atmospheric pieces do their job admirably.   There are two parts of the story in the game, and the story involving Narita Boy is boilerplate "man has to go to Big Bad and hit him with a sword to save the realm" stuff, which is probably for the best because the vast majority of the story is put into the flashbacks and worldbuilding, and trying to tell a complex story in the present of the game while also going over how the present came to be would be way overstuffed.  I liked the game a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe it's because I'm ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up on percocet after having my tonsils removed three days ago but the story makes no sense to me, whatsoever. The beginning of the game feels extremely tedious and I was left wondering what the ♥♥♥♥ I was supposed to do. Virtually every single line of dialogue made no sense to me.It feels like Narita Boy is trying to be esoteric for the sake of being esoteric; I'm not really about it. There could be something there underneath all the fluff and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I don't care enough to continue playing to find out. I backed this game on Kickstarter several years ago and I'm glad to see that it finally materialized, but I'm less than impressed with the end result. Just feels really disjointed and strange.I also don't like that there seems to be no aspect of challenge, whatsoever. _childDocuments_.review: Even though its beautiful to look at, it was the sum of little small things that made me refund it.1- The jump lag, its subtle but according to redditers its built in, not an issue with my hardware, i failed 5 times to jump over the first red hand, and i freaking come from playing platformers for 20 freaking years.Hence the platforming aspect suffers, i found myself falling in the same chasm several times because of the distance being shorter than the maximum jump span, then when you try to maneouver in mid air you end up falling.2- You can get to a door and you upper stick to enter, but if you walk a little bit more you hit a wall and the prompt to enter disappears, you need to go back to the exact trigger placement so you can enter that door, it gets anoying very quickly.3- I had a key, i had thee doors that looked the same, but key only opened one. Anoying.4- Hitting monsters is cool, but combat in general isnt, Its very straigh forward: hit, dont get hit.5-I felt i was being guided the whole time, i read around 300 lines of lore, was introduced to a lot of information that i obviously didnt get because it was excited about getting into the mechanics first. I think the game needs to be fun first so i can get interested in the story later on. I swear the initial lore dumping could have been an email.6- I had no idea where i was going the whole hour i played.Maybe you guys would like it, i come from playing a lot of Blasphemous, Dead Cells, Castlevanias in general, so i was familiar with what i wanted and this one just didnt get me.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this because it's not a bad game, it's just not really my kind of thing.This is basically a mix between hack and slash and WASD-adventure game.  Short bouts of intense combat with lots of running back and forth to find symbols, keys and other stuff.  There is a story there, which begins as a Tron-type clone but quickly descends into a quasi-religious prophecy script that you tend to find in high fantasy, all wrapped up in techno-babble type speech from the "programs" you interact with.  I'm a programmer by trade and a sci-fi/space opera reader, yet even I felt that the flowery writing with difficult to parse language was OTT, so much so that I stopped really taking in the story element quite quickly; it's not like you lose out on anything important as all the objectives are spoon fed to you anyway.  The art style is interesting, but makes playing the game more difficult as it's hard to see what is going on sometimes.So it's not for me, but I can admit that for the type of game it is it is pretty well put together.  The combat is smooth enough and enemies varied enough to keep it interesting, the art fits the premise, the language and story (what I followed of it) basically make it deep cybercore and based on what I played and progression I made I would estimate there to be at least 10-15 hours of game play in there for most people.  So a decent game if you can get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: First off: this is not a Metroidvania. Its a 2d sidescroller with good combat and 'Points of No Return.'False advertizing aside, this game was an absolute BLAST!!The 80's aesthetic is used to great effect and the gameplay is great, even if the movement is a bit slippery.The story is very simple but its well told.Get it on sale
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Was one of the kickstarter backers for this. My rating is very mixed. The good:- Aesthetics - variety of monsters - vehicles / powerups- some moments just felt SO cool. The bad:- uninspired puzzles - story killed me, just a bunch of jargon somewhat related to computers and code. - platforming was very "floaty" I died more often over jumping a platform than from the enemy battles.- the last boss was very slow and long (the glove boss was much better IMO)- when you beat the game you are stuck at the last boss, unable to go back and collect the secrets. - some of the effects to make it feel retro (static, scan lines, screen warp) made it too busy making it hard on the eyes, or hard to differentiate enemies from backgroundIt was an enjoyable playthrough, but not good enough that I would recommend it to others or play it again myself. It's a shame though because I think there's so much potential for a gem here. But I think there were just budget/staff/time constraints that prevented it from being realised.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Visuals: The retro aesthetic is too busy and unfortunately makes for kind of muddled visuals, especially when trying to figure out if an element is interactable or just in the foreground/background. Coupled with an absolute ton of flashing lights it’s easy to get a headache. The game seems to be aware of this because various NPCs go out of their way to point out things that should otherwise be immediately evident in the game world. Gameplay: Level design is also retro in the sense that it’s frustratingly brainless and very repetitive. After a few hours, I realized I was pushing through just to finish and not really enjoying the experience. It’s very easy to permanently miss key unlockables which makes no sense for this style of game. Then, when you realize you’re locked you out of places you have already been it’s insult to injury. This could be saved if the combat was engaging enough to warrant a replay, but most encounters are best dealt with by button mashing and trading damage to get things over with asap. Story: I would have been happy to stick around for an engaging narrative, but I just didn’t feel any connection to the characters, their past, or ongoing events in the world. Some of the flavor text is pretty funny, though.

_childDocuments_.review: This should be a thumbs up, but I finished it and it tastes of lost potential.This cant be a review like those that list the good and the bad things so im gonna give you some of the characteristics which stood out to me and some of my thoughts, and you decide if it is for you.1- The game barely fits the metroidvania tag, some bactracking, some secrets, but not much else.2-you have many types of movements and many types of enemies which are to be taken on with different stratefies, the main difficulty of the game is how quick can you go from one mindset to the other3-Ther artstyle, the tone and the ambiance are awesome, but the wrting leans so much into its style that sometimes you just want to skip chuncks of text, 4- A BIG NONO: the game was release (at the same time) for PC, Mac, Xbox and PS4, it seems to assume you have a controler, however it DOES allow you to use a keyboard through one of four predetermined configurations, on of which is named "custom" but you cant change the bindings... meaning the keyboard controls are uncomfortable as f*ck5- it has what I call "floaty jump" meaning its that jump which overshoots and easyly overcorrects the fall6-The story is the main problem:  While the setting and the writing could have made this game into something bigger and impactful, a story with loads of lore and loads to explore, instead they chose a small, personal story with more than a dash of sci-fi-fantasy which ultimately fails to deliver the awesome eperience the artstyle promised. AND it doesnt resolve the story, there is a main objective which is cleared, but the overarching conflict is only escalated for the game to slap you in the face with a "to be continued"All in all, I did have a good time playing it, but after it became more frustrating that fun (more than anything due to a complicated writing wasted in such a small story) i simply finished it out of compulsion.

_childDocuments_.review: this one is not clicking at all, and i haven't played enough for this to be a comprehensive bad review, but here's some of the things that bothered me:first up, positive notes - love the style, love the soundtrack, the combat/attack animations are neat (but there was so little of it compared to all the running and talking...)the initial bit of friction i encountered was that there is so much talking about nothing in particular. the entire setting is extremely silly, it's fine to not turn this into the entire lore of middle earth. sometimes visuals and gameplay are completely sufficient to tell a story. Having this much talking to npcs (before you even get to do anything) come up in something that looks so much like an arcade callback is for one unexpected, but none of it was particularly interesting regardless.also a bit at odds with the style, this is somewhat metroidvania-ish. the layout is not linear, there is backtracking, and there is no map (at least not that i've seen). i really don't think this kind of setting, aesthetic and the environmental traversal options the gameplay offers support this kind of thing at all. imo it's a bit of a disconnect of game and gameplay mechanics.there are also some minor mechanical annoyances - the jumping feels very floaty, the level design doesn't make it especially clear where is safe to walk and where not, the visible section of the area is small enough that you sometimes can't see where it's safe to jump down and where not. at one point i ended up aimlessly going back and forth because i was fairly certain i was supposed to go through a door, but it wouldn't let me - turns out you needed to stand on top of a tiny stair for the interaction to work.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a hard game to not recommend because it's clearly got a love and passion from dedicated developers. At the end of the day though I think the art style is so overdone it distracts from the game and makes it hard for me to play. Everything is bright and flashing and moving all the time. After even just half an hour I was left feeling physically ill.The gameplay is harder to review because I didn't get very far but I will say it has a really slow start trying to build atmosphere & story but a 2D-Metroidvania might not be the best medium for that. The initial dialog is definitely a whole short story to read and not told via environment or gameplay very well. The gameplay I did experience feels like it was underfocused on compared to the rest of the experience. Combat feels floaty, it's often hard to separate the background from the foreground important pieces.All in all, I expect lots of people could fall in love with this. I find it personally hard to recommend as a game. If nostalgia pulls you to this game you'll probably love it. If not, I hope you'll find more to love than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Good pixel art and soundtrack, but the overall experience is not great.Some enemies feel like mini bosses : they are damage sponges and take minutes to kill (ie the big tank guy where you have to wait for it to exhaust all its shots and rush you to be able able to damage it a little and then wait again).Problem is that they are put in the middle of enemy waves and you often have to fight them again and again when you die.The character is too floaty, jumping feels imprecise and weird to time correctly to avoid projectiles.Using some powers takes way too many time and leaves you too vulnerable, like the beam attack, the switch between the different "colors" and the heal.Story is boring and poorly written, it is overreliant on made up words to try to build lore, unfortunately without success.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not quite finished with the game yet, but I do feel confident enough to review.Hooo boy, does this make me wish there was a "neutral" option instead of good/bad, because what's here is great, but damn if it's not flawed.First, let's get the positives out of the way:And now, the bad:this game has some bafflingly stupid design decisions compounded by just genuinely poor design. Despite combat being the main gameplay mechanic, there is  way to heal outside of it, so if you have a sliver of health left, ♥♥♥♥ you I guess! Why? This isn't fun, it just makes any combat encounter something to dread. You wouldn't even have to add healing, just completely replenish health after each combat encounter, or have some sort of save point that refills health like  And that's not even touching on the combat itself which just feels bad. It's , but it feels incredibly slippery and demands a lot of precision at times, a poor mix. It also really feels like it would benefit from a block or parry button, but there's already a ton of "mechanics" in the game that end up using almost every button on a standard controller, so maybe not.The game seems intent on wasting your time in the most tedious ways possible. For example, the main goal is to restore some guy's memories, you do this by finding totems and activating them, then entering a "hall of memories". To activate a totem you have to do a button mashing game after pressing the use button, but then you have to press the use button  to enter! Why do I have to press the same button twice? Just open the damn thing and get on with it. Also, and this is really nitpicky I know, but the door to leave the hall of memories is slightly raised forcing you to jump to leave rather than just walk. Again, just why? You'll have to visit this area at least 12 times, why is there a single step forcing me to jump at the end of a long hallway, it interrupts the flow.I wish Steam would let you just downvote a tag without flagging it, because whoever slapped the "metroidvania" label on this doesn't know what a metroidvania is. The level design is incredibly linear, forcing you to walk back and forth unlocking doors. Imagine if each level in Mario made you backtrack 4 times each level before letting you advance, and you'll have an idea. This is directly counter to metroidvania level design, which is all about maps that loop in on themselves and have alternate paths. Sometimes there's backtracking in these, but they often try to mitigate that by having shortcuts and at the very least are almost never completely linear. Again, it all adds to the incredible tedium the game is assaulting you with.Bafflingly, despite how much backtracking the game requires of you in each level, you are completely unable to go back to levels you have already completed, and there are hidden items not necessary for winning but purely for 100%. Which is another thing at odds with people who think this is a metroidvania, but also really frustrating because some of these items are quite well hidden and it's not clear you can't go back until you try to.While I praised the story earlier, I do have one complaint in that it's also not very good at hiding its twists, , so while I dig the mystical code reverence, the actual plot is kinda straightforward and obvious.Lastly, the game lacks any sort of replay value due to how linear everything is and the combat just not being that good, but also the game could benefit from a few more QoL features. You'll notice each enemy is given a very quick intro and has a name, but there's no "lore" or stat section in the menu to go and look at them in any detail, which given how excellent the pixel art is feels like a huge waste.I'm giving this game a thumbsup more so because all of these problems are easily solvable and I think a Narita Boy 2 could knock it out of the park, so I do want people to support the devs in the hopes of that happening. As it is however, your time might be better spent looking up a playthrough on youtube than actually spending 25 dollars on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a love letter to times past, hitting resonating notes of nostalgia for the 80’s and 90’s pop culture. I couldn’t help thinking as I played through this game that it was the way I imagine playing older games that don’t hold up in modern times. Powerful tight mechanics, Bosses that challenge you, and music that you feel in your bones. The story in this game sets you as an unknowing protagonist in a fantastic cyber world, where you both are, and are not the main focus of the story. It plays out with you slowly discovering who you are, and what your place in the wold is while hitting notes that can be emotionally resonating for some in a bitter sweet way. Overall this game just oozes in style. The world is built of pixelated vistas, populated with memorable characters that are easy to care about. Without spoiling anything, when you find yourself surfing through a digital sea on a floppy disk hover board, only to jump off and engage in satisfying combat with a Techno Sword that doubles as a shotgun while synth wave music pumps in your ears, you can’t help but smile. Please do yourself a favor and play this game

_childDocuments_.review: :- . Pure eye candy. You will often stop playing just to gape at the backgrounds.-  that blends perfectly with the visuals.- Really imaginative worldbuilding.- Varied combat system with a wide range of attacks and special moves.-  with forced retracking.- Floaty jump physics.- Excessive info dump in dialogues.✔️ - you appreciate great art.- you're a synthwave lover.- you miss the 80's❌ - you care way more about gameplay than aesthetic.- you don't typically care about the story in a videogame.There are games where you can tell how much passion has been put into them by the developers. Narita Boy, despite its flaws, is one such game. It's not a perfect game. But it's a game with a soul, and I think that's way more important.Narita Boy is an action adventure game with beat 'em up style combat sections and a classic hero-saves-the-world storyline. Where it really shines, though, is in its presentation.If there's one thing that Narita Boy does extremely well, it's . The Digital Kingdom that our hero must journey through really feels like a living, breathing world in all its virtual glory. The beams of the Trichroma bathe all its regions with its yellow-blue-red sacred light, revealing incredible landscapes of sheer binary beauty: forests, deserts, coastlines and cityscapes populated with a variety of outlandish creatures and menacing foes made with the most exquisite pixel art. All of this is enhanced by an amazing synthwave/chiptune soundtrack, both moody and catchy, that perfectly fits every scene.Playing Narita Boy late at night is a surreal, dream-like experience, especially with its convincing CRT effect that gives the whole world a hypnotic retro glow.A lot of thought has been put in the worldbuilding, and you will learn all about it along your adventure through the abundant dialog that the game throws at you.As rich and interesting as the world is, these info dumps can get a bit annoying at times when all you want to do is keep hacking enemies with your mighty Technosword. But as I mentioned, this game is all about immersion, so taking the time to carefully pay attention to what is said really helps you get sucked in the game world.The combat sections are fun without beeing exceedingly difficult. You have a wide range of different attacks and special moves which you use to defeat enemies with ever increasing strength and difficulty, many of them requiring the use of specific moves to be defeated.There's also a high risk/high reward powerup mechanic with which you will be able to both deal and take massive damage, which adds a bit more depth to the combats. The bosses are varied and imaginative as well, although not much of a challenge for the most part. Overall, the whole combat experience feels satisfactory and really engaging. My only issues with it are some occasional input lag, as well as some difficulty at times to keep track of Narita Boy's position in the fight due to the visual overload.Unfortunately, Narita Boy has way more serious flaws, which can make or break the game for many. The levels, beautiful as they are, are designed around you going back and forth in a series of repetitive key-fetching quests that get old really quickly.And the floaty jump physics make the game unnecessarily difficult at times, especially during platforming sections, which fortunately are short and not very prevalent.Overall, I was left with the bittersweet sensation that Narita Boy is a missed opportunity that could have been a true gem if not for its flaws.Nonetheless, the good parts are so well executed that you can forgive its shortcomings. All depends on what you enjoy in a videogame.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the game. It was challenging, rewarding, and visually amazing. An 80's techno-splosion that looks and feels rad as ♥♥♥♥! The game is short and has a few problems here and there though. I backed this game a couple of years ago and I have been very excited about it during development. The development team did a great job with announcements and keeping the backers up-to-date the entire time with their work. They deserve a positive review from that alone.I do recommend getting this game, but I also have some notes about it that I think people should know before they buy it.The main gameplay has three sections. Running around with some basic platforming, solving visual puzzles that comprise of three icons you need to input into consoles, and finally fighting hordes of enemies and bosses. The game has a great balance of these sections throughout the game and none of them seemed excessive at any time. I did find some real problems with the basic controls though. Narita Boy only runs when not in a cutscene and is a bit floaty in the air, this can cause some platforming issues. Jumping was also hard for me because in order for me to "small jump" I had to barely touch my jump button, Narita Boy almost always full jumps and this caused some problems with the boss The Glove on the train. I am not sure if this was the game or simply my older USB controller so I'm not going to dock it points for that. As for the combat, I thought it was pretty solid. There were a few gauntlets and bosses that were really hard for me to get past, but ultimately I just had to "get good" and then I beat them. There are quite a bit of moves/attacks that you can do and I honestly forgot about a lot of them until I was getting smashed over and over again by the same guys. Then I remembered that I have summons that I can use, or that I can imbue myself with a certain color to do more damage to those types of enemies. I really liked this mechanic. Other than those small issues I thought the gameplay was fun throughout the entire game. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing! The sound and the music are beautiful and very well produced. The audio perfectly matches and balances the aesthetics of the game. Every song is a banger. I have nothing bad to say about the audio from this game.Perfect 80's style pixel art. The design of the characters and environments were beautiful. The colors make everything pop while you can still see the difference between the foreground and the background. The animations were great as well, I felt like my character was able to do everything that they were doing without exaggerating anything. The storyline is very convoluted. There are two main stories happening and you get tossed into them pretty quickly.First, you have the Digital Kingdom that you need to save. Pretty straight forward, kill the Stallions and save the people. All the people within the Digital Kingdom and the three houses are awesome and I thought they did a great job creating their stories.Second, you have the Creator's Memories that you need to find and unlock. Each memory gives you a flashback of how the creator grew up. I honestly didn't find this storyline very useful to the game and it was pretty forced. I think the writer(s) didn't worry about whether or not they should put something into the stoyline and instead they focused more on putting as much as possible into the storyline without worrying if it actually fits or not. Some comments on the ending: I genuinely enjoyed playing the game and it was worth the wait. I know I complained a decent amount about certain sections, but overall the game was well made and I had fun playing it. I will be keeping an eye on this studio and development team to see what they make next.

_childDocuments_.review: Before getting on with the review I would like to say that this game is not a pure "Metroidvania" in the generally accepted sense of the term. (I've never been a big fan of using that term, but people know what a game is like if it has that description, so I'll use it.)  It definitely has elements of those games, but this game is mostly linear with the exploration, since new abilities and items are obtained after completing specific parts of the game; progression of the story happens the exact same way for everyone.  That is not necessarily a bad thing, but some people will be disappointed since they may go in expecting a traditional "Metroidvania", when the game is closer to a basic platformer with some enemies thrown in every so often.  Even the enemy fights are scripted in the game in that they only appear at certain parts of the story so there is also a linear aspect to the enemy encounters.The graphics are amazing.  Some people do not like pixel art but these graphics are far superior to anything that was on the 8-bit and 16-bit consoles.  However, a couple essential things may be hard to notice (such as which walls can be climbed) due to the high level of detail throughout every region.The audio is great.  It definitely is not the type of music that would have been in older games from the '80s like how the story takes place, but it fits the mood well.  Some areas are more ambient and other times there are more elaborate songs.  Graphics and audio are definitely the high points to this game.Gameplay is mostly good.  Fights have variety since there are a few moves that can be done instead of merely using a single attack button.  While running around, though, the controls seem a little slippery sometimes, especially when trying to jump across pitfalls to land on platforms.  Luckily in these instances there are infinite lives so the game puts the player back at a recent checkpoint.  However, that can also be a bad thing--that definitely makes the game much easier since there does not seem to be a true "Game Over".  One can even start a boss fight with half health and then lose to that boss, but then respawn at the start of the fight with full health.  It almost seems counter to the '80s theme that this game is presenting; games back then were NEVER that easy with infinite lives and numerous checkpoints.  Hopefully there will be a "New Game+" mode afterwards with limited lives and such, or maybe the developers will add that as an optional mode.I myself like this game so far even though I have not completed it yet.  I was expecting something a little different, but I still enjoy games like this.  I have only a few small gripes with the game, but it definitely is not detracting from the experience; it is still recommended and I am looking forward to the rest of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I will very tentatively recommend Narita Boy if the graphics and the music hook you. I enjoyed the lovely pixel art and the synth-wave music enough to fight through some somewhat mediocre gameplay. There's nothing inherently wrong with Narita Boy's gameplay, but it is tedious in nearly every way. You will spend a lot of time walking across the map to get a key, and then walking backward across the same screens to use it. A Metroidvania, this is not. The world isn't inter-connected, and areas are locked off after you've completed them, The platforming and combat are passable, although there was quite the difficulty spike in the penultimate boss.Overall, I think you can give this game a try, and if the music and visuals aren't doing it for you in the first couple hours, then refund it.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this in the Humble Choice. I didn't enjoy the time I bothered trying it.It's very stylish; the 80s nostalgia is actually really nice. Unfortunately, it is overdone in some ways, specifically the nauseatingly psychedelic backgrounds and overly-flashy neon. There should at least be a setting to reduce the twitching. If you're photosensitive in any way, do not buy this game.I can't tell if it's linear or not. The layout is so drenched in neon blue that I can't tell if I'm supposed to go somewhere other than "forward". It's hard to tell if you're supposed to jump over, jump onto, walk across, or turn around because of the monochromatic flooring and walls. I actually gave up bothering to progress because it got too difficult trying to see where on the level I'm supposed to go, and I was only about 20 minutes in.Consider this: About 96% of players get an achievement for pressing the first button. Only about 86% have the achievement for bothering to walk five more rooms and grab the weapon required to play the game. That's a pretty steep drop off.Would like to enjoy the nostalgia, but can't stand the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy has some of the best pixel art I've seen and the soundtrack is great. The game just oozes 80s aesthetic. But unfortunately that's all it has going for it. The repetitive gameplay and shallow story really let this game down and stops it from being an indie masterpiece. The aesthetics only cannot carry this game.The core gameplay loop just consists of "get key to open door to get key to open door" on repeat with some clunky combat and platforming between said keys and doors. Due to the games insistence on doing things in threes for thematic reasons you find yourself in very arbitrary scenarios. For example, needing to find keys to open doors in sequential order of "zygote", "pregnancy", and "birth". After getting the pregnancy key from the zygote room you backtrack to the pregnancy room which has nothing in it except for the final key. I found this to be so pointless. There are times where you get a key to open a door NEXT DOOR to the room you're in. This is the worst kind of padding that is found throughout Narita Boy.The story is incredibly simple but it tries its best to complicate things in order to hide that. The first half hour is just a massive techno-garble exposition dump framed in big walls of text, a real challenge to stop your eyes from glossing over. Complicating a simple story of "You're a Hero with a magic sword, save the kingdom." There is also a secondary story going on in the background that throughout the game you piece together through memories but I found it to be very predictable. If you have played any indie game with a "3deep5you" sad story then you will know what to expect.Overall, I cannot recommend Narita Boy. If the game had tight combat and controls like Hyper Light Drifter with more varied objectives and also toned done the superfluous over-the-top dialogue then this could have been a much better game.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is so disappointing. The presentation is nothing short of AMAZING. i jammed to the music and the otherworldly visuals sucked me  in quickly. Unfortunately, then you have to play the game. The jumps feel a little floaty, but aren't too bad overall. The level design and concept is a total mess however,. It is just non-linear enough to be confusing and distracting while falling well short of a proper exploratory action game in the Metroidvania style. This game would be awesome as a proper version of either a straight up action platformer or an aforementioned "metrodivania", but as it is , it's just a mess with some rocking tunes
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I'm dumbfounded as to why there is no D-pad support. I was raised on the D-pad since the 8-bit era and here we have a really great game with a plethora of 80's-ism but no D-pad support? This is not gonna stop me from playing or recommending this game but personally playing 2D platformers with the analog stick is the bane of my existence. Paaah-lease remedy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I never thought I'd give this a thumbs down. It's dripping with style and amazing music. The animation is great. The story and the memories start off interesting with hints of this person's real life and it seems really cool, but then after an hour or two it just starts to go downhill fast. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks very good for its style and the soundtrack is awesome.However, I cannot recommend it for three main reasons:- Awfully wonky controls for a game that requires precise movement. Jumping feels very strange, movement feels awkward, combat does not feel good at all because of that.-  The game starts with LOTS. OF. TEXT. And when you think it's over, you walk a couple of screens and have LOTS. MORE. TEXT. Got your weapon? More. text. It gets old really quickly. - At least up to the point where I've played, there's no easy way to heal other than dying (!). Which means that you're going to be repeating a lot of fights just because you started it with a low life bar.I had high expectations for this game, but its shortcomings got on my nerves real quick.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is an experience. I have not finished the game, but I am decently far in.Combat: 7/10: Very satisfying if basicStory: 10/10: I really like it, and find it intriguing and engaging. It's what I keep coming back forLevel Design: 7/10: Some things can be annoying, but other than that it's very good and intelligently laid outArt Design: 9999999999/10: It might just be my favorite looking game of all time, tied with Titanfall 1
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game, you can tell this is a passion project, instantly fave for me, loved the style and world, really surprised by a really moving story and lore. Yea, the mechanics can be a clunky, but I found myself liking the combat and exploration a lot once I got the hang of it. Don't miss on this excellent game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Although I concede that the gameplay could’ve been better, the places where Narita Boy shines it does so as bright as the light of the trichroma. It succeeds in its 80’s themed artwork, electronic music and poetic lore.Putting combat aside (which quickly becomes repetitive although the bosses add variety) the ebb and flow of spirituality and computer-speak is sublime… at times describing the malignant code of a devious program and in a flash diving into the balance of the three houses upheld by meditation and neon lights.In this regard I feel the game has three layers; like a computer program speaking about itself, there is the land Narita Boy traverses, the code written for this land to exist and the life of the coder himself which deeply influences the other two. Many times I wondered if the flashbacks were biographical in nature or if the Spanish studio created this vibrant world in a lazy afternoon. Either way, the result is impressive indeed.To realize that the Creator had sold the Narita One console for riches and fame, while playing his Narita Boy game is a great way to break the third wall. When I saw him on the cover of Time magazine it felt real, especially when he describes his life from childhood to the present with such sadness and subtlety. Now on my second playthrough to catch those pesky achievements, I can appreciate more the direction the game is taking. A crazy 80’s pixelated world seen through the eyes of a boy hero fighting through lines of computer code, what could go wrong? Its an experience, and simply for all its layers of complexity I give this wonderful, trippy title a recommend. By the way, taken straight from their website: "Every asset of the game is individually designed and painted." Impressive, huh?
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Cool graphics and aesthetic but boring gameplay. Most of my time in Narita Boy has been finding keys to open doors and backtracking to find more keys that open other doors. It's basically just a series of fetch quests with little direction on where to go with some boss fights sprinkled in occasional. I just found the game to be boring and tedious.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing art and sound. Cardinal sin of giant lore dumping at the start of the game. Probably first time in my life where i went "Yeah, i ain't reading all of that." and closed the game after half of an hour of reading something i really do not care about. I will try to continue a little bit later, because art style is so perfect and intriguing, but if reading/gameplay ratio will stay the same, i will not be able to do it. I'm sorry.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself has some interesting qualities but overall it's not that good and has too many cons for me to give it a positive rating.Pros:- Somewhat cool story (most of it's fine but a lot of it just seems like it was written by a child)- Unique gameplay and level design- Good gameplay music, sounds, etc.- Nice visuals- Clean and easy to use UI interface- Challenging gameplayCons: - The games theme song is bad, from the tone, to the lyrics to the person singing, it needs a lot of work- First quarter of the game is blinding with how many flashing lights and odd setups there are- When the Narita Boy logo appears and the guy says the name, it's really annoying- When you die, the tag line for death is pretty bad and the guy yelling it is also bad and annoying- Button input lagged and i generally had to press the same button multiple times to get it to work, which causes serious issues when you are trying to respond quickly during an intense fight- Huge blocks of texts to read through constantly throughout the game, really broke the immersion and flow of the game- It's really hard to differentiate what you can interact with and what you can't most of the time (i.e platforms, buttons, etc.) as everything is merged together and there's no sort of attempt made to separate them, even just a little.- You can break the game easily by leaving the game, going to main menu and re-loading the game again, most animated objects are now broken and don't animate. In very specific areas certain NPC's or interactable objects are now gone or not interactable any longer.- I have no idea how you fully heal in this game other than the 1 health point you can get from holding Y, i was fully healed like once or twice in the entire game and i have no idea what triggered it (i.e not dying but being fully healed by some event)- People keep yelling at you "naaarrrriiiittttaaaa boooooyyy" and it's really bad, there's no vocals so the extended text like this just feels a bit much.- The core memories, totems, etc. of the creator/developer seems more like a homage to the actual developer and some need to put themselves in their own games, which i always dislike when devs do this.- The last 5 or so core memories don't really make much sense, they hop and skip around not really telling you anything and leave out any real info, instead displaying nonsensical scenes or dialogue (the previous memories were not like that)- The ending of the game made very little sense and seemed rushed, i have my own ideas as to why but implying in the 2nd game will be a beat em up, is an immediate turn off (considering most, if not all, legit metroidvania games use swords)- The end credits was not really tolerable due to the theme music being badOverall it's an interesting approach to a Tron like metroidvania game however there's simply too many issues and negative aspects to the game for me to really say i'd play it through multiple times or that i'd recommend it to others.At the very least hopefully some of these notes are helpful in your future projects, good luck!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This is just one of those amazing games, wrapped me with intrigue all the way to the finish line. The world and its aesthetic is absolutely enthralling, given that I was ready to expect basic, even walking sim gameplay. However, the gameplay is no slouch at all, you will regularly be demanded to step deftly through hail after hail of enemy attacks, don't be afraid to lose, especially to bosses, you need to screw around to figure out the best strategies and moments to strike. The exploration is juuust exactly engaging enough to motivate you through the wondrous and fascinating lands of the digital kingdom.Easy 9/10 from me
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I have to sadly write a negative review for this game. It's not a bad game, it has actually some strong argument for him. But being a "big" indie game with a publisher and more budget than a solo dev, and some online hype : I feel I have to be stricter. Basically to the contrary of what you see read or see in videos: this game is not at all a 2D action game with platforming and exploration. it's more of a point'n'click adventure text narrative heavy game with strong art direction, great universe, impressive visuals... but the controls both in navigation and fights makes most of the effort to turn it into an action game failed. you might enjoy this is you are the sort of player where story and art is enough to please you, and follow a linear go to flow or many many keys to open a door, where ? you don't know, you don't have map.

_childDocuments_.review: first off i should say i stream this game and that might make a me a tad bias (VrooMinTheRoom, one hour episode 1 out now daily episodes until beat) but honestly, I love this game a lot.             {The music is godly and the first boss fight song is one of my favorite ost songs from anything ever up there with doom and wolfenstein.}            {{The animation may not be the best but it is really good especially where it counts: bosses, fighting sprites, and backgrounds.}}           {{{The movement can be tricky at first and there are some moments where it feels kinda unfair when u try to jump down a ledge and there's a tiny pit that you couldn't see(it should be noted I don't use controllers often so It might just be me)}}}          {{{{The combat is just really really fun and doesn't feel repetitive at all and its quite fun to learn the enemy's choreography so you know when to dodge and when to give up on a combo.}}}}         {{{{{The in between game play could be lacking for some people's tastes but personally I just use the down time of running back and forth to listen to that bumping track which btw almost every room is a different song so it does feel like you're moving and not just listening to the same song on repeat.}}}}}

_childDocuments_.review: Confusing and awkward art style, that's a personal thing so perhaps this appeals to you.In terms of the story, I just couldn't be bothered, it's trite and tedious and tries to get you to empathise with the main character. I don't care about the main character, I just want some platform action without feeling 'emotionally guilted' into caring.As for the repeated pressing of [X] to achieve a task, that's just stupid. I am there, I have the stuff, don't make me constantly batter my gamepad, that's just pointless busy work.This game has a very positive review, so clearly whatever it does, people like it.I do not, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to give this game a negative review because I see that there has been put a lot of thought and effort in the design and somewhat in the story, but unfortunately, I cannot give it a pass.I've played through it 6,5h and it was fun around like in the middle when I was at the yellow kindom; Unfortunately, the flaws of the game became very much apparent. Negative:-there is no way of going back to places you wanted to visit to find things you left or forgot about. No backtracking-too linear. While that isn't per se a bad thing, here it just feels like too much. There is little to no exploration and that is sad and doesn't motivate me-you run around and don't even exactly know where you are. I feel like some "quests" of the main story are plain dumb and lead to nowhere, could even have been totally ditched without changing a single thing-there is one combat move that is not really explained; it just exists and doesn't do much dmg... no advantages. Why does it exist at all? Nobody knows-the techno keys and other kind of disks are, as a concept, not visually helping. I get something and I literally don't know what I can do with it. No descriptions; I was confused sometimes. I ran around trying all kinds of machines and it would eventually work somewhere-although the concept of the different colors is cool, it is just too rudimentary and unevolved... could have been so much better. Too clunky with the activation and swapping; why ?-rarely I was actually losing fights a lot (okay the last fight was a little tougher) and the enemies are easy to push- just too much textpositive:-the most striking thing: the art style. Some areas are beautifully made and evoked fancy feelings inside me-the combat is fine, but just fine. Could be much better and kind of profounder. Some skills are quite satisfying to use and look cool-the story is acceptable. Took me 6,5h to play it through; the NPCs swapped all the time which didn't give me time to fall in love with them or hate them; not even the Motherboard nor HIM where especially enchanting. Wow, she is nice. Cool. He is the antagonist; he mean. Give me more! While there are sweet stories hidden, they are never further told or dynamic. Sad, I'd love to know what happened to the poor Llama in the desert-fun moments such as the concert fight or the credits karaokeAll in all, it is not terrible, but good is an exaggeration.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game.Art is great. Music is fantastic. Gameplay is butts.FTUE needs some serious help. TLDR; too much text, not enough gameplay. walking around and talking to npcs while they explain a world Im not yet invested in is a classic "infodump blunder". I'm here to play a game, not read a novel. If you need to explain something that early, show me, don't tell me. You have fantastic visuals to do so, use them.Couldn't get through the tutorial level. Got lost and bored. No real clue where to go or what to do. (telling me to ""get the sword" with no context not only means nothing, it's annoying)Auto-save on death revived at VERY inconvenient places while just trying to get through the opener.i.e. I went up an elevator, couldn't interact with anything, went back down, died, got respawned at the top of the elevator. This happened twice and I turned the game off. It felt like there was no respect for the players time. Walking is slow and unenjoyable. Need a sprint function. If there is one, I never got to see it.Let me run right, learn to use your physics (which will take 1-2 rooms max), gimme a weapon and kill some baddies AT LEAST before making me run around looking at text.Very disappointing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks great, has some good music and actually has kind of a touching story.  Unfortunately, the controls just don't live up to the action.  There are many new powers to unlock as you go.  But, the further you get and the more powers the more the combat kind of devolves into button mashing.  For one, the controls aren't responsive enough for the later game play.  Often when you are in a bad situation, just give up and start over because the enemy will keep knocking you out of attacks and there isn't much you can do.  Another game that has great potential marred by mediocre controls and some seemingly purposefully bad check pointing.  Sometimes the checkpoints are great.  Other times you will find yourself clearing out and area and die on a boss only to be put back several screens just for the sake of making you take extra time to travel back several screens.  Makes no sense when the way is already clear.  Why waste the players time but then other times you spawn right before the boss.  Another minor, but annoying gripe is that you cannot skip the boss intro if you die.

_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is less of a metroidvania than most linear games. It occasionally just removes upgrades you got in previous levels and does not allow for backtracking outside of briefly playing errand boy for various NPCs but this does not apply across levels. Boss design tried very hard to be unique and is thusly very rough around the edges. The story itself is nonsense but workable if stereotypical but the side story or whatever it's supposed to be is cringeworthy and laughable and found me questioning whether this part of the game you spend maybe a half-hour of forced gameplay in a ten-hour game was supposed to be considered as a joke. The soundtrack is excellent and the composer should be very proud. The art direction is beyond anything I've ever seen before, making this inherently ridiculous digital world feel not only interesting and enjoyable but alive and lived in. The combat feels punchy and genuinely excellent but none of the enemies seem to be designed around it. A handful of examples of this are: the warlocks, standard enemies, that just appear and disappear and take around 3 minutes to kill; the 'pirate' optional miniboss whose hitboxes are just ridiculously hard to reach and have projectiles that seem to be made to be dodged by something shorter than the released product's main character; the ridiculous waiting game of the Glycoma boss; the imprecise, floaty jump controls do not work for The Glove fight meaning the skill floor for that fight is so much higher than any of the other ones. All jump-related puzzles feel awful and there are three or four secrets hidden around the map that you cannot come back to but affect your ending of the game. There are some other weirder notes about soundtracks only being used for one very small, hidden room or the example with the forest where you seek out a MacGuffin for a few minutes and after a lot of back and forth you finally get to enter the forest and it's just an eventless corridor that leads to the next area. This is just bizarre game design that seems to be intentionally made to pad the length of the game.In full honesty, this is a game I love the idea of and wish beyond hope that I could recommend but suffers from far too many simple, textbook problems that the industry moved on from years ago. This is Koba's first game and it shows.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked so promising to me, the pixel art style, the synthwave soundtrack, the 80's atmosphere... and myabe that last thing was what made me realize I couldn't like this game at its fullest.Starting by the elephant in the room. The lore is DENSE. Not that it is bad, but the over-exposition to lore makes it less interesting. Games with a lot of lore that gives you just enough to keep engaged, work. Games that overexplain everything to the point to tell you, 'go this way' in a section where you clearly were going that way because it is the only way possible, don't work the same.Narita boy does everything well at its artistic side (ignoring the flashing colors, and the aformentioned overexplaining), the story is good, the memories are endearing, the wolrd feels alive, their aesthetic is so unique even for a over-seen technoworld, it manages to combine hardware and nature as an element for their visuals and characters.Backtracking in this game doesn't feel bad at all. The game is more like a couple of dungeon-like levels, you enter, explore, get the keys, explore, battle, exit, proceed to the next 'dungeon' and the loop, if not repetitive to someone, works well. The combat may be the strongest point of this game, the way you unlock the moveset piece by piece, just to start using it to a new foe, works perfect as tutorial, and when you realized you can defeat a previous-known foe with your brand new habilties, makes it satisfactory. Not to mention the amazing variety of combos you can perform if you manage to get to game to keep your pace...Nonetheless, they may have gone a bit too far into this "retro" feeling. The controls aren't unplayable, yet they manage to not respond as they should at times. Times that may be crucial to carry on your adventure.The platforming and level design lacks engagement to go over them.. The levels are at times too linear just to be cut to a platforming section of 2-3 platforms that adds literally nothing to the experience. It's like they realized the main character was walking in a straight line for quite a long time and said 'now we need to move in another direction, for variety'. The jump is heavy, delayed, and floaty. Sometimes making it imposible to calculate where to land. Add to that, the 'game over' screen, which is rather a formality to keep the retro feel, and that's its weakest point.This game feels like it was designed to artificially make it longer by failing. Take a look a the long platforming sections where there is not a single saving point, if by chance of luck (and bad control response) you die on it, you'll must walk it over all again. And the creator have mercy, that section didn't contain one or more battle rooms, which you also, must complete all over again to continue, most of the time to a point that just makes you, go back where you came.Bottom line's Narita boy was a good try, with subpar execution. I'll be looking forward to anything that Studio Koba has to offer to addd into this franchise/universe, if any. I hope they could polish the rough edges to deliver a truly magnificent experience :)
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Style over substance and the wrong kind of nostalgia! Narita Boy gives me the vibe of being made by people who would love to live in the 11th century, conveniently forgetting all the boons of modern civilization like hygiene, food and medicine.If you like crisp controls and a sense of direction, this is not the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The Story is complex, but very intriguing and overall amazing for an indie-title like Narita Boy.The Creator, a genius of his time, creates a video game console called Narita One with its flagship title being a game called Narita Boy.Narita Boy becomes a tremendous hit! Copies of cartridges are flying off physical shelves worldwide. Within weeks Narita Boy is the best-selling video game of all time, critically acclaimed for its power-fantasy wielding the Techno-sword and taking players on a journey like no other.Meanwhile, inside the binary code, the digital realm connects with reality. Him has returned and deleted The Creator’s memories. Supervisor program, Motherboard, and her agents have activated the Narita Boy protocol.The Stallions are coming, and the Digital Kingdom needs a hero. You are taking control of this young pixel hero who gets beamed into this wonderful pixel code.By emulating the look of a retro game and combining modern elements Narita Boy is a game in game action platformer with a tremendous focus on fantastic synthie sounds, cryptic storyline, A to B puzzles and sword wielding action elements.Narita Boy has definitely it flaws, especially when it comes to unprecise controls, cryptic narration and tutorials as well as to the overall complex game design with little help about the next steps to take. It lacks modern game elements like a map or way markers – obviously the game decision also wanted to bring back some of those frustrating 80s moments. Dialogues throughout the game are interesting but rarely getting to the point about what is important. Thankfully you get a quick quest objectives menu which helps a lot to manoeuvre through the game. Besides of this. the first 20 minutes of the game have been very frustrating for me and filled with unnecessary backtracking just because I missed some fundamental game elements, like going through doors, climbing up a cliff. Probably my bad. The moment you find out, you feel a bit stupid. But having understood these basic game mechanics, let’s call them shortcomings, the game starts to shine with its overall bad-ass cool atmosphere, the fantastic theme and an artsy design rarely seen.The Combat is swift with variations in combos. You can triple click to slash through hordes of enemies or you can use a powerful beam to light up bulks of foes. The counterparts come in different physical variations with different grades of difficulties and tactics. Sometimes you need to dodge at the right moment - rinse and repeat -, and sometimes you feel cornered and it becomes slightly more frustrating. Whereby the combat system is overall well-designed and yes fun, there seems to be however something off from times. I mean I click the button but nothing on the screen happens. I mean I dodge and the character is running in the other direction. I was wondering if it was my controller – yes, you better play it with a controller, or if it was the game itself. Here I see still room for patches in order to improve the combat system. But hell yeah it is fun and the boss fights are challenging as well as it should be in a modern retro Metroidvania. Later on, you will learn to better combine shotgun attacks with beam attacks, dash and dodges, just as it should be. And even more later on you can get different coloured attacks which give the overall cool sword fighting mechanics even more depth and makes you want to fight even more instead of doing the puzzles or platformer part of the game. In conclusion, combat is fun, but needs one or another patch.The respawn system did not really appeal to me. Instead of respawning on the same screen where you died, the game will respawn you at the latest checkpoint. This checkpoint can be far away from the platform where you have died which means you will need again to back-track or revisit the location over and over again. The well-crafted backgrounds are nice to watch with their contrast-full and colour-full blinking neon-lights on dark-blue. However, they wear off after some time seeing them again and again. Only solution, git gud and do not die. Learn the tactics of the combat and especially learn how to jump properly with the analogue sticks, from one platform to another without falling down. More difficult than being said. But do you remember the controls in the 80s?The game shines spectacular when it comes to its synthie 80s music. You can get for 15 Dollars a great OST on Steam, performed by Salvinsky and composed by Salvador Fornieles, published under the label Autoeditarte/KzooMusic. Feel fresh waves of synth wash over you while travelling the Digital Kingdom. With 50 kickin’ beats that will send you back to the future.The game is around 9-10 hours playtime, steep learning curve and backtracking included but also offers some value for replayability in my humble opinion. With a price tag of 25 USD or Euros you will get definitely enough game for your money. But as always, it is totally okay to wait for a sale, especially since Narita Boy will not grow old as it emulates a retro game by itself, so it will still be totally cool 10 years from now.By concluding, Narita Boy is a fresh neo-retro experience in the best 80s home console artsy pixel style, powered with one of the greatest soundtracks in indie gaming. However, it still has its game design flaws, with unprecise controls, difficult puzzles, dislikeable respawn functions and a narration that could be too complex for the average gamer. On the other hand, the game will find its fanbase for sure, since the neon-lights, the cool overall presentation, the love and sweat that went into it, let’s you forgive its shortcomings in platforming, puzzle and combat. Whereby some parts might be frustrating, new environments are rewarding and give you the desire to continue the adventure. EDIT 28.11 - I nominated Narita Boy for best Soundtrack Award. Cheers.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I have never seen a game use so much exposition to say nothing at all. Many pages of text suffuse every level of this game, and it amounts to the religious equivalent to meaningless technobabble. Even before the game gave you a button prompt for meditating, I could have told you that the creators were big on meditation and spirituality.The plot isn't much better. The nameless protagonist is abducted in to the digital realm and set on a quest to restore the memories of the computer's creator, complete with flashback scenes to pivotal moments of the man's life. This is barely passable as a motivation, and words cannot express how little I care for this stranger. Like so much of the rest of the game, it serves only as an excuse to push the player forward, and is much better when ignored.I don't know why this game is trying so hard to evoke nostalgia for TRON, since it has nothing to do with that IP aside from the inciding incident and color scheme. Everything about this game is pulling at some form of nostalgia, whether it's the CRT filter, the imagery borrowed from TRON, or the fact that the god-figure looks like a cartoon caricature of a washed-out musician. The game can't even figure out which culture it's trying to evoke, at times using metalhead references, and at other times having the PC perform disco moves to celebrate milestones.The best thing I can say about the art is that they tried. The amount of care and effort put in to the assets is clear, but effort does not equate to quality in this case. At its worst, the environment is unparseable, and the difference between platforms and irrelevant background details can only be found with trial-and-error. At its best, it's still just copying TRON.The gameplay redeems none of this game. Platforming is passably ok, and the combat is deeply unsatisfying. Enemy attacks are incredibly spammy, your own animations are floaty and uncomfortable, and fight mechanics lead to slow combat that isn't exciting.Event at 3$, this game was not worth the time required to complete it.

For one, the graphical style is very unique and one-of a-kind - both 80s retro and futuristic, with a strong whiff of Out of this World. Even the story of a boy and his Hafu creator managed to actually have some emotional moments - a surprise. But at a few points I nearly deleted the whole game of my HDD in frustration - that one fishkoi boss, for example. Still, the last moments of the game are worth it - especially the awesome city that you eventually reach. I found that many of the moves are in the end not super useful or they come too late in the story, but at least they did provide you with enough for us to have some fun during the combat. Anyhow, for those with some patience, the game does prove rewarding, even if the glaring flaws can be hard to overcome at times. 6/10 (I use the full 1-10 scale, so this is above average).

_childDocuments_.review: Fauxstalgia for hipsters who weren't born in the 80s. I mean, it's okay but it's nothing that hasn't been done better elsewhere. The jumping is floaty, the metroidvania aspects are done poorly and the game starts with a million dialog boxes telling their very average plot. It's a very mid game. Mediocre at best.40 minutes into the game expect to be directionless; The game functions much like a metroidvania, you unlock more parts of the level as you progress and backtrack. For the first 30 minutes, aka the hidden tutorial, you'll be okay. Then you'll eventually reach the top of some tower and have to backtrack... A lot. Once that's done all directions are gone, and you have no map. Hope you enjoy trial and error.At the VERY least the game gives you "objectives' and "hints" as to where to go next, but oftentimes those objectives and "hints" are SEVERAL levels behind. Still, that would be fine if the game had distinct looking environments. It doesn't. This game is what every zoomer thinks the 80s were like; Blue, chromatic abherrations, Tron... Blue. A lot of blue. So much blue in fact it is extremely hard to distinguish one area from the next.Another smaller issue the game has is that the jumping is extremely floaty. It just feels weird; It feels more like you're trying to clear an half life surf level than a platformer game, and no insult to half life surf levels buit when I'm playing a platformer I expect consistent arcing platforming, not this weird stuff where I can cancel all my momentum in midair. More aggregious is the game and especially the marketing's insistence that this is somehow an "Arcade game equivalent". I'm not sure what arcades had metroidvanias and much less, what arcade games CONGRATULATED you on your play. Again, this is just plain fauxstalgia. It's not cool, it's annoying.I don't recommend this game to anyone except those morbidly curious for aggregiously mediocre experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so I'm almost 4 hours into the game and I'm liking it so far. The setting is pretty cool, the graphics are pretty nice, a lot of nice pixel art. _childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy perfectly nails the 80s retro vibes. The art, music, and thematic are on point and masterfully crafted, with just the right amount of comedic moments, including a wink to Rick Astley's iconic dance moves.What made Narita Boy a memorable experience for me, however, is the sad backstory of it all that slowly unveils as you complete the game's main objectives. I could relate to the story and it made it much more compelling to me than it would have otherwise.If I could give one small criticism about the game, it would be about the healing system. The player character doesn't heal between fights, but gets to retry at full health should they die, which makes the first attempt almost systematically harder than subsequent attempts. I think giving the player character full health between combat challenges would have made sense, game-mechanics wise.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

Do know that you cannot go back to previous areas nor is there a chapter/level select. Explore thoroughly if you want to get all achievements.Nonetheless, this is one of the games ever made!

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is such an epic game! The story is super cool and kept me hooked the whole time. The characters are really interesting, and the whole world is just so detailed and awesome.The controls are another big plus. They're really easy to get the hang of, and you can totally customize them to fit how you like to play. It never feels too fast or too slow, and it keeps you excited to see what's coming next. Plus, the difficulty is perfect. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game nails the retro, cyberpunk aesthetic in every way. The platforming took a second to get used to as Narita Boy is pretty floaty but the action is solid overall. Most of the power-ups were badass and the action sequences were very engaging toward the end of the game. I'm a gameplay-first gamer, and this game has quite a bit of dialogue/exposition dumps that broke up the flow of actually playing. I do feel that other games do this type of storytelling in a less pretentious way but that's definitely subjective. I will say that this game does not allow backtracking, which was extremely frustrating. I missed 1 secret floppy disc and would have to play the entire campaign again to find it. Overall, I feel like those who resonate with the story will love Narita Boy, while others will casually enjoy the experience as I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed myself. Animations were phenomenal, it had a great soundtrack, and the gameplay was fairly tight. Story was quite emotional, and it drew me in enough to ask questions (one of which I definitely got right ;P).It had a very 80s pastiche feel to it, and I appreciate that. I think there were some criticisms about that aesthetic, with it not being realistic, but it doesn't have to be.I don't remember too many glitches, but the floppy board was bugged at one point, and I was able to use it outside of its intended purpose, which was actually kinda cool.I don't know why, but I thought this was a Metroidvania? It sort of has some of that, with some ability-gated progression and collecting upgrades along the way, but there is zero backtracking (which is annoying, considering I wanted to try finding the First Memory disks) and no map (which some other reviewers said was a detriment, which is fair enough), but the fact it's not one is fine. That was an L on my part lol.I definitely didn't expect what happened at the end. If you know, you know.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros+ Top notch visual/animations : I would recommend buying it just for animations. (However, it's still a high price to pay for just that)+ Great story telling/ Creative world building.Cons- The fight play is bogged down by unintuitive controls; key mappings are unintuitive and charging abilities are not worth using (it's better to normal attack). Attacks are cancel-able by a dash. However, charging blades and charging guns are not possible mid-air. Weird design choices indeed. If the game decides to be soul-like and has no jumping and/or animation cancelling, this design would be fine. Currently, It's like in the middle (Not choosing whether it wants to be dynamic like traditional metroidvania-megaman type OR be soul-like)- Way points are unclear. Because the animations in both character skills and maps are 10/10. At times, It's unclear where to go such that trials and errors are often the last resort. To make it worse, it does not have minimap or any maps of any kinds to guide you through the digital world. Most of times, the important objective is hidden at the edge that I did not even notice that it were there.

_childDocuments_.review: Brings me back to the days of Duck-tales and Sonic from Sega just from the visuals. I did enjoy the combat, but the controls were not to my liking. I would have changed a few things. Also the dodge mechanic can be 'dodgy' Sometimes you go through enemies, sometimes you take a hit. The checkpoint system is very forgiving and no achievements for not dying (thank god).As for the story, I liked it. Conflict of two worlds. Internal demons. The struggle of being an immigrant in a new country is very compelling. Is the hidden memory worth it? Probably not. Can you 100% this game without trying. HELL YEAH!If you like platforms with a bit of hack and slash, I'd say this game is for you. Just remember to get all the items in the level before you leave, cause there is no going back to collect what you missed if you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is simple yet satisfying platformer with numerous twists, used to tell epic saga and moving story; all of this in really original audio-visual sauce and setting. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy offers an intriguing and exotic narrative, immersing players in a digital world where they must thwart the aggression of the Stallions, formidable adversaries seeking to dominate the digital realm. While initially perceived as a metroidvania game, Narita Boy diverges from this genre, presenting players with intricate puzzles to solve in each stage or area they traverse. Exploration is key, as progressing to the next stage often renders previous areas inaccessible, urging players to thoroughly explore every nook and cranny before advancing. In addition to its puzzle elements, the game features intense battles against enemies, with various abilities to collect and enhance the protagonist's combat prowess, adding depth to the gameplay.The soundtrack, reminiscent of 80s music, complements the retro aesthetic perfectly, offering a diverse array of tracks that never fail to captivate. Visually, Narita Boy excels in conveying the emotions of NPCs through its 2D graphics, immersing players further into the digital world. For enthusiasts of 2D exploration games, Narita Boy comes highly recommended. However, given its current price point, it may be advisable to wait for a sale before making a purchase. Nevertheless, the rich narrative, engaging gameplay, and immersive atmosphere make Narita Boy a worthwhile addition to any gaming library.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is a 2D action-platformer that revels in its 80s TRON-esque aesthetics.You'll be slashing your way through the Digital Kingdom as the titular Narita Boy, gaining powers, defeating bosses and learning about the world. Your general move-set is pretty varied, but it does lose its luster around the last half an hour or so.The story is surprisingly emotional for a game that seems to stem straight from an 80s action movie.The only complaint I have is that due to the hyper-stylized graphics, it can be hard to distingush between objects you can land on and objects that are just part of the background.Overall I reccommend this game.
