_childDocuments_.review: No ability to backtrack at all. Checkpoints are few and far between, and so far between it reaches the point of intense annoyance. The reason for the annoyance is the incredibly difficult combat due the lack of responsiveness and lack of fluidity in the controls. The combat consists of spamming you with enemies to the point where you can't avoid taking damage, hence the large health bar. The only means to resist the damage are the incredibly stiff controls set up to punish you if you make one micro adjustment not perfectly in frame alignment with the programmed timing and persnickety control variation. You can dodge as soon as an enemy telegraphs their attack, and it's a coin toss as to if the game registers your reaction as perfect enough to count as a dodge, especially in late game. I also encountered several glitches where buttons needing to be pressed to continue the game wouldn't register when I pressed them and the character did the animation. I had to leave the area and come back to get it to work. How can you have too much backtracking, yet not enough ability to backtrack? I don't know, but the developers pulled it off. It's a shame because the story is serviceable and has some real depth. I got all the way past all 3 houses, found all but 1 of the missing creator memories, and have no way to go back to the blue house to get the one I missed. It's an absolute shame, because this game was so close to greatness, and has some great points. If you just watch Youtube videos of the story you can probably experience most of the good this game has to offer, but I can't recommend a game that's pulling teeth to beat for all the wrong reasons, and you'll still miss the secret ending without having a guide open the whole time you're playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: a great game but has little promotion in my country, i found this purely by luck and did not disappointed. 8bit is definitely my cup of tea but its vfx is seriously hurt my eyes, especially in nighttime and in creator memories cutscenes. overall, it's a good game to relax after a week-long of working and making adult money.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, I bought this game because i was learning pixel art and searching for inspirational games to learn from. I heard from a couple people that Narita Boy had some really great art. I was not let down! Will most likely buy anything else these artist work on.      The game itself isn't bad either. There is some fun combat and abilities you learn along the way that really sync up quite well. by the end your chopping threw your foes smoothly, flying up down and sideways with your abilities. One annoyance was that there was no way to really heal up before a big fight so if your about to die you might as well get it over with in order to get a real try in at the boss/stage. There is self healing built up from damage but it take a while to build up each bar for one health point when that same bar can be used to clear a whole screen of enemies with a special attack.  Maybe the devs made it like this for balance or no death runs but can be annoying to have to die just to really try a fight. There is also a decent amount of back tracking and figuring our where to go in the early game, but that eases up as you get to the later half.     I ended up 100 %ing this game and enjoyed my time with it. So with that i certainly recommend it. The best part about this game is the art, Combat is number 2, story 3, and level design is last. If art and combat are important to you than you will enjoy this game as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita... BOY!This game certaily was not what I expected. Well, that's not entirely true. It's partially what I expected. A linear action platformer, with a dodge-focused combat system. The visuals of the game are what initially drew me in. What many might not expect is the story, heavily reminiscent of TRON, but with a hefty dose of pulling on your heartstrings. As Narita Boy journeys through the different parts of the digital kingdom, you upgrade your repertoire of skills but your main goal is to unlock The Creator's memories so that he can ultimately save the digital world. The story isn't groundbreaking, but it felt incredibly genuine to me and really pulled me in. Even when certain enemies frustrated me, I was compelled to move forward and finish the game. Some people might come into this game expecting a metroidvania style adventure with lots of backtracking or even RPG elements, but you won't find any of that here. Therefore I also never felt like I had no idea where I needed to go, although there are a few secrets strewn in for good measure. It's a little thing that I appreciate. I'd really recommend Narita Boy to anyone who appreciates some story moments in their action games, although you could bring up the criticism that the two parts feel somewhat disconnected from each other. I never felt that way and would still rate this game pretty highly!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: HIGHLY RECOMMEND=================A true retro gem in all aspects: visually it's a masterpiece, the OST is to this game what Daft Punk's OST was to Tron -- truly fitting and captivating, the animation is exceptionally satisfying and the combat feels awesome, the lore is deep and the story is heart-wrenching at times. REMEMBER: This is a true indie game made possible via kickstarter and made by a small team. This is a truly legendary feat to pull off and while it might have some drawbacks, it's an incredible experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Pros - Retrotech/Tron/Digital Fantasy Vibes        -  Amazing Synthwave Soundtrack        - Solid Character Designs and AtmosphereCons - Really Frustrating Techno-Keys Hidden In Every Level In Order to Progress         - Combat System is Very ClunkyI really enjoyed the story and used a walkthrough just to know where things are because after 30 minutes of finding some obscure location of a key, I was over it but still wanted to know what happened. Cool story just marred by odd design choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I just love this game. It's amazing. People complaining about the "spirituality" or "light exposure" in the game is just sad people with nothing else to do.Gameplay is cool and easy to learn. The story is really interesting and personal. It feels like TRON but cooler, because you get a Sword that can be a shotgun and you can blast a freaking Kamehameha from your face... Yeah!!! It's that cool!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This game's been hyped up big time, but it's not quite the masterpiece everyone says. Story and world-building are so-so, but the gameplay? Definitely fun. My advice: grab it on sale to make it worth your while. Don't buy into all the rave reviews - seems like they didn't play till the end, which honestly, drags a bit. No major twists or anything. It's a straightforward good vs. bad scenario. Still, it's a decent play, especially if you're more into the action than the story
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game because it combines a lot of elements that I love - pixel art and 2D platforming. unfortunately the game is boring, starts with tons of dialogue you have to read to even understand what you're doing. you keep getting quest upon quest on every step you take. The price was great too, but i just won't play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy A game that looks good but its poorly designed . That's how I could describe it in a one sentence but going with a bit more detail it seems that some of the most important things in this game are actually the worst. This is the good thing I can say about the game. The graphics are amazing and make you feel like you are really inside of a digital world in the 80's. Good pixelarts and animations too. The colours sometimes felt too bright for me at some locations but it could be just me.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: it's no katana zero but honestly i really like this game so far, the mechanics can feel a but wonky or annoying at the beginning but you get used to it. the music and the visuals are awesome. my only complaint i guess is that the story is a little cheesy, but that might be just me. might update this review later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: An overlooked gem of the Retro-Metroidvania craze. The presentation of the game is just sublime, offering a unique and highly stylish ride through crazy 16-bit vistas with an amazing synthwave soundtrack. The attention to detail is often staggering and rarely matched by other games. While the gameplay is nothing outstanding or snappy, it is fun from beginning to end and avoids overly hard difficulty spikes like many other games in the genre. This is mostly a relaxed, sometimes slightly challenging 5-7 hours escapism with a pretty decent story attached to it. There isn’t much replay value or innovation to be found but still highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game! It looks, sounds and feels amazing. This game definetely deserves more attention.I've beat the game on the Steam Deck and it fits this platform just perfect, but I suspect on a bigger screen it feels differently in a bad way. The gameplay is very straightforward and even cozy with the exception of last 2 or 3 battles where you need to use many abilities you discovered throughout the game.And at the end there is karaoke!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: For a Metroidvania, Narita Boy feels quite linear with not-so-challenging gameplay. However, the game is still absolutely amazing. It's an understatement to call the visuals stunning; there is obvious love and care that was put into every small detail. There were particular moments where I called my brother to come over to see how beautifully drawn some scenes were. Despite the fact that most characters have squares for heads, they all felt very unique, and memorable. The game also has a ♥♥♥♥ ton of abilities, which you're forced to master since pretty much all of them are required throughout the entire game. Despite this design choice, the game does not restrict you from coming up with some creative solutions to boss fights. Overall, it was all very fun to play. My only criticisms are in regard to the easy difficulty of the game and the lack of backtracking. Some boss fights were honestly too easy, that I beat them without realizing they were bosses? I legitimately thought they were introducing a new mob, till I noticed the heart icon on the side of the screen. My favorite boss black rainbow, which had amazing abilities and a gorgeous design, was too weak that I beat them on my first try. Even the final boss, he took me only two or three tries to beat. This is honestly sad, because the gameplay itself is very cool that I feel that it would still be enjoyable if they increased the difficulty a bit. As for backtracking. I felt honestly sad, when I realized I can't access the portals, to gather the hidden memories of the creator. I put it to the side to focus on the main story, because I expected full access to the map (as is the case in most Metroidvanias). but no, I would have to replay the game if I wanted to do that. Despite all that, the game is still amazing, and beautiful. Also, it's genuinely funny. with a lot of coding easter eggs. Give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing Narita Boy I just couldn't help it but play it again.I must admit I am kind of a sucker for pixel games but this game was just something else... The first thing to point out would be probably the amazing score- I have never bought a game's soundtrack but I feel like I am going to make an exception here. But that just the music. Regarding the game itself- it's flipin' amazing! From the cool-retro style visuals to the literal overflow of atmosphere. And whilst it's not perfect (you get lost around quite a bit), I would still regard it as one of my top 10s of the decade!-EC out!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely hate that I can't like this game. The style is there, the music is perfectly 80s synth but with an actiony/ mysterious vibe, I want to explore the world and story.But god I cannot get past the way it controls. I even came back almost a year or so later to give it another try but I still feel the same about the controls. It feels bizarrely delayed when it comes to starting to run and jump and the combat feels not too clunky but you can still feel something is up.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I understand I am recommending this game but I am going to list everything good and bad before you buy so that maybe you won't feel so bad at the end like I felt.Firstly the good, The game has amazing art, world building, sound design, music, controls could use a little work but aren't bad (until later and I'll cover that) and overall the story is very strong (until the end in my opinion and I'll also cover that.)So what could be wrong about this game? Well it fails to use a number of the mechanics it introduces and ultimately feels like the developers thought it'd be cool but didn't know how to use it in later levels, also you cannot backtrack and as a player that likes to finish thing and then spoil myself so find secrets after that really sucks (i'm not sure why that is but it'd be nice to go back to areas if you think you missed something)On top of those things, the controls feel floaty for any kind of movement but wasn't a problem until the end game where there are a number of combat encounters and 2 bosses that do either require you to be a master with the floaty controls or at least ask you to be good at them, it's a very sudden difficulty spike and made the end of the game feel very bad from the beginning.The Story for me lost a lot of it's interesting bits after the combat had the huge difficulty spike and i blame it partly on the difficulty spike ruining my interest in the game as a whole but also the story not leaving any details to think on at the end and instead just telling you things when they could've held on to a few of those for a small twist at the end.The rest of this contains spoilers for bosses and mechanics of the end game:The Glove sucked and from what i have read people generally agree with me. At the time I am writing this there is a drop of 1.3% according to the steam achievements. As one of the people that beat this boss after an hour or more of trying to beat them i can say this is where the difficulty spike began and that this boss was poorly designed as i feel i largely beat this boss due to luck (which i shouldn't feel like if it were a good boss fight), I have seen people argue "just get good" but this boss is poorly designed and requires controls that this game just doesn't have to support that kind of fight.There are 3 late game areas that you get a cool new ability to use to get around the area, in the Yellow World you get a horse that you use for maybe 2 mins before it become a mech suit, fight a dragon mech suit, and then never use it again. in the Blue World you get a surfboard that you use there and ONCE in a later area and that is it and even if you try to use it you cannot summon it. In the Red World you get a new move designed to break enemies armor that cannot be damaged in any way but this move sucks and sometimes doesn't work (causing me to take damage) and most of the time it doesn't even activate for me, also it doesn't work in tight spaces even though i remember at least one fight needing you to do exactly that. So much of the late game goes under used and while each thing added is fun and interesting it feels like there was no point in that progress.Now while this review may be rather harsh and ultimately negative, I still love this game bc of the positives i stated at the beginning and i wouldn't be so harsh on it if i didn't love what it could've been. I'm even planning on getting the last few achievements i don't have in a 2nd run through of the game. I just wish it was better in some areas and didn't just throw away a lot of ideas or under use them. This game is good but so many things came to ruin it in the end, but that doesn't make it a bad game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This was an incredible audiovisual experience. The music and the design are something truly incredible. While you are around playing, captivated by the sights, the game will often require you to look for hints too, which are most of the times hidden in plain sight. I am no platformer/metroidvania expert but as far as the fights go, I found the controls VERY clunky, to the point of some fights becoming outright frustrating. You can't exactly (at least later on) mash buttons to win: most ''end-game'' enemies, and obviously bosses, each require a specific strategy. Luckily the major part of the game is not battle focused, so you can still very much enjoy the experience. I think how much you'll like the story depends entirely on your expectations / experiences, it seems like the whole comunity is split in half regarding that: I personally really liked it, especially the pacing. Overall if you're here checking reviews because you saw some screens/videos that caught your eye, trust your gut and get this game: it's also relatively short, so savor every frame you can
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are the best part of this game. The combat is good but the most enjoyable parts of it are the end. The story is cool and it actually had me reading most of the text (there's alot of it). Some of the "find the key" sections were confusing and I wish it was more intuitive. Also the price seems like a little too much for the length. Would recommend for anyone who likes 2D games
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: - The 80s are alive and well in Narita Boy. The music and visuals really hammer home that point- The pixel art is gorgeous, particularly the backgrounds. The devastated sci-fi environments you traverse all feel distinct and storied, each with their own palette and fine details- Unfortunately, there's a slightly annoying CRT filter over all that gorgeous artwork that plays into the 80s veneer while diminishing all the effort that clearly went into the art- I really hope you like droning synth music, or else the soundtrack is going to wear on you. I found it appealing in that Stranger Things vein, but it may not appeal to all tastes. If you play to the end, at least, you get a fun J-Pop theme song to cap things off- The story has a fairly interesting premise. The developer of a video game is attacked by the villain of his creation, causing him to lose his memories. It's up to the legendary Narita Boy to save the game world and restore his creator's memories- As you play, you'll find shrines containing the memories of the creator, which will gradually explain the relationship between Narita Boy and the programmer who created him- The narrative surrounding the in-game world isn't quite as interesting. You mostly just navigate from objective to objective as directed by the Motherboard. It's a little dull, but at least the gameplay is fun- Nariata Boy largely plays as a beat 'em up with puzzle platforming sections- Despite starting the game with no combat capabilities at all, the combat feels like the focus of the gameplay and feels pretty good. The controls are tight, and your attacks feel weighty- After getting the Technosword, you begin with a basic combo, charge attack, and "shotgun" attack that basically serves as a powerful horizontal ranged option- You'll eventually get a jump attack and dive attack, but these are only helpful against certain mobs. Additionally, you'll find your basic combo, dodge, and jump can solve most combat- Despite combat feeling good, you wind up fighting a lot of the same mobs over and over again. It can feel a little tedious at times. Luckily, you can get rechargable screen wipe attacks to speed things up, and boss fights inject some much needed variety. They're still button-mashy, but at least they require pattern memorization and careful dodging- Platforming feels secondary to all the combat, and once you get used to the floaty jump, getting around isn't too hard. There's nothing that'll require more than a single attempt or two to get past- The puzzles are also fairly simple. It boils down to symbol and color memorization- The game comes so close to being good. The combat feels like it's so omnipresent simply to pad out the length of the game. Big waves of tanky enemies get boring after a bit. It took the shine off the otherwise fun combat. Similarly, the CRT monitor definitely detracted from the visuals. It would have made more sense if it disappeared when you were in the game world- This was a really good Steam Deck title. It's well-suited for handheld play and ran very well- . In all, it's a good experience with some definite 80s style. It plays well and sounds good, but there are some annoying gameplay and visual aspects that diminish what could have been a better experience
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Visually stunning, strange and silly and striking. Great synthy soundtrack. While the gameplay was not much of a challenge for me, I enjoyed the combat and worldbuilding very much. A linear adventure with an incredible aesthetic, combat that felt great and fun movement (if a little less snappy than I'm used to). I had a great time with this game, even if the story went a little off the rails, and may well replay at some point to find a couple of bits and bobs that I missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game with a bit of a caveat. This isn't a Metroidvania. You can't return to areas once you've completed them. It's designed for a very linear experience. While others will dislike this aspect of the game, I didn't mind, and I was more interested on the world, story and atmosphere. I think the combat has some rough edges since certain power ups and moves are less useful than others, but the game did a good job throwing enemies that required specific moves to remind you those moves exist.The most important aspect I mentioned prior was the story and atmosphere. The music is phenomenal as it pulls from 80s funk and synth, but it isn't all high octane since there are more quiet sections of the game that help slow down the pacing. The music in these memory sections are tranquil and nice. The story about a boy exploring the damaged psyche and missing memories of its game creator and how it eventually connects to the end was nice and delivered well enough throughout the game time.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a beautiful pixel art ADVENTURE game, but not  Metroidvania as most people would think. I will start with the positives:Rarely a game would make me complete it two times in a row and especially a story driven game. However, the strongest point of it in my opinion, isn't the story, but the gameplay itself. The thing I most like is the combat system, it has a variety of moves to dispatch those Stallions. They aren't really difficult, but not easy either and overall the game is merciful and not as taxing as other similar games might tend to be, which I find positive since I enjoy games that don't put you into pointless grind. The graphics and music are wonders to behold, I am a sucker for synth-wave tunes and it definitely has won me there. The graphics also add to the overall digital 80s synth-wave atmosphere, the Digital Kingdom is full with really picturesque places among the despair and chaos that the Stallions bring. Here are the cons and nitpicks that I didn't really like or let's say the negatives for me: As mentioned, it's a story driven game but it's story isn't it's strongest part. This is simply because it goes though really beautiful and touching moments, clever and insightful symbolism, it's really inviting to invest time into it and then ultimately falls short towards the end (at least for me). Some would be spoilers from here on:  . Techno Key searching brings in a way "Find Blue Access Key" type memories of 90s 3D games and I am not really fan of those, but then again they are not that hard to find. Despite the nitpicks it's a really nice adventure game, it's not taxing and it's pretty enjoyable and beautiful to the eye. Might revisit it again for a "3rd time's the charm" run in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: + Cool Pixel Graphics+ Good Movement- Find a key to open a door, Repeat- Fight the same enemies OVER and OVER- Later Bosses are annoying.  The game eventually turns into a Souls like.  - If you miss any achievement during your play thru there's no way to get it again without starting from scratch.I enjoyed this for a while, but after a point, it just was annoying.   For those of you who played Another World (Out of this World), it feels very much like that, but add in hack in slash.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I just couldn't.Now, before I start, let me clarify: I DO like this games art, and I DO like this games music. The pixel art and animations here are phenomenal, and definitely the highlight of the game. The music is pretty good, too. I especially love whenever Narita Boy starts dancing with the music, its cute and really well done.However, the reason I'm giving Narita Boy a negative review if because of its gameplay. From the beginning of the game to the part I'm at (The Blue House), the gameplay has consisted of two things:1. A really basic combat system every now and then, and2. Searching the entire area (btw there is no map in this game) for a key, and then trying to figure out where that key goes (you can't check what the key is called after getting it so if you've forgotten where you need to go, you have no hope of making it back).Another problem I had was with the brightness. For the first hour or two of playing, the lights were so bright that they started hurting my eyes a bit (though it stopped bothering me after a while). And throughout a whole game there have been a bunch of flashing lights, so be warned. (Edit: looking back, I think this might have been caused not by the bright lights, but by the old TV filter that makes the screen slightly blurry. My mistake.)I feel bad giving such an artistically cool game a bad review. If you don't care about tedious gameplay and just look at the art, then you'll think that this is an amazing game, but for me, the gameplay makes Narita Boy a boring mess to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I played this for an hour and a half, and I am not impressed. The first hour is nothing but exposition (of a religious-themed Tron-like nature), fetch-quests for obscurely-named items, and pixel-hunting. (Seriously, there's one door I couldn't figure out it was a door because I couldn't enter it -- but it turned out that the noisy pixels at the bottom of the door were teeny-tiny stairs, and I couldn't enter the door unless I was at the top of the stairs.) And there are multiple "techno-keys" you need to fetch, but there's no inventory system to tell you which keys you have and which keys you need. There's some kind of vaguely-map-like thing in the upper-right corner of the screen, but it's not actually usable as a map. I guess it's kinda usable as "the thing in the upper right looks like 'that', so I must be in the room with the shiny beam."And it's hard to control, too. I used an Xbox controller, and I had to use the left-thumbstick to move, when there's a left-dpad right next to the thumbstick that the game doesn't acknowledge or permit you to use. Thumbsticks are not good when you need precision movement, and the movement in this game is a bit sloppy.Also, the game thinks it's cute to have you write glyphs down on a pen and paper. This game is a love-letter to all things 80s,  and it's quite lovely, but let me assure you, I am not nostalgic for having to take notes.The "neon" them occasionally gets so bright that my wife had to look away. No, she doesn't have photosensitive epilepsy or something, it was just so bright and flashing that she couldn't stand to look at it. The stunning visuals go a little too hard on the "stunning" bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: "Narita Boy" is an exceptionally well crafted action-adventure, with a gorgeous visual design, great pixel-animation and a lush and vibrant retro-aesthetic. The lore is dense, the synth-sound and OST is great and the enemydesign is very good too! The story about an emotional laden IT-designer and his personal history and spirituality that becomes the religious fundament of his very own creation (thus the world you play in) is atmospheric and told very well once you get invested in it. The whole tone of the game draws inspiration from varoius 80 milestones and media like the Commodore64, Tron, Kaiju-films, the Back-to-the-Future movies and even Akira.   Gameplaywise it is solid with classic mechanics and ability-progression and the controls are fluent. It is not that challenging with infinite respawns at various checkpoints. Sadly there are some missable optional collectibles and For a game that is about 6-8 hours long, the price tag may sound steep, but it is wholeheartedly recommendable!(Wait for a sale, if you are unsure!)
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I find it very confusing that Wiro Doloran's review has so many upvotes, as I find it to be vile and delusional. I find it hilarious that he gave his own list of songs he would rather have in it and called himself "A bit of a dreamer" 🤡 . Also funny that people don't read what they are buying, as it does not state that it works with keyboard and mouse.To Studio Koba:This game was amazing. I absolutely loved the dialogue throughout the game as it helped create such a great tone. It made me feel like I was actually apart of something real and exciting, something that I don't get too often as a 30 something year old. The Stallion designs were phenomenal and the music by Salvinsky was literally perfect. Synth Sensei will forever be stuck in my head. The colour pallet mixed with the old TV aesthetic was also a 10/10. I can't wait to see what else your team comes up with!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Just an overall good game. Great side scroller action game with amazing presentation. The presentation alone carry the game in my opinion. The music, the graphics, the lore,etc. You feel transported in this digital world in a instant. The game play is solid throughout the game, carried by a great enemy variety (you get to face new enemies almost till the very end). I do have a couple of problem with the game though:- For some reason, could not go back in the menus, like ever. Good things the default settings were good, otherwise i think the experience would have been ruined- I know that the hole theme of the game is to use the three primary colours, but sometimes, the enemies can melt with the background or the warning indication is barely visible because of the background. Best example is the fish boss in the blue place. Could barely see the warning indication that he was coming.- The character is a bit TOO floaty. Some platforming section can be a bit frustrating even though the jump is quite simple. The bar in the Desert is a great example. Got stuck in there for 5 minutes trying to get the jump right even though on appearances, it seemed simple.So in conclusion, a game that may seem like many other side scroller action game, but the art direction and the vibe of the game makes it shine in the end. Glad there seems to be some sequel under the way.3/5
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I love how every area is filled with doors and every door unlocks a key for another door, so on and so forth until you unlock the one final door that takes you to the next level, great level design! In all seriousness though, the gameplay and exploration are pretty bad but the visuals and music make up for it. The art direction is absolutely stunningIt didn't take me long to beat this game but I still felt like it overstayed its welcome (that's probably due to the bad level design and exploration tho), the combat had a lot of abilities and enemy variety even though you deal with most of them the same way.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Very touching and enjoyable story. Though the tone shift can be jarring, it wasn't jarring in a bad way, more of an interesting way. I'd say the combat could use some refinement/more features, but this game really does have soul, the exact element that most AAA games today are lacking. Where most games feel made by committee, this one really feels made by a passionate small team that have an idea they want to explore. Oh yeah, also the art is sick. Hopefully they'll flesh out more variety and maybe upgrades to combat in future titles, but this one is certainly worth a try. 8-8.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Just bought and played a lot through Narita Boy and made lots of progress! As someone who is a big huge fan 2D Indie retro modern style video games! Narita Boy took it on the whole next level! It's visuals and gameplay and overall aesthetic, feels like if Hollow Knight, Hell Is Other Demons and Oniken Unstoppable Edition all fused together!!! That's what this amazing game delivers!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! The beginning is a little bit strange but after half an hour it start to be really cool! Gameplay is pretty well balanced, you will loose a couple of times but always be able to win before it gets frustrating.2 big deals though: _ Only mono sound when using headphone, really unconfortable... Ok nostalgia bla bla but at least having an option to display it in stereo would be great._the last disk of the secret memory which a lot of player missed, thinking they would find it later. In this game, U can't go back like in other Metroidvania-like...
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game. Thoroughly enjoyed playing through it. Soundtrack is amazing, graphics are gorgeous and I connected very much with the themes of loss in the story. The gameplay is a mix of side scrolling exploration, platforming, and short combat sections. Combat is decently fun. It's simple and could have used some polish, your character is a bit floaty but you get used to it. Play this game for the aesthetic, story, and the vibes. Don't confuse this for a high octane action platformer because it's not.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of personality and strong visual style. Combat is OK - it's a bit floaty and lacks feedback (I played on controller), but there's enough enemy variety and moves to learn to keep it interesting. Story was decent, even if it felt purposefully obtuse at times, which made it hard to follow.Overall, I think this is a pretty tidy experience and worth picking up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Strange game, but kinda cool if you like weird stuff that isnt like anything else.  Lots of technobabble and Japanese culture imagery really gives it its own flavor.  A lot of it is just thwacking enemies and it gets quite carried away with fetching disks here and opening doors there, but you get to learn lots of neat moves.  Really needed more time with the giant robot mecha though, it should have been a part of the boss battle or something.  Also I dont understand the ending, explain more but write less.  A couple of the bosses take way too long, cut down their health a bit so it isnt such a long slog, I hate it when it takes forever.  Not really any replay value once you get all the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita boy is a nostalgia, a time travel back to my childhood.I grew up in the Commodore 64 and Amiga era and for some reason, this game reminded me, what a great era that was.Now time to put sentimentality aside.Its not a metroidvania game, but I enjoyed the linearity and the story telling method, even though it was avarage.The art style and the retro synthwave music is phenomenal, this is why I bought the game in the first place.When the fighting start and the music kicks in, chills running down on my spine and thats what I want from a game!

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine. _childDocuments_.review: On creative level and character design alone this game deserves credit - it's absolutely beautiful and unlike anything I've seen before.The combat is starting to pick up as I progress and is varied enough to keep me interested. It's nothing amazing but it's decent.It's not really (trying to be) a platformer/ metroidvania and this is where I think a sequel could improve the formula - a bit better wayfinding and exploration/collectible elements with more RPG elements. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked it. 8/10This game has some of (if not) the best pixel art i've ever seen in a video game. The animations and the character designs are incredible, so is the music. The story is also pretty good and emotional. The world of Narita Boy is definitely the best part of the game.The combat is simple but flashy and fun. The boss battles are usually pretty good, however there were a few (like 2 or 3) that felt pretty boring imo.The movement controlls feel pretty floaty, however I got used to it after a while. (I played on controller)The writing is also definitely not going to be for everyone, there's a lot of technobabble.One last thing: This game is absolutely not a metroidvania, and I have no idea why some people are calling it one. It's a linear action platformer.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the better sidescrollers so far but like so many in this genre, it is more about patience and repetition that gameplay.Pros: The music and theme of the game is spectacularly good. I love every bit of it. The 80s retro vibe hits true to home for me and the clever digital-fantasy universe demonstrated here is one of the most unique I have seen since Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon.The various attacks and power-ups etc are quite fun to utilize and works great with a gamepad.Cons: Require patience and repetition than anything else.Why am I giving a positive review overall? Because the positives above outweigh the negatives and I recommend it so long as people know what they're getting into.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The game is just awesome: graphics, music, whole aesthetics + atmosphere, controls (via gamepad). The level design should be improved, sometimes you do not know where to go - the backtracking is not fun (a better "quest" indicator or a small map would not go amiss). I suggest enabling the "CRT soft filter" in the settings, it is much better on the eyes. I had a great experience with Narita Boyyy.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The factor that makes indie games special is that they take risks and innovate, because that's the thing that makes them sell. Narita Boy is a confusingly managed Hack n Slash / Platformer game with a focus on the narrative. Its controls don't do much to make them stand out of its generic mainstream counterparts. Sure, it twists a few rules like requiring release of charged attack at the last second to deal the maximum damage - but, even that has been done in AAA titles like Monster Hunter.Now, with nothing to offer new functionally, the game struggles to guide the player across levels because convoluted art. The foreground has a wide wall, yet I am supposed to figure out that I can walk through it without backtracking. The glow indicates physical structures but only a specific type of glow.Then there's the awkward mix of hard-core platforming with hack-n-slash elements, limiting good reception to a very specific audience.What really bothers me are the walls of texts in the dialog boxes often showing up in the game. The story awkwardly switches between use of those, and some expensive diegetic level art. Balancing the art with the narrative by use of a storyboard format would have been much more consistent and easy to follow through.Therefore, after not having much to play with, and being driven away from some personally irritating factors, I do not recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Overall, very solid game, easily 11/10 from me.  More explanatory review below.Initially didn't think much of the game because pixel graphics aren't my thing, but I liked the Tron inspiration, so I tried the demo.  MAN that was a great choice, the demo played smoothly and really gave a good sense of the game.  Soon as I finished the demo, I went and bought the game + soundtrack, because they have some fantastic music.  Gameplay is very smooth, doesn't feel clunky at all.  Puzzles and exploration aren't completely "hand-holdy", but I haven't come across anything too hard yet.  The graphics, you like or you hate.  There are a lot of programming jokes and a few references I've noticed, so there's that to look forward to as well (if that's your thing).  There is kind of a dual storyline in the game; once you play you'll understand, and no that's not a spoiler.

_childDocuments_.review: 12h for 100% AchievementsThis game commits hard to the world that it setup, doing some great things world building the characters, levels and backstory. Visually is sporting that 80s neo retro look, which is tighted a lot with the story and it's simply beautiful throughout. Same goes for the music, it belongs so much to what you see and it elevates or relaxes the moments according to what is happening. Great combination of audio and visual! Combat is fun and responsive. At first it feels a bit plain, but new abilities are unlocked in a study pace and at the end it all comes together very nicely. Enemy variety was an unexpected surprise, since the game throws you many new normal and elite enemies as well as new bosses up to the end of it. Level Design has some small vibes of a metroidvania game, even though it's not one of them. There is a lot of backtracking based on what you found later on, and since there is no world map of any kind, you need to remember what path leads to where. This can be daunting for some, but luckily it was not for me.Loved every moment of Narita Boy, highly suggested!

_childDocuments_.review: is a stylized 2D action-platformer. With striking visuals and a nigh-perfect soundtrack weighed down by repetitive, easy combat and undertuned platforming,  offers players a mixed bag that prospective buyers ought to fully consider before purchasing. If you're looking for a solid platformer or a complex, replayable combat-driven gameplay experience, look elsewhere. If you like the cyberpunk '80s/retro game aesthetic and a weird, sometimes heartfelt story, this should please you.You play as the titular Narita Boy, a lookalike of Commander Video with spindly limbs, who must traverse dystopian cybernetic wastes in order to defeat the machinations of the evil Him. Starting with only the ability to jump, gain a plethora of combat and movement upgrades to fight off a wide variety of evil minions and hunt through multiple worlds, all the while uncovering the secret history of the game's digital setting and its enigmatic Creator. is the textbook definition of "style over substance." This game's aesthetics are top-notch, drowning the player in a spectacle of '80s cyberpunk technicolor landscapes and creatures. The attention paid to environmental detail is substantial, as the game foreshadows multiple themes introduced in the endgame through the level design in earlier areas. The Japanese decor, for instance, both reflects the heritage of a major character and acts as a nod to the frequent source of influence on the cyberpunk style. The soundtrack also deserves a shoutout for how well it achieves tunes that are hypnotic, heart-pounding, or heartwrenching when need be. Finally, the CRT sheen and pixel art style capture the '80s arcade game feel very well - sometimes too well, as the bright flashing lights can be hard on the eyes. An optional filter provided can mitigate this if it's an issue for you.'s gameplay fails to meet the standard set by its looks, though. Though an action-platformer, the action is simple and repetitive and there is barely any platforming. Narita Boy wields a sword, with which he gains upgrades to add an array of attacks to his arsenal. Overall, though, he only receives two basic attack patterns and with the slow rollout of moves throughout the game, the combat devolves into button-mashing. This isn't helped by the game's easy difficulty that makes most enemies serve as mere punching bags. Even bosses will take few attempts to learn their obvious patterns; only the game's final two bosses pose notable challenge (the first of which will hit unsuspecting players like a brick wall, in an example of poor game balancing). The large variety of common enemies do offer enough fodder to make encounters mildly interesting and fun to mindlessly mash through - but "mindless" is the key word here.'s platforming is so thin that it barely merits mention. The player character has floaty controls which make precise platforming harder than need be, which perhaps explains the lack of platforming challenges more complex than "climb ledges" or "jump over pits." For as easy as these tasks are the game can be oddly punitive towards death, as the respawn points are set seemingly randomly: sometimes you'll be sent rooms back, other times on the very platform you died on. Levels are typically linear affairs that give the player very little reason to deviate from the main route, which sans the techno glitz every level is painted with can really be boiled down to a series of fetch quests. The aesthetics were very evidently the driving factor in the creation of , with gameplay a casualty of the former's high demands.This game teeters on the midpoint of whether or not to recommend. The amazing looks and sound clash with the repetitive combat and uninspired gameplay loop. Ultimately, I suppose this is worth recommending so long as prospective buyers are aware that  is more about the glorious design on its exterior and not really a deep action experience worth revisiting. Wait for a sale on this one.  gets a C+.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is obviously very pretty, so I won't bother elaborating on that. What has been holding my attention, is the story. It's quite interesting and has a lot of feels to it. I won't spoil anything you don't learn early on, but the main idea is that there is some programmer who, among other things, developed a video game. Much of this dude's code has become sentient, to the point where there are distinct personages within his programs that interact with each other and view the programmer as a creator deity. There are many religious themes here, and the application of chromatically-saturated, 16 bit nostalgia aesthetic to communicate spiritual iconography is really something to behold. Anyway, something has happened to the programmer in real life, and for the "digital world" inhabited by his sentient code, this is akin to God being put into a coma. Enter the player character, who is some kid who is just obsessed with a game the programmer put together. We see a scene of his mom telling him to go to bed as he's sneaking some late night gaming on an old school MacIntosh-looking computer. The presence of this kid and his interaction with the game is basically the contingency that allows the sentient code to trigger a "hero" protocol to combat its internal issues and somehow revive the "Creator". As you're running around, fighting bad guys in the form of malicious, renegade subroutines, you learn about the programmer himself, his life, and his formative experiences. The tone here is rather melancholy. I haven't finished the game, but I anticipate this being a very robust story.  Some thoughts on the game play itself, which I see other people criticizing: I don't think that the objectives are overly-confusing. They don't spell things out for you completely, but the environment is basically linear, so there's no reason you should be back-tracking that much. There's a couple quirks in the environment, for example, it took me a minute to realize that I have to physically step on these platforms to interact with them, and couldn't just be to one side. But once you figure stuff like that out, it's not too confusing. The character is very "floaty", and the jumping felt unnatural for me, initially. But you can toggle back on the joystick or hit down to make your placing more precise as you're moving around platforms. My biggest complaint is how your sword literally shoots beams of light whenever it moves. This amounts to not being able to see the enemies' animations as you're striking them, which means you have to either constantly be sticking-and-moving, or just anticipating the average amount of time between enemy attacks in order to not get hit. All that said, combat is still fun, and there's a bumping track that starts playing whenever you get locked in to a combat situation. The pacing of the game is interesting. I would directly compare the pacing and how the game balances combat, to exploration, to narrative exposition, with another excellent game, Tails of Iron. The environment is not littered with enemies, but when you do encounter some, you're locked in and have to take some time with them. This makes every fight feel meaningful, and not just wave after wave of low-tier baddies to bop, cause, what else was the game designer supposed to do? A lot of these sparse combat situations are bosses. The bosses are shown as having distinct personalities and presumably, have roles to play in this world you're fighting within. Overall, the game is a great multi-media experience and a great example of the story-telling potential of video games as a medium. I don't know why they're charging $25 for it, though. I got it when it was 50% off, and given that most people seem to beat this game in like 7 hours, $25 seems a bit steep. Still, great game. Play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I just completed this game now. This was a nice journey. There are so many nostalgia-based video games on the market right now. There has never been a better time to get my retro-fix that I crave. In many games the references to our righteously rad past feel as if they are a bit forced or contrived. It is not enough to include nostalgia in a video game or movie. This game does it the right way. Here there are constant resemblences to our 80's consciousness. But more importantly, the game is a very nice metrovania offering. The difficulty is in the right spot for me (somewhere in between medium and hard). The power-ups are offered to the player little by little through the entire game. The final power-up is given at the very end so the game always feels fresh. When I received a new power-up I actually looked forward to the appearance of bad guys (aka Stallions) so that I can try it out like I am taking a new car for a spin. Here we see that the nostalgia is organically woven into the game; it doesn't just provide 80's references, it provides 80's feelings and impressions.The music is a bit other-worldly, and sometimes terrifying. The gameplay is pretty smooth. I know that I am enjoying a game when I learned the different moves so well that one maneuver flows right into the next one. The lore is intriguing enough where I will do some digging on reddit and youtube to enhance my experience of this game.The last line of dialogue in the game may have been a bit trite and banal, but it certainly brought a smile to my face. It is ok to pay full-price for this one. The experience that it provides is well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing 2D side-scroller magic!  Brilliant art design, great music, and a unique storyline set this game apart from much of the rest out there.  The "memories" sections kind of get a little weird, but they make sense within the context of the storyline as you progress through it.  Boss fights could sometimes get extremely challenging, but you really felt like you were progressing with each iteration of a battle as you learned to pick up the enemy fight pattern and tactics, so the battles remained fun throughout without getting frustrating.  The level design was excellently handled, as well, making progression through the game due to loss of direction a rarity, while also making you feel like the world within the game was really flushed out and tangible.  Really hope to see more from this developer in the future!

_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The art and music are right up my street, synth ambience and a psyedellic eighties' vision of inside a computer. The combat system seemed a little functional at first, but now I'm several hours in and have unlocked (and am still unlocking) new moves, it's really fun and varied, with nice evade mechanics and special moves. The bosses are really cool and imaginative too; I particularly liked that rainbow and black hole witch character.The story is in the spirit of Tron and Rez, where you're inside a computer fighting rogue viruses. It's realised with a ton of creative and clever lore, essentially creating an electronic, holographic, computer-terminology-heavy version of a medieval kingdom. However, it's very full-on with lore and exposition, and quite abstract and surreal, with no real tangible NPC characters to latch onto; the boxes of dialogue that appear are routinely quite long with this kind of delivery - in fact, it's all monologue, with no dialogue with the player, nor between NPCs. The objectives themselves also feel quite routine - retrieving keys to progress is pretty much what they all boil down to. The levels are open, allowing you to explore and backtrack until you've moved on from that area, and I think there's some non-linearity in the order you can complete objectives. But it does feel like a linear road.There's also a subplot which follows the life of a fictional real-world man, the "creator" of the digital kingdom system you find yourself within, but who has been incapacitated by the virus. You retrieve his memories as you progress, which play out as nice little gameplay vignettes, with a more human-relatable narrative voice than the characters in the system. It's poignant, and clearly loaded with emotion - though personally it's not really resonated with me, despite me losing a parent in my own life, which the story touches on. Whether it's the stark contrast with the rest of the computer world narrative, or whether I feel it's maybe a little heavy-handed in trying to bring some emotion to the surface, I'm not sure.My PC isn't the fastest (2016 machine, mid-spec), and the game does occasionally drop frames; it also seems to run the machine quite hot for a 2D game, but I'm guessing it's because of all the art that's going on. It's generally smooth though.I've not completed the game yet, and I am enjoying it enough to keep going. From the hub area, it seems I have about as much to go again of the creator's memories to unlock; my total playtime will probably be about ten hours by the end.Overall I applaud the developer and publisher for creating a slick and polished 2D action game.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: First things first: Unless you're in your 40's or older, no, you don't really know Tron. Yes, Legacy is one of my favorite movies, but you really enjoy it, to enjoy it on the level we did well, "you had to be there."While using 8bit aesthetics on purpose is by no means new, this might be the one time I fully endorse it. Narita Boy doesn't just resort to "retro looks" for the clout, , with the proto-sprites moving freely, and with the light FXs shiny and colorful the way old arcades did.The gameplay is simple yet effective, the kid of platform gaming we'd have loved on the Intellivision but only got later on with the NES and SMS. The story is Tron-candid with all the bubblegum naivete proper of the 80s and is not afraid to chew the scenery with flair and gusto, like Jack Nicholson in Burton's Batman.What does take the cake and cinches it all together into a legendary experience, however, is the music. Salvinsky making of each part of the game a moment with high-caliber synthwave worthy of the greats.If you're a middle-aged gamer or a fan of Synthwave, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fantastic if you don't go into it expecting a metroidvania.  Narita Boy is a room based, narrative-driven-puzzle/platformer/adventure-thing with a bunch of combat upgrades and a killer art style and soundtrack.  The combat feels amazing, the story ranges from overwritten to downright fantastic, and the overall worldbuilding is really fantastic.  Most of the negative reviews assumed Narita Boy was a metroidvania.  It isn't and it doesn't really pretend to be either. _childDocuments_.review: This review is a truncated version based on the upper character limit for Steam reviews. For the full version, watch the video.A lot of retro-inspired indie games tend to be set in worlds that attempt to have a quasi-mythic quality about them, a world reduced to ruin or at best set just before the end times. And Narita Boy is once again a game that tries to do the same, at least to a certain extent. However, it’s not entirely set in a fictional world removed from our own. This is where Narita Boy actually employs another common aspect of many indie titles, which is that a lot of them like to set themselves inside a digital space like a simulation or an in-world video game.At the start of the game, after it sets up the inciting incident, the protagonist gets sucked into his computer, where the rest of the adventure ends up taking place. I’m sure that to many creatives in the indie space, incorporating things about computers into their games’ narratives seems like a logical thing to do. However, at this point, I’ve seen enough attempts to incorporate computer terminology and programming concepts into video games to where I honestly feel like it’s just too lazy to do if you’re not trying to use this aspect of your world building in novel ways.Narita Boy unfortunately doesn’t do that. In fact, much of the narrative during gameplay is largely removed from what the story segments of the game are about. That inciting incident I mentioned earlier goes as follows: A schlubby looking dude called Lionel is sitting in front of his Macintosh in the 1980’s. Because of course a game that takes place inside a computer rendered in pixel graphics is set in the 1980’s so it gets to make liberal use of Tron’s neon lightshow color palette. I mean, if they’re ripping off the concept of living computer programs, they might as well go the extra mile and leave no ambiguity where the inspiration came from. While happily coding away, Lionel’s computer somehow gets taken over by a self-aware program called HIM, who somehow causes Lionel to lose his memory, which for some reason causes HIM to get insanely powerful and threatens the digital kingdom. The goal of the narrative is to travel the digital kingdom to restore Lionel’s memories and defeat the Stallions, HIM’s evil computer programs that have invaded the various locales of the digital kingdom before taking on HIM himself. While that’s straightforward enough, there’s unfortunately not a lot to the story taking place inside the digital kingdom. Like I said in the beginning, the game is fond of using flowery exposition that tries to give the world a lived in and quasi-mythic feeling sense of tangibility, but much of the dialogue completely undermines this with the overly techy way its written that never lets you fully immerse yourself in this world or the plight of the programs you encounter. Then again, the story that’s being told here is mostly not about the digital kingdom or its plight, it’s more about Lionel and the things he’s forgotten. While traversing the various locations of the digital kingdom, you can encounter a bunch of totems, each of which unlocks another memory, which are key scenes from Lionel’s life since early childhood. And I have to say, much of what’s in those scenes is really effective. Many of these moments have a gravity that I haven’t seen in a lot of other games. Mostly because it also deals with rather mature concepts like child abandonment, alcoholism, spousal estrangement and divorce as well as parenthood. Unfortunately, pretty much none of that narrative and its themes are represented in the digital kingdom, where the threat of the Stallions is never used as a parable to whatever the memory you’re unlocking next is about. From a gameplay perspective there’s not much to say about Narita Boy. It’s a fairly basic hack and slash with a bit of platforming thrown in for good measure. The main combat mechanic is pretty enjoyable and it’s fun to figure out each enemy’s moveset, strengths and weaknesses when you first encounter them. However, the farther the game progresses, the more you have to fight waves upon waves of the same enemies you’ve already dealt with only in ever greater numbers.Also, I feel like the health system is in need of an overhaul. There are no health pickups in Narita Boy. The only way you can get back health is through a segmented bar that gets filled whenever you strike an enemy. Once a segment is full, which takes quite a few strikes, you can use that segment to get a single health point back. That’d be fine enough, if there were other means of getting back health. Because that bar fills way too slowly to be useful during combat. The problem arises whenever you get out of a fight and have only a few health points left. If you continue and enter another fight, chances are you’re going to run out of health if you don’t manage to dodge everything perfectly. Since the game autosaves after pretty much every fight, the best strategy when you only have a few hitpoints left is to just die on purpose and just respawn with full health. But other than that, there’s not much to say about the combat. The number of abilities expands at a decent pace, and some are even needed to bypass certain roadblocks.In fact, seeing that initially made me feel like I was going to be playing a Metroidvania. I mean, looking at a clearly breakable wall that I don’t have the ability to get through yet almost instantly sends me the signal that I’m supposed to explore something else first and come back once I’ve found the ability that lets me bypass that wall. And honestly, I would’ve liked Narita Boy more if it had actually leaned harder into being the Metroidvania it clearly wanted to be. Unfortunately, there’s not a lot of freedom to go wherever you please, the whole affair is pretty linear from start to finish. That doesn’t mean the game isn’t fond of letting you backtrack across cleared out screens to get to the other end of the map to retrieve a key that opens the door you’re currently trying to get through, not at all.I personally felt that the game didn’t need the cliffhanger it ends on to claim that the story is to be continued. The narrative is already on shaky ground as it is since much of the stuff happening in the digital world didn’t relate to Lionel’s memories, so how would an advertised continuation of the story serve the narrative instead of just having it naturally conclude once you’ve beaten the adventure? Not everything needs to be a franchise these days, it could’ve just given you a final resolution. If you want to continue making games set in this world, just set up a new inciting incident, instead of promising a sequel that you won’t know you’ll even be able to deliver.If it seems like I’m down on Narita Boy after having criticized it so much, let me assure you that I don’t dislike it. My problem with Narita Boy is that I see a lot of unrealized potential. Visually the game is stunning, even though a couple of accessibility options to reduce all the flashing lights would’ve been nice for people with photosensitivity issues. And just like the visuals, the soundtrack is really cool, it has some downright synthwave bangers in there. Overall I did enjoy my time with Narita Boy, both because of the surprisingly effective story of Lionel as well as the pretty enjoyable gameplay. What I wished was that the same amount of polish that went into the visuals and soundtrack could’ve gone into fleshing out the narrative and its themes to incorporate them into the digital kingdom, enable more freeform player exploration to make it the proper Metroidvania it should’ve been and maybe tweak the combat a bit, instead of relying on the many multi-wave battles that happen during later stages that don’t feel substantially different from the ones earlier in the game, only more drawn out due to the increase in the number of enemies they spawn.

_childDocuments_.review: CAUTIOUSLY RECOMMENDED FOR THE RIGHT AUDIENCE - 6 out of 10Narita Boy is clearly a passion project that its development team poured their hearts and souls into making. I enjoyed it, am grateful for the opportunity to have played it, and am excited to see what work this development team does in the future. I might even advocate buying the game just to support them. Nevertheless, from a review standpoint, I have to be honest... this game has some rough edges. When it shines, it shines brightly, with plenty of fun moments, amazing art, a nostalgic soundtrack, and an excellent sense of style. However, its design-shortcomings make it a difficult ride to get through. If a player can push through regular moments of frustration on the journey, the game rewards the player with an explosive and fun ending, which somewhat makes up for many moments of annoyance experienced along the way.Despite what may initially look like a Metroidvania, Narita Boy is actually an action platformer with exploration elements. As an action platformer, the main things I was looking for to review this game were (1) great action and (2) great platforming. Therefore, you might be surprised to learn that this game has (1) long stretches with no action and (2) floaty/clunky movement across very simple map layouts. There are certainly vertical stretches in the game that demand careful jumping and dashing, but these moments tend to be more annoying than fun. There also isn't much in the way of cool movement abilities in the game. It feels very basic. Thankfully, when it does happen, combat feels fun and stylish. If the amount of effort that went into making combat feel interesting went into the platforming elements of the game, the overall package would be a lot stronger.Narita Boy has occasional moments of true greatness. I especially loved the last hour of the game, in which the soundtrack blares epically and the combat comes nonstop with one satisfying encounter after another. Boss fights throughout the game are also largely a hit, and they were my favorite part of the experience. The boss fights complement another huge strength of the game: the visual design. Enemies and areas are filled with animations and cool effects, which makes the world feel alive. I felt like I had been transported into a new world. That was a big achievement.However, it was somewhat hard to appreciate these strengths when I was constantly being annoyed by things like:1) getting consistently lost without access to a map or a clear indication of where to go next (searching for floppy disk keys that could go in one of many identical key slots throughout each area).2) having to use a pen and paper to write down symbols for teleporters through the game.3) constantly missing necessary items, platforms, and doors because they blended into the background.4) lacking a reliable way to heal, meaning that health was always low.5) trying to understand an incredibly bizarre story with weird religious overtones.If you're looking for a good dose of nostalgia and are willing to overlook clunky controls and a somewhat tedious level design, you'll probably be able to enjoy Narita Boy like I did. Hopefully, the developers can learn from this project and make something truly stellar in their next attempt! I'd score Narita Boy with a 6 out of 10, which isn't quite strong enough to make me want to universally recommend it to everyone, but I'm sure it could be a great experience for the right audience.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh wow, where to begin...I'm writing this review right after finishing the gameI loved this game, but I also recognize it has warts. To really get the most of it, you want to set aside enough time that you want to really engage with it. The sets are gorgeous, there's a lot going on in the backgrounds throughout the game. The narrative of the game also really resonated with me. It felt meta without forcing itself, and without getting into spoilers it's all about the life of a programmer in an era where to make video games you had to also make computers. There were parts where I was questioning the reliability of the narrator, and that uncertainty was handled masterfully by the writers.As far as gameplay goes, it's pretty standard action-platformer fare. You get your light attack combo, your heavy attack, a couple of spells, and genre staples like dodging and ground pounding. Mechanically, it's not very innovative, but animations are slick, and before an enemy attacks you there will be both an animation and audio cue. Sometimes those cues are subtle, and the boss of the blue level made me want to pull my hair out before I realized what those prompts were.There is one innovation to the combat system, and that is that midway through the game you gain the ability to type-match enemies. Basically, there's a system where you can give yourself a coloured aspect, and certain enemies may have them too. If you match colours with an enemy, you'll deal but also receive massively increased damage. This system kind of fell flat for me: it doesn't come up as often as it should, and you can almost always just delete enemies before they hurt you. There are three types too, so a more interesting system might have been a combat triangle instead of simply matching colours.If there's one other criticism I have for the game, it's the amount of backtracking involved. It's a problem that you tend to see, particularly in a metroidvania, and some might say that it adds to the experience. But the combination of not having any real fast-travel or map along with getting your hints from NPCs throughout the map can cause you to make some unnecessary trips. There is a system where you can have objectives displayed for you, but these often are vague to the point of uselessness. For example, you might hear from someone that you have to go to a place and do a thing to get a key, but then the objective is simply "find the key"All in all, the pros outweigh the cons for me. It really can't be understated how good the visuals of the game and story are. The game has some challenge without being overly difficult, and honestly it just FEELS great. It's a much deeper dive into the fantasy of video games than I expected going in,  and I'm so grateful for it and glad I gave it the time to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a gem!The art style was spot on, being both very modern while keeping that 1980s Tron vibe.The accompanying synthwave soundtrack was brilliant and catchy.The gameplay was perfectly tuned, with an approachable moderate difficulty without any real frustrating moments, yet putting a very mild challenge to casual gamers.And the story was there, very present but not imposing itself into a novel.My only criticism is that most fights didn't take full advantage of the combat mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game with an interesting story and visuals that remind me of games like Out of This World and Flashback. It gives me vibes of Tron meets Star Wars in a way. The platforming is decent and the fighting mechanics are fun, but take a little getting used to. The game itself is difficult, but not too difficult. My only complaint is that the ending should have explained more and been more self contained. It sets up for a sequel, but we never know when or if sequels will come these days. I would welcome a sequel, honestly. Especially if it goes in the direction I think it is going. Very well done!

_childDocuments_.review: The drop-dead gorgeous pixel art and sick synthwave sound track were not enough to overcome the frustratingly imprecise controls, incomprehensible dialog, and uninspired mechanical design. On the controls front, I felt that Narita Boy moved poorly, with not a clear sense of inertia, which made it difficult to space jumps correctly and time movements and attacks in combat. For dialog, while I respected the commitment to the hacker aesthetic it leaned too heavily on its own jargon to be truly understandable. Where the game falls the most flat, however, is really in the mechanical design itself. For example, you gain an ability to heal yourself, which is charged by attacking enemies, yet the amount it heals does not justify the time and energy put in to it. Contrast this with a game like Hollow Knight, where it takes comparatively few hits to generate resources for healing, but you must contend with finding the space to actually heal. Add on top that there doesn't seem to be an obvious way to heal to full when outside of combat situations (say at a save point or similar). Similarly, death seems to have little meaning in this game. You just start from the nearest point none the worse for the wear. Despite this, the pixel art is really quite beautiful, and the team behind the game has definitely captured that 80s aesthetic. So, if you're looking for a game that is dripping with 80s hacker vibes and willing to play through a mediocre hack and slash platformer, by all means give it a shot. Overall though, I can't see why you would *play* this. It's all style, and very little substance.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics are amazing, world is incredibly detailed, good controls, good fighting moves, fantastic music, there's a lot to love about this game.It drops the ball with gameplay outside of the fights though, you're just going between doors and keys.  I would have like to have seen more metroidvania aspects.  If you loved Hollow Knight, you'll like this, but it doesn't measure up.  Haven't finished it yet, at around 8 hours with 6 achievements left, probably 2-4 hours of gameplay left.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed it - feels like a very heartfelt creation from a small dev team and that's my jam. The art direction, pixel visuals, music and (surprisingly affecting) memory scenes steal the show. It's a short (just 5 hrs) but great little experience and really did get to me. It's not a perfect game, it almost feels like it could of done with smoothing over and re-examining the structure between homage of a retro video game and being one. It's way too wordy upfront and could of done with more show less tell, a tighter script etc. The combat actually gets really fun but I think it takes a while to get there and just fighting hordes of them in closed off one screen arenas isn't as much fun as having them dotted throughout an actual level. It would of been great to spend longer in the digital kingdom exploring it's wildernesses complete with more branching paths and platforming.  Would of helped making the game longer between towns + created a more well rounded experience. Having said that I was constantly surprised by the creativity displayed and atmosphere - very glad I played it and will return to see what I missed, seems like there might be another ending>? Looking forward to a sequel.
