_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best gaming experiences I've had in many years.You are led along the story the creator's (creator of the game in the game?) life through the rediscovery of memories stolen by run away malicious code in the game of which you're the hero.-The story line and the way it was delivered has good pace and it never left me feeling stuck or as if I was not progressing and losing interest.The combat animations have a real sense of motion and power though I found myself using perhaps half of my arsenal in most trivial combat as it was all that seemed needed which was slightly disappointing.   The visuals and soundtrack in Narita Boy are some of the the most enjoyable I've seen and heard. The music changes in each area and whether you're in combat or not adding to a sense of changing pace in game play which synced with each area really well. I did experience one music bug where several songs where being played over each other though it only seemed to be in one level for some reason.The art style reminds me a lot of "Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP" though with a Digital world theme, a fantastic pixel art style that really fits well in this game as the generally square and blocky characters look like PC hardware from the 80's.Generally the level designs were basic and unfortunately sometimes a little too "back tracky" for the type of platformer that it seems to want to be. The symbols based level mechanics where fun though kind of shallow and felt like they were not always laid out through the levels very well. The symbols are often the key to progress to the next area though they're not awarded for overcoming a boss or puzzle but merely found by observing the world or pressing a button on the wall, in this way they can be easily missed. I feel like there were several ideas for game play mechanics that all had potential to bring a lot more depth and interaction to the game though the developers have not connected them in a way that all makes them feel more than proof of concepts.All that being saidThis is one of the few games I have sat down with and finished in a long time.A solid game play experience with an emotional story that I'll remember for some time I'm sure. The minor disappointments I had were vastly overshadowed by the quality of the visual and auditory feast of the overall product.Narita Boy.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: A big oh well. Disappointing conclusion that felt that the developers honestly didn't know how to end the story they had started, ran out of time and needed to meet a deadline, or simply are grasping at more revenue for a possible sequel to wrap it all up. Despite the only draw being the art, animation, and music, at the Blue zone on the level design seemed rushed and uninspired. The jump mechanic is loose and created a disconnect unnecessary for a game. Combat happens in forced segments that near the end just begin to become a slog more than fun. About a third in the story becomes rather predictable.Also, the whole Japanese thing comes off as disingenuous and more at adding "coolness" or an exotic touch more than anything else. A woman in the 50's would not be wearing a kimono.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly ENJOYED and LOVE this game. The environment, the music, the sounds and the small gimmicks that happened through out the game made it really fun. It reminds me of the old games I use to play back when I was younger. Felt the ending a bit. Aside from that I really didn't have issues with the game aside from not being able to find certain key things for progressing. Not being able to go back and do things I missed. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to thumb this up, but as a game I have mixed feelings about this one. On one hand the music, art style, and setting are fantastic and I absolutely loved these. On the other is gameplay, which was really quite weak. Character movement is floaty and doesn't feel great, visuals get in the way of combat all the time, making it really hard tell sometimes what is even happening. Enemy design was kinda meh, most were just ok and some were just not fun to fight, often utilizing invincibility and timed windows to attack, pigeon-holding you to cheesy strategies. The game is also very challenging towards the end. I'm not surprised to see the achievement % for the last couple levels is very very low. Overall the gameplay was just not very good.Story was engaging, but involved a bit too much reading, even just muffled techno voices would have made this a bit more bearable, but it was just so hard to care sometimes when you are piled with paragraphs of text.The redeeming factor of this game is however the art style and music, which really are fantastic. If you do jump in, go in expecting to just jam to some music and enjoy some art, while putting up with some mediocre gameplay along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most visually stunning action-adventure games I've played in years.  The graphics and audio design just ooze style, and while most games can't get by on style alone, this one also delivers a perfectly serviceable combat system, scores of unique bosses, and a genuinely interesting and heartfelt story to keep you engaged.This games greatest sin is its dense and boring intro.  You're thrown into a confusing world you know nothing about and are immediately hit over the head with dozens of dialogue boxes filled with techno-babble.  The gameplay starts out extremely basic, and the combat is frequently interrupted so that NPCs can just bombard you with gibberish you can't follow and won't care about (at least not initially).  The beginning section also has one of the more open and confusing layouts, which can be offputting.  The game gets a bit more linear though as you progress.  Pros:+Incredible visuals.  The screenshots don't lie.+Solid audio design/ music.+A dozen+ bosses to vanquish.  While they mostly have simplistic patterns, they're all visually distinct and you'll need different strategies to beat them.+A well-conceptualized, surreal world that you'll grow to love with time.  + Nothing in this game feels recycled or copy-and-pasted.  All areas have unique layouts and normally have a couple really cool little side events that help spice up the gameplay.   + A story-line and lore that keep getting better as the game goes on.  There are a few really interesting plot developments towards the very end.Cons:- Sequence-based puzzles that force the player to backtrack to learn how to break them.  Don't feel bad about checking a guide if you don't want to waste your time.- Massive exposition dumps towards the start of the game with dense lore and indecipherable terminology that will initially mean nothing to you.     - A slow intro sequence.  If the first hour doesn't hook you, you're not alone.  Persevere!  It gets better. - The price may seem a bit steep for an indie you can beat in 8 hours or less.  So yeah . . . I recommend you give this game a try if you're even the least bit interested.  It's well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting game and a great example of how you don't always need realistic graphics to make a game look amazing. The story is so heartwarming and the gameplay is really good I know for sure that we need more video games like this one. I loved the scenery the in game places are so captivating, The abilities you unlock are so cool, some of the boss battles are really memorable like "Lord VHS, Ghost and The Glove", The 80's vibe and the music really adds to the charm of Narita Boy. All I have to say is may the Trichroma be with you !!!

_childDocuments_.review: First of all I have to say I love the setting of the game. It is very interesting and reminds me a lot of dreamlike worlds. I enjoy that there is a fairly in depth story and one that is highly relateable in that when we experience a close death we as humans either become constructive and destructive. The music matches the setting extremely well with a techno feel but really representing early 80s like music. Whether you are in the forest, by the sea, in the desert or in the concrete jungle.The combat is pretty descent if you like the style they went with. They went with a semi floaty combat to make it feel a little more like the physical world. I really enjoyed the horseback riding which was done well. The horse felt like it had real weight to it and it took time to accelerate and stop. You unlock many of your techniques along the way like many others. A lot of the skills are things meant to push you forward like shoulder bash breaks certain walls. Up+attack gets to things above your regular jump, floppy disc lets you ride over water and more.I did try to find some bugs while playing and I didn't find much. The only annoying  ones I found were with the floppy disc in that you can wipe out when jumping on waters edge. Even though your whole board is in you wipe out, respawn where you wiped out and then proceed to drown.It is a game that feels like real effort and heart was put in or that is at least how see it.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game a thumbs up due to the outstanding visual presentation. You really feel that the developers were passionate about their project and something beautiful came out of it. Unfortunately it is not much fun gameplay wise. I was instantly addicted to other 2d pixel art games like Axiom Verge, The Messenger, Blasphemous etc., but this one just doesn't work for me. Movement and jumping is clunky, fighting looks good, but feels unsatisfying and interaction with switches, NPCs and other stuff just interrupts your flow. Also the Tron-like story in a pseudo religious cyberspace feels a bit forced and over the top. I was not interested in really diving into it. Great piece of art, but not a great game - nevertheless I'm not refunding, because I think it is important that games like this exist.

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Booooy is just an amazing thing to look at. The creativity and quality of the world is amazing. Gameplay is fun in general with lots of power ups and abilities to learn and get you through the game. There is a lot of text in the game, its ok at the start and at the end of it but latter half of the second act it gets ridiculous how much you have to real about the things you are doing. It does not need the amount of expository narrative that it has, the art in the game help the world building so much, and the objectives are not hard to remember that its really hurts the game having to read so much that you can infer or already know. There are a lot of areas that don't tell you anything, you just see a picture or people doing something and leaves it to you imagination to create the story of this world and that is when it excels.The sound design and music are amazing, period. Gameplay is really fun, comprising of "arenas" where enemies spawn and you have to defeat them for the most part. _childDocuments_.review: All in all a very enjoyable ride.The biggest achievement here is a stellar presentation in graphics and the very inventive setting. But the NPCs talk a lot, without saying much, never informative and seldomly funny.The level design is also rather uneven, at first appearing to be a metroidvania, quickly turning into a very linear game, that does not allow you to go back in order to search for the bonus content you missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if TRON were a Sword-and-Sorcery tale that played like a 2D Brawler with a smattering of well implemented Souls-like mechanics all set to some truly divine synth tunes, and you will have an idea of what Narita Boy appears to be on the surface.Now imagine that just beneath the above mentioned experience's beautifully pixelated exterior dwells an unexpectedly deep and touching storyline which contrasts majestically with the nail biting intensity of the game's combat.And that combat is glorious.A sort of Arena Brawler at it heart, combat encounters typically lock the camera in place as the player battles waves of increasingly complex of enemies in order to progress.  Combat encounters are broken up by world exploration, moments of verbal/visual story telling, and the occasional platforming or puzzle section.Fights are fast paced, reflex heavy, and brutal.  Controls are tight and responsive, and you pick up new moves along the way which are just as useful in battle as they are between battles.Player Death holds little sway In Narita Boy as each defeat merely sends you back the the beginning of the encounter or your most recent checkpoint; which is good, as it minimizes frustration and keeps the gameplay experience flowing smoothly.  And nowhere is this more welcome than during the game's unforgettably intense Boss Fights, all of whom deserve their own seat in the great Soulsborne Boss Fight Hall of Fame.And then there's music.  The music simply cannot be praised enough.  Salvinsky's synth tones are nothing short of 'enrapturing' (I swear that's a real word).  Heart-pounding, tear-jerking, awe-inspiring.  Words alone cannot do these divine notes justice.  They MAKE the experience.  Salvinsky's music lifts your soul from mundanity, whisks you away to far off world of wonder hidden just behind the pixels in your monitor and invites you to bask in it's grandeur, weep for it's sorrows, and steel yourself before it's terrors.If nothing else, get the soundtrack.  At two and a half hours long you are getting way more than your money's worth.Anyway...If I haven't convinced you of this game's sheer awesomeness by now then there is probably no helping you.  But if you're a fan of epic journeys, gorgeous pixel graphics, retro eighties futurism, mind blowing music, heart pounding boss fights, and a truly touching story that is way definitely better than it needs to be, then put your money 'Narita Boy'.May the Trichroma be with you.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: The game is super fun! I really enjoy the premise, the aesthetic is interesting and the gameplay is smooth, challenging, and rewarding when you play well. Hopefully the developer will add a photosensitive mode in the future that reduces the flashing while maintaining the color scheme and art style (maybe reducing the frequency?). Still, from what I did play of the game - I did enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Tldr; Nostalgic pixels, good gameThe Digital Kingdom is under attack. The Trichroma is at risk of being consumed by HIM. Code ripped asunder, trampled underfoot by Stallions. Only the One can help the Creator regain his memories. Only you. Only... Narita Boy.Journey back to the 80s as you dive into this gorgeous lore filled world as Narita Boy, the hero destined to save the Digital Kingdom. The story is filled with detail, allowing you to dive fully into the Digital Kingdom like the hero you are. I thoroughly enjoyed the interactions I had throughout the game with various NPCs. Engaging and often humorous, there was always something to learn about the world and its inhabitants. The game itself is what I would call an action-adventure sidescroller. It consists of some puzzles, some platforming but I felt the games true focus is on telling the story of Narita Boy and the Digital Kingdom. There is a lot of fun combat with a plethora of abilities; the game does a great job of introducing these so the combat is constantly evolving.Where I thoroughly enjoyed the gameplay, I was blown away by the games visuals. Narita Boy uses traditional 2d animation; Every asset, every background, every effect done frame by frame. The ambient lighting, the character design - especially the bosses, I absolutely loved. This game was built on pixels and nostalgia. Every time you unlock a new ability, the writing slams onto the screen on a floppy disk, uploading to your digital psyche. Over and over again I found myself blown away by the Digital Kingdom. The music is a wonderful accompaniment to the game, changing with the various stages and amping you up in times of battle. I haven't heard much else by Salvinsky but will definitely be keeping an eye out for this talented artist.Studio Koba made something special with Narita Boy, capturing the nostalgic feel of games of old with a polished, modern play style. I thoroughly enjoyed being absorbed into the Digital Kingdom and becoming... NARITA BOY!!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Good: Atmosphere, music, cohesive aesthetic, world building and intriguing story. _childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this fully expecting Narita boy to be a simple, fun retro 2D platformer riding the ever-popular wave of faux 80s nostalgia – what I got was one of the most incredible looking and sounding games I can remember, with a poignant and heart-wrenchingly human story flowing through its old pop culture references and homages to classic video games. While from a gameplay perspective it does leave a bit to be desired in some places, Narita Boy is just balls to the walls awesome from the get go and constantly had me with the hugest smile on my face.  The games weird visual style of melding outdated technology with eastern mysticism is some of the best art direction I can recall in a 2d game, with incredible enemy and boss designs, wonderful use of color and all-round stellar work. While not terribly deep, the games combat is really fun, giving you a small but insanely cool arsenal to play with, and by Odin’s beard this might be the best game soundtrack of all 2021.  It’s not terribly difficult, but the strong native and constant eye candy made sure that this was never an issue for me.Also, there's the Hex, which might be the greatest moment in video games since the proto-metal bit near the end of Alen WakeThere are minor gripes though.  The jumping is a bit too floaty for my tastes, and at times the screen it too cluttered, with enemies and their attacks melding into background and foreground objects. There’s also that horse level, and I did feel that at about 7 hours the run time was quite short.I can also see some players being a bit annoyed that the game is not more difficult, but for me this wasn’t an issue as it was more the feeling of being on a grand adventure, like some long lost Goonies/ET/Never ending Story/ Transformers type movie, where by exploring the world, taking in the sites, and learning more about the very heavy “real world” story behind the game was my main motivation for playing. Again, I was fully expecting this to be a fun 80s nostalgia romp, but Narita boy is so much more.  It might not top Hyper Light Drifter as my favourite indie game of the last few years, but this is up there with it.  Can’t wait too see what happens in the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy was a fun and somewhat challenging retro style 2D action game. A nice little story of love and loss. The visuals were awesome in this game with great looking scenery, cool looking enemies, and some flashy combat. Not sure if I'll go back for them as they were missable and I'd have to restart the game.I highly recommend the game as I enjoyed it all but I honestly would way for a $10 sale on it. I feel $15 is more reasonable for the game but I have no regrets buying it.

Gameplay takes a back seat in favour of immersion and exploration, and I think labelling it as a Metroidvania is a bit of a stretch. What it lacks in combat and platforming is made up  for in pure audiovisual style, as I spent most of my time taking in vistas and spamming screenshot captures. An emotional story about loss and the management of oneself compound Narita Boy's sense of sublimity. Please play this!

_childDocuments_.review: The story and the music. Now I’m not going to spoil the entire story here, but I can say that I was invested in it. While the game takes itself seriously, it does have some funny moments in it. Learning about the creator of the Narita One’s past were the most interesting bits of the game for me.The bosses, for the most part, were a bit basic. Most of the bosses in the game follow the formula of the first boss: Dodge big attack then attack them in the opening. Bosses in most video games can be boiled down to that, so I want to elaborate a bit. In the game you obtain new moves a lot of them in fact, but you only utilize one of them for its high jump. The only boss that I can exclude from this is Lord VHS, the first boss and The Glove because that boss makes you dodge multiple things. There is just a little bit more to that boss than the others, for example Dragon Bot. The fight looks cool, but all you do is dodge a couple of attacks then attack it. This boss and the others are just too simple. I think the devs could have taken advantage of the skill set the Main Character gets and made more unique, interesting bosses with that in mind.Narita Boy was a wonderful experience and everyone should buy it!Full Video:

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy was a game that I didn't get a chance to back when the Kickstarter was active, but I discovered it sometime after and I've been following ever since. This game almost feels like it was made for me specifically as the one person who is a fan of both Tron movies as the game feels like an attempt to improve upon the Tron formula in addition to being a really fun game in its own right. The story is fascinating and full of a shockingly high amount of worldbuilding, the graphics are beautiful with neon mechanical landscapes detailed in wonderful pixel art that could be mistaken for straight up digital paintings in some places, and there's a smooth synthwave score that's thick and atmospheric during exploration and rockin' during combat.Functionally the game is a hack-n-slash beater with some light exploration and platforming, and it is fun for the most part. You're constantly getting new upgrades and moves throughout the game, there are enemies being introduced right up to before the final chapter, and there are plenty of setpiece moments like mech battles to break up the pace. The only real problems I had were encounter design and checkpointing. To be blunt, you should just be automatically healed between encounters because if you're on low health, you're likely going to pointlessly die at the start of the next fight. And while it wasn't a problem for most of the game, there were a couple of really bad checkpoints like the Ancient Ones in the Blue Beam Realm. I went like 5 screens over and it brought me back there for whatever reason; I'm honestly baffled why the game doesn't just checkpoint you at the start of every screen.Other than those few minor issues, Narita Boy was a wonderful time to play and you'll probably have a blast playing this one if you're any kind of fan of action platformers or like the aesthetic of Tron.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Style over substance isn't everything, but the visual and audio aspects of this game make up for any flaws it has in my opinion. I urge anyone who is considering getting this game to just do it! It's well worth the asking price and even better if you can get it on sale. The game is fun and challenging without being too difficult. The story is delivered to you through bite sized chunks as you unlock the creator's memories, which I thought was a clever way of keeping you invested. I know people have complained about the controls, but I got used to them pretty quickly and learning new skills as the game progresses made the gameplay more enjoyable. As a retro gamer I want this gem to get the love it deserves and the ending leaves it open to a possible sequel which I would love to see come to fruition.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Congratulations on releasing this masterpiece, Studio Koba! Just finished it and absolutely loved everything. It's just the right amount of challenge - hard enough to make it feel awesome when you play, but not too hard to make you want to give up (I'm looking at you, Hyper Light Drifter). The artwork is absolutely gorgeous throughout the game. Music is another strong suit of this game - I find myself listening to the soundtrack even when I'm not playing. Gameplay is also fluid and good. You gradually unlock various powers throughout the game. There are a very wide variety of creatures in the game, each with their own weaknesses and requiring a different strategy to beat. Overall, I highly recommend this game - 10/10!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Play it for the cool art and the soundtrack. The gameplay is very sloppy (specifically with regards to input) and not very challenging. The story completely falls apart.Also this game commits the cardinal video game sin of not letting you go back to certain areas to finish things up. Worse than most because it doesn't wait until the end of the game to lock you out, it does it as soon as you leave. Completionists beware. Pick it up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Narita Boy is f*cking awesome and there is a simple reason for it.The sheer amount of IMAGINATION (in capitals) on display is just insane. The world, details and music of the Digital Kingdom tell volumes of the creativity of the dev team. I have been interested in the game since its Kickstarter back in 2017 and it is everything I had hoped for. It is nothing less than magical and it immediately transports my 32-year-old mind into a simpler time when I was drawn to beautifully crafted games like Another World or Heart of Darkness.It's not a Metroidvania but rather a side-scrolling puzzle and action game. The progression is linear but I didn't mind at all: in fact, the pacing is great. The variety of enemies and abilities are huge and the game keeps adding new elements right until the endgame. When I booted up Narita Boy, it simply sucked me in and didn't let me go before I finished the final boss. I also didn't expect to be moved by its story.The controls can be a bit janky at times and I feel that compared to the 2017 final trailer, some scenes could have been polished a bit more. Nevertheless, these are just some small nitpicks in an otherwise great package.There is simply nothing else like Narita Boy out there. It's a wonderful, magical experience and I'm looking forward to more! So put on your headphones, turn up the volume and become NARITA BOOOOOY!
_childDocuments_.name: Narita Boy

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game.  The floaty platforming takes some getting used to, and only being able to high jump from the ground can get pretty frustrating, but the visuals and music are completely out of this world and more than make up for the average platforming.  The combat has enough variation with the different abilities that it is consistently interesting and fun, although each boss tends to have only one or two abilities that can actually consistently damage it, which can get pretty tedious on the harder ones.  Overall though I highly recommend this game, and I'll be sure to go for 100% on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Thus far I'm really enjoying this game. It's one I've been looking forward to for a very long time and I'm pretty excited to finally step into this world. The art is wonderful, the character design is especially cool. I want to cosplay everything! The soundtrack is really amazing, and I may end up purchasing it at a later date to have in my own collection.The combat isn't super difficult, though for someone who is less experienced playing this type of game I've found it to be a good balance, and just tricky enough in the right places. My biggest downfall has been mixing up the buttons. It may be my controller, but I've noticed I sometimes dodge the wrong way even when the joystick is pushed in the direction intended.I also realised I had missed some of the floppy pieces a bit too late and ended up restarting since you don't appear able to backtrack, but taking a bit of extra time to explore the first go around and following my instincts instead of ignoring them would have solved that problem. All in all I'm really enjoying my playthrough. I like the story so far, especially the memory segments and can't wait to see where it goes from here. Thanks for a great game!

_childDocuments_.review: Backed this on kickstarter on a total whim. Had no expectations really, just thought it looked like a cool concept. Studio have been pretty good about keeping the fans updated, and i think they have made pretty darn good progress against thier targets. Have only played the first level so far, but i am very impressed by how close it is to the pitch. The retro theme running through it is nostalgic and fun, tongue in cheek with nods to the genre. The music is great with its roots in 8bit soundtracks but with modern interpretation. The animation is a lot more polished than i thought it would be, feels really satisfying, and the combat is good fun. I feel like i am engaged in the story and i am exploring without too much intervention, and backtracking actually doesnt feel bad because i am being rewarded for remembering places, which i dont tend to in the aaa questfests where you get a map, minimap, hud icons and a glowing path for the real dumb. I am dying quite a lot but without huge penalty so i feel challenged enough and i dont feel like im being swaddled and fed warm milk. So far so good narita BOOOY.

name: Rogue Lords
detailed_description: The first roguelike in which you play as the devil, which means you can change some of the game's rules to your advantage! Run after run, manage your team of famous evil geniuses as they encounter unforeseen events and turn-based combat. Unlock new skills, create powerful synergies and use your powers to turn the situation in your favour at critical moments. Only by collecting ancient artefacts can you finally take your revenge on the Demon Hunters. A DARK TALE Weakened from defeat to the forces of good, you fled the world and sought refuge in hell to survive. Decades later, you have returned with your most faithful Disciples to exact revenge on those wretched Demon Hunters. But the world has changed in your absence. Your enemies have become all-powerful, and a new religion – the Sanctua Lumen – has become very influential. It mercilessly hunts down all those who serve you. To reinstate your hold over the world of humans, you must first regain the strength you previously wielded by taking possession of artefacts with legendary power. CONTROL FAMOUS EVIL GENIUSES Create your team of 3 Disciples from Dracula, the Headless Horsemen, Bloody Mary, the White Lady, Lilith, Hecate, Baron Samedi, and Frankenstein and his Creature. Each Disciple has their own unique story, abilities and gameplay: combine their skills to create devastating synergies, and deal with the mortals that dare stand in your way. Collect souls and exchange them for new skills, upgrades and powerful relics that can strengthen your Disciples. THE DEVIL PLAYS BY HIS OWN RULES Sacrifice some of your health to control the game interface: nothing will stop you – and certainly not the rules imposed on mortals. Manipulate the health bars of your Disciples and enemies, optimise status effects to suit your fight tactics, open portals on the map, tip the odds in your favour during events… there are many occasions to use your diabolical powers throughout your run. TAKE BACK YOUR RIGHTFUL PLACE Increase the terror gauge by winning fights and completing interactive events to earn valuable bonuses for your Disciples. Complete each event to your liking to reduce the influence of the Sanctua Lumen, give mortals good reason to fear you, and decide the fate of traitors who have allied themselves with your enemies. Take revenge on the Demon Hunters in epic turn-based fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Buying this game was the closest I ever came to a drive-through marriage in Vegas. Love at first sight, checked all my boxes, thought it would become my favorite game ever - but that didn't happen. I'm not at a point yet where I'd want a divorce though. If at least some of the many issues get addressed, there's still a chance for a happily ever after here.The positives:- Theme is fantastic. The artwork is great; characters, overworld, animations, cutscenes - everything looks great. Music is nothing to write about home about, but it's not annoying either and fits the vibe well.- Innovative ideas. The Cheat mechanic is fun, abilities and status effects are interesting. I love the 'social activities' that give characters traits and improve their stats (if successful). The Terror effects and drawbacks are also a good and interesting part of the gameplay.The negative, and I already feel bad that it's going to be a much longer list:- Runs take ages. Fights can take ages. Ultimately, there's not enough enemy variety to justify it. If every book had distinctive enemies, sure, but as it is, I'm fighting the same mobs over and over again.- The overworld, while pretty and atmospheric, is a clumsy mess. Getting stuck on random trees or houses is no fun. There's no point in walking around. A StS-style map would spare the player much time and frustration.- Too much randomness. RNG is brutal. Shops do not have refresh. If you're not offered the right skills, there are enemies you simply won't defeat. Enemy behavior is unpredictable - sometimes you just get team wiped because a mob decides to dish out unpreventable AoE attacks with more damage than you could possibly block or heal back on turn 1. Getting the 'good' artifacts and skills makes or breaks the run - as it is, there is more or less just one viable way to play, and everything that doesn't contribute to it is worthless. The balance is just completely off. Experimenting with new skills or teams is an excercise in frustration, not fun as it should be.- But also not enough randomness - specifically when starting a run. Slay the Spire offers you a choice of 3 advantages if you made it at least to the boss. Monster Train gives you an artifact choice and random starter cards from your clans. There's nothing like this in Rogue Lords. You start with the same skills every time, you don't get an artifact. You have nothing to lean into or build around. That makes the game feel very repetitive early on - especially because some characters are locked behind later books and your team choices are limited.- SO. MUCH. CLICKING. Refilling the Devil power (aka 'Pyre Health') really shouldn't take 5 clicks. Every run, I have to click through the same screens - chapter story nodes that always tell the same story, entering the store, refilling health/removing bad traits, it's all so insanely clicky.- Social Activities are a fun part of building characters, but they aren't very transparent. In many events, I get several choices, but no indication what they do. Am I getting souls from this? Does it trigger a terror effect? Does it give me a trait or an ability? I don't know! Could be anything!I really hope some of these things will be addressed in patches, and if that happens, I'll gladly change my review. In its current state, I just can't recommend the game - although I wish I could.

_childDocuments_.review: Not recommended in current state. Too much RNG that can cost you whole round. The whole pace of the game is too slow, it just doesn't work with a roguelike because it discourages replay. It's slow because they make you run between nodes for no reason. You just walk from A to B, why? To torture us and waste our time? Seriously, the game have so much potential, the idea of being devil and having the ability to cheat but in a limited scope is amazing, character models and animation are pretty. The overhauls style of the game is pleasant. Game play loop is pleasant enough if not for the RNG that can cost you round for no reason and few other caveats it would be gold. Plenty of bugs:1. infinite loading screen that requires to delete GameStatistics.sav2. often UI breaks during game, unable use demon cheat or other buttons because they are not there, have to relaunch the whole game.3. random save corruption4. random skills sometimes do not work5. enemies/our characters sometimes reset to full health on my turn6.bug that makes you or enemy deal 5x the damage that it shows killing you or enemy in 1 shot.Inconsistent difficulty, seriously, if your game requires for first 10 rounds to loose because of RNG until you unlock levels for better characters, skills etc, that is bad game design. The game should not be impossible for first hours as that is frustrating, the only way to win first few games would be to backup savegames and savescum but that is not something I am willing to do. Plenty of mechanics not properly explained or some skill explanations aren't quite right.Enemies takes an insane amount of time to kill unless you get a specific party with specific skill and specific relics which are all random, sometimes you will loose only because you did not roll skills you needed.It's a game that hates the player, it feels like the devs haven't even played their own game and did not playtest it, otherwise they would realize crucial mistakes. Devs need to realize that slapping RNG to every single mechanic is just lazy, do not make it random, make it dependant on the player choice instead, some randomness is fine, but everything? Nope.The game requires devs to put more effort into it, its too frustrating currently. There are better alternatives.

_childDocuments_.review: Professional art that could belong in a dark comicbook bestseller, fantastic characters, and impactful animation that didn't get old for me until the late game - all framed by a tasteful, elegant UI. This game looks eye-popping, it's bathing in style. Enemy designs reminded me of the Order of Light from Black Moon Chronicles, which is one of the highest praises I can give. The Devil never shows himself, but his powerful baritone, coupled with rich writing and captivating story, gives him all the characterization he needs.Endearingly, even in defeat, he sticks to his cheeky repertoire no matter what. And in there, he's got the moves! Twist the hand of fate with the help of Diabolic Essence, which doubles as the Devil's hitpoints and mana. Intuitive in design, the Devil Mode can be turned on at any moment - even during your enemies' turn. Having enough essence, you can swap buffs and debuffs between characters as you see fit, drain health pools in one swipe, recharge skills, raise probabilities, switch encounter types, and draw new paths on the map! Jesus wept.The abundance of features was hard to wrap my head around at first, but what could've ended in a headache-inducing cacophony, soon turned into a chorus of angels, screaming in perfectly synergized unison. There's a ton of derivative mechanics that the game makes their own. It only seems like a mess initially, then you'll see that the game revolves around making informed decisions, recognizing priorities, and committing to choices that will help your party stay on top of things.You pick 3 villains from folklore and urban legends for your party and run through a Book, designed in the form of a map from Slay the Spire, to beat its Boss. You get 6 types of encounters: Combat, Event, Elite, Shop, Styx Fountain, Skill Altar. Most of them let you choose your rewards on completion. Terror, Relics, and Souls are priority picks to go for. Gaining Terror applies random buffs to Zones ahead. These valuable delayed rewards could be anything from free use of Devil's Power to a Shop discount. Terror has a gauge and every 4 levels grant you a free Relic.Relics can also be obtained by beating the Elites. Taking on these dangerous guys is especially risky here, but one lucky drop can turn an average disciple into a powerhouse and turn the tables on the whole run single-handedly, so be ready to bet your neck. Last but not really, Souls are the currency accepted by the Grim Reaper, a local shopkeeper - get them or lick your lips staring at all the Skills and Relics on the counter. Seems like a lot already? And that's merely the half of it!Just like your disciples, enemies have two health bars - Health Points and Spirit Points. When picking your party and your Skills, you must first make up your mind about which type of damage you are going for and commit to it. Pretty basic.There're many alternative ways to obtain Skills, that's why I didn't call them priority picks. Yet, they're your bread and butter, or rather blood and soul, allowing you to reforge your minions as you see fit. There's plenty and each minion can have up to 7 Skill slots. The system presents you with tactical depth due to the interesting features, not just damage or healing. You'll be juggling various status effects, from Bleeding to Depression, and so will your enemy. Expect to make nail-biting, hard choices every step of the way.Even just upgrading a Skill isn't a trivial mechanic. Each one has 3 power levels - Ordinary, Wicked, and Demonic. To upgrade, you must either gather 3 Skills of the same level or leave one in the bony hands of the Grim Reaper until the next shop, which can be dangerous. Obviously, you want to see them maxed. But boy, is it a tricky performance! Buy, obtain, replace, sacrifice. Collecting a required set of Skills and Relics while maintaining a healthy level of Essence, Souls, and Terror is a difficult task akin to solving a strategic puzzle.Skills consume Action Points and deplete charge on use. Your disciples have special abilities that recharge their skills and typically do something else. And when I say "special", I mean it - none of them play the same, almost every single one introduces a fresh set of mechanics that prove indispensable in a fight. Besides, your party shares the AP pool, which, coupled with Skill depletion, makes you adapt to predicaments instead of cycling through the same motions over and over again. Unless you find a cheesy tactic to involve just that.Other things I liked about this game's combat:- It doesn't rely on RNG. Most of the Skills have value ranges, but they aren't crucial. Besides, there are NO MISSES!- Your minions' health tops up between fights, only Devil's Essence persists and can usually be replenished at the Styx Fountain.- Enemies telegraph attacks, their intents are shown above their silly heads. The same goes for damage estimation that your disciples will receive during your adversary's turn. - Elite combats have their own sets of rules that can make a fight extremely challenging (Fanatic). But it's still a neat feature.- Easy Bosses. Yes, considering the length of an average run, it's good. Except for that cleaning lady, she needs a nerf.I'll start complaining soon, but first, let's make something clear for the sake of fairness. Yes, occasionally the game can royally screw you over. But most of the time, you have too much control over what's happening when traversing the overworld and during the fights to blame a dice roll. Your victory majorly depends on your mastery of the mechanics and focus, not on your luck. Dig enough graves for yourself with your own hands and you'll learn to see your losses from a mile away.I expected different Books to have different enemies, but they only got beefier. The Books change, but the game doesn't. Trying out different party compositions saved the day for a while, yet new party members are unlocked by progressing through the story. You'll get the last 2 only after finishing the second to last Book! By then, I already had an optimal setup and it became a grind to victory.A run lasts for up to 3 hours due to the abundance of really slow combat with no option to speed things up. On top of all, meta-progression ended too early for me when I've reached the maximum level long before finishing the game, so dying stopped being fun. No new Skills or Relics, only suffering. The game has a strong early to midgame, but due to all this, I was so exhausted that I had to force myself to finish the last Book.When I lost in the beginning, I learned my lessons, unlocked new stuff, mastered new tricks, and desired more experimentation. After dying in the late game, I just sighed. I can look past the lack of variety and difficulty spikes, they're collateral and "balance" is but a buzzword. Developers, please, what you need to fix is the pacing. Implement a "fast animation" option, allow action queueing, and shorten the books. Then, maybe unlock all characters earlier, put in more enemy types, several meta-levels, and a few fresh backdrops.The rating sucks right now, but it can be helped. At the end of the day, Rogue Lords is an imperfect yet devilishly beautiful strategic gem that demands focus and thought. Good artistry is everywhere, but it seldom translates to good game design. Fortunately, despite outstaying its welcome, this game plays almost as good as it looks, having the team behind it pour heart and soul, and not necessarily their own, into the cauldron. Now, go forth and plunge this land into chaos! And try not to burst into tears while you're at it.P.S. They've patched in an easier difficulty, now everyone can play it without worrying too much.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a roguelike turn-based strategy game. You are the devil and Deamon Hunters beat you up 10 years ago. You literally went to hell to gain more power. Now, you and your disciples return to earth to achieve world domination.The story is told through texts. Missions are called books, which are divided into chapters, and each new chapter the book will open to tell you more about the story. Most of the text is read by a teller and the voice acting is pretty good actually. Before the battle starts, you can select one of three different rewards you receive if you win the battle. Depending on the reward, the battle may be harder though.Battles are turn-based. You can see the enemies' intentions at all times (What they do, who they going to attack, and how much damage they do). Your team consists of three disciples and you have five action points in total per turn. Attacks cost one to several action points. After using one, it needs to be recharged before using it again. Every character has an action that allows recharging all of its (or the whole team) attacks for some AP. Every character has a physical and a spiritual health bar. If one of them gets reduced to zero, you need to attack the enemy one more time to kill him.If one of your Disciples loses all of his physical OR spiritual points, they don't die. Instead, every time they get attacked, you will lose diabolic essence. If you have no DE left, you will lose. This is a mode used within battles. It's like cheating. You can modify health points, recharge skills, and move statuses. It's literally cheating. The price to pay for that is diabolic essence - so use it wisely or you'll lose everything! Every book is like a mission consisting of several zones each with activities in them (like battles, events, a merchant, etc.). Sometimes you can choose one of a few zones (Think of nodes in roguelike games). Some zones have optional side activities, too. Every disciple is different in his looks, characteristics, and skills. You can obtain skills in different ways. If you get the same skill three times, it will be combined into the same with a higher rarity. You can also choose one of your three disciples in an event to do a social test. The social test can result in gaining positive or negative traits. Diabolic essence and souls are your main resources. If you have no DE left, you will lose.You can get souls as rewards after battles or events. With them, you can buy or upgrade skills or get new relics. Terror grants you new relics and a chance to get higher rarities when it comes to skills. After reaching certain points in a book, you will get a new point. After obtaining four points, you will rank up. After every run, you will get EXP and level up. For getting achievements or leveling up, you will be rewarded with new disciples, skills, or relics which can show up in your next books.    Rogue Lords is a fantastic and addictive roguelike turn-based strategy game. It offers a lot of content, has a gorgeous art style, the music is very atmospheric, the voice acting is great and they successfully implemented a few innovative features. A few things could be improved, like the grind, some bugs, making spiritual attacks more viable, and adding a fast mode. Even though this sounds like a lot, I had a hell of a time with the game. I got it pretty late last night and immediately played it for over 5 hours without taking a break. Rogue Lords is definitely a must-have for every turn-based strategy fan out there!

_childDocuments_.review: At a first glance Rogue Lords looks like a great new indie roguelite game with some interesting mechanics that I haven't really encountered much of before. However the more you play of it the more glaring it's issues become and it's blatantly obvious the game is poorly balanced and rushed when it comes to a lot of different mechanics.Let me start with the positives.The game has a "cheat" system it calls the devil mode where you can trade your devil essense for to tweak success chances, restore/lower HP/SP values, teleport between the lanes and more. The devil essense is a resource which you primarily use for this but it is also your overall health pool. When any of the characters you control goes down to 0 HP/SP and takes damage that damage is then subtracted from your devil essence and if it reaches zero it's game over. This is a fun mechanic that adds further strategy to the game and I bet most players have their favorite uses for this resource.Next we have the overall skill system. Generally you can use each skill once before it becomes depleted and depleted skills are recharged by a "recharge" skills that all characters have however most characters have some special mechanic to their recharge skill. For example Draculas recharge skill is more expensive at 2AP but in turn recharges all 3 of your characters skills. Skills themselves are granted mostly from combat and buying them from the merchant but you can also get them from social events.Social events are a type of encounter where you will send one of your 3 characters to do some evil task and all characters have different attribute levels for their social skills which are almost exclusively used in the social events. The different attributes are used in different options but usually you have option that doesn't require an attribute. Passing these events give your characters traits that can increase their damage, social skills and health values. Another neat thing is that the different characters can gain extra negative/positive traits depending on how they like the  choices you make.The above mentioned systems are what the game does fairly well although although even despite them being the strongest parts a lot of them feel half-baked.What the game really suffers from is an overall lack of balance and polish to the point where it is at times hard to enjoy the game at all.First of all the way the difficulty scales. The game is divided into different books, you need to complete one before you can move on to the next one. Every book you complete increases the difficulty for all books, even the ones you have already completed. You can't lower difficulty and the difficulty itself is very poorly implented as it mostly comes from an increase in enemy HP/SP values which makes the already slow combat even worse. Also due to this difficuly system you are punished for using newer characters that haven't unlocked any skills yet.Another HUGE issue is the overall build variety. Each character starts with 3 skills and can obtain more during the game. They can also unlock new skills by completing different achievments tied to the characters. The issue is that the synergy between different status effects are pretty much none. You can't for example stack different effects of the same type and every status has a type. For example you have a bleed effect that is considered a weakness (red) and a burn effect that is also a weakness. These two can't stack and they will overwrite each other which means that you generally only want one type of status for each type in your party not to break status combos. I can't forget to mention that status effects scale very poorly as adding stacks never increase the effect but just the duration. A status effect that decreases damage you take with 4 damage isn't all that useful when enemes hits for 50+ damage.This is further made worse by the fact that to obtain more skill slots above the 5 your start with, you need to sacrifice an old skill at a special altar that is one of the nodes you can encounter. By sacrificing a skill it won't show up again, this is both a blessing and a curse because it means you need to pick up unwanted skills so you can sacrifice them at the first opportunity.The overall variety of the game is poor and not just wwhen it comes to different builds. Every book feels the same as the next other than the few lore bits you encounter and the end boss. You run into the same enemies, the same events, the same background and so on. Enemy variety is overall low and the designs are pretty bland which makes it difficult identifiy them at a glance. Events while being fairly numerous reuse a lot of graphical assets.Lastly I have to mention the overall lack of quality of life features. No way to remove/speed up animations, No way to turn off the annoying devil narrator who constantly mocks you, You can't arrange your skills on the skillbar and many more annoyances exist in the game.The game has good potential and I love playing as the different classic evil characters but as it stands the game needs a lot of polish and balancing to make it a game I would recommend to anyone else, even people who love the genre like myself.

_childDocuments_.review: A whole lot of reviews seem to be complaining about the difficulty curve and enemies doing lots of damage, so let me just nip that in the bud: the game is balanced around the huge pile of defensive effects and debuffs that can reduce incoming damage. There's "wall" which halves received damage, "dodge" which negates physical damage entirely, "alteration" which flatly reduces outgoing damage, another (whose name I forgot) which reduces outgoing damage by half, and many kinds of healing. In addition, your units have damage gates before they pass damage to your true health bar for the run: as long as your disciple has even 1 point of health, he can take a 1 billion damage hit and still not damage you whatsoever. As if all the ways to mitigate damage weren't enough, each character has 2 health bars to work with, which can safely be depleted separately, plus there are spammable taunts to redirect damage between units. Look, I don't want to dismiss the pain of a steep difficulty curve, but the game offers a million tools to manage incoming damage, and if somebody is telling you damage scaling is too steep they just don't know how to play.The actual, meaningful criticism that should be leveled at this game is the lack of enemy variety. As far as I can tell, all the difficulty scaling comes from increases or decreases in the values for certain mechanics. So, Rogue Lords needs more content. But at the price point it's at, with a whole lifecycle of probably new content, patches, or expansions ahead of it, I think the base of this game is quite strong. Don't sleep on it.

_childDocuments_.review: In my quest to find more fun roguelites, I have played a few runs of Rogue Lords here. Initially I was turned off by the very long winded tutorial that took a lot of control away from the player, but after that run where I got to play and learn, I actually started really enjoying this game...for a time.The story is that you play as the Devil...well, more like the Devil's disciples. In the tutorial run you are defeated by Van Hellsing and in order to defeat him, your disciples have to collect these rare trinkets to become strong enough to defeat him in battle. So they venture forth, terrorizing villages, slaying hunters and civilians all with the Devil's help to defeat Hellsing once and for all.The first thing I instantly praise this game for is its looks. Visually, this game is awesome. I love the animations and overall UI of the game. You start with 3 disciples, but as you level up and complete more runs, you will unlock more. Each disciple is some iconic horror villain like Dracula, Bloody Mary, Lillith, etc. They all have their own unique set of moves that you can find and obtain to help you fight against the hordes of demon hunters that stand in your way.The skill system works pretty well. With each battle you can choose to get a passive buff in a later level, gain new skill(s), or gain a currency of souls that you can spend when you visit grim reaper shops. You can always check the map to find out what is the ideal move to make and plan ahead. If you get the same skill 3 times, it will increase in rarity and come with better perks like more damage or debuffs. You can also get smaller trinkets that give you passive buffs during your run as well to further strengthen your disciples. The turn-based Action Point (AP) combat is good so you don't have to make rushed decisions.On top of combat, you can run into events where you have to make choices that will effect your run. Each of your disciples have individual stats that can help change the outcome of particular decisions. If you're feeling unlucky, you can use your overall HP known as demonic essence to increase your odds of success. You can even use the demonic essence to heal your disciples in combat as well, but once it runs out, you lose the run.Each combatant has their own HP and SP bars. You have to get one of the bars down to 0 so they enter a "vulnerable" state and then you can knock them out. Some disciples are good at attacking SP, others are good at lowering HP, whole some are good at debuffs or  supporting the party. You can only take 3 disciples with you per run and learning how to synergize them together is key to winning because this game is rather challenging. You will gain skills by leveling up each run, so even when you lose you gain something sometimes. But...Let's talk gripes, for I have many of them. Like most roguelites, you're going to lose a lot in the beginning because you're learning the game and don't have a lot of skills to pull from. But then a couple of runs in, you'll start finding your footing and the game becomes fun. Then you realize that each completed run makes the game harder, but for the wrong reasons. The enemies gain more health and do more damage whenever you try for the harder runs to continue the story. Your disciples do not though. The problem with this is that some disciples are really trash early game and with the added difficulty, it makes it frustrating hard to get any traction done on a run. Instead of trying out combinations and having fun, you are stuck to a set 3 to just make it through the game. Next thing you'll learn is that harder runs are mostly dictated by debuffs and buffs. Once you learn how to block them and keep your disciples alive, each battle becomes very long and tedious. The animations that were fun to watch at first are now grating because you have to watch them over and over in a 15-30 minute battle that used to take 5-10 minutes. This game desperately needs a fast forward button because a standard run will run you about 2-4 hours and they only get longer with the increased difficulty. Lastly, as charming as the storybook feel of the game is, because of how slow the game goes, it becomes annoying after awhile and you just want to mute the Devil's repetitive voicelines after awhile.Final verdict? That sweet spot a few hours in was some of the most fun I was having in this game for a while. I was almost about to say it rivaled Monster Train. But after I got to about the third run and enemies were getting spongier, I felt like I was wasting time and the game just lost its luster. It's a shame because I want to recommend this game, but I can't without a fast forward feature and something that gives you some sort of good start on the harder runs. Some may like the challenge, but I just find it to be a waste of time. Maybe grab this when it's on sale if it peaks your interest, but for now I cannot recommend it. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Game is really fun, it really is, and a lot of love clearly went into it. My main problem is as others have said, the difficulty scaling. You can be doing really well and then all of a sudden you're getting hit for 20x3 from what's considered a minion to an elite fight. Crazy unbalanced. I do truly enjoy the game, but it needs some balance tweaks before I give it a thumbs up. I do want to argue against what others are saying about the Terror system. It's good! I like that you can influence the map and that the map can fight back. I do agree with another reviewer who says that the negative buffs should never "block" your path. I think there should always be an option to go down one way without a negative buff, but even then it's not the end of the world. This game's biggest issue is definitely the difficulty. Some skills also are worded weirdly, specifically there's one for The White Lady that I don't even understand. I also think the map should be more tightly knit, a lot of time is spent on the map which can stack up to a lot of time spent. I don't want it removed completely, but I do want the walkways between paths made significantly shorter, and also should make it so that you can fly over obstacles, just to make it easier to travel. Other than those major issues (hence the downvote), the game is great, and I look forward to changing my recommendation to positive once they fix these issues (hopefully).

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off with a clear statement because this is probably going to be long: If you enjoy hard Rogue-Like games and are looking for a challenging team manager/slay the spire type game. This is fine.Pros:-It's an infinite game. Theoretically, you can go on for quite a while not having runs be similar enough to each other to feel too boring.-The devil mechanic is quite interesting as you are able to "cheat" certain mechanics and functions of the game to force them to be in your favor.-Each character, even when doing similar roles, have a large variety in the way they play-Every approach can be quite powerful, whether that is sp or hp damage.Cons:-The game is extremely hard. You should be going into this knowing it is not going to be your friend, and many times you will lose to things that are not completely your fault.-Some of the enemies are brutally designed against making one character the strongest on your team, a strategy that is basically required for most of the rest of the game.-Elites are extremely plentiful, as interesting as some of their designs are, expect to run into literally all of them every other run. Sometimes, you will run into elites that simply counter the strategy you are given.-Most of the obtainable early characters do not have more than one solid ability that can defend themselves/the group, meaning if you aren't killing all the enemies quickly, you will often lose.-Unlocks feel kind of bizarre. You almost immediately unlock a new character, but if you are not completing runs, it is quite easy to stockpile the unlocks for characters you haven't even unlocked yet.-Some of the tooltips are incredibly poorly designed.Gripes:-Bugs. Bugs. Bugs. Playing the game on day one? I have been subject to a pop-up that explains the character Lilith and it literally won't go away making it impossible to read the other tooltips. Bad UI is a shame.-As soon as you unlock Lilith, Dracula isn't particularly useful. She unlocks basically immediately and his real powerful unlocks take several more runs (failed or succeeded) to unlock.-There is a leveling system and an achievement system to unlock things. Admittedly this is enjoyable, the fact that several of my abilities and new character are locked behind abilities that are for characters I do not own is frustrating.What I would change if I could:-Second mission is not this abrupt skyrocket of difficulty. -Tone down the elite where you can't damage the side adds until the main one has been dealt 40 hp and sp damage... 4 times..-Up the amount of soul, and have some kind of like soul reduction as the difficulty goes up. I think it would be very helpful to the game if the first actual run you complete was a bit more forgiving, seeing as you won't learn much from it and likely will complete it by sheer luck.-There's still a problem with scaling.(HP damage+ is noticeably harder to obtain than SP damage+) this is regrettable when you are in a game where the game can offer you only HP damage scaling and you have SP damage attacks mostly.. And vice versa.-There is a case where even going through fights, the lovely narrator can get stuck saying multiple things while his minions are also talking. It's sad because the dialog is actually rather good, it just sometimes gets washed out.To conclude:Game is good. Game is hard. Frustrating, and even unfair. Expect this game to crush your dreams sometimes. And bask in the lovely narration of the Devil.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a fun roguelike very much like Slay the Spire, but not being a rip off in the slightest.  It has a unique cheating mechanic and is pretty difficult while also having balance issues and run destroying bug.  The concept is unique, fresh, and fun, but the gameplay could use some retuning and class balancing.This is my biggest gripe in general, but I think I feel differently than the majority.    At least not in the way of traditional Roguelikes.  They're meant to be incredibly challenging as you learn the mechanics and add points to the metagame.  However, it's only soul crushingly difficult if you use certain characters.  It's just too difficult to win with physical damage.  The enemy does too many things to mitigate physical damage dealt, while physical damage characters just feel weaker.  Even buffs and debuffs favor SP damaging more - The 'poison' of this game comes in two flavors, Depression which damages SP health over time and Decomposition which damages health.  However, Depression .  Which brings me to...I can only win if I use Lilith, White Lady, and one other (I usually pick Hecate but have also gotten away with Baron) and in a game with different classes that you want to experiment in, this just sucks.  Here's an example of what I mean:-White Lady starts with a skill called Mask of Torment that does SP damage passively every turn.  It's a 1 AP cost and you turn it on and forget it's there.  I  like this as a mechanic and there are other masks and other items that compliment the masks that really make it fun and dynamic.  10/10 would recommend.-Bloody Mary, however, has a recharge that is 2 AP, only affects her, and adds a mirror that duplicates effects and damage to one opponent.  This means that she can output some pretty good damage, but you have to burn 2 out of your 5 (usually) AP just getting it set up, and when the enemy dies, you have to do it again to set up for the next enemy.  Also, understandably, some of your greatest abilities cost more AP, so you can have a turn where you just recharge and use one ability.  And to make matters worse, a lot of her abilities have the 'bloodthirsty' trait meaning they only target the enemy with the lowest HP, limiting your options in terms of attacking.  Bloody Mary's recharge should be 1 AP or the mirror should transfer or something.Relics can mitigate this in some way but it's RNG based on if you get them or not.I've only encountered one bug, but it can really mess things up:  If you exit the game during a run and then relaunch it, sometimes it will just go into an infinite loading screen and force you to restart the game, and more importantly, end your current run and restart it.  This  if you're far ahead since some games can up to an hour or longer to complete.While I like the style of the game, the running about in the overworld feels unnecessary and sometimes frustrating as a small tree or fog patch will prevent you from getting to the objective, forcing you to run all the way around to activate it.  Not to mention some of the events and story beats are near the first time, but when you do them for the 47th, it can get old, having you spamming click to get past it so you can get to the gameplay.  Although the voice lines are well acted, they repeat very often ('Do I have to get my hands dirty again?') and become tedious very fast to the point to where I just disabled the voice volume.  Also, because of the nature of these games i'll idle, and having a narrator constantly talk at me and berate me is grating to say the least.Despite the gripes, however, it is a fun game.  The cheating mechanic creates an interesting dynamic in gameplay with swapping buffs, raising/lowering health and changing paths on the map, and I think it's a great dynamic.  Although the classes are unbalanced they're unique and interesting and I would love to see future DLC, expansions, or sequels employ more famous monsters like Swamp Thing, a werewolf, the Babadook, and others.I don't regret buying it and have had a lot of fun with it.  If you like Slay the Spire or other deckbuilder games, or even villain-as-a-protagonist games, this one will give you a lot of hours.I just think it really needs work.  With how receptive the developers have been to player feedback, however, I think it's got a bright future ahead of it and will edit my review to be even more positive when game benefiting changes are made.Edit:  Infinite loading bug has been fixed, so the devs are listening.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an odd game to review, I don't think I have seen such a big gap between gameplay quality and graphic quality. I love roguelike games and deckbuilders, so I decided to try it despite the mixed reviews and I regretted it.Art, sound and animations: 9/10. Just really good, awesome voice lines, really cool animations, fantastic art, few things to nitpick. The story I didn't get to see all of it since I couldn't get myself to play this any further but it's a cool concept and I liked what I saw.Gameplay, interface and pacing: 1/10. The gameplay makes no sense. It's a deckbuild game where you barely get opportunities to tweak your deck. You'll mostly just use whatever abilities you start with, which gets very boring and repetitive. Upgrading an ability requires you to get three of them and combine them... why? It's very slow and RNG based. The whole pace of the game is very slow, which just doesn't work with a roguelike because it discourages replay. It's also slow because they make you run between nodes... for literally no reason. There is nothing to explore or interact with, you're just walking from point A to B, cause. It's one of the most ridiculous game play decisions I've ever seen. Cherry on top, the interface is pretty, but buggy and unresponsive. Some of the abilities seem cool but the game restricts you so much in trying them out or experimenting that it just doesn't actually matter.
