_childDocuments_.review: Initially, this game is great. If you are a fan of the genre of deck-building roguelikes (STS, monster train, griftlands etc) you will find this game being a fresh breeze with a lot of new characteristic mechanics such as the devil mode, pairing of skills to make a higher rarity and 2 separate hp-bars. Also the artwork and voice acting are great. However, it feels a bit unfinished. After 40 hours I've beaten the main game ("last book") on my first try. Here are a few points that should be improved:-Increased enemy variation. A lot of standard enemies and elites are recycled throughout the whole campaign. The books (or campaigns) use the same enemies, so advancing to the next does only change the final boss (even the minions in the boss room are the same as you encountered earlier!). -Pacing. As others have pointed out, the game becomes really slow because of all the animations. A run takes about 2-4 hours depending on how fast you play.-Viable strategies. At this point in time, it feels as if increasing raw damage through various artifacts, skills and events is the only way to scale. Depression and decomposition (acts as poision for the respective hp-bars) feels a lot too slow and with a too low ceiling to have an impact compared to other skills. Also, having a character with a heal and a way to remove statuses/silence feels almost as a must.-Because of the point above, with raw damage being the viable way to kill enemies, fights tend to revolve around a certain pattern of  buffing your damage or action points, decreasing incoming damage (either pure subtraction of damage or halving the damage) and dealing damage. The planning becomes quite simplified after a while, and what really makes it tedious is the amount of hp of the enemies. The fights can drag on for 15 turns, when you know you have won in 3. The randomization of drawing cards is not here, as in the other games.-Repeating voice lines. I do not want to hear anymore about the santua lumen or woods that needs more terrorizing... Lessening the chance of activation on voice lines would improve the game.CONCLUSION:A game that is good for about 40 hours to scratch the itch of an RPG roguelike. It is okay, but gets monotonous after a while. It does bring up a lot of interesting mechanics, that I hope other developers look more closely at. Is it worth your money? Maybe. However, it could easily have been so much better with a few adjustments.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:I really, really love a lot of things about this game. The aesthetic and world building choices here are just really top notch. The premise is fun, the theme is interesting, and the story builds and feeds back well into the game loop.CONS:Combat. Is. A. Mess. Hard enemy scaling within a combat encounter Combat in this game is an arms race of hitting  Characters suffer heavily from extreme niche role design that doesn't play well into the combat requirements.SUMMARY:I'm recommending this game because I had a lot of fun exploring it, but in all honesty, I would love nothing more to see a Rogue Lords 2 with a completely reimagined combat system.I love the diversity of characters, I really do- *but*- a lot of the characters are just seriously blocky and underpowered. Combat is just designed to be an extremely tight damage race. Enemies frequently have abilities that allow them to stack physical/spiritual power very quickly and then will 100-0 your disciples leaving your demonic power vulnerable. Only one character reigns supreme at consistently beating that damage threshold (Bloody Mary). Bloody Mary has flexible typed on-demand massive spike damage that no other character can touch. And unfortunately, enemy design *requires* leveraging this damage because of those enemies that will rapidly damage scale within a single combat encounter resulting in a super fast outpacing of any defensive or healing abilities. Hitting one of these encounters without a spike comp is an instant loss.The shared AP pool contributes even harder to this issue because with only 5 action points to spend between your entire team, and many defensive abilities costing 2 action points- and the need to stack those defensive/healing abilities in order for a tank to be able to survive focus fire..... it just doesn't make tanks or healing support, or even damage over time a viable strategy. Not when Bloody Mary is *easily* able to 100-0 targets in each of her turns if you spend all 5 points on her.Additionally- only one negative debuff can be applied to an enemy at a time. This results in characters who may want to apply competing debuffs being completely incompatible for a team comp. In general, it makes any characters reliant on debuffs to apply damage incredibly unreliable. Additionally, debuffs only stack in duration, and not intensity. All of this removes any threat a debuff comp could possible have of threatening the dominance of pure spike damage.  Bloody Mary having the passive ability to double her damage on a given target just makes her an absolute powerhouse for single target damage. Because units heal to full after every combat, healing and defense feel extremely lackluster when Bloody Mary not only has the ability to do 4x HP or SP hits, but also drop a massive 12 damage reduction for the cost of 1 AP. Stacking everything on her is just a winning move *every time*.Any time I have tried to break formula with dropping Bloody Mary or explored trying to pump a different character, or evenly buff the team over time, I have noticed that the game get significantly more challenging and I frequently lose very early on.On a sidenote for oddities- I have found that if an enemy has a buff and you don't, you can steal it. If the enemy has a buff and you also have a buff you *must* swap the buffs. Which I don't think is intended mechanical behavior, but helps hammer nails in the coffin of tanks with damage mitigation buffs like Wall who want to steal and enemies Shell.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Tough, demonic-themed, rogue-like tactical battles and unique artstyle are not enough to offset the lack of depth, repetitiveness, odd design choices and overall balance of an otherwise decent gameWhen I first saw Rogue Lords, I was keen to try it out and see how it compares to other rogue-like battlers like Iratus. I think the game is best described as a tactical combat game, with rogue-like characteristics. This is a formula that can be challenging, but if implemented well, can result in a very rewarding gaming experience. The main features behind the rogue-like concept is the lack of independent saves / loading, irreversible game choices and (which result in) multiple playthroughs. Let's see how the game measures up:+ I like the unique artstyle -- too often you see Japanese-anime themed characters or art influences in games these days, so this is a refreshing change+ The overall concept -- you play the Devil, using various minions to battle demon-hunters in the quest to regain various relics -- and combat mechanics work decently. When you mouse-over an enemy, you can see what they're planning next, and who they're targeting; as the Devil, you can influence outcomes of events or battles by expending some life- Odd design choices: There are randomly generated paths which detail various routes your party can take but for some reason, you have to manually navigate this route with an on-screen avatar. Pathfinding in this mode is messy and annoying, and quite frankly, why is it even necessary? Just clicking a point on the route map should suffice. Another example: combat sequence is not determined by character initiative (any of your characters can go first) but by "action points" which are pretty much limited to 5. There are rare instances where you may be able to increase this, but it seems strange to use AP in a rogue-like battler. And why 5? What determines action points? There's nothing that informs this in the game design- Lack of depth: You have just over a half-dozen of minions that you can employ (you have to unlock them progressively when certain milestones are reached) and you can only use 3 at a time in battles. You have a dashboard, but no base per se, and cannot build buildings for bonuses (as in Iratus, for e.g.). There are magical items you can equip minions with and a "terror level" that can have some positive effects but this is too insignificant to add depth or benefit you much. RL also has random events that can result in buffs or negative influences on your minions, and the Grim Reaper encounters that can enhance your minion's abilities, but these are too random to help much- Lack of difficulty levels: Rogue Lords is tough. After 5 attempts, I cannot even reclaim the first relic; I can only imagine the level of frustration players would face if they wish to unlock all the  minions. The extreme randomness of events, chance of encountering elite enemies early on, and unusual combat metrics (you have to do additional physical or spiritual damage even after their maximum levels have been drained in order to kill an enemy) do not help.         - There aren't enough encounters to build up your minions before meeting elite enemies. You die EARLY. And often        - As the Devil, you can influence outcomes by expending life, but beware: getting that refilled can be extremely difficult.         - Lastly, and I have not been able to independently verify this (it all happens too quickly) but it seems like if just one of your minions dies, you lose the entire battle and the playthrough ends. You don't get to regroup, choose another route, etc. It just ends and you have to do it all over again- Which leads to extreme repetitiveness: Trying out new combinations of minions, spells etc. can be fun if there's strategic or tactical depth; not having the latter makes every playthrough a chore. With work, Rogue Lords can be both challenging, and fun. Currently however, I cannot recommend it due to the reasons listed above.4.5 / 10.0
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Before delving into the negatives, there's obviously been a lot of love poured into the game by the dev team. It's a great concept, and there is fun to be had. I'm a big fan of Slay the Spire which is what motivated me to pick Rogue Lords up. I've enjoyed some of my time with the game, but it's got too frustrating for me to keep playing for now.I unfortunately need to echo a lot of the other reviewers criticisms of the game. The enemy encounter balance seems way off. You can be having quite a fun, challenging run until certain enemy encounters absolutely destroy you out of nowhere. The enemy damage output can just scale immensely from encounter to encounter and it feels impossible to counter at that point in your run. It's incredibly frustrating to have your run end so abruptly and feeling like there wasn't much you could have done about it. I think Slay the Spire handles difficulty ramping really well in comparison.I'm also not a huge fan of the debuffs that get placed on the map as you progress. They are a nice mechanic in theory but they sometimes get applied in your direct path only a step or two ahead without any branches to allow you to avoid them or choose another negative buff instead. Personally I feel like they proc too often as well, staking the odds too heavily against the player, especially in the first chapter.The UI could use some streamlining as well, there is a lot of clicking past flavour text that after reading once you'll probably want to avoid in further runs.In my opinion the over world, while nice for world building, is unnecessary and slows down your run too much. I'd much prefer to see a Slay the Spire style map instead.There is a great core game here I think, and I'm looking forward to returning to it in the future to see how the devs respond to players feedback. I think some criticisms I noted above can be patched out easily (damage scaling, map debuff frequency), while others are core to the game design (the overworld) and will persist.I'd suggest watching some play throughs before purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: Decided to update the review, following on from new changes the game has had. I've marked the updated bit further down.Rogue Lords is a tough rogue-like dungeon crawler, where we take on the role of the devil and pick 3 disciples to complete each book (a book is essentially a campaign run, lasting around ~3 hours, of which there are 7 in total). The disciples are figures of fiction and myths, such as Dracula, Bloody Mary, Baron Samedi, etc. There are 9 disciples altogether, although we only start with 3 of them and have to unlock the others over the course of the game.The gameplay involves travelling from one node on the map to another, and at each node something happens - combat, an event with choices, a grim reaper from whom we buy stuff, and so on. The map has several different paths going through it, and it is important for us to plan our route and decide what we need to prioritise as each type of event has different bonuses and risks. For example, an event where we fight an elite enemy can grant us a precious relic as a reward which gives us useful bonuses, but elite enemies are dangerous, and such encounters could leave us worse off afterwards.The fighting is turn-based, 3 vs 3 style. Our team has a shared pool of action points, so we can choose and change how much each of our disciples acts each turn. Each of their skills consumes a different number of action points, so planning ahead at all times is required. The enemies all play their turns out as well. However, being the devil, we are able to know exactly what moves they'll play during their next turn, so we have to prepare for that accordingly. Also being a devil, we can influence some aspects of combat in a way of "cheating". By using up our existing essence (our life force essentially), we can increase health of our disciples, decrease enemy health, or move around status effects (such as stealing beneficial statuses from enemies and remove harmful ones from our team). It's a great idea that I believe hasn't been done before and greatly spices up the fights. We have to be careful though, because if our disciples run out of health or spirit points, they become vulnerable, and additional attacks will cause us, the devil, to lose essence. If essence runs out, it's game over.In addition to combat encounters, I also felt that game mechanics taking place outside of combat have also been developed nicely and given a lot of thought. The book events for example put us into some random scenario (from a big pool of different scenarios), and we pick one of our disciples to handle that event. During it, they can make choices, which can provide us with various benefits. Some of those choices have a % chance of success. However, once again, being the devil, we can cheat and manipulate the reality to our advantage. How? By simply tweaking the success rates of these events. If gambling with RNG is not your thing, you can simply guarantee the chances of success by using up some of the devil essence.Now there is some randomness to the way each book run happens, because the event paths on the map do not go in the same sequence each time, and the rewards themselves that we get are also randomized. Even the skills we get for our disciples will be offered randomly, so you might not always be able to find the skill you want one of your disciples to learn. But with so many choices and options available, there are many opportunities on how to modify your build and tackle the challenges ahead.Now be warned, the game is hard and it doesn't have a difficulty level selection. Its default difficulty will already be challenging from book 1, which means the game is easily not for everyone. Its learning curve can be quite steep, because it can take a while before you finally start realising how to best synergise different game mechanics and make them work to your advantage. So, majority of the game is hard but fair. That is until a certain boss...----Updated paragraph---The devs have updated the game with a couple of balance patches recently, including introducing Apprentice mode which is slightly easier. I think stuff like this is always good to make the game more welcoming to a wider range of players. Although I still believe the penultimate boss in the game needs balancing, because it's way harder than every other boss and enemy in the game, so regardless of which difficulty mode you go for, this boss will feel like two difficulty levels higher than all the rest, causing an inconsistent difficulty spike. I've personally enjoyed everything the original Normal difficulty level has with the exception of this boss. So I still think there'll be many frustrated players, but at least now with Apprentice mode, more players should feel confident to give the game a try.--------------------------------Old part of the review---Now here's the reason why I am recommending with reservations. WARNING: RANT INCOMING. I think the boss at the end of book 6 (the penultimate book) is crazily unbalanced and infuriating and feels like a very cheap difficulty spike. After having attempted it multiple times, it became clear that it requires a very specific and exploitable build setup in order to be beaten, as the nature of the boss fight introduces a lot of limitations on what you can and cannot do, which massively restricts any sense of strategy. These limitations will change after every few turns, and then all get joined together at the end. Can't attack more than x times, can't use more than x skills per disciple, and worst of all - can't apply ANY statuses AT ALL. Given that majority of the skills your disciples will have will apply some sort of status (either beneficial or negative), your choices on what you can do become cut down by 90%. And just as you bring the boss's massive health pool to 0 and think you've finally beaten them, they heal some of their health and summon two more minions (because that is absolutely what each of us "enjoys" seeing a boss do when we think we've finally overcome them). At this point I am tired of wasting my time trying to overcome this cheap boss, because it just became an exercise in frustration, and I don't think beating it will give me any satisfaction anymore. I've had my fun with the game and enjoyed it for far longer than most games, but at this point I think I'm going to put it on hold and wait until another update patch when the devs decide to nerf some aspect of this boss.---------------------Verdict---So, to conclude, Rogue Lords is a brilliant game really with many interesting mechanics that keep you engaged, highly tactical fights, intriguing characters, and a beautiful visual style. And really, the aforementioned boss is the only filthy stain on an otherwise pristine work of art. I do hope they balance it eventually to keep a more consistent level of difficulty across the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is effectively a board game, and it's a pretty good one at that. Once you you figure out the character synergies it becomes a lot better.That said, it's entirely possible to end up with a non-functional party if you don't approach your development correctly, such as balancing relic and skill acquisition, and I think that's where a lot of the gripes here come from. There's also the fact that there's no log and some crazy design decisions, like a bleed affecting a character per target damaged rather than per skill use. That can also lead to some extremely frustrating moments until you figure out the mechanics, which are not well spelled-out.This game is absolutely worth a go if you don't mind feeling your way through a game. If you want everything clear and up front, then you might give it a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really creative expansion on the slay the spire formula - i have really enjoyed it - with 25 hours in, I am one book away from the final boss, at the highest difficulty (which i recommend). The twist is that you (as the devil) can intervene in fights real time and cheat - stealing status, reducing health etc, at the cost of your own life - which is a really cool formula, and something you will need to use, because your enemies will hit like trucks!Each of the characters are very very unique and interesting to play, with lots of different skills to unlock (and not all that grindy) - Dracula and Baron Samedi are my favourite. Give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: So like most of you I was really hyped for this game. I'm a big fan of most roguelike deckbuilders and the concept of using gothic horror characters with cool abilities sounded like a blast! And it was, at first. I probably played the game nonstop for the first two days. It was really cool and fun discovering the abilities of the characters and unlocking new ones. The player characters are really well done and have their own strategies you can implement. Bloody Mary uses her mirror to reflect and double her attacks, Dracula uses his life stealing ability and gets stronger when he's at 0 health, Headless Horseman and Lilith play as tanks, trying to absorb as much damage as they can and heal themselves and the team back up. I thought the characters could have been more synergistic with one another however, since a lot of the time most of them conflicted. The enemies in Rogue Lords have 2 health bars you can use to take them out basically, HP or SP, and the characters themselves should pretty much just stick with other characters that deal the same type of damage as them. for example, having the White Lady in my team with Bloody Mary and Dracula did not work well at all since Bloody Mary and Dracula were more HP focused and White Lady is more SP focused. So most battles White Lady didn't do anything at all but absorb some blows. I had no use for any of her abilities since she couldn't take out any enemies on her own faster than the other 2 could together, and she doesn't start with any healing skills like Mask of Opulence (should've been her starting item). Hypothetically you can turn any character into an HP or SP focused character, but really that's just luck based on what skills are offered to you.  Regardless, I thought everything was balanced well for the most part, up until about the 4th storybook. For those of you that haven't played, you are the Devil and you're sending your Disciples (player team of 3) to collect artifacts from these different storybooks (which should've been more varied in appearance and quest interactions in my opinion) so you can eventually defeat Van Helsing, the final boss. Each storybook took me roughly an hour or so to get through, unless I died and needed to restart but that hardly happened the first few books. It's at around the fourth book I found the difficulty curve becoming a little too steep. I thought maybe I was just going about my strategy the wrong way so I gave it a few more tries. After dying quite a few times I somehow muddled through to the fifth book when I realized for sure how terribly unfair the game was becoming. I'm not one to shy away from difficulty, but this is like the equivalent of fighting Smough and Ornstein with 50 HP and nothing but a broken sword. The enemy AI is WAY more powerful than the player character in almost every way imaginable. I'll just list a few of the examples I can think of.*They sometimes start battles with buffs that protect them from damage for 5 or more turns*Can give themselves and allies 2-3 buffs at once*Can deal 20-30 (usually around 50-100% of total player HP) damage to you or your whole team before there's even a   possibility you have anything equivalent in rarity*Most have WAY more HP/SP (100+) than anyone on your side of the screen, and the ones that don't are usually protected   by buffsIt really was manageable at first, utilizing the devil mode to move around buffs/ debuffs when I needed to and lowering the last bits of AI health to finish them off with a death blow. However, due to the lack of any upgrades for the player such as better starting stats or cards, the AI outpaces the player exponentially. I'ts great to unlock new abilities/characters/relics that do new cool stuff and introduce new mechanics, but if they're not improving how well you are able to play overall then you probably shouldn't increase how well the AI is able to play overall either. I like the game up to around the fourth book, but it is going to be hard to recommend until they work out the balancing issues with the AI. I doubt I'll even finish it since I feel like I'm just at such a huge disadvantage. Really wish the developers had done a little more playtesting and tweaking with the difficulty modifiers before release. 6/10UPDATE: So after not playing for a while I saw they had released an update which fixed the balance issues, which I was honestly surprised they had addressed so quickly. Admittedly I was still skeptical when I decided to give it another shot but I'm pleased to say they did an awesome job fixing the game. I was worried at first they may have toned it down too much since the first 20 minutes seemed a lot easier than usual, but as I progressed further the difficulty increased by just the right amount. By the end of Chapter 5 I was down to my last 20 health, but I never felt overwhelmed or at a disadvantage like I did before. I pulled out a win Chapter 5 on my first attempt coming back, but even if I had failed in the end I wouldn't have been upset. Props to the developers for listening to their audience and doing a great job rebalancing the game. I can now say this ranks up there with the top 5 roguelike deckbuilders I've ever played. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: The main strentgh of this game, theme aside, is the combat. It feels very satisfying, and you have to be aware of what's happening all the time, because things can go very wrong very fast. Thankfully the game telegraphs the enemy's attacks. Don't get it wrong, this doesn't make a game easy, since it's balanced around this. It makes the game less BS, and you have to do anything you can to mitigate damage on your characters. This doesn't make the game a glorified Simon Says either, it's a good mechanic.When you use a skill, it gets disabled, and you have to recharge it. This sounds bad, but again, in practice is a good mechanic once you play with it. The way you upgrade skills is also interesting. You have to have one skill three times, and then it gets upgraded. There are plenty of ways to get skills, and it adds to the decission making of what you use the skill slots for.Sadly I'm not a roguelite guy, and this game isn't chaging my opinion for them. But that doensn't mean I don't enjoy the core gameplay. Characters are very unique, but sadly there aren't that much enemy variety, at least from what I have played. There are levels that get unlocked eveytime you clear the previous one, but all look and feel the same. I'll update the review if I see things changing.There are more things to talk about, like how you can cheat and drain an enemy's HP to 0, or swap statuses however you like (again, the game is balanced around this), but the review is long enough, I would say. Overall, a great turn-based game with fresh mechanics, I just don't feel the roguelite progression.

_childDocuments_.review: The other reviews cover the pros and cons of the game quite well, and I'd echo much of the same sentiment here.  Rogue Lords is a flawed gem.  The core offering shows a lot of promise, but the myriad of balancing issues and overall lack of common quality of life features leave the game in a state that cannot realistically be recommended at this point.If this was the state of the game in Early Access, I'd say that it has a ton of potential and would be something to keep an eye on.  Seeing these types of issues in a fully released product, however, raises the level of concern.  The response from the developers is the final straw in nudging this negative review (offering to tell players how to best exploit the game's mechanics because build variety is so severely limited to deal with the difficulty cliffs the game provides rather than acknowledging a problem exists and a providing commitment to fix it is not a reasonable mitigation to the underlying problems).This is a game I'd love to see fixed in updates, but it's not something I would recommend in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: A really great game!  Here are 2 reasons that make this game better than others in the genre:Your disciples start each fight fully healed.So why is this great?  In many similar games you carry over injuries from previous fight. This leads to a balancing where in most of the fights your goal is not to win the fight, but to win the fight with zero loses. Only boss fights are really fight to the “death”. SO most fight are kind of boring.  Rogue lords does not have this problem, nearly ever fight is tense and exciting.The diabolic essence mechanicDiabolic essence represents the life of your devil, but is also used as a resource to manipulate the world of the living in multiple ways. You can swap buffs and debuffs with it, you can heal your disciples or recharge their abilities. This is a really potent tool that can get you out of tough situations. But since this is also your life you really only what to use it, if you really need it.So why is this great?In games like this, randomness can throw you into really bad position and if you want the game to be challenging the randomness will sometimes put the player into unfair positions. The diabolic essence mechanic can mitigate this problem and allows for a challenging game, were you can get out a really tough positions for a prize.A few words on the topic of the difficulty curve, since some reviewers seem to think the game is too difficult:Using diabolic essence is not cheating! If you can swap a buff/debuff for 5 essence to avoid getting 20 damage to the devil, just do it! Once you realize that, the  game really isn’t that hard at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for March 2023, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before April 4th, 2023, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.An RPG version of Slay the Spire. Rogue Lords is going to look like yet another Slay the Spire title, and it borrows a lot from that game, especially the map design.  However, Rogue Lords also does a lot differently.  Instead of a card or a deck, players have three characters, and each uses attacks and skills.  Players are playing the Devil, using disciples like Dracula, fighting against Van Helsing, and trying to increase the terror.  And the design of the world is quite good.  It’s a unique idea. Yet with this being a rogue-lite, RNG is going to be important, and there appears to be a focus on getting three of each skill to level it up, meaning players may have to invest in certain abilities with the hope of getting a payoff that may never come.   Also, Rogue Lords talks about each book, their form of a run, having six chapters, which sounds like a lot, but the tutorial is far faster than a typical run.  Pick this up if you want yet another rogue-lite.  This is the issue I have.  I have so many rogue-lites I doubt I’d have space to add this to the rotation.  Nothing here jumped out at me as must-play, but if you have more time or really like the idea of a more RPG-style combat system as I’ve been showing here, check this out.  It’s an interesting twist on a common style.If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords has a non-traditional game mechanics, the in-game 'cheats' by the power of the Devil. You can use this power to do almost everything to help you win the game: depleting enemies HP/SP to 0, recovering our HP/SP, exchanging status, increasing success rate, changing path, and keep us alive. Though it sounds like cheating, it is surely the game mechanics. You may find this interesting. The power is limited to a currency. Using the power cost you depends on the cheat. It will reset every time you start a book. You can also recover in a fountain. It may also be changed by some events.It may looks like overpower, but No. How did I always be killed in the first book, in the easiest difficulty? I've been died in the final boss for a few times, and some before the final boss too. It is getting bored as I always repeat the first book and start with zero progress: stats reset, no good skill kept, no item kept, etc. There is a 'general' progress which could give you better skills in the game, but the starting always start zero, thinking like a deck of cards but your initial cards always the same. The good thing is you can change your characters if they're unlocked, so at least you can have new formation.This game was interesting, but it is ridiculously difficult. I cannot get pass the first book. Tried some tricks but nothing works.Though, it had been fun for my 10 hours. And perhaps, my future smarter version of me would come back to beat this.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a turn-based roguelite game. As Satan the prince of hell, your power has severely diminished after The Great Hunt. To reclaim what is righfully yours and remind the mortal the evil and despair once dominate the world, you send out the eight trusty disciples to retreat powerful artifacts lost in the war. The demon hunters will not go down easily. So optimize your disciples power to create synergies, spread chaos across the human world, and take revenge on your arch-nemesis Van Helsing. This game, is one of those "I wish it could be better" kinds of game for me. It really ticks a lot of my boxes:play as mythical creatures in a facinating turn-based battle, various skills to customize each disciples, events that are not only interesting but also beneficial, and a "demon mode" which is basically cheating. Sadly the difficulty spike between each night is still high, even after the massive tweak happened weeks ago. This fact solely dampen my enjoyment. That`s being said, I still recommend this game for its aesthetic and the direction it choose, but it truly deserves a mixed review.Powerful immortals live through the river of time. These are the disciples you have at your disposal, taking inspiration from various folklores, myths, and legends. Each of them possess inhuman power if you can match out the perfect synergy. Just take the starting three disciples for example: Headless Horseman, Count Dracula, and Blood Mary. Headless Horseman is your standard tank. He can easily redirect the incoming fires to himself, and even better, with each hit he takes, he can retaliate more damage back at his opponents. Count Dracula can be a wonderful support offering sustainbility and damage boost to his allies, and a terrifying beast, unleashing double the amount of attack when near death. Bloody Mary is a damage powerhouse, able to deal with two enemies, picking up the weakened one and severely wounded the rest, at a time with her mirror. These three can easily help you out the whole game, but there are still five more disciples waiting for you to discover their lethality and potentials.The main gimmick of the game. As a devil, you don`t play by the rule of mortals. With devil essence, you can distort and shift the reality with ease. Stealing powerful statuses from enemies, reducing their entire health bar to zero, raising your disciples back from near death, and rescaling the success ratio of social tests, there are many things you can do to turn the tide of battles to your favor. Be ware though, the devil essence is not unlimited. Players still need to use it wisely. If it reaches zero, you will be forced back to hell.The combat in Rogue Lords is quite interesting. There are five action points share among the three disciples. Every skill from the disciples require certain amount AP to use, and then the skill will be consumed when used. The disciples have to spend their main ability to recharge the skill. This system offers some insight of whether you should use up one of your disciple's skills at once or not. Is it worth it to go all out to take out the enemy`s damage dealer and leave the team to suffer some hefty status effects? Is it worth it to redirect the firepower or share the burden equally? Will I have enough AP to recharge my skills and also do some damage? These are the thought processes players need to take init consideration with each round of the combat.→Not the next Ancestor from Darkest Dungeon, but VA still does a great job.→Interesting Upgrade And Sacrifice System→The animation is smooth.→Social Tests is a fun mini game.→Especially in mid to late game, the difficulty seems to ramp up rapidly once you make past the first night. Enemies deal significantly more damage, have more health, and possess permanent buffs. Your disciples will often find themslves lacking the power to fight back. Even with the latest difficulty tweaks and updates, the problem is still there, more or less. It`s really discouraging to find out that avoiding the battles which are the most interesting part of the game, is the best way to ensure victory for each chapter.For a roguelite game, Rogue Lords currently does not have enough variant comparing to the total chapters it provide. The Social Tests and elite enemy team compositions could use more variety. I suggest adding chapter-specific events and unique enemy encounters. By doing so it not only helps differentiate the chapters more, but also spices up the replayability.Even after I finish the game, I genuinely still do not understand the purpose of implementing the top-down area traversal system. I like the appeal, but this feature does not serve any gameplay value whatsoever. I suggest adding some kind of mini games or secrets for players to actually explore the area besides going straight to the point of interest. Something like collecting wandering souls, scaring of any human beings, or even some sort of pre-battle preperation to help ease the incoming fight. →Needs a refresh option in the shop.→I wish all the dialogues are dubbed.→Please commentate on the other disciples as well.→Alt Skins For Other Disciples→Let us choose the three base level abilities for every disciple. This could open up more replayability and refreshing team comps.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is an absolute gem for fans of tactical roguelikes! The unique premise of playing as the Devil, controlling powerful evil entities like Dracula and Bloody Mary, adds a fresh, dark twist to the genre. The ability to manipulate the game’s rules to your advantage – bending reality to rewrite outcomes – feels both devious and empowering.Visually, the game is stunning, with dark, gothic art that perfectly captures the eerie atmosphere. The combat system is deep and rewarding, encouraging strategic thinking as you assemble your team of villainous disciples. Every run feels different, with a wide variety of choices, events, and outcomes, which keeps the gameplay exciting and unpredictable.The narrative is also fantastic, embracing the wicked theme without holding back. It’s not often you get to feel like the bad guy and have so much fun doing it! The difficulty is challenging but fair, giving you that satisfying roguelike thrill of improving over time.In short, Rogue Lords is a brilliantly crafted, devilishly fun game that offers a unique experience you won’t find anywhere else. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Rogue Lords is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rad and you should buy it.I'm absolutely baffled this is currently sitting at Mixed. This is an *excellent* game.If you've enjoyed titles like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, FTL or Tainted Grail, you'll get a kick out of this.This is a well thought out title, that introduces genuinely fresh and interesting mechanics. Devil mode let's you 'cheat' by swapping status with enemies, setting new paths, altering hit points ect. Your health is the resource, so you need to consider how to use it optimally in between shrines (sort of like StS campfires).You get to pick from different rewards for fights. Take some souls to spend at the 'merchant'? Grab some skills? Inflict terror which which has no benefit now, but pays off later?You unlock new disciples as you go, which each has unlockable skills and mechanics. Bloody Mary does ferocious damage, and you can mix in some debuffs if you like. The White Lady has passive effects and debuffs, but can also lean into large damage. The Horseman is a tank, and can unleash powerful abilities as they take more damage. Perhaps you prefer Lillith as a tank? Or maybe make her a tanky/debuffer/support. There's more disciples than what's listed here, and it's a really interesting mix of mechanics.The RNG is obviously there, but it feels much less punishing to me than Slay the Spire, a game which I enjoyed immensely. And I mean, that's part of the genre. You don't get the things you exactly want, but you'll get most of what you want, and you have to make up the rest with what you find, while managing your risks and opportunities. Sometimes you mess up, sometimes RNGesus is cruel, but as I've learned more about the game, I feel like every one of my lost runs was due to my inexperience.Looking back, I now feel like none (or very few) of them were to due bad RNG. Knowing what I do now, I feel like you get the tools and chances you need, but it's up to you to figure out how to put them together into a successful run.The things I'd change are it can be tricky navigating through some forest sections, but only slightly. I also feel like it should take less clicks to get through some screens, but it's fine really. What I'd really like to see is clear rewards/punishments from the social challenges.This is a fresh, interesting and unique entry to the genre. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed roguelite games such as ,  or  and are looking for another title to stratch that itch, look no further. has you take the mantle of the Devil, remotely controlling a party of his Disciples to bring terror upon mankind and take his revenge on a bunch of corrupt clergymen and demon hunters.The gameplay follows a fairly common formula : Pick your itinerary on a branching map, and stumble upon battles, shops, events, and story beats as you grow in power through traits, skills, relics, etc. Battles use an action point system ; you get 5 action points per turn for your entire party to share as you wish. Skills that get used get depleted, forcing you to take certain recharging actions to use them again. This, coupled with a very in-depth system of ailments and buffs of all kinds, makes for very interesting and complex gameplay. With a cherry on top.The main twist  brings to the table is the Devil Mode, which allows you to... cheat, essentially. If a battle goes awry, use some of your Essence to give your characters some health back. Or perhaps move a buff from an enemy to one of your Disciples. Unhappy with your itinerary on the map? Create a portal to the other side. Odds are against your success in an event? Oops, 100% success rate now. Of course, Essence is precious : You can only regain a certain amount at specific spots on the map, and it happens to double as your "True" Health Points : If it ever falls to 0, your run is over. But using it is well worth it, and it brings a lot of fun to the table, both in the form of a wonderful balancing act—figuring out how much you can cheat before it gets risky—on top of a great feeling of, well, unfair amounts of power.Naturally, since the game hands you that much power, it needs some backbone to take it. It's quite undeniably very spicy, enemies hit hard, use pesky buffs and debuffs and have loads of health. Elite fights and Boss fights have gimmicks that can be a real thorn on your side.I however do not think it's  hard. I think it's just right. A well-built, well-piloted team, with or without luck, will usually come out of harsh battles beaten and battered to the brink, but victorious nonetheless, and since your health, skills and all that gets restored between fights (with a small exception aside), that's perfectly fine. Enemies are very strong, but so are your Disciples. There are many ways to setup very strong teams, very strong combos, be it blasting your opponents so hard they can't hurt you much before they fall, or completely neutering anything they try to achieve, or even one-turn-killing.You are the Devil, after all. You can literally alter reality to give yourself an advantage. Your foes need to be stout to stand a chance. And stout they are.This game is well worth the purchase. Very complex and interesting combat, the overall themes and atmosphere are fun, art direction is very good, and it overall succeeds at giving you that feeling of overwhelming power when your team composition gets going, while still being challenging enough to make those high power levels satisfying to use.If you like turn-based RPG roguelites, don't mind your games to be a little bit spicy, and would enjoy making mortals bend to your will with the power of a little causality manipulation... Yeah, you probably should get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: We have one of those interesting situations here where you have a game you want to like because of the things its does well but cant like because it misses in crucial areas. The two major complaints about this game you'll see are the bugs and technical issues. Things like sound bugs and relics that just dont work for example. Its not acceptable at all but Im sure at some point in the near future it will be fixed. The other is the difficulty of the game. Im not so sure its that the game is hard but rather that the game heavily rewards some choices and punishes every other one that isnt that. By that I mean they want you to play the game one very specific way and nothing else will work very well if at all. This comes from design choices like the odd one sided scaling difficulty as you progress through the game. The enemies get stronger and by that just bigger numbers (more HP, damage etc) which is always a bad way to scale difficulty but you as the player dont get stronger. You do unlock skills and relics as you go but they arent a strict power increase and they unlock at a fixed time. So the enemies gain stats every win while your strength as the player stays pretty much the same. I have no idea why this system is even in this game and its like they picked at random from a rogue lite mechanics list and slapped it in. The issue with difficulty here is how narrow your options are to play the early game of each run. Play it the intended way or lose, sometimes lose anyways because RNG. Then the midgame rolls around if you make it and the difficulty drops off a cliff. Once you start to get skills and they get upgraded, maybe you nab a good relic or two the rest of the run is mindless DPS races with the enemies. This game is one of those games thats so close to being amazing but just barely doesnt get there. Its hard to say its a bad game but its definitely not a good one

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game on the very first Steam Next Fest and I am glad I did, it cought my interest immediately.The game lives by its theme, it has a demonic nature, observable everywhere, in its art, animations, music etc. The combat Animations are pretty great, so is the art, the music is catchy but nothing to write home about.It's structure is a mix between Slay the Spire and Darkest Dungeon. Map is STS-like, Combat is a bit like DD with regards to the skills (no cards/decks) and having multiple heroes but also like STS as it works with Action Points instead of a single Action per character, plus skills need to be recharged. It has many other unique elements and a clever and fun twist to all of it.i really liked my time with it. After 15-20 hours some repetition starts to sink in, granted there were 5 more Disciples I didn't play with yet, they seem to have quite unique and complex abilites and I just felt comfortable with the team I had at the time.Speaking of repetition, there are events that you'll see multiple times, which is no big deal but I the game could benefit by some additional variety. More combat and map environments, some animations outside of combat would probably suit the aforementioned events, some more character quips and I would honestly like a bit more story or more details. Perhpas these would be present with a bigger budget, I look forward to additional content or their next project.Voice Acting is brilliant, especially the Narrator did an outstanding job and with great vocabulary, very enjoyable, the discpiles I played with were great too. The game in general nails the atmosphere.It's quite challenging, but has an easier mode if you are struggling. It felt like I need to pull crazy combos and builds to win but at the same time I only lost 3 times in total and 2 were due to my own oversights. It's intimidating at first, seeing these huge attacks but if you are well equiped and learn how to manage your resources you should be fine most of the time. So I think the balance overall is fine.Definitely recommend, even if you don't like the roguelike/lite genre maybe give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I was interested in this game after playing the demo during a Steam demo week. Love the theme, good music, interesting mechanics. They fixed a lot of the performance issues I saw during the demo week, so thus far no major bugs. A minor bug where sounds keep playing long after they should stop happens, but it's something that can be fixed. I feel this game has a lot of potential and will continue to play it because I love games in this genre.However, there's what I'd call glaring design issues that are just killing my enjoyment of the game.#1 There's essentially 2 "health" stats, life and spirit. Since damage done by enemies are going to be either, you can't beef up one stat, because as soon as you run into an enemy that does damage of the other type, you'll die. I'm not inherently against this design decision, but it's an extra difficulty hurdle that just gives you more to manage in a RNG rogue-lite game. The problem with this system, comes from issue #2.#2 If you lose 1 disciple, the run is over. Given the party size is 3, having to manage 3 heroes worth of stats/skills/gear in a RNG rogue-lite game is tricky, but a fun challenge. However, I keep finding myself losing runs just because I'm taking multiple high damage hits in a health stat that I've just not been able to raise high enough for a character (once again, due to having to juggle 2 health stats between 3 heroes.Issue #1 isn't as much of an issue if issue #2 were to be changed to requiring your entire party wipe before the run ends. Often times in multiple hero based games like this, when a hero is "defeated" in battle, they obtain a negative trait/perk (which is already a system in this game) as a death penalty. Simply removing them from combat when they die, and then giving them a negative trait if you end up winning the battle is the change I think I'd want to see right now.#3 "Multiple" hits can kill you in 1-turn, thus negating the utility of the "vulnerable" system. The first time one of your heroes goes to 0 in either HP/SP, they enter a vulnerable state. That's great, it gives you a chance to avoid being 1-shot. However, if that 1-shot ends up hitting multiple times, then you just flat out die if the damage being done exceeds the pool of health stat being depleted, and I think this is the issue.The change I'd like to see would be that when a character enters a vulnerable state, no further damage can be done to them (including debuffs) that turn, so you at least have 1 more turn to try and resolve the situation. This effect could be limited to 1 time per combat to avoid cheesing vulnerable states if issue #3 were to be changed so multiple hits don't just end you. It's not about making the game easier, just rather making the system put in place actually work better.#4 Overall balance and tuning of encounters seems a bit too heavy handed for the first act. Some encounters just feel like boss fights that you have to use devil power to get through no matter how good your run is going. Reaching the final act boss only to wipe due to the other issues mentioned is just super frustrating because it just feels like the balance of the game is off, rather than my play style is just wrong or I've not grinded out enough runs to unlock items to actually win.Right now, I'm not sure what I need to do to beat the first boss encounter other than unlocking way more characters to hopefully find better synergies between them. However for the first act in a game, I just think that's not good design. Hitting brick walls so fast and early in a game in this genre is just really frustrating, especially when there's so many others that do it way better.Anyways, that's my initial review after playing for 5 hours, and getting to the end of the first act multiple times, but just not seeing any path forward other than to keep grinding and hopefully unlocking new mechanics or characters that can be used to beat the boss encounter. I do like the game and want to keep playing it, but right now it's just not a recommend without some major reworks I think.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is solid and clearly a lot of sincere effort was put into it. There are many interesting mechanics and I love the idea behind Devil Mode, but overall the game seems somewhat unpolished.Let's start with Devil Mode.As shown in the trailer, Devil Mode allows you to change some of the stuff in the UI at the cost of your own Hit Points. There are several ways to use it - during a fight, to create an alternate path forward, or during a Social Activity.The Social Activity one I use the most and I'm certain most players will as well. It allows you to max out the odds of success.You don't NEED to max out the odds, but not only do you get nothing from it if you fail (other than the trait listed at the start, which is a minor benefit, albeit a stacking one), but it causes a Threat (basically a meta debuff, like losing some money) to appear on the map (maybe it has a list of options, not just a Threat, but I have no intention of actually checking as I'll never intentionally visit a Social Activity when I have a chance of failure).I only failed once, just to check the outcome, but with that knowledge, I always just max out the odds, which costs 5HP per 30% increase (so usually 10HP) and it's not difficult to avoid these Activities, if you don't feel like using your health.While I didn't do it often, Devil Mode in fights is a VERY powerful tool... under the right circumstances, which are not always obvious (makes sense, this is a puzzle/strategy game, so you do need to spend some time figuring out the correct/best line of actions).DifficultyThis is a quite the subject and definitely requires more playtime than I have. Still, I'll present my initial impressions.I did notice that the enemies have a pattern (some of them, at least), however, for the most part it felt very random. You could just get unlucky and every enemy simply decided to use an AoE attack for an insane amount of damage. I did some save-scumming for this (for those that don't know: you can turn off the game mid-fight, launch the game again, and it loads the last save, which is the start of that fight): Sometimes I would just "die" on turn one, because, like I said, enemies decided to drop a tactical nuke on me. Other times, after restarting that same fight (everything is randomized each time), I would just breeze through it, because they would spend their turns doing nothing but apply various buffs and/or debuffs.Anyway, setting those extremes aside (something the devs should definitely look into patching out via improved AI behavior), the first few Chapters of every Book felt relatively well balanced. It's the latter ones where things start to fall apart (including the debut of the aforementioned extremes).That stems from scaling. You either need to upgrade the Skills of your Disciples to keep up with the enemies or hope to find relics that do it for you. I have completed three Books and all of them involved upgrading defensive skills to survive and relying on Relics to scale damage (because Relics can provide infinite offensive scaling, which cannot be said about defence).Important to note, that because I haven't played for very long, it's very possible that alternative win formulas than the one I relied on exist. It's just what worked for me with the options available.Still, I was able to find scaling Relics in 2/3 of the Books I played (I probably could have had it in all 3, had I realized the need) and if you fail to find scaling damage, you encounter a different problem...PacingThe game is slow and repetitive. I haven't unlocked all the characters and I'm already tired of the ones I have. Throughout the run you get a very limited number of Skills. Which is further impacted by the max limit of abilities you can have at any given time. This rebounds back into the scaling issue - you need 3 copies of the same ability to upgrade it, but you cannot afford the space to keep duplicates with you.Each run takes a while - around 3 hours each, by the looks of it - and during every fight you go through the same cycle of abilities: 1) Heal any vulnerable Disciple2) Mitigate incoming damage3) Recharge abilities (to ensure availability to do 1 and 2 next turn)4) Deal damageDue to the limited number of abilities, each of the steps is going to be mostly identical. The fact that enemies feel mostly identical doesn't help - deal damage or apply status. Yes, there are many unique abilities, but those most often revolve around increasing the damage the enemies deal.And in the second half of a Book, the fights become straight up tedious, if you fail to find any damage scaling from your side, especially the boss - dealing 1000 points of damage 15 damage at a time isn't very engaging.And that's all I have to say. The TL;DR is that the core gameplay is solid, but a fairly large amount of polish is still required for the game to be "good", IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally enjoyed this game, but I get why not everyone would. The tutorial in particular is really slow and is a 'click this, now this, now purposefully mess up so we can teach you how to fix this and you can't do anything else' for like, half an hour to 45 minutes. I bet this game is also particularly difficult for people who aren't used to playing roguelite deck builders since it was pretty easy for me to figure out how to build the characters and what was worth avoiding, but there's a lot of different combos between skills + relics (which give you different bonuses) that could be overwhelming. I liked (most of) the characters, the 'terror' system was relatively well implemented granting better skills + relics the more it levels up, the game was challenging but didn't feel particularly unfair, save for the notorious 6th boss fight. I didn't find much use for the headless horseman, the creature, or baron, but I'm confident enough that if I played with them longer I'd find some insane/broken builds for them. The art/style was also great, and I loved playing as the baddies. The limited amount of voicelines did get a little grating by the end of the game, and I was a bit dissapointed the headless horseman didn't have an irish accent despite being described as an irish soldier in the lore blurbs on each character, but each other characters abilities, stats, and voicelines felt fitting. What didn't feel too well thought out was the trait system, the positive traits were good but the negative traits didn't really impact much, usually just a -1 to social interaction stats which have no impact on combat. I never had more than 2 negative traits on a character at once, and there are several opportunities to get rid of them during the game. There's about two dozen unique social events in the game that rewards you traits for passing/failing, so it felt fairly varied throughout each playthrough. What I don't agree with some of the other reviews about is the RNG. The combats can be kind of swing-y depending on if the enemies decide to buff or all decide to attack your weakest combatant at once. But, for that and for everything else in the game there's a resource pool that lets you move around buffs, debuffs, health, the chances of passing social checks (to get those positive traits), recharging your depleted abilities, and you can even jump to different points on the map. That resource pool is like your overall HP since it goes down if your characters take damage past their HP/SP and if it goes to 0 you lose, and if you aren't using its potential, you're going to have a bad time. There are a few bugs (particularly visual bugs with the devil mode), but very rarely did they impact the core mechanics of the game. Granted I played this in the summer of 2023, so I don't know how buggy the game was on release, or if the combat or RNG really was horribly broken. I played the game on the 'normal' mode out of easy/normal, and I lost about 5 times, providing a fairly challenging experience granted that each 'chapter' takes a good few hours.30$ Canuck bucks is also a bit expensive for me, 10$cad on sale is a decent price, but I got a steal getting this for a super heavy discount from humble bundle.  Overall, this game is like a 8.5/10 for people like me who enjoys these types of games, and probably a 4/10 for anyone trying to get into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall 10/10 - The characters are fun, the story is interesting enough with enjoyable commentary by the Devil and there is quite a large mix of viable strategies. Even at higher difficulties.Despite what some reviews may say, this game is balanced quite well. Those who think otherwise are likely not playing smart. And this game does demand smart play at higher levels. That means choosing the right skills and relics pending how the random factor plays out. Just that if play too haphazardly, you might miss a critical debuff in combat that has a huge affect or you might choose a relic that does not support the skills you have chosen well enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords takes the Roguelite element to new horizons. Welcome to the Devil's Lair, disciple. Brought back from playing your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ backlog to serve the first angel and destroy humanity, were you? Fear not, for I will tell you everything that you need to know to do precisely just that in this... very evil review, muhahaha!Ahem, excuse the cringe, on with the review. Rogue Lords, as its name implies, is a very roguelike / roguelite centered; and when you hear roguelike, you hear "I'm going to die a lot and hate my life over and over again until by some miracle of godly intervention I make it past where I was stuck for 3 runs straight!".You are the Devil; in what seems to be the apocalypse approaching, the Devil, sent back into the world of the living, must gather his own artifacts of power that were scattered by the lightbearers. Your main hub is the devil's lair, where you do nothing but check stats of your disciples  and choose the next mission. However, the devil is quite weak that's why he must send his own disciples into quests to find those artifacts in an attempt to recover his lost power... and once that happens, doomsday is at hand. Who's going to try to stop him? A sanctuary of light, erected by the follower of the Sanctua Lumen; hordes of witch-hunters, priests, clerics, archbishops and inquisitors armed to the teeth.In brief, each artifact requires you to go in a lengthy quest (or run, whatever you wanna call it), which occurs in a sort of "book-like" chapter-based adventure. That adventure, however, is completely randomly generated. Your followers will all basically synergize, expect for the RNG that plays into what skills they'll be getting in each adventure. The combat is very cool-looking, and your characters, despite being generic themselves, will have a panel called "Social Skills"; More on that later, now let's talk about the quest.Each quest is detailed inside a book in which you control your three disciples in a topdown fashion. There are events that happen while you're doing that and multiple routes to choose from; events that require you to use your disciples' social skills to resolve situations and get either negative or positive traits from them... a shopkeeper you can meet to trade your collected souls for skills or items, combat etc... Social Skills of your disciples can be useful to resolve these events without wasting your lifepoints, simply called the Devil's Essence. Combat is basically Rogue Lords in all its grandeur; your disciples have battle skills unique to them! To kill the followers of Sanctua Lumen, you have to either deplete their HP or their SP, so you have to build your team around doing that. So many followers of light have the ability to heal, but you've got the ability to cast Zombie, which turns heals into damage... Anyways, after winning a fight you either get bonuses in the map called Terror Influence, you get new skills OR you get souls (the game's currency). However, there's a lot of strategy that goes into combat! When it's your turn, everything is laid out for you, how much damage you'd be taking, what skills are going to be cast the next turn, and you have to carefully study each of these actions to be able to prepare a reaction for them. That doesn't mean that strategizing efficiently will win you every battle, because sometimes you're out of skills and you'll just lose regardless. You can't shoot if you're out of ammo, right? Sometimes all you need to do is pray for the RNG God to help alter the outcome of a battle, so if you're not a believer then I urge you to start now lolNow why is combat so fun in this game? The Devil's power! That's right, you can interfere directly with the course of battle by using what is called "Cheat" (it's the devil's power's name lol). With cheat, you can swap around buffs and debuffs at the expense of the devil's essence... Think of it like those kids who cheat in VAC-protected games; they know the price and they're willing to pay it for a small temporary satisfaction... Sometimes, buffs that are cast by the enemies are so annoying, so one way to deal with them is exchanging them with debuffs affecting your own party. It's very fun to cheat fate!!All in all, Rogue Lords is an amazing roguelike game that gets a  score, and I'm not even big on these sadistic roguelike games but I do find this game quite addictive; the characters are very charming, their interactions with the events are unique and the Devil himself is very charismatic! I never thought I'd be saying that, ever haha but here we are! Get this game, play it and don't be mad if you lose all your progress a room before the boss.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguelites have taken the gaming world by storm in recent years and I’m certainly not upset by it. Death as a part of your journey as opposed to being the end of it brings with it a considerable amount of replay value as you hone your strategy with new tools after each loss. Tangible gains after each run are the defining feature as you continue to unlock more exciting options for future attempts at victory. Rogue Lords takes the best of the genre and creates a familiar yet new experience by combining the successful ideas of the past with an engaging horror atmosphere to make its own unique experience.As with most roguelikes, Rogue Lords has an overarching plot that defines the narrative but each run is different in its events. This time around there are different books, or adventures, that you can choose from that flavor the big story events within them but they have a relatively minor role when compared to the generated elements. The central thread here is that you are The Devil and you’ve returned from banishment by Van Helsing after a rough encounter with him where he pulled out all of the stops. Perhaps unsurprisingly, even without The Devil and his monsters around, humanity has continued on with its trend of being absolute ♥♥♥♥♥ to one another. A fanatical religious sect has taken over and forced itself onto the population as they build their churches and burn those they deem heretics across the land. Sometimes they catch a follower of darkness while at other times they’re simply tormenting the innocent needlessly. The world’s not doing great even without him, but the return of the Prince of Darkness is surely toward the bottom of everyone’s Christmas list this year.Although he’s very influential over the world of mortals, The Devil tends to delegate to his most trusted disciples when he needs a more hands-on approach. These disciples aren’t just any Tom, ♥♥♥♥, or Harry either, and you’ll likely recognize them from classic works. Their ranks include such legends as Vlad Tepes Dracula, Dr. Frankenstein, and The Headless Horseman, among several others. I found their voice lines to be entertaining and faithful to their origins even if they could have used a few more of them to spice things up. As much as I love the line, “I heard you, you call me three times,” hearing it a dozen or more times every fight got a bit old.Rogue Lords involves branching paths that lead to a variety of locations that offer varying benefits and challenges. This is similar to what we’ve seen in titles like Slay the Spire and FTL, though the key difference here is that you actually control your party as they move between locations as if it were an action RPG instead of instantly jumping from point to point. On one hand, I can see this being meant to further immerse you in the interesting setting that you’ve been placed into. On the other, it often feels like you’re wasting your time as you trek through randomly generated worlds that don’t look all that different from one another.The party-based system of this title offers plenty of variety for building groups that synergize well together. As you travel down these paths, you’ll be able to build them up from a small standard selection of skills and poor attributes to brutal powerhouses of your own design. Traits, attributes, and skill loadouts all go into making your disciples your own. It’s important to note that Rogue Lords is not a card game and each loadout is a selection of skills that is always available as long as you have them recharged with the needed action points remaining.Traits more often than not come from event locations that play out like short, multiple-choice visual novel scenes. A set of attributes are used to determine which options each character is skilled with such as how terrifying or deceptive they are. The higher their skill the more likely they are to succeed at a related task. It feels like a tacked-on system at times, but I have to admit that these events are quite fun and offer some great rewards. You often received maximum health benefits and permanently boosted damage modifiers which drastically increase your combat efficiency.Souls are the currency that you’ll collect in Rogue Lords. When you’re lucky enough to meet with the Grim Reaper, he’ll trade you new skills and relics, as well as “borrowing” a skill of your choice to cheaply upgrade it for the next time that you meet. All of these options can offer solid bonuses, so the more souls that you can get your wicked hands on, the better.Combat is a turn-based affair that consists of the player having action points to split among their party as they see fit and enemies that carry out one action each per turn. Health is split into physical and spiritual; once either of these types is depleted, a character will become vulnerable. A vulnerable enemy will die upon suffering that type of damage again while a vulnerable disciple will start stealing the amount they are damaged from the Devil’s Essence pool to stay alive. You aren’t defeated on a disciple by disciple basis in Rogue Lords, you only lose a run once your Devil’s Essence has been completely drained.Devil’s Essence has more uses than simply acting as your disciples’ emergency health reserve. It can also be used at will as a source of mana to “cheat” and give yourself an advantage in a variety of situations. In combat you might use it to shift a disciple or enemy’s health up or down or to move buffs and debuffs around freely. Outside of combat you are able to use it to boost success choices in story events and to teleport between paths that don’t connect to one another.Disciples skills come in a wide variety and every disciple has their own unique selection. The starting party consists of a bloodthirsty leader who brings strong party buffs, a tank fellow who seems to have lost his head, and a mirror-based murder machine. I’ll let you figure out who’s who but they’re all capable of specializing in very different ways from one run to the next as they progress. I’ve found that whether you’re going hybrid to strike at both the spiritual and physical health of enemies or if you’re building for one both builds tend to work, but you should always have at least a skill or two to hit the other when you might end up facing off against enemies that are particularly resistant in one of the categories.Rogue Lords has succeeded in carving out a space for itself on the digital roguelike shelf. It’s familiar enough for genre veterans to hop right in but it’s unique enough that it doesn’t directly compete with the long-standing heavyweights. I recommend this title to anyone who’s looking for a new experience in a similar vein to Slay the Spire especially if the horror theme counts for bonus points for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is punishingly difficult despite it's playful art style.  I don't mind the difficulty, but I do mind that so much of the difficulty is the result of RNG.Here are just a few things that are based entirely on RNG...Skill selection (via the Reaper shop).Skill availability (via mission rewards).Buffs (given at the start of mission sections).Debuffs (also given at the start of mission sections).Event outcomes (based on percentages)All are based on RNG in one form or another. _childDocuments_.review: A pretty good rogue style game, but the overall difficulty and complex interactions of each character are probably too off putting for casual play. Playing as the Devil who narrates a struggle against the Van Helsing, you employ infamous figures of darkness from legend, tales, and myth to wreak havoc against an equally corrupt holy order and attempt to reclaim your artifacts from Van Helsing after your defeat by him. There is no glossing over it, you are playing evil beings in a dark version of the New World, and the concept is just great.The game features some nice stylish art and decent voice acting, although the latter is very repetitive and the voicework for Baron Samedi doesn't fit well. Music is good too.Much as any rogue style game, you're mixing skill and luck in an effort to cobble together a synergistic strategy as you make your way through around six chapters to fight a boss at the end to get the artifact. You have options to guide your path, such as inflicting terror to gain more artifacts and scene bonuses, get more souls to trade with the grim reaper for powers, or simply take a skill for defeating your enemies. Generally this works. You will, however, get a 'bad hand' every so often where the skills and relics you really need won't show up. Unfortunately, you might not know this until late in the chapters when you've already sunk several hours of play.So, the biggest issue with Rogue Lords is the difficulty. Fights are really just too sloggish because your characters are surprisingly wimpy on their own. You need those good outcomes to build anything, as the enemy is obnoxiously tanky and can win fights by attrition if you're not careful. You can choose of 3 unlocked villains to play with, but they don't all work together very well in terms of their skills, so you need to coordinate who you use. As in many rogue games, beginnings are particularly bad and boring... your characters are such wienies and have no starting options beyond whatever you win going forward. This makes new chapter starts dull and monotonous. It's also worth noting your characters tend to get a lot of DoT (damage over time) abilities that do not scale much at all, while the same enemy hitpoints and damage keep rising higher and higher. This feels like an obvious oversight. By the later levels, if you haven't built for direct damage, you're not going to overcome how utterly defensive the enemy is. Even on Apprentice difficulty by the fifth storyline, you're going to struggle unless you're obsessive in your strats. Sadly, team build diversity is very poor in this title. For all the randomness, you're almost forced to pick certain team comps for the higher bosses. It's a strong sign of the combat's notably poor balance.I love the style of this and it has a lot of potential, but it desperately needs updating and tweaks in the combat gameplay. I've read rumors that it's been abandoned, which is a real shame. I've variously enjoyed myself and have been bored out of my mind with Rogue Lords... so much is luck based and the excessively repetitive long fights aren't winning it any favors. There is fun to be had and the idea is interesting, but unpolished game mechanics, bad luck, and overly weak ability pacing can devolve into frustration easily.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  Brilliant art direction but abysmal game design.I would dearly like to enjoy this game, but I simply cannot.  It's gorgeous and has character oozing from every byte, but the wild difficulty spikes -- even on the supposedly easy Apprentice mode -- make it unplayable.  Additionally, there's a really bizarre mechanic which serves only to add frustration to your strategy, wherein draining all the hit points from an enemy doesn't kill them.  No, you have to hit them AGAIN.  This may not sound like a big deal, but it profoundly affects your turn-by-turn strategy when you have only a very few skills and action points available on any given turn.  Add to this the fact that if just ONE of your three characters falls, it's game over.  Not the round, the entire game.   Bad player!  Start over, you!  Yeah... no thanks.I've tried several times to get into it, but I just keep quitting in frustration and going back to Slay the Spire.  THAT is how you design a fun game.  The art in StS may look like it was drawn by an autistic 12 year-old, but it's really fun to play.  And in the end, that's all that matters.  Sorry, Rogue Lords; you coulda been a contender.
