_childDocuments_.review: I've found this game very enjoyable but it is quite difficult and it's entirely possible to make mistakes that lead to a chapter becoming seemingly impossible to complete.  You must make the right choices for your current build and composition.  You must be able to debuff, you must be able to damage - of both types at times -, you must be able to remove buffs (without the use of your diabolic essence).  Balance is the key as if you tip too far in one direction and ignore the others, running across a certain elite will ruin your day.  You must also understand how the debuff/buff types remove each other as you can use your own debuffs/buffs on enemies (and your own minions) to remove a buff/debuff you couldn't otherwise  It has a good tutorial, but especially in your first few hours of figuring out Rogue Lords, the game feels balanced around the ability to crash the game and restart it to rework the strategy for a fight.  If you don't make use of this you will almost certainly lose hours and hours to chapters that were otherwise winnable, becoming quite frustrated at the same time  Reading the tooltips is critical so be sure to approach battles carefully and read the intentions of your opponents. This is not a game to be charged through or you will have a bad time  There are a few minor bugs (with sound) and the graphics can be a little choppy at times during transitions, but the meat of the game is the strategy, deck building, and interesting events. And the meat is good! Just be sure not to choke on it

_childDocuments_.review: I'm extraordinarily disappointed by the game. It has a lot of potential and was very promising, but it is just empty. The feeling of progression is non-existent, to the point where it's the opposite that's happening. I'll get to that later. First, let's adress the main issue : the randomness and the frustration it creates.There's a lot of ways to win in the games, but if you're unlucky, none of them will be available. It's okay. If you lose, you can just try again, that's the point of a die and retry. Except, here, you don't really gain anything by starting over, and this is the second issue : the lack of progress.You unlock three things through losing AND winning in the game : unlockable relics, unlockable skills, and new characters. More characters means more options, that's nice. More unlockable means more randomness, making the game harder and less stable, which also leads to more frustration for the player. Now, of course, if you manage to succeed, you will move on the story, and that's nice. You may argue that your own knowledge and skill as a player progress, or that the new unlockable are somehow better than the previous random ones and that I just have to try until I get a run with them, and I'd call out your bs. That's not how it should work. The game shouldn't get harder, unstable and more random as I play. It should become more challenging, asking me to think more and play better. After succeeding a chapter, everything you have won for your disciples will reset, meaning you will just have to start with the base stats and skills everytime. As a player, you barely have control on what's going on, and that's just sad. You should have the ability the choose things, to prepare your disciples before hand, something, not just NOTHING. This is just sad.Now, for the last part, this is subject to interpretation. I haven't played that much, but I quickly noticed that most of the events share the same arts and / or character skins. I would like to say that I think it's a bit lazy, but as I content creator I understand that this type of work tends to be dull and grueling. In a nutshell I wish the events and characters had more variety.I can see that a lot of work and love went into the game, but I'm afraid it's a failure as it stands. I couldn't find any enjoyment playing it. Most aspect of the game could and should be improved so that it becomes at least enjoyable / playable. This feels like an unfinished project. I'll probably not play this game again and will definitely not recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: If comparable in design to Slay the Spire, Rogue Lords has more depth to its mechanics and adds some features that render it unique and worth the experience.The team being composed of three disciples allows for many combos, role experimentations and build options. While each disciple has a core mechanic or a damage focus (HP, SP, or both), the sheer number of skills allow them to fit many roles in a team. There are obvious choices for successful teams and roles, but any character can shine in its own way and carry you through a run. Relics can also play a big part in a way or another, maybe even switch your build focus mid-run. Just like other rogue-likes, mistakes are punishing. You’re better thinking twice than rush in and put an end to your run towards revenge. However, the depth of mechanics can make it troublesome for beginners, or people not accustomed to this kind of game. I’d then advise you to read carefully, every time you’re doing something meaningful. Even reading events is important to get the best reward you expect to get. With just this bit of care and experience, you’ll be able to get through the game, even with subpar builds or against a poor rng. However, be advised, there is no difficulty setting yet, and the game can only become harder through the completion of books, out of 7, even previous ones.Now, the Devil Essence. This resource looks like nothing I’ve already seen and adds a nice flavour to the genre. While it allows you to cheat with the UI under a dozen circumstances to ease your pain and min-max the run, it’s also a pool to absorb your mistakes. Don’t abuse it, don’t drain it, keep a safe amount, and you’ll likely reach the end of the book. You’ll be able to replenish it in numerous ways, so don’t be shy to ever use it either.You may like it or not, but I find the character design gorgeous, and the animations are top-notch. While it’s not at the core of a rogue-like, it adds a bit of immersion and pleasure to the eye that really is a soft candy in such a harsh world. The music is solid and complements the atmosphere of the game quite well. Voice acting is well done, especially the devil, even if he has no patience at all while you’re thinking about your build for a few minutes.Bugs are a thing, as usual so early after launch, but the team is working on them and is prompt to give workarounds until it’s fixed. The team is also happy to advise if you struggle in your runs, and listens carefully to suggestions to improve the game experience. We can expect QoL improvements and UI clarifications in the next updates. There are hopes of extensions to bring new disciples, enemies, relics and so on to increase the already good replayability of the game.Overall it’s a challenging game that remains fun all along, once you get the grip on it.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like the game at first and even recommended it, but after completing 75% of the game all I can say is - its a dumbed down, boring version of Slay the Spire mixed with Iratus but somehow with less content in it. It took things from both games but ended up worse than any of those two.For example, here you control 3 characters but will use and upgrade mostly 1 or 2 because of the lack of AP/Mana. So I dont see how is it better than having just 1 character. The synergies are almost nonexistent between characters.The "cheating" mechanic also gets boring really fast once you figure out the best way to use it.RNG can easily ruin your run failing 90% skill checks. Its at the level of X-COM where you can fail 90% skill check several times in a row.There is no difficulty settings, the game increases the difficulty by itself as you progress with the story and theres no way to reduce it, so prepare to fight enemies with +40% HP/SP on a regular basis.Theres also no meta progression, so if youre struggling at the very beginning - it will only get worse unless you "git gut" and start abusing the same broken characters(Bloody Mary). Basically, you can complete the whole game with the exact same set of characters and tactic because nothing changes between the Books(story chapters) apart from bosses which are also static. You can only unlock a couple of new characters, relics and skills, but you dont really need those to complete the game. So the replayability is nowhere near the level of StS or Iratus.All in all, its a very mediocre game. There are games better than this one at the market.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed here but there seems to be more good than bad. Lots of neat moving parts for tactical battles, and the variety of Disciples/characters leads to a lot of choice in builds and satisfying combos. The balance is manageable if you're experienced with strategy games (albeit seemingly biased towards SP builds), and the graphical style/lore tidbits/story elements work really well together. Plus, there's enough largely original elements (skill recharge system, devil mode, terror, skill upgrades, dual health bars) for it to feel like something new.I do have one major issue, and that's the run length. Runs can drag on, in part due to the large amount of events per book, as well as slow animations, lots of loading screens or meaningless clicking between events, and the map system dragging out time. This makes battles eventually feel like slogs, and makes it feel all the more frustrating when you make a silly mistake and kill your whole run or are blown up by the final boss. If there was a fast mode here, I'd highly recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a punishing rogue-Lite with a steep learning curve, but also provides an equally fun and rewarding experience. Rogue Lords' signature addition to the rogue-lite formula are the Devil Powers. Allowing the player to make deals with the devil in order to turn defeat into success. Cheating for a Faustian price. For me, the devil powers were so unique, and added so much depth to the strategy, that it alone justifies this game's existence and makes it worth the price of admission.Is your character about to die? Heal them. 30% chance of success to complete a challenge? Cheat and slide the value to 100%.Don't like where you are on the map? Use the devil powers and teleport to where you want to go.This system adds a lot of flexibility to a game that can feel rigid in it's difficulty. The risk reward nature of it makes every failure feel like it was your fault, because at some point, there was someway to turn the odds in your favor... and you didn't.Admittedly, there are some janky aspects to anticipate when purchasing...CONS *A mouse to move navigation system - can we get a WASD patch, please?*A lot of unskippable dialogue*The default normal difficulty of the encountersBut, despite those choices (I'm not even going to call them issues), I can tell there is a lot of love that went into this game. PROS*The Devil Powers system is an awesome, innovative mechanic *Huge diversity of builds and strategies*Replayability*Great Theme and Art Style

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Changed to "not recommended". It's just too frustrating to be honest. By the time you unlock the final characters you wonder why you should ever use them. The Boss I just fought hat 1,500 HP/SP, was constantly spawning high damage adds, buffing itself every 2 turns and preventing me from actually PLAYING the game (do not damage the enemy more than 5 times, do not debuff the enemy, do not play more than TWO skills per turn or else you get a massive hit to your SP). It was honestly unwinnable. A battle of attrition you can only lose when you get bombarded with 40x3 SP damage from just the boss plus another multi hit from 1 or 2 adds she constantly summons. And since you can't actually play to your strengths, because you get massively punished, it's just not ... fun. To be honest. I don't understand why the devs felt the need to just make the story mode this harsh (I was breezing through all other fights, didn't need Devil power etc. just to get cockblocked after about 2 hours at the final boss), instead of offering difficulty modifiers like any other "rogue lite" to make the runs more challenging (and more rewarding) IF you want to. As I said below though: Replaying the same chapters over and over again is boring. This game should have a story mode and an actual rogue-lite mode where bosses and enemies get mixed, where you can add and remove modifiers and increase HP/SP, etc.Thank the Lord for Cheat Engine ... otherwise I'd have long just uninstalled this one. Which is sad, because the presentation is SO good. But if there's no reason for me to actually test out different load outs in a sort of endless mode ... yeah. Pass.I wish I could give this a "neutral" rating. For 20 bucks I've already gotten 10 hours out of enjoyment out of it and am "only" halfway through.I do believe this game has an identity crisis though. It's more like a traditional turn based combat RPG, but with shoehorned in rogue-lite elements.These elements make the core of the gameplay of course. Different events, skills, relics, encounters, etc. all pretty much random to an extent.But I feel they are a bit contradicting the actual story element of the game, in that you have 6 chapters that get unlocked after you win the preceding one.Currently there doesn't seem to be any reason to play previous chapters again. The only difference in chapters are the 6 or 7 story dialogues anyway. And the final boss of course, which is unique to each chapter.Other than that everything plays out exactly the same way. You advance from node to node, you fight, you clear events, etc.And since the difficulty of ALL chapters actually increases after every completed chapter there's no point in returning to an earlier chapter to perhaps make unlocking more skills, relics or characters easier to beat the harder levels.It would have made sense to make the current chapter harder ... but even here I would have preferred actually different encounters or deepened game mechanics, etc.But you fight the same enemies as in chapter 1, complete the same events, and so on.A lot of wasted potential, since there are two progression paths: one for simply playing the game, which is fine, the other for completing several achievements, which can ... technically ... lock you into a state of not being able to progress since the difficulty is too high for you to unlock them perhaps. That's just my feeling though. You might not even need those skills or relics, and having unlocked them doesn't mean you will find them during a run anyway, but still ...The design is pretty great, everything feels, sounds and looks great, combat is a lot of fun, and once you have a working combination it's a joy to see your strategy pay off. What is NOT fun though are the so-called "Fanatics". Who thought it'd be a good idea to include those bastards in the game?A fanatic basically makes all other enemies invulnerable until you deplete BOTH his hit point gauges THREE times in total. There are hit points and spiritual points, which act as two separate life bars for ALL other creatures apart from this one. Normally I'd say you focus your character build on ONE type of damage, otherwise enemies will quickly overwhelm you, because you spread your damage too thinly and would effectively be working on two different enemies at once, instead of focusing one down, which in my experience, turns out to be absolutely deadly to your cause.In any case, that's a whopping 150 HP and 150 SP ONLY to make the other enemies vulnerable, enemies that happily wail away at you and get stronger every turn in the meantime and can at best be temporarily debuffed.Since the game's other enemies don't work that way, encountering a fanatic is akin to a death sentence ... and I haven't yet found any pattern in which fights they'll appear. Heck, every elite encounter is easier than those asshats.Even with your "cheater" bar, the devil mode, this is basically setting you up for instant death if you have to spread around debuffs (which are also damage) instead of fighting the main threat.Maybe I'm missing something. In any case, the game could be expanded upon, but the only way I see how is if they either include randomized daily dungeons of a sort or bring out a proper expansion in the future, otherwise the time investment is too high to continue playing imho (a run takes 2 to 3 hours easily). Too much repetitiveness, too much sameyness, since the story doesn't really hold your attention that much.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is tough to review. Combat is fun, as is the diabolic essence mechanic that lets you essentially spend true health to bend the rules. There are some truly ridiculous synergies to discover, and the difficulty isn't unreasonable once you realize the importance of defensive buffs.The sound is atrocious. The seventeenth time you hear a voice line in the first mission, you're gonna mute the voices. And then when you realize the music doesn't vary between areas, you'll mute that, too. Story is a fun premise and it doesn't live up to it. It might as well be nonexistent.The sense of progression sucks, too. It's basically "get a new skill after every moderately long run".Ultimately, the game play is fun enough, but the game itself doesn't feel polished, or... finished. I don't recommend it for now, but it has potential. The devs can definitely turn it around with some work.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so I hate to dunk on an indie game, especially since it is pretty fun but This game has some issues.The Positive:-The theme is immaculate.-Sound design and animation is Great.-The core concept is actually really interesting as you are the villain but also the world is just as evil as you are so you are heavily encouraged to be villainous, and you'r characters actively rely on cheating to win.Tragically the good ends there. The Negative:-The main hub is barren, there is very little to do here besides start your next run.-There needs to be some kind of carry over from runs. Runs are super long and all the power ups you get from leveling up are completely RNG based, there needs to be more rewards for progression.-The over world is kinda janky. You can get stuck on random objects and your character will just spaz sometimes.-I wish Disciples had more personality, they are interesting at first but get really dry after a while.-Social interactions need more transparency, we get options but no idea what those options do inaddition to the fact that reactions seem to be random and randomly good or bad at that.-Level progression needs to be more consistent. Since the world is semi randomly generated youd think that the world would be diverse but they aren't, the only real RNG is in what each stop does and which ones get negative effects, this means you can get screwed super easily just because of bad luck, as like I said there is no way to actively make yourself stronger or gain new mechanics to play with.Honestly the game isn't completely bad, but It has a lot of problems that need addressing or it is unlikely that it will ever strike a bigger audience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game sucked me in. The theme was done excellently, story was interesting, and the strategy is very engaging. Unfortunately, I am unable to recommend it for two reasons: 1) Pretty minor, but it needs a fast animations option. After beating the game and playing on harder difficulties, you don't really want to see baron blow smoke for the 6th time in one turn. Just becomes tedious.2)Major reason is the amount of bugs. At first, I thought some things didn't go as I thought they would. A relic look like it didn't activate or a skill failed to perform up to expectations. But I was still learning and thought I was just miscalculating things. At high difficulties, you keep track of EVERYTHING and that's when you see the endless amount of bugs. I'd say about 1/3 to 1/2 battles are bugged. Skills not applying like Count's protection eat and + damage. Skills magically applying to you than the enemy, like casting decomposition on a zombie weak enemy only to have the decomposition hit you instead and the zombie buff remain. Or your alteration gets stuck on you. Etc etc. The "funniest" bug was the elite fanatics 5 lives just dying in one hit. Basically nullified the whole challenge. Unfortunately, most of the bugs seem to work against you though, but it could also be that the enemy skills are not explicitly defined. Sometimes they cast double up arrow and it just removes a weakness. Maybe that was intentional but it happens rarely and seems like a waste of their turn so I lean to some sort of bug. Also I've had it where the enemy got in a loop of just casting provocation on itself despite being the last one. Regardless, there are just SO many of these type bugs that it makes me wonder how the game got through QAQC.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun. Good - All of the character designs are really cool, really unique art. Would've been cool to see a shapeshifter in the roster.Wasn't sold on the system initially, but the essence system adds some unique interactions, people complaining about the game being overly difficult don't understand how to balance their resources out.Some of the item/character interactions are really insane if you can get the correct build, which has both pros and cons to it, but when it works well it's super satisfying.Skipped through literally every interaction, but for those of you who enjoy it, all of the main encounter/lore points are voiced and the narrator is pretty good.Cons - Biggest con is the lack of build diversity. You're either going HP or SP depending on your trinkets/event bonuses, status' in the game are super underwhelming and they're mainly there for damage reduction. Depression would be the main outlier here because of the amount of interactions it has with different skills/trinkets, but it's still just better to go for pure damage and ramping generally. Felt myself gravitating towards the same system of buff the hell out of Mary/Dracula and 1 shot everything. After beating the last boss, even though a NG+ is introduced, i've got no desire to play more.Some encounters didn't feel great, the only one that was potentially run ending in my case was the Fanatic, if you can't split your damage quickly enough he's just a menace, with that said out of the 10ish runs it took me to beat the game, he was the run ender only twice, it's not overly difficult, there's just no counterplay without the correct set-up and that feels bad.Game really just doesn't have much replayability because the power climb is exactly the same every run - get terror up, focus on events and buff damage, then get skills, in that order every time. Should be more/random combat rewards, being able to chose what reward you get just feels badly designed and takes a lot of randomness out of the game, which isn't a great thing for a roguelike.There are some very rough explanations on certain skills/interactions I'd imagine due to the game being developed in French and ported to english, but it wasn't a great job. None of the lore(that I actually read) was bad, but there is a huge lack of proper tooltips on quite a few things which I hope will get fixed for newer players, but it's strange to see something so simple pass QA on the 1.0 release. Playing Hecate was a literal roll of the dice on trying to figure out how her moon phases worked and what shifted what.This is likely just a personal opinion here and YMMV, but by far the most efficient comp was Drac/Mary/Lilith. Baron and the Lady were both really good for SP comps(which would suffer against fanatics, so rip that), and Frankenstein/creature I used for one run and didn't find either enjoyable at all. Horseman was just a worse Lilith from what I wanted out of my 3rd. Hecate was just so badly explained trial and error was the only way to see what her kit did, which isn't fun with as specific as some counters need to be.Overall It was fun, kind of got old towards the end and the lack of replayability(for me) is never a thing I want in Roguelikes, but the game was fairly well made without many issues, and had some unique features on top of gorgeous aesthetics and still gave a solid 20 hours of content for 20$. It doesn't have the balance or replayability of StS, but for a smaller scope the game is great. For all the people saying the game is to hard and you can't pass the first book... what? If you've got any experience in turn based games you'll be fine, like any other roguelike bad RNG can kill a run, but it's more user-error then anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: Unique and Devilish art style.You are playin' the Devil here so you get to CHEAT!!!Characters and a Devil that aren't lackin' in villainous charm.Unique take on JRPG combat with a bit of Magic the Gathering's combat style systems.A lot of replayabilityLooks like a lot of others reviews have issues with the difficulty in this game.  Compared to a lot of RNG styled games this one is fairly balanced.  I played 85% thru the game on its hardest mode before the last patch.  I found it difficult but in a fun way.  You have to arrange as many advantages as you can to dominate the enemy.  The RNG for items and skills feels a lot like a CRPG to me where you're hoping that you can force something you really want to come up, or you play what you're given and try to make do until you can change something about you're skills/relics. _childDocuments_.review: Despite the tutorial, the learning curve is too harsh. At no point did I go "oh, I got it 100%". None of the characters feels particularly powerful.  There were too much thrown at a player in the tutorial, new elements should have been spread out further so you don't have to learn too much. The first mission should have been a series of 3 mini-chapters. Personally, I'd have focused on each character one by one. For example, I would have had Dracula be your first disciple, on his own. The first chapter should have been about how he works, his skills and should have focused only on mechanics of battle. These fights should have been dead easy. World interactions should have been introduced here.The second chapter should have been about skills and showing how Dracula versus the H.Horseman have their differences and highlighting what they are. You then introduce optional missions. These fights should still be easy, but ramp up the difficulty a smidge, to the point that there was no way Dracula could beat it on his own. You there introduced how the Devil effects interactions with the world. Effects should be explained, but only how they impact the enemy. Next chapter should have introduced Bloody Mary and talked about tactics. And the Grim Reaper and how to upgrade skills, etc. At this point, the chapter should end with a difficult fight. During this chapter the effects to enemies should have been explained and how you can influence things. To win the second before last last fight, you then introduce the Devil and how he can cheat. The final fight of this point should have a fight that unleashed you on your own. This way each chapter gives the 3 starter disciples their focus and allows them to be introduced gradually and at no point is the player ever left feeling "wait, I just learnt some information, I haven't processed it and I don't know what to do with it, but your now giving me more?". Its too much too soon.I don't expect holding hands, but honestly, I felt confused and over whelmed by the system. Before I could learn what one thing did, I was given another, sure, some players can learn this, but, I feel this puts off a lot of potential new players. Theres a lot to learn and not a lot of time to learn it in. Lastly on skills....When I was comparing skills, none of the 3 starter disciplines really stood out in that first mission, there played so similar at times, that it didn't matter if the H.Horseman was able to tank damage, Bloody Mary and Dracula and he had some skills that were so similar at times that when it came to pick NEW skills, I didn't know what was the best thing to get rid of or add. Theres no clear "this would be better" skill option and in the first few missions there should. Its unclear if "X skill would be better" or "Y skill would be better", because the game throws too many new things at you at once. The result? a Cluster-F---- of "I dunno?".

_childDocuments_.review: Edited to add this:  There seem to be a lot of negative reviews and complaints on the forums from players who think the game isn't well balanced, or is unfair.  I think those folks are being too critical, and that they also do not fully understand the game's complex systems.  You aren't meant to win every single run, quite the opposite.  You do gain levels and unlock more powerful items, different disciples, and new abilities whether you win or lose.  With the way the game is designed you'll probably lose more often than you win until you really get the hang of it.  That does not make this a bad game, or a poorly balanced game.  It's simply a complex and unforgiving game that has rogue-like features.  Enough about this, on to the review!I absolutely, without a doubt, recommend this game.  It's fantastic.  From the fairly complex combat to all the little details.  The UI and inventory systems could be a bit more streamlined, there's a bit too much flipping back and forth in some menus, but that's my only major gripe.This game is tough but usually fair and when the going gets tough you can cheat.  Yes, you can cheat.  No, it's not like cheating in other games.  In this game you're supposed to cheat from time to time.  I mean, you don't have to but it's so easy to just... cheat.  Like crazy.  All the time.  Until you run out of power.This game's a combination of Slay the Spire, Darkest Dungeon, and Iratus Lord of the Dead.  With cheating.  Why with cheating?  Um, because you're the Devil, that's why.  Yeah, that's where it's a bit like Iratus.  You are playing the "evil" side.  With supernatural minions.  And they can't die.  They get knocked down to 0 hp or sp and you start losing essence equal to the damage they would have taken.  Lose all of it and it's game over... temporarily.  Minions heal every time they start a new fight, so it's okay if they get knocked down to zero health or spirit points or if they take a lot of damage during a fight - as long as you aren't losing large amounts of essence you should be fine.  Note that I said a new fight, some fights have multiple waves and the minions do not heal between waves.Each run can be quite different from the last, and each run generally gets pretty tough at some point but if you're prepared, and a bit lucky (or if you create your own luck by maybe cheating just a little bit) then you can often get by.  But if you fail?  Well, have I mentioned the cheating?  You're very good at cheating at everything, including cheating death.  You simply use your powers to start again with some bonuses that you may have unlocked after each failed run, or new minions you have unlocked as you progress.  Change tactics, pick different minions to bring with you on each run, pick different skills and bonuses.  Choose your path, choose your relics, choose bonuses from each fight.  Choose what to upgrade, what skills to focus on, and choose where and when to use your power to alter the outcome of almost every situation in the game.  Change things on the fly with your powers, or leave things up to chance if you wish.  There's so much choice in the game that it may feel overwhelming until you really get used to the mechanics.Please, take a few minutes and check this one out, I think it's a solid 9/10 and definitely worth a look if you can handle the difficulty.  Yes, it's difficult, and sometimes feels unfair, but it's designed that way and a very new release so there maybe a bit more balancing to come.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels too complicated.1. Ok, you start with 3 peeps. And you unlock more as the story progresses. Perfectly fine.2. Ok, there are 'rounds' instead of turns. Your peeps go first. Got it. I'm not sure why I wouldn't just use my good abilities most of the time.3. Each ability can only be used once before recharging? That seems unnecessary. Like, sure, it fixes the above problem, but now it has its own problem with pacing.4. And would this stupid #$%@ing tutorial please stop forcing me to do something? It doesn't give me any time to process the context of what's going on before it just goes down the line.5. There's RP events, combat events, shop events, skill upgrade events...? What? Why?6. wait...I start over when I fail? Alright Slay the Spire is the same way, but the combat is much snappier and less chaotic.So let me get this straight: this a turn-based party game where each ability is about as complicated as DD spells, party comps, and trinkets with just as much investment, but it resets every run as if it has the simplicity of StS's cards, AND it railroads you through the first level to try to cram as much game knowledge as possible into your brain as possible?Like, what's wrong with the tutorial level having enemies with 8 hp/sp and the party members having only 1 ability that don't need recharging across rounds? Sure, once per round usage limit sounds great. Why does there need to be an active recharge? You can already gain skills after combat. Starting off with 3 spells that are functionally identical seems ideal for a tutorial.And don't get my started on D/Levil Editor mode. The sheer amount of options is ridiculous. Don't get me wrong; don't cut it. Don't nerf it. But why the hell is it so open ended at the beginning of the game?Honestly, I think that if the first few levels were revamped to reduce the complexity by a huge margin, let the tutorial not railroad the player, and simply let the player build up to the same level of complexity, the game would be a 100x better.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a nice candy with a tasteless filling that will bore you after the first 2 hours. After that, it is the same over and over. Nice setting, graphics, interesting set of skills and good voice overs but lack of real depth in combat, poorly balanced essence feature, empty useless world, too linear, merchant is a bummer and it is a bad roguelike. More specifically, you encounter events on the map where your lords can improve their skills or get more souls and create terror advantages throughout sections of the world. Combat is turn-based where each character has their unique set of skills that needs recharging before next use costing the action points from the same action points pool. The events are varied but it is always about cheating the skill checks. In combat, you deal physical and spirit damage with actions points from a conjunct pool, similarly to Iratus or Darkest Dungeon but the problem is enemies deal too much damage and your lords have short physical and spirit bars which get restored after every fight but after just few fights, your demonic essence, which is used for cheating skill checks as well as moving statuses, will get depleted, and it also works as back up health and stress pool if your lords are on a brink of dying, so if it reaches zero, it is game over. You can regain this essence only in a specific shrine in one of the world paths. I also do not understand why we have to walk through the world if there is nothing in it and you only walk from combat to event to merchant to combat to shrine. And that is it. Instead, they should simply make it like in Slay the Spire, click on these events directly on a map and not waste our time walking and getting stuck on trees and "exploring" a linear lifeless world.Merchant aka Grim Reaper is another supposedly complex feature, we get to buy new skills or upgrade existing ones by merging 3 of the same kind, or upgrading one but we will lose it until the next merchant encounter. And then, there are relics which can be either good or terrible. By good, you get to be lucky to buy one that synergizes with ones of your lords and by terrible, it will give you some bonus but will reduce something else important like give 1 more action point but all incoming damage is doubled. Merging skills is too expensive and it is better to lose one temporarily and fight with another lord or skill with similar values. I can barely afford anything useful if anything at all at merchants also thanks to negative effects on the world map which can sometimes not be avoided altogether.The 3 lords I start with are a vampire who deals only physical damage and can cast stealing physical damage to allies but can not receive any spirit stealing from his allies so easily “dies” to exhaustion and is otherwise almost useless. His special skill is recharging all other skills. Another lord is a headless guard who is supposed to work like a tank but somehow does so ineffectively. He deals massive physical damage. Third starter lord is a witch who can deal both physical and spirit damage and can double attack with her special ability. She is a very potent fighter but she has short damage bars. I unlocked a fourth character who deals spirit damage only with stealing spirit and her skills cost only 1-2 action points, but can not withstand damage much more than any other physical only character.This game is a huge disappointment for a roguelike game. I do not get stronger after each run. Yes, the new lord is slightly more effective at dealing spirit damage but the main problem is still persistent. Demonic essence pool is too small at the start and used for so many things, do not forget that enemies deal more and more damage just in the first stage of the world and you do not get many occasions when to replenish the essence back. In many matters it feels like a Banners of Ruin approach when you start each game with the same enemies, and waste so much time before you reach something slightly so interesting. I like the narration and events are quite a nice touch but gameplay wise it is very linear, there is no strategizing, you only have to get so lucky to get high damage spirit skills and kill enemies before they kill you. I would rather lose some of my lords and go on then having to perish in a failure every time I run out of demonic essence. I also discovered I can not snowball my damage with extra status points which deduct each turn, they get reset to the same number, so I have to keep using and recharging my skills and keep playing with just one lord while the other two lords just stand there aimlessly. It is a bad design that annoyed me in Banners of Ruin as well but it was better executed there.Rating: 4/10 The game is not fun.

To achieve this goal, the Devil must navigate through various environments, gather resources, and build a team of loyal minions.The gameplay is divided into two distinct phases: the first is a strategic planning phase, where players can choose which minions to bring into battle, upgrade their abilities, and equip them with various items and relics. The second phase is the actual battle, which is turn-based and requires careful planning and tactical decisions to emerge victorious.One of the most notable features of Rogue Lords is the unique storytelling approach. The game is presented as a dark fairy tale, complete with striking visuals, atmospheric music, and voice-over narration that brings the world and characters to life.However, the game can be challenging at times, and players must be prepared to face difficult battles and unexpected obstacles. The learning curve can be steep, and players may need to experiment with different strategies and team compositions to progress.Overall, Rogue Lords is a well-designed and engaging game that offers a fresh take on the classic roguelike genre. The combination of strategy, role-playing, and deck-building mechanics creates a unique gameplay experience, and the game's striking visuals and atmospheric music help to immerse players in its dark and gothic world. _childDocuments_.review: The thing about rogue-likes that makes them awesome is having a great core gameplay loop. Hades, Risk of Rain 2, and the Binding of Issac, are great examples of this each taking a little over an hour for a speedy run (ROR2 having a loop you can choose to lengthen or shorten making it even more to taste). This is so that no matter how hard the game is (or how unfavorable a run), or how often you die, you can saddle up and try again and not feel like you've wasted your time. If you're reading the text prompts at all or any of the carefully written scenes (Not enough though I repeated 2 of them twice) and listening to the narration this game's 'run' is **3+ hours**, and there's no way to shorten it, other than button mashing through all the story. If it wasn't a rogue-like and just a dungeon crawler where you had save points and didn't waste 2.5 hours only to die from some elite fight that generated out of nowhere, it would be a good game, but as it stands, with the brutal efficiency with which it kills you, causing you to button mash past all the cut scenes you've already seen before, it's awful. Unlike Hades or ROR2 there's no story reason behind why this has to be a Rogue-like. In Hades you just can't die, and ROR2 you just play as a different crew mate after the other ones have died. Here you just show up back at the central hub, and you have to play through the same story beats again. Maybe the dungeon is supposed to get easier as you bring things back, but after my first run I leveled up 3 times (which I guess meant was doing well???) unlocked a new character. Then I had an hour run and died to two elite fights back to back. I was thankful that two half runs brought me to only 1.9 hours and not 3 so I could return it. Its a shame that such a good idea, combat system, story, and art style got lumped in with the rogue-like trend and thus became unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: A promising game, but ruins it with some very bizarre design decisions.TLDR.: The game has an ever increasing difficulty system which you cant change, so if you just want a game you can just enjoy and mess around with. This aint it chief. The difficulty rises to a lvl after just  a few wins, where your disciples feel ridiculously weak, making early fights a drag, and if you've liked the game on a lower difficulty that you already past, well too bad, you cant enjoy the game on that one.You play as the all mighty devil, who's leading some famous monster movie characters from history as your disciples.The game is  all about completing the same book, numerous times, with randomized encounters, but a different narrative and final boss. So far so good. The narrative is actually really good too.The problem however rises with the ever increasing difficulty system every time you complete a run. This difficulty you can never change, even if you wanna play the first book. Every increase in difficulty, basically just increases the HP of every enemy. (it adds some other random stuff in it, like increased elite encounters. (Minibosses with more HP), etc.)This is a huge issue because your disciples will stay the same. Which makes early fights, ESPECIALLY elite fights, a major slugfest, since your unupgraded lackeys deal very little damage, while your enemies can usually 2-3 shot your mighty monster units, which just makes you feel pathetically weak, and can drag out elites fights waaaay too long.Disciple unlocking is also messed up cuz some requires you to progress in to the book, so you will never be able to play with them on lower difficulties, and some require you to lvl up. Now if you get to a difficulty where you are struggling, you will have a hard time gaining any experience at all, cuz yeah, failed runs dont give much exp, requiring you to fail again and again and again to maybe unlock a unit which you can play with, with no option to maybe tone the difficulty down back to a lvl you enjoyed playing with.I my self dont mind a challenge every now and then, but I'm not a fan when the game is forcing said challenge down my throat. I'll never understand who thought this will be a good idea.

I'm not an obsessed Autist.And, unfortunately, because of these reasons, I just can't recommend this game. I know what you're thinking "Roguelikes aren't for everyone". _childDocuments_.review: 5 out of 103D roaming on the map is pointless and a waste of resources. Woke character design, I've played nearly 20 hours and the only characters I've unlocked are women who greatly outshine the 2 men that you start with. White Lady can almost entirely solo encounters if built right while Dracula and Headless Horseman get stomped down no matter what you do. Bloody Mary does seriously broken levels of damage and Lilith can tank, heal, or DPS without issue. A combination of the those 3 makes it almost effortless to complete a run.Difficulty is weird. In some instances it's totally one sided and in others it's effortless. The progressive nature of each successful chapter makes wanting to do newer chapters seems like a punishment rather than a reward.Character designs are interesting but some characters like Hecate and the White Lady being entirely oriented to one type of damage is problematic at times, especially when you reach later stages where even normal fights are equivalent to elite fights. The 3 vs 3 nature of the battles make each of your "Evil Geniuses" seem less powerful or impressive than they normally should be. Dracula should be a force his own as should the rest of them. Enemies, even named chapter villains seem very faceless and devoid of any actual character. Between each chapter, outside of the chapter villain, you fight the same things over and over again.--- Apprentice Update ---So I popped back on to see what had changed. Were there balancing fixes to broke ass characters? Nope. Instead we got relic/artifact/whatever you want to call them, updates and an "apprentice" difficulty.What does this apprentice difficulty do? It just doubles your starting life and makes some things cost less. I just unlocked Baron, and he is able to solo encounters by simply applying his signature debuff then recharging to give it more ticks and just annihilate SP on bad guys. Combine that with the White Lady being in your party and you get free attacks every turn that specifically target SP and nothing else and you mulch encounters. It doesn't even matter that enemies have loads of SP because Barons debuff reduces their maximum and if you just play safe you can get everyone's down to 1. If you play really safe you can get the Healing mask for White Lady and you're basically invincible. This difficulty adjustment didn't do anything. The problem isn't that you have too few resources or that your life is limited or whatever, it's that every time you complete a chapter the difficulty increases by a set amount regardless. I want to unlock all of the characters, but I don't want to be punished for trying to do so and this Apprentice difficulty doesn't actually make the play any noticeably easier. All it really does do is allow me to spend life to power through stupid trait encounters on the map or make boss fights absolutely trivial because by the time I've gotten to the end I have 150 life or more and can just nullify every action the boss takes by swapping debuffs or stealing buffs. It's stupid.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually loved this game and I'm at about 55 hours.  I find the characters to be diverse and interesting in their playstyles.  I think the combat system is well thought out and smooth, the energy and recharge system work quite well IMHO.  I think skill and item accrual is also well done, ie: how you can select your rewards from each fight and they all feel pretty powerful depending on your map.  The Reaper's shop and trading in skills to level them up also works very nicely.  "Cheating" with your life force is also a fantastic adaptation and I think it has TONS of potential.     I guess what I'm saying is, mechanically speaking: I think this clicks on all cylinders.  As folks have pointed out, it is VERY repetitive and there are scant few enemy types.  The story is kind of *meh* but I don't really care about story so that doesn't matter to me.  I also found the encounter events to be less than interesting and, after 2-3 runs you will have pretty much seen them all.  The Social Skills and acquiring traits didn't seem that impactful either and could probably be skipped altogether.       The engine here has so much going for it.  The repetitive nature of the levels, quite frankly, is a bit disappointing given the price point.  However, I will say that it has not stopped me from playing!  It is still damn fun and I would eagerly await the next project from this team.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun to play and easy to learn but can be challenging in some fights.  You have to decide how best to progress and those choices can impact how easy or difficult a story is to complete.  Do you choose to fight every battle and build up terror to get a lot of terror bonuses?  Or do you build up souls to buy and upgrade skills?  Do you do a lot of events to build up physical and spiritual hit points and damage?  Do you accept a debuff so you can get a buff?  How you proceed can definitely impact your game.You also can choose among a variety of characters (disciples) to have in your group of 3, once you unlock them.  Each has different skills and benefits.  And how they work together can really impact how you do in a story.  Do you use characters who do a lot of physical attacks or ones who do a lot of spiritual attacks, or do you try and get a balanced mix of the two?  Your enemies will sometimes be able to ward against one or the other and some have more physical HP than spiritual HP while others are the reverse of that.  By making the wrong choices, you may find you have a much harder time completing a story.  On the other hand, the right choice may make the story very easy to complete.As you progress, whether you win or lose, you'll get experience that will unlock more skills for your characters, possibly making it easier to complete the next story.The unique part of this game is the use of demonic essence to basically cheat.  You can use your limited essence to drop an enemy to 0 physical or spiritual HP and then finish them off with a single attack.  You can move a buff from an enemy to your own character or a debuff from your character to the enemy.  There are a number of abilities you can use, both in combat and during the story events.  The balance is that once you run out of essence, you lose.  And if one of your characters gets defeated, you lose essence.  So it can be risky to spend a lot of essence but spending it can turn a loss into a victory very easily.Overall, this game is all about strategy.  The choices you make definitely have an impact on your game.  If you like this kind of combat, you will probably enjoy this game.  But if this isn't the kind of combat you like in a game, you probably will not like the game.  Most of the game is really about the combat.  Even though there are other things to do in the game, the main focus is the combat, so if you don't like that, you aren't likely to enjoy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Don't buy it.Some games deserve long reviews because they're mostly good and have noticeable shortcomings; other games deserve long reviews because they hold much promise and fall short of fun despite holding promise.  Rogue Lords receives a short review because it's an unenjoyable game: I wouldn't recommend it to anyone, even a fan of roguelikes.The game's strongest point is its theme of cheating.  I found that idea immediately appealing -- as someone who enjoys roguelike deckbuilders, I loved the idea of deconstructing the genre (I loved what Undertale did for RPGs, for comparison).  The cheating mechanism in the game allows such wickedness as prolonging your party's health, killing enemies, and, most importantly, altering the chances during skill checks.That's where the creativity ends: the fights are repetitive, the characters aren't interesting, the gameplay is clunky, the graphics are ugly, and the writing is subpar.  The game thinks that it's cool and sacrifices fun: a great example of this is that the game forces players to walk manually between encounter nodes.  The landscape isn't interesting and there aren't traps to avoid or treasures to claim (as there are in Darkest Dungeon, which can justify manual travel, and even then keeps it one-dimensional instead of two-dimensional): the developers just wanted you to watch Dracula walk from one town to the next.The game lacks polish and I didn't want to play more.  There are enough great games with gorgeous graphics and great games with primitive, stylized, or retro graphics.  Poor game design and poor art (visual and written) conspire to make this the worst roguelike deckbuilder among the nine or ten I've played.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is an interesting specimen of its kind. On the surface you'd go into this probably expecting some sort of tactical deckbuilding roguelite like some of its predecessors. And while the game takes certain pieces of their DNA, there are some things where it differs greatly.This game puts you in the shoes of The Devil, the big D themself, as you command a trio of villainous evil-doers around a fantastic version of pilgrim era North America. I have to admit, I was sceptical of Rogue Lords at first. It all looked really nice but played very weirdly. I'm putting this down mainly to it just being very different from other tactical roguelites I've played. But over time, the game really grew on me. Its cast of villainous Disciples is colourful and offers enough variety that 9 characters actually feels like a lot of options and they all feel quite distinct from each other, from Dracula to Hecate to Frankenstein (and his monster!). The game's mechanic of "cheating" is what drew me in, gameplay-wise and it's cool that it's actually an integral mechanic to the game instead of just a minor gimmick.On the other hand, the story felt like it offered little more than a backdrop. I rarely cared for the nature of a certain stage's boss or the actual flavour-text of an event but the fun and engaging combat system encouraged me to finish every last thing in the game. The strong visual style really enhances the overall enjoyment of the game. It's like playing the baddies in a movie animated by Tim Burton or Guillermo del Toro. Your characters, both The Devil and your gang of three, offer quips and one-liners that feel a little cheesy but didn't diminish my fun and on the combat noises, from Bloody Mary's shattering mirror to the swashbuckling of the Headless Horseman, the sound design worked very well to underline each characters' personality.Overall I'd recommend Rogue Lords to everyone who enjoys an unconventional tactics roguelite. In the same vein, if you look at the game's screenshots and think "this looks really cool!", I'd also encourage you to try it out. The game really has a lot of personality, even with its story being ultimately a little forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics, character design and gameplay mechanics are good, but the RNG and difficulty make this a difficult game to recommend. The spike in the mid-game is just insane, and you are battling RNG along the way in stacking your pathetic increases of power. The game becomes a grind under the pretext of Rogue-like. Difficulty is fun when it's fair; this game is RNG hell and not fun after it becomes a grind. For me, this was the 15 hour mark on Book 3. Wish I could be bothered to unlock Frankenstein and Baron Samedi.. but I can't.

Great art. Story is cool. Who doesn't love an evil protagonist? _childDocuments_.review: Mechanics and difficulty are fun and challenging. There is a decent amount of ability complexity and interaction. Headless Horseman is cool....however, the UI in the game is terrible and hides critical information in all sorts of places (and some of it is randomly not translated to english, but that at least seems rare and not a huge concern as far as I can tell, but I was only 5 hours into the game, so maybe there's more of that).As one of the main elements of the game is discovering new skills and modifiers for both your own team and on enemies, prepare to lose some runs due to not seeing some additional caveat on them (important ones like things that end your turn upon useage of an attack, your skills being locked in a particular battle after useage, etc. - i.e. not just small stuff where a skill combination doesn't work out or you get a bit of additional damage. I just figured the enemies had some sort of interrupt ability/skill debuff that I triggered from time to time somehow, which is incorrect). Just to give additional context: I'm the sort of player that reads every tiny text, tutorial, side story and item description in any game I play, and it helped me none here. If an overpreparing completionist can't find this info, I doubt more casual players will.I'll give this game another try in the future; if the mid-to-end-game makes putting up with the UI worth it, I'll update and/or change my review.If putting up with terribly conveyed information is not a huge problem for you, the game is recommendable; difficult games with itneresting skill combinations are hard to come by, and this one is at least pretty decent. If, like me, it's a game breaker for you, then the game cannot be recommended.----Suggestions for the devs: While I still don't know why my skills were locked, it would be nice if the tutorial would let you know how, when and why they could be locked, and what modifier categories exist (enhance, cure, etc. - one of these is "completion" which if I understand correctly now, means the skill ends your turn); also skill descriptions ought to mention these things as well.If you're afraid of bloating the current tutorial, just give some text-only advanced tutorial that can be read optionally somewhere. It would be a great help.

_childDocuments_.review: So close to greatness. Fun battle system that's great to power scale, but the UI... it is so bad that it straight up brings the game from an 7/10 or maybe even 8/10 on a good day to a 5/10 at best. No battle log is one thing, but in battle all the important information that will end your game in an instant if you miss something is tied to each character on the far side of the character, it's a massive pain with how ridiculously small the icons are, it's easy to miss a status or special trait of an enemy and straight up make a game losing move in one turn. It pisses me off and destroys the flow of the game. I guarantee you will lose and not know why you lost in one of your earlier runs. I cannot stress, I have made a lot of runs in this game, and still occasionally go from a won run to dying in one turn because the combination of too much information in too little space screws you over. I don't even really pay attention to the battle animations after the first run with a new character but they take up 95% of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ screen for it, I can't believe the testers didn't complain about this. It might be the lack of battle logs but I'm pretty sure there are some bugs involving some off the statuses too. It really ground me down with spending 20 minutes to lose to a single misread, especially with all the unnecessary walking between events that got super annoying. Can't believe testers didn't say anything. Feels like the art team had too much control over the game's great visuals, but ended up making the gameplay, and therefore the game, suffer. Might return to it someday, but since I got it in a Humble Choice I feel like I got enough of my money's worth to say if it's on sale for cheap and you're big on roguelikes, try it out. You might not get ground down by the grind like me and make it to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: This game clearly isn't for everyone, but if you like a challenging roguelite it's pretty good.  You have a few different games to play with regard to picking up and improving skills, and preserving your devil essence and using it as appropriate in combat or tests.  Like most roguelites, there's usually a way out of a bad combat situation, though in elite battles they often need your diabolical help, whether to patch them up enough to survive the next onslaught, or switch buffs and debuffs between your guys and the enemy, and then take advantage of them.  It's fair if you strategise well, and I haven't seen much in the way of bugs or slowdowns.  My party got stuck in fog once, but I was able to work my way out of it.After a few false starts, I've completed the first book and felt it was well-balanced.  The way the game works is that each book you start again with a new story and tougher enemies, but progress gives you access to better spell drops etc, as well as the effect of your improving skills. So very roguelite.Edit: Book 2 won a day after I wrote the previous.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: This games premise and artstyle made me put it on my wishlist a year back, and now when it was on sale I got around to buy and play it. After having played it, I wish i did not hold off on buying it as I had a good time with it and it delivered on what I wanted. Cool premise of controlling the Evils from folklore and "cheating" on the battlefield with the devils power. Especially the devils power is really fun, and when you think you know all the ways to use it cleverly you suddenly find a new, unfair and tricky way to use it.This is actually my first rogue like ever, but the premise of the game made me try this new genre. So from my limted knowledge of that genre how do I find it? The main thing that stuck out to me, is that the enemy variety is really low. After the first chapter you have pretty much seen all of the enemy types, except the bosses of course. So, a few chapters in it got really repetitive with what enemies you got delivered in the fights on the way to the boss. That said, the bosses themself was pretty fun with how it throws new problems for you to solve. Another postive for me was how impactfull and thoughtfull the ability upgrades felt to me as the run went on. Which Evils abilities do you choose to upgrade? Do you go magic or physical? Lastly the run itself go on a straight map, with 6 story checkpoints between. Between the story checkpoints themself are 2-4 roads you can choose paths to take to the story checkpoints. In those roads you find a regular and elite fight. In addition to a shop, a sacrificial altar where you lose a ability to get a stronger one, and a quick spot where you can get a small trait bost to your evils.Hope this quick written thoughts help you guys to decide :)
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: It's easier than Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but only because the pools of abilities and relics is much smaller than those other games, so it ensures you get 1 or 2 good ones each run.  Oddly enough, it made me think more than those games because turn order and buff management is so important.  Thumbs up overall, but definitely doesn't have the longevity of those other games, also quite a few bugs.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Tight and fun rogue-like. Good tactical options though sometimes there is a tendency towards a dominant strategy; which can be fun admittedly when you end up building a rare insane build which kills everyone in one to two turns. The enemy design is interesting and varied. The disciples (player characters) are also varied and have lots of interesting builds and combinations between them.Overall, I recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I really like just about everything the game has done. I love the mechanics, the visuals, the characters, the voice acting for the most part, etc. The only downside to the game is that it is a buggy mess. The game seems to really struggle hard when calculating items or abilities that activate more than once; the staff of storms sometimes only activates once when it should activate tons of times, the bleed effect does the same, and many more effects. In my last run, I had a bleed effect appear on me from nothing, costing me the entire run. Again, this game is phenomenal, it just really needs some updates for bug fixes.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a quite stylish rogue like a la Slay the Spire with the added twist that you are the seemingly handsome devil and thereby entitled to cheat. You will build a cast of three charming folklore evildoers who somehow break the game mechanics in one way or the other as the ridiculous boss health pools demand and retrieve the [insert devilish contraption] from the bad bad human peoples of non devilland.Presentation being top notch and surprisingly tame given the horrid action that is narrated (but never shown) sets the game up for a nice halloweenish experience. The voice of the devil may remind some people of the success of darkest dungeon's ancestor.Biggest critique of this title would be its moderate longevity. Unfortunately the depth of combat though overwhelming at the start decreases with time as you master the devil's finite set of powers to your advantage, which begin to feel more like a routine than the giddy bad boy trick you felt the first time. The need to "pop off" in one way or the other based on the increasing difficulty more often than not stagnates interesting gameplay, as you will likely find yourself attempting the same strategies multiple times. Whilst the game nudges you in different directions with certain relics, encountering one that worked before / seems easier to do / doesn't require you to think will likely tempt you back into the old ways.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game. I just completed it and I think like it's more of a turn-based campaign than a typical roguelike though. The good:+ Cool atmosphere and art+ Lots of variations in builds and strategies+ You can make crazy strats with strong relics (passive abilities)The meh:- The runs are too long to offer a lot of replay value- The enemies are not that varied
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords has all the fun of the Slay the Spire run/cards/relics with a 3 character JPRG battle setup.  The art and visual design is nice and the characters are very polished and have a consistent aesthetic.  I have really enjoyed building party composition as I worked my way through run after run.The only real downside is that there is not enough variation in enemies.  As you progress through the chapters, the world, the enemies, the mini-bosses are all the exact same.  Hell there's only one quest and even THAT is the same.  Despite that flaw (which does really bother me actually) its a great game.Also, some of the mini boss designs (fanatic) are so unbalanced  you have to close-client scum to beat them - just FYI.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game with lots of different characters and abilities, a beautiful art style and a fitting narrator.The only thing I can complain about is that you can't change the difficulty even after beating the game. I just beat the final boss and am now stuck at difficulty 9, which is too difficult for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: I received this game as part of the March monthly Humble Bundle. This is a fun and deep rougelike, but it needs a balance pass pass and many bugfixes IMO. I've beaten the final boss with all characters. They all feel unique and viable and there are plenty of synergies to be found within any party of three. Some characters and team compositions feel much better than others which is fine IMO. The biggest issue I've had is that some skills and effects like the White Lady's damage mask bug out and deal no damage while still triggering burn status. This can typically be fixed with a hard reset, but it's very annoying given how long runs already take. As for enemies, groups of 2-3 can become insanely damaging out of nowhere when they all line up big, multi-hit attacks on the same turn. This sometimes happens on the first turn of fights when there's no counter-play options beyond the party's skills. Beyond enemy AI changes, I think a thematic way to deal with this would be a Devil cheat to reroll intentions. There are also some enemies that are far too tanky, especially if they show up early game. The one that gains a permanent +1 damage every time its hit while also casting shell, taunt, and having 150-200ish in both health stats is probably the most obnoxious. I believe the devs should reassess when enemies can show up throughout the game and which effects are allowed. For example, -50% damage taken is probably more appropriate for early game encounters than -X flat damage.  I'll also echo others' thoughts about manually moving feeling out of place for this type of game. Overall, I like this game a lot and I think it has tons of potential, but I can't recommend a full-price purchase. A few bugfixes and some streamlining would go a long way to improving the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend and had fun completing this TBS with one set of characters but a little tedious to get all the achievements.  Cool theme as well as concept I haven't seen before with the devil's health being a flexible/precious resource and something to manage and use both on the travel map as well as in the battles whose mechanics are simple to learn but can become challenging.  Different characters enable interesting strategies and synergies to try out along with the variability of the skills picked.  Can select your team (or choose random) and some work well but others not so well, e.g. limited by who can tank/taunt.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic game. The art is amazing. The story is good, has a good flow of chapters and books. Building different teams and trying them out is fun. The game gets very challenging as you progress which feels satisfying.Devil mode letting you cheat some things is a fantastic new addition to the genre. I hope there is a dlc for more characters, or they make a sequel with more. Anyone complaining about rng in a roguelite is insane. The whole genre runs on rng. This game has the sacrificial stone which lets you mitigate rng by removing skills from future loot pools.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: Great rogue-lite with with some cool mechanics, amazing art design, great voice acting and an interesting new theme (or new-ish - it actually reminds me of the original Dungeon Keeper, but I haven't seen a lot of that lately) of playing as the Big Bad.Some minor unfixed bugs suggest that support might be lacking.All in all, I'm shocked at how much fun I'm having, considering that the game flew under my radar for so long.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gem of a game right here. Challenging turn based encounters with character progression that's based entirely around risk & reward, the inclusion of a literal cheating mechanic as well play in fantastically with the aesthetics & there is alot to love here. There's also alot to get frustrated by, as there are enemy combinations that feel more cheap than fair & one mistake in combat can cost you the game, or one bad decision will cost you your run two events later. I also hate how if one of your party members goes down then it's game over. That sucked in the Persona games & it sucks here! TL;DR, good game with good ideas with a good number of bugbears to boot.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give it an ok. While the gameplay is catchy and somewhat addictive, the difficulty can be overly brutal. There are a TON of status effects, and because of this I think the game can sometimes be a bit buggy. I specifically remember the "mirror" status effect never seems to work, as it never applies a status upon the caster. (Making it entirely useless).  There isn't much enemy variety, as you would think you would get different enemies each stage, but again that's not the case. New characters are mostly unlocked by beating entire stages (which again, can be brutally hard.) A single stage can easily exceed 30 minutes. So if you don't have spare time to kill, you will not have time to beat this game. I still haven't beaten it.
_childDocuments_.name: Rogue Lords

_childDocuments_.review: This game challenges you but in a very satisfying way. It encourages you to keep playing, try different characters and find the best build for the chapter you go through. While there are some balancing issues, on the enemies side, the very same can be said for your own skills. So in order to beat that tough boss, you have to make sure you select the right characters, secure those relics and have fun. _childDocuments_.review: This is a circumstantial recommendation! I'm not going to sugarcoat it... this game does not want you to enjoy playing it (at least if you're more of a casual player who doesn't have much free time to put into it, like me.) If you enjoy rogue-likes with the line of thinking "in defeat,  you become stronger," you'll enjoy this game. Every time you fail a story, you'll get EXP for how far you got in a story and unlock new stuff to hopefully make you better next run. At the same time, every time you fail a story mission, your entire progress in that event is lost and your characters' skills and abilities are reset. It's super disheartening playing a super long story mission just to fail at the end and lose it all and have to try all over again. Sometimes it's not even your fault you failed. You just didn't get very lucky with what the game gave you in that run. The stories are long, the RNG sucks, and enemies at times are almost unbeatable no matter what you do simply because the game decides to 4x their attack, or because you got shafted on the RNG, relics, and skills you earned up until that point. If you are ready to fail over and over and feel very rewarded when you finally beat a chapter because it was through careful planning and gameplay (and quite a bit of luck), this is the game for you. If you want to have mindless fun, I recommend finding another game. But for the more hardcore people, I will recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, several mechanics are either bugged or there are hidden rules that need to be exposed.For example, some statuses are not removed from enemies properly, perhaps due to them being too important to combat, but this only add issues:- The whole point of the game is to 'cheat' things. But if some npc generates regen every turn, I can't steal it?- The attack still goes off without any indication that the status won't be stolen. Why not put all these statuses in a group since you're already doing so, and make it clear no status can be stolen/removed from that group?Another example of poorly balanced mechanics are the altars. These altars are map nodes that require that you sacrifice a move (which will not drop/be available for purchase for the rest of the run!) to unlock another move slot, and it gives you another move as additional compensation. This is not enough, however:- Firstly, there are several instances where there is no other choice available but altar nodes. I've had a chapter node surrounded by altars, which forced my entire setup to rotate. This is a major issue, since you have to give up crucial moves that you can never get back again. The only way to counter this is to only grab moves as a reward from combat, so you can perhaps grab a duplicate skill to sacrifice. Of course, this massively reduces your choices, and further limits play by only allowing you to improve that move through the grim reaper nodes, something that you can only do once every-time you reach a reaper node.- The sacrifice forces you to play differently, but this also forces you to lose your composition. The player having to decide which of their favorite moves to sacrifice for a measly slot and a random skill does not spark joy, it's frustrating due to the artificial limitation. Not all skill work together, so the chances of a random skill (not even fully random, since we're removing cards we already sac'ed) working for your build gets smaller and smaller the more you sac. This can completely destroy your build early.The odd thing is that some runs seem very easy, probably due to avoiding these RNG traps. Once that happens, the difficulty nosedives, which makes me feel like the difficulty relies far too much on constraining the player's agency.
