_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and ambitious game that is extremely fun, although it could definitely use more time in the oven.  I am going to talk about the things I feel it did wrong instead of right, since the volume of the latter totally eclipses the former.  Don't let the negative tone of the below get you down; I still very much recommend giving the game a shot!The otherwise fantastic game frustratingly falls a bit flat in at least three broad categories of oversights, errors, and/or unsatisfying design choices: (1) the battle system doesn't feel tight.  Among other issues, It's ambiguous at times when your turn ends and when it begins.  Your characters will sometimes randomly emote for a bit before you can start telling them what to do.  Sometimes you get locked onto one character's move list and have to push buttons until you find the golden one that enables selection of another character.  It's at times difficult to tell whether the debuff you plan to inflict on your opponent will override some existing debuff.  Minor issues, but the game would feel incredible if the flow of combat was touched up to feel more snappy and precise.(2) There seem to be myriad issues with damage calculation.  Through my own testing, it seems having the "burn" debuff up will make certain attacks by White Lady do 50% or less damage, like the system counts the procs from the debuff as procs that the abilities used are supposed to deliver.  I've also found that in some playthroughs my +damage traits received from events do not actually affect my characters in combat.  If an enemy AoE saps HP from your team, it heals them for 3x more than it damages them if they are zombie-debuffed for the same attack.  These issues are cumulative to the inherant ambiguities of having simple text-based mechanics and are exceedingly frustrating beyond the obvious reasons, because they tend to punish identifying and building synergies rather than reward them.  (3) Scaling in this game is really awkward.  Certain debuffs only do 2 or so damage per proc, and get completely eaten up by really early game mitigative effects.  There aren't any super consistent ways to scale those debuffs up either -- even for those characters whose whole schtick revolves around said debuffs -- and even the methods that exist don't exactly render the debuffs worth using into the late game.  A lot of debuffs that mitigate a certain raw amount of damage (e.g., -10 hp damage) and which also occupy the only weakness slot available (e.g., doesn't stack with -50% to damage) do not scale at all when enemies are hitting for 50 x 2 and are therefore largely useless late game.  You can try to play around this fact once you are aware of the lack of scaling, but it doesn't feel very organic or rewarding to try to deal with these relatively useless statuses in light of the way the game encourages you to level your abilities.  Part of the problem here is the "souls" currency isn't awarded very consistently, so the shop (which could help the learned avoid scaling issues) can be totally inaccessible if you don't find the OP souls-rewarding relics early.Again, great game that is unfortunately replete with some design and very unfortunate execution-based errors that really suck the souls out of it.  I'd still recommend, but would LOVE some attention to the execution issues to make the game feel more fulfilling.  GLHF all!

_childDocuments_.review: After the latest patch that fixed a crucial bug i would say that this game is definitely worth your money, if you are looking for a turn-based combat game that is. The game world is pleasing, being The Devil's disciple is a very neat concept, taking characters from different folklore, Dracula, Bloody Mary and The Headless Horseman for example. The skills you can obtain are plentiful, have three rarities that you can get and have a lot of combo potential if you are willing to explore the possibilities. Between combats there are all kinds of interactions you can come across, events, merchants, places to refill your devil essence and more. Especially the events you come across are very fun and unique each time. You get to choose which one of the three members of your current team you send out and each of them have unique social skills or traits that impact the probability of your success. And depending on your choice of action the result varies. After each event, regardless if you succeed or not, the character you sent out will receive a buff to their stats, if you did succeed in a test then you get bonus rewards and the rewards can even extend to your other party members. After each chapter your party members' traits (positive and negative), relics and skills will be reset to default. You can switch characters in your party in between chapters and all the experience you gained on your previous runs, failed and succeeded, carry over and unlock even more skills, relics and other content to your upcoming runs. There is so much depth to this game and stuff to unlock that i can very easily see myself sinking 100 hours to this game and beyond. Definitely grab this game if you see it on discount, and even for full price if you are a strategy enthusiast you can't go wrong with this!

_childDocuments_.review: Felt compelled to write a review given all the dumb negative reviews...this game is easily an 8.5 or 9/10.i felt like it had good balance of abilities, decent story, enough variation in enemies and abilities to keep it interesting, and a nice variation on relics (the items you get throughout your run that augment/improve your power)people seem confused by "one disciple dying ending the run" but they dont get it...a disciple running out of HP or SP means that the next time they get damaged for HP/SP, you lose your REAL health bar, which is the devil essence pool you see in the upper lefthand corner.  Its honestly so simple that I think people are being intentionally dishonest in their reviews?  or dumb on purpose?  idkthe difficulty isnt low but thats how it is with roguelikes.  if you learn what abilities and relics work well together, you simple pair what you're offered and then you feel strong by the time the end boss comes around.  just take a deep breath and review all your options and all the already applied buffs/debuffs on your team and the enemy before acting.my ONLY complaint i think would be that 1)  theres no persistent buffing between runs, as some have pointed out . might be nice but its just not included although that may be a purposeful design choice.  And 2) i thought van helsing, the end boss, was kinda easy...the 2nd to last boss has 2 phases and is much harder than the real end boss of the game, which i kinda breezed throughstill.  very fun, interesting, and different from other roguelikes.  would def recommend, esp for the price

_childDocuments_.review: You can read the description of the game somewhere else, I ain't typin that.If you can see how it is similar to a deckbuilder, recharging being akin to shuffling etc. You'll be alright.The characters can be played in a few different ways and depending on how you modify each character they will work with each other differently.You can play heavily damage type slanted teams but some of the later enemies will prove difficult if you don't have a way to fight the other type.Each character has different utility and you have multiple options for tank, damage, support.The event options are the best feature in that all of them are useful. You can focus on a few of them to build stats, skills, pruning the skill options, event boosts to amp options or gain less to go to a recovery area. All of these options have merit and playing to balance or focus these locations is a great part of the game.There is an escalating difficulty and the option to play lower difficulties on previously beat levels would be nice for work-shopping strategies. The devil cheating ability, whether used as a parachute or as a constant asset in scenarios, is such a fresh thing to have. Bending the rules to ruin a heal or combo is so satisfying as it gives you an out on an otherwise deadly situation.After all achievements and levels have been finished there is not much else to do but what you have is a lot if you pursue it.I would like infernal mode to have elite combats with more character, even just a boss at every chapter end with escalating difficulty tweaks that lessen as you increase difficulty. I had a great time and any new content will most likely get my dollar. They responded and fixed any things that have bothered me and are still listening on how to adjust the game according to any sensible player requests.All of my time with this game was well spent.Please make Mr. Lantern, Wolfman, and swamp monster characters please

_childDocuments_.review: This game is challenging and fun, and pretty deep with different builds and strategies.  Each disciple and team can be built in many ways, and the risk-reward and planning you have to do to win is very satisfying when you pull it off.  The devil power to make map warps, swap statuses, futz with HP/SP bars is really innovative and the fact that mana is your life makes it a great mechanic.  I'm a rogue-like lunatic and have 1000s of hours in everything from Slay the Spire to Binding of Isaac to FTL and many others.  Actually if you like FTL - made Into the Breach it's got that 3 vs 3 feeling, except with abilities and it's not isometricStrong recommend for deep strategy players of rogue-likes.  There's also some fun world-building, great characters, and tons of fun text, items, abilities, and quest stuff happening.  My few beefs are that sometimes it's hard to navigate on the open map because paths aren't always clear (isn't procedural gen fun?) , couple of times my devil warps weren't accessible (small bug), there are still a few enemy buffs I don't understand that lead to me or them taking more damage than I expected (polarization synergy maybe?)   Like a hard game, I feel such a sense of accomplishment unlocking each chapter - I'm on C5 now.  Expect to replay the lower chapters to unlock more abilities to progress.I do wish there was an option to speed up the game a little bit in terms of battles and even just clicking through events.  If ti's a mandatory event I don't know that I need to click in, then click the altar, then sacrifice, then click again to get my new skill.  Some events should just happen, maybe?Can't wait to unlock and beat everything.  this one keeps me coming back.Put all of my remaining essence to beat the penultimate boss, only to have them suddenly revive.  That's some straight f***ery right there.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Lords is a fun turn based Roguelike that incorporates many design mechanics from other popular Roguelikes while adding its only twist, primary its diabolic essence mechanic that allows you to manipulate fights and events. All the disciples play differently from each other and are unique. Unfortunately the game does lack in the post game and its meta progression stops after hitting the level cap of 25. Its new game plus mode, infernal mode, is primary just for your own personal challenge and the difficulty seems to cap at level 9. It could really use some more quality of life changes such as more detailed information on effects, being able to choose your starting abilities after unlocking them, displaying to the player what the event outcomes are to specific choices after doing them once, and listing what previous enemy moves were after having encountering them before. The Ui could also be improved upon more. Overall I really enjoyed my time with the game and hope there is more content for it in the future. Supposedly there was some cut content, I would like to see it added for free.

_childDocuments_.review:
Weakened from defeat to the forces of good, you fled the world and sought refuge in hell to survive. Decades later, you have returned with your most faithful Disciples to exact revenge on those wretched Demon Hunters. But the world has changed in your absence. Your enemies have become all-powerful, and a new religion - the Sanctua Lumen - has become very influential. It mercilessly hunts down all those who serve you. To reinstate your hold over the world of humans, you must first regain the strength you previously wielded by taking possession of artefacts with legendary power.

The first roguelike in which you play as the devil, which means you can change some of the game's rules to your advantage! Run after run, manage your team of famous evil geniuses as they encounter unforeseen events and turn-based combat. Unlock new skills, create powerful synergies and use your powers to turn the situation in your favour at critical moments. Only by collecting ancient artefacts can you finally take your revenge on the Demon Hunters.

name: The Procession to Calvary
detailed_description: Press Quotes “An animated montage of Renaissance art that’s been cut, mangled, and pasted to create a smart and funny tableau of Monty Python-style jokes.” - Polygon “If Renaissance-era art was anywhere near as funny ... I’d probably know a lot more art history right now.” - RockPaperShotgun “With crazily funny dialogues that will make you question your sense of humor … this Renaissance-themed adventure game will take you on a journey you have never been on before.” - IndieGameMag About the Game A time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for just one more murder... -Ecclesiastes 3:8 About Huzzah! The holy war is over! Your oppressors have been vanquished, the churches of the Old God lay in ruin and thousands of innocent people have been murdered! But it's not all good news; the tyrant Heavenly Peter has escaped your clutches, and you have been tasked with the mission of finding him... Your journey will take you through a richly detailed landscape built from hundreds of different Renaissance paintings. You will steal a ship, feed a donkey, compete in a talent contest, assist an inept street magician, sing, dance, play the (magic?) flute, poke a man's face, hunt for treasure and have a chat with Our Lord God Almighty... But will you find Heavenly Peter? And if you do, how will you take your revenge!? Features Pointing and Clicking – A traditional point and click interface, with a 'verb coin' interaction menu and a simple inventory from which you can drag and drop your preciously hoarded items. Renaissance Artwork – Paintings by Rembrandt, Botticelli, Michelangelo and many more are brought together into one consistent world, in a way that is also as sympathetic as possible to the original works. Classical Music – a soundtrack selected to fit with the style of the artwork. Music from classical composers such as Vivaldi, Bach and George Frideric Handel will accompany you on your journey. Standalone Story - The Procession to Calvary is set in the same world as Four Last Things, but it's story can be played independently. Optional Murder – You will be equipped with a sword. This will become useful in a number of different situation, but you will be strongly discouraged from using it on people. Ignoring this advice - and murdering anyone who stands in your way – will serve as a useful method of skipping any puzzles you don't like. But be warned; your actions might come back to haunt you... Nonsense – A style of humour reminiscent of the surreal, anarchic comedy of Monty Python. Lofty subject matter is treated with refreshing flippancy. Gags about butts are taken very seriously. But rest assured, while some of the jokes may be ridiculous, the puzzles make perfect sense! (or at least adhere to a consistent internal logic) Moments of Surprising Profundity – Actually, no... Don't read too much into it.

short_description: Pilfer from pirates, conspire with cardinals and perform miracles with an incompetent magician. The Procession to Calvary is a Pythonesque adventure game made from Renaissance paintings, and a spiritual successor to the critically acclaimed Four Last Things.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to buy Joe Richardson a bottle of very fine wine. I can just picture him, working a soul-sucking 9-5 DMV death-rattle of a job, with a head full of art and glory. Putting stamp upon meaningless stamp on dead paperwork while his soul yearns for beauty, truth, freedom and adventure.The man is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ intellectual treasure. The Procession to Calvary builds upon and expands on his unique style. You will be in stitches the whole time and you will spend a few hours immersed into some of the most exquisite artwork mankind has produced to date.Buy this now and help Joe get some quality wine.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Four Last Things then you are a shoe in for this game.  If you haven't played Four Last Things then GO AND PLAY FOUR LAST THINGS!Seriously.  Play Four Last Things first and then if you like that come back to this after that.  _________________+ amazing visuals.  The entire game is renaissance art from start to finish and is amazingly mashed up together.  + hyperbole...."You wasted amazing on a basket of chicken wings!?"  This game is hilarious.  Some of the dialogue is so funny I made a noise out loud.  There are some strange references.  The descriptions of the paintings in the gallery were fantastic.  The game's humour is on point for the kind of folks that have an interest in British humour or enjoy intelligent sarcasm.+ puzzling.  The puzzles in this game are harder.  I know people are going to look at my playtime and comment "git gud n00b" but I did not use a walkthrough and was really stumped by the Satanic sacrifice riddle. Looking back it is actually a great riddle and if you want another bit of Bosch riddling then head  __________________-  Caedite Eos!  You have the option to kill.  And this can lead to some puzzling choices.  I put a dying man out of his misery and then was removed from the game's main story.  I couldn't seem to advance.   HINT: DON'T KILL ANYONE IN YOUR FIRST PLAYTHROUGH________________The Procession to Calvary is a deeper, funnier, more explicit Four Last Things.  This is an example of a game growing off its own strengths and weaknesses and producing something far superior.  If you like Monty Python and playing games then just throw this in your cart right now and save me the breath of telling you why you should buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: A hilarious game and a continuation of the first one Four Last Things. This could be played as a stand-alone, but to understand the characters more it will be more fun to play the first game. The procession to Calvary is a medieval game made with Renaissance paintings, yes, actual paintings belong to real painters. You play as a knight who is obsessed with killing. The holy war is over however and she is forbidden to kill anyone accept of Heavenly Peter.. or maybe she can kill a man or two. This game has multiple endings depending on how you 'treat' people and how you acquire the items you need in your journey. It is an extremely fun game with outstanding classical music, if you like any track playing in any scene, you can click on the musicians and you'll get a comment on which piece they are playing. There is a bit of going back and forth and unfortunately, there is no map. Sometimes figuring out what to give the characters can be difficult without a guide. But overall the length of the game and gameplay is fun.Pros:+Beautiful Renaissance art.+Amusing story but not for everyone.+Classic music.+Manual save.+Multiple endings+Steam achievements. Cons:-No map.-No voiceovers.This game might not be for everyone. I highly recommend it to people who enjoy dark humor and point&click games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Classical Art Meme: The GameIt's like Monty Python raided The Louvre... I would like a supple young boy with rosy cheeks and a pert little butt please.LOOK AT MY MASSIVE KEY!Do you enjoy 90’s style point-and-click adventures?Do you like Monty Python?Do you think crucifixions are absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hilarious?If so, don't even bother reading further.  Just buy The Procession To Calvary and go in blind. You won't regret it. This is quite possibly the best Point-and-click adventure I have ever played. It's like LucasArts or Sierra had an illegitimate, yet adorable lovechild with Monty Python. I started playing it during a bit of a down period while looking for something to distract me, and this was exactly the level of silliness I needed. And that’s pretty much it.But for those dot want more information...The Procession To Calvary is a one-man indie game by Joe Richardson, with graphics pulled entirely from classic Renaissance paintings.  They've been cut-and-pasted and animated in a deliberately crude paper doll fashion, in a style clearly inspired by Terry Gilliam's classic Monty Python animations.  Likewise, the music is completely public domain as well, various classical pieces.You play as an unnamed female warrior, who I'll call Bellona since that's the Rembrandt painting she's taken from.  Bellona really really loves to murder people.  So when a recent holy war ends with the enemy routed, and she's told to stop murdering people, it's the worst day of her life.  However, she discovers that their hated enemy - Heavenly Peter - was actually left alive.  And after a bit of negotiation with her leader, Immortal John, Bellona is given special dispensation to do one more murder.And that's the goal of the game: travel to a foreign land and murder the f**k out of Heavenly Peter.  Gameplay proceeds entirely in classic point-and-click fashion.  If you've ever played a Sierra or LucasArts game, you know exactly what to expect.  And on the whole, the puzzles are fair, and only a couple seem particularly tricky.  Bellona can die in a couple places, but the game helpfully autosaves before it happens so there's no real punishment.  It's also possible to get into a dead-woman-walking situation, but the game outright TELLS you to save before you do the thing which will lead to this, so it's entirely on you if you ignore the warning.  Plus there's an alternate ending which can only be seen this way.But the emphasis here is on the style and humor, which lands way more often than not.  Dialogue is strong, the animations have great comic timing, and there are plenty of genuinely screwy situations you'll end up in.  As mentioned above, the comedy does tend to be quite dark and twisted.  It might not be for all tastes, although the Renaissance art prevents it from ever being particularly gory or troubling, even in a scene with a lot of crucified people.  Or as the game puts it, "naughty boys."I personally found it one of the funnier comedy games I've played in a while. It's fairly short, as adventure games go, and could probably be finished in an hour.  I got through it in three short sessions.  But for me, it was long enough for the price.  Definitely recommended, if you want to go on a murderous rampage across classic artwork.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, as long as you are a fan of point and click adventures and don't mind very black humor. Also you shouldn't be offended by jokes about religion. And, well, the game is not very long or difficult as well. As long as you are fine with that (I am), this game is extremely funny. You play a female military officer who wants to continue to kill people but isn't allowed to do so because the Holy War has ended. The authorities might look away, though, if you kill the leader of the defeated warparty, who has fled. So you go on a mission to kill Heavenly Peter. The core gameplay is classic pnc - look at/talk to/operate are the three options you have to interact with hotspots. You can also use your sword or your inventory. That's it. The graphic consists of (parts of) famous Renaissance paintings, the characters are papercut figures from those paintings. Looks really cool, especially if you are a connoisseur of this time period. The same goes for the music, the game uses quite a few excerpts from classic titles, and you can hum along with all of them. Expect an autosave function (manual save is possible) and a hotspot finder when you explore the landscape and have really weird conversations with its inhabitants. Monty Python would be proud if they had written this game. A scene can't be cruel enough that it still isn't funny. If you have played the earlier game from Mr. Richardson, Four Last Things, you know what to expect.Classic paintings and music combined with a very surreal humor form a hilarious, but very short, point and click adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: This is another delightful adventure from Joe Richardson. I loved Four Last Things and he did not disappoint with Procession to Calvary. It is clever, funny, irreverent, and incredibly entertaining. Using classical music and artwork, he has put together a world that is fun to explore and will keep you laughing out loud. Dialog is presented as text and the absence of voice overs is a definite plus.  Be prepared to think out of the box to solve some of the more complicated quests.  And, don't be in a hurry. This is a game that begs for you to click on every object and use every dialog option for the pure fun of it.I highly recommend Procession to Calvary for those looking for a unique game with an intelligent sense of humor. Those who have played Four Last Things will enjoy the cross-references.I played through more than once and experienced three unique endings that all had me in stitches! This title makes it to my list of my most enjoyable gaming experiences this year.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: (No spoilers.)  An absolutely fantastic game that's just dripping with style.  It's borrowed style, but in this case that's even better!  Watch classic paintings come to life to tell an absolutely ridiculous story.  Perfect for Easter (in a deeply-irreverent sort of way)!Put more directly, the art is top-notch, the animation is hilarious, and the (also-borrowed) musical pairings are perfect.The puzzles are all fair, ranging from several strictly-logical affairs to a handful of clever head scratchers.  Nothing is so difficult or random that it should drive you to a walkthrough, and I suggest you avoid looking up the solutions to any puzzles lest you shorten your total gameplay.  (If you ever get stuck, just revisit areas you haven't been to recently and look at things fresh.  That should generally do the trick.)My first playthrough was about five and a half hours.  That was with no walkthrough use whatsoever and having a good time stopping to interact with everything.  It would be possible to beat the game significantly faster, but I don't recommend it.Go for it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply hilarious. It uses animated renaissance paintings to tell a satiric story where the protagonist is a nonsensical murderess, fond of slaying anyone she crosses (cute animals, musicians and mothers being the exception). And the dev found satire in everything, even his own work! It is extremely hard to not keep laughing while playing.I had never been interested in renaissance art before, but this game was a real learning experience. There is one room in the game where the dev presents all the paintings (with their title and authors) that he used in the game. And I found some paintings really beautiful. This game really changed my mind how I saw renaissance paintings.The game has 3 different endings, one obtained after only maybe 20 minutes of gameplay while the others need a bit more work to get.I highly recommend this game. It will make you laugh and you will learn something at the same time!
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: SOThere is an obvious Monty Python reference here, and it actually fits.In this point&click adventure you live out your dreams of murder, but since the war is over, there is only one legitimate victim left. Talk to everyone, collect everything, no matter how ridiculous, and use items on the right things. All the while you can brush up on your renaissance and baroque music knowledge, as well was interact with your favorite old paintings. The girl with the pearl earring (Vermeer) was my favorite.Pretty short, not too much adventure moon logic, great look, great music and humor, fair price.Follow my curator at PS: Ashen backed the game on kickstarter, so you know this will go on my "wtf did I just play?"-list.

_childDocuments_.review: Short but good point-and-click adventure. The game is very pythonesque and the animation style resembles the Monty Python a lot too. I found the puzzles pretty straightforward and despite being stuck for a while at one point, the game has new dialogue options for the relevant characters that made it clear how to progress.Highly recommended if you liked The Four Things and also if you like point-and-click games in general. The Linux version worked perfectly as well.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, this is seriously funny.I appreciated Four Last Things, which was peculiar but not very good as an adventure. This is an all-round improvement, sharing the same wonderful idea behind the graphics and music, but with better puzzles, not too cerebral but nonetheless not easy. Its structure feels more complete and classic in a good way, but keeping a fluid narrative and in my opinion it is the most complicate thing for an adventure to find a correct balance between puzzle and fluid storytelling.It is crude, violent, ironic and i think pretty blasphemous... but also has a few flaws! It is short, but longer than Four Last Things, and it may offend your religious belief if you have one and you completely lack any sense of irony.Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: The Middle Ages- what a crazy time to be alive! It's after the Holy Wars and you play as a representation of Rembrandt's  who just wants to do some murder and Heavenly Peter is in your crosshairs. Wildly irreverent, self-aware, and deeply sacrilege,  is the second title from  in his bizarre triptych. I love that it's called a triptych. I finally got through this in preparation for  I've already played through  and honestly don't remember it too much except for the similar design style and humor but I feel like  was a bit more straightforward and less obtuse in the puzzle department. I finished this in a little under 4 hours and only had to look up two things towards the end and I am typically a pretty impatient person when it comes to point-n-click games because I frequently find at some point I can't follow the dev's logic. But this was a little easier and it seems like some knowledge of the paintings and historical context will help intuitively guide you to the next steps. The foley and BGM are very appropriate and add to a weird sense of cozy hilarity. Overall,  reads "Monty Python" in the sense that it's constructed of those familiar crudely animated art history textbook collage but the humor is distinctly North American. I did totally laugh out loud at places and mostly had a wicked grin running across my face the rest of the time. But the humor is  for everyone: If you are sensitive at all about Christianity/Christ in particular you probably want to skip this. It's not all silly fart, burp, and crucifix jokes, though. There is throughout and at the end some flippantly profound commentary around religious hypocrisy, class hierarchy, and social responsibility. I enjoyed this one and am looking forward to

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the first game of the series, I was so thrilled to see the game play mechanics get enhanced. This game basically solved most of the technical difficulties I was having with the first one. I also really enjoyed how this game expanded to have multiple endings. The art and music was lovely as ever. I didn't think 4th wall breaks would ever make me laugh, but the one mentioning the Kickstarter was so brilliant.I still had to use a guide for some tricky parts, but overall, if you know some things about renaissance art and religion, you will be able to solve most the puzzles. The Procession to Calvary is even more crude than the first game, and it was great. Can't wait for the next one!

_childDocuments_.review: is a follow-up to , a wacky renaissance point & click adventure with great graphics and music supplied by the masters of the era.pretty much more of the same, about twice as much, in fact, clocking . instead of various sins, the story focuses on a lady who still wants to continue killing people despite the war being over, so she heads out to talk things over with the guy in charge, immortal john, who you might remember from somewhere. our hero interprets the conversation as a mission to kill heavenly peter, so that's what she sets out to do.while there are some recurring characters and locations here and there, it's perfectly enjoyable on its own. still, you'd be a fool to skip either game, and somewhat of a lesser fool to only consider the pacifist way of going through calvary, as . punching people in the face is also advised.resolution options and windowed mode are available via the unity launcher, separate volume settings in-game, controls are the usual, plus middle mouse to highlight hotspots (only very briefly, which is annoying, but if you hold the mouse button over the magnifying glass in the top right corner, it'll keep flashing the icons), right click to draw/sheath your sword, double click to run. manual saving available (only 4 slots, no confirmation before overwrite, nor time or date to identify which is which) and the game autosaves every now and then, like before you accidentally (or on purpose) do something stupid that results in a game over screen.not gonna bother with a whole essay this time, , it's a point & click adventure like no other (except ).

_childDocuments_.review: I have only two complaints about this game. 1.I am a reviewer in Steam and I hate this meta ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! © 2.Why is the organist in the cathedral not nude, Joe! But seriously, the sequel of my beloved “Four last things” simply could not turn out bad, and if you knew her, then you know what to expect. A crazy mix from the dark Middle Ages, Monty Python's macabre humor style, unmotivated violence, incredibly beautiful artworks, each of which is based on medieval works of art, classical music, juicy gags and skunk. In fact, I don’t even want to spoil some jokes in the review so that you can enjoy them yourself during the game. This time we play for the harsh woman-warrior, who after the end of the war has absolutely nothing to do, so she goes on an absolutely random assignment (which, frankly, nobody gave her), trying not to kill anyone on the way (hehe, not to kill anyone in the Middle Ages, oh yes)The game is completely absurd and not shy about it. You can literally go through it , using the most surreal way I've seen in games in my life for this. Animations, dialogs, descriptions of objects, even the smallest details of anything are created in order to make you laugh. It would seem, how can you make ridiculous and absurd thanks to the backers from Kickstarter? Believe me, you can. Although the game, like its predecessor, is not too long (3-4 hours), but it is so saturated that this time will seem to you something incredible. The interweaving with the first game is very pleasing, it is nice to see old characters and recall those events, to see their impact on the world in this game. The concentration of humor here is just off scale, by the end of the game there is simply no strength left. And most of all I am glad that this is not a repetition of the last game, it really changed in spirit, being perceived by Something Completely Different. I have remained exceptionally pure delight, of course I advise you to try and appreciate this gem by yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: It was a super quirky, weird and funny game. I was entertained throughout while enjoying the classical art theme and classical bg music .. super glad I played it. All the endings were unique and I had fun going over them. A chance to go around sticking your sword into every person you meet? Hell yeah! Brilliant short game!

_childDocuments_.review: Great idea but lacklustre execution.I am a huge fan of point-and-click adventure games, so when I heard a YouTuber praise this game, I immediately went ahead and bought it. The art style is marvellously grotesque, and I love it. The game is often witty, always bizarre, and frankly, it's a romp!That being said, it features all the tropes of mediocre point-and-click adventure games, namely an overabundance of . Every single puzzle is either convoluted and far-fetched, or it's ridiculously obvious; none of them feels 'just right' in terms of logic and difficulty. I guess the developer figured a grotesque game need only be filled with grotesque puzzles, and in my opinion, the two don't really mesh well together. Case in point, the final objective betrays a cruel lack of inspiration, . And it's a shame, really, because this game is extremely short. Outside of a few "missable" achievements, it has little replayability because it lacks a cohesive story. Some of the achievements .In short, I love the game's Monty Pythonesque aesthetic, but the illogical progression reminds me of  and its  sans the brainteaser.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece. It is like an endless nightmare you never want to become to an end. Mixture of really dark humor and real Renaissance artworks the game establishes something so unique and genuine that usually kept me dropping the jaw. Being as witty, gorgeous and hunting it easily leaves players to just want more when they reach its state of completeness.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Who could have known that the Renaissance was so murderously funny?! You won't stop laughing while you're playing this game! Everything felt so artistic and funny. The puzzles weren't difficult at all, but, at least, they weren't too easy and they were creative. This game is a sight for sore eyes and is undoubtedly worth its price. Great job, Joe!
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Solo developer Joe has returned with what I think is his best game so far. The Procession To Calvary is in the same style as his last game, Four Last Things, even using some of the same UI graphics and characters, but he has stepped everything up a notch here.Procession... is incredibly funny with several laugh out loud moments, and contains some of the best writing I've ever seen in a point n click game. Added to that is the brilliantly done animations which make great use of the odd facial expressions the characters possess, and the comic timing is just perfect.The puzzles are fun, mostly logical, and certainly not challenging, so you're never taking too long or having to guess very much to continue enjoying the game. Yes, there is a certain amount of back and forth between locations to complete them, but that is expected in this kind of game. Plus, it reveals more of the hilarious dialog, which is always a good thing.Joe has essentially mastered the art (pun intended) of this style of game and, like before, he also makes very effective use of music throughout, with different pieces of classical music being played in each location. And it feels like they fit in SO well with the theme of the scene.So, what are you waiting for? Grab your sword, give it a quick polish, and set forth at once on your own Procession to Calvary! You will NOT be disappointed!
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to believe that someone made a Monty Pythonesque (specifically Terry Gilliam animationesque) game in the 2020s and it is actually good, yet here we are.  A short, frequently (though not always) hilarious diversion full of beautiful medieval/Renaissance art that does not get the chance to wear out its welcome.  Definitely my kind of adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Clever concept and execution, especially the breaking-the-fourth-wall part. It's linked with the first game - The Four Last Things, with a bit of continuation and returning characters. But if you haven't played the first game, you'll still be able to enjoy this game. Definitely not everyone's cup of tea; it's a satire and may be offensive to people belonging to certain religions. Otherwise, enjoy it as a piece of art (pun not intended).
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: You can't seriously review this game without mentioning Monty Python's Flying Circus, so here you go: Monty Python's Flying Circus.It didn't come as a surprise to me that it's fun, that it's brutal or that it's not meant to be politically correct. What did surprise me was that it actually involved some thinking when solving puzzles. So, it's short, but fun, if you're into the stuff that had to and has been mentioned.Runs flawlessly on Linux.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Dude didn't know what to do with his master's degree in art history and his unparalleled talent for making memes from the past decade... And then he decided to make a video game.It's a gem with such a silly and charming concept and execution that it's much more fun than it has any right to be. This right here is a work of art (or several) masterfully packaged in the format of one of the most potentially frustrating genres I know.How many great stories have been lost in the intricacies of puzzles with alien logic or pixel hunts? But among the many games I've regrettably played of this type, The Procession to Calvary has the distinct quality of being one of the few that I actually enjoyed my time with and would like to play again rather than watch. It's a short, consistently hilarious adventure with no interruptions that add nothing to the experience. The simple puzzles, even though they are insane, make more sense and are easier to decipher than 90% of the great classics of the genre. This is the kind of game that whenever you encounter a "problem", a big smile spreads across your face.The thing was simply put together and executed quite confidently.For obvious reasons, it's also an extremely beautiful game, full of great music. I'm surprised this hasn't been done sooner... And that it's legally viable.It's recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: I adored Four Last Things and am finding further joy in The Procession to Calvary. The fine art animations are as smooth as they are silly and charming. The dialogue and the gameplay are as bizarre and funny as ever. If you like point-and-click adventures, Renaissance art, or Monty Python, or preferably all of the above, then this deliciously twisted labor of love is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: This game is b***dy hilarious.Classic point-and-click puzzles, plenty of fourth-wall meta nonsense, lots of gorgeous Renaissance art & music used in *very* clever and funny ways, and just a wonderful, uplifting, silly, occasionally gory and deeply enjoyable story. Most of the puzzles were silly, but not completely random - you can figure them out with a bit of common sense or by just paying close attention. There's only two or three hours in it, but it's all gold and no filler.And honestly, who could hope for a better visual aesthetic than the cream of Renaissance art?
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Good short length PnC adventure game. Fun and original setting with good puzzles and use of a smaller scope environment. Writing feels a mix of Monty Python and Ron Gilbert and brings more than enough laughs to justify the price along with the great visuals mashup and excellent classical musical choices throughout. Only negative is that the gameplay concept of being able to stab everyone and create alternate puzzle solutions doesn't really work since you can't really clear the game if you kill even a single person along the way, which is a bit of a shame. It's a fun little diversion to check out what happens when you do stab people instead of solving the puzzles, but it doesn't really bring the multiple solution ways for progression that it seemed like it might have.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Like Four Last Things, the sequel is Monty Python meets Monkey Island meets Renaissance paintings meets religious satire.  Unlike Four Last Things, this installment is heavier on offensiveness and digs at religion but lighter on clever humor and uniqueness.  The idea of a warmonger creating a Crusade for herself is a funny concept, and there is a lot of good humor throughout the game.  That said, personally I found the bad to outweigh the good in this particular case.  That said, I'm willing to admit that I'm not the target audience for this game, and I'm not dismissing those who enjoyed it.  I just feel that it was personally not a game worth playing for me.  Finally, I do have to give this game credit for one of my favorite achievements I've ever gotten in a video game: Serial Killer, where you progress through the game by just murdering every significant character that in regular gameplay you need to move forward.  It's an unbelievably funny achievement and it almost made the game worth it for me.  Almost.  4/10.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Calvary is the second part in a soon to be trilogy of comedic historical-themed Point&Click-Adventures mainly notable for their visuals, built entirely from renaissance-era paintings, cut-up and spliced together collage-style, with some crude animation to tie everything together, which ends up being exactly as unique and impressive to look at as it sounds like.Sadly the rest of the game doesn't really live up to the quality of its presentation, with bog-standard Point&Click gameplay and somewhat mediocre puzzles, most of which are pretty easy, but there's a handful of questionable leaps, though nowhere near the kind of obtuse insanity the genre has become somewhat infamous for.The game's also a bit on the short side, with a playthrough generally clocking in at around 2.5-3 hours and without much in the way of replayability, though, to be fair, it's a solo endeavour and not terribly expensive, so make of that what you will.Finally, there's the writing, and I frankly don't care for it. Expect lots of try-hard "dark" humor and half-baked satire, a truly painful sequence of incredibly unfunny 4th wall breaks and many lazy attempts at capturing some of that Monty Python-style weirdness the storepage alludes to without fully grasping what makes it work. Of course, humor is inherently subjective and judging by some of the other reviews, there's a lot of people who seem to really enjoy the humor in this, so your mileage may vary.Ultimately, the game's worth a look if only for the unique aesthethic, but don't go in expecting a masterpiece of comedy or adventure design. And if you haven't already, I'd also recommend trying out the "Four Last Things", the first entry in the trilogy, which is quite a bit shorter, with similarly dodgy puzzle design, but slightly better writing I'd say, and a plot that gives some admittedly optional background to the events of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely Fantastic. One of the best adventure games I've played in a long time. Procession to Calvary is a traditional point-and-click adventure with a twist: All the art is renaissance paintings brought to life with jiggle bone and a few modern effects. The music matches too. Any scene with music has visible bards you can interact with. You play a psychopathic killer who is just barely able to exist in a normal society. Your goal is to kill the pseudo-catholic warlord round these parts and it kind of kicks off from there. Procession to Calvary uses the "gating" method of adventure game design (I'll let you in this area for a floopdoodle, I'll give you a floopdoodle for a shimsham, shimsham for a minigame), but it really works because of the writing and the jokes. Comedy is extremely difficult for games to get right, especially adventure games. Procession to Calvary hits the mark. I was consistently cracking up again and again and again. Just when you think they're out of jokes, the developer does something really clever that pulls it all together.Best of all, I think, is that Procession to Calvary comes with a thematic cheat button. Your character wants to murder everything in their way. If you get stuck or bored, you can just kill anyone in your way and rush to the ending. Innovative design, fantastic comedy, good adventure game questing, and inspired concept. This is an adventure game for the books and one I was proud to 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: This finally fulfills the potential that Four Last Things had. Even though we know the gig from FLT, the environments are still striking. The huge improvement is that now everything fits together better, starting with the fierce warrior woman who we're playing as -- and who in fact is Rembrandt's Bellona. Instead of just borrowing some random characters, the game is making use of familiar paintings and themes to create an unexpected effect or to give the player a chance to interact with the characters from the paintings in a way that's actually related to the nature of those characters and paintings. Talking to the girl from Vermeer's portrait who complains that she feels incomplete was just great (it's entirely possible though that I just missed some connections in FLT).It is way more funny than FLT in all departments: the puzzles, the actions of the protagonist, the dialogs, the general silliness. The puzzles in FLT were often more annoying than entertaining. Most of the puzzles in Calvary are quite simple (and they allow taking short, although in most cases that will affect the ending), but pretty much all of them are well-designed, well-signposted and actually funny (the wheel, the lamb, the treasure map, the , you name it).

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a Kickstarter campaign last year which I backed, and for fans of the previous game Four Last Things or just tongue-in-cheek adventure games, Procession to Calvary is an easy recommendation.This games style comes from the mash-up of sophisticated renaissance era paintings used as characters and backgrounds, mixed in with anachronistic, absurdist, and fourth wall breaking humor. It worked really well for Four Last Things, and Procession to Calvary is very much the same deal. The game is not that long, about 3-5 hours depending how much of a completionist you are, but it is filled with jokes and fairly simple puzzles. Majority of the puzzles were reasonable to figure out with no moon logic, but there were a couple of puzzles I wasn't really fond of. One puzzle required brute memorization, and in two other instances you're stuck searching for a needle in a haystack even after you've figured out what you need to do. However, these puzzles are at least doable, and as a last resort the creator of the game has posted a walkthrough if you're truly stumped.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game in its own right, and an excellent follow up to Four Last Things. It would be entertaining enough to see familiar paintings brought to life, and figures from different paintings conversing, but the puzzles are good and Joe Richardson’s writing is consistently irreverent and insightful. Once again there's meta-commentary on the process of game making and publishing, which is sharp and accurate. The music is well-chosen and, as in a Haneke film, always has a source in the scene. The new protagonist has a refreshing character, in contrast to the usual game do-gooder, and the addition of her sword “verb” adds many new possibilities (be careful using this, but never give up, even if it looks like there is no way out. You will always be able to reach an ending). It is an adventure game, with all that goes with it, so there is much going back and forth, working out what’s required and how to trigger it in each scene. As in Joe’s first “Preposterous” game, there are puzzles in this that depend on timing, one of which threw me for ages before I realised what was required, and another in which I misunderstood the hint and was stumbling around in the wrong location. None of this impaired my enjoyment of the game though, it’s just the nature of this sort of game, and the environments are so well made that I didn't mind spending more time in them than I had to. Recommended for everyone, but especially recommended for anyone that has ever taken a class in art history and spaced out at the slides, imagining the stories within.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a backer of this because I enjoyed Four Last Things and Procession to Calvary is a bigger and better sequel. One added difference is a mechanic rarely seen in adventure games and that's being able to stab most of your problems away, its' kind of like in Westwood's Blade Runner game where you can pull out your gun at anytime, though just like in that game there may be consequences for it here too... But yeah, if you enjoyed Four Last Things then this is a must play as its an overall improvement and overall fun adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: I'm at neutral/meh level with this game. Play it only if you run out of other point and click adventure games on Steam and all your paints have dried so you have nothing to watch. It's often on huge discount, so surely wait for that if you're curious.I don't think I've seen another game that took paintings and made them alive. This is very good idea, and works very fine. The world is made into quite coherent whole, out of tens of paintings. Each location has a band or a musician playing the background music(all classical compositions). It's a very nice touch, and the musicians were my favourite part of the game. I made sure to clap at all of them, which you can do in this game.Some of the visual gags are funny, although none of them is "laugh out loud" funny. It's not even "have a smirk" funny. Text-based humour sucks. Half of the dialogues are written like conversations on Twitter. The characters speak in a way that you find only on social media when teenagers try to be "kewl" with each other. It's very jarring. When the NPCs talk semi-normally but in a loose manner it creates fun contrast for the art presented. But once they degenerate into half-brains it's really unfunny, lame, and cringe-worthy.The puzzles are OK, I guess. First half of the game is made out of linear, really easy tasks. Then the game opens up, and you have 4 tasks to complete in parallel. You can choose to solve most of the game trough violence and kill many of the NPCs. If you're solving everything without the murder it's very easy to forget about the option to use your sword, and some puzzles still require you to use it. Some of the puzzles are irritating. There's one that makes you interact with the fish, but you have only one chance, before the fish runs away. If you don't do the proper action fast enough you will have to run trough multiple screens, watch long and boring animation, before you have another chance. Or there's a scene where you have to choose dialogue options so fast you don't even have time to read them all. It's even more jarring, because you have to wait pretty long before next dialogue option appears (as it tries to sync to what's going on the screen). I think it could have been done much better, show the dialogue options a bit earlier.Even though the game has some merits here and there, the abysmal quality of dialogues is killing the game. Most of the game is spent on talking to NPCs, so some nice visual jokes can't save the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Having been impressed by the author's previous game, "Four Last Things," I was filled with excitement to try its sequel, "The Procession to Calvary."I adore the concept of animated Renaissance paintings presented in a bizarre and humorous context. The rich symbolism found in old paintings becomes a delightful experience as visual concepts are reinterpreted with a touch of humor. The game's immersive atmosphere is further enhanced by the classical music soundtrack.However, when comparing "The Procession to Calvary" to its predecessor, "Four Last Things," it becomes evident which game design choices excel.The Procession to Calvary" boasts a straightforward plot. You assume the role of a bloodthirsty character driven by a desire for revenge against the emperor from the previous game. A sword is introduced, providing you with the option to eliminate any obstacles in your path. While a peaceful approach leads to the best ending, the allure of witnessing the consequences of choosing violence is irresistible. Notably, this path allows for swift progression, leading to the "bad" ending in just 15 minutes.In theory that is not bad, since it shows you pretty quickly that the violence is not the way to go. But the problem I have is the fact that most of the game's scenes are uncovered within those initial 15 minutes. Since the game is very much an interactive painting, this quick revelation somewhat diminishes the anticipation and intrigue surrounding the ending.Of course you don't get to see everything, since there is a peaceful and longer way to progress in the game. You got to access a couple more scenes and rooms. My favorite being the art gallery, where you can see all the original works of paintings that the game uses to build the world.Regrettably, I found the puzzle-solving logic towards the game's conclusion less captivating. While it started promisingly, I struggled and eventually gave up on the last few puzzles, including the talent show, devil sacrifice, and a farting skunktalent show, devil sacrifice and a farting skunk..The ultimate two good endings didn't really provide additional content, that I hoped for. Hence my complains towards the bad ending being too revealing. Consequently, the frustrating puzzles towards the end and an underwhelming climax, left kinda sour taste in mouth.Nonetheless, "The Procession to Calvary" deserves applause for its ability to once again create beautiful collages of Renaissance paintings. And for that I am willing to pay money and would love to see more of. Even though as a game, it might not be the best.Games are indeed works of art, and viewing "The Procession to Calvary" from that perspective mitigates some of its flaws. Nevertheless, I would recommend redirecting your attention to the author's first game, "Four Last Things," which, in my opinion, offers a superior experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just start off by saying that the creator made a number of obvious (and in my mind childish) historical and geographical errors in the creation of this game. While the creator seems to be a well-meaning purveyor of history instruction interactive video games for children, as a historian I felt nothing but whiplash from the careless transitions from Bruges to Florence to Venice -- like we're expected to just  our armiger protagonist could traverse half of Europe at a jog! Parents, beware.There were other errors riddled into this game. At one point, a lyre  sounds like a guitar, and there's a visa reference to a profession that's at least  anachronistic. Finally, there were a few meta gags which, the creator should know, do NOT sit well with Steam reviewers. To my mind, these betray low standards in a game designed for the pedagogical uplift of children. (However, the anatomically specific sword wounds are to be commended.)All this being said, if your child is of the sort that doesn't to care enough to distinquish between 1540 and the 1545, then I could see the charming selection of music, the exciting Early Modern talent show, and immersive smithy puzzles to hold merit among households seeking to raise athletes, rather than scholars.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was oddly disappointing compared to the previous entry. Theoretically, its greater length should increase its value, but the gameplay grew grating as time dragged on. The puzzles this time felt more roundabout, which should have added a great satisfaction to the solving, but at several points they just seemed reliant on what we used to call "Sierra's Moon Logic"... And while on a scholarly level I appreciated the tribute to Morton Smith's ludicrous 1970s work "Jesus the Magician," this game veered from the manic irreverence of the first to a tiresome reliance on simple shock tactics. Farts! Crucifixions! Catholic pederast jokes! Ooh, how daring. Yawn. It's not the 1990s anymore, gang. Arguably the best parts were the opening and the three different endings -- everything in the middle just felt like a slog after a few minutes.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually a big gamer, only finally getting around to it due to Coronavirus lockdown, and this game immediately jumped out at me as something more esoteric and unusual, as well as being similar to the old Monkey Island games I remember playing when I was younger. I'm not hugely educated on classical art but I can appreciate it, and seeing these backdrops animated and satirised was massively enjoyable, especially when accompanied with the appropriate music.Moreso, the game is one of the funniest I've played. Stumbling upon both alternate endings before finding the designed one, I loved how well the game balanced mocking the stuffiness of all the art and music but stopped short of undermining it, instead encouraging the audience to look into it more. I laughed out loud a fair few times and there were many moments that genuinely surprised me in a good way. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant!  Similar in style to Four Last Things, and as terrific as that game is, Procession to Calvary is even better.  It's not just that the use of Renaissance and 18th century paintings for every bit of artwork in the game (and as in Four Last Things, there's a cool art gallery room where you can see the original paintings used for every character and scene in the game), is a great idea in and of itself.  It's on top of that how cleverly well implemented everything else in the game is --  puzzles, jokes, characters, music.  There are tons of supposedly comic p&c adventure games but almost none of them are actually funny.  Procession to Calvary is laugh out loud funny repeatedly.  Joe Richardson somehow manages to pull off very smartly written crass toilet humor and a general tone of a sort of existential absurdity.  It's legitimately Python-esque, a level of sophisticated silliness many try for but few have managed to successfully pull off.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Procession to Calvary" is a delightful successor to the whimsical adventure game "Four Last Things," crafting a Pythonesque experience from Renaissance paintings that is both hilarious and engaging.Embark on a journey through a meticulously crafted world of Renaissance paintings, where you'll undertake tasks ranging from stealing a ship to conversing with divine entities. Immerse yourself in the beauty of Renaissance artwork by renowned masters like Rembrandt and Michelangelo, set to a classical soundtrack featuring compositions by Vivaldi and Bach that complement the game's artistic ambiance.While "The Procession to Calvary" shares a universe with "Four Last Things," its standalone narrative offers a fresh and engaging experience for both returning players and newcomers.With the option to wield a sword and make choices that impact the story's outcome, players must decide between peaceful solutions or more violent paths, akin to the moral dilemmas found in games like Undertale.Experience a blend of surreal comedy, well-crafted puzzles, and moments of unexpected depth in a game that seamlessly combines humor with thought-provoking scenarios."The Procession to Calvary" offers a grottesque and splatter-filled adventure with well-designed puzzles, humor that breaks the fourth wall, humor on breaking the fourth wall, and multiple endings to discover. While the game may be short, its entertaining gameplay and diverse narrative paths ensure a memorable and enjoyable experience for players of all types.

_childDocuments_.review: is an unique, humorous and creative puzzle game that does not get the attention it deserves. The game comes after Joe Richardson’s other game  ; although the games are not technically required to be played in order, there are a couple easter eggs referencing that prior release. This is a shorter game that can be completed on a weekend afternoon, which includes achievement hunting if that is a goal. There really is not a lot to critique about the game; it is a quirky point and click puzzle game. Some of the humor is dark and has gory moments, which might not be what some people are looking for. The puzzles were balanced and intuitive, with only once instance where it required the player to make a leap in logic. The “double click to move faster” function was a bit clunky (at least on my laptop.) The majority of the time it worked, especially while moving from one section to the next, however, if you wanted to rush over to talk with an NPC it was finicky and took some  to make the mechanic work.On one hand I lament how short the game is, but on the other it was the right amount of exposure to the humor and style to not lose its novelty. The humor is reminiscent to Monty Python, but its edgier and stands on its own. The first ending was well constructed regarding to how it punishes players for rushing through the game, while also giving them hints along the way to change course. Once you’ve achieved ending 1 (assuming it was indeed your first play through) you can then go and experience what the game has to offer.  The game encourages players to interact with NPCs and their surroundings, offering them humorous results, and given how short the game is there really isn’t a reason not to.

_childDocuments_.review: Joe Richardson returns with his latest game, and the direct sequel to Four Last Things. That's right: this is a sequel, even if the description says "spiritual successor"; the plot is a direct continuation so I highly recommend checking out the first game if you haven't already.Joe's writing is in top form in this release, having gotten better with each subsequent game. One thing you'll notice if you've played all his games (like I did over the last couple days) is that he has gotten less existential / political with time. Earlier Richardson games had more of a philosophical slant; meanwhile, The Procession to Calvary owns its status as a comedy game through and through. And, honestly, I think this is Richardson's best work; impressively, I think he has gotten better with each subsequent release. Comedy writing is difficult and this guy is -good- at it now. There are small parts where the dialogue is a bit too involved, but by and large, it's quite well done.Highlights include: The game's pretty short (most people seem to do it in 3-4 hrs), but it actually has quite a bit more screens than any of his previous games. Seeing a new screen with new (old?) art is my favorite part of these games so I'm happy he was able to cram more in. It took me a little longer than most to beat this one, as I got stuck quite a bit more than normal. I don't think any of the puzzles were particularly difficult or obtuse; I just couldn't put 2 and 2 together on a handful of them for whatever reason. There's no hint system, and quite a few of the puzzles come with effectively no clues from NPC dialogue, so if you're stuck you're just stuck. Got through it just fine but I was in Adventure game hell for a little while there.Wish we get voice acting in his next release. Would really level things up. Nonetheless, I greatly enjoyed this one, and I'll play whatever Joe puts out next. Well done.

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Calvary is Joe Richardson's follow-up to the excellent Four Last Things. Richardson retains the same art style and music that made the first game so unique: public domain paintings - subtly animated - and fittingly classical music gives this series a wholly unique style.The plot is rather simple. You play as a woman on a quest from the Immortal John to kill Heavenly Peter. Along the way you'll meet several characters and complete quests for them, from saving a "street magician" to winning a talent contest. Puzzles can be a little obscure, I wasn't always sure what to do and had to look up a good at some points. The player character moves very slowly, even with the "run" option turned on, and there's a lot of backtracking involved. Despite this, I enjoyed the game. Robinson has a good sense of humor; he breaks the fourth wall at certain points and has no problem poking fun at himself. As a fan of the time period a lot of the art of is drawn from, the visuals carried the game through some of the more frustrating puzzles for me. Runtime is very short - expect to spend anywhere from 90 minutes to 2 and a half hours, maybe a little more if you decide to play again to get all the endings. I wasn't motivated enough to do so, but the Steam achievements indicate there are 3 endings. In summary, The Procession to Calvary is a nice follow-up to Four Last Things, but doesn't reach that game's highs. Take a look at the Steam store page - if you like the art and music and enjoy point and clicks, you'll enjoy this game.﻿$10 is maybe a bit steep, but the game often goes on sale for $4 or less, at which price it's a solid buy.Score: 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: First off, let me say that if you're intrigued by the look of the game and into the whole point-and-click adventure genre, Procession to Calvary will not disappoint. Well worth full price, and if you happen to be reading this during a sale, stop reading the reviews and just buy it already! Get a copy for a friend while you're at it.In case it wasn't already clear, this is a point-and-click game in the vein of LucasArts' Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, Sam & Max Hit the Road, etc. The focus is on using inventory and dialogue options to solve puzzles and make your way through the story. Like Richardson's previous games, there are multiple "bad" endings to be discovered along with the one "good" one - you can speedrun your way to one of them in mere minutes of play by simply killing everyone you meet, and I recommend doing this at least once because it's hilarious. In the spirit of the games that inspired it, though, incorrect choices rarely lead to permanent setbacks - you can usually continue the game right after one of the bad endings and get back on the straight and narrow path immediately. The one exception is (unsanctioned) murder, which will not only lock you out of the good ending but also most of the story. But, the game straight-up warns you to create a manual save before you begin sprinting down the assassin's road, so, fair enough. Having now played through the whole "Games by Joe Richardson" bundle, one thing I will say is that he's gotten much, much better with every game. I found the two previous games clever but flawed, in particular by writing that occasionally lapsed into the sort of above-it-all cynical philosophizing that I probably would have enjoyed a lot more in my teens but now seems... kind of cringey. At least the visual style of Four Last Things (to which this is a direct sequel) was an improvement over The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything's intentional jankiness. (I know it's satire - it even directly name-drops Rabelais for chrissakes -  but I still had to *look* at these characters the whole time I was playing, you know?)Procession to Calvary keeps all the best aspects of its immediate predecessor but the puzzles are better designed, there's more to do, and the writing is sharp and funny and manages to be About Stuff without resorting to text-walls of artless, on-the-nose social commentary. The whole thing just comes together in a way that the previous two (while still good and worth playing!) couldn't quite get to.I'm very much looking forward to seeing where he takes the series in the next installment, "Death of the Reprobate"!
