_childDocuments_.review: IntroductionThe notion of spraying tea across your keyboard because you’ve witnessed something sphincter-clenchingly hilarious has become something of an internet meme.  It’s the sort of thing people say to express a level of amusement they rarely, if ever, attain… but nobody really sprays tea across their keyboard.  (And those who do have learned a valuable lesson.  Don’t drink beverages at your workstation.  It’s unsanitary, and has the very real potential to brick that expensive RGB mechanical gaming keyboard you sold one of your kidneys to pay for.)However, if any game genuinely has the capacity to cause you to spray tea across your keyboard, it’s Joe Richardson’s ‘The Procession To Calvary’.  It’s so consistently funny it should really come with some sort of health advisory attached.  If you’ve ever watched Monty Python’s Flying Circus and giggled yourself stupid over Terry Gilliam’s surreal animations featuring, among other things, the hand of God, ladies devoid of clothes, and a lot of farting, then you’ll have a vague idea of the chortle-fest that is The Procession To Calvary.GameplayA sequel to the also very amusing ‘Four Last Things’, The Procession To Calvary is a point and click adventure game in the style of Monkey Island or Thimbleweed Park.  You wander around, chat to people, collect items, and then combine everything in order to solve puzzles and advance the story.As the game starts, our sword-wielding, armour-clad heroine is fresh from the battlefield, having waged a successful campaign against the tyrannical ‘Heavenly Peter’ and his Southern armies.  During the game’s intro sequence we witness her capering about famous Renaissance paintings, gleefully lopping off heads, and inflicting grievous injuries on a selection of hapless unfortunates — all to disturbingly jolly musical accompaniment.  Given the rampant bloodshed and horrified screaming, you know you shouldn’t laugh… but you do anyway.In short order, our nameless heroine is promptly informed by her superiors that the war is over, and an age of peace is being ushered in by new leader, Immortal John.  With no more indiscriminate murder on offer, she manages to convince Immortal John that sending her to find and kill Heavenly Peter would be completely acceptable, and not in any way a breathtakingly hypocritical breach of his new ‘age of peace, no more murdering’ policy.  Sword in hand, off she goes to put down a tyrant.If you’ve played a point and click adventure game before (and if you haven’t, you must have spent the last three decades locked in a cupboard), then you’ll get the hang of things in about five minutes.  Holding down the middle mouse button reveals ‘hot spots’ in the current location — people, items, and parts of the scenery with which you’re able to interact.  You can examine things, talk to people, and perform an action (like picking up an object or slapping someone), and what you’re able to do largely depends on the situation.You also have a sword.  This comes in handy for things like cutting ropes, toppling trees, or hacking off someone’s legs.  However, for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction… except in this game where you really have no idea what to expect — although the game does do you the courtesy of warning you when you’re about to commit some atrocity that may have dire consequences.  Usually.Wandering about the first few screens, I decided I’d descend a cliff to have a gander at what might be at the bottom.  A casual click resulted in our heroine hurling herself into space, ending up a mangled pile of broken limbs and bodily fluids, after which “YOU ARE DEAD!” in huge white letters was plastered across the screen.  Fortunately, the game autosaves at regular intervals, so don’t let an abundance of caution constrain your more mischievous inclinations.  Some jokes really are worth dying for.GraphicsOne thing I’ll say about Joe Richardson, the unhinged mastermind behind this game, he must have an awful lot of time on his hands.  To create the graphics for The Procession To Calvary, he has taken a stonking great pile of Renaissance artworks, gleefully mutilated them in Adobe Photoshop, then cobbled them back together as a sort of high-brow, wine and cheese evening, “Look at me! I’m wearing a turtle neck jumper!” abomination.  Then he’s added puerile jokes and  gratuitous violence.  It’s amazing stuff and the man’s quite obviously a genius.  If you’d rather put a live badger down the front of your trousers than visit an art gallery, playing The Procession To Calvary will serve as an appropriate substitute.SoundIf you’ve ever wanted to hear ‘Stars And Stripes Forever’ played by a hyperactive brass band, while in the background, a city burns, Death saws the head off a white-robed layabout, and you slap a man in the face only to be told, “You hit like a girl!”, then this is the game for you!  Pretty much every scene in the game features some surreal musical interlude, whether it’s a cellist sitting in a rowboat, a flute-playing minstrel hopping about after you with his foot stuck in a bucket, or a Baroque quartet playing Bach from a tree, Joe Richardson has managed to shoe-horn important musical works into his game, while also making them utterly ridiculous.  I mean, the music’s great… but it’s the comical irreverence that really makes it all work.  The game fairly screams at you, “See?! This sort of music is for everyone, not just old people in cardigans waiting to die!”The sound effects are likewise brilliant.  Pythonesque “Ooohs!” and “Ahhhs!” are in abundance, along with a selection of slaps, farts, disapproving grumbles, angelic choirs, the grisly sound of limbs being violently severed, and the resultant demented shrieking.  Headphones might be a plan if you don’t want your neighbours to suspect you’re either off your face on drugs or some sort of serial murderer.PerformanceGiven the game is primarily composed of ‘Frankensteined’ 2D art and pop-up text, it’s safe to say you could probably run The Procession To Calvary on a pocket calculator.  This is not a game likely to cause your hardware to raise a sweat, complain about being overworked, and write to its MP, no matter how archaic it happens to be.  If my nine year-old Thinkpad can cope with it, I’m sure whatever rickety embarrassment you have sitting on your desk is more than capable.ConclusionIf you like laughing, and puzzles, and music, and laughing while solving puzzles and listening to music, and appearing all clever and pompous because you’re playing a game full of Renaissance art (when really you’re a cultureless philistine who wouldn’t know art if it crapped on your lawn and burned down your house),  then you desperately need to buy this game.  It’s not only educational, it’s dangerously amusing.  If you’re a fan of Monty Python, and surreal humour in general, you’re probably sold already, but even if you’re not, Joe Richardson is a giant among men who should be showered with cash for his selfless contributions to “not making crap games”.  And he’d probably like to eat, pay the rent, and clothe himself in something other than bin bags and vegetable peelings.Two caveats: The Procession To Calvary is quite short.  Not sneeze and you’ll miss it short, but it’s more suburban hedgerow than Great Wall of China.  (The quality makes up for it!)  The only other reservation would be if you’re a pious sort averse to anything making light of ‘The Big G’.  A game that reduces Our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, to the role of an incompetent street magician is probably something you’re not going to find terribly funny.  Different strokes, and all that.Final verdict: Nine tins of spam out of ten!

_childDocuments_.review: Despite what the weird kid in your class that chuckle-grunted constantly while doodling Joker fanart in his math notebook would have you believe, we did not invent the meme.  The abstraction of meaning to metaphysical absurdity has many names such as "doing a put-on" and "having a jape because you're dying inside."  There is no way a bunch of gross old guys sitting around drunk off their keisters with their teeth rotting out of their heads were being totally serious when they drew cats shaped like bread loaves stabbing jesters in the margins of their illuminated manuscripts.  The Procession to Calvary is a good game that you should just buy, right now, unless you truly detest adventure games in all their variety because it's one long peerless meme and so dank I had to wash my hands after playing.You're a female army officer wandering through the Pythonesque absurdity of Renaissance Europe, helping demons stay fed and making friends with skunks.  The visual gags are second to none and the fact that you can cheat, kinda sorta, buy killing obnoxious NPCs to skip puzzles is a great addition.  The self-awareness keeps the proceedings from becoming a slog and only on a couple of occasions did I struggle more than was justified to solve a puzzle.  Having to do the same thing twice with no obvious indication it will make a difference can be annoying, but hey.  I have the internet on my phone.Pick this up.  You can breeze through it in about three hours on a day off and you'll bask happy in the familiarity that they were slonking the dank memes back when the bathroom was a bucket.  Cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Cavalry is up there as one of the funniest games I have ever had the privilege to enjoy. I'd place it in the same tier as South Park: The Stick of Truth, Trover Saves the Universe, and Aviary Attorney and I would have a very hard time ranking the order to place them in. That being said, the game appeals to a specific group of people that simultaneously enjoy point and click adventures and bawdy dark comedy. If you like both of those things, then good news: you'll enjoy this game (I hope)! There were a couple minor annoyances in my playthrough that I wanted to mention. Because there are no quest objectives in this game, it can be a hard game to pick up and come back to later. I took a break for a couple days and came back and I had a hard time remembering all the conversations I had with characters, which consequently made some of the puzzles more difficult and tiresome. Additionally, for the final puzzle you need to obtain jewelry. I was able to get two crowns by different methods and when I took the second crown to the characters I assumed it wouldn't work. But it did and the same character acted like I hadn't given him a crown before and placed the second one on his head where the first already was. I think this was just a minor bug but it was confusing because I didn't know whether that was the correct way to pass the puzzle. Besides that I only noticed the occasional spelling error but nothing too egregious. Overall, it was an excellent experience that I wish was a tad longer, mainly because the world and characters were so enjoyable to interact with and writing the brilliant. This is the first game made by Joe Richardson that I've played and needless to say I am thoroughly impressed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Procession to Calvary

_childDocuments_.review: Prcoession to Calvary is an excellent adventure game which tears up and recontextualises classical art to hilarious effect.It is a sequel to Four Last Things, and is just as good. Know that Four Last Things doesn't need to be played first to enjoy this, but if you like one you will definitely like the other.The style of the game involves collages of classical artworks which have been crudely animated in Monty Python style. This idea, of taking a portrait of a nobleman, and wobbling his head back and forth to make him talk about cheese, is inherently very funny. It's what kids do when they're bored in an art history lesson. It's made even funnier by Richardson's excellent writing, which made me laugh out loud on several occasions.The humour is almost entirely "stoner humour" - slightly surreal, taking everything in its stride, with some unexpected dabs of "deepness" here and there. It works great contrasted with the rich classical and baroque music (all public domain) and paintings being collaged.The gameplay is standard adventure game fare, but with the additional option of using your sword on things. The puzzles I found middling. Not too easy or hard, and all of them feel fair. The sword is actually only used very infrequently, and so I was most tripped up when it was a solution to a problem and I'd forgotten all about it.The story, like in Four Last Things, is short and thin. That's a shame, because I could have enjoyed a much more fleshed out game. As always with this complaint, though, it's clearly a great game if the main drawback is players wanting more!The game may look suitable for all ages, but is really not for children. Anyone teenage or older should have a great time with this game though, and anyone sad that there's nothing like Monty Python around these days... here it is!Easy recommend.

Would recommend to anyone with an interest in fun, art and music! 🏄‍♀️As is the joyous tradition of the adventure game, there will be at least one puzzle that will get to you, annoy you, and when you realize the simple solution, you WILL be mad about it. Don't sweat it. 🧓Much love to the developer 🥰

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Cavalry is the Deus Ex of hardcore renaissance infantry combat simulators (HRICS). In this game you will move swiftly through a realistic depiction of renaissance era Europe, as you are tasked with dealing vengeance upon the evil Heavenly Peter. The world has been crafted with masterful artistry. TPoC has a very painterly look, and many of the scenes (but not all) would fit in just fine if you were to print them out and hang them in an art museum. Just like Deus Ex, interaction is a key theme and highly realistic. You can grave-rob, steal jewellery, jump off balconies, snort snuff, interact with animals... you name it, you can do it. However, the real core of any HRICS game is the killing, and there is plenty to go around here. Swordplay is a sheer wonder. Unarmoured civilians such as a lone cripple are deftly sliced in half with visceral detail. However, the town bounty system is brutally difficult, and I still have not been able to kill the final boss. All in all though, great game.25/11/2020: I updated this review for a badge.

_childDocuments_.review: I've long loved this art. I've long loved this music. If that policy were applied across art museums nationwide, the art critics whose heads didn't explode would die laughing. All in all, I imagine *that* would raise attendance rates. Oh, and for anyone like me with art pretensions, it should be noted that Richardson has a deeply impressive range of paintings (and music) in his source material. I didn't even realize there were two veduti from different points upstream of Santa Maria della Salute looking towards the Punta della Dogana...one of the best parts of the game was playing "Find That Painting". I still haven't found them all, and if anyone has a complete set of references rather than just the artist list, I really want to track down the Netherlands city scene that features briefly in the runs north and south.ANYWAY: Thank God, you don't have to be an art critic to enjoy this game. Please go enjoy it now.

_childDocuments_.review: This is another cut-out-animation game in the style of Terry Gilliam, a follow-up to the same developer's Four Last Things.  The short answer to whether you should play it is yes, but it may take you no more than about three hours, and it's fairly easy.  I paid $8 for it and certainly felt like it was worth it, and frankly I'm surprised more games haven't been patched together this way since it makes for some seriously amazing art from start to finish.  Really there are only two things that could go wrong here: how the game plays, and whether it is funny.The game plays well, without glitches, operating within the typical framework of a strictly dialogue and inventory-driven point-and-click adventure.  There are no worn-out adventure puzzles like sliding blocks, matching symbols, or arranging levers.  There's not even that much to combine in your inventory, and if it weren't for the fact that you can pick up some items again after you use them, you'd never have more than about a half-dozen items at once.  I won't spoil how the game gives you multiple solutions to try, but the achievements kind of do that anyway.  They all have scripture verses as descriptions, but it's the names of the achievements that reveal a few things for you, like the fact that there are three possible endings.  I found it to be pretty clear how to get all three, and I think most people will find the autosave sufficient for trying a second and third ending without much hassle.As for whether the game is funny, you can see it's unashamedly claiming to be like Monty Python, which can be good or bad.  I love Monty Python's Flying Circus, and Terry Gilliam in particular, but I've often found that attempts to copy that style can fall really flat.  The good news is that the aping of Python doesn't go much further than the animation style and irreverent absurdity, meaning that the dialogue sort of establishes its own style of humor based on fourth-wall breaking and some general awareness by the characters that you are playing a game.  I think it's a good thing that the game isn't voiced, because I can imagine that voice actors trying to be funny would just end up distracting.  I guess the bad news is that it's not really laugh-out-loud funny anyway, more silly.  But that's fine with me.Some people might have the concern that this particular subject matter will be more sacrilegious than trying to commit the seven deadly sins in the previous game.  I guess it depends on how sensitive you are to that.  Python always avoided the worst of that problem by mocking the religious establishment and its followers more than Christ himself, even when they referenced biblical times or crucifixion specifically.  This game obviously references crucifixion as a method of torture and execution, but it does go a half-step further in having a character that could be a more direct mockery of the Christ story than Python's Life of Brian ever was.  However, as much as I like for humor to be fairly tolerant of religion, I didn't find this game's content to go far enough overboard as to ruin it.  Make no mistake, if you don't want any jokes about the subject at all, you're checking out the wrong game, and most fairly conservative people wouldn't want their kids playing this game.  But I can take a joke up to a point, so I can live with the way this was done.  To be honest, the game is less about the religious content and more about accentuating the outlandish depictions in classical art, so the shock comes less in anything particularly blasphemous but more in seeing these people and creatures, with their facial expressions and oddly detailed environments, out of context of the original work.  That's the best thing about the two games.So the real selling point here is not that the game is a good adventure, but that it's a great use of Renaissance art and classical music.  In that regard, it is masterful work and a blast to look at. In my opinion, you might as well play Four Last Things first, but then I think you'll find this game to go pretty quickly.  I only sort of got stuck once for a few minutes, but even then, I knew exactly what I was trying to do, so it didn't take long to move on.  I never found two of the achievements that were unnecessary to getting the endings, but there wasn't much else to explore or really any reason to replay except maybe to show it to other people who would find it fascinating or funny.

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Calvary is a goofy point-and-click adventure game using only renaissance artwork as its game assets and as a result feels very Monty-Python-esc. The game doesn’t take itself too seriously and instead focuses on some simple problem solving to keep you busy between a funny storyline. Total playtime was maybe 3 hours because I got stuck in the middle. I think considering the game was made by one person it totally justifies the price tag, but it may be too expensive for a game of this quality if you don’t look at it as supporting an indie game dev at the same time. If you’re looking for a good laugh it’s worth the $10 either way, I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing. The gameplay is a point-and-click adventure with a simple inventory to use items on world elements. You spend the game clicking on where you want your character to go and can right click to either speak touch or inspect certain objects and people. There is a button to see all interactable objects so usually you cannot get too lost.It becomes pretty apparent what the goals are to progress the story but sometimes it can be confusing what objects you need to acquire as some world elements are there to serve a purpose while others are just a visual gag or the music players in that scene. Overall, it feels better than most point-and-click adventures you’d find on a flash website because the artwork is so nice and the animations both in your character and in the backgrounds are eye-catching. The entire game is using assets taken from renaissance paintingsThe game feels very “alive” for lack of a better term. While the background is always a painting landscape they added lots of animated characters either playing music or do something in the background or foreground so you don’t feel so stuck in a painting as much as just running through a world to explore.No real downsides to the graphics, everything is a painting, so it obviously looks great for the time period this story takes place in and the goofy animations just add to the overall goofy feel of the game.The music in this game is atmospheric using classical music and matching it to the tone of the room you’re in. It’s never intrusive and is nice to listen to for a while since you’ll be running from point A to point B quite often if you get confused. The only real downside is that there isn’t any voice-acting; I always play my games on stream so having to read out this much dialogue can be annoying but I understand VA can also be very poor so not a big issue. If you read fast and click through dialogue it might save you 20 minutes over the course of this game. The story is about as simple as it gets, really, you’re just overcoming obstacles in an effort to kill a guy. Not because he’s important but just because your character likes to kill people. The game is mostly about making you laugh while looking at funny animations in a style that reminds you of Monty Python both in aesthetic and humor. The story isn’t terrible but it’s very simple and does allow you to fail in a couple ways if you kill someone you aren’t supposed to.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard of The Procession to Calvary while attending Day of the Devs 2019 in San Francisco.After chatting with Joe about the game and his design process I got to play the demo he had, this game was a comedic hit even in that demo!Fast forward several months and it is finally available in all its artistic glory and is even more comedic and ridiculous than that short demo was.While the game is short (3-4 hours to get though and nab any missing achievements) the jokes and skits are in no shortage and give plenty of good laughs.Joe is an awesome guy and is extremely passionate with making his games and you absolutely should give this Renaissance Art point and click a go!

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely hilarious, superbly-written and devilishly unique and stylish point and click adventure. Perfect for fans of the absurd, and/or with a slightly warped (or just plain childish) sense of humour - think Terry Gilliam/Pythonesque shenanigans and you won't be far off. Not a lengthy game by any stretch of the imagination, but multiple (well, 3) endings and routes through the game allow for some enjoyable replayability. The humour hits the mark right until the closing scene, and while some of the puzzles can initially feel a little obtuse, they have a forehead-slapping satisfaction and logic that doesn't take too much effort to achieve. Thanks for such an awesome game! :)

_childDocuments_.review: The Procession to Calvary is a hilarious point-and-click game.It's full of some of the world's most celebrated art and music, clever puzzles, senseless violence, and as the game's trailer puts it – nude men wrestling by the sea. Truly a game with lots to offer.Since this is a classic point-and-click game, you're going to be facing a few puzzles. You'll help a street magician (who might be the messiah) perform his greatest trick yet, solve a riddle written by the devil himself, and win the local talent show.You can put the work in and solve them with logic, or you can just say "♥♥♥♥ it" and kill everyone. You do have a sword, after all, and what good is a sword if you're not going to use it?Mostly, The Procession to Calvary a game for anyone who enjoys unique visual styles and Monty Python-esque humor. The weird mix of high culture and low comedy just works. The artistic visuals only serve to amplify the physical humor and fart jokes. Not every joke lands, though – there are a few moments where the game breaks the fourth wall that just feel awkward and pointless.Still, any adventure fan who appreciates the power of silly jokes will enjoy this wacky title.

_childDocuments_.review: Three years ago I’ve accidentally stumbled upon Four Last Things, a bizarre comedy point and click adventure game built entirely out of the Renaissance paintings. It was simple, yet incredibly fun and funny and reminded me of the the best elements from the 90s attempts by 7th Level to make a Monty Python game, without all of the crap that was also present in those games. It was also a solid adventure game that wasn’t just a series of funny interactions and gags, even if most of it was simple. So I’m glad to say that The Procession to Calvary, a sequel of sorts, is in many ways even better.The setup of the game, just as with the previous one, is simple and silly. The holy war is over, no more blood will be spilled in the name of it. Except, our main character really wants to murder more people. Killing the tyrant who escaped the war and wasn’t punished seems like a good excuse, so that’s what sends her on the quest. Getting to the target, however, isn’t that simple and she will need to overcome obstacles to get to her goal.This is, of course, done in the usual for adventure games fashion – by killing everyone. I mean, by solving puzzles and helping others. You can, however, kill everyone, since, as a warrior, you are equipped with a sword you can unsheathe at any point. Which is a fun addition to the usual formula even if the payoff is rather disappointing and never really goes to truly funny subversion of expectations like something that you can find in Zork: Grand Inquisitor, for example. Nonetheless, the “puzzles” are usually clear, the goals are fun to get to and the writing rarely gets “too silly”.There are a few moments where the game slightly falters as an adventure title, there are moments where the jokes are a bit too dumb, but it doesn’t happen often. And besides, just like the previous title, you can complete this game with seeing pretty much everything in about 2 hours (if you’re a fast reader, at least). Which is a perfect length for a game of this type. Additionally, due to the switch to Unity, the game now properly supports higher than 1080p resolutions and, in general, should run better and have less issues. If you didn’t like Four Last Things? Yeah, this is more of the same, just better, really. If you have played it and liked it, then definitely get this one as well. And if you haven’t played Four Last Things, well, get both, especially if you can enjoy this sort of silliness.

_childDocuments_.review: Genre: Action/AdventureGameplay: Linear/Point&ClickTheme: PythonesqueThe Procession to Calvary is a short but enjoyable narrative for the casual gamer. Before I dive any further into the review, I'd like to note that this is an indie title developed by one person, Joe Richardson. Furthermore, the game only costs $10, but that does not excuse it from receiving an honest and unbiased review.The very first thing that grips your attention while playing The Procession to Calvary is the music. The game does a brilliant job of introducing but not forcing bits of classical music throughout the game. Nearly every graphical setting you encounter has street performer(s) in the background playing music, where you have the option to interact with the musicians to either clap, sing along, or learn what they were playing. Its a form of artistic immersion that I appreciated. I wanted to see more of that. Being someone who has no prior background to the subject matter/theme of the game, this was an excellent opportunity for the developer to educate their audience. Not only on the music, but the entire setting (places, people, and historical references).The narrative is unique and different from most games I have played. Being that I classified the theme of this game to be Pythonesque, it deals with comedy. Humor is subjective. Therefore, I won't judge the game for its style of humor or the developer's attempt at being a comedian. The game did make me smile from time to time but never made me open my mouth. The gameplay, however, is what interests me. The Procession to Calvary progresses its narrative in multiple ways because it has multiple endings. The progression comes down to two simple choices: kill characters (making the game a short experience) or solve riddles/puzzles (making the game a challenging but rewarding experience). The latter choice is the only way to "beat the game" properly, encouraging players to play through multiple times. This is where I began to see the shortcomings of The Procession to Calvary. After finishing the game once, I didn't want to play through it again. The main protagonist doesn't have enough character for you to care (no background or sense of purpose other than the main objective to kill someone) to go on another quest. Is the protagonist a famous soldier? Where do they come from? Questions I would have preferred to be answered to make me connect with the character. The same criticism can be stated about other characters. The narrative is unique because of its art style and setting but lacks depth and creativity in storytelling.Overall The Procession to Calvary is worth its asking price but is unsatisfyingly average. Joe Richardson created a similar title in 2017 called Four Last Things with the same genre, gameplay, and theme. This game does not noticeably improve on its predecessor. Granted that this is an indie game developed by one person, but that does not excuse it from the same mistakes that AAA titles commit. Every new game developed should be an improvement from previous titles, The Procession to Calvary makes one of the deadliest sins in the industry by replicating a previous experience.Score: 3/5 - Average

name: Biped
detailed_description: Two little bipedal robots, Aku and Sila, will walk side by side and embark on a fun and bonding journey. MASTER INNOVATIVE AND SIMPLE CONTROLS You control the robot's two legs using two sticks or left and right mouse buttons. This allows you to perform various moves—from simple walking and sliding to more advanced actions, like operating machinery or cutting wood. CONQUER TWO-PLAYER CO-OP Enjoy the adventure solo or grab a friend or a family member and have a blast together in co-op mode. Communicate and coordinate to conquer challenges together and find out how good a pair you truly are. EXPLORE FUN ENVIRONMENTS Your adventure will take you to many beautiful and mysterious location on the planet. Explore secrets in forests, valleys, waterfalls and icy mountains and find your way through the puzzling paths that lead to the planetary beacons. PAIR YOUR LOOKS Collect treasures and buy a goofy hats! Dress up your biped the way you like. Better yet, match your partner’s look and become the most dazzling adventurers in this epic quest. CREATE YOUR OWN ADVENTURE You have passed all the levels already and want more? Create your own levels using Steam Workshop, share your levels with the community and try the others' ones. Nothing is impossible with Biped. =======================================================================

_childDocuments_.review: My wife and I are hugely into local co-op games, but we almost bounced off this one.  We failed so many times that the first level took us well over an hour.  We wondered if maybe it was just too difficult for us, and we've finished some truly challenging games together.We took a small break, came back to give it one more try and... the second level was challenging, but totally doable and we finished in a much more reasonable time.  By the end of the game, we even went back and replayed the first level, and while it was certainly easier for having gained a lot of practice, but it was still insanely hard for a first level.  The level order seems completely random to me, and seems to have nothing to do with creating any kind of difficulty curve.The game is plagued with inconsistent, and often seemingly insurmountable, difficulty spikes...  but...  it was a lot of fun.  If you like co-op games that require a combination of skill and efficient communication, this is definitely for you.  Play it with a loved one and you'll both be belly laughing over all your stupid mistakes... when you're not teetering closer and closer to passive aggressively blaming each other for everything that goes wrong.  If you can clear the first level, I think you can make it all the way, but it will never be a 'walk' in the park.

_childDocuments_.review: Who doesn't fondly remember the days when the Internet wasn't as omnipresent as it is today and we met up with friends to play video games sitting on the couch, whether against each other or in co-op mode. You know - live and in color. Some manufacturers like Nintendo continue to hold this local-multiplayer flag high, but commonly today, people play mostly online with each other, and the face-to-face, social component is falling away.The story in Biped is told quite quickly. You play the two humanoid robots Sila and Aku. The tin pals are sent to Earth to light beacons that will allow them to teleport across the planet. To complete this task, they have to travel to different locations and overcome obstacles. Among other things, you'll move through the ruins of ancient civilizations in the shape of the two robo-friends, roam through desert regions and slide over icy mountains to get to your destination. In the process, Sila and Aku are dependent on the help of other robots and, of course, on each other. Only together can the obstacles be crossed - well, at least if you go off together with a friend. Biped also has a solo mode, in which you can live through the story campaign alone. The eight levels, including the tutorial, are then adapted to one person and you'll encounter more other robots, who will take over the tasks that would otherwise take up your partner. The solo campaign, like the co-op campaign, is also played through after three hours at the latest.Biped is only played with the mouse or the two analog sticks of a controller - we played with the gamepad. The whole control system is thus reduced to a minimum, but there are still a large number of actions that can be performed. The two legs of our robot are each controlled with one of the two sticks, and different movements lead to different results. This requires practice, but after a while you get used to the unusual concept and can perform precise actions and movements. The sticks are also used when activating switches, holding onto ropes and walls, and grabbing objects. To do this, you just have to hold the stick, and thus the leg, to certain objects. With each mission, new mechanics and obstacles are presented, matching the setting. For example, in order to get to the top of a snowy mountain, we'll have to swing up ropes, use air locks to catapult ourselves upwards, and hang on magnetic walls to avoid falling down. In another area, we have to help the robot inhabitants with sawing and transport the finished wood along conveyor belts. Each level offers new, innovative puzzles and tasks that guarantee a lot of variety and fun and most importantly: It's absolutely kids / family friendly.Cooperation is also important when it comes to swinging from one platform to another. The collision detection irritated us a few times, though, and also caused moments of frustration. The small robots can slide over flat levels, which allows them to progress faster. However, it was not always obvious where these accessible levels begin and end, but it's also a bit due to the camera, which causes problems every now and then. As a result, we sometimes got stuck on edges or were thrown over the target.Biped surprised me quite a bit, because rarely have I laughed so hard during a co-op title. This is ultimately due to the interesting game concept, because in the game you and your partner each embody a robot, whose individual legs you have to control separately. What necessarily follows are rather chaotic and whimsical moments, which always arise when you dare to tackle one of the many fairly designed challenges. At the same time, Biped is intuitive, excellently done by the game design and manages to build up a pleasant learning and motivation curve. You're also offered a solo mode, but it's clear that the game focuses on the co-op aspect, and in this respect it shines. The stages serve common platform stereotypes that have been around for decades: Ice World, Desert World, Jungle World, etc. With coins found in the levels you can buy some headgear for the little robots - but I've seen that in funnier or more motivating ways elsewhere.  Unfortunately, the very short gameplay time gets in the way. You can play through Biped with your game partner in one evening, but after 3-4 hours, depending on how well you do, all the fun is over. However, if you're looking for a decent co-op title, you can still get it, especially since Biped isn't too expensive at 12,49€ (I would highly recommend waiting for a sale).

_childDocuments_.review: Biped is a fun, cute co-op and solo game. I mention co-op first because it's really designed around playing with another person. However, you can still enjoy solo play. The controls are very innovative and novel. The first place I ever came across using dual sticks to control separate motion was from a tank arcade game back in the 1990s. The control is a bit confusing at first, but then becomes very intuitive rapidly.The only critical critiques I have about this game, are:1. The camera2. Only co-op host seems to get stars that both players got playing together.For the first critique, if you ever played Super Mario 64 you know that camera makes a world of difference. In Biped, sometimes the camera is just right, other times it is completely unbearable. Sometimes it cuts off speech bubbles or useful areas, while other times you don't even think about it.The second item is a personal frustration. My friend and I have separately gotten all of the stars in the solo game. However, when we played coop together we noticed that he would get 4/4 when I would only get 3/4. We haven't figured out why this is happening if it is suppose to happen. Worse yet, it doesn't seem that many, if any, are attached to my account for the achievement. This means we would have to play through ALL of the co-op levels together again (all the regular AND pro ones) with ME as host. That seems rather odd and I would guess that it's not intended? But it is immensely frustrating. I'm not sure if there's any way for the devs to fix this?Other than those 2 issues, Biped has been a really fun, simple, cute co-op game.2020-07-08 Update - We noticed some serious issues of the game lagging out when we would hit difficult parts. I'm not sure how they coordinated the network for co-op but it was frustrating at times to have lag kill us.A third issue that I neglected to mention is that only the HOST can see the status of completion for each level (time, deaths, stars), which lends itself to possibly explaining why only the host gets full credit for stars.WHAT was strange, was when I was hosting, part of the levels were completed and unlocked and it seemed somewhat random. We really didn't enjoy the boat level. It was interesting and novel, but super annoying. That's just our preference. What was nice was that those were all completed on my side, making me wonder if the devs deliberately wanted co-op gamers to replay the non-sucky levels? Or maybe there's just a sync issue with level completion stats. If you're just looking for a cutesy co-op game, Biped is a good game for you.However, if you care about completion, and fully polished games, I would give Biped a TEPID rating.SUMMARY: Good solid start on a game. Needs more polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I can’t really join the euphoric chorus in a lot of reviews here. Sure, it’s an alright local coop game all in all, but a long way from a masterpiece in my opinion, mostly because of the tedious movement system (you control each foot separately, hell if your controller got mechanical issues) and the sudden difficulty spikes in between. Sometimes levels were easy and fun, other levels were simply frustrating or annoying (already the first one), especially if you try to collect all the stars (good advice: DON’T, because you need the ones from the bonus levels for any achievement as well). I wouldn’t even call it a puzzle game, as coordination and agility challenges based around those leg movements and the according physics are predominant. The main story also is rather short, only 8 levels including the tutorial, and has rather few variations (mostly the standard, like river, ice, forest etc.). Instead, after finishing, the game offers several bonus challenge levels as mentioned which really are extremely hard, and this is no joke, they’re truly diabolical. To be honest, we gave up after a few tries, yeah, that’s how much fun they were. By the way, I also finished it in single player, which is surprisingly much easier and features a bit different level designs, but of course is short, too. And before I forget, there are indeed slight customization possibilities by buying some funny hats in the shop with coins you find during the levels, but the achievement to buy them all is rather grindy and requires to at least repeat the tutorial 30 additional times.I’ll still give this a positive rating, just because it was not all bad, but it definitely wouldn’t be my first choice for a local coop game to have fun. Too much hassle in between, too little variety, and I’d wait for a good sale keeping the short game length in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: The game seems really fun if you're playing local, but online there's a gigantic issue regarding how the engine handles the connection.My friend and I live in the same city, we both have relatively low ping; I have 15ms, he has 50-130 (a few spikes). My friend doesn't lag in most games, but this game is utterly unplayable. Somehow, the game decides that the lag between my friend's computer and me should be added as input lag into the game; so it's impossible for him and I to play the game, since it feels like we're playing on ice. It's horrible, it wouldn't surprise me if programs like Parsec (A program that allows another person to play from his computer in your computer like if you were in local cooperative) would make it more playable.I wish we could've played it the way it was intended, but jesus, our internet is decent, it shouldn't act like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Biped is a charming and cooperative puzzle-platformer that delivers a fun and lighthearted experience. You control adorable robots, "Aku" and "Sila," as they traverse a series of levels that require precision, teamwork, and creative problem-solving. The game’s standout mechanic is its unique movement system, where each leg is controlled individually, adding an extra layer of challenge and hilarity as you wobble around.The puzzles are well-designed and progressively more difficult, encouraging communication and coordination, especially in co-op mode. Whether you’re balancing on narrow platforms or solving timing-based puzzles, every moment feels like a fun test of your teamwork skills.Visually, the game’s colorful, minimalist aesthetic adds to its charm, and the lighthearted soundtrack complements the cheerful vibe. However, the game is relatively short, and while it’s perfect for a few hours of fun, some players might wish for more content.Overall, Biped is a delightful co-op game that shines in its simplicity and creativity. It’s an ideal choice for those looking to enjoy some light puzzle-solving with a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: Biped can be very frustrating or very rewarding or both at the same time. Good communication is needed with your partner or there will be a lot of potential yelling and blaming. _childDocuments_.review: Didn't realize we had beaten it as we ended after the end with the idea of coming back. But we did, so time to review:Game has very cute graphics and nice music. Now, that said... there are a few puzzles that were rough and at least one that felt unnecessary for online co-op. There is tunnel crossing controlled by a switch, and if the partner has ANY sort of latency this becomes very painful. It was clearly tested with couch co-op because even a half second increases the difficulty by a very huge margin. I'd really have appreciated if, after enough fails, we get a "Skip" option, or if the developers were able to test with someone in another State/Country and make adjustments to the breathing room.And on the topic of co-op, the lobby is painful. "Lobby is full" with one person, failures to invite, and more. They have a beta for better client that we didn't know about until the end, but this really should have been added to the main system at some point in the last few years.With that said: It was still enjoyable, we got a good number of laughs and I don't regret playing. The amount of frustration was acceptable and I'd still recommend, just try to play with people closer or go into the Betas and get the betterping one before struggling.

_childDocuments_.review: Biped is a 3D Puzzle game, where you or / and friend controlling a robot, and your job is to restart all of the beacons on Earth, before the catastrophe, meanwhile you need to solve puzzles.My favourite part in Biped, is the gameplay. It's short with not too many levels, but the puzzles and the levels itself don't feel boring at all. Some levels are challanging, you need to really get used to the controlls, which I will get to it later. You can collect coins, stars and completing the levels in time for achivments or for coins, you can buy hats, which adds to the fun factor. The game is a bit childish, but it's for everyone and can bring fun to you alone or to your friend, too. There are also additional levels, which ramp up the difficulty, after you beat the game, if you need extra challange. Long story short, pretty fun gameplay with new elements and not boring at all.Controlls seemed bit difficult for me at first, but it was really good. I played the game with controller, due to the game recommended it. You basically controlling the two legs of Biped with the two joystick, which seems bit difficult, but later in the game, you will get used to it. It's responsive and easy to get into, but hard to master it.Surprisingly graphics is also a strong point of the game. It's a fact, that further textures not looking detailed at all, but the graphics in general fits for the game. I didn't saw any graphics bugs either, it's just wholesome.Sound desing is also nice. There are no dialouges, only beeping but those are not annoying in my opinion. Pretty good stuff.Story is basically told at the beginning, which is Earth has beacons and Bipeds needs to restart it, before something bad happens. Simple is that, however there is no need for additional story. Few of the levels has some story with different robots, which is just enough for the end of the level, and that's all right.Biped surprisingly a really solid puzzle game, with cute graphics and design, yet challanging gameplay at some point, but not annoyingly hard. The only issue is that the game is quite short, but the solo and coop campaign together could give you enough gameplay. I can defiently recommend the game, even for the full price!

_childDocuments_.review: This game's beauty resides in its weird movements and the amount of fun/fun moments it can produce, getting used to them at the start for me was hilarious but once you are used to them the real game begins where you will realize how bad you are at video games. _childDocuments_.review: The trailer and gifs on the Steam store page give a very accurate representation of what you can expect playing Biped.Biped is built entirely on the premise of two player controlling two robots and independently moving each leg of their robots. The control setup reminds me a lot of I am Bread and Octodad: Dadliest Catch, except that the controls are actually friendly here instead of arbitrarily complicated. You can move your robot one foot at a time, or you can slide forward by moving both legs simultaneously. The game presents a unique combination of puzzles based around moving your robot legs in specific ways. Some puzzles require you to alternate who takes a step, others require a specific number of legs to be on the ground at a time, and more. The water area was the only level I thought was done poorly because it requires you to alternate your steps and keep walking through the entire level.I enjoyed the game, but not enough to make me want to play each level again to beat the challenges or find the collectibles. It's good enough for one play.Don't bother playing this if both you and your partner don't have controllers. Controls with the mouse are terrible. On a controller, each joystick moves one foot. With a mouse, left click does the left foot and right click does the right foot. Your fingers will be exhausted!

_childDocuments_.review: If you are going to play this game, you have two options. Your friendship is going to end directly or your friendship will be stronger and you will have an amazing time. The game offers a single-player and co-op experience, but we especially recommend co-op. Here is our Biped Review.Biped is a coop action-adventure game with a strong focus on moment-to-moment collaboration between 2 players. Playing with a friend makes the game more difficult, but you will never forget this moment. The game is developed by: NEXT Studios and is published by META Publishing.If you like to play the game less stressful, you can play the game in solo mode (or when you don’t have friends). I really enjoyed playing this game even while playing solo. Solo felt way more “calm and cozy”, while co-op felt like I was going to lose my voice while screaming at my friend.The movement is really challenging, but not in a bad way. It makes the game how the game needs to be. You can choose between “just walking” or “skating”. Walking doesn’t work like walking in other games because you need to move your thumbsticks like you use your legs in real life. This sounds simple, but it takes a surprising amount of precision and cooperation, especially in the later levels where the difficulty skyrockets. This creates funny and chaotic moments but also makes the puzzles dynamic and increasingly challenging.When you try to complete the level, you are also able to pick up coins and do challenges to get stars. With the coins you get, you can buy skins for your character. No microtransactions, just play the game and grind coins to get good-looking skins.The levels in Biped are colorful and varied with a friendly atmosphere. The puzzles range from simple to quite complex, especially in the later levels. The music really fits the vibe and the game sound effects make the game even better. The co-op levels often require precise timing and teamwork, which makes the game extra fun for friends or family members. Although some challenges can be a bit frustrating, they ultimately provide a great sense of accomplishment when completed.I really enjoyed playing this game. The mechanics are fresh and innovative and the level design looks really good. The level design is colorful and the puzzles are fun. And the fact that you are not forced to necessarily play with anyone is Biped’s biggest plus. And another surprise: they announced a sequel (Q2 2025)! Excited to play Biped? We are going to give away a Steam copy! Keep an eye on our socials!

_childDocuments_.review: Biped is one of the best coop puzzle games. Controls are intuitive. Gameplay is very smooth, the bipeds always do what you want them to. Characters look and sound adorable, and are customizable. Bi-tiful visual style, sound design, soundtrack. 8 different levels each with their own environment and puzzle mechanics + separate coop challenge levels.Only problem is, coop is a bit buggy sometimes, but it can always be solved by restarting the level. The levels are short with a checkpoint before each puzzle.This game deserves 10 sequels, and I'll play all of them. Hopefully they can iron out the bugs next time, even though the bugs lead to hilariously absurd situations, like your teammate spawning underwater in a raft mission.

_childDocuments_.review: If it weren't for the dearth of gameplay, this game would be strictly better than Chariot (which is also a solid physics based co-op). _childDocuments_.name: Biped

_childDocuments_.review: Biped definitely expands and fully explores all the possible challenges and obstacles that come from its simple gameplay mechanic - there are two robots that possess only two feet each. You'd think there's only so much you can do with that. But they've found a lot of creative ways to use this mechanic to provide entertainment and new challenges.Every level is set in a different biome and explores one or two concepts each, making each level feel different from the ones that came before. In any case, level design is great. The soundtrack and sound effects are simple but charming, and the graphical style is definitely cute and brightly colored. We do have some gripes with the game - there is no way to select which of the two character (Sila, or Aku) you want to play. You might have to disconnect and reconnect your controllers to get the character you each want in local coop. Always having the same character (and associated color) is . Getting confused on who you are can make you fail challenges. Some particular obstacles were also quite frustrating to overcome. This is made even more annoying by the fact that the game judges you each level on a number of parameters - time, number of deaths, 'harmony' (has to do with the time in which you as a duo complete certain challenges) and number of stars collected. If you're doing a normal playthrough I simply wouldn't worry about those meters and just have fun. Luckily none of those judgments of player skill are reflected in the game's achievements.We found the standard story levels to be the most fun to play. Each of the seven coop levels have two associated 'pro' levels. These definitely don't have the same thematic vibe as the original levels and take place in a futuristic, clinical robot setting. We definitely did not enjoy those as much as the story levels as a result.I'd recommend Biped for the unique concept, cute graphics and emphasis on cooperative play. It's definitely a short game - completing only the coop story levels takes less than 4 hours. I imagine you can get another 8 hours out of the single player levels and the pro levels.

_childDocuments_.review: Biped is the most fun I've had in a co-op game in a while. To me, it is a satisfying blend of mechanics, puzzles, graphics, and overall enjoyment. The controls are simple. Just the two mouse buttons or the two analog sticks on controller. The real spice are the puzzles that you face. Each level you pass introduces a new mechanic that adds a twist to how you play. I got to say that playing this game blind and seeing all the new mechanics slowly unfold filled me with a surprising amount of joy. Now, sprinkle some lively and cute graphics and you've an attractive puzzle wonderland. A co-op game wouldn't be a co-op game without chaos and Biped provides a lot of that chaotic energy. (Given that you are playing with the appropriate person.) Hit up a friend and enjoy as chaos ensues. What's not to love about this game? It's the prefect blend of straightforward mechanics, challenging yet enjoyable puzzles, eye-catching graphics and tons of chaotic fun. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Me and my girlfriend are in a long distance relationship. Due to the coronavirus spreading like crazy nowadays, we're cannot travel and see each other because she's dozens of cities away. One of the things that always brings us closer is, of course, co-op video games. Doing, playing or achieving something together is always an experience that is romantic. That being said, in these hard times, we were having difficulties finding a new co-op game because we pretty much played most of the titles currently in the market hence looking for a new one.And with all my heart I can say that Biped is the one. First of all it reminded me Portal 2. At the time of this review, we played one hour and it's basically what you expect. Solving puzzles together is the core mechanic of the game. Levels are colorful, puzzles sometimes identical but that doesn't take away the fun. Hopefully, they'll get more diverse as we progress. The robots that you're controlling are super cute, world is colorful, controls and camera are amazing, graphics are good for this type of game. Basically, it's a polished game unlike some others in the market.So to sum it up, If you're looking for a cute, colorful and fun co-op experience, Biped, definitely deserves a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: The cute and cheery outer shell hides within a surprisingly difficult and unique coop puzzler that will put your friendship to the test. _childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly short to get to the story end, this is probably less than three hours of play.  You and a partner can get through this in a weekend easily. After that, there's probably a number of hours left in various challenge maps and collectibles for the completionist set.The game is played with the dual-sticks of a controller.  It's obviously meant for the Playstation design, but the Xbox controllers work acceptably well. After that, it's mostly just timing and coordination with your partner.  There are a few moments of frustration, mostly around color-based puzzles, where you and your partner must alternate footsteps, usually under a time constraint. Most of the other puzzles are just physics things -- make an object or character move the right direction at the right time.  The penalties for death are generally pretty benign, so failure doesn't have a very strong sting.All in all, the game's polished look and feel, easy to pick up mechanics, and Super Mario-like design make for a great couch-coop game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really well polished co-op experience for 2 people. The animations and the sound effects are top notch. Puzzles are based on teamwork, moving together and helping each other to cross gaps or obstacles. _childDocuments_.review: Biped is a Co-op Puzzle game with Physics based movement controls. The game has only two controls, one for moving each of your legs which requires a bit of work to get used to but adds a lot to the difficulty factor of the game as the puzzles are more timing and teamwork based then mentally straining. The levels have a variety of themes such as Desert, Snow, Forest and Water. It has a simple but stylish art style with a total of 8 co-op levels and 8 single player levels which are the same as co-op with small changes make it work with AI rather than a second player.There are also Two Pro levels per regular level which contain a number of challenge sections rather than a fully-fledged level. There are coins to collect which you can use to buy hats and stars which really just add to the achievement for collecting all of them as they are not required to complete levels or anything. The game is about 2 hours long but if you also play the Pro Levels you can extend the playtime to anywhere between 4-6 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Unique and fun gameplay, but 12,49€ for an 1 hour campaign is a bit too much. You can get the Portal bundle for almost the same price. Biped is a puzzle platformer where you play as a robot and control its 2 legs individually. Feels kinda weird in the first few minutes but it is easy to get used to. The story doesn't really make sense, you are supposed to light up some beacons to " light the earth " and help galaxy travellers. It is either baddly translated or baddly written. But I don't mind as I mostly bought this to play a relaxing puzzle game. And for the most part it does exactly that but when I saw the credits rolling I was like " no way, that was it ? ". Now the game says that there is a second campaign but you can only play that in co-op mode, but I only have 1 friend who owns this game and he doesn't play it anymore ... so I decided to play co-op with ... myself. And it is frustrating trying to play with a controller and mouse at the same time. Here is what I don't get though - in the main ( single player ) campaign you meet robots ( NPC's ) who help you solve puzzles by timing their movements with yours. _childDocuments_.review: Biped is a handheld (Nintendo Switch)/console game that's also been put on Steam as a bit of an afterthought, as it's very much designed for the handheld/console gaming audience.It's an insanely overrated gimmick driven 3D platformer with somewhat minimalistic art, made for the Nintendo Switch.  It's from the Russian publishing group, "META Publishing" but if you dig into the EULA and privacy destroying "policies", you'll see the names Tencent and Epic Games everywhere... just to make sure who we're dealing with here, the enemies of Western gaming.  Funny how you have to dig so deep to find out who's really behind this... I can see why they would take steps to try hide their identity.  But for the most part this review must be about the game, no matter how unethical, nay, evil the developers are. And make no mistake, this is an awful game.  It's a gimmick game where you use Nintendo Switch controllers to move the legs of one little robot one at a time.  Why?  Because the developers seemed to think it would be a good idea if, instead of making their game challenging, they would instead make the interface challenging.  The developers were wrong.  This is a terrible idea, it results in a janky gameplay experience.  The interface to a game should never be an obstacle, and it definitely shouldn't be an obstacle on purpose.  This is an awful design principle. On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.PC gamers will be insulted by the demand from the developer that a console peasant children's toy controller should be used, despite this being on PC.  Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for, and must never, under any circumstances dictate to gamers how their games are to be experienced.Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.You're forced to sign a highly questionable yet legally unenforceable End User License Agreement.  This agreement includes questionable (and possibly law breaching) privacy requirements that no gamer should ever have to engage in.  Developers must learn they are here to serve gamers, not control them.  I had my cat walk over the keyboard while the EULA was displaying, which fixed that problem for me.As mentioned, this game behaves as spyware and collects "telemetry" and personally identifying information.  There is no apparent way to prevent this hostile and sinister privacy invasion.  The developers will make the unverifiable claim that this data isn't personally identifying, of course that's BS as they're collecting IPs and all kinds of other information about gamers, when combined with other profiling data this can 100% identify an individual.  They say it's for "QA" purposes but there's no guarantee they're not profiling you or selling your data to third parties as they spy on you.  Should you trust them?  Of course not... if they had any concerns about user safety and privacy,   There's simply no reason to trust them and gamers should avoid this game because of this unacceptable privacy invasion.So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?Biped has the ridiculous price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the questionable ethical nature of the developer and/or their associates (as outlined above), this is impossible to recommend.For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games from slightly more ethical developers like "Resident Evil Village", "Remnant: From The Ashes" or "Halo: The Master Chief Collection".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this. The developer has colluded with and are tightly related to Tencent who work aggressively to withhold games from Steam in brazen acts of bribery and anticompetitive behaviour.  This is harmful to gamers and to the gaming industry, and is completely unethical behaviour intended to cause this harm for short term profit and long term disruption of the gaming industry and to Steam itself.  While games absolutely should be considered on their own merits, as I have in my review above, gamers must be cautious when buying games from unethical developers like this.  There's no telling when they will accept more bribes and pull their games off Steam again... they've done it once, they can't be trusted.  Gamers have a right to know about this.  Gamers have a right to open, ethical and competitive marketplaces for their games.  If you buy this game you may be putting your money at risk.

_childDocuments_.review: The Games Main Focus is on 2 Player Co-Op and there are 8 main levels, 14 pro levels that are behind co-op Multiplayer. and then there are 8 more levels on single player if you plan to 100% the game, personally i have played ALL co-op missions, and the 8 additional single player missions (with all 3 badges Lit), i can say this game was hella fun besides the horrible User Interface like applying where the game window is going to go, game resolution, stars collected, time that's passed for speed runs, death count, harmony percentage. all these key elements and none of them have any numbers, not during the levels, not in the level select menu. not in any other menus. the only way to get any numbers and have knowledge of completion of the levels... is if the badges are lit up in the level selection menu. and that's it. also 90%+ harmony for the telepathic achievement is based on the number of co-op challenges completed with the 90% or higher rating, not the entire level. Game doesn't tell you that either, luckily i played with my wife and the game itself is very fun to play and i love the replayability regardless of how short the main game was and with knowledge of a sequel coming probably by like mid-2025 if i was taking an educated guess. i love the ice-skating rink at the end credits. i'm only sad we don't get an ice skating rink ourselves to play around in as an added bonus for completing the 8 main story missions other than all that? games great and i highly recommend it [got the game for $4 btw] so you should probably get it at the time i'm writing this or wait til it goes 75% off or more again later on.In conclusion: Now after having beaten ALL levels when speed running there is a major flaw in how the NPC's will literally stop you in both solo and co-op mode consuming. every. waking. second. gotta go fast? STOP ok now stare at these NPC's for 5-15 seconds. no way to skip and only a few exceptions to spam enter key or A Button to skip the dialogue, other than that? stare at the same dialogue to learn the same level over and over and over again until you land your speedrun. i'm hoping a patch or the sequel patches out both this problem and the one with the co-op pro missions where if only one player makes it to the other side of the level but your partner falls to their death? _childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun co-op experience with a friend, and you've already played the heavy hitters like It Takes Two or Overcooked, Biped is a great little game to give a try. I bought this to play with my wife, who isn't a regular gamer but does enjoy a good co-op game that we can play together. This one reminded me quite a lot of It Takes Two, in that each level mixed up the game play and introduced a new way to advance through cooperation. It can take a little effort at first to learn the controls, since walking is mapped to both joysticks, which will feel unusual since movement is normally just mapped to one stick in most games (e.g., to move your left leg, you move the left joy stick, and vice versa for right leg). You'll be pulling your hair out at first in the tutorial, but once you get the hang of it, the controls become more natural and the game is a good time. Difficulty wise, you'll definitely have to communicate with your partner, and some of the challenges will put up a fight until you figure out the right approach. As for story...there really is no story, but alas, that didn't both me or my wife since the gameplay was focused and fun. All in all, this is a really fun time, as the gameplay and levels are creative and the runtime doesn't overstay its welcome (right around 3-5hrs). If you're looking for your next co-op game, give this one a try!

With its unique mechanics and engaging challenges, Biped offers an unforgettable cooperative experience that you won't want to miss. Get ready to embark on an unforgettable journey with your friends and experience the magic of Biped! Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely little couch coop game well worth picking up for a couple bucks (often bundled on Fanatical / check isthereanydeal) that gives you control of a wonkly wobbly little biped, each bubbly tobbly wobbly leg of it controlled by your analog sticks on your controller (that's right, you'll need a controller for this game, otherwise forget getting it), leading to some lovely clunkly tumbly situations as you try to get through a somewhat challenging series of stages from A to B.There some extra trial maps which we did not do yet and the game recieved unexpectedly rich postlaunch support that added an easy to use map editor for all to create new stages with, however overall content is still on the shorter end which is why I would recommend picking it up only 2 dollars or so - those 3,5 hours represent 2 nights of play for a full "main campaign" completition.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games and have this one in their backlog (minor spoilers ahead). Biped is a solo and co-op 3D puzzle game with physics and object interaction, where you control one or  two robots and have to pass obstacles and solve puzzles. The graphics and models are simple but have enough detail and variety to easily identify and distinguish the 7 different biomes and stage themes.The control system is very different and original but takes some time to get used to, basically each mouse button (or sticks in a controller) moves a leg and to move you have to tap both alternately. You can also press both to glide, but it makes it harder to control the robot.   It doesn’t have a story but the game is fun and challenging. The main stages have different mechanics and types of puzzles, and the pro levels take those mechanics and offer even harder challenges.   15 Achievements, with varied tasks. Around 13 hours (played the co-op levels with a child). Medium, the solo levels are easy but the co-op levels require coordination and teamwork, and the pro levels in particular will require some extra effort and a lot of tries.    Medium. Besides finishing the main levels, you also need to pass one within a time limit and another with less than 10 deaths, but both are doable. The hardest ones are getting all stars (two are particularly well hidden) and completing all the pro levels, but guides are available. A bit of grinding is required if you don’t start hoarding coins right at the beginning. Biped it’s a great co-op 3D puzzle game that’s fun to play and just challenging enough to avoid being frustrating, so I recommend it even if you don’t want to 100% it. The achievements require a bit of effort but not too much and the grinding is minimal.

Biped also has an in-game editor so you can continue playing even after finishing the campaign. The graphics are nice and cute with very soft shadows and a colourful world that is immersive. I would give Biped a score of 8/10 with some minor difficulties with lobbies and menus.

_childDocuments_.review: From a new-ish game developper we have a sensationnal experience which may quite be the best game mechanic since Valve's Portal series. And I'm not even joking!Biped is played as a solo or multiplayer Co-Op game. You control a small bipedal robot (hence the name) where each of your analog joysticks indpendently control one leg. It seems weird, but after about ten minutes you get the hang of it. You can grab stuff, fligh yourself aroud with ropes, or slide on smooth surfaces. It really is an amazing way to control a character and is quite intuitive belive it or not!All of that combined with an amazing sound design, fun and light music and nice low-poly aesthetics. That game really is a joy to play! Dare I say it, it feels like a well-polished, casual Nintendo game. Few games can claim that title!The down side is that the game does not seem that long, and does not seem to have a lot of replay value. I'd say that the solo campain lasts two hours at max, and then if you have friends maybe another two hours for the co-op campain. Also, while it may be possible to play the game with a keyboard, it really was designed for game controllers users. And you'll have to get two to play the local co-op, or two copies of the game for online co-op.Still, the price is right, and I would definitely give it a go at full price if you have a game controller or two laying around! I'd say tho that the best is to wait for a sale and get it for the last 5$ on your Steam gift card a distant relative left you for christmas! Overall, 4/5.

Since the controls are so unique, even if you've played games your whole life, you'll probably be taking the same amount of time wrapping your head around the controls as well. This might seem like a bad thing but it gave her time to accustom herself to it without having that feeling that she usually gets when playing games that you're already off to the races because of how much farther the experience gap is.All in all, this is a great game if you want to do maybe a couples play though, you're playing with a friend who isn't exactly a pro gamer, or I can even see this working really well with a child.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game if playing with a friend. The environments are so varied. The levels can get challenging. This game is just a fun time. The music is good.If you're buying this game to play alone, you'll probably want to skip. The single player is very short and easy. The co-op is a lot more fulfilling. The simple story line is tied to the co-op. The beginning scene and end scene are non-existent in the single player, which goes to show how much more emphasis was placed on co-op.The co-op also has 3 times more levels in the form of pro levels that offer more of a challenge than the standard level. The pro levels expand upon a new mechanic introduced in the base level. The controls are very solid. You never really feel like you failing is the result of the game but because of you. Even though the co-op is longer and more challenging, overall the game is still pretty short. I 100% it in about 13 hours. That being said, towards the end of this year, the developers plan to release player-made levels, so that can add to the replay-ability of this game. I definitely plan to re-install to check that update out when it comes out, especially if there's enough community involvement to produce enough levels. I also feel like the game does a little more hand-holding than needed. New mechanics are not that difficult to understand out-of-the-gate. It kind of breaks the pacing of the game, the fluidity and the immersion. However, the intervention of the other robots does add more character to the game.Definitely buy this game when it goes on sale. Even at the retail $15, I'd still say it's a good buy, especially if you can play with lots of friends and with the update coming in the end of the year. This game has a lot of promise. I look forward to continue seeing it grow. I would definitely buy a sequel if it comes out, especially if it introduces multiple environments and is much longer.
