_childDocuments_.review: Although I spent countless hours playing original, I must admit that after only several hours I lost enjoyment playing this installment. Following issues irritate me constantly:1) 3D view makes maps appear smaller and harder to navigate on. It is very easy to place air units on the wrong hex due to 3D perspective.2) It is hard to distinguish units of different types, especially between Me109 and Ju873) What are my main objectives again? Maybe there is a way to replay briefing. Probably hidden somewhere that one can find when looking very hard. Readily available is the enigmatic summary of goals that in some scenarios is not very helpful.4) I can capture equipment. I can invest in heroes with skills to capture even more equipment. Great. Oh, wait. I have to purchase captured equipment for the same price as brand sparkling new one from my own factory? What's the point then, especially that many captured equipment is worse.5) I understand the challenge but it is taken to ridiculous level. I know it is hard to expect even semblance of historic accuracy from today wargames but PC2 takes it to the next level. Pzkpf38tz are having hard time with Polish tankettes, not to mention 7TP. Enemy cavalry or infantry decimates my tank in urban hex. Fine. My infantry is totally inept against enemy tanks or artillery in similar scenario. How can I even define any sensible tactics seeing such different results in similar scenarios?6) Bewegungskrieg for the win. Right. How did my pinzer movement ended in my own unit isolation even though I have string of units one touching the other?7) With the amount of equipment and reinforcements, Polish army will conquer Berlin by second week of September. I am surprised I am actually winning. Most scenarios I played so far are grinding WWI style positional battles and not battles of movement.8) If anyone believed scenario narrative, one would think that if not for the heroic stance of Wehrmacht panzer divisions on the Gustav line, French army would occupy Berlin even before first shots of September were fired.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Panzer game and I absolutely love it after ~30 hours.+ Customizable gameplay preferences (separate from difficulty)+ Tons of units that unlock at a nice steady pace+ Reliance on combined arms tactics (something I mistakenly ignored on my first few playthroughs)+ Pretty graphics that suit the style of game+ Good performance (RTX 2080 is running north of 100Hz)+ Maps that allow creativity- I've averaged one CTD per 15 hours of gameplay (occurs during deployment phase)- Frequent visual bug that refuses to add texture to transport trucks, half-tracks and transport planes- Steep learning curve in terms of how units interact and unit interdependencies- Some tactical info/numbers are not shown (i.e. suppression amount is not shown if you're also dealing damage)- Music is good, but there are only a handful of tracks, so it gets repetitive- UI is too busy in some cases and too simple in others

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed such now classic games as Panzer General 1 and 2  or Panzer Corps 1, then this games is an absolute must to have! The game mechanics has improved significantly: you have much more complex relationships between the objectives / unit cost / unit traits and terrain, so steamrolling the map with only Tiger II core is not going to work anymore :) The variety of units is vast, and on higher difficulty settings you have to have a balanced core, which makes the game interesting (for example, unlike PC1, not every arty provides AT support now). Last, not least - the AI intelligence is no longer a joke, it does some nasty tricks to overconfident players. The game just started, so there will be cool new DLC to come, so learn your basics and get ready to fight!

_childDocuments_.review: 26NOV21 - Update. This game has only become better with the AO DLC. There is so much content. This is must have for any strategy enthusiast. I can't wait for the Pacific DLC to come out.An improvement over PC1 in every way. All units now feel useful and that they have a place. No more glossing over certain units/classes, this has a lot to do with core slots and new unit abilities.I'm only about halfway through the campaign. I'm yet to try scenarios or multiplayer, or even use the editor. I'll probably update this review as I explore those.Positives;Core slots: This took a little bit to get used too but now I see how good it is. It is one of the most important stats in terms of balancing in my opinion.Abilities: These help define and differentiate units and where they fit into the scheme of things. E.g. A 20mm Flakveirling AA has the "rapid fire 1.5x" and "low altitude attack" abilities; it can throw a lot of shots out at fighters and tactical bombers, using their close defence trait (which is usually 0). Compare this to a 38mm AA, it does not have those abilities but its air attack value is much higher.The same goes for artillery, it's no longer bigger = better. The really big guns have great range and have counter battery fire and can provide AT support, but they cannot provide fire support against soft targets. This is where the smaller artillery pieces excel.My Panzer Corps now feels more rounded than PC1, I'm no longer just going for the most expensive unit. I'm weighing up core slots/unit abilities/cost.Encirclement: Cutting off the enemy now causes cumulative penalties that cannot be shaken until the encirclement is broken. If your units become encircled you must take immediate action to break it, or your unit will die/surrender in a matter of turns.Camouflage: If you bought the General or Field Marshall edition you'll have more choices than you can poke a stick at.Campaign options: You can now customise your campaign rules. Some people are critical of this but I think it is a great feature that makes the game more accessible to everyone. I'll play the game my way (which is pretty much the default setting at this stage, with "undo movement only" the one change I made) and enjoy it, and you can too.Transports: You can now embark and move/ disembark and move all in one turn now. No more spending multiple turns trying to load up your paratroopers at the same airfield.Negatives;Campaign flow: There are no more minor or decisive victories, I know why they changed this and how they balanced out prestige but I really enjoyed the campaign charts from PC1. I'd like to see this bought back. Depending on the scenario in PC1 a loss was not necessarily game over, you lost a battle but the war continued. Here in PC2 its game over, no matter what scenario you're on.

_childDocuments_.review: A very enjoyable game!  I played PC (as well as Panzer Generals 2, back in the day).  Thankfully, Panzer Corps 2 is a worthy successor to the excellent, tactical, WW2 combat found in Panzer Corps 1 (unlike Panzer General 3D Assault, which was abysmal compared to Panzer Generals 2).  For the most part, PC2 has refined and improved on the gameplay found in PC1.  I read complaints in early reviews of PC2 that the maps were very small.  I am not sure if this was an issue that was changed since then or if I have a different definition of a "small map", but I found the map sizes to be just fine.  There are some pretty tiny maps in a few missions, but most are not this way.  The "Corps Slots" mechanic is a little annoying after being used to making my army as large as I want in previous games.  Still, I feel it adds and element of strategy and balance required of the player that is good for balance.  All in all, my complaints are minor and mostly deal with elements that prevent the human controlled army from being to OP (movement for tanks in overrun is limited to total movement at start of turn, limited supply, i.e. number of shots, per turn, etc...).  A great game and worthy successor in the line of WW2 turn-based strategy games!

Some scenarios are quite merciless; giving some vague impression of what kind of how resource-intense WWII was.Main negative point is, that there are currently no Allied-campaigns available.If you like round based hex-field strategy games, the old Panzer General and/or the earlier Panzer Corps version I highly recommend this one; it’s a pretty good and challenging strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played the previous game (Panzer Corps 1) for a bit over 200 hours and finishing most of the Grand Campaign and now having around 100 hours in PC2 with the main campaign and the AO Spanish Civil War (SCW) finished, I feel like that I can give a somewhat fair review.In terms of the baseline mechanics PC2 is a solid upgrade over the previous game, at least indirect fire for AT weapons, the substantial improvement of recon units and the slot system are well-implemented and feel like a natural evolution of what PC1 had to offer. The new medal system is also appreciated and gives minor stat-boosts in addition to providing similar aesthetic "upgrades" to veteran units, as it's always nice to see highly-decorated units deep into a campaign.The base game main campaign is also a massive improvement over the one from PC1 as it's longer and has (in my opinion) better individual scenarios. In addition you get a variety of different historical battles as was the case with PC1 (though I have to admit, that I haven't properly played the yet), as well as 10 puzzles, that are increasingly challenging and require adequate knowledge of the mechanics.On the other side I also have to admit that PC2 feels a lot more "gamey" or "arcadey" in comparison to the previous part. Especially the new hero system is in theory very interesting and gives a wider variety of play-styles. But at the same time, as you get more and more heroes (the base preset is one new hero per scenario, which is fine for the base campaign, but spirales completely out of control in the Axis Operations (the new Grand Campaign)). Hero abilities are at times significantly stronger than anything seen in PC1, since they aren't just raw stat boosts, but they literally change the rules for some units. When combined with the fact, that you can freely switch heroes from unit to unit and even put a lot of them on the same unit, that really starts to break the game.You can of course choose to start with the setting of no new heroes per scenario or lower the chance to get one at least below 100%, which is standard, but that also feels weird to an extent, as the differential between having that mass of heroes and having basically no heroes at all is massive and would make playing on the same difficulty a completely different experience. That's the point where I feel that PC1 felt a lot better balaced and contained, but that is only really an issue in the Axis Operations as you use the same core army over dozens and dozens of different battles.Something I want to criticize is the sound design, it's horrible in my opinion and that's a topic many other people have noted in various discussions. To put it simple, it absolutely lacks the punch that it had in PC1.Hearing your Tiger I, Panther or Flak 36 8,8cm fire in PC1 felt absolutely satisfying and the movement sounds were also very good, while all of that just sounds "bland" in PC2, so regrettably this area is just a straigt downgrade from PC1.The new 3D-graphics are okay I guess. Being able to change the camoflage of units is quite nice and the variety of different patterns is appreciated. I honestly think that on larger maps with more stuff going on, PC1 gave you better overview and felt less cluttered. I honestly speaking miss the old 2D-art style quite often and wish I could get the new mechanics with the old art style and sound design (would be very nice as an optional, alternative view, but probably too expensive to implement and maintain, so more along the lines of wishful thinking...).So, as a final conclusion, a wide variety of improvements, some that might be a bit devisive and some that will probably be enjoyed by anyone who likes this type of game. The base game is absolutely worth the money even at full price and since there is a mod-pack with the entire Grand Campaign from PC1 for PC2 you can theoretically play for hundreds of hours without ever buying any of the DLCs.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy!I had very high hopes for this game but in the end its impossible to play.  Even at entry level difficulty the game isn't enjoyable, 30% fewer units than attackers, units do not heal over time but cost more money you do not have, you cannot partial move, the build chain is not clear and you can "Upgrade to a lower unit".  There is no benefit to surrendering units, your artillery and anti aircraft do not always function correctly and will not auto target incoming units.Deployment zones are very limited and don't allow you to actually setup defense lines yet the bad guys always have troops in trenches 3 squares away.Surviving equipment must be repaired, again taking away from your limited cash and will die the first attack as you cannot use after "repairing".The studio needs to to MAJOR reworks to make this game playable.

_childDocuments_.review: Order of Battle and Unity of Command have such superior mechanics over PzC 2, that really PzC 2 feel like a children's game with little room for application of tactics or strategy. 1. The content is lacking: only 4 single player scenarios and 2 cooperative multiplayer scenarios included. Both cooperative scenarios are really difficult and not fun. 2. Combat mechanics are still funky and not enjoyable, and do not allow for the application of a strategy or tactics. Odd combat results that cause units to be nearly impossible to kill, unless you've applied multiple forms of suppression - maybe realistic, but the enemy will usually outnumber you and have near-unlimited resources that allow for quick replacements. Entrenchment is also extremely lenient and instantly regenerates. The encirclement mechanic is funky, and not reliable nor does it punish encircled units harshly enough (whats the point of encircling if its going to take 5 turns to be effective?). Another gripe is the turn limit - very strict, and almost makes the game feel like a puzzle. 3. Multiplayer Crash Bugs - There's a massive crash to desktop for multiplayer games that seems to have gone unfixed thusfar. 1. Random Mission Generator - although you cannot chose your opponent, so sometimes odd adversaries2. New Online Multiplayer Mode allows players to play simultaneously (no more PBEM reliance)3. New graphics engine looks nice4. Custom camouflage and insignias are fun5. Aircraft return to base after every turn (less micro)

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Panzer General or Panzer Corps, get this game. It moves the genre forward in ways that haven't been since since PG1/PG2 days:The Good:+Captured Equipment is fully simulated, and encourages encirclements and being careful with your captured equipment as reinforcements are limited to what you captured+Overstrength separated from Experience, adding more customization+General Traits that allow you customize you general from an general who can have more infantry or more tanks in their core, to someone whose tanks move slightly faster over land, etc. Makes each playthrough feel significantly different.+Built-in encirclement mechanics: the game intelligent traces a supply route to the nearest supply base and if it can't the unit or group of units get encircled, getting progressive penalties and suppression by just sitting there. Now encircling the half a million troops in the Kiev pocket in 1941 is a thing+Units take up a varying number of core slots: simply brilliant. Adds so many meaningful decisions and hard choices as to your force composition. It really does seem to promote more historical compositions, at least compared to before.The Mixed:~Heroes play a bigger role. You can assign heroes to whatever units you want, with 3 heroes in one unit. On the one hand they seem a bit ahistorical strong (but not imbalanced, just weird that a tripled hero Tiger will wipe the floor with enemies the normal tiger breaks even with..maybe it's historical, don't know). But in terms of gameplay, it really does add depth as you have a lot of meaningful choices to make as to where you put your heroes. ~The graphics are gorgeous, but poorly optimized. It's a mixed bag since strategy games don't need great fps, but it seems that the devs could have done a lot better because it struggles to get half fps I get in other unreal engine games with the same resolution (PC2 is based off unreal engine).The Bad:None for me. Maybe only 24 hours in the day lol? I started a new battle in my campaign at 11pm last night and when I glanced at the clock it was 4AM. No regrets. The game is that good.TLDR: Get this game if you're a gronard. Period.
_childDocuments_.name: Panzer Corps 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's an OK title that doesn't live up to the previous installment in game depth and it's poorly optimized, so it crashes my pretty decent computer with a dedicated graphics card.Despite the criticisms below, the main game is decent (if short), so it may still be worth it, but don't expect the DLC to somehow expand or better the game. It was more frustrating than entertaining.I got the field marshal edition with all the dlc and what they don't tell you in the AD is that the DLC is not at all connected to the main game. it's a stand alone game where you advance in chapters. TOTAL bummer.The game looks better than Panzer Corps 1 but it doesn't PLAY better. It's more gamey and several mechanics were simplified and nerfed. The NAVY combat is non-existent. It's just a waste of time to have ships in the game at this point. Planes now simply return to the airport after every turn AUTOMATICALLY, You can no longer shift planes over the target to bomb it (which is how they did it in WWII with tactical AND strategic bombing). You can no longer reach further targets and you don't have to calculate fuel and strategy with planes. TOTAL bummer.The campaign is shorter than the original game. Now they're spending time designing unconnected DLC instead of bettering the main game. Another bummer.  The original was an actual connected campaign of multiple scenarios. This is a bait and switch to sell you perpetual DLC.. NOI think many comments about weak infantry are partially true. That's because game designers made several questionable decisions in scripted scenarios where you're tasked to relieve surrounded troops and where you're given support infantry that you can not reinforce. They are unusually weak and no positioning or lifting of penalties will work. Really? You can't reinforce troops under your command as well as your core troops? It's bunk. That just shows loss of creativity in game design (or pandering to the casual gamers). The game designers thought it was a GOOD idea to completely remove player control of infantry units in the DLC Spanish Civil War, so you have to rely on DUMB ai control of infantry and somehow work around it as a "challenge". But NO.... All the time spent developing core units and you have to wait for the next DLC, coming out who knows when. So all the named "heros" are saved for the DLC only. Another bummer. _childDocuments_.review: While there are several things that Panzer Corps 2 does right, it overall falls short of its predecessor.  The Good -The game has a large amount of player customization and difficulty settings, which allows the player to customize their experience to their liking.  This leads to the campaign having replayability.  -The game features an accessible level and campaign editor, which allows for the creation of not only custom levels, but entire campaigns if you are willing to learn the very basics of scripting and directory usage. -There is a great number of units, scenarios, alternate paths, etc. -The later DLC adds lots of content if you are already enjoying the game’s style and mechanics.-The ability to capture enemy equipment is a great feature and defines many of my campaigns.  The Bad-The 3D graphics are generally ugly compared to the older pre-rendered / pixelated art in Panzer Corps 1.  It does not feel like you are controlling a “Panzer Corps” on a real map, but rather playing with plastic toy soldiers and tanks, which lack any real weight.  While the terrain generally looks acceptable, the way entire units are represented by 3D vehicles does not work the way it worked in Panzer Corps 1.  There is a very basic alternative view, but it is also pretty ugly and hard to figure out what is going on.-When playing on Iron Man Mode (1 save, no restarting), you can’t redo unit moves.  This is fine for attacks, but is extremely annoying for movement, because a single miss-click could lead to your most important unit being killed.  In Panzer Corps 1, you were able to redo movement actions.-This game, despite being a hex and counter turn based strategy game, takes up a bunch of space and is very heavy on your PC for what is going on on-screen.  Another reason it should have been a pre-rendered style.-Most of the gameplay changes from the original were for the worst.  For example, they introduced an anti-tank support ability for anti-tank guns, which is great.  However, they  removed the ability for many artillery to target tanks in support at the same time.  I really do not like this, and even changed the game data to allow artillery to always support against tank attacks.  Another example is how equipment is not limited.  There is an option to make all equipment limited, but it is not done so in a realistic manner.  In the base game, there is no reason to keep some units un-upgraded, and when you change a unit to a new model, you don’t lose any money, you just spend the difference.  Not at all realistic.  -The controls feel very unnatural.  They basically took the controls from Panzer Corps 1, but didn’t account for the changes in smoothness or that we have better control setups for these sorts of games anyways.  Instead of selecting the hex you want to move to, for example, you just click on the map hex, which can lead to frequent miss-clicks.  Overall, I did not like Panzer Corps 2, but it is not a terrible game by any means.  You will probably enjoy it if you loved Panzer Corps 1, or love casual hex and counter war games.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played Panzer Corps 2 for very long but I really enjoy the base game campaign PVE content. You'll never learn from your mistakes if you simply undo your actions. I think if you enjoyed the combat style that Civilization brings to the table, this is similar without the annoying city building, diplomacy, or burdens of trying to convince the populous that total war is in their best interest. The music is good and the voice acting makes me laugh. I think Panzer Corps 2 would have been in my legendary game category if the developers had introduced specific unit abilities like popping smoke for armored vehicles to dodge direct attacks, grenades for base infantry, and panzershreks for elite infantry to deal damage in a tight spot. Abilities like those used in Company of Heroes or Gladius. The sounds effects are good, but could be improved -should be improved. Take CoH for example, probably the best combat sound effects in any game ever created. That said, I enjoy this much but would have loved to have seen more in terms of unit abilities in addition to the positional encirclement and mass attack tactics. I haven't played multiplayer yet, but I do recommend this game to fans of WWII genre and war games in general. Panzer Corps 2 is my kind of sauce and it's delicious.

_childDocuments_.review: Panzer Corps 2 is a turn-based strategy game set during World War II. It offers an extensive campaign, a number of stand-alone scenarios, some tactical puzzles, a random map generator and a variety of multiplayer options. The campaign will let you lead the Wehrmacht through the WWII, starting with the invasion of Poland in 1939 and ending with the defense of Berlin in 1945 or with the conquest of the US, depending on your choices. There are about 60 scenarios in total, but you can experience only 20 of them in one playthrough due to a branching nature of the campaign. The campaign and its difficulty are very customizable. In addition to the general difficulty slider, you can disable some of the game mechanics and introduce additional challenges. You also have a choice of how much randomness you want in your game, from a completely random-free chess mode at 0%, to full simulation with all the dice rolls at 100%, or anything in between. You can pick traits for your general that will change the game even further, making the game much easier or significantly harder. Some traits and heroes you can get might be a bit too powerful and allow you to “cheese” the game, but you can disable them completely for a pure wargame experience.The rules and mechanics at the heart of the game are quite complex. There are a lot of moving pieces to put together and you’ll have to use all of your tactical genius to find the most efficient solutions. At the same time, they’re not too complicated. You can say that Panzer Corps 2 is easy to learn and difficult to master. The AI is okay. It’s not exactly brilliant and often too passive, but it still can punish you if you make mistakes.Panzer Corps 2 offers a wide selection of vehicles to play with. Pretty much all the military equipment that was used in WWII is here, authentically recreated. And it looks amazing. The landscapes are beautiful and the unit models are very detailed. It’s a real eye-candy. The soundtrack is very good as well. Sadly, all this beauty comes at the cost of rather poor performance. Optimization in PC2 is not great. The game is surprisingly demanding, especially when it comes to video memory. Panzer Corps 2 is a beautiful and challenging game, and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes wargames or turn-based tactical strategies in general.

_childDocuments_.review: 🥇 75 / 100➲ Panzer Corps 2, the successor to its acclaimed predecessor, is a stellar addition to the world of WW2 turn-based strategy games. This installment not only builds upon the foundations of Panzer Corps but also embraces 3D graphics and maps, bringing a refreshing visual update to the genre.Pros:✔ Each level and map in Panzer Corps 2 offers a distinct visual and gameplay experience, ensuring that players are consistently faced with new challenges and environments. This diversity enhances the overall gaming experience.✔ The leap to 3D graphics is a noticeable improvement, providing a more immersive and visually appealing gameplay environment. While the sound effects could see some enhancements, the graphical upgrade stands out.✔ Panzer Corps 2 strikes a balance between accessibility and depth. It's easy to learn but presents a formidable challenge for those aiming to master its intricacies. The game continually surprises with new strategies and features, even after extended play.✔ The game is a treasure trove of content, featuring a plethora of units, challenges, and randomly generated scenarios. This wealth of material, combined with historical accuracy, ensures a rich and engaging gaming experience.✔ The strategic elements are robust, and the inclusion of generals with assignable perks adds another layer of complexity. The game demands thoughtful planning, and losing units permanently intensifies the challenge.✔ While still present, the randomness factor in Panzer Corps 2 feels better balanced than its predecessor. However, some units may still exhibit imbalance issues.✔ The game's soundtrack enhances the overall experience, delivering a memorable and immersive musical backdrop.Cons:✘ While the main game offers a rich variety of features, the DLCs, though containing worthwhile content, might feel less substantial compared to the first Panzer Corps DLCs. The quality of the initial DLCs seems to overshadow those of Panzer Corps 2.✘ The AI, though competent, showcases some questionable decision-making, such as inexplicably moving into rivers and sacrificing defense. While it adds unpredictability, it may not always align with strategic logic.✘ Some units and aspects of game progression may feel unbalanced, impacting the overall equilibrium of the gameplay.➲ Panzer Corps 2 stands as a commendable addition to the WW2 turn-based strategy genre. With improved graphics, deep gameplay, and a wealth of content, it successfully evolves from its predecessor. While facing some challenges, particularly with AI behavior, unbalanced units and DLC depth, the game remains a must-play for fans of turn-based strategy and those who enjoyed the original Panzer Corps. It's an improved version that adds more features to love, even if it carries a few cons along the way.🥇 75 / 100🏆 85-100 Points - A gaming masterpiece, worth every moment and more.🥇 70-85 Points - Solid gameplay and immersive experience.🥈 50-70 Points - A decent game, not really good but still enjoyable.🥉 0-50 Points - Terrible and boring. Falls short of expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Panzer Corps 1 was essentially a 2000s remake of the 1990s Panzer General with modern graphics. It was an easily accessible wargame which did not ask too much of its players when compared to "hard-core" WW2 titles, bridging the gap between tactical wargames like Close Combat and strategic-level games like Hearts of Iron. Although Panzer Corps 1 was easily accessible and highly replayable with an intuitive interface, some wished for more tactical nuance and expansion of classic wargaming concepts through the years.Panzer Corps 2 continues the legacy of Panzer Corps 1, and will be familiar to those who have played it. And while there has been a significant update to the graphics and sound which is very well executed, there are also foundational wargaming additions to the title when compared to PC1 - such as "wide front" and encirclement bonuses and a welcome, complete re-working of the supply system to better fit classic wargaming encirclement dynamics. There is also an improvement to the more mercenary side of playing, as you can capture enemy equipment for your own use, and doing so provides a large prestige (game currency) bonus. Many other small features, such as bogging of vehicles during retreat and realistic reworking of the aircraft basing system are also noted and enhance the feeling that this is not simply a "rework" of Panzer Corps 1.Overall, Panzer Corps 2 is a very welcome audiovisual and gameplay update to the vaunted PG/PC franchise and should be on every non-grognard wargamer's wishlist. And, perhaps, with the added features and notable historical fidelity of the many units involved, even some grognards will find themselves pleased and thinking of the old SSI.

I understand that the scenarios had to be challenging, but constant reinforcements of enemy units is not the answer. Enemy units can spam anywhere that they had started the scenario on the map, even around at"flag" points that you units  occupy ! _childDocuments_.review: Panzer Corps was a modern interpretation of SSI's classic beer-and-pretzels wargame Panzer General, specifically it was the spiritual successor of the first game in that long-lasting series. Panzer Corps 2 builds on that by taking elements from some of the later games of that same series, like People's General or Panzer General 3D, adding some original elements and mixing everything up a little. The result is an absolute delight for anybody who loves classic turn-based strategy games with a World War background. If you liked any of the original games of the Five Star General series, then Panzer Corps 2 is a must-have for you! If you always wanted to try a classic turn-based wargame, then Panzer Corps 2 is the perfect place to start, it welcomes beginners with open arms and gives them a lot of help and support.Not everything is perfect. The latest patch (patch 3) made the AI a bit suicidal. The balancing is still very much work-in-progress. And there are some quirks that players need to get used to. But other than the campaign scenarios being a repetitive, especially compared to the later DLCs for the first part, there really isn't much that's not to like.I especially love the attention to detail that went into everything, the fantastic sound track, the cute looking graphics, the highly-configurable difficulty settings. I've sunk more than 100 hours in to the game already, and 50 or so more into the betas, and I can hardly wait for the first DLCs.Highly recommended! Instand hit!

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to Panzer Corps. It retains its predecessor's intuitive streamlined turn-based gameplay, while adding intriguing new game mechanics.Bridging units are actually useful now, being able to move and cross a river in the same turn. Fallschirmjaeger are much less frustrating, and are allowed to reposition after parachuting. If a unit is mounted in a truck, it can dismount (and defend itself) if it only makes a partial mounted movement. AA units can switch between AA and AT. Fun! AT units now lend support fire to adjascent friendlies who are attacked by armor. Recon units now grant accuracy bonuses to adjacent friendlies. And tanks overrun destroyed units and may move/attack again!  Panzer Corps 2 addresses one of the glaring balance issues of the original, and that is core slots. In the original game, 1 unit = 1 core slot, and you could only go into battle with a set number of units. This worked ok to a point, accept that it never made sense to add some of the cheaper units to your core army. Every army was filled with the best jets, the best panzers, the best infantry, which made each army feel kind of samey. In Panzer Corps 2, each unit is worth 1 or more core slots. That big artillery piece might be worth 6 slots; a cavalry 3 slots, a light AA unit 1 slot, and so forth. This creates very interesting choices in core army composition. Sometimes a cheap Panzer 1B is perfect for mopping up. A cheap AA unit can keep your slower-moving elements safe. There's even a cheap scout plane (the mighty Fiesler Storch) that not only helps you scout ahead, but supports other units by increasing their accuracy. I love that little Storch.By utilizing cheap units, the player can then invest in some powerful front-line units and still have enough units to attack along different lines of attack. ...Which brings us to a map design encourages multiple lines and sometimes pivoting lines of attack. The original game tended to encourage "blob army" movement with large packs of supporting units moving together and systematically taking out objectives. The new Panzer Corps 2 mechanics, combined with intelligent map design make for some thought provoking planning.The hero system is reminiscent of Panzer General 2. Instead of simply adding to stats, heroes grant unique game mechanics. For example, "Ingore ZOC" allows your panzer to bypass zones of control to hit rear line targets. Assign Heroes to any unit, then reassign later. A Hero with "Double Support" attacks twice with support fire. Assign it to your Fighter or AA, when you anticipate a large enemy air force; then in a new mission, assign it to your AT to help fend off an armored assault. Heroes can make individual units unique, and the system encourages experimentation. Good Hunting!Breca

_childDocuments_.review: I really made an effort to like this game. Historical scenarios, especially WW2-era war-games, turn-based strategy - anything remotely resembling the classic “panzer general“-series has a huge appeal to me. Unfortunately, this game fell far short of my expectations. There are some nice new features, such as encirclement, heroes which add special traits to individual units and of course very good graphics. What still ruined this game for me though was the terrible AI. Your opponent never cares for his own losses but throws half of his force at you during the first 3-4 rounds without any care for survival – his only objective is to damage your most expensive units, even if it costs him all of his own. So the main point in literally every scenario, even the ones that should see you attacking him, is to form a strong defensive position at the start, deploy many AA-guns and ATGs and wait till the AI has butchered his own forces trying to damage yours. Having killed his first wave, you repair your own units and the scenario begins in earnest. To still keep the game challenging, the AI usually has far more units at his disposal, half of which are guarding important positions, waiting for you to activate them by approaching. But the basic problem remains: An enemy unit either guards its position to the last or goes into kamikaze-mode once activated. You never get the sense of a real opponent at work who would care for the survival of his troops – his only goal is to damage or kill a few expensive units of yours, even if it costs him all his own. So if you like nice graphics, turn-based strategy and a ww2-background, this game might still be for you. But if you like smart strategy, flanking maneuvers, clever planing, logistics and an intelligent AI, you risk being disappointed. This game is merely about attrition, not strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as tactical wargaming goes, I struggle to think of a title that did a better job of representing it than Panzer Corps. Scenarios are tense throughout, resources and time are limited, and although your forces are always improving, so too are your enemies’. With a robust selection of units complete with a wide variety of strengths and weaknesses, determining the right tool for the job is a must to ensure that you don’t run out of resources and doom your campaign. Needless to say, I wasn’t sure how it could be improved upon enough to warrant a sequel and was skeptical that there would be enough that was new to make its price tag worth it.Yet I was pleasantly surprised (maybe even ecstatic) when I began my invasion of Poland in Panzer Corps 2. Seemingly everything was improved at least a little and I found myself instantly hooked. It’s quite an accomplishment to develop a game that is so well designed that the majority of its flaws go under the radar until they’re later revealed by its own sequel’s improvements, but Flashback Games did just that.There are several campaigns available and they frequently offer choices that can alter the path that they take. Poland, for example, has a northern and southern approach that you can take which will give you two separate experiences with different scenarios and challenges to overcome. Although an earlier build had direct mechanical benefits for choices (Poland offered prototypes for the north and increased prestige for the south), it seems this was scrapped and your choice no longer offers such benefits. Instead it simply offers an overview of the challenges that you may face with each approach and what you’ll need to prepare for, an important choice if you’ve specialized your forces in a certain direction. The last thing you want to do is fight in the woods and mountains if you’ve focused the majority of your energy on improving your armored divisions.Those who’ve played Panzer Corps will find the campaign setup quite familiar. Scenarios offer a set of objectives that must be accomplished within a deadline and the units, prestige, and experience carry over from one to the next. This means that every single casualty has long-lasting detrimental effects on your campaign and units them suffer them will need to be reinforced or replaced by spending your hard-earned prestige. When this happens, you have the choice of bringing in elite recruits that will maintain the unit’s experience or bringing in much cheaper ones that will reduce it by a proportionate level. Casualties are inevitable but it’s integral to your success that you minimize them as much as possible.Having multiple approaches in these campaigns is nice but it comes with a loss of the merit-based paths of the original Panzer Corps. Scenarios now end in either victory or defeat, marginal and decisive victories no longer exist. Overall, I think this change is a step in the right direction and adds more replay value since there are plenty of options to tailor your campaign along the way, though some may miss the additional benefits bestowed upon particularly effective generals.The balance of units in Panzer Corps 2 is a noticeable improvement over that of its predecessors. I found certain units not to be worth the trouble in the original but I’d found myself seeing the value of every unit that I could recruit this time around. The improved capabilities of support units stands out in particular here with recon getting the most impressive boost with new traits that improve the effectiveness of those attacking an enemy near them, bring them from a useful scouting unit to an absolutely fantastic one that improves your forces overall.Aircraft have been reworked and now return to base at the start of every turn. You’ll still have your fighters, and tactical and strategic bombers, but they’re no longer sacrifice themselves to further your goals, at least no when it comes to fuel. I like this change as it allows you to keep your mind on the strategy at hand without having to waste your time and manually tell aircraft to rearm and refuel. Speaking of aircraft, anti-aircraft weaponry now suppresses aircraft instead of destroying it outright, which is still incredibly useful but will require series veterans to recalibrate their brains.The large selection of units that defines Panzer Corps is as impressive as ever. Rebalanced and ready to go, you’ll be excitedly spending your prestige each time a new level of technology’s reached your command. Scenario victories and conquered points of interest (like cities and airfields) grant you prestige and you’ll want to take advantage of many as you can within your deadline to guarantee that your forces are not only able to reinforce, but also able to grow by upgrading and purchasing new units. As you progress, you’ll gain more core slots which allow you to field larger force with each scenario as long as you can afford it. It can’t be expressed enough, management is key here.Panzer Corps 2 shows up with a brand new feature of its own, designing your general. This not only adds new tactical opportunities but also significant replay value. In addition to selecting a portrait, you’ll be able to select strengths and weaknesses that will alter your capabilities greatly. Strengths will cost points while weakness will give you them, and abilities range from anti-aircraft causing casualties instead of suppression to specific unit types requiring fewer of your core slots to not being able to reinforce units outside of the deployment phase. I’ve mostly played it safe so far by choosing a strength or two without any weaknesses, though I could see this being such a versatile element of gameplay that you could force yourself to adopt entirely new strategies for overcoming your enemies. I look forward to making some absolutely wild generals in the future.Your general isn’t the only one that’s looking dapper though, as Panzer Corps 2 is looking fantastic for a historical wargame. We’ve come to expect simpler graphics in the wargame genre, often even having them reduced to stacks of chips on a board, but this title manages to make combat surprisingly thrilling with its good looking units gunning down and blowing up other good looking units with visuals that blow our expectations out of the water. These graphics far exceeded my expectations, though the audio quality did as well, especially since its predecessors weren’t that impressive. I often found myself immersed not just in the tactics of any given battlefield as I’d thought but also in the overall atmosphere that was carefully designed. Neither of these qualities are needed for an excellent strategy game but they’re certainly a welcome addition.Panzer Corps 2 set out to top one of the most regarded wargames of all time and succeeded. The elements of the original Panzer Corps have been improved, including streamlining certain aspects that dulled the enjoyment and adding depth to units that make some of the formerly less impressive choices a new valuable addition to your forces. If you’re a strategy wargamer this is one that you absolutely must add to your collection. I’ve had a blast with it already and I’m very much looking forward to its DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game for hardcore wargamers who know the difference between tank variants. It is incredibly difficult and inaccessible to even casual strategy gamers (like myself) who have played every PG game since the 90's. Yes, I should probably 'git gud,' but it's unreasonable that a ten hour study of a game be insufficient to be relatively passable on the early stages. The game forgets what the every other PG games knew - some players like to have fun, feel strong, be smart, learn, but ultimately blow stuff up. You don't get to build up a massive army on the easiest difficult and roll through your adversaries as a way of learning mechanics; even the easiest difficulty is incredibly hard. In the name of realism, it fiercely caps your army size and forces you to make agonizing choices that the average non-WWII-expert would not know how to make.As an example, there is a bonus objective in the first level that is essentially unattainable unless you do certain things exactly right - including substituting certain units, overstrengthing, etc. Anyone who does not have a PhD in wargaming needs a YouTuber to show them how to fulfill this objective. Some might say that half the fun is learning the system. And that's all well and good - but the system takes far too long to learn, and there are too few rewards on the way.I was hoping for a fun but challenging romp through World War II. Instead I got a miserably frustrating slog even when I put the difficulty on 'simpleton.' This is a Soulsgame for hex-based masters. If that's you, you'll have a blast. But if you want to pretend to be an armchair general and have some low-stakes fun, this game is utterly unplayable.Somewhere along the way, Slitherine forgot to make a game that could be fun for all crowds.

_childDocuments_.review: Encirclement: A highly dangerous situation for a fighting force where—on the strategic level—it cannot receive supplies or reinforcements and—on the tactical level—can be subject to an attack from several sides. Because of this—since the force cannot retreat—it must either fight to the death or surrender.I’m willing to sport the idea a surrounded unit 'could' try to run in panic, but not without the surrounders getting in some free attacks of opportunity. In Panzer Corps 2, they simply retreat, free of charge. And they can do it repeatedly. This leaves your units lowering their weapons and looking around in confusion. “Hey, vhere’d zey go? Scheiße! Zey retreated again! Hey Hanz, how do you disarm zis Stielhandgranate? Vhere are you going? I… BOOOM!”Can you imagine if our prisons were designed this way?This poor tactical feature has managed to take a good chunk of the fun out of this game. Combine it with all your planes resetting after every turn by flying back to the nearest airfields, and you got yourself a frustrating mess.The good part about being surrounded by bad design decisions? I can retreat—without a scratch—to Panzer Corps I where I actually enjoyed myself.“C’mon Hanz, your friend’s dead, let’s go.”

_childDocuments_.review: My initially impression was its a good but not great game. Animated with very good voice acting except for some pronunciation issues of names like Manstein. The senario list is currently short but with additional DLCs and the editor, this can be expected to change.- Tutorial: Tutorials are useful. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game for what it is, a casual Civ-combat-style strategy game with a WWII theme. However, given the price tag of $80+ for the base game with all the DLC, I won't recommend it. It's fun enough for a quick hour after work when I can't commit an entire day to gaming, but balanced against the price tag to get the full experience, it's surely not worth over $80.The game just feels like it's missing a bit of polish. No way to save your game between campaign missions, no UI scaling (and this really bothered me because the UI is huge, I wish I could make it smaller), framerate is locked at 62 fps if you keep vsync on, no cinematics, the unit "cards" are bulky yet have no real information at a glance (e.g. no way to quickly find my paratroopers because I have to click each individual infantry unit to see if they had that "trait"), etc. These are all somewhat minor qualms but as I mentioned, together they all just feel like some polish is missing.Aside from the polish-related gripes, the campaign isn't really a "campaign," so much as just a set of levels. I don't mean that in a sarcastic way, I mean it that basically you start the campaign, play the level, then you play the next level, that's it. No cinematics, and by no means expecting some over the top Call of Duty level production... a slide-show of still images with some narrator talking about the previous mission and what you're doing next would do wonders for the pacing. The beginning of the levels is broken up by a short briefing by a single voice actor (in 11 hours I haven't heard anyone else talk), and he is really not great. I don't know if maybe the existing player base from the previous game doesn't expect those things and I'm just expecting this game to be something that it's not, but to me for an $80+ game (and yes, if you want to play the full experience you are spending $80+), I expect all those things to be fleshed out.None of these complaints make this a terrible game or anything, just weighing what you get versus the cost. If you can get everything together in a bundle for $30 then sure, this game would totally be worth it for a bit of casual strategy war-gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: Panzercorps 2 is  a simple PBEM game which depends on hexes-based maps/ gameplays and turn based strategy. PC2 has some good points. The next good thing is that so many units can be used in the game for each army. Each unit has unique stats and tactical advantages or disadvantages. The last good thing is that hexes created with a acceptable balances. If you play the game for 5 hours or more, you can easly estimate conflicts at the hexes. In this paragraph, i will handle negative sides of the game. These lines might be longer... Firtsly, So many vital bugs there. I waited patches to fix them, but there is no fix from developers. You can not play multiplayer games more than 2 players. You have just 2 chances to play multiplayer more than 3 players. First chance is that you can select a mp scenario which depends on 4 players free for all. However, you must 4 players, no 3 or no 5. The other chance is that you can create a map with editor. However, it takes soo many times and problems. I am preparing a map for 2 hours to play 45 minutes. Not a great deal.Another problem is there is no logical loading screen. You cant understand whats happening. Is the game loaded? or crashed? or just see a image? Moreover, you can set a game with some settings in mp for first PC2's launch days. However, a patch came and create another bug. The patch gave to create password options for players in mp. HOWEVER, PASSWORD BUTTON REMOVED THE SETTINGS BUTTON TO HOST A GAME. WTF? You can not setup a game with special options even you are just 2 players. Scenarios are so hard. All scenarios start a simple first level. You can pass it with slightly casualties. However, all level 2 maps of sceanarios are extremely hard and unbalanced. MOREOVER, THERE İS NO OPTİON TO JUMP LEVELS OF SCENARIOS. If you selected a map with hard mode, and fail in level 2. You can not change the setting to down easy. You must be defeated in the end of game. Changing to easy just seen in the end of the game. Are you kidding ?Optimization is terrible, this game depends on TURN BASED, how can use processor nearly %100 when turn is mine. İ am not cliking or doing nothing. How is CPU usage extremely hgh? I can handle most of levels with low detail settings with 30-35 fps. However, i cant play Minsk Begration Operaiton with my friend. Terrible optimization when i ever seen. Musics... There is no music, sounds are just sounds not bad. Menu design not bad. 2d Artwork is  not bad but just a picture fixed all menus. Some unestimated crashes happens.I played it nearly 40 hours even these problems. However, i stopped to hoping developers fix it. I stop my tie with the game.Score: 3/10 (cancer)

_childDocuments_.review: Very worthy successor to Panzer General (one of my favourites from many moons ago). An improvement, in fact, as there is now real value to including support units like AA, AT and Recon, which were just a waste of Core slots in the old games. _childDocuments_.review: I loved the original Panzer Corps and the improvements to Panzer Corps 2 are more than just superficial. Not only does it include experience and overstrength of unit, but also use of heroes. Heroes together with medals makes for great diversity, and the ability to add perks in the beginning of each operation/campaign makes for the ability to adopt play to your specific play style. There's one general drawback tho, a hold over from the first game. There are no real consequences to anything you do. Meaning you can certainly do well in specific scenarios, but there appears to be no real benefit for being very succesful. Some scenarios runs the full aloted turns without a major effect on the outcome.If there is, and I'm just finishing up the French campaign - nothing indicates that your previous success change the relative future events. I managed to sweep Dunkirk with my air force, but nothing indicated that this will effect things going forward. So while you play important battles, completely devastating the opponent in record time, has no material effect.And while it certainly would be ahistorical to 'win', who would like to play until 1945 ending up with a given loss? I hope I am wrong and that there will be a way to 'win' a theater of war.The old excuse was that your part of the overall war is relatively small so local success does not translate into a operational win, but I find that a poor argument. No one plays a game to admit defeat, you do it to 'win' in the sense you can win.

name: Crossfire: Legion
detailed_description: A New Generation of Warfare! The world is in conflict. Black List and Global Risk are in a perpetual fight for the domination of their ideologies; but all is shaken up with the arrival of a new faction on the battlefield. Lead your customized army to victory on the proving grounds of a not too distant futuristic world consumed by corporate conflict. Crossfire: Legion is the ultimate fast-paced real time strategy game. Whether you are looking for a highly competitive experience or prefer a slightly more relaxed approach, Crossfire: Legion has something in store for you. Prove your abilities in the online versus modes as you manage resources, consolidate a base and send your army to annihilate the enemies. Prepare yourself, on the field of battle, hesitation is your worst enemy. Crossfire: Legion also comes choke-full of exciting multiplayer modes that will test the full gamut of your abilities as a commander, from strategist to tactician - and have you realize that not all enemies are terrible foes. Unit control and tactics are core elements of Crossfire: Legion but success in battle starts before the first shots are fired. In Multiplayer, you are in full control over the composition of your army. Choose between three factions and customize your roster by selecting your troops, infantry, vehicles and air units that will guarantee victory. All armies are led by a Commander; choose yours wisely as they bring special commander abilities to the battlefield which just may turn the tide in critical situations. Society is crumbling in the near future of the Crossfire universe. Fight atop skyscrapers, dig into a bayou, or infiltrate heavily defended military bases as you get to know the main characters and goals of all three rival factions; the world is yours to conquer in this narrative-driven campaign. Climb the multiplayer leaderboards through a “season-based progression system.” Improve your tactics by reviewing your last battles using the built-in replay system. Team-up with friends to vanquish the AI in Operations. Be ready to assault enemy positions or to defend your own. Create your own maps or modify existing game modes using the level editor tool, or expand your RTS experience by browsing the Steam Workshop to find unique community-made challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: Game requires online connection to play every game mode except campaign. Skirmish versus AI is played through the online servers. Offline skirmish is not planned for official release. There are practically no players online so be wary if you are buying for PvP.The game employs a very strict population cap that severely limits how many units you can play with. Using higher tier units will often reduce your army to less than 10 units on the field. There are no plans to allow players to play without this pop cap, even against the AI or in custom games.In regard to units, the game does indeed have a lot of them but you can only bring a small number of them into a match. Not too dissimilar to sub-factions of C&C games but with such a large number of possible combinations you and your opponents can field, you can easily find yourself fielding a deck that is largely impotent to your opponents deck. As more units are planned to be implemented, the balancing issues are likely only going to increase.It's not a terrible game. It looks good. It sounds good but it is devoid of original thought or creativity. It is yet another one of those "golden age RTS" that tries to replicate the formula of those games you were playing 20-30 years ago. In particular, Crossfire Legions is a Starcraft clone without understanding what makes Starcraft a good RTS.If you're looking for the 'same old' in an off brand package then this will certainly do but instead of playing something like those other games, you might as well just play those other games.Update: As of official release, I still stand by this review.

That being said, yes this game has a little bit of work to do in the pathing/movement department. Unit groups are tad bit clunky, but nothing abysmal enough to make you not want to play. It is actually a pretty decent early access release. Combat is not too slow. Base building is pretty unique and isn't left by the wayside like in many RTS games of the current years.Blah blah blah, review, blah blah. Don't listen to people who have the attention span of 3 y/o child and make assumptions on something they never actually played.The end.

_childDocuments_.review: Has great potential. Good to see a modern / futuristic RTS without fantasy creatures or aliens. So on that basis I am in and hopeful. Needs at least a FAST FORWARD option like X-Morph Defense for the in game cinematics to get the thumbs up from me (I don't enjoy being forced to rewatch things!).The developers seem capable of making a great game and judging by what they have achieved so far, they appear to have the resources to do so. Problem is it took many hours of perseverance to get to a point where I was actually enjoying the game due to many rough edges (as expected for an early access game). It is developing pretty fast and I look forward to seeing it mature and live up to its potential.The biggest problem with the campaign is you die learning the units, controls, etc and then have to sit through the same in game cinematic cut scenes again. Which kills your enjoyment and focus, increasing the chances that you will die again and have to sit through it again. The in game cut scenes desperately need an option to FAST FORWARD or SKIP. Fast forward like x-morph would be ideal. This and bad AI really messed with and ruined mission 2 for me. It takes the fun out of it. Watching the train come and go is torture! I fell in love with RTS starting with C&C back in the day. Haven't played much RTS lately. Overall, I found mission 2 much harder than all other missions (finished all 8). Ultimately, to overcome m2, I played some player vs AI to better learn the game without those repetitive interruptions. Personally, I think the campaign should be the way to learn.PLEASE:- Fast forward option for cinematics that run in the game engine like X-Morph Defense has (great because it doesn't waste much of your time but you still see what happens in fast forward as a memory refresher)- Better path finding / AI- A specific example from mission 2, I had many units come at the main battle from below. A unit positioned in the archway blocked them all even though there is wide open street right there that should have allowed them to follow my instuction and reach the destination / battle easily. Instead I found half my army spinning on the spot- A related issue in mission 2, I guess I found the 2 Scorpion units earlier then developers expected. As a result, after the main battle, if I go too close to the area where I took control of them, they go rogue and return to that place. Then I have to send another unit over to them to claim them again. They should never leave my control, especially not in the heat of battle- Why do I constantly lose and have to re-set my control groups after each in game cinematic in the mountain mission? Within a mission with the same units on screen I constantly have to reconfig things==================== PATH FINDING & AI ====================The path finding is pathetic at times. Position a unit in a small passage way and you can have lots of units spinning in circles behind that blocked passage way because they are too dumb to go around it. Even though the blocked path involves a pillar only a few meters wide, they will spin on the spot indefinitely.It seems like it can't handle any complications, if its first choice of path is blocked by a unit, it just gives up and spins. Heck some times units on the same team get tangled up facing each other. They try to resolve this by mirroring each others movements... so they dance together indefinitely... left then right then left then right...Set a destination around the corner... your unit will navigate the terrain ok... but then crash into an enemy unit that is not moving and spin on the spot trying to figure out what to do as it still wants to get to the destination but has no idea how to go around the enemy.The units also waste time trying to go to the exact same spot only to then realise they should space out so they can fire. So only a few units are effective while your other units are busy bumping into each other, leaving you open to taking substantial damage and losing units while they get their ♥♥♥♥ together.======================= MICRO TRANSACTIONS =======================Blackbird are saying they are moving away from micro transactions due to feedback. However they are contradicting themselves a bit. Compare the devblog saying it was never part of the plan to the recent article with quotes from their COO & CEO saying micro transactions were part of the plan.Given the contradiction, it would be good if they declared via a new update on steam that there will never be micro transactions - make it definitive. I know a bunch of people that ran from this game because of that. I only kept watching it evolve because I like the modern / futuristic asthetic which is rare in RTS, so I'm more more patient and hopeful.DevBlog 18: Major Update 1.1 - Thu, June 30------The “store” section in-game worried players because it led some to wonder if we’d later introduce gameplay affecting microtransactions and pay-to-win mechanics. While this was NEVER THE INTENTION, we did think a soft-currency tied player progression system would work well. We acknowleadge that the way this was presented was fairly confusing and so we are happy to remove it while we review better progression systems.------ article - July 7, 2022Quotes from:Blackbird Chief Operations Officer Eric TorinBlackbird Interactive CEO Rob Cunningham------"But upon releasing it to Early Access, the community was very clear that they were concerned about any kind of pay-to-win scenario, or that we might have a paywall between a player and key units."In response, Blackbird announced last week that it was removing the store section of the game entirely and promised that all units will always be available immediately to all players, with no unlocking for gameplay-affecting items of any kind. The studio still plans to release downloadable content for the game, but not in the form it had been planning."There was a lot of internal discussion about what was appropriate and what was possible in the monetization space," Torin says. "We didn't want to forego the potential of MICROTRANSACTIONS, etc., because that is something that's very much part of the Crossfire IP as a first-person shooter. But we weren't sure about how it would land with the community, and that's partly why we thought Early Access would be a good way to test what was possible. But because the response from the community was so aligned with 'Please don't do this,' we decided to make the change and roll it out as fast as we could."------IN SHORT: The devblog says micro transactions were never the intention, but the COO / CEO say micro transactions were part of the original plan, which was abandoned after feedback. Thanks for listening.============= CAMPAIGN =============The early missions are painful with small chunks of RTS wedged inbetween painful storyline exposition without any kind of skip your forced to watch again and again. As you learn the games units and controls and struggle with stupid AI, you die and watch the same cinematics again. Needs FAST FORWARD like X-MORPH!The first level reminds me of Syndicate more than anything, which is not a bad thing. I'm open to variety in levels, scale, gameplay, etc.I had to play against the AI (PvP) to get a feel for the game before completing campaign mission 2 because the repetition was killing me.======================== PLAYER VS PLAYER & AI ========================I never see any lobbies or players so haven't tried PvP. I'm Oceania. There were supposed to be changes coming to improve this... not sure what they are.The ability to play against AI is there even though the wording and UI can be confusing and is not available for all game types.A quicker way to get a feel for the overall game then the campaign. But again the bad AI / path finding ruins it. Why go so far with graphics, sound, units, etc and not bother with decent path finding.

_childDocuments_.review: A genuine hidden gem. This is one of the better RTS games of the last decade with a few really interesting innovations. There's a few things I genuinely love and a few that I think need more work, I'll list them below:The Good:1. The main course - the unit selection. There's 3 factions, and before each match you get to select 7 units from that faction to form the core of your army (from about 17 available per faction). Immediately, before the match has even started, you start having to make meaningful strategic choices. Do you select cheap troopers to swarm your enemy or the hulking shields to tank for your harder hitting troops? Do you take a medical unit that can't fight but can sustain your armies in larger engagements? How much anti-air do you need if you plan to close out the match asap with a rush? Its fantastic. You make real, meaningful choices before you even go.2. The commander abilities. There 3 different commanders for each faction. These commanders contribute 2 unique powers - but they have a limited amount of power they can deploy per game. Use it up early to get an advantage? Or save it for the larger late-game fights? Sacrifice cheap troops to bait out a use? Or do you invest in healing and shields to survive a commanders onslaught? Even more meaningful choices are always welcome. 3. Streamlined building and production. There isn't a ton of base building in this game. You have a pretty simple economy system, some supply buildings, and some basic production buildings - infantry barracks, vehicle factories, and air hangers. The game lives and dies in its armies, which are the main focus of the game. Simplifying the base building cuts down on the time needed to get to the good part, and made the game more interesting and dynamic. You can lose an entire base in a minute after a bad push, and then reclaim that ground and rebuild that base in the next minute. 4. Tech progression. Tech goes up pretty cleanly - so all factions at level 1 have access to basic infantry, level 2 they get basic vehicles and advanced infantry, level 3 basic aircraft and advanced vehicles, and level 4 gives elite units and advanced aircraft. Depending on load outs and how aggressive people play, you may not make it to the higher tech levels. As the game progresses, the units you use and the units you fight are constantly shifting - as initial infantry assaults will slowly include light, then heavy vehicles and by endgame you'll be contending with war mechs and heavy aircraft. 5. The visuals are honestly pretty good. The art style is clean, and there's a lot of love in the unit models. My main critique is that all the love went into units and none went into buildings or the map. The units are beautifully animated, but most buildings aren't at all. Even more than that, nearly every map is mostly static. In a unit focused game, not a huge deal, but it would have been nice. The Bad:1. There are basically no skirmish maps. You have 4 maps in the game, and while each is entirely unique, they get repetitive. 2. There are no players. Not a huge deal for me, because I play with friends or against very competently designed bots. But, most of the custom game modes - read: the really cool and interesting ones - are multiplayer only and I genuinely wish they spent some time making bots for those as well so I could actually play them. 3. The big subjective opinion - the game is trying to be a multiplayer experience but the best part of the game is the single-player content. The game I'm playing is either almost entirely against bots, or very rarely in coop with friends vs bots. The skirmish bots are actually genuinely pretty good, and I think that if this game leaned into singe-player content hard they could really sell the game as one of the best solo RTS games on the market. But, as far as I can tell, that isn't the intended direction of the game. As a result, I expect that the already limited offering of solo content in the game will remain sparse, which just feels bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Aeshetically, it's similar to Command and Conquer. Upon further review, however, I find it is more like Starcraft. The three factions are similar - one tech faction, one defensive faction, one swarm/hit-and-run faction.I find the negative reviews are either outdated or, well, I don't know. One person said it lacks content. The story is thin, but I don't think it 'lacks content.' You have three factions with several dozen cards to make up a deck to play in multiplayer. I doubt there is a big player base - I have no tried multiplayer. But I can't fault the game's quality for that.Though the game is like Starcraft II, it's card system sets it apart enough that I enjoy it as a separate entity.The campaign is solid. RTS doesn't tend to do campaigns well, but the people who did Kharak are clearly aware of how to make a coherent story that, while somewhat thin and lacking in length, paints a compelling universe into existence.My biggest complaint - and this is a complaint for Starcraft, CoH, and a bunch of other RTS games - is the lack of ability to rewire your hotkeys to allow for AWSD scroll. I hate using the mouse scroll now that I've gotten used to more recent games that do use the AWSD keys to scroll, e.g. Iron Harvest, Northgard, etc.One of the dumbest complaints that I read was that the card system is too limiting - your armies are too small. But it's not much smaller than Starcraft's supply cap, so I don't know what that guy was complaining about. Maybe he just wanted to take all the units into a match?I don't know man, the game has a price but the review is free, so you pay for what you get and maybe that guy only played 20 minutes and was like 'man i am an expert at this game, i can review, i know things, and stuff, and things and stuff, man i'm so good at reviewing things. probably the best. i am donald trump.'

_childDocuments_.review: Crossfire: Legion. A new real-time strategy game...with nothing in it. I really am not happy with this game, its so disappointing. Where to start?I suppose I'll address one of the misconceptions about the game: It's not pay-to-win, it doesn't have any purchasable currency period. It does, however, have an in-game currency earned from completing challenges, picture it like stockpiled xp that you spend on unlocking units and commanders for the existing factions, cuz that's what it is. Sounds fair enough, and considering the game looks visually like a mobile game, its expected. I don't like it, but its expected and not enough to ruin the game for me.HOWEVER, I have no way of knowing how fair the currency rewards for the challenges are, because I couldn't complete any of them. Not because I'm bad at the game (which, I mean, I AM), but because the challenges active while I was playing required me to play in pvp, which I initially never intended to do because I hate pvp and prefer pve content in most games, but then I realized the other problem: the game is already dead. Completely empty, not a lobby in sight. Can't complete pvp challenges if there's nobody to fight.This didn't bug me much, because "Operation Thunderstrike is a cooperative pve mode where you and up to 2 other players fight against an ai" was the thing that sold me on the game. "Up to 2 other players" my arse, the gamemode requires a full lobby to be launched, it won't let you play it solo. Great. So a campaign that takes about an hour, visuals that remind me of Command and Conquer: Rivals, pvp focus and a pve mode that can't be played. Amazing. Why was this rts made?Onto more coherent gameplay descriptions: It feels like someone made a Red Alert 3-themed mod for Warcraft 3. The detestably-competitive "units on higher ground than you are untargetable until you get an air unit/other source of high-ground vision there" mechanic is present, nearly every unit has an active ability, units that are firing at a target become incapable of being moved by anything and act as a solid wall (and unlike blizzard's own games, Legion here lacks good pathfinding so your soldiers will just bounce back and forth trying to decide whether to try and push through their friends again or just walk around them, demanding you micro-manage them around to get their guns in range), sticky selection (where once you select something, you can't unselect it unless you select something else, meaning you never have an empty selection) is always on and has no toggle to turn it off (I realize this may be an uncommon personal gripe, but good gods is it as uncomfortable as bending a toenail to not be able to unselect units). Let's see, what else. The only currently-available singleplayer content is the still-in-development campaign, which features unskippable in-engine cutscenes, and is extremely short due to being only four relatively easy missions. I would have loved to see what else the game has to offer, but again, you can't play the game with ai, just stare at the populationless pvp and pve modes without ever launching a match because some idiot decided to release an rts without skrimish ai.Honestly this entire review is just the pouring out of my eternal disappointment with the gaming industry's apparent hatred of the real-time strategy genre. Why can't we get a new rts that doesn't cheap out on content, doesn't clearly stink of "we'll be the next e-sport like starcraft 2, screw the vastly larger casual playerbase that gets rts games to that point in the first place!", and doesn't look like it belongs on an iphone? For the love of the gods, if you're not gonna make an rts for rts fans, then don't make an rts AT ALL.

_childDocuments_.review: Hell no, I'm getting it refunded this game is dead on arrival.So, there's an in-game store with in-game currency that locks you out of units and such that you need to buy to even be able to select to use in your roster because.... reasons?
