_childDocuments_.review: Playing this over the free weekend. The campaign does very little to explain any of the setting, characters or even technology that is present in the crossfire universe. The campaign is also very short and ends in about 5 hours even while playing on hard. The campaign does not allow you to select your unit roster and will make some of the stupidest choices in order to make a mission harder for no good reason (i.e an early blacklist mission tasks you with fighting multiple bases which all have air units supporting them... while you have ZERO units that can hit air aside from a single weak light helicopter which the game does nothing to inform you about, many global risk missions will intentionally not give you splash damage dealing ground vehicles and instead slap you with the tanky but useless phalanx or the completely worthless weak shield generator herald).The unit roster is extremely bad as there are many units that simply aren't useful. For example you can pick for blacklist in the light helicopter section, a helicopter that carries infantry (never useful because infantry die quick and aren't too useful especially blacklist infantry), a helicopter that does some splash damage but is extremely weak, or a "air superiority" helicopter that does heavy damage (even more damage than the heavy copter the falcon) to both ground and air targets. Bear in mind that in this game there are few if any dedicated anti-air units and units that can hit air rarely do splash damage. Another example is with new horizon who can for their heavy vehicle list pick between the hyperion (which does 100 dps but seems bugged and kills units much slower than expected and has NO splash damage meaning it struggles against T0 infantry and needs to be micro'd to use its splash damage attack which is weak), the titan (powerful with splash but very slow rate of fire can be micro'd to be more durable), and then there's the behemoth (does extreme damage in a short burst despite its dps being listed as 40, and can do an AOE explosive nova that is also deadly, fires rapidly and does splash with each shot). There doesn't appear to much incentitive to pick anything other than the behemoth.The AI isn't too great either. It doesn't seem to have much of a strategy and can easily be steamrolled by any player who understands how RTS games like this work. The low pop cap and high income rates typically means that you have to build about 3-4 of the unit type production building that you want and then just spam the crud out of a single unit type and then kill the map with your blob. The high power of AOE units and the ease of their production means that there's little room to be cheeky with infantry or lesser tier units (exception is the vampire which is such a good T0 infantry that you can steamroll from the start with it provided your opponents haven't established themselves yet). Unless the unit does splash damage or has a high rate of fire + decent damage and is airborne, there isn't much reason to build that unit. There's very few units in the game that really benefit from their damage modifiers as well (i.e sniper does extra 80 damage to an infantry target but he's so weak and prone to overkill that he actually LOSES to infantry blobs despite that being the one thing you would use him for) meaning you don't really really have too much to consider aside from whether the unit you are blobbing beats the other unit that you are blobbing. Maybe in competitive play you might have to worry about Air superiority fighters that two of the factions have but I'm not convinced they actually succeed in their job and they can only hit air units meaning countering them is as simple as switching to a good ground unit and they are still weak to anti-air splash damage that some of the heavy air units can deal.*Spoilers for Campaign*The campaign is a very generic story. One faction global risk is viewed by a resistance faction blacklist as a megalomanical faction bent on taking over the world. Blacklist launches a raid on global risk using data provided by a third party and steals global risk's tech (including a stealth gen technology) and blows up their HQ. Unsurprisingly it turns out the third party is actually the evil one and global risk has a cannon fodder infantry and aircraft doctrine and huge tank policy to go give candy to kids and pet dogs or something. New horizon enters the scene with their cool mechs and cyborgs and reveals that they have control over one of the blacklist leaders and has that one "kill" one of the other blacklist leaders and then get incarcerated. New horizon goes and steals a bunch of stuff from Global risk despite the fact that they are business partners and they could have just paid $$$ for the stuff. Somehow the "killed" blacklist leader survives (there's not even a mission where you take him to hospital, he's just alive) and you get to play as global risk as the Cardinal and kill everyone with swarms of fighter jets. Global risk rescues their useless leader warden (who was somehow captured and was really important, even being described as so important that global risk can't function without him, despite never being mentioned till now) and then proceeds to steal what new horizon stole from them because they have swarms of jets that kill people and New horizon doesn't. Global risk finds out that new horizon wants a prototype mech and figure its because its a mech and therefore cool and desirable (it's the titan so anyone who has the played the game knows that unit sucks so this is clever writing) but they are wrong. Either way, Global risk tries to evacuate the prototype mech on a cargo barge but their attempt fails and they scuttle the boat but somehow fail to blow up the cargo. Blacklist somehow stole the cargo despite not being anywhere near the fight (it would be more clever writing if they actually used the fact that the titan is the most durable unit in the game to explain why the scuttling didn't kill it).New Horizon Campaign starts with some kid we've never heard about called Angel who is the daughter of the global risk leader Cardinal (the real leader, not warden who is so useless he dies and no one freaking comments). Angel was the victim of an exploding truck that hurt her and killed her mom and decided to join the emo new horizon faction because rebel teens do that sort of thing. Angel is tasked with blowing up the rest of Global risk's fleet and assets and stealing back the mech from blacklist. Angel being a female power character, is given a super mech behemoth prototype that instantly kills all enemies in one shot. Unsurprisingly Angel succeeds in stealing back the stolen Titan mech and also blows up the global risk fleet which was lead by Warden (who was so important that global risk continues to function without any problems after his death). The titan mech is turned into a mobile bomb that angel escorts into global risk secondary HQ (they already lost their main HQ in act 1). Angel tries to tell her dad to surrender and almost convinces him to surrender by being excessively emo unfortunately the real leader of new horizon Cipher (who is so important we just learned about them now) hijacks the control of the mech and detonates it to try and kill Angel's dad. It is here that it is revealed that new horizon is a NWO type organization that wants to mind control everyone with cyborg implants and it wants to test how good the implants are by forcing Angel to watch her dad die (because controlled tests with people who don't pilot\command one-hit-kill death mechs just isn't a thing these days).Mind controlled blacklist commander viper (who is so important we are learning about him now) is set to execute cardinal but the two remaining blacklist commanders somehow teleport into the fight (despite there being no way they'd know this was good place to be or to even uncloak) and the "killed" blacklist commander is Viper's brother and I'm out of words. wow

I’d say lean into that harder, and to keep the the competitive crowd happy just allow everything to be unlocked in ranked matches (or something like that). But seperate the currency by faction, make people play that faction to unlock the units. Add skill trees to each unit that require xp to unlock from using that unit etc. factions feel too familiar, almost a copy direct from other similar RTS like StarCraft C&C etc. but with less character. Maybe that’s hard to avoid, either way didn't excite me. I could go on but will leave it there. Will keep an eye on the game and hope it improves.

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a kids game. C&C from a decade ago trumps this game in every way possible. Worst thing? You can't even save your game. There are checkpoints. And if you continue from a checkpoint your workers are not assigned to certain mine anymore, your shortcut group keys 1,2,3... are no longer assigned to units... it's just a joke. You just mass produce units, press A to send them on their way towards the enemy and wait until the dust settles. Balance doesn't matter because resources are unlimited when you're building a base. _childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is simplified. The campaign is generic, short, and without any interesting mission design.Response to developer:I'll mainly focus on this statement: "The campaign is actually meant to be more of a tutorial"I can't even begin to tell you what is wrong with this statement.- your game is not complex enough to require a 7 hour tutorial. - I'm going to assume you mean a tutorial for competitive multiplayer. Singleplayer modes are never good tutorials for multiplayer. Look at Starcraft II for example, playing the campaign teaches you nothing useful for multiplayer. Same for AoE II, same for WoW if you wanna go to a different genre, same for everything. The only remotely useful singleplayer tutorial are the challenges in Starcraft II and AoE II and IV, and that's not a campaign.- taking a game mode in itself, and something quite a significant number of players play as their main mode and saying it's "more of a tutorial" is honestly insulting. Look at Starcraft II, look at CnC 3. Those have GREAT campaigns. While you may not have their budget, surely you can do better than what you did.Look up GiantGrantGames' "The next major RTS will fail. This is why." video to see why modes other than competitive multiplayer are very important."What kind of complictions are you looking for in the game-play?"- more involvement in the gathering of resources. You collect two resources from two gathering nodes equally distanced from the dropoff building, you start with 5 miners, you need 10. There's no difficulty in reaching/determining the ideal number of miners, no concern about the positioning of resources, no concern over positioning the dropoff point. - more buildings, and more upgrades. Have more buildings that unlock more upgrades, more defensive buildings, more upgrades in these buildings. Have a tech tree that's more complicated than you need the building that produces the unit and maybe an upgraded HQ.

_childDocuments_.review: [[b]DISCLAIMER[/b]: played this during the game's free weekend][[b]EDIT[/b]: this review has been updated as of 11 Dec]It's an interesting project, granted. The presentation is pretty cool and so are the factions, but other than that... this is a game trying its best to be both a StarCraft and a C&C clone, but isn't sure which one it wants to be (and for the worst). Campaign's interesting enough, even if it does use the standard military fiction tropes, but it's way too short - I assume it's to ease players into the game before they hop into the MP lobbies.Speaking of which, a lot of pretty horrendous AAA practices in terms of QoL and such. For example, no way to invite friends (they have to join by opening Steam chat and joining a friend's game); no way to lock lobbies; minimal options for skirmishes; no saving during the campaign; no offline PvE options... I'm aware that this game just came out of Early Access, but this is just like most shoddy AAA releases where you have to wait for a multi-gigabyte "day one" patch to fix stuff that should've been fixed in the first place.  This shouldn't be the norm. It's in extremely poor taste to release unfinished games like this.The loadout system is intriguing with how it promotes various tactical options, but it's easy to pick the wrong loadout and quickly get rekt by an enemy. Forget to pick a stealth detector when fighting Black List? Too bad, GG. Would've made more sense to have different commanders with different loadouts. On that note, the commander abilities are pretty unique, but why they're so limited in Versus mode is beyond me. You could reduce the amount of points gained from kills or increase the cost and cooldown of abilities instead of making them a finite, non-renewable resource. Ultimately, people are going to save up their points much like RPG players hoard health potions for "emergencies" (been there before).Then there's the gameplay itself. The SC similarities are obvious and I don't know if it's a good thing or not; it sure feels like nothing's really ground-breaking here. I can turn a blind eye with the outright copycat gameplay and the minimal army composition, but more variety in units you can use wouldn't hurt. A friend said this is rather similar to what Airmech did, but I've never played the latter, so I'll reserve further judgment on this. Gameplay loop is relatively fine, but I'm not particularly encouraged to make use of ability micro; a strong, balanced army comp and focused fire is generally good enough to get the job done. Some abilities are useful, while others leave much to be desired. Probably needs more playtesting. Readability is also kind of messy; at times I have no idea which health bar belongs to which of my units.Pop cap costs could do with some changes to encourage some power spam; some folks like myself like having big armies duking it out. You can still maintain tactical supremacy even with a big army if you know what to do with it. Would also help with opening up more tactical opportunities, since you still need to balance carefully between offensive/defensive actions. I probably would have to experiment more to see what kind of results I'll get, but as it is, it's been a fairly insipid experience from start to finish. Might be a case where I'll end up sticking with a tried-and-true loadout and not change at all. Time to kill (TTK) is all over the place, too, where Global Risk is on the short end of the stick with regards to this (it sure feels that way to me). AI is serviceable; decent fun, but gets predictable after some time. I do like how it knows when to retreat, though.Pathfinding's also a doozy. Forces tend to clump up together and cause a traffic jam when moving from point A to B. When they arrive at the destination, some units just trail behind along the route they followed and don't stick together. At times, they just bunch up together like Mutalisks stacking on top of one another. I think the devs are aware of these things, so hopefully they'll fix it.Overall, it's an OK RTS title. Nothing particularly new or inventive, while retaining the traditional bits with some changes it up here and there, and none of it in favor of the game as a whole. Disappointing? For now. There's lots of room for improvement, especially if the devs want to grab the attention of interested RTS players and still turn a profit (that's the endgame, after all). Hopefully there'll be some major revisions that might help take this game in the right direction. Until then, I can't recommend this game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a decent experience all in all. It not perfect in any sense, but its definitely not as bad as some other reviews make it out to be. Yes, not all units are available at launch. You need to unlock them by spending in-game currency that can be earned solo. I'm not sure why that is a deal-breaker for some people, but to say the whole game is trash because of that is a little premature. Some of these negative reviews are from accounts with less than an hour in the game, some less than 25 mins. I need to put a little more time into the game myself to be fair, but I feel like this game is being review bombed but I can't find the reason why. There are things that need to be polished up, there are some very valid criticisms with this game right now, but telling people that the game is a scam seems pretty unfair to me at this point.If you are on the fence about picking it up, my advice is to watch this game for a few weeks and see what the developers do. It just came out in early access, lets give them a chance to make some changes that the community asks for, and see how it goes from there. Fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: So very short time playing because even though it says there is 16 hours left to play it. Its telling me I need to purchase it. Even though its still within the trial period. So thats cool. I only played the campaign and a few missions. You can't skip cut-scenes and if you fail a mission you will have to rewatch the entire cut-scene. On some missions if you loose a single unit or a specific unit that looks exactly the same as other the same type you will fail. This made micro managing very difficult and rather annoying. _childDocuments_.review: As many others have said if there was a middle rating id use that. The game is gorgeous I love the art style, the units are cool, but man it is CORNY AF. Like maybe this wouldve cut it in the early 2000s, but man it is so so cheesy. The campaign is fun but cringe at times. The devs have potential but they need to create their own IP. If this is what crossfire has to offer than im good its really vague and theres no world building like...at all. It just feels really cheese and plain. If youre a solo player like me i advise you stay away due to the fact is not a "classic" RTS. Its kinda like a MOBA hybrid. You hardly build your base and the resources are just little facilities that the your workers collect resources from and bring back to base. Its kinda like dawn of war 3. You also create decks so you can use your full roster you only have two units per production facility and its kinda wacky. I think these devs should use their talents to learn from this and make a better game thats an actual RTS set in a universe that they can create so theres no limitations. The crossfire IP just isnt interesting and with all the strategies and cool universes we have in the genre it just does not compete. CNC is kindve corny but theres a lore to things explanations on why things are the way they are. Its not just good mercenary vs bad mercenary vs high tech mercenar! Id stay away personally. This one will most likely go down as a failure and thats okay, as long as the devs learn from it.

_childDocuments_.review: *Received for free to play during the Free Weekend*Greetings as always!  Today we’ll be looking at ‘Crossfire Legion’ an RTS that seems bent on finding a dedicated scene in e-sports.  I’m unsure if that is a good thing or not but I do love RTS games and this was available as a free weekend so I did get some time in, though not as much as I’d like.  Let’s discuss.Look Ma no Aliens:  The core of this game is an RTS, not a very inspiring one (more on that later) but an RTS none the less.  You command a PMC of sorts and from what story I saw it seems to center around what is a pseudo pre-Bladerunner world where Corporations seem to have more power than governments.  The multiplayer adds in options for commanders and picking a single unit of multiple for a ‘role’.  The sound and music is there and feels very reminiscent of C&C Generals.  If it feels like I’m being very generic on my commentary it’s because I am as generic feedback is all I can really provide for this game.  I will say one thing about this game; the shift-order system is pretty high up there with the other games and this singular thing requires praise and I wish all RTS would adopt this.Step into the Crossfire:  The game seems to care more about an ‘e-sport’ design than making a quality RTS and it left me with feelings of DOW3 and not in a positive way.  The mechanics are pretty much WarCraft 3 re-skinned with modern world units.  To make matter worse they seemed to have cut the free weekend a day short so I wasn’t able to dive any deeper to see if my thoughts are founded.  I’d be happy to play more but definitely not willing to buy this game.  Everything from the cosmetics to the story just feel generic and uninspired.  Even the resource gathering is just two generic resources; you were doing a modern take on an RTS; could have been something very interesting.  As it is, it’s just a generic RTS setting that the game seems less interested in and more interested tournament play.Overall, I would have spent more time with this game to validate my above concerns but the free weekend seemed to be cut short, unsure if the issue was on Steam or the Game side but it did solidify my findings.  This game is an RTS, the bones are here but the flesh, blood and more importantly the soul of the game are not, I’d pass on this for now.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: It is not a bad game. the only problem is that every single game from the Command & Conquer series does a better job than this, with the exception of Tiberian Twilight. Even the graphics are better in those old games than this one. There's also the questionable problem that you cannot play this offline. If you like the Red Alert series, why on earth would you play this? Like I said, it is not bad, but it is so limited. The only reason you would get this is because you cannot obtain a legitimate copy of Command & Conquer or because it just doesn't run on your computer for some damn reason. On top of that, the installation is nearly ten gigabytes.It's lacking so many basic features of an RTS that it's actually unbelievable, I just cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I do what I  always do in a new rts and immediately try the skirmish mode, it's what I like the most. The game reminds me of red alert 3 a lot in terms of gameplay which I am not opposed to. I like the return to free base building and simple resource gathering so we can focus on combat and army management. Some have claimed that you have to pay for units, which is true, but here's the kicker, its with a currency you get from playing! There's no actual micro transactions for real money that I saw. I think this is in part due to the fact that you can make different "decks" of units like in a card game, this means that even if your in a mirror match, your opponent might be bringing an entirely different force of units. I haven't tried the campaign yet but I've enjoyed the game so far and am eager to see what comes next. A refreshing injection into an old genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my take on this early access game review. I'm not sponsored by anyone and paid my money on my own.As always i'll categorized the review into four category (Graphics, gameplay and My enjoyment)Graphics: This is nothing out of ordinary. It serves its purpose well for a RTS game, but nothing innovative. I'll give it a 7 out of 10. (Good)Gameplay: At first this game may looks like a replica of a Command and conquer game, but this game is more in line with Starcraft game. The factions in this game even resembling the three factions of Starcraft. However this also make the game imbalance. Three factions are not balanced properly with the global risk faction the strongest faction while the new horizon the weakest faction. This makes playing the new horizon a struggle against other faction while playing the global risk a breeze through over other faction. The reason for this comes down to cost efficient of each faction units. The new horizon faction have the most expensive unit but still unable to compete with other factions in the same tier while global risk units are way cheaper while still holding up against the unit of the same tier. That is a bad game design. I recommend the developers of this game to balance the factions a top priority to work on immediately. Another one of the unsavory game design is paywall units and commanders. I don't consider this a bad design but more of a nuisance. You see RTS players are not an RPG players. We want to play the full game without having to grind out things for it. Some people might be okay with it but there will also be others that don't like it. All in all I think that the game is playable, so i'll give it a 4 out of 10. (Slightly below average)My enjoyment: I did have fun with this game despite all of the game set back. I think this game has potential to be a good RTS game, but not right now. I cannot recommend this game to other players at this stage but this game is still in early access there are times for developers to improve this game and one day this may stand tall and proud as a good RTS game. I give this game enjoyment score a 5 out of 10.(Sometimes fun sometime boring and tedious)

But what is way worse is that the scale is slightly off, it is too zoomed in and the units are too big, which makes the gameplay more messy and together with the terrible pathfinding and units derping out it really detracts from any microing. Some basic functionality is missing, like shift clicking an attack order or unit ability. There are too few maps and the map layouts they do have are mostly pretty awkward. The game looks pretty gorgeous but for some reason the menu is pretty ugly and lacking some basic functionality as well. For instance, you can no longer see the number of players for the map you are selecting once you've opened a lobby. _childDocuments_.review: Since I played Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak, I had my eye on Blackbird for if/when they would release their next title, so I caught this one right on early access. This is almost like when you find out about a music band, and you really like them, and buy their next album, regardless of how good it turns out. In this case, this is not really their next album, more like their next .Overall, I believe that BBI have stepped up their game. The art style and overall production quality are reminiscent of Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak, which is a good thing. However, the content delivered here is very little, so let me elaborate. I will also shorten the game names to "Homeworldy" and "Crossfiry" ... you guys, and your long trademarks.This has been fun, I have enjoyed my (short) experience. The game seems overall quite dynamic. I made an army of tanks and ... whaddoyouknow! my soldiers found their way through my own damn tanks. My impression of the game performance is outstanding [1]. My praises go to the developers.Like I said I had fun, but not everyone is like me. There is way less content here than in Homeworldy: take the approx. 11.5 hours it took me to finish the Homeworldy campaign, versus the 1.5 hours that took me finish this Act 1 of Crossfiry. Like I said: way less.Most of the potential play time, as it seems, is moved to the skirmish games. The game has this system which allows you to unlock new units as you win skirmishes, which reminds one of the way that units are unlocked with each mission of a campaign. This is OK, because we are allowed to progress and unlock units while playing VS. the AI. However, there's not much to do here either. After X hours of skirmishes vs. AI, I will have unlocked all units of my faction, and that will be that.There are basic, fundamental features that in my opinion are essential for the single-player experience and learning curve, which are missing:- Save games (FFS!).- Replays (also known as "demos" in Dota 2/Counter Strike).- Time analysis of game: total game time (FFS!), evolution of economy over time, evolution of army over time, timestamps ...- Zoom out, also known as "sensor map" in Homeworldy.I am not going to criticise the multiplayer experience [2] (many others will do it for me). Let's just say that Crossfiry has a very small team behind it, and they cannot tackle the insurmountable task of implementing even a small fraction of the features needed for a competitive multiplayer game.[1] There is no built-in benchmark, and no replay capability, so it is not easy to give an accurate measurement of the average FPS that you can expect in a reasonably crowded battle scenario. Here are the results that I got, and the scenarios that I used:Crossfiry: 94.1, Homeworldy: 83.2, Dota 2: 125.5 FPS.- On Crossfiry, 10 minutes into a skirmish game,  when armies are reasonably big and fighting each other. 5 Minutes of gameplay.- On Homeworldy, 10 minutes into the final scenario of the campaign (Khar Toba), 5 minutes of gameplay. No big battles are easily happening on skirmishes there. DXVK (translation from DirectX to Vulkan) give a steady 144 FPS during cinematics, but may get as low as 30 FPS in a battle.- Game 4 of the finals of Dota 2 Major in Stockholm, 24 May 2022, 19 minutes in, 6 minutes of gameplay.All games maxed graphical settings, all run on the same PC.[2] We know that the overwhelming majority of RTS players will stick to the single-player campaign, and we have many ways to quantify that.Take the RTS games in Steam that have achievements for "your first online skirmish" and how spectacularly low that percentage is, compared to "play the tutorial" or "play mission X of the campaign". Oh and by the way, what percentage of Homeworldy players got any of the multiplayer achievements?Take latest Age of Empires 4, and their advertised 50 hours of campaign content, in the form of history docummentary.Take the majority of positive Homeworldy reviews, and how they mostly praise the storytelling .Take the last poll results from Crossfiry, the overwhelming response for "more content" and realize that there was no option in the poll for "more  content".

_childDocuments_.review: To be sure, Crossfire: Legion has a long way to go between now and its projected full release in Q4 of this year. Unit collision and pathfinding is wonky, the factions lack balance (nobody plays New Horizon), and certain commander abilities are overpowered... but these issues ultimately boil down to stat recalculations and playtesting, meaning they can all be remedied prior to full release.Thus, a much graver concern is the game's lack of faction design novelty—as is, Global Risk, Black List, and (to a lesser extent) New Horizon are all slight permutations of each other: they're all led by the same roguishly handsome, morally gray, English-speaking tech-startup CEO in his or her late 30s. No surprise, then, that they all deploy slight variations of the same troops, tanks, and aircraft. The result is a similar playstyle and experience from early to late game, regardless of faction. I dissect this issue in greater depth in the following video: .So, why am I recommending this game? Well, what matters at this stage of Early Access is that all of the pieces for an addictive, fast-paced RTS are present—really, despite all the above doom/gloom, Crossfire: Legion is fun! Now is time for Blackbird to do what we know they're capable of doing: deliver a unique, player-friendly gaming experience. Removing the disastrous in-game store and soft currency was a great first step that should win back a number of players that were immediately put off by such a grindy, fun-defying feature. Next up: delete faction loadouts, which are a holdover from the in-game store; let us play with each unit at our disposal. Relatedly, allow for offline skirmishes—again, this is a holdover from the store needing to track a player's soft currency. As that's no longer the case, I'd love to see this addressed soon.Here's to hoping that Blackbird continue to listen to and implement more community feedback in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: They did A LOT of things right! The RTS genre is VERY difficult to develop, though. They got more wrong than they got right, sadly.It looks great, it's more responsive than most RTS titles on Steam (only about 1/4 inputs dropped). They did a good job not trying to innovate where games like Starcraft had already solved the equation......And now my pros are over and it's time to start my cons list. I don't want to do that. There are a lot, I'll rattle off a few: No strategic substance to gameplay, rigid online-only skirmish modes, very low popcap (basically a squad at T3), very spammy/slanted economy particularly at odds with the low popcap, contrived campaign story (my campaign Hard completion achievement is shared by under %1 of players >.>), meaningless unit variation and unclear roles (the support units and detection/stealth are extra cringy), the online features are abject failure.Get it if you have a relentless itch for a new RTS. Don't expect the itch to be satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: Plays like starcraft 2, looks more like command and conquer, has less content than grey goo. Sure I would recommend it because it is fun, but is it a great rts? Not by any standard. Comparing this to C&C3, Starcraft 2 or even Grey Goo, this game is lesser than any of them. There is not a single thing that this game does that isn't done better by one or more of those other games. Does that mean this game is bad? No.This is a competent RTS that lacks the polish, creativity and innovations of more popular RTS titles, but it is fun to play and the price point is right. If you're really looking for some new RTS to play crossfire legion is fine, but you will discover it is a retread of common ground if you have played any of the big RTS games of the past decades. It is in nearly every respect generic and derivative, and worse it severely lacks content and maps (although it does have a map editor). While I do like the designs of a lot of the units, the commander artworks and general gameplay, I could say the same for the other 3 games I mentioned and not only that I could say I like them more. If you're interested in the game the short answer is that for the amount of money you spend you'll probably feel like you got your money's worth.

You can ONLY see the cost of the unit you're building, but NOTHING else. Not damage, range, health, shield, abilities, etc. The one race has an AoE bombard ability (like the Ghost's Nuke in StarCraft2), that has a 'warning timer' of less than 5sec... so unless you can react to the warning sound, go over to the bombard area, select all your units, issue the move command AND get them moved out of the large bombard area in less than 5 seconds, then you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (spoiler alert: you can't). The 'warning timer' on the Ghost's Nuke was 15 seconds for a bloody reason... no human can react AND extract their units in 5 seconds. The robot race is represented 250% more, than the black race in this game. That's just brutal. You're not given ANY information with regards to the different difficulty mode changes. Does the AI just get smarter on higher difficulties, or do they actually gain bonuses? Nobody knows. The campaign is unbeatable. _childDocuments_.review: I remember following this game back when it was early access. I had enough disappointment with early access to know better than enter a new one, ever. Still though, it had my attention and I remember the issue with units locked behind a resource you gather in game. People did not want that and the game and probably business model for it swapped to a standard price tag. I do not know what people are on, but 30 bucks for a new video game is not mad expensive. It's a weird excuse for passing on the game itself. Now is it good or not? I don't think it can be that binary. What do we want from an RTS game? First, that they keep existing! but coming from Starcraft Brood War myself, I remember seeking 2 main things from the game: entertainment (yeah, it gotta be fun, come on!) and challenge (it's either my opponent or me, but I want to test myself against him and hope I can defeat him). Now for the game to be challenging, it needs to be balanced as well. So first: is it fun? I mean my experience is very small, but I appreciate having 3 distinctive factions, and 3 is the magic number to work towards "perfect" balance. Secondly: is it balanced? Well it's a harsh one, I'm about to start doing some pvp so it'll be easier to have an opinion on that part. In short: no, it does not look perfectly balanced. Another thing comes with the pretty unique card system. It's cool to have a distinctive feature in a well, well explored genre. My issue comes from from how it was implemented and balance than the fact it exists. It's all right to decide to either have access to a fast scout or a heavy tank, or a rocket or sniper infantry. But, strategically, it would be better to choose in game rather than have a locked setup before the game. My opponent spams heavy troopers? let's get snipers! he works towards mechanised units? rocket it is! He blobs a lot? grenade time!The reason for it is it would open up a different strategical approach to the game (either decide quickly and harrass, or defend and react) and a lot more flexibility in your adaptation to what your opponent brings to the table. It feels it would be more engaging than spamming 1 or 2 units because they are the best of your roster. I read that the game will be DOA (dead on arrival), but as I installed the game and created a lobby, I did not have the time to have a look around and get a little information that somebody already joined my game (it was locked for 2 players). Then I made an another up to p6 game and we were 3 in like... 2 minutes maybe? Later on, as we kept going, we chatted a little instead of rushing in a new game and we ended up as 5 in the game, but because I had to leave, we couldn't make way to play all together. My point is: I found people to play with instantly. I am amazed by the amount of negativity thrown by people here. We are lucky enough to see a new RTS game coming out, and the best some found was apparently to blame it as hard as possible instead of trying to make it work and have the best out of it. Few hints and reminders: -devs don't know everything.-devs don't do everything. -devs don't decide everything. Final take on the game: It looks good, the art style is quite cool whilst not destroying gpu usage which is kind of mandatory with RTS games in my opinion. The server seems to work decently well, so that certainly is a +.3 distinct factions is the best foundation you can have. For the single player guys, you have a campaign and a skirmish AI. If you're experienced with RTS, you will not find it too challenging, but hey you can face up to 5 AI alone. Tell me then that this is too easy. A couple of design decisions I would have preferred differently, but hey it's not so bad and as a foundation it is decent material. Besides, my take on it is just one man's opinion. Not everything is perfect, but coming from Total War Warhammer 3, it's refreshing to have a game delivered in proper condition. And hey, there's a chat in multiplayer. Yes, a chat. That's amazing. What I would be looking for in the future: -more maps. As we usually say for RTS, maps are everything. But not all!-with the card system, either staying as is or tweaked, we could surely enjoy more options with each factions. I'm pretty sure players would welcome more units and commanders for sure. -balance effort. Yeah, the usual. But it does not feel atrocious to the point nothing can be fixed. Tweaking the numbers and unit skills are things the devs can do. Probably simply give feedback? To sum it up: Good looking rather fast-paced RTS game. 3 distinctive factions with some balance to work on, but nothing as horrible as one might think. Has content for both SP and MP, but leans towards MP, which is good in my opinion for an RTS. Come on it's 30 bucks, stop saying it's too expensive and respect the people who worked on it a little. It's one thing to dislike it, it's an entirely other one to feel entitled they should give it for free or be insulted at every occasion. I'd give it a 7/10 overall on release and it could be a 9 no problem.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This appears to be primarily a multiplayer title, but I played only the single-player campaign.A fast paced RTS without being too reduced in options.  The game looks and sounds good and is quite readable except when there are large masses of units clumped together. The campaign cutscenes look great - 3D animation with a painting-like post-processing, like in Deserts of Kharak.  The gameplay is fairly fast and oriented more towards micro-management and abilites. Units are varied and fairly interesting, I have found some favourites. However the roster for a mission is limited and predefined in the campaing, which sometimes forced me to rely on units I found suboptimal for the task (i.e. defending with glass cannons, raiding with slow units). The three factions have different strenghts and distinct look and way of playing. Sometimes the units had a tendency to rush into combat, but there is a hold position command to counteract this. The economy is simplified, but present and cannot be ignored. There is no resource depletion and very limited expansion ability, at least in the campaign. Base building is limited to set locations with resources, with main building, some production and fairly fragile defensive buildings. This all is streamlined towards fast missions and army customization in the multiplayer. The game is fast and units can die quickly. I would have preferred to have an active pause at times.  The campaing is 15 mission long and quite fun. Missions are fairly varied and fast. Maps are generally more restricted, akin to Halo Wars. Towards the end there were some missions with timers or forced escorting, but only few. There is no manual saving, but the game autosaves after fullfilling an objective. The story is interesting, but not very deep, given the space. Still, the cutscenes looked great. I would compare it to C&C Generals or Halo Wars.

_childDocuments_.review: Classic style RTS with some potential with the decks. It's more of a small scale micro fight than Starcraft. Biggest gripes are the vehicles are too large, and take up too much pop cap.  They bump and grind into each other and it becomes a choke pointy style battle in larger groups, very visible in the campaign and in skirmish. If the sizes were shrunk with the vehicles, preferably the pop caps at least cut in half for the vehicles, and the maps opened up, you can get some flanking in your battles instead of the bigger death ball wins. You will get some enjoyment for the price, and the custom maps can address at least one issue, but the longevity of this game will have to come with the modding scene bringing in some changes. Still, I am having fun, so thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite having a bit of a rocky launch, numerous quality of life improvements have turned this game into a reasonably fun RTS game. _childDocuments_.review: Its an actual base-building RTS that plays like a Starcraft 2 and Command & Conquer Hybrid.Yes, It can be played in a singleplayer manner even though it is clear it was designed as an e-sports oriented RTS. Unit Rosters and Cards:The game features a unit card system which in practice permits you to build your roster of units and in the process disables some units from overall use for the upcoming match. I find it limiting but not uninteresting and still I would not consider it a blocking factor for purchase.Campaign:Overall it provided a pleasant experience that also introduces to you most of the currently available units. However the overall experience is not something memorable.Sound: The sound is good. The music and sound effects are of good quality and matches the game's atmosphere. I also like the tactical unit reporting on the occasion.Graphics:You either hate it or like it. Personally, I liked the artwork style and graphics and in combination with the music and game-play it creates a nice atmosphere for the game. Also, in 4k resolutions it looks just fine.Multiplayer: Have not tried it yet after the title's actual launch. Will revisit the review later on :)Conclusion:All in all, I must say that this game has covered a long road since early access which back then I did consider it dead on arrival. However, the devs continue to support the title, by adding new units, listening to community feedback etc, which I find it pretty cool to be honest. There is still space for improvements though, lots of improvements and fixes. Factions need balancing. And unit path-finding needs adjustments.  Also, for those who care for the "minor" staff, there is no player color picker for single-player matches and you need to be connected to the internet in order to play anything.Some suggestions to the Devs:Please differentiate single-player skirmish and multiplayer matches. In single-player, I would give the option to the player to not require a connection in order to play a match. Also, the AI definitely needs to be worked on and improved. Cheers!

For those who play planetside 2 the way I can put the factions is Black List is TR, New Horizon is VS, and the Global Risk is the NC. Basically Global risk will hurt when you get hit and can take a hit, Black List are the squishiest factions so you need more micro managing or larger numbers depending on you're playstyle, and New Horizon is a faction just to hate... Okay to be more fair, New Horizon is the most glass cannon faction out of the 3 from what i've played so far. They are hard hitters but can't take a hit. Now I haven't had much experience outside of AI and story so I can't you how each faction works against players but that is just the basic.I will say if you like March of War you will like this game, and the only down side is there isn't as much in customizing army as their could be. But being Early access I hope more units get added so you can more specifically tune you're army to you're liking. it would also be nice to see more factions sub divisions added in the future. _childDocuments_.review: Crossfire: Legion takes the best concepts of the best RTS games and mix them together to make an easy yet complex game where your customized army battles against other armies.There are three factions each one has its own gimmick that makes them unique.Black List: Invisibility and Guerrilla warfare makes this faction excelent if you want to harrash your opponents.Global Risk: Unit after unit, this faction produces units nonstop to overwhelm the enemy.New Horizon: My favourite, big high tech units that bring down armies alone. Use this faction if you want to feel powerfulThe game overall is very good, it's easy to learn, the matches are quick (between 10-20 minutes on average) and the custom armies makes it fresh every match.Graphics are decent, at the moment it lacks some visual effects but we have to see how it evolves.The soundtrack is functional, we don't have any song that could be considered a master piece like in the 90's but it does it job.Bugwise the game is very polished for an rts. There are some bugs with physics and pathfinding that could hinder the game if left like this but at the same time too specific to ruin your experience.The matchmaking does its job, but at the moment there are too few people playing the game to detect problems with it.The game has potential and right now needs a bigger community the most. We will have to see in the coming months if the game delivers, but looking at the recently released roadmap the game promises if everything goes as expected.Final score: 8/10 Pretty solid, needs more advertisement and more time.

_childDocuments_.review:
The world is in conflict. Black List and Global Risk are in a perpetual fight for the domination of their ideologies; but all is shaken up with the arrival of a new faction on the battlefield.

Crossfire: Legion is a real time strategy game featuring tactical action in furious battles across a shattered version of the near future. Raise and customize your army to engage in intense online combat and carve your own path as you rise through the ranks.

Whether you are looking for a highly competitive experience or prefer a slightly more relaxed approach, Crossfire: Legion has something in store for you.

Prove your abilities in the online versus modes as you manage resources, consolidate a base and send your army to annihilate the enemies.

Prepare yourself, on the field of battle, hesitation is your worst enemy.

short_description: AO Tennis 2 is the only tennis experience designed for and by its community. Create your own players, stadiums and legendary matches. Enter the competition to reach the top of world tennis in Career Mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh, . There always seems to be luck involved when it comes to the quality of the king-of-the-rackets sport turned into video games. The financial backbone is  the likes of  or  and game studios are trying to keep their financial risks to an absolute minimum. So, it's no wonder that this iteration is struggling with both light and shadow, but let me start from the top...- Solid gameplay mechanics: the system with charging up a shot and releasing the button at the right time was basically taken from Top Spin 4. If you played TS4, you will feel at home with AOT2 pretty quickly. You feel the weight of your shots and the rallies can get really engaging and intense.- Highly customizable difficulty: you can basically customize everything in this game. CPU level, auto-movement, ball speeds on different surfaces, stamina and several different other assisting systems. You can also set the length of every event from 1 game in 1 set to 6 games in up to 5 sets.- Australian Open: the only licensed Grand Slam tournament in the game is presented beautifully. There's cutscenes, impressions from Melbourne and the Rod Laver arena is crafted with high detail. You shake your opponent's as well as the referee's hand at the end of a match and the whole ambience just hits the right spot. I love it.- Highly customizable character: Hands down, this is the best character creator ever conceived in a tennis game. It may even be one of the most detailed CCs in any game. Body sliders for almost every body part, facial structures are deeply customizable, there's a myriad of different hair styles and for the first time, you can even adorn your player with jewelry like earrings or necklaces. The clothing system lets you freely choose what you're wearing, how it's colored and what logos you put on it. Also: don't be afraid to make a mistake during creation. You can alter your character afterwards , including body sliders.- Improved on-court immersion: BigAnt Studios implemented a few more things to improve the on-court experience. Players will ask for towels to wipe their sweat, there are more animations when you win, like falling onto your knees or the famous falling backwards on the ground, sending the racket flying. After points or mistakes from you or your opponent, you can now also give a positive or negative reactions which will influence how your player is received by the media and fans. It's your choice: will be famous or infamous?- Press conferences: For the first time in any tennis game, we have press conferences! Yes, you read that correctly. Occasionally, but most of the times before and after tournament finals, your player will answer questions at conferences that will contribute to your aforementioned  or  points. The questions are pretty shallow and repeat quite often, but it's a step towards bringing more immersion to the game.- Management system: the whole organization system has seen a lot of improvement over the first AO Tennis. You now have a calendar where you can plan well in advance which tournaments, sponsorship events or trainings you will attend. There's plenty of training options to improve your stats and you can invest money to reduce tournament or travel fatigue or to impact several other parameters. Maximizing your stats will cost you . I'm talking millions of $. Luckily, World 1000 and Grand Slam tournaments will earn you enough price money to cover for these expenses.- Manager: you also have your own manager now. Whenever you earn a new trophy he will congratulate you in a short cutscene - nothing too special but it enhances the overall experience. He will also tell you when new sponsorship opportunities arise. Sponsorships basically earn you money by winning games or over certain time spans.- Busy community: whenever you need to download a brand logo, certain players or venues, you can rely on the community creating it. Even just one day after release I found all the Adidas and Nike logos I needed to make the perfect outfits of my player.- Infallible computer: your opponents will hardly make . Over the span of more than a whole career mode year, I've counted only  unforced errors. That is pretty much the amount I make in one match. You basically have to enforce a winner to make a point, you can not count on indirect points whatsoever from your opponents. The difficulty setting does not impact this either. They just don't make mistakes.- Ball boys still don't move: two of them patiently sitting at the net and when a ball hits the net, they don't move. Why implement ball boys, when they don't fetch balls?- Generic audience: whenever I see the audience up close, I ask myself what the programmers were thinking with this. They look like N64 characters with ultra-low polygons and super pixelated. They are missing limbs and their bodyparts are clipping badly into one another. You don't really see it from afar, but whenever the camera rests on the players sitting on the bench in the breaks, you see them. And it makes you wanna puke. Couldn't they render a high-q variant of the audience for this scene? Also, the cheering always sounds the same. No matter if you're playing in a big stadium or a small country club, the crowd cheers will always sound like you're playing on a sold-out Philippe Chatrier. - Inconsequent concepts: remember me mentioning sponsorships? When Nike comes to you offering a sponsorship, you will swell with pride. However, signing this deal will have no impact on your gear. Wouldn't it be cool and realistic if you had to wear Nike outfits from then on? But the game doesn't follow through with that because there is no license in a way that it can be shown in the actual gameplay on custom characters. The mentioned  or  points also don't have any influence on your player really. Other than some emails regarding your perception in the media, there's no real consequence to how you behave.- Career character not playable in  mode: that is a real stinker. You can't play your avatar in any other modes other than career. Why not?- Weird, generic CPU players: in one tournament I've encountered a  player from  whose name was . Lol! And the actual chinese players look anything but chinese. I know that there are several hundred players that need to be created generically, but it's just weird seeing these crazy combinations of names and ethnicities.- Certain ball throw animations look they move in slow-motion. For example the animations from Marketa Vondrousova or Belinda Bencic.- Occasionally after replays, there are graphic glitches flashing across the screen for a fraction of a second.- The net is in the way of the camera on certain viewing angles.- Weird lighting, especially outdoors with hard shadows making the character look ugly.- Player movement restricted when serving. This bug was transfered AOT1 to AOT2. At least once per match, you won't be able to move your player sideways as far as you want to change serving position. Doesn't seem to follow any rules.So, these are my observations. Do I recommend it? Yes. Because it's pretty much the only Tennis game right now? Kinda. But at the same time, AOT2 does hold its own. The inconsequent new concepts and technical deficits are somewhat annoying but not really game-breaking. There are some welcome additions in terms of improved immersion and player management, the controls (with a gamepad) are good and the gameplay is fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is really a good tennis game but it has some issues that could be addressed with a patch.  My biggest gripe is that low level computer players NEVER EVER MISSES.  Ever. You also better stick your volley for a winner because if the computer gets to it will be either a perfect lob or a perfect banana hook winner into the corner (which they never miss).  It seems that there needs to be a control stat of some sort because real players who go into futures (ex college players) make TONS of errors.  It's a little ridiculous.  I can play an entire match and the computer will have 2-3 unforced errors.  Other than that sometimes your character won't "auto run" for a ball which is frustrating.  Gripes aside it's a decent tennis game and should be checked out if you are a tennis fan.

_childDocuments_.review: AOT2 is an atrocious tennis simulation and provides painful gameplay at best.Its base is to hit the ball at the correct time, like most other tennis games. And once again, it proves to be a bad mechanism at simulating realistic tennis, especially coupled with the other mechanisms.Indeed, for each strike, we have to do that :- press the strike button before our opponent strikes the ball, to maximize the charging time; so it's usually more efficient to select our strike before we know the outcome of the opponent strike, which is totally anti-tennis, and thus lead us to usually always using the topspin strike- then push left or right as soon as we see where the ball will go, then the game will automatically position our player (except when it doesn't because it's bugged)- pushing left/right will start to aim left/right, so we need to really react very fast if we want to aim in the opposite direction of our run, but not too fast either else our player will stop to run!- aim 50cm away from the left or right line (the aiming is blocked on the line); so if we don't time correctly the strike, the imprecision system won't push the ball out- release the strike button  the strike; if the "" is correct, then the strike is ok, else the ball goes a bit too much to the outside of the court (but strangely almost never too much to the inside)- wait for the AI to get his I-just-got-stuck animation, so the next strike will be a winner. Or wait for the direct lucky winner (see below)If you can do that correctly, you'll beat the game till at least the Veteran difficulty (level 5 out of 8).Use the overpowered volleying to beat the levels above.Although all that is really painful, not much enjoyable and very repetitive, the worst part is that the "" to time before the strike isn't constant and doesn't feel much natural, and it's just plain absurd very often :- your player automatically runs backward to catch the ball? Timing is constantly changing so tough luck to get it right- the incoming ball is too slow, which in real tennis is actually an easy strike becomes here a total mystery and the best bet is to just put back the ball in the middle not to take any risk- you take the ball a bit inside the baseline or 2 meters after, the timing change; in one case you might need to release the strike button 0.3 seconds before the strike and in the other one, 0.2 seconds. Or the opposite, I have no idea how it works but it's not the same.This is the core mechanism of the game and nothing is explained about it. The tutorial is ultra basic. There's no documentation. Thus it's a constant lottery.At least till I found a trick: our player animation is a good indicator of how long till he's going to strike the ball, so releasing the strike button when his racket is straight behind him works pretty well. Except when it doesn't. Why, oh why? Again, I have no idea (except the ones exposed above).Even worse, when you strike a fully charged strike, with perfect green timing, then the resulting strike is random. Sometimes, it's a good ball, sometimes it's so so, and sometimes it's a winner. So this enforces, even more, the lottery feel.So as exposed above, the AI player gets regularly stuck on the end of his run to the right or to the left, and needs ages to come back to the center. When he does this, it's the guaranteed winner to the other side. So it's easy to wait for that, as he attacks very little bit if you can manage to put the ball constantly to the left/right (which is easy enough to do).Not only the AI doesn't attack much, but it barely does any winner! The classic match will give you on your side: 20~30 winners and 10~30 errors; and on the AI side: 1~5 winners and 0~5 errors. It's bloody ridiculous.Not only he does very few errors, the ones he does are scripted : he sends back your attacks with ease, and then on an easy ball, he strikes it way out.Moreover if you keep the ball in play long enough without doing a winner, after a while the AI will start to send missile after missile, super long, super near the lane lines, on the exact same balls where he was doing crappy balls just 5 seconds before. And he won't freaky stop to do these missiles.So you'll stand there, pressing left or right as quickly as possible, then a quick tap to time the strike, feeling more like a goalkeeper than a tennis player, and still hoping for that lucky green timing that will produce a lucky counter winner: because let's be frank, tennis is all about luck, right? (spoiler alert for the devs: no, it's not).And the cherry on the cake is that every opponent plays basically the same. The only difference is that this one is a bit more or less efficient, with a few occasional volleys in option.So as if all this wasn't painful enough, we get a bunch of bugs and smaller glitches:- like said above sometimes our player stops to move or go in the wrong direction- the AI does some moonwalking away from the ball, then a couple of quick steps to it, but too late- the clothes jerk at the start of each point (it's unnerving once you have noticed once, so try to not look at it!)- the volley feels totally overpowered- Most AO tournament settings are not saved from one match to the other one- the physics is overall good and convincing, but regularly the ball really does weird stuff- have to press the A button to skip the constant mini-cutscenesI tried to play online 2 weeks ago.Unlike 400 of the people who did that out of a total of 1800, I managed to do 1 match. Like 400 people out of 1800, it was and will be the only 1.If you counted that correctly, it means 1000 people played more than 1 online match. 4 months after release, that's really low.But it's logical: the online is even worse than the offline, and by far. The ball teleports after each strike, there's only 150km/h missiles everywhere so the point lasts 5 seconds at best, and then we are forced to wait for our opponent to press that damn button to skip that cutscene where his custom-made and atrocious Federer is grinning like a mad man (this face will hunt my nightmares till the day I die).- visuals are alright- ball physics in the common case is good- players look like their real counterpart- many player customizations- can download other user-made customizations- atrocious gameplay- absolutely not realistic tennis rallies, ending in missile frenzies- obscure timing rules to strike the ball (this is the core mechanism, it should have some explanations or the rules should be more clear!)- doing the exact same perfect strike in term of timing, charging, aiming and incoming ball produces significantly different qualities of strikes- all opponents play the same, only strengths differ- AI almost doesn't do any winner nor error; it's barely better than a stupid wall- awful netcode making the online a painful experience (so there's barely anyone online)- requires to be online even when playing offline (this one alone makes the game deserve its thumb down)- makes tennis look like a lottery game where luck is the most important factor, and completely ignore that tennis is actually about positioning, strike selection and adapting to your opponent strengths and weaknesses (if you actually like tennis, you shall find the only tennis simulation that gives you this, you deserve it!)

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game and I still like it in patches but I just find myself extremely frustrated with the gameplay and other major issues. Positives:- It looks amazing (Especially for an Australian game)- Many many customisation options- I love the stadium editor and how you can make your own slams and venues- Real players look great (well the few that are there)- The mid match save feature is neat and usefulNegatives:- The AI literally make 0-3 unforced errors a game, I go through streaks of matches up to 4, where there is not a single unforced error from the AI (remember at the start of the career you play against opponents who are ranked 500+ so they should definitely be missing some shots) and these players who are ranked 500+ are pulling off bending shots down the line where it curves out and back in the court, perfect lobs, amazing shots facing away from the court, it's insane.- The timing system is extremely harsh and creates infuriating moments even on the lowest difficulty where timing is a component (the lowest difficulty gives removes the timing element and makes it ridiculously easy) it makes every hit feel like a lottery and sorta of a rough guess on when to release the button- The combination of the AI having aimbot and the timing being a lottery, makes the gameplay boring and repetitive to the point it's frustrating when the AI toggle the aimbot and start winning points because they are just prolonging the inevitable outcome of the game which is a player win, and I've been too scared to turn up the difficulty as I feel as if the timing gets any harder I won't stand a chance- The repetitive tournaments that you have to keep winning in the career mode in order to get your ranking points and be able to enter into better tournaments, I get it, that's how it is in real tennis you have to go around the world and play in little tournaments against other lower ranked players in from of like 10 people who have no idea who you are. So it's not this repetition that i'm putting down as a negative but rather, the absolute rubbish simulation system, I could 4-0 up about to win the match and i think to myself "that's me in the next round, I'll just sim the rest" and I understand that I won't win 6-0, but the game then has the nerve to tell me "sorry you've lost 5-6" or sometimes even 4-6. I know you're probably thinking why not play the last of the match out, because I have to play through 5 rounds against creepy looking randomly generated players (more on that later) just to win a tiny tournament that gives me 35 ranking points and enough money to upgrade 2 attribute points- The players you come across in the lower ranks of the game look dam right terrifying, There are players that have a grey afro and brown handlebars on their face and just random combinations of hair and facial hair on their face/head, this really breaks the immersion of the experience- Don't even get me started on the cutscenes- (This issue may just be me) The controller support is obviously appreciated but when half the time you boot up the game and it doesn't detect the controller and won't detect it resulting in you having to reboot the game, along with the fact that if your controller disconnects during a match it won't re detect it when you plug it back in meaning you must save the match mid way and reboot the game and sit through all the loading again to get back into it with the controller- (Again might just be me) Now I have a decent pc that runs nba 2k20 and fifa with quick loading times but for some reason this game takes forever to load, sometimes upwards of two minutes to load a match which only adds to the frustration when you have to reboot the game to use your controller againOverall, I wanted to like this game and I think it's a massive step in the right direction and if even some of these issues could be fixed it would be a fantastic tennis game. I'll keep playing it when I feel calm and want to get frustrated and I'll update the review these issues get fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, and it has it's positive points. So while I don't recommend it, it's not without some reservations as it does have a few redeeming qualities.Graphically this game is better than most, if not all others out there. It's not "next gen" quality, perhaps they need a bigger budget for that, but if tennis and graphics quality are your thing, I doubt you will find a better option. cut scenes/cinematics, are a nice touch. If you have no patience for these things, you can cut them short and get right back to it. Otherwise bask in the glory of a good game as you sit down and take a drink from your bench on a change over, or stare at your cool shoes as you slow motion walk onto the court. The career mode is a nice addition. It's not unique to tennis games, most have a career mode, but this one does offer some depth that others do not. Specifically in how you can manage the details of your whole career and not just play a decade of matches and move through the rankings. I also like how you can keep tweaking your players appearance whenever you want. If you want a different look, or to age your player every few years, you have that option. I'm not sure I like how the only way to progress your actual skill points is with money though, rather than training. Training will only increased attributes and skill cap, not the skill itself. Buying skills seems rather absurd to me. I do like how you can create your own schedule, hire a staff, and manage travel expenses, choose sponsors, etc. Mismanaging your time or money here can submarine your career. Character Creation is very detailed, in fact, incredibly detailed for a sports game. I do love tinkering in char gen., however, after giving it a go a few times, and having experience with char creations of many other titles that offer similar detail, I've found that the char creation is oddly limiting in some key areas. Specifically mouth and eyes. Face morph in general is great, but when it comes to eye and mouth options and details, well, you just don't have very many decent looking options, and the few that actually don't look rather bad, you cannot tweak to the extent one would like.Finally the area of biggest disappointment and unfortunately, the thing that always trumps all of the above more positives things, GAME PLAY. At first I was pleasantly surprised, and as i mentioned in my opening sentence, it's not ALL bad here, but the bad can't be easily overlooked. The game play graphics, animations, and movement are not terrible, they are okay. yes, there are glitches that cause you to do some pretty impossible things that a human should not be able to pull off, but these are not often and can be overlooked with mild amusement. After immediately winning a couple practice games, easily, I was thinking, okay this could be rather easy to get good at. So I began my career on Amateur. I was again pleasantly surprised at not only the challenge of having close matches, but making it to the third round in the very first tourney I played. My success was short lived though, next tourney, second round departure, then first round, and not even close. I began to notice patterns I've seen time and gain with other tennis titles. that sense that games were scripted, and often what I first thought was "god mode" kicking in for the opponent, followed by "idiot mode" on the very next point. Note, this isn't all sour grapes, I was equally baffled by easy wins where my opponent would suddenly just do nothing right, and I could seemingly do no wrong. Then, as expected, something would change and it would be rocket winners and me hitting one unforced error after another. While this tries simulate the ebb and flow of a real life tennis match, it comes off as sudden and jarring. You can also never "wrong foot" an opponent, where all you as the player needs to do it take one false step the wrong way and you're suddenly running in slow motion for a ball that should still be very gettable. until this point though, I had not even discovered the worst issue. i didn't know you could change difficulty on the fly, mid match, anytime you wanted. So I began to experiment a bit with various settings, how the timing/accuracy/power gauge thing worked differently, because I was having a heck of a time trying to decipher it. At times it would shoot up and give virtually no time to react for a "green" sweet spot, and at other times it would move so slow I would literally have to hold my shot for it to get to the green, often giving the opponent time to recover, thus forcing me to rush the shot. Rookie difficulty is a complete waste of time. It's basically god Mode for the player. Your meter is always in the green, no matter what, and it stops at the boundaries so you won't spray any shots long or wide. This itself would not be terrible except that at the same time you are hitting one perfect shot after another, your opponent is quite literally inept. Yes, they do hit the occasional god shot, but you will most likely retrieve it and hit another perfectly timed and placed shot for a winner. I then bumped it up to semi-pro, and then pro. Nothing changed from Amateur. nothing I could at least detect? I was still winning and losing in the exact same way, and at the same, almost predictable rate as in Amateur, the AI was still playing god with me, losing when it seems appropriate, and winning no matter what I did. So I believe now that the game decides when to kick up the difficulty to something above pro on me when it sees fit. Other games do this as well and it's always been my biggest contention with Tennis titles, even other good ones that people seem to love. IMO there should be a cap on each level of difficulty that the opponent is not able to surpass, and your play and their should always be dictated by your attributes and stats, not by auto turning legendary mode on and off in predictable patterns that are so jarringly odd it leaves you wondering how you just completely forgot how to play the game when a moment earlier it was a real actually nice battle for momentum and control. In summation, get the game if you like the details and the fluff, but if you want a nice game play experience that doesn't feel fabricated there are other titles that offer perhaps less eye candy and detail, but the game play is more nuanced and closer to the real life ebb and flow of a tennis match.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is solely about the gameplay when going against the AI and my experience starting the career mode.  Even at the amateur difficulty level, It's really hard playing against the AI if you try to play normal tennis as a new player. You can cheese drop shots and chip and charge because the game is broken in that way, but that's not what I'm looking for. If you just care about winning, then cheesing as I've mentioned is the way to go, and you won't find the game difficult at all. All of the issues I have with the game are about how hard it makes it to play normal tennis.This game is not fun for me mainly because I feel like it over-complicates hitting the ball with placement. The aiming system is terrible and very sensitive, so don't even think about trying to play by feel without looking at the shot meter or the aiming marker. Your player moves like a drunk and like every surface is the beach, which makes getting into correct position for shots a chore. If you're not in good position, good luck keeping your shot in unless you hit short and up the middle. If you hit short and up the middle, the AI will quickly take advantage. So, you have to take pretty big risks consistently to have a chance at winning without cheese, and the game tries to make that as hard for you as possible.Due to how hard the game makes it for the player to take risks, the AI should make way more errors. The AI is just too consistent overall (even at the lowest difficulty settings), particularly with high risk shots. If the AI is going to be like that, then it shouldn't be so hard for the player to execute higher risk shots.I'm not sure if I'm willing to spend a lot of time trying to get better at a shot system that I think is broken to begin with. Having to take my eyes off the ball to look at a power meter while I'm also trying to move and aim my shot is just too much. Tennis is a very feel-based game, and for me, the gameplay here does a poor job of replicating that. I love tennis and wanted to love this game, but man it is really trying my patience.Edit: I refused to be pwned by this game, so I did put in the time to get proficient with the controls and gameplay. It took until I reached about level 75 before I could win most matches efficiently playing mostly from the baseline with no cheese. Before that, I had only 2 bad choices: either 25 - 35 net approaches or drop shot cheese just to end points quickly, or boring grinds from the baseline trying to find an angle to beat the AI backboard.I did all this only because I'm stubborn. Everything in my review before the edit still stands. The devs have the bones of a potentially good tennis game here, but improvements in the shot system (seriously, just scrap it and start over), player movement (way too clunky) and AI (almost all errors are forced, everyone is a good mover, illogical difficulty spikes, I could go on...) are needed. And please, increasing the difficulty should not change anything about how to hit a shot; just make the AI smarter!I appreciate that this game exists, because serious attempts at video game tennis are hard to find these days. My criticism is only because I care about this stuff and I want others who are thinking about playing this game to hear the opinion of someone who really put in the time to understand how it works.
