_childDocuments_.review: I really hoped that some of the more mixed reviews were wrong, but sadly they were not. This game looks great and feels like it should be fun, but it has a couple issues that really hold it back. The biggest problem is one of physical space. The devs made the landmasses on the smallish side. Normally, this wouldn't be too much of an issue, but then they decided in their infinite wisdom to require that all roads use their own tiles. You will basically use around 1/3 of the landmass just for roads. This completely hamstrings you when trying to design your settlements and makes everything more of a slog. It also feels like you rarely get ahead of things in terms of supplies to your various settlements. Then, if you do, you find that you don't have enough space in your warehouses for the supplies so you need to build a settlement worth of warehouses. Remember that landmass issue I mentioned? Well, now you are devoting a lot of it to warehouses and they all need roads. It's a real downward spiral from there and eventually you just feel tired and unsatisfied. The last time I played this game was months ago and I have no urge to return to it. That's probably the most telling factor of all. In the end, it just isn't fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that can be a hit-or-miss. I think it's great; but there are some serious issues which can potentially drive people away. In fact, they do: roughly 70% of players have the achievement for making a first tool, but only 26% have managed to achieve spaceflight... and a minuscule 2.4% have beaten the game. It took me 38 hours to reach the ending - but I restarted halfway through my first playthrough and never sped up time, so this number might be a little inflated. So what's the problem, you ask?The main issue is the convoluted logistics. Your enjoyment of the game is greatly dependent on whether you can make peace with it, figure how it works and eventually master it. It's one of those things that seem simple on paper, but in practice work nothing like you'd think.Basically, you have islands and planets. Every planet has 3-4 islands. Each island has a different set of resources available to it. You can transport resources between islands using ships, and one island per planet can have a spaceport, which you can use to transport stuff to other planets. You can either micromanage each transport, or you can automate it by setting how much of a given resource you want on a different planet/island.And for the most part it works... if you configure it well. If you want something imported, something else has to export it, which means setting the desired value low. But how low? And what about hubs, which import stuff from an island, but then export it into space? What about multiple importers given a single exporter? What about storage?All of those things can be eventually worked out with patience and trial and error. And the occasional manual transport. Ironically, thinking about production chains and general logistics of your little interplanetary empire is one of the main things in this game, even if you're not having any problems with the transport system. I suppose that's a given for a city builder like this... but it's really a huge part of the game. It almost made me feel like I'm playing Satisfactory, with comparing production numbers and looking at graphs.So that's one thing. Another one is that this game does a pretty good job at cultivating this optimistic, happy atmosphere of post-post-apocalyptic hope... you start asking yourself, what happened to humanity in the first place? Things aren't so bad, right?And then, as you gaze into the void of space, it . So you find yourself having to deal with... unfriendly forces, shall we say? There are different kinds, and they force certain actions and a certain pace. I found it relatively forgiving, but I can see that for many people this can be a huge deal breaker. Granted, you're provided with tools to defend yourself - but you have to research, build, and maintain those tools. That can be a bit of a pain.And finally we get to the pacing. Things really slow down once you leave your first planet, mainly because you need different kinds of research which need to be found first. And then you need to construct proper production and transport facilities to even begin to harvest it, and then you need to move it around... this can be very annoying, and brings the game down to a halt, especially if you don't know what you're doing. Which you probably won't early on.It feels like the game has some almost arbitrary hoops for you to jump through at certain points. Expansion becomes less of a curiosity thing and more of a complete necessity. That can be annoying; But once your little machine starts working properly the satisfaction is quite delicious.So I've been pretty critical of the game so far. I want you to know what to expect if you decide to play this. Is it worth it, you ask? If you can handle it and don't mind the pace - absolutely. The game ends up surprisingly deep, and keeps unfolding for quite a long while. What's nice is that once you set islands/planets up, they're for the most part self-sufficient and even ready to provide surplus resources for newer colonies. So you're free to focus on whatever your current frontier/objective is.Let me give you a glimpse of what I mean by "surprisingly deep". At first, your peeps are happy eating potatoes and drinking water. But after a while, you'll discover vegetables, and at some point they'll expect some variety. Then comes fruit. Tea. Mix the two together, you get smoothies, which gives happiness and speed boost. Different islands can have different climates, which call for clothing. Everybody likes looking good, right? So you can also provide some luxury accessories for your people... and so on.All of this goes quite well with the aforementioned wholesome, hopeful feel of the game. The aesthetic, especially the music, is just amazing. It really makes you feel like it's humanity's golden hour, finally ready to fulfill its cosmic destiny, becoming one with all creation while retaining that childish playfulness and curiosity.And that feeling is what drove me to completing the game. And I'm glad I did, because the ending manages to somehow tie together all elements of the entire experience in a fantastic resolution. This applies both to the mechanics - you have to master all branches of production to get it done - and the story and its themes. It took me a while, but it was all worth it.So yes, I think the game's pretty good. The core gameplay loop is fun in a way that makes time just fly. Yes, there's frustration. But it all can be mastered. If you think you have the patience for this one, then by all means, play it. I'm glad I did. Just keep in mind that this game's a little more than just a wholesome city builder, and you'll do just fine. Enjoy, my friend!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting more from this game, specially from the gorgeous trailer and nice music and atmosphere. However, this is just a simple random city builder with a nice visual twist (the spherical world). The title doesn't even make sense, there is nothing to do before or after or during you "leave".To be honest I thought, from the title and trailer, we were supposed to have a balanced city, without pollution or something, so we could "leave" in peace. Since this is supposed to be a "non-violent" city builder, I thought the Space whales attacks were related to you doing something wrong, like polluting or expanding too much. The fact some structures start polluting the ground made me be almost sure "that was it"No. They attack at random (after you colonize your second planet), destroy parts of your town, and go away. There are also other minor enemies that can reduce your city effectiveness or even destroy structures. so much for non-violent. Why do they attack you? who cares ... nobody. Its random, they want to "eat" or they just to. You can counter them with "non-violent" choices like feeding the Space whales of building light to prevent Gremlings, but that is it, the non-violence means submiting to them, not avoiding them in the first place. You can pollute and expand all you want.This was a huge missed oportunity. I thought the "guardians" were supposed to keep you in check for hurting nature, but no, they are just hungry mobs. Feed them and continue destroying the world, no problem.As such, this is just your typical resource/hapiness management, with some annying "trade" mechanics between your islands (each have their own resources, so basically you do not have a single united planet or civilization, you have to micromanage trade between your own "colonies")The graphics are gorgeous, the sound is ok, the music track is awesome, but other than that, this is a generic city-builder. Since I love the genre and have seen this formula all too often, there is nothing in it for me. So, "before you leave" the game permanently, there is literaly no reason to keep playing, all you need is to spam resources and trade routes and grow for no reason or deep purpose.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A relaxing and fun cross-island and cross-planet colony sim, in the spirit of games like Anno. Manage your peeps' happiness, develop industrial chains to produce building materials and supplies, and survive the perils of new and undiscovered islands.You may like this game if:* You like strategic placement of buildings to get bonuses.* You enjoy managing logistics chains.* You want to have something very pretty to look at while you work.You may not like this game if:* You're looking for a challenge, or high difficulty.* You want to be able to have individual control over all of your peeps.* You like in-depth, nuanced resource management.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I love a good logistics/citybuilder game, and this one is definitely cute, but after the first couple of hours, it honestly all feels like busywork. Having to build the same infrastructure over and over again gets tiring really fast. As I move through the tech tree, instead of getting excited at new possibilities, I mostly get annoyed at having to fit new things into my setup.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: "Before We Leave is a non-violent city-building game." Huh, neat.Later...We have a robot minotaur who runs around one of our islands constantly scaring people away from their work and self-maintenance routines. We can counteract this by sending wrestlers to  wrestle the peacefully rampaging robot minotaurs into submission in a way that doesn't involve violence. We're not sure how but they worked it out!We have a freaking laser gun turret on another island which routinely blows up our buildings (non-violently of course) if we fail to answer its riddles... we have some guys working on that, but they're not very good at it so there are a lot of non-violent explosions.We have certain islands where anywhere not specifically protected by a powered searchlight (non-trivial to establish, on a new island or planet) will be mercilessly plundered by some little gremlin robots. I suppose theft and robbery are technically not violence? But they do seem to be allowed to steal everything, including non-renewable resources like ancient tech, which is We have regular visits from enormous space whales who non-violently eat large areas of our planets, including houses and people if they happen to be in the way. But it's not violent, you see, because the people just start happy new lives inside of the space whale, like that old guy in that book some people won't stop going on about. Gepetto! That was it.So in summary, that was a freaking lie. The game is not non-violent, it just does violence at you and then gives you only appeasement options for vaguely dealing with the problems by enabling or encouraging negative behaviors in questionably aware robotic entities and huge things that will happily eat you. No, you don't get to argue, you damn well  to your players and for that you get a very very near miss from a thumbs down simply for deceptive marketing that does not represent your game design. Alright? You only get a thumbs up because reviews are already mixed, and the game as a whole is not terrible. It has serious issues, like how tile-filling roads are a very inefficient use of hex-based space, especially when you're also trying to preserve obstructive but pollution-reducing forest areas, while also limited by resource stacks, etcetera. Mostly it just doesn't do what it says it does - it adds stressful and violent elements to what would otherwise be somewhat dull, rather convoluted, suspiciously Anno-esque, but potentially relaxing gameplay.I'd grade it a C or so, on a scale of F to S. Not awful, but not as good as it should be. Apply yourselves, Balancing Monkey Games!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is a charming and relaxing colonization/exploitation game, with a great theme sprinkled on top.I'm not sure why the reviews are on the lower side, but so far I've been having a blast with this title.It has very strong Anno vibes, you settle islands and eventually different planets.You build cities, set up your trade routes and work on that production chain.Since this is hundreds (thousands?) of years after some big apocalypse, your people just emerged from their vault as they stake their claim on this world yet again.I love how the further you go, you encounter strange anomalies on new planets that your people don't really understand fully, but boldly adventure to these sites nonetheless.For example, there is a big ancient automated turret that periodically shoots down some of your buildings, your people call this the Sphynx and when it activates, it says it's asking a riddle.You have a team of specialists that need to answer this riddle correctly to not anger this Sphynx, in other words, they just defuse this thing regularly.Such a neat mechanic tied in with the theme, it's not like your people are stupid, you are developing industry pretty much from the get-go and researching lost technology, but they are also on strange new worlds, you can find old human ruins, or perhaps alien artifacts. It has that sense of wonder that an episode of Star Trek could have or even a bit of Stargate.The story has me actually hooked, strange stuff is going on, what does it all mean? What happened? What is the mysterious object my people saw in the sky?There are some serious connotations, being the post-apocalypse and all, but it's very tongue in cheek, people can't die (as far as I'm aware, if you fail to feed them for a while they just refuse to work), there are hazards and biomes that can give you boons or maluses, but it's never game ending, nor do they feel like a nuisance, more of an interesting twist or challenge.Some people wrote a review like this "You settle islands and do the same things over and over again." which I don't feel is fair, I mean you can do that, but here is where the Anno part comes in. Different islands can produce different resources, some can produce what others can't, it's up to the player to set up an efficient network and the smart shipping tool helps a lot with this.For example, I could create lumberyards and food fields in every single island and essentially "start over" every time, but doesn't it make more sense to specialize an island and export food and wood from there? Especially if on that island you found a Nanotech spire which you choose to use to boost your kitchens and smoothie makers.Make a fleet of ships and optimize those trade routes and this is pretty much the fun of the experience.I like this game, it shows passion, charisma and it's an incredibly chill and fun experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: This is one of those games in which the tutorial can easily take two hours or more to complete. If you are a "try before you buy" kind of gamer, remain vigilant. Watch that clock, or your refund window will close before you know it.You may be wondering why I'm giving a thumbs-up to a game I've refunded. It's because I fully acknowledge that it's exactly what it claims to be, and it does everything it wants to do pretty well. However, I find the main mechanism (and plot point) driving exploration to be a bit clumsy and forced.Before I even bought the game, I saw "non-violent" and "post-apocalyptic" in the description and thought how unusual to see those two adjectives on the store page for the same game. It didn't take much play time to realize that the post-apocalyptic setting is nothing more than an excuse to make you "harvest" all your technology from nodes on the ground. Your people are utterly incapable of learning or innovating on their own. They can't even figure out how to build a damn bridge without some green blobs on the map somehow explaining that process to them. Is such a culture actually worthy of spreading to other islands, let alone other PLANETS? I leave that question to the philosophers, but I'm personally not feeling inclined to help them on that journey.Honestly, it didn't seem like such a bad thing until I realized that the game was going to use this mechanism to gate my tech progress so strictly. There's a finite amount of "green" knowledge to be mined from your initial island, and it will get you far enough up the tech tree to enable the ocean voyage that will get you to the island with the "red" knowledge. It is impossible to learn any red tech until you undertake that voyage. I can see where this is going, game, and I'm not a fan.Ultimately, that whole system adds a draconian linear element to what could otherwise be a cool open-world experience. But sadly, it's not my only gripe. There's also the weirdly big, chunky hexes into which you must fit every structure and road you ever build. This makes planning your cities into a rather claustrophobic puzzle as you try to fit everything into the tiny nooks and crannies generated by the world-building algorithm. It's clear that that particular puzzle is an intentional part of the core gameplay loop, but it's not one I particularly enjoy.SO ... if you like colony-building games without war, it's worth checking out. The management tools are robust and detailed enough to give accountants and city managers happy dreams for years. The tech tree is not super-interesting: You're not going to be making a lot of meaningful decisions there anytime soon, but it's deep enough to keep you busy, I guess? There's a pretty slick trade system -- and it's a good thing because the way resources are divided among biomes is slightly diabolical.If you don't get hung up on the inelegance of the tech system like I did, and if the Tetris-y feel of the city planning actually appeals to you, there's a lot to like about this game. Just not enough for ME to like.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The game describes itself as a peaceful city builder but I'm not sure what that means in a game where you are only allowed to create misery and spread pollution. You can apparently only make things worse. Misery seems to be a constantly snowballing feature of the kinds of society this game allows you to make.It'll tell you that people will be happier if you turn that fruit into a smoothie, but then why does the smoothie stand have an aura of constant "Gloom" around it? Why do people lose happiness from walking past an "Upgraded" house in a way they don't from walking past a basic hut? The further you go up the tech tree, the more red minus signs your buildings have on their little frowny face stat icon. Even after starting over on an easier difficulty, it's unclear if any of my actions were doing anything at all to slow the ever-worsening mood and living conditions of my people.As I sit here writing this review, I'm honestly still trying to figure out if Before We Leave is some kind of artistic statement about how the only moral path forward for society is degrowth. The people on my little islands never seemed happier than when they had potatoes to eat and well water to drink in their basic huts. If you click the tab at the top to display the Happiness of your people, the most basic thing it shows you is where you are on a spectrum from green to red, from smiley face to frowny face, but that meter isn't describing your people's aggregate mood like you might think it is. It's simply showing your current population number. The more people you have, the more you grow your cities, the further you slide into the frown zone. Is that not a deeply intentional choice? I can't really tell.As far as I can tell though, the optimal way to play is to start up the tutorial mission and then never ever fix the broken generator. Leave your people alone. They are objectively better off without you.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a generic city builder.  The trailers made it seem like it was more exploration-based, but there isn't anything interesting to explore.  You just send a ship out till you find another landmass, create a settlement, and move on.  Each settlement builds pretty much the same way as every other settlement with way too much space taken up by roads.  It doesn't help that the maps feel tiny and the space-whale stuff isn't fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a few months since I bought BWL and after giving the game a few runs I've got to give this a thumbs down for now. It starts off all calm and cutesy with no real problems, but once you start to industrialize and need to ramp up production of all things from crops to building materials and other resources while also being accosted by a plethora of "NON VIOLENT" threats that kill your peeps, destroy your structures, and steal your resources, that is when the problems start showing up.1. Roads are ridiculous. Every little thing needs a road to it. Including wells, farms, and fountains. It makes sense until you realize that roads are the only things acting as pathways and how much space they consume. Building one efficient ring of potatoes around a well means that one tile must be a road and then you need to build another ring of roads around your ring of farms. This inefficient use of space is crippling since the islands are small and you need to save on greenery as much as possible. This is made even more impossible on desert islands. This becomes a major nuisance very quickly.2.  Elevators are inefficient. It takes one peep at a time up and down. At first that's fine, but when you start to focus all your polluting industry on the mountains to save space that's when you have dozens of peeps lining up for that one elevator and are too stupid to take any other alternatives. On my very first playthrough i was under the impression that the tiered storage, which connects mountains to the ground, served as both storage, an elevator, and a road, and I was so excited that I tore down all of my elevators and replaced them with storages immediately. No sooner I did that I was spammed with errors saying that there was no route available and I had to delete all of the storages and replace them with the elevators. Apparently making this HIGHLY NEEDED adjustment would make the storages too overpowered and it is too complex of a change to make.3. This is a personal gripe, but when I made a post voicing my frustration with the roads and elevators it got some positive feedback, even from the devs, that is until I pointed out that stairs should be added as a cheaper alternative that can allow more traffic than elevators. This got my post taken down. I don't appreciate devs that take ideas and criticism down.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous looking little game and what should have been right up my alley.Only...it's not fun.I've played/loved banished, frostpunk and other city/world builders. But there's nothing to grip you here.You just collect stuff, no downsides or conflict, no problems or worries.They try to make it seem like you need food, but your peeps don't really need it.Same with clothing. And in the end there's no great sense of accomplishment. It's just happy happy build stuff on island one, go to island 2 with boats, launch to other worlds and rinse repeat. Needs more meat to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's a casual, relaxing take on the city builder genre. If you are familiar with these type of games you probably won't find it challenging. But it has good vibes, a quirky and endearing low-tech look and a passable story. It can be a bit puzzle-y at times especially on smaller islands as space is limited and roads can take up quite a lot of it. Setting up the logistics between the islands and planets can offer some challenge if you play with the older Lane Shipping option. The devs introduced a Smart Shipping feature which takes away even this hurdle. I'd avoid it unless you want to keep it really casual.I also played the game on the hardest settings trying to give myself a challenge and was very disappointed in that aspect. It was just a lot more tedious, but still very easy. Clearing away all the starting pollution is just a chore. And resources were too abundant even with everything costing twice as much, surface resource deposits being halved and building deletions not giving back any resources. I didn't run out of a single surface resource in a standard 5-planet playthrough so didn't have to build a singe deep mine, electronics maker or anything like that. Whales still didn't cause any problem, only the very first could hit the surface before I built elevators. And it was still very easy to keep peeps happy. Just the +8 bonus from good meals and smoothies was enough 99% of the time. Most disappointingly planning efficient island layouts to maximize bonuses between buildings was largely a wasted effort. Efficiency only really matters for the food industry because only meals and drinks are consumed continously at a fast enough rate. All my other industries had plenty of downtime so in the end it didn't matter much how efficient they were. Lastly playing on these settings has a nasty bug: the road layer building creates resources out of thin air whenever you build road upgrades.Other issues in short:The nanotech spyres introduced in the latest update can sometimes offer interesting choices but often they are insanely overpowered giving huge bonuses to your island for little or no drawback. Taking the offer to boost your field production to 1000% feels like cheating.Converting a spyre to a 3-tile building (fe an aegis or research institute) can brick your game completely if the tile which the spyre wants to expand into is already occupied. Always save before using a spyre for this!The airships are a lot worse than ships, so it's largely pointless upgrading to them.I've had problems with the game slowing down and becoming unresponsive for a few seconds. Happens more often the longer you play in one sitting without restarting the game.Conclusion:I can recommend this game as a casual, laid back city builder on Normal settings for experienced players looking to chill. May also be a good introduction to the genre for newcomers.I don't recommend it if you are a genre veteran looking for a challenging experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I just don't know. There's a lot to like here, because it's cute and got depth.On the other hand it's just ... annoyingly vague and grindy the more you play.Trade is the biggest offender. Either you do it manually or you let the "smart AI" take care ... and that AI ain't anything but smart... it's already aggravating just trading between islands, mainly thanks to the spherical nature of the planet and the shipping menu itself. The game wants you to set up specialized islands, but then requires quite a lot of micro-managing and jumping between islands and later planets. Couple this with research that needs to be TRANSFERED from one island to another, while the AI seemingly can't handle this request (or couldn't at first), so my peeps wouldn't "gather" red research, because the AI wasn't prioritizing its trade, and despite having a cargo hold of 30, it would only ever load 8, deliver, then forget about it again, so my peeps would stop working ... again. I ended up doing it manually, then I ended up just rebuilding my research center on a new planet, because I did NOT want to deal with shipping research via space ship back home.Once you get to the space stage the game really got boring in my opinion. Trade slows down to a crawl and you have to hope that the AI does anything remotely useful... I wasn't really able to get any great production chains going, since there was always another bottle neck. Then space whales attack and you need a big tech building all of a sudden ... on an entirely different planet. Then your islands start being polluted without the game really warning you about this. Suddenly there's a toxic sludge and a big chunk of your buildings stop producing, and you need two more buildings with highly specialized materials to get rid of it. That would be "fine" if the game at least told you "hey, if you don't do something soon, all of this will be a toxic wasteland", instead there is no warning (that I could see) and suddenly "bam" ... I was looking forward to really getting civilization back on track, but in the end the game was too micro-managy for my taste. I'm the kind of person who wants to set up efficient production and trading lines, then take care of expanding my territory, not constantly manually going back and forth to deliver 1 clothing item to a different island, because the AI again wasn't capable of doing so, and instead distributed said clothing item to a random "peep", instead of the vital "air lock" that let's me clean up the spillage, which prevents the entire island, and thus the entire civilization, from functioning.It's not a terrible game, but it's also not great and imho not worth more than a few hours of gameplay. It just doesn't achieve what it sets out to be and stands in your way all the time. The hex based nature doesn't really help either.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like a demo of a game that has never been released. Plus, devs lose time working on an editor when the game seriously needs more content and improvements... a waste of a game full of potential. :(@coffee_whale : To me, it's like the game lacks of different ways of entertainment. Let me explain this to you. For some reason, this game reminds me of Spore. Spore was fun, because there is the part where you have to develop your own creature (first phase), then you have to develop your civilization (second phase), then you have to develop your own empire in the space! (third phase). All these three phases, are quite different from each other and offer different ways to have fun within the game.But what "Before We Leave" offers? Building and management on a planet. That's it. No enemies to confront, no storyline, no sense of expansion in the space (the universe is super limited in this game), there is literally nothing that distracts you or in any way involves you to continue to build and manage your colony/civilization.I really mean the words I said, this game could be a BIG game, but it needs more work in my opinion. No one likes repetitive games. As a plus, I didn't like much you're already selling out at 40% your game. I paid the full price to support you and because I believed in this game... putting a 40% it's just like saying "heyyy, take this game now before it will be forgotten!!"... and don't tell me it's not like that.IF, and a big IF, the game and the direction with it will change in the future, for sure others and me will change their reviews into positive ones...
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Minature Anno with spacefaring Robinson Crusoe theme.  Colonize islands, then planets while avoiding space cetaceans.  Very good UI, keybinds, and trade routes.  The fast pace compared to fuller-featured city-builders is welcome because of the minimalist style that makes it more like a roguelite where you want to move quickly and optimally rather than languish and gawk at your beautiful city.  Got it on sale, but worth full price.  Have not encountered any bugs.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: So, I got this game in one of the recent Humble Choice bundles and was quite excited to see a "no-combat city-builder", as I do find combat in sim/city-building games to be incredibly tedious. If I want combat in a builder game, I'll go play an RTS like Age of Empires or Command and Conquer.Anyway, the unique take here, compared to other casual builders such as "Banished", is that you start on a little island on a planet and everything is based on hexagonal tiles a-la Sid Meier's Civilization. Now, I MUST mention this! As other reviewers point out, this game is TERRIBLY optimised. I know sim/city-builders can be resource hogs, but this game is tiny and doesn't have thousands of people on-screen at once - YET, my 6800XT is at 99% usage every second that I am in-game. BE WARNED!Onto the other, less egregious, issues I have with this game:The islands are TINY. At least they appear tiny, with very little build-space for expansion, because every other tile you build HAS to be a road, or the game will not allow you to place buildings. What ends up happening, is that when you get to what I'd consider the mid-game (building your spaceship), your initial island will be (seemingly) 50% roads, 10% production buildings, 15% houses, 25% warehouses.side-note: Warehouses here are terrible. They take up valuable space (and have to be oriented in a specific way) and really do not hold a lot of produce, especially if you want them to handle multiple items. They can also only be upgraded once too, meaning you still need tons of them on your island when you hit mid-late game.So, you have to load up boats and expand to other islands on your initial planet. No big deal, except, at least in my play-through so far, the other islands on my home planet are even smaller and covered in mountains, which are themselves littered with resources, that you cannot get rid of or build around. This is made worse by the fact that on desert islands, you cannot build a lot of the resource buildings (mainly food) on the sand tiles, meaning the actual available space to start making the micro-colony self-sufficient is minuscule.Now, I managed to mostly keep my enjoyment going and muddle-through up until the spaceship segment of the "tech tree", but after having colonised my second planet, I started to see some major tedium seeping-through. At this point, it becomes your typical resource-management shipping/logistics simulator, rather than focusing on one main city/island - and here, it is done poorly.Rather than implementing a system like, for example, Anno 1800, where you just select a trade ship and say "hey, send 30 of this resource from Island 1 to Island 2" and set it to auto, here you have to select an island, say "hey I want X amount of this here", then select another island and say "hey I want X amount of this here too" and then hope you overproduce that particular resource at Point 1, so the ships go "oh look, they have 50 of this when they only want 30, I can export some of that". On paper, this sounds like a good system, so you aren't leaving Point 1 without any resources, but when you advance into the game and are looking at multiple islands on multiple planets, it ends up becoming a complete mess.-> Set resource limit of Z on Planet 2, Island 2 to 0, so it forces the export. Set resource limit of Z on Planet 2, Island 1 to at least 1, so that it imports from Island 2, then set the resource limit of Z on Planet 1 (whichever island you want) to fill.The big issue here is that sometimes, your spaceship will leave with only 1 in the inventory, because Island 1 only wants to keep 1, so then stops accepting the import from Island 2, despite that Island being "export only". You basically have to micro-manage the resource levels on each Island on each planet, for example:-> Planet 2, Island 1 "I want 50 of this" -> Trade Ship delivers 50 of that item -> Planet 2, Island 1 "I only want 5 of this" -> Now the spaceship will correctly pick up 45 of the item you want to export to Planet 1 -> ((rinse and repeat this process))This is further compounded by how research/tech-tree works in this game. As each tech-tier uses the material from the previous tier, the main way of doing research is to do everything through the Library on your main island. But research is a material you need to gather (and it's fairly limited), just like wood or food, so you need to colonise all of the islands on every planet and then have it shipped back to your main base by using the jank shipping system I described above.It's really tedious.A lot of the tech/research in this game is locked randomly too. I had to search through ruins and shipwrecks for some of it, which is fair enough, but the rest of it? I have no idea. Not that I truly know what the point of getting the final ones would be anyway, as my population is happy, I'm powered by solar and wind and I have yet to encounter the space whales (the kraken is stupidly annoying though).Well, this is a lengthy review, so let's sum it up:A casual-friendly sim/city-building game, that clearly had good ideas and intentions behind it. It also has pleasing graphics and a nice, peaceful soundtrack that doesn't grate on you during a long play session.However, it has glaring issues, especially the (I assume) graphics memory leak, the janky logistics system that requires micro-managing everything, the unique hexagonal layout that becomes frustrating after a while (seriously, warehouses are screwy) and I can't help but feel as though the game is unfinished in a lot of areas.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to love in this game. Unfortunately, there's a point where the "smart" shipping breaks down and you either have to wait for an hour (or longer!) for goods to make their way to where they need to be on very silly ships, or wrestle with manual loading/unloading between islands and planets. As an example, ships that carry 90 items will often randomly start a long space voyage with 3 pieces of fruit, to a planet that needs stone. This can be exacerbated by weirdness between the shipping and build priority AI. You will start to colonise a new island, only to have the ship unload its fuel or stone before its wood or tools, so your people can never build the most critical infrastructure (or warehouses). Your peeps often soft-lock because of things like this, unable to complete the hut or field they started building, but unable to change tasks, with your boats stuck at the port unable to unload because the port is full. The whole thing just ends up being unsatisfying and disappointing. I want to see what the game has to offer, but what I WANT is to build a bunch of colonies and feed space whales, not fight with AI shipping.I started over a few times, trying to build "around" the bad AI -- Only building space ports on the same island I build libraries, carefully managing my import/export numbers (itself a HUGE chore for no apparent reason - why no "equalise across planets/islands option? Why can't I set every good on a planet to 1 number? Why can't I even see all the goods on a single menu until after I manually select each one? I could go on...) . But there's a point somewhere around the second planet and the electronics/chemicals tech where it always seems to break down. (There's also a point around the first scout boat  / first autosave where my computer always completely locked-up and needed rebooting, 5-6 times altogether, but that might just be me.) Genuinely, this is a good game with absolutely exhausting QOL and AI issues. I hope they patch it some day.

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing how many negative reviews there is recently, I feel like I should share my experience...Yes, the game is chill, don't buy it if you want to sweat (although if you choose some hardcore settings, it can become really challenging)Yes, some technologies seem useless, I don't use all of them, but I guess they can suit other gameplays.Yes, there are only 6 different biomes, you won't be surprised when you discover a new one, that's not the point of the game...The point of the game is optimization. And it does it perfectly. I just love getting everything as perfect as I can before moving on to the next island or planet... and then come back with the new technology to optimize some more... I don't agree with the lack of replayability. But yeah, I guess you need to like getting everything neat to enjoy it. It's a very relaxing game, the soundtrack is amazing. I can't wait for the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a city builder game without violence. There is no other country to destroy. It's just you, your people, and the resources to manage. But that's not the only thing to manage. You also have to take care of pollution and keep your people happy. Also, there may be some mysterious beings in the universe.  That's what the game is about. Your people lived underground for generations and don't know anything about the world. The only thing they can do is grow potatoes. Everything else, they have to learn first. By discovering and researching old technologies, they'll be able to build new things.  Researching works a bit like in Age of Empires in the sense that your people will discover era after era. Firstly, they will build streets of sand. After some more research, they will learn to build streets with stones and so on. The same goes for almost everything else. You will be able to upgrade houses, warehouses, and so on.  With a special building, your people go to discover technologies and collect them. This is called green technology. With that, you can research in the library. Later, they will be other technologies on other islands or planets like red technology.  Talking about other islands and planets. That's what makes Before We Leave special. You will be able to discover the whole planet and expand to different islands as well as new planets. This will be a long but worthwhile journey.  The tutorial keeps your hand pretty tight. The game will teach you everything slow enough. It makes sense and isn't overly complicated. In fact, this is one of the best tutorials I played in a city builder. In most similar games 100 textboxes are popping up, while someone talks to you and several tasks pop up, too... This is not the case most of the time in Before We Leave.  But don't think BWL is an easy game because of that. There are several things to manage and keep in mind. Your people need to be happy and for that, they need more than just food and water. You also need to take care of pollution while managing dozens of resources and all that while progressing more, discovering new technologies, islands, and planets. The art style is gorgeous and the music and sound effects are perfect. They change accordingly. Is it daytime and all your people are working hard and fast? The music will be faster, too. Is it nighttime and people are sleeping? The music will be shut off and you'll hear the wind and so on.  Before We Leave is a beautiful city builder without the need for war to make it a fun and engaging game. It could benefit from a nicely done multiplayer mode but the relaxing and chill experience would be destroyed that way. It's easy to get into, has one of the most user-friendly tutorials, and gets complicated down the line. Expanding to new islands, and planets, discovering new technologies this way, and trading resources between your islands is fun. You'll always think: "Just one more trade, to upgrade/discover/build this one, then I'll quit for now" and play some more anyways.  If you're into city builder this one is for you. It's definitely worth the asking price of 13,49€/14,99$!

_childDocuments_.review: Baby's first Anno!In Anno, if you don't have food your settlers leave, your supply chains break down and you end your game with bankruptcy. Here, they just stay at home for a bit.If you don't have Luxury items or clothes or other essentials, you can't grow in Anno. Here, your "peeps" are slightly unhappy about it but still go their merry way.The whole game feels like an Anno without consequences. The only way is forward, I don't think you can lose (haven't had to deal with whales yet though). The hexagonal building system is okay. Reminds me of Civ 6, with adjacency bonuses and what not. The game tells you to remove trees sparingly since they reduce pollution, but in reality you're just gonna mow down everything but a few for space. With no consequences. It's also difficult to figure out consumption of various goods (electricity for example...) and the overlays don't help. Not that you need it.Ah, there I go again ranting about a game that I'm recommending. Because the rest of it is kinda neat and just falls into place nicely. For 15 bucks I can't complain. A good intro into management/supply chain style games for people who are scared of them. Also cute. Thanks for reading and subscribe to my OnlyFans.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely do reviews but I fell I need to on this one.  So this is not a finished game, I've spent almost 30 hours playing and the game is nice and the reviews about it just being a city builder and a well paced game are dead on, but when you get deep into the game is where it falls apart and it falls apart badly.  I'm a huge city builder gamer, have been since the day of the original Caesar and Sim City.  I'm extremely familiar with this genre.This is a nice little game with a lot of interesting aspects that add to the city building genre.  Good graphics, comfortable play and some unique play style.  However when you get deep into a game you don't expect it to fall apart this badly.One please fix planetary trade, when you click to see what you are trading between planets you see Island labels, now you can probably figure it out but that is just poor development.  Second please tell me what Planet I'm on, i'm switching at this point between 4 planets and you start to get lost, not fun.  You need to have something where I can click on shipping to see what ships are doing what, clicking on the trade icon doesn't tell you if you have a ship that is doing nothing.  Now for the whale, yes there is a giant outer space whale that sucks things off your planet, not an issue until you apparently get a island that get impacted, not fully, but greatly and just can't recover.  Your basically done at this point.  The peeps can't respond, rebuild, or anything else.  It's a dead island which was critical to getting to the end.  That is NOT FUN!  I basically have to start again, which I'm not going to, this is not what city building is about.I was so ready to give a thumbs up but I can't to many issues and you can't spend 30 plus hours in a game to just be basically screwed.  I hope they fix things because this game has the potential of really being a solid city builder.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a delightful departure from the typical 4X strategy game, offering a non-violent, city-building experience. Set in a hexagonal world, it welcomes players to nurture a civilization emerging from an underground bunker. Rather than exterminating foes, your focus here is on housing and harmony with the environment.The game's world is a lush and vibrant one, with hex-clouds obscuring unexplored areas. A day/night cycle introduces changes in population behavior and adds to the game's charm, despite making night-time play a bit challenging. The citizens, known as "peeps," are adorable wooden toy-like figures, each with a unique name, personality quirks, and happiness levels that can be influenced by various factors.Before We Leave shares similarities with small-scale city builders like Frostpunk, with a focus on roads and infrastructure. You can meticulously plan your road network or opt for freestyle construction. Increasing efficiency by reducing travel time between resource locations leads to faster progress, akin to a reverse domino effect.Explorers are crucial for uncovering caches of technology from past civilizations, which you can research to advance your own society. The game's pace depends on your peeps' happiness, regulating the flow of new constructions.What sets Before We Leave apart is its non-confrontational approach. Unlike many 4X games, it doesn't revolve around amassing armies and battling other civilizations. Instead, it encourages eco-friendly practices and building up your civilization. Even cosmic threats like space whales are manageable without violence.The ultimate goal is to expand your civilization to other planets in your solar system. It's a satisfying journey to reach the end of the tech tree without warfare, all while keeping your peeps content. The game's eco-friendly message and optimistic outlook offer a calming and enjoyable experience, making Before We Leave a unique and worthwhile addition to the 4X genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after deciding to ignore some of the initial scathing reviews and I'm so glad I did, because I ended up playing 18 hours in the two days I've had it. I think many reviewers are judging the game on whether it fits into their idea of what a management game should be, not on whether it accomplished its mission, or whether or not it's fun.And it is fun!It takes all the best parts of city building and resource management - like gathering raw materials, finessing production chains, the balance between residence and business, strategic building placement, and shipping logistics - and left out the frustrating Death Spiral many of you will know from similar-genre titles like Banished and Frostpunk. There is no money, so there's no bankruptcy like in Anno, and there's no losing population like in Foundations. Many negative reviews have complained that there are no devastating game-ending consequences, but that's not necessarily bad, and I find that the mechanics fit the story and aesthetic of this game.Sometimes I want to play a comfy-cozy game that doesn't make me pull my hair out after a dozen bad starts or kill off the residents (who have names!) that I've grown attached to. If I want to climb Frustration Mountain, there are already dozens of titles like that, but I find Before We Leave to be unique in that it is a fully realized resource management/colony sim that is also cute, comfy and somewhat casual.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun. Do I think it's worth 20 bucks? No. I have reached the penultimate stage of the game, I am one step off from having the highest tier of technology, and I... don't really want to play this game anymore. After conquering my citizens' sadness by balancing their workload (growing the population so nobody is overworked) and giving them a lot of nice food and jewelry, it kind of feels like the challenge that the game presented is all but gone. I'm not too interested in seeing whatever the endgame is, yeah I could make a planetary shield to stave off the space whales, but why? I can just as easily stave them off by not playing the game anymore.It has become more of a chore to constantly set up new colonies (identically to my previous ones) than it has been entertaining. I got burnt out on this game in under ten hours and something about that is kind of sad for the type of game this is. It's just a little too shallow to keep you invested but takes too much effort to enjoyably replay. Or even finish once, in my case.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a BAD game, I just think expectations need to be tempered.- Limited building placement, forget about planning out your settlements how YOU want them.- Somewhat linear island colonisation methods. You do the same thing every time with very minor variation.- Worlds and islands should be bigger.- Research trees are OK and give you milestones to work towards.- Cute game, looks and runs brilliantly.- Basic but solid and intuitive logistics via shipping routes.- It's easy to pick up and play. Relaxing non-violent colony sim.Overall, I think the game is priced correctly. But before you buy, make sure your expectations aren't too high.

_childDocuments_.review: Crawling out of their vault like in Fallout, humans have to repopulate the world after a great desaster. Unfortunately, living underground for generations has not only made their skin a bit pale but also led them to forget most of humanity's knowledge, so they have to start anew. They still know how to build roads, huts and farms, but have to reasearch stuff like mines or gardening.Build roads and houses, farms and factories, everything connected directly or by roads. Using the limited space available it feels more like a puzzle game than a colony building sim. A magical transmogrifier converts wood into tools. Wood, stone and tools are all the ressources available, you need to research new technologies, construct more advanced buildings, harvest all ressources you find, build new houses everywhere. Then research and build a ship to reach other islands, build another colony to successfully pollute and ruin our whole world - AGAIN. Technically, the game works fine after a year of Early Access. Zoom in and out, watch your little peeps and their buildings from all sides. 4 scenarios challenge you with different setups to keep the game interesting.Would overpopulate and waste our world again. And again. Exterminating animals or other humans would make this even more fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, the "fun" consists of managing very limited space and to get the logistics between different islands and planets working. The mostly automated logistics system since the last large update of the game makes that challenge mostly a matter of producing enough storage space and setting up transports of the required goods. It quickly becomes more tedious than interesting to set up a new island for extraction of science or some resource. The management of space is more interesting, where trying to create a thriving civilisation on a very small format really forces you to prioritize and set up colonies for production of goods not essential to your main island. The tech-tree is mostly a matter of finding the right research resources, and is then very fast. It is not particularly deep, but even so, you are not really awarded to progress down some of the tech for your population anyhow. Increasing your population above 118 people mostly doesn't make sense - they become more demanding, and.. do nothing in particular in return. To get the best clothes, salt etc seems mostly a waste of time, so I didn't bother, and instead kept my population under control. This would have been resolved by the population generating something else than labor, which is hard to utilise, since you don't have enough space to build a massive industry requiring a lot of labor anyhow on your island.  The style of the game is positive, cosy and easy to feel at home with. The complexity and challenge of the game is possibly a bit too low - especially if you come into the game from Anno 1800, Factorio or similar games. It seems to draw most of its inspiration from the Anno games, and makes an "Anno light", with mostly no enemies and no economy, making the game relaxing. The problem is that lacking such thresholds makes the game developer create tedium by unnecessary expansion to get research instead to be the goal of the game. Altogether I enjoyed it for what it was, but don't expect too much debth or complexity in the management of your colonies in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A peaceful colony management game that doesn’t put its best foot forward, seeming tedious, but improves in the mid and late game. Before We Leave (BWL) is an extremely gentle colony management game. You lead your ‘peeps’ as you emerge from an underground shelter used to hide from an unspecified disaster on the planet’s surface. Rebuild society, rediscover technology, and reclaim the stars as you learn from the past and try to do better than the ancients who fled below ground. There are no real hostile entities, at least in my play through, though there ARE antagonists you need to work to overcome, but the biggest difficulty is fighting the midgame lull.  This is a real tough one. For the vast majority of my playtime I’d have given BWL the thumbs down… There are very clear reasons why only around half of players reached a new island, a quarter reached a new planet, a tenth met a whale, a twentieth made it to the rim or core, and only half of them finished the game… But now? By the end of my play through? I think it has to be a thumbs up, because I’ll be back to play again. Not right away, but some unspecified time in the future when I want a gentle colony builder, I’ll be back… and that in and of itself is essentially a recommendation. So if you like peaceful, simple, and gentle colony management games… then this is for you. I’d say it’s easy enough to be baby’s first colony management experience, but the grinding early game and ridiculous minutia in the most annoying ways possible might put budding colony managers off… As such it does need some experience with the genre to get the best experience from.I do not recommend this game if you’re after a strong story experience, if you want strong challenge, if you want meaningful choices, or if you want something fast paced and pewpew. I definitely don’t recommend this if you’ve not got the patience for a long haul and no eye for detail… but if that’s you I’d be surprised you read a long form review for a genre that probably drives you mental… For me, while much of BWL is left wanting, I enjoyed it once I had everything up and running and could just cook. That combined with my inevitable return, and it gets the old thumbs up. with reviews by genre. In case you want to find more games, or even reviews, like this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I was really surprised by the enjoyable complexity of BWL, and the depth at which I ended up enjoying it. It's a very stylized city-builder, but where I got my satisfaction was optimizing trade and production routes, and the scaling challenges that come with a growing game world.There's things I wish you could adjust, like HUD options or minor aesthetics, but overall it's already very customizable. You are continuously discovering new areas and planets, with new challenges and land types throughout the gameplay experience, and there's additional scenario modes to play through too, once the main game is completed.It's satisfying in a way that allows you to balance out each island, each planet, and keep going to make bigger and ever-more surprising advancements in buildings and gameplay. I'd say highly recommended for those city-builder fans that want something a little different, more island-based like ANNO, but stylized and cartoony-fun, with sprinkled gameplay extras as opposed to realism.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I have personally been enjoying this game very much! I appreciate that I don't need to worry about war or combat, nor must I consider the monetary value of my peoples (ie. slavery). It still can be challenging, and I was pleasantly surprised by the little challenges it throws your way (ex: the gremlins!). The aesthetic is very pleasing, and it isn't very demanding graphically. I would definitely recommend this! I've written out some of my experiences and some tips! ♥- The Tutorial -Doing the tutorial is a good idea and I do recommend it, but the tutorial will take you through pretty much the whole game, or at least deep into the mid-game -- this could literally be hours and hours lol. But I would suggest stopping **after you have started to explore your second planet.**, then proceed to your own games. - Your First Few Tries -In my experience, you will probably want to restart at least a few times before you reach your second planet or shortly after. This is because you will find that making your Peeps happy on all islands may be trickier, and once it falls behind, it may not always be possible to recover it. For strategy games like these (ie. Civilization), falling behind like that can set you back the whole game. I restarted five times before I found a method that worked for me! - Game Settings -As someone who enjoys strategy games, but isn't necessarily the best at them lol, I do want to be challenged but I need my games to be Kinder to me. Dead honestly, right off the bat, the first threshold for Peeps Expectations should be increased to 100. I think 60 is much too early. Luckily, you can customize these settings when you start a new game!Settings I use: • Space Whale Difficulty: 50% • Peep Expectations: 100 • Start Resources: Extra • Pollution Rate: Half • Weather Difficulty: Easy - Tips for Beginners - ☆ Try to build Kitchen and Smoothies on each of your islands, and only trade the fruit/veggies between the islands that produce and need them. I found it simply wasn't possible for any one island to produce for more than its own. ☆ Take your time! Like most sim-city-building-civilization games, you have to be careful not to get ahead of yourself or your Peeps. ☆ If you have any snowy islands, try to build on those last as they will require extra resources in comparison due to the conditions.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game with a rough start. It can be relaxing and fun, but it can be hell until you understand how to properly configure transport, what features of the game are worth investing in, and which features you simply need to ignore because they simply aren't worth it. Overall, I recommend it, but if you are expecting a cozy and relaxing game, just play the tutorial to the point where you leave your first planet and then create a new game with custom settings.   What seems to be the major problem with this game is expectation, because as you start playing it, you may think this will be a relaxing game where you can just spend your time making your cities bigger and prettier, focusing on making life for your people easier and happier. And this is not what you get, at least when playing with normal settings.So, that being said, I know it will sound weird, but: Your first playthrough will not be a fun experience. For me, it was frustrating, and sometimes stressful, especially because of all the micromanagement you have to do, trying to figure out why a trade route isn't working as expected, why suddenly everyone stopped working somewhere, and especially why god hates you so much to the point of throwing a toxic garbage from space which you can only remove with a late-game building in the middle of one of your most productive cities.But... After you play the game for the first time (which can take around 10 to 20 hours), you'll finally understand what you should and shouldn't do, and the game gets more relaxing and fun from there. You can even tweak the difficulty to make things way easier and get rid of some nuisances.Sadly, this is a flaw that prevents a lot of players from completing the game, I know that I almost gave up the first time. But I liked the game enough to complete it 100%, and after customizing my game, the rest of it was a really fun and relaxing experience (the exception being the "Getting Busy" scenario, which is the worst and more stressful part of this game, but you only need to play it if you're into achievements and/or hate yourself). This game would immensely benefit from a modding community, but sadly there is no support for it. I say this because there are some features in Before We Leave which consist of good ideas that do not exactly develop well. Also, there are a lot of buildings that never get an upgraded version in late-game, so you will have some futuristic high-tech structures digging resources directly from hell being powered by a wooden wind turbine that looks like it will fall at any moment. Also, you will be able to have modern trade ships, but god forbids if your spaceship isn't made of fricking wood. So, yeah, the game is good, but it would be awesome with a few tweaks here and there.Anyway, it's visible that the devs have their heart and minds on the right path here. Yeah, Before We Leave isn't perfect but, even with its flaws, I liked the game so much that I wishlisted their new game (Beyond These Stars). For such a small studio, they did a really good and enjoyable game as a first attempt, and I truly believe their new game will be amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Ok first.. I did enjoy this game!I'm only not recommending it because the issues it has actually do make the con list longer than the pro.First like others have said.. this game runs hot! Like my PC fans are turbo just with this game lol even on low graphics my pc wants to take off like a jet engine. Others have had this issue too and I hope the devs fix whatever it causing it in the futureOk now onto the game consPaths... They are needed to connect EVERYTHING and are the worst thing to place in game.
