I get why houses and buildings need paths but why do farms and wells? surely they can walk through the plants?Research.. Why is this per island?! why so I need to transfer it by ship?! why cant it just be a separate thing and not a resource?Trade System.. I had to watch tutorials on how to get this to work. A simple "I need this" "I want to export this" on each island would be easier than the  current system which had me confused AF. I was just doing it manually for the longest time cause that was easier for me.Bridges.. I have so much trouble with these. On paper they are a great idea but the 1 tile limit makes them almost unusable on most maps. I just use elevators insteadPollution Cleaner... I was excited when I unlocked this but it doesnt really feel or look like it does anything. I placed multiple around my heavy polluted areas but they were always polluted even after being cleanedThis game is fun and having played SOOO many of these types of games I really hope it gets some updates cause I want to play it for hours like it deserved but right now it's just abit too much effort but a lil less reward
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very mid city builder. I wouldn't say it's necessarily bad, but I think you'd be better off spending your time playing other city building games. Before We Leave presents itself as a relaxing city builder, where you build beautiful cities on an inviting, friendly atmosphere. After 2 or 3 hours of playing, you'll realize that this is far from the case. There are many (over 30) different resources to balance between multiple islands, and eventually, multiple planets. This is not a bad thing for players who want a challenge, you just have to know what you're getting into.Pros:  - The hexagonal planets provide a unique environment to build your city, and space management is a fun challenge - The UI, controls, and overall feel of the game worked well for me - Nice supply chains that require you to build a variety of industries and be creative with your trade routesCons: - Replayability: The game gets pretty boring pretty fast. When travelling to a new island, you basically start almost from scratch and have to build the same buildings all over again. Same thing with travelling to a new planet - The green/red/blue technology system for research is annoying. I don't understand why they decided to have 3 different types of technologies for research. - Some of the creatures you face off against in the later stages of the game are just annoying instead of a fun challenge.It's not a terrible game, but I wouldn't put my time or money into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a fairly simple city builder and exploration game. You start off with a few people (peeps) exiting a bunker after the apocalypse and have to rebuild civilization one island at a time. The buildings and tech tree are relatively simple. Create a mine to get iron ore, smelt it into bars, combine with wood into tools, use tools to construct more buildings. Most of your choices come in how you lay out the buildings in your town. Each building gets an adjacency bonus depending on what it is next to, but you also want to make sure your peeps don't have to walk too far. Some buildings are noisy and make pollution so you want them farther away. After you've done this a few times you start to develop a pattern for new towns and adjust it to fit whatever island you're on.The main challenge you deal with later in the game is shipping. Between your islands and even between planets. Only some islands can produce specific resources, for example sand to make glass from a desert island. You'll have to manufacture and ship glass around to make sure every island has enough to build with. The shipping management makes this pretty easy, you can set it to make sure an island always has, say 40 glass in stock. As you start getting more peeps on your islands the overcrowding makes them less happy and you'll have to provide them with better stuff. The better crafting takes more ingredients. For example, the nice clothing requires cotton and wool which usually grow on different islands. So you will be shipping a bunch of raw materials to your tailor-factory island which then ships nice clothes back out to all your other islands.Keeping all your supply lines filled up can be a bit challenging, but luckily the game is very lenient on punishment. If your peeps are unhappy or run out of food, they don't die, they just work really slow. Once you make them happy, they'll start working fast again. Similarly with resources, if you destroy a building all its resources just fall on the ground and you can use them to build again. Not having a harsh punishment lets you focus on building out new islands while mostly ignoring your old ones.The story of the game is found in little pieces of diary entries from various points in the past. You discover them out of order so you may read a note about being trapped in the bunkers for years and then read a passage about the hints of the upcoming apocalypse that put them there. There isn't all that much story to be had, but I feel like it was well done.Overall I highly recommend this game. It scratches that perfect itch between simple enough to not be daunting and complex enough to find interesting optimizations.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Going to do a full review, but I'll put a checklist first so people looking to buy can get the gist of what they want.❤ Audience ❤☑ Beginner☑ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☐ Expert☼ Graphics ☼☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☑ Beautiful☐ Fantastic♬ Music ♬☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☐ Beautiful☑ Fantastic☠ Difficulty ☠☐ Easy☐ Average☑ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Hard☐ Unfair§ Bugs §☐ Bugs destroy the game☐ Lots of bugs☑ Few Bugs☐ You can use them for speedrun☐ Nothing encountered☯ Story ☯☑ There is none [there's a background to why you're doing what you're doing but that's it]☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☐ Fantastic⚔ Gameplay ⚔☑ Frustrating☐ Sleepy☐ Boring☑ Fun☐ Challenging۞ Game time / Length ۞☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☑ Few hours (10 - 20 hours) [it gets a little boring, read on]☑ Long (40-60 hours) [if you complete everything]☐ Very Long (61-100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)$ Price / Quality $☑ Full price☐ Wait for Sale☐ Don't buy☐ Refund it if you canI loved this game, I spent a lot of time really quickly playing.  If you look at others reviews you can see a pretty standard 20-40 hours of game-play. Once you get far enough into the game, about 15 hours if you play normally; You kind of plateau. You get invested in the "small fires" of the game, fixing happiness, avoiding space-whales and Minotaur's. But the farther you get from your home planet, the more excruciating it is to get supplies. It's not that obtaining supplies is hard, its that figuring out the perfect trade-route to get to different planets becomes a chore. The UI is a little funky when it comes to interplanetary trade too, it uses the same trade routes as the intercontinental trades which gets a little confusing.I've expressed my biggest problem, and honestly I don't know a solution. I would like if "auto" trade routes were truly auto, but you still have to specify what it needs to trade. If a continent or planet NEEDS tools, and I have a continent with an abundance, why not just have it traded automatically when set to auto?Like I said, I love the game, its a lot of fun at the beginning and middle, but near the end its just a chore to get anymore done. I would recommend this game, but at the same time I wouldn't. Its fun, but it gets old.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Nice soundtrack, fine graphics.  But unfortunately the game has only as much fun as you finish the tutorial, i.e in a single hour.What is too bad, lot of good ideas, automatic ship lanes that spread wares between settlements.  House vicinity bonus, fun level for peeps, etc.   But the overall mix doesn't cut it.  The pollution is FUBAR. And fiddling with the building placements gets tired in minutes.  You have to waste lot of space to roads and everything needs direct road access. What sounds like good puzzle/challenge on paper but sucks bigtime in the game.  Maybe if there was a "planning mode" that only checks the restrictions at the end, allowing to arrange and then draw the roads.  As the game allows demolish with full refund, you actually can reach the desired  results within the game rules, but only with suffering. For no reason.  I usually spend plenty of time at these kind of games but plan to drop this with just few hours, before even reparing the spaceship -- I clearly see the clicks to get it, but have no urge to actually carry out.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A logistics city builder in the vein of the Anno series with gorgeous graphics and its own little spin on things.You lead a weird little civilisation that seems to exist outside of any time, simultaneously populating your world with brick houses next to wooden warehouses just down the road from the airship port and the spaceship dock where your wooden barrel-like spaceships will be launched from in order to retrieve microchips from the planet where you're mining them from pre-apocalypse office buildings.There is a lot of very satisfying plate-spinning as you flip between your island cities on a growing number of planets, eventually searching for a way to deal with the cosmic horror of a whale that shows up to literally eat tiles off your planets, threatening to leave your planets a swiss-cheese of empty hexes.I absolutely loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: "Before We Leave is a non-violent city building game set in a cozy corner of the universe." Well, that is what the official blurb says, so let's go with that.As with all city builders, your job is to create a society, and help it grow, and expand. Your people are known as "Peeps", and they have spent generations underground, so their civilisation is lost, you will slowly help them grow, expand the settlements, discover new as well as lost ancient technologies and eventually even leave the planet and colonise new and wonderful places.Everything is very laid back, the mechanics of the game are very simple, the planet your play on is based on hexagonal tiles, each tile represents an area you can build on. You start off with everything very basic, and as you go along, you will find that you can research new ways to do things, everything from the way you build roads, to the buildings and so on.One of the things that makes Before We Leave stand out, is the look of the game, as I said you play on the whole planet which has kind of been shrunk down, you will start on small islands, create shipping routes to other islands, and eventually leave the planet and go to the next.You will start off playing with a pretty cool and detailed tutorial that will help teach you everything you could possibly need to know. It does this in steps, and at no point will you feel overwhelmed. My only gripe, and this is a small one, when you are first learning how to play through the tutorial, you may find yourself frustrated when it comes to placing certain buildings, that can only be placed in certain areas, for example, adjacent to a mining spot on a mountain, the tutorial tells you what you need to do, but until you have done it, you may not completely understand how to do it. Of course, once you figure it out, it is easy, but for a good ten minutes I was shouting at the screen at my obvious incompetence at placing a single building. Of course, I soon figured it out and felt stupid.As city building games go, this is pretty cool, it looks great, it sounds great, it has some original touches, it is easy to pick up and play, and things do get more complicated and detailed as you grow, that it keeps the challenge going.The GoodLooks great, easy to play and learn. Fun, easy going gameplay.The BadThe tutorial is great, but perhaps for stupid people like me there is one or two things that could have been better, but this really is me grasping at straws.OverallA Fun city builder, that fans of the genre will love.I score the game a solid 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Short-lived, unfinished and tedious.Once the visual appeal flushes off, you will never get back to the game. Game process is full of meaningless, tedious tasks (such as having to manually move resources between islands/planets). Game is literally empty once you've opened all the tech tree. Every other game is exactly the same; "random" islands/worlds are not random enough and do not alter gameplay in any way. Once you realize this - you're done with the game.Probably worth $5 or so on a sale to play 15-20 hours, but that's it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Starts off pretty fun, but after colonising a few islands the game devolves into a very poor and extremely tedious logistics simulator.  The pollution mechanic is also extremely poorly implemented. Put simply: industrial buildings produce pollution. If pollution gets bad enough, it causes the surrounding area to become covered in toxic sludge. Toxic tiles cannot be entered unless you build an airlock, which requires a fair amount of tools and metals.In other words, the regions most likely to become covered in toxic sludge are the same regions that produce the materials required to remove toxic sludge. Tiles that are covered with toxic sludge cannot be worked, which means you'd better have the necessary materials for building an airlock and decontaminator in storage, or you've softlocked yourself. And if you've made the mistake of placing your metals and tools warehouse near your industrial area- which is the natural, optimal place to put them at-  you wind up unable to get the materials required to construct the airlock which allows your workers to travel through toxic sludge, because the warehouse that stores them is inaccessible due to toxic sludge.A frustrating waste of time. It's a pity, because the underlying idea (colonising multiple planets and linking them all into a great supply chain) is brilliant, but the game itself is a little too tedious after a certain point.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Buggy late game. After multiple restarts and numerous troubleshooting attempts: late game trading just bugs out! At random ships will indefinitely sit idle at a port (sea, air, or space) and they will not load resources if you take manual control over them. Or ships will start having random resource numbers that go over their max load limit, e.g. 341/60, Or ships will not transport research between islands or planets which freezes your tech tree which keeps you from progressing further. Otherwise a good, chill, city-builder game—it just has a backbreaking, progress ending bug being an incredible flaw, to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Played a ton of this on EGS before buying it on Steam as well. Hands down the best colony sim/base builder game I've played. Not only does it onboard you really well with a well paced tutorial and helpful research tree, but the anxiety level is turned way down compared to other colony games. My favorite feature since I first played is the addition of Smart Shipping, where you can just identify what an island needs and all the trade vessels figure it out for themselves. It's such a relief from the trade routes of yore.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is the game I've been wanting for a while. I love 4X games, but find combat in these games uninteresting. I just want to explore, develop my civilization and finish up the tech trees. At it's root, that's what this game is; a 4X game without warfare.But it's so much more than that. The story line (humanity rising from the ashes) is well done, and the buildings are all cute and well designed. It's easy to tell what each building is and the fact the the world is a true globe makes moving around to your various islands and planets feel like you are really on a planet.  There are enough fiddly bits in the game to keep it entertaining (and make replays different enough) without making the game as complicated game as Civ VI or Stellaris. The graphics are excellent and scale well for older machines. My little Dell XPS laptop with integrated graphics handles the game great on low resolutions. I definitely recommend this game for fans of the genre. As a dad of three, my game time is limited, and love games that are complicated enough to feel challenging and interesting without requiring me to do homework before picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game.The progression is the best part. I felt like every step I make brings more depth and challenge, enough to make you invest a few more hours but not enough to make you upset. The pace was excellent.The gameplay is really fun overall. Supply chains are well thought of.I think there could be some QoL changes to the UI, especially around trading, that could make the game somewhat more enjoyable.If you are a hardcore fan of city builders, there is a lot of inventive mechanics here for you, and also many of the classical features of this kind of games...
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's unfortunately a dull game. I don't think all games need a direct antagonist or hostile opponent. It's commendable that Before We Leave chose to not have combat, especially in a genre which is dominated by fisticuffs and conquest. However, they've removed staple 4X mechanics and haven't replaced them with anything. This had lead to a game which feels incomplete. I'm building things, but.. why? My people are currently living in an underground shelter, there's an infinite amount of them inside the shelter, and they have no resource needs or consumption when they're underground. What is the narrative - or mechanical - reason for building on the surface?I wouldn't be upset about absent features if the core gameplay loop of Before We Leave was amazing, but it's basic as heck. All I'm doing is throwing down buildings as I unlock them, without regard for placement or synergy bonuses. There's nothing else to interact with in the game, and there's not enough meaningful decision making. Each resource has one building (or a combination of buildings) that increase production. If I want more of a resource, I build that building - usually anywhere - and now I have more of that resource over time. That's.. it. There's nothing else to this game. I could build a sprawling settlement with over 100 people, but it's functionally no different to a settlement with 4 or 5 people. More people makes it faster to get resources, however there's no reason to get resources faster (beyond boredom). There's no external pressures, no resource sinks, no AI factions, no wildlife (hostile or otherwise), no other players, no scripted events, no story, etc etc. Just place building, get resources, place new building, unlock tech, repeat. Sometimes I have to setup a supply line between multiple islands, but otherwise the core loop is unchanged. I don't think all resources were infinite, but they're plentiful enough to be effectively infinite. I had enough building supplies on my starting island to fully supply my other islands, and those new islands had their own supplies to tap into as well. There also seems to be no meaningful penalty for ignoring the citizen needs? Ignoring needs made people work slower, but as time is mechanically irrelevant in game it doesn't matter. I could build food and clothes for my people, or I could hit fast forward and wait a little bit. This is the more boring approach for sure (and one I actively tried to avoid), but there's no incentive or encouragement to do otherwise. I'm an hour in and I've seen almost everything the game seems to offer. I'm about two thirds through the tech tree, I've colonised multiple islands, and I've got a navy ferrying resources between the two. Every new tech is a building I plonk down somewhere, then forget about. I think I could have ignored this if any aspect of Before We Leave was amazing, but sadly it's all too basic. It doesn't do any individual aspect better than its peers, and it's certainly not greater than the sum of its parts. For island-hopping settlement shenanigans, the Anno series does everything better. For logistical supply chains, games like Factorio, or even Rimworld handle it better. Civilization has a better hex-based 4x gameplay loop. For combat-free settlement games, Banished or Frostpunk are significantly better. The plethora of Sierra-style city builders also offer a range of more interesting buildy games.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A citybuilding game similar to the Anno series in that you need to set up different interlinked colonies across multiple islands with different resources available that you need to deepen your production chains, with the goal of eventually leaving the planet and colonizing other planets.  Like Anno, your greatest resource is the amount of space you have to build your colony so you have to be efficient. My issue is that the gameplay loop is just increasing your population to take on more industrial jobs, then plop down a bunch of farms where you can to meet the needs of your growing population, increase your population to get the laborers needed to work those farms, add even more farms to feed those laborers, and repeat until you reach equilibrium then start over again. Eventually this combined with the dwindling options for locations to place new buildings leaves me exhausted.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: So, after 35 hours  I finished the tutorial!! And I must say, I absolutely loved this game. I can totally recommend it to anyone who likes strategy / builders.The reason the tutorial was so long is that it's just a guided playthrough the whole game, which even though works perfectly as a open-ended sandbox to just keep building and settling, also has an ultimate goal, if you prefer playing objective-oriented and bring the game to a sort of narrative ending.I find the basic building system both challenging and rewarding. Basically, every building must face a road and roads take themselves a tile, which means each placing is strategically important and your road layout to maximise  available tiles is one the most crucial and basic elements. Add to that, that you should try to remove as little forests as possible (because they reduce pollution, peeps like them and it's just cool to try to build and develop while remaining somewhat "green") and you really have a nice challenge.The second layer of the game is keeping those resources flowing between islands and planets, organising a global and system economy, which will depend on the conditions both of planets and islands, what resources they have available and what you can grow and produce there.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to efficiency manager 3000. I love resource management games. This one is just....very.... blah.There are parts that make it very relaxing and enjoyable. The aesthetic and music are 10/10. Its just that, once you get big enough, like 40 mins into your world, there comes two problems. One - it stops being world building and starts being efficiency manager. Like a tax auditor on a tropical beach. The second issue is...it just doesnt go anywhere. I played it as full as i could and got real far but...the only threat - challenge - danger - *issue* to wrestle with was just that - your peeps get not happy the bigger you get.Thats all. Good but, I just lost interest immediately. Buy it for the 10 steam sale but otherwise save your money
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Hello friends,Today i will review the game Before We Leave. This game is a strategy city builder. Spaces are limited on the places you can build stuff, so some spatial strategy is needed. Also, there are technologies to unlock to make the game easier. Be warned though, there are many challenges and you may encounter massive monsters from outer space. To most action adventure players, they may find this game too boring or too slow as it has a chill vibe in it.As this city builder comparing to other ones, this one focuses more on strategy of building in smaller spaces. Also, using boats and airships to logistics to transport between different locations, and even building rocket ships to ship between planets. Although not as as fully fleshed out like other city builder games, it has some neat technologies to unlock to use. Also, as i found it personally, the smalle islands are not able to get the resources on these islands efficiently as it is unpossible to farm resources on them. I even asked this question personally on the forum here on steam. You can find the link below:So far, nobody has answered my forum question. When they do, i will change this review to reflect this. Anyways, here is my PROs and CONs list: PROS:- Strategicly placed buildings is key to success in this city builder game.- Easy to understand, hard to master.- Pixel type graphics using hexagonal map pieces- Much of the game is very chill and slow, making it very relaxing.- Many technologies to unlock to make building easier and get new resources.- Different seeds of planets that add more variety of maps you can play on.- Watch out for pollution disasters and space whales!CONS:- Unable to farm resources efficiently from very small islands, thus it is impossible to get these.- The graphic and hexagonal style of maps not might be liked by everyone.- It is possible to build too many things on a new planet or island thus locking you out on building anymore on it. Best to use a previous save you made to avoid this issue.- The slowness of the game might be a turn off for people who like lots of action. This is not a action tittle. It is a strategic slow city builder game. Recommended game. If you like city builders, and have to use strategic building to build on small islands, then this is your game. Interesting enough, the developers of this game are making a direct sequel to the game called Beyond These Stars.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good for what it is, and has a few interesting mechanics like the automatic trading between cities and even planets. It doesn't redefine the genre, but it is good for what it is.I had intended to leave a Thumbs Up review, but I experienced several game-breaking bugs towards the end of the game (mostly pathfinding that broke, and would not reset even when some buildings were destroyed). This led to a Thumbs Down.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I can’t help but feel that this game is throwing some philosophical shade at its civilization/city building counterparts as its beginning usually comes at the end of every other game in the genre: with nuclear annihilation. Before We Leave, by developer Balancing Monkey Games and publisher Team17,  is a non-violent, tile based city builder that begins with little figures (called “peeps”) emerging from nuclear shelters to rebuild the land their ancestors once bombed to oblivion. It's a hopeful and optimistic premise for its genre (and for humanity by extension) as it’s focused on rising out of our human failures to build a better world. There is no colonizing other nations, rather, it's about rediscovering the land and knowledge we’ve once destroyed and taking care of that land now that we’ve got it again. In that vein, the game highlights the more peaceful gameplay loops of the genre, getting rid of all the violent stuff (like stealing worker units from your city states), and in its place, bringing to attention things like “global warming” and being stressed about the bad air quality as the main antagonist of the game. In all seriousness, this is a serene resource management/city builder where the player acts as an omnipotent figure who balances components like food, luxury items, pollution, and wood to build their civilization and keep the people in that civilization happy.Before We Leave is able to reap the benefits of real time strategy as it puts a docile spin on the genre; in other words, you do not have to worry about enemy players or other civilizations coming to steal resources or land from you. There are little external threats to the player’s civilization throughout the game, with the main challenge being properly allocating buildings and resources given a limited amount of space. This gives the player a constant sense of progression and agency regardless of their actual skill or understanding of the game. In part, this is due to the non-intrusive interface the game uses to deliver hints to new players. As per the nature of its genre, the game tends to feel open ended, leaving the player to take initiative to explore and expand their civilization. For many, this can make the experience feel aimless, especially without a concrete story, but for others, this is a welcomed challenge to build the best civilization they can in the least amount of time.One of the most distinctive parts of Before We Leave is the space travel where colonization goes further than what’s across the ocean. Exploration is interesting in general, usually accompanied with new tiles and circumstances that require the player to manage their resources with a different strategy. Exploring across the ocean will likely be one of the players first goals, then, getting to space, and eventually, exploring space and avoiding the space whales. Certainly, THE most distinctive part of the game is the space whales. I guess you’ll have to play this relaxing entry to find out what they do.  Something about this game’s mechanics just feels refreshing. Before We Leave progresses in real time, giving the game a vibrant and lively feeling as your peeps scurry about, building, resting, and playing music. It’s so easy to get attached to the little guys, each individually named and following realistic routines. Funny enough, the peeps are made the more endearing because of how sad their initial circumstances are: literally all they could make before you arrived were potato farms. As a consequence, it's easy to get attached to the main game play loop of building up luxuries, reducing pollution, and getting them off the potato only diet to keep them happy.In terms of story, Before We Leave does not have an actual plot, but not due to laziness or a lack of creativity; the game takes advantage of the tried and true premise of all civilization building games in order to keep the player immersed: survive, explore, and thrive. At first glance, the game seems simple, partly due to the limited actions a player can take to get started and learn the basics. However, each step seems to unlock a number of new steps, and the great depth of content keeps this mechanic in play for hours upon hours. In essence, Before We Leave is composed of mechanics to make the player feel satisfied and immersed through a simple yet effective strategy while continuously surprising them with encounters that break up the monotony of the player’s previously successful strategies (like… did I mention the space whales?).
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: "Before We Leave" is a city builder that, at first, looks to be a relaxing entry-level one, but quickly turns into a tedious and grindy test of your patience.This is the first city builder that I played that uses hexagonal tiles, and will most likely be the last one that I will ever play again because of it. Using hexagonal tiles didn't "feel good" for the majority of the game. It limits the amounts of different layouts you can have and waste a considerable amount of space. Coupled with the fact that you have to connect every building to your roads doesn't help as well. Why do I have to connect a road to every single building? Why?!Most building are occupying a single tile, with the exception of some special buildings (lift, warehouse, space port, etc.). While this makes planning their placement fairly easy, you never really have to adapt to any weird sizes.Some of the design decisions that went into the buildings still boggle my mind:Why does the warehouse need a second tile for its outdoor storage, when it's a WAREHOUSE?! Shouldn't there be enough space in the building itself? Why is there no single tile warehouse, like a shed?Why can't my peeps access the lift from the side? It's clearly accessible when looking at the model? Why can only one peep use the lift at a time?Why is there no staircase? Why do I have to rely on inefficient lifts for vertical movement?Why is there not upgraded version of the well? There's no way a small well is all I can build even after constructing apartment buildings.Why are there no conveyor belts? You're telling me my peeps never thought of conveyor belts even after build airships and space rockets?!Why do I need a "Decontaminator" for removing toxic sludge? Why can't peeps with protective suits clean that tile like they do normal polluted ones?Why can't I dismantle a space ship that landed on a planet? Have a good huge space ship sitting next to my apartment buildings for the rest of the game is not something I like.You have no control over which peep works at which building. So a peep living in Miami might start working in a mine in Ohio, and there is nothing you can do about it. This wouldn't be THAT big of a deal if the wouldn't need to go back home to sleep and eat.Everything has to be carried around by your peeps. There is (almost) no automated way for transportation. Conveyor belts? Nah, who needs those? Best I can do is get 'ol Ben with his lumberjack arms to carried it around for me.Pipes also don't exist in the game, so enjoy watching your peeps carried water to their houses when the well is only two tiles away.Using ships to transport wares between islands is convoluted and never quite worked for me. The game uses a "smart shipping" system, that relies on you setting the amount of a resource that needs to be on the island and the ships take/deliver those resources until the amount has been met.I would have much rather preferred a more flexible "take that much and deliver this much to there" approach, but maybe that way is preferred by other players. At some point I just gave up and manually shipped needed resources, as I was able to more accurately control the flow of resources.The pacing of this game is terrible. While your first planet might be set up fairly fast, every other one slows down the pace considerably; to an annoying degree. It takes forever to build up every production line again on the new planet, unless you want to import everything from your first planet. And most of the time you only colonize other planets for a single new resource, only to repeat that for all other planets in the solar system. Apart from maybe a new resource, there's nothing interesting to discovers. Because of that, it quickly becomes bothersome to have to go to yet another planet.It also doesn't help that a space whale randomly targets one of your planets to take a nice bite out of it, setting you back a couple of hours if you're unlucky.Having to find a specific research resource depending on the item you want to research not only slows the game down to an annoying amount, it's also not very interesting. There has been cases where I was missing maybe 5 blue research for an item I wanted to research, which forced me to colonize yet another planet. Why...The audio in "Before We Leave" is quite good. I enjoy the music and all the little sounds the buildings do when used or when you click on them.I especially like the jingle when the big thread is announcing it's presence.It might not be the most beautiful city builder, but it certainly is not ugly.With the exception of the peeps model, I like every single building and vehicle model in the game. They all fit together quite nicely.If you can deal with the slow pace of the game, the repetition that setting up all production on every planet entails, and the hexagonal tiles, you might find a relaxing city builder. I however, after playing my fair share of city builders, expected a bit more ... something. Challenges, good reasons to colonize other planets, more complex production lines and layout possibilities. Maybe the game is just not meant for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a really odd, yet delightful mix of a city-builder, a civilisation-sim, and a management-game. It is also almost deceptively easy to pick up, and you can in fact manage to complete a game without 100% knowing what you're doing. But then when you DO find out what you're doing, oh-ho-ho, there are so many things to help you make sure that you're running everything as efficiently as possible, and before you know of it, you're spending hours planning out how to keep your peeps at highest happiness so they work the fastest. The graphics are not super complex, but everything is nice and distinctive, and in a world where games sometimes has so much detail that it's hard to tell what you're supposed to interact with, BWL is a lovely breath of fresh air. And while there are game-speed buttons to speed up actions in-game, then leaving it at 1x speed actually turns it into something that can be safely left alone for 10-15 minutes at a time without anything crashing and burning. Also, there are giant space-whales. Buy it for the whales.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Escape dystopian reality and create your own version of it. Build your civilization as small as possible, or expand it to every corner of the continent. A continent not enough? Set sail to new continents with different climates. Leave the land virtually untouched, or expand to cover every corner. Run out of continents there, Alexander the Great? Ride a rocket into space, and show SpaceX how it's done! Somewhere along the way, you might feel like it's time for a break. At this point, you've played through the entire night and are now late for work. This is definitely a game that I recommend setting an alarm for a good time to quit or just to take breaks.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just landed on my second planet, and still in the "tutorial" (which is more like a special scenario, since it spans an entire game). But so far so good :) Very good, in fact. The main adjective people seem to use about it is "chill", and I'd agree (since outside threats play a minimal role), with the reservation that the player has plenty of  scope to screw things up themselves ;) But there are no timers ticking or barbarians at the gates, at least until well into the game. Plenty of complexity in terms of variety of structures and resources, but everything fits in a straightforward interface. For anybody else that's played a lot of civilization/citybuilders both large and small: I guess I'd have to say it has the sweet but simple graphics of Islanders (plus the adjacency bonuses), the complex transport challenges and "research as resource" design of Factorio (except we're dealing with roads, ships and rockets instead of conveyer belts), the demanding individual pawns of Rimworld (luckily not QUITE as crazy though), the everpresent ecological challenges of Frostpunk and Anno 2070, and the non-threatening gameplay of Slipways... where the main threat to success is your own poor design choices.What's unique about it, at least in my experience, is the iterative design where as you spread your people, first to new islands and then new planets... and more or less start fresh at every stop, with the same basic city planning and bootstrapping through the stages of resource production. You're not starting 100% fresh of course; you have the tech you've researched, and you can support your new colonies in terms of goods through trade with the old ones. But there are some things you'll want to be able to manufacture everywhere, so the early settlement process will start to feel very familiar. Personally though this doesn't bother me; the random terrain and resources provide different constraints every time, and anyway I have always enjoyed the early stages best in these games, where people's needs are simple and problems limited ;)Anyway, came to this late but highly recommend, especially to anybody who likes plenty of scope to build happy
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed playing BWL, it is a fun, relaxing, and pretty game. I am a city builder fan (Anno, Banished, etc) but not not so much a hexagonal fan, but I still liked the game play and its style. The sense of exploration and caring for your peeps is satisfying. I love the planet like sphere maps and discovering other planets to visit. I would recommend this game to city builder fans who like to try something uniquely similar.

_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: At the time writing this I have little over 10 hours in the game! You tell me what I end up getting to :) Check out this Let's Play for More Visual and Audio Experince!Before we leave is one the best games I have played in a long time for getting right into the game and understanding what to do. It's not because it's easy or simple. It's because of the amazing job they did with the tutorial system and explaining the basics of the game.Even if you decided to skip the tutorial the tooltips alone are in such detail even the icons within the tooltips can be hovered for even more detailed tooltips on what the icons mean... It's honestly one the better games I have seen in a long time for detailed information, but not in a way that in overwhelms you.Now the actual gameplay is a ton of fun... You start on a island with a bunker with your Peeps... Yes they call them Peeps and I so want to each some Yellow Marshmallow peeps right now! Anyways you start in a bunker after the world has gone through a major disaster. Your peeps emerge to start civilization all over again and work your way to bronze age (Iron) and steel and start colonizing other islands and expanding... Eventually you even expand into space and start colonizing multiple planets. Alone the way the more progress you make the more new "threats" or should we say challenges you face. No your base is not going magically vanish or ruin hours and hours of progress. I don't want to spoil it too much, but basically each thread has a small mechanic tied to it. To a big Feeding Elevator, to a Bright Spotlight to keep the challenges at bay.Honestly I scratched the surface of this game and I only start playing a day ago... This game has a ton of replayability already I can feel it. Just getting to a new Planet and starting a fresh colony I am already optizing it better then my first planet / island... Keep in mind that when you leave your island or planet their still 100% there running and you can go back and forth anytime in fact you start to set up intergalactic trade lines! Honestly this game is just plain and simple fun and amazing. There is even more content coming even a big roadmap for 2021 and a massive Patch coming Day 1 on Steam release called Content Update 7.I don't think you will regret buying this game if you enjoyed games like Factorio, Satisfactory, Dyson Sphere Program, etc.Oh and one last thing the peeps are not like most towns games. They get slower, etc if they are not happy and this happy meter is mostly dictated later due to massive populations... it's quite easy to always keep them happy and it does not "ruin" or "destroy" your work. If you played other town games where simulation bugs, etc held you back then don't worry at all with Before We Leave! Let me know if you bought the game and if this review helped you decide!Feel Free to Check out my Let's Play if you want to get a visual and audio experience of this game :)

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better games of the genre. One of the few games I've played til I got tired of it, then came back about a year later and played another 18 hours.This game is relaxing, but I came back to it almost a year later because I wanted to play something that made me feel good. There's something about the game that fills me with optimism and puts me in a good mood. I could go on and on about it.I've read that the devs are making a sequel and I'm stoked about that. To that end, here's what I'm hoping is improved in the next game:- Performance. Game is very hungry for the level of graphics. It runs great with most settings turned down and textures still on high, but everything on high made things choppy.- At some point, a good portion of the gameplay becomes about setting up new trade routes with new islands/planets. This is tedious. There should be more tooling to set this up for us...maybe something along the lines of a template I can start with at a new island. Or, make this mechanic simpler in general.- One of my favorite parts of the game is unlocking the tech tree. I would love to see this expanded upon.- I'd have so much more to say if the game were fresher in my head, but I at least wanted to drop by and leave a very strongly positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first: I've been a tester, both voluntarily and paid, and a moderator for the Before We Leave Discord for over a year now, so take that as you will. Having said that...I really love this game. It's calming, peaceful, as challenging as you would like it to be, with unique mechanics and endless replayability. I got interested in the game last year, before it was launched on Epic, and became a voluntary tester, and fell in love with it, and have played it every since, with 100+ hours on Epic. The art style and music, SO GOOD, and the whole just... feel of the game is spot on.It's come a long way since the early days. The devs are super lovely and responsive to feedback, positive and negative, and the community as a whole is just a really nice bunch of people to be around.If you want a unique, happy, peaceful yet challenging-in-places game, I thoroughly recommend it. Have fun, Peeps!

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I like city builders, and I like how nice and streamlined this is as a planet builder. Managing which hex tiles should have which buildings, or a path, or should remain a tree, and planning out the flow of the islands and their trade specialties is interesting. What I don't like is how much micromanaging trade takes. Look, I'm building a structure on planet 3 that needs resources from planet 1, because planet 1 has much more developed infrastructure and produces more and better stuff. Maybe for example the resource I need is on planet 1, island 2; The structure that needs it is on planet 3, Island 2. - In order to get that resource to reach the structure, you need to access the trade options for planet 1 island 2 and set the desired number of that resource to 0, or something less than the amount you have to get it to export. - That won't do it on its own, though. You also need to do the same to the trade options for Planet 1, island 3 (Because that island has the spaceport (only one per planet)). Set the desired amount to 0 or 1, I'm not sure. It's weird that you need to set the spaceport island to import a resource it doesn't need, because it's a middleman.- After that, you need to set the trade options for planet 3, island 1 (spaceport) to import that item with a desired amount of 0.- Finally, you can set planet 3, island 2's trade options to import that resource at the desired amount. God help you if that resource is a consumable like food or clothing. I've had to manually micromanage a shipment of bread from port to port to port because IT KEPT DISAPPEARING IN TRANSIT.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This game should be right up my alley, with its various production systems, but I can't say I enjoyed it at all.I think it's mostly that, despite having overlays and graphs, it's often difficult to tell even the basics of what's going on. Mostly it's because there's no way to tell how fast my peeps are consuming clothes.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. It strikes the perfect balance of logistic management and peaceful city builder. The setting and art is also really nice, and the music is FANTASTIC.A common complaint is in the happiness system, but it just isn't a thing that makes sense to complain about. Yes, peeps get a little sad when they have to work, yes they get sad when they walk through pollution, yes they get sad in dense urban environments. Don't you?? The whole point of the game is building a quaint city for your peeps to live in; give them some nice meals, scenic countryside, places to enjoy each other's company, time to stop and smell the flowers.Another complaint is that the game is marketed as non-violent, but it is definitely not. I understand the frustration some players must have gone through, and I definitely think this description needs to be changed. However, what is really intended by this claim is that you will NOT be competing against other players or player-like AIs, in the vein of the Anno games. I very much appreciate this, as while I loved building and expanding in Anno, the constant pressure to compete against other players made the game unenjoyable to me. No, this game is NOT NON-VIOLENT; you will struggle against and overcome various types of environmental hazards and creatures collectively called Guardians. However, this game is not COMPETITIVE; you will not be pressured into a PvP like system and you will be able to play at your own pace.Btw...For maximum fun (in my opinion) I suggest playing on half-sized resource deposits and the default 5 planets. And if you really like the idea of chasing resource deposits and exploiting and exhausting them (as I do), I also recommend double-cost buildings.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This was a nice surprise as I didn't expect as much depth as is there, given the cutesy graphics, low price and gentle non-violent angle.  But there's a lot of game there.  It's a hex-based simcity like on spherical planets with multiple planets.  The trade system to ferry goods between island and between planets is very smart and let you easily automate complex flow.  Roads are free, as is decontruction+recontruction, which is very freeing and let you adjust and refine your cities in a very satisfying way.  They kept the depth and complexity where it's fun, and removed a lot of the tedium in the genre.  Like many Unity games, it's a resource hog for what it is and my 3080 was sweating, but it played fine.  Great value for the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks nice, and I think it accomplishes what it sets out to, but I guess what it sets out to is meh. It's too restricting to have a sandbox builder vibe, it has (maybe) a bit more depth than what I expect a good mobile game would have, but there's really nothing fun or engaging about it. If I uninstall it, I will probably forget I ever played it.

_childDocuments_.review: So like some others have said, once you get your spaceship this game becomes...frustrating, not only do you have to micro manage shipping on one planet but then among Multiple planets! and while that doesn't seem very frustrating it is..cause it isn't done well in this game. It's a bit sad because the style and concepts are there for a great game but with such little build space and some really ridiculous constraints it just is not enjoyable for me, i can't relax and play this game because i get to a second planet then realise i basically have to funnel every resource from my first planet into this second one to get anywhere..and that takes FOREVER! like nah man.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. My only quip is that it can be hard to tell just how much of a resource you're producing - both island and planet-wide. I love the music and sound, the play-style, the art, and the giant space whales (as rude as they are). Fantastic job!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Its a mediocre game. I enjoyed parts of it and think it was worth playing, but I can see how the space limitation aspects could really turn some people off as you lose a lot of space to roads and the islands aren't that big. Mid to late game is actually pretty weak as there is very little motivation to go back and redesign and you just don't use much of the unlocked stuff. _childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Giving a recommendation, but there's definitely some flaws with the game that reveal themselves as you go.The biggest one is that if your people become unhappy, they work slower, but in order to make them happy you have to make better items or clean up pollution, which takes work. The result is a cycle of a failure. The more you try to combat unhappiness, the worse things are because less gets done which leads to things getting worse.The only surefire solution is to abandon that island of sad sacks, start over elsewhere, amount a bunch of high quality food or clothing, etc. on a different island and deliver them to unhappy island to give them a burst of happiness and attempt to get things back on track.You also end up with 4-5 islands per planet, and multiple planets so keeping track of all the depression going around across the galaxy is less fun and more tedious. As other reviews also mention, once you do 'beat' a game and get all the research and explore all the planets, there isn't much more reason to do it again.The final goal to complete the whale charmer is an expensive building and FIVE UPGRADES which is just insane. After I finally did that the whale also failed to be charmed because there was toxic sludge in a place I hadn't even explored. So I had to go and clean it up, which was amusing because the game kept sending whales that failed to be charmed for the entire time I was cleaning which was SO MANY WHALES that I got the achievement for surviving 20 whale attacks even though I didn't 'survive' them, they never attacked, just passed by to let me charm them.After doing the main game I started some of the scenarios but ultimately realized I was not enjoying gaming the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever wanted to micromanage the production, distribution, logistics, and basically the entire supply chain for an interplanetary society, this is the game for you! Before We Leave is a relaxing city building game where you help the Peeps rebuild civilization after a calamity. You must  explore and trade with other planets, grow and manage resources. The game is non-violent and charming, with a hexagonal grid system that adds strategy. It’s a game that will make you smile 😊 and feel good. If you like resource management games like Anno or Banished consider giving this gem your attention.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: First run with the tutorial. 3 hours later i feel it's a mess and I start a fresh game. 10 hours more and I'm still in the tutorial mode and the micro-managment is messing up with my brain as I have to keep in mind: where is resource X because I need it in the island 2 of planet 3, so I remember it's on island 4 of planet 1 but the landing pad is on the island 1, so then I pick a ship to pick the resource from the island 4, manually move it to the island 1, pick a starship to ship the item from planet 1 to planet 3 but the lander is on island 3 of planet 3 so i pick a boat to ship the resource from island 3 to the island 2.Are you confused reading this? That's what I feel when I have expanded on the third planet.Poor display of resources. As you start you think there are 3 main resources but no, there are a lot "hidden" on sub-menus, and every resource has a limited amount of storage depending on a multitude of cross-bonuses between buildings you have no idea how to summarize all so you start spamming warehouses but no, there's no space on the island...Is that so hard to put for example "10/52 wood" (meaning 10=stored amount; 52=max storage availability")?This game needs to get rid of all that micro-managment and it could be a 10/10.P.s.It is "its" not "it's". Grammar basics.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The game is overall a good game but I cannot recommend it because even on the easiest difficulty setting I find it virtually impossible to achieve a balance of peeps, resources, jobs and progressing through the game.I am always short on food and or drink, clothing or some other resource I can't keep enough in supply.Trying to have sufficient storage on each island is a joke, warehouses add very little in the grand scale of what production is needed and as a result I find has in my case made this unplayable due to not being able to progress past the first space landing colony.I ended up being able to settle most of the planet 2 on a custom game of a 4 planet system on easy and have now encountered the desert islands are the only ones that can grow orchards and wheat on planet 1 yet the severe space restriction for growing means I can't hope to keep a balance on resources for every island on both planets, never mind even trying to settle the rest of the solar system.What good does setting the game on easy do if it's just going to be difficult no matter what?Oh well, another game for the"never finish" pile.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun bigger city/planet building game.You have to manage pollution and happiness, but that really isn't very difficult.Space whales come by every once in awhile, and can be kind of annoying (they destroy a large area on a planet), but once you figure out how to keep them at bay, they aren't that difficult to manage either.Playing with the tutorial the first time through the game really helps understand the mechanics, and gives you some direction.  There's a lot of trading to manage, as most islands, and even some planets won't have all the resources you need to build every structure or farm/mine every type of resource.  Again, once you get enough airships/spaceships, this isn't difficult to manage either.  There's some other "guardians" on the planets that will make life difficult, but once you defeat them, they actually start helping you.This game definitely does a great job at balancing trading/colonizing/expanding and scratches that sim-city building itch.  I would highly recommend it for anyone looking at those types of games.  I've beat the main game, and enjoyed it thoroughly, and am about to embark on the new scenarios.I feel like people who are criticizing the "non-violent" part of the game are taking that term waaaay too literally.  Yes, there is conflict with the guardians, but you aren't building troops like in Starcraft or even like in the Civilization games to combat them.Also, there is a hidden history to discover in the game.  I don't want to spoil it, but it definitely gives this game a little bit of that extra something that makes it extra enjoyable!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: why do i need to explore the new planets with a boat when i've got spaceships in orbit?  why wont the peeps on the last planet solve their own desire for water?  why wont the red science load on to a transfer space ship?  why do the roads take up half the real estate?  why is lumber always ALWAYS running short?  why are there 36 unemployed peeps with 30 open positions?  why are the iron and stone mines so small if the islands are supposed to keep running while i move to the next planet?  what's all the junk in the ocean i can't salvage?i've stopped caring about answering these questions.  it's not a bad game and could have been a good one but it's just.... annoying.why do i have to write a review to leave a thumbs down review?  just take my word for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Biggest complaint about this game is that it fails on properly designing a shipping system. It is a game literally about colonizing all of the islands on the planet, moving onto the next planet, colonizing more islands via trade ships basically. But it fails on letting the player fully customize the trade route. Your options for the trade route are. You can manually select what port on the export island is used, but aside from that, you cant really manually select where the import island is. You can kinda tell it where by saying this island wants 20, that island wants 20, and this island also wants 20. But its extremely janky with multiple windows to go through essentially creates window hell, when it could just as easily be all compacted into a single window.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty good city builder which has you establish and manage multiple colonies, but isnt really the kind of game that would be good for repeated playthroughs.You start off on a single island on a planet, setting up your first city before you push out and colonise more islands to which opens up access to new resources and the technology to go with it. Eventually you'll move out into space and set up colonies and other planets and repeat the process. As you set up colonies the logistics of transporting resources to other islands and planets come into play. Each island will only contain certain resources. So for example you may only be able to grow certain crops or there may be no stone or metal but it may have electronics. So as you progress a good chunk of the game becomes trying to move resources around to where they are needed.After you set up a few colonies in space some giant space whales show up and start causing problems which means the mid to late game comes with the goal of mitigating and eventually stopping that threat. And to do that you have to set up more colonies and get access to more resources. This is where the game started to lose me a bit.Initially its a fun challenge of setting up and managing the different colonies but when you get to setting up colony number 10 the novelty starts to wear of a bit. As each time you establish a new colony you have to go through the same steps of setting up the basic necesseties like food, water and basic materials before trying to setup extracting the more advanced resources on that island, it starts to get a bit repetitive. At that point I just pushed for the end game goals as quickly as I could as I'd started to get tired of the main gameplay loop.This isnt really good for repeated playthroughs either as you have to follow a pretty linear path of progression in the main campaign. There are additional scenarios available, one of which I tried, and though there are slightly different goals I found I was still going through the same setup and establish colony then setup more colonies loop that the main game has, and at that point I'd had enough.Not to leave the review sounding too negative though, I still had fun with this game and think at least a single run through the main campaign is worthwhile. Once the logistics side of the game clicks it can be pretty satisfying to set up multi-planet production chains and theres additional challenge in juggling things like happiness and pollution as you expand your cities. It's also a pretty chilled game even when the space whales start showing up. Even if you only play it once it's pretty reasonably priced so I think its worth a try if you enjoy city building games.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Played a lot when it came out, I will pick it up again because of the wasteland update but a positive review is long overdue :DThis is a nice ressource management game, I really enjoyed the way you need to balance your ressources using various level of interstellar transportation.There is a endgame, however I also tried to have happy Peeps and luxurious planets, so it was a fun challenge.Also, quite a number of hidden bit of lore, which is always enjoyable.When I grew a bit tired of the normal mode, I went to try some Scenarios, but appart the Seeds one, they are quite hard!So yeah in the end, hours of fun for me, 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty to look at, the hex tile layout to build up the planet feels unique, and interesting weave of resource building, tech tree, balancing peep needs, pollution control and shipping routes. Very easy to get lost for hours and hours. The only thing I would change so far is to add an extra tab to the island management screen so you could compare warehouse capacity with warehouse contents with what settings are on shipping management. I ended up making a spreadsheet once I got to my third planet. And being to change the name of a building before it gets built so I could write on warehouses what they are intended to be for.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: An experience that matches the hollow and pre-planned planets you play on. The games makes to odd choice to punish making better buildings and more comfortable houses with unhappiness. Structures that protect them from total destruction makes them even more unhappy. But even before that the 'peeps' are hollow creatures. The generated quips only highlighting their total lack of persistent or meaningful existence. They will get sad, work less hard but does that even matter? The options for optimization are very limited, the logistics is cumbersome. There is no state of optimal to begin with. But perhaps a greater issue is that the experience doesn't scale with the game. You are expected to be as micro intensive on your first island as the last. Encouraging a approach where you make an island work somewhat and ever caring about it again. Which is how I played this game. Made it work somewhat but doesn't make me care about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the gameplay loop, though it is a bit basic. While the whole idea of launching from the planet to grow is nice, once you unlock all the things there isn't much endgame content or replayability aside from optimizing shipping lines, upgrading buildings, and just exploration/building cute settlements. My favorite thing was just the art style; it's a pretty game and I spent a decent amount of time just watching the peeps run around. I'm glad I tried it out, but at about 10 hours in, I feel like I've fully experienced what the game has to offer and probably won't play it more. It's great for casual play, youngish kids, or just people new to the genre. I don't have anything bad to say, but it also isn't amazing. Just a cute little laid-back city building game with a great art style.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The game is unique and fun with a neat progression from simple to more complex. Its a lot of fun to see the new biomes and islands make use of their natural resources and specialization.  The game is also pretty forgiving in that you can make mistakes and build in the wrong order, but it always will allow an "undo" with 100% refunds of materials when you break down buildings. There are some questionable design decisions, I think, with requiring certain buildings as arbitrary road blocks to expansion.  I feel like those should be done away with as the game progresses, rather than resetting to near 0 with every new planet.However, the reason its going to get a thumbs down from me is the random opposition you see from  certain creatures and buildings in the game.  These seem to serve no function other than to throw a wrench into the players plan.  This is fine, a little challenge is a good thing.  What isn't fine or a good thing are random end game states.  Its possible for the RNG to irreparably harm your play through to the point of non completion. Why would I want to continue playing this game when at any moment my entire game can be rendered unwinnable, and all of the planning time amount to nothing.  Absolutely indefinsible in my view and a reason I'd encourage all but the most hardcore or detailed players to steer clear.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I can see the appeal for other people but this feels way too repetitive and straight-up boring...Yes, it's a chill game, no actual threat really. But it lacks personality, I can construct stuff pretty easily and growth matters with the limited spots on the islands and such...but there is not much else for it. The way the stuff gets researched is kind of tedious, the more advanced, the more time it takes to unlock...even if you set to 4X speed. Will keep the game though because I like the design at least...
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, I dunno, I just didn't find it that compelling. The setting up of supply chains seems kind of tedious and the game isn't particularly attractive. There also doesn't really feel like much stakes, you can spend as long as you want setting everything up with no tension to get it done sooner, but there's too much stuff to build for me to stay engaged. It's not like you have any meaningful choices either because everything needs to be done in a certain order to make it work. I dunno, I just didn't like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I got this because it looked like a fun, simple city building/strategy game, too bad it is anything but fun and simple. It is one of those games where you have to build X, but before you can build X, you need Y, but to get Y, you need to have a certain number of A & B that get put together in Z, but to build Z, you need C & D, and so on and so forth, until you realize that you aren't having fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Playing along time near to the end of the game and you will get stuck. You have to reload an old save game to get going on.Example - at the end an isle with desert has any food option, It is necessary to import those - no problem with that. If the storage logistic does wrong - you will fail. Workers doesnt work without any food at the docks. No import of the necessary food takes place - so nothing happens anymore on this isle. An isle without any food option should always have a high priority of food by the devs. A normal player will not be aware of this decision to be stuck at an dead end.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Really disappointing title. I expected more engaging gameplay after watching the trailer and reading the description, but was severely disappointed.In the game there's a very generic "mobile" city builder experience, with a confusing UI, unbalanced resource management, oversized gameplay elements that actually make all available land very cramped (it's way too easy to block yourself and paint yourself into a corner due to the big tiles and roads needing their own tiles too), flat&boring soundscapes (I can't imagine how they won an award for that... the competition must have been terrible?), and nothing unique or special in progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This review will be brief: This game is highly addictive and amazingly made.No seriously, this is something I've always wanted to be made, where you work on your world and build it from the ground up, expand to other places, set up trading hubs and supply chains and then go beyond just the 'map'.So far on my save I have 6 colonized islands (about to colonize the seventh), two planets and I'm having to deal with heavy and quick automation on my second world while the homeworld is slowly burning its resources.There's a lot to do. It may look simple at first, but when you end up going for the second shore you're already thrust into thinking way ahead about what your goals are. Supply chains will get ever more complex, new resources are thrown in, and when the 'industrial revolution' begins you likely will end up having over 100 Peeps per island.The tech tree seems a bit sparse and limited, but it is a bit welcomed a change since it won't make you focus too much on it and instead have you focus on optimizing your worlds for supply and demand.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: pretty good, scratches the same itch as Civilization. it's satisfying to harvest the science on each island to expand your capabilities.the seed scenario is more fun than the main win condition because the main game gets ANNOYING in lategame. you basically need to harvest every single resource and manufacture every single product and funnel it to one island on one planet. pain in the neck. the seed scenario still requires you to explore and build without (imo) unnecessary micromanaging
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game at first but it quickly became tedious. The relaxing nature of the game was taken over by a sense of anxiety that I might have forgotten one item from a planet shipment causing everything to not work correctly or other work stop errors. I generally love logistic-based games but this one got so unnecessarily complicated so fast.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: City builders and colony sims are my bread and butter games, and I can easily spend hundreds of hours on a good one. This is not one of those good ones. I can not stand the hexagonal tiles on a small diameter globe this game uses. I want to be able to visualize my colony at a quick glance, and having to rotate the world to see it's entirety is was an instant turn off. Requiring every building be on the side of a road with hexagonal tiles severely cramps the colony layout. I prefer colony games that require more thought what buildings to build and when, and not on the exact placement of the roads. This is the first Steam game I have ever refunded.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin!! - This game is a pleasant surprise, that gives off 'Banished' vibes. It is extremely beautiful, with a great soundtrack. What seems quite simplistic to start, quickly turns into a very in-depth, thought out strategy. Buildings too close to other types can be a boon or a penalty - causing you to really think hard over your layout. Sail the open sea's and then explore distant worlds. This little gem has it all. For the cost - I have zero regrets in buying this game! I find myself wanting to just find that 'optimal build'. If you are looking for a game that has a relaxing vibe, I seriously suggest you give this one a go. Please Note: This is a non violent game (as it already mentions) - don't expect war scenario's or fighting.. It really isn't that type of game.TLDR:- Built huts, made smelter next to their homes - polluted my Peeps, they got mad at me. I'm sorry Peeps.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I'm struggling to say how much I'm enjoying this game - it is superb.Each time I think that I've reached the 'levelling off' point that you get in most management / city builder games there is a new development that changes the game-play - even if it is only temporary or localised changes they are well implemented and keep my interest going.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Its fun and kept me going for hours. Big plus for having a planet editor as well, custom worlds gives tremendous replayability. Just wish oceans were useful instead of just dead space, would add much more options for things to build. Custom buildings or mods would be sweet if that was a thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good, enjoyed the tutorial so far. It seems engaging, not addicted yet (of course by the time you read this my game time may say otherwise), but can see me giving this a chance.It reminds me of earlier versions of Civ without the violence and with a sort of Dyson Sphere Program feel about it. At the asking price probably worth a punt.----A few (game) hours later: I stand by the Civ+DSP description, it has DSPs chill ambience and the 'I need this for that to build this to build that' addictiveness, plus it has a lot of Civ style mechanics. I know it's sold as a 'casual game' but as someone who has many hundreds of Civ hours under my belt I'd say it's not too casual.  I agree with those who say there is little jeopardy, but actually much like Citties:Skylines the lack of jeopardy just adds to the chill. If you're looking for a low stress but non-trivial city builder then this is your game. As you may see my hours are starting to clock up. Will come back and review after a few more hours.7 hrs in : Yep it's a very chilled game, you don't really focus on win/lose so if you're looking for a competitive game this isn't for you. If you're looking for a relaxing resource management / logistics game then this is for you. And it is compelling, it has a just one more thing addictiveness about it and I am still thoroughly enjoying it. I suspect the downside maybe limited re-playability and game duration but that I have yet to see.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this more than most city builders because it's easier to manage. Resources don't have to be precisely balanced; once you set up a colony it can sustain itself and doesn't keep bothering you, just set it and forget it and focus on making progress instead of constantly having your attention drawn back to previous parts of your settlements collapsing.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. Having put many hours in it on gamepass, to my delight it was part of the humble monthly bundle. Not for all tastes. If you want another civ you arent getting that. But its a nice little city builder, time manager that is more for casuals.  I high;y recommend it for people who liked the old simulation games.
