_childDocuments_.review: Well-crafted builders are always a good time. Whether you are building single structures piece by piece, cities by block, or empires by province, the feeling of pride that you get looking at the glorious progression from potential to reality makes all of the meticulous planning and hair-pulling worth it. If the title in question brings new innovation to the genre, that only sweetens the deal further.Before We Leave isn’t Minecraft, it isn’t Cities: Skylines, and it definitely isn’t Crusader Kings, though it is another experience where your actions will shape the world around you in a unique and satisfying way. With enough elbow grease, you’ll find a way to supply what is needed to sustain a sprawling society built from the ground up as it stretches not only over oceans, but across worlds.If Fallout’s setting were a more pleasant and peaceful one, it might look something like Before We Leave. Remnants of an advanced civilization dot the landscape, but the world itself seems to have recovered from the catastrophe that befell it. You will start with nothing more than a small entrance to an underground shelter and it will be your task to settle the world above. The shelter is only a single tile, though it has a small batch of starting resources to start off with and a healthy population that will move into housing as you build it. It is your responsibility to take care of things from there though, as those training wheels soon become negligible and your peeps will have to find a way to sustain themselves for the long haul. New homes need to be built, agriculture and industry will need to take off, and you will be giving direction on which natural resources will be harvested and processed into increasingly complex goods.As your shelter empties its population and resources, you will be putting your infrastructure into place. Forests and mountains will provide the necessities of wood and stone for construction while ancient ruins will provide iron and research. Farms will feed your people and keep them at their most productive and as their numbers grow, they’ll begin to demand luxuries.Research is consumed by your library as you unlock increasingly advanced technologies that improve the efficiency of your colonies. New foods, goods, and resource extraction methods are all discovered on the technology tree. For example, though your people will mostly be satisfied on a diet of potatoes early on, they’ll demand a more robust diet including vegetables, fruit, and tea as you progress. In fact, you’ll even need to take those new crops and process them into new foods, like meals and smoothies, to satisfy the population that you’ve spoiled with luxuries. Occasionally you may even be surprised by a tech that adds a new system to the simulation entirely, like power stations or inter-continental shipping. Happiness is a necessity and you’ll be balancing your capabilities for meeting the needs of your peeps with their wants. New tech will allow you to process resources into more consumer-friendly goods that will encourage your population to be fat, dumb, and happy. As long as you manage to meet these goals, they’ll continue to put their all into expanding your ever-growing civilization.Ensuring that you have a satisfied population that’s large enough to operate as a workforce is not the only piece of the puzzle in Before We Leave. Building placement has the potential to drastically alter the overall efficiency of your varied businesses depending on what’s in their proximity. Homes, for example, have their housing capacity increased for each other home next to them, while their food and water storage capability will be boosted by being near farms and wells, respectively. On the other hand, pollution and gloom nearby will reduce their happiness, and you have plenty of industries that produce both of these in bushels. This system ensures you’ll spend plenty of time tactically placing buildings in ideal locations, not only fitting in with your logistical concerns, but also in maximizing the benefits and minimizing the detriments of whatever may be in their immediate environment.Logistical networks will grow as your settlements do and you need to hone them as close to perfection as possible. All buildings have to be connected to a road and your peeps take time to travel. The faster they can get from A to B, the more productive your society will be. As you might imagine, road placement is a major factor in building synergy as well, and planning ahead will save you the headache of expanding once the island is mostly settled later.Though roads are reliable overall and will more or less work as intended as long as two buildings are connected to the same one, the convenience of living on a single island is a short-lived one. You’ll need to end up establishing trade ships for delivering goods between your settlements, whether they’re on the same world or another. Though it’s certainly not the most overwhelming of logistical systems out there, there’s enough going on that you’ll be tailoring your routes to deliver needed products from one colony to the next frequently.Before We Leave is a solid hex-based entry in the city builder genre. It’s presentation is enjoyable and it’s easy enough to pick up while still remaining complex enough to entertain the more invested city builders among us. The required sense of pride in what you’ve built and that feeling that there’s always just one more thing you need to do before you save it up for the night is there and I found myself playing an hour or two over what I’d intended on several of my sessions. I recommend Before We Leave as a fun title to dive into for awhile that will entertain fans of the genre no matter where their depth preference lies, just don’t expect the depth of the most hardcore titles in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is actually pretty fun to play. The animations are colorful and the whole environment feels great. I really like the idea of humans rebuilding after a cataclysm. I've only played 20 hrs, but so far, it seems the biggest issue is simply not having enough space.The islands fill up quickly and eventually always become just a mess of buildings and roads. Trying to optimize routes is difficult with how little accessible space available. I understand that is part of the game, figuring out how best to place roads/buildings to allow for the smoothest goods transportation and providing scenery. However, the space available really requires you to cram a lot of stuff together. It would be great if there was at least an option to have the generated islands larger, thus allowing a more relaxed and open type of game instead of being so cramped all the time.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game!  A strategy builder game, with a casual and light hearted slant.  Some items can only be crafted or found on certain island types.  For example, you need fruit to build more forests, but not every island can support an orchard.  Set up your shipping and let the game automatically shift everything around via ships and shace ships.    Eventually, you'll be up against a hazardous force from deep space...but don't worry, even if everything goes wrong you won't suffer too greatly.I enjoyed the art, music, and light hearted nature of the game.  Once you beat the main game (which has procedural elements, and hence is replayable), there are also some scenarios that may interest you as well.I'd absolutely recommend this game to anyone that is looking for a casual and fun 4X-ish game!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, its a pretty solid game, clear gameplay goals, clear instruction, and its got a charming art style. Whats not to love? You control a civilisation of little dudes that make ♥♥♥♥ happen, you start at the basics, by which i mean, you start with just dudes and woodcutting, and eventually you research tech to a point where you're building space elevators to feed giant space whales that wanna wreck your whole freakin shop. 9/10 pretty solid.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a well-thought-out, well-executed game that was built to a particular vision, and it delivers on that vision well. I'd recommend it to those who like city-builders or colony games and are willing to (or prefer to!) do without combat; after all, that's what drew me in. What issues I have with the game aren't actual *flaws* so much as cases of its vision not being my vision; as a player, I'm not really in the game's target audience so much as adjacent to them. I've still clocked >30 hours of play, and I'll probably add one or two dozen more before I set it aside.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Played it for 81 minutes, didn't really find myself enjoying it.  Seems a little bland and baordgamey (and I love boardgames), without adding enough heart/interest.  The game seems to be relying on some sense of exploration, but everything is so small and cramped, and from the other reviews I read, it sounded like it doesn't change much as you play.I am sure some people would enjoy it, some interesting puzzling/efficiency elements here.  But I have way better options out there and in my library.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It is not a bad game - but not a good one, either. Fairly standard build-your-colony stuff that has a few nice moments, but lacks the "oh, this is cool" moments that make such games enjoyable.Building your colony is fairly straightforward. Then you have the usual management stuff where you need to balance everything so that you don't run out of this and have enough of that, etc. - when you colonise a new island or planet you have to be careful to not run out of vital resources or you can be stuck (especially on planets, stuck with no way of recovery!).You have your usual tech tree, spiced up slightly by several different research types, your manufacturing chains. It's all there, and it's all solidly made - it just doesn't have anything that makes me want to play this one instead of any of the others I already own. The "this is what sets it apart from the competition" thing is missing, and so it's fairly bland in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A neat city builder, with a emphasis on logistics and production optimization. You want to have a better system for meals for your peeps? Well better build some kitchens, but wait those kitchens produce unhappiness and pollution. So you produce some pollution cleaners and some markets to produce luxuries to counteract the negative effects of the kitchen, but now you need more people and thus more meals...you get the idea. The statements that this is a relaxing city-builder are a bit misleading in my opinion. This game focuses heavily on progression of tech and resources to advance the game, but the problem with that is you will end up polluting/overcrowding your world making people unhappy. The constant struggle to maintain progress while keeping those ungrateful peep bastards happy is not exactly relaxing. However, I do recommend this game if you like supply chain management and in-depth production chains. It is definitely satisfying when you get your production systems working just right, but be warned if you are like me you will find times when you are stressing.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: i thought this game would be way more relaxing than it actually is. between pollution, space whales, minotaurs, and population happiness, there are just constantly fires to put out. the silver lining here is that you don't have to manage supply routes at all, since all of it routes automatically (though you should still practice good zoninga nd manage your production and output)
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Does exactly what is says it is going to do and in a beautiful, yet still feature rich, way.The gameplay is full, while not overly complex. The interfaces are informative and efficient. There are some odd design metaphors, but they are easy to figure out.Don't come in thinking it is going to be a brutal struggle that you will need to play over and over to eek by. The gameplay is forgiving and low-stakes. Most of the time playing other 'survival' colony games (Banished, FrostPunk, Oxygen Not Included, all of which I love) I end up having to either do out-of-game research or lots of in-game experimentation to figure out a viable way to progress. Here, not so much. The only real risk is time. I hear other's complaints of repetition, I can see where they are coming from. There is a kind of pattern to expansion. I have been loving the game as things slowly escalate into different and more intricate connections and infrastructures.This is a breath of fresh air, exactly what I needed. Well developed, consistent, engaging. Love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This game was first marketed as a peaceful civ builder because you're not going to war or anything, and it's more about nurturing the environment than conquering. That really appealed to me, and I'm glad to say it stuck the landing.It's very cute and fun but that doesn't take away from the inherent complexity of these kinds of games, so it's rewarding to make advances and see your civilization flourish.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A solid, and very pretty, 3X strategy game. There's no "Extermination" so you're free to explore, expand, and exploit to your hearts content, starting on a single continent, expanding to additional continents and setting up trade routes between them, before building spaceships and colonising nearby planets to repeat the process.It's a relaxing game in most places, and constructing all the necessary buildings for a happy and productive society can be almost puzzle-game worthy as you try to fit everything in, keep your residents happy, and keep pollution away from them. I'm still trying to get to grips with the happiness and pollution systems, where I'm still at the stage of the game telling me X is wrong, but I'm not familiar enough to know how to fix it, which I'm hoping will come with more play time (and more research; the tech tree itself is a nice push to expand as you need to gather the resources for research from increasingly far flung places).The developers appear to be engaged and adding additional content, so I have high hopes for the future of the game; what I've seen of it so far definitely puts it on the recommended list though.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The idea is great, I love city builders and I dig the cute graphics.The main issue is the game getting repetitive after a few hours.Exploration is dull and it's basically just clicking around with your ship.Each island/planet feels very similar up to minor differences.Resource management in this game is tedious.This game is not for me.I picked this up few months ago, played for a few hours and never felt like going back to it. I guess it's just isn't fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I actually enjoyed this game way more than expected, and I expected to really like it. Before I knew it, it had been eleven hours, and I didn't regret anything. I'm usually a cozy gamer but I have a weakness for management games... and this is kinda the best of both worlds? Your peeps are SO CUTE and I loved making sure they had everything they needed to be happy lol. I did have to restart once when things got a little.... out of control... but, honestly, that's on me, and part of the chaotic fun of management games. I really recommend trying this game if you even kinda enjoy resource management/base building type games, or cozy games, and ESPECIALLY both. okay, bye <3
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: If you like city builders, then this is an awesome game. It's a very relaxing game, but it keeps you on your toes at the same time. The game is really good at adding layers of complexity just when you think you've got your current situation covered.I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes city builders!There is a story line in this game and it's a sci-fi themed city builder!You wouldn't play this game for the story, but the fact that there is somewhat of a story makes this even better.I haven't finished one game yet (still playing the tutorial after 16 hours) but I am letting the game take me through the works.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't expect this game to take up so much of my time. Had fun doing resource planning and managing trade. It was pretty chill.You don't need to do things so fast, just slow down your time. Your peeps won't die from having zero potatoes on the island. Just make sure each planet is self sufficient in all resources except the few end-game resources which are only available on some planets since space shipping is slow. It ain't that hard. Nice background music and cute sound effects.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I find the logistics system incredibly tedious and annoying.I have no idea what each island is producing, or needing or bottlenecking on.When I got to other planets I just couldnt be bothered to set up interplanetary trade, and then inter island trade between the new planet's islands. I literally just quit the game there and then.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I really should like a cute nonviolent city builder game, but this one just didn't do it for me. It feels fiddly: trying to find an optimal placement of roads, making sure you get exactly the right resources in the right order to build what you need, constantly having to micromanage shipping between islands... I just didn't enjoy the core gameplay enough to want to keep going.

_childDocuments_.review: I would only recommend this one on sale. Tried playing the tutorial all the way through to the end game, and it was fun for a while, but the game just wasn't holding my interest. There are good things like decent artwork, informative overlays, and an interesting logistics system, but once you figure out the basics the game starts to feel repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: I love city builder games and Before We Leave scratches that itch very nicely.There's a good balance of complexity and simple optimization problems. Your first colony won't take long to get into a pretty productive equilibrium -- but once you start settling other continents (and then other planets) moving resources around becomes a bigger focus. Resource scarcity will force you to expand, and things can go south for your little towns pretty quick, so be prepared to accept a little failure on your way up.Definitely take a minute to appreciate the artwork, it's very atmospheric!

_childDocuments_.review: A hidden gem and probably one of the better games I've purchased recently, and one of the ones that feels like a great value for the cost vs playtime.The game itself is an "Anno" style game with the addition of additional planets instead of just islands. It does reduce a lot of the mircomanagement of this style of game, but at the cost of feeling a bit redundant by the time you've colonized your 5th or 6th planet in a system, but that's ok - it's easy to build a small colony strip that planet of resources and send them back to the planet you care about without needing to build a giant fully functional city each time.It also runs great on my old computer (medium settings), and I've had no issues and no performance lags even as I hop between planets and islands.

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is the kind of civilization builder I can get behind because it favors a fairly simple and non-violent approach to city management. Also, because it reminds me of the greatest (and most accessible) PC strategy series of all time, Civilization. While I certainly like the idea of Sim City and the Anno series, they make budgeting and infrastructure demands that I’m never prepared for. Were I am actual city planner, I’d be hiding under my desk and crying a lot. Civilization is a much more relaxed experience because it removes the intricacies of city management in favor of territorial expansion and diplomacy (with a side helping of optional global thermonuclear warfare). Before We Leave, an Epic Game Store exclusive from developers Balancing Monkey Games, takes an unconventional and fun approach to civilization management and expansion that I found enjoyable and relaxing.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to echo many of the other negative reviews. At first I thought the game was super cute. It's a very relaxing game in the early hours, when you're just trying to set up an efficient system to gather resources, and the game is very forgiving even of sub-optimal city planners like myself. But the game pretty quickly seems to spiral out of control. Within about the first hour you're required to leave your starting island and start exploring others, which requires essentially starting over. This second island, at least on all of my procedurally generated worlds, often lacks even basic resources, and severely limits your fertile growing space. You could remedy this by creating a shipping lane from your first island -- except that in the game's current state, the ship sometimes just disappears never to be seen again. If you're unlucky enough to have this occur too soon after colonizing your second island, you're basically stuck and have to reload a previous autosave.  It's a super cute little game, but I can't recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: As if "Myst" and "Anno" had a lovechild... an entertaining and low key fun game. No fighting and you can even be "vegan" and not have any animal exploitation. You will have pollution but you can go "green" in your energy after you progress. A combination of research and exploration is required to progress. Some folks have made negative comments about the smart shipping. You can avoid these problems by only using thesmart shipping to send food,  water, and tools and building a small fleet of ships for the other resources you will needin bulk.Some tips in no specific order:1. Build lots of warehouses. You will want to have room for every resource in the game. 'trust me'2. Use the cleaners to keep pollution down or else... (spoiler)3. Expand your main port when you get that technology. You will thank me later.4. Research the submarine! You need it to get the goodies hiding in sunken wrecks. 5. After you upgrade your main shipwright, make sure to have an un-upgraded one to make the smaller vessels.6. Use your upgraded transports to load resources that have not been mined/produced. They will wait to get filled up.7. Unlike other games, roads are free. Where they make sense, use them.8. Spoiler... When you get to another planet, build what you need to exploit the local resources. Don't try to turn it intoa paradise. 9. Always send the "tech" (which is a game resource like water) to a central location, preferably the home planet.10. Surprise - there is an in-game "short story" about the events leading up to the game start. You will get it in pieces and out of sequence as you explore... see #4 above.********************** to the devs if you are still listening? ***************************A. The whole "minotaur" thing seems to be a waste of time. Is there a point to it?B. The "outermost" planet achievement does not seem to work, did I miss something?---- ok i found another planet number 5 that is now "outermost"-------- ok done!

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a hexagon grid based city builder. You are tasked with colonising new islands on a planet until you do what brought doom to earth in the first place, mine everything it has to offer and then move on to the next planet to destroy.Steam Curator Page:+ Great music+ Ultrawide works perfectly+ Interesting mechanics+ Grid works well+ Extensive difficulty customisation+ Thought provoking- Trading mechanics could be better- Locked at 60FPSThere are only a handful of things that I found to criticise about this game. The lack of framerate control (locked at 60FPS) and the somewhat confusing at first trading menu. Eventually you get used to it however.The gameplay is simple. Every building has to be attached to a road. If there are roads, your minions move a lot faster than if there were not any. Specific resource buildings require to be attached to the resource they are designed to mine as well as a road. You must find the balance between resident numbers, food and resource production. Some islands cannot produce certain resources so you are obligated to utilise the trading features in order to move resources around as necessary. The goal is to colonise all of the islands and eventually repair the shuttle to migrate onto a new planet where it is rinse and repeat.I am not usually too keen on grid based city builders but this one caught my attention immediately. The graphics are enjoyable, the performance is great, albeit locked at 60fps for now, the feature set is extensive, and the overall structure of the game is put together very nicely.#gameplay #citybuilder #reviews

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so I've now spent about just under 14 hours on this game at time of writing and I feel that I have an good enough understanding of problems with the game to write a review though I will state firstly that what I consider this game to be is a Puzzle City Builder with Eco management and my experience of these games are very limited and I have only been playing through the tutorial scenario this entire time. (I expect it to take another 10 hours at least probably to finish that which will probably be the end of the game, but it has different scenarios)Now then I do actually recommend this game, at a discount only, why? It has some serious issues which the Devs have appeared to ignored from looking at other reviews and from my own personal experience the biggest of which is that my 2080 TI GPU's 3D capacity was getting maxed by the game due to a setting called "atmosphere" being turned on which when turned off and seeing no graphical change I noticed that the 3D usage went from 100% nearly constantly to around the 30's%. This issue has been reported in reviews of many other users with them also saying it affects CPU's temperatures, I can't verify that as I can't see mine actively currently but with the effect one setting which has no graphical change causes on my GPU's usage....I wouldn't be surprised. This is half the reason why I can't recommend the game at full price since it could destroy your hardware and the Dev's have seemingly ignored this from what I can see.Moving on though the other problems I have is with how the gameplay is of the game which I feel are mainly a lack of information and examples of how to use buildings your given access to if not that they are too limited in their area of effects and thus in my mind appear to be useless. For example there is a building that improves production and extraction buildings....now would you include a farm building as part of this especially when there is no building catagory/tab which states production buildings with it's tool-tip? Apparently the game thinks not and instead has production buildings be what refine or use raw materials. Now next this improvement building has to be touching the other hex of the building you want to improve which as you need a road connecting to all of these means that you must decide to make a singular one of these buildings for the one you wish to improve around this resource hex or sacrifice one to have the improvement reach two of them for an small increase in production that does not make up the lose. So the improvement building for extraction and production are largely useless since you'd have to sacrifice a lot of space for them to provide too small of a benefit in my view since I find my bottlenecks to not be in the production but the extraction/farming buildings (except for the marketplace). This also goes for various other buildings that appear to be useful until you realise that they're range is just the touching hex's which if your trying to boost other hex, like housing boosting farms, you have no extra space for these to be fitted in which resulted in myself avoiding them when I realised. But that's not the worst bit, happiness buildings are.Building that are meant to increase happiness like the fountain which seem amazing since they give +3, same with forests and keeping them around, until you realise how short that buff that they give lasts and once again their range. Because once I saw, I've only decided to go with smoothies and meals ever since to buff/offset happiness as the fountain's buff lasts on one speed a few seconds after the Peeps walk by it which if they're heading to their job or somewhere which means that they won't be leaving soon, it's useless. It's useless if you even place the fountain on a hex touching their workplace since it only activates when they go past it via the street, being beside it somehow gives nothing. The forest buff last a bit longer but it didn't seem to last even 30 seconds which isn't long enough to have the peeps pass by again unless they are transporting goods, those peeps are my happiest peeps since they aren't sitting in a gloomy forge with pollution...so yeah useless.....But don't cut down all your forests as your woodcutters do need forests to cut down to give wood, forests only give them a storage buff which is useless if you've got a warehouse allocated for wood.Anyway back to why smoothies and meals are what I decide to keep to....their buffs last so much longer from what I can tell and thus they make an actual difference in how happy my peeps are and are the most cost effective once you upgrade their production buildings. This is unlike the other two happiness products which give good amounts but cost a ton of work making them impossible to use, jewellery produces so little and take up 3 hexs compared to 2 in total for a smoothie, meanwhile cotton to make fabric and then clothing is even more alone since you get so little cotton per farm tile.Now I have more to say but I feel like I am running low on characters so I'll say this next two things to end this....the game gives a lot of hand-holding and information about the basics at the start of the tutorial before it leaves you alone and then expect you to look at all the little tool-tip buff/debuffs each building can have or give while not giving you an guide or information book for you to look into for if you want to find out more information instead of just getting on with the game, why? I also must point out that in the tutorial I have noticed that as long as I never produce a gadget I never trigger the whales to start to appear and thus only have had to deal with managing my own peeps which I feel has been a big enough fight an annoyance that I don't want to now let the whales appear, as I want to completely rebuild my setups on multiple island but I wonder what else will come along that will mean I should rebuild all over again and then need to deal with no way to deal with overpopulation once again.....the game was fun before the whales, now it's a grind, a time grind.The music soundtrack and how it's done is unique and awesome, I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for February 2022.   If you are interested in the game and it's before March 1st, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A post-apocalyptic city builder focuses on logistics. Before We leave reminds me of Cities Skylines, it’s a game about building and managing a civilization rather than trying to beat enemies.  According to multiple sources, there is no combat, even though some monsters are listed in the difficulty settings.  The core of the game is laying out your islands for your people to live on, and then letting them expand to other islands, and eventually worlds.  Beyond that, players mostly will deal with managing trade routes.  If island A has green technology, and island B has red technology, ships can transport these goods in either direction or both.  Before We Leave allows the player to move on from Islands fully rather than micromanage it.  I have played this game for multiple hours to cover it for Game Pass, and the only times I returned to the previous islands was to maximize output or to set new trading routes, which is a relief. Pick this up if you like a casual city builder.  Some people might want more challenges, and there are harder and easier difficulties. Players can also just sit back and enjoy building a civilization that they choose to, whether it is optimal or not.   I enjoyed my time with this one and am very glad I now own the game on Steam. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect to like this game as much as I did, but I ended up binging some 9hrs straight in one session and definitely felt the "just one more turn" vibe you get from CIV games.The economic systems are fairly basic and logical, but the sense of progressions is great. Even though you are effectively doing the same stuff, each new planet you colonize feels "fresh." My first one was just chaos trying to figure out what is going on. My 2nd one was a more strategic approcah where I could plan things out. The 3rd one I skipped several chains of development and went straight for the end-game tech by importing all materials from my first two planets (a really cool "wow my empire is a powerhouse vibe") and fourth one was peak tech and engineering, with clean energy, irrigated fields, brick roads and tall apartmnets. A really cool vibe.The game has some smaller issues, mainly when it comes to laying out and keep track of cross island and cross planet supply chains (if something breaks, it's a tedious process of checking every single "step" across multiple planets and islands to figure out what broke), and I was never entirely clear what I needed to do to keep my peeps happy (I know I need clothes and fancy foods but how much? can I trade one for the other? is spamming fountains and musicians enough?) And I've seen a lot of people complain about roads taking up tiles, but I actually enjoyed this aspect - since a lot of islands have limited green fields, it adds a bit of extra spatial puzzle to planning out your cities and becomes even more interesting in the HOA scenario where houses need to next to place of work. I enjoyed planning out my cities around the roads, but YMMV.All in all, I greatily enjoyed loosing an entire week of nights to this game and I'm surprised the reviews aren't higher.

_childDocuments_.review: Really, This game is very well made.I Played it once a couple of years ago on another account and now that I'm playing it again I can see that the developers really care about this game.First of all, This is a (What I like to call) Logistics Game. The type of game where you need to use your brain to make things work, optimize the way that things are done and organize your setup to make it at least understandable like Rimworld or oxygen not included. If you don't like the kind of games I mentioned, this one is not for you.Before we leave is very relaxing and cute. The planets and the World feel so small yet full of content to explore that you can associate this aspect with the one Outer Wilds had.The story is pretty cool (even though its understanding is not necessary for the gameplay), and the devs are making the game better each year (even though slightly).The WasterLand Update, for instance, brought a lot of new little things that made the gameplay cooler and easier to comprehend and I just loved the work that the devs did.Overall, for the game's price, you should at least give it a try if you enjoy games similar to Rimworld, Oxygen not Included, or even Cities skyline (Because of the "city management" category).

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches my non-violent city builder itch. I recommend it. Very chill, much build and rebuild. Nice steady learning curve, pretty straightforward resource management, and a space management aspect that focuses on limited tiles and road access.But be aware there are threads of development hanging out that haven't been tied off yet. At this stage, you can produce some things (like Wool and Salt) for which there are no evident uses and which can fill up storage space. The gameplay that exists is substantial, fun, and functional, but there's obviously more gameplay planned. Or, perhaps I'm wrong about this and it's merely the very thin documentation on the wiki that prevents me from understanding the use of the end of some production chains.But even with these minor problems, the game is entertaining enough to seize my attention as firmly as "just one more turn" Civilization. It's a slick experience and makes the happy brain chemicals.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking forward to this game as I've played other's similar (Banished, Kingdoms and Castles) and thought it would be a nice change to purely build and develop a colony. In reality it's quite boring. Once you have finished with one island you discover and colonise the next land. The new islands have further research and different climates but that's as much as it differs. Each island needs to be colonised exactly the same as the first one. It's very much rinse and repeat. It didn't take long for me to exhaust the research on 2 islands and I was moving on to my third and thinking I don't want to do all of this again.. The game overall isn't very difficult, food and resources are easy to manage and trade links with further islands makes this even easier. The game lacks in micro-management, workers don't need to be assigned they just figure it out on their own, there's no disease, no one ages/dies, forests & natural resources don't exhaust. The game needs to be fleshed out with some RNG in my opinion to make it enjoyable. For the price point, wait for a 50-75% steam sale if you fancy giving it ago, otherwise don't bother.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game... the graphics are really cute and the game has a charm all of its own and implements creative ideas. It's fun until the point where everything gets repetitive and you build colonies island by island and planet by planet according to the same scheme. At some point you just lose track and feel a bit helpless and it's nicer to start a new island than to optimise the old one. Every island also looks super similar, because you always have to build the same buildings. On top of that, you're constantly forced to optimise the space on the narrow islands. The transport routes and the trading system are very exhausting. For this reason, I have lost interest in the whole game. Nevertheless, praise to the game developers, I would like to see the game developed further!A few Ideas:- terraforming to expand or even unite the islands - or just bigger islands.- citizen satisfaction could be a resource for terraforming- expeditions to distant planets not to colonise them but to find technology- change the annoying sound of the minotaur- the inclusion of greek mythology demystifies the game - maybe maya or alien technology would spark more curiosity.- longer build-up time per island and planet before you move on to the next one.- simpler trading system- cows should definitely produce more pollution!- improve the overview of resources- a challenge could be: to equip rockets with new engines/technologies before the planet's resources run out- in any case, a more concrete objective must be pursued- the technology tree could be more strategic and include decisions instead of researching everything one after the other.- why not let the player decide whether to rob the planet, poison it and move on to the next one. (to return later with new technology to repair and colonise it again. :D)

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a deceptively cute but grind-y colonization game. It's a non-violent sibling to the Civilization series. This game sold me by its small, charming village communities with warm colors and soft tones combined with resource management. Like many of it's kind, this game's primary objective is to EXPAND. The charm was short-lived because expansion happens so quickly. As I expanded past my initial island and onto other land masses — which requires ships and trade lines — I started to get stressed. It quickly became overwhelming and unmanageable, and the cute visuals, cozy color palette, and calm music couldn't overcome that. The pressure to build, grow, expand, colonize (but don't pollute and make sure the people are happy!) is ever-present and impossible to ignore. This is basically a macro-simulation of the world we currently live in and that's not how I particularly want to spend my free time. I wouldn't recommend this game to folks who want a slow-paced, leisurely colony game.

_childDocuments_.review: Some years ago, I had a thought dwelling upon Sid Meier’s Civilization. Since the last three installments have switched to a hexagon tile based map format, in the next game, they could raise it a step further, and put its maps on a *proper sphere* tiled with hexagons (plus twelve evenly spaced pentagons, to make it actually work). Earth is kind of a sphere, and not a weird looping cylinder, and these games like to take place on what is basically Earth after pressing the 🔀 shuffle button, so why not?Then I found this game while scrolling through the Store. I see the images on its page, and my mind harkens back to that old thought. I haven’t ever played a game set on a hexagon sphere (No, Rimworld doesn’t count, because it barely does anything with its hex-sphere). To be honest, this is literally the only reason I bought this game.What is this game? Well, it’s not “Sid Meier’s Civ on a hexagon sphere”. That much is obvious. But what it is is quite charming – A simplistic city-builder in which smart land use is paramount. The whole “hex sphere” thing isn’t just a random gimmick, but a foundation upon which the whole rest of the game is built upon - literally. Each island is a puzzle of optimization: How do you get the most [X] out of this finite space? The islands seem to be just the right size for this question - Big enough that you have a lot of freedom to do with them as you wish, but small enough that you'll find yourself locked in after building all the basic, self-sufficient supply chains, and find yourself wanting when trying to add more facilities.Take roads, for example: Roads are useless buildings by themselves, and do nothing good for anyone. However, you need roads to connect all your other buildings to. How do you maximize the ratio of not-roads to roads in [X] particular geography? Trees are another example: They're dispersed randomly when you find each new island, sometimes in inconvenient places. You can demolish them if you want, but trees existing makes peeps happy, and it's not easy to grow them back. Do you just mow down the entire forest when you first land, build around & work with nature, or some mixture of the two?Some of these questions are offset or even removed outright as you advance in technology, but as you do so, new ones often take their place. How to move goods around a planet to make the best end-game consumer goods? How to organize cleaners & polluting buildings? What to even do with all these alchemical crystals?This isn't a perfect game by any means, of course. I can name plenty of flaws I've encountered: For example, I wish you could place bridges over certain "low-lying" buildings, like woodcutters & sand mines. It would be really neat to be able to see my other planets & spaceships in the background while zoomed out in the planet view. And, they could have done a much better job of hiding the existence of the [FCNPR JUNYRF] as a surprise / spoiler, rather than plastering them all over the title screen, store page, and "new game" settings. That said, given that most of these are really petty complaints, I think that alone is a good indication that this is a pretty good game. A solid 8.5/10, in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: You must dig your way to the surface before you can reach your way to the stars.If you want to see gameplay and watch my first impressions as they happened, click on my video. Before We Leave is an open city-builder, a peaceful game of exploration and resource management that sets itself apart with its graphical style (featuring a spherical world) and interplanetary civilization. Relax to soothing music while your peeps (yes, they're called peeps) run about, avoid hungry space whales, and do everything they can to prevent the reinvention of the microwave. ... okay, I made that last part up.Control has a few issues. Every building must connect to a road (standard for the genre), and it must be oriented towards a road. There's no way to re-orient a building without tearing it down, and you awkwardly hold the mouse towards whichever side of the hex you want it to face. It's not as intuitive as it should be, and it led to me reloading after settling a new island and having no way to actually colonizing the island. (My road was facing a dead end instead of inland.) Trade routes are clunky to set up. Hotkeys don't always work, and when they do they're a bit unintuitive because they're all numbered. You press the number of which type of building you want, then the numbered building within that type.Before We Leave's art style has captured me and is keeping me playing. City builders can often be a "pick your flavor" genre, and although Before We Leave is no different in this regard, its art style lets it stand out amid the genre. Beyond that, it's a simple question of if you want to manage a set of planets. Well, do you?

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a hex based city/planet building game that offers nice graphic elements and gaming experience.I was initially attracted to this game because of the hex element of the game, it gave me tabletop gaming vibes, which I have an inclination to like because I collect and play board games regularly.  Not to mention the post apocalyptic theme of emerging from the ground. Hits a lot of nails on the head with the theme and design department. The game play is fun and as I suspected since you are using hexes , you may get buffs on your touching edges on the buildings you play. For example putting houses close together may give you more slots for inhabitants (or peeps as the game calls them) of your town. There is a skill tree that makes buildings soft locked in gradual layers depending on your progression in the tree. I am a fan of skill and progression trees, I feel like it's often the beating heart of sandbox games like this. I felt like the progression was a little fast at first and then hit a wall where it became so apparent. Its key to build your city and not rush it. There is a balance to the flow of the game and the tutorial does a great job getting you into the grooves and progressions that can lead to success.Graphically your hexes are larger in size on a planet that your view derives from. I think it has a very ideal and good design. The peeps running around are nice to watch as they are automatically doing jobs and tasks that you have put into your city. The spherical shape of the planet and map make the growth and expansion of your city rather attractive to watch progress. This game looked great on all settings and more than expected settings in the menu. This is a very well polished game. The idea of this game was very indicative of many things we have seen before but the combination of graphical design with the planet and hexes and fantastic tree makes this game set itself apart. It played right into my interests in board gaming and presented it to me in a growing world vibrantly displayed on screen. Certainly worth the coin it costs getting those peeps out of the ground to rebuild humanity!

_childDocuments_.review: some review compared this game to satisfactory/factorio, they couldnt be more far away from that.... this game is like playing an old settlers game on rails(you cannot control the units, only place buildings),and let me stress this: "THIS GAME HAS MINIMAL ANIMATIONS", might as well be a chessboard game.next is: TIMEGATES, made from colored "technology" scattered across islands/planets, so your progress is halted by the fact you HAVE to expand to get new tech by gathering this misterious colored tech.THAT'S IT.... thats the whole game in a nutshell....Ive played a lot of city building games in my life, and this is by far the worse, there's basically no way you can lose whatsoever.... might as well be a mobile phone game where u pay money for the peeps to build faster.... _childDocuments_.review: Just not fun. Why play this game? It's not unique. There are others that do the same thing better.Hey Lauren,I'll try to recount the more specifically the experiences that ultimately lead me away from this game. It's been a couple weeks, but I do have a brief recollection of things.The first off-putting item was the road system. I liked the concept, but the way in which it was implemented made planning hard. For each building, you need at least one road, so at least half of the map is often used for roads. Because of some natural features, I often found myself accidentally blocking off part of the map and building complicated road networks across chasms to go around to the other side of a building. This was more pronounced on the second continent, where I had to build wells in certain locations to counteract the desert. Combining this with the need for food, it wound up having a huge scope-creep as far as construction went.This is where the second major struggle ensued. To counteract the resource problems, I tried utilizing the ships for trade. It felt really cumbersome. I don't remember the scenario exactly, but I was trying to use two ships to maintain all the resources on the continents and couldn't automate the second ship separately. I think it was because they were technically the same route, I couldn't select the auto-loading separately for each ship, and it became a very cumbersome balancing act.So for me, this simply became a game of balancing resources, with very little nuance. I didn't feel like I had a connection with the characters like I would in RimWorld, and I didn't feel like I had the agency or power I might experience in Civilization. There was nothing unique enough about this game to draw me in enough to care about crunching the resource numbers, or to separate itself enough from others of its kind.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun for a time, but fundamental flaws in the gameplay loop bring down an otherwise enjoyable time waster. Tools are an essential part of the economy, and you require tools to build something that can make them. On the first planet, this is gifted to you by a magical device to stop you from realising this mistake immediately. On the second planet, this device is not there and after some investigation of the economy you slowly worked through on the first island - you come to realise that it is impossible for this planet to be developed on its own as you did with the first. The planet I landed on had no iron on the first island - preventing me from making any tool-making buildings, which in turn meant that I had a limited number of ways to use my initial stock of tools before everything crashed to a halt. There is no experimentation to be found at this point, you cannot proceed without precisely using the limited stash of tools provided in your travel to the planet to create a spaceport and allow resources to be shipped to your new planet. There is nothing you can do about this, all avenues of expanding or exploring the new planet require advanced buildings or tools - a glance at the forums and early access feedback reveals that this is a common complaint that has evidently been ignored by the devs. You should never be able to soft-lock yourself in this manner at such an early stage of the game. This would have been trivially easy to fix - a single guaranteed iron/stone tile on the planet you land on, or a tier 0.5 building that makes tools out of wood at a terribly slow, inefficient rate, the ability to move the magical item on the first planet, allowing the colony spaceship to generate tools slowly. All quite easy to accomplish, none of them put in place. A frustrating experience that only compounds the fact that this was already not a match for its primary rivals in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely addictive, on par with cracktorio levels of amazement. Strongly recommend if you have a whole day and a half (let's say 36 hours, because you probably won't be going to sleep) exploring your whole star system, optimising your production while listening to some sick beats blasting out of a chipper-sounding pipe band. There's a strong interconnected sense of scale from tiny farms to solar rocketry and logistics too.I think a major upside to the game is the hex tile and adjacency system which gives it a major advantage over standard square-grid systems  in older (predominantly german) titles or even free floating placement. Coming off a civ-6 kick with district placement it felt pretty natural. But BWL is great and forgiving because you get to move your buildings around without losing materials (you "spend" worker time but hey, there's cool animations to go with that!).I have some minor gripes with the UI, some of the icons take some getting used to (Industry is some random crates instead of say, a steel bar and a cleaning chemical vial; but logistics and storage is also crates, so it's ambiguous what "crates" mean and that's not ideal for intuition), and on the UX side some of the transport stuff and planet-switching could be refined too. Specifically, you switching camera *out* to space view with a single tap, but then it's clumsy not being able to then zoom *down* to a particular planet without going through menus. But for upsides, the keybind system is fairly well customisable and two-thirds there of what I want. The other minor gripe is that you are going to run into setbacks even if the game isn't "violent" per se, but it's pretty easy to repair and rebuild, plus these setbacks sometimes have upsides too, so it still feels natural.Overall: extremely worth it, I ought to have bought it earlier to be honest, but the Summer Sale pushed me to try it out sooner. This is the actual vision of scaling gameplay that I wanted from Spore all those years ago.

_childDocuments_.review: A really lovely little game. I had a pretty fun time with it, but eventually it kind of got a big boring. Just to note, it says City Builder as the main tag for this game, but really it is more of a logistics and resource management game.You start on one island on a planet. On that island you harvest resources, refine them, upgrade your technology, and grow your population. From there you colonise all of the other islands on the planet. This gives you access to different technologies, different resources, and more land for more people. From there you expand to different planets, eventually colonising all of the islands on all of the different planets, sending resources on boats and airships between islands, and then with rocket ships between planets.There is a lot of logistics and planning when it comes to this game. You can be pretty terrible at building and managing your islands, and even your planets, and it doesn't matter. What does matter is being able to set sea trade routes from an island that has raw microchips, to an island that can refine and rebuild them, and then have them be send via trading rocket to a planet that does not have access to any of those resources; but you need the microchips in order to build the devices needed to mine the rarer ore on that planet. If you do not like heavy resource management and a game where you mainly focus on logistics, this is not a game for you.The city building is there, and it is important, but it is light. The more people you have on an island, the more unhappy they get. This combined with more pollution and industrial/technology buildings, can have them pretty upset if you don't make all the different items they want; so I just never went higher than 50 people on an island if I could help it, and 90% of the time, I could. Yes, it is useful if you make sure that your glass factories are near a sand mine that has three tiles of empty space around it for maximum resource harvesting, and decreased transport time, but you don't really need to care. Especially if you have few people working. Just set the game to max speed and eventually they get everything you want done.So yeah, the city building isn't all that important, deep, or crucial in the long run. Being able to send the resources you need from one place to the other, is way more important. If that doesn't really sound fun to you, then I wouldn't recommend you get this game. If everything you have seen on the store page makes the game look like it would be fun, and you think you will like it even with everything I have added in, get this game. I would probably suggest you get it on a sale though. After about 30 hours in I got bored; so unless you know you are going to get double the amount of hours out of this game, try to get it for at least 25%-50% off.

_childDocuments_.review: "Finished" the game, as much as one can finish a strategy game - seen the credits, and done most of the challanging things. All of it in one playthrough in about 16.5 hrs and i must say it is a rather cute little game, with a nice management system. The hexa grid makes it somewhat of a challange to plan your colonies. Good fun, recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Initially it was maybe a slight thumbs up but after playing it for a bit its a full thumbs up.Visuals in general are nice.Guardian visuals are fairly lame. The big one barely even animating is kind of lame.Gameplay is okay. It is a very messy builder. Very much a micromanager style builder. It's difficult to layout your master plan and you'll mostly just have to stick things where they fit. There are some large flat islands to build on but they are usually devoid of resources. You can very easily run into issues of production/storage when your ports fill up with non critical resources and critical resources cannot be delivered. The gameplay is extremely repetitive because you tend to have to build up every island you settle. You also have to build up a lot of the same buildings again and again, otherwise you'll probably run into shipping bottlenecks. Once you've finished the tedious work of establishing all the islands the game actually gets more fun. You can actually build things instead of waiting on shipments.Guardians are overall just annoying. I would say turn them off but, they are sort of the only end game thing to do though so without them a bunch of builds are pointless.Audio is nice. Good music, fx and alerts.No noticeable bugs. Transport spaceships on auto seem kind of broken. They seem to really favour research over other critical resources.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Exploring the world of Before We Leave was a serene journey filled with charm and discovery. The game's approach to city-building felt refreshing, providing a gentle pace suitable for all levels of players. The tranquil atmosphere, accompanied by soothing music and vibrant visuals, made for a relaxing gaming experience. While the lack of urgency may not appeal to everyone, the game's emphasis on exploration and expansion kept me engaged throughout. Overall, Before We Leave offers a peaceful and enjoyable adventure through civilization, perfect for those looking for a laid-back gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I've always liked city builder type games and this one took it to another level with control over the entire planet and then with space travel you can control the galaxy and work on achieving a peaceful/protective universe.The music and ambient sounds when zoomed into each planet is unique and soothing.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty relaxing but I hope that I can copy & paste templates in trading UI though, it gets a bit tedious to set up the trading demands for every new city, or to update every single city's trading demands for new goods/resources. After all, most cities need about the same diversity and amount of goods/resources.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is one of my favorite city-building games. The theme is charming, from the little Peeps and animals wandering around to the wooden spaceships. The soundtrack is pleasant and hopeful. Placing structures has a puzzle-solving aspect to it, with adjacency bonuses to get the most out of every building. And the end of the game is pretty satisfying.Unlike some city builders, Before We Leave isn't particularly difficult. Peeps can't die (aside from space whale attacks), but they'll stop working if their basic needs aren't met. Population control is important, but relatively easy to manage. Most of the game comes down to managing pollution and logistics. At launch, the trade system was difficult to master, but the "Wasteland Update" in 2022 added a "smart shipping" option that makes transportation of goods much easier; as long as you're producing enough, resources will find their way to where they're needed.Some of the scenarios are genuinely difficult and provide a few new challenges once you've beaten the game. I only wish there were more than four.Overall, I think Before We Leave is a fantastic game and a great example of a "cozy" city-builder. I loved it at launch and after coming back to it recently (achievement hunting), I find myself loving it even more. I'm looking forward to the sequel, Beyond These Stars.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Geheimtipp.Extremely good building strategy game, that streamlines its whole experience and boils it down to the genres most interesting mechanics.+ Simple gameloop, yet complex gameplay.+ Map tile resolution is neither too high nor too small.  It just fits together beautifully.+ The mechanics make sense and are easy to follow.+ Keeping track of ressources is easy and placement follows simple rules of common sense.(For example: the longer the ways, the longer ressources take in transit. No need for boni or mali to create this effect artificially.)+ The controls are easy to learn and feel very intuitive.- Just the camera feels a bit too restricted and doesnt offer enough modes.+ Music nice and fitting.+ Graphics solid and with fun little details that makes it fun to just tour the city.(- Touring the city doesnt really work that well because the camera sucks for that. :/ )I am still in the testing phase and just playing the tutorial.Im very looking forward to a strategy game about ressource-management that is fully simulated, has the wusel-factor from the settlers and doesnt annoy around with unneccessary fighting.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't play civ building games so I can't compare Before We Leave to similar games but for someone looking for a casual entry point in this genre I can easily recommend this.Big props for implementing tool tips that are actually informative, compact and explain pretty much every mechanic in the game.the only negative thing I can say about this game is the shipping ressources mechanic, which becomes pretty convoluted as you expand and you need to understand the automatic shipping feature (which is also well explained) if you don't want to micro manage yourself to death.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Fun passive city builder game. Population can't die, they just get less/more efficient based on happiness level. There is no permanent fail state.The skill tree is odd, but still works in a weird way. For example I once had to do an interplanetary shipment of...8 glasses of milk, so my wrestler could upgrade and beat up a minotaur. Shortly after this, I discovered how to make cement, lol. How I'm an interplanetary traveling species without the knowledge of cement, I'm not sure. The game sort of falls apart in the end game I found. It quickly becomes a trade/storage micromanagement sim as you have multiple islands on multiple planets that need to shift resources back and forth. You need to perfectly optimize your trade routes or things will get jammed up and butterfly effect into every planet missing a vital resource. Trading AI was hit or miss sometimes, which could get frustrating. If you're someone that likes to min/max, I'd say there are other games that do that better. But if you're just looking for colony sim with light ramifications for mistakes, I'd recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A well-rounded game that walks a nice balance of being easily accessible in the early game, and robust in the late game.  While there are some late game balancing issues, especially with population, it didn't impact gameplay that much.  I love the graphics and how the gameplay blends in with the overall theme of the game, making for a nice, relaxing experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game where you control a single surviving colony of people and slowly expand out and colonise the whole solar system. Resource management and logistics are easy enough and still manageable when you have multiple colonies on multiple worlds. The only real enemy is random attacks by giant space monsters that basically count as natural disasters.The few down sides are that you people are little wooden figures which feels weird.All the planets basically look and function the same making each planet not very meaningful. You might as well just have been colonising a single world instead.All the wooden enlightenment era tech feels strange when compared next to space colonisation. You build space vassals out of wood and metal.So its a fun game that also feels oddly disconnected and strange at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Before we leave is a chill colony/city builder that almost feels like you are playing a board game. Unlike some other city builders in this game Your building decisions have drastic implications on your city due to pollution. Otherwise, this title is for sure an easy and fun pick up and play.✅ Great tutorial easy to play✅ Intuitive gameplay✅ Thoughtful building✅ Unique Graphics❌ not much replayability❌ Can be repetitive at timesAll in all, you should definitely check this game out if you can 7 Pollutions out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and kind idle management simulating game.Easy, abstract and forgiving compared to "Oxygen Not Included".Rocket-speed progressing compared to Sims.It annoys me a bit by some of its "magic" and "old civilization" sources for materials and knowledge.No in-game money lulling crap.(Taken on a big sale)

_childDocuments_.review: "Before We Leave" is easily worth the $5 sale price, and probably worth the $20 full price. It's a novel take on city/colony planning: plop down buildings and roads on a hexagonal map, do some 4X stuff, advance down the research branches, and try not to make a mess of things. If you like those types of things, pick this up in the next 48 hours for the massive 75% discount. Cheers.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave seems to be inspired by the Anno series of games. There are a bunch of planets and each planet has a bunch of islands. Each island is rather limited: There is a fixed set of resources on each island, some of which are finite. Each island has a climate which may restrict you further. The islands are small. You also have to deal with pollution, "gloom", and other negative effects of industry. In effect, there's no way for a single island to be self-sufficient and produce all products, so you need to specialize each island (and possibly entire planets) and establish trade routes to move goods from where they're locally abundant to where they're scarce. One island may be dedicated to producing high-quality food. Another to producing good clothing. Etc.As you expand, you're faced with new challenges. On the second planet, you run into island guardians that you have to resist or tame, lest they destroy your buildings, steal your supplies, or do other nasty things. At some point you'll run into space whales who get pissed off at pollution, or something. (I'm not quite sure as I haven't met any yet.) This prevents it from becoming  repetitive.The idea is interesting and the user interface is clean. The game does seem to use an excessive amount of CPU and/or GPU resources sometimes, even while paused. Several of the negative reviews talk about this, and I've experienced it as well. My biggest complaint is that after settling a bunch of islands it starts to get repetitive, even with their attempts to throw in new challenges. Part of the problem is the lack of a narrative to provide an impetus for me to keep expanding. Why not stop right where I am and call it good? Overall I think the game is worth picking up if you think it might appeal to you, but I feel like at some point soon I'll be feeling the urge to just hurry up and get to the ending.EDIT: I just quit where I was. Colonizing three planets was enough. Why go further?
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: It's refreshing not being constantly bombarded with attacks, you can just build at your own pace and enjoy the feeling of progress. The art style is lovely, balancing resources and peeps is fun and optimizing your islands is addicting. I would strongly recommend it for anyone who likes to help and watch a world evolve.The only complaints I have are A.) The logistics. You can't copy-paste shipping settings so you need to add everything manually for every island. Moving research around is a pain and seems to take priority even if you need something else more. Being able to build a research station in space would help both with the shipping and not having to remember where you've gathered it all  B.) You can retire some ships but not all. I had two ships constantly marked as idle C.) I wish the ending was less abrupt. A simple cutscene or some new animation would make it it feel more finished. D.) I keep confusing the Industry-button for storage even after 40 hours of gameplay. The natural resource-button is also confusing, it doesn't look like anything to me.Aside from the logistics, all of these are small gripes. And while I'm not personally a fan of micro-managing resource shipping, I still like playing this because other parts of the game are so enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I've spent way too many hours in this game after first trying the console version on game pass. I like that it's non-violent, so you can build in peace and not be preparing for war. The most difficult and continuous challenge is trying to balance production efficiency with keeping your people happy. Other, more devastating and time-critical challenges will present themselves as you advance, though. I'm not sure how I feel about those, but for the most easy-going experience you can actually turn them off in the game difficulty settings if you want.As I progressed and discovered new technologies on new planets, I found myself returning to where I started and improving things there instead of just pushing forward to end the game as soon as possible. There's just always something improve and optimise. The name of the game is spot on in this regard, and it's addictiveness caught me totally by surprise.I've also had tons of fun just starting new games focusing on lessons learned or making up silly goals like mining all the iron and stone out of mountains. Highly recommended, but only if you have the time to spend. Because let's be honest: this game does not get you anywhere in life. And yet the reward is in taking it slow and doing all the little improvements here and there. That one more thing before you leave.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best city sim games I have played to-date. The system for trade and resources management feels robust and intuitive. I haven't experienced all the in game content yet, but the "calamities" I've run into so far are quite unique and add an interesting twist to how I plan out my cities. Highly recommend for those that love city building / resource management games!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This game is by no means perfect: the auto shipping system is confusing, tedious, frustrating and slow, and completely unusable for planet to planet shipping. But the game is for the most part very charming and relaxing. The soundtrack is A+, and the progression is well paced and very rewarding and fun. Seeing your civilization grow from an industrial nightmare to a haven of clean energy is a sight to behold, if you ever get that far. Gameplay aside, the game does have a story that does not start until you are already about 80% done with the game, because you need the submarine researched in order to start unveiling small clues, which by the way, takes for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ever, so you will never ever learn the game's story unless you sink a solid 100 hours into it. Other than that, it's a fun city building game. Not the best you will ever play, just a short experience that some people may find up their alley and others not so much. If it ever goes on sale, highly recommended. Other wise, not worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games you can spend hours and hours playing and not even realize it. Perfect game for relaxing!There are a few things i do not like however;1) The planet-to-planet trade UI is confusing and cluttered when you have alot of planets to trade with. 2) The speed you research things makes you demolish alot of infastructure on the first planet in order to fit in the new buildings you researched. The space you have is allready super tight and even if you plan out the island to only produce x things and you trade it between the islands you still run out of room sooner than later as waiting for the space transport just takes forever and is not realiable, thus the majority of things you still have to produce on all planets. _childDocuments_.review: SETTLERS!That's what I've thought when I've started to play this game. You're starting as a small settlement, you build houses, tree cutters, stone mines, food fields, and you start to build more and more complex facilities. This part of the game is absolutely settlers. But than comes a twist: you're on a really small planet, and the starting island is tiny, and doesn't have all the materials you need - so you need to set sails and explore the world, which is fun. You find some other islands, and you start your second settlement. And to balance your islands, you start trading - for example, your first island is lush and fertile, but your second one is a literal dessert, so you build more potato fields on your firs isle, and export it to your second one. Easy-peasy, right? Well, theoretically, it would be, but that's the part where this game fails miserably. You can either micromanage trading, setting manually every single items you want to trade, and manually navigating your ship from one port to another. Really not fun. OR, you can set what items you want to trade on each island, and set your ships to auto mode. Sounds good at first, and it seems it's working. Until your settlements gets bigger, you conquer more islands, and at one point, the whole logistics gets too complex for the AI. What was working at the beginning, is not working anymore. You usually see your ships standing in the port of your main island, as waiting for every single item to get transferred to the ship. While, for example, on your other island, are waiting for their food, which is just not coming, because your ship waits for 1 more vegetable. You can manually command your ship to go NOW, but you literally have to stand there and do this every single time, if you want the commodities to flow. There is another obvious bug affecting trading, which makes impossible to select which commodity you want to trade with which port (to create some more specific trading routes), and you can only choose "Any" port, and let the AI do its thing - but AI is too dumb for the task.I've tried to reach the next phase of the game, where you start exploring other planets, colonize those, and start trading via space, but I was just too tired waiting for some specific items to get transferred from one island to the other. Honestly, it's a shame, as the game COULD be very good - it has everything, cute graphics, nice music, chill atmosphere, exploration, etc., but the broken trading system ruins the whole experience really fast, just after a few hours of gameplay. (Also, it would be nice to have some scenarios or a real campaign mode - there is sandbox mode only-, but that wouldn't work either with this broken trading system.)
