_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave begins as a Settlers-esque city-builder and reveals itself as a logistics challenge in the campaign’s second half. It’s worth sticking out the rather gruelling tutorial and derivative-feeling first couple of hours, as the game becomes more interesting and rewarding in its later stages. Emerging from a bunker on a cute micro-planet in the aftermath of an ill-defined “galactic disaster,” your “Peeps” quickly get to work farming potatoes, chopping trees and mining iron. The familiar outward spiral of industrial and technological complexity is interrupted by the need to colonise new islands and – soon –other planets in pursuit of rare resources. Accompanying this is the need to organise an increasingly complex logistics network of shipping between your under-developed colonies, existing industrial bases and new resources. Technological remnants begin to make life difficult in the later game.Graphically gorgeous, Before We Leave is a rather anachronistic muddle of tone and theme. Mostly bucolic, bordering on twee, it feels as though the game’s focus on recovering from disaster and avoiding ecological devastation is trying to send a message about sustainable development. Throw in menacing – though largely inconsequential – space whales and interplanetary colonisation, however, and any message becomes harder to discern. There’s no plot or drama motivating your expansion aside from the intrinsic desire to scale the tech tree. To give you some idea; I unlocked windmills and space elevators at about the same point in the midgame. The soundtrack, likewise, is an odd mix of mellow guitar-and-synth, and hyperactive shanties. Though the overall effect is quite interesting, Before We Leave sometimes feels as though everything was throw at the wall by its small developer to see what stuck.Overall, Before We Leave can still be recommended to players prepared to meet it in the middle, and especially to tough out an offputting first couple of hours. Its ugly UI and clunky tutorial don’t do a great job of explaining the game’s idiosyncrasies or even main premise, but there’s a solid campaign here for both experienced city-builders and newcomers. Rimworld is still the superior far-future top-down colony sim, with a much more dynamic sandbox, while those who enjoy wrangling networks of resource flows here might want to graduate to the colossal logistics challenge of Factorio.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a nice little city building and management simulation game.  It does get a bit complicated if you try to grow too fast.  But of course if you play with the space whale turned on, taking too long will cause your planets to get eaten.  So There is a balance of sorts.  I enjoy it, If you like city builder games, then you would probably like this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The sense of scale in this game is just great. When you manage to get economy running on your island, you get to colonize another one and the whole new world opens before you - getting trade routes set up, manage resource distribution... and then you colonize another island and whole planet. When you think you have this game mastered, you fly to another planet and get to this again, while setting up interplanetary trade routes and resource management. Before you know it, you have several solar systems colonized and it is fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge Anno/Settlers/city building fan so I was surprised to see this in a Humble Choice having never heard of it before. I was even more surprised that it ended being one of the best builders I've played. Gameplay is somewhat similar to Settlers/Anno in that layout and product chains are key. The story is fairly minimal, delivered mostly through unlocked journal documents. Aside from the main game whose goal is to essentially traverse the research tree, there are 4 scenarios that dramatically change the way the game is played and force you to stretch your builder brain a bit to succeed. I actually enjoyed it more than Anno 1800, if you're into that kind of game this is absolutely worth a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a relaxed city builder you can leave running and watch, a terrarium of peeps going about their business. The world is engaging and beautiful, the challenge laid back, the concepts easy to grasp. If there's a complaint, it's a little shallow. You manage your population's happiness and that involves feeding, housing, clothing, and providing amenities, while also using them to pursue other goals like expansion. But this ends up being a solved problem; better food/drink makes your peeps happy, the production chain is straightforwardly simple, every input and output usually has just a few steps (save the highest levels of food/drink production, but that's hardly necessary). Almost everything you need is merely a matter of waiting while your peeps generate the materials. I've never gotten into a situation where I would have to restart the game, that is, a loss scenario. Now, what about the whales? The game by default is very kind, and you'll quickly find counters to make them a non-issue. The first attack if you're unlucky may kill a few peeps and damage a few buildings, but again, nothing is a true permanent loss -- the survivors need only time to gather materials and repair, while the population needs literally a few minutes to replace your casualties. That renders a lot of other sort of "calamities" kind of toothless. Yeah, you can get a weather storm that shuts down your farms, and they stay at home angry that they're hungry. But it'll pass and if you've built any sort of excess in your production chain you'll rebound in a few minutes. So it's an irritance that means that you hit the fast forward button until it's done. And so forth. Higher difficulties means littering your path with more obstacles, but because of the nature of the fundamental game, it's a bit like adding sand to your shoe before going on an untimed marathon. All you've done is make the task of reaching the goal take a little longer and more annoying without making it necessarily harder. So the bottom line basically is that BWL is a city sim that has a specific concrete goal in mind, and once you've sorted that out, you've solved the game and that's really it. And it's not hard at all really to solve it, but it's fun while you're still sorting it out. Definitely worth a try if you want to just relax and solve a logistics game at your leisure, in essence.

_childDocuments_.review: Simple little colony sim to get into with enough content and busy work to easily sink a few dozen hours into. What comes across as limited in scope really opens up when you realise there's actually space travel and planet colonisation here too (within a single solar system mind you).Graphics are charming, music is easy to listen to with mostly violin and upbeat folk reminiscent of medieval times.The hex based base building and exploration is quaint, with the way the hex grid pops up to reveal the area as you explore the void compared to a traditional fog-of-war is a nice touch. Primarily it's all about supply chain and distribution - making sure you have enough of X to construct Y and location Z.This means that road construction does take up valuable construction hexes meaning the placement of them will probably be one of the more demanding decisions to make in-game.Not everything can be farmed/mined/researched from a single island and/or planet though - and the real complexity comes in the form of logistics and shifting resources from several locations in order to build something on a different planet.You do encounter hindrances in the form of gremlins, minotaur and kraken, all of which aim to disrupt your supply line and break the monotony of the loop, but are more of a minor hindrance at the end of the day (and net you some lore too).End-game is all about managing extremely expensive to build structures while fending off space whales as they gobble up parts of your planet (the menacing sound of them approaching from deep space with the dimmed folk music playing in the background pulls off that suspenseful realisation of impending doom perfectly - great stuff on that account).I do think that's where some of the unnecessarily dragged out sections of the game come from - there's no real way to speed up transport other than to assign dozens of ships to every trade lane which creates a lot of busy work as they all take a pinch of something for the arduous trip back.To the devs:

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Before We Leave a lot, it gave me a fun fifteen or so hours of gameplay. The planet-scale city builder is very pretty, and the hex-based, constricted building system forces you to really think carefully about how to develop each island. The elaborate network of trade needed to supply your islands and planets is fun, and keeps you conscious of your civilization at every scale. There's definitely an annoying hump around midway in the game as you have to repeat the process of setting up islands for new resources a few too many times, but it's made up for by the late game where you get to play with more and more technologies and have an inter planetary industrial base to support end game projects.The story is light but charming, and watching a space whale twice the size of a planet swallow up half of your under-prepared island is a humbling experience. You really feel like little ants exploring a world of ancient giants.I can see where some of the criticism is coming from, but I had a fun time. I'll definitely come back as they bring in content updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating 3/5Management games are a dime a dozen these days. From managing large scale, in-depth and expansive civilisations (Civilization series), to more niche subjects such as prisons, hospitals and amusement parks (Prison Architect, Two Point Hospital, Rollercoaster Tycoon series), management games are a well entrenched genre.Before We Leave, from Dunedin’s own Balancing Monkey Games, leans more on the larger scale side of this, but also attempts to make it more accessible for newcomers. To that end, I believe they succeeded.Before We Leave starts with the last vestiges of humanity appearing out of a shelter having survived some unknown galactic event. You have to gather all the necessary materials to restart life, and use the remnants of the old world to research technologies for the new one to thrive. However, there is only so much technology to use on one island, so eventually, you branch out to other islands and then eventually other planets to begin the human race anew.Each island on a planet has a different climate. The desert island doesn’t have much space to grow food, the rainforest gives a boost to production, etc. Despite the variety, no one planet has everything. In a lot of cases, an island won’t have the necessary resources to properly begin a settlement. This is where Shipping Routes come in. Ports and Space Ports allow you to set up these routes to exchange items between islands and planets.The main draw of Before We Leave is the removal of combat mechanics commonly seen in management games. In their place, we have what is more akin to minor annoyances on a few islands, which you deal with nonviolently. There are gremlins that will take away your resources, minotaurs that will disrupt your villagers (called Peeps), cryptic Sphinxes that require riddles answered, and giant space whales that will devour planets unless you can sate their hunger. Yes, the giant space whales that devour planets are a ‘‘minor annoyance’’.You don’t control the Peeps directly. You can influence their decisions through a simple priority system. The Peeps are pretty good at sustaining themselves, leaving you more time to start colonies on other islands and, despite a few issues, it works really well.One of the things that makes it easier than other games is that there isn’t a fail condition. Your Peeps can’t die if you neglect their needs — only lose happiness, which affects the speed at which they complete tasks.Everything seems to affect happiness in some way. Most buildings come with a gloom effect, which reduces happiness. Many buildings have a pollution effect, which reduces happiness and gets worse if you don’t deal with it. Having too many Peeps affects happiness. Having the Peeps do hard work reduces happiness . . .you get the idea.To counteract the happiness drop, you can give your Peeps better food to eat, better clothes to wear, and decorate your settlements. However, this eventually became unbearable as all of my Peeps slowed to a crawl or simply refused to work if I didn’t spend a lot of time building ways to make them happy. And remember, not every planet or island has what you need. You have to ship in items to keep your Peeps happy so they’ll make something for another planet . . . it was about this point it started feeling like I was simply spinning my wheels.Despite that, the game is charming. The graphics, while simple, are clear and easy to distinguish. Each building has unique sound effects and your Peeps add a sense of life and presence to the game.Before We Leave is a game I can recommend for newcomers to the management genre: it’s simple, accessible, with a dash of cosmic horror, and is just an all-around nice game to relax with as long as you’re not trying to micro-manage everything. The constant need to keep your Peeps happy is a big detractor, but if you can deal with that, then you’ll find a lot to like.

_childDocuments_.review: once you get the hang of it this is a really fun game. a lot of people complain about the micromanagement, what they are referring to is you need to transport goods between islands, but im sure those people are the same people building every building on every island which leads you to micromanaging heavily. if you do buy this game, my one massive tip is make each island its own speciality within reason. one island produces food, the other tools / luxuries or an island that makes raw / refined materials, this ties in well with similar buildings granting each other adjacency bonuses boosting production even further. then all you do is set up the islands to trade tools for food. then you set and forget! only adjusting rarely to accommodate new population or new infrastructure. just note that initially you will need all basics when starting an island, once the island is established you can lean more onto trading resources instead of creating every resource on every island.

_childDocuments_.review: I love a lil' colony sim game and that's what this is, so that's why I like it! Talk about an open world game though, it's an open 3-world game. There are certainly some repetitive aspects to the game, wherein you successfully colonize one island, then have to repeat your success on another island with a different climate, but you're meant to do a little better each time you gain access to a new area.  It's easy to rearrange your previous colonies once you've started to like the look of a later colony, and I appreciate the lack of a major hassle like in some games that force you to live with the consequences of unmovable structures. The weather events are cute, the animations are pleasant, the music is jaunty. Why aren't you giving it a play? (Maybe you already have, I don't know your life).

_childDocuments_.review: After several weeks and MANY (~90?!) hours I just finished my first play through and I'm actually eagerly excited to start again and see if I can do better, and what having more planets is like.  I absolutely recommend doing your entire first run-through in in tutorial mode. It's not condescending or overly-simplified. It just means they tell you what sorts of steps to take next to progress, and I can see how one might get stuck and frustrated going into it blind. A lot of things are locked until you first encounter the necessary materials, and some of those steps are... giant leaps, as it were. The soundtrack is fun and appropriate. If you like generally relaxed colony/city builders I cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyably mellow little city builder, with a touch of inter-island shipping/resource management, similar to the Anno series. Unlike many other feudal era/low tech city builders, there's no real fail state, or harsh survival elements to contend with. At worst, a mismanaged island will result in angry, inefficient workers. While some might find this a little too forgiving, it's nice if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, where you aren't needing to juggle multiple islands and their production lines in real time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that has a nice balance of having a good challenge without the other chaos of a normal city builder. I wouldn't say that it is relaxed in nature but it does allow you more flexibility in thinking when it comes to strategy. Each island on the planets is randomly generated and it provides a curve to the building process along with pollution tracking and trying to create efficiency through placement of buildings.I won't lie, YOU WILL FUDGE UP AT TIMES. The beauty is sometimes you can fix it quickly or later during the game. However, this might include taking buildings down and that can complicate things for a short time. Also, the need to be at peak and to improve can cloud your judgement and put a damper on things if you're not careful.There really isn't anything I feel could be truly improved or even a negative note. I will say that your materials numbers a can be confusing at first when you're trying to see how your doing, but it is easy to understand once you see it in action.Overall, I find it a rather addicting game. It is slow but it's a nice pace compared to similar titles.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not a big fan of real time strategy. I tend to prefer my civ builders when they're turn-based, but trust me when I tell you... This is one of the best games ever made. I am not certain of how replayable the game is yet, but if they managed to figure that repeated loop out and make it entertaining? This would be THE game of 2021. While I received this game through Keymailer, I was not asked to review it or even say nice things. Viewers of my streams know that I will talk badly of a game that deserves it. _childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Trade is honestly so tedious you feel like you spend more time in trade menus than actually playingSpace whales appear unannounced and cause permanent damage to planets, sometimes leveling half an island (more trade menus to get it back operational!)No point in colonizing all planets, all it means is more trade menus since the first 2/3 and a science lab gives you more research than there are techsThe "guardians" are an annoying distraction with little to no payoff, making it take that much longer to get a new island up and runningTechs like the shield, the party building, musician, and honestly even the 2nd level shipyard are pointless as they help with issues you should have already addressed well before then(even with how small the tech tree is), with the shield being extra useless for all but the whale tamer planet
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. Usually with this kind of game, as soon as it gets to the mid or end game, i want to start again. The mechanic of going to different planets means you do start again in the same game, which keeps me on board and building new and better things. The constant pollution and gloom is a worry, but i have found that keeping populations small means you avoid those expectations, but i'm not sure if this is how you are meant to play it, or if i am avoiding a key mechanic to make it challenging. Overall i really like this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game.  I think it's worth every 2000 pennies.  It's simplistic in some ways, but is a really good game with regards to resource management challenges.  Some reviewers say you are constantly creating gloom and pollution, but it's managed with certain jobs and upgrades that these users probably didn't play long enough to actually figure out.  A lot of the island building requires a lengthily process of resource sharing and upgrading which you really can't successfully do in a short period of gameplay.  I am 50ish hours in and I am still unlocking many building and trying to balance trades.  When something is going wrong, it's either because you did something wrong or upgraded resources too soon.I look forward to upgrades and expansions, and I have yet to play the scenarios which may add some fun challenges to the gameplay.Yes, I'd recommend it to a friend.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of colony games and resource management.One of the first resource colony games I played very intensely was Banished. I logged in almost 300 hours into that game. In many way I see similarities with these two, but without a doubt, Before We Leave improves on a lot of my problems with Banished.I can't express enough how impressed I am with the game quality and functionality. Problems are introduced, and a clear solution is available. Example : Finite resources such as stone, iron and electronics? Colonise another planet/island and eventually advance your research to produce them yourself (ie deep mines). Great touches to details such as the little animals around the islands, short bios for Peeps and the various biomes and weather which truly make this a challenging yet sweet game to play. I certainly appreciate the lore that was crafted into the ancient guardians and the ancient Peeps.I'll be logging in many more hours to come.If I were to give my two cents on a potential improvement or addition to the game, I would be delighted to be able to 'tame' the domestic animals such as dogs, cats (and maybe birds?) so that I can share them with other islands and planets, however, I will be realistic with my expectations from the developers. Fantastic game. Kudos!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Sound effects are awful. Instead of real background effects the devs have gone with that god-awful "we put the mic in the fishtank while we were at the pub" background sound that doesnt match whats happening on screen and sounds dreadful. Didnt even get as far as other peoples problems with this game  due to the sounds annoying me so much. Real shame as this seemed quite fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely recommend. What a well done game! I am so pleased to say that this game also has a WONDERFUL onboarding tutorial (which is lacking in so many games!) so I was absolutely delighted right from the get-go. There are always many different elements in building games like this, and it can be overwhelming at the start, but they do a great job of breaking it down and showing you the important things that you need to know to build a successful colony! This game is a charming city(/planet?)-builder that you will easily play for hours. The graphics are cute, and it's so fun to play! My only complaint is that the roads take up so much space, haha. NEED MORE ROOM TO BUILD THINGS. Maybe bigger planets. ;) That's all part of the challenge, though, and I will be playing this for many more hours to come!

_childDocuments_.review: Very crisp, smooth running city builder.  Not much different from the core game of other city builders, everything is built on tiles like Civ games, There is a simple progression tree to give you something to work towards.  I'm curious to see how the space portion of the game plays into it, as I haven't gotten the spaceship repaired yet.The game is well rounded at this point, graphics look good, controls are easy to use.  I personally did not run into any bugs.  I played the tutorial, but if you have played any respectable city builder before, you could probably play without doing the tutorial because most everything is controlled the same way.I would recommend. It is a good quality game that is different in it's own way, but still retains the classic charm that makes city builders fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Before We Leave is a fun super casual city-building game.The trailers are pretty explicit regarding what the game is about: it's laid-back, easy to grasp and not super complicated (some light resource management is involved).I really appreciate the art-style as well as the game's soundtrack.One thing that could really use a revamp IMO is the UI. And I don't mean just the looks. It's OK for the most part, but sometimes pretty mediocre. There are a lot of stats and a lot of menus, and they could really use better color coding and clearer iconography.It gives me the impression that this is an early access title.All-in-all, it doesn't detract from the fun.This is still a very much fun little game.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10: The game feels polished and complete and that alone is worth 8 points after playing games like Foundation and Folk Tale which were a waste of money because they were never finished and became abandon-ware. I enjoy the challenge of managing road and building placement to gain the best possible bonuses for production. This means I enjoy being able to place roads and buildings wherever I choose and not being locked into a box by the designers. Even choosing the entry point to a building needs to be thought out for road placement when placing an elevator. For me running out of research points and having to find more nodes on another island is also a unique challenge. The design requires you to think and decide what you need to research now so you can get to the next island and/or planet. The music is relaxing and for me the game works as it maintains a good flow and balance throughout the game play experience. Is this the type of game for everyone? ... probably not.
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: The game is interesting for only the first two hours. All that comes later is a complete waste of time, which the only purpose is to stretch your in-game time.At least half of the buildings' upgrades are redundant. You don't need to have more than 60 people per island. Some upgrades have completely no logic. For example, better houses make people unhappy. And you have to improve infrastructure just to be able to sustain everyday life. The same problem with overpopulation, you just don't need it to finish the game. Better food required only to get rid from the minotaur. Raw food is more than enough to sustain happy life even under heavy production utilization.Ancient dangers can't be dealt with at the early game. But, if it's not some vital colony, that you need, you can just ignore it, nothing bad will ever happen. There are no real consequences.Same thing about whales. They do nothing dangerous. The only expensive thing that they can destroy is anti-whale buildings. Other buildings can be rebuilt within minutes or even seconds.Production problems. Some products require themselves just to be able to produce them. Such as electronics and tools. I assume you can even completely fail planet colonization if you waste all of your tools on something except spaceport or tools production line. Developers even added deus ex machina at the start of the game, which can produce tools from wood. While by default tools require iron.Also, you can't destroy a colonization spaceship, which existence is completely pointless when you are fully settled.Biomes. You can't produce some plants in some biomes. And there are almost no islands where you can produce everything. It's kind of strange. Some planets don't have such biomes at all. Just one more way to stretch game time. Some planets don't even have enough biomes to produce everything. You will need to import products from another planet (no you don't because these production lines are redundant).I finished the game. After the first two hours till the end gameplay doesn't change at all. You won't see anything new. I played just to see how it ends. I stopped getting pleasure from the game.Good graphics, pleasant music. But, I'm sorry, I don't care about it if the gameplay doesn't worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I saw this game on Steam and watch the stream for a bit.  I have to say this is a fun little builder game with a bit more of the traditional city builders.  It sort of reminds me of Populous meets Civ meets Settlers meets Spore, all in a good way.  The people are simple but the idea of being underground after a war is great.  As I am writing this, I am about to launch the psace ship for the first time.  It is a kinder, gentler Mad Max world.  Still learning, but almost 6 hours in, I like it and it has been well worth the entry point!
_childDocuments_.name: Before We Leave

_childDocuments_.review: Really adore the game. Just reached my second planet and I am loving the concept and all. It's really relaxing for now (can't tell whether there will be any mechanic in normal play that will make the game more of a hussle, but I don't expect any). The only thing I am missing a bit is an option to easily relocate buildings (like ANNO has for example). Especially my first island was a complete mess when I moved to my second planet, because you get a lot of new buildings and mechanics which you can't foresee and which impact the efficiency of your industry.All in all the game is wonderful and really worth it's money if you fancy strategy games with industry management. The no-violence part is something I absolutely love and miss in a lot of other games like this.Definetly would recommend this game!

name: SELF
detailed_description: Dreams use so many bits and pieces of our memory, but not in a logical, linear way. ―Rosalind Cartwright, Psychologist SELF is a suspenseful Kafkaesque text-based adventure game with simulation and puzzle mechanics. My father has vanished, yet I seem to be the only one who has noticed. Even my own mother is completely indifferent to his absence. The journey I must embark upon to bring him back is one that can only be traveled alone. In this game, the boundaries of reality, dreams, truth, and memories are blurred. Many puzzles and challenges await, and you must commit to a series of choices leading you to a range of different endings. In this introspective adventure, you must collect clues from throughout your journey and piece them together to find out the whole story. But— will you seize the opportunity to find your SELF ? A story that plays out upon an interactive CRT monitor screen. Varied gameplay including bullet hell minigames, inspired by titles such as Undertale and Just Shapes & Beats. A unique experience with rich pixel art and a gripping story. A fragmented narration with multiple endings.

_childDocuments_.review: Such an interesting little game, with great music, atmosphere, pacing, writing, all the things that matter to craft a compelling narrative experience. Very poignant moments and scenes that take full advantage of the surrealist setting. It has some slow repetition to get to the points where the story branches, and the avoidance minigame is largely boring, but these are very minor gripes.
_childDocuments_.name: SELF

_childDocuments_.review: For much of the time I was playing SELF, I was considering the metaphorical implications of the different images used in the game. The flooding water representing a memory that can no longer be repressed, and the sinking feeling associated with the vivid memory of someone who was once so close to you. The cracking screen, perhaps representing the growing ineffectiveness of using entertainment to avoid encroaching emotions.What a disappointment, when, at the end, these images are revealed to be quite literal. However, I did find the way that the other characters interact with you to be amusing. The only individuals which actually seem to listen to your character are the tall/thin and short/stumpy men that follow you around. Everyone else (your mother, King, the clown, the people that speak to you over church bells, the fellow student at school) ignores the requests you make of them and questions you ask them, only to ask you shortly thereafter "what they can do to help." It was frustrating, and a unique emotion to be induced by a game - it made me feel like I was on the phone with the customer service department at the local cable company. King buys you a soda after you tell him you don't want one, the clown gives you a balloon after you tell him you aren't interested, etc.Outside of this interesting emotion provoked by the game, I didn't find much to appreciate. The mini-games that allow you to either face the past or avoid it were unengaging and repetitive, and the game featured a few typos as well ("take them were?" vs. "take them where?" and "reelection" vs. "reflection").I feel that I should note to potential players that I generally only play games of this type once. I'm not interested in playing through the same scenes over and over, doing slightly different things to uncover each of the game's seven (!?) endings. Not an awful effort, but "My Name is You" (which I've noticed is now F2P) is still the best "Kafkaesque" game around.
_childDocuments_.name: SELF

_childDocuments_.review: The music is REALLY good, let me start with that. The story is... cryptic. Sometimes that can lead to wanting to know more, or feeling like it's too much effort to dig for. In this case, I was intrigued. Some mini games are... weird, and aren't very obvious as to what the solution is. The MAIN mini games are reminiscent of how Undertale did boss battles. Except in this case you choose red or green and WANT to run into the objects. As someone else has already pointed out, the "avoid"/"give up" option is too easy, and it would be great if you had to fight both ways for the choice you were going for. I haven't reached all endings yet, but the thing that I personally enjoy about the story (where others may not), is that it leaves a lot for interpretation as to what's REALLY going on.

_childDocuments_.review: is a Kafkaesque text-based adventure that unfolds on an interactive CRT screen. The game claims to draw inspiration from titles such as Undertale and Just Shapes & Beats, striving to combine text-based narrative and choices with a variety of gameplay mechanics.It is a decent interactive fiction that will provide around two hours of gameplay. The game has an interesting albeit confusing storyline that successfully captures the player’s attention. However, it oversells itself with exaggerated claims of puzzles and bullet hell sections, which although fun, are not overly challenging and often feel like a side note that would be better marketed as a unique take on decision making in games. I would recommend the game as a narrative experience, particularly to fans of text-based adventures, but would ward off anyone looking for more action-packed or high octane gameplay.My full detailed review of this game is available on

name: Adore
detailed_description: JOIN OUR COMMUNITY About the Game Adore is an Action Creature Collecting game where the main character, Lukha, is able to summon and control creatures to fight by his side in a simple and innovative way . In Adore, you can customize your game style according to the creatures you capture. Each of them has very different characteristics and abilities. On top of that, there are the Synergy System, Traits and Special Abilities, which allows for even more varied playstyles and powerful combos. SYNERGY SYSTEM Your creatures work best together. You can create synergies between them. Each synergy that a creature has, will activate an extra ability or modify your creature. TRAITS Go on expeditions after statues of Draknar, the god of creatures, so that your creatures receive traits that make them unique . SPECIAL ABILITIES Each creature also has a special ability that can be used when its energy bar is full. You have to decide when is the best moment to use the special ability more effectively. The path to becoming a good adorer is long. A true adorer knows each of his creatures and finds the best way to get the most out of each one. RUNES & ARTIFACTS Equip and upgrade special Runes and Artifacts that best compliment the qualities of your creature team. COOKING Gather ingredients during your adventures and create unique dishes to help you and your creatures in the journey. TRUE ADORER Put all your knowledge to the test. It's crucial to know when to summon each creature, have good positioning, when to recall them back, what artifact or rune to use, how to prepare you and your creatures for expeditions, training your creatures. All of this is just the surface of a true adorer. Draknar, the God of creatures is dead and a curse is spreading, taking control of all his creatures that inhabit Gaterdrik. But the last spark of it's the flame felt upon Lukha, an apprentice of the adorers and Draknar's last hope. Lukha, during his journey to revive Draknar, discovers not only many secrets of the immense and mysterious world of Gaterdrik, but also, the conspiracy that killed Draknar.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not a fan of rogue like games at all. The only reason I picked this up was because the idea of a creature summoning game that wasn't turn based was interesting to me and I am so glad that I did. The game balances out the rogue like elements and the persistent elements really well. There are persistent unlocks, such as buffs and debuffs on creatures and temporary stats, such as synergies. Synergies make your 'team' function differently each run. This makes it so, yes there are very powerful combos, but no you aren't going to always get them. You can't really 'min-max' completely, yet each run, the decisions you make need to be considered for what would be optimal in that situation. You also unlock other things over the course of the game, it doesn't hold your hand in what to do, each run you are figuring stuff out so you never have an 'ugh gotta get through this AGAIN' moment. At the same time I rarely find it super frustrating, even when a run ends, it's just 'okay, lets go again'. It's a really good blend of what I think appeals to people in rogue like games and ARPG games. There are bugs but so far the dev team have been really responsive to them, they are pretty active on the discord, asking for information and taking interest in feedback. It's a small dev team but they are responsive to the community. The game is a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: Adore

_childDocuments_.review: With the latest update, Adore is in the best state it's ever been, and keeps me coming back to play in a way the original gameplay loop, while innovative, just didn't manage to accomplish.To those out of the loop: before the Welcome Home update, the play loop of Adore was structured more traditionally 'roguelike' in terms of run progression, with a groundbreaking summoner/moba-like combat system, but relatively light on the 'creature collecting' part of the game, simply because that' difficult to incorporate in any roguelike. There was a metagame hub where some creatures (not many) could be 'stored', essentially, and the only way to get new ones 'stored' was to start runs with empty party slots and capture new creatures, which you could then choose to bring with you or not when the run ended/failed. There was an element of 'trading up' through a run to a degree, starting with a few keeper creatures and some filler, and then capturing/releasing others as you went to keep pace with the difficulty curve (which, let me not forget to mention, is surprisingly steep and still is. not unfairly so, but definitely unforgivingly so). This resulted in some awkward tensions, such as situations where you could theoretically capture a new creature (that would then have full health) to replace your trained up creature that was at critical health to keep the run going, but would result in giving up the 'keeper' creature etc. It had phenomenal per-run gameplay and combat mehcanics, but had self-admitted struggles making the roguelike and creature collecting parts of the game - the blending thereof being what makes Adore so innovative - play nicely together. As a result, it was primarily a 'roguelike with creature collecting elements'.Welcome Home did away with all that and entirely overhauled both the metagame and the per-run gameplay loops, and Adore is now decidedly a 'creature collecting arpg with roguelike elements', and while at first I felt disappointed at hearing the change announced months ago, I can say now having played it that it was absolutely the correct decision. By de-emphasizing the length and self-contained nature of each individual 'run', and leaning heavily on metagame progression, creature collecting and tuning, and very creatively allowing items from each run to persist across each other through the use of 'durability', Welcome Home brought Adore much needed persistence and *reasons* to keep playing, and a sense that even when your runs fail you still made tangible progress in some way.The actual combat itself is largely unchanged, and that's fine, because it was excellent bordering on unbelievable that no one had really tried something like this before already.I *will* say that the durability system feels strange at first, and the shortness of runs in the beginning of progression gives an illusion of gutted difficulty compared to the previous build. THIS IS MISLEADING. The game still completely kicks your ass as you get farther (honestly I'm only at depth 4 of 6 and feel like I may need to spend some time grinding some resources at depth 3 to get the ball rolling again), and the durability system starts to make MUCH more sense as the game gets harder. It allows you to build up the power momentum necessary to take on the longer/harder runs (called expeditions) that are the real meat of the game, without letting said momentum build and last indefinitely so as to trivialize the game. It's deceptively well thought out, and I sincerely hope they devs don't tweak the current formula *too* much, because it works incredibly well. I'm super excited for more creatures! Only thing I can really think of currently as a 'big want' would be the ability to customize your creatures a bit more, at least aesthetically. Stuff like renaming them, skins (or just alternate skins in the wild), maybe even stuff like accessories, just because they feel like they would fit really well with the style and art of the game. Get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: When this game launched in early access it started out as you capturing creatures to then summon and manage them in battle. They could take damage and die, which made this game slightly about your character, but mostly about having a team of creatures and keeping them alive during fights. It was clunky and needed A LOT of polish, but that is the idea I bought into. It was truly one of a kind game. Now it's game where you capture creatures and then use them as skills in battle. To clarify, you DO summon a creature, but it attacks once and vanishes. You can spam the summon key to make them attack in succession (just like you would with a SKILL). The only real difference is your skills have a healthbar, so if you constantly cast your skills in dangerous areas too much they start transferring their damage to you. It's an different implementation of skills, but calling ranged attacks innovative (as store page implies) is a stretch.I thought it had some fun ideas but it wastes way too much time on trivial tasks. You'll have to do the same dungeon 100s of times to upgrade everything you want upgraded, because you get 1 resource at a time and most things require 2 or more.You look at the dungeon and in most cases you know exactly what you're getting from it. Upgrade resource, crafting material, "rare" monsters, health potion (which by the way is 1 time heal on pickup). Somehow knowing I'll get 1 mushroom and 2 stones for 10 minutes of my time is really depressing.Creatures look cool. They have distinct powers and attacks. You can even get 2 with slightly different upgrade paths. That's where my praise ends. They are clunky to use and are expensive (in terms of time required to capture, store and upgrade) , which makes switching creatures a massive chore. This game has "Blessed" (rare) monsters. With all the grind they are probably the biggest disappointment in the game. It's a recolored version of the same monster with higher POTENTIAL (when maxed). Did I mention the game punishes you for switching creatures?Capturing blessed ones is annoying too, because you can accidentally kill them while clearing other monsters. There's no real way to aim your monsters when you're fighting 4 of them - they just target the closest enemy.The game is heavily grind-based and grind is poorly rewarded. You need 2-10 runs for upgrades which you need many of. The upgrades are 20 HP (base is 100), 1 run speed (whatever that means), 2% movement speed (on 11% accessory), 1 creature storage slot, etc.None of the upgrades felt impactful so far. They didn't change gameplay and if they changed performance I didn't notice.

_childDocuments_.review: I came back a second time to edit my review after almost a year of not playing. TLDR: This is a genre-defining title, and the devs are CLEARLY on to something.*insert sound of audience clapping, whooping, and throwing roses*Wow you guys have done something incredible with the soundtrack. The music is a sincere joy to experience, in fact when I came back it was the FIRST thing I noticed/remembered. I thought to myself "I cannot believe how good this music feels to listen to, like calm in your soul." Every zone's track brings me this internal feeling of ethereal serenity in my soul. I mean FFS guys, I could feel the music in my chest. I heard it with my heart, not my ears. Y'all obviously LOVED making the music for this game, and as a musician myself, I feel that that passion is what has made this game so wonderful. In my original edit (seen below this review under the line) I mentioned that the zone layouts weren't really random enough to feel organic. That has been fixed. They are broader and more intricate, they are beautiful and full of soft textures and attention to detail. Your art direction and execution has bolstered that ethereal serenity along with the music. I sat and watched the water in the hub/start, while my creatures goofed off in circles and just enjoyed the scene as though I were sitting on a bench in a garden. The combat, the creatures and the difficulty are simply perfect. On normal difficulties, I am getting whupped by my lack of attention, or my simple mistakes made one too many time. I died while trying to capture a creature, instead of just accepting the loss and dodging out of the way. I died getting cocky on the boss with low health. I died wondering why these monsters kept spawning even though I'd completed the objective (I hadn't). It was fun getting owned by my own skill (or lack thereof lol). What made it even better was not having to give up my 1 health super quick ♥♥♥♥♥-slapping badger-monkey that I had had since the tutorial. It used to be that if they were at critical health, they just died when you did, and that always crushed me a little bit. But now my 1 health super quick ♥♥♥♥♥-slapping badger-monkey gets to come with me. My only negative-ish observation is that every time you enter a new room in the zone, it restarts the music. This may only be in the Forgotten zone tho bc that's the only time I noticed and it wasn't even a big deal.For anyone who took the time to read this review, please just buy the game. It's incredibly fun, and so much more than worthy of your time. These developers have poured more love into this game than any other developer I have ever seen. This is passion, and that's what you came to the reviews to find out. To the dev's, a final curtain call from me reviewing your game. And once again I have come to say:I Adore you.___________________________________________I played my fair share before I came back to edit my review. Here are my thoughts:TLDR: This is a genre-defining title, and the devs are CLEARLY on to something. It needs more polish, some solid rebalancing, more items and creatures to add variety to builds, and a lot of love with the environments. Overall I think the biggest downfall so far is the maps. While they are B E A U T I F U L, they are also very hollow and repetitive. Each room within each tileset is some mirror or slight alteration of another, but not quite different enough to feel procedural. There is a lot of work to be done with the variety here. That being said, the art is truly incredible.The combat is punishing, but very fun. Hard enough to whup your ass, but fair and entertaining enough to keep you coming back for more. As of the last update (Runes of Dukur) the difficulty appears to have swelled a great deal. Fine for the hardcore metagamer, but would probably cause a refund from a casual normy who's just getting into creature collection. If you want a game that's going to kick your ass and still feel satisfying, Adore is for you.OMFG THE CREATURE COLLECTION!!!! I absolutely A D O R E all of the creatures I have come across. They need some rebalancing because some creatures are not viable in most builds, but that doesn't mean they aren't awesome in their mechanics. I'm particularly fond of the rapid-attacks from the saber-tooth demon-wolf that I named Schmoopy. What really excels here is the way creatures are stored, I love the mechanics. PLZ ADD MORE DOODZ AND MECHANICS TO MAKE DOODZ DO STUFFAlmost there guys!! I Adore you.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept of mixing a creature collecting ARPG with the roguelike/lite formula holds so much potential, but unfortunately this game squanders it. It's not all bad - the creature designs are solid, the art style is cute, and the combat is ok, even if I do wish I could do more with my main character besides dodge while I micro my summoned guys. You can also ride some of the creatures around! For some people, that might be enough to enjoy this game.For me though it's not enough, and the game got stale extremely fast. Maps are just a string of incredibly samey looking encounter rooms. Exploration is pointless as there's nothing to find. Sometimes maps have branching room paths which mean you have to trek back through the entire map to complete the mission. The ability to mount might seem like it solves this issue - but mounting up is a special move, you get dismounted when you enter new rooms, and have to walk while you wait for the special to recharge! It's mind numbing. The game also includes this odd Curse system which can make a creature much less useful until you go find some berries to make a consumable that clears the debuff. It feels like a weird half attempt at permadeath which honestly leaves me scratching my head as to what the point of it being included is? Also, the dialogue in this game is awful. It makes some attempts to be funny but these are all utterly cringe inducing. The writing is littered with awkward phrasing and spelling mistakes. It might be a bad translation from a foreign language, I honestly can't tell. Overall there's not much else to talk about because that kinda seems to be all there is to the game. Perhaps things get more interesting later on, but after an hour with it I'm utterly bored. If I want to scratch that creature collecting itch I'll boot up Temtem or Pokemon Legends instead.

_childDocuments_.review: is an indie monster-taming action roguelite. Just those words strung together should get some people excited, it sure did for me. Please keep in mind that this game is definitely in Early Access, and there are going to be some expected bugs and QoL issues, but we should all expect these to be resolved for the final version.Playing as Lukha, you are in a semi-dead and constantly reviving state, much like many other protagonists trapped in their respective roguelike/lite settings. You enter into the domain of Draknar, the god of the creatures, as an apprentice to try to lift the curse that are taking over the creatures. To be honest, there's not much in the way of a story once you get into it, except for the insults you get from Draknar every time you die.The game is played in a top-down manner, with beautiful graphics and I played with a DS4 controller, which worked reasonably well. It's certainly an unique take on the action genre because the main character cannot perform any attacks at all. Instead, he can only tame creatures who then become linked to him as part of his life.The only way to move forward past any first area that spawns any monsters/creatures is by taming one and continually summon/unsummon for it to do your bidding. After completing each room, the exists turn from black to green, indicating that you can move forward. There may be also an essense orb for you to gather, this gives you an immediate character stat boost plus you can use the orb at any statue/altar of Draknar to either unlock another creature slot (up to 4 total) or to give one of your currently tamed creatures an upgrade/ability. I was completely ignorant of the ability to unlock a creature slot, so I played initially using only one creature. See below for video.Monsters will level up with summoning and fighting, but they may also take too much damage and perish. The game uses an interesting system in which you can summon and unsummon your creatures so that they can avoid taking too much damage and you can get them out of trouble in a hurry. Lukha also takes a signifiant health damage should any one creature die, and if it happens to be the final tamed creature, it will be game over.Each creature will automatically unsummon after performing its usual attack, unless you command it to perform another attack while it's out and about. There are some creatures that are clearly meant as support with status effects while others are the primary heavy hitters. There are not a ton of creatures out there at the moment, but putting a team together based on what you like as well as what the game throws at you that run does make it rather interesting at times.The run currently consists of 4 zones, with progressive difficulty in terms of run-progression. But the zones are also randomized, so if you cannot get past the first area, replaying will likely spawn you another area as the starting point. Each zone has a shop room and a boss room. Their entrances are indicated by yellow and red lighting instead of the usual green for a standard room. You can use the map to fast-travel to any previously visited room, though I am having trouble with my controller to do this. I know you can do this easily with Keyboard+Mouse.The pace will seem rather slow at first, but it gets rather frantic later on. You can usually bait and prey on most of the commonly spawned creatures, but when it comes to the bosses, it's very much an all-out brawl in trying to ensure survival without losing too many of your tamed creatures. Once you get past a boss, a portal opens up to allow you to travel to the next zone. You can also go back and pick up any left-over goodies or to buy something from the shop before moving on. (Item drops upon completing the rooms stay and are available as long as you are still in that zone/map.)Overall, it's an ambitious game with a fun idea, and a mechanic that doesn't seem all that intuitive to start. The QoL issues does make it in need of work, but that shouldn't stop you from trying it out. There is enough polish to already have plenty of fun with this game, and at a starting price today as it enters Early Access at $9.99 US, I think it fully deserves some serious attention.Sure, it could use some more creatures (in the works) and better balance (I found one boss significantly less forgiving than the others) so if you want to wait for the game to take on its final shape before diving in, I would say that's a reasonable choice as well.KB+M works well, controller input mapping needs some work but does work for the most part.Artwork is fantastic and overall a very pretty-looking game.Decent, not too fancy, tracks run out if you stay in the same zone for too long. I suppose this is something that will be fixed eventually too.You can get a pretty good idea by looking at some gameplay and I think the team did a good job putting together some decent trailers to show you exactly what you will be getting into. So take a look and see. I also have a short video showing my first look at the game. (Before I realized how to unlock creature slots.)Game launched into Early Access today at $9.99 US, this is an absolutely reasonable price for the game. The price is expected to increase with further development.  is a really nice indie title in Early Access. The game mechanics are fresh and play out decently without hindrance to enjoyment. The bugs, QoL and balance needs are expected in the game's infancy and should be worked out before full release. The current price is reasonable and the gameplay certainly feels fresh, with the difficulty expected of roguelites. The pace may be offputting for some, so look at some gameplay videos and decide for yourself.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow the idea of catching monsters to attack other monsters has been stuck in a JRPG turn based style. Adore breaks that mold with finesse and it feels incredible. This isometric roguelite has you unleashing a whirlwind of creatures casting spells while you dodge roll and face off against behemoths all in hectic real time.  It has the right amount of complexity in place and I can’t wait to pick it up again. No need to bury the lede here. You’re still reading this? The premise alone should be enough of a sell. It’s like another game that rhymes with Shmokemon, but instead of watching things bounce around in turn based combat, you are right there in the heat of battle summoning up ice mammoth squirrels shooting magic etc. Lukha is an Adorer who can capture creatures and summon them to fight. Creatures are summoned like assists in a fighting game: your ferret isn’t following you around when you summon it, rather you are sending him out like a skill shot in a MOBA.  The MOBA aspect also rings true in regards to the perspective and the fact you have up to 4 creatures you can juggle around. You need to manage stamina and cooldowns as you send out monsters and wait for them to be recalled. The creatures are more than just attacks though. Each creature you capture and summon has a health bar, a special gauge, a synergy, and stats. As you play with these creatures they will level up and grow stronger: maybe it’s a crit increase or AOE increase, or their special gets a buff.  Each time you attack with a creature you will feel its special gauge, then when its full the next attack will have something special like a shield or buff. The synergies give bonuses to specials or attacks  depending on the types of creatures you summon together. However, your creatures are vulnerable and if their health is depleted you use your beloved, overpowered friend for good and your own health bar will take a hit. New creatures can be captured but you are either starting from scratch or hoping that the creature chest you opened has the right one to complement your roster. There is more to the game than watching your pet kill other animals. Your character starts off with 1 slot to capture a monster. He is vulnerable as he channels the spell to capture a creature, and it will also cost you essence. Essence can be found around levels and is used to buff your creatures or to unlock additional slots for you to capture more, up to 4.The latter option should be prioritized; If all your creatures die and there's no more to catch (like in a boss fight), or you don’t have enough essence, it’s an automatic gameover. Picking up essence also allows you to power up Lukha with more health, stamina, or movement speed. Outside of essence you will want to get your hands on fragments and gold coins. Coins will allow you to purchase a variety of items from standard health kits (for you and your creatures), keys to unlock chest, or equipment that will do things like buff your speed after rolls or add life steal to your creatures. Fragments are the progression system currency that you will use to unlock new monsters, new mechanics, and new items.The game looks enchanting. The color pallete, setting, and creature designs feel partially inspired by Studio Ghibli and Runic games. The litter of rocks and stone remnants combined with the cartoonish feel overall gives the game a  look. The outlandish creatures seem to look like they belong in a Studio Ghibli feature more so than in Nintendo's famed franchise. It’s a treat to watch a deerlike monster frolic around stone ruins as canopy of cherry blossoms sits cozily in the foreground. The stylized look of everything feels polished from Lukha’s paint to the glow of every spell.  The world and lore of Adore seem nice, but they take the backseat for now. There's harrowing talk of a slaughtered village, mystics gods, curses, and blessings. It's a thrilling backdrop, but we will have to wait and see where exactly the story and world go as the game is developed.Adore is not without its flaws. I ran into a few rare bugs where enemies were invulnerable or my character would be stuck and unable to attack. These were rare instances. It also feels underwhelming to have Lukha be completely defenseless when he doesn’t have creatures: it would be nice to wack things with your staff even if it does low damage. Healing yourself or your pets can also be difficult which encourages you to play very carefully. In terms of balance some boss fights and enemies can punish you hard if you aren’t careful, and at least one boss rushes his attack faster than Da Baby jumps the beat.At the moment Adore is a ton of fun and some challenge. There are only a few mechanics to unlock, some monsters, and a handful of items. I was able to reach the last stage after a few hours and I got my first win around 6 hours in, but there is a lot planned for the game and I haven’t unlocked everything. I love Adore in its current state, but I can’t wait to see all of the planned content.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know exactly which reports or which trailers deceived me, but I expected a monster catching game, in which you assemble a group of animal minions and try to keep them alive in fights. You would care for them, train them and level them up. Basically being a bestiamancer.I also expected hordes of enemys to slay with my pet friends and  levels to explore.The monsters don't stay. You have to manage some kind of "summon energy", so mostly you only have two monsters active at the same time. If your monsters would die, they enter a special state instead, in which they are still some kind of "alive" but if they get damaged further, YOU (your character) is losing life instead. You can remove that curse by giving them a break in the archive. The monsters are beautiful and very different from each other. There IS a story. _childDocuments_.review: Adore has good bones but it does need work. The parts of the Adore that  I enjoy: The monster design is good, I wouldn't say its completely unique but compared to some of the other monster collecting games I have seen they are enjoyable. The combat system is entirely unique to the genera, you "control" your monster, while also being able to control the main character, both of which have their own health bars and can get hit by the same attack/monster. Your stamina bar is the main recourse to use your monsters. No stamina = no monsters. They have "ultimate" abilities that are exclusive to each monster, that range from healing to throwing up water on your foes. When your ultimate isn't charged you have a generic attacking ability that is also different from monster to monster.  If your monsters heath bar is drained they don't "faint" they get cursed. They can still be used in combat but if they have any damage dealt to them in this state you will die and get sent back to town. Each of the 4 monsters in your party level throughout combat making their attacks stronger, as you progress you can have them learn traits. The trait system is generic and leaves more to be desired but its enough to customize your party to what play style you most enjoy. There are artifacts that you as the player can equip that provide passive benefits to add more build diversity which is a nice touch as you as the player don't level up like your monsters. From what little story I've read it seems fun, but corny. That is to be expected for a game geared towards a younger audience. The things I dislike about this game:Not being able to just skip the dialog in the game is annoying, not deal breaking but be aware that you have to spam the continue button if you don't care about the story.The tutorial and info screens can be less informing then they should be. Some game mechanics you just have to figure out on your own.The controls are obviously optimized for a controller and not a keyboard and mouse. If you double tap any summon button you basically waste stamina as your monster is thrown out and retrieved so fast the model doesn't load and its neck is broken. This along with some irritating mobbing that can happen means you as the player are getting the ever loving **** kicked outta you while you wait for stamina to regen. The targeting system that is used for your monsters just doesn't work for me. I will try and target a monster that will one shot my party monsters faster then it takes Trump to get indited and they go after a monster that is as fearsome as a puppy. Some of the wild monsters attacks are less then fun to deal with, monsters with floating wind attacks and damn electric snakes that one shot any party monsters and almost the player character that again mob are less then fun to kite. (I fully recognize that this is most likely user error I just don't have the mental to deal with it 100% of the time) Conversely some monsters in general are weaker then a toddler with a blow up hammer. They just hit you and its a minor annoyance. If you capture them, you have a toddler that hits wild monsters with a blow up hammer. When opening chest to get a random monster, you have to hit the F button twice. Once to open the chest and a second time to collect the monster. Unlike in most games were when you open a chest the loot is automatically collected. When this isn't done you lose the monster forever. You get a really rare blessed monster that is game changing and you don't confirm that you want it, its GONE. FOREVER. Hitting F a second time isn't obvious when it SHOULD be. The game shouldn't let you leave the map before you confirm you want the monster or you "release" it.One thing that has been a MAJOR annoyance to me is that the save system doesn't work 100% of the time. About an hour of progress was lost because the save system just didn't work. All in all Adore is a unique monster collecting game that is difficult but enjoyable at best and at worst just doesn't save your progress. I enjoy it when I have the mental, when I don't I have to take 10 mins of my day to sit outside and pretend that video games were never invented.

_childDocuments_.review: I am editing this as I play. absolutely love this game. Then the monster is gone if you die and extra painful when its a super blessed and a direct upgrade to your favorite monster.  I would prefer a more diverse and larger roster of monsters with more unique traits and abilities. The leveling is pretty slow and a pretty low level cap for the grind. More levels please. The main char is fairly useless so far, with only 1 actual ability I would really like to see more skills even if its like a double dodge simple thing. The last monster I started to use purely defensive for the main char but as I have used it, it has come to be very very handy with it's knockback, last thing you want is monsters getting close to you! _childDocuments_.review: INTRO TO EA REVIEWAdore is an easy recommend for it's innovative system that utilizes your summoned creatures as abilities/skills. I like to say it's the real time version of Pokemon lol. For the amount of content currently in early access it's well worth the price.CREATURE GATHERINGIt is nice that there's no limits. Though when it comes to gathering all 39 creatures it can be a little painstaking trying to decide which creatures should be released if you don't want to grind for more fragments that will allow you to unlock additional slots. Though this did force me to try out new creatures more often than not which was nice nudge.PROGRESSIONThere are so many avenues of progressions. Artifacts and Runes for the Adorer. Synergies and Traits for the Creatures. I won't go into much detail here. But I will say that there's a lot of freedom and runway for these systems. So there's always a new combination to try. And there's always another upgrade to pursue. I did end up spending quite a bit of time doing just that LOL. The Synergies system is really great way of forcing you to try different creature party combinations for the best results.COMBATIn spite of the combat being very simple as you progress up the difficulty tiers, tougher enemies in larger quantities are thrown at you, making it more difficult to complete a map without getting wiped. So you always need to stay alert and attentive to where enemies are coming from and which type. Each creature has a basic & special attack. And these attacks can either be melee or ranged as well as single or multi hit. Sometimes it's best to go with burst damage from single heavy melee hitter for an Adorer or Legendary creature. Other times multi hit attacks might be better to keep a mob of enemies at bay. I ended up focusing my efforts on 6-8 creatures. And even though I had my 4 starters, I couldn't always use all of them due to them getting "cursed"(i.e. knocked out) which requires 1 turn to transpire(i.e. run a map) in order for them to be healed. Some Adorers and Legendary creatures are tougher than others. But they were all unique. And presented their own challenges when facing them.CONCLUSIONIn spite of the procedural maps being a little repetitive and needing some extra aspects to produce more diversity, I really enjoyed the gameplay loop of searching out money, crafting materials, fragments, and more to move further down the avenues of progression in preparation for Adorer and Legendary creature fights. I finished all the content before Update 0.11.0 introduced Gems as an additional form of progression. But I plan on returning for the 1.0.0 release when storyline will be complete/introduced.

_childDocuments_.review: ADORE is a game with a high degree of specialized play.  You, the Adorer, have been chosen to restore the ancient order of Draknar.  To accomplish this, you must venture out into different places where you encounter wild and fantastic creatures.  Some of them, you must put to rest, others, you will recruit to aid you.  That, is where the game becomes special.Each creature you collect has a different ability, type, and stats.  This allows the player to customize their team.  You can build a team that suits your play style, and also helps to win certain types of battles.Your creatures become further specialized as you create synergy with the other creatures in your team.  When creatures of different types work together, they both have the potential to become stronger.Feeding your creatures can boost their stats, and eventually as the creatures spend more time adventuring with you, they gain levels.  As you play, you find ways to further improve your team - but I leave that to you, Adorer, to discover those ways for yourself.This game is a top-down 3rd person dungeon crawler procedural zone generation.  The game is in Early Access at the time of this post, and Cadabra studio is actively finishing the game.  You can expect very good support from them in both Steam, and Discord.  They listen, and respond to players.  Be ready for adjustments in gameplay though.  Early Access games necessarily change, and sometimes we like or dislike those changes as players.  Remember that part of your adventure is helping this game to finish by giving feedback, suggestions, and bug reports.  In my honest opinion, this game is easily worth more than they are asking.  Many hours of content and gameplay, even if it doesn't look like there is a lot to the game at first.  As example, there is currently no co-op, or PvP, so it might seem like there isn't much to it.. but there truly is.  The depth is in the creatures you collect and customize, and in the rich storyline.  The story is great!  I easily find myself buying-in with the characters and progress, and it will only get better with time.  So go on, get it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more mixed for me. I've 100% the game and built all the creature to satisfaction however bugs and lack of quality of life makes this game hard to recommend with certainty. I love the art style and unique game play of summoning creature. Its more of a top down dungeon crawler but the gimmick is your creature is stand in for you ability.Creature have their own health and you need to manager theirs and yours. Later you can customize creature ability with synergy and these can be quite game changing. Synergy can add new effect or enhance existing abilities. But it requires a creature of the synergy type to be in your party. However synergy cost essence and it can not be refunded. Resetting the synergy destroy the applies essence. This makes the game very unfriendly to experimentation as essence is quite time consuming to farm.The game is consist of procedural generated map layout with hand made area. Each map will contain various resources and consumable. Later you gain access to expedition that is up to 3 maps of different type of biome that only count for one day. Expedition are preferable for its vast amount of resources, upgrades and bless.The capture mechanic can be quite fiddly, you need to stand within a cone that swivel and rotate. Thankfully there are trinket and creature ability that makes it easier and manageable. Tougher and late game creature needs their health managed and carefully timed ability for successful capture. Mid to late game you have access to hunts that let you pick specific bless and super blessed. Super bless creature are important as they always give max out traits. However expect to reroll several super bless as traits given are randomised, you get to pick between two trait for each of the 4 trait slots for some control, however there more than 8 traits and you may not see the trait slot you want in the trait selection pool for that creature.Creature capture are limited by 3 Gatedrik particle. By mid to late game you will hate this limit. Early game it made sense as you had to make some sensible decision. But by mid to late game when bless and super bless consume 2-3 Gatedrik particle it will feel very limiting. The maximum amount of Gatedrik particle can not be upgraded. Often you will end up having to kill super bless you wanted to keep because of this as multiple can show up in expedition.Hunts consume resource intensive essence, product of capturing creature. Failing hunt hard earned essence. Despite it showing 3 skull symbol for tries, it is only for death which is incredibly rare for you to die during hunts. Killing your target or letting the map that the target is on expires ends the hunt and you must start again. Because of the time and resource investment of hunts I recommend just save scumming and saving time especially since may want to reroll the creature and especially for super bless legendary that are quite expensive to hunt.Your Main character have equip-able trinket that majority of effect is kind of underwhelming even when upgraded. Unfortunately the game felt you need limit the full amount of upgrades you can have despite being quite. This can be very disheartening if you farmed quite a bit for those trinket upgrade. Especially when the upgrades are miniscule, pushing only a few percent.All consumable item are on a timer that tick down for each run, this is fine for health consumable. You can further extend consumable by cooking for them. Unfortunately the time limit includes insects which is vital for cooking +6 traits. Insects is a nice way to compensate bad trait rolls, unfortunately its all up to luck. If you want certain skill you have to hope that 3 of the insect you want are available within 3 day, as all 3 must be cooked at once. This can be quite tedious. If the game had a fridge you could use to extend timer on a few consumable this would mitigate some frustration with luck base gathering.Now for the biggest reason I wouldn't recommend the game. Its still buggy and its been almost about 10 month since last patch as of time of writing.One of the most frequent bug is mounting one of your creature and ending up in inescapable  area which can kill your run unless you have another mount charged, trinket that can regenerate creature ability or manage to kill every creature in the area.Late game there are temple you can raid for gem for bonuses effect on trinket, limited by upgrade amount. About 1 in 15 runs the exit will not be interact-able and the run is killed. Especially frustrating if it happens at the end of expedition or ascension.On rare occasion you can't back out of the menu and you have to force close, killing the run.If you have to force close because of a bug, most of the time it will count it as death. This skips a day and forces you to spend another to retrieve your stuff.One of the creature by name of Zoras is still bugged with circle of fire synergy. Does nothing, unless you fight an enemy Zhoras and it uses the circle of fire attack. Then your Zhoras fire of circle works.Overall if you're looking to get invested in this game, expect some kinks and element of frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique blend of creature collector and ARPG.Creatures are captured and short-summoned to do an attack or two then recalled.  You play offense by recalling creatures before they take damage and casting them at the best times (casts per regenerating resource being the limiting factor).  You play defense by looking out for your own health and the health of your pokemon.Level up pokemon.  Empower them with items.  Empower character with passives that affect character and pokemon.  Minor crafting elements.Solid game.  Repetitive, but what ARPG/Creature-Collector isn't, amirite?This kind of thing is what we need more of.  Games are pidgeonholing themselves by refining further and further toward a singular genre.  Games that mix elements from a *limited number* of genres are where we'll see the innovation in the next few years.  This is one of those games.  Finite.  Imperfect.  Quality.
