_childDocuments_.review: A few thoughts on both sides of the coin:-There is a lot of gameplay here; different card/gem combinations means that there is some extra customization, but there are a lot of "best in slot" gems for particular cards (e.g. even gems that give more spirit are only good on particular allies, since others are "spiritless," and since you only play ally cards once before they are dissolved from your deck, gems that you want to play multiple times are better suited for other cards). Reminds me of Monster Train and how some card/gem combos were kinda busted, but also necessary to win in some cases.-People complain about grinding but with 2 runs I basically unlocked all of the primarily interesting features that enhance the gameplay (alchemist, swapping starting cards, few extra treasures, etc.) the rest of the progress tree looks like incremental buffs that only matter for when the difficulty is ramped-up with the "epilogues" (e.g. spending progress points on bonuses to gold generation, while epilogue increases costs of things). To unlock everything would take a long time, but so does beating all of the ascension/epilogue levels, so I assume it's more of an arms race.-The dynamic of 2 heroes hits a sweet spot. I've played a few games that allow up to 3 or 4 heroes and it gets very cumbersome. It does at times feel like a gimmick with the number of abilities that encourage you to just swap back and forth for value.-As the devs said, the game is basically feature complete without the DLC. I didn't even look at it, but it's not unusual for art/soundtrack stuff to be available on release for an extra price. The fact that there's a couple treasures/a boss that is locked behind it will make some people feel the game is incomplete without it, but that's basically a logical fallacy. Getting up in arms at the devs for being "greedy" is pretty lame. Just buy the game without the DLC and then if you actually DO love the game, make a decision from there.Overall, I enjoyed my first 5 hours, and I'm interested in trying the other characters and combinations. Probably good for 30 hours for someone like me unless I get really hooked, and I probably will never buy the DLC and am fine with that.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook has beautiful art, animations, music and atmosphere, something I have been craving from this genre for a looong time. And I absolutely love the exploration system this game has, where you slowly explore and paint the map with your looted brushes and inks. There's just something very satisfying and relaxing about it, and discovering treasure has been the most exciting out of any roguelike deckbuilder I've played.It just makes every run feel like an adventure, rather than just picking from one of two corridors.The gameplay is very similar to the classic Slay the Spire formula, but with a few twists. You can combine multiple heroes into a team of 2, which creates some more potential combinations. You also have skill trees, gems and difficulty modifiers to customize your experience further.So while I can't yet speak for how long Roguebook will remain fun, the building blocks of longevity is certainly there.That said, with 32 hours at the time of writing (although some of it from alpha/beta) I'm still having a lot of fun.While the market has become heavily saturated with these kinds of games as of late, I would definitely recommend at least trying this one, because it certainly feels like a breath of fresh air.Edit: To address some of the negative reviews this has gotten, about the game being unfair or imbalanced, and that you need to grind the meta progression to be able to win. Literally not true. I won my first 3 runs in a row, 2 of which were on higher difficulties - before I even realised I could unlock the meta progression. In fact, if anything, I would say the game is a bit too easy. So I don't think it's fair to bash the game because you're bad at it, and I certainly don't want the devs to make it easier because of it - 'cause I'm already winning consistently. Or to blame your losses on the meta progression, when it's perfectly possible to beat it without even putting a single point in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Just not worth the price point.Richard Garfield  a big name game designer, but Roguebook just seems like an unpolished product. It has  ideas, but none of them actually improve the genre and principal game loop. In many ways I would say it actually misses on what makes Slay the Spire good. For example, there is a weird tension between wanting to keep your deck small, lean and mean, but not only the opportunities to remove cards from your deck are very low, there are actually -kind of mediocre- incentives to actually have a deck as big as you can in the form of bonuses unlocked via amount of cards. Most of the game is actually spent on the overworld map, trying to plan the best way to optimise your brushes. That is, again, neat, kind of interesting in of itself, but it is completely disconnected from the thing that I want to be doing, aka, playing my cards. And even that feels kind of terrible, with no options for zooming out or panning the map, and a feelbad situation where you just have to  you hit something good with your brushes. Subjectively I also kind of dislike the artstyle and animations, it feels kind of sluggish and slow, and certainly not charming. For example, reshuffling your deck takes more time the more cards you have, so by the end of the game you are sitting there for 30 seconds just waiting for your cards to move from left to right??In the end, above all, this is a very expensive game for the amount of blemishes it has, so I simply cannot recommend it. If you haven't, just play Slay the Spire.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played a lot of Monster Train and Slay the Spire, and Magic the Gathering, and almost every TCG out there... I'm trying really hard to like this game, but increasingly find myself frustrated at the end of every play session.My primary issue with this game is that the majority of cards in the game are just frankly boring. There's also an incredible lack of synergy in deckbuilding. Most of the time you're getting "do damage" or "block damage" cards with an occasional bleed effect or mana generating type effect. Every time I've tried to do a run with cards that are more unique, such as allies (cards that summon companions that attack with you) I just never seem to find anything to make it truly work. The game also entices you to keep building your deck larger and larger, that's how you unlock passive skills for your characters. There's also a boss that erases your deck during the fight, so having a higher number of cards is beneficial there. That whole aspect is also detrimental to the actual deck building... You'll find yourself having tons of cards that just frankly don't do what you need them to do in the given situation if you choose to go this route. The game overall is okay, I think I'm done with it after my 6.5 hours played. I may give it a few more tries to see if I'm just missing something, but I think it's more that there's something missing to make the game feel more coherent. Too many runs are decided by RNG. Normally these games make you feel like you're at least steering a ship in a given direction, this one feels like you're just on the RNG roller coaster and hoping it works out.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know how I feel about this game. And since my New Years resolution is to be more positive in life, I'm going to recommend this game but with a hard caveat. This game, like most rogue-likes, is abusing your broken mechanic more than the opponent can abuse theirs. It's fun, and frustrating, ultimately feeling like you're at the mercy of RNG. This game leans way heavier on finding an item than it does creating your own monstrosity. To improve cards you add gems, except gems are expensive to implement if you want to buy them or rare to find if you want to stumble across them on the map.This game also pretty clearly makes you play it over and over so you can increase world loot drops through a persisting upgrade system that uses "pages" as the upgrade materials. Each run you'll get a paltry amount of pages and quickly realize it'll take a lot of runs to make precious progress through this upgrade system.My biggest gripe with the game are a select few enemy types that I haven't figured out how to beat cleanly yet appear in every run. One enemy type is a raccoon like create who increases their "power" each time you play a card. But there's no way to beat them unless you play cards. I get the idea here, you're suppose to exercise restraint, but every time I play him, I take an insane amount of damage and they're always the "elite" challenge right before the boss. So you enter the boss fight very wounded. This is just one example of a mechanic that I feel needs tuned. There's plenty more.Also, not all cards are clearly explained in how they work. This is a small gripe because you end up just figuring it out as you go, but it becomes a much larger issue when the lack of transparency in how a card works ultimately sets you up to fail your run.But, there's so positive things to mention. I really like the hex-based world to explore, the movement system, and hero system. It's straight forward and easy to pick up. The art is really well done. There are some UI problems where clicking a card before an animation completes can cause you to accidentally "activate" the ally card underneath. This can burn a valuable resource. But, playing with a bit more patience makes this a non-issue.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - Two heroes/decks and map exploration aspects put a nice twist on the Slay the Spire formula. Overall it's a good game, I had a blast for ~25H, but it faded quickly after that.Main reasons are lack of content and changes to the gameplay as you progress + lack of RNG + low difficulty (no challenge and end goal) + lackluster use of the game's strong points (2 decks and exploration).Somehow, even though you combine 2 decks, I wasn't able to find that many viable ways to play. I also usually couldn't create very good synergies between the 2 decks. Most of the time I just used one hero to absolutely obliterate everything, because all hero decks have everything you need and more. Cards synergize very well within one deck too. The other hero was a minor support in most of my games.The game also pretty much always gives you opportunities to snowball and build a broken hero and it's hard to resist going for the tried and proven strategies. Deliberate experimenting felt like handicapping myself severely.I have to say that the way the game rewards bigger decks is great though. It's a nice option opposed to the usual thinning down.The game is too easy. I lost 1 run in which I experimented a lot. Other than that, every hero pair I tried was a win on 1st try. Despite pumping up the difficulty on every opportunity and experimenting with builds. The few broken strategies are very easy to spot and implement every run.It kills the challenge and incentive to look for new solutions. Lack of RNG kills the excitement and improvistation/resource management.At first it looks like there's a lot of that. But it seems it's only a facade. A lot of these are just % modifiers to more/better stuff during a run, which is useless, as you're steamrolling the game anyway. The interesting unlocks run out after 2-3 runs. New cards usually felt weak and didn't tie into any viable strategies.Difficulty modifiers looked interesting but fell flat in actual gameplay - they didn't really change your approach and actions during a run all that much.Hero unlocks were of course nice.Game seems to run out of new interesting/surprising battles quickly. The enemies, their setups and patterns feel very same-ish. Even though some enemy mechanics are very interesting at first. This includes bosses.The maps also become stale fast. Even with the difficulty changes that seemingly can modify them significantly.There also doesn't seem to be an exciting end goal. Lore is non-existent too, even though it tries to deceive you otherwise at first (not that StS had any lore :D but it helps! Monster Train did lightweight lore perfectly).Music feels super generic. My wife said it sounds like something an AI prompt generator would put together when you asked it for "fantasy game soundtrack". Compared to the quirky but memorable StS music and freaking masterpieces that blasted in Monster Train, it's just very disappointing.A nice but shallow and short-lived deckbuilder. Give it a try on a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook, simply put, is a very solid Roguelite deckbuilder. It is my personal favorite in fact, and I have tried games such as StS and Monster Train for comparison.The art is gorgeous, music is magical, and gameplay, addicting. My favorite innovations in this game are the drawing ink tiles within a book to create a path, and socketing gems into cards to alter the way they work, these are both very satisfying feeling mechanics.I will also admit that I am not very skilled at this game genre, so the fact that it has a meta progression helps players like me to make some progress without getting too much handholding. It helps mitigate frustration of feeling stuck while also slowly improving ones own skills in peace.The flaws for me being- game was/is a bit rough around the edges here and there, mostly when it comes to minor bugs and a bit of balancing. Yet, this is being improved upon very quickly, which I think is satisfactory enough. If you can handle the possibility that the game still may change a smidge, do get it. But if you abhor even the tiniest of differences, then wait a bit longer until it's fully settled after some more hotfixes/patches. This has personally not been an issue for me though. The game is fun, looks good, has unique mechanics vs others in the genre, and is addicting. It has meta progression in case you struggle. Still a bit buggy and is getting gradual balance/hotfix patches. I recommend it if you like similar games.

_childDocuments_.review: As you can see from my hours played, I’m a fan of Roguebook. It has some great and interesting ways to approach the deckbuilder genre. Copies things from tried-and-true mechanics, without making it feel like a ‘been there, done that’-game. It has some flaws and, unfortunately, some game-breaking bugsRoguebook is part of the ‘Faeria universe’, with a lot of the characters being familiar faces if you’ve ever played their first game (Faeria). You don’t need any prior knowledge of their first game to be able to enjoy this one. It’s not some complicated storyline, or has very in-depth lore for you to follow. Our heroes are trapped in the Roguebook and must fight their way through different chapters to free themselves, that’s the gist of it really. We have 4 heroes in the base game, 5 if you buy the DLC as well (which I can really recommend, the 5th hero is one of the best). We always play with 2 of them at a time. Where one hero is in the front row and the other’s in the back, these rows are an important part of how you’re playing your cards.  This ‘Faeria universe’ has a lot of heart, there are memorable allies and adversaries we face along our journey toward the end of the (rogue)book. There isn’t a lot of (spoken) dialogue but that doesn’t bother me at all within the deckbuilding genre. Every piece of lore or items you come across in-game have a small piece of info attached to it and that’s it really.When playing for the first time, you are getting a quick tutorial about how the UI works and what the basic attacking and defending mechanic is. If you are familiar with the deckbuilding genre you can skip all the info popping up, there’s nothing you haven’t seen before.Roguebook start with a basic deck, the enemies you face have their basic health pool and attack values. By completing different ‘epilogues’ as the game calls them you unlock more difficulty tiers to make the game harder. As a reward you find more pages, which are used to upgrade your heroes, gold, items and buffs. A bonus amount of pages is awarded if you play an epilogue tier with heroes you haven’t used to complete that tier before.  My experience after starting a fresh game (with all card and epilogue tiers locked again) is that the first 1 or 2 games are tough. You only have basic cards and gold, plus all the good cards are unlocked as our heroes gain experience. So our first steps are a bit of hit or miss. We are forced to use 2 heroes that do have a decent synergy but they are definitely not the best pairing the game has to offer. When we start to unlock our 2 missing heroes (you will find them across the different acts (of which there are 3), we have more options to choose from, this makes the game way easier to play. The thing is, depending on what your personal preference is of course, there are 3 really good heroes and the other 2 just feel like ‘ok if I have to play them’. There is one pairing that feels like they’re made for each other, which is amazing, but it makes the other pairings feel way less fun to play with. These 2 (Fugoro and Aurora) let you breeze through the game in the middle difficulty tiers.At the last 5 epilogue tiers Roguebook shows that it really can be a difficult game to master. Where each of the cards you’re choosing to add to your deck really are making a difference between life or death. I like my games to be tough but fair, I think Roguebook manages to achieve this most of the time. Downside is that after about 30 minutes in when doing a new ‘run’ you know if you’re deck is going to get you to the end or not. There is very little you can do to fix a deck that isn’t great to start with. Once you notice these patterns the game has it makes me want to drop the runs I know I’m going to die on, instead of trying to find something to make them work.It sucks to have to say this, but the patch history of Roguebook shows that the dev didn’t seem to care much about some of the game breaking stuff that can sometimes pop-up. The UI can sometimes not respond at all (especially when using flash gems), quitting the game will then let you completely lose the run you where on. The controller support is okay for the UI, but my DualSense controller isn’t able to select spots on the map that are at a diagonal position of where I am (So top left and right, plus bottom left and right). There are some UI-glitches, the mine you can enter can make your heroes get stuck and there are many more. By playing this game so much I know there are ways to get the game to respond again, but it’s not what you want to see really.I love Roguebook’s universe, a lot of the gameplay elements and the fact that it has a lot of interesting new ways to deal with things that can make deckbuilders feel like the same type of game but within a different world. It does however has flaws, and these flaws are sometimes things that are difficult to ignore. But it is an amazing game if you can see through that part. Love, PJ

_childDocuments_.review: First of all - Day 1 content DLC - Yuk.  Like everyone else I see this as a really bad decision.  The developers should quickly change the content to free and figure out some compensation for those that bought the DLC because the negative reviews flowing in from that decision will make a huge impact on total sales of the game.It also makes clear that all new content is going to be paid.  I think the 'living games' that continue to pump in new updates for free do a lot better financially through greatly increased total sales.  A later DLC that included a set of completely new lands to explore is something I would consider buying - but asking us to pay for some extra cards - nope.  Maybe the game designers Magic the Gathering background influenced them to think, "How can I get lots of extra ongoing income from all the people that buy this game?"I'm still giving a thumbs up though.  As well as bad decisions, there are some great ones.  The top one is permanent progress and real rewards for taking on higher difficulty.  Most deckbuilders they say, "Well done on beating the game - do you now want to cripple yourself in the next run?"Well, no, I don't really want to cripple myself.  It does not feel nice to make yourself weaker for no good reason.Roguebook says, "Do you want to make things harder... but we'll reward you for it."   Now that motivates me and is a nice target to work towards.I also enjoy the permanent progress aspects.  I beat the game on the second run, so agree with the dev's inputs that it is easy enough to beat without the permanent progress - although quite frankly I'm happy with being able to fail at the start like in Across the Obelisk.  I like to be rewarded for things in games and permanent progress is the best sort of reward - not just more cards which quite frankly often make you weaker most of the time.Graphics in the game are great.  Very polished, and good art really does make a difference.Gameplay - some interesting opponents with good imagination in their mechanics.  Moving towards combos feels a bit harder - and overall I feel that my combo strategies are more simplistic.  Perhaps I will find some more clever options as more cards are unlocked.... let's see.

_childDocuments_.review: Having completed all the Epilogues and just about everything there is to do in Roguebook, theres a lot I want to write about, but suffice to say it is a fantastic game. If you at all like card games, strategy, or deck builders, this game is worth playing. That being said I just wish there was more. After you beat the third boss, there are marginal goodies to be obtained by doing it again, and again, and again, but even though there are oh so many more choices than slay the spire, it still feels like the game should just be getting started, not ending so soon. This game at times feels more like an RPG with the excellent graphics, music and Faeria story behind it, rather than a deckbuilding game. And in that sense I feel the developers missed an opportunity. I just wish there was more. I wish the levels continued in ever increasing difficulty. I wish there was a sudden death mode with infinite bosses, no healing, more diverse battle effects, etc etc. They really could've gone much deeper with this. Instead, the epilogue difficulty challenges theyve added for replayability - like starting with less brushes or taking damage when you pick up gold - just in general make the game less fun rather than introducing a more innovative challenge. Most of my minor comments about Seifer being able to solo the whole run by himself, Sharra not being able to do anything, and really OP combos and RNG are being addressed. Just wish I was on the development team to take this game a little deeper into its potential, but I'm looking forward to seeing what else is added to the game in the future.Beautiful, innovative and original deckbuilding strategy game.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried all the popular single-player Roguelike deckbuilder games out there:-Slay the Spire-Monster Train-Griftlandsetc. etc.And to be honest, I just couldn't get into them. Even though I'm a huge fun of large multiplayer CCG type games like Eternal Card Game or Legends of Runeterra, the single-player equivalents just never did it for me. Every time I would play one, all I could think about was that I could be unlocking content or gaining rank in a much more challenging multiplayer CCG against real people who were much smarter and more interesting than the predictable computer opponents these single-player StS (and) clones have to offer.Roguebook is honestly the first StS-inspired deckbuilder I've actually enjoyed and doesn't constantly give me the feeling of being simply a lesser online digital cardgame.I think a lot of it has to do with the atmosphere. Just like Faeria, Abrakam has a mastery of a particular type of animation style, sound effects, and music. Ultimately, this game is  relaxing and enjoyable. When you play their games, it feels a bit like being transported to the Miyazaki/Studio Ghibli universe. The ambient environment is wonderful and as you progress through the game it feels as though you're slowly exploring a magical world, as opposed to grudgingly climbing the Spire for the 15 billionth time.I think that's one of the main reasons I never could get into StS. The gameplay may have been fantastic, but the animations, art style, environment, music, and theme itself was lackluster. I suppose the gameplay would technically be the same if the developer were just using stick figures and black cards with white text to display the decks, but for me that takes away from the enjoyment of the game.To each his own I guess, but if I'm going to play a single-player card game, it better have something pretty damn appealing outside of battles with a very predictable computer opponent, when I can play card games against real people who are much more interesting and intelligent for that purpose. So far, Roguebook has been the only one so far to achieve this and scratch that itch. A lot of the reviews seem to be critical, not of the game itself, but of the expensive pricetag and the day 1 DLC BS. All I can say is that if this is a Richard Garfield inspired game, what else do you expect?Garfield is a brilliant designer, but is well-known for his outrageously expensive pricing models, the like of which arguably killed Valve's Artifact. If you doubt this, simply consult anyone who has had to spend tens of thousands of dollars each year to play Magic the Gathering competitively.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a very rough start on launch, but now that the dust has kind of settled I have no problem recommending it to players. The company seems responsive to community feedback and has already made some decisions that signal that they are motivated to support the game in positive ways. For example, there was some major backlash for their day one content dlc, and in response they baked it into the base game and refunded everyone who purchased it. This kind of action lets me know that 1) they listen to their community and 2) they are motivated by things beyond simply maximizing profits. They really seem to want to make this game a real gem in the deckbuilding, roguelike genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Even now, the very first character you are given is terrible. And I do mean terrible. She runs a dagger style with a lot of low cost spammable cards. One of the Bosses. Spoiler. Spoiler. Makes your cards cost more. This means that she is about 1000% worse than any combination of the other three characters. I adore her style and theme, but in the end, she is a squishy character who doesn't even outdamage the tank. This means she loses Seif's survivability or Sirocco's utility for literally zero gain. She has a swapping place mechanic that literally needs the other hero to be good at buffing her minions. I get that you want to promote synergy and an approach where you make an overpowered deck. But. If the first elite of the game hits me for 45 damage when my highest block card is a 12. I am going to get punished for almost no fair reason. I see like any slay the spire type clone, you forgot that the LOWEST of RNG is actually supposed to still be playable at lower tiers. Good god. Not to mention, this game is clearly under $40 because it's bad. Not because it's just cheap. I do, however, think I will continue it, The nuances are plentiful and the gameplay can be very interesting. But until I see some sort of major redesign of the female sword wielder, she will not be used by me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of game where I wish Steam had a middle review score rather than positive or negative. Pros:The core game itself is good and fun, having two characters makes it so you want each of them to synergize as much as possible with how you build your deck as each character has their own cards that enters one deck.Beating the game allows you to replay with optional additional challenges so if you want more of a challenge you can build and customize it to your tastes and unlock even harsher challenges.A very easy to learn how to play kind of game.  The art is great and everything is visually appealing and fits well.Having to use brushes and ink which are very limited to open up more of the map makes exploration limited and meaningful.Cons:The bugs are the worst part of the game.  There are ones that are common that will cause crashes which can also end your current run making you lose progress.Performance issues,  sometimes slowdown happens whether it be a moment before a battle begins when it is usually basically instant or notable delay in playing cards and the actions actually taking place. These issues will never be fixed.   The games last patch was years ago so they just walked away even though the bug issue can be experience ruining.  Not much to unlock after beating the game.  Sure you can upgrade your characters and runs a bit (like start with more health and gold)  but many of the cards unlocked for characters aren't very efficient.    This makes additional challenges pointless as you'll never be properly rewarded.I want to recommend this game but can't because it was left in a state where the bugs are terrible.  Going into the mines gives me about a 1/3rd  chance of the game crashing.   The mines while optional also often contain some of the best things to pick up.    There is no excuse to leave a game unfixed with well known issues.   Good game, bad developer practices.

_childDocuments_.review: A great Slay the Spire-alike that focuses on deck *building*, rather than deck *culling*.  That is to say, Roguebook heavily encourages large deck sizes (over 30 cards by the end of the game) because of talents that unlock as your deck size crosses certain thresholds, and the near total lack of opportunities to remove unwanted cards.  This means you can't build your whole strategy around specific combos, because you're unlikely to get the cards you need on the same turn.  Instead, the goal is to build around a more general theme by collecting a lot of complementary cards.Roguebook, while obviously cribbing from StS and Monster Train, does enough differently to be worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Roguebook for a while now and there's something lacking in this deck builder that looks like it sets itself apart from other games of this type but doesn't really do anything new. While it's beautiful and challenging  and you have the whole ink reveal mechanic that offers a degree of flexibility I feel like there's some things missing from it to make it stand apart from the rest. First off you're thrust into this book that gives the impression that there's some deep story here. Some reason why you're trapped in this book. You start off with 2 very distinct character types and have the chance to unlock 2 more during your runs but there's very little substance connecting them as to why they're running together. I finished the game and played through the Epilogue twice but it's pretty much more of the same. Maybe it’s my mistake for equating book to story. Okay I’ll own that assumption but then what else does this game have to offer? After 20 hours of playing I’m not quite sure. Progression just feels stagnant.The thing it does offer is a significant scale up in challenge once you unlock the Epilogue and add modifiers. But once you figure out which synergies work with all the character pairs you kind of just stick with that to win what battles you can. RNG and luck play just as much or are worth more than actual strategy in most boss battles. Is there more to this game I’ve yet to uncover? Probably, but there’s not enough going on to keep my attention long enough for me to find out. It's not bad but there's much better games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid rogue-like deckbuilder with gorgeous, striking artwork, a map to explore and loot in-between combat, and interesting choices to make, though doesn't have the same challenge, longevity or depth as Slay the Spire or Griftlands.𝓰𝓪𝓶𝓮𝓹𝓵𝓪𝔂It's a typical rogue-like deckbuilder where you are given access to a variety of cards depending on which characters you have in your party, and you unlock more cards and perks through runs with the characters, levelling up, and collecting "pages". The card combos and character identities in this game are solid, and you play around having two characters of your choosing in your party, allowing you to set up for synergies between them. The battles are clear and easy-to-read, and the gameplay is intuitive, if not maybe too much so? I find Roguebook a lot easier than Slay the Spire and Griftlands, and there seems to be much less nuance and creativity in combining certain cards together. The combos you can do are fairly obvious, and there aren't really a lot of hidden synergies or hidden OP combos to discover. It doesn't feel immensely rewarding as the other two games do, and runs in Roguebook are much easier to complete. In saying that, there are difficulty modifiers you can add as you keep beating the game, but it doesn't feel like the same difficult challenge as other games. Most of the modifiers are to do with the way the map works rather than combat, making the fights feel largely the same even as you unlock more things. There aren't a lot of bosses to see, either, and with the way the map works, runs can be strangely short with the RNG aspect -- though, runs will get progressively longer as you unlock perks that allow you to game the map overworld in a way that benefits you.Which brings me to: the thing that I both like about Roguebook and find a chore sometimes is that you have to be pretty strategic about exploring the map to find treasures and gold. The way the map works is, you start on a bunch of hexes and have to use a paintbrush to uncover more hexes which may contain loot, card upgrades, money or enemies. You basically walk around clearing the fog of war to gather the most resources you can before facing the boss of the stage. The part I like about this is that it can be fun -- it also breaks up the gameplay loop a bit so you aren't quite fatigued out by the battles -- and you can find yourself picking up a ton of treasures and cards. The part I don't like about this is that it can also sometimes feel way too tedious or RNG if you end up uncovering squares that are largely useless and then, that's it, you're out of paintbrushes to explore with, and you're on your way to fight the boss feeling like you have almost nothing in hand. Even if you play every encounter correctly, you can feel like you aren't rewarded because you had an unlucky go with the map. As a result, runs can feel super long or super short, entirely based on this overworld exploration system rather than battling. Of course, as mentioned above, as you progress the game, you unlock more perks that skew the overworld exploration in your favour, but the fact that the progression in this game relies so heavily on improving the map's gameplay loop makes it feel a little unrewarding -- I personally feel like the card battling should be the game's bread and butter, not the exploration and looting.A few other minor mentions, mechanic-related and QoL-related: - Cards in Roguebook have gem slots, which is certainly unique, allowing you to modify your cards with effects such as "this card gains +5 damage" or "draw a card, discard a card", giving you a bit of flexibility to come up with unique combinations.- There are cards in this game that allow you to summon allies, and each round these allies will attack for however much "spirit" they have -- this currently seems incredibly overpowered since there's not many ways enemies can get rid of your allies, and you can just turtle and win out a battle this way.- There are some battles in this game that just feel like boring DPS checks or defense checks, which makes it feel unsatisfying to get any custom or interesting builds off the ground- It's difficult to trim your deck in this game- The loading speed between battles or chapters can sometimes be so long that you think the game has crashed. I'm not sure why this is the case, but I know I'm not alone here- I wish you could scroll around the overworld map to have a quick peek at corners, but as it is, if you want to see what treasure was in the left corner of the map, you have to walk back there yourself just for a quick look𝓼𝓽𝓸𝓻𝔂Basically, you're stuck in a book and you need to find your way out, and you do that by completing runs. It's... it's a story that justifies you doing repeat run-throughs adequately enough and it's entirely just in the background. It's a roguelike deck-builder, there's not much to expect here. It's a nice setting, though, and there's an interesting world lurking in the background what with the different races and characters and hints of lore from the world of Faerie. 𝓶𝓾𝓼𝓲𝓬It's pretty and sweeping and dramatic, but I did end up muting it eventually. Don't get me wrong, it's solid and nice. I just like listening to my own music while playing deckbuilders.𝓪𝓮𝓼𝓽𝓱𝓮𝓽𝓲𝓬𝓪𝓵𝓵𝔂For me, the aesthetics of Roguebook is one of its strongest points. All the artwork looks very picture-esque and out of an artbook or compendium or book of myths. It's colourful and the designs are striking and gorgeous, and it looks beautiful both in still-frame and in-motion. The enemies are weird but memorable, and even the map is pretty as you plod along it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this at release and it just wasn't ready. Now it is, no more game breaking bugs or loading issues. As for the game, it is beautiful and I was easily addicted for 50+ hours. I've played a few deckbuilder rogue games and this is definitely worthwhile. It's not quite the fast paced action that Slay the Spire provides, but it's immersive enough and did I mention the art? It's really pretty :-)
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Either I'm a strategic genius (I'm not) or the game is just too easy, but I managed to beat on the first run. On my second run, it crashed mid-session, and my save is gone. Many compare it to Slay the Spire, but I don't feel it has the same depth. The price is kinda steep, and the whole game feels like it should still be in early access. I'd prefer to give a neutral review because it's not really bad, but not that good either. If you are interesed buy it on sale or from Humble Bundle in the January choice, but you might be better off to buy Slay the Spire or Monster Train. 5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a pretty obvious copy of Slay the Spire. Everyone who likes Slay the Spire will likely also enjoy Roguebook as it solves some of the short comings in Slay the Spire.Every Run consist of a team of two (out of four) heroes. All combinations are viable and play different. The addition of a world map stage, which tiles need to be revealed with ink and brushes won in the fights, is a nice touch. Unlike like Slay the Spire a run isn't automatically doomed after a bad fight, players can try find some source of (mild) healing before tackling the next enemy. Cards are upgraded with gems either found on the map, narrative events or won in elite fights. Each type of gem adds a different boost or effect to a card, most cards have only a single slot. The focus should definitely be put in exploration and clearing as much of a stage as can be revealed before continuing as the Boss fight at end of stage 3 is underwhelming, there seem to be only two variants and both are relatively weak in comparison to other bosses and even some of the elite monsters.During every run players collect pages of the Roguebook which are the games currency for progression. Players can use those pages to buy embellishments of their story which will ease the experience of the next run (e.g. finding more gems, starting with more gold, health, better cards, finding more stuff). This is balanced by the Epilogue system which is this games version of the Ascension mode. Each Epilogue run allows players to pick up to three modifiers which nicely mixes up the experience.Overall a a very nice iteration of a working game concept with some great improvements and only minor draw backs (e.g. almost no way to remove cards again). Recommended. On that note, the DLCs (included in DeluxEdition) are a heaping pile of dung and add next to nothing to the game. If the base game is cheaper than the DeluxEdition buy that instead!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is yet another "Slay the Spire"-like. The main difference is the overworld, which replaces predefined paths with hex grid exploration. It's a great idea that I like very much. Unfortunately what I don't like is the core of the game, the combat. It feels unbalanced, enemies hit hard, grow in power very quickly, but cards do not and healing is scarce. I thought it might get better with some unlocks but those require lots of grind so I just gave up.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I think I prefer it to other deckbuilders I've played, since the decks feel a lot more like a CCG like Magic. The characters that you combine cardpools from remind me a bit of the color wheel from MtG. Likewise with the way drafting works and how you can kind of force an archetype, compared to other games where you often end up forced to build around whatever you find on that run. I also really enjoy the hex based exploration and find it's a lot more compelling than picking lanes in Slay the Spire.I think Slay the Spire might be a bit tighter tuned and might have more longevity due to it's more rogue-like difficulty and random items, but I may actually enjoy RB more.Game also seem ripe for expansion.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, though there are a few mechanics that are anti-fun for the player (chief among them being that the last boss regularly removes cards from your deck for the whole fight when it damages you, meaning you literally have no deck to draw in 7 or so turns.  Not sure who on the dev team thought that was a fun or engaging mechanic).The simple fact is that this game is not done.  It crashes regularly.  Had 4 CTDs in as many hours, and my last run was softlocked because the game would crash any time I tried to initiate a combat.  Do not buy this game until it is stable.  Fun when it works, great art style and cool world design... But failing to launch a stable game is failing to meet the bare minimum, sadly.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I don't write reviews. I am making a an exception for this exceptional game. This has every bit of replay-ability of slay the spire. It offers so much more though! I has tons of beautiful fights, nice voice acting, exploration and customization with a randomness that I love. Every play-through offers novelty, challenge and plenty of nice visuals. Best Deck builder I have played to date.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Only fun for a couple of hours. There is a dominant strategy in the game (Sharra Daggers) and you should always aim to build that deck, as it is the most reliable to get and the most powerful when assembled. This lack of variation is 'fixed' by subtracting from your metaprogression resource when dropping a run. Overall just bad design behind some fantastic artwork. At this point, we must seriously question if Richard Garfield ever tests his own games.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have many hours in the game, but it seems overly difficult for no reason. I'm a big souls-like player so bashing my head against a wall over and over again is nothing new to me. This is a fair warning to anybody new to the genre, or anybody thinking of picking this up rather than it's competitors; it's absurdly difficult. No way to remove wounds so they clog up your hand, after the first boss everything hits like a truck. Just be warned that you will get frustrated at first. Perhaps it will get easier once I unlock more cards but for right now, the difficulty spike is almost a deterrent, and I'd rather avoid as much combat as necessary.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: So I actually like this game but am giving it a negative review for one very specific reason and it's a matter of principle.After playing it for a number of hours I couldn't figure out why some of the achievements and one of the characters weren't being unlocked. Apparently there are additional expansion packs you have to purchase in order to unlock these achievements and this additional character in which some of the achievements are dependent upon. In my opinion this is ridiculous. It makes it feel like I only purchased part of the game and the rest of the game is behind an additional purchase. It shouldn't be impossible to get 100 percent achievements without additional money spent. For whatever game I purchased, I should be able to get all the achievements with enough time.For example, there are these things called "embellishments" in the game that you purchase via in game capital that you've earned from your play through's, in order to boost future play through's. There is an achievement for purchasing a single iteration of each embellishment on the embellishment tree. Well not only did I purchase a single purchase of each embellishment I purchased all possible iterations of each embellishment so that there were no more possible embellishments to purchase but I still have not unlocked the achievement. The only logical conclusion is that I need to purchase an expansion in order to unlock additional embellishments in order to acquire the achievement for the original product.It's one thing if the developers want to have expansions to make additional money on the product, I don't have a problem with that. But don't include the achievements and character in the original product.Because of this, I will refrain from future purchases of their products which is disappointing because I was actually enjoy this effort and would have likely made future purchases for the long term. However on principle I will avoid them in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly the game I was looking for after completing both Slay the Spire and Monster Trains.It copies the key aspects of the above-mentioned games and adds an extra layer of depth on top of that.Exploration is extremely rewarding; it feels great to find (literally) a boost to your current strategy.I can see myself easily sinking 50+ hours into this game.Highly recommended for all fans of deckbuilding games.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: The game balance falls apart after your first run.The devs made deck-bloating a feature in this game, but forgot to balance the enemies and rules around this system. Some runs become a slog because perks are hidden behind RNG and card number requirements, and some enemies just outright counter big deck. There are so little ways to draw or search cards that late game bloat decks become a shallow shell of your original build.I tried it and didn't like it, but the game may be solid for other players.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only at level 6 of unlocking the difficulty ranks, but it feels like there's decent diversity to the gameplay and it scratches the itch for when you want more Slay the Spire / Monster Train but aren't in the mood for Slay the Spire or Monster Train.Doesn't quite have the same level of polish as StS/MT and feels like balance is still a work in progress.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: A less grim-dark, more charming, fun deck-builder that is different in several ways from most deck-builder games:- Runs take a bit longer -- but when I thought I had played for a few hours my playtime was 7 hrs! (time flies with fun)- Easier than most Rogues -- you won't have to lose a lot at the start while you build up things that carry over from run to run.  I've done 8 runs and won 6 so it's different.- Overworld exploration mechanic is unique- Deck builds are all about adding cards, not about pruning your deck down- Card upgrade and gem mechanic works pretty well, but is less often than in most games- Much less variation in runs due to rogue mechanics (if you play character X it won't vary much from run to run)- A neat mechanic for each character attacking with their own cards with some nice design around that- Even though there are just 4 playable characters, there is some fun in trying different character combo-pairs for runs.Overall it's a nice spin on a deck builder game.  Even the new mechanics had me interested and were easy to get into and start min-maxing with.  I'd recommend it if you enjoy games like StS and want to try something a bit different in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Good game is good.The thing I like most about Roguebook is the exploration element that it offers for a roguelite deckbuilder. Not only are you crafting your deck, but you are also strategically moving across the map, painting it with your brushes and inks that you get from battles, which informs where you might want to go next. This breaks away from the linearity of games like Slay the Spire and Monster Train where you have a series of branching paths to take. You have a choice of 4 heroes (2 of which you unlock as you play the game), that offer their own selection of cards to create your deck with. The synergies are pretty interesting to experiment with and the mechanics of the cards are varied enough that no one particular hero falls into a pigeon-holed niche. The mechanics of having two heroes swapping back and forth takes some getting used to, but once you go through a few runs you start to figure out how everything works together.Not that I have any complaints, but I definitely would like to see more enemy variation down the road. After playing so many runs, you'll start to get into the same routine with what you expect with the somewhat limited enemy pool from each chapter. Each fight is challenging and engaging in its own right, don't get me wrong, but it does get a bit predictable. I will also mention that it is occasionally buggy with the predictive damage outputs. Sometimes I will have armor values that pop up at the beginning of battles that shouldn't be there or sometimes enemies will do more damage than their attack says they will, but nothing earth-shattering.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: For the price and other similar games already out, I don't recommend this. I was about too with all the hours I put in but I seem to have only put down the bad stuff this game has. Not saying this is a terrible game, it does have a lot of good in it. Just the bad stuff really keeps me from saying "hey man, if you really want to have fun with a rogue like game then try this one!"This game seems really unbalanced with the enemies you get to face and what your characters have to offer. Even normal enemies will have boss like skills and sometimes you'll see an enemy that is about to do 40 points or more of damage. I enjoy the tier list you get as you collect more cards. I enjoy how you have different means to attack (ally, normal card hit, bleed, ect.) and the kind of blocking cards that work well with other set of cards. I do enjoy the two team combo and sometimes they do wonders together. There are some things I do enjoy but I am not a fan of seeing a normal enemy that has a certain move set that I have no counter for. Either taking a huge lose of life or having the game to be over. I know I know, try to collect cards for all the different monsters. But it isn't simple as that because you might never see any cards that can counter or your deck will be too large and before you can draw it the damage is already done.Lets talk about the scrolls you collect with each play. You will gather some scrolls that will allow you to improve your game to make it easier and more interesting. However, only very few I go "hmm this can do me a whole lot of good" while the others I am like "sure, I got the scrolls to throw away". Having this talent tree always set is a good idea, but the things on it doesn't seem to be very helpful in the long run. Even those that will be good no matter what because they require a lot of scrolls which means you have to grind it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Having played nearly every deck builder from slay the spire and monster train to fights in tight places, I can safely say this is up there with the slay the spire and will a classic to remember in the deck building genre. In nearly all respects the game is just a higher budget version of slay the spire, and that's a good thing. However, the game does have a few different enough mechanics to separate it from the slay the spire like its two hero system that it borrows from monster train. My only complaint is I want more and then I remember I only spent $25 and it was worth every penny. I have 18 hrs at time of review but by the time you are reading this i'll probably be well over 100
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I like it, but honestly, how many times am I going to play a re-tooled Slay The Spire? I don't care that this was made in part by the creator of MTG. The idea was perfected by STS and now I'm in clone hell.I'm recommending the game simply because it does what it sets out to do. But even with the inking system, there's nothing new here. I know, I know, you're probably saying, "Well what did you expect?".You're right. I won't argue with you. So all of that aside, it's still a very good game. And just because I'm not moist with glee about it doesn't mean that you won't love it. You probably will. It's just that I'm tired of playing someone else's version of the same old worn-out trope. Now who are you people and where is my horse?
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a no brainer to try if you like games like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Griftlands etc. At 23 hours I feel I have enough time in to write a review!First thoughts: The game art/ music/ battles are super nice and fun! There is some issue with input delay, like you'll go to select a card to play, and it won't play, and sometimes it led me to accidentally play a card I did not mean to play. This is a small technical thing that I feel could be patched in the future and provide a better, less frustrating experience! -Another first thought was that the map seemed a bit empty. Not a lot of items to find, just a lot of empty hexes, but I quickly realized that the further you progress, the more items you'll find in your hexes when revealing the map! So this didn't bug me anymore.-Progression seemed slow at first compared to other roguelites, but I found myself completely addicted to just keep doing more and more runs until I got it right. Now I can't put the game down!There is a tournament mode, and a New game + mode (which is similar to ascensions in other roguelites),and it's super satisfying that they give you some options on how you want to play the epilogue chapters at first without choosing you to go down one path. Overall, I am suuuuper happy I bought this game! I purchased the DLC Character, and I will definitely purchase more in the future if they are released.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of card games since the early 90's and a deckbuilding fan in more recent years, I'm having a lot of fun with this one. The visuals and the musical score support the card game really well to create a beautiful fantasy setting, as you'd expect from the makers of Faeria.The game itself is fun to play and addictive. It's new, but feels familiar and the balance feels right to me. I'm still playing at the starting level, but managed to finish 2 of my first 4 runs while trying out the characters. There's plenty of chances to push your luck and many different synergies and mechanics to twist and abuse to build a deck around.Easily worth the full price if you like games like Slay the spire (this one is much prettier) or Monster Train (another hidden gem of the genre IMO).---Little edit since I played about 30/40 more hours since this review was posted. Basically, I stand by what I said. This is a VERY nice game that I find myself getting back to and really scratches the Tabletop/card game itch for me. Highly recommended.---Over 100+ hours in. Still having fun and finding myself relaunching this game every now and then for another go. Great stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game with potential to be even better. It is massively fun, the graphics are beautiful to the eye, kind of charming even though cartoonish. Sound design is awesome and the game structure is solid, as a card game it is pretty solid. The mechanics are simple and satisfying. I would like more content to revisit and play even more, because after a few runs it gets old. Unlock all cards and some kind of skill tree and that's that.

_childDocuments_.review: Good: game is fun. If you like slay the spire/monster train, you will like this game. There are a bit more hero mechanics (like front hero and back hero) compared to StS. Artstyle is the best IMO among the hundreds of similar roguelike deck builder.Meh: The 'unique' aspect of this game is that you traverse through the map in 'civ like' style, but I dont find that aspect to be particularly fun or exciting, just a minor annoyance compared to the more straight forward choose left and right path (like StS/Monster train). It makes a already heavy RNG game even more RNG based (you may struggle to find heal for example if your path reveal is unlucky)Bad: it crashes fairly regularly. game crash when I progress from chapter 1 to chapter 2 around 50% of the time. In my 4h of play, it crashed around 3 times. Also encountered some janky visual/UI in game. For example, every time I face Azure wisp, there are a turn where they have the shield but it won't show up on screen (and I only know because my attack dont register). The enemy attack effect is also not communicated properly. For example, there's an enemy that gives you 5 bleed if it hits you, but in no way you will know that just by playing it first time, you only know through trial and error, once you get hit by her. Finally, achievement is also bugged. I lost against 'Avatar of Greed', and yet I got the achievement of my beating it when I got the game over screen.Overall: 7.5/10, above average rougelike deckbuilder, that is if you ignore the crashes and bad UI. It is currently only polished in artwork but underneath the pretty art, the game is not very polished.It is inbetween and yes or no for recommendation, but because of the regular crashes and numerous bad UI decision that affect gameplay, I will just put this as a no for now.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting deck builder. I'm not sure how long this will stay fun, but so far I'm enjoying myself. If you've played Slay the Spire and Monster Train, you know the genre well. If not, go back and play those first - see if you enjoy them and then play them some more. After that, you can try finding new variants on the genre.Roguebook is one such variant. You have a map exploration 'minigame' which is satisfying. You also have a simple system; you pick two heroes and the card-pool is based on the two picked. The basegame has 4 heroes to choose from and there is 1 dlc hero. You can already try the 5th hero sometimes in the daily challenge runs, as the heroes are predetermined. The balancing is.. fine. There are very clearly better and worse strategies, and with okay luck the game is on the easier side. Personally I thought the challenge enjoyable, you can try to go for weird strategies if you want to have a more challenging game, and there is also an ingame 'challenge' system to raise the difficulty.The artwork is 90% the same as it was in the developers previous game Faeria (which as a purely cardgame is still a very underappreciated gem). So on the one hand there is a lot of re-use of assets, on the other hand it also means the game looks very nice and has a strong visual style - much better than a lot of copy-cats in the genre.Something that can be seen as a flaw is the length of an average run. It easily takes 1,5 hours+ to complete a single run which is on the longer side for the genre. Saving mid-game works, but it's a bit wonky sometimes. Lastly, every run has an idiotic "review" button at the bottom, but perhaps that's them trying to find a way to get activity on their game seeing as to how their previous game Faeria died a slow death.Definitely though, for fans of the genre this game is an easy recommendation. I'm considering buying the DLC character, and would probably buy more if they would release them.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This game gave me my "Slay The Spire" fix (after playing Downfall). The tactical combat is fun without being too complicated.. You can't remove cards, so there is less deck building strategyzing during the same run, but you get four characters, each with their own cards, and for each run you pick two, which makes for a good amount of combinationThe overland is a map that you need to "paint" to discover, which adds a nice layer to is (while being visually pleasant).

I now have to re-unlock Siefer, and regrind a win, AND regrind 30+ pages which is kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nightmare since I don't have a bunch of the upgrades I unlcoked, AND I just lost what is 100% my fave character AND several levels on the characters I do have. _childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game; but there are a couple of things that bug me.1) I would like the opportunity to scroll out and see the whole map.  Very irritating to have to walk around to look at whatever your runes discovered.2) I know it's a rogue-like; I play a LOT of them, but the monster damage vs. your damage/defense is very unbalanced.  They can do 50+ damage and you can only block a fraction of that. And monster damage is very unbalanced right out the gate. Granted, there are cards that help balance that but not enough. 3)There needs to be a way to recover your health besides 10 hp for both of you at once.  What if one char has 4hp left and the other one is at full health? 4) There should be a way to remove cards from your deck.5) Why do your character upgrades come from your card add amount in deck?  They should come with # of monsters killed, or number of hexes uncovered.  Having a thin well-working deck is an art.6) Death system is too punishing.  Wound cards you can't get rid of and keep racking up more and more.The art is nice and the story is fine. It's very fairy-taleish.  It's kept me fairly busy this weekend, but overall I'm not super happy I spent 24.99 on it.  At this point I would only recommend if it was on sale (9.99? 12.99?) and you are a patient person not likely to throw your laptop against a wall.If the devs actually fix some of these issues then i think this game has some real promise.  I will come back to this in the future when I've exhausted Across the Obelisk, which is also punishing but in a *fun* way.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I never really got into Slay the Spire, despite enjoying watching others play it. The main things that turned me off were having only 1 character, and not really having what felt like a world to explore. Roguebook is basically Slay the Spire, but with 2 person teams and a map you explore. Needless to say, I am loving it. On top of the StS-esque mechanics, it adds sockets to cards which allow you to place gems that modify their effects in various ways; basic gems might grant you a card draw or cost reduction, while legendary gems can do incredibly fun things like adding a second copy to your hand or putting the card back on top of your draw pile.If that wasn't enough, you also have 'embellishments', which are basically a meta-progression talent tree where you purchase levels using the pages you acquire from your runs. Between the gems, talents, picking which of the 3 secondary characters you want each run, the unique card pools for each character, and the decision-making involved in how you choose to use your limited ability to reveal the hidden map tiles, this game offers a level of strategic depth that's very compelling, while also being straightforward enough to pick up the basics very quickly. And the art style makes it a joy to look at.My only real complaint so far is that there are only 3 stages to beat per run. I hope they add more as time goes on!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not big on writing reviews I have always been of the mind that you should just let the game speak for itself and if someone wanted to know more about a game they could just look up a video.. that being said I really love the art style that being of the faeria universethe game will start you off on a kind of practice run but the real fun starts after you finish your baby run I'm enjoying the extra challenges the Epilogues are providing, the randomness of the tournaments are fun to experience too :Pif you see this game on sale or just love the look of it I highly recommend adding it to your games collection :)
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: If you've gotten bored with Slay the Spire and Monster Train, this is worth considering. It's not nearly as good, but it's not bad either.Fundamentally, this is a well designed deckbuilder. The overworld exploration is a nice change from the branching predefined paths of most other games in this genre, but almost everything in this game feels more restrictive. A lot of relatively basic gameplay features are locked behind the meta-progression which makes very early runs feel more like required grinding than legit runs, and it feels like there are generally fewer viable final boss capable builds.I'm also not a huge fan of the art style, but I didn't like the art style in Slay the Spire much either and still played a lot of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very deep deck-building rogue-like strategy game with beautiful graphics, amazing music, and superb sound. The variety of enemies and their strategies they use against you are diverse, intriguing, creative, and challenging. I first played this on Stadia (RIP) and fell in love with it. I play at least one round almost every day (through one level) since I bought it. You can unlock challenges, new cards, and more, and after 115 hours of play on Steam, I will have not unlocked all the levels. The four different characters can be combined in any pairing you like, which gives this immense replayability as you try out strategies to see how the pair can work together. For example, one character might unlock many ally cards, while the other character can pump up those summoned allies. The combinations are very diverse and deep enough to keep me coming back to play out different ideas of how to beat the game.I am still not sure how the levels work, with the different challenges. I just recently realized you can combine more than one challenge (for example, when you pick up gold, take damage, but also you have to beat all the elite bad guys). The game does a great job teaching you how to play, but I wish there were a better explanation of how the challenges unfold and how to choose them.So you read this far and are getting ready to tell me in the comments, “How can you say this is the best game of its type when “Slay the Spire” is so much better?” Well, I disagree. I like them both as equally as you can like two games that do have some vast differences, despite both being deck-building rogue-likes. I played “Roguebook” first then discovered that “Slay the Spire” came first. I then bought “Slay the Spire” as well, and think it is equally amazing. It is subtle differences between the two, but these two tie as far as which one I favor because “Slay the Spire” is a bit unbalanced at times--I can blow through the first level no problem, then get destroyed in the next one by the first battle, whereas “Roguebook” is a bit more balanced in the rogue-like portion and feels less punishing; plus, having two characters as opposed to the one character in “Slay the Spire” gives it more dimension in strategy. Having said that, “Slay the Spire” just feels more elegant and simple in a good way, whereas “Roguebook” has a map that adds to the game, but can also make it a bit harder than it needs to be. Flip a coin--they are both fantastic at what they do. So what if you could only buy one of them? Wait for a sale, and buy both!This is complicated. It plays well, but has two issues, one of them solved with a pair of eyeglasses. The text in some portions is so small, even on a big TV, so be sure your eyeglass prescription is up to date. The other more troubling issue is that at times when I connect a controller (PS5 or Stadia via Bluetooth), when you move the joystick, the selection box moves at 100 miles per hour across your choices, almost like it is reading the input too rapidly--the box shoots across the dozen cards, past the one you want. This only happens about a third of the time I fire up the Steam Deck, and restarting does not solve it. No idea why it happens. So you might say you could just use the D-pad to single tap, but guess what--that input it mapped to another function, so you have to use the joystick to pick cards. I sort of solved this by remapping the controls so I can use the D-pad, but then that removes a function in the game that requires the D-pad; having said that, I rarely need or use that function, so it works well enough. All of this joystick issue can be avoided if you use a mouse, but this is a couch game for me, so I really want to use the controller, not the mouse. This issue never happened on Stadia for me, so it must be something about how the Deck interprets the controller signal over bluetooth.The full price of $25 is not too much. It is the most I would pay, but you can easily find it on sale for under $20, so if you are still playing “Slay the Spire,” wait for a sale!

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best fully released roguelike deck-builder since Monster Train. I love that it's not just Slay the Spire combat, but they added a somewhat unique positional element by having you switch your heroes between the back and front row for all kinds of tactical effects. The overworld exploration part also feels very rewarding and varied and it's interesting to optimize your brush / ink usage to reveal different hex tile patterns and work your way towards watch towers (that reveal even more tiles) or specific treasures (this game's relics) you want for your build.In true Richard Garfield "think on your feet" fashion you are confronted with countless little randomized options on how to refine your build (via cards, treasures, gems you put into cards à la Vault of the Void, or traits you get for having a bigger deck which is another unique twist on the typical "thin out all the trash" gameplay of these games). You will rarely (be able to) do the same thing you did in the run before. The four characters (making for 6 possible duo parties) are well-defined and offer a variety of builds and synergies. Even the difficulty options add to that aspect on top, since you put together a set of (sometimes quite game-changing) modifiers instead of just going through generic "enemies have more HP/damage" levels.One thing that's rather "meh" currently are the two final boss variants. One of them eats your cards, the other makes them cost more. Both feel quite "anti deck-builder" in that whatever well-oiled machine you constructed up to that point might suddenly not work anymore and you can't really play around it much in the fight itself (as opposed to e.g. Monster Train). I also could do without the meta-game progression personally (especially the "+X% chance to blah") but I've seen worse. Some unlocks even make the game more interesting.All in all a great entry to the genre and an easy pickup if you consider yourself a roguelike card game afficionado!

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game. In the realm of deck builders, this is definitely on the better side of things. The map exploration mechanics are a nice touch, each of the characters feel different enough to matter, and there's plenty of replay value. Much of the art is pretty great, colorful, and none of the combat ever feels trivial.I only have a few quibbles... A head banging ogre just doesn't work for me (it really is just an odd decision), and in a world with so many cool characters and endless possibilities, we have a human princess? Yawn! Missed opportunity there. Ogre? Neat! Fuzzy Kobold? Awesome! A turtle?! Fantastic! Human? Eh.Those small (and purely subjective) things aside, this is a good choice if you like deck builders.

_childDocuments_.review: To my opinion, Roguebook is the true sucessor to Slay The Spire.+ Gorgeous graphisms+ Solid gameplay+ Interesting difficulty settings- Too many drafted cards per run which ruins the importance of choice- Relics are a bit boring (like in most deckbuilders :/)Edit : don't listen to the bad faith negative reviews, the game is stable (I encountered 0 bugs during my last 30h), there is only one real dlc to buy and it's optionnal, and it contains a looot of content.While the game doesn't add a lot to the deckbuidling genre, everything it countains is executed with great mastery. The main innovation is obviously the fact that your deck is a mix of your 2 character's deck. Adding cards gives rewards (although they aren't all great), and there are no ways to remove some to compensate, so be careful not getting greedy ! It also has a strong take on exploration, moving from tile to tile, discovering events that make you powerful among other treasures ! There are 4 characters + 1 from DLC, which in turns leave plenty of combinations, and overall, it is very generous in content (3 last bosses !). The little yikes are that you can draft so many cards and loot/buy so many items that you might see all of it very quickly. Also, plenty of items don't offer a cool interaciton, more like the usual +1 Power kekw.Unlike most deckbuilders, Roguebook is a rogue-lite. Beating bosses and exploring is rewarded with pages, a money to buy neat upgrades with that make you stronger. Broken difficulty you'd say? Nop, thanks to the Epilogue system that offers an ever increasing challenge along with a few rule twists that I'd like to see more in the genre (not just "+50% enemies' muscle size").There is no big narrative, but a few fight puzzles here and there.Personal note : 8/10Gorgeous, effective, and vastly superior to Slay The Spire. If you liked Faeria art direction, you will love this one. The animations and enemy arts feel like 3d although everything is 2d. The level in this studio is simply insane ! Personal note : 10/10Excellent soundtracks are probably one of the hardest thing to produce in a video game, probably because of the overwhelming amount of video games these days. Standing out from the crowd on the musical level is hard, and Roguebook doesn't win this bet. On a more positive note, all sound effects are neat, and I like most voice-lines. "Wake up, weakling !"Personal note : 7/10Despite its early balance issues, Roguebook is now an excellent game. Actually, I would suggest anyone that would like to introduce in the genre to start from this game. It starts kind of easy, but adding epilogue will put your skills to the tests ! Maybe the game lacks depth in the items, and it certaintly gives too much per run. It is possible to go for the strongest builds  almost every run. However, I always enjoy playing again, testing out a new build and enjoy this great piece of art :)

_childDocuments_.review: So, how should I start? First thing of, I think this game is really, really, really good.I really love deckbuilding games and I played most of them (slay the spire, monster train, ring of pain, griftlands, Banner of Ruin, Inscryption, etc. ), and I think this game excels in every aspect of gameplay when most of them lack (expect inscryption).The cards battling aspect is very good, even if most of the effects are a little basic, You can have fun with it, and You can try different types of decks/builds using different types of heroes.But the real highlight of this game, for me, is the map and how you can navigate it, most of the roguelite I played have a linear map and very specific set of choices, in this game you can navigate the map in a "sandbox" kind of way, You decide freely where to go, how, and when: at the cost of resources dropped in the map! _childDocuments_.review: Great fun, would recommend for any fans of rogue-like deck builders. This is one of those games that keeps pulling you back for one more run. After 80 hours with Epilogue 15 cleared with all hero combinations, I have definitely had my $20 worth of entertainment. - Beautiful art style and animations- Addictive - Refreshing change as the game encourages "fat decks" - Combos and synergies between heroes are really satisfying- Epilogue, Roguebook's endgame, allows you to choose your own difficulty ramp which is a great addition and reminiscent of Hades Heat system- The game can be brutally frustrating due to RNG elements and scaling of enemies. Only two of the four characters have AoE abilities which can make certain boss fights or encounters much more difficult and only some characters have access to certain keywords. - Game crashes fairly often- Lack of content compared to other established games in genre (Monster Train, StS) although the most recent patch has added new Ep levels and run tracking which is a nice addition. [h4] Wishlist and fixes [/h4]- I would love to see more heroes added in or different Acts- Rebalancing cost for Gem Mines - I think that this should be reduced to 1 Brush or an ink + Brush as there isn't really that much value in a Gem Mine aside from a guaranteed Well or Alchemist. The Gem/Treasure offered might not have any benefit to your run and taking the Gem Fights can stop you from ramping enough to fight the elites/bosses. - Legendary card balance and keyword availability between heroes which can make or break a run at higher difficulties (example being Aurora sole access to Timestop, Protection (Fist + Forcefield) and Humbling Vision making her utility way ahead of other characters). For example in comparison to Sorocco, who is the other "support hero" and his defensive legendary cards at a similar cost for 4 energy with melee, Gain 8 Block + 3 whenever you add a treasure (Hoardshell) versus completing skipping an enemy's turn = 0 damage (Timestop). When enemies are hitting for 60-80 in a single hit or 40x 3 hits end game at EP15, the difference between blocking vs completely stopping a turn or halving enemy attack is insane. - Flurry is also broken for me, please fix as I love that card.
