_childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a 7/10, having played most big Roguelite Deckbuilders in the past years. To sum it up, get it on sale 100%, If you are a sucker for the genre get it at any price.First lets start with the Cons:- Game is not fully polished, some minor bugs can be found here and there (only had to restart once in 12 hours) and also sometimes little freezes before combat- After having played Slay the Spire it is very hard to unsee where they have a lot of their inspiration for enemies. They definitely have created their own enemies with distinct combat startegies, but some combats are straight up copied with the minimal effort to make it somewhat differentNow to the Pros:- Nice take on the decision tree by making it an explorable hexagon map. It really adds another dimension on how to advance through levels and felt very refreshing to play- A lot of people complain that the "Deck gets filled with useless cards you cannot buff" throughout a run. I cannot understand how one can be so dumb to complain about this when taking cards in this game is PURELY OPTIONAL. YOU DONT HAVE TO ADD ♥♥♥♥ CARDS. YOU CAN SKIP THEM. So if you dont have the mental capacity of a 4 year old, you have way more options to go for small/big decks, depending on your strategy- The game has basically all mechanics to play around that a Deckbuilder should have nowadays. You can build decks that kill enemies with strong single hits, multiattack, AOE damage, Damage through stacking your Block, Buffing your Power, Discard and Draw mechanics, Damage over time, Damage through minions, Manipulation of your mana and hand size and so on. I can see why a lot of the bad reviews complain that the game has one dimension a combat, because again you actually need to think for 0.1 seconds and combine cards with relics (permanent powerups) to make block or discard buidls work.- Ah yeah the relics, they have a lot of them and offer good variety. What is OP with one Character can be useless with a different one or different Deck. - Cards are buffed via gemstones with unique abilities, some of them permanent, some of them being super strong but only 1 time use. This opens up the door for a lot of strategic choices, customization and counters for certain enemy types.- Economy in this game feels balanced very well and choices matter. Again, stuff that can be very strong with a certain playstyle can be weak or useless if not used with the correct build or character - Front ally takes all the damage, which adds another nice dimension in playing out your turn (many cards having shuffle effects and last hero to get block always goes to the front)- NG+ Gameplay is made by choosing which aspect of the game becomes harder (Enemies, Economy or Exploration), which again allows you to have many variants to choose from depending on your Squad/Build. Also Cards and Items can be picked to specifically counter your handicap, wich adds to the strategic decisionmaking- General difficulty of the game seems to be in a good spot

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically it's very solid, probably my new favorite in the 'roguelike deckbuilder' genre. It's somewhat similar to Slay the Spire, but builds on that formula in a lot of good ways. You take two characters out at a time, so there's a lot more versatility than Slay the Spire. Overall I recommend it.While I'm comparing these games, I should also mention that I think Rougebook seems a bit harder to me, or harder than Monster Train at least. Looking at the reviews, it seems I'm maybe in the minority with the opinion. To me, the balance seems somewhat punishing. Cards in Roguebook with comparable effects to cards in Monster Train or Slay the Spire are usually strictly worst, costing more or producing a worse effect. Card draw and ramp effects are less accessible in Rougebook compared to Slay the Spire or Monster Train.Edited post 1.5 Patch: Had some issues with cloud saves, but seem to have gotten my save back after the latest patch. The quality of life changes in that patch were also nice, I still think the balance is a little more punishing than others in the genre, but not in a bad way. Definitely still a little rough around the edges, but easy to recommend to anyone who enjoys rouglike deckbuilders.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game but it comes with a bunch of annoying quirks.First of all, I'll start with what I liked. The obvious one is graphics: the environments are visually pleasing, character and enemies design is interesting and it feels pretty polished.Gameplay wise, what I liked the most is the pairing mechanic: basically you have 4 character in total, but for each run you can pick only 2 of them. Every character focuses on different ways of fighting so you can mix and match what you like playing.But this comes with some side effects: some pairings are comically broken - I ended up winning on my third run...And I could have won in my second run, but at the time I didn't understand how the final boss was fighting.The other thing that felt a bit off was the luck factor: some randomly generated drops were miles above and clearly better than all of the stuff I got in my first run.I get that finding a game breaking combo is part of the fun in this genre but here it felt mostly derived from RNG and less based on player's skill.When you complete your first run, you can start a new one with modifiers to make the game harder. Honestly I started a new one but I quickly lost interest because the first modifiers you can access don't change the gameplay at all, they just make the game more tedious to play.That's what I liked the least about the game: everything feels a tiny bit too slow, starting with map exploration: it's a cool concept, but it feels detached from the rest of the game.Overall I'd recommend playing it, especially if you like games like Slay The Spire.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Roguebook is a perfectly servicable deckbuilding roguelike with an interesting map feature and some creative card designs, with overall good balance for the cards.However, as an achievement hunter, this game is a mess. Several long mega-grind achievements. No way to see progress for completion achievements. Broken tracking for those achievements, which can require you to need to edit your .json if it doesn't update for a 1 time event. Unclear unlock conditions for the various events in the game. And a Daily Challenge achievement that requires you to be in the top 50% of players that doesn't proc correctly, and 2 years after the game came out the pool of players doing it are small. Even achievements aside, the music and world are pretty bland, with lackluster worldbuilding. A lot of this game seems to being to try and ride Richard Garfield's name into sales. And the DLC is overpriced, $10 for a character unlock is way too much for what content this game has. Get it (and the game itself) on sale at best. There's fun to be had here, and if the Devs hadn't abandoned the game and fixed the bugs it'd be pretty solid. But as is, it's a 3/10 at best.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a low budget heroes but with cards: walk around on a hex-based map, pick up stuff, fight with mobs, but fight by playing cards.There's no way to heal except very low amounts in the form of potions found on the map occasionally (nowhere enough), no way to accumulate ?spell? points to play cards, hand is always discarded so no way to plan ahead and keep a card for later, also not possible to customize the deck, so one has to play with all and every cards.In other words, this is basically a random-fest. Either have to spend all ?spell? points on defense but that way the fight may last forever as the enemy DPS is too high, or suffer some damage but kill them - yet without the chance to ever restore HP so die slowly...The other issue is the map revealing "ink" (can't move but to revealed hex, ink removes the fog of war). Runs out fast and as cannot be planned where to go as no idea what to find where (e.g. healing potions...), so one can get stuck easily - this is what happend to me on the first (and last...) try: Revealed a large area, but in the fights I lost most of my HP, can't go anywhere but to fight the boss and that's it. Checkmate.Would refund but bought a key on 20% the Steam base-game price with ALL DLCs so... couldn't resist that bargain (now I know why it's that cheap...), so remains in my library but in the garbage-section I'm afraid.

_childDocuments_.review: Exceeded expectations. The best STS-like I've played.Has generally what you'd expect, plus these unique differences:- 2-character duos, chosen out of five characters.- Unique meaningful exploration/planning outside of battles. This is a little stale eventually, but a great fresh idea for the genre.- Adding gems to cards for choice of extra effects.- Random pool of skill upgrades to choose from each run.- Extremely limited ability to remove cards from your deck. You may see this as a downside. But it really changes the experience compared to other card games, and I assure you that infinite and almost-infinite decks are still possible.Downsides: - Achievements are an example of why achievements usually shouldn't exist. They're almost all meaningless grinds, and almost none about interesting challenges.-Maybe too easy. I do have lots of experience in the genre, but I'm up to the 10th run or so and I think I only lost twice. I'll say I do spend tons of time making decisions and may not have survived if not. I'm maybe almost starting to have trouble after 10+ wins, but this is a LONG time needed to reach that point. Still, keep in mind I've played games like this for probably hundreds of hours.

_childDocuments_.review: 20hrs into the game, I can see this becoming my favorite deckbuilding game (and I already have hundreds of hours on Slay the Spire and Monster Train)Great mechanics and such variety.. you can clearly see some of MtG inspirations which is awesomeCombinations seem endlessMap mechanics are also very good, it's all about risk and rewardLove it
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: A great twist on the roguelike deckbuilder.Unique map exploration mechanics that are very interesting and make runs feel different.A team of 2 (out of 4) heroes means you have 6 unique combinations which play differently that help the variety.Beautiful artwork and worldThe "upgrade" system let's you insert gems with unique effects to your cards, resulting in many possible combinations.The "ascension" system looks very promising, letting you choose your modifiers instead of being the same every run.Unlocking permanent bonuses gives you progression, but mostly you eventually replace a decent percentage of your starting deck, avoiding the boredom/repetitiveness of the first act (compared to its direct predecessor Slay the Spire)I highly recommend it for the lovers of the genre
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: To me, this is the first game in the post-STS wave of roguelite deckbuilders that feels like it's really evolving the concept instead of just adapting it. I can't recommend Roguebook highly enough if you're interested in the genre.That said, I do want to point out the one problem I have with the game: a successful run in Roguebook easily takes me 3-4 times as long as it did in STS, and it's not because I'm fighting more battles. The load times and animations are just punishingly slow for a roguelite game about grinding through runs with permadeath, and there's no way to skip or accelerate them. This really needs to be addressed if Roguebook is going to compete with STS for long-term replayability, because I just can't see myself doing this hundreds of times at the current speed.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: It has the elements of a fun card management game like Slay the Spire and such, but it's lacking the deck tuning aspect. You can get new cards, and empower them with gems, but you can almost never get rid of a card. So your deck grows and becomes unpredictable. It's hard to set up combos when you can't thin out unwanted cards.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot .. It's not as balanced & considered as Slay the Spire, or quite as insane as Monster Train - but it's a pretty good point on it's own. The thing I most like about it is the dual characters, character level ups, but most of all that slim decks are not the best way to play. You get to play with all your toys and have to take card to level up your characters. I really liked the combo decks you got in Monster Train, and this is a variant of that with the different heroes. The game is distinct enough visually from Slay & Train, though there are certain things I wish were animated instead of tokens. ( I wish ally cards had animations, I want to see my horde of frogs!)Of the three games, it's the lightest in terms of narrative by a mile. I'm mostly alright with this, though the events in Slay the Spire & the lore in Monster Train added a whole bunch here. I get the feeling if I played Faeria I'd have more insight into things though.It is a little buggy, though it's getting patches. Ive had a single crash in my 15 hours, and twice where characters models went white  for a battle. Not too serious.I do wish it were a bit more difficult, I've progressed the meta progression a bit & it's pretty assumed I will win. The New Game+ additions aren't enough in terms of difficulty, It's more like they add different randomizers that change things up.Of all the 3 games, this one will screw you the least in terms of RNG - which is a good and bad thing in my opinion. I've had a lot of fun with it, and still have probably another 20 or so hours with the content so far. Hopefully they add more heroes in the future. _childDocuments_.review: I expected so much more from a game by Richard Garfield, creator of the most successful commercial card game of all time (and recipient of that honor for 30 years now and most likely for the rest of his life as well)! I am also a big fan of Jean-Michel Vilain's Faeria, which deserved so much more success than it got and which I madly respect.Rogue Book is an incredibly mediocre and by-the-book rogue-lite deck-builder and it's baffling that it came from the mind of the creator who single-handedly established the collectible-card-game industry as an entertainment and competitive-play juggernaut. Faeria didn't do quite as much but it aimed to re-design card-games for the online digital age and absolutely nailed its concept!The dual-character aspect of Rogue Book is basically a façade. It basically just defines what card colors (in Magic terms) you will have on your deck. Whatever other mechanics are tied to it, like positioning are a bother at best and at worst a laughable down-grade from the expansive game-board of Faeria.Your hand and mana are reset every single turn so there is literally zero tactical depth beyond "what can I do right now"? Compare that to the utmost basic play-by-play flow in Magic The Gathering or Faeria and it's not hard to understand why I'm flabbergasted by the fact that Garfield and Vilain are credited in this game as the two creative directors!The over-world aspect of the game is interesting and at first gave me chills when it reminded me of the 1997 Magic game by Micropose (AKA "Shandalar") because that was and still is the best marriage of digital card-game and RPG world and mechanics to this day.However, it quickly becomes clear that the implementation of exploration in tins world is a major drag. Revealing a tile takes 5 clicks (depending on how you do it) and that's something you'll have to do basically every time (or even multiple times in a row) whenever you progress even a little bit within an area of a level of a run.Yes, I get the idea - you turn exploration itself into a game mechanic. The problem is the implementation, not the concept. Desktop Dungeons does it better. Dungeons in Shandalar and worlds in Heroes of Might and Magic did it better 2 decades ago! Why are these things being reinvented after all this time - but worse? You could copy-paste the design of HOMM's randomly-generated worlds into Rogue Book and it would be an automatic upgrade while also fitting-in with the structure of sub-areas and portals in the game.No, the fantasy that you are painting this colorful game world on-the-fly doesn't make up for the hassle. I can see that it could but Rogue Book's delivery of that vision ain't it.The controls in this game... actually terrible. I'm getting some serious second-hand embarrassment just thinking that they have the gall to sell the deluxe edition for over 50 dollars!You have to hover each card individually before being able to read their text. Then you have to click to select the card. Then you have to click on its target. Think about it: the majority of cards in the game can only ever affect a single target (their respective hero or the first enemy in line) - as such, a single click on most cards would be exactly enough but for some unthinkable reason you need to do 3 actions instead for every single card you will play in every single fight of every single run in Rogue Book.Maybe the keyboard is better? Well, the card numbers keep changing as your hand changes so good luck keeping track of the three cards or so you'll cast every single turn. And guess what, the keyboard can only select the card itself so you still have to choose your target with the mouse. Remember that target, yeah the one that 90% of the time is always a single possible option? Yeah, we're sure gonna need you to click on that!Skipping the turn can be done with a keyboard stroke though. Oh wait, did I say stroke? I meant you have to hold the space-bar for exactly one second. Thankfully this is not a major inconsistency in the game's inputs or something you're going to be doing multiple times per minute while playing the game. No, of course I'm joking. It's exactly that.You cannot exit any of the many game menus (shops, crafting, scenes...) with the escape key. However you can rebind the "cancel" key so that you can have a key that exits screens. You can rebind the exit action to any key... except escape (╯°□°)╯︵ ┻━┻I've had an eye on Rogue Book for years now. I always thought that it was over-priced but that the game was better than people were giving it credit for - exactly as with Faeria. When this Summer Sale rolled around, it was the first game I checked for a discount and immediately decided I'd buy it once I saw it was 80% off.The exact opposite of Faeria, I think this game deserves a much lower overall rating than it currently has. The recent (30 days) 70% score IMO more accurately reflects the game's shallow card-game rules;  awkward exploration; and ridiculous control scheme. I'd go for 60% even and maybe all the way down to 50% if I'd let my sheer disappointment factor in.Right now, Monster Train is 70% off; Faeria and For The King 1 are 80% off. I cannot imagine any world in which I'd rather pay a cent for Rogue Book over any of these. Anyone who enjoys RB is entitled to their own opinion but if they're not aware of much better deck-builders or much better party-based rogue-lites, it's only because they didn't bother looking.Outside Steam, MTG Forge is free and lets you play (and even draft) any edition of Magic. Shandalar is very old but some genius made it playable in modern systems also for free

_childDocuments_.review: VERY cautious recommendation. Recommending based on the Devs probably balancing many of the issues over time, and the game still being quite fun despite the issues.Anyway...The game is basically Slay the Spire with enough ideas of its own to be its own thing. The game has potential and a fair number of good ideas.Good potential, as mentioned above. Has some really cool ideas, such as how you explore the map using "inks".Shuffling around two characters is an interesting mechanic.The art is really nice. Most Enemies snowball in power forcing you to always play an offensive deck-style to deal with them quickly before they just straight up annihilate you.Remember the Cultists from Slay the Spire? They were fairly durable and every turn they got stronger until they obliterated you. They punished defensive and overal slow decks. Now imagine if 2/3 of the fights was versus Cultists; that is how Roguebook fights often feel.Okay, so why is this a problem again? Well, it basically encourages you to go full YOLO-deckbuilding with maybe a token bit of defense to avoid some chip-damage. If you don't go heavy-offense you're almost inevitably going to run into some enemies which snowball much faster than you can handle.This is made even worse by the fact that many offensive cards and artefacts synergize amazingly. Defensive cards usually just buy you some time to draw the cards you actually need.There is still some tactics and a lot of thinking to the game, but the back and forth isn't quite on the Slay the Spire level. Most of the time you just try to slam the enemies into the ground before they can rev up their tactical-nuke miniguns.The deckbulding just isn't as interesting as it should be a result. The game balance snowballs into explosive nonsense, sometimes very early.Just because you're two turns from death every late-game fight it doesn't mean the game is well-balanced. Roguebook throws out extra energy, double-damage, and all sorts of incredibly strong power-ups to the player, and sends enemies to match. This might sound neat on paper, but in practice it just breaks the game's balance over its knee. Sure, killing the final boss via 423 bleed stacks on turn 3, after nearly getting crushed by a standard encounter due to a below par draw just before, that is amusing. The first and second time. When you realize you're basically just playing the game fishing for a "broken run" via some busted synergy the game end up less interesting.I figure the game pushing you heavily towards having a huge deck size is supposed to handle this, but really, it just makes your broken-op deck less consistent because you will sometimes draw nothing useful for two turns and die. If you already have a winning deck you can just stop adding cards.The fact that the game swarms you with so many artefacts, deck-size-based upgrades, and sometimes amazing gems just pushes it over the edge. If playing a [2+]-cost card and dealing 20 damage causes me to achieve apotheosis as my enemies prostrate themselves before me, then all I really end up doing is picking big expensive damage cards and things that let me play more of them (eg. extra energy cards, ...). Amusing, but winning like that hardly feels deserved. Some grind, but not in any way damning.It isn't really as bad as some reviewers make it out to be, but you're basically not going to win the first round unless you get really lucky. The reason is that some extremely important upgrades are locked behind (very early) post-run rewards. Most players should have enough resources to come out victorious after they've gather a dozen or so "parchments".If you've played the likes of Slay the Spire and Monster Train and want more then this game is worth giving a look. If you're low on cash, wait for a sale. If haven't played the two previously games mentioned, do so instead. Roguebook is as of writing not yet on their level. IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a great take on the deckbuilder genre and one that I keep coming back to run after run.When I discovered Richard Garfield was helping work on a roguelike deckbuilder, as a huge Magic fan, I got very excited. But that excitement was quickly quelled when the game launched with Day 1 DLC. Fortunately, Abrakam realized their error and corrected it with an apology, making the DLC part of the base game and offering refunds for anyone who purchased it. Awesome job Abrakam. That kind of responsibility earned yourself a fan, and I look forward to seeing what else you do with this game.  If you too were turned off by the day 1 DLC, I beg you to reconsider and try this game out. Roguebook checks all the boxes for me in what I want out of a deckbuilder:- Innovative, syngeristic card choices and mechanics that function together on multiple axes. One of the questions I've come to ask myself when getting acclimated to a new deckbuilder is: "is this game challenging me to beat it, or to not lose to it?" which may seem a bit redundant, but it's a important distinction for me, and nine times out of ten, if a game falls into the latter category, I will quickly lose interest. Roguebook feels very much the former, and the cardpool and underlying mechanics reflect that. You get big, flashy turns with lots of sequencing and decision trees; massive, swingy spells; and powerful, game-changing artifacts; all of which culminate into an experience that makes you, the player, feel as though your ability to win is being tested rather than your ability to avoid losing.- An overworld navigation system that is interesting, fun and functional, but doesn't detract from or bloat the core gameplay *too much*. As the genre evolves, I've seen more and more games get creative with their overworld systems. Some are great and some, not so much. Roguebook's overworld isn't flawless, but it is interesting, and puts greater emphasis on exploring than many other titles in the genre. There is a touch of resource management that comes with the ink and brush mechanics (essentially you're "painting" the world around you to reveal the game board) but it's not so pronounced that I feel hindered by it most of the time. The best overworld systems in the genre are those that you barely even notice, and Roguebook isn't quite that, but it's totally serviceable and can be quite fun when the RNG works in your favor and you reveal good tiles.- Fascinating worldbuilding that isn't full of overdone classic fantasy tropes (i.e. There's no "rogue" "mage" or "warrior"). I really appreciate when these games deviate from classic fantasy roles and try to push character archetypes that aren't rooted in one predefined playstyle. StS did a great job at this, and Roguebook does it a little better. None of the characters in Roguebook fit a classic role. Any of them can be played as damage, tank or support to mostly equal effect. More importantly though, character defined archetypes rather than role defined archetypes gives the player a blank slate experience that allows a greater sense of creative freedom when experimenting with cards and archetypes.Roguebook isn't without flaws though, and there are a couple gripes I have with the game:- The character pool is too small. There are 4 characters at the time of this writing, and you get to pick two on each run. While there are some interesting pairings, I feel as though there just aren't enough characters to really feel totally satisfied. I'm someone who loves tinkering with new mechanics, but at only 20hrs in, I feel like I've seen the extent what each character has to offer and there's little more to discover in that regard. Additionally, the character cardpools are quite small. After only a couple runs I had unlocked all the available cards for each character, which leaves little incentive to grind for more unlocks.- The game is too quick. I'm not asking for a Gordian Quest style 6-hour, 5-act roguelike run, but it would be fun for me if each act was a bit longer. I think most of my runs clock in around an hour, and when I really like the deck I've built (and the game is good, so I end up liking a lot of them) it just feels too short to really scratch the itch. Adding some more board space or encounters would dramatically improve this.In summary, Roguebook is a solid take on the genre and one that I am happy to own. Is it the best addition to the genre since StS? Probably not. Could I see myself dumping 100+ hours into it, granted the devs continue releasing content and updating the game? Absolutely.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good deckbuilder that introduces a good bit of variety + cool ideas to make the game stand out and feel unique despite the massive amount of other deckbuilders out there.Namely:1.) You choose a combination of 2 characters out of 5, instead of picking just 1.  This allows for a pretty big variety of synergies.  Unlike other deckbuilders that use multiple characters, it also still plays with 1 deck.  This makes it so you don't have the hassle of managing a deck for each character, and you don't need to take the extra time to play each of their turns individually.  More options without more hassle.2.) The Map exploration via ink/brush on pages is a really enjoyable breakaway from the standard choose your path gameplay that has been the genre standard.  It adds a totally different twist to it while still leaving the element of risk/reward choice. Well thought out.3.) Difficulty stepping via a combination of tiered malices is more interesting than just stat boosts.4.) Giving bonuses based on how large your deck size is is a great way to break the deckbuilder "meta" of getting the smallest repeatable deck possible.5.) Gem variety (that get put in cards to modify them) allows for an even larger amount of gameplay styles and crazy synergies.Definitely worth a look if you're into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: While i'd love to be able recommend this game, it's ultimately a very shallow experience. There are multiple cool ideas that are simply not developed enough to give them time to shine, and a terrible meta-progression system The gameplay loop ultimately boils down to a "Go big or go home" type mentality, where winning is all about assembling a combo - and such combos are far too easy to assemble in this. The net upshot is a very one-note experience where victory or failure is mostly determined by how fast your combo comes onlineThere's a dramatic lack of content in the amount of relics, and UX issues are persistent, including soft locks. As an example: a card that summons Allies and a card with Ally on the text are not the same thing, despite the fact they have the same overall effect. Several crashes have also happened. For a game claiming to be a released candidate, this is very disappointing. The meta-progression system is just bad - both incredibly grindy, and adding no actual depth to the game, just raw power. The epilogue system has some interesting ideas in it, but ultimately boils down to just picking the harshest penalties to get the highest difficulty - there's not anything to shake up how you play the game, just choices that serve to narrow the space. Characters lack a distinct identity and are often parasitic in their mechanics, which means you end up mostly playing one character and having the second one tag along. Enemies are likewise very shallow mechanically, with most of them being in effect "This scales rapidly". The game also does nothing to engage with enemy positions or ally positions other than the bare minimum - a real own goal given this is one of the points of distinction vs something like Slay the SpireThe map system is a very cool idea, but in practice devolves into playing whackamole and hoping you hit something, removing any real strategy from it once you've tagged all the revealed titles. Given the level of power that things like Faerie Wells or Gem Shrines can offer, this makes for incredibly swingy runs with very little player control.I can say that the game is very pretty, not to mention visually charming. But at it's current price and content, unless you're not planning on playing more than twenty hours, this is not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I could tell you about how much I love this game, but instead I'm going to tell you what I know about it's journey.Matt White was a simple gamer, just like us. He liked Super Metroid, he liked Dark Souls, he even liked fighting games. It had been years since Nintendo had touched the Metroid franchise. So, he thought to himself, why don't I make one?It was 2012. Matt had already been toying around with Flash sidescrollers. Having fun dipping his toes into making stuff, just for fun. Matt was also an excellent artist already; he drew comic book art, in a style similar to those old 80s sci-fi anime's. He didn't really know anything about programming, but after conversations with a mutual, they agreed to partner up and try to make something special. Try and make a Metroid-like that was somber, yet lively, and hauntingly beautiful.So a Kickstarter was made. Matt didn't really know anything about making games. Few people outside of the industry really talked about it back then. They did some math, guessed about how long it would take them, and a goal was set - mere $15,000. A measly amount compared to even most indie games of today. It seemed like enough back then. And the Kickstarter was a rousing success, funding waaay above goal. Not quite enough to reach the oft-joked about Wii U stretch, but a windfall nonetheless. The money was divided evenly between the two bright-eyed and idea-filled partners. This was it. It was time to hunker down and get started.But then the programmer's work started to slow. He would miss calls, skip out on meetings. He stopped returning messages. Slowly, he himself became a ghost of the project. He had taken the money, but wasn't producing the work. There was so much to do! But only Matt remained. And only Matt would continue the project.Stencyl is a good engine to work with visually, especially if you are new to making games. Although shaken by the silent departure of his once-partner, he soldiered on; dutifully creating all the artwork, pulling from sound libraries and implementing his ideas into the game engine. It was rough going, for a single man. But it was going. And that was all that mattered, with the weight of the fully funded Kickstarter behind him, and the growing coverage of his dark, yet vibrant take on the (for the time) neglected genre.However, Stencyl just couldn't keep up with Matt. Fixing bugs was a struggle for this new developer. And the more content and artwork and ideas he shoveled into the engine, the longer and longer it would take to compile, sometimes up to 45 minutes for each change! Instead of smoothly moving forward, working on the game was becoming frustrating. This couldn't go on. A change had to be made.So Matt makes the tough decision to switch engines, communicating this to all the Kickstarter backers. It is an understandable, if regrettable choice. The game was already at least halfway done! But it was also necessary. The engine was pushed as far as it could go, and Matt, burning the candle at both ends to make his dream a reality, had no choice but to start over.The next years are spent learning to code. Unity has plugins to work visually, like Stencyl. But so much MORE could be done by directly coding it. Ideas exploded forth. The animations could now be expanded upon. Even more options for including melee and different weapons were now a possibility. Matt hadn't stopped playing other games during these years, and they all helped to shape and grow this new vision of Ghost Song.A vision I hope you will enjoy in its completion as much as I have.Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Great roguelite deckbuilder! Combat is heavily inspired by Slay the Spire, but has a bit more complexity as you control 2 characters at a time, and which one is in front matters at any given time. Has a very interesting mechanic where you level up and gain perks (almost like minor artifacts, where you choose one of 3) depending on how many cards are in your deck. So there is a good balancing act of adding cards to your deck to unlock the next levelup, while trying to avoid ending up with a bloated deck.Lastly the 'overland' events has a lot more strategy to it than other games in the genre, as you explore a large map and reveal tiles through brushes and inks, which drops from the enemies you defeat. Overall a very enjoyable experience! highly recommended for fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I only needed 4 hours in game to give this a positive review. Card battler akin to STS or Monster Train. Simple but nice graphics, music and sound nothing remarkable. Very easy to learn the mechanics. Nice progression system. The game has an interesting exploration aspect to it, and it's pretty cool, I enjoy that part a lot. The game as a whole is a chill diversion and it's exactly what I wanted. Cheers: From the game menu it's one click to save and exit the game entirely and this makes me happy. It's funny that I have to call this out because so many games make you click 5 times to exit.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game.  More forgiving then Slay and I find it more fun too with 2x heroes, maps to explore, and unlocking upgrades as you go.  As an avid MtG fan, this scratches the deck building itch in single player style.  I have not had issues with bugs and seems like the dev team is releasing patches regularly with both new content and bug fixes.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I am a veteran gamer and rogue-likes/lites are at the top of my preferential genres. I will say that I like a lot of aspects of this game, several of which are highly innovative, at least as far as bringing together many ideas from other games (including the Dev's Faeria) into a relatively well-polished game. My problem is as follows:If the rogue-like isn't real-time and/or doesn't have PVP, especially if a lot of the controls lend to immediate and irreversible actions being possible, there needs to be an undo of at least the last action. I think its situational to the game whether redoing a whole round/encounter or checkpoints/save files, but being unable to undo accidental clicks when half the screen becomes clickable is a significant problem. For example, clicking the character model sometimes having functions, clicking allies sometimes having functions, etc. Even if there were checkpoints/saves, then your misclick wouldn't cost the whole run, where in this game that means several hours of your time. I can't recommend a turn-based rogue-like that does not account for this issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Worth grabbing on sale but can't recommend at full price.Main Pros:-Visually beautiful and polished-Using ink to explore the 'pages' is a fun little mechanic.Main Cons: -The deckbuilding system is lacklustre. You mostly add cards to your deck with minimal ability to remove the old/bad cards, making it hard to amass any real synergy.-Some issues with the balance and difficulty curves.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Slay the Spire, this is an easy recommendation.The art is fantastic, and the game has some interesting mechanics that makes each run feel more unique and less of a required structure than a STS run.You explore each "floor" map using tools that are limited use. You're rewarded by using "ink" and "brushes" carefully to reveal the tiles that may contain battles, gold, or special events, etc.Also, unlike STS a large deck is encouraged. There's a bit of a learning curve with all the pieces in play here, but once they click the game is super fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Cool deckbuilding game with a  lot of synergies to explore between cards, skills, relics and other gameplay aspects. The only real downside is clunky and somewhat sluggish way of playing cards in battle. It feels like there's a lag after every card played, probably because of the animations. You can get used to it after some time, but still the game could use a fast mode of some sort.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: So I got this like a year ago and barely touched it, at first it was too complicated for me. But today I finally got around to watching a tutorial and tips video on YouTube, it kinda started to make sense. Won my very first run with white lady and fat boy. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ once it makes sense and you get the hang of it, you can figure out some super dirty combos and it is so much fun, I'm loving it. I will say this is one of the more challenging roguelite deck builders because there's quite a few moving parts, but it boils down to about the same as StS with an extra dude which is sweet, and the swap mechanic is actually really awesome when you get the hang of it. The Ally system is really cool too, just finished a run with wolf boy and beat the final boss with an aggressive ally who had over 300 spirit at the end (you'll get how sweet that is when you start playing).I really like it now that I've given it a proper shot. And there's good progression in this game too. There's a skill tree as well as your usual unlocking cards/artifacts as your characters level up. This is a good one and I'm glad I didn't uninstall it and have it lost to my history of backlogged games.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This is great deck building game that which is sufficiently different from others in the genre to be interesting and enjoyable. I particularly like the gem system in the game which gives every card a huge set of possible uses and synergies when enhanced with different gems. I hope this system continues to be expanded. Control of two heroes simultaneously also adds additional variety to gameplay and deck building. Finally the game feels polished with a consistent and appealing art style.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I am FLABBERGASTED this game didn't reach the heights of Monster Train in popularity. It steals most good mechanics of Slay the Spire and then makes a whole new game around them, while being far prettier to look at. This is an absolutely EXCELLENT roguelike deckbuilder, easily the second best in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This is more roguelike and less traditional card builder than what you think at first glance. With that I mean that both the deck and the world mechanics are far more RNG between runs than many others; you cannot have a narrow, build focused deck but is forced to play with the deck the run gives you as well as the items the run gives you.I have seen several negative reviews where people have not understood this and  complain that they can't focus on "2-3 different decks" depending on runs and complain about "deck bloat".Those things are not bugs, those are literally the game's core mechanic.It is a GOOD roguelite deckbuilder, but it is rogue FIRST, deck second due to it's heavy reliance on RNG on runs.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: On sale, this game is worth a buy, but at full price I would in no way recommend it.The truth is it has a lot of fun ideas and is a decent deck building game, but the replayability isn't as good as other games of this nature (STS) and it's annoying painting system doesn't allow to really explore each map as much as you would like to.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun to re-play at first, and I really like the idea of teamplay that is pretty innovative to me. The problem is that when you'll unlock and replay several times with all characters the game is finished for you. The compendium thing might be encouraging for replaying, but not as much. For me 4 characters for the game that uses 2 at a time is not enough the modding community could probably solve it but the game doesn't have steam workshop (well I get it, it might be counter-productive for selling DLCs). Overall the game is good and I will leave positive review.l I really enjoyed the voice-overs, the lore and the idea of exploring the map by yourself the possibility to revive your buddy and back-up each other also I've played Faeria so seeing familiar characters was pretty nice, but still it doesn't feel like I'll be able to play the game for like 150 hours like I did with slay the spire
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: As others have said, this is the first Spirelike that has grabbed me on its own merits. It does some things that are at least conceptually interesting, like juggling two heroes at once, a mix-and-match approach to increasing the difficulty instead of the linear progression of Slay the Spire's ascension modes, nonlinear card upgrades (using Gems to modify their properties) and a board game-like exploration layer instead of StS's map tree.UPDATE: I'm still not at the highest difficulty level but it still seems very unbalanced. I will sometimes die in Act 1 if I don't find good combinations of cards/gems/items, but then dying in Act 2 is very rare and I don't think I've ever lost in Act 3. It's way too easy to build broken combos that make the later stages a cakewalk.However, my early impression is that this game isn't nearly as balanced as StS. It's possible that I will change my mind as I play more, but right now it feels pretty easy to make a broken build, especially with Ally cards. Maybe this is just because I've played so much StS that I have the hang of this game from the start and the difficulty curve will catch up to me. However, right now it doesn't feel like I have to consider how to balance my build to handle different monster types... most of them are not sufficiently special to counteract any particular build, so you can just focus on one type of combo and make it as broken as possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: At this stage, I wouldn't recommend this game. Haven't played for a couple of weeks, as I am waiting for a solid update. Day One DLC aside, my initial opinion was positive. It looks great and the map gameplay is actually kind of cool.Play a few runs and you'll see the cracks form, however. There are minimal successful strategies outside of stacking bleed or ally damage, and because the UI seems not to have been tested with large stack numbers (horrible overflow), I can only surmise that these strats 'break' the game and so weren't tested for?Needs some polish and balance, currently have my second refund request approved due the DLC snafu.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Deckbuilding game combined with a roguelike experience, with its own little twists on the genre make Roguebook a delightful game to play. If you have enjoyed Slay the Spire, you should feel right at home here with the deckbuilding aspect of the game, but with the added challenge of two characters and thus two decks to draft and manage. The art direction and animation is very good as well. I see myself playing this game quite a bit if I ever get time off at work.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game.  Beautiful presentation, satisfying meta progression, exploration/ progression branching repackaged as filling in a magical book feels fresh, combo and positional tactics feel extremely satisfying.  I do hope the devs add a history tab and an end-of-run tally, as it's satisfying after a run to take a look at the successful compounding of power.  Highly recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I have played a fair few deck-building roguelikes, and this one is pretty solid.  I quite like how, unlike most deck-builders, you are incentivized to actually make your deck grow practically the entire time.  It's a really interesting balancing act.  I wish there were a little more to the framing device as an actual story, but it's still quite a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Just one more run it says. And there go another 4 hours of your life. Hours you try to pick up the one slick combination of cards that crushes those foes you have beaten thousands of times. Yet any run is different. And once you hit the tournament circuit there is no end to varieties. You want to beat this book fast. You want to beat it with elegance. You want to beat every hex of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: fun casual game, not too deep, super pretty, but might not be for the hardcore rogue enthusiasts.It's a fun, simple, easy to spend way longer than intended playing, but the main draw and reason for endorsing this game is how pretty it is to me. The art is great, the illustrations are lovingly rendered and as simple as the animations are, they totally work for me. But also, I'm sure casual of a "rogue" style enthusiast, so it may not be for the more hardcore of this audience, but for us filthy casuals it's great. Decent tactical depth, but not too heady, great for a quick dip in and out.My only gripe would be that the story content is too short. I beat the three main acts in the first hour or two of playing. But the diversity of tactics (for me at least) kept me going well past that, along with the extra optional goal and trial systems which opened up the gameplay after that.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Good card mechanics, an enchanting art style/lore and some new aspects to the genre (map exploration) makes this my favourite deck builder yet. From the 62 hours played so far, i used about 60 hours my STEAM DECK, which works great with this game.I enjoy Monster Train, Slay the Spire, Griftlands, but I am coming back to Roguebook more often.Once the player beats the first run (which can be considered a prolongued tutorial), the game opens up with challenges, which rank up in three different branches. I find these challenges quite entertaining. When one is completed, the subsequent challenge becomes available. A challenge from one category can be combined with 2 challenges from the other branches.The heroes come with different card sets, that need to be unlocked. Each run starts with two heroes, that can be interchanged. This makes 10 different couples (incl. Furoro DLC) and each hero can be played on the front or from the back.During the run you get to choose- which cards to draft / swap- which cards to buff with gems- which charakter ability to level- what artefacts to buy- how to effectively explore the map to maximise your progress before challenging the level boss.After the run you get to spend obtained book pages to upgrade your heroes, start and map conditions.This makes for a lot of replayability.Negative reviews complained about unfair situations and the roguelike mechnics. I am not the sharpest tool in the shed, but I was able to beat the game, from the first time played, seven times in a row and ramping up the difficulty up until Epilogue Level 7 before I lost a run. And this loss was well deserved, because I insisted on a build, when the game dealt me other cards. I do not find this game to be unfair.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a newer entry in the deckbuilder roguelike genre and also happens to be my entry point into the genre. Despite being a huge fan of roguelikes & roguelites, this was the first one to peak my interest enough to try it right away. Now after spending more than 15+ hours with Roguebook, I can say it’s a great game for new & veteran players alike. However, there are a few issues that hold Roguebook back from being a perfect game.ProsEntertaining & Diverse gameplay. You choose between 2 characters to use in each run from a total of 4 (2 are unlockable). You lose a run once both of your characters run out of HP.Every character has a unique ability and a completely different set of obtainable cards that encourage the player to try out each character multiple times.Each run (game session) is divided into 3 levels with the goal of defeating the boss in each of the three to win your current run.Every run has the same 3 levels in the same order, but the placement of enemies changes along with which boss you fight at the end of each level.Movement takes place across an overworld where you actively click on tiles around the map to move to them. Most of the map is covered when a level begins and you use your paint brush (which has limited uses) and paints you find to uncover other spaces.Combat is done by selecting cards from your deck and dragging them on the enemy you want to attack. Each card has an energy value and you only have so much energy each turn. Your two characters are each positioned on the field one in the front and one in the back.Cards have different effects such as hitting multiple opponents, causing bleed, and healing you from damage. Defense cards are also an essential part of the Roguebook experience as some turns enemies will hit with enhanced attacks and the best course of action will be to dodge.Roguebook allows each of its cards to be customized by finding gems throughout a level. Gem’s can be slotted into cards to gain extra abilities. Examples: Costing one less energy when character is in front, Retaining card in your hand after use etc.Enemies are broken up into two types of encounters, normal and elite. Elite encounters are like mini-bosses and when defeated drop an extra paint brush and an artifact or gems. Normal enemies drop regular ink when defeated. The mix between normal and elite fights adds great diversity in how you tackle different battles.Each enemy is slightly different from the last and have different abilities and effects that are worth looking out for. You’ll have to develop new strategies to take on each type of enemy. For example some enemies attacks will debuff your character, while others will burn them requiring them to swap places with their partner to avoid taking tons of damage.Roguebook has a unique mechanic that incentivizes you to pickup new cards. The more cards in your deck the more skills you get to choose from a random skill tree that is provided in each run. Often, you’ll have to weight the pros & cons of picking up a card that doesn’t work with your current deck in order to gain a new ability.Artifacts are equipment that can be found on random tiles that provide extra bonuses to your characters. They’re usually spawned off the beaten path of a level and require players to put the effort in to make a path to them.Around the map are other events that can be found such as: Picking up gold, Transmuting cards, Finding healing capsules, & Chasing after a thief who steals your artifacts. Events add great variety and help make exploring the Overworld interesting.Pages can be found across each level and from beating bosses. You can use pages after each run to purchase permanent bonuses from the game’s skill tree.When a run is finished the two characters you used gain experience points and level up. The level up’s do not increase any stats, but they do unlock new cards that can be found in your next run.After completing a run you unlock NG+. There are 15 levels of NG+ (called epilogues) and there are special modifiers that you can activate to have increasingly difficult run’s.The modifiers are really interesting and shake the gameplay up significantly. Examples are (Making Elite battles unskippable, hurting you when you pickup gold, etc.)For those interested in achievements, Roguebook has 56 achievements which will take the average player at least 20-25 hours to earn them all.Roguebook boasts an excellent storybook style art design. Particularly the enemy designs really stand out as the elite monsters and bosses have very unique designs.NeutralMany deckbuilders do not have meta-progression and even though the meta-progression doesn’t give a huge advantage some players may be put off it.The soundtrack and sound effects aren’t anything to write home about.ConsElite battles feel unbalanced. Many elite battle monsters will chip away a large amount of your health especially on higher difficulties. While they do provide better loot I found myself usually avoiding them on higher difficulties as they weren’t worth losing tons of health to.Characters need more levels with added rewards such as cosmetic for characters or more cards to unlock. This would increase replay value beyond the epilogues.Semi-frequent bugs and crashes. Roguebook has come a long way since launch, however it still suffers from crashes mid-run and save corruptions. The team is actively working on patching these issues, but as of now it’s still an issue.Having an extra level that could be swapped in and out every run would make each run feel a little unique, since playing the same 3 levels each run in the same order can get repetitive.Link to Review:

_childDocuments_.review: So you want to play another STS-like? Play Monster Train, it does everything Roguebook does, but much better. Roguebook suffers strongly from some questionable design choices;First off, I want to talk a bit about the overworld and the ink-throwing board game that comes with it. Seems very original, right? True.. but even Monster Train's simple choice between left lane or right lane is more interesting in the end. Coloring in the overworld map plays out exactly the same every single time, and even after just doing it three times I was already bored with it. Tile randomisation changes absolutely nothing about this.Secondly, there's a terrible design choice that gives you an extremely powerful perk every time your deck reaches a certain number of cards, which is unbelievably dumb. The best thing about deckbuilders is finding synergetic strategies, so incentivising the player to always take additional cards is just terrible game design, leading to your strategies being watered down to the point where it doesn't even play like a deckbuilder, but more of an ability based turn based tactical game that sometimes locks you out of your abilities randomly.Thirdly, there's no story or exposition to save some face here, just like most deckbulider roguelites you simply boot up a new run from the menu. All that persists between runs is a terribly grindy and unappealing looking metaprogression tree.Another major problem I have with the game is with its extensive randomisation of enemies, even chapter bosses. It's such a weird design choice, since it makes it so that chapter two is in no way different from chapter one, apart from having blue tiles instead of green ones. A game like this needs a chapter boss that has some personality, so if you get beaten by it you can swear revenge and try again. Showing up at the end of a chapter only to face a randomly generated foe is extremely unfulfilling.Lastly, the game doesn't seem to be mechanicly stable. I had to abandon my first decent run just before entering chapter two's boss, because every single time I tried to enter that battle the game would crash completely. After six or seven attempts I gave up, losing two and a half hours of play time, which felt extremely bad.I have only played seven hours of this game but I'd rather just play more Monster Train than boot up another Roguebook run. Feels kind of bad to dunk so hard on this game, because it does look very pretty, but I just can't think of many good things to say about it other than that. It was somewhat fun for a few hours, but just has too many problems.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Do I recommend? Yes. BUT. And the but is super big.It's not the best card battler out there. It's not really that challenging, it's not really that deep on strategy, it's buggy at times (luckily so far nothing game breaking I saw in other comments). It's missing some good QOL updates, mainly some map would be super useful to not have to run around them checking if you didn't miss anything. But I imagine it can be great game if you find Slay the Spire/Monster Train/Vault of the Void too hard or you got to this game first.The price on this is horrible, I got it in a bundle which I bought for another game and can't really imagine paying full price for this no matter how many hours I put into it. Mainly because I'm chronic achievement hunter and if not for those I would already uninstall the game. Which will most likely happen anyway at some point, because some of them require you to play this way too many times for what it offers.Still, going with positive as there is no possibility to go with "meh, but playable" and it's not really that bad of a game to go for negative one.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: In the end just no fun to be found, either with deck building or discovering a story.Compared to other card games in this genre, Roguebook feels like you have no sense of control.Character classes are vague in their definition, whereas in Monster Train the classes are very well defined and offer an immediate sense of how you should play them.It feels like this game took the relic system from Slay the Spire, but made it more expensive so you end up with far less modifiers (and less excitement each run). It took the gem system from Monster Train, but made each gem too situational rather than simpler card upgrades.Too many systems and card/gem/relic combinations moving around to grasp control over a run, and not enough player power to make great decks shine. This is one to pass on.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed playing this but find it way too easy even before you start unlocking progression perks.   I'd really enjoy allowing the player to remove cards (which isn't possible at the moment and would leave you without the bonuses that a larger deck playstyle enjoys).I think this would be a good balance of luck for draws and skill for deck management which is lacking at the moment.  TLDR - Overall, a fun game that could be great with some tweeks.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not quite good enough. It seems incredibly easy with certain builds. Granted there's a 'hades-like' difficulty map that adds certain feats/challenges, but it just seems like it's there to stretch out the game rather than make it any more difficult or not.Bleed is stupidly overpowered. You can easily beat the boss in 1 turn with it and some of the gems/artifacts/treasures (ex. the spend all energy to energyx10 dmg from the redpigdude + double damage artifact that seems to always spawn last map + 50% bleed first hit trait + bleed gem = 1 shot everything, even the last boss) Some characters gimmicks (like the turtle character) don't seem worth bothering with given other characters synergy with bleed. It's very similar to slay the spire to where if you raised an eyebrow at the dev they might blush a little bit at the copy pasta from that game...On the positive side, Good graphics, music and animation. Probably worth 10-15 bucks and not 25. Games a bit too easy, really not much strategy to it overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Although it only has three "chapters", this deck builder rogue-lite game has consumed quite a bit of my time. The story is interesting, the characters are fun to play and the many card/character combinations keep me coming back again and again to try out different strategies.I'm really hoping the developers release additional content, as this game will be on my play list for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great rogue-lite deck-builder game. Good visuals, good sound, interesting cards, fairly balanced. The main distinguishing feature is that you have two characters that provide cards for your deck. The position of these characters, in front or back, determines who will be hit, attack increases, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. It might be for you if you like to play once in a while and prioritize the quality of the experience over endless grinding opportunities, and/or if you enjoyed  but would like to enjoy once again the pleasure of discovery, the freshness.I love , both because of its looks (style, world building and general aesthetics) and its pure gameplay. I am a long time  player, and I typically enjoy the process of deck building, but I do not have much time to play so I would rather enjoy a 1st person game on my own terms. I need some degree of challenge, but I don't like much to grind.  will be my 1st point of comparison.I also quite enjoyed . The gameplay was quite refreshing after , with interesting twists, notably the necessity to combine two deck styles in one. On a surface level, it could be more fun than , but it was also shallower and after a while, games became more like always the same than . There is no doubt to me that even though  is a nice game,  is a greater game.  will be my second point of comparison. draws good points from both games (and more but I did not play those). It has a fun and light (humorous) style that is closer to  but a much better world building and general aesthetics like . It has the double-deck twist like  and other fun features like the discoverable map, while remaining deeper than  although not as much as  at least for the moment. But the balance is excellent and that is a strong point of the game. That might be the point that deserves unpacking the most.A problem with  is that each hero (i.e. "deck") comes with one or two strong strategies to pursue, and that these strategies become viable depending on cards or relic combinations. Although the game is fun by itself in the beginning, progress ends up coming from a difficulty rise that narrows down viable strategies to a handful of the most successful ones, which makes each game look like a bet on whether or not the picked strategy can be assembled.  still has a tactical element that makes it enjoyable but the deck building part of the gameplay does not remain fresh and interesting beyond a few dozen hours (in my case). Which is not bad at all, by the way. In comparison, a key characteristic of  is how it forces you to compromise and hybridize telegraphed strategies to succeed. Where  has more cards that are a pay-off in the right circumstances by meh otherwise,  has more cards that would give you a small edge if you pushed your deck in certain directions. There are still a few overpowered strategies, but the goal of the game is not to find them, it's rather to cultivate the emergent synergies of your pool. That is what makes  a superior game in my opinion.  is much closer to  on that aspect. Although at the same time, it seems that you could easily get lucky enough to have some overpowered relics or combinations that win by themselves. So in that sense it is more fun and less demanding than . I am in fact totally fine with that, because the gameplay does not get boring. It has a little bit more of tactics than  (character placement) and most importantly it does not depend on you betting on one of the few viable strategies. I think that the cards are better designed.One problem I have with  is that it exceeds my competences. Like high level competitive  or simply any game, like tarot, a high level of engagement gives you the most out of it. Tarot is to me highly enjoyable with skilled players, but quite boring with beginners, because much less interesting things are happening. With  I ended up on the other side of that line: it seems to me that the game was balanced for a type of player that is much more engaged than I am. For instance, certain cards are good because of some details in the mechanics that are not apparent, because they were not supposed to matter, but that were nevertheless discovered by the player and exploited in a perspective of absolute optimization. That's an integral part of games and gamers' community, and that's fine. But sometimes balancing for those cases can lead to less balance for less engaged players. It's a question of design, of situating your game design on a scale from fun and random to deterministic gameplays.  has in mind a player that is a bit too much like a Chess player to me.  has in mind a player that is a little bit more like a  player. Which I like because, and I must stress that now, the card design is still great. It is balanced to provide fun, even though it might not get as balanced to players who are highly engaged and know the hidden details.Before I wrap up, I want to say I highly appreciate the characters: having a strong female, an older person, a fat hedonistic guy... The references are not cliché like 's american-centered devils and angels, I like to see yaks and frogs. The music is a bit generic in its style (cinematic) but very well made, and the sound design is excellent. And these choices resonate greatly with the game design. I appreciate in particular the play style of the Kappa grandma for its flavor (Seifer's gameplay is a great flavor match too but a bit less unexpected).In short: great music, graphics, and aesthetic choices. Excellent design on multiple terms, balanced for fun and flavorful. It's a bit early to speak of replayability, but I expect a lot of it considering the cards' design.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Magic The Gathering and when I found out that the creator made a game, I had to get it. Has very much a MTG feel to it which made it very easy to pick up and play. Very addicting game if you're into card games like MTG/Pokemon etc. Love the strategy element, makes me use the ole' noodle more often than other games make me use it.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a delightful addition to the roguelike deck-building genre, offering a fresh take on familiar mechanics. Developed by Abrakam Entertainment and co-designed by Richard Garfield, the creator of Magic: The Gathering, this game brings a wealth of strategic depth and replayability to the table.One of Roguebook's standout features is its rich and diverse character combinations. Players can choose from a roster of unique heroes, each with their own playstyle and deck of cards. The game truly shines in its duo system, where you combine two heroes, mixing and matching their abilities and cards to create powerful synergies. This system offers an impressive variety of strategies and encourages experimentation, keeping the gameplay fresh even after multiple runs.The game's innovative map system adds another layer of strategy. Unlike traditional roguelikes where you navigate through predefined paths, Roguebook presents you with a blank map that you gradually uncover using brushes and ink. This exploration mechanic ties seamlessly into the game's progression, as uncovering more of the map allows you to find valuable treasures, encounters, and power-ups.Visually, Roguebook is a treat. The hand-drawn art style is charming and fits perfectly with the game's storybook theme. Each character, enemy, and environment is beautifully crafted, bringing the world of the Roguebook to life.The deck-building aspect of the game is well-implemented, offering a good balance between strategy and luck. As you progress, you'll acquire new cards and relics that can dramatically change your playstyle, encouraging adaptive strategies and on-the-fly decision making.While the game can be challenging, especially for newcomers to the genre, it provides a satisfying learning curve. Each run, whether successful or not, feels like a learning experience, and the unlockable content provides a strong sense of progression.One minor criticism is that some character combinations can feel significantly stronger than others, which might limit variety for players focused on optimal strategies. However, this also allows for some incredibly powerful and satisfying builds.

_childDocuments_.review: Great roguelike deckbuilder similar to Slay the Spire. Very little narrative/story, just like StS. From a Slay the Spire player with 500+ hours over multiple platforms, the only real change from StS you're getting from Roguebook is 2 things: there are 2 characters you control at once, but it honestly changes the gameplay very little, and the other thing is the map you explore between battles/events. Exploring the map did feel fresh and fun, like its own little puzzle where you're choosing which areas to try and get to. I found, after getting familiar with the mechanics, that it started to get stale in that I wasn't really forced to make any hard choices - I felt like I could get all the things I wanted to get from that part of the game. With that said, it's still a fun alternative to Slay the Spire - by comparison, this game has more focus on visuals and theme, but Slay the Spire is slightly deeper and more gratifying gameplay-wise. I would recommend this game, especially on sale, to any fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an okay game, but it didn't pull me in.  Here are my main complaints:1. I don't like how the cards are split between two characters that act at the same time.  I had several times when a character was positioned wrong because the card draw was bad, forcing me to play some secondary game that wasn't a deck builder game.  It's a clever concept that some people will like, but it's not what I want in my deck-builder game.  Just personal preference though.2. The map... eh... it didn't really add much to the game, imo.3. Although I didn't get far in the game, the cards didn't jump out at me like some of my other favorite deck builders out there (Slay the Spire being the gold standard).  When I got cards in this game, it felt like I was still getting starter cards, while Slay the Spire and Monster Train and other great deck builders don't waste time getting into the meat of different play styles instead of just attack/block.  In fact, this is one of my biggest complaints about most deck-builders out there, so not really surprised to see the issue here, even if I didn't get far to see if it holds for mid or late game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good but not as good as slay the spire. It's a solid 8/10 game and worth the money if you like roguelike deckbuilders. This game is a fun 30-40 hour experience and is worth playng. But just doesnt get to the same level of slay the spire in terms of strategic depth or infinite replayability. I imagine i will stop playing this around the 50 hour mark and go back to playing slay the spire instead. But I'm glad i bought this game and played it. Pros, The art is fantastic, Movement is interesting and gives variety outside of fights. The 'Ascension" mechanic changes how the runs are played, you choose from a 3 lists (gold, exploration, and combat) and can customize your runs with different modifiers, this lets you strategize before going into  a run based on different modifiers like "take damage when you pick up gold" or "cannot skip card choices" changing how you build your deck for those specific runs. Or instead of straight combat buffs for the enemies you could choose to instead make traversing the map much more difficult instead. It has some interesting choices and synergies between classes, and map layout gives you more decisions before a single combat begins. The game actively encourages you to draft cards and rewards you for building a large deck, which is great for the new player experience. Cons, Meta level progression makes your characters significantly stronger out of the gate, leading to much lower powered runs early on, and it locks large chunks of gameplay elements out of the first few runs. This does make the game feel like its opening up slightly but the static numerical buffs are completely unwelcome for me in a roguelike. If you prefer roguelites and meta progression this could be viewed as a plus, but honestly makes me hesitate in recommending the game. If it weren't for this one thing alone the game would be a 9/10 for me. The meta progression at max rank almost doubles your strength, making early runs feel like you just need to grind more and later runs feel like you are cheating with all the free extras the game gives you at the start. As an example, one of the higher difficulty modifiers is +10% gold cost, which means nothing when one of the passive upgrades is +50% gold picked up off the ground. It feels like cheap padding to keep you doing runs even if you lose, getting further without improving. That said I had no difficulty winning the first few runs without any upgrades, but it still feels incredibly unwelcome in the total experience. The game has a significant amount of glitches such as cards not discounting correctly or showing incorrect damage numbers. This usually is not that meaningful but can be really rough when it does ruin your turn. I have not experienced any crashes personally. The glitches will be hopefully patched out, and aren't as bad as the other reviews make them out to be (at least for me). The game also had day 1 dlc, but that was removed and added to the base game so is no longer an issue. Overall the game is fun and if you're interested in buying it i'd say its probably worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty interesting take on roguelikes.Heavily inspired by Slay the Spire, yet a bit different.In games such as those you usually want to have a small deck, however here you need a bigger deck in order to unlock new masteries, which makes it interesting - a tradeoff between permanent buffs and your deck power.Map exploration is very original.Still, after 20h+ it feels pretty repetitive. Maybe rng hits too hard, because often it feels like you either struggle like hell with rng or you just breeze through.Another problem is that perma progression makes the player too strong too fast, which in turn made my next games (with challenges maxed) kinda boring.To top it off - there is a "challenge level limit" - meaning you have to win many times in order to pick a stronger challenge, which in turn made me lose interest in game (it became too easy, and I couldn't be bothered to grind to get to challenging gameplay again).First impression: 8/10After playing 20h+: 6/10So I guess it deservers a thumbs up, but imo grab it on at least -50% promo - not worth full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic card game! It has several features that really break the mould of the genre, in a good way:1. The exploration of the map is an awesome feature that has created a whole new dimension to the genre. It is very enjoyable and encourages finding creative solutions in order to optimise your run.2. There are several synergies for large decks; this creates another dimension to deck building, rather than the typical thin deck cycle meta that is prevalent in most card games. 3. In a vein similar to Monster Train, you can choose two allies and your deck is create with cards from both. Although Roguebook doesn't do primary/secondary characters; both are primary and vital.4. 'Ascension' difficulties are very flexible. You unlock tiers and each tier has 3 optional difficulty modifiers, allowing you to really tailor your runs.Highly recommend! Also, there are skins! Some people are complaining about day one DLC, but honestly? You pay cash, you get content, devs use cash to continue improving game. Who loses out here?
