_childDocuments_.review: Alright, strap in folks, because we're about to dive into the wild world of Roguebook, and let me tell you, this game ain't playing around.Picture this: you're diving headfirst into the roguelike deckbuilder genre, and suddenly, out of the murky waters, emerges Roguebook—a sparkling gem among the sea of games. What sets it apart, you ask? Well, let me break it down for you.First off, we've got these energy mechanics that'll have your brain doing cartwheels—in the best possible way, mind you. And the characters? They're like a bag of surprises, each with their own bag of tricks waiting to be unleashed.But wait, there's more! You can mix and match these characters however you please, creating a strategic cocktail of chaos that'll keep you on your toes. It's like trying to solve a Rubik's Cube while riding a tightrope—tricky, but oh-so-rewarding when you crack it.And let's not forget about the overworld, my friends. It's like stepping into a high-stakes board game where every move counts. You gotta be smart with your resources, exploring every nook and cranny for hidden treasures and epic showdowns.Now, I won't sugercoat—this game does have its visual and auditory charms. The graphics are decent, the soundtrack adds a nice touch, and the storyline, well, it'll keep you engaged enough to see it through.But here's the kicker: you're not just playing a game, you're weaving your own destiny. With endless possibilities at your fingertips, every choice you make shapes your adventure. It's like being the architect of your own epic saga.And let's talk about leveling up—watching your heroes evolve is like witnessing a caterpillar turn into a butterfly, with each card you snag paving the way to triumph. Plus, the dynamic duos of heroes for each run keep things as fresh as a buddy cop movie, but with more mythical beasts.Sure, there might be a few bumps in the road—like some difficulty tweaks that could use a little TLC—but overall, Roguebook is a stroke of genius. With its replayability and promises of future delights, this game is here to stay.So, if you're craving a gaming experience that'll have you on the edge of your seat and itching for more, Roguebook is your ticket to adventure. Trust me, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow no amount of prior videos or reviews gave me a proper feeling of what playing this game would actually feel like, so I couldn't get around just jumping into it, and hey, it's been a decision I shall never regret!The thing is that Roguebook doesn't play out similarly to any of the other popular roguelike deckbuilders out there. Managing a deck with cards of two different heroes, knowing who of them is suited for which position, who thus gets which treasure, and then additionally improving important cards with gems for turns that truly feel powerful if everything has been prepared smartly... it all packs a special charm. Enemy mechanics and how certain battles effect the own deck management offer noticeable variety to other deckbuilders as well. And then there's of course the exploration of the map as icing on the cake; learning where to use paint and brushes to uncover as many secrets as possible before facing the chapter boss, well done! The animations and voices/sounds carry the atmosphere as well, concluding my thoughts of why I think that Roguebook satisfies its niche in the roguelike deckbuilding world.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: The developers have admitted making a mistake with the day 1 DLC, apologized, and will be offering refunds for the content. As a result of that, I've changed my recommendation from a thumbs down to a thumbs up. I'm keeping my original review below because I think it's important to see that feedback, and it shows that the developers are a good group of people willing to admit fault and correct mistakes. The game does still have bugs, but I truly love the game enough to overlook them, especially now knowing that the developers are willing to work on improving it. I love the 4 distinct characters and their unique mechanics. Each character's deck can be built in multiple ways from being defensive, offensive, or support. I'm hopeful that they'll add more characters in the future (which I will have no problem paying for)! :) Very happy with how things turned out.Original review: Even though I love the gameplay mechanics, art style, characters, voice acting, and more- I can NOT recommend this game. It has insulting Day 1 paid content (seriously?) which contains perks, and the game is PLAGUED with bugs. I'm normally very forgiving on things like that, but this is a final product which not only insults its fans by trying to milk more money from them, but which also has very clear developer oversights. I ran into a problem which blocked me from entering the boss gate on the first level because the randomly generated tiles built a wall in front of the entrance... that's not a bug, it's a clearly stupid decision on the developer's part. Design it so the 3 tiles before the boss gate always generate as clear tiles... it's not that hard. The game as also crashed for me at least a dozen times, one of which removed a very valuable card from my deck. How the heck did this get released?!

Despite clearing almost all of the map on the first page, getting all the gems and power-up items, and strategically balancing my deck, it is still possible that you will encounter an enemy in the second page that will just wipe you. Drawing 2 Defend cards on a five card hand is not going to help you against an enemy that does 30 damage every turn when your character only has 66 HP. _childDocuments_.review: Not a big fan of STS... but i do like card games and figuring out their nuances before getting bored with them... Dont like this one too much so far.. i like the idea of the game and it has a few good points however,  Like slay the spire there are too many card game "gimmicks"  that make this a game of attrition and slog. Examples of this are unfair advantages to enemies added to make this game difficult that cannot be defended in any way, like getting debuffs that by pass defend points, enemies only allowing you to hit them for 1 point of damage each time regardless of the attack value, having just enough hit points to carry over into the next round if every attack card played is max damage ( common cards ). The death system when an ally perishes and you can revive them with silly cards that get added to your deck along with the wounded cards that fill up your deck with uselessness.. just makes we want to start a new game and not bother with the headache and time waste of a slow and inevitable death.  The other problem i have with this card game and in general ( some are not like this ) but u cannot see the enemy cards, you cannot see where their attack values come from and they do not need to cycle cards like the player does they are just fixed on a pattern meant to kill the player.. In short the player is constantly at a disadvantage with out any strategic way to mitigate this other than find the right cards or get them in their hand at the right time ( neither are directly up to the player ).  I do have a few games where enemies play from their own deck and need to cycle their cards which makes the game much more strategic and fun.   Now im not saying this is a terrible game, I do like the ink system, adds a bit of fun and mystery along with the strategy/luck factor needed to keep a rogue like game going fresh,  just not for me to recommend at this time, as for right now every time i play the game and try to enjoy it i turn it off rolling my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: Something is definitely missing from this game, which is really frustrating b/c it feels so close to filling this massive void in the deck-builder genre. Overall, a thumbs up obviously means it's still a game I'd recommend if you're on the fence about it. But here are some flaws I saw in the game in case the game devs are looking to make updates.I purchased the game b/c I'm annoyed to death with multiplayer, Netdeck-builders like Hearthstone and Magic. I crave nothing more than a deep, deck-building, single-player campaign with tons of replayability. I've been playing Slay the Spire, and while I enjoy it, the way you advance levels doesn't give me enough sense of adventure. I'm looking for a roguelike deck-builder that allows exploration, discovery, some more RPG elements. A good mix of pick-up and play simplicity yet robust enough for replayability. The closest thing to that would be an old MTG game called Shandalar. For those unfamiliar with Shandalar's campaign mode, it's played on a randomly generated map with random battles. You progress your character by collecting cards and gold, visiting towns, exploring dungeons, and customizing your deck along the way. The game is very old, however, and I wanted to play something newer.Enter Roguebook.The game seems to have almost everything I mentioned above that Shandalar had, except dungeons, towns, and true deck customization.The combat isn't overly complex, but it definitely requires careful planning and focus. You are generally trying to optimize your mana, actions, and character placement since whoever is in the front takes the damage. While I enjoy the complexity, I've found that I can't play this game as long as other deck-builders. The game can definitely get mentally fatiguing, but that's not a complaint about the game's complexity. I eventually get to a point where the effort required to persist just isn't worth an experience that feels restricted.The most frustrating part of this game is the "ink brush" exploration system and how it prevents you from thoroughly exploring a map before advancing. Each level represents a "chapter" in an unwritten book, and the tiles represent pages that you're uncovering. The game has different ink brushes to let you reveal these tiles (straight line, individual tiles, surrounding tiles, etc.) One of the goals of every level is to optimize your ink usage.I would have preferred if the ink was used to scout a much larger map, not to restrict you from exploring the map when you run out of ink.While the exploration system is definitely unique and thematic, you are frustratingly at the mercy of the random types of ink you get from battles. For starters, you need to fight as many battles as possible because each one gets you more ink. You also need to get to the watchtowers because they reveal the surrounding tiles for free. However, it's rare to find efficient routes to these battles and watchtowers.All too frequently, 50% of your best ink brush (the "surrounding tiles" one) is wasted because all the tiles beside and behind you are already uncovered. This severely limits how much of the map you can explore. Every now and then, you can build a long "bridge," which lets you maximize this ink brush. But ultimately, the ink system ends up being a frustrating restriction on exploration instead of a fun mechanic that encourages puzzling together the most optimal route.I'd love it if this game found a way to make every level larger and completely explorable. If that was the case, it wouldn't be the ink that restricts you, but instead your own discretion based on your character's health levels. The ink could simply be used to scout.More opportunities to control your character's improvement would also be welcome. For example, the game offers plenty of opportunities to add random cards to your deck. But that's all it feels like, adding cards. It doesn't feel like you're building a deck. You can't consistently remove cards (only can transform them if you find an altar). You can't sell cards, can't go hunting for specific cards. Can't put cards in or take them out temporarily.Inns, dungeons, more combat, more shopkeepers hidden on a larger map would transform the game into something significantly deeper. This could have been a world that allowed a player to attain infinite knowledge and power, at the risk of the hidden dangers that loom on the unseen pages. It's still very much a game worth playing if you like the fusion of exploration and card-based combat. I think there are many opportunities for minor tweaks that can significantly improve the game. Look forward to seeing if some are implemented.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun 'Spires-like' game. Graphics/animation are neat. Still has frequent bugs and stability issues currently, however with the level of polish that the rest of the game has, these should be fixed soon. Playing it cheese mode, where you exit or restart the game if you things aren't going your way, is the only way I can play it. I think it would be too annoying otherwise. If one of your characters dies, it can be revived and you only get a game over if both die, so in that regard it's more forgiving than Slay the Spire. I really like the map reveal mechanic, and I like that you have a pair of heroes. I think that makes the replayability much higher. Also the progression feels really good. It's overall easier than Spire. Another thing that's nice is that it feels like it's easier to put a coherent deck together, and with that, very satisfying to craft very powerful cards with it's gem/socket system. You can make monstrously powerful cards. I'll also note that sorocco has an ability that is supposed to make all future cards have 2 sockets, however it currently makes ALL cards even the ones you already have, to have TWO sockets; which can be insane. Personally I hope they keep it that way but I doubt it, Anyway, buy it, have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game a lukewarm thumbs-up. It has a couple tweaks to the Slay the Spire formula that make it interesting, but as others have noted, it lacks the replayability. (At 28 hours I've beaten it with every combination of characters already--I'm not sure I had beaten StS more than once or twice at that point) Unlike StS, where you needed to carefully craft your deck and pick relics to make the end-of-game surmountable, Roguebook seems to allow pretty much any build to run all the way to the final boss(es). But at the same time, while in StS you could beat any boss with any good deck, the final bosses in RB are more or less designed in such a way that all but one style of deck absolutely will fail. Which is not to say that it's hard if you know what you're doing, just very limiting. It's a bit disheartening to see that it's out of Early Access already, because it feels like it needs about 50% more content to really shine. It also still has some weird quality of life issues like lagging interface, which can cause you to easily mis-click, and it still crashes inexplicably (but does autosave).Overall I do not regret buying it (on sale), and it is an entertaining game, but for the about the same price I have gotten considerably more time out of other, similar games.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well designed game. Feels like slay the spire, but the exploring the map element is vastly superior. Having 4 heroes and 2 per run allows for many different deck combinations, which blends well with the fact you draft a new deck each run. I find the amount of similar runs much less than in other games. I had been finding some combos a bit easy, but one week in to the game they released a patch that seems to have already nerfed many of the broken combos I had seen, so this is a good sign! Well worth my money and worth writing my first review for.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with promise on the deck creation side. I feel that an opportunity was missed in having alternate exits and making the game less linear.My big gripe would be that the top level 'Epilogue' is perhaps too easy and the feats you unlock too powerful and encourage re-rolling too much.Anyone who got a heap of playtime outta STS or MonsterTrain or plays MTG will probably find this more than worth the cash.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: A "Slay the Spire" like with beautiful art and an interesting overworld roaming mechanic where exploration is a limited resource.Sadly, it's hampered by an atrocious rogue-lite progression mechanic that requires about 36 hours of mindless grind to unlock all embellishments requires to even play the game at the intended power level it was balanced around (and as a deckbuilder it's already fairly easy to begin with.)This slows down more for other players as there's no option for animation and action speeds.  While certainly better than others in the genre, it still slows down gameplay quite a bit.The UI also has some issues as the game feels very much like a tablet game ported to PC, making mouse interaction feel 'off'.  Like a lot of dialogue boxes will require you to clikc outside of them to progress instead of on them, there's no way (that I saw) to scroll the map, there's definitely no zoom options, etc etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Back when this game was first being released I was quite skeptical. The beta/demo was decent, but poorly balanced and felt a bit strange. I am glad to report that things definitely seem to have smoothed a bit and the full release has much more going on in interesting ways. I do agree that it can't really hold a candle to the titans of the industry like Slay The Spire, Monster Train, or Griftlands but I think it fits quite well into that same mid-tier as Fights In Tight Spaces.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: A really solid deck builder, with a great spin on 'level exploration" compared to others of the genre. Instead of picking points on a boring branching grid, you get to choose areas of the level to reveal, never knowing what you'll find. You never uncover the whole thing, which is a good choice IMO. The art style is really fantastic, great amout of care put into rendering units, and the 'cutout puppet' animations are the best I've ever seen. Great respect for the art team on this one. The cards are varied enough to remain stimulating across multiple runs, and the materia-like gem-socket customisation of cards is just so satisfying. However I've had a few gems not work correctly on certain cards, so some obscure bugs remain to be fixed there.My only other gripe is that beating a run is super unclimactic. Screen goes black and you return to the main menu for a menun animation that isn't even a permanent change... Weird choice, lack of story-oomph for a game that leans so hard in creating a world, and wrapping this whole concept of being lost in a book...Overall though, the true test of a game like this is how many times you return for another run. And although Monster Train remains my most constant re-visited deckbuilder, this one is easily 2nd to it. GG devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: This game was surprisingly good.  The characters and their cards interactions are awesome.  There is enough variety that runs feel fresh.  There are enough interesting items that can be found to keep you thinking of new possible ways to build your deck.  And most importantly to me with any roguelite game, there is enough progression to keep you motivated to keep playing, and to me the progression feels substantial!  I had  3 instances where my character would get "stuck" on the world map.  A quick save and quit /  reload game fixed that each time. It is worth mentioning though.Do not be fooled by the generic name!  This game is awesome, and I sincerely hope the individuals responsible for it continue on in the industry for many years, just maybe come up with a better name next time.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Some really great roguelike mechanics here, and some quite fun ideas as well. It's a bit like a monster train - Slay the Spire baby, and while those are big shoes to fill, the devs are putting in the work to help this game live up to its potential.The level painting mechanic is a nice reprieve from the standard "choose a path along a tree" that StS made a mainstay mechanic way back when. Each of the characters are feel very different, and as do each choice of two of the 4 characters.  I would definitely buy this game and check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Slay the spire, and monster train, and if you liked those, I think you'll like this one.It adds a little bit more depth because you control two characters and you have to manage both of their health.I think I really like the art style, it does feel a bit more alive to me than the others. For difficulty curves I think it adds good replayability because it doesn't just make the game harder, it makes it different, though I've only gotten through the first tiers of difficulty. You can combine some of them. or just choose certain ones as there are different ones to choose from, though eventually I'll probably do them all.Additionally I really like the roguelite system. you get better stuff to start with, while you're making the game more difficult, which I think is a nice balance.One thing I really like about this game is so some of the upgrades is a couple of your basic cards are transformed into non-basic cards and are usually better. It's nice instead of starting with I don't know useless cards in your deck so the game is harder and less fun. I think someone else said this is a super easy game, but I think once you get the knack for deckbuilding in this game it does become pretty easy, but beginning was hard. I won't disagree I do think this game is a bit easier than slay the spire but I also dislike slay the spire because I think it is too difficult, and you can call me a baddie for saying this but I think it's too RNG dependant. So even though this game may be easier, I think it is due to the fact it has better balancing gameplay.Though I do love this game, it certainly does come with it's own cons. And that primarily is that is and I'm going to steal this from someone, "I love you you buggy diamond piece of *****."Bugs encountered so far:Flash gem on kill does not use up flash gem (feature? please keep in. Tested on block 30 flash gem (block does 2x dmg combo) and I think it was the double damage flash gem.)Shield is removed when the other character blocks randomly. Like this is just normal gameplay, for a fully released game, this should not be an issue It makes me want to not recommend the game but I am still having fun so far. please fix.You can move over tiles that you're not supposed to sometimes, and other times can't move over tiles you should be able to. (this is huge because you can get stuck pls fix)Did a predator hunt and it just gave me the reward for free. I have confirmed you are supposed to fight it because I did so in a recent run.Sometimes the damage is a ? and I'm not sure why, like what can't you calculate?! Again, basic mechanic that should be working on a fully released game. I hope they do fix these bugs, because this is a great game and I want to recommend it.Grievance: "Dealing damage" doesn't count as hits/doesn't combine with hero power, so I couldn't get my double damage x2, or hero power modifiers.  I just want dem deets ya know? I know it's probably better for the game in terms of balancing, I'm just complaining.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game in Early Access.  But now that the official 1.0 launch is here, it looks like I have to pay even MORE because some of the game's content is locked behind an additional pay wall.  Basically, those of us who got in during early access were conned into paying for a 'basic' version of the game that is actually incomplete.  We're now being asked to pay again to unlock the content that should have been included in the 1.0 launch top begin with.So yeah, my advice is don't get this game unless you plan to spend additional dollars on DLCs. You will not get the complete launch content and the full experience otherwise.  It's very deceptive and frankly kind of ruins the overall Roguebook experience for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant take on roguelite card games that will be very familiar to players coming from Slay the Spire, Griftlands or Monster Train.The game brings in enough new mechanics and systems in its exploration and 2 character party system to present a new take on the genre, and I found myself really enjoying messing around with different character combos and trying to break the game.The art style is great and the characters and enemies are all full of distinct flavour that players coming from Faeria will appreciate in particular.My only complaint personally was that I felt like I ran out of content really quickly. 1-2 more unique characters and a slightly more robust NG+ system would get me playing this game for hundreds of hours! Still a worthwhile game regardless, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, the game is pretty good, a normal deckbuilder with the twist of how you maneuver the world and make actions. Admittedly, the main deckbuilding generally lacks that much synergy between cards themselves, and more with the relics and the cards, and the gems with the cards. Generally, you take what you lack for future fights and whatever works better with the relics and gems you have, since they do most of the heavy lifting. The interesting part of the game occurs when you begin adding what the game calls "embellishments", in which you can add additional things to the roguebook itself, making subsequent runs easier, and different in a number of ways. They do have multiple characters with which you can make different strategies with, but they're not particularly deep.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent from what I could gather in the short time I played. Looks like there was inspiration taken from Slay the Spire (I don't know, if Slay the Spire itself was inspired by other rogue-like card games....). Roguebook has a bigger budget though. Th artistic side is more developed than in Slay the Spire. The only problem I have is the overall polish (clunky animations, small visual bugs...). is not good. I am also not a fan of the brush mechanic. So much time is spent otuside of combat. Overall the smaller scale of Slay the Spire works better.TL;DR: If you like Slay the Spire, give it a shot. But wait a few weeks/months for some patches (atm I haven't encountered anything game-breaking yet).

_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Watched Day[9] and Brian Kibler play and saw the obvious similarities between this and Slay the Spire. Having put 60+ hours into that game, while this is extremely similar it can only be considered a compliment. The overworld/ink exploration system gives an added dimension that is extremely enjoyable (and decisions feel meaningful), and the "which gem should I put on which card" dynamic is equally fun. Still some minor bugs, but overall very happy I bought this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Really on the fence about this one... I wish I could give a conditional thumbs up, but since that's not possible, thumbs down best captures my thoughts. This game shares 90% of its DNA with Slay the Spire in terms of core mechanics and a large number of individuals card effects. So if you have played Slay the Spire to death, I doubt that you'll find reason to play what is pretty close to a re-skin. The 10% that's new consists mostly of the dual team of heroes, and a gamified movement system that requires you to spent limited resources to reveal parts of the map. Neither were enough to make me want to keep playing once I realized I was playing Slay the Spire 1.5.The other thing that really tipped this from a yes to a no is that Roguebook does not respect the player's time. It contains a huge number of slow, recurring, and unskipapble animatinos. That's poison in a roguelike, where players are expected to play and replay the same sequences. It got extremely aggravating waiting several seconds for my deck to reshuffle during combat, or going through the time-wasting game opening animation at the start of each new game, or waiting for the shopkeeper to waddle across the map to his shop every level. Deck shuffling should have been close to instantaneous, and it should not scale up with your deck size and there should be no unskippable animations at all during game start. Or at the very least there should be a fast animation option... Slay the Spire has one, so I don't know why Roguebook failed to steal that idea when it stole everything else!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I adore Slay the Spire and will say nothing bad about it, but it's not an exaggeration to say that this game takes nearly every element from StS and finds a way to improve on it. It's absolutely amazing. It's still got a few bugs and balance issues to work out (as did StS when it first came out), but it's still immensely fun and engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Nice deck builder game.The story is questionable, but due to the constant repetition of the run it hardly matters anyway.I find both the card design and the monster design very cute.The idea with the big map is nice, because you have to uncover everything first.All in all a good deck builder that can keep you engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: If you like "choose your path" style deck builders like Slay the Spire and Monster Train, then this might be right up your alley. It's definitely better than Slay the Spire, but it's hard to compare to Monster Train. I like them both a lot, but for different reasons. The art style is beautiful, there's more actual exploration, and I find I have to really think through my turns. With Monster Train, as much as I love it, the right path I find is pretty evident. Here, I've been rewarded a number of times for really thinking through the problem and exploiting every mechanic at my disposal. Feels good to find a way out of a full party wipe!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad per say, what it has seems polished. The problem is it just doesn't have enough to make it replayable at the moment. I am making a list of negatives for me because plenty of other reviews tell you the good about the game.-I unlocked both of the unlockable characters on my first three runs.-There isn't much left to unlock other than some cards by grinding.-I unlocked everything on the embellishments tree that wasn't a small percent increase on the first 3 runs.-Not enough bosses or enemies, every act seems to contain the exact same fights. There appear to only be 2 last bosses.-Not enough emergent synergy between characters, at least two characters should be able to interact with any given gameplay mechanic. For example, courage only appears on one character (maybe more cards are unlocked which get it, but I wasn't going to grind to find out). For my next point...-Too many useless relics/gems. They should only appear for characters that can interact with their mechanics. You could use a tagging system for this. Got a gem that increases damage based on courage, on two characters that cannot get courage unless they have another gem that generates it...-Balance, the game does not appear to be balanced yet. This will likely take some time to mature, but I find it really weird that enemies have abundant options to gain strength as a battle progresses but most hero buffs only last 1 turn. The ones that don't are usually really, really slow.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: You start out with lame cards that don't really combo very well.   After some runs,  you gain enough points to stack the odds heavily in your favor.   It is stacked so hard that it makes the game boring.   Now I can win without enemies even taking a turn.    The classic Slay the Spire clone mistake is that you make cards to underpowered or overpowered.   You should be able to get broken combos, but it should be extremely difficult and feel like a real accomplishment to create a deck like that.   It needs small steady upgrades instead of a single stupidly strong item.Love what they did with playing 2 heroes at once and the penalties of one getting knocked out.Good at giving the players difficult decisions for events (but still could be much better!)

_childDocuments_.review: Did they forgot to add an ending to this game? Or are you only shown it after New Game+?Really short experience in any case, unless you want to grind it out (apart from what you already have to do in order to ease the difficulty). High production values, though. Not sure about the replayability vs repetetiveness and not sure I want to find out. I wish there was a thumb sideways option.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game, but I've played 5 runs and had to abandon 3 of them due to game-breaking bugs. The first time I was most of the way through a run and suddenly everything stopped interacting. I could click on things (the shop, combats, etc.) but nothing would happen.The second I came out of a gem mine and it restarted the floor, but there was no exit and no enemies. Just me sitting in the beginning few tiles with nowhere to go... softlocked.Then several times I tried to get out of the bugs by backing to the main menu and reloading into my game... One time it reloaded the in progress game, but one level back. I continued to play through back to where I was (a half hour of play to do it the 2nd time) where I hit another softlock, I abandoned that run. The other time I tried to quit to the main menu and rejoin it simply didn't allow me to continue my run. It showed that I had an "in progress" run in the Legacy menu, but it gave me no way to rejoin.I never leave bad reviews on games, but this game is so bugged it's unplayable. When you can only finish (win or lose) two of your first five games, there's clearly a problem. I would recommend you stay away and spend your money elsewhere until Roguebook becomes a finished game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: There's quite a few bugs like Heal from Reap that rarely works, and visual bugs with allies disappearing, the Heroes page is completely lacking in information, and there's a whole of 3 levels and very limited amount of cards.  The game has promise, but right now it's a rough work in progress with limited replay value.  Hopefully it'll become better and I'll edit the review to reflect that.Update June 29, 2023.  since there hasn't been updates in over a year, it seems this can be treated as abandoned.  the foundation is too limiting to continue to build upon, otherwise this could've become something similar to King's Bounty/Heroes of Might & Magic type series...  but it's really too bad it's not and was quickly given up on.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I've managed to finish 2 runs now (count me as a casual roguelike player) and I have to say: This game is pretty darn good! Obviously the clean and consitent artstyle does the game huge favors and mix and matching the 4 different heroes in groups of 2 is a real joy. I'm slowly at the point where I have seen (not played) MOST of the cards at least once and they all look well thought-out and balanced. After finishing your first run, you'll be able to pick from different modifiers (and stack them) as is the norm in these kind of games. The modifications I have seen so far look really fun and seem to mix up the experience by a good deal (much more diverse than just damage modifiers!).If you like roguelike cardgames like Slay the Spire or Night of the full moon, you should pick this one up. For players new to the genre: Picking this game is a good as any and the game has some decent support for new players (some tips at the start a.s.o.). ___Edit:Since realease a week ago, the devs have already shown some real passion for the project. Although there was non-cosmetic day 1 DLC (and we consumer shouldn't forget!), the DLC has since been integrated into the basegame and doesn't require additional money anymore.I should also mention that a lot of small and big balance decisions have been made to further stabilize the character's and enemie's balance. Overall very good changes so far.___________________I'm already exited to see if the game can motivate me like it did for the last few days. So far I'm anything but bored.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Competently executed but nothing special as roguelike deckbuilders go. If you like this sort of game and wish you had another one, basically the same thing but 10% different so you can learn and play another one, this is that. If you are looking for something radically different from Slay the Spire or Vault of the Void: no.The mechanics will be very familiar, to the point that you already know them from other games. Variations:- You get two heroes instead of one. Pick two of four, shuffle their decks together, go.- With two heroes, positioning can matter, and swapping between them can activate effects.- The map starts hidden, so you must find the nodes with limited "ink" rather than just picking which nodes to encounter. You start with a short, cleared path so you can always advance.- Talent rewards for having more cards in your deck, so there is a tradeoff between having a lean, efficient deck and having a bulkier deck with more bonuses. Also almost no ways to remove cards from your deck, but you can pay to transform a few.- Great indication of what your choices do. Events will tell you what each choice means. When you go to play a card, numbers will pop up showing its effects after your assorted modifiers. Hovering over "end turn" shows how damage will play out. This is a great bit of interface.- Rather nice art.I like this kind of game, so I liked this game. It is soundly in its genre. If "yet another roguelike deckbuilder" does not excite you, pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a deckbuilder with some more unique elements that add a bit more strategy to optimize play. Each run consists of using two characters where you try to synergize actions by swapping positions and trying to find combos. In additions, there's a unique "exploration" mechanism where you use brushes and inks to reveal tiles on a hex map. It adds just enough over other deckbuilders that it offers some fun for a few runs.I did find that this game is pretty polished in some areas, but unpolished in others. There's no option to speed up movement or animations, so you can count on maybe 1/4 to 1/3 of every run being time waiting for animations to finish. The problem with the fight animations for each card you play is that sometimes when you play cards too quickly, there are lag issues with having the HP totals and other items getting updated. There are also a number of unnecessary clicks required to access the merchant and start each game at the gate, again pretty much a waste of time after you've seen these portions once or twice.There are still a number of bugs with the game - anything that changes a card cost to 1 actually changes the cost to 0. Also some issues with combining cards and gems - most noticeably with Aurora's card Empower - if you insert certain gems in this card, it makes Aurora attack instead of her partner, which ruins some strategies. My enjoyment levels were basically:Hour 1: There are some serious issues with this game, why is everything so slow?Hour 5: Okay, I'm liking the mechanisms a bit, having a bit more fun. Already finished my first run. Progression cost is pretty much exponential, but the rewards are also exponential. Kind of balances out. Hour 10: On E4 now, playing different character combinations is nice but honestly not hugely different.Hour 20: On E7, but things are getting stale. I have too many games in my backlog to continue playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has put hundreds of hours into deckbuilder roguelikes (slay the spire, Monster train, dicey dungeon, etc) this one feels very bland in comparison. The characters cards don't add anything new or interesting to the genre outside of the swapping mechanic, which doesn't really add a lot of strategy or fun to the combat in my opinion. The cards boil down to: Attack, block, allys and miscellaneous buffs/debuffs. This isn't exactly bad as most deck builders follow the same format, its just that I never felt excited to add cards to my deck as they all felt the same. Games like Slay the Spire give you a huge amount of options and deck building styles that make each run feel unique and fresh. I completed about 6 or 7 runs of Roguebook and I honestly couldn't tell you what strategy or deck I had as they all felt the exact same. The characters also leave a lot to be desired, as the starting artifacts/relics/whatever they're called don't make any interesting gameplay changes or significant impact on the run. Lets take Sharra (the starting character) for example: Her identity is a damage dealer who likes to swap to the back line so someone else can tank the damage. Great, except for the fact she doesn't do enough damage. During my runs with her I've found that the red guy and the wolf sword guy both do more damage AND have other utility such as tons of block or healing. Granted I only leveled each character up to 7 so maybe the fun cards are the final unlocks, but I was not impressed with the card selection/unlocks that I did unlock. Other issues I have with the game include bugged animations, cards showing open gem slots when they already had a gem attached, cards staying on the screen after the fight ended, resuming runs in different places than where I left off, long lag when playing multiple cards in a row, block and other buffs taking a long time to display changes in battle, certain cards not showing they swap positions despite other cards having a dedicated mark on the cost of the card (very frustrating), and other minor issues that I can't recall at the time of writing this.One thing I did enjoy was the gem mechanic that lets you alter cards with new abilities, extra, damage, or more block. This feels very similar to one of my favorite roguelikes Monster Train, but unlike Monster Train I never felt like the gems made enough of a difference. Outside of the rare or legendary gems, it just didn't feel impactful to the run.The map exploration was also enjoyable, but overall felt stale and a bit time consuming about 10 hours in. With other roguelikes the options for moving around the map and choosing your path leads to fun events, encounters, and rewards. In Roguebook, you just get more map exploration tools, gold piles, health containers, the occasional gem/faerie orb/alchemy lab and in very rare instances, an event. Last but not least, the final bosses. One boss in particular has a mechanic that removes cards from your deck for the remainder of the fight. WHAT??? Who thought this was a fun mechanic for deck builder? You know that strategy you have been building up to for the past hour and a half? Yeah, we're going to purge those from your deck which can either be annoying or an inconvenience at best and a complete run destroyer at worst. The other final bosses seemed fine though.Overall I just can't reccommend this game to other people who enjoy this genre. Characters are bland and uninspired, cards are boring, and the runs take too long. I would suggest playing Slay the Spire or Monster Train instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: The two big gimmicks of this game, the map revealing mechanic and the "two characters with one shared deck" idea, are both interesting. So far I don't enjoy it as much as Slay the Spire (or FTL, if comparing to roguelikes more broadly), but that may change.My only complaint is that the game runs poorly on my PC, despite exceeding the recommended hardware (i5-9400, GTX 1650, 32 GB RAM) and purported Linux compatibility. I had to lower the resolution to sub-1080p to get a cursor that updates more than 5 times a second (FPS was higher, but UI elements were unresponsive). Fortunately the game has no real-time elements or it'd be unplayable. I'll have to test whether it runs better in my Windows 10 install, but Debian (11, with non-free firmware) runs other hardware-appropriate titles in my library without issues.

It has all the elements of the rouge-lite deck builder and a few extra new things to make if feel fresh. I cannot recommend this game enough to those of us who like the genre. TREAT YO SELF

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: The visuals are beautiful and there's enough here to have some fun. There are a few irritating flaws that are either minor oversights by the devs, bugs, or just bad design decisions? Hard to tell which one. The game's a bit on the expensive side for how much content I've seen so far1. The art and FX are gorgeous! The animations are great and are a lot better than most other games with a similar style of 2d animation2. The deckbuilding aspects are better than most other roguelike deckbuilders, but not as good as StS or MT. My deck was pretty fun by the 3rd world, but there doesn't seem to be many "WOW" cards that really change the game. This is a bit of a flaw in the game as I'm not super stoked to get any of the cards. Often times it feels more like a, "I guess that's a better card." 3. Gems add some interesting upgrades, but the system needs a few design tweaks to be great. Right now they feel like a 3/54. Some of the cards don't have any way to show they'll make my character swap positions until that character is in the back row?! Why oh why? This completely ruins a major design pillar of this game - strategizing character swaps. I noticed this problem in the demo and assumed they would have a solution in place for the main release. This almost made me give a negative review. Am I missing something here?5. Enemies are varied, but I barely remember any of them due to the fights feeling too similar. My strategy feels the same every time based on my deck. I often can't tell what the debuff in their "Attack or Defend and Debuff" action actually did due to the timing of their turn. I dunno, maybe everything happens too fast or I'm not looking in the right place for it? Like when I was fighting the 3rd boss I had 4 cards go to my dissolve pile, which was the same action as his power (dissolve 4 cards when attacking), but he didn't attack that turn. Just a lot of confusing things like this are happening...6. The world map could be so much more fun. Right now I run back and forth across the map wasting a bunch of time trying to maximize the number of tiles I can reveal with paint, but there doesn't seem to be any logic to what I'm revealing. Maybe this gets better when you find different relics or something, but for now it feels like a mostly random time waster7. DLC on day one when the game feels like it's lacking content is not a good look8. Being able to pair up different characters is pretty neat. Looking forward to unlocking the 4th characterI've been playing pretty much every roguelike deckbuilder because I'm developing one myself (Demon's Mirror). There are a lot of ones not worth your time. Fortunately, Roguebook is towards the top of the worth-your-time pile.

_childDocuments_.review: We all love Slay the Spire. If you've never played Slay the Spire, go ahead and buy and play that game first hands down. It basically spawned the roguelike deck builder genre, and it has yet to be beat.When I first started playing Roguebook, I thought it was amazing and possibly even better than STS, but after playing it some more I've come to realize it actually isn't remotely as good. Now, that still leaves Roguebook as a really cool and fun game in its own right, but the game is so clearly inspired by and building off of STS that I think the comparison is useful.Pros (compared to Slay the Spire)1. Two heroes adds variety and more varied deck building. There are probably even more valid archetypes to win in Roguebook than there are in STS, and having two different pools of cards makes for a lot of cool variety.2. High production value in terms of graphics and animations. STS has a nice indie vibe going, but Roguebook is pretty.3. Open map exploration feels pretty cool. There are a lot of fun widgets and dynamics to trying to explore as much as you can.Cons (Compared to Slay the Spire)1. The biggest problem is difficulty. This game is ridiculously boringly easy. Whereas in Slay the Spire it was a serious challenge, and required careful strategy and gut punching losses to make progress at higher ascension levels, I've reached epilogue level 9 in Roguebook, and if anything the game has gotten easier than it used to be. Almost every run I've had has resulted in victory with me feeling like my skill was largely irrelevant to the end result. For example, in my most recent run I got one OP artifact and by the time I got to the final boss I killed him in two turns (for me) without him damaging me. The big problem is that feels like the norm, not a really cool runaway lucky run.2. The map exacerbates this difficulty problem. In STS you're trying to score as many points as possible, but if you take too dangerous (i.e. points filled) of a route you will probably lose. So the map encourages you to challenge yourself mightily, but lets you take easier routes if you need to. In Roguebook you mostly do every single encounter you reveal, so you aren't really making meaningful choices on the map. You're just trying to reveal as much map as possible as efficiently as possible and do all the things on it.3. Balance and card / artifact design is quite poor. Whereas in STS there are many really fun run-defining artifacts that let you build a deck around them in cool ways that warp the play experience drastically from run to run, in Roguebook there are few artifacts that add that level of cool customizeability to your builds. Mostly the artifacts add value, and the ones that could be strategy-defining are too powerful for it to actually be meaningful. (Note I realize I'm comparing a newly-released game to a game that has spent years in development. But I played STS in early access and it was never this poorly balanced from the get-go.)Overall, I'm glad I bought the game. I've had fun playing it. But whereas I beat all ascensions and unlocked all achievements in STS, this game has been a bit of a letdown for me after the first 12 or so hours. Fun yes. Enduringly challenging and awesome? Nah.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Glady updating the review after developers addressed my big gripe with the game. I'm grateful the developers took the actions they did and I look forward to spending many more hours with this fantastic game. Thanks to the development team and everyone for reading and engaging in this dialogue. I'm not really sure what to do with the old review so I guess I will just keep it below for reference. Original review: I hope folks (especially developers) read this review and realize where I am coming from. I want to heap some praise on this game before I get to the bad. This is an amazing game. Fantastic mechanics with deep customization and skill trees. The cards, artifacts, and world events are thoroughly enjoyable. So many great things coming together to make an awesome player experience. Graphics, music, art are all top notch. I was tinkering with all sorts of different possibilities and every run has been different in its own way. This is one of those games you think about playing when you aren't playing it. This game is unique in the genre and carves out its own niche but still manages to feel familiar. Unlike many deckbuilders that encourage deck thinning, this one flips that mechanic on its head and actually rewards you with talent choices based on the number of cards you have gathered. This means you need to build the best and most efficient deck for your run, not necessarily the smallest. It all comes together right at the end where the player should have somewhere around 30 cards, which is where the tree is maxed out. Since there aren't many ways to thin the deck you need to be mindful of what you are taking. It's great stuff. There are also persistent skill trees called embellishments in addition to the run specific trees (awesome I know) and these allow you to feel that overall sense of progression between runs.  The map reveal system is unique and thoughtful. It makes you think about how to best reveal portions or the map with your limited ink supplies. The more you can reveal the more chances you have for precious loot. It's so cool and different from other games in the genre. Folks have complained about content but I am closing in on 10 hours and I think the content is fine. In my first several playthroughs I have been enjoying the pace and experimentation. I have also encountered many different enemies, all of which have an interesting design and aesthetic.I gave this game a bad review for one main reason which is the day one DLC. A negative review seemed like the best way to make my voice heard. Let me tell you guys it sucks leaving a negative review for this game. It is amazing. That being said I still think the decision to release content DLC at roughly a third of the price of the base game was not a good one. This game is already priced on the high end for similar games. The crummy pricing happened in Faeria too, which was another awesome game of theirs. There are some smaller gripes that I have but they are mostly quality of life type things. There is no map function or ability to zoom out, no way to see what embellishments you have during a run, and no fast mode option (think StS) to pass through turns quicker.  So yea a great game will stand on its own, people will buy it. Several other great games like this either have no DLC or very limited, large content drops that came after release. The business model is concerning and it is a bad look for the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun but has way too many gamebreaking bugs to consider unless you're really into going through runs for an hour and a half and having to just delete the run because you ran into a bug that prevents you from continuing. Play a weird card? Game crashes, run is dead. Finally unlocked the cool underground mines to explore? Don't hit a trap, it will crash your game and kill your run. Since these errors just immediately re-trigger as soon as you reload the game, the only way to "recover" from these errors is to "Drop" your run from the main menu, i.e. start over on a fresh one. This wouldn't be nearly annoying if this was a fast paced card game like slay the spire where you may only be losing 30 minutes of time, but these runs are seriously long and tedious in comparison. Buyer beware--but honestly it is pretty fun when it actually works.

_childDocuments_.review: In short:Slay the Spire mechanics and hero driven + Monster Train duo clan system with flexible card upgrades.It's difficult to start a review without mentioning the controversies that happened on launch.The game released with day 1 DLC which provided some more content (such as new cards) and was part of the Deluxe edition as a reward for players that wanted to support the devs more. As you might have expected, this didn't go well with the general player base (and rightly so).The good news is that that devs have reacted to the feedback within mere days, and have incorporated the DLC into the base game + immediately addressed some other game related frustrations (such as a particular boss design).So in case you come across some negative reviews with mentioning the points above, just be aware that it was fixed.As for the gameplay, most should already know the general concept of a rogulike deckbuilder. Map, pick fights, get cards, build decks, beat bosses -> start a new run at harder difficulty.So let's talk about what makes this game different from others of the genre.Firstly, you control two heroes instead of one, each with their own deck (similar to Monster Train's clans). You get to swap them through cards which is important as only the front hero gets hit.Second, there is also the map. Instead of a node structure, the map is made out of hexagonal tiles of which most are HIDDEN. In order to unhide them you have to use your brush or inks to reveal more tiles and get access to rewards and other boons. It's a gimmick more than anything, but it feels so unique and fun that it's worth mentioning. Finally, unlike many deckbuilders, Roguebook rewards players for making bigger decks. After acquiring a certain amount of cards in the deck, new traits are unlocked that are very useful to have, but not gamebreaking enough so that it's still viable to skip them in order to have a thin deck. + Card play and deckbuilding is great. Slay the spire players will definitely see some similar mechanics, but it also does its own thing, both of which are done very well.+ Art is amazing. Some may be thrown off by the "mobile" aesthetic, but I personally loved it.+ Revealing the map is a cool gimmick. it feels like exploring and certainly there are ways to get better at it by optimizing your brush and ink use.+ Rewards bigger decks. In most deckbuilders there is a clear value of having a thin but optimized deck. Roguebook does not prevent such decks, but it rewards players that enjoy adding (too)many cards to their deck via a skill system in order to power balance these two playstyles.+ Enemy design is great. Apart from some boss fights, the enemy design can be very creative (e.g. you have enemies that eat their summons or have targetable limbs). * Runs can take a bit too long, usually taking more than 1h.* Unlocking new cards is a bit slow.* Upgrades can sometimes feel underwhelming. The game gives you gemstones that add an effect to the card, but while some allow rather broken combos, others are not as exciting to use.* Some boss design is frustrating. There is one deck that builds around daggers, a 0 mana card, that scales well with damage boosts. The idea being that you play several daggers per turn as they cost 0. Then there is a boss that increases the cost of cards by 1. While it has a unique mechanic to allow a temporary mana boost at a price, it makes the deck that had no trouble dealing with encounters before, now struggle as you are no longer able to free spam daggers. Another boss (which is being reworked thankfully) deletes cards from your deck, so if you build your deck around a few key cards, good luck beating the boss without the oil for your engine, or, if especially unlucky, without the engine. Thankfully, these are exceptions to the game, and are issues already being addressed by devs. -  Content dries up relatively quickly. With only 4 heroes, and slow unlocks, after 10s of hours the game starts feeling a bit repetitive as you have already tried out most of the decks combinations. The game is still fun even after, but definitely needs more heroes and content. While it had a rough start and has some flaws that need to be ironed out, Roguebook is a worthy addition to the top roguelike deckbuilders and easily earns the Royal Seal of approval.Royally approved!

_childDocuments_.review: 26 hours in, so this isn't a knee-jerk review.TLDR I like it: a bit slay the spire with less power tripping but +you can save out of battle exit the game and come back to continue++entirely playable with just the mouse & not timing based (so I'm totally eating nachos and pizza with my other hand)+++very much rogue-LITE, so  (vs arcade game runs that don't matter/build)+++ In my very 1st run, I was able to reach the endboss (but got slaughtered). Beat him 2nd & 3rd runs, didn't reach him on the 4th. So having a good game experience isn't gated behind weeks of grind.++one of the few deckbuilders that actually encourages trying different strategies and has  It is refreshingly freeing vs must have less than 10 cards games. (in fact, card removal is very rare in this game)+persistent gain in 3 ways: new cards & treasures/relics, perk points (more health, higher chance of rarities, random swap on starting deck, etc), and story progression.+story progression: unlike many rogue games, difficulty options aren't just a make it harder because why. (I lost interest in climbing the difficulty ladder in Slay the spire and Dead cells) This isn't a simple number. Options that change the run are choosable but also encouraged because they boost perk point gain significantly and flesh out the world/story by the encounters you can see. +some enemies force interesting challenges and not over focus. But they can often be flat overpowered in spite of that. (eg ally eating boss? Well I have super crazy ally generation and was sacrificing them for minor benefits anyway. eat however many you want, they'll still beat you)+risk/reward balance: not always risk early, not always wait until the last. If you have a small heal every battle, attacking elites then spreading out with normal battles lets you recover. Avoiding the elites until the end, means you don't see a potentially game changing treasure until a bit late to strategize around it.Attacking too early means you risk ending the run because you were too weak.+ It can even be a strategic decision to win the battle. But it is penalized. You can revive them mid battle, but even with that, you now have useless wound cards until you beat that map's boss.++++Variety:the combo of 2 characters, plus mid-run choice of several viable builds (focusing on either character), game altering difficulty options, plus encounters that can drastically alter things. For example:*swapping a character's attack damage to no damage but bleed at half.  I'm weak in normal encounters, but vs bosses? And I discovered happily *Getting bonuses for using cost 2+ cards makes cards I'd usually avoid suddenly more viable and powerful than their cheaper cousins.*Knowing the shop had a cost -3 gem and encountering a super power block card had me switching my strategy to focus on the secondary character and basing damage off of block.*getting 2 of the same ally that attacks every time the front hero plays a card had me quadrupling down on card draw and cost 0 cards. But the ally that swaps your characters also became very valuable.CONS:- I don't the typical speed options other deckbuilders would have.-ish, possible to get wrecked by an enemy that demolishes your strategy before you are strong enough to brute force it.-Individual runs are good, but completely fleshing out the world/story is going to be a long time. (true also of many other deckbuilders and rogues) +but at least this one seems to incentivise it.-if you don't care about losing and just want the extreme OP power fantasy, this isn't going to do that as often as something like slay the spire.-/+ it is possible (uncommon) to have a very mediocre run. You might still win with it by being careful. But it isn't as satisfying as doubling down on a winning mechanic. (note: your spending decisions greatly affect your ability to pull out of that situation, so it is partly caused by you)-With several game mechanics encouraging big decks, there is also the increased risk of ending a run to several bad turns on the wrong boss. (But again - player choice: if something is  maybe you should have prioritized the not losing vs loving the damage output. EG put the get every turn gem on block instead of attack)

_childDocuments_.review: Comparisons to Slay the Spire calling this too similar aren't really fair, and imo are being made by people who didn't really love StS. I've played StS for ~900 hours until I was completely abhorrently bored with it and can say that this is something unique and different.Some key things:Two heroes and you build a deck with each of their cards. The lead hero takes the enemy attacks/is protected by block, playing any card that blocks moves the character it belongs to to the front. You can literally build a deck to swap character positions with every card played and there are ways to get benefits from doing this.Card upgrading is via gems and sockets, rather than just an upgrade. There are gems with various effects - "draw a card", "add block", "remove all block from the enemy before doing damage", and they can be added to any card, leading to a crazy number of upgrade possibilities. It leads to far more exciting deck synergies than simply "bouncing flask into catalyst"Map exploration is dynamic and interesting. There's the theme that you're inside a book and the map is revealed via brushes and ink items, which are rewards for doing battles. The more of the map you reveal, the more improvements for your deck can be found.Difficulty increase progression - similar to slay the spire's ascensions but instead of a linear path there's 3 paths, one that effects battle difficulty, one that effects exploration, and one that effects money gain - and you mix and match to make each run have different modifiers. For example, "elites hit 20% harder" is tier 1 from the battle column and "lookout towers replaced with something weaker" is tier 2 from the exploration column, combine to make a tier 3 difficulty run.I've tried other StS clones and noped on them (lol Neoverse) because they were too similar. This, I'll be sticking with for a bit.

But lucking into that is pretty rare and virtually always near the end of a run.Not totally polished, but close. Slightly buggy, occasionally enough to cause major annoyance.Looks quite nice, especially in battle. Sound is good, voice is good (only tried English).If you like this type of game, you'll probably enjoy it, so I'll recommend it ... barely.*** Their other game, Faeria, is an excellent card+board multiplayer strategy which is still quite alive. ***

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal strategic experience, well balanced and satisfyingly tactical; although the challenge quality does fall apart by the upper echelons of the difficulty tiers.The game does a really good job of giving the combat a lot of mechanical substance. Many enemies have some form of unique mechanics that change the way players may approach the fight, with harder enemies introducing mechanics that players must juggle to avoid the threat gaining a huge advantage. Meanwhile the cards themselves also have a lot of interesting mechanics with synergies being very attainable. It's completely if not often possible for players to develop a working synergy just by casually picking cards with similar effects. There's a decent variety of trinkets, bosses, cards and gems players can use to alter their cards; although it does feel like the game is lacking in terms of regular enemy variety.The map system adds a fantastic extra layer to the experience with players progressively revealing and exploring the map to reach enemy encounters and find loot. It also adds another layer of strategy and management onto the game in the way that players decide to go about revealing the map and where they choose to go first. The game also has a fairly interesting difficulty tier system, as players have to mix and match special challenges in order to increase the difficulty level of the run so they can unlock the next numerical tier. There is an overarching upgrade system as well, but it's not especially interesting and mostly padded with small percentage increases to chance based elements.The game manages to be fairly balanced but there are some outliers. In terms of the map exploration the worst part is that there's a huge amount of variance in how many healing items players may find. Players could find seven in a biome, or they could find zero. The same goes for finding persistent boosts to energy generation, players could find plenty or almost none; which can severely lower the power ceiling of their build by the late game. A lot of enemies also have gimmicks which equate to them gradually scaling their damage the longer the fight goes on, which can result in the enemy numerically outscaling the player if the fight goes on for too long. This unfairly disadvantages builds that are based around a strong defence, and generally forces players to scale their own power during the fight so they can compete with the opponent. There are two enemies in particular, the Blood Sprite and Rainbow Yak, who are especially unfair as their gimmicks simply involve them gaining obligatory advantages with zero trade offs or available counterplay. This results in completely viable decks being absolutely outscaled by these particular enemies simply because there's no strategic response to their exclusively advantageous gimmicks. If the player is not overpowered enough to outscale them with raw numbers then the player is the one that gets outscaled. In general the higher the difficulty tiers get the less forgiving the game becomes towards decks that aren't overpowered, and getting an overpowered deck is entirely about random chance. Eventually it reaches the point where every major enemy becomes like the Blood Sprite and Rainbow Yak, hopelessly outscaling any build that can't overwhelm them with absurd numbers. But it at least takes awhile for the game to reach this point.The game itself looks gorgeous but there's also a lot of ridiculous glitches to it. Currently there's multiple random ways the game will crash, although it saves constantly so crashes are mostly just an annoyance. There's ways for the game to soft lock itself via cards becoming unresponsive, especially on controller where cards at the far side of the player's hand won't be selectable sometimes. The game constantly struggles to process what is happening, resulting in a delay on actions being performed. Several random upgrades, trinkets and or achievements aren't working currently.And the "Deluxe" addition of the game is absolutely ridiculous. The alternate card art pack adds barely any alternate card art and what it mostly does add are embarrassingly immature and immersion breaking tweaks to a couple card graphics. Meanwhile the alternate character outfits are just lazy, in some cases borderline unnoticeable tweaks to the existing character outfits. Honestly both packs are just really cringey, low effort, shallow cash grabs that cast a bad light on the game as a whole.Although not extremely diverse the substantial strategy elements, unique map exploration, ease of deck building and lovely art result in a satisfying and engaging experience; which manages to be quite balanced through most of the progression.If you're interested in finding more games like this I've probably reviewed quite a few on my curator page .
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is an interesting game. Having played 117 hours, I really enjoyed this game but I don't think it meets the quality of other Deckbuilders i've played. It lacks the simplicity of a game like Slay the Spire but also fails to present the wild combinations of decks and builds afforded to those who enjoy Across the Obelisk. If you like the genre, I think this game will hold your interest but it would surprise me if I met someone who said this was their favourite Deck Builder.

I played through the first run, had a fun experience, then tried to run it back again. When I tried to load into a second run, it froze and crashed. What it'll do is get stuck on the loading screen in a black background, then literally shut down my computer screen, and then the screen is transparent so I can see my desktop but the game cursor is still visible and I can't click anything or see the game. This has happened when I loaded into a second run, so I reloaded the game, and it crashed. I reboot the game and I get in, but this time I crash when I try to talk to the NPC. Same situation, but now I've tried multiple times and it crashes every time I try to initiate the first fight. I really hope this is just an error that can be fixed and not a bug in the game, because this game seemed really promising and I'm so excited to play it.Update: I came back 3 weeks later after seeing there was an update, and hoped the issue would be resolved. Booting it up, things looked smooth, but once I got into the game I came across the same issue. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, a great addition to the deckbuilder genre. Interesting mechanics. Nice art. Lots of achievements. Runs are a bit long, maybe 2h+ (please add an Animation skip!). _childDocuments_.review: It reminds me very much of  by Valklabs, but with a slightly less serious tone and world exploration added in which you have to manage exploration resources. Also, Roguebook has 2 optional public "tournaments" per day in which players compete to finish a run with special rules the fastest (they don't actually play matches against each other).The graphics in both games are stunningly beautiful, although while Relapse is in 3D and displays blood, Roguebook features well-drawn 2D sprites and more of a fairy tale charm (or rather a japanese mythical charm).Also, you don't have to be afraid to buy the same game twice; although they have several similarities regarding game mechanics they're both unique in their own way, bring different features to the table, and are definitely worth the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This roguelike deckbuilder is excellent in every aspect. Hindered only by it's awful name, Roguebook evolves every part of the existing subgenre in ways that make too much sense.-The one-two hit of having multiple heroes that build off and support each other keeps each fight fresh and engaging. -Carving your own way rather than picking a set path feels so much more freeing-Battles not rewarding you cards and instead getting them optionally allows you to craft your deck exactly the way you want rather than being forced to deal with a consistently overinflated, unpared deck.The only things that I wish would have been in here is some item or talent that allowed you to reroll rewards and for more scroll events to happen.This game was clearly made by masters of design.No doubt tied with Slay the Spire in GOAT of the subgenre.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been eyeing Roguebook since it was announced.  As a player of many of Richard Garfield's games and having spent hundreds (most likely thousands) of dollars from almost as soon as MtG hit the stage until back a few years ago I know the man knows how to make a good card game with interesting mechanics.  However I already have more Deckbuilder games, specifically Roguelike (eh, Roguelite technically, yes I am a traditionalist when it comes to the term) than I can shake a stick at I held off for a few weeks after launch just to see how it would go.    There already is such a great number of Roguelite Deckbuilders out there in the vein of Slay The Spire that it is getting harder and harder to really set one another apart.  Monster Train did a good job but most of the others that I have in my library while fun, don't overly reinvent the wheel, though each usually manage to put just enough spin on the genre to make them fun enough to play.  So the question is, does Roguebook mange to set itself apart from games such as Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Erannoth Reborn, Deck of Ashes,  and similar games that mix Card Games with FTL elements?  So far after about 2 1/2 hours of game time I feel that it mostly does.   It has enough uniqueness to it to be it's own game, yet you can jump in and figure out how to play it without much of a learning curve.   There is a story there but the lore isn't going to be what pulls you into the game.  It does have the "just one more try" feel about it which is always a good thing in my book.Stability wise I had no issues.  No crashes and the game ran smoothly.  The artwork is nice and doesn't get old to look at, and isn't a machine killer so you should be able to run it on a fairly dated machine.   I haven't tried it on any of my secondary rigs or my gaming laptop however on my aging desktop which is a i5-7400 @3Ghz running 16GB RAM, an SSD and Nvidia GeForce 1060 GTX the game ran smooth as silk.  As I like to disclaim, I play a lot of true Roguelike games such as Nethack, Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and Angband (often in pure ASCII mode, or low quality tile modes) so graphics are honestly not a huge sell point for me.   So I will just put that out there as a disclaimer.Music wise, I couldn't really tell you,  unless a game has a wonderful soundtrack such as that from Witcher 3, I almost never have the background music in games playing.   So I will not comment as to the music.  The other general sound effects are passable enough for me and what little voice acting there is is fine.Challenge wise the game seems pretty good.  I haven't beat the first boss yet though each run besides my first (I think I had four runs total) I got him down to without 10-15% health usually.   Each time I realized I fail I realize afterwards what mistakes I had made so I don't really think the game is unfair, nor do I feel it is too easy though I am sure once I really pay attention to it like most of these type games aside from the RNG you will learn how to cakewalk the bosses most of the time.Thus brings me to my final point, I can see where people will get upset because RNG like most Roguelite/Roguelike games will set you up for the loss no matter how well you play the game.  There was a run or two that I just got unlucky with what ink brushes that I got from fights and mini boss fights and I couldn't explore anymore of the map to setup my characters to really face the final boss with any real luck.   But that is just the name of the game when it comes to these kind of games.  So if you don't like games where there is just no way you sometimes will be able to win, no matter how skilled you may be, then this isn't going to be a game for you.  Then again when you get down to it neither would be Solitaire I would imagine.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is an excellent little addition to the ever growing genre of "Rougelike Deckbuilder". Even if you played any of these types of games you should feel right at home here but of course Rougebook comes with its own twists and mechanics to separate itself from the rest of the genre. My two favourite feature is the "Board-like" exploration where you have limited tool for exploration but with some clever positioning and movement you could definitely reveal the whole map (even though its not always the best idea). And the other mechanic i really enjoyed is the two hero combat system where your heroes position matters a lot and switching their places is constantly happening throughout the combat and it is just adds another depth to the fights.The game also boast on hell of a look with its fun designs and colorful graphics , it is absolutely lovely to look at.I also want to mention the Devs behind the game who are constantly engaging with the community and steadily adding new things (for free) to the game , absolute lads.- Recommended.
