_childDocuments_.review: (Purchased for ~11CAD)This is a solid rouge-like deck-builder. For those starting (and seeing complaints of lack of synergies) be warned that this has VERY heavy meta progression. I don't think it would be possible to win on a clean save file. The game is also a tad clunky (no way to speed up animations) which makes this feel extremely slow compared to the leaders in the genre. One thing that is very hard to ignore is how awful the UI/UX is designed. The game does zero favours for you in displaying information in a clean and efficient way. Example; there are no card types (ie attack card, defence card, summon, spell) and rather the cards effects are just descriptively written in the text box and its given a title and card art. This causes two huge issues (opinion me). 1) It is unclear what your hand is 'at a glance'. When you immediately draw a hand of cards good UI should have some sort of labelling/symbol system so players can quickly see roughly what their hand is. 2) The card descriptions themselves are not written in a consistent format and it can make the nature/effect of the card unclear until you have thrown it down once to test it. With all that in mind, I have done a number of runs and will likely attempt to max out the ascension system for difficulty completion but I would be pumped for some extra polish on the game. Good Game

_childDocuments_.review: [Updated the review for the new content patch in August]Average at first but then it get drags down to something much lower.Gameplay Loop:1) Start off by choosing 2 heroes (Out of 4. Last 2 needs to be unlocked)2) Choose your difficulty3) Unveils part of your map covered using Ink provide4) Fight battles5) Gather resources from the map6) Shop7) Fight Boss8) Repeat 2 more timesWhy I don't recommend the game.* I usually post a game review when I finish it at the highest difficulty and all the achievements. I can't do that here because of bugs. A handful of achievements aren't working. There are also bugs in the game like Cloud saves being broken and deleting saves files.[The new patch added even more bugs and stuff that are critical like cloud saves are still not fixed. A handful of achievements are still broken]* Lag / optimization issues with certain cards. There's nothing more infuriating in a card game where playing cards feels bad. One second lag here isn't too bad except when it's a card you play 4-5 times in a round.[Daggers are fixed and do not take forver to use now. However, certain cards just pauses for a couple of seconds when you use them. Two steps forward and one step back]* Gameplay animation. The game have a nice gameplay animation for all their cards. Which is great until you have to play a card 10 times in a round and you can't skip any of it. Add that with the lag and you got yourself a stew.[See above]* RNG. Cardgames have an inherent RNG in card order. Roguelike deckbuilders also have another layer added on top where your selection of cards and relics are not stable. You have to make the best out of your situation. Roguebook Devs decided that wasn't enough. They want more RNG. Fairy wells, Gemstone mines, free treasure, and talent trees are all randomized. These items are game changing and/or extremely powerful. Yet you have no control on when you get it and what you get. When I win, I like to know it's because of my decisions not because I got lucky. Imagine if one game you get 5 mana and another where you get 3. That will be a situation you'll be subjected too more often that not. [No changes here. However on higher difficulties is much harder so when RNG fails you it really hurts now]* Lack of content. There really isn't much here and probably the reason why there is so much RNG in this game. You have 3 worlds (maps) with 3 bosses. That's it. No map variations . No daily challenge. No storyline to uncover. I play for achievements to extend game time and some of those are broken (no ETA fix by the Devs).[Gem mines were added as a bonus dungeon. As of writing they are not worth it unless you do not like your run and want to cripple it.][1 was fixed, some remains. Can't wait to 100% this game in December 2077]* Deckbuilding and the Final Bosses. There are 2 final bosses. And you have to build your deck to defeat them. It doesn't matter if you discover cards that let you loop your deck and kills enemies in a couple of turns. If your end bosses if Greed you really should not take those low cost weak cards. If you're fighting against Mist you should have more than 1 win condition because if can be taken from you outside of your control.  Keep in mind, these bosses aren't hard. They just limit what you can do and how you can build your deck. To quote a forum user: "It sucks to have your card choices not even matter in a game 100% about making smart deck-building choices." This is even worse on Epilogue 15.[The Devs fixed major issues with the bosses. But now the problem still remains their mechanics are not fun to play against. I think most players (I am part of this group) want something more interactive with the bosses. The world 1 and 2 bosses are well designed and had interesting mechanics. The end bosses are just a drag to fight. I gave this game 2 royal ink out of 5.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful but extremely flawed deck building roguelike that is better left on the shelf.  The exploration system is clever and rewarding and the long term progression mechanics are adequate but most critically Roguebook fails to deliver a balanced and fun deckbuilding experience. Early on the encounters vary from trivial to impossible with little rhyme or reason and far too much left to the chance of a drafting systems that puts the player fully at the mercy of RNG. Competent games of this type use drafting systems that differentiate between types of cards (defensive, offensive....common, rare) early on to ensure that players have access to the tools they need to progress, but this one does not.  The biggest flaw, however, is the death system. I suspect that they intend that their unlimited-use resurrect in combat would be more forgiving, but because it adds dead cards to your deck and resurrects your dead character with 10% life, all it really does is drag out the loss and make it more painful.  If you manage to grind your way through the game enough to unlock a wider variety of cards and tools, you will find that the late game experience is even more broken than the early game, with every run turning into some combination of infinite combos and OTK's. This can be entertaining, a few times, but really loses its luster game after game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite Roguelike, yet it's almost still hard to recommend for what a buggy piece of ♥♥♥♥ it is. Granted this is not as buggy as the Nintendo Switch version, but Christ almighty it still is a disaster. Clearly the devs has no intention of fixing all the issues wrong with it. All that being said, I've had this game corrupt my saved progress more than a dozen times and it's crashed on me more than 100 times. No exaggeration as I been playing this game since its release. But now that negative is out of the way. This is my favorite Rogue like deck builder. Easily over the likes of Slay the Spire or Inscryption. I do hold those games in high regard, and at least they are mostly bug free unlike this title. What I love most about this game is it's map system. It brings a new level of discovery and risk reward other than being given roughly 2-3 alternative paths which both Slay the Spire and Inscryption do. The graphics certainly have a Hearthstone look. Love it or hate it. As for the combat, you can find so many ways of synergizing builds. I constantly find new and powerful ways to become powerful years later. To me it's the best Roguelike and the most buggy.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I've played Slay The Spire, Monster Train and now Roguebook. Of all three, I think Roguebook is the best *card* game. I know that Slay the Spire fans will consider that sacrilege, so I'll try and explain. Both Slay the Spire and Monster Train lean havily into RNG and roguelite elements. RNG is a huge factor in those games and there's a priority on meta and unlocks in order to progress and eventually beat the game.While Roguebook does employ those elements, it's far easier to build a viable deck every. single. run. And your strategic choices have a much larger impact than the cards you come across.TL;DR: If you're good at CCGs like Magic: The Gathering, that skill will transfer to Roguebook, and you will feel powerful as you make your way through the game.Whereas, Slay the Spire and Monster Train can just bend you over regardless of how good you are at CCGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good, even if on the somewhat easier side.Pretty standard deckbuilding game where you can create some damn fun/broken decks, and there are plenty of items to go around, plus you can augment cards with gems, and get random talents for drafting bigger decks, so there's certainly a lot of variety.The two major gimicks this game has is that a) you need to 'draw' (explore, really) the map as you go with limited resources and b) you have two heroes instead of the one. I'd give the game an 'alright' rating if I could.Kinda goes like this:* You got 3 characters, can unlock a 4th.* Games are played using combinations of 2 of the 4 characters.* A new card every time a character levels up.* New cards stop arriving after 10 levels, no new rewards for characters after that point. Leveling up has no purpose after 10.* Nothing left to unlock except for difficulty modifiers and standard roguelike options (higher chance of rare thing appearing etc).I wanted to keep playing but there was very little to unlock which would affect my decks and characters. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed roguelike deckbuilder games like Slay the Spire, this game will feel satisfying in the same way while also not being a clone. Lots of new ideas and systems are changed like choosing 2 out of 4 characters to play each time (allowing different decks) as well as each card having 1/2 slots to put gems that you can pick up and add bonus effects on to cards that can keep things fresh but also lead to some pretty satisfying combos. The level progression system is much more flexible and interesting to explore then Slay the Spires mostly linear choices for encounters.One major criticism was that they had day 1 paid DLC with extra content but after hearing feedback they immediatly just added it to the main game for free which shows they are willing to listen to feedback and adjust accordingly. I've done less then 10 runs (have been able to complete a couple of runs) and so far I'm really enjoying the game and cant wait to see what else they bring!

An exceptional entry in the genre, which is kinda unsurprising given Richard Garfield's involvement.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 6/22/21 -Since my initial review, the developer has given everyone access to the DLC.  All is forgotten and forgiven.  After playing a few more games of both wins and losses, the balance is still a little off. If I could, this would be a neutral review.The decision points in this game still aren't as sensible. You are either going to get that "one" card that is just going to win you the run right off the bat, or you are going to be offered 20 cards and die a very slow death as the deck goes nowhere. The one good mechanic of the game is that it does reward you for taking cards in your deck. Balance between characters are still very noticeable. I will still say the first run of the game still feels off as well. Depending on how good you are at deck builders, you may have the frustrating experience of not beating the game until run 3-4.  I am hoping that this game will also have a proper conclusion. Currently lore wise, it is still lacking. The below review was when I first played this as it came out with payed DLC - and since I have played it a bit longer - you can still read this, some of this is still relevant.There was a steampost about this game how most people compare this to Slay the Spire.I played one game of this and thought, "yeah, people need to give this a chance".I've played 3 more runs after, and I am sad to say I know why people make the comparison.All the runs I've played have been nothing but frustration, as I try to understand the synergy(or lack of) of the cards I am deciding to pick up, and what other possible decisions I'm making that is failing me. This game is heavy into the meta-progression, as in you need them to win. Its not the same meta-progression you expect from STS, where it opens up gameplay, rather this feels required (more HP, more gold, more treasure)This is super unfortunate, because I haven't seen much of the game after 4 runs, each taking more than an hour. There is a huge lack of lore or progression. and the lack of decisions to make makes this game a huge slog. Imagine playing STS, and not getting past act 1 after 4-5 runs, and not getting past act 2 after the same amount of runs, while being locked out of your very first unlocks until 10 runs after. Thats what this game is feeling.The beauty of roguelites is that you find different ways to win. Whatever this game is, its just a miserable slog. I haven't learned anything except that I need to find where the save file is located so I can skip all this metaprogression.If you haven't done ascension 20 yet in STS, do that before checking out this game.  Other than the gameplay, the art is beautiful. The lack of lore and story (gated behind weird difficulty) is making this hard to play as well. There are some elite and boss varieties, but they aren't noticeable. Likely, if you have built a broken deck, it will probably carry you through the entire run without consequence.Edit 06/18/21Okay, forget everything I said above. Why is there a PAID DLC ON THE FIRST DAY OF RELEASE?  What?!!!

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about ? It's a well-made, fun and intricate deckbuilder with roguelite elements, and while I have a lot of issues with it I still like it, and would recommend it to players who enjoy other deckbuilder games like  and .Anyone whose been paying attention to this title over the lead-up to it's release knows that the game launched with a lot of issues, and if you ask me I'd not hesitate to say that it came out of the oven too early. The ordeal involving the Apex Predator pack however has proven beyond any doubt that the developer's heart is in the right place, and the game has received plenty of patches and hotfixes over it's lifespan to salve-over the egregious inconsistencies. It's perfectly playable now however, but I still adamantly stand by my statement that it should have baked a little longer. But now that those issues are irrelevant, let's talk about how the game currently holds up;Describing my experience with , both past and present, in one phrase would be "two steps forward, one step back". Meaning that for every two things  does really well, there's one thing it does that I absolutely hate. Gameplay-wise,  has an excellent gameplay loop, emphasising exploration and resource-management with a fog-of-war style approach to it's maps, requiring the player to utilise "inks" to maximum efficiency to reveal the map's tiles and uncover a very wide array of resources, ranging from simple gold piles to gem troves that can be used to apply new effects to your cards.What I don't like about the exploration is that after chapter one there's a guaranteed event where this incorrigible greaseball of an NPC appears, steals one of your treasures and runs away to an undiscovered area of the map. Which has the potential to completely screw over your run as this prolapsed pink-sock can steal a treasure that is absolutely essential to your build, then f--k off to a tile that requires a large amount of resources to reach.The card mechanics in the game are well-implemented, and aside from the clunky nature of the UI they flow reasonable well enough (if I might impose a recommendation for future updates, add a "quick-play" option to skip the card animations, or at least speed them up like what  did). They can create combinations that are very deep and intricate and require careful ordering when playing to maximise damage output or mitigation. Choosing a combination of two out of four playable hero characters, each with their own deck of cards that excel in some areas but not in others, most of the combinations work well with eachother and if managed properly can effectively cover eachothers weaknesses. But what I don't like (read: HATE) about the deck management is the lack of card removal options. The game seems to encourage building a colossal deck, which is at odds for my preferred playstyle of other deckbuilder roguelikes. This is definitely a personal preference and you might have a completely different opinion, but I like to keep my decks small and consistent, and I'm very picky about what cards to add because for each card put into the deck makes it less likely I'll draw the cards that I need. So for me, removal is one of the most important aspects of the genre, something that  did exceptionally well. What  has instead however are these little "Alchemy Shops" which allows to to replace one card in your deck from a pool of randomised cards and gems, which at best can be rationalised as a super-upgrade, and at worst can just end up replacing one useless card with another useless card. I know this is very much a personal gripe, but for me it damages my overall takeaway from the game.The characters and combinations of decks are mostly well thought-out and work well with eachother. Mah boi Seifer in particular is an absolute beast and his deck is exactly what I like it to be: It has unique mechanics that don't isolate the other characters but instead works with them cohesively, it requires planning and efficient management and it's payoff is incredibly satisfying. Sorocco is the hefty, reliable heavy-hitter whose deck is as big in impact as it is big in energy cost, and his easy access to area-of-effect attacks and massive block cards make him a sturdy character. Aurora is like a glass-tank, with interesting support mechanics and a lot of access to energy generation and card draw, and as a result she's rarely anything but essential.The short-end of the stick of the cast, for me at least, is Sharra. I find her in terms of gameplay, aesthetics and character to be extremely boring. Her deck emphasises multi-strike attacks and mobility, so she benefits immensely from power stacking, so she works very well with Sorocco. But I find that she lags behind when paired with either of the other two. She and Aurora both have little health pools, and while Aurora does have access to hefty block cards they're effectiveness is highly situational, so their momentum often peters out in more intense difficulties. As well, she doesn't get along with Seifer since they both want to be in front, they both want to dish out the damage and they both generally lack in reliable defence. I find this to be a recurring trend in deckbuilders like this, that the starting character is always my least favourite, like the Ironclad in  or the Hellhorned in .Finally, the game's presentation is phenomenal. The character and enemy animations are smooth and fluid, the design and overall art-direction is colourful and brimming with personality, and the voice-acting/sound design is wonderful. What I'm not to impressed by is the music, I'm sure the composer worked really hard on it, but it's mostly just generic-sounding and forgettable orchestral tracks. Compared to  which has an absolutely breathtaking series of compositions, this one just feels feeble and toothless. I also REALLY hate the Yak enemies. Not because they're overpowered or broken, but because they're so freaking adorable and I hate myself for fighting and killing them. Plz remov yaks my bleeding heart can't take them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good - very good even - roguelike deckbuilder. It looks great, the two character/deck system adds some dynamism to rounds, and basing rewards on the collection of cards reduces the need to pare down your deck as a winning strategy. The setting is colourful and imaginative, and while I'm not personally the biggest fan of the aesthetic (scans a little "hidden object game" to me), it's certainly fully realized. All of these markers  help differentiate it from the undisputed kind of the genre, Slay The Spire (with which it shares a number of features).Where it doesn't quite live up to that comparison, though, is in speed and ease of use. The more detailed graphics result in longer load times. The world map approach, while interesting, results in more time between matches. And while I haven't taken a stopwatch to the average round, they FEEL longer. There's also no way to speed up animations in the options, or reduce the image quality for faster loading. For me, this kind of game lives on the laptop, and I don't want to have to rely on my gaming PC to make it speedy (note: the controller layout works quite well on Steam Deck, but I still found the loading to be quite long). Very good, but deeper optimization and more speed options would make it great. 3.5/5.

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite good, it expands from Slay The Spire, but I think it gets boring fast. While Slay The Spire had at least one "objective" to really finish the game, this one does not. After one successful run (which is really easy to get), all you can do is repeat the same runs on the same places but with difficulty twists. While in Slay The Spire you had to collect the gems with different heroes to open the door to the "real final boss", in this one you just repeat the same stuff over and over. Got bored after 20 hours, which is a pity, because I expected to play more.It has some really nice ideas on cards and synergies, although it becomes a bit RNG dependant as the game gets harder. The fact you can play with 2 heroes and change their positions, while also being able to explore the tiles, has a nice flavor too.In short, it's a good game to distract with for a few hours

_childDocuments_.review: This game is plain AWESOME.Take Slay the Spire (awesome game too), multiply the amount of fun by 100, the possibilities by 1000 and the cosmetic aspect by 9999, and you get this game.The replayability of Roguebook goes far further than the price tag seems to entitle. The universe is GORGEOUS and the combats feel balanced, challenging but fun. You can make sick combos that are super gratifying, even if you end up losing a fight. _childDocuments_.review: Good game, recommend on a sale. cool it's based in the same universe as Faeria. Sadly there are some annoying clunky elements that stop this good game from being great.- Can't see party perk tree until you've already gotten to a specific level. Makes it impossible to plan a big vs small deck build.- Can't see the different run (epilogue) challenges before selecting your heroes. Most will choose their party based on the challenges, not the other way around. - Flash gems are annoying and tedious to use. In Slay The Spire you often use a potion once you've spent your mana and need that one last move to not get rekt. This game makes you use flash gems (potions basically) WITH cards, so you can rarely use them once you realize you need to. - The game progresses each run by giving you permanent upgrades and challenges that have a fun risk/reward element. As time goes on you just get un-fun challenges that are straight debuffs, with no reward associated with the debuff. This is an un-fun trap that a lot of deck building games fall into.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets a solid mixed review from me. I enjoyed it for a couple runs but only kind of. It has all the pieces of a fun deck builder, but only the bare minimum. It has great artwork and exploration elements, but these only hold your attention for so long.I feel like a game that highlights synergistic builds, by mixing and matching decks, needed more approaches. Currently there are only 4 base decks with each base deck having their own flavoring, but they don't feel different enough (as in the pairings do the same thing at the end of the day it seems), and even if they did, they don't have enough options. We needed more than 4 characters/ decks for a game like this. As others have pointed out the balancing is a bit flawed, but I don't agree with the meta game bashing. I like the progression system and it reminds me a lot of hades by making the game easier to a point. Then after you hit that point the game only gets harder. So I'd take that critisim with a grain of salt. The only valid part of it is that it takes way to long to unlock the 4th hero. I'm already bored of the first three and haven't unlocked the 4th after beating the game once. Not sure how to do it honestly.TL;DRPros+ Great looks+ Fun exploration mechanics+ All the fun mechancis of a basic deck builderCons- Decks dont feel different enough- Characters are not diverse in theme enough (of the three i have played there are two bruisers and one striker. Missing utility and blasting at the very least). - The "synergy" element of the game encourages endlessly adding cards to your deck to unlock passives. Most the passives are fairly weak and as many people know, adding cards to your deck is often a bad idea as it increases the RNG of getting good draws. So basically its compensation for doing something bad, and even then its not enough compensation'- No way to remove cards from your deck only transform- Functionally not that innovative besides the exploration mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun gimmicky 2 character Rogue-like deck builder. There are many cards locked behind progression with characters, and a progression of difficulty with modifiers. Some items are single character dependent, some are character order dependent, some are both character usable. Cards work a similar way, and there is a mechanic of position switching. The game requires a bit of understanding what things do, and each card can be enhanced with a gem that augment or change how they work. It is a nice take on deck builders I've played and it's definitely offering a challenge since focusing on one character can destroy a run, but it reminds me tunnel vision can often lead to shortfalls.

_childDocuments_.review: With allies, hero swapping, and fog of war this deck builder roguelite does a lot to stand itself out from the other big hitters. The card tuning isn't as tight as other big names, but their is a lot of depth when you have 4 different heroes to mix and match in your two person party. The gameplay is smooth, the controller support is passable (I found some controller mechanics aren't intuitive, like reviewing your items or showing where your brush will clear the fog.) and the art style great. It plays well on the SteamDeckn aside from some hard to read text. A way to zoom cards or accessibility options to increase text size would go a long way. Once you are comfortable with the cards though this faded a bit. Easy choice for a deck builder if you're craving it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a game about a book that has trapped you inside of it. As you explore the book, you use ink to reveal combats, vaults, gold, and more to help you reach the end of each chapter. At the end of the chapter is a boss that becomes increasingly stronger and harder to overcome the more chapters you progress. Overall the deckbuilder roguelite is very fun and well put together. You play with two heroes each with their own cards and in combat in a different order. Depending on their order will depend on how they take damage and cards can force you back or forward. This requires balancing to your deck as well as to each combat with cards that have many different mechanics, some that echo other games like Slay the Spire while other mechanics are unique to Roguebook. As you progress, you will find pages that help you embellish your abilities and make later runs easier. However there is also an epilogue that gives significant debuffs to you to make runs increasingly difficult after you beat the game. Overall this is a very well put together deckbuilder roguelite and excels at competing with others like Monster Train and Slay the Spire.Pick this up if you like roguelite and/or deckbuilders and want a new flavor to try.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: 18 Hours Played There isn't much left to do at the 18 hour mark.  The challenges are very easy and the replayability is gone. This is a cool game for the first 10 or so hours but once you beat it the first time it is downhill from there.Slay the Spire ruins so many games- this one included.  You are just so very conditioned to have high replay value and then, when it isn't there, the game feels empty.The Lead Dev needs to tweak the progression system.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm always looking for great roguelike deck builder games as they are my go to for when I want to relax and test out great combos. My top fav is still Monster Train so I'm always on the hunt for the next one that will come close to it's awesomeness. Roguebook is up there for sure.In Roguebook you play as 4 heroes (You start with only 2 at first), trapped in a magic relic known as...the Roguebook. They must stop the evil force inside the book to free themselves by defeating monsters and grabbing ink and brushes to draw out the pages. Can you help them escape?Like most deckbuilders, the first few runs were very meh. You don't have many cards or artifacts unlocked, so it takes awhile for things to pick up. By my 4-5th run, I started getting decent cards and learned how things worked and the game truly started to shine. Learning when to use defend cards to swap my heroes, gaining awesome "ally" cards, and so much more. When the game clicks, it clicks!One of the things I find interesting in Roguebook is how they want you to obtain cards. The more cards you add to your deck, your overall party levels up and gets passive perks. There are chests that let you draft cards hidden on the overworld map and you can even use the shop on the map to buy more cards and gems. Each card has a gem slot that you can attach a gem to to give them an added bonus. You can make it do more damage, more block, or even super unique properties like add debuffs. The amount of custimazation is really fun to work with especially as you add more passive buffs.You have to find paint brushes and ink to fill out the hexes on the overworld map to find more goodies, enemies, or special events. You can also find pages, which are the currency to give you even greater passives prior to your run. This can unlock more places on the map for you to discover like the mine, the well, and the alchemy lab that lets you transmute cards. Since the map is different each time, it keeps the gameplay fresh.The art is really beautiful. Battles are fun and grow more challenging the more you play. The enemy variety can get a lil repetitive after a few runs and soon you'll learn what cards you need when facing certain opponents. Some enemies have really unique battles like getting stronger the more cards you play in a turn and so on. You can even fight secret enemies and bosses depending on choices you make on special events to get rare buffs/ cards.Lastly, the four heroes have very unique cards. You can only take 2 of them per run, but it's fun to mix and match them to see how they synergize with each other. Completing runs allow you to do challenge runs in which you add a stipulation to make it a lil tougher. The payoff allows you to unlock more pages, so it's worth it for the fun and to see if you can complete them.I don't have too many gripes. My first gripe would be that for some reason, my game seems to run a lil slower once I started unlocking more things. There aren't any graphical options I can really do to tweak it so it's just annoying to have it stutter sometimes. As stated above, the enemy variety can start to get a lil samey after you do a few runs unless you find secret bosses and enemies. Final verdict? This is a very fun roguelike deck builder. I've finished about 5 runs and still want to keep unlocking more cards and passives for my heroes. When I get some great synergy and see the damage rack up, or play 8 cards in one turn when I'm only supposed to play 3, it really makes me feel awesome. I recommend you try this game out. Enjoy the art and card combos, and enjoy the updates as they just recently added a tournament mode and a new character so there's still lots more fun on the way. Thanks for reading!

However enemy order is completely unchangable and   uninteractive.- Other then damage there is 1 of the 4 currently available heroes with maybe 3 cards that can affect the enemy with one   effect (-4 damage that's it, no stacking either, pretty much only useful vs multi-attacks). Meanwhile the enemy gets  though less than expected coming from other games in this genre a handful of status effects to apply to the players  characters- And as for players themselves, there's not many buffs they can apply to themselves either, - so the entire game kinda feels  like i'm just crunching numbers alone and the enemy is just kinda there. Overworld- it has a neat/unique over-world map exploration mechanic.  You can't see the map, essentiall you have to strategically   place lines and circles to maximise the area you can see and to reach objectives hidden within.  But it doesn't take long to   realize optimal ways to do this, act 2 throws in a slightly different map layout to alter how you play these but then act 3   goes back to nothing.  This is the games equivalent of choosing your paths commonly found in other rogue-like card   battlers but a nice twist overall

_childDocuments_.review: I own slay the spire on basically every electronic device that will support it, it's my go to game when I'm traveling, killing time, on the can - what have you, I play it the way people play solitaire or do crossword puzzles it's just a thing I like to do. I'm no expert at the game but over the years I've been playing it I've come to a very deep appreciation of and sensitivity to,  it's rules, synergies and systems. I say all of that because   the developers clearly have the same love and respect for the genre defining deck builder that I do.I do reccommend Roguebook wholeheartedly - I've dumped about 40 hours into it over the last month or so and I think it's a charming, beautifully rendered fun game but if you like sts you will get your money's worth out of this little gem. However, it lacks the consistency and depth of it's superior predecessor. I find the base starting decks cumbersome and unbalanced, a lack of a consistent card removal mechanic, not enough deck manipulation tools or inter-party synergies mean I am almost always praying for rng to provide  me a bleed or rage based I win button. This one was close to becoming an all-timer for me but ultimately just lacks that last level of balance and depth that keeps it just shy of greatness, but a legitimate case could be made for my expectations being too high based on what I am comparing it too. All in all if you like the genre, this is a fun addition to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Gave this one a negative review on release, played it now for a little bit and it is much better and indeed very enjoyablePositive:+ You always play as a team of 2 out of 4 characters, where each character has their own cards, traits and special abilities+ If one character dies, you can still continue the fight and try to resurrect the fallen one by playing certain resurrection cards 5 times+ Effects of cards change can change, depending on the characters' position. This leads to some cool combo effects+ Between battles, you move around the area which is divided into several hexagon tiles. In the beginning only one path to the boss is active, but you can activate more tiles by using paint brushes and inks which allows you to go your own way and discover the area+ Art style is great and all the characters and enemies look really cool. There are also animations for attacking which makes the game feel alive+ Enemies have very cool mechanics and unique status effectsNeutral:+-New special effects for your characters and your group can be unlocked if you have a certain amount of cards in your deck. This is nice, because you are rewarded for a bigger deck, but on the other hand this leads to situations where you fill your deck with more cards just for that effect...+- Luck and RNG / The tile-system: While in Slay the Spire or Monster Train your path is clear and you can always choose a direction (for example resting at a bonfire it Slay the Spire), in Roguebook most of the map is hidden. If you don't manage your ink well or get unlucky with the drops after fights, you can't unlock large parts of the map, which doesn't feel good, but is probably intendedNegatives:- The death system is very punishing. Not only do you have to end the fight with only one character (who has to eat all the damage OR block without being able to deal damage), you also receive wound cards which permanently stay in your deck for each time a character dies. Then, your normal draws will be replaced by the resurrection cards, which means, your next turns will be weaker as well. If you manage to resurrect your fallen character, it returns to battle with like 8 HP, which means you probably won't survive the next battle, if you don't have enough heal flasks left- This game's meta-progression system, where you have to collect "pages" that drop at random which you need to strengthen your next runs still feels a little bit clunky. So your early runs could feel like grinds to collect those pages, while later on you are much strongerOverall, the experience is much better and I can see that the devs used their time to improve this!

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to wait until I put 30+ hours into the game before I posted a review, since I'm the type of gamer that gets bored rather quickly. I tend to jump around a lot and play 5 or 6 different games during a typical 3 hour nightly gaming session.Additionally, if I'm still playing a game which has cost me less than a dollar per hour played, I figure I've gotten my money's worth.I bought Roguebook when it first hit steam, mainly because I was an early Faeria player, and I thought it would be similar. I refunded it after an hour, because it was obvious that this game shared very little it's CCG cousin.I'm glad I tried it again though, because it's a very good Rogue/Card game in it's own right. It was a bit bit frustrating at the beginning, until I got familiar with the puzzle-like aspect of the map; balancing picking more voluntary fights (with more damage to my heros' precious health), with the chance of obtaining a powerful item or card to help me progress. I rarely keep playing these types of games after I've completed the first run and unlocked all of the characters, but I just unlocked the final Hero and see myself putting a bit more time in trying out her style. It gets repetitive like most games in this genre, but uncovering the map is still quite enjoyable.I only wish the actual design of the map would be more random, and not just the location of objects. Every level basically starts out the same: Visit the merchant, open a box, start the first fight (usually mandatory since he is blocking the way to the S>N path), walk up that narrow path to open another box and then move north a hex or two more to reveal a location. From there on, it's trying to figure out the most efficient way to visit the tower on the left and the one on the right to open up even more of the map.The game design probably dictates this approach, since randomizing the map with something like the Boss to the West, and 2 towers to the East, would have players screaming about the bad RNG if the map proved to be too difficult to uncover.I'm starting to hate that little path though.The graphics are pleasant, the battles range from simple to very challenging, and overall the progression is well-balanced.I would recommend it to the casual player like myself. I can't speak for the hardcore players and whether it would hold their interest for hundreds of hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say I was not expecting a turnaround in this DLC business, I'm very pleasantly surprised and consequently . The old review can still be found after this new (more elaborate) one.The first thing that stands out is how pretty the game looks, the graphic design and animations are by far the best in the genre (among around ten dekcbuilders I tried). Two core mechanics distinguish this game from others: The explorable map and swapping the positions of the two heroes in fight. While the discovery of the map is fun at first, after a few run it becomes a bit repetitive and more a source of frustration than anything when your brushes discover nothing repetitively (I wish you could tell in advance when a tile is empty or not to avoid some of the randomness of a run). The swapping is a strong mechanic that is both fun and allows for cool build ideas/interactions.There could be more build defining cards to allow for a greater variety of builds and synergies , and the balance is a bit off still, but hopefully gathering usage data will help the developer flesh out the most boring/unused cards and tune some enemies to improve the game in those regards.As of today there are still a noticeable amount of bugs, crashes (but I'm on Proton so it might be the reason) and card not behaving like they should - although it's not to the point that it hinders the enjoyment of the game.The developer stated they worked really hard on it and you can definitely tell it's true, after the backpedal from the day one content dlc we can hope that the remaining issues will be dealt with to make this game one of the top in the genre.The game is good but not good enough to excuse the greed of the publisher hiding content behind a paid DLC on release day.It's already more expensive than most deckbuilder roguelikes out there and not that much novel to justify it.In term of Gameplay it is still miles away from Slay the Spire, less build defining cards (meaning less replayability), the balance is questionable and the meta progression is over the top.I would advice waiting for a special offer even if it means waiting some time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really solid evolution of the kind of gameplay you'll be familiar if you're a fan of Slay the Spire or other deckbuilders.The mechanical changes here add a lot to the game, in my opinion.  First, the biggest one is that you have two characters, not one, and as a general rule the vast majority of your cards are "played" by one of the two characters.  Secondly, your characters have a tactical position, basically either in front or in back, and as a general rule, most damage will occur to the "front" character.  Another change is that when one character loses all of its life, while that character is "down" the game is not over unless the other character dies in the same battle, and the first character will usually come back in a turn or two, or when the battle is won.Another change is that rather than a branching decision tree, you are exploring a large map by using "brushes" and "inks" to open up sections of the map.  You can then collect resources you find, or engage in battles in order to get rewards of gold or more brushes and inks to open more areas.Progression occurs after successful "runs" and allows you to permanently enhance your characters and add additional resources to the map.Additionally you can open up additional characters (at the time of this review I have 4 open) and they play quite differently, so that gives the game a lot of replayability.  Additionally after the 1st time you beat it, you can add difficulty enhancements which add additional rewards for completing the game at the higher difficulty. Overall as a fan of Slay the Spire and Monster Train as well as other deck building roguelikes, I think this is a really good one and would recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew this was a good video game when my run took a turn from "well, let's just see what this final boss looks like" to a nail-biter of a victory, clinched by a final blow where my rat/demon hero devoured the soul of a creature made of shadows. I mean, that's video games, am I right?!?!If that somehow isn't enough for you, and you need to talk about things like "mechanics" and "the state of roguelike deckbuilder genre", know that this isn't just another Slay the Spire clone (said as someone who would put that game on their all time top ten list). As Cameron Kunzelman said in in his article for Vice , Roguebook owes a lot to that now genre standard. but inverts a lot of its logic. The game encourages you to build a "fat" deck, not to pare it down. Some of the most interesting tactical decisions are made when figuring out how to traverse the map, the area where Slay the Spire often feels most stale. The most enticing "new" feature in Roguebook for many will be that you get to use two heroes at once, which leads to Magic the Gathering style deck color combinations that are delightful to play around with both mechanically and narratively. I like to think that by that time that final boss's soul was absorbed into my rat hero's demon arm, that he and his companion for the run--a half-ogre pirate first mate and blocking specialist--understood each other a little bit better than they had when they first began their journey. That made me feel good. Almost as good as banishing that shadow creature to the abyss with my sick card combination.

You are painting your path on a randomly generated map.  35+ hours in and passed Epilogue 10 I still and finding new things.

_childDocuments_.review: + quality and variable gameplay+ a combination of deckbuilding and game map detection- some UI elements - minor technical errorsRoguebook is a deckbuilding roguelite card game on which the well-known designer Richard Garfield, the creator of Magic the Gathering, collaborated with the Belgian studio Abrakam Entertainment. It's recognizable on the game, its game system is well thought, even if not complicated. The gameplay has 2 parts , one is the movement in the game world, the player uses limited resources to reveal a map of each of the three campaigns and gain new items and cards for a pair of his heroes. The second is a classic card combat, where the acquired items are used in a series of combat. The variability is based on a combination of 2 of 4 characters with unique decks, the cards can be modified by inserting gems into their slots and create classic synergies and combos. Of course, as always with a similar type of game, random luck is a significant element within a single run. After the first completion, it is possible to make the transition difficult with various challenge settings.The graphics of the game are no miracle, but art is nice.I've been playing a lot of deskbuilding games like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Grieflands and Roguebook lately, I rank Roguebook among the most successful.7,5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game must be one of the few that survived the pitch, development, and launch without changing at all. I genuinely believe someone wrote down on a white board "Slay the Spire, but we let Richard Garfield do it?" and everyone burst into applause. I'm not kidding. If you like Slay the Spire, and think the idea of picking a pair of protagonists at the start of the run is a cool gimmick, then you will like this game. Just stop reading reviews, you've made up your mind, buy it.There are welcome tweaks to the formula: shop is always accessible, map isn't just a list of connected objectives and more central to the theme of the game, art is pretty great and well animated, upgrading cards is completely different (and much better, tbh), there is no separate archetype for decks with lots of cards versus decks with few cards (as you get more cards you steadily upgrade your team with "talents" unique to each hero).Some minuses of course: Things I would consider fun, core mechanics to the game might take a few runs to even get to (the alchemist upgrading cards, for instance, and 1 of the possible party members). The icons for enemy actions can be a bit muddled and hard to distinguish at a glance. Some stuff is left intentionally vague so that you have that surprise value from finding it out yourself.... but that ends up getting in the way of having fun, faster. It seems built to be a very sturdy base that they add on to with DLC and such.Overall, I am quite liking this game. The genre has been getting garbage rip-offs of STS's innovative concept for a few years now. Finally I have one that really scratches that STS itch in a way none of the others have. Excited to see with what the team has in store post-launch!SIDE NOTE:There was a bit of controversy, justly gained, when this game launched a few days ago. Instead of just the game, there was also a day 1 DLC with a few more cards (4, I believe) and a new final encounter/boss. Within hours they were flooded with complaints, as most assumed this was a scummy cash grab for a product the team must not have faith in. The only reasoning I can come up with is that they really did have no faith in initial sales and knew they would have to take a PR hit to make sure they could break even on dev costs. They quickly responded to the community and lumped the DLC back into the base game and refunded those who had already bought it. I believe this was an honest mistake from the developers, who are hopefully now enjoying some positive word-of-mouth and working diligently on DLC worth a standalone price!

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of good single-player, deck-builder games out there and Roguebook is one of them. Similar to Slay the Spire and Monster Train, Roguebook sits comfortably between the two, borrowing mechanincs from both but at the same time being unique.Roguebook was developed by Abrakam, in collaboration with inventor and game designer. Richard Garfield creator of Magic: The Gathering. This was one of the things that caught my attention and I decided to play the game in the first place.The story goes a little something like this. The Roguebook was an esteemed book of lore in the world of Faeria. After the events in the Chronicles of Gagana take place, it was lost and forgotten inside the depths of a faeria well. There it lingered for over a decade. Faeria besides being the name of the world is also the source of magic. After being in contact with faeria for so long, the Rogubook transformed in a terrible way. Over time it slowly developed a mischievous personality and it devoured the four heroes Sharra, Seifer, Sorocco and Aurora inside its pages, thus trapping them. Later a fifth hero was revealed. Fugoro who got added as a dlc. Your task as the player is to choose two heroes, defeat the book and escape if you can.One of the things Roguebook does differently is the map, which looks like a board game with hexagonal tiles. The map is hidden behind a fog of war and you have to uncover it using brushes and inks with various abilities. It is a departure from the typical left or right dilemma posed by other card games and instead gives you the freedom to forge your own path towards the end level Boss. I personally like this design.Another thing that I liked is the fact that you use two heroes with different decks each which adds a lot of depth and replay-ability to the game. Another unique feature is that blocking is applied only to the front hero and the swapping mechanic which adds a lot of synergy and fun opportunities to your decks. The game also uses gems, which you can use to upgrade your cards and you can use them any time you like, be it on the map or in the middle of combat, which provides an extra layer of strategy to your runs. All in all the game has a lot of fun mechanics which work together well.The artwork is really beautiful. If you are familiar with Faeria you will notice that a lot of artwork from that game have been used in Roguebook which I find great because it makes Roguebook feel like an extension of Faeria, which it is.All is not good and well though. The game relies heavily on scripted draw mechanics. There are times you will feel that the game deliberately didn't give you the one card that would save your run. Like when you have 11 cards in your draw pile, you draw 9 and the game decides to leave out the one card that you need. It can happen, but here it feels that it happens way too often. As do turns which end with the enemy monster having only 1 life point.Roguebook is one of the games that I really enjoy playing the daily challenges. The mix and match of modifiers provides a fun run, if you don't want to play a normal one.If you can get past that minor drawback the game offers you hundreds of fun hours, with some fun modifiers to keep you challenged for a long time. Roguebook is a card game you won't regret buying.

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is really good.I think it's up there with Slay the Spire and Monster Train. I backed it during the Kickstarter, back then the pre-alpha version was already very enjoyable.The biggest difference in Roguebook compared to other roguelike deckbuilders is that you control 2 characters. (Also there are 4 characters to choose from, so you have a lot of variability.) Both have their own cards shuffled in your deck. The positioning of these characters is always very important and make a very nice puzzle feeling to combat. A simple misplay could cost you your run.What I really like is that you unlock abilities as your deck grows, so there is an incentive to pick up new cards along the way.Also the overmap exploration is interesting. At first it might seem random, but there is strategy involved in when and where you use your inks and brushes to get the maximal effect.There is also progression in the game. You unlock more cards and gems as you finish runs and can unlock passive bonuses to help you. (However you do have to get some basic unlocks to get the "full game" feel.)After your first win, in New Game+ you unlock different mutators you can pick and choose from to vary up your games even further.TL;DR: If you like roguelike deckbuilders this is a 100% buy.

_childDocuments_.review: <<Wait for updates -- some bugs fixed but still untuned and lacking features>> [Review current as of v1.4]As many others have noted, this is quite similar to Slay the Spire, but with some innovations. There's a world map you explore, and your deck/character is two characters that interact. These are good features, they're interesting, and they add some neat twists on the deckbuilding genre. However, the game itself just feels small. The fights are pretty monotonous -- even when the monsters do different things it doesn't affect how you play, you still just need to kill them quickly. Each character has about 45 different cards, compared to Slay the Spire at around 75. This is mitigated somewhat since you're combining two characters, but there's still fewer cards overall, and there's less room for a range of different cards -- a lot of the cards are just variations on "deal x damage" or "gain x block." There are almost no ways to remove cards, so you'll be stuck with starting cards the whole way (unless you swap some of them for random other cards with the progression system...). Some of the build diversity is controlled by artifacts, but there are a lot of clunkers here too. On top of this, there's no run history or even any way to view your deck after the final boss fight. The infrastructure of the game is just lacking. Many recent "roguelikes" have really raised the bar for statistics and fine-tuning (Hades and Monster Train, for example), and this falls so short it feels like no one who tested it has played the genre. The core gameplay is fun and has a lot of potential, but the game itself needs a lot of improvement and polishing before being worth it. The developers have promised updates, which I look forward to, but that just makes this feel even more like an early access game.

_childDocuments_.review: OK Look. If this were released before Slay the Spire, I'd hail the designers and devs as 900% briiliant. Yes, yes Garfield is at least 700% brilliant already and he more or less invented deckbuilding from scratch. And sure, if this was released as Slay the Spire 2, I might be a little disappointed, but not really unhappy. This is is not totally revolutionary in a world where Slay the Spire exists. But if it were released as Slay the Spire DLC, and I plonked down my 20 USD, I'd be perfectly satisfied. There's enough innovation here to much more than justify the money and and time. The 2-hero system, the more dynamic world map, and the spendable roguelite points are are sweet additions. It's a bit more polished in terms of visuals and worldbuilding. It's seem silly to ding such a fun game just because it's self-consciously derivative. 10/10 would slay again. And again. And again. _childDocuments_.review: Heard some buzz about this game from the internet awhile back so I decided to back the kickstarter. Now the game is finally out and it has not disappointed.The roguelike deck-building genre has really become quite saturated in recent years. There's stiff competition from the likes of Slay the Spire, Griftlands, etc. So now more than ever these games need something to make themselves stand out. Roguebook does this by making you play a tag team of 2 characters you select each run, as well as adding a map exploration element.As of the time of this writing I have maxed all the characters and gotten most of the unlocks so I've seen most of what the game has to offer. I personally think Seifer's a bit too strong right now, not a huge deal as there is no multiplayer element to the game but something to think about when balancing later. The cards and customization with gems adds a deep layer of strategy, but often you use this to maximize the potential of one card. Making your own broken combo feels very good and I'm glad the developers even added perks when you increase your deck to a certain size to incentivize players to not just build tiny, super consistent decks. It's a problem that plagues some other games of the same genre. My main issue with the game currently is just a desire for more "content." The event and artifact pool are still relatively small and you will see the same ones frequently. With 4 playable characters and using two every time that will eventually get repetitive too so hopefully they will add some more. The only other nitpick is that finding wells that increase your mana production is a very huge swing in terms of what your deck can support and what it can't. And currently finding more wells is completely luck based. Also crashed a few times but no progress was lost.I enjoyed my time with the game and if they support Roguebook with updates I'll certainly come back.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to anyone that loves deckbuilders like Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but I don't think it has the same replay-ability as those games. One thing I love about StS is that it can be really tough at the higher ascension levels. Roguebook feels like it gets less challenging the deeper you get. I think the big issue I have with Roguebook is that there's no downside or opportunity cost to exploring the whole map. As long as I'm patient I can usually pick up every visible piece of loot and most of the gold. This also means it's fairly easy to put together the same overpowered strategies from run to run. It feels like it's missing a huge piece of the puzzle which is negative encounters. There needs to be some bad things that can happen when you reveal the map. The one kind of negative encounter, when Fugaro steals a treasure from you, ends up being a net positive when you find him and get an extra treasure out of the deal. The fact that you know beforehand where all the blocked terrain is also means that using the inks and brushes is very deterministic. I think the game could benefit from more randomness in how you reveal the map so that it isn't such a sure thing. The game is still fun to play but it doesn't feel like you need to make any hard choices.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I'm leaving this review to inform new buyers that the main reason why this game has gotten negative reviews has been fixed. They also issued refunds to all those that purchased the DLC before this change.That said, this really is a great deckbuilder roguelike. It's unique in the way that it will actually reward you with powerful passive abilities the larger your deck becomes. Also their is a positional dynamic in the game where the location of the heroes (front or back) will change how different abilities work. I encourage anyone who likes deckbuilders to give this game a shot and not heed the negative reviews (the ones pertaining to the DLC) in your decision to try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but so far it just doesn't do it for me. As much as it hurts, I have to give this a No, at least for now. I hope future updates will improve on the game, but in its current state I just can't quite bring myself to recommend it.Paradoxically, this game is at once too similar to Slay the Spire and doesn't deviate enough from its formula to really stand out. The things that it does deviate on tend to be to its detriment.The biggest problem is that there's no way to remove cards from your deck that I've found, meaning you're stuck with your starter cards for the whole game. Maybe the meta-progression solves or mitigates that somewhere down the line, but I'm not going to grind it out to see. On that note, having a meta-progression like this game does goes against the spirit of deckbuilding roguelites to the point that it's almost a dealbreaker on its own. I want to progress by improving my game knowledge and strategy, not by grinding and continually shifting the "base difficulty" lower and lower.Then there's other things that are less major but just don't feel right. There are no (?) hotkeys, so you have to semi-awkwardly click everything. The upgrade system seems interesting, but in practice the gems are incredibly rare or prohibitively expensive. Questions of balance aside, enemies just feel too same-y, most seeming to follow the loop of attack -> gain power -> attack -> gain power. Swapping feels like a half-baked mechanic. Healing is terribly awkward with two heroes, because your only healing item heals a small amount of health on both of them (so if you have one hero at full health and one at low health, you essentially waste healing every time you use an item. Whether it's balanced or not is immaterial, because it just  terrible). Not everything is bad, of course. I think Seifer has a really neat character mechanic (although he makes the other two starters look super boring in comparison). Having allies you can summon is a cool addition to the formula. The mapping system is generally pretty fun. The visuals and art style are super nice (aside from a couple things that lack polish). Plus, it's a lot of fun to see all these familiar faces from Faeria in a new context. But all in all, the scales tip a bit too far to the negative for me. In summary, it's a prettier Slay the Spire with some very confusing design decisions that hold it back from achieving greatness. However, if you're not a deckbuilding purist and you don't care about the lack of a "base" difficulty, then odds are pretty good you'll enjoy it. The devs clearly put a lot of love into this game, and I think there's plenty here to potentially like. It's just not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Update:It's over 6 months later and multiple game-breaking/soft-locking bugs still aren't addressed Movement is often unreliable, with characters refusing to walk over what should be passable terrain, or moving THROUGH impassable terrain which usually crashes the game. This is normally just an annoyance that requires a quick QuitToMenu->Resume, but that they screwed up movement this badly in a visually HEX BASED game is insane to me.Moreover, there are also multiple bugs with the NEW content, without even fixing those old bugs. Them asking for money for the new character seems borderline abusive.Overall, worth playing only if you like the genre (base game isn't BAD, just unfinished but decent).Original Review:This game is solid, but it lacks NEARLY enough polish, or fun in a few places, to be called a finished release. With the amount of work that did clearly go into the game, I'm surprised it was considered done beta-testing, let alone early-access release. A lot was sloppy or unfinished on release.A couple PROS to start:+ Judging from the active dev activity this game will almost certainly be worth buying in a few more weeks or months of the paid early access that they're essentially doing now. (Update: Meh.)+  Gameplay is mostly quite fun! I've managed to get 40 hours in as of this writing, and I enjoyed most of my plays through act 2 of 3 (Act 3 being an unfun experience is something the devs have said they're working on). It's very much a StSpire-like template (with a lot of numbers and cards feeling similar or identical) but that's sort of expected in the genre at this point and doesn't detract from anything.+ Hex-based exploration is a mechanic that can add a lot of variety to the roguelite-card-battle experience, + The cards, gems, and mechanics that are "new" to me compared to other genres are pretty sweet. Balance-wise, most numbers on "old" things are also reasonably balanced for the game as of this writing. Also a pretty big balance con here though, in a minute.+ Visual design-wise, the art's nice, the music is charming, and overall game presentation for things they finished (where there aren't bugs or weird interface issues) is pretty good. Several enemies have interesting mechanics that make the fights cool compared to others in the game (although not as many as one would hope).Now cons:(- -) Tons of major bugs on release. (Update: the game seems buggier now??! The flash gems introduced a gamebreaking bug, and the gem caverns have like 3 separate bugs, etc.)I was shocked to learn that there was a beta-testing period. As I've had a couple of runs bricked or ruined by interface bugs with a sample size of <20. Restarts do fix a couple of bugs I've experienced, but not all.(-) It seems like the designers had limited experience with games in this genre. (Minor update: this got slightly better, but not really enough that there isn't a noticeable card-balancing gap in comparison with something like Slay the Spire, which has a few misses of its own.)A large amount of mechanics, cards, costs, and enemy numbers are useless/trivial, way too big, or way too small (excepting the things virtually copied from templates like Strike/Defend, some energy adds and costs, and a few fights).(-) Related, there are dozens of examples of things completely run-winning on their own. One power-adding event comes to mind if encountered at any point in a run with any deck composition. Devs have stated that the intent of the game is to be breakable/comboable in a run, but several single things (cards/evens/gems) currently win runs on their own or with minimal effort or synergy.(-) This game is really, REALLY easy for anyone experienced with similar games. This is largely due to the number-tuning mentioned above. I've lost one run of 12 because I tested something that didn't work the way I expected, and a single other run because I didn't know an A3 boss mechanic that hard-countered the deck I had steamrolled the entire game with. Otherwise I've tried the first thing that came to mind with each class combination and only had one run that was at all challenging through Act 2.(-) Act 3 is mostly worthless to play through on an average run. Decks are pretty much "done" and fights are easy by this point (in every run I've done through NG+14).(-) Act 3 bosses are lackluster "gotchas" that punish players for playing. Just some rookie designer mistakes with both of the bosses. The devs' stated goal is "a game about breaking things in half with insane combos or clever set ups," and both bosses explicitly punish the player for doing this. Again, this isn't a difficulty thing as I've lost one fight against either (because I didn't know what the "Legendary" affix was going to do and it hard-countered a deck I made that would have otherwise won easily). There are some minor tweaks they could do to make either one make sense, but that wouldn't fix the core final-boss mechanics being unfun, in general. Just to restate: I think final bosses need to be HARDER and have their designs seriously tweaked. (Minor Update: boss unfunness was tempered somewhat, but two of them still have similar, unfun mechanics.)(- -) A lot of things in the game seem like afterthoughts. (Minor Update: this has gotten worse somehow instead of better. A lot of the additions since "launch" are rushed nonsense and the game somehow feels more like a beta than before.)e.g.1: Shops start each zone. No exploration required, you just always know you'll get a shop and you (mostly) always know that shop 3 is better than 2 is better than 1. This compounds with how easy it is for a couple of things to break open the game and win a run to mean that most runs are mostly won upon reaching Act 3, if not sooner with a lucky shop 2.e.g.2: Random trait-shuffling of "level ups" with how the game handles them, mean the clear best traits can be available almost immediately. It's a neat idea to increase run variety, but their lack of balance across traits (some number/design issues here too) means that there's a lot of effectively unfun variability here.e.g.3 is a big one for me, but some people like it:(-) Meta progression. Nearly every unlock strictly makes the game easier, with buffs to things appearing their numbers/rarities. This game hides several CORE MECHANICS behind a few runs-worth of unlocks. I don't even mean characters (which it does do), I mean things like energy, alchemists, or gems spawning on the map AT ALL, or starting runs with gold or ink. We have to unlock 2 less strikes and defends in the starting pool becoming actual random, possibly useful cards (ala Monster Train). I don't mind meta progression in games. Hades comes to mind as doing a great job, even with a ton of it. StSpire is a similar game that hides some things behind unlocks, but doesn't gimp or buff the players' runs too much based on amount of play time. This game just has no variety or really any thought put into most of the meta progression, which just highlights a lot of the basic design and balance flops mentioned elsewhere.(-) Surprisingly little variety. Many decks end up feeling the same since every run is a blend of characters, and most of the 6 class combinations play out similarly, with 1 or 2 clearly directional builds for each combination. The devs expect us to play many dozens of runs (~300 hours at my slowish pace estimates) to unlock some of the steam achievements, but I've seen virtually everything the game has to offer in under <20 runs of 1-3 hours. I've seen most events multiple times already. There isn't generally a need to do every fight on a map, but their locations are all visible at the start of each act and it's pretty much always better to fight more, so every run ends up with the same encounters on each map. This compounds with the easy difficulty, which makes most of the runs I've done feel painfully similar, albeit with some sweet card/gem combos assembled in each.

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to hold off reviewing it until I beat +15. If you're looking for a new deckbuilder, I'd recommend this one. I've played Slay the Spire, Monster Train, and a few others, and this one really made me want to thoroughly complete it. There is enough variety and unique combinations that really makes each run fun and challenging. It's not perfect (I'll talk about that below), but it's worth the coin. Positive:*Gem system adds a fun element that makes some not so useful cards viable. *The large deck angle adds more ways to build around bad cards. *The map puzzle offers a fun min/maxing experience. *Heroes feel unique. *Flash gems offer more flexibility and a hail Mary mid-battle. *Difficulty tweaking allows for interesting combinations of difficulty. *Gem mine is a fun challenge (albeit should be free to enter).*Ability bonuses for deck stacking are great.*Good content for your money. *The game is beautiful to look at, and the devs keep adding more visual elements with each patch. *Swapping mechanics are so much cleaner than games that use "lanes." Neutral:*Starting elements (gems, cards, relics, etc.) are entirely randomized, so you can consistently restart for a better initial run. *Not every hero pair has great synergy (they should probably have unique hero pairing cards). *Sometimes you'll get a dumb luck run in your favor, which makes for a stress-free run. *Legendary equipables that change the hero look are a nice touch. Negative:*Game-breaking bugs still exist. Spawning errors (especially the gem mine), incompatible hero abilities when embellishments are implemented, bogus gem/card pairings (especially discard/drawing mechanics), visual bugs, enemies hitting past shields, towers not generating, event bugs (especially the infinite card bug). I've had to drop runs because of these. *EVERYTHING is RNG. Gems, cards, relics, abilities, events, inks,  gem socket count, the shop, and maps (you'll have runs with zero health pots for example). So much of the run is dumb luck, which at the higher levels where the path to victory is limited, is trash. There needs to be a better way to control the game state. There is zero opportunities to fix a bad run. The alchemists, which should mitigate this, adds more RNG!*Some heroes are clearly dev favorites and have much better cards as a whole (I'm looking at you Sorocco).*There is nothing you can do with pages once all the embellishments are purchased. There should be a consumable system and a page dump to help make the bad luck runs more manageable. *The two older bosses obnoxiously limit what your deck can look like. There is an embellishment that shows you what the final boss will be, which means absolutely NOTHING when everything is RNG. There is no "building" a deck around them. You're just picking the least worst combination of cards. *Extremely unbalanced events. One event will clear the entire board for you for a two-card punishment, while others are just punishments.*In the no path to the boss challenge, I've gotten map/ink combos that cannot reach the boss.*Cards that produce allies are not considered allies, this makes ally relics, sockets, etc. useless. More useless for Aurora when these ally cards never appear (RNG), and her frog mechanic goes no where with these things.*Because everything is randomized, you'll get starting games with rare inks, rare/legendary relics, and gems, while in other games you'll get loaded up with common garbage. It's not balanced.  What could change:*More ways to control the game state at a cost, but not a manipulation that produces more RNG like the Alchemist. *Something else to do with pages once embellishments are tapped out. *Cards that upgrade upon winning at various levels of difficulty. *Starting unique hero pairing cards when certain hero combinations are selected. *Ongoing balance, which already is happening. *Since events are so rare, they probably shouldn't be punishments alone. *Purchase consumables!*Retooling less than useful relics and abilities. *Gem mine should be free since some of the RNG (there is is again) rewards are pretty awful. *Maybe creating equipment for heroes that guarantees a card attached to it. All in all a great game. The RNG is dreadful. Any game that drives me to consistently restart for a better initial game state is nearly a deal breaker. This is what I found most frustrating towards my journey to beating +15.

_childDocuments_.review: I would give Roguebook a “soft” recommendation. If you really enjoy Slay the Spire style card games and want more, this game is right up your alley. If you are new the genre I would suggest Griftlands instead as I believe that game has a better presentation and is more entertaining overall. If you are bored of the genre and want to try something a bit different, try Trials of Fire or Monster Train instead. Overall, this game is just fine but nothing special.As far as positives go, the game has beautiful artwork and the characters are well animated. The game encourages large player decks as there are several bonuses built in to having a large deck: you can select character perks as your deck grows and some cards get more powerful if you have a large deck. You always have two characters in your party and their cards can play off one another in various ways. There are a total of four characters but since you always have to choose two there isn’t really a lot of variety in how you play.The game isn’t particularly difficult, I managed to win it on the second or third try. There are fifteen additional difficulty options you can gradually add to the game and they do change up the way you play which is a nice addition. There are also plenty of progression systems built in including unlocking the new characters, leveling up characters so they have access to more cards, and unlocking additional bonuses you can find on the map.Once again, it’s a perfectly fine game, well designed and looks pretty. It doesn’t move forward the genre in any way though.
