_childDocuments_.review: Check out my full gameplay review video for Roguebook. I go into great depth about the Story, Graphics, Audio, Gameplay, and other noteworthy things I feel needs to be mentioned:  So, if I were to explain Roguebook to someone who has never heard of it before, it is a deckbuilding roguelike and it is very similar to Slay The Spire, Monster Train, and Tainted Grail: Conquest. In my opinion, however, Roguebook has surpassed the previously mentioned games in almost all aspects. And I really do mean it. There is a lot here to cover and I’ll try my best to get into the nitty gritty of things so you can make your own decision whether or not to pick this game up or not.To start off, let’s bring up the story: After many fabulous adventures, recounted in Faeria – Chronicles of Gagana, this relic was lost in a well of Faeria. Through contact with this source of magic, the Book developed a wicked free will of its own and became the Roguebook!You play as a band of heroes filling out the book, defeating enemies along the way, and ultimately try to bring order to these tales written in this book. The flow of Roguebook is exactly what you’d any deck building roguelike to be. Each run is around 20-60 minutes depending on your playstyle. You’ll start a run by picking your chosen heroes, upgrading your permanent skills, uncovering randomized maps, defeating enemies, making choices in encounter events, and getting as far as you can before dying and doing it all again with a new setup. Each run will feel really different.Now that’s summarizing it pretty simply but let’s get into more detail so you can see why it stands out in the wake of all these deck building roguelike games that have been popping up within the last couple of years.Let’s talk about heroes. After playing and unlocking some new content, you’ll ultimately end up with the choice of 4 heroes to start a run with. These runs consist of a party of 2 of the heroes for a total of 6 matches to play around with.Each hero brings along their own cards that are put into your player combat deck and they also have their own special abilities. They differ in health and playstyles. When drafting new cards they are chosen from the pool that the individual heroes offer.In combat you play as both heroes. They are color coded and are easy to differentiate visually. They have their own individual health bar so you have to manage and make sure no one dies. If they do, they can be revived mid battle by playing specific cards or after battles, but for the rest of the run you’ll draw wounds within your deck. Pretty much clogging it up and eating a draw.There is a backline and frontline. There are a lot of different effects within cards and abilities to help manipulate the line but at its core: Enemies will attack the hero in the front. You can typically use a block card to move to the front and tank the hit. If the backline has defense it is added to the frontline.Enemies vary widely in their playstyles. Encounters have strategy and really make you think about how to approach each battle efficiently. No matter what kind of deck you’re using there’s definitely an encounter that will somewhat counter it so make sure to keep that in mind.With your team you go through 3 chapters. Each chapter gets progressively harder and has you exploring a map that has not yet been revealed. It’s randomized each time and though there’s an open path to the boss of the act, it’s highly recommended to take the time to fill out the map, gather new cards, abilities, and random events.You can move freely on the map as long as the node is revealed except you cannot walk over enemy nodes. You unlock the map using your brush. At its base it will reveal up to 2 nodes from your standing spot but with more consumables and buffs later you can reveal in a straight line, a specific spot, and more.Within the map you can find: more enemy encounters for money and ink, random events for choices that are good and bad, money on the ground, alchemist huts, gemstones, and more.Speaking of gemstones, this is one way to upgrade your cards. Your starting cards and ones that you obtain throughout your run can sometimes have gem slots on them. With the gems that find you can insert them into the card permanently for that run to power them up. More attack, block, draw, there’s a lot of effects.One particularly cool aspect that I like is the addition of allies. There are many of them with tons of positive effects, but essentially they are helpers. Some attack, heal, draw, have passive effects and even active effects. Complete builds can be made around them.The game has a sort of high risk high reward / push your luck aspect here. Like I said there’s nothing stopping you from rushing the chapter boss, but it’s up to you to decide whether or not your build is strong enough to take them on or you’d want to take the time to explore as much as you can, just be aware health is static between battles so you can end up at the boss with almost no resources left.After winning or losing a run you’ll net experience for the heroes you brought and for your overall account. After leveling you can unlock new cards and artifacts to find in future runs. It’s a huge incentive to keep you replaying.Along with that, within runs you’ll find pages that are carried over forever and are used to permanently upgrade your heroes, unlock new map encounters, and essentially make future runs more easier.Roguebook has charm. From what I’ve played so far, it’s pretty balanced and every build I tried was vastly different but worked in their own ways. Enemy encounters are really fun with each having their own strategy to beat them. The game is perfect for those who love deckbuilders, it doesn’t hold your hand and the constant progression and joy of experimentation is just top here.This is an amazing addition to the deckbuilding roguelike genre. It’s a very high quality game. Though it is $24.99 US, there is a digital deluxe edition for $10 more or you can purchase it separately. These give you the original soundtrack, new costumes and alternate card art. Unfortunately one of the DLCs locks behind some enemy encounters, cards, and gems. It’s a very small amount of locked content like 5 each or something but that’s weird seeing it on launch day. This is a must play for deck building roguelike fans.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: well worth the money, and an exciting addition to the ever-growing catalog of card-battlers.I began playing card-battlers with Slay the Spire (or perhaps it would be more accurate to say that I began with Magic the Gathering, when I was a little kid), and since getting into the genre, I've played a fair number of games with card battling mechanics: Gordian Quest, Arcanium, Gloomhaven, Quinterra, Hearthstone... but I must confess that this new release, Roguebook, is perhaps the most fun I have had with card-battling since the days I was perusing my local board game shop for the perfect MTG singles! Roguebook is a triumph. Roguebook is aesthetically beautiful, for a start--prettier by far than Slay the Spire, and even prettier than Gordian Quest (which, of the card-battlers, is probably the most similar in terms of mechanics). With regard to gameplay, I think Roguebook is both invitingly accessible and excitingly complex. It took me all of five minutes to get a hang of the basic mechanics, but I expect I'll have a long way to go before I get genuinely good (I still typically lose the game in Chapter 2!) I quite like card-battlers like this, because they strike a balance between the tactical thinking of turn-based strategy games and the immediacy of action-rpgs (since the tactics are microscopic, at the level of a mere handful of characters).I hope that future updates of Roguebook will implement even more characters, and perhaps some kind of campaign mode for players who are itching for a more central narrative element (though the lore in the game is lovely already!) And aside from the occasional bug (sometimes terrain hexes with items don't activate the first time you step on them), I'd say that this is a polished and well-wrought release. If you already like card-battlers (or if you have always wanted to try deck-building), then I really can't recommend Roguebook enough. Now, I'm back to playing it!

The End boss has 500 max HP for reference. You can have up to 6 Allies per battle in play!!! = if get them all buffed that 900 dmg per turn , without using character attacks!!!+Chill game play, but requires thought before play, (no rush)+Play at your own pace+ Decent deck customization , cards are tied to characters you play as (up to 2 or 1 per run), allowing for interesting combos and strategies+/- Repetitive, with medium enemy Variety (the variety is there, but they do not really change complexity, very simple to understand enemy moves and play around them).+Worth the price of admission+/- DLC is worth the price of admission, (no they are not greedy, indeed they could have added this into the game, but I think it is a worthy addition for the price as a DLC, the deluxe version is the best one to get for value).+No bugs to current, will edit if i find any.+butter smooth.- Minimal system settings, they should have at least added key bindings to the camera at least (arrow keys), but most of the game is played with mouse anyway (Didn't play with a controller)- Once you understand how the enemy's work, since they have little change, its a cake walk after you complete once, from once on however, the "Epilogue" is where the variety/challenges comes in. _childDocuments_.review: Despite it's charming exterior and interesting take on the rogue-lite deckbuilding genre, it is hard to recommend Roguebook in its current state. The game clearly lack polish to the degree that this feels more like an Alpha build - in the classic sense where it knows what it wants to be it's just not well implemented.What it gets right:- The game innovates on the deckbuilding genre by adding a map exploration phase which is extremely enjoyable. If you've ever gone through Slay the Spire and just wished you could have more agency in your route, you will enjoy maneuvering the pages of the Roguebook to go from encounter to encounter.- It's implementation of various upgrade systems is interesting and can lead to some very fun combinations, even if the systems themselves aren't altogether very innovative.- The artstyle is charming, if a little reminiscent of Monster Train- The meta-diffuculty system changes the way you explore in the overworld map between games which keeps the game refreshing between runs.What it gets wrong:- Within 8 hours of a playing a fully released, $30 title, I have experienced 4 fatal crashes. I can't remember the last time I experienced a fatal crash in a fully released game, let alone so many in such short time. On top of fatal crashes, you get more minor bugs like struggling to select various cards, card texts not updating properly, swap indicators not updating properly. Bugs that, while not literally gamebreaking, indicate a lack of polish in the final product.- The rogue-lite elements are interesting enough. More often than not, they are slight percentage upgrades to improving the materials you interact with over a run. This adds a relatively flat and boring degree of RNG to a run but I'm not altogether complaining about that. What I find unacceptable is the one particular upgrade that seems necessary if you don't want to create an impossible scenario for yourself - the boss indicator. After about 1-2 successful (or unsuccessful truly) runs, you can purchase an upgrade that will tell you what the final boss is going to be for your run. This should be in the base game, period, because of the way the bosses appear to be balanced. Those of you familiar with Slay the Spire will know of the shiv based decks and how encountering the Act 3 Time Eater boss can put quite the damper on your parade, but it does not make the run impossible. There is a similar interaction in this game, but rather than having an interesting mechanic around number of cards you play before the opponent gets a buff, this boss just increases the mana cost of all of your cards. You get a coin that you can play for more mana that gradually fills out your hand, but if you're running a Daggers based build (where your general goal is to throw 20+ daggers at your enemy in one turn), this boss is practically impossible, and if you're playing the game for the first time, you have no way of knowing how rough you'll have it. And as a side-note, if you're trying to throw 20 daggers at your opponent, it takes A While. Some sort of QoL throw all implementation seems like a no brainer - it feels it wasn't tested at all.- The balance in general is weird. As you progress through the normal enemies on the map, the encounters seem to get progressively harder. To the point where the normal enemy encounters are absolutely more dangerous than the elite encounters or even the boss encounters. It is particularly weird since these common enemies don't give cards like your usual Roguelite Deckbuilder - just some gold and an ink you can use to explore further which CAN lead to cards or health or just nothing depending on your rng. - As a minor nitpick that was extremely frustrating to me, the boss lair in the first two chapters of the game can be approached from all angles, but the boss lair in the third chapter can only be approached from the front (unless I encountered another weird bug). There is nothing in the game to indicate this other than the design of the lair. It just seems weird to be inconsistent when the overworld hex exploration mini game is so intriguing. - The balance and implementation of certain mechanics can lead you to blaming the mechanic for being bad and wanting to drop it rather than understanding that there was some mistake you made in deckbuilding. For instance, one of the characters has a set of cards focused around establishing a single ally that progressively grows stronger as you go through the fight. To take this mechanic at face value, you would want to build a deck around these cards as your offensive cards, and then a more defensive angle for your other character. How this mechanic gets implemented, however, means that any enemy that summons more enemies is practically an automatic loss as your ally can only hit the first enemy in the fight and doesn't trample. And that is all that this set of cards can do. Compare it to the poison mechanic in Slay the Spire where you can take AoE poison cards or you can take poison cards that focus on single target. You might have a run where you only take the single target cards and get killed by a mob of monsters, but because you know of these AoE options, your conclusion would not be that poison is bad, but that your deck needs more poison variety. In this instance, my conclusion is not that my deck needs more of this specific archetype's variety - it actually needs less of it in order to succeed.What's neutral:- The characters are nothing to write home about. They all have the same types of decks that have been done in other deckbuilders. You get to choose two characters per run which can be somewhat interesting figuring out how to make these characters work with one another, but at their core their card sets are obviously built to be relatively evenly offensive/defensive. This seems to be by nature of having to have two party members - they need to be able to kill things and defend themselves no matter which combination you take which in turn seems to limit design space.- I could not for the life of me tell you a single name of one of the bosses or enemies. While that isn't particularly new to deckbuilders, these enemies seem particularly forgettable in design. Cool design in fight, but hard to remember after the fact, possibly because there are very few enemies who actually impact how you will choose to play your deck which is arguably a very negative thing for a deckbuilder game. Ultimately, it isn't a bad game by any means. There is something here. It just feels unfinished. There are bugs galore. Minimal QoL implementations. Minuscule options menu. Weird balancing choices. This game could use another couple of months in the oven polishing up all of these bits  and then I'll be happy to recommend it, but until then, stick to a deckbuilder that had more care put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game art is beautiful and the 2-hero mechanic works well but I felt the game didn't encourage or require the same level of strategy as other popular deck builders.To touch on a few strategies:It's relatively-easy to win with a big pile of above average cards and large decks are encouraged by a core-mechanic which upgrades a hero with a drafted talent every 4ish cards you add to your deck, until you've received 5ish hero talents.Small decks are impossible to build because removing a card from your deck is a rare event that you'd be lucky to see once a run.The bleed mechanic from elite enemies prevents slow paced defensive decks because bleed is unblockable, never decays, can stack and In-combat healing is a rarity which can't keep up with bleed even if you were able to draft it.And the final frustration is that the 2 final bosses in the game have unique mechanics which completely shut down several deck strategies. The bosses aren't strong because of what they do, they are strong because what they prevent you doing.One boss removes 4 cards from your deck every time it hurts you which shuts down smaller decksThe other boss increases all cards by 1 mana and provides you a method of reducing your max hand size by 1 in exchange for 3 mana on any given turn. This boss is the more interesting of the two but shuts down any deck relying on 0 cost cards.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was really fun until the last patch (1.5 "The Gem Mines"). I played it until epiloges 14/15 (the equivalent to Slay the Spires Ascension Mode). Now the game is completely overtuned and you need a very very good deck to even make it through the first act on higher epiloges - so it is even more meta heavy. The problem is that when you don't get the cards needed to craft such a deck, the whole run is doomed from the beginning. Given the time it takes to complete a run, the last patch really sucked all the fun out of the game. Until the endgame mode get's properly balanced I can not recommend this game.Update after patch 1.6 - The last patch brought a new endboss and balance tweaks on the mine and monster scaling on higher epilogues. Altough I didn't play that much after the patch, I managed to beat act I and II on epilogue 14 in the first try, so this is a good sign. I have to admit, that the devs keep listening to feedback and the game is getting patched. _childDocuments_.review: Cool game, but only three chapters? Within the first hour I got to the end of chapter 2 and almost beat the boss. Yes, there's post-game content, which is basically grinding unlocks to make the runs more challenging, but that doesn't seem compelling. Granted, I don't care for Slay the Spire, it's okay, but I do love card games (was ranked 300th best Elder Scrolls Legends player and 1,200th best MTG Arena player), and Griftlands was great. This is a well produced game and I liked what I played of it. The allies (supports/enchantments) are a nice touch, too. Music is okay, artwork is quite nice, and granted my second run was more difficult than the first so maybe I just got lucky. But its just too short to be worth the price. At half price it's a definite.The new gems expansion did not change my mind. Some of this game is luck - but not the predictable kind of luck based on card draw. It's the map exploration - whereby you have no idea if you're going to get 6 healing potions (hearts) or 0 to 1 per map. The one perk that lets you see where the healing potions are is a random and rare find. I don't mind randomness in rougelikes, it's fun, but not when health is involved, considering that only one character heals after every round (and only with certain cards or perks - note he also takes damage to use his best attacks.A couple more free expansions and probably worth it at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, I have a lot of mixed feelings about this game. Let's just list the pros and cons:PROS- Graphics and art are good- There is potential for interesting strategic choices to be madeCONS- I played for only 32 hours. And everything is unlocked, and the game feels stale. Ultimately feels like an early access game, and it's like, so where's the actual content at?- Strategies are overly simple, and certain strategies are really OP, like bleed. It's like you flip a coin, and if you win, you can put together a super OP strategy and win easy, otherwise you lose. And you can't do well with a random deck, and there is no opportunity to innovate your own play style, because the card pool is so limited.- Bugs. Sometimes, when you play cards too fast, the game crashes, and you see a huge error message covering the whole screen full of numbers and letters, like the matrix. If I wanted to look at the matrix, I would watch the movies, not play this game!- Bad UI. You know how in Slay the Spire, you can play multiple cards all at once? In this game, trying to play multiple cards at once results in the screen locking up, you can't see what's happening, and you have to wait for each animation to finish, to see what actually happened. Hard to explain, but it's kind of annoying. - Bad design aesthetics. The battle takes place in the upper half of the screen. It's just uncomfortable to look at. Like, if you took a picture of the ocean at the beach, would you have the sand be 90% of the picture, and the ocean be 10%? No!- Lack of impactful decisions. I get the feeling that 99% of my decisions do not matter, and only 1% of decisions really do. Example: one game I was doing very badly, I was sleep deprived, and had a very bad deck with no hope of winning. Then, in the last one or two fights, I drafted one card and one relic that allowed me to kill the boss only playing that one card. So, all the strategic decisions I made the whole game didn't matter, and the only thing that determined win or loss is getting lucky and getting that one card. Lol.- Lack of variety. There's only 4 heros you can play, and 2 of those are whack, so there's only 2 that are good (in high difficulty). Also, the card pool, gem pool, relic pool are really small. And there's very little variety of enemys and bosses. And the final boss is the same every time, so you see the same stuff over and over again, each time you play. I'm bored, in only 32 hours!TLDR: I had high hopes for this game. It was really fun the first few times, but ultimately the game has no depth. There's huge potential for sure, but as it is now, playing this game is like a novelty thing, like talking to your neighbor's kid, just play along a little and move on.Edit: this game is a bugged mess. Today I tried to concede a run. Error message and crash to desktop. Can't even go to main menu. Then I was in the final fight, and one (important) card in my hand was not able to be played. Every other card could be played, but this one card couldn't be clicked. What a great game. Uninstalled, and I will be refunding.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly I cannot recommend this game. _childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is an extremely solid game. I have a lot of specific good things to say. Short version: I loved exploring all the options. Especially how you can combine them all so freely. Cards, powers, treasures, card-upgrades, unique events, and even which parts of each Floor you choose to explore. You can do what you want, when you want, all the time. And woe betide the turtles who stand in your way.The best feature by far is how your heroes level up as you draft cards. A small, consistent deck is still the gold standard. This one mechanic meant, for once, smaller decks weren't objectively more powerful. There are other things, like how small decks are hit harder when a hero knocked out. It's the first time I didn't feel punished by a deckbuilder for playing with all of the cool toys I found. The best part is that since you have so much control over drafting cards, you can still aim for an elegant little machine with just the right parts, if  that's what you want.The number of options made every run different. Especially how you combine two heroes and their decks for each run. Though I favored some characters, I never felt any were overshadowed. There are a lot of other subtle touches that I appreciated. A good example is an ally card which you can use to attack, or sacrifice for one burst of healing. If you need your little buddy to deliver the killing blow, you still get the healing even though the battle is over. Interactions like that meant I almost never felt like I'd accidentally screwed myself by doing things in the wrong order. I mean, you can still mess up your turn, but I cannot tell you how many Slay the Spire runs I've killed because I picked up a cool card at the wrong time.In fact, I never really found any truly bad cards, powers, or treasures. This is good and bad, but mostly very good. I never felt terribly challenged. I had consistent success throwing kitchen sinks at turtles. I'm not saying that wasn't fun. It was. I had a blast. But the flat power-level makes for less of a puzzle. Fewer "aha" moments where I realized why a card was good (or terrible). Not a lot of powerful combos. Again, it's not like they aren't there, but I never felt I needed them. I slew legions of turtles without ever feeling like I'd made a bad decision I couldn't come back from. Again, to be crystal clear, that could be good or bad. It depends on what you like to do in these sorts of games.I didn't love the mechanics for increasing difficulty. Like everything else, you unlock difficulty modifiers one at a time. You can mix and match them, but enjoyed playing with the higher level ones the most. That meant I spent most of my time playing with the less interesting modifiers in order to unlock the cool ones. By the time I had everything, I'd explored most of what the game has to offer. It would have been much better, for me, if I could have played with the toughest conditions from the beginning. Not because I wanted more of a challenge, but because I didn't enjoy every challenge modifier equally. The Level 5 mods are the most interesting, especially the one that gives Bosses new powers and attacks.All in all, I'm really impressed. I will definitely come back if content gets added in. I actually don't want new heroes and cards as much as I want new enemies, traps, and bosses. Almost 100 hours and I don't think I played with a tenth of the possible combinations that are already here. I would get a lot more out of applying those same toys to overcome new, and more punishing, challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: **Edit** This edit will be my final review edit as I have now completed the game and all difficulties. The game is fun. That's it that's the post you can move on if you don't want to read a giant wall.In many ways it feels like a "Slay the Spire 2". It has some methods of added complexity and mechanics, but not so complex or drastic that it makes gameplay confusing or difficult to understand. Adventuring through the "Spire" by revealing the map yourself is extremely fun and strategic, though it does add RNG. Over time though, it feels like it's missing something. In the higher (A11+) difficulties I found myself purposely NOT exploring and risking fights; going straight to the boss to kill them once I knew I was good to go. Literally skipping content as the optimal min/max strat to win feels a little sad. I stopped using brushes once I grabbed the treasures and Faeria wells to save them for future acts and then... just never used them. Bit of a bummer. The "Ascension" levels of difficulty aren't the traditional "monsters get stronger, more bad stuff happens to you, you get nerfed". Many of them adjust the way the game actually is played. Like taking Skytowers (reveals the map for you) away and replacing them with little vision trinkets or Faeries that you gotta beat to get your vision. Or making the back rank enemy (if there's more than 1 baddy) untargetable. Switching Brushes/Inks as rewards for fights, or removing the path to the boss so you gotta earn your way there, or lose HP when you get gold -- they change the way you have to approach and play the game. This helps keep things fresh instead of *bad guy stronger now he smash more*. This is a wonderful idea, but it does bring a few weird quirks with breaking other mechanics or treasures to be completely worthless if you happen to get them during that particular run. Also once you climb to the highest levels (A12+) the interesting changes go away and THEN it becomes just "Game is harder now".Another cool game feature is Embellishments: The ability to upgrade your characters passive abilities and RNG. These are super fun, and kinda OP. Getting to start runs with higher stats and free loot and improved RNG? Yes plz. You get a bonus each time you beat a new difficulty, and now that I've beaten all 15 (in 16 total runs...) I still need a TON of pages to max out the book. Like 5k. So the last level of some bonuses take oodles of grinding, though at least the important stuff you can get pretty easily and then add small benefits as you can afford them. The four characters are all cool in their own right. Sharra (Silent), Sorocco, (Ironclad), Seifer (Watcher) and Aurora, (Defect I guess?). You get to make any party combo of 2 you pick once you unlock them. It's a fun balancing act of taking cards for both, (or not, you can win with one dude having ALL the stuff) dividing up treasures, using their strengths and synergies, alternating who takes hits and which position they stand in, etc. Sharra seems a little weak to me, and I rarely used her. Though one of the bosses she has a major advantage to. Aurora is SUPER fun with "infinite" HP, but on the highest difficulties I was too scared of her low HP and getting one-shot. Seifer feels the best overall to me. He has high damage, decent blocking, LOADS of sustain between fights, and his Enrage mechanic is just straight up fun. There's a ton you can manipulate with him and it really feels like you're making an impact with your choices, not just playing cards you were given. Purposely taking hits to set up Enrage for the next fight to get an advantage -- or purposely stalling fights to draw your sustain cards really let you min/max and shine. Many reviews mention that you're encouraged to take more cards instead of meticulously craft your deck... but I've not felt that way. I feel strongest around 21-24 cards, and while sure you get some extra passives if you add more cards you also definitely bloat the deck making it harder to maintain synergies and take longer to get to your good stuff loaded with gems. 10 good cards and 10 average cards is just going to be better than 12 good cards, 8 average cards, and 10 okayish cards but getting an extra passive or two. Though specific cards/treasures may make you adjust your deck and theories on the fly based on what synergies you have available. Overall however I want a consistent and well-oiled deck over a bunch of booster packs thrown together. It's rare for me to go over 22-24 cards and if I did, my deck probably sucked real bad that I was desperately trying to add something impactful or hope to find combo pieces down the road. Twenty years of MTG and 700 hours of Slay the Spire give me confidence that I know what I'm doing with decks and sometimes you take a short-term hit for long term benefits. ******Bugs: I used to have TWO paragraphs in this review describing bugs. However as far as I've been able to replicate - the bugs I've observed have been fixed. So MAJOR props to the devs for keeping up with what players found and stamping them out. There's a few non-bug-quirks such as if Skytowers are removed due to a modification from your difficulty settings, you still can be given a treasure that buffs skytowers which feels super lame if it happens. However I'm sure disabling specific cards/treasures/passive RNG based on the specific modifications for the run is probably no small task. Overall though it's been awesome to see the constant updates and hopefully there's more to come over time!It's got room for quality of life improvements. Better descriptions of mechanics, more helpful tool-tips, allow users to add/customize keyboard controls. A friend had to tell me the arrow keys move the map around because the game sure didn't.So if you stuck around and read that whole thing, you'll know Roguebook is a strong game. I had a ton of fun playing it, and  there's a LOT of stuff that makes the game tick and is cool to mess around with using different mechanics/combos. Exploring is fun even though sometimes the "right" play is to purposely not explore. Now that I've finished the game, I definitely feel a little empty that there's no more content for me but if DLC or more characters or something do come out one day I'll definitely pick this back up :)

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a solid entry into the deck builder genre. It is beautiful, runs smoothly (it has crashed a few times on my system, though I'm running Linux using the proton 6.3-5 setup), and provides a solid experience reminiscent of Slay the Spire. I particularly like the sense of adventuring with a companion as opposed to the thematic sense of isolation many roguelikes fall into but that is more of an ambiance I like.Its shortfalls primarily relate to limited content: few strongly differentiated enemies including final bosses, limited content for each hero, few relics and gems, and few "Narrative Events". The decks often look highly similar depending upon which hero you favor in a given run. Most of these "issues" are easily "fixed" as additional content comes--I'm particularly hopeful that this game gets opened to the Steam Workshop so that it can receive similar content expansions that Slay the Spire received which would address a lot of the gripes individuals have had with the game as it is at the moment; DLCs would presumably similarly expand the game (though I'm hopefully that content expansions would be more regular and included like Slay the Spire's model). A couple of other issues I noticed is that 1) randomness in the tile map contributes into somewhat lopsided runs that can often be determined by a couple of lucky early finds and 2) the meta game progression doesn't open up additional play styles but makes your starts fundamentally stronger and easier which somewhat deviates (in my mind poorly) from the typical roguelike model of predominately opening up options. The upgrades opening certain options which generally make the game easier and are not linked to doing different things (which often make exploring the world better in my mind), but rather on just doing the runs and incentive running with additional handicaps. I suspect this will be one of the more polarizing elements of the game.Overall, I would recommend the game, but that is contingent on the expectation of continued development.Good:Strong basis for future expansionSolid mechanicsSmooth gameplayBeautiful setting/cards/charactersBad:Limited contentLimited enemy interactionsLimited sense of differentiation in play throughsNo current steam workshopUpgrade system makes each run fundamentally easier as opposed to more diverse

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure what kind of a review it would be, positive or negative, until I sat my ass down and started writing. In the process, previously fragmented issues clumped up rather quickly, leaving me morbidly certain about the verdict.Roguebook is a deckbuilding roguelite from the creators of Faeria. I used to enjoy the latter, so buying this game eventually was a no-brainer for me. It starts out strong, emanating rich Faeria vibes, playing majestic music, and creating quite the atmosphere with its impeccable art. Snappy, beautiful, tactical, highly satisfying is how I would label its exploration and combat systems. When it comes to the form and spirit of the battles, the closest comparison I can draw is Steamworld Quest. Without the endless inane blabbering in-between. There's no reason to describe combat in detail, you can literally understand how it works by looking at one gif. As for the challenge it provides, Roguebook is much easier than most of its peers. It's a selling point for some and a no-go for others. Personally, I don't mind since the runs can last for up to 1.5 hours, so the whole endeavor, much like regular human runs, could be rather frustrating if the difficulty was any higher.The exploration mechanic shines, allowing you to brush your way through its gorgeous maps by using different kinds of tools that you fight for and find in the wild. Now, that system is an explosive injection of dopamine! I'm completely on board with the Resonance of Fate style map-painting. A weird parallel, I know. Resources like inks and different brush effects are common, but not easy to come by in bulk. In each location, there's just enough of them to fill at least half of any given map, according to my statistic. The end goal is to pick up as many important items as possible while making tough decisions, having to leave some parts undiscovered due to the ink scarcity or to save some for later.The deckbuilding mechanics push you to create bigger decks, awarding perks for the deck size. What a weird novelty that goes against everything I know! Think well before adding any card to your deck, the game doesn't provide many honing options. You can attach gems to your cards, draft some, transform a few, but don't expect to thin your deck properly. There's no such service - not at the end of the level, nor even in the shops! Preposterous, but only emphasizes the importance of cycling and passing on card rewards. Besides, even if you take every card, you'll probably end up with a deck of 40-50, which isn't the end of the world. As for the strategies, be that some swapping combo mess, an ability to play expensive cards for free, or droves of allies, it's all good since quite a few of them seem to be viable and reachable intently. With only the luck of the draw to decide your destiny at the most pivotal moments.Alas, Roguebook's destiny was decided when it got its kidneys ripped out and sold on the streets. Crippling the game and diminishing an already lacking foundation that could've used half a year in production to just add content. This game desperately needs more enemies, heroes, items, events, map skins just to feel right. And come on, on top of that, you have a gated character limited to an overpriced DLC!? I won't pay a 10 dollar bond for a crumb of something that belongs in the base game. I'm not saying Fugoro's ransom somehow completely ruins the core game. Truly, my displeasure with him signifies Roguebook's core problem I already voiced - the lack of variety. This game should've thrown every single asset into the breach, it was never in a position to lock anything out.Variety is one of the Leviathans of all roguelites, and its absence here is what limits the game's replayability. The local progression tree is pretty neat and the maps remind me of Heroes of Might & Magic 3 visually and mechanically. Sounds nice, and initially it is. Yet, these are the same few maps on every run, and meta-progression fizzles out after you obtain the juiciest bits. Naturally, these tarnished virtues ceased to deliver me from yawning. Even then, the gameplay kept being enjoyable to a degree. Having mastered all cards (all but 3, sorry for the blatant exaggeration) and characters felt empowering, the game's charms were able to make me stay on the grind. However, one day I skipped playing it, then one more day, and soon my interest faded. This is where Fugoro could give me a little push for another run, but lookie here, he's incarcerated! It could be the run to tip the scales for so many people, you know.All things considered, I don't think the game delivers the feeling of closure either. I won't be completing the lame NG+ fully, I'll never see the true ending. Applying a few modifiers to the same map isn't enough in my roguebook is what I'm saying. I've beaten the game 5 times and called it a day, yet the last 2-3 times felt like flavorless busywork. Also, one person made sure that I mention the presence of daily runs for some reason. Do you care? I don't. They aren't a game-changer in any capacity. In the end, Roguebook isn't trash. But it's another mindless clone, albeit with a pretty set dressing. I wouldn't recommend it to the majority of players.Although, if you're anything like me, you don't have anything better to do with your time, and to you, I suggest buying the game at a discount. I know what I said - it turns into shallow busywork and suchlike. But it holds up pretty well for its first 8-12 hours. If you buy it expecting just that, there's a chance you won't regret it. Regardless of my harsh criticism, I don't. It's a chill walk in the park. Until the park starts to curve in upon itself, and then comes a realization that strangers and dogs you pass by are the same strangers and dogs, swapping places. Stretching their glossy lips in toothless smiles.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not terrible, but in a sea of so many roguelikes, and deck-building roguelikes, this game takes a lot of the wrong routes.The two main things that kill this game for me are the map exploration, and the 'covenant, ascension, whatever you wanna call it".The map exploration seems so interesting when you first look at it. Revealing parts of the map to explore and find the things that will become your run. The intrinsic flaw in this is that the brush is poorly designed. By doing 2 spaces outward in every direction, from you in the middle, it means that you are always most rewarded for staying relatively central in the map, and finding a little path to use it on. Most of the time you explore a circle centered on the middle of the map, and it gets kind of boring. Your exploration and the things you find are significantly more rng dependant than most other games. Imagine playing slay the spire but every single space is always a question mark, on every run. That's essentially what this map functions like. It is not well designed unfortunately.The epilogues, the ascension system, is very unfriendly to the player. Rather than gradual difficulty rises, they are individual challenges that can be combined, each with very different ways they need to be played. They usually just take away options you have for exploring and improving your deck, in a game where you are already heavily limited. There should have been a better ascension system in place, and these could have been individual challenges at the highest ascension level. This would have been significantly better.Bonus note, the final bosses are some of the worst designed fights in any game. While not overly difficult (there's actually a couple elite fights I think are significantly harder, looking at you beserker and confusion fish), they are incredibly unfun to play against. One in particular, that randomly dissolves significant portions of your deck, is almost completely rng dependant unless you have an incredibly powerful deck for setting yourself up to win turn 1 or 2, or just hope you get really lucky and he doesn't dissolve any of your important cards when he dissolves 5 random ones turn 1, and potentially many more on future turns.Anyway, game looks pretty, and the animations are decent. Sound design is alright. Unfortunately gameplay-wise it heavily lacks the staying power of good roguelikes. I wouldn't recommend paying full price for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Solid roguelite deck builder. There's some continual progression between runs (that you can disable if you don't like). Pretty similar to Slay the Spire, except you manage two characters at once. This adds a lot of replayability. Each characters has a few different build approaches, and those will synergize differently depending on who you pair them with.The exploration mechanic is fairly neat, too. It's less constrained than Slay the Spire or Monster Train. While that may ultimately make it a bit more RNG in a way that is unsatisfying for some, I think it adds some interesting flexibility and variety to runs.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: While initially I liked the game as it does feel a little more refined than others in the genre (which would be expected given the creators), it fails at a few basic levels: 1) It shows you all the relics up front in your library up front, instead of letting you discover them. Same with cards. This very small step adds a lot to the roguelike deckbuilding genre. 2) Uninteresting synergies - The heroes just didn't do it for me. I kept playing, thinking "ok, maybe the NEXT unlock will make this hero really shine." Nope. Also, the heroes weren't really anything new. 3) Minimal synergies between relics and cards - too many relics feel meaningless, like i'm just collecting 'stuff' with no point. 4) Way too many cards that feel unnecessary or not wanting to be played. 5) You are penalized HEAVILY for restricting your deck - in fact, the game inherently assumes you are going to expand your deck. Good points: 1) The gem system is good and probably one of the more interesting parts of the game, although certainly not unique. Also, some gems just feel pointless, and when I get 3 of the same pointless rare gems on the same run, it begins to feel taxing. 2) the graphic style is nice, although the animation for cards tends toward very basic. In fact, I rarely notice any difference between basic cards and very exotic card animations. If you want a newer roguelike deckbuilder and have played all the other ones out there, this will scratch the itch. But at the moment, there are several more that at more rewarding, more challenging, and have a better overall system.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy deck builder rogue games you'll enjoy this but even with the association of genre and dev, do not expect this game to be all too similar to Slay the Spire. A main point of this game is your ability to paint your map, aka reveal more spots to walk to, which means you might just waste an entire brush on nothing, rather than in StS where every room will have some kind of event. A great plus when it's about the tactical aspects though is the synergy between characters. During your runs you can unlock more teammembers, two of which you will control each run. As all of them have different abilites and strengths it sometimes can be quite interesting to try to mix them up and see what works best. While Poison has been removed and replaced with bleeding, there is still a similar ability to the orbs in StS, this time called Allies. You can spawn those creatures, up to six of them, which will have passive (and sometimes active) abilities that they'll use after every turn. Most simply do damage but some have more creative powers. You'll just have to play and see.

All depends on what you choose.5) Short, but funThere are only 3 maps to go through, but that's more than enough to enjoy each run with different combination of characters and perks.[-]1) CrashesSome occasional crashes. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely awesome game 😊 If you like Faeria you will find lots of references here and the overall aesthetic is also very close to it.Gameplay-wise it is basically Slay the Spire, but with a map progression twist - instead of choosing between a couple of paths, you have a big map in each of the 3 stages. It is obscured at first, and the resources that reveal it are limited, so you need to plan accordingly. I found that part extremely satisfying, especially with NG+ modifiers (a la Hades).Meta progression is smooth and much more modifier based than the usual RNG item pool found in the genre. I personally like this shift, makes the runs more strategic 😊Lastly, I see some reviews point out greedy devs not sticking to pre-purchase promises. I did not hear about the game until yesterday, so all I can say is that what you buy is what you get 😄 The game feels complete and well-balanced, and I hope it will be expanded like Faeria was in the past.Oh, and in case you were wondering - the game does not feel like Faeria when it comes to the gameplay loop. I always found Faeria very slow and web-like with all the loadings, which was a huge turn-off. This one here seems to be a stand-alone package 😊

_childDocuments_.review: A quality Slay-The-Spire-'em-up. Card balance is great, heroes all feel distinct and different while still having multiple build options, and art/music are consistently high quality. Occasional bugs pop up, but nothing major in my experience. Difficulty also scales well, with the game feeling decently challenging at the low levels, and steadily ramping up as more and more challenge tiers unlock. Definitely worth a purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: It's an addictive game. I'm both disappointed and thankful that there are (currently) only three levels. I hope that this gets expanded at some point. Or that a new game gets created with this as the prototype. I suspect that this game is "testing the waters".One element of Roguebook reminds me of the (late 90s) single player Microprose Magic the Gathering game, Shandalar. In both games you wander about a map building a collection of cards. I prefer Shandalar to Roguebook, but Shandalar is not (easily?) operable on any of my devices.The Shandalar (MtG) mechanic is deck construction; Roguebook's mechanic is closer to Dominion in that you curate a pool of cards from which to draw hands. There is occasional permanent card removal/substitution via events, and temporarily via cards.As Roguebook is a roguelike, each run is quite short. There's no permanence beyond an embellishment tree that makes further exploration a little easier.Edit: The game says "This is not the end." ... that harder content exists in my next run. I think I'd prefer to have harder content in additional areas/levels of the one run.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not generally a fan of these rogue-like deck builders, but have really taken to this one.  I know it's shallow but the graphics and sound design have a ton of appeal.  Probably more important, there's some very solid strategy on the gameplay.  Good synergy between some of the cards and you have to be careful to add the right mix to your deck and not water it down with a bunch of cards that don't really work well with the engine you're trying to build.  Definitely worth trying out!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I like the core gameplay more than Slay the Spire and about as much as Monster Train. I'll list the bad first:  Balance isn't very good. Not enough content, just 2 end bosses IIRC (but the "elite" enemies have nice variety and can be hard if your build isn't busted), too much RNG on the exploration (but the exploration is way more fun than StS's), poor controls and accessibility (apparently this is a priority coming in patches though).My #1 complaint now that the day1 content DLC was fixed is that the progression/perk tree is just baaaddd.  Progression in Monster Train and some other rogue-lites is much better.I wish there was some actual deck building mechanics, too. But other than that... honestly I liked the *idea* of Slay the Spire a lot more than I actually liked that game. I find this game more fun but it needs some patches and more content.

_childDocuments_.review: Verdict: Well-crafted deck builder that has some really interesting spins on the genre. The game needs a bit more balancing but it is really enjoyable as it is. Update: There are more negatives than I usually like, but what you get for your price (and promise of future DLCs and balancing) keeps the game in recommended+Steam achievements (52, require at least 100 hours of grinding)4 very different heroes with unique cards and abilitiesUnique world and combat encountersRelics are really interestingMap traveling is enjoyable and as far as I can say unique15 map modifiers that make the game incredibly challenging 5 levels of new game+Risk/reward is a huge part of the gameCharming graphicAmazing soundtrack Events are exciting and there is a lot of themCards are upgradable with gems - this puts in a huge number of combinationsMore cards = more talents but a larger deck is another risk/reward attribute of the gameDevelopers backed down on day 1 DLC ... I applaud the ability to admit a mistakeAbility to summon allies -No steam training cardsThere are some glaring issues with hero balance and hero combinations (e.g. best hero combination has a 52% winrate and the worst only 20%)The game crashed on me a few times when I went to the menuThere is no tracking for several achievement-connected things (cards played etc.)Some cards and enemies clearly need balancing After 20 hours I have a feeling that success is strongly influenced by rng finding mana wells Characters synergy is feels half doneI often feel like a relic/card is not working with some card combinationsUpdate after finishing the game on max difficulty-Complete lack of balance (seriously, bleed is broken)The game doesn't have any ending even though it indicates one after a first playthroughTerrible DLCs (seriously, just ignore them, they are extremely lazy cash grabs)Runs on high difficulty basically depend on randomly finding the majority mana wellsSome achievements are not working at all (missing boss, game not tracking cards played, tea pots used ...)

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent roguelike deckbuilder which is deceptively simple at first, but it has  a lot of depth and strategy with interesting deck  combos once you learn how the game works. keep in mind that if you come from other games like slay the spire or monster train, the game will feel a lot slower but more tactical, you not only draft cards upgrade them or transmute them but also you insert gems to your cards which add another layer of strategy and also you manage two decks at the same time. I could go further into details but  if you are a fan of genre give this game a try, explore it yourself,  and you wont regret it!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun and streamlined single-player Slay-The-Spire-esque game. I would recommend this.Pros:+ Quick and satisfying runs+ Interesting take on deckbuilding. With most games you need your deck to be as small as possible. In this game you get strong passive bonuses based on how large your deck is.+ Great visual presentation+ I think the cards and items are pretty cool and diverse. Being able to augment your cards is nice too.Cons:- Not that many unique elements to it. There's some cool stuff, like the passive-bonuses-things. The multi-hero-thing's been done by games like Gordian Quest and Dimension Reign.- I'm not super-sure about the difficulty. I had to get used to the game in my first 3 runs. But I finished 4 runs in a row now in increasing epilogues while hardly taking any damage. I'm not sure if I wanna keep grinding up to reach higher difficulties later.Overall the game works, and is fun and charming. If you like deck-building games, I'd say give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on deep discount for the price of an expensive coffee -- I'm fine with that, but wouldn't recommend.  Anything done by this game is done better by StS and Monster Train.  I find the overland map exploration to be a chore, needlessly complicating and borking runs if you don't reveal the right tiles at the right time.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been a fan of Nacon and Abrakam since Faeria and I was looking forward to this game, so much so that I even backed it. It does a few things differently than other deckbuilding roguelites in that you have meta items to help you explore a map and be more selective about your encounters. It really is very well-made but some enemies are too restrictive in how you should beat them and sometimes that might even brick your entire run (looking at you berserker). Having 2 heroes, each with their own decks and cards to unlock adds a new flare to these kinds of games, add to that the fact that positioning a hero either to the front or back matters and only the hero in front takes the damage from most attack, and having 4 total heroes gives a lot of room to play around and replay to your heart’s content. There are higher difficulty settings which spice the game up even more, and I’m not talking about just increased HP and Attack for enemies it’s more like you can only have 1 item or cant use more than 3 cards a turn and things like that.Overall a great game and definitely worth a check.

Card balance feels off a lot but as a rougelite game i feel i win from snowballing stats and other benefits i get early on rather than having a good deck at times. The other oddities that i have faced were collision turning off in the beginning or tabbing back in as well as turning off flash gems but still getting them.  the game looks well put together but doesn't really feel like it at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Good but not great.I recommend this to fan of games like slay the spire and monster train looking for something new. If you have not played slay the spire or monster train, play them instead, especially slay the spire is the real deal.That said, this is a solid game, with some interesting choices. For example you get bonuses for collecting cards which is a good boost to thick decks. (thin decks are still very playable, no worries) Playing a pair of characters is also pretty interesting and adds some variety. The exploring part is a fun novelty, although not that deep once you get it, and a bit annoying in the end, since it slows the gameplay.The game also has very good art, which is a real plus.Some things keeps the game down though, as most notably the balance is not great. Some combos are too powerful and some enemies are much stronger than some others. This is a real issue imo.Also the enemies and events lack variety, especially the normal enemies. You will mostly see the same enemies every game and the same events every other games. Bosses are a bit better.Lastly the game lacks a fast mode at the moment, which, combined with the running around you do while exploring makes it longer and less engaging.If those points do not deter you, this is a solid game right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty cold on this game at first even though I had been excited for it since I played the demo. The balance felt off and I was not a fan of the upgrade system. It almost seemed like the game was going to force me to grind out the upgrade tree just to be able to complete the game.While I'm still not a huge fan of the upgrade system, I have grown to like the game more and more. A lot of the important stuff in the upgrade tree isn't really difficult to unlock, and I have beaten the game several times since.There are two things I really like about this game.First is the exploration system. I love exploring the map and strategizing how to optimize my use of inks and paintbrushes to uncover the map. It's a lot more fun than the boring maps you find in other deck builders. I hope this gets expanded upon in the future. The epilogue system in this game also helps vary this up by imposing different rules and limits on you, which influence how you approach exploration.The second thing I really love is the character system. There are four characters and trying out the different combinations is a lot of fun. Some cards might work better with one combination but no so well with another. Exploring and learning new interactions between characters is a lot of fun and adds to the variety. While I haven't tried every combination yet, I have felt like some combinations make a little more sense than others, but I still think the ones I did not like as much were potentially viable.There are some negatives, however.You will hear it a thousand times. This game has day one DLC and it's a bit overpriced too. I personally bought the game on GMG for a decent discount, so it did not really bother me much, but I definitely think $8 for the day one DLC is way too high for what it offers. I hope future DLC offers a much better value. I don't recommend the DLC unless you buy it at a discount. Luckily, it's fairly minor content.As already noted, I also do not like the upgrade system. You gain pages by playing the game. You can increase the amount of pages you earn by using the epilogue system, which is a way to increase the difficulty of the game. You then spend these on an upgrade tree. In general, I don't like meta progression in roguelikes, and I don't really like it here either. The only meta progression I tend to enjoy are ones where you unlock new weapons or characters, but in this game the upgrade tree straight up make the game easier as you unlock more and more.The game is also somewhat buggy at the time of release. I haven't found anything too game breaking yet, but there's enough bugs to where I have found several. Finally, I'm a little lukewarm on the epilogue system. This is a post-game system that lets you increase the difficulty of the game. There are three branches of "rulesets," and you can choose up to three "rules," one from each branch. These change things about the game, like making elites do more damage or making it so that sight towers don't spawn on the map. While it offers some neat challenges to overcome, I would have liked a bit more of a linear system as well, similar to the ascension system in Slay the Spire. I may warm up to this system as I play more, but I'm not super excited about it as is.Overall, I think Roguebook is worth your time. It's a pretty game with a lot of potential variety. I hope to see future content for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say that I'm really fond of the deck-builder roguelite genre--but I actually do really enjoy this game. It's quite good. I haven't played Slay the Spire--I've played Astronarch and FTL, which are genre-adjacent; but I like this game's exploration mechanic when compared to Slay the Spire. It's a really good mechanic that drives the value of this game forward, I think. There's a lot of good to be said about this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook is a rogue like card game. However, it comes with a lot of inovating ideas which feel awesomly refreshing for the genre.The goods :+++ : The art style.+++ : The map exploration with ink is simply amazing.+++ : You unlock talents as your deck grows which does not make you feel bad when your deck grows and decrease your chances to find your best cards.++ : Each run you pick a team of two charracters (amoung 4), both charracter come with their unique set of cards and playstyle. However, I would have loved a deeper interactions between charracters with multicolored card or relics for instance. This could completely change your gameplay for a given duo (maybe in a DLC ?). Nevertheless, the dynamic of combats makes use of the fact that you two charracters in a very clever maner !++ : There is a very nice feeling of permanent/meta progression between runs through both card/relic unlock and most importantly a game changing skill tree ! Nevertheless, I have a comment on the skill tree. Certain upgrades feels just amazing (such as more energy altar on the map, begin your run with a gem, replace a strike in your deck,...)  and certain traits feel just awefully overpriced : spending all the rewards of a 2 h run to gain 2 max hp on one charracter feels bad as a late game reward. I would have loved a larger skill tree with more game changing traits sometimes very expensive but then game changing (such as : draft your starting gem, one of your strike is replaced with a card you draft from a pull of 3, get a free alchemist at the beginning of the run, reveal the elite fights on the map,...) intead of a totally overpriced  4th/5th life upgrade ! ++ : The gems allows you to modify your cards for a given run which makes each run even more different.The defaults :- : There is a lack of enemy variety in my opinion. It is far enough for 2 or 3 runs but then you realise that on each run you always fight the complete set of enemies in the game.- : There is still a lot of small bugs (but that will hopefully be solved ! )In a nutshell, this game is just a masterpiece. I strongly recommend it. The devs have just crafted a pure diamond for the genre. I just hope that they will take our feedbacks into account and make it shine !!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is great. Several similarities to Monster Train but there is an overworld to move through on every run which adds a lot more variety. There are also lots of ways to progress between runs. The best PvE card battler I've played so far.Edit: I've seen some complaining of difficulty and a grind being required to unlock things that make each run easier. Not my experience at all. The game is difficult, but not too difficult. A couple of elites, especially in chapter two, are imbalanced. One of those has been nerfed, but I think it needs a total rework. Other than that I think the encounters are well-designed.Another reviewer claimed you needed "100 runs" to start unlocking useful things. Not even close to true unless you are almost immediately dying every run. Even the first few unlocks from either spending pages or unlocking new character cards make a significant difference, which you can get after just one run, even if you didn't beat the final boss. I'm 33 or so hours in and my interest is starting to wane, but even if I stopped now I'd be happy with the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid deck builder. It does not quite have the elegance and satisfaction of Slay the Spire, but is a solid alternative for those who are looking for something new.Most notably, Roguebook adds a whole bunch of new mechanics. Where Slay the Spire gave you one hero that determines which cards will be available during a run, you now play a team of two. Where you only unlocked new cards/relics and difficulties between runs, Roguebook also adds a permanent passive bonus tree. Within each run there gems that can permanently or temporarily improve your found cards, and an entirely new resource system to explore the map.All of these systems work just fine. They are easy to understand and fairly satisfying, with solid risk/reward choices. However, the fact that it invests so many more systems but still doesn't quite reach the same depth shows nicely why StP remains the king of the genre. And in terms of innovation I would still consider Monster Train the more interesting title.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I still want to like this game, and for a completionist, it took me around 100 hours to "beat" the game, that is win a run on max epilogue level. And while there was some fun had, I have no desire to continue playing. There are "only" 15 difficulty increases in the game, unlike 20 for Slay the Spire and 25 for Monster Train. You also only need to beat a difficulty with any pair of heroes to unlock it. As there is no log book of wins, there is nothing telling me what pairs won at what difficulty, although the last few runs I just used the same pair because they felt like a strong combo.As such, I feel very little desire to continue playing. The devs have fixed most of the early bugs, but there are some which could still be fixed I think, plus wording on certain cards made clearer. If you loved StS and want to try something similar, this is not terrible, but I feel this lacks the replayability StS and MT have. It also feels easier, a lot easier, than either game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game but it is definitely on the lower tier of deckbuilder games.  There is just way to much RNG luck.  Even as you progress it is extremely difficult to build a deck with any type of strategy or identity. I'm all for the random draw at the beginning and then trying to build a deck strategy around what you have been given but it's really hard to do that.  Also, many of the enemy and boss mechanics are very frustrating and it is very hard to build a deck to combat all of the different challenges each provides.The gems are a nice twist but often you get really bad gems so you don't even use them.The pre-run challenge mechanic is nice but generally makes the run a little to difficult.Overall, I would say this game needs so tweaking for it to actually be fun.  Every time I play this I run into a new issue that makes me want to quit the game.  That's poor design given that most games in this genre are designed to keep you wanting to start up a new run each time one ends.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Roguebook does a good job at being "similar, yet different" to StS. So if you're in that purgatory of wanting to play StS but not wanting to play more StS, this could be the move.I would never recommend it to someone who wasn't sick of playing Slay the Spire - just go play that then.The most important thing to remember when playing Roguebook is that the "card rewards" are not really rewards - they are basically "shops" and it's best to think about them that way. You get to see what's on offer, but you really can just keep those 25gp instead, and you'll have one less card in your deck and be 25gp richer.That said, Roguebook feels very clearly designed by someone who played a bunch of Slay the Spire, liked it, understood what was good about it, then tried to make a game that was similar - but different in key ways.In StS (and most other games of this type) you have to prune your deck a lot, and big chunky decks are bad. That's just a dynamic that comes up on its own in this type of game. Roguebook has like a dozen different bits of design clearly intended to counterbalance this somewhat, so that mid-sized and even pretty large decks are actually quite playable.There are literal rewards, several rules keywords found on cards e.g. related to the size of your draw pile, there are ways of getting more card draw or cycling, etc.Having a big deck might be why you're dealing a lot of damage, blocking a lot of damage, drawing more cards, why you have more cool talents unlocked for this run, etc.Ultimately, the game is balanced so that mid-sized or even real bigboi decks are very playable and kinda fun and chaotic. Smaller decks still work for the same reasons they always work, so it's more of a rebalance.The central gimmick of combining two different characters and swapping between then when you use defensive cards is well integrated in the game. It helps make the game feel different from StS. You can combine different characters to get different talents to choose from. It works.While Roguebook is overall a very good game with excellent design, it's just a really tall order to try to make anything that wouldn't be unfavorably compared to a game as incredible as StS. But I'm a pretty critical guy and I think it's good enough - at least, good enough for those of us in "StS purgatory". What else are we gonna do, play StS again?For everyone else, I recommend Slay the Spire instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is a good addition to a healthy collection of rogue-like games on Steam.  It feels very dialed in with the relationships of the 4 characters.  It takes some of the fun battle mechanics of Slay the Spire and provides you with a much more fluid map to search and journey across (semi-puzzle mechanics).  The game needs some visual polish and controller support seems to sometimes cause odd visual glitches.  The controller support could also use more clarification in options (key bindings do not seem to show their related controller buttons, though buttons show up during gameplay) as well as longer time windows before triggering Brush.  All that being said, this is a game I can see myself continuing to enjoy for a long time and I would recommend this to anyone who wants a game that is very Slay the Spire-esque with a map exploring mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: Lost track of how many times my jaw has dropped at all the amazing creativity on display in this game. Definitely on par with StS and Monster Train, with enough well executed innovations to justify membership in that exclusive club. The party/swapping mechanic is brilliant. Ignore all the "Day 1 DLC" whiners...when something is this good, I don't give a rat's ass how the developers decide to monetize it. Note to devs: I will be buying any and all future DLC for this game--more heroes please!
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: After 30 hours of playing I can say that this is a great game. The mix of playable characters, variety of cards and power ups make for a very replayable experience. I love that the items that drop have a big impact on the game and how you build your deck. They can turn a struggling run into you wiping the floor with the bad guys if you get the right combo.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review: I was a kickstarter backer and have generally followed the game through its development. They had some rough times but I think the game is a lot more fun and interesting for the efforts.I like the concept of swapping who will be in front (taking the damage) with special effects that might be gained by either being in front or the rear. The new ally cards are also welcome, as they can stack interesting ongoing abilities at the cost the action to put them in play.
_childDocuments_.name: Roguebook

_childDocuments_.review:
The ancients speak of a Book written since time immemorial containing all the world's legends. After many fabulous adventures, recounted in Faeria Chronicles of Gagana, this relic was lost in a well of Faeria. Through contact with this source of magic, the Book developed a wicked free will of its own and became the Roguebook!

You are trapped in the Book of Lore of Faeria, and each page represents a new challenge. Lead your two heroes to victory in this roguelike deckbuilder developed in partnership with Richard Garfield, creator of Magic: The Gathering. Put together the best synergies between cards, relics and abilities, and take on the Roguebook.

name: Cris Tales
detailed_description: Experience Past, Present, and Future simultaneously in this gorgeous, indie love letter to classic JRPGs. Cris Tales is a gorgeous, indie love letter to classic JRPGs with a new perspective. Peer into the past, act in the present, and watch as your choices dynamically change the future -- all on one screen as you play! Join the newly awakened Time Mage Crisbell and her fantastical companions on their journey across a dark, fairytale world facing a grim future. Crisbell must embark across Crystallis and the four Kingdoms in a bid to stop the powerful Time Empress and rewrite the future of the world and all those living in it. Along the way, she’ll meet and recruit powerful allies with their own unique stories and skills like Matias the Frog and Willhelm the Child Mage. As she explores the world and meets her unique companions, Crisbell will have to make choices with far-reaching consequences for the people she meets – consequences that will impact the world you’ll experience in real-time throughout your journey. Each companion will be invaluable as you face these choices and the myriad enemies who stand in your way. Will you buffet them with attacks, or discover creative ways to use Crisbell’s time powers to alter the reality of each fight? Beautifully hand-drawn 2D art is animated frame by frame to bring the branching pasts and futures of each region, enemy, and NPC to life across more than 20 hours of gameplay. Experience a unique combination of branching stories, innovative combat, and classic RPG excitement in Cris Tales’ exciting and unforgettable exploration of how our actions echo through time. A Love Letter to Classic JRPGs – Inspired by timeless JRPGs like Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy VI, Valkyrie Profile, and modern classics like Bravely Default and Persona 5, meet and recruit a unique cast of teammates, challenge myriad enemies, and make your way through an expansive world. Experience the Past, Present, and Future Simultaneously – Peer into and learn from the past, decide on actions in the present, and alter the course of the future in ways that will reshape the world dynamically depending on the choices you make. Master Strategic Turn-Based Combat – Warp your enemies into the past or future, synchronize attacks for enhanced group abilities, and master the timing of attack and defense to go beyond your party’s limits in combat. Uncover a Fascinating Story & Characters – The Empress’ plot to destroy the world is complex and layered. Use your wits and recruit powerful allies throughout the world to uncover and undo her multi-faceted web and make your way to the True Ending of this enchanting tale. Discover a Beautiful World – Climb aboard an airship or boat and traverse this handcrafted, dark fairytale world. From the shining kingdom of Crystallis to the slums of Saint Clarity, discover each unique location and shape its future.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very fond of this game, however it has a *lot* of imperfections. I could write an essay but I'll try to keep it brief.The art is phenomenal and I continue to be charmed by it. The combat *mostly* works well and is satisfying, if a little basic. The voice acting is great. The soundtrack is good and nicely sets the tone. The time mechanics are a little under-utilized, but I still enjoy wandering around cities surveying the different timelines.Unfortunately this game needed a *lot* more playtesting, and more time in the oven in general. Very lacking in QoL features. Lots of minor nuisances during gameplay. Long loading times (make sure you install to an SSD if you have one!). Balancing issues, with the difficulty curve being all over the place. Plot points vary wildly between 'ooh the plot thickens' and 'wtf was that?'. And a general assortment of bizarre occurrences that make me wonder whether this got rushed out of the door e.g.- dialogue assuming you've done things you haven't done yet- tranquil music when a major antagonist is standing right in front of you- a useless new character with no equipment being dropped into your party right before a major encounter (you can remove them, just... why?)To sum up, while it's far from a GOAT I can recommend this if you're looking for a classic style JRPG that looks beautiful - just bear in mind you'll have to be willing to overlook a  of minor annoyances. I'll update this when I'm done if I've anything to add.
