_childDocuments_.review: The story starts off pretty good, I was invested in the beginning but it gets kind of sloppy towards the end... like really bad writing for dialogue and narrative and characters never really seem to take the situation at hand seriously (except for Crisbell) so in turn I can't take the story seriously even when they're talking about people being massacred. And the ending is pretty underwhelming... everything seems a bit rushed towards the end... they do pull some familiar tropes from JRPGs, one that comes to my mind is Bravely Default but I don't want to spoil anything if you're still interested. All I'm gonna say is, it didn't leave a strong impression on me like Final Fantasy IV or V did or even Bravely Default. I like the artstyle which looks anime inspired but also has a unique identity, and my favorite designs are Crisbell, Zas, Kari, Wilheim (and it's a damn shame we can't have his true form playable...), and Adri. Cristopher's design is so uninspired it just looks like a kid playing superhero in his backyard and JKR is kinda cool but something about his design throws me off... maybe it's because he's supposed to be an android but looks like he's wearing a biker jacket, khakis and white shoes. I get it's kind of like a homage to the SNES Final Fantasy games but it just doesn't hit the mark for me. Combat is kind of boring, it does everything right but something about it just feels like a chore and I don't know why. Super Mario RPG has a very simple combat system as well but I would rather fight 100 nonstop battles there than in Cris Tales. At least one attack has a chance of hitting all enemies in the remake or Geno Flash to wipe them out quickly. In Cris Tales most skills are useless so you just kinda bash main attack to get rid of mobs. Or maybe Cristopher and JKR had some skills to clear trash mobs, idk I ran a party of mainly Crisbell, Zas and Kari (later Adri late game) Although there was one memorable scene from combat. In the museum there's these weird giant bug enemies, it starts off as a cocoon but if you use invoke the past it turns into a giant grub thing and somehow webs up your time crystal so you can't break it, not sure how that works... but anyway, it was called Triggot Creeper or something and it swallowed up Zas and there's like a little icon of her and the face she was making was hilarious. It was like an anime style screaming icon. Honestly surprised with its unique mechanics that it wasn't a boss.Anyway, when the difficulty increases combat gets even more tedious because nothing wants to die and you don't ever really do that much damage. Although once you get good gear and upgrades, it's manageable but still, it's a long grind to get there... but when you're finally strong enough they do have an item to stop random encounters which is a god send because the white loading screen is an eye sore and it happens way too much... It also tends to crash frequently... At least for me... I can't even look at the Quest Log without it crashing. The overworld is pretty much empty, and when you can freely explore it, you really feel just how empty it is. But maybe I'm spoiled by FFIV and Trials of Mana's overworlds. You really only get to explore maybe 4 or 5 different regions and you have to reexplore them again late game, it's kind of like Bravely Default... but mid... The gimmick that was the main selling point of the game to manipulate time between past, present and future is only used when exploring towns and... it's not that exciting. It's actually kind of painful to look at and you can't turn it on or off which would have made things more interesting in my opinion. Sometimes I want to see what an NPC would look like between different time layers but I have to switch to Matias to see it better because Crisbell doesn't have enough room for me to see... I wonder... maybe most of the developement went into this past, present, future gimmick which caused the other parts of the game to be less developed... I don't think it was worth it. It's a very cool concept but the tradeoff doesn't seem to be worth it, especially when it isn't even used late game.  The music is good but boy are they bad at using music to change the mood... there would be times where the boss would say something menancing but it would still be playing some lively music... Dungeons are okay, kind of got like a Paper Mario feel from some of them but the lack of maps kinda makes it a pain to navigate around. But they aren't that big though so you'll probably be done under an hour for most of them. The lack of maps is also a problem when navigating towns and you have to find some NPC to recruit and you forget where they are exactly so you just have to talk to everyone... there is a map for the overworld... but... like I said... empty... it's like 4 regions... left, right, center, and lower center...Ultimately! I think I will give it a 6/10. Has a lot of room for improvement. Not the worst game I ever played but I do kind of regret spending so much time on it when I could have been playing Sea of Stars. That game does have a few faults that miss the mark when trying to recapture that classic JRPG feeling but it does it better than Cris Tales did. I think Cris Tales was too ambitious on the artstyle, graphics and gimmick of time travel, that it left a lot the other areas unrefined such as the story, characters and world exploration. Would I recommend it? Eh... if you can get it under $20 and have time to kill maybe...

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game to recommend, but it's not a bad game. The art style is amazing, the voice acting is great, and the story is solid. I played this game because of it's art and characters. I was in love with the MC, and the style of the game and it hooked me but after that I struggled to keep playing. In the end, I'm happy I did. The story was satisfying to experience and the combat was fun and required thought, even if the time mechanic ended up being in the background and it just turned into a more generic JRPG.Unfortunately, the game is marred by a few glaring problems. Everyone else mentions it, but it has a slowness. The loading times between zones, between battles, the slow combat animations. It can make it feel kind of like a slog to play through. There is a wierd balancing between characters, some are very very powerful in a straight forward way that makes you migrate towards them even if they aren't the characters you enjoy. Speed is way too powerful, Crisbel ends up being a haste bot for your damage dealers. They take away your characters at various points, but because XP isn't split up and they take their gear with them, you can find yourself at a big disadvantage. Only one character has the ability to scan all versions of a monster, making it feel a bit punishing to not use them until you give into the freedom of just not caring about switching times.For each area, there are side quests to complete which impact the story, but one of those areas locks you out of the side quests well before you get the warning of it and if you aren't aware can cost you the 'best ending' which is very frustrating.Ultimately, I wouldn't recommend this game in general to someone looking to play a JRPG. However, if you found something you love about it - like the art style in my case, or if you love JRPGs in general and just need something to scratch the itch it is worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game, if a bit simple and short. The combat is fun at first but gets easy but ends up being a steamroll if you put any effort into building your team. The story and characters are charming charming, but rather standard, save for some twists near the end I really liked. The art and music are really good.If you are looking for a game to have fun and be done in <20 Hrs, I recommend it. If you are looking for a challenge, keep looking.
_childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still far from finishing this game and will probably amend this review after I do, but so far I can wholeheartedly recommend it. I have played the demo and fell in love with the premise, the world and the characters, and the full version builds upon it even more, which is very nice.The biggest plus of Cris Tales is the game does not pretend to be something it is not. When the devs say it's a love letter to the jPRG genre, it really is, the only detail being - it's a love letter to the old-school jRPGs and not the modern ones. So if you're a Final Fantasy I-VI buff you'll feel much more at home than someone who doesn't know those titles.Biggest con so far is that the battles feel a little slow and rely on your reflexes (for dealing additional damage or parrying). I feel like this part could have been polished a little more. The game could offer a system where the game would do the button pushing for you as this part is extremely crucial to fights throughout the game and people with worse reflexes might get frustrated.So far, so good. After almost 8 hours of gameplay I give this a solid 7,5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: Cris Tales is a wonderfull game, although with it's flaws.The art style is gorgeous, the soundtrack is good, the characters are nice, and it doesn't drag too much with the story (meaning it doesnt bloat itself too much). There are some aspect that are less good.Like some reviews also state, the music transitions sometimes are lacking, and the intro for the battles are just a loading screen, wich is a good and a bad, good because you dont instantly get a heart attack when one pops out, bad because of the wait. (the loading screen itself is ok)In the end it was a surprisingly good game, i know working through a pandemic is prone to cause some bumps, so treat those problems as what they really are, little bumps.

_childDocuments_.review: I have not completed this game yet. It seems I will have to start from the beginning due to a bug, but having said that,this game is very enjoyable. At the moment, I will recommend it at the buyers risk as in regards to the state of the game at release, as pertaining to bugs that can interfere in battles, quests, achievements, and character stats. These are what I have seen listed in discussion threads, with the exception being battles.Characters are likable, art direction is amazing, music is great.Some aspects can feel a chore at times, and there have been a few difficulty spikes, but nothing someone who plays JRPGs hasn't run into before. _childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing the game for a good bit now, and I got to say I'm having heaps of fun. The combat has fun sense of depth and experimentation for the most part, the story and cast are quite charming. Plus the art style of the game is jaw dropping. I will bring up that game has short comings that as much I love the game so far. Might be deal breaker for some.First while I do find the cast charming, they are quite shallow in a lot of ways. The story's pacing is also very quick, even when it would be great for it to slow down and let us get to know an area or character. Second is how enemies move in combat, the players characters run up to the enemy and do a strike which you can time a button press to do more damage. Weirdly, the enemies don't run up to the player characters to attack. They just stay in place and do an attack animation, which again with a nicely timed button press will block a lot of damage.Lastly, the side quests have you run around the world map a lot and the speed that you naturally makes it a slog to go through. Believe it or not, despite the above mentioned issues. I still love this game and seriously recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful animation, one of the few games where I see the intro every time I start the game up.I controls are a bit confusing compared to normal keyboard controls, although luckily you're rarely getting punished for it with the playstyle. It's very cute, but occasionally a bit slow in progress. But that seems to be part of the genre. Still haven't figured how to use the equipment I've collected on my characters, so there's a few things that could be improved on in future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: A great ode to the JRPGs of the SNES and PS1 era. Graphically this game is exceptional, consistent and pleasant to the eyes. Its music its great and reminds me of the melodies of great composers like Nobuo Uematsu and the like. Gameplay I find it pretty interesting, with enough new mechanics that makes it stand on its own as new approach to the old school JRPGs systems, but still keeping what makes it feel traditional and inspired by those games from the past. The only critique I have is it's loading times before a battle start, which I hope gets fixed in a future patch.If you like old school JRPGs, with random battles, turn based combat and lots of dialogue, this is a great game to have. If you are not into this kind of games, it may not be the best game to start with on the JRPG genre (specially if you want a fast paced game).
_childDocuments_.name: Cris Tales

_childDocuments_.review: The game is exactly what the demo was advertising.The game is beautiful, fun to play and they added a subbtle indicator for the timing in combat.There is some choices you have to make that I assume change the ending , the combats really are the selling point of the game for me. They're simple but yet strategic.It just runs fine here with 144fps, no stuttering or framepacing issue, I did see a visual bug like 2D overlapping but really a minor thing.Now for the negatives: The game is too expensive IMO and should have been around 30 (no regional pricing...).no graphical options for PC, you can't change resolution/framerate cap/ enable anti- aliasing (and there's a lot of aliasing).(devs stated that adding graphical option for pc is part of their plans)Overall seems like a good game, but the release could have been handled better. Hope the game will sell well

_childDocuments_.review:
Cris Tales is a gorgeous, indie love letter to classic JRPGs with a new perspective. Peer into the past, act in the present, and watch as your choices dynamically change the future -- all on one screen as you play! Join the newly awakened Time Mage Crisbell and her fantastical companions on their journey across a dark, fairytale world facing a grim future.

Crisbell must embark across Crystallis and the four Kingdoms in a bid to stop the powerful Time Empress and rewrite the future of the world and all those living in it. Along the way, she'll meet and recruit powerful allies with their own unique stories and skills like Matias the Frog and Willhelm the Child Mage.

As she explores the world and meets her unique companions, Crisbell will have to make choices with far-reaching consequences for the people she meets consequences that will impact the world you'll experience in real-time throughout your journey. Each companion will be invaluable as you face these choices and the myriad enemies who stand in your way. Will you buffet them with attacks, or discover creative ways to use Crisbell's time powers to alter the reality of each fight?

name: Wayward Strand
detailed_description: Welcome to the Hospital It's the summer of 1978, and Casey Beaumaris is trying to make the most of her holidays, when her mum asks her to spend a long weekend helping out at the airborne hospital where she works. Casey prefers the company of books to people, but she agrees, secretly planning to write an article about her visit for the school newspaper. With her trusty notebook at the ready, Casey arrives on board the airship. The staff are overworked as they prepare for the visit of an important official, while the patients react to grief, or deal with active trauma. In the midst of these and many other interlocking and overlapping stories, Casey spends time with the patients, learning about their lives, and, as the stories unfold, discovering what she can do to help. Explore A Living World Within the world of Wayward Strand, time passes for everyone - characters continue their lives without waiting for you to interact with them. In Wayward Strand’s unique narrative structure, the stories of over a dozen characters constantly unfold around you in real time, as you, as Casey, roam freely throughout each day. Choose which story to be a part of by following people, having conversations , and exploring the hospital. The hospital’s residents are an eclectic cast of characters – some charming, some eccentric, some rude – each with their own desires, goals and imaginations. Every character moves and acts of their own accord, at their own pace, on their own timeline - sharing news with each other, arguing, joking, gossiping - or having a chat with Casey when she comes by. Every playthrough gives you the opportunity to discover something you didn’t see previously - what you missed the first time, you might see the second, third, or fifth time around. Your Journey When you see someone, you can follow them, to see where they go and what they get up to. You can eavesdrop on peoples’ conversations, or come into the room and be a part of the discussion. Spending time with particular characters will lead you to new storylines, locations, revelations and resolutions. As the journalist for her school newspaper, Casey keeps track of events and information in her notebook . Players use Casey’s notebook to delve deeper into peoples’ stories, to make new discoveries, and to piece together mysteries. Voice & Screen Language: English Accessibility The Family Video Game Database's page on Wayward Strand has details on our accessibility features and requirements:

short_description: Wayward Strand is a heartfelt story told in a curious way. Hop aboard an airborne hospital and meet its fully-voiced cast of eclectic characters. As time passes for everyone on board, explore the interwoven lives of the patients and staff; discover something new on each and every playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand is an undeniably cozy narrative game with a true Australian flavour. Its unconventional narrative approach genuinely makes the environment, and characters within it come alive. Taking approximately 7 years to develop, this is more than just a passion project, but an experimental success, and a great accolade for Australian Indie developers.The protagonist is Casey, a 14-year-old girl, and daughter of the head nurse on the airborne hospital. Set in regional Victoria, Australia in the 1970's, this airborne ship is a state-of-the-art facility, caring for countless elderly patients. I am not sure if the inspiration behind this is the Royal Flying Doctor Service (a famous health care service for remote areas in Australia), but I could not help but make the comparison, which made me feel even more at home with it.  Perhaps this is the first ever narrative game that I have played that perfectly portrays my home state and rural-town feel, from the background sounds, characters, voices, phrases and even the menu soundtrack. Developers' really have done Victoria (and Australia) justice in making this game. Whilst this is completely playable for Non-Australian players of course, I imagine that many sayings, tones, subtle references and so on, will just not connect with an International audience. However, this is extremely minor, and I believe everyone can enjoy the game for what it is, especially the Aussie accents. Well, that depends on you, the player! Casey wanders the facility and speaks to the various patients. Whilst there is a small overarching story between Casey and her mum's relationship, the rest of it is completely up to the player. To further explain, time passes normally for the characters. The world is still moving while Casey is doing any action. Therefore, it is impossible to experience everything in the game in one playthrough, as it is a living universe where characters do not wait for players to approach them. They are going about their daily lives, whether you are there or not! I was apprehensive about this concept at first, as it seems so difficult to make it work. How can developers' have no idea where the player will be at any given point, but still display a logical and heartfelt story in a chronological order, I thought. Yet, it works, and each playthrough is unique. Whilst it is not flawless, and there is  some repeated dialogue that may have already been heard, it is minimal, and I cannot imagine the amount of work that went into fixing as many of these inconsistencies of interwoven storylines.Wayward Strand's narrative is astonishing. Not necessarily because of the content it covers, but the narrative design behind creating this living world must have been a nightmare to make coherent. Yet, the developers  manage to do just this.Wayward Strand is a heavy narrative game. It is a cozy, relaxing experience that delivers genuine and deep conversations. There are no puzzles, true choice/consequence styled dialogue, item collection, or anything else that gamers are accustomed to in adventure titles. This entire game is exceptionally unique, and this non-linear narrative approach involves immense risk-taking, as it will not appeal to the masses. Text cannot be skipped, so fast-readers may have a bit of a headache here, but it is for good reason. Because of the “real-time” world, timing is awfully important, everything is meticulously scripted to avoid inconsistencies and to allow the stories to function. If players were to skip text, this would dramatically alter the timing of every single event happening simultaneously at that moment, ultimately devastating the narratives flow.The gameplay really is as simple as it sounds, Casey spends three days aboard the 3-floored ship and spends her time speaking with and/or helping the residents. Learn about their pasts,  their conflicts, their petty gossip. and relationships towards each other. Eavesdrop on nearby conversations, or peek into rooms to learn more. If I saw a speech bubble of an interesting conversation happening on a different floor? You bet that I am going to head straight there to listen in. The characters themselves are expertly written and they are not cardboard cutouts of elderly people being compassionate, sweet and "homey." Quite the opposite, there are some downright surly residents, even mute ones. Discover what experience or feelings gives them this attitude. Choose which people to speak with, or to just... spend time with. Sit in the same room as them for a while, and sometimes they will begin a conversation on their own.Once it reaches around 5pm, Casey will meet her mother and begin the trip back home. But for the entire day, what Casey chooses to do, is completely up to the player. It is designed around multiple replays as you WILL miss things. It is simply impossible to see it all, and I definitely will be going back to see what I missed out on. Upon reflection, I am under the impression that one of the game’s core messages is curiosity, and to inspire it, even in the smallest of ways. Despite the idea of “talking to old people” not seeming like the most captivating thing to do, Wayward Strand queries this, demonstrating the mutually beneficial outcomes of being kind, and simply conversing with others.I believe it is important to note that this game is not riveting, it is a slice-of-life, heartfelt narrative experience. There are ample times when running around from room to room, trying to start conversations, repeatedly, is just what the gameplay is. I appreciate this style, but it would be very beneficial to add manual saving, as the days can be quite long and for those with short attention spans, it would be hard to stay focused in a game such as this.The artistic design in Wayward Strand is soft, snug and everything cozy. It reminded me of children's picture storybooks, or hidden object books. Its soft, but detailed design perfectly encapsulates the heartwarming narrative of the game.The sound is just as welcoming, with warm guitar strings and an upbeat melody always playing in the background. As an extra plus (at least for me), the Australian magpie vocalisations in the menu screen just topped it all off. Could not think of a better idle soundtrack myself! Approximately 5 hours for one playthrough Player choice Yes, extremely so.Wayward Strand is a standout Australian narrative game. Its unconventional non-linear approach to storytelling is not something I had ever encountered before, but developers' have made it work, and made it work WELL. Its focus on replayability, player choice, excellent writing, voice overs and cozy aesthetic make this a game I highly recommend to narrative lovers, especially those who like wholesome games, this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing Concept, Okay ExecutionSo, I went into this game really wanting to love it. I love the time and schedule system in Majora's Mask, where you can follow people around and see the little details of what they get up to over the course of three days, and that's literally the same system this game has. This game, sadly, even though its only focus is on that system, does not do it as well as Majora's Mask did.I really enjoyed my first playthough of the game. I enjoyed 90% of the characters (side eyes Mr. Avery). They're very well written and there are a few scenes that popped up that were very fun and unexpected. Even the character which I didn't enjoy wasn't because he was poorly written but just because I didn't like him as a person, lol. I enjoyed a lot of the concepts that the game explores with their characters. Every line is voice acted superbly. There were no moments where a line felt awkward or poorly read, and I'm very picky when it comes to voice acting. You can tell a lot of love and thought was put into creating this game, and I was super excited to go through every lovingly made detail with a fine tooth comb and see even the minute ways that my choices would affect in the story. Sadly, that's impossible. The gigantic blaring elephant in the room issue with this game is, the fact that the journal entries do not remain on subsequent playthroughs. Every time an event happens, like something as small as a character sleeping in bed or just sitting in their room for a few hours, the main character notes it in her notebook and what time it happens. I was very excited for this. I thought I would be able to fully fill out the notebook through multiple playthoughs and learn everything about these characters. But no, when you finish the final day, your notebook gets wiped. You can't take that information with you into the next playthrough. So, if you want to learn all of the characters' schedules and all of the possible outcomes from your decisions, you basically have to either keep your own separate text document and constantly be opening that up and writing in it or replay the game many times and repeat many scenes and have it all memorized in your head, and I'm sorry but even though the scenes are nicely written, I don't want to repeat them over and over again. And that wouldn't be an issue, if the notebook remained filled out through the playthroughs, because for example if I had 1pm to 3pm filled out for a character from a previous playthough, I would know that I would just need to find that character at 3pm and I could continue filling out their schedule and seeing the gaps in the story without repeating a bunch of stuff. As the system is now, filling in gaps in the characters' stories is impossible, unless your mind is like a steel trap and you have every single event and time it occurred that you've seen memorized.A smaller issue I have is that the character animations can be pretty janky, especially the main character's walking animation, which I can only describe as constantly doing the stanky leg, so there were a lot of times where I was taken out of a scene, because it was a very dramatic situation, but the animation would be messed up for some reason, so objects would be floating or impaling characters in the face, or just the constant sight of my character doing the stanky leg to get around, while comical, would get annoying to constantly look at. Like, there's charming jank and then there's just "Do the game creators have eyes???" jank and the main character's walk is definitely "Do the game creators have eyes???" tier.The game takes about 4 hours to play through. As it is, I don't think many people would enjoy replaying the game, which is sad, because that's the whole point of the game, but again with the useless notebook system, it's too frustrating. And don't get me wrong, the first playthrough was enjoyable. There were a lot of heartwarming and funny and interesting moments and I really felt like I was going to be able to deep dive into this game and unravel every detail of the story. But, again, that first playthrough is all that I was really able to enjoy, and if you look at play times on other reviews, you'll probably see the same with other people.Overall, I recommend this game if you have a bigger games budget and are okay with spending 20 USD for a 4 hour experience that you can tell had a lot of heart put into it. If the notebook system was overhauled and made so that it wasn't wiped after every playthrough, I would recommend it completely, but sadly I can't. There is a lot of potential in this concept, and I think almost everything besides the gameplay and walking animation was executed very well. Sadly, though, this is a videogame, and I just can't recommend a game where the core gameplay mechanic is so flawed.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for Wayward Strand a few years ago during LudaNarraCon and I had kept my on eye on it since. Now that it’s finally been released and I’ve played through it I can definitely say it’s a great game. Wayward Strand feels a bit like the 90’s Jordan Mechner directed adventure game, The Last Express, in that it’s a historical fiction adventure game set in a singular location where people are doing their own thing around you as the in-game clock ticks on whether your there to see it or not. Unlike Last Express though, Wayward Strand is much more low-key and mundane, there are no grand mysteries to uncover or daring adventure to swashbuckle your way into, you’re just a young Australian girl, Casey, tasked to accompany your head nurse mother to the airship hospital she works on to help her keep the patients company for the three day weekend. That’s pretty much the gameplay, exploring the airship hospital and getting to learn about it and the characters you interact with over the course of three in-game days. The mundanity of the game is one of its greatest strengths as there are very few games I can think of, even ones more grounded in our reality, that just lack any kind of peril. Even games such as Gone Home and Firewatch which are entirely grounded, still dance around with player expectations that there may be more sinister things at work, and that still sort of applied to Firewatch. Wayward Strand focuses on how the everyday going-ons with the hospital and how the patients deal with their lives in their twilight years, knowing that the reaper will be visiting them sooner rather than later. An example of this is that one of the patients passed away early in the morning of the day that Casey first arrives so she never gets to meet him, but you can have her question the patients and staff about him and they’ll regale you their memories of him. I’ll just tell you straight up there’s no underlying twist to his death, he was just old and he passed away in his sleep and that just exemplifies my point, this isn’t some standard high concept game narrative where there’s got to be something  deeper going on, it’s just life and life doesn’t tend to give one satisfying narrative climaxes. But that’s not to say it’s boring at all, the characters are fleshed out and interesting and they’re brought to life with quality voice-acting and charming art and its real engaging interacting them. That’s another face of the game too, it’s a positive and human game as the relationships of the patients and staff keep them going, but avoids being twee or cloying. It’s a game that is appropriate for kids but has some real maturity to it.As I stated before the characters do things on their own and have their own schedules so there is definitely stuff you’re going to miss on a first play through. For example I only managed to get a scant few of the game’s achievements in my playthrough so there definitely is more for me to uncover. I plan on revisiting the game again sometime after I’ve chipped away through some of my backlog. One of the few negatives I feel the game has it you have to play each day in one go, the game doesn’t have any middays saves. The devs have already said they are working on this and they’ve already patched a day select so this problem will be mostly likely fixed. There’s also some janky graphical stuff like characters clipping through each other when they walk through doorways, but that’s just such a minor quibble, especially because this is an indie game, and everything else about it is great.Wayward Strand is just a charming and maturely written game that you don’t see a lot of this in medium and I heartily recommend if you’re down with exploring an airship hospital and its cast of characters.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting experience that I'll probably write more about when I've had more time to think or even do another playthrough or two. So you have a lot of agency as a player in that sense, but you won't be a big hero. It's more about the small things. You may also share your character's frustration sometimes. _childDocuments_.review: RECOMMENDED, BUT WITH MAJOR CAVEAT. This is a slow-paced game that focuses on story and conversations. There is no major excitement here, no action, no puzzles. It's more of a slice-of-life experience than a dramatic narrative, so if you want those aspects in your games, you probably will not enjoy this one!While somewhat of an oversimplification, the best way I can describe my experience with this game is "visiting a nursing home simulator". Going through this game felt not unlike going to visit my elderly grandparents. It's the perfect example of the sort of unconventional experience that the indie game scene has made possible; a true slice-of-life with none of the aspects that make for successful mass-market titles, but making and distributing this game to the right audience is now possible enough that it can still exist.And I'm glad it does exist. I only played through the game once so I've missed a majority of the content there is to see. It was far from being the most engaging experience I've ever had with a game, and I was ready to move on by the time I was done, but I did enjoy my time with it and will probably one day visit it again.While I give this a thumbs up, it's really only an experience that certain types of gamers will enjoy. Hopefully this review has given you enough information to know if you're one of those types. :)

_childDocuments_.review: You explore a charming repurposed airship, serving as an old folks home. As a young girl, walk around, talk and offer the local residents company, eavesdrop on conversations, and collect information about them in your journal. Enjoyable high-quality voice acting and an atmospheric soundscape, all set in beautifully crafted, hand-drawn environments. The game consists of three chapters, each representing a day, with a total playtime of around four hours. The goal is for you to discover the distinct personalities of each resident and some of the staff. That said the airship is relatively small, with only six main resident rooms. You can go around and do whatever you want but it still ends up being pretty liner with not much purpose or reward to go exploring outside the intractable areas. Despite some limitations, the game play allows for a relaxed, engaging social simulator experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A slow and sweet game set in a nursing home that happens to be on an air ship tethered to the ground in Australia, it's a clockwork little world in a way that reminded me of classic game The Last Express, where characters are on schedules and have activities all their own and you have to make choices about where to go and who to talk to and what to see. I recommend this game because there are sweet scenes and interesting characters and a charming design. I'm glad I experienced it. But I can't say it's an especially strong recommendation, because, this game just needed a little *more* in every direction. More drama -- there is some drama to your character's relationship with her mother, and each of the residents of the nursing home has some interesting backstory to them, but nothing really seems to matter and there is no problem to solve. More depth to the world -- it's interesting that this nursing home is set on an airship that seemingly arrived out of nowhere, but, as far as I can tell...that's it? There's not much more backstory to it than that, and it doesn't feel like anything would be different about the story if this nursing home were on the ground. And it needed more options for players. The game only saves when you complete one of the three days of plot, each of which takes about an hour, which is frustrating. And, I assume because everyone is on such a schedule, there's no way to lightly fast forward through dialogue sequences or actions your character is taking, which means a lot of the 4 hours I spent playing this game was just me twiddling my thumbs as I waited for a character to spit out all their dialogue, or for my character to slowly navigate the stairs. There's enough charm and warmth to this game that I felt it was worth my time and interest, but I did leave it feeling like with a few more nudges in the right direction, this could've become a much stronger experience. I am curious to see what this team does next, I hope they build on the successful parts and make something better.

_childDocuments_.review: I was provided a key for Wayward Strand directly from the developers themselves back around October of last year and, due to a multitude of conflicting schedules, got the opportunity to finally play this game a week ago. I started and played the game with the vague idea from their twitter page that the game is naturally narrative-focused and reminiscent of a story book more than a game. However, what I received instead from Wayward Strand was an experience that I greatly appreciated and was impressed with, especially with the amount of 1st party titles from the Big 3 consoles that I played recently (4 to be exact) that were left me disappointed and wanting more.Wayward Strand reminded me the beauty of indie games tend to allow go underappreciated as the more notable, big-budgeted games usually grab our attention due to the exorbitant amounts of money that goes into advertising them. The game starts off on a rather innocent note, putting us in control of 14-year old Casey who has 3 days left of her summer vacation. There is something of a story that is Casey's mother, the head nurse of the hospital, going through stress due to the hospital being understaffed, the director trying to receive additional funding for the hospital, and naturally, having a managerial position, and this stress does bleed a bit into Casey and her mother's dynamic with one another. The gameplay allows you as Casey to realize why this is the case for her mother, but with your interactions with the inhabitants of the airship, you discover secrets about not just them, but also about the ship itself and former inhabitants, giving the game a slight air of mystery. With each inhabitant having their own personality and habit that contrast and sometimes clash with one another, I eventually found myself invested into each senior citizen to the point where these were no longer characters, but actual humans.In doing so, when I finished the game after 4 and a half hours, I had to hold back a bit of tears as someone who faced personal deaths within the last 5 years that greatly affected me. This game not only emphasizes not to take life for granted, but to also recognize, realize, and remember that those around us, especially our parents and elders, were once young. Once lived a life experiencing their youth, adulthood, hardships, and a plethora of other emotions before age brought them to their final stage of life. This game does a splendid job in showcasing while we all are subjected to mortality, cherish those memories you created, reflect on how you overcame those challenges you didn't think could be defeated, and live in the moment -- every day -- until your final breath leaves you.While I give this game much praise, it is not without its faults. Unfortunately, this game would benefit from smoothing out its animations more. Also, as this game is clearly designed around a fixed-time frame where it's impossible to do everything on one playthrough, there should be a New Game + added along with keeping the journal entries from your first playthrough. Although I recommend to play this game because it truly is deserving of a playthrough, I am also understanding of those of you who might want to do multiple playthroughs (or even attempt to 100% the game), and do not want to spend $20 on a game that is still lacking polish in crucial departments that warrant a game worthy of obtaining your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: After an hour with this gorgeous little game, I can't wait to delve deeper in to it's warmth and soothing little touches. Gentle plucks of a classical guitar spur on a narrative told by the most beautiful and unique artwork. You drive through the Australian outback of my childhood to a 'Round-the-Twist' lighthouse with an airship floating in the bay. You ascend into it with your mum and begin the cutest little adventure as Casey, an Aussie kid with a passion for stories. As you meet each character, you are reminded of an elder from your own life, each one with a million stories. Some can't be shared because of ailment, a foggy memory, or perhaps trauma, but you will sit there for hours with them in the hope you are able to harvest some gem of wisdom. You bring comfort to each of the characters by simply caring about them and what they have to say. There is plenty of beauty, but the spectacle is not the main character here. Rather, the game taps in to something more primal than that. It gives you an opportunity to enjoy giving the other characters care and love and respect. This game  empathy. It  the joy of giving joy. What a clever idea for a videogame. Bravo.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been a really fun game but if you are 100 percenter like myself you will hate this pretty much by day 3.The clock ticking on might sound fun but you quickly get that you are missing an awfull lot of stuff.I looked up the internet and nobody has even tried to come up with a guide to get most of the achievements in 1 playthrough.From what I could understand this needs even more than 3.If anyone ever writes a decent guide please contact me :)I will gladly replay and end it cause now I abandonded it during day 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic little slice of life Aussie adventure. Awesome voice actors, intriguing characters and cool visuals.This is a very specific type of calm game. There's no high stakes or intense gameplay; however, the whole vibe works together with the pace and keep me engaged.I do have a bug where the audio will skip and cut out for half a second. Usually only lasts for 20 - 30 seconds and then it goes back to normal for 10 or so minutes. Some animations are a bit janky. There's a nice animation when you walk up or down stairs but using the elevator gives weird pop in as you teleport up or down instead of move there.Overall, I love the setting. It feels very Australian. It's a shame it has been slept on a bit but Steam is a brutal place. Regardless, I have enjoyed my time so far (I haven't finished the game yet).
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so nice and I mean that in the most pleasant way possible. What really makes this game is the voice acting and the artists/animators. If I had to critique something it would be the ending, Overall though I am shocked this game doesn't have a lot of attention. It is very lovely and has re-playability. The characters are interesting and have their own personalities. It's all very realistic and I loved it! Could not recommend it enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: I was incredibly impressed with this game - I did not want it to end. I wound up wrapping in just under 11 hours. This is one of those games where you will want to do some Groundhog-Day-ing - revisiting days to see what you missed. I never found myself bored with redoing a day. I thoroughly enjoyed getting to know every character.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand was a beautiful game. I just finished my first play through of it and I am excited to start my next. I enjoyed the the feeling of being the background character, merely just existing in the lives of everyone on the ship. Each character is so distinct and how the story plays out really puts you inside the mind of Casey. It was hard on the final day, saying my goodbyes-- craving for more days of bonding with those on the ship. While the game was slow and calm, I never once felt bored, there was always someone to find and at minimum just sit with. Personally, this game reminded me to enjoy the slow moments, that sometimes just sitting with someone is enough. I heavily suggest this game to anyone who likes low-intensity games, ones that encourage you to take the time to exist and interact with no objective to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand is an incredibly ambitious narrative videogame with great writing, a refreshing art style, and a fascinating setting. It had some visual glitches, when I played it at least, but it's still worth checking out if you're interested in narrative focused games that take the medium in interesting and fruitful directions. I'm looking forward to the team's next project.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely stunning narrative experience. Subverts conventional expectations of what game narratives can deliver - both in terms of mechanics and actual content. Superb cast of characters, truly heartwarming moments, and a storytelling method unlike any other game (perhaps Overboard! is in some ways mechanically similar)Some minor glitches and bugs, but this beautiful game is well worth looking past those. A masterpiece, and I say this as someone who's been a fan of narrrative based games since 1992.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe this game is utterly charming in every way. From the art style to the voice acting (which is surprisingly great!) and the little stories throughout the game, everything is just charming. This is a slow and relaxing game that filled me with a sense of peace and comfort instead of boredom. I felt the length was just right to really immerse myself in the world of Wayward Strand without it overstaying its welcome. I really enjoyed my time with each character. You won't encounter any puzzles or action of any sort, but I think that's pretty clear from the trailer and description. There isn't a big overarching plot or mysteries to solve, it's just a really lovely slice of life game that will make you feel warm and fuzzy. Absolutely charming game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a game where much happens. Although, judging by my achievement count, perhaps this is just a game where I missed everything that happens. But the last thing it asks you to do is say goodbye to all of the characters you've met. I was quite sad to be leaving. So clearly the developers have achieved what they set out to do. Highly recommended for anyone willing to try a slow quite game about fractured relationships and the encroachment of mortality.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: All the characters are layered and seem genuine, the conversations are interesting, and (unlike some others who have criticised the pace) I enjoy the flow of the interactions. There's a warm heart beating at the core of this game.It's a blanket of contemplative nostalgia that wraps itself around you and makes you take stock of things. Time is fleeting, and this game compels you to look around and appreciate people and things with a gentle curiosity, before they melt away.This isn't just a fun game, or a good experience; it's a balm in these dark and crazy times. When I immerse myself in this world, I feel comforted. But not just in an escapist sense - on the contrary, it encourages me to engage with what surrounds me and reminds me of what's truly important.Uplifting, warm, heartfelt, soothing, well-written, and very much worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: A cozy and delightful game and that I'm looking forward to replaying to tease out the rest of the story!It's very immersive due to the excellent writing, well-designed interface (you can use the undocumented Q/Z/X/Space and arrow keys to do everything), and the voice acting. The art is also lovely :)As a heads-up - you can't save except between "chapters" which is about once an hour
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game, I really like the concept of the game, I've been keen to play it for a while, I enjoyed speaking to all the different characters and slowly learning more about them. The art style and music is great too. I kinda wanted a bit more, in a way, but I'll give it another go as I'm sure I haven't seen it all yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: This game is filled with heart and is lovely to play. Characters are spot on and gameplay is done right here. No need to rush to do things and time moves slowly in this game.You are girl who helps his mum with elderly people. You need to make company with them and same time ask about airship Because this whole elderly people home is on airship. If you want something really lovely game where you can relax and make yourself feel like your doing good job this is for you.Also this game saves on end of every day. So beware if you don't play enough you will need to start again same day over againI would buy this game for sure if I don't have it for review
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand is a fantastic story-rich game. I really liked how the entire game was voice-over so I didn't have to read everything, and the voice overs help to immerse me in the game's atmosphere. There was this weird bug that sometimes the audio would skip a bit, but it wasn't to the point where it made me want to stop playing the game. If you like story-rich games and have some time on your hands. I would highly recommend checking out Wayward Strand.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that attracted me is the art style and after I finished the story, I have to say the developer has done a great job in making this warmth and heartfelt game. The song, the mood, the art style, they are all blended in to perfection. It is like a getaway game when you want to take a break from chaotic reality. Thank you for making this wonderful game. I'll look forward for more games!
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Very sweet and heartfelt. This game is exactly what it advertises: Going into a geriatric ward and just talking with the residents. All the personalities are unique, and some are a bit...strong. But if you like just sitting and learning about people, enjoying their experiences, then this is a perfect game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: A game that thrives on the simple and small beauty of conversations, silence, and friendshipWayward Strand is a slow paced game. The gameplay consists of walking around, talking to elderly people or just hanging out with them in silence. This simple premisse works thanks to it's elaborate narrative device, supported by great writing, voice acting, visuals and music.This device works as a system where every character has their own path and routine, all happening at the same time, meaning that while you're on a room talking to someone, the other characters are getting on with their day, moving around and even entereing the room you're in to talk to its resident.This gives a very dynamic feel to the world, first: it makes the characters feel alive and with their own autonomy, something greatly supported by the writing, every character has a unique personality and different facets and layers to them, which adds a good amount of replayability since you can't see everything on a single playthrough. And second: it gives a lot of freedom and fills you with a feeling of exploration and curiosity, learning about the ship, getting to know the residents and staff or just hanging out with the people you like the most, as a player you're free to do all theses things or focus on just one, there's always something going on inside the airship.Couple that with a charming visual style that has a very children books feel and a varied soundtrack, with every room having it's own track, and you got a amazing experience that manage to stay with you long after you beat it. And it's very much worth it for anyone that enjoys chill and relaxing games focused on conversations and bonding with characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand is one of those games that makes you realise that we've been missing out on something all this time, and in this case, it's cool and funny old people. Where are all the cool and funny old people in videogames! Well, they're right here in Wayward Strand. There's a granny of every flavour.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely little game that epitomises the best qualities of Australian storytelling.  Calm, pleasant, mundane, and charming - the only wrong way to play this game is to rush through it, to try and get all the answers and win at the story.  No, the way you play this is the same way that Casey needs to spend time with the patients - just be present, talk when it strikes you, and don't be afraid of silence.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that makes you take your time, and chill. It's a challenge to tune down to the games speed, but once you let go and just let it come it's so good. This game is lovely, a fabulous few days to spend exploring and learning about the community around Casey as she explores the airship. The characters are rich and engaging, and the performances of the cast are marvellous. There is so many threads to explore and no way you can experience all threads in one play through. My kids and I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Wayward Strand is a weird and wonderful wander through questions on ageing for teens and old people; agency for those in the care of others, and the agenda of you the player in an environment where time passes and your actions or inactions have consequences.I think everyone will find this poignant at times, and hopefully make you a little bit proud that a game with a heart like this can exist. It's one you could play with your grandparents if you're lucky enough to still have them around, or if not like me, one which will remind you of them in such a powerful way that you can feel their presence.Unapologetically Australian in a way that is rare in games, and giving representation to a group of people never covered in games with any depth, Wayward Strand genuinely makes the world better by existing. Designed to wallow in rather than race through earning achievements, Wayward Strand is emotional, meaningful, and important.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to the Hospital - It’s the summer of 1978, and Casey Beaumaris is trying to make the most of her holidays, when her mum asks her to spend a long weekend helping out at the airborne hospital where she works. Casey prefers the company of books to people, but she agrees, secretly planning to write an article about her visit for the school newspaper. With her trusty notebook at the ready, Casey arrives on board the airship. The staff are overworked as they prepare for the visit of an important official, while the patients react to grief, or deal with active trauma. In the midst of these and many other interlocking and overlapping stories, Casey spends time with the patients, learning about their lives, and, as the stories unfold, discovering what she can do to help.
_childDocuments_.name: Wayward Strand

name: Georifters
detailed_description: Buzz IntelGaming It’s an ingenious use of the “2.5D” perspective, asking players to use 3D spatial reasoning to navigate 2D situations. About the Game Steal the ground right from under your enemies! or yourself! In “Georifters” you can spin walls, twist tunnels, crush critters, battle against the ground or with it! It can be your tool or a weapon you use to smash others in a series of fast paced ground busting arenas. Flip! Spin! Crush! Choose From A Variety Of Heroes Dress them up (or down) and combine outfits to look fabulous on your way to victory. Duel it out in a variety of exhilarating multiplayer modes Up to four friends or strangers can show off their skills as they go head to head at full speed, battling for victory, for honor - and of course bragging rights. More Thinker Than A Fighter? No worries! Try some precision ground manipulation in co-op, against a friend, against an enemy, or a friend who is your enemy, or if you don’t have any friends or enemies (good for you!) you can go lone wolf in the story mode. Bust your way through 6 fantastical worlds 30+ levels, 300+ stages, each based on a unique theme. Features - Unique ground manipulation system allows you to move the world in many ways around your enemies or your self! - Use your ground manipulation skills to discover and unearth hidden items and power ups! - Unlock heroes , worlds, weapons, upgrades and more - Upgrade your chosen champions unique abilities to suit your play style - Over 50 different costume combinations , choose how fabulous you look whilst crushing your foes - Grab up to four friends to team up with or against each other for fast paced ground manipulation battles - More a thinker than a fighter? No worries! Grab a friend for some precision ground manipulation in Co-op. Or single player if you prefer to do everything yourself. - 6 Unique bubble worlds each inspired by one of the human senses. - 7 Unique heroes each with they're own individual special way of manipulating the ground - Explore 6 fantastical worlds comprised of 30+ levels with 300+ stages - Controller and Keyboard support - Supports remote play together!

name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2
detailed_description: Without a shadow of a doubt it is one of the most dangerous motorbike races in the world. In TT Isle of Man – Ride On the Edge 2, you prove your worth in different championships before setting out to conquer the Snaefell Mountain Course, a 60 km-long track with both winding and straight sections that will push your riding skills to the limit. TT 2 features 17 additional tracks, 18 different motorbikes including classic models, and the official riders. And now it’s more realistic than ever, thanks to entirely revamped physics and faithfully reproduced rider movements. Fine-tune your motorbike, upgrade its performance and monitor its data in real time so you can stay competitive. TT2 also offers a brand-new open world, a biker's paradise where you can test your bike settings and gain the experience you'll need to win the TT Isle of Man title!

_childDocuments_.review: Here's my suggestions... Overall, this is the best bike game I've played. Like other reviewers have mentioned, low speeds don't feel that good but there's not many opportunities to go that slow! As far as anything on a 2D screen controlled by an xbox controller can, I'd say it feels pretty realistic, with the caveat that I've never in real life experienced a tank slapper at 200mph down a narrow village street with my visor so covered in flies and the sun so low that I can't see the next corner coming at me. But then neither has anyone else here so that's alright then.Buy it if you like a challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Here’s a rider and adults Review! It’s awesome and feels better than the first one. It does a great job of making you feel like your going fast as hell all while leaning and throttling out corners like a beast. I ride in RL both SS and SB Motorcycles and this game feels pretty awesome. Don’t listen to the negative reviews saying it sucks. I have been riding since I was 7 years old and I like the feel of it. Also no one will ever be able to make a game driving or riding feel like the real thing it’s impossible. I mean the games beautiful and you feel like your ripping thru twistys on the TT course. I have GPBikes and MotoGP and I still say this is a great game and prefer playing TT2 right now over my other Bike Sims.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Let me begin by saying I have no clue about anything to do with mechanical or performance issues when it comes to motorbikes (real or virtual). Piston what? Suspension huh? No idea... See? :) I just like to drive things at insane speeds in a way that feels extremely dangerous. This game is the first racing game I've ever played that lets me do that to my heart's content. I'll be honest, my 15 hours of play so far have largely consisted of choosing Single Player > Quick Race > Isle of Man and just bombing around the track in first person view with every HUD element switched off. Nothing in the way, just learning the track and building up an intuitive feel for the optimum speed in each section. It is so much FUN!!! I keep catching myself just grinning like a schoolboy on his first roller coaster. And, by the way, I am rubbish at it. A HUGE achievement for me was to make it round ONCE without falling off and that took me days of trying. I particularly love all the leaning into corners as you race. It's genuinely hard not to actually lean for real as well! If, like me, you don't know much about bikes but just want to blast around an incredibly beautiful course at silly speeds you should definitely check this game out.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game to experience the track. I didn't expect the mechanics to be so bad. I ride a 1000cc bike on the street and fast (when on a private track obviously) and I can tell you that the bike does not move from one lane to the other when I want to take a long sweeping bend and certainly not during a short corner. That said some of the wheelie characteristics when accelerating in the low gears is very close. Other than that, a complete miss. I can pull away without it feeling like the clutch is slipping for 10minutes before it picks up. Riding over bumps in the road moves the bike around IRL but it doesn't pivot you onto the floor. The wheel will lift over certain changes in road pitch but you wont instantly fly off the back because the rear overtook you. I could go on, and on, and on. How long it takes to go from banked left to banked right at any speed. Your lean angle v's the AI's lean angle (scratching vs 20deg) etc etc.So this game is definitely not a sim. Ok, fair enough. So then its arcade, right? Wrong!Arcades are accessible, and this is not. It doesn't have the playability of games 20yrs old let alone something new. I've been playing this game wondering who the developers were targeting. My answer is they dont care, anyone who will pay up front for the IOMTT experience. Of course there are skilled gamers who, with time can crack any game and become elite at it. They are prepared to learn the physics and glitches that make it go fast and repeat the formula for every challenge. But that's not the majority. This game is flawed throughout (broken menu's, no ultrawide screen settings, Nvidia cant even find the game). In reality its nothing more than a 1.2 patch of the first IOMTT game.But if you want a good idea of some good places to spectate the real IOMTT then this helps.I'll see you up the mountain with my sandwiches, a man nappy and just a pinch of salt.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I jumped straight onto time attack mode and snaefel mountain course tested 3 bikes classic supersport and superbike, and it's awsome i can feel the wobble more like what i see in videos of real TT, it feels more closer to real TT , and the feeling of speed is also improved more than 1st version, in slower bike i found myself desperately trying to keep bike as straight as possible as some unexpected bumps could cause me to fall.i ride bycicle in real life and this feels much closer to that feeling which is awesome.I feel this game to be awesome, i don't know about any career mode bugs since i didn't started it yet. Good job to developers you guys are awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game, being a sequel to the first TT Isle of Man, doesn't feel like a big enough step in the right direction when compared to its prequel. In some areas, it's worse. The career mode feels great, with you choosing between races on a calendar. When it comes to controls and physics, many drew comparisons between the first game in this series and Milestone's titles. Some preferred Milestone physics, some preferred KT Racing's. I'm in the latter camp, which is why I'm disappointed in the physics of this game. It feels like a step backwards, you can barely influence weight shifting. The only times you'll pull a wheelie is on bumps in the road or from a standstill, you really can't do it deliberately. Braking feels great, though. You can lock up the rear tyre, making the bike squirm and snap, but you can catch it and it feels just as great as doing it for real. The same goes for when your front wheel starts going skywards over crests, it just feels right as you close the throttle and manage to keep it under control. On the fine details level, it feels like they learned from what was bad in the previous game. If you lean too much you hear the foot pegs scraping, however it still is way too lenient in letting you get out of situations where you'd low side for sure. Graphics are 'meh'. It does its job just as well as the previous game except for one huge problem: the sense of speed is way worse in this game than the first one, which is a big shame because the first game had the greatest sense of speed of any racing game I've played, arcade or sim. To have a step down from that is a big shame. The engine audio is also very bland, but the wind noise helps maintain the sense of speed.Content-wise, this game outshines the first one. It keeps all of the previous tracks and adds a new area which has several different track layouts. Obviously, it still features the Snaefell mountain as you'd expect. That is this game's biggest claim to fame. If you love road racing and the Isle of Man TT in particular, this game doesn't have any competition. While I miss the sidecars, the classic bikes are a hugely welcome addition. It adds some much needed variety. When I summarize the game's flaws and its strengths, I can't recommend it. You can neither high-side nor low-side, you'll only fall off the bike by crashing into something or from out of control wheelies. The bikes don't feel too different from each other, it's just different degrees of speed. The sense of speed is still great when compared to other series, but that mainly comes from the game's setting. It's the bloody Snaefell mountain course, fully recreated! Sadly, it feels like the devs (or more likely, the publishers) know that this is what will make you buy this game, so I fear they'll just keep pumping and dumping these games and release them every time the month of May comes around. The post-launch support for the first game was atrocious, and I fear it'll be the same for this one. Unless you REALLY want to ride around Isle of Man, avoid this series.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Best physics of any bike game out there by far. The sensation of speed and acceleration it conveys don't even come close to this in any other bike game I've tried (Moto GP series what is that snail paced rubbish all about?). This is the closest sensation I can get to riding bikes for real and I've ridden for over 20 years 1000cc sports bikes - not that I do 170mph on the main roads or anything. It's the acceleration this game conveys, the rush of wind, the camera angles - all superb. Shame there is a lack of bikes though.
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle of Man: Ride on the Edge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the freakin' Dark Souls of racing games, no wonder it has so many bad reviews.  It is also not a looker and lacks the polish of Milestone's bike games. But I would still recommend it. It takes a bit of getting used to, but once you get into it a bit, it's really rewarding. It also really makes racing a bike feel dangerous somehow even though its just a game.  I'm digging it.  I saw lots of people complaining about how 'unresponsive' the controls are, well, it's a bike not a car, you idiots.  Weight transfer is a major thing. If you are turning and leaning left, you can't suddenly and immediately turn right, you have to shift your weight over first. You also can't just go into a track blind and expect to rock it first try. You need to learn the tracks. This game rewards patience and perseverance. Great but very tough game with a lot of heart and love put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up with a few major "BUT" points.Handling is a lot more forgiving than the first TT, but in some ways, less realistic. Even on full "pro" physics/sim settings, you can veer a little off course and onto dirt in a long sweeping curve at over 170kph and not crash... yet go over a little lump/rise in the road and rather than become airborne for a moment, you INSTANTLY flip and die. In those little ways, the first TT game was actually more realistic in capturing the brutal lethality of this type of road racing (where you could have a pants crapping moment when becoming airborne over surprise bumps and lumps in the road, but also die the death you deserve for going off road at crazy speeds).Some of the forgiving physics during high speed cornering that killed you in the first TT if you did not have the absolute perfect entry point into a hard corner, now allow for what feels like a more natural experience here. Steering correction in sweeping turns or even little mistakes at lower speeds in hair pin turns are also non-lethal and more realistic... things you can actually get away with in the real world.  But there is a trade off where some of that forgiveness rubs off into unreality... like accidentally side swiping a stone wall that, again, should tear off your fairing, catch your handle bar and rip you off your bike... instead you just scrape along like as if you are in a car and have a chance to disengage with the wall and keep on driving. It can be a bit weird.So... physics while good, are not perfect. Milestone with MotoGP 20 onwards seem to have a more sophisticated physics setup in terms of tyre compound/heat/road surface temperature/etc. variances and such, but TT still feels much more natural in terms of your connection to the ride.The sense of real world crazy speed is still superior here than in the MotoGP/Ride/Milestone games, but again, feels less "crazy fast" than the first TT. Try going street legal road speeds and you will see how much slower it feels. To me everything felt almost half speed... like 100kph felt like about 60kph in the real world. 170kph felt like 100kph. That is still better than Milestone that makes 170kph feel like 60kph (to me).Visually it feels softer and less real than the first TT as well. That softness makes it less distracting and easier to enjoy the ride when racing through high contrast foliage/shadow areas (which is also unrealistic because that kind of light/dark contrast messes with your focus in a big way in the real world, even at low speeds, and the first TT captured how uncomfortable that experience is). Still very pretty though, just different from the first.Personally, I am not a fan of the career mode... a lot of forced tutorial explanations for quite awhile, but thankfully you can force click/skip each comment. But in all honesty, I never intended on properly playing the career anyway. The developer has done the smart thing (again) and let you access EVERY bike and EVERY track/circuit right away for a quick non-career race. The career mode however does appear to be far more involved and advanced than the first TT, and should prove infinitely more rewarding.I think the biggest draw though is the free roam mode. It is like a motorcycle only, sim-focused Forza Horizon 4... beautiful British countryside to just cruise or race around. No traffic, no psychotic AI to get in your way. Especially for those of us that live in areas with 3rd world road conditions (Australia for me), it is nice to plunge into a fantasy land for a moment where a motorcycle can be ridden on an open road where there isn't a death dealing pot hole, or serious reconstructive resealed cracks for more than 50 metres. Aside from those surprise lumps that kill you instantly if you launch over them at high speed, riding is almost entirely a beautiful thing in free roam mode.Overall, TT2 is kind of a must for anyone seriously into motorcycles. Different enough in feel from the first TT that it is worth owning both.One big downside though is the external view... this is where Milestone wins with Ride/MotoGP... the animations here are still stiff looking and limited, and that makes seeing your bike and rider a distraction as they "kind of" lean into a corner. You are, however still better off staying in one of the first person camera modes for a less distracting, more satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The most intense racing game experience available, and this time the bikes feel like they are connected to the road and can be pushed to the limit.  This time the bikes can be enjoyed without the constant nagging stress of when the bike will kill the player next!Be under no illusion, this is sill a 'difficult' racing game.  If you ride too hard and fast you will lose control.  Unlike IOM TT1 this time you can tell both why and where you made mistakes.  Learn the corners, correct the lines,  easy on the throttle and brakes and it's an incredible experience.  The most difficult element remains being able to concentrate for so long, few racing games demand anywhere near the effort.  The career mode is also far more enjoyable than the first game, good events and progression although the perk system is a bit strange and could do with more work/explaining.If you like motorbike games I think you'll love this.

_childDocuments_.review: OMG! I don't know where to start........When I first played TT Isle of Man Ride on the Edge, I was amazed......! There it was....FINALLY......a modern bike race game with the WHOLE Mountain course digitally mapped. Absolutely stunning achievement. Bike models were beautiful and animated perfectly. Graphics sharp, detailed and fluid with infinite draw-distance....A MARVEL!!!So after a few runs and major crashes I settled on what 'felt' to me like the most stable bike in the Supersport class.....The Honda CBR600RR (I decided to leave the 1000cc bikes alone until I'd mastered the track). I set about making the settings perfect so I could really control the bike properly. Expert level - Steering sensitivity, deadzones etc.......I found the right settings after much tweaking and finally began my mission of completing a lap and setting a time.....A year and a half later, after many many hundreds of laps and about a million crashes I finally completed a full lap without a crash and set a respectable time of 17min 24s (placed me 403rd). The game is SUCH a THRILL when u get it right and gut-wrenching when u mess up but that's all part of the experience. Going flat-out as fast as u can for as long as u can and 'Riding-on-the-Edge'. I've been doing that since I started playing the game and am constantly chasing a better time and perfect laps. This game is almost perfect as it is....My only quibble about it is I couldn't find ANY online games. Not even if I hosted.....Anyway, so I found out a sequel had been made......'TT Isle of Man Ride on the Edge 2'. Better graphics they said, better physics.......I thought 'Ooooh! I wonder how they've made an already EXCELLENT game better?'...'Wonder if there's a better Multiplayer selection?'.....So I bought it for myself on my Birthday.....WHAT A LET DOWN!!!!.......I have spent 18 months RACING HARD on FULL SPEC RACE MACHINES trying my absolute best to set lap times and complete laps/sections at BREAKNECK SPEED with the racing line BRIGHT RED on every corner, only to find that in the sequel 'Ride on the Edge 2', you CAN'T do that!! You have to start out on a BOG-STANDARD machine with stupidly LOW HP and trundle round the track with a mainly YELLOW race line coz the BIKE ISN'T FAST ENOUGH!Basically, it's now a CAREER BASED game, where u enter events on a calendar and SLOWLY work your way up purchasing bike upgrades as u go. You can't even use a full power bike in the Time Attack mode. You have to EARN the bike first in career mode. Lord knows how long that would take but quite frankly I can't be bothered to find out. I have re-fired up the original game and am back to trying to set fast laps on that. I feel like I wasted £28....I bought some DLC too.Oh, and I guess some might be saying....'But it's got better physics now'.....'The Graphics are better'.......NO and NO. The graphics look 'washed-out', AREN'T as smooth as the original game and the physics? The bike is now SO unstable and unforgiving it doesn't let u do ANY of the control movements from the first game and the ride settings AREN'T transposable from one game to another. It's a mess! Has left me quite disappointed actually... :(Oh, by the way....I tried to connect to Multiplayer and got the same ZERO result. 'NO GAMES FOUND'....at any time of day and whatever u select. And if u try and host a game, u just sit in your own EMPTY LOBBY forever. Thumbs down for the minute unless Devs do something drastic! :(P.S : What the hell have u done to the spectators? They now look like they've all had REALLY bad facial surgery and are all 'Derpy'. :(
